en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Root Fifty of the Middle Collection.
(First Part) Commentary on the Introduction to the Composition. 1.
At the commencement of the commentary, the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of making known the origin, the support, and the purity of the Dhamma that is to be commented upon.

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise toward the expositions of the Dhamma; and for the purpose of producing all benefit and happiness through right practice, which must be acquired by means of their proper learning, retention, and so forth.

Alternatively, it is because it is auspicious, because it constitutes the preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it has been practiced by the wise, and because others will follow one's example in the future upon seeing it.

And this act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is performed within this commentary. Alternatively, the making of this homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of generating a specific merit consisting in the worship of those worthy of worship.
That, in turn, is for the purpose of augmenting the power of the karma that has brought about one’s own present prosperity.

It is also for the purpose of ensuring that such prosperity does not diminish in the interim. Both of these are for the purpose of completing the *Aṭṭhakathā* (the Great Commentary) without obstacle. This very [purpose]...
And this is the purpose intended by the Teacher here. For he will say: "Thus, with a mind full of confidence...
[etc. ...by its power. Through the worship of the Triple Gem, there arises an immeasurable majesty of extraordinary merit due to the realization of the unsurpassed field of merit;
and thus, even amidst the manifold obstacles inherent in worldly existence, it serves to destroy all defilements that constitute the bond of those obstacles.
It succeeds. And it wards off calamities such as fear. As it is said:
“For one who honors those worthy of honor, whether they be Buddhas or their disciples,” and likewise:
“Bhikkhus, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost; and for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost. Thus it is said.
“The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises ‘the Buddha’—
that rapture alone is better than the entirety of Jambudīpa.
For one who praises ‘the Dhamma’… [and so on] … even the entirety of Jambudīpa.”
“...for one who praises [the Sangha] as ‘the Sangha’... even with the whole of Jambudīpa.
Likewise:
“At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... nor is his mind obsessed by delusion,” and so forth.
“In the forest or at the foot of a tree...
[as before] ...there will be no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation. And so it is said.

In this context, in order to demonstrate the possession of extraordinary qualities in the Triple Gem (vatthuttaya) which he wishes to worship, he spoke three verses beginning with “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ. For it is through the possession of extraordinary qualities that one becomes worthy of worship;
and worship rendered to those worthy of worship accomplishes the intended purpose. In this regard, of the teaching...
Desiring to provide a commentary, he notes that this [commentary] is not dominated by compassion like the teaching of the Vinaya, nor is it dominated by wisdom like the teaching of the Abhidhamma;

rather, it is dominated by both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, in order to first offer praise to the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is the very source of the remaining jewels—he says, "whose heart is cooled by compassion," and so forth. In that regard:
It is called *karuṇā* because it scatters; the meaning is that it scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it afflicts;

the meaning is that when there is suffering in others, it afflicts or troubles the compassionate one. Or else, it is called *karuṇā* because, when there is suffering in others, it causes a trembling or heartache in the virtuous.
Alternatively, *ka* means happiness (*sukha*); it is called *karuṇā* because it obstructs that. This is [the etymology].

For [compassion] has the characteristic of the desire to remove the suffering of others; it "obstructs" or hinders the happiness of compassionate ones because of their disregard for their own pleasure—this is the meaning.

"Cool with compassion" (*karuṇāsītala*) means cool by means of compassion; one whose heart is such that its heart is cool with compassion is "one whose heart is cool with compassion" (*karuṇāsītalahadayo*);
that is "one whose heart is cool with compassion."
In this regard, although it is observed that both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) serve as causes for the cooling of the mind—

due to their intrinsic nature of desiring to bring about the welfare, happiness, and non-decline of others, and due to their being direct opposites of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and aversion (*arati*), thus functioning in the mode of severing the torment within the mental continuum of other beings—
nevertheless, because they function in the mode of removing the suffering of others, their essential flavor (*rasa*) is the inability to endure the affliction of others.
Non-violence toward beings and compassion are especially stated to be the cause of the heart’s coolness for the Blessed One, just like the tranquility of his mind;

thus it is said, "one whose heart is cooled by compassion. Alternatively, it should be understood that through the medium of compassion, loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are also stated to be the causes for the coolness of the heart.
Or else, [compassion] is that which is the basis for his extraordinary and unique knowledge, being preeminent and entirely complete.
Because it pervades its own object just like omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), compassion (*karuṇā*) has attained the state of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
thus, it is said that "the heart is cooled by compassion" because compassion alone is the cause for the Blessed One’s heart being exceptionally cool.

Alternatively, although loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also causes for the heart’s cooling in an eminent way, compassion is the cause for these as well, since it is the primary factor for all the specific qualities of a Buddha.
Compassion is said to be "the cause of the coolness of the Blessed One’s heart. For all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source.

Indeed, for the Blessed One, whose heat of suffering in *saṃsāra* was extinguished by the power of compassion, there arose—through his desire to remove the suffering of others—a state of tirelessness even throughout many incalculable eons, as he remained devoted to gathering all the factors that constitute the qualities of a Buddha without exception.
And for one who has attained mastery over the Dhamma, even when confronted with signs that would cause the heart to burn— such as the conditioned phenomena of sentient beings—
there was not even the slightest alteration in the coolness of his mind. And in this interpretation of the meaning,
it should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is included throughout all three stages.
It understands, thus it is wisdom (*paññā*); the meaning is that it penetrates by way of its various modes according to the true nature of things.
Wisdom itself is the "light of wisdom" (*paññā-pajjota*) in the sense of illuminating the true nature of phenomena through its various modes by means of abandoning the veil of the knowable.

It is "dispelled" (*vihata*), meaning specifically struck down, eradicated, and destroyed, because of the abandonment of even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). That which is dispelled by the light of wisdom is "dispelled by the light of wisdom" (*paññā-pajjotavihata*). They are deluded...
By that [delusion], one is either deluded oneself, or the mere state of being deluded is the *tanti* (the bond); thus it is *moha*. It is *avijjā* (ignorance).
Because it conceals the true nature of objects, it is like darkness; thus it is *tamo*. One for whom the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom is *paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo*;
such is "one for whom the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom. For indeed, although the lamp of wisdom exists in all those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*),...

Since there exists a distinction in the abandonment of defilements by the Fully Enlightened Ones (sammāsambuddhas) through the eradication of even their latent tendencies (savāsanappahāna)— compared to disciples who have attained vision (diṭṭhippatta) or to Paccekabuddhas, who are like those liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) in that the darkness of ignorance has been destroyed— the author,
praising the Blessed One for his preeminent abandonment of ignorance, says: "He whose darkness of delusion was destroyed by the lamp of wisdom."
Alternatively, because he has produced within his own continuum the complete disappearance of the darkness of ignorance even without the instruction of others;

because he has likewise attained omniscience and mastery over the [ten] powers; and because he has correctly set that [knowledge] in motion within the continua of others through the power of his preeminent teaching of the Dhamma—it is the Blessed One alone who should be especially praised for the removal of the darkness of delusion; thus he said.

"‘The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom. In this interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood that by the phrase "the lamp of wisdom," both the Blessed One’s wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*) and his wisdom of teaching (*desanā-paññā*) are included through a general designation, or by the method of mentioning one of two similar things (*ekasesanaya*).

Alternatively, because the Blessed One’s knowledge has as its limit the entire range of the knowable, [he is so called] by virtue of being capable of awakening to the true nature of all phenomena within the knowable.
Because the darkness of delusion— which obscures the true nature of all knowable phenomena— has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom known as unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*),
it is said that "the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," referring to the Blessed One’s destruction of the gloom of delusion, which is not shared by others. And here,
because the destruction of the darkness of delusion has been attained, unobstructed knowledge is figuratively attributed to his own continuum (*sasantāne*) by way of metaphorical causality.

It should be understood as "dispelling the darkness of delusion. For the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies through the perfection of the resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is indeed the abandonment of the cognitive obscuration (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*);

however, because it serves as the cause for dispelling the darkness of delusion in the mental continuums of others, unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is called "the dispeller of the darkness of delusion."

But what is the reason that only the eradication of ignorance (*avijjā*) is taken as the basis for praising the Blessed One by way of the perfection of abandonment, rather than the supreme and exhaustive abandonment of all defilements (*kilesa*)?

It is because, by the very mention of its abandonment, the eradication of the entire mass of defilements is manifested due to their being associated with it. For there is no such defilement [that is not included therein].
"It is not abandoned by the abandonment of ignorance without remainder.

Alternatively, just as knowledge (*vijjā*) is the primary cause for the arising of all wholesome states, so too is ignorance (*avijjā*) the primary cause for the production of all unwholesome states and for the continuation of *saṃsāra*; therefore, by the statement regarding its destruction, there is the eradication of the entire mass of defilements.
"He is indeed called [thus]" refers to the statement: "He whose darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.
Humans and gods are *narāmarā*; together with humans and gods is *sanarāmara*. That which is both this world and *sanarāmara* is the *sanarāmaraloka*.
One who is revered (*garu*) by that *sanarāmaraloka* is *sanarāmaralokagaru*; him, the *sanarāmaralokagaru*. By this, [the status of] gods and humans...
This demonstrates the Blessed One’s benefactorship by bringing about specific qualities appropriate to the remaining beings as well.
And here, one should not raise the objection regarding the distinction between the primary and the secondary; for the order of words is one thing, while the order of meaning is another.
For in such compound expressions, even that which is primary is presented as if it were secondary, as in the phrase "the assembly together with the king" (*sarājikāya parisāya*).

In this context, although the world (*loka*) is threefold—consisting of the world of beings (*satta-loka*), the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*)—the meaning should be understood according to the world of beings, because it is the weightiness (*garubhāva*) that is intended here, and only that which is capable of being treated with weight is appropriate.

For it is called "the world" because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are experienced (*lokīyanti*) therein. And by the mention of "immortals" (*amara*) here, the deities of rebirth (*upapatti-deva*) are intended.

Alternatively, the word *loka* has the sense of "aggregation," in the sense that it is "perceived" (*lokīyati*) or "designated" (*paññāpīyati*) as a collection. "Together with men" (*sanara*) means those who are with men;

"those who are with men and immortals" (*sanarāmarā*) refers to them. It should be construed according to the previous method as "the world of those [who are] with men and immortals" (*sanarāmaraloka*).
And here, by the term "immortal" (*amara*), the purified deities (*visuddhideva*) are also included, for they are, in the ultimate sense, devoid of death.

"Immortals. And the inclusion of "humans and immortals" (*nara-amarānaṃ*) is by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭha-niddesa*), as in the expression "the Teacher of gods and humans" (*satthā deva-manussānaṃ*).

For indeed, [the Buddha] possesses immeasurable and incomparable excellence of power and special qualities, owing to his being of ultimate benefit to the world including its gods and humans through a preeminent perfection of application that is unsurpassed, intent upon providing for the welfare and happiness of all without exception, and preceded by the avoidance of every kind of harm.
And the Blessed One, the supreme among all beings, is the object of the highest reverence for immeasurable beings throughout immeasurable world-systems.
Therefore it is said: "Venerated by the world of humans and gods.
He whose going (gamana) is beautiful (sobhana) is the Sugata. For the Blessed One’s approach to those who are to be trained is exclusively—
It is beautiful because it accomplishes the welfare and happiness of those beings; likewise,

through the adornment of his physical body with the primary and secondary marks (lakkhaṇa-anubyañjana), his bodily movement and cognitive movement— free from defects such as haste, slowness, stumbling, dragging, pressing, contraction, crookedness, and confusion— are like the gait of a majestic swan,

a bull, a noble elephant, and the king of beasts, and are accompanied by the excellence of qualities such as vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, and energy, due to his original resolve (abhinīhāra).
"Up to great enlightenment, it is indeed beautiful because of its faultlessness.

Alternatively, he is the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*) because, through his self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he has fully understood the entire world by means of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*), and thus has rightly gone to or understood it through knowledge.

Likewise, he is the "Well-Gone One" because, by abandoning the origin of the world through the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), he has rightly gone beyond, having brought about the state of non-arising (*anuppattidhammata*).
He is the *Sugata* because he has rightly gone to, that is, attained, the cessation of the world (*lokanirodha*), which is *nibbāna*, by means of the clear realization of its actualization;
and he is the *Sugata* because he has rightly gone to, that is, practiced, the path leading to the cessation of the world by means of the clear realization of its cultivation.

According to such passages as: "Those defilements which were abandoned by the path of stream-entry—he does not go back to them, does not return to them, does not go back again to those defilements—therefore he is the *Sugata*."

This meaning should be clarified by way of this method. Alternatively, he is the "Well-Gone" (Sugata) because he has gone to or attained a beautiful state—namely, perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or even Nibbāna.

Or, because he speaks the Dhamma that is real, true, beneficial, and appropriate for those to be trained according to their needs and at the right time, he is the "Well-Speaker" (Sugata), speaking correctly; thus, the letter *da* becomes *ta*.
Having thus [explained] that he is "Well-Gone" (*sugata*) by virtue of his beautiful gait and other such qualities, [the text says] "to that Well-Gone One.
Because one must go (*gantabbato*) by way of rebirth through meritorious and evil kamma, these are "destinies" (*gatiyo*); they are specific types of existence-in-becoming (*upapattibhava*).

These, moreover, are fivefold, categorized as the hells and so forth. By means of the attainment of the Noble Path, [there is the cessation] of all kamma leading to existence through those [destinies].
Because he has turned back from [rebirth] by making himself a being no longer subject to karmic ripening, the Blessed One is well-liberated and dissociated from all five destinies;

thus it is said, "liberated from destiny. By this, he shows that the Blessed One is not included within any destiny whatsoever, which is why the Blessed One is called the "God beyond gods" (*devātideva*). For this very reason, it was said:
“Those taints by which one might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by which one might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain human status—
those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.”

Because the defilements of karma that lead to various states of existence were completely abandoned by the Supreme Path even at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Blessed One has no inclusion within any state of existence;

thus, the Blessed One is absolutely liberated from all realms of being, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings—that is, he is liberated from those states of existence.
"Vandāmi" means I pay homage, or I bow down, or I praise him.
Alternatively, "liberated from the course of existence" praises the Blessed One by virtue of his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue.
For here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two aspects: through the perfection of his own welfare and through his practice for the welfare of others.
Of these, the perfection of his own welfare consists in the attainment of unobstructed knowledge and the absolute abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies.

It should be understood as such from the attainment of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). Furthermore, the practice for the benefit of others (*parahita-paṭipatti*) is characterized by teaching the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering with a mind indifferent to gain, honor, and the like;
by a constant inclination toward the welfare of others even toward those who oppose him; and by the arrival of the time for the maturation of his knowledge.

Moreover, in this context, the practice for the benefit of others is twofold—by way of disposition (*āsaya*) and by way of application (*payoga*)—and the accomplishment of one's own welfare (*attahita-sampatti*) is threefold.
It is thus revealed. How so? By the phrase “one whose heart is cooled by compassion,” the practice for the welfare of others is shown in terms of intention (*āsayato*).
By the word “Sugata” in the sense of having gone rightly, the practice for the welfare of others is shown in terms of application (*payogato*).

By the phrases “one whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom” and by the word “Sugata” in the sense of the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, the threefold attainment of one’s own welfare is shown. [The remainder follows] in the remaining sense.
Thus, by the phrase "the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," the entire practice for the attainment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others is also revealed.
Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood through three aspects: from the perspective of cause, fruit, and benefit.
Therein, the cause is great compassion, which is shown by the first word [of the verse]. The fruit is fourfold: the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment.

[These are] the perfection of majesty and the perfection of the form-body. Among these, the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment are manifested by the second term through the sense of penetration into the truths, and by the word *sugata*;

however, the perfection of majesty is manifested by the third term, while the perfection of the form-body is manifested by the word *sugata* in the sense of the beauty of the body’s gait as previously described, [provided it is] without the deficiency of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Because of that absence [of suffering]. Having made the immediate benefit internal, there is the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation by way of the threefold vehicle.
It should be understood that this is expressed by the word *sugata* in the sense of "one who has spoken rightly" (*sammāgadanattha*).
In this context, by the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," he shows the root of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). One whose mind is impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)...
Indeed, the Blessed One, having made the resolution for the sake of uplifting beings from the mire of saṃsāra, gradually fulfilled the perfections and attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment. By the phrase "the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," he demonstrates perfect enlightenment.
For path-knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and path-knowledge has [wisdom] as its proximate cause.

Unobstructed knowledge is called "perfect enlightenment" (sammāsambodhi). By means of the term *sugata* in the sense of "one who has gone rightly," he demonstrates the practice for perfect enlightenment;

for through the term *sugata*, he reveals the Middle Way—accompanied by compassion and wisdom—which is free from the two extremes such as the adherence to lethargy and agitation, the accumulation [of karma], devotion to the pleasure of sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and the dogmatic clinging to eternalism and annihilationism.
By means of the other [terms], he shows the purpose distinguished by the exertion and non-exertion for perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
Herein, the primary purpose is the crossing over of sentient beings from the great flood of saṃsāra; the other is the secondary purpose.

Among those, by the primary [purpose] he shows the practice for the benefit of others, and by the other, the attainment of one's own benefit. By both together, [he shows this] among the four types of persons, beginning with those who have set out for their own benefit.

This demonstrates the Blessed One’s status as the fourth type of person (*puggala*). By this, he shows his own state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), his state of being most worthy of veneration, and his having become a field of merit (*khetta*) for the act of paying homage.
Furthermore, here, by the inclusion of "compassion" (*karuṇā*), the Blessed One’s uncommon qualities that have attained the state of greatness among worldly beings are illuminated.

The perfection of all mundane qualities is demonstrated; by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown, because it illuminates the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) which has the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
For the meaning established by the inclusion of both is elaborated upon in the passage beginning with "the teacher of the world of men and gods" (*sanarāmaralokagaru*).
And by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows that his approach is free from defilement (*nirupakkilesa*); by the mention of wisdom...

...the departure. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the Blessed One’s activity in accordance with worldly convention, because compassion is within the sphere of worldly usage.

By the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows the non-transcending of convention; for it is through the failure to understand the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that one transcends convention and clings to [notions] such as a "being" (*satta*).
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, [he shows] the dwelling in the attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*).

By the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), and the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*).
By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) is included, there are the remaining unique knowledges:

the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the knowledges of being unshakable by the eight assemblies, the ten powers (*bala*), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, and the sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct (*ñāṇacariyā*).

He demonstrates the range of knowledge by way of numerous classifications of wisdom, such as the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, he shows the perfection of conduct; by the mention of wisdom, the perfection of true knowledge.
By the mention of compassion, there is self-mastery; by the mention of wisdom, there is mastery over the Dhamma.

By the mention of compassion, the state of being a protector of the world is indicated; by the mention of wisdom, the state of being a protector of oneself. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the quality of being a benefactor is indicated;
by the mention of wisdom, gratitude. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the absence of self-torment is indicated; by the mention of wisdom, the absence of tormenting others.
Or else, by the mention of compassion, the accomplishment of the qualities that make one a Buddha is indicated; by the mention of wisdom, the accomplishment of the state of Buddhahood itself.
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the saving of others is shown; by the mention of wisdom, one’s own crossing over [to the further shore] is shown.
Similarly, by the mention of compassion, a mind of benevolence toward all beings is indicated; by the mention of wisdom, a mind detached from all phenomena is indicated.
Furthermore, among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is the primary cause, and wisdom is the culmination, for there is nothing superior to it.
Because there is nothing further to be done. Thus, by showing both the beginning and the end, all the qualities of a Buddha are demonstrated.

Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*)—preceded by the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)—is shown. For virtue has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from the abstention from taking life and so forth;
and that compassion is associated with the first three meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). By the word "wisdom" (*paññā*), [the aggregate of wisdom is shown].

The aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*). Since virtue (*sīla*) is the beginning of all the Buddha’s qualities, concentration (*samādhi*) the middle, and wisdom the end—thus, by showing that they are beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, all the Buddha’s qualities are shown through this method of demonstration, because they are shown by way of a guiding principle (*nayato*).
For this indeed is the means for seeing the Buddha’s qualities without exception: namely, the grasping of the guiding principle.
Otherwise, who indeed would be capable of showing the qualities of the Blessed One in their entirety, following them one by one? For this very reason it was said:
"Even a Buddha, speaking the praise of a Buddha, might do so for an eon without saying anything else."
“An eon might pass away in its long duration,
yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

And for this very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, when questioned regarding the delimitation of the Buddha’s qualities, rejected it, saying, “Certainly not, Bhante,” and added, “Nevertheless, Bhante, the logical sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.”
2. Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by means of all his qualities of omniscience, he now spoke the words beginning with “Buddhopi” in order to extol the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*).
Therein, “Buddho” is a designation of the agent; “buddhabhāvaṃ” is a designation of the object;
“bhāvetvā sacchikatvā” is a designation of prior actions; “yaṃ” is a designation of the object in an indefinite sense; and “upagato” [is the verb].
The exposition of the act of passing away at another time; the exposition of the act of paying homage. "That" is the specification.
"Dhamma" is the designation of the object of the act of homage.

"Gatamalam" and "anuttaram" are its qualifiers. Therein, regarding the word *Buddha* first: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths (*saccāni*); he is a Buddha because he causes the world to awaken," and so forth.

The meaning should be understood according to the method of exposition (*niddesa*). Alternatively, he is called "Awakened" (*buddha*) because of the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), or because of the state of blossoming of his awakening (*buddhi*); thus, he is awakened by way of the meanings of waking and blossoming.

Alternatively, it is because there is no knowable phenomenon (*ñeyyadhamma*) whatsoever that has not been awakened to, and because there is no specific object of knowledge that is not grasped as an object of action (*kamma*).
Since there is no intention of performing an act (*kammavacanicchā*), the designation of the agent is obtained solely in the sense of understanding;

thus, "he has awakened" (*buddhavā*) makes him the Buddha, just as in the expression, "one who has been ordained does not give. In terms of meaning, however, he is one whose defilements have been entirely destroyed and shattered by self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) together with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), having been refined by the perfections (*pāramitā*);
he is the repository for an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The Buddha is the continuum of the aggregates (khandhasantāna). As it is said:

"Buddha refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū); without a teacher, he personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.

The word *api* is used in the sense of esteem (*sambhāvane*). By it, one expresses: "Even that Blessed One, endowed with such distinguished qualities," referring to the qualities about to be described.
He demonstrates veneration for the Dhamma. "The state of a Buddha" means perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). "Having developed" means having produced and increased it.
"Having realized" means having made it directly manifest. "Attained" means arrived at; the sense is "reached.
This is connected with the phrase "the state of a Buddha. "Gone-beyond-stain" means free from stain; the sense is "faultless. "I revere" means I bow down to, I praise.
Or: "Anuttara" means devoid of anything superior; the sense is "supramundane. "Dhamma":

it is called *dhamma* because it upholds (*dhāreti*) those who practice according to its instruction by preventing them from falling into the states of misery or into *saṃsāra*. This is the summary of the meaning here:
even the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is thus endowed with a multitude of diverse qualities, [proclaimed] that *dhamma* known as the Noble Path...
Having cultivated [the path] and realized that which is termed the fruit and Nibbāna, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment;

I pay homage to this True Dhamma of penetration, which is the cause of even the Buddhas’ Buddhahood, which is free from all stains of defilement, and which is unsurpassed because there exists nothing higher than it.
Since it is the True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-saddhamma) as well that elucidates this, its inclusion here should be understood.
Alternatively, it should be understood that since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “He reached the ocean of the method of the Abhidhamma;
he comprehended the three Piṭakas,” the term “realization through comprehension” (*sacchikiriyā-sammasana*) applies to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) as well;

therefore, that too is mentioned here. Likewise, because it is said: “Having developed and realized which Dhamma...,” [it refers to] those qualities that constitute the state of a Buddha (*buddhakaradhamma*).

It should be understood that here, by the word "dhamma," the trainings in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth are also included along with the perfections (*pāramitā*) in the preliminary stage.
For these too, because they are the opposite of defilements, are free from stain (*gatamala*), and because they are not shared with others, are "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
Thus, he who has made the great aspiration for the sake of all beings' escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra, whose disposition is refined by the dwelling in great compassion—
Having attained mastery over kamma and other factors through the thorough cultivation, direct realization, and complete perfection— without exception,
respectfully and continuously— for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons,

of the supreme qualities such as giving, self-control, and restraint, which have been purified by the excellence of wisdom; he possesses a marvelous, inconceivable, and great power, having reached the ultimate pinnacle of perfection in higher virtue and higher consciousness.
The Blessed One, having dispatched the Great Vajira-knowledge through twenty-four million four hundred thousand modes regarding the nature of conditions, attained supreme and perfect enlightenment.
And here, by the word "having developed," he praises the Dhamma through the perfection of clear knowledge (*vijjā*); by the word "having realized,"...
[The first is] for the perfection of liberation; likewise, the first is for the perfection of jhāna and the second for the perfection of emancipation.

Or, the first is for the perfection of concentration and the second for the perfection of attainment. Alternatively, the first is by way of the knowledge of destruction and the second by way of the knowledge of non-arising.
Or, the first is by way of its similarity to lightning and the second by way of its similarity to a thunderbolt.

Or, by the first [term], through the attainment of dispassion (*virāga*); by the second, through the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). Likewise, by the first, through the state of outlet (*niyyāna*);
by the second, through the state of escape (*nissaraṇa*). Or, by the first, through the state of cause (*hetu*); by the second, through the state of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Or, by the first, through the state of vision (*dassana*); by the second, through the state of seclusion (*viveka*). Or, by the first, through the state of predominance (*adhipati*).

With the second [attribute], the deathless state, he praises the Dhamma. Alternatively, by the phrase "having developed which Dhamma he attained the state of a Buddha," he praises the Dhamma for its being well-expounded (*svākkhāta*).
By the word "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*), he praises it for its being directly visible (*sanditthika*).

Likewise, by the former [attribute] he praises it for its being timeless (*akālika*), and by the latter for its being inviting one to come and see (*ehipassika*). Or else, by the former he praises it for its leading onward (*opanayika*).

With the latter [phrase], he praises the Dhamma by way of its being personally realized. By the term "with stains gone," he shows the purity of the Dhamma through the indication of the absence of defilement;
by the term "unsurpassed," he shows its vastness and perfection through the indication of the non-existence of anything else more distinguished.
Alternatively, with the first [term] he shows the Dhamma's perfection in abandonment, and with the second, its perfection in intrinsic nature.
Or, the state of having removed impurities (*gatamala*) should be applied to the Dhamma by way of its being something to be developed (*bhāvetabba*).

For through the quality of development (*bhāvanā*), it becomes the eradicator of defilements (*dosa*). The state of being unsurpassed (*anuttara*) should be applied by way of its being something to be realized (*sacchikātabba*).

For, because nothing further remains to be done once realization (*sacchikiriyā*) has been produced, and because it is not shared with others, it is called "unsurpassed. Likewise, by the word "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*):
Together with the preliminary virtues (pubbabhāga-sīla) and so forth, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom pertaining to those in training (sekkha) are shown;

by the phrase "having realized," together with that, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha) in the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) are shown.
3. Having thus praised the True Dhamma (saddhamma) in brief by means of all its qualities, [the author now praises] the Noble Saṅgha.
He spoke the words beginning with “of the Sugata” in order to offer praise. Therein, “of the Sugata” is a designation of relationship;
its connection is with the word “sons. “Orasānaṃ” (of the legitimate) is an epithet of the sons. “Crushers of Māra’s army” is a statement of the reason for their status as legitimate sons.
By this, he acknowledges that the very abandonment of the defilements is the reason for the Blessed One’s having them as his legitimate sons.

It shows [this]. "Of eight" is a description of a numerical limit. By this, it shows that even though they possess the status of being distinguished beings and number in the many thousands, they do not exceed this numerical limit, because they do not transcend the state of being established in the path or established in the fruit.
"Assembly" (samūha) is a description of a collection. "Noble Saṅgha" (ariyasaṅgha) is a description of a community distinguished by its virtues. By this...

This also demonstrates that the noble persons (ariyapuggala) possess the nature of the Noble Saṅgha through the concord of their bodies, owing to their being united by the commonality of view and virtue.
In this context, "urasā" means those who exist, are born, and have grown in the breast (the heart).

For just as the legitimate sons (orasaputta) of beings, by virtue of being born from [their] own selves, are especially entitled to the inheritance belonging to the father, even so these noble persons [belong] to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
At the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma, they become absolute partakers of the noble birth, of the bliss of liberation belonging to the Blessed One, and of the jewel of the noble Dhamma;

thus they are "legitimate sons" (*orasā*), as it were. Alternatively, because the noble disciples—who are entering or have entered the plane of the noble ones through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma—are born from the effort generated by the Blessed One’s breast, they are [called] "legitimate sons" in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*).

“They are worthy of being called ‘sons from the breast’ (urasaputtā). For even when the teaching of the Dhamma is being carried out by disciples, it is still called ‘the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma’ because it is rooted in him and because there is no difference in its characteristics and so forth.
Even though, at the time of the noble disciples’ attainment of the Noble Path, [beings] might act to create obstacles for them just as they did for the Blessed One,”
Neither Māra the son of a god nor the host of Māra rejects [the Buddhas] absolutely;
however, when the grounds for their rejection have been demolished, they too are indeed said to be demolished. Thus it is said: "of those who crush the army of Māra.

In this context, although one should have said "of those who crush Māra and the army of Māra," the form "of those who crush the army of Māra" is used by means of a *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (elliptical compound retaining only one member of a similar class).

It should be seen. Alternatively, just as with the Māras of the aggregates and the formations, the host of the power of the defilements (*kilesa-balakāya*) is called an "army" because it acts as an ally in the slaying of the Devaputta Māra. As it is said: "Sensual desires are your first army," and so forth.

And that army of defilements, consisting of one thousand five hundred divisions or indeed infinite divisions, [is to be overcome] by the weapons of such qualities as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity.
The noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) are "crushers of Māra’s army" because they have, in part, crushed, shattered, and scattered it.
By this, he shows that they are sons born after the Blessed One.

They are called "noble" (ariya) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), because they are far removed from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, and because they proceed in the right way. Now...

Or, the Noble Ones (ariya) are so called because they are to be approached as a refuge by the world including the devas, because they are worthy of being approached, and because for those who have approached them, their purpose is accomplished.
The "Noble Saṅgha" (ariyasaṅgha) is the Saṅgha of the Noble Ones; or, it is the Noble Saṅgha because it is both noble and a Saṅgha. That Noble Saṅgha.
Following the Blessed One’s passing, the attainment of even the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma is dependent upon the jewel of the Saṅgha.
It should be understood that the words "I worship with my head" were spoken right here in order to demonstrate the great helpfulness of the Noble Saṅgha.
Furthermore, in this context, by the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he demonstrates the excellence of the Noble Saṅgha’s origin;
and by the phrase "the destroyers of Māra’s army," he demonstrates the excellence of their abandonment, as it illustrates the relinquishing of all defilements. [Of the eight...]
By the term "assembly" (*samūha*), he indicates the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*) through the illumination of the state of being on the path and in the fruition.
By the term "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*), he shows the perfection of power (*pabhāvasampadā*) through the illumination of its preeminence over all assemblies.

Alternatively, "the legitimate sons of the Sugata" illuminates the Noble Saṅgha’s state of having a pure basis; "the destroyers of Māra’s army" illuminates their state of practicing according to the right, straight, and proper method.

“Of the assembly of eight” is an illumination of their status as those worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) and so forth; “the Noble Saṅgha” is an illumination of their status as the unsurpassed field of merit (*puññakkhetta*).
Likewise, by the phrase “the legitimate sons of the Sugata,” he illuminates the existence of supramundane going for refuge within the Noble Saṅgha;
for it is through that supramundane going for refuge that they became the Blessed One’s legitimate sons. “Crushers of Māra’s army”...
By this, he shows the right practice in the prior stage accomplished through the perfection of the resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
For those who have made the resolution and have practiced rightly conquer Māra or the assembly of Māra.

By the phrase "the group of eight," he shows, by way of reference to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhānena*), the states of the trainee (*sekkha*) and the one beyond training (*asekkha*) which have penetrated their respective opposites—the factors of the path and the fruits.

Because it has been proclaimed thus, the phrase "the Noble Saṅgha" demonstrates its status as the most worthy of offerings. Furthermore, going for refuge is the beginning of all the qualities of the disciples;
the stages of training together with their preliminary practices, such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth, constitute the middle;

and the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (asekkha) constitute the end. Thus, in brief, all the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are shown to be excellent in the beginning, the middle, and the end.

4. Thus, having performed a salutation to the Triple Gem by way of briefly enumerating its entire range of qualities through these three verses, he now speaks the words beginning with “iti me,” dedicating that very act of homage toward his intended purpose.

In this context, the term *ratana* (gem) refers to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, in the sense that they generate delight (*rati*). For it is said of them: “Thus indeed is the Blessed One,” and so forth.
As he adverts to the qualities as they truly are, a no small measure of rapture and gladness arises, which serves as the cause for the attainment of the Deathless. As it is said:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... nor by delusion... his mind is upright."
“Indeed, Mahānāma, the noble disciple gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma;
in one who is joyful, rapture arises,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the sense of “jewel” (ratana) is the state of being honored and so on. For this has been said:
“Valued, of great price, incomparable, rare to behold,
and enjoyed by beings who are not ordinary— that is why it is called a ‘jewel’. Furthermore,
qualities such as being highly valued and so forth are found only in the Buddhas and others, and not shared with anyone else.
“Consisting of homage” (*vandanāmaya*) means consisting of homage, just as there are things “consisting of giving” (*dānamaya*) or “consisting of virtue” (*sīlamaya*).
Here, “homage” (*vandanā*) refers to the inclination toward the qualities of the Three Jewels by way of body, speech, and mind, or it is praise (*thomanā*).

It is called “merit” (*puñña*) because it produces the fruit of being worthy of honor (*pujja*), or because it purifies one’s own continuum (*santāna*). “With obstacles well destroyed” (*suvihatantarāyo*) means with obstacles thoroughly destroyed. By this, [the author] indicates his own perfection of faith (*pasāda*).
It shows that through the excellence of the Triple Gem’s status as a field of merit, that merit is capable of destroying obstacles and calamities that hinder the exposition of the meaning.
*Hutvā* (having been) is a verb indicating a prior action; its connection is with the phrase “I shall expound the meaning.
*Tassa* (of that) refers to that merit consisting of the homage to the Triple Gem. *Ānubhāvena* means by its power.

5. Having thus shown the purpose for paying homage to the Triple Gem, he now states, beginning with the words "marked by suttas of middle length," in order to introduce that teaching of the Dhamma whose meaning he wishes to comment upon, by way of praising its qualities.
Therein, "marked by suttas of middle length" means by suttantas that are neither too long nor too short in measure.

Of that which is characterized [by the word *Majjhima*]. For just as in the *Dīgha Āgama* there are suttas of long measure, and as in the two Āgamas—the *Saṃyutta* and *Aṅguttara*—there are suttas of short measure, it is not so here. Here, however, the suttas are of middle measure.
Therefore it was said: "of that which is marked by suttas of middle measure" means "characterized by suttantas that are neither too long nor too short in measure."
“Meaning. By this, he shows that the designation “Middle” is a conventional term following its meaning. But is it not the case that the suttas themselves are the *āgama* (scripture)?
To what, then, does the *āgama* belong as marked by the suttas? This is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*); however, the *āgama* is designated in dependence upon the suttas.
For just as the conventional term “sutta” is used for a collection of both meaning and phrasing, so too [the term *āgama* is used] for a collection of suttas.

This is the conventional designation "āgama" (scripture). "Idha" means in this teaching. It is called "āgama" because one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth, will come (*āgamissanti*) to it, from it, or by means of it.

It is "vara" (excellent) because it is chosen by the wise as being excellent in the sense of possessing the highest qualities such as being "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*), and because it is the cause for the successful attainment of whatever is desired.
Thus, it is an "āgamavara" because it is both an *āgama* and a *vara*. Alternatively, it is "vara" because it is the best among those recognized as *āgamas*.
The excellent Āgama and the medium [Āgama] constitute the "excellent medium Āgama" (*majjhimāgamavara*); [this refers to] that.

"Those who have awakened after the Buddhas" (*buddhānubuddha*) refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Chief Disciples, who have penetrated the Truths by following the penetration of the Truths by the Buddhas.
By them, it was "commented upon" (*saṃvaṇṇita*) by way of both commentaries on the meaning (*attha-saṃvaṇṇanā*) and commentaries on the qualities (*guṇa-saṃvaṇṇanā*).
Alternatively, it should be construed as "the Buddhas and those who have awakened after the Buddha" (*buddhānubuddhā*).

For indeed, whatever meaning was first analyzed by the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) himself—by way of miscellaneous teachings on the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma—that very same meaning was subsequently compiled by the reciters (*saṅgītikāra*) through their respective commentaries. Regarding the phrase "crushing the arguments of opponents" (*paravādamathanassa*):
The meaning is: "the crushing of the arguments of those belonging to other sects" and "the shattering of their adherence to views.

For this scripture is specifically called "the crusher of the doctrines of others" because it elucidates the faults of the adherence to views held by proponents of such views in discourses such as the *Mūlapariyāya* and the *Sabbāsava*, and because it demonstrates the crushing of the false doctrines of Saccaka and others in discourses such as the *Saccaka* and the *Upāli*.
"Thomi-toti. This is the custom of the Master [Buddhaghosa] in his commentaries:
that at the beginning of each respective commentary, there is a praise (*thomanā*) consisting of a recital of the specific qualities of the particular doctrine (*dhamma*) to be commented upon.

For instance, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, and so forth, it occurs respectively as: "of the one possessing qualities that bring forth faith, of the one generating the various modes of knowledge, of the preeminent among those who discourse on the Dhamma... and so on.

Praise was offered [for it] with such words as: “Of that Abhidhamma which generates varied eloquence, which has been plunged into by profound knowledges, and which is constantly diverse through various methods. 6.
It is called *atthakathā* because the meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathīyati*) by means of it; that very thing is the *Aṭṭhakathā*, where the sound *ttha* becomes *ṭṭha*.
Having composed it, as in the passage beginning with "the meaning of oppression is suffering" and so forth, at the First Council;

by the five hundred elders, Mahākassapa and the others, who were masters (*vasin*) because they were endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind through the possession of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and because they possessed the fivefold mastery over the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and other states; "yā" means that which [is the] commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); "saṅgītā" means recited.
In places where it was appropriate to clarify the meaning, [the commentary] was spoken by summarizing it as, "this is the meaning of this," and "this is the meaning of that.
It was also recited subsequently by the Elder Yasa and others during the second and third councils.
By this, he demonstrates the purity of the lineage of his own sub-commentary.
7. He is called "Sīhaḷa" because he was taken from the womb of a lion; thus he is Sīhakumāra.

Because the kṣatriyas on the island of Tambapaṇṇi were born of his lineage, and because that island of Tambapaṇṇi was their dwelling place, the state of being "Sīhaḷa" should be understood [to apply] to both.

"Brought" means brought from Jambudīpa. "Then" means afterwards; for at a later time, in order to prevent confusion with the tenets of other schools, [the text was translated] into the Sīhaḷa language.
"The commentary was composed" means that, because the original root-commentary (*mūlaṭṭhakathā*) is not common to all, this exposition of the meaning must be performed exclusively [by this work].
For this very reason, he says, "for the sake of those dwelling on the island. Therein, the construction is:
"for the sake of those dwelling on the island"—meaning either those dwelling on Jambudīpa or those dwelling on the Sihaḷa island—it was composed in the Sihaḷa language.
8. "Having removed" means having removed the Sinhalese language, which is like a bodice. "From that" means from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "I" refers to himself.
"The delightful language" refers to the Māgadhī language; for that, being the natural mode of expression, delights the minds of the wise.
For this very reason he said, "conforming to the method of the Thread" (*tantinayānucchavika*); that is, it is in accordance with the course of the Pāḷi and conforms to the Pāḷi language.
The meaning [is as follows]: "Free from fault" (*vigatadosa*) means devoid of unrefined expressions, linguistic obscurities, and other such defects.
"Not violating the *samaya*" means not contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhanta*). By this, he states the absence of faults in the meaning.

Indeed, because they are not contradictory, the teachings of the Elders (*theravāda*) will also be elucidated here. "Of those who illuminate the lineage of the Elders" (*theravaṃsadīpānaṃ*): by means of the stable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.

Because they were endowed with these qualities, [they are called] the Elders (thera), such as Mahākassapa and others. The lineage of the Elders (theravaṃsa) is the succession of teachers derived from them.

Being included within that [lineage], because they are perfected in both scripture and realization, they cause it to blaze forth by means of the lamp of wisdom; thus they are the "Lamps of the Elder Lineage" (theravaṃsadīpa), namely, the inhabitants of the Mahāvihāra.
It is "determination" (vinicchaya) because it is determined in various ways at the points of difficulty (gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna).

A discourse that severs doubt proceeds by way of crushing the core of the matter (*khīlamaddana*). They possess a very subtle and delicate analysis (*vinicchaya*), thus they are called "those of very subtle analysis.
Alternatively, *vinicchaya* means that which analyzes; it refers to the knowledge whose object is the meaning as previously stated.

It should be construed thus: they possess a very subtle, skillful, and analytical discernment. By this, [it is shown] that [the teaching] has been handed down through the succession of elders beginning with the Thera Mahākassapa.
And for that very reason, it shows his status as an authority by stating that his determination is unerring, gentle, and subtle—a standard for those dwelling in the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra).
10. Regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and for the sake of good people" (*sujanassa ca*): the particle *ca* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). By this, he shows:
"It is not only for the sake of those dwelling in Jambudīpa, but also for the sake of pleasing virtuous people. And by that [he implies] "also for those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi..."
The meaning “for the benefit” is established because it is easy for them to grasp and so forth, and because it is of great assistance to them as well.
“For the sake of long endurance” means for the purpose of long-lasting persistence; that is to say, for its stability over a long period of time.

For this exposition of the meaning leads to the long endurance of the True Dhamma, since it serves as the means for the correct application of words and phrasing and for the proper method of interpreting the meaning. Indeed, this has been said:
The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the stability, the non-confusion, and the non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Which two? Well-arranged words and phrases, and well-expounded meaning.
(11) Desiring to provide an exposition of the meaning [of this], he spoke the words beginning with “the discourse on virtue” in order to avoid the excessive bulk of that exposition.

For this very reason he said, “I shall not analyze that here. Alternatively, showing the instruction to those who would give a discourse—that the *Visuddhimagga* should be taken as a portion of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) which one intends to compose—he indicates the topics already analyzed therein by way of summary, beginning with the words “The Discourse on Virtue” (*sīlakathā*).
Therein, “the Discourse on Virtue” is a detailed exposition of virtue (*sīla*) by way of what is to be practiced (*cāritta*), what is to be avoided (*vārita*), and so forth.
The "ascetic practices" (*dhutadhamma*) are the thirteen qualities that shake off the defilements, beginning with the practice of eating only almsfood.

"All meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to the thirty-eight mentioned in the Canon and the two mentioned in the Commentary; these are, without exception, the bases for the practice of the development of yoga.
"Accompanied by the exposition of temperaments" means being accompanied by the exposition of the nature and other characteristics of those of a lustful temperament and so forth.
The *jhānas* are the four fine-material-sphere *jhānas*; the *samāpattis* are the four immaterial-sphere attainments.
Alternatively, the eight *jhānas* are so called when they have merely been attained, while they are *samāpattis* when mastery in entering them has been achieved.
Or else, the *jhānas* are the fine-material and immaterial-sphere *jhānas*, while the *samāpattis* are the attainment of fruition and the attainment of cessation.

12. All six super-knowledges (*abhiññā*), distinguished as mundane and supramundane, are summarized and condensed by way of wisdom (*paññā*) according to the method found in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* and other texts, starting from the singlefold classification; this determination is the "determination by the summary of wisdom" (*paññā-saṅkalanā-nicchaya*). 13.

The "mode of conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) refers to the state of being a root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth for conditioned phenomena (*paccayadhamma*), which are the phenomena arising from conditions.

The teaching of that is the "teaching of the mode of conditionality," meaning the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, because it is free from the confusion of tenets held by other schools...
Because it is thoroughly purified, and because the discernment of the compact mass is extremely difficult, it is subtle and delicate;
and because it investigates therein by means of the method of unity and so forth, he said, "by means of the very pure and subtle methods.
Because it has investigated without abandoning the methods as they appear in the *Paṭisambhidā* and other texts, its course is not one that is released [into mere abstraction].

14. Regarding the phrase *iti pana sabbaṃ*: the word *iti* indicates completion; the word *pana* is an ornament of speech. Thus, the meaning is: "all this. *Idha* means "in this commentary. "I shall not analyze that [portion] because it would involve repetition"—this is the intended meaning.
15. Now, determining the sole reason for that non-analysis, he says: "In the middle, the Path of Purification," and so forth.

Therein, by the expression "standing in the middle" (*majjhe ṭhatvā*), which demonstrates its state of being central, it is shown—specifically—that [the author] stands in the midst of the four Āgamas.
This shows that the *Visuddhimagga* is a common commentary (*sādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), and not an uncommon commentary like the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and others. Furthermore,
the phrase "especially" (*visesato*) is stated with the understanding that the *Visuddhimagga* also serves as a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, as appropriate for each.
16. *Icceva* means “just thus. *Tampi* refers to the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*) itself. *Etāya* means by this [work], the *Papañcasūdanī*.
Herein, by the words “brought to the Island of Ceylon,” etc., he shows the cause for composing the commentary;

by the words “for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island, for the satisfaction of good people, and for the long endurance of the Dhamma,” he shows the purpose; and by the words “of the excellent Majjhima Āgama... [he shows the specific source].
By the phrase "I shall clarify the meaning," the purpose (*piṇḍattha*) is shown;

and by the phrases beginning with "Then, having set aside the Sinhalese language" and "The discourse on virtue (*sīlakathā*)," etc., the manner of composition (*karaṇappakāra*) is shown. For even the non-investigation of the discourse on virtue and so forth constitutes the manner of composition here.
The commentary on the introduction to the book is concluded.
Commentary on the Nidānakathā:

Since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of those things that possess distinctions occurs only by way of showing their divisions, first, in order to show the division of the Majjhima Āgama by way of the Paññāsa-vagga suttas and so forth, [the text says]: "Therein, the Majjhima Saṅgīti..."

He said, beginning with the words, "It is named... and so forth. Therein, the phrase "therein" (*tattha*) refers to that statement where it was said, "I shall elucidate the meaning of the excellent Majjhima Āgama.

By the expression "It is named the Majjhima Saṅgīti," and so forth, he shows that the Majjhima Saṅgīti—which was spoken by way of the Majjhima Āgama—is such as this, starting from the *Paññāsa* [Fifty].
Alternatively, "therein" (*tattha*) means: "Understand through this commentary..."
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the *Majjhima-saṅgīti*," this shows that the *Majjhima-saṅgīti* whose meaning you understand is such as this, beginning from the *Paṇṇāsa*.
Five tens make a *paṇṇāsa*; it is the *paṇṇāsa* at the beginning, i.e., at the root, thus it is the "Root-*Paṇṇāsa*" (*mūla-paṇṇāsa*).
That which exists in the middle is "middle" (*majjhima*); and it is both "middle" and...
“Fifty” refers to the middle fifty. “Above fifty” means more than fifty. “Comprising three fifties” means the enumeration of three groups of fifty.
This “comprising” (saṅgaha) is fourfold by way of genus, origin, action, and number. In that regard: “And whatever, friend Visākha... [and so forth].
“Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these qualities are included in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha)”;

this is a grouping by genus. “And as for right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, friend Visākha—these qualities are included in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha)”; this is a grouping by kindred. “And as for right view, friend Visākha...”
“Right view and right intention—these phenomena are included within the aggregate of wisdom. This is inclusion by function (*kiriyā-saṅgaha*).
“If the eye-base is counted as belonging to the aggregate of form, then indeed, it must be said that the eye-base is included within the aggregate of form.
This is inclusion by enumeration (*gaṇanā-saṅgaha*). And this alone is intended here. Therefore it was said:
“Comprising seventy-five” means “a calculation of seventy-five. “From groups” means from a collection;
however, in this context, it should be understood by way of decades. For, in the Dispensation, the term “group” (vagga) is generally used for a decade.
Therefore he said: “having made five groups for each fifty. “The combination of fifteen groups.”
The meaning is "conjunctions of fifteen groups. However, some explain the word *samāyoga* as having the sense of a "collection" (*samudāya*).
Regarding the term "from the words" (*padato*), here a verse-line (*gāthāpāda*) consisting of eight syllables is intended by the word "word"; therefore, the reading should be:
"From the syllables, six hundred thousand and one hundred eighty-four, plus forty-four thousand syllables."
They say this. However, because a verse-line (*gāthāpāda*) is found to consist of anywhere from nine syllables up to twelve syllables,

it is stated that "from the perspective of syllables, there are seven hundred thousand, forty thousand, and fifty-three syllables," having taken into account that a *bhāṇavāra* consists of two hundred and fifty such verses.
For in this way, the calculation of syllables accords with the calculation of sections (*bhāṇavāra*), and not otherwise.
A "section" (*bhāṇavāra*) consists of two hundred and fifty verses, based on verses of thirty-two syllables;

it should be understood that both this calculation of syllables and the calculation of sections are obtained by following the calculation of words (*pada*). Indeed, in order to make this very point known, immediately after the calculation of suttas—
The sections have been counted without including the recitation divisions (*bhāṇavāra*). Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as the recitation divisions have been proclaimed for the Middle [Length Discourses], there are half a recitation division plus twenty-three additional phrases."
"One should discern seven hundred thousand letters, forty thousand, and fifty-three letters.
Regarding "by way of connection," this refers to the connection of the teaching.
For within a single sutta, there is a sequence of preceding and succeeding portions of the teaching.

Connection (*anusandhi*) is so called because it follows from a sequence of inquiry. Herein, connection by way of intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*) is twofold: that which follows from one’s own intention and that which follows from another’s intention.
Furthermore, in some cases it occurs by way of a question from those listening to the Dhamma when the teaching has been interrupted;
in other cases it occurs by way of the intention of the Teacher who is teaching, or of the disciple, or of those receiving the Dhamma.
In some cases, it occurs by way of the Dhamma to be taught; thus, in brief, it is of three kinds. Therefore it was said: “In brief, the connection is threefold:
by way of connection through questioning, connection through intention, and connection according to the context. Furthermore, the connection should be understood as fourfold even in brief.
In that regard: “When this had been said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, what indeed is the near shore...’”
“Which is the bank? Which is the far shore? What is the sinking in the middle? What is the emergence on dry land? What is the seizure by humans?
What is the seizure by non-humans? What is the whirlpool? What is the state of internal putrefaction?
The sequence of questions is to be understood as the teaching set forth by the Blessed One in response to those who asked thus. Then, to a certain monk...
Thus a reflection arose in his mind: "In this way, indeed, form is non-self... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self.
How then, when actions are performed by what is non-self, will they touch a self?
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of that bhikkhu, addressed the bhikkhus: "It is possible, indeed..."

“Monks, it is possible that here some foolish person, being ignorant and immersed in ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think that the Teacher’s instruction should be overstepped, thinking:
‘Thus, indeed, form is non-self... [and so on] ...they will experience [feeling].
What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? In this way, [he addresses] the inclinations of others.

Having understood this, the connection [of the discourse] should be known as being according to the underlying inclinations of others through the manner in which the Blessed One delivered his teaching:

"Then, O Brahmin, it occurred to me: 'What if, on those nights that are well-known and distinguished—namely, the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—on such nights as these, I were to go to those sacred groves and shrines...'"
“‘I might dwell in such dwelling places—forest shrines and tree shrines that are terrifying and hair-raising—thinking, "Perhaps I might see fear and dread.
Thus was it said by the Blessed One: 'In this matter, friends, greed is evil and hatred is evil;
for the abandoning of greed and for the abandoning of hatred, there is the Middle Way.'"
"Leading to the eye, leading to knowledge, it conduces to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna"—

thus the connection based on the teacher's own inclination (*attajjhāsayānusandhi*) should be understood as occurring through the teaching delivered by the General of the Dhamma according to his own personal disposition.
Alternatively, it may be understood by way of a corresponding state of phenomena (*dhamma*) to that principle with which the teaching began at the outset.
Alternatively, the sequence of connection should be understood according to those suttas in which the subsequent teaching arises by way of the opposing factor (*paṭipakkhadhamma*).
For example: in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, the teaching arose below by way of virtue (*sīla*), while higher up, direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is presented.
In the *Vatthu Sutta*, the teaching arose below by way of defilement (*kilesa*), while higher up, the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are presented. In the *Kosambaka Sutta*...
Below, the teaching arose by way of quarreling; above, the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) are presented.
In the Simile of the Saw, below the teaching arose by way of impatience; above, the Simile of the Saw is presented.
In detail, however, there is here—in this [text]—a threefold and fourfold connection (*anusandhi*) in this manner in brief.
In the *Majjhima Nikāya*, when analyzed in detail as appropriate in each respective sutta, there are three thousand nine hundred and something connections (*anusandhi*) discernible.

Just as this statement regarding the divisions into fifties and so forth serves to show the actual form of the Middle Collection (*Majjhima Saṅgīti*), it also serves to avoid the fault of inclusion (*pakkhepa-dosa*). For, in the case of the fifties and so forth—

Once these have been determined, there would be no occasion for anyone to claim that even a single word of a discourse brought forth as being distinct from them belongs to this Middle Collection (*Majjhima Saṅgīti*).
Thus, having defined the Middle Collection by way of the sequence and phrasing of the discourses in the fifty sections (*vagga*), [the text continues].
Now, wishing to provide a commentary on this [work] starting from the beginning, he said, "In that regard, among the fifty sections, the Mūlapaññāsa is first," etc.,
in order to show that his own commentary proceeds according to the sequence established during the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
Therein, because the Dhamma and Vinaya were taught and promulgated in various places according to specific circumstances, they were scattered.
*Saṅgīti* means singing together after having gathered [the teachings]; because its scope is vast and it is worthy of veneration, it is a "great *saṅgīti*," thus a *mahāsaṅgīti*.
The first *mahāsaṅgīti* is the *paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*; the time when that took place is the *paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*, and it is at that *paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*.
It establishes the teaching—making known what was previously unknown—by way of the teacher, the time, and so forth.

It is called the *nidāna* because it points back to the origin; that which is termed "introduction" (*upodghāta*) by worldly people should here be understood as the textual passage beginning with "Thus have I heard," and not, as in expressions such as "Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its basis," the cause for the arising of the teaching through intention and so forth.
For this very reason, he said: "The passage beginning with 'Thus have I heard' was [spoken] by the Venerable Ānanda..."

"The introductory narrative was spoken at the time of the First Great Council. Now, although it would be appropriate here to state in detail that particular First Great Council in which this [text] was deposited according to its sequence—
since it has already been explained in detail by myself in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and should therefore be sought there—
I shall do so while avoiding the excessive bulk of this present commentary.
He said, “But that [discourse], however,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Nidānakathā is finished.
1. The Chapter on the Fundamental Exposition (Mūlapariyāyavagga).
1. Commentary on the *Mūlapariyāyasutta*:
Commentary on the Internal Introduction.
Having thus referred to what is to be said regarding the external introduction, [the author] now proceeds to comment upon the internal introduction starting from the beginning.
The passage beginning with “But as for this” (*yaṃ panetaṃ*) has been stated.

In that regard, since one who provides a commentary must first show the word-analysis (*padavibhāga*) and the meaning of the words (*padattha*) concerning the phenomena to be commented upon, and thereafter provide the commentary by way of showing their collective sense (*piṇḍattha*) and so forth, he therefore spoke the words beginning with “*Evaṃ* is a particle-word” (*nipātapada*), in order to first show those words. In that context, “word-analysis” (*padavibhāgo*) refers to [the analysis] of the words.

This refers to a compound (*padaviggaha*), not a word-analysis (*padavibhāga*). Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of the term *padavibhāga*, both the words (*pada*) and the analysis of words (*padavibhāga*)—or the compound of words (*padaviggaha*) and the analysis of words (*padavibhāga*)—are expressed through the principle of "retaining one" (*ekasesa*).
In that context, the compound of words is: "It is both beautiful (*subhaga*) and a forest (*vana*), thus 'beautiful forest' (*subhagavana*); [and] of the *sāla* trees..."

It should be understood in the context of compound terms (*samāsa-padesu*) by way of such examples as "the king" (*rājā*), "and that king was a *sāla* tree, thus [he is called] Sālarāja," and so forth.

"In terms of meaning" (*atthato*) means in terms of the word-meaning (*padatthato*). Showing the meaning of the word *evaṃ* first, according to the sequence for extracting the meanings, he says: "First, as for the word *evaṃ*," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "restriction, etc. (*avadhāraṇādi*), here the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes meanings such as "this," "question," "measure," and so forth.

The inclusion [of the word *evaṃ*] should be understood. For instance, in such expressions as “various crafts and occupations have reached this state (*evaṃgatāni*), being of such a kind (*evavidho*) and such a form (*evamākāro*),” the word *evaṃ* has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*. Indeed, the word *gata* is a synonym for manner (*pakāra*), as are the words *vidha* and *ākāra*.
For worldly people explain that when the word *gata* is joined with *vidha*, it signifies manner (*pakāra*). Thus: “In this way (*evaṃ*), you have been well-bathed...”

In such passages as, “Well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, wearing ornaments of jeweled earrings, clothed in white garments, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they sport about—
just as you do now together with your teachers,” it refers to a question.
In such passages as, “Thus its revolution is so rapid, thus its lifespan is so limited,” it refers to a measure.

But is it not the case that in the passage, “Thus indeed you are well-bathed, well-anointed; thus is the limit of your lifespan,” the word *evaṃ* (thus) expresses both the mode of questioning and the measure [of the lifespan], and therefore the word *evaṃ* has the sense of “mode”?

No, because there is a distinction. For when the word *evaṃ* denotes a mere mode—as in “It is thus, indeed” (*evaṃ byā kho*) and so forth—it is intended to have the sense of “mode”; however, it does not denote a specific mode. And so:
Having thus established the appropriate examples and illustrations beginning with “By a mortal born in this way,” it is so:

for in the passage “Just as... much,” the collection of causes for merit—such as rebirth as a human, reliance upon a true person, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, the attainment of wealth, and the performance of deeds like giving—is comparable to a string of garlands because it possesses qualities such as beauty and fragrance, being the substitute for a heap of flowers.
Since abundant meritorious deeds are to be performed by a mortal being because of the nature of having to die, they are like a heap of flowers or a string of garlands;

thus, because the manner of comparison is stated indistinctly by means of the word "yathā" (just as), it is appropriate to say that "the word ‘evaṃ’ (thus) has the sense of concluding the manner of comparison.
However, when that manner of comparison is specified, it becomes a simile in meaning; therefore he said, "in a simile..."

"...has arrived.
