Likewise, regarding the manner of instruction such as "one should approach in this way," the specific mode of demonstrating that perfection of deportment (ākappa-sampatti) appropriate for a recluse is, in its essential meaning, itself an instruction; thus it is said: "In this way to you... [and so on] ...in the instruction.
Similarly, in the passage "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata," the meaning as spoken by the Blessed One—
“Encouragement” (*sampahaṃsana*) refers to the act of gladdening and inspiring those who know [the truth] without error, by means of proclaiming the qualities actually present therein.
It should be construed as: “that which is the manner of encouragement therein.

In the same way, it should be construed here that “the manner of censuring” is what they call [it]; and that manner of censuring arises from the presence of abusive words such as “outcaste” (*vasalī*).
It is understood that [the meaning] is made manifest here by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*).

And just as it is here, so too should the forms of similes and the like be regarded as being stated by way of simile and so forth, due to the proximity of words such as "heaps of flowers" which are spoken by way of simile.

However, the phrase "Yes, venerable sir" (*evaṃ, bhante*) is used by the bhikkhus—who have been directed toward the careful hearing and attention of the Dhamma—as a way of acknowledging their own state of being established therein.
Because it has been stated here, the word *evaṃ* (thus) is used in the sense of accepting what has been said. By this, it is meant: "Yes, venerable sir;
well said, venerable sir; very well, venerable sir. And as for the instruction, "Speak thus," it means:
"Speak to the ascetic Ānanda in the same manner as I am speaking. This mode of speaking which is now to be described is indicated by the word *evaṃ*.

It is said, "in the sense of illustration. Regarding the phrase "it is so for us" (*evaṃ no*), here too, in order to produce a firm conviction regarding the fact that those aforementioned phenomena bring about harm and suffering, a question is posed by way of seeking consent: "Do they lead [to such results] or not?
What is your view on this? Since it is then stated, "It is so for us on this point," the word *evaṃ* (so) expresses a firm conviction in that specific manner.
"Vibhāvita" is understood as "discerned. However, since that mode of leading to harm and suffering for those phenomena is being delimited, it has the sense of restriction;
thus he said: "In 'thus it is for us here,' etc., [the term refers to] restriction.

"Skilled in various methods" refers to those consisting of unity, diversity, non-exertion, and the nature of things (dhammatā), and those consisting of the "turning of joy" (nandiyāvatta), the "tipukkhalasīhavikkīḷita," and the "hook-like observation" (aṅkusadisālocana).

Or, "various methods" (*nānānayā*) refers to various ways of approach according to the distinctions of the basis (*ādhāra*) and so forth; or "methods" (*nayā*) refers to the modes of the textual tradition (*pāḷigati*).

These [modes] exist by way of basic rules (*paññatti*) and supplementary rules (*anupaññatti*), by way of categories such as pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, mundane (*lokiya*) and so forth, mixed with both (*tadubhayavomissaka*) and so forth, wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, compendiums (*saṅgaha*) and so forth, liberation through occasion (*samayavimutta*) and so forth, establishing (*ṭhapanā*) and so forth, roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) and so forth, and the triads and dyads (*tikappaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.

"And of various kinds" means of various methods. "Skillful in those [methods]" means subtle, delicate, and refined through those various methods. "Inclination" (*āsaya*) is the same as "disposition" (*ajjhāsaya*);
these are manifold due to distinctions such as eternalism and so forth, and within that, due to distinctions such as having little defilement (*apparajakkha*) and so forth;

or rather, it has its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*)—that is, its cause of arising—in various dispositions, such as self-disposition and so on; thus, it is "originated by various dispositions. "Endowed with meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasampanna*).
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: it is "complete in both meaning and phrasing" because there is nothing further to be added;

that is, it is endowed with the six factors of meaning—namely, announcing, revealing, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and defining—and with the six factors of phrasing—namely, the description of syllables, words, phrases, modes, etymologies, and explanations.
Regarding the phrase "various miracles" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*), they explain the meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya* as follows:

"It is called a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes adversaries and because it takes away the defilements such as lust. However, the Blessed One has no adversaries such as lust that need to be removed.

Even for ordinary worldlings, when the mind is free from secondary defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and its adversaries have been destroyed, the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) [arise].
Because it occurs [in that context], it is not possible to call it a "manifestation" (pāṭihāriya) here by using the conventional terminology applicable there.

However, if it is said to be a "manifestation" because it removes the defilements residing in those to be converted—which are the adversaries of the Blessed One, the Great Compassionate One—then this is appropriate.
Alternatively, [it refers to] those which are the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Dispensation.
[It is called] *pāṭihāriya* because it takes away those who belong to other sects (*titthiya*).
For they are taken away and removed by means of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, through the removal of their views and because they are incapable of proclaiming [their own] views.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "afterwards" (*pacchā*), as in such passages as: "When he had entered therein, another brahmin arrived."
Therefore, "manifestation" (*pāṭihāriya*) refers to that which is to be carried out and set in motion after the mind has become concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task;
or, it is the "carrying away" (*haraṇa*) that occurs subsequently once one’s own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the paths [of the noble ones].
Furthermore, the miracles of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction are performed for the welfare of beings by one who is free from defilements and has accomplished his task.
Furthermore, they must be performed again; and because they remove the defilements of other beings from one's own defilements—which are like green grass—they are called "miracles" (*pāṭihāriya*).

A miracle itself is a "miracle," or that which exists within the collection of miracles consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) is called a "miracle" individually.
Alternatively, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "miracles" because they remove opposing factors.
*Pāṭihāriya* means that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which has come from that; thus it is a "miracle.

Since this miracle is found in the teaching of the Blessed One in many ways—through the classification of psychic power (*iddhi*) and so forth, and through the classification of its objects—he said, "the manifold miracle" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*).
"Not otherwise" means not other than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One; it does not mean [not other] than the Blessed One...
From the perspective of the manner of teaching: for the Blessed One’s teaching possesses an inconceivable power.
And by taking it thus, the statement, "Who is capable of understanding it in every aspect? is justified;

furthermore, this does not contradict the demonstration of the power of retention, because what is intended is the non-deviation from the manner of what was heard. For here, there is no need to avoid the charge of redundancy between the two.
This is because they have the same object. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder was both capable and incapable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching in its entirety.
This is because [the term "self"] is applied to one's own continuity, which is designated as "internal" (*niyakajjhatta*), as stated in the passage: "That which is not another is the self."
Although the word *me* is seen in only a single sense in all three ways, he says,
"The word *me* is seen in three senses," with reference to the existing distinction based on its designation as an instrument (*karaṇa*), a recipient (*sampadāna*), or an owner (*sāmin*).

Although a prefix (*upasagga*) qualifies an action, nevertheless, because it is merely indicative, even when that prefix is present, it is the root-word itself (*sutasaddo*) that [expresses the meaning].

He says, “Both with a prefix and without a prefix,” etc., demonstrating that when the word *suta* (heard) without a prefix is used to denote its meaning, it is not contradictory to include the form with a prefix, since it expresses that very same meaning.

The word “its” (*assa*) refers to the word *suta*. Since the instrumental (*kamma-sādhana*) and locative (*bhāva-sādhana*) derivations are possible here for the word *suta*, he says: “either ‘that which is held’ (*upadhārita*) or ‘the holding’ (*upadhāraṇa*).”
"Or else, it is the meaning. Regarding "when 'mayā' is the meaning": this means when the word *me* functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of the agent (*kartr*).
Regarding "when 'mamā' is the meaning": this is when it functions as a possessor (*sāmin*) by way of a relationship (*sambandha*).
It is stated that, in the proximity of the word *suta*, the word *evaṃ* must be employed as that which illuminates the act of hearing (*savana-kiriyā*).
"‘Thus’ is a demonstration of the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the five-door consciousnesses, such as receiving-consciousness and the rest, as well as the mind-door consciousnesses brought forward by them.

Since all sentences are accompanied by the sense of the particle *eva*, the meaning "heard indeed" (*sutameva*) is obtained for the word "heard" (*suta*); thus he says, "by way of negating the state of not having heard."

By this restriction, he shows its lack of attachment. Just as "what is heard is indeed heard" must be delimited, he says, "it is properly heard," in order to indicate the grasping that is neither deficient nor redundant and is non-erroneous.

Alternatively, since a word expresses a meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words, the meaning of "heard" is that it is not un-heard; thus it is said, "by way of negating the state of being unheard."
By this, he effects a turning away from [what is merely] seen and so forth. This is what is meant: "This was not seen by me, nor realized through self-become knowledge;
rather, it was heard, and that too correctly. For this very reason, he said: "It is a demonstration of a grasp that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous.

Alternatively, when the word *evaṃ* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), this construction of meaning is made; thus, for the word *suta*, which depends on that [word *evaṃ*], [the following applies].
This meaning was stated as "by way of the negation of the state of not hearing. For this very reason, he said: "a demonstration of grasping that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous.
And here, the word *savana* (hearing) should be understood in the sense of the object (*kamma*), as in "it is heard" (*suyyati*).
Thus, the application of the meaning of the three terms in one manner is by way of the cause of hearing, the person who hears, and the particularity of the hearing itself.
Having shown this, he now says "in the same way" and so forth in order to demonstrate it by means of other modes as well.
Therein, "of that" refers to that cognitive process of the mind-door (*manodvāra-viññāṇa-vīthi*) which occurred in the presence of the Blessed One in the manner of hearing the Dhamma;
for that [process] is capable of proceeding toward objects of various kinds. And thus it has been said: "by following the ear-door."
"In various ways" (*nānappakārena*) means by way of the different modes of grasping the meaning of the expressions that will be explained.

By this, he indicates that in this construction, the word *evaṃ* is taken in the sense of "manner. "The manifestation of the state of occurrence" (*pavattibhāvappakāsanaṃ*) means the manifestation of the existence of the occurrence.
"Hearing" (*sutaṃ*) is the manifestation of the Dhamma; it refers to the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) of the aforementioned type with respect to whatever object [is present].
Because it occurs in various modes, it is called *dhamma* on account of its being a phenomenon (*dhamma*), not because the word "heard" (*suta*) has the meaning of *dhamma*.

The clarification of that very same meaning is given by the passage beginning with "For here... and so forth. In that context, the term *viññāṇavīthiyā* is used in the instrumental sense (expressing the means).

*Mayā* is used in the agentive sense. The word *evaṃ* is employed for the purpose of pointing out (*nidassana*), having been taken as the indicator of the mode to be demonstrated; thus it is said regarding that which is to be pointed out.
Because of the absence of anything that ought to be demonstrated [as a separate entity]. By that word "thus" (*evaṃ*), he shows that the entire sutta is referred back [to this opening phrase].

Since the word *suta* (heard) is a verb, and because the act of hearing is connected to a common continuum of consciousness (*viññāṇapabandha*), and because the designation "person" (*puggala*) is applied there, it is said: "‘Suta’ is an exposition of the function of the person. For [the term] is not devoid of the conventional designation of a person.
"The act of hearing is obtained in a composition of Dhamma.

The phrase "of whichever stream of consciousness," and so forth, was stated by taking the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the sense of manner (*ākāra*), in order to show an alternative application of the meaning different from the previous construction.
In that context, "conceptualization of manner" (*ākāra-paññatti*) is precisely a derivative conceptualization (*upādā-paññatti*) of phenomena.
It is spoken of in that way by way of the grasping of the mode of occurrence. "Suta" (heard) is a designation for the object;

it is stated as such because, taking into account the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, the phenomenon (dhamma) which has become the object of hearing is the locus of its occurrence by way of that act of hearing.

Although there is no agent whatsoever in the ultimate sense apart from the continuum of consciousness, [this is said] through the usage of conventional language, out of a desire for words expressing a distinction conceived by the intellect.
It is stated as if that [consciousness] were something other than the mental continuum, saying "by means of the mental continuum, for one who possesses it.

Furthermore, although the dharma to be heard is the object of the act of hearing, it is here [referred to] by way of the mental continuum that functions through the act of hearing, because in the ultimate sense (paramattha) the mental continuum is the agent;
or else, because the occurrence of consciousness itself, by way of hearing, constitutes the state of the act of hearing.
And because that [object] is the domain of the agent of the action, it is said: "in the domain of the agent possessing that.
Furthermore, because the Elder was one who had correctly ascertained the nature of what was heard, he said: "the conclusion of grasping.
Alternatively, it should be understood that by taking the word *evaṃ* (thus) for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇattha*), this construction of the meaning has been made.
The word *evaṃ* has the nature of manifesting the form, the indication, or the determination of the meaning and the phrasing of various previously heard discourses (*sutta*) designated as such;

thus it is said: “*Evaṃ* is a designation of the function of a person,” because it denotes the operation of the collection of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*) which serves as the basis for the conceptual designation of a person (*puggala-paññatti*) through the determination of that form and so forth.
However, since even for the Puggalavādins there is no act of hearing that is independent of consciousness, it is specifically the operation of consciousness; thus he says:

"‘Heard’ is a designation for the function of consciousness. And because the occurrence of the word ‘me’ (I) refers exclusively to a sentient being, and the function of consciousness must be subsumed under that very [being], he says:
"‘Me’ is a designation for a person endowed with both functions."

It has been stated. The meanings of the words *evaṃ* (thus) and *sutaṃ* (heard), which respectively possess the nature of a designation for what does not exist (*avijjamāna-paññatti*) and a designation for what exists (*vijjamāna-paññatti*), are shown by way of their function as a collection of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*) serving as the basis for such designations;

thus he said: "‘Thus’ is a description of the function of the person (*puggala-kicca*), ‘heard’ is a description of the function of consciousness (*viññāṇa-kicca*)". And here, it is by way of clarifying the distinctions between the instrument, the action, the agent, and the object that [this is explained].

It should be understood that the four applications of meaning beginning with the accusative case are shown by way of: (1) the person, the activity, and the object; (2) the demonstration of the person’s activity; (3) the specific designation of the mode of apprehension, the apprehender, and the object to be apprehended;

and (4) the designation of the agent, the instrument, the activity, and the agent [of that activity]. This is because every meaning attainable through language must be approached solely by means of its conceptual designation (*paññatti*), and because all such designations...
Because they are included among the six types of designations starting with "existent" (*vijjamāna*),
he says, "‘Thus’ (*eva*) and ‘mine’ (*me*) and so forth," while determining the specific nature of those designations such as "thus. In that context,

because the meaning being expressed by "thus" and "mine" lacks the perception of phenomena such as the letter-forms (vowels and consonants) and so on, it is a designation of the non-existent (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).

He said: "It is a designation of what does not exist by way of the true and ultimate sense. In this context, "by way of the true and ultimate sense" means by way of the meaning of reality and the meaning of supremacy. This is what is meant:

that which is not a non-real object like an illusion or a mirage, nor a non-supreme object to be grasped through hearsay and the like; rather, it is the intrinsic nature of form, sound, and so forth, and the intrinsic nature of being affected, experiencing, and so on.

The meaning [of the word *sacca*] is called the "actual meaning" (*saccikaṭṭha*) and the "ultimate meaning" (*paramattha*), but the meaning of the phrases “Thus have I heard” (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*) is not so.

To make this very point clearer, it was said: “What is there in this? and so forth. However, the word “heard” (*sutaṃ*) is spoken with reference to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), as in the phrase “an existing designation” (*vijjamānapaññatti*).
For it is for this very reason that it says: “That which has been apprehended here by the ear.”
It has been said: "When it is stated, 'perceived by way of the ear-door,' everything—including both the meaning (attha) and the phrasing (byañjana)—is thereby obtained.

It is to be expressed as such because it is spoken in dependence upon this or that [object]. That is to say, in dependence upon those phenomena that have come within the range of the ear, one says "thus" (*evaṃ*) by way of referring back to their determined aspects and so forth;
and in dependence upon the aggregates included within one's own continuity, one says "mine" (*me*).

The meaning [is as follows]. Although the conventional usage of "heard" (*suta*) occurs with respect to the sense-base of sound (*saddāyatana*), which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of being seen and so forth—just like the expressions "second," "third," and so on—it nevertheless occurs only by depending upon what has been seen, smelled, or cognized, such as "the first" and so on.

Therefore, he said: "Because it must be spoken of in relation to what has been seen, etc. For this meaning is explained thus: "it is not un-heard, therefore it is 'heard' (*suta*). By oneself, the Thread (*sutta*)...
The Elder replied, "It is indeed so," referring to the specific modes [of recollection]; thus he said, "it illuminates non-delusion.
By the phrase "one becomes capable of various kinds of penetration," he shows both the manifold nature and the difficulty of penetrating the discourse that is about to be spoken.
He says, "it illuminates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard," because the manner of what was heard is being shown as it truly is. "By non-delusion" means by the absence of delusion.
Or rather, it is through wisdom itself—arisen at the time of hearing—that the subsequent accomplishment of wisdom occurs.

This same point should also be stated regarding the phrase "without confusion. Since the aspect of the phonemes to be penetrated is not exceedingly profound, and since there is nothing further to be done there than the mere retention of what has been heard, the function of mindfulness is predominant; wisdom is subordinate there. Thus it is said: "preceded by wisdom," and so forth.
“Having taken [the phrase] ‘preceded by wisdom’ (paññāya pubbaṅgamā)”: here, being preceded means being predominant, as in such passages as “mind is the forerunner” (manopubbaṅgamā).

Alternatively, since the eye-consciousness and so forth are subordinate to the adverting consciousness and so on due to their being preceded [by them], this meaning is also appropriate: “wisdom is the precursor to this [mindfulness].
Thus, regarding the expression “preceded by mindfulness” (satipubbaṅgamā), one should follow the method already stated.
The meaning should be understood according to what is possible.

"Endowed with both meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasampanna*) means either "endowed with a complete meaning and phrasing," or it should be seen as meaning "possessing six factors of meaning— namely, through the methods of revealing, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, making clear, and defining— and six factors of phrasing— namely, through the methods of letters, words, phrases, syntax, etymology, and exposition."
The word *evaṃ* (thus) illuminates *yonisomanasikāra* (wise attention);
the intention is that it refers to the fact that the objects of the true Dhamma—which are expressed by the meanings of "mode," "indication," and "determination"—are unerring.

It illuminates non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) in the sense that, without concentration, one cannot hear the Sutta that is about to be explained and has reached the present context through such inquiries as, "Where was the *Mūlapariyāya* spoken? and so forth.
It was stated on the grounds that [such a thing] is not possible. The passage beginning with "of one whose mind is distracted" is stated by way of corroborating that very point.
"By all excellences" refers to the excellence of meaning, phrasing, teacher, purpose, and so forth.

Just as [proper attention] has the sense of indicating the mode, the demonstration, and the determination [of the object], it is like the hearing of the true Dhamma in relation to its domain, which is the true Dhamma free from error. And just as...
Just as the accomplishment of right disposition toward oneself and previously performed merit is stated to result from non-distraction through its fruit-like appropriate attention—
because they are inseparable from it— in the same way, the accomplishment of hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a good person should be shown to result from non-distraction as their fruit,
because these do not exist for one who has not heard the Dhamma and lacks reliance upon a good person. Not...

Furthermore, by the statement beginning with "one whose mind is distracted," which establishes the capacity [of the listener], it is shown that the accomplishment of hearing the True Dhamma—which is the fruit—is achieved through non-distraction as the cause and through reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*). Here, this following interpretation would be appropriate:
hearing the True Dhamma and reliance upon a true person are not exclusively the causes of non-distraction, because they are external factors (*bāhiraṅga*).
Furthermore, non-distraction is the sole cause for hearing the true Dhamma, just as reliance upon a virtuous person is for the hearing of the true Dhamma.

Even so, this demonstration of the accomplishment of reliance upon a virtuous person by means of non-distraction is not yet fully established; it is not that it is not established, because for those with distracted minds, the purpose is accomplished through the absence of attending upon a virtuous person.
And here, the former [demonstration] is [made] by means of the result [to show] the cause.
The first is the demonstration of the accomplishment [of a result] through a sign, like the swelling of a river indicating the certainty of rain upstream;
the second is the demonstration of the accomplishment of the fruit through its cause, which should be seen as the occurrence of rain through the rising of a cloud that rains unconditionally.
This is the manner of penetrating the excellence of the entire Dispensation by way of the distinctions and divisions of the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s word.
It is said that "such is the auspicious form" because it is the cause for the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others without remainder;

this is connected with the phrase "because it does not exist. The "attainment of the latter two wheels" refers to the pair of qualities consisting of one's own right aspiration and previously performed merit.
Furthermore, they are called "wheels" (cakkāni) because they function in succession, and because by means of them sentient beings move through states of fortunate rebirth.
Or rather, it is with reference to this that it was said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels; possessed of which, the fourfold wheel turns for gods and humans,” and so forth.
Furthermore, the sequence of first and last here should be understood according to the order of the teaching.
“By means of the accomplishment of the latter two wheels” means by way of the existence of the latter two wheels. One whose self was previously rightly directed...
And because one who has performed merit becomes pure in disposition due to the distancing of the defilements that are the causes of impurity, it is said:
“Purity of disposition is accomplished. For it has been stated: “A mind rightly directed makes one better than before,” and:
“You have performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be free from taints. Therefore, he said:
“Through purity of disposition, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in realization. Regarding “purity of application”:

it is by way of the clarity of the application of hearing the Dhamma, which is preceded by wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). Thus it is said: “the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures (*āgama*”).
Or, it is by way of the faultless nature of all applications of body and speech. For one whose applications of body and speech are completely pure is free from remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).
"One whose mind is undistracted is confident in the scriptures.

By the phrase "illuminating various kinds of penetration," and so forth, he demonstrates the application of meaning by way of the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*), because it illustrates the Elder’s lack of confusion and non-forgetfulness regarding both the meaning (*attha*) and the phrasing (*byañjana*) through the words *evaṃ* and *suta*. Therein, "illuminating the penetration of the various types of what is to be heard" means:
By this, he shows that this word *suta* (heard), through its proximity to the word *evaṃ* (thus) or by looking forward to what is yet to be said,
reaches out to a specific portion of the Dhamma that is to be heard in a general sense. Since the thorough investigation and deep penetration of the Dhammas of the scriptures—

which bring about mental vision— are specifically dependent upon attention (*manasikāra*), these [qualities] are joined with the word *evaṃ*, which illustrates "wise attention" (*yoniso-manasikāra*) according to the method already stated.

Since the mastery of the Dhamma through hearing, retention, and verbal cultivation is specifically dependent upon attentive listening, he—linking it with the word *suta* (heard), which illustrates non-distraction—arouses enthusiasm for hearing the Dhamma as a perfection of the Dispensation.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). "Examined with the mind" means: "Here, virtue (*sīla*) is taught..."
"Here is concentration, here is wisdom; such are the connections here"—in this manner, he has examined [the teachings] again and again with the mind.

"Well-penetrated by view" means: either by the view consisting of receptivity through reflection (*nijjhānakkhanti*), or by the view known as full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), he has thoroughly [understood] the material and immaterial phenomena taught in various places, [thinking]: "Such is form, so much is form," and so forth.
Having established [the meaning], they have penetrated it.
"By the entire phrase" is said because, previously, it was applied separately by means of three words.

"Not attributing to oneself" means not placing [the thought] "this is mine" within oneself. "The plane of the bad person" refers to ingratitude; as it is said: "In this case, a certain evil bhikkhu..."

The state of ignoble speech mentioned in the passage, "Having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, one burns oneself," that very state of ignoble speech is the non-Dhamma (*asaddhamma*).
But is it not the case that because the Elder Ānanda lacked the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of thinking "this is my word," and because Elders such as Mahākassapa were free from such suspicion,
their statements regarding the transcendence of the plane of the unworthy person (*asappurisa*) and so forth [apply to them]?
“Is it pointless? No, it is not so; for by saying, “Thus have I heard,” this meaning is also shown to have been clarified.
However, some say: “That statement was made with reference to the reflections of the deities; therefore, such an objection has no place.
For at that moment, a reflection arose in the minds of certain deities: “The Blessed One...”

"He has attained final Nibbāna, yet this venerable one is skilled in teaching; now he teaches the Dhamma—he who was born into the Sakyan clan, the brother of the Tathāgata, and the son of his younger paternal uncle.
Does he teach the Dhamma that he himself has realized, or is it merely the word of the Blessed One as he has heard it?
Thus, from the perspective of such doubts and from the point of entering the plane of a person of no virtue (asappurisa),...
"Transcending and so forth" has been explained. "He leads" (appeti) indicates this.

It is a "guide" (netti) because it leads beings, as appropriate, toward the welfare of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal; thus, the Dhamma itself is the guide, a "guide to the Dhamma" (dhammanetti).
Doubt (vicikicchā) is a state firmly rooted and fixed. Vacillation (vimati) is a mere difference of opinion that does not involve excessive wandering. Lack of faith (assaddhiya) [is also included].

It is destroyed because it was taught by the Blessed One, because it was received from him in his presence, and because it is free from the fault of grasping at errors, mispronunciations, and the like.

Herein, the first three applications of meaning are shown by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "thus" without grasping any specific distinction among meanings such as "manner" (*ākāra*) and so on;
the four following [applications] are elucidated by taking the word *evaṃ* specifically in the sense of "manner"; and the final one...

However, it should be understood that the three [instances] have employed the word *evaṃ* respectively for the purpose of indicating a mode, for the purpose of illustration, and for the purpose of restriction.
The word *eka* is seen in such senses as "other," "best," "without companion," and "number. For instance, it is used thus: "The self and the world are eternal..."
In such passages as "This alone is the truth, all else is vain," it is seen in the sense of "other";
in "one-pointedness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), in the sense of "preeminent"; in "alone, withdrawn," in the sense of "without a companion";
and in "There is, monks, only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," in the sense of "number. Here too, he shows that it is used in the sense of number.

He said: "The term 'one' is a designation for the delimitation by counting. Regarding "time" (*kāla*) and "occasion" (*samaya*): "proper time" refers to the appropriate time, and "occasion" (*khaṇa*) refers to the completeness of conditions.
For the appearance of a Tathāgata and so forth is the occasion for the holy life of the Path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.

Furthermore, the "occasion" itself is the "occasion" (*samaya*). The meaning is that what is called both "occasion" and "occasion" is one and the same; thus it is called the "Great Occasion" (*mahāsamaya*).

"A great multitude. "Even a time" (*samayo pi kho*) means even the cause for fulfilling the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "Proponents of doctrines" (*samayappavādaka*) refers to proponents of views (*diṭṭhippavādaka*);
for it is there that the various sectarians (*titthiya*), sitting together, proclaim their respective doctrines.

"The realization of the goal" (*atthābhisamaya*) refers to the attainment of welfare (*hita*). "That which is to be realized" (*abhisametabba*) is "realization" (*abhisamaya*); thus, "the goal is realization" (*abhisamayaṭṭha*) [is said] because oppression and so forth are things to be realized.

These have been stated by bringing them into a state of unity. Alternatively, the meaning that constitutes the object of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) or penetration is the "meaning of clear realization" (*abhisamayaṭṭha*).

Those very [meanings] are thus stated as a single entity. In this context, "affliction" (*pīḷana*) refers to the oppression of the truth of suffering, which is the harming of one who possesses it and the making of it non-expansive.
"Torment" (*santāpa*) refers to the burning and scorching by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth.
In this context, it is a *samaya* (conjunction) because the cooperative causes (*sahakārīkāraṇa*) meet (*sameti*) and assemble (*samaveti*). It is a *samavāya* (assemblage).
It is a *samaya* (occasion) because the noble life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*) meets and comes together here with the persons who are its support. It is a *khaṇa* (moment).

It is a *samaya* (time) because a being or a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) meets there, or because it comes together with [factors] such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) or [phases] such as arising (*uppāda*). Thus, it is time (*kāla*).

For although time does not exist as a substantial entity (*attha*), it is nevertheless conventionally designated by means of a form established through mere conceptualization (*kappanāmatta*) as the locus or instrument of the occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*).
"Samaya" means the going, proceeding, or remaining together of parts; it is a collection, just as in the term "samudāya.
For it is precisely the simultaneous remaining of the parts [that constitutes a samaya].

It is called *samaya* because it brings together (*samūheti*). It is a *samaya* because when the remaining conditions come together (*samāgame*), the fruit comes (*eti*) from this and arises or occurs;

thus it is a cause (*hetu*), just as in the term "origination" (*samudaya*). Or, it is a *samaya* because beings come together (*sameti*) through the state of being fettered (*saṃyojana-bhāvato*) and proceed (*eti*) within their own domain, or because beings proceed (*ayanti*) and move about according to their respective inclinations (*abhinivesa*) due to the state of firm grasping (*daḷhaggahaṇa-bhāvato*). Thus it is a *samaya*.
View (*diṭṭhi*); for by means of the fetter of view (*diṭṭhisaññojana*), beings are bound exceedingly tight. *Samaya* means meeting, encountering, or coming together; it is acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
Or, *samaya* means the act of coming together (*samayana*), or proceeding rightly (*sammā ayana*) or departing; it is abandonment (*pahāna*).

*Abhisamaya* means that which is to be approached rightly and fully realized (*abhisametabba*) by means of knowledge facing toward [the truth]; it is the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. By way of its state of being directed toward [the truth]...
"Abhisamaya" means that one goes rightly toward [truth] and awakens; it is the non-erroneous realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dhamma*).
In this way, the application of the term *samaya* should be understood according to its respective meaning.

Regarding the extraction of the meanings of the word *samaya*, the example for the word *abhisamaya* should be understood by the method already stated. "Of" (*assa*) refers to the word *samaya*. "Time" (*kāla*)...
The meaning [of "time"] here is because meanings such as "conjunction" (samavāya) and so forth are impossible in this context,
and because time must be referred to by way of its being the introduction (nidāna) to the discourse, just like the place, the teacher, and the assembly.
But why is time indicated here in an unrestricted manner, rather than being restricted by way of seasons, years, and so forth?
He said: "In this regard, although... and so forth. He spoke the passage beginning with "Or rather, these...
in order to show that by using the word *samaya* (time/occasion) without restricting it to specific seasons or years, this further advantage is obtained;

for a general designation settles upon a particular instance. In this context, the occasion for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) consists of the daily attainments of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the fruits of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
The time of passing away was specifically for seven weeks. "Well-manifested" means made clear by the appearance of radiance that shook the ten-thousandfold world system and other such phenomena.
To show how these aforementioned types of occasions can be subsumed under different categories, he said, "And this," and so forth.
For thus, the occasion of the function of knowledge and the occasion of the practice for one's own welfare are both included within the occasion of full enlightenment.

The occasion of noble silence (*ariya-tuṇhībhāva-samaya*), the occasion of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra-samaya*), and the occasion of discourse on the Dhamma consisting of the practice for the welfare of others through compassionate activity (*karuṇākicca-parahita-paṭipatti-dhammakathā-samaya*)—these alone are the occasions for teaching (*desanā-samaya*).

The connection is that the description is made by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the Abhidhamma, the Suttas other than those [already mentioned], and the Vinaya.

"Thus" (*tathā*) refers to the locative and instrumental cases. The sense of locus (*adhikaraṇattha*) is the sense of support (*ādhārattha*). "State" (*bhāva*) is indeed action (*kiriyā*); it is the characterization of another action by means of that [state].

The characteristic of a state by means of a state. In this context, just as time—though itself non-existent in the ultimate sense—is recognized as a support delimited by states possessing intrinsic nature, because of the absence [of those states] prior to and subsequent to that moment when they arise at that specific time, as in such expressions as "born in the forenoon" or "going in the afternoon";
and just as a collection, though non-existent apart from its constituent parts, [is likewise recognized].

It is designated as the locus of its parts by way of a mere conceptual construct, as in such cases as "a branch on a tree" or "grown in a heap of grain," and showing that it is the same here [in this context], he said: "For the locus... of phenomena.
At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen within that mass of phenomena, at that very time, within that same mass of phenomena...
And the meaning there is that contact and the other [mental factors] are also present. Just as in the expression, "He went while the cows were being milked;

he returned when they had been milked," the act of going is indicated by the act of milking, so too here, although the words "at whatever time" are used, the meaning "being present" (satī) is understood precisely because the referent of the word lacks any absence of existence.
At that moment, the activity of arising of consciousness is characterized by the activity of the seven mental factors and the activity of the manifestation of contact and the rest.

"In which moment" means: in which ninth moment, in which cause such as appropriate attention, or when there is a convergence of conditions, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen; at that very moment, in that cause, or in that convergence of conditions.

Since contact and the other [factors] are also present, he says, "In both cases, the locative case is employed for the word *samaya* (occasion/time) because it is connected with the state of being a characteristic," thereby showing that "it is characterized by a moment... and so forth.

Both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible, as in: "He dwells because of food" (*annena vasati*), "He dwells because of Vedic study" (*ajjhenena vasati*), and "He cuts with an axe" (*pharasunā chindati*).
As in the passages beginning with “he digs with a spade,” when the Blessed One hears of a transgression, he convenes the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
having questioned the individual involved regarding the matter at hand and having rebuked him, the Blessed One— without exceeding the time when that specific matter occurred—
lays down the training rules (sikkhāpada) at that very time, taking into account the cause for the laying down of those training rules.
As in the case of the third *pārājika* offense and others.
From the very beginning of the undertaking until the conclusion of the teaching, [the Buddha remained] through the dwelling of compassion, which is defined as the practice for the benefit of others.

"For the purpose of indicating that meaning" means for the purpose of indicating the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*). The use of the accusative case is made just as in the expression, "He studies for a month."

“Porāṇā” means the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). “A difference in mere expression” (*abhilāpamattabheda*) means a distinction by way of mere words. By this, he shows that the analysis of grammatical cases (*vibhattivyattaya*) was performed in the Suttas and the Vinaya.
“Best” (*seṭṭha*): the word expressing “best” is called “best” because it is associated with the quality of being best. The same applies here to the word “supreme” (*uttama*).
“Worthy of reverence” (*gāravayutta*) means endowed with a state of weightiness due to the possession of weighty qualities, and because of its fitness for being treated with respect.
Or [the word *bhagavā*] is connected with veneration (*gārava*). It has already been explained that it need not be discussed here, because this commentary is but a single part of the *Visuddhimagga*;

such is the intended meaning. Another method: he possesses fortune (*bhaga*), thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*); he has nurtured (*bhatavā*), thus he is the Blessed One; he has sought fortune (*bhāge vani*), thus he is the Blessed One; he has sought excellence (*bhage vani*), thus he is the Blessed One; he has possessed (*bhattavā*), thus he is the Blessed One; he has vomited out excellence (*bhage vami*), thus he is the Blessed One; he has vomited out fortune (*bhāge vami*), thus he is the Blessed One.
The Blessed One has partaken of his portion, and he has partaken of fortune in the forest;
likewise, he has vomited out misfortune and vomited out portions—thus the Conqueror is "Bhagavā.
In this regard, how is he "Bhāgavā"? Those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and the rest are portions of qualities, portions of excellences.
These qualities, which are not shared with others and are unsurpassed, exist and are found in the Tathāgata.
For instance, his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, moral shame, moral dread, faith, energy, mindfulness,
clear comprehension, purification of virtue, purification of view, serenity, insight, and the three roots of the wholesome.
The three types of good conduct, the three right thoughts, the three blameless perceptions, the three elements, the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four analytical knowledges,
the knowledge that cuts off the four modes of birth, the four noble lineages, and the four grounds of self-confidence.
The five factors of striving, right concentration with five factors, right concentration with five kinds of knowledge,
the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements leading to escape, the five kinds of knowledge regarding the bases of liberation,
the five perceptions that ripen liberation, the six bases for recollection, the six respects, the six elements leading to escape, and the six constant abidings.
The six unsurpassables, the six perceptions conducive to penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six unique knowledges, the seven factors of non-decline,
the seven noble qualities, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person,
the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements], the seven perceptions, and the teaching on the seven persons worthy of offerings.
The teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed; the teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom;
the eight rightnesses; the eight transcendences of worldly conditions; the eight bases for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments;
the eight thoughts of a great person; the teaching on the eight bases of mastery; the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention; the nine...
The factors of the foundation of purification, the teaching on the nine abodes of beings, the nine ways of removing ill will,
the nine perceptions, the nine diversities, the nine successive dwellings, the ten qualities that make one a protector,
the ten bases of totality, the ten courses of wholesome action, the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, and the ten qualities of one beyond training.
The powers of a Tathāgata; the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; the twelve aspects of the Wheel of Dhamma;
the thirteen ascetic qualities; the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha; the fifteen factors that ripen liberation; the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing;
the sixteen states that burn away the future; the eighteen qualities of a Buddha; and the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge.
The forty-four bases of knowledge, the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away, the more-than-fifty wholesome states, the seventy-seven bases of knowledge,

the great diamond-like knowledge that moves through the twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments, the knowledges of teaching, reviewing, and analyzing the *Paṭṭhāna* according to its infinite methods,
and likewise the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings in infinite world-systems— such as these.
Infinite and immeasurable divisions, qualities that are not shared by others and are unsurpassed—such portions of qualities and such portions of excellence exist and are found.
Therefore, because he possesses these aforementioned divisions of qualities, although he should be called "bhāgavā," the vowel *ā* is shortened to *a*, and thus he is called "Bhagavā.
Thus, first of all, he is "Bhagavā" in the sense of being possessed of portions (of qualities).
"Because all the factors of virtue, beginning with morality, exist in their entirety within the Sugata, he is therefore called 'Bhagavā'.
How is he "Bhagavā" in the sense of being "venerated"? Those who, having applied themselves with zeal for the welfare of the entire world, [attain] the eight [stages] beginning with human birth...
Having synthesized these qualities, the ten perfections— namely, the perfection of giving,
virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity;

as well as the ten secondary perfections and the ten ultimate perfections— these thirty perfections, beginning with giving and so forth, are to be fulfilled by Great Beings (Mahābodhisattvas) through their great resolves for perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

The four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*); the four foundations such as truth (*sacca*) and so forth; the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*), namely the renunciation of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife;

the preliminary application (*pubbayoga*), the preliminary conduct (*pubbacariyā*), the proclamation of the Dhamma, the conduct for the benefit of kinsmen, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct of wisdom—these and others, or in brief, all the accumulations of merit and knowledge that constitute the qualities producing a Buddha.
From the time of his great resolution (*mahābhinīhāra*) onwards, for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkheyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons,
he has performed and accumulated [merit] thoroughly, continuously, and without remainder, such that it does not lead to decline, defilement, or stagnation,
but rather leads exclusively to ever-higher distinction; thus, because he possesses what has been so performed and accumulated, he is called "one who has performed" (*bhata-vā*).
It should be stated that he is called "Bhagavā" by changing the letter *ta* to *ga* according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*). Alternatively, the meaning is:
because he has "borne" (*bhatavā*) those very qualities that constitute a Buddha, in the manner already described, he has "maintained" (*bhari*) and "fulfilled" (*sambhari*) them;
thus, because he has borne them, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
The Protector has fulfilled all the requisites for perfect enlightenment, beginning with the perfection of generosity;
therefore, too, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).
How does he "possess" (*bhajati*) the portions? Those portions consisting of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that are employed daily, numbering twenty-four quadrillion—[he possesses these].

He "frequented" (*bhaji*) and "cultivated" (*sevi*) the forest (*vani*) throughout all time for the sake of the welfare of the world without remainder, and for the sake of his own dwelling in happiness in this very life;

thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*), meaning one who has frequented the forest. Alternatively, among the things to be directly known—such as the wholesome states and the aggregates—there are fourfold portions of clear realization (*abhisamaya-bhāga*) categorized by way of thorough knowledge and so forth. It is because he has frequented these that he is the Blessed One.

In detail, however, there are numerous portions to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*), such as: "The eye is to be fully understood; the ear... [and so on] ...aging-and-death is to be fully understood";
portions to be abandoned (*pahātabba*), such as: "The origin of the eye is to be abandoned... [and so on] ...the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned";
and portions to be realized (*sacchikātabba*), such as: "The cessation of the eye... [and so on] ...the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized."

The categories of phenomena to be realized (*sacchikātabba-bhāga*)—such as "the way leading to the cessation of the eye," and so forth—and the categories of phenomena to be developed (*bhāvetabba-bhāga*)—such as "the four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth—these he "frequented" (*vane bhaji*), meaning he cultivated them appropriately through the practice of the proper range of objects (*gocara*) and meditative development (*bhāvanā*).

Thus, because he frequented these categories (*bhāge vanī*), he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). Alternatively, [he is so called] because of those aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhamma-kkhandha*) beginning with virtue (*sīla*), and so on.
He made a wish with great compassion, thinking, "How might I establish these portions and divisions of qualities, which are shared with disciples, within the mental continuums of those to be trained?
And that wish of his brought about the fruit exactly as intended.
Thus, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he wished for a portion.

Because the Blessed One (Bhagavā) has fully enjoyed and aspired for the portion of qualities consisting of the knowable and the meditative attainments for the welfare of sentient beings, he is therefore called "Bhagavā.
How is he "one who has gone to the bhagas" (bhage vanī)? Briefly, by those who have performed merit and are endowed with skillful means, according to their respective wealth...
They are called *bhaga* because they are to be enjoyed (*bhajīyanti*), namely, mundane and supramundane accomplishments.
Regarding these, first, while the Tathāgata was still a Bodhisatta prior to his full enlightenment, he frequented and cultivated (*bhaji sevi*) the most excellent forests;

established therein, he brought to maturity the Buddha-qualities by fully acquiring all the factors that constitute a Buddha. But once he had become a Buddha, those [forests] were endowed with blameless happiness.
He frequented and cultivated the forest even in its supramundane aspect, which is not shared by others.

In detail, however, he frequented and cultivated the forest regarding the manifold, unique blessings (bhaga) that are not shared by others—ranging from the sovereignty of a regional king, the prosperity of a universal monarch (cakkavatti), and the prosperity of a celestial king, up to the superhuman states consisting of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, attainments, knowledge and vision, the development of the path, and the realization of the fruit.
Thus, because he frequented the forest of blessings, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
"Whatever prosperities there are in the world, and those various supramundane ones—the Sambuddha enjoyed them all;
therefore also he is called Bhagavā. How is he "Bhattavā"?
He is Bhattavā because he has many devoted followers who are firm in their devotion (*bhattika*). Thus [is] the Tathāgata.
Indeed, because he possesses the state of being endowed with immeasurable and incomparable special qualities of power such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),

he is the supreme among all beings; and because he is of ultimate benefit to the generation of gods and humans through his unsurpassed perfection of application— which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent solely upon the provision of welfare and happiness without exception— he possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*), the fathom-wide radiance (*byāmappabhā*), and other such qualities not shared by others.

Because he is endowed with a form-body exquisitely adorned, and because he possesses a vast, utterly pure, and resonant sound of praise—extending throughout the three worlds and proceeding in the manner of "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," etc.—which arises from the attainment of qualities as they truly are;

and because he is firmly established in such supreme perfections as fewness of wishes and contentment; and because he is possessed of the most distinguished qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence.

And because he is pleasing in every way through his quality of inspiring confidence within this fourfold world-system— being measured by form and confident in form, measured by sound and confident in sound,
measured by coarseness and confident in coarseness, and measured by the Dhamma and confident in the Dhamma—
he serves as a locus for the respect, esteem, and reverence of immeasurable beings, including both gods and humans.

It is a state of supreme love and devotion. Those who are established in his instruction and endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda) cannot be diverted by anyone—whether by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
For even at the sacrifice of their own lives, they do not relinquish that confidence.
Or it is because of the state of firm devotion toward him. For this very reason it was said:
“The wise man who is grateful and mindful of benefits, he is one who possesses virtuous friends and firm devotion.”
“Just as, monks, the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore,
even so, monks, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

Thus he is called *Bhattava* (the One Honored) by the Blessed One through the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), having elided one *ta*-sound and changed the other *ta*-sound to a *ga*-sound.
"Because many have placed their trust in the Teacher who is endowed with an excellence of qualities and who seeks the welfare of the world, he is therefore called 'Bhagavā'.
How does he "emit fortune" (bhage vamīti) and thus become "Bhagavā"? Because even while the Tathāgata was a Bodhisatta in former births, he [perfected] the perfections...
Fulfilling it, he vomited forth glory, sovereignty, and fame known as "fortune"; he cast them away without regard, like a globule of spittle.

Even in his final existence, he regarded the sovereignty over the four continents—which was like the lordship of the deva-world, the basis for the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), resplendent with the seven treasures, and accompanied by fame—as no more than a blade of grass.

Because he, disregarding all things and becoming indifferent to them, went forth after abandoning them and awakened to perfect self-enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), he is therefore called the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he has vomited out (vamī) these fortunes (bhage) such as glory (siri) and the rest. Alternatively, "bhā" refers to the lunar mansions (nakkhattāni);

those which move and proceed together with them are "bhagā. These are the specific features of the receptacle world (bhājanaloka), such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavanta, which serve as their support.

He is "Bhagavā" because he has vomited up beauty (*sobhā*) due to its state of being fixed for an eon (*kappaṭṭhiyabhāva*); he has vomited those [beauties] from his parts (*bhage*) by transcending the abode of beings that dwell therein; and he has abandoned them through the relinquishing of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to them.
Thus, too, he is "Bhagavā" because he has vomited up beauty from his parts.
Furthermore, because he has vomited up the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-siri*), as well as fame, sovereignty, and happiness...
"The Sugata, the Blessed One, has abandoned the worldly mind.
How does the Blessed One "vomit up the portions"? "Portions" (bhāga) refers to divisions of phenomena belonging to the same class;

these are manifold, categorized by way of the aggregates, bases, and elements, and within those, by way of form, feeling, and so forth, as well as by way of earth and so forth, or the past and so forth. All of these the Blessed One—
Having utterly severed all proliferation (*papañca*), all fetters (*yoga*), all bonds (*gantha*), and all ties (*saṃyojana*), he attained the deathless element (*amata-dhātu*).
He vomited it up, cast it out, and, without looking back, abandoned it and did not return.
For thus he [regarded] the earth, water, fire, and air as the foremost of all things; likewise the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and forms, sounds, and odors.
In regard to tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, there arises eye-consciousness … pe … mind-consciousness;
eye-contact … pe … mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact … pe … feeling born of mind-contact;
perception born of eye-contact … pe … perception born of mind-contact; volition born of eye-contact … pe … volition born of mind-contact.
By means of the classification of phenomena according to their sequence—beginning with "craving for forms... [and so on] ... craving for mental objects; thought concerning forms... [and so on] ...

thought concerning mental objects; examination of forms... [and so on] ... examination of mental objects"—he vomited up and disgorged every single category of phenomena without exception, casting them away through a relinquishment free from longing.
For it is said: "That which, Ānanda, has been abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and cast aside..."
"That the Tathāgata will return to that [existence] again—such a possibility does not exist. Thus he vomited out the parts;

this is why he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). Alternatively, "he vomited out the parts" means that by means of the gateway of noble-path knowledge, he vomited out, disgorged, became indifferent toward, relinquished, and abandoned all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless, inferior or superior, dark or bright, and those with their opposites—and for the sake of others, he likewise [taught them to do so].
He taught the Dhamma. And this has been said: "Bhikkhus, even phenomena are to be abandoned, how much more so non-phenomena;
I shall teach you the Dhamma, O bhikkhus, as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping," and so forth.
Thus, too, he vomits out (vamati) what belongs to the parts [of defilement], and is therefore called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).

"Because he has abandoned both the dark and the bright, having attained mastery over the categories of phenomena such as the aggregates, bases, and elements— for that reason also he is called 'Bhagavā'.
Thus it was said.
“He has attained the portions, he has attained the portions; he has won the fortune and is devoted to it;
he vomits forth fortune as well as portions—thus the Conqueror is called the Blessed One.
He makes the body of the Dhamma manifest: “Ānanda, that Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught by me to you...”
This was said because there exists a figurative expression for the Dhamma as the Teacher, based on the statement: "That which has been laid down by me is your teacher after my passing away.
His body is like a vajra-thunderbolt because his physical frame is indivisible by others; for indeed, no one is able to cause an obstacle to the Blessed One’s material body (rūpakāya).
He indicates the excellence of the teaching by means of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which serves as a pointer for the entire sutta that is about to be spoken.

He indicates the excellence of the disciple: "I, a great disciple established by the Blessed One in the foremost place among five categories because I have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), have heard this; and it was heard by me alone, not from hearsay, nor brought down through tradition."

Because it illuminates this meaning. The Blessed One indicates the perfection of time through the word *samaya* employed in proximity to the word *bhagavā*, because it illuminates that the time is adorned by the arising of a Buddha. For the perfection of time has the arising of a Buddha as its supreme excellence.
Therefore, this is said:—
“In this degenerate age of strife, the arising of a Buddha—oh, what a great marvel!
Like a lotus with its nectar fully blossomed, born from the midst of a consuming fire.
By the word “Bhagavā,” he points out the excellence of the Teacher, because it is a designation for one who is revered by the highest beings due to his distinguished qualities.
"Today is an auspicious day, a lucky moment, a favorable constellation"—today is an auspicious day; therefore it is a lucky constellation, and even therein, this is a lucky moment.
"Let it not pass"—the connection should be understood as: "let the night not pass for those who are looking toward the break of dawn.
"Standing while the torches stand"—this means *ukkāṭṭhā*; standing while the torches are blazing.
The grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) of the word *patiṭṭhitā* should be understood according to the rule *mūlavibhūjādipakkhepena* (Pāṇini 3.2.5).
Alternatively, according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*), it is called *Ukkaṭṭhā* because she was established (*ṭhitā*) when the torches (*ukkāsu*) were being held aloft. Others, however, say:

"That city received the name ‘Ukkaṭṭhā’ because of its association with superior qualities (*ukkaṭṭhaguṇa*), namely the excellence of its location, the excellence of its inhabitants, and the excellence of its provisions."
"Without distinction" means not by way of distinction, but by way of the commonality of the state of abiding (*vihāra*); this is the meaning. "In the postures... pe...
in the abidings" refers to these four abidings: the abiding in postures, the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.
"Illuminating possession" means the illumination of the state of being possessed. "This" refers to the word "abides. For it is said: "Here, someone..."
In such passages as, "He dwells in association with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows," it refers to dwelling in the postures (*iriyāpatha*);
in such passages as, "At that time, monks, when a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... having attained the first *jhāna*, dwells therein," it refers to divine dwelling (*dibbavihāra*);
and in such passages as, "With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one direction," it refers to sublime dwelling (*brahmavihāra*).
“At the conclusion of that very discourse, Aggivessana, right there upon that same prior object of concentration,
I steadied my mind within myself, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it— that by which I indeed dwell for all time”—
in such passages as these, [it refers to] the noble dwelling.
In this context, *iriyā* means moving about or proceeding; it is bodily exertion. Because standing and so forth are the means for its occurrence, they are called "postures" (*iriyāpatha*).
For one who possesses the state of standing might perform some action with the body, or likewise one who possesses any other [posture] such as walking and so on.

Alternatively, *iriyā* is that by which the personal existence (*attabhāva*) moves about or proceeds, or by which bodily functions are carried out. It is called a "path" (*patha*) because it is the means for the occurrence of that movement.

Posture (*iriyāpatha*) consists of standing and so forth. In its actual meaning, it is simply the continuity of the fourfold material aggregates (*rūpa-santati*) proceeding in the manner of moving, stopping, and so on.
"Abiding" (*vihāra*) means either the act of abiding or that by which one abides; thus, posture itself as an abiding is "postural abiding" (*iriyāpatha-vihāra*).
"Celestial" (*dibba*) means existing in the heavens (*divi*). Its meaning is: existing in the divine worlds such as the Brahma-parisajja, due to the frequent occurrence [of such states] therein.
In this context, it is "divine" (*dibba*) because it conduces to divine power, or because it is "divine" due to its great range by way of the exertion for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
It is the "divine abiding" (*dibbavihāra*) because it is both divine and an abiding; these are the four fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*).

The formless-sphere attainments (*āruppa-samāpatti*) are also included herein. They are "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*) because they are the abidings of the Brahmas, or because they are the abidings that lead to the state of a Brahma.
The four immeasurables (*appamaññāyo*). Noble ones’ [states], or noble abidings, are the noble abidings (*ariyavihārā*); they are the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphalāni*).

For although that Blessed One is able to maintain his physical existence for a much longer time by means of even a single posture (*iriyāpatha*), nevertheless, [the text says] "this is the nature of a body that has been grasped at" (*upādinnakasarīrassa*).

This was said in order to show [this]. Or alternatively, because the Blessed One—wherever he may dwell—dwells teaching the Dhamma to those to be trained and spending his time in various meditative attainments (samāpatti), he thus "carries" (*harati*) or brings about, that is, produces, manifold welfare and happiness for both the beings to be trained and himself;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "he carries manifoldly" (*vividhaṃ harati*).

“Subhagattā” means being beautiful by way of splendor (*sirī*), desire (*kāma*), and honor (*mānava*). For this very reason, it is said: “Because of having beautiful splendor and because of having beautiful desire.

Regarding the phrase “at festivals, gatherings, and celebrations”: here, a “festival” (*chaṇa*) refers to the performance of auspicious rites for people together with their retinues on specially marked days such as those in the month of Phagguna (Phālguna) under the constellation Uttaraphagguṇī (Uttaraphālgunī).
A “gathering” (*samajja*) refers to theatrical performances and the like. A “celebration” (*ussava*) refers to a festival (*nakkhatta*).
In whatever village or town the inhabitants, having made an announcement for three or seven days regarding the festival,
enjoy their wealth according to their means and engage in festival sports while adorned and prepared;
for them, that [wish] comes to pass exactly so— meaning that for those people, that aspiration is fulfilled almost entirely through the power of the deities residing there.

"Exists" means that the aspiration succeeds. By the phrase "because it is dear to many people," he clarifies the meaning of the very same term, "because it possesses beautiful desires," by means of a different mode of expression.
Herein, this is the etymological analysis: it is called *subhaga* because it is well-frequented (*suṭṭhu bhajīyati*) in the sense of being desirable;
or alternatively, it is *subhaga* because there are beautiful trees (*subhā agā*) therein; or else, it is so called due to its association with a beautiful reputation (*sundara-kitti*).
“Subhaga”—thus they explain the meaning here. Some, however, read it as “subhāgavane,” and they state its meaning to be “in a forest on a beautiful stretch of ground.
Others say it is “Subhagavana” because it is a forest belonging to a yakkha named Subhaga, being possessed by him.
In the sense that “vanana” means devotion, in the sense of causing that devotion, it is said to “vanayati.”
The etymological derivation (*padasiddhi*) should be understood. For this very reason, it is said: "He produces affection for himself.
Regarding the word *vana*, it should be understood as meaning "to beg" (*vanute*), according to the application of metaphorical designation.
*Ujuvaṃsā* means those with straight branches. *Mahāsālā* means great trees. *Aññatarasmiṃ sālamūle* means at the root of a certain tree... [of another].
"At the foot of the tree. "The eldest tree among the forest-growers" means a tree that has become the foremost among those growing in the forest.
That very state of being the eldest—its excellence and preeminence attained through its status as a forest-grower—is why it is called the "Sāla King.

It is a "king" (rājā) in the sense of delighting (*rañjana*) those who approach it; and in order to show that the designation "king" applies even to other such trees, [the text says] "of the well-established," and so forth.
It has been said. Therein, "O Brahmin, those who are righteous" is an address.
Etymologically (*nippariyāyena*), the word *mūla* (root) refers to a specific part that effects the firm establishment of a composite whole possessing branches and so forth.

Because it occurs figuratively (*pariyāyato*) through conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) for things similar to that [root] and for the location upon which it depends, therefore [the text says]: "One should uproot the roots."

Here, it is intended in its primary (nippariyāya) sense; thus, having distinguished it by means of the word "root" (*mūla*), he says, "it is seen in the root-of-roots," just as one speaks of "suffering-of-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*) or "form-of-form" (*rūparūpa*). "In the uncommon cause" means in the specific cause.

The meaning is that it is seen in those conditioning states (*paccayadhamma*) which, in the sense of being roots, act as supportive factors because they establish the state of being well-established for these [defilements] in their unique (āveṇika) arising together with greed.
*Tattha* means: regarding the statement that was spoken, namely, “At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a king of sāla trees.
*Siyā* means: someone might have such a reflection, or it might occasionally prompt an objection in the manner that is about to be stated.
*Atha tattha viharati*: if he dwells there in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of the king of sāla trees.

"It should not be said" means that the intention is that because the heights, the beautiful, and the forests are distinct locations, and because it is stated as "at one time," [the two cannot be identical].
Now, the objector clarifies his own position with the words "for it is not possible," and so forth.
The other [respondent], showing that all this was spoken by one who did not understand the unerring meaning, says: "But this should not be viewed in this way."
He said: Therein, "this" refers to the statement, "He dwelt at Ukkatthā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a king of sāl trees.
"Thus" refers to that which was questioned by you beginning with, "If, first of all, the Blessed One...
The meaning is that this should not be understood in that sense; rather, the meaning is that it is not for the purpose of showing dwellings that are neither first nor last in both instances.
Now, demonstrating his own intended meaning as it is without error, the fact that he had already stated it previously, and the fact that [the opponent] had not yet penetrated it, he said:

"Have we not said... [etc. ...at the foot of the Sāla-king tree? Even so, one should say only "he dwells at the foot of the Sāla-king tree in Subhaga Grove," and not "in Ukkaṭṭhā"—thus one should take account of this objection.
Thus it was said: "For the purpose of indicating the alms-village," and so forth.
Furthermore, the description of the alms-village must certainly be provided here.

For just as the description of Subhagavana and other such places serves many purposes—such as providing assistance to those who have gone forth—it likewise serves various purposes, such as providing assistance to householders.
Showing this, he said, "By means of exalted praise," and so forth. Therein, by accepting the requisites, by providing an opportunity for approaching and attending upon [the teacher],
by establishing [the pupil] in the refuges and the precepts, by bringing about the attainment of higher distinctions according to their respective potentialities,
and by selecting a suitable dwelling place for the study, inquiry, and application to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), the taking up of householders as pupils is accomplished here.
It should be understood as providing assistance to those who have gone forth. It clarifies the purity of approach and withdrawal:
that approach is out of compassion and not for the sake of gain and so forth, and that withdrawal is through wisdom and not for the sake of conflict and so forth.
"Dhammic happiness" means blameless happiness. The abundance of benefit to the devas is due to the seclusion from people; it is secluded from the common folk.
For indeed, it is a place that the gods consider worthy of approaching. "The accomplishment of that purpose" means the accomplishment of the welfare of the world;
the meaning is the fulfillment of the Buddha’s duties. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), through the mention of [the Buddha's] excellence, he shows the non-neglect of the form-body (*rūpakāya*);

through the mention of the beautiful groves and so forth, [he shows the non-neglect] of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*). Likewise, by the former [phrase], there is the performance of actions dependent on others.

By the second [verse], the performance of actions independent of self is shown. Alternatively, by the former [verse] the function of compassion is indicated, and by the latter, the function of wisdom.
By the former, his possession of supreme compassion is illuminated; by the latter, his possession of supreme equanimity is illuminated.
For the Blessed One feels compassion for all beings with supreme compassion, yet he is not beset by the fault of attachment therein.

He is equanimous because of his state of supreme equanimity, yet he is not indifferent to the bringing about of the welfare and happiness of others because of his state of great compassion (*mahākāruṇika*).
Through his great compassion, he possesses lordship over the world; through his equanimity, he possesses lordship over himself.
For thus, when he was a bodhisattva, his mind being stirred by great compassion, he became intent upon the welfare of the entire world from the moment of his Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) onwards.
Accomplishing the equipment of merit and knowledge for the sake of achieving that goal, he experienced immeasurable time and no small amount of suffering;

yet, due to his equanimity, he was not shaken by those sufferings that fell upon him rightly. Likewise, through his great compassion, there was an orientation toward *saṃsāra*, and through his equanimity, a disenchantment with it.
Similarly, through his equanimity, there was an orientation toward *nibbāna*, and through his great compassion—
The realization of that [state] is as follows: through great compassion, one does not cause harm to others; through equanimity, one does not fear others oneself.
