By protecting another through great compassion, one protects oneself; by protecting oneself through equanimity, one protects others.
Therefore, among those who have practiced for their own benefit and so forth, he is the fourth type of person.
He becomes accomplished. Likewise, through great compassion, there is the fulfillment of the foundation of truth and the foundation of generosity;

through equanimity, there is the fulfillment of the foundation of peace and the foundation of wisdom. Thus, for one whose intention and application are utterly pure, through great compassion, there is the attainment of success in existence—such as the perfection of sovereignty—for the very sake of the world’s welfare; and through equanimity, [the same].
Not regarding even a blade of grass as something to be clung to, he withdraws from it.

Thus, for one whose approach and withdrawal are perfectly purified, there is the relinquishing of all attainments by way of giving for the very benefit and welfare of the world through great compassion, and through equanimity, there is no expectation of a fruit for oneself.
Thus, from the moment of its full accomplishment, he is endowed with marvelous and wonderful qualities.

Through his great compassion (*mahākāruṇikatā*), he performed deeds exceedingly difficult for the sake of the welfare and happiness of others; through his equanimity (*upekkhakatā*), he did not even adorn his body.
Likewise, through his great compassion, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon seeing those who were old and afflicted in his final existence;
through his equanimity, he departed on the Great Renunciation without regard for magnificent enjoyments comparable to those of the gods. Likewise, through his great compassion...
The commencement of insight was by way of compassion alone, with the words, “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship,” and so forth;
yet, having become a Buddha through equanimity, he spent seven weeks passing his time in the bliss of seclusion.
Then, out of great compassion, having reflected upon the profundity of the Dhamma and having become indifferent toward teaching it, he [responded] by means of the request of Great Brahmā.
Making way means that, despite conduct that is unsuitable for those to be trained—such as the group of five monks and others—he does not act otherwise because of his equanimity.
Because of his great compassion, he has no perception of enmity toward anyone anywhere due to the absence of aversion;
because of his equanimity, he has no affection or intimacy toward anyone anywhere due to the absence of favoritism. Because of his great compassion, [he feels] for villages and so forth...
Even for one dwelling in a nearby place, there is dwelling as if in a forest-place due to equanimity (*upekkhakatā*). Therefore it is said:
"By the former [phrase], he illustrates his possession of supreme compassion; by the latter, his possession of supreme equanimity.
The word "therein" (*tattha*) refers to that. It is an illustration of place and time, meaning those places and times which serve here as qualifiers for the act of dwelling.
Showing that [the word] "taṃ" (that) serves as an illustration of those [terms] already mentioned, he said: "At whatever time... [etc. ...it illustrates.
For the word *taṃ* is a restatement (*paṭiniddesa*) of a meaning already stated; therefore, here it ought to be a restatement of either the time or the location, and not anything else.
This, then, is the analysis of the meaning regarding the status of the word *tatra* as a restatement. Since—
However, in such instances, the word *tatra* (there) indicates both the location and the time distinguished by the teaching of the Dhamma;

therefore it is said: "Or it illuminates the place and time appropriate for what is to be spoken. By this, the meaning is: "In such a place and at such a time as that wherein the Blessed One addressed and spoke to the bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. The phrase beginning with "For not... (na hi) etc., establishes that very meaning.

But is it not the case that the Blessed One, standing in the very same street where he had refused Bāhiya’s request for a teaching on the Dhamma by saying, “It is not the right time,” nevertheless taught him the Dhamma while standing there? This is true;

however, this is an example of not teaching at a time when it should not be taught. For this reason he said, “It is not the right time. As for what was said there regarding “between houses” (antaragharaṃ):
“We have entered [the forest],” he said; this too was spoken by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) to show that it was indeed an improper time for him.
For at that moment, his material body (*rūpakāya*) had become unworkable due to the fatigue of the journey, and his mental body (*nāmakāya*) was overwhelmed by the force of intense rapture (*pīti*).
As both of these were subsiding, the Blessed One spoke “It is not the right time” by way of a figurative expression in order to avoid further elaboration (*papañca*).
He rejected it. As for the example of the "non-admission of what should be admitted," such passages as, "Then the Blessed One, having descended from the road,
sat down at the foot of a certain tree," and "Having emerged from the monastery, he sat down on the seat prepared in the shade behind the monastery," are included here by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
In such passages as, “Then, monks, that fool, having been a lover of flavors here before and having performed evil deeds here,” the particle *kho* serves merely to fill out the meter;
in such passages as, “Indeed, one who lacks respect and deference dwells in suffering,” it expresses emphasis;
and in such passages as, “To what extent, friends, do disciples not train in seclusion when the Teacher dwells in seclusion? it [expresses a question].

"In the sense of 'at the beginning' (*ādikālatthe*). The meaning is "at the commencement of a sentence. In that context, by means of the word-filler (*padapūraṇa*), a mere ornamentation of the speech is effected;
by the sense of "at the beginning," there is merely an introduction to the sentence; but by the sense of "determination" (*avadhāraṇa*), there is the demonstration of a restriction.
Therefore, in the phrase "thus he addressed," the restriction regarding the act of addressing is demonstrated.
Why is it said, “‘Bhagavāti’ is an illumination of the world-honored one”? Is it not the case that the meaning of the word *bhagavā* has already been stated previously?

Although it was stated previously, that was done for the purpose of showing the specific agent of the action of dwelling in the aforementioned place, and not for the purpose of the action of addressing;
here, however, it is for the purpose of the action of addressing, and therefore the word “Bhagavā” is repeated for that reason.
To show the meaning of the phrase "stated in the Pāḷi," he said: "'Bhagavā' is an epithet signifying one who is revered by the world.

"A term for a person fit to hear the discourse" means a term for a person worthy of hearing the teaching on the *Mūlapariyāya* which is about to be explained. Among all four assemblies, it is the monks alone who are especially the vessels for such teachings;
thus, this is said for the purpose of showing their preeminent status as recipients of the Dispensation.
Having thus shown the inclusion of the word "bhikkhu" here, he now says "apica" (furthermore) and so forth in order to show the etymological meaning (*saddattha*).
In that context, "bhikkhu" means one who begs; the sense is "a bhikkhu by virtue of the nature of begging.
"One who has entered upon the alms-round" means that he has entered upon the practice of wandering for alms—the practice of gleaning—which was entered upon even by the Buddha and others.

Because of his non-exertion, O monks. For anyone who, having abandoned a mass of wealth, whether small or great, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, is called a *bhikkhu* because he has adopted the alms-round by accepting the outward signs [of the robe] and has abandoned the making of a livelihood through farming, cattle-herding, and so forth;
or else, because his livelihood is dependent on others, he receives food and meals in the midst of the monastery.

One who has entered upon the practice of wandering for alms even while eating is a *bhikkhu*; or, because one has generated the aspiration for the going-forth by depending on the consumption of morsels of alms-food, one has entered upon the practice of wandering for alms and is thus a *bhikkhu*—in this way the meaning here should be understood.
According to this method: "One who wears torn robes is a *bhikkhu*, one who breaks evil, unwholesome states is a *bhikkhu*... and so forth.
[The term "bhikkhu" is used] according to the method found in the Vibhaṅga, beginning with: “Because of having broken away from evil, unwholesome states, he is a bhikkhu.
In the sense of making known, it means causing understanding; that is, the sense of announcing.

Regarding the phrases “one whose nature is begging” (bhikkhanasīlatā) and so forth: the state of having the nature of begging is the state of maintaining one’s livelihood by begging, and not by means of agriculture, trade, and the like.

The virtue of right livelihood (*ājīva-sīlatā*). The nature of begging (*bhikkhana-dhammatā*) refers to the essential character of begging as described in the passage, “The Noble Ones stand depending on what is given,” and not the character of seeking honor or gain.
Skillfulness in begging (*bhikkhane sādhukāritā*) means being diligent therein by recollecting the teaching, “One should rise up and not be negligent.
Alternatively, while “virtue” (*sīla*) generally refers to one’s natural disposition, here it refers specifically to that which is undertaken through formal resolve.
"Dhamma" means a vow (*vata*). Others, however, explain it thus: "Vow" (*sīla*) refers to the undertaking of a practice; "Dhamma" refers to conduct handed down through tradition;

and "acting well" refers to performing tasks with diligence and reverence. It is "practiced by those inferior and superior": those who, though established in the state of a bhikkhu, are arrogant and conceited due to pride in birth and so forth;
and those in the state of a householder who, because they do not even approach others with a sense of need, [remain in their low state].
They consider the practice of alms-gathering to be the ultimate form of wretchedness; for both of these [groups], by the word "bhikkhus" used in their respective order,
he demonstrates that this mode of livelihood— practiced by low-born people, the destitute, and those who maintain themselves by wandering for alms among other families—
is a way of life associated with wretchedness, thereby effecting a restraint against arrogance toward those who are superior.

It should be understood that by explaining the mode of livelihood practiced for the sake of purifying one’s way of life by the Buddhas and others who went forth from distinguished families of great wealth and nobility, [the author] effects a restraint against dejection.
For the word "monks" (bhikkhave), because it is an address, serves to bring [the audience] face-to-face;
and by virtue of its context and its inherent power, it generates a desire to listen and enjoins them toward careful hearing and mental attention.
It exists. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he said, "By this [term] 'Bhikkhave'... and so forth.
Therein, "careful hearing and attention" refers to careful hearing and careful attention.

But how is it that hearing and the rest, when they have occurred, are said to have occurred carefully? [The answer is: "Surely, by means of this right practice, the excellence of the entire Dispensation..."
"It will come into my hands"—thus, by means of earnestness and reverence, and by not treating the discourse or the speaker with contempt and so forth. For it is said:
"Bhikkhus, one who hears the true Dhamma endowed with five qualities is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states.
With which five? He does not treat the discourse with contempt; he does not treat the speaker with contempt..."
"One does not disparage oneself; with an undistracted mind one listens to the Dhamma with a one-pointed mind, and one attends to it wisely.

Possessing these five qualities, monks, one who listens to the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states. Therefore he said: "It depends on careful listening and attention..."
"Indeed, it is the excellence of the Dispensation. The "excellence of the Dispensation" refers to the accomplishment of virtue and the other [perfections].
It is so called because it first arose by way of realization (*adhigama*); because it conforms to the Teacher’s conduct through the practice of the qualities of virtue and so forth;

because it possesses the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*anudhammapaṭipatti*) by way of the three vehicles (*yāna*); and because it receives the entirety of the Dispensation. Thus, it is "proximate" (*santikattā*).
"By way of being near" means by way of being in close proximity. "By way of constant association" means by way of being associated [with the mind] at all times.
"According to the instruction" means in accordance with the teaching; the meaning is that they received the instruction in its entirety.
"Referring specifically to certain bhikkhus" refers to those mentioned at the conclusion of the sutta: "Those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words."
[This refers to] the five hundred brahmins who had gone forth; with reference to them.

Although the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma was previously common to the entire assembly, having shown the reason for addressing the bhikkhus alone with the words "the eldest and best," etc., [the text] now shows the purpose of the teaching of the Dhamma by addressing the bhikkhus.
In order to demonstrate this, he raised the objection: "But for what purpose did the Blessed One [speak]?
In that context, "with minds directed elsewhere" means having their attention fixed on something else. "With distracted minds" means with unconcentrated minds.
"Reflecting on the Dhamma" means reflecting individually in the mind upon the Dhamma heard either that day, yesterday, or the day before. Having addressed the bhikkhus regarding the Dhamma...

The phrase "without having addressed them" and so forth was spoken in order to demonstrate, by way of contrast, the very point that they were able to perceive the teaching from the beginning as it was being delivered.

Furthermore, in the expression "Bhikkhavo," the elision of the vowel *i* should be understood as occurring through the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), as in "Bhikkhavo iti. For this word "iti" [functions here as a particle].
It possesses a manifold variety of meanings, such as cause, completion, reversal of word-meanings, specification, manner, determination, illustration, and so forth.

For instance, it is seen in the sense of cause in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, it is because it is affected (*ruppati*) that it is called 'form' (*rūpa*). Likewise, it is seen in the sense of cause in:
"Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things; for I have [entrusted] to you..."
In such passages as "compassion [is the thought]: 'How may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things,'" it has the sense of completion.
In such passages as "Thus, or in this way, he abstains from dancing, singing, music, and the viewing of spectacles," it has the sense of beginning.
In the passage "Māgaṇḍiya is the designation, the appellation, the description, the conventional term, the name, the naming, the denomination, the etymology of that brahmin... [it refers to a name].

In such passages as “*byañjanaṃ abhilāpo*,” it refers to the reversal of the meaning of the words (*padatthavipariyāye*); in such passages as “Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise man is fearless;
the fool is beset with calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity; the fool is subject to misfortune, while the wise man is free from misfortune,” it refers to a manner or mode (*pakāre*);
and in the passage “When asked, ‘Is there this condition for aging and death? you should answer, Ānanda... [it refers to a specific formulation].
In such passages as, "If one should say, 'It exists,' it should be said: 'With what condition is there aging and death? To this, it should be said:
'With birth as condition there is aging and death,'" it has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). In such passages as, "'Everything exists,' Kaccāna, is one extreme;
'Nothing exists,' Kaccāna, is the second extreme," it has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). Here too, it is used in the sense of illustration.
It is to be understood as follows. *Bhikkhave* is a form of address; the word *iti* indicates that very [address], as in the phrase "he addressed them, saying, 'Bhikkhave'.
By this same method, the meaning of the word *iti* should be understood accordingly in cases such as "Bhaddante" and so forth.
Since it was previously stated that "the Blessed One addressed [them]," the genitive case "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) is used here in the expression "they replied to the Blessed One."
With the intention that "addressing itself indeed requires another related party," it is said: "They heard the address of the Blessed One.

Furthermore, the term "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) is a dative of reference by virtue of its connection with the act of assent, just as in the expression "he assents to Devadatta" (*devadattassa paṭissuṇoti*).

The connection is: "That which is the source for what was spoken. Here it is asked: For what purpose is the statement of the source (*nidāna*) included when the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being performed?
Is it not the case that only the words spoken by the Blessed One should be compiled? It is said in reply:

For the sake of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching. Having bound it together by means of the time, place, teacher, occasion, and the assembly, [the teaching is preserved].
For when a teaching is established, it becomes long-lasting, free from the nature of forgetfulness, and credible—

just as a legal decision is rendered secure by being bound to the place, time, agent, and witnesses. And for this very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa posed questions regarding the location and other details,
such as, "Friend Ānanda, where was the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* spoken?", he provided the answers to those questions.

The Dhamma-treasurer (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) spoke the introduction to this sutta beginning with "Thus have I heard. Furthermore, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Teacher.
For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, his status as a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is established by the absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, or reasoning;
indeed, for a Perfectly Enlightened One, there is no need for prior composition or the like in any respect.

Because his range of knowledge is unimpeded and because it is of a single measure regarding all knowable phenomena, and likewise because he is free from the "teacher’s fist," the stinginess of withholding the Dhamma, and any partiality toward his own disciples, the fact that his taints are destroyed is established.
For those [defilements] cannot possibly exist in one whose taints are entirely destroyed; thus, there is the activity of benefiting others in one who is perfectly pure.
In this way, [the Buddha is distinguished] by those signs which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving—the very stains of a teacher that corrupt the perfection of view and conduct.
The Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) and his practice for the welfare of himself and others are revealed by the introductory statement (*nidānavacana*).

For, through the perfectly enlightened and purified states that manifest the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment, the first two grounds of self-confidence are established; and from that very fact, because the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and liberating phenomena is established, the latter two grounds of self-confidence are established.
Thus, the Blessed One’s endowment with the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own and others' welfare are made known.

In those various instances, it is because the teaching of the Dhamma is illuminated through spontaneous eloquence (*ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna*) in accordance with the circumstances encountered and the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*).

Here, however, it should be connected as being for the purpose of illuminating the teaching that defines the distinctions in the practice of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) regarding subjects such as earth and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "The introductory statement is for the purpose of making manifest the excellence of the Teacher."
Likewise, there is the introductory statement (nidāna) for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation.
For the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion, there is no practice that is purposeless or for his own benefit alone.
Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Enlightened One—who engages in every activity solely for the sake of others—exactly as they occurred, [are recorded].

That which is spoken—which, in the sense of instructing beings as appropriate through the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—is the Teaching (*sāsana*), not mere poetic composition;
and this, being the conduct of the Teacher, is elucidated here and there by means of introductory narratives (*nidāna*) together with the appropriate details of time, place, teacher, and assembly;
however, in this instance, it is stated: "in the bases such as earth and so forth."
Everything is exactly as before. Therefore it was said: “The introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation.
Furthermore, the introductory statement is for the purpose of showing the authoritative nature of the Dispensation by means of demonstrating the authoritative nature of the Teacher;
and that demonstration of the authoritative nature of the place and time is according to the method explained below by means of this word, “the Blessed One” (bhagavā).

It should be understood as "fully developed. By this word "Bhagavā," this meaning is elucidated in every respect through the statement that demonstrates the Tathāgata’s abandonment of all stains of defilement, misconduct, and faults such as lust, hatred, and delusion;
through the demonstration of his possession of extraordinary and perfectly pure qualities such as knowledge and compassion;
and, for that very reason, through the demonstration of his state as the supreme among all beings. This is merely a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory formula here.
The commentary on the internal causes is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the presentation of the sutta:

"Of that which is presented" means of that which is taught. For even the teaching [is considered] as the virtue and so forth—the meaning to be taught—within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
It is called a "deposition" (nikkhepa) because of its being laid down.

Since it becomes clear when explained after investigating the deposition of the sutta, [the author], having first shown the general classification of the Blessed One’s origins of teaching, demonstrates that this particular teaching has such-and-such an origin.
Once the origin of the teaching has been shown, the commentary becomes easy to understand through the thorough comprehension of the sutta's introduction (nidāna).

It has been said. For in this way, the teaching as it proceeds—beginning with "Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling," and "Bhikkhus, even that bhikkhu who is an arahant whose taints are destroyed," and "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one"—becomes easy to understand because the connection [between the sections] is shown.
In that regard, although there are hundreds and thousands of different divisions...

The discourses (suttantas) do not exceed sixteenfold variety by way of the primary methods such as those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and likewise they possess a fourfold nature by way of the bases for the delivery of discourses (suttanikkhepa) such as one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya). Thus he said, "For there are four bases for the delivery of discourses.
And here, just as there is a distinction in the combination of one's own inclination and the occasion for a teaching (aṭṭhuppatti) with the questions of others' inclinations (parajjhāsayapucchā);

It is possible [to classify them] as: "one's own intention and another's intention," "one's own intention and dependent on a question," "dependent on an occasion and another's intention," and "dependent on an occasion and dependent on a question"—because of the existence of these connections based on intention and questions;
thus, although a distinction through combination with one's own intention may also occur by way of an occasion, [it is categorized] by means of one's own intention and so forth.
However, because there is no connection by way of occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) for those [discourses] standing before it, a complete method of detailed exposition is not possible here;

thus it is said, "the four ways of laying down the Suttas. Alternatively, since all other possible ways of laying down are included within these, only four are shown by way of the fundamental laying down.
And in this context, this classification of connection (*saṃsagga*) should be understood as that which has been thus demonstrated.

Herein, this is the etymological explanation (*vacanattha*): it is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*), thus it is a "deposition" (*nikkhepa*); the discourse itself is the deposition, hence "discourse-deposition" (*suttanikkhepa*).
Alternatively, the act of depositing is "deposition"; the deposition of a discourse is "discourse-deposition," meaning the teaching of a discourse.
One's own inclination is "self-inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*); that which has this as its cause is "motivated by self-inclination. One's own inclination...
*Etassa* means "of this," referring to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*). The same principle applies to the inclination of others (*parajjhāsaya*).
*Pucchāvaso* means the power of a question; that which possesses this is called *pucchāvasiko*. *Atthuppatti* is the arising of the meaning that serves as the basis for the teaching of the Sutta;
*aṭṭhuppatti* is simply *atthuppatti*, having changed the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*. That which possesses this is called *aṭṭhuppattiko*.
Alternatively, *suttanikkhepa* means that by means of this the discourse (*sutta*) is laid down; it refers precisely to one’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth.
In this particular interpretation, "one’s own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*) is the inclination of oneself; "the inclination of others" (*parajjhāsaya*) is the inclination of others.

That which is asked is an "inquiry" (*pucchā*), meaning a matter to be inquired about. The speech of those who receive the Dhamma, occurring by way of such inquiry, is "occasioned by inquiry" (*pucchāvasika*).
That very same [term] is stated as "dependent on a question" (pucchāvasika) in the masculine gender by virtue of its dependence on the word *nikkhepa*.
Likewise, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*) means simply "an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

Furthermore, in this context, because it is independent of external causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others, the state of being a separate Sutta-deposition belonging to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) is established.
This is because it was delivered solely according to his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the system of the Dhamma.

However, there is no restriction on the "arising of the subject" (*aṭṭhuppatti*) regarding those discourses delivered on account of the inquiries of others— those inquiries arising from the inclinations of others which serve as the cause for the delivery of the teaching—
or regarding those where the inquiry itself serves as the occasion for the arising of the subject, since these occur in accordance with the inclinations of others.
How is there no restriction regarding the inclinations of those who cause the teaching to circulate? This point need not be raised as an objection.

For, since the occurrence of the causes for the delivery of a discourse—when it is entirely free from the specific requests or inquiries of others—is taken to constitute the "occasion for the teaching" (*aṭṭhuppatti*), there is a separate mention of those instances dependent on the inquiries of others' inclinations.

Thus, in the case of discourses such as the *Brahmajāla* and the *Dhammadāyāda*, the motives for the teaching were the praise or censure [of other teachers] and the acquisition of material gifts, respectively.

It is called “aṭṭhuppatti” (an occasion for discourse). That which is taught by taking as its basis the inclination of others, even without their asking a question, is “parajjhāsayo” (based on the inclination of others);
that which is taught by means of a question is “pucchāvasiko”—this meaning is well known.

It should be understood that he spoke solely according to his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma. He is a bearer of the Suttantas on the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

This is a collection of discourses connected with the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, arranged in successive order. Likewise [there are collections] on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the requisites for concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*), and so forth.

The factors conducive to the ripening of liberation (*vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā*) are the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhindriya*). "Inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) means resolution (*adhimutti*). "Acceptance" (*khanti*) means the acceptance resulting from the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*).

"Mind" (*citta*) means that which cognizes. "Directed application" (*abhinīhāra*) means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*). "The state of awakening" (*bujjhanabhāva*) means the nature of awakening, or the mode of penetration.
This connects with the phrase "placed when conceit has arisen. The three genders are the feminine gender and so forth. The four terms are name and so forth.
The seven case endings are the nominative and so forth. Having set these aside, he says nothing else according to the natural language.

Because it proceeds in that very same way. A "knot-word" (*gaṇṭhipada*) is so called because, just as a knot in a tree is difficult to penetrate and difficult to cut, even so, a word whose meaning cannot be explained is called a "knot-word.
"Without having struck" (*anupahacca*) means without having extracted [the meaning].
By the statement, "Whatever it connects with, it illuminates that in its entirety," he shows the limited scope (*sappadesatā*) of this word *sabba*.

For the word *sabba* is seen to be employed in four domains: the all-inclusive all (*sabbasabba*), the partial all (*padesasabba*), the all-inclusive sense-bases (*āyatanasabba*), and the all-inclusive aggregates of existence (*sakkāyasabba*).
Thus, for example, [it is said]: "All phenomena (*sabbe dhammā*) in all their aspects [are known] by the Buddha, the Blessed One..."
In such passages as “coming within the range of the door of knowledge,” it refers to the *sabbasabba* (the all-in-all).
In such passages as “Sariputta, all that you have spoken is well-spoken by way of its method,” it refers to the *padesasabba* (the partial all). In the passage, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you ‘all’...
the eye and forms... the mind and mental objects,” it refers to the *āyatanasabba* (the all of the sense bases). [And] “all from all.”

In such passages as "he perceives," [the term] refers to the whole of personality (sakkāya). Among those, in the first instance it is used without limitation (nippadesa), while in the other three it is used with limitation (sappadesa);

however, here it should be understood as referring to the whole of personality. For he will say: "But those states included within personality (sakkāya-pariyāpanna) are to be understood without exception as being precisely those of the three planes."
"In the Noble Truths" means in the [Four] Noble Truths. "These four things"—this refers to the four factors beginning with truth that are now being discussed.
Therein, "truth" (*sacca*) is verbal truth. "Stability" (*ṭhiti*) is energy (*vīriya*); alternatively, the reading is "steadfastness" (*dhitī*), which has the same meaning.
"Relinquishment" (*cāga*) is non-greed (*alobha*). "He transcends what is seen"—that is, he transcends whatever is perceived in relation to those factors such as truth.
Thus, it overcomes its own perceived enemy; it does not fall into its power, but rather overcomes it—this is the meaning.
It functions according to its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), because there is no possibility of an un-natural phenomenon (*asabhāvadhamma*) arising.
For phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature are not produced by anything. They "bear their own characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*), even though they are [in some respects] devoid of characteristics.
There are no such things as "dhammas" [in the sense of a self];

nevertheless, just as the notions of a self, beauty, pleasure, permanence, and so forth—imagined by views and craving—as well as primordial nature (prakṛti), substance (dravya), the soul (jīva), the body (kāya), and so on, which are established merely through worldly convention, are not found in reality or as ultimate truth, being like flowers in the sky, these [dhammas] are not like that; rather, they are real and ultimate.

Because they are apprehended as mere phenomena (dhammamatta) due to the absence of specific qualities such as a "being" (satta), it is said that "they bear their own characteristics" in order to show that they possess intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

For even when there is no actual difference, a description based on a distinction established by mere metaphorical designation (upacāramatta) is employed for the sake of easy understanding, as in the expression "the body of a stone statue. They are borne [by their characteristics].
They are called *dhammas* because they are determined and known according to their specific nature, such as hardness, contact, and so forth.
"In the uncommon cause" means in the uncommon condition; the meaning is: in the individual, unique condition for each respective thing among the phenomena of personality (*sakkāya-dhamma*).
But what is that? It is craving, conceit, and views, or else ignorance and so forth. For just as in the case of earth and the other elements...

Craving and the other [defilements] arising in relation to the bases for conceiving (*maññanāvatthu*) are themselves conceivings; they are the root cause for the occurrence of those [conceivings]. The same applies to ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest.

For this is demonstrated through both positive and negative concomitance: positively, by such passages as "the uninstructed worldling," "I say that it is not fully understood by him," and "delight is the root of suffering";
and negatively, by such passages as "through the destruction of lust... because of being free from delusion. Thus, their status as the root cause is made clear.
It is called a *pariyāya* because it causes one to understand and realize the meaning that is to be taught; thus, it is a teaching (*desanā*).

It is called a *pariyāya* because it proceeds by encompassing its own fruit, or because it functions as the cause for that [fruit]; thus, it is a cause (*kāraṇa*). It is called a *pariyāya* because it revolves from one to another;
thus, it is a turn or sequence (*vāra*). Thus, the word *pariyāya* [is used] in the senses of teaching, cause, and turn.

The occurrence [of the teaching] is to be understood. "Of interpretable meaning" (neyyattha) refers to that meaning which must be determined by not taking [the words] according to their literal expression.
"All phenomena of the three planes" are to be understood without exception, because all phenomena such as earth and so forth—which serve as the bases for conceiving—are intended.
"Teaching of the cause" means a teaching that makes known the cause; "that meaning" refers to that which is reckoned as the root cause of all phenomena.
Or it refers to the meaning known as the teaching of the cause (*kāraṇadesanā*). For this very reason, he said: "That is the cause, that is the teaching. "This has the same meaning":
these two words have one and the same meaning. Indeed, the word *sādhu* itself, when augmented by the letter *ka*, is spoken as *sādhuka*.
For it is precisely for this reason that, when explaining the meaning of the word *sādhu*, the word *sādhuka* was cited by way of an extraction of its meaning.
*Dhammarucī* means one who desires merit. *Paññāṇavā* means possessed of wisdom (*paññavā*). *Addubbho* means one who does no harm; the meaning is "one who does not cause injury.
*Idhāpi* means even in this *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*. *Ayam* refers to the word *sādhuka*. *Ettheva daḷhīkamme* means in the performance of a task with thoroughness.
*Āṇattiyaṃ* means in the act of commanding. For when it is said, "Listen, pay close attention," by the word *sādhuka*, [it implies the same].
Just as there is the performance of listening with attention, so too is the giving of the command stated.
Its purpose as a command should be understood in the same way as its purpose as a request.
Now, the connection here should be understood as follows: the warding off of distraction of the ear-faculty by means of directing it toward listening.
The meaning is: "Lend an ear," because it serves to preclude other activities. It is the warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty by means of precluding thoughts of other things.
"The former" refers to the word "listen. "In this" refers to the pair of words "listen, attend," or to this context.
It is the prevention of grasping the phonemes in reverse order, because it acts as a barrier against distraction at the ear-door.

For one who hears according to reality, there is no grasping at the sound through distortion. The prevention of grasping at the meaning through distortion occurs because it wards off the distraction of the mind-faculty.
For one who carefully reflects upon the Dhamma, there is no grasping at the meaning through distortion.
He enjoins [one] to listen to the Dhamma by means of the arrangement "Listen! Regarding "retention and investigation," by the inclusion of the term "investigation":
It includes the thorough penetration of views through such processes as comparison and investigation. Regarding the term *sabyañjana*:
here, that which makes manifest (*byañjayati*) the intended meaning is "expression" (*byañjana*), namely, the natural linguistic convention. That which is together with expression is *sabyañjana*;

the meaning is "endowed with expression. Because it is to be striven for (*araṇīya*), because it is to be approached with reverence (*upagandhabba*), and because it is to be practiced (*anuṭṭhātabba*).

The meaning (*attha*) refers to the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) and so forth. "Possessing the meaning" (*sāttha*) means together with the meaning; thus, it is "endowed with meaning.

Regarding the phrases "profound in the Dhamma" (*dhammagambhīra*) and so on: "Dhamma" refers to the textual tradition (*tanti*). "Teaching" (*desanā*) refers to the teaching of that textual tradition as it has been determined by the mind.

"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the textual tradition. "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) refers to the realization of the textual tradition and the meaning of the textual tradition exactly as they are. Because...

This teaching of the Dhamma and the penetration of its meaning are difficult for those of dull intellect to plunge into and impossible for them to find a footing in, just as the great ocean is for crocodiles and the like;
therefore, it is profound. Hence it was said: "Because this Dhamma... [and so on] ...attend closely.
And herein, because penetration is difficult to achieve, [the profundity of] the Dhamma and its meaning [is established] through the knowledge of the teaching.

It should be understood that the teaching is "difficult to fathom" because it is difficult to practice, and its penetration is "difficult to fathom" because it is impossible to bring about [realization] and because the arising of knowledge regarding its object is difficult to achieve.
"Teaching" (desanā) means reciting; its "explanation" (niddisana) and "exposition" (bhāsana) are what is intended here, thus he said: "even in detail..."
"It is said that [he] will speak. Or, *bhāsana* is clear speech.
"Like the cry of a myna bird" means sweet, pleasant to the ear, and lovely, like the call of a myna bird. *Paṭibhāna* is sound. *Udīrayi* means it is uttered or spoken.
When it was thus said—"Listen well, attend closely, I shall speak"—they became inspired with zeal.
Thinking, "The Teacher will not teach in brief alone, but will also speak in detail," they became joyful and elated with newfound enthusiasm.
Regarding the phrase "here" (*idha*), it is said that this locative particle refers to the specific location being discussed, intended as the place of origin for that individual;

thus he says, "it is a locative particle used to designate a place. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the physical world of space (*okāsaloka*). For in the expression "here the Tathāgata [appears] in the world," it refers to the field of birth (*jātikhetta*).
In this context as well, it is this world-system (cakkavāḷa) that is intended. A recluse (samaṇa) is one who has entered the stream (sotāpanna). A second recluse is a once-returner (sakadāgāmī).

For this has been said: “And who, monks, is a recluse? Here, monks, a monk, through the total destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer. And: “And who, monks, is a second recluse? Here, monks, [a monk...]”
“A bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hate, and delusion, becomes a once-returner.
And: “While standing right here” means while standing in this very Indasāla Cave.
2. “Unlearned”: here, *sutaṃ* (the heard) refers to that which has been ascertained by way of the ear-door, or the act of ascertaining itself.
“*Assatthī* means ‘one who has heard’ (*sutavā*). For the meaning of the particle *vā* is manifold, depending on whether it signifies mere existence, abundance, physical affliction, and so forth.
Thus, in such passages as ‘this world is finite and circumscribed,’ the meaning is mere existence. In such passages as ‘wealthy, possessing enjoyments, a recipient of food,’ the meaning is abundance.
In such passages as ‘he is diseased, overcome by disease,’ the meaning is physical affliction. [In the case of] ‘a leper’ (*kuṭṭhī*)...”
In such passages as “with a tattered robe,” it is censure (*nindā*). In such passages as “envious, stingy, fraudulent, deceitful, and hypocritical,” it is frequent association (*abhiṇhayoga*).
In such passages as “staff-bearer, umbrella-bearer, and water-vessel bearer,” it is conjunction (*saṃsagga*).

In such passages as “or even by that he is wise,” it is comparison (*upamāna*), meaning similarity. In such passages as “the wise indeed recognize him as a sage,” it is aggregation (*samuccaya*). “Who indeed are these... [and so forth].

In such instances as “Of whom? there is doubt (*saṃsaya*). In such instances as “This one, among these recluses and brahmins, is the most foolish and the most deluded,” there is specification (*vibhāvana*).
In such instances as “Or perhaps this prince did not know moderation,” there is syntactic completion (*padapūraṇa*).

In such instances as “Whatever recluses or brahmins there may be, monks,” there is optionality (*vikappa*). [And] in the case of “The glorious son of the Sakyas, endowed with virtue through the perfection of his virtue...”
In such passages as, "A fair report of his fame goes abroad," it has the sense of praise (*pasaṃsā*).

In such passages as, "He is wise, possessed of wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering," it has the sense of excellence (*atisaya*).
Here too, the meaning is either excellence or praise; therefore, it refers to one who possesses what is praised, or who possesses learning with excellence.
"Learned" (*sutavā*) refers to hearing the Dhamma of the scriptures, which is capable of destroying defilements;

having heard that, the practice for the sake of suchness is also indicated by this term "learned. Alternatively, one who has heard what is worthy of being heard and has accomplished what is to be done through that hearing is "learned" (*sutavā*);
by contrast, one who lacks that is "unlearned" (*assutavā*).

For this prefix *a-* is intended to signify the exclusion of association with that [factor] in such cases as “states without cause” (*ahetukā dhammā*) and “a residence without a resident monk” (*abhikkhuko āvāso*).
In the phrase “states without conditions” (*apaccayā dhammā*), it signifies the exclusion of being related to that [condition]. For that which has arisen from conditions is related to its conditions;

thus, by virtue of not having arisen from conditions, the lack of relation to those [conditions] is made manifest here. In the phrase “states that are non-demonstrable” (*anidassanā dhammā*), it signifies the exclusion of that very nature [of being demonstrable].
For "nidassana" (manifestation) is to be understood as the state of being visible. Alternatively, it is called "nidassana" because it sees; that is, eye-consciousness.
This term is used to exclude other states from its function, such as in the case of "states free from taints," "states non-reactive," or "states without an object.

It is also used to exclude other states from its nature, as in "formless states" or "states not associated with consciousness. For otherwise, these [terms] would be explained here in a different manner.
“Non-human” (*amanusso*) refers to the exclusion of that state alone; it means there is no mere human, but rather something else similar. For here, similarity is indicated.
“One who is not an ascetic, yet claims to be an ascetic, one who is ignoble”—this refers to the exclusion of those qualities by which he would be esteemed.
For here, censure is understood. “Is your lordship free from illness? Is the maiden slender?”—this refers to the exclusion of the non-arising of those [qualities].
The phrase “unarisen states” (anuppannā dhammā) serves to exclude those things that are similar to them.

For while past states have previously arisen, and even those states whose arising has already been initiated possess a partial accomplishment of their conditions and thus a state of having begun to arise, and moreover, there exist states entirely liberated from time—how much more so, then, for present states?

Therefore, it is precisely their remoteness from these [present states] that is understood here. The phrase “states of one beyond training” (asekkhā dhammā) serves to exclude those that do not reach that final consummation.
For here, the cessation of that [ignorance] is what is revealed. Thus, it is an indicator of many meanings.

However, in this context—as in such expressions as "formless phenomena" (*arūpino dhammā*) or "non-mental factors" (*acetasikā dhammā*)—it should be understood as the negation of its existence; the meaning is "elsewhere.
By this, he shows its lack of knowledge derived from hearing and so forth. Therefore it was said: "One should be known as 'unlearned' (*assutavā*) due to the absence of scripture and realization."
Now, in explaining its meaning: since even proficiency in the aggregates, elements, and so forth constitutes great learning capable of preventing conceiving—as it was said:
"To what extent, venerable sir, is one a person of great learning?
When, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu is skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, and skilled in dependent origination—to that extent, bhikkhu..."

“He becomes one who has heard much. Therefore, it was said: “For one [who is proficient] in the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), truths (sacca), the modes of conditionality (paccayākāra), the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and so forth.
In that context: *Uggaha* (learning) is the act of committing to memory. *Paripucchā* (inquiry) is the questioning of the meaning.

*Vinicchaya* (analysis) is the making of a determination by means of posing questions and providing answers together with those who are skilled. *Adhigama* (attainment) refers to the paths, fruits, and nibbāna.

They are called *puthujjana* because they have not destroyed (*avihatattā*) the many various kinds of defilements and the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), or because they are produced by those [defilements].
Alternatively, the word *jana* expresses the very state of being undestroyed. Regarding the phrase "looking up toward the faces of various teachers," the etymological meaning is:
"those for whom various (*puthu*) people are recognized as teachers are *puthujjana*. They are various in all [six] destinies (*gati*).

Regarding the term *avuṭṭhitā*: here it refers to those who ought to be born; or, "beings" (*jana*) are so called because beings are born (*jāyanti*) therein—that is, in the various destinies (*nānāgati*).

Since these [destinies] are manifold (*puthu*) for them, they are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, those beyond this [point] are born by means of these—namely, volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth—and since these exist manifoldly for them, they are "worldlings.
Or rather, the word *jana* should be understood as having the sense of "volitional formation" and so forth. The "floods" (*ogha*) are the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the others.
The "torments" are the fevers of passion and so forth. Or, all defilements (*kilesa*) are "fevers.

"Ordinary persons" (*puthujjana*) are those who are born as individuals attached to the fivefold strands of sensual pleasure; they are so called because passion, greed, and the like arise within them.

Alternatively, the word *jana* may be understood to mean passion and so forth, in the sense that these [defilements] are born individually among people and they are attached to them. "Attached" (*ratta*)—
They are "colored" by desire and lust, which cause the transformation of the mind just as various dyes color cloth;

they are "greedy" through covetousness, which has the nature of longing, having fallen into a state of greed; they are "infatuated," being bound to that object as if knotted together and difficult to release;
they are "deluded," having become, as it were, senseless through the influence of the defilements, with no other purpose.
"Fallen into fainting and delusion. "Clinging" (*ajjhosanna*) means remaining after having swallowed and finalized [the object] as if it were something not shared with others.
"Attached" (*lagga*) means stuck like a crooked stick, or submerged like a person who has fallen into a great mire up to the tip of the nose and cannot be pulled out;
"clung" (*lagita*) means having clung like monkey-glue, from which one cannot rise again.
Like a monkey, it is caught by means of the five faculties. *Palibuddhā* means bound or afflicted.
*Āvuṭā* means ensnared; *nivutā* means obstructed. *Ovutā* means enveloped or covered over.
*Pihitā* means closed; *paṭicchannā* means concealed. *Paṭikujjitā* means turned face downwards. Or, for many...
By the phrase "beyond the path of calculation" and so forth, he shows that the "many-folk" (puthujjana) are called "worldlings" (puthujjana).
By the term "unlearned" (assutavā), the state of being blinded by ignorance is expressed; thus he says, "the blind worldling is what is meant.

[They are called *puthujjana*] because they are far (*āraka*) from the defilements due to their having been severed by the Path. "In misfortune" (*anaye*) means in non-prosperity (*avaḍḍhi*); "in harm" (*anatthe*) is the meaning. Or, it means in misfortune, that is, in the absence of the right means (*anupāye*).

"From the state of being noble" means from the state of not turning back. "Aya" refers to growth, purpose, or means. "From the state of being worthy of approach" means from the state of being fit for attendance.

The derivation of the word should be understood according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*) in the first alternative meanings, but according to the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*) in the latter.

Although the term *ariya* appears in such passages as, "Those who are noble (*ariya*) have purified bodily actions," where it refers to those whose intentions and applications are pure; [it is used here in its primary sense].

This term also applies to worldlings (*puthujjana*). However, here it is intended to signify the state of being noble (*ariya*) by virtue of having attained the Noble Path and by virtue of being entirely supramundane;

showing this, he says "the Buddhas," and so forth. Therein, the phrase "Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata are true persons" is stated in order to show, without confusion, the meaning of the terms "Noble Ones" and "true persons" as they are used here.

It has been said. However, because from the perspective of the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), the states of being a noble one (*ariya*) and a true person (*sappurisa*) are of an identical nature, it was therefore stated:
"Or all [of them]," and so forth. By this much, the disciple of the Buddha has been described.

For he must absolutely have a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), since the first path cannot arise without the voice of another. And specifically, the Blessed One alone is intended as his virtuous friend. For this has been said:
“Indeed, Ānanda, it is by coming to me as a good friend that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth,” and so forth.
And that very state is called “firm devotion” through the attainment of verified confidence (*aveccapasāda*). For this has also been said:

“Whatever training rule (*sikkhāpada*) has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives. [This is due to] gratitude and other such qualities.

Regarding the terms *paccekabuddhā* and *buddhā*: one who knows what has been done (*kata*) is called *kataññū*. One who makes known (*vidita*), that is, makes manifest (*pākaṭa*), what has been done is called *katavedī*.

For even over many hundreds of thousands of eons, the *paccekabuddhas* recognize the assistance rendered to them and make it manifest by generating mindfulness through such acts as accepting material gifts;
likewise, they act with diligence toward one who is suffering from the miseries of *saṃsāra*.

They perform the duties that they themselves are capable of performing. However, the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the assistance rendered even throughout thousands of incalculable eons, as well as the necessary conditions (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits;
he makes this manifest and, like a lion, performs the work of a Buddha by teaching the Dhamma with thorough care in every respect. By means of which practice...
"Seen" means that there is a failure to act upon what has been seen, a lack of heedfulness toward it, and a habit of not seeing the Noble Ones;

it should be understood as a failure to perform well in the act of seeing. Regarding the phrase "one who has not seen with the eye," here "eye" does not refer merely to the physical eye, but rather to the divine eye (dibbacakkhu); thus he says, "or by the divine eye. "The state of being a Noble One" (ariyabhāva) [is to be understood].
Those qualities of the path and fruit by virtue of which one is called "noble" (ariya) are to be understood here.

In that context, "in the state of seeing" (tatra) refers specifically to the nature of seeing through knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). "Basis" (vatthu) means the cause for making known the intended meaning.
"Even though it was stated thus" (evaṃ vuttepī) means even though it was stated by applying it to oneself under the guise of another. "Dhamma" refers to the supramundane dhamma (lokuttaradhamma).
Or the Dhamma of the Four Truths. The qualities that make one noble—such as the contemplations on impermanence and so forth—are themselves impermanent and so on when they are being clearly seen;
or else, they are the Four Noble Truths.
"Undisciplined" (*avinīta*) means not disciplined, not trained by way of the training in higher virtue and so forth. Of those [qualities] such as restraint and discipline...
Because of this absence, one is called "undisciplined. To demonstrate those [types of discipline], he said, "Discipline is twofold," and so forth.
Therein, "restraint of virtue" (sīlasaṃvara) should be understood as the restraint of the Pātimokkha; and in terms of its actual meaning, it is the non-transgression of body and speech.

"Restraint of mindfulness" (satisaṃvara) is the guarding of the sense faculties, and that is simply mindfulness occurring in such a manner. "Restraint of knowledge" (ñāṇasaṃvara) refers to the [cessation] of the streams...

Having said, "I shall speak of restraint," because of the statement, "By wisdom they are covered," it should be understood that restraint is the covering—namely, the knowledge of eradication—of craving, views, misconduct, ignorance, and the remaining defilements, which are comprised within the ear-faculty. Restraint by patience (*khantisaṃvara*) means endurance;

and that consists of the aggregates proceeding in such a manner, or it is non-hatred (*adosa*). Some say it is wisdom (*paññā*), but that contradicts the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Restraint by energy (*vīriyasaṃvara*)...
It is precisely energy that proceeds by way of the dispelling of sensual thoughts and so forth.

The abandoning of each respective unwholesome factor through its corresponding wholesome factor is "abandoning by means of its constituent part" (*tadaṅga-pahāna*). Abandoning by suppression is "suppressive abandoning" (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

The passage beginning with "By this restraint of the Pātimokkha" is an exposition of the restraints of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so forth. In that context, regarding the word "endowed" (*samupeto*):

The word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*). By it, he indicates the analysis of restraint (*saṃvaravibhaṅga*) as it appears in the Vibhaṅga, beginning with the words "accompanied by," "approached," and so forth.
This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Whatever needs to be said regarding this matter will be made clear in the immediately following sutta.
Regarding "bodily misconduct, etc.": this refers to bodily and verbal misconduct, which are reckoned as immorality (*dussīlya*), and that which is reckoned as forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*).
It is [the restraint] of negligence, or of covetousness and so forth, as well as of intolerance, ignorance, and indolence.
"By way of restraining" means by way of closing off or shutting up. "By way of disciplining" means by way of disciplining or removing the improper activity of body, speech, and mind;
or it means by way of disciplining bodily misconduct and so forth; or its meaning is by way of cutting off the crooked activity of the body and so forth and leading them straight.
Restraint and discipline should be understood as the non-arising, in various ways, of bodily misconduct and so forth that would otherwise arise when conditions come together;
this is what is connected with the term "abandoning. Why was it said, "in the insight-knowledges such as the discernment of name-and-form"?

Is it not the case that the discernment of the conditions for the delimitation of name-and-form, the comprehension [of those conditions], and the overcoming of doubt are not insight-knowledges, because they do not function by way of the mode of comprehension (*sammasana*)?
True, this is so. However, it is stated thus because they serve as the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for insight-knowledge. Knowledge that occurs in the manner, "This is merely name-and-form;
herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self," is the definition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*). When mindfulness...

*Sakkāyadiṭṭhi* (personality-belief) is the view that occurs when one regards as a self the existing body, which is comprised of the five aggregates, or when there is a view directed toward that very body.

It is the wrong view that functions in such ways as: "One regards form as self. *Paccayapariggaha* (comprehension of conditions) is the knowledge that discerns the conditions—such as karma and ignorance—for that same form and non-form.
It is the [wisdom] that functions according to the method: "There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings," and so forth.

The view of no cause (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*). The view of an irregular cause (*visamahetudiṭṭhi*) is that which maintains: "The world proceeds and ceases by means of God, the Primal Man, Pajāpati, primordial matter, atoms, time, and so forth. "Of that very same" refers to the discernment of conditions itself.

"By the overcoming of doubt" means that just as the arising of name-and-form occurs through conditions such as karma at present, so too it occurs in the past and the future; thus, [one understands] across all three times.
By means of the knowledge that removes doubt. "Of the state of being a sceptic" refers to the occurrence of doubt proceeding in such a manner as: "Did I exist in the past?

and so forth. "By means of comprehension by groups" refers to the knowledge of insight into method (nayavipassanā-ñāṇa) occurring through the process of comprehending the five aggregates by subsuming them under eleven categories, beginning with: "Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present."
"Of the grasping 'I' and 'mine'" means of the grasping for a self and what belongs to a self.

"By the defining of the path and the non-path" means by the purification of knowledge regarding the path and the non-path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇavisuddhi*). "The perception of a path in what is not the path" means the perception that arises, taking the illumination and so forth—which are not the path—to be "the path.
Because one who sees the arising of formations correctly [sees] that "in this very way, formations arise from their corresponding causes,"...
But one does not grasp [them] as being annihilated; therefore it was said: "By seeing arising, [one abandons] the annihilationist view.

Furthermore, when one sees the passing away of formations and sees that "even though these formations proceed uninterruptedly, each time they arise, they cease without re-linking," for one who sees in this way, how could there be a grasping at eternalism?
Therefore it was said: “By seeing [their] passing away, [one abandons] the eternalist view. “By seeing danger” means by the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).

“In what is fearful” means in the five aggregates, which are fearful because they are the source of all fears and because they are the opposite of the supreme consolation known as the subsiding of all suffering.
“By the perception of fearlessness” means by the perception that has arisen [thinking], “It is fearless; it is secure.”

The perception of gratification (*assādasaññā*) is the perception that occurs by way of finding gratification in the five aggregates of clinging; it is also called "clinging through attachment" (*ālayābhiniveso*).

The perception of delight (*abhiratisaññā*) is the perception that occurs by way of taking delight in those very same things; it is also called "joy" (*nandī*). Grasping (*ādāna*) is the desire not to be released.

Non-equanimity (*anupekkhā*) is the failure to become disenchanted with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*); the meaning is "possessing attachment. Regarding the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ*).
The contrary state regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the grasping at eternalism or annihilationism, or the delusion that obscures the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
The contrary state regarding Nibbāna is delight in the formations (*saṅkhāra*), or the delusion that obscures Nibbāna.
"Grasping at the sign of the formations" refers to that defilement which, because it has not been abandoned, prevents insight from relinquishing the sign of the formations.
That which is also called "clinging to conjunction. Abandonment (*pahāna*) is precisely the transcending of the grasping of the signs of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).

"Occurrence" (*pavatti*) is the state of occurring; the meaning is "obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). Regarding the phrase "of the phenomena such as the hindrances," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes the defilements belonging to the side of the hindrances, as well as applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth.
The connection is: "that which is abandonment by way of the absolute non-occurrence due to the cultivation of the four noble paths."
By what means is there abandoning? This meaning is understood to be "by means of the Noble Path," because it is stated that [defilements] do not occur due to their having been developed.

Regarding the phrase "belonging to the side of origination": here, taking into account that all four paths constitute the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Truths, they are to be abandoned together with the respective origins (*samudaya*) that are to be abandoned by them;
thus, they share the same nature as origination. Furthermore, in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths), all defilements—
Because the state of origination has been described, views and so forth are called "belonging to the side of origination. Pacification (*paṭippassaddhatta*) is the state of being calmed.
Freedom from the conditioned (*saṅkhatanissaṭatā*) is the absence of the intrinsic nature of formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"Abandoned all that is conditioned" means devoid of all conditioned things; the meaning is "beyond formations" (*visaṅkhāra*). Furthermore, it is both abandonment and discipline, thus "abandonment-discipline" (*pahānavinaya*); this refers to the first sense, while by the second sense—
"Abandonment" (*pahāna*) means that which is abandoned; it should be construed as "the discipline (*vinaya*) of that [abandonment].
"Because of the broken restraint" (*bhinna-saṃvarattā*) means because of the lost restraint; the meaning is "due to the absence of restraint.
By this, even one who has not formally undertaken the restraint is included. For restraint is to be accomplished through formal undertaking; in its absence, it does not exist. Indeed, in the world...
They say, "Alas, what a great wealth we had! It is lost because it was not utilized in that way. *Ariyeti* means "noble"; for this is a nominative singular form.

*Esesa* means "that very same one," the sense being that he is not other than that in meaning. *Tajjāta* means "of that nature" in meaning; a true person (*sappurisa*) has the nature of the noble ones (*ariya*), and a noble one has the nature of a true person—this is the meaning.
“That meaning” refers to the meaning spoken of as “the exposition of the root of all phenomena. But why is the teaching here presented by way of the person (puggalādhiṭṭhānā)?
Whatever needs to be said on this matter, he himself will state it later with the words, “Because the worldling has not fully understood the basis,” and so forth.
It is called “dhammādhiṭṭhānā” because its basis (adhiṭṭhāna) is the phenomenon (dhamma); that is, it relies upon phenomena as intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma).
The teaching that has been set in motion. The first [type] proceeds by way of the Dhamma alone;

the third arises by way of a person and concludes by way of a person alone; the others proceed by way of a mixture of both Dhamma and persons. But why does the Blessed One teach the Dhamma through such a classification?

It is because of the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*) and because of his skill in teaching (*desanāvilāsa*). For those who are to be trained are [divided into those who prefer] a foundation in the Dhamma...
Through the teaching of the Dhamma, they penetrate the meaning with ease; to them he teaches the Dhamma accordingly.
This method applies everywhere. And because of his thorough penetration of that element of Dhamma, he has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching;
since that [element] is thoroughly penetrated by him, therefore the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, who has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching, acts exactly as he wishes.

"In such and such a way he teaches the Dhamma": it should be understood that by this inclination of those to be trained and by this skill in teaching, he teaches the Dhamma through such a classification.
"Consisting of six elements" refers to these six: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

By way of the elements, it is sixfold as the six elements. By way of the eighteen mental explorations—namely, the six explorations of joy, the six explorations of grief, and the six explorations of equanimity, as stated in such passages as “Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy”—it is eighteenfold as the eighteen mental explorations.
By way of the foundation of the Truths and so forth, it is fourfold as the four foundations. By means of the eye of wisdom, regarding what pertains to the present life...
He should be understood as "blind" because he does not see the welfare of the future life; as "one-eyed" because he sees only the welfare of the present life;
and as "two-eyed" because he sees both.
The connection is: "he is pointed out. And "he is this one" refers to the Blessed One, who is skilled in the analysis of the teaching as it has been described.

Meaning: "One who has not fully understood the basis" means one whose aggregates (*khandha*) have not been fully understood by way of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). For the aggregates are the basis for full understanding.
"Rooted in non-full-understanding" means that it exists because of the presence of the cause for the lack of full understanding;

for the defilements such as ignorance (*avijjā*) are the opposites of full understanding, and all conceivings (*maññanā*) are rooted in them. Regarding the phrase "one who does not see the Noble Ones," here the word *iti* [indicates the end of the quotation].

The word "ādi" (etc. includes the remainder of the text that occurs as a qualification of the worldling (*puthujjana*), such as "unskilled in the noble Dhamma," because it constitutes the description of the worldling. Therefore he said: "In this way he described the worldling.
The commentary on the introduction of the sutta is finished.
The commentary on the section on earth:
"Of that" means of the worldling (*puthujjana*). It is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because an object (*ārammaṇa*) dwells therein by way of being made an object;

it is so called because it is the locus of occurrence. Therefore, he said: "in the bases such as earth. This is also true for the phenomena of identity (*sakkāya-dhammā*) by way of being objects and so forth.

Even though conceiving (maññanā) exists as a cause [for their arising], it is stated that "conceiving is produced by all the phenomena of identity-attachment" (sabbasakkāyadhammajanitaṃ maññanaṃ) precisely because they have conceiving as their cause.

And here, although the earth element is equal in measure to the remaining elements, its state of being superior or inferior should be understood by way of its capacity (sāmatthiya), according to whether it is accompanied by or lacks the other constituent factors (sasambhārāsambhāra).
They are called "constituents" (sambhārā) because they support (sambharanti); that is, they are attendants (parivārā).
Within each respective group, the remaining phenomena occur in relation to the characteristic earth-element as conditions and as attendants, as appropriate.
Therefore he said: "For that is 'earth with its constituents' (sasambhārapathavī) because it is earth together with its constituent factors such as color and so forth.

Regarding the term *pathavito*: in the sense of being broad (*puthula*), it is *puthuvī*; *puthuvī* itself is *pathavī*. For even though its occurrence is limited, it is called "earth" because of its vastness.
That which exists as the supporting basis for all its constituent qualities deserves to be called "broad," "spread out," and "vast";

however, this does not apply to the [elements] such as water that exist by entering into it. As for the earth consisting of material components (*sasambhāra-pathavī*), there is simply no need to speak of its breadth.
In the case of the objective earth (*ārammaṇa-pathavī*), the sense of "breadth" is established through the meanings of increasing and pervading.

In the other case, it should be understood by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*). "The earth as object" (*ārammaṇapathavī*) refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) designated as earth, which has become the object of jhāna.
Therefore, he said: "It is also called 'the earth as sign' (*nimittapathavī*). "By way of arrival" (*āgamanavasena*) means by way of arriving at the cultivation of the earth-kasina (*pathavīkasiṇa*).
For it is thus stated: "The water-devas and the earth-devas, the fire and the wind—then they arrived."
All four kinds of earth are indeed objects for the conceiving that arises from mere hearsay and so forth.
For instance, even "characteristic earth" (lakkhaṇa-pathavī) is extracted by such passages as "that which is hard, that which has become solid.

As for what some say—"When the characteristic is seen, there is no conceiving; and the perception (saññā) mentioned in the phrase 'one perceives' is the root of the grasping of views"—[this is not correct].

“If ‘taking as a lump’ is not applicable to the characteristic, then the earth of characteristics should not be grasped”—this is incorrect, because the penetration of characteristics is not intended here.
Therefore he said, “having taken up worldly convention. Nor is every perception one that takes things as a lump, nor is it the sole root of the grasping of views;
therefore, even in the case of the earth of characteristics, by way of the door of the body—
Otherwise, conceiving (maññanā) would indeed continue to occur regarding what is present. For that very reason, it is said: "obtained merely through hearsay and so forth.
By saying "he perceives [it] as 'earth'," he shows that the word *pathavī* is used in the ablative sense (*nissakkavacana*).
Because one who perceives even the fourfold earth as "earth" does so, by way of that or that method, precisely as a portion of earth.
It is said that "one perceives," not by way of a physical portion; therefore it is stated, "one perceives by way of the division of earth.

"Taking up worldly convention" means not abandoning the common designation of the world. By this, he shows that even in the case of the earth as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa-paṭhavī*), its occurrence is solely by way of conventional expression.
If its occurrence therein is by way of worldly convention, what fault is there? For do not even the Noble Ones say, "Venerable sir, this is the great earth," and so forth?
"Do they proceed by way of worldly convention? No; it is not intended here that they abide merely as conventional designations.
Rather, showing that through the medium of convention there is a false adherence, he says: "One perceives by means of a perversion of perception. The meaning of this is:

one perceives by means of a distorted perception produced by improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra), which proceeds in the manner of [the notions] "beautiful" and so forth. By this, the weak conceivings of craving, conceit, and views are indicated.
It should be understood as "shown. If this is so, why is "perception" (saññā) mentioned? Because it is the manifest state. This should be seen as follows:

just as when fire is being churned and smoke is perceived, although the fire is indeed present at that time because they are inseparable, yet because it is the smoke that has become manifest, one says "smoke has arisen," not "fire has arisen"—so too should this be understood. Even though there [in that case]...
There is the function of conceiving (*maññanā*), yet it is not the function of perception (*saññā*) alone that is manifest, because [perception] is unmanifest due to its state of being obscure;
rather, that [function of conceiving] is conducive to conceiving and accompanied by conceiving. Therefore, he said: "One perceives through a perversion of perception.
Thus, the connection is: "One perceives while not even relinquishing the portion of earth," for one who [perceives] the earth of the aforementioned varieties...

Just as one who does not let go of, nor abandon, the division of earth might perceive a lump of clay as gold, so too one perceives that which has the intrinsic nature of non-self and so forth as a self and so forth;
it is on account of this that [the world] speaks of "earth" and so on. Showing that it cannot be said that the ordinary person’s grasping prevents the investigation of the logical method, he said:
"Like a madman... he grasps. This refers to the distinction of the noble ones' lack of vision and so forth.

The construction is as follows: by the Blessed One himself, when speaking of the distinction of the noble ones (ariya) such as their lack of vision [of the Dhamma], the cause for the aforementioned perception has been stated here.
"In this way" means in the manner described by the passage beginning with "he perceives through the differentiation of earth.
He says, "having perceived... later on... he grasps," because "having perceived" is an expression of a prior action. "Papañca-saṅkhā" means categories of proliferation; beings proliferate.
They are called *papañcas* because one lingers long in *saṃsāra* by means of them; they are called *maññanās* because one conceives by means of them, such as imagining "this is mine" and so forth.
Thus, it is said that by both these methods, craving and the rest are what are spoken of:

"By the *papañcas* of craving, conceit, and views, which here are spoken of under the name of 'conceiving' (*maññanā*). The conceiving of views arises from grasping at the ignoble as noble, or the inferior as superior, and so forth.
Since craving, conceit, and the conceiving of "I" are likewise modes of apprehending things otherwise, he said, "he apprehends otherwise.
