Just as the common nature of reflecting (upanijjhāyana) belongs to thought (vitakka) and the rest despite their distinct individual natures through their functions such as directing the mind toward an object, so too should it be understood that "conceiving" (maññanā) is the occurrence of craving and the rest by way of a common mode of imagining the object, despite their having distinct natures through their functions of relishing, loftiness, and misapprehension. Therefore he said:
“‘He conceives by means of three conceivings,’ and so forth. The word “his” refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*).

Since there is indeed a subtle occurrence of conceiving even in such things as the contemplation of rise and fall, the author—desiring to show that [the coarse form] is easy to discern—said “by way of the coarse method.
For it is shown that once the coarse classification has been demonstrated, the subtle classification is easy to understand.

"This is called the application of the meaning" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Internal" (*ajjhattika*) refers to those bound to the sense-faculties, included within the continuum of a sentient being, and designated as "one's own internal" (*niyakajjhatta*) in both the *Vibhaṅga* and the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

"In the *Vibhaṅga*" means in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*. "External" (*bāhira*) refers to those not bound to the sense-faculties, included within the continuum of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Hard" (*kakkhala*)...
"Stiff" (*thaddhaṃ*). "Rough-natured" (*kharigataṃ*) means harsh. "Harshness" (*kakkhaḷattaṃ*) is the state of being harsh; "state of being harsh" means having a harsh nature.

"External" (*bahiddhā*) means that which has become external to what is bound by the sense faculties. "Not clung-to" (*anupādinnam*) means not grasped. "Iron" (*ayo*) is black metal. "Metal" (*lohaṃ*) is fourfold:
elemental metal (*jātilohaṃ*), derivative metal (*vijātilohaṃ*), artificial metal (*kittimalohaṃ*), and "pisāca-metal" (*pisācalohaṃ*). Among these, "iron" (*ayo*)...
Copper, gold, tin, lead, bronze, and vaikrāntaka iron—these are called the seven types of natural metals (*jātiloha*).
Nāga-nāsikā iron is called a mixed metal (*vijātiloha*). Bell-metal, round metal, and brass—these three are called artificial metals (*kittimaloha*).
Peacock-feather metal, *puthuka*, *malinaka*, *capalaka*, *salaka*, *āṭala*, *bhattaka*, and *duṣiloha*—[these are further varieties].
There are eight kinds of "pisāca-iron. Among them, *vekantaka-loha* is a type of iron capable of cutting all other types of iron;
for it is called *vikantaka* because it cuts (*vikantati*) or cleaves. *Vekantaka* is simply another form of *vikantaka*.
*Nāganāsika-loha* is like iron, yet it is a different species of iron, just as turmeric and other such things are different species [from iron]. For indeed, it has the appearance of iron...
It remains as a dense mass like iron dross; however, when heated and beaten, it breaks apart and scatters, becoming neither soft, nor smooth, nor workable.
*Kaṃsaloha* (bronze) is made by mixing tin and copper. *Vaṭṭaloha* (bell-metal) is made by mixing lead and tin.
*Ārakuṭa* (an alloy) is made by mixing jasatamba and tin. For that very reason, it...
Because it is produced by means of [other] metals, it is called "famous metal" (*kittimaloha*). However, that which has emerged solely from the *rasaka* element is also called "brass" (*pittala*).
That is not intended here; rather, what is stated as "possessing fame" refers to that which is prepared by mixing exactly those [elements] as described.
These very substances, such as peacock-feather copper (*morakkhaka*) and so forth, have these names. Among them, since the five types of metal by birth (*jātiloha*) are [mentioned] in the Canon...

These have been mentioned separately; therefore, it should be understood that "metal" (*loha*) here refers to everything remaining after [the specific metals] have been stated together with pure copper (*vekaṇṭaka-loha*).

"Tin" (*tipu*) is white tin. "Lead" (*sīsa*) is black tin. "Silver" (*sajjha*) is silver. "Pearl" (*muttā*) refers to the eight kinds of pearls, such as those from the elephant’s frontal globe and so forth.
For it is said: "The elephant’s frontal globe, the boar’s tusk, the serpent’s head, the cloud-peak..."
There are eight sources of pearls: bamboo, fish-heads, conchs, and oysters. Among these, those produced from the frontal globes of elephants are yellow in color and lacking in luster.
Those from the tusks of boars are the same color as a boar’s tusk. Those produced from the heads of serpents are blue and other colors, extremely pure, and round.
Those produced from clouds are brilliant, difficult to distinguish in form, and dispel the darkness during the night.
They remain [in the world], yet they are merely objects of enjoyment for the gods.
Those born from bamboo have a color similar to that of a *karaka* fruit or a lotus, but they are not radiant; and those bamboos grow only in places frequented by non-human beings (*amanussa*).

Those born from fish scales have a color similar to the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish, and they are round, light, and lacking in luster; and those fish are born only in the midst of the ocean. Those born from shells...
Those born from conchs have the color of the shell's interior and are the size of *kola* fruits, yet they lack luster.

Those born from pearl-oysters possess a distinction of luster and come in various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls according to their origin, those born from fish, conchs, and oysters are ocean-born;
some of those born from snakes are also ocean-born, while others are not. This is because, for the most part...
Pearls are seen in the world as those from the ocean; even there, they are produced by oysters, while others appear only occasionally. Therefore, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated:
"‘Pearl’ means a pearl from the ocean. As for ‘gem’:
with the exception of the beryl (*veḷuriya*) and so forth mentioned in the Canon, every other variety of gem, such as the *jotirasa* and so on, is also a gem. Regarding ‘beryl’...
*Vaṃsavaṇṇamaṇi*: a bamboo-colored gem. *Saṅkha*: a sea shell. *Sila*: there are eight types of stone, including black stone, yellow stone, white stone, and so forth. *Rajata*:
silver, including the *kahāpaṇa* coin and other items generally recognized as silver. *Jātarūpa*: gold. *Lohitanga*: a red gem. *Masāragalla*: a variegated gem (*kabara-maṇi*).
Also included are palm trees, coconut trees, and the like, which serve as external burdens for grass and other materials.
"Grass" means [any plant]. "Wood" refers to anything with internal core, such as *khadira* wood and so forth, down to even a mere fragment of timber.
"Gravel" refers to sand ranging from the size of a mung bean up to the measure of a fist.

"Sand" refers to material smaller than a mung bean. "Potsherd" means a fragment of a broken vessel. "Earth" means the soil together with its constituent elements. "Stone" is so called because it cannot be crushed within the closed fist.
Starting from [the size of] a cloth down to a stone the size of an elephant, and starting from the size of an elephant upwards, it is called a "mountain.
This is the detailed description regarding iron and the other [elements]. "Sign-earth" refers to the earth-kasiṇa which has become a counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).
For that too, by way of the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional [states], constitutes the fine-material-sphere first, second, third, and fourth jhānas.
Because of the statement, "These states, which are the result of jhāna, have external objects," it is called "external earth.
Therefore it was said: "taking that which is the sign-earth in the triad of internal objects.
And here, the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) should be understood as being included within that [category], since it was already included by the mention of "ground" prior to the arising of the sign.
Having stated "by three conceits," the triad of conceits is shown by applying them briefly to one's own and others' continuums through the passage beginning with "I am earth.
Therein, "I am earth" and so forth shows the conceit of views and the conceit of pride regarding internal objects, because they manifest the adherence to a self and the notion of "I.
By the phrase "earth is mine," it shows the conceit of craving.
Or, there is conceiving through pride (*mānamaññanā*) because one conceives of the earth—which has become an object of appropriation—as "better" and so forth.
The analysis of conceiving in the remaining two phrases should also be understood by this same method.

In that regard, one who has attained the meditation on the earth-kasina (*pathavikasiṇajjhāna*), while adhering to the object of that meditation grasped by the eye of jhāna as "self" and regarding it as "better" and so forth, is in fact [conceiving]: "I..."
One conceives of it as "earth"; furthermore, by grasping that very thing as "this is my self," one conceives of it as "my earth.

Likewise, by adhering to it through the mode of speech "another person" or "a deity," thinking "this indeed is the self of others," one conceives of it as "another's earth" or "the earth of another. In this manner...
The same fourfold analysis should be applied, as appropriate, to the remaining elements as well.
Having thus demonstrated conceiving (*maññanā*) by way of this fourfold set in the phrase "he conceives earth," he now says "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth,
in order to show the manyfold manner of his conceiving after having analyzed both the objects of conceiving and the acts of conceiving themselves.
In this context, "he" refers to the aforementioned worldling (*puthujjana*). "Lustful passion" (*chandārāga*) means dense passion. "Relishes" (*assādeti*) means he desires;
he finds gratification therein by thinking, "These hairs are soft, glossy, curled, and blue-black," and so forth.

"Rejoices" (*abhinandati*) means he delights and exults, facing toward craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). "Utters praise" (*abhivadati*) refers to the surge of the arising impulse of rejoicing through craving.
Unable to sustain it within his heart, he utters the words, "Oh, what beautiful hair I have!
He "remains clinging" means that he remains having swallowed and finalized [the object] through the forceful adherence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

"Or else some other object of lust" refers to something other than the hair and so forth—such as the various parts like hands and feet—which is included within one's own internal self and serves as a cause for the arising of passion.
The object (*vatthu*). By the word "thus" (*iti*), he refers to the manner in which [the body] is to be desired, namely, by way of its glossy appearance and so forth.

In that context, "he brings about delight" (*nandiṃ samannāneti*) means that he attends to and accumulates craving (*taṇhā*), treating those future hairs and so forth as if they were already accomplished.
"He aspires" (*paṇidahati*) means he establishes a wish.
The construction is as follows: based on prosperity, one generates the conceit “I am superior”; based on adversity, one generates the conceit “I am inferior.
Since the conceiving of pride arises through the prosperity and adversity of the hair and so forth—which constitute portions of the earth—it is said:
“In this way, one conceives of the internal earth by means of the conceiving of pride. Apart from its constituent parts...
Showing that because a composite whole does not exist, the adherence to a "living being" (jīva) occurs even with respect to its parts, he said:
"But according to the method [of the opponent's] statement, 'That which is the living being is that which is the body,' with regard to what do they adhere [to the notion] 'this is the living being'?

Here, the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*) should be understood through such methods as: "What are these hairs? Are they created by Īśvara, dependent on Pajāpati, a collection of atoms, or a transformation of primordial nature (*pakati*)? and so forth.
"By this occurrence" means by the occurrence that consists in the exhaustion and eradication of craving, conceit, and views.

Although the possibility of all three types of conceiving (*maññanā*)—beginning with "This is mine"—is shown here, it should be understood that specifically the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*) is singled out here, because craving and conceit have already been shown previously. Therefore he said: "In this way, internal earth..."
“He conceives by means of the conceiving of views. The construction is:

“He also conceives external earth by means of three kinds of conceiving. To show that method of conceiving, he said, “How? Its meaning is to be understood according to the manner explained below. “This is the soul”:
some Nigaṇṭhas, like others, adhere to the notion that this black iron [ball] is “the soul, the self. Thus...

Regarding the phrase "one conceives of external earth through the conceiving of views," here too it should be stated by applying the method beginning with: "Whatever is the internal earth element and whatever is the external earth element.
As for what should be said regarding such passages as "one regards the earth-kasiṇa as self," that has already been explained above. This too...
And this method should be understood as being included right here in the passage, "He regards form as self," because even the kasiṇas possess the designation "form.

Regarding the phrase "he conceives earth," he says, "From here on I shall explain in brief only," because the detailed method for the objects of conceiving and the act of conceiving that was stated previously applies exactly to the method stated from this point forward.
But one who is not such [a person] will explain it in detail;

this is the meaning. "Therefore" means: because "on earth" (*pathaviyā*) is a locative expression, therefore he constructs that basis for conceiving as the support for himself, others, and the instruments; this is the meaning. Thus he said: "I am on earth," and so forth. But is it not...

Is there no contradiction here in saying that for the continuum of phenomena—which is divided into those bound by the faculties and those not bound by the faculties—the earth together with its constituent parts is the supporting basis (*ādhāra-nissaya*), while the other [elements] are the objective basis (*ārammaṇa-nissaya*) for that which takes them as its object?

No, because this is a conceptual construction (*parikappa*) regarding the state of being a support for the basis of the conceit (*maññanā-vatthu*). For this [earth] is the basis for the conceit of views and the conceit of pride, which take the form of the thought "I am."
Taking the earth as a support for oneself, one conceives: "I am in the earth.
Taking the earth—which has become the basis for the conceiving by craving—as a support for an accessory, one conceives: "My possession or impediment is in the earth.
The meaning in the cases of "another," etc., should be understood in this same manner.
The phrase "this method of meaning" (*atthanaya*) refers to the connection [of parts] as stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
"By this very method" means by that same method of meaning which was stated to illustrate the status of the whole as the locus for the [thought], "That self of mine is in this form.
For a whole is not obtained apart from its constituent parts; therefore, the rule stated regarding the whole applies to the parts as well.
The intention is that [it] is obtainable. Therefore he said: "But he conceives: 'This self of mine is this earth.
Regarding the phrase "in that very self," here "his" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*). "In that very self" means in the self which is dependent upon both internal and external earth.
This is the commentary on the expression "he conceives in earth. Thus, regarding the phrase "he conceives in earth":
Having shown the conceiving of views, conceit, craving, and ignorance by way of the self (*atta*), the passage beginning with “But when... is now stated to show them by way of another (*para*).
Therein, “his” (*assa*) refers to another. “Then” (*tadā*) refers to the conceiving by way of another.

Only the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhimaññanā*) is applicable there, on the grounds that adherence to permanence and so forth can arise therein. By means of this restriction, the conceivings of conceit (*māna*) and craving (*taṇhā*) are excluded.

The intention is that conceit and craving—characterized by the occurrence of thoughts such as "I am superior" and "mine"—do not arise when another person is apprehended as possessing the state of belonging to another.
"By the other two as well" means by conceit, craving, and the conceiving of "I-making. This is what the commentators maintain.
For even in the case of another person, there is excellence, sovereignty, and so forth, which depend upon the earth.
The intention of the teachers is that for one who perceives and aspires to a state of superiority and so forth within oneself, pride, craving, and conceit arise in order to bring about such a state.
In the passage, “Another’s earth, another’s earth,” these two modes must also be extracted along with their underlying intentions.
In such instances as “he perceives from earth” (*pathavito sañjānāti*) and “from the beginning” (*ādito*), the word *to* is seen even when it is not an ablative;

therefore he says, “‘From earth’ (*pathavito*) is an ablative expression. “Together with its requisites” (*saupakaraṇassa*) means together with the wealth and requisites consisting of gold, bullion, slaves, servants, and so forth;
the meaning is: belonging either to oneself, to another, or to their requisites.
"According to the aforementioned classifications" means according to the divisions already stated, such as the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so forth, or the internal (ajjhattika) and so forth.

"Arising or emergence" refers either to the doctrine of the Brahma-Egg (*brahmaṇḍa*), according to which it is said: "That egg was made of gold; in it, Brahmā himself arose," or to the doctrine of atoms (*aṇukavāda*) proceeding thus:
"From two atoms comes a dyad (*dviaṇuka*)," [and so on] regarding the arising from earth.

The construction should be understood as follows: "This entire world has emerged from Īśvara," meaning that one imagines the emergence of the earth from Īśvara according to the doctrine of a creator (Issarakutta).
Alternatively, the intention is that there is a self consisting of water and so forth, distinct from the earth.

In this context, it should be noted that in the first interpretation of the meaning, the ablative case is characterized by agency (*kāraka*), whereas in the second, it is characterized by a secondary suffix (*upapada*).

The conceit of craving (*taṇhāmāna-aññanā*) here should be understood in terms of one who imagines the attainment of happiness from the earth that has become his own possession, and from that very [earth], his superiority over others.

"Others" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. "Grasping another self as immeasurable" means either by way of the previously cultivated attainment of the immeasurable kasiṇas, or by way of the views of the followers of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and so forth.
Or, having grasped the self as immeasurable and pervasive. "From the earth" means from the earth known as the earth-kasina, which has not been previously developed or expanded.
"Even outside of this self of mine" means the intention is:
"even beyond this earth, there is my self. "Entirely" means without remainder. One clings to the great earth through craving; and this same method applies to sovereignty over the four continents.
It could apply to a world-ruling monarch (cakkavatti) established as a lamp, and it certainly applies by way of regional kings, great ministers, and householders as well,
because conceiving (maññanā) arises for them too without exception regarding their respective possessions.
It is stated that there is only a single conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*), due to the remoteness from the grasping "This is mine" and the grasping "This I am, this is my self."
"Is it obtained?"—in order to clarify this elliptical reference (*atidesa*) thus stated, the passage beginning with "And that this... was spoken.
Therein, the connection is as follows: "And that this" means "and this conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*) is to be applied.

Just as the conceivings of craving and conceit (*taṇhāmānamaññanā*) arise for one who produces affection and pride toward the basis (*vatthu*) conceived by the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhimaññanā*), so too [they arise] through that which is conceived by the conceiving of craving.

It can be understood that for one who regards the self as superior by means of a [material] basis, and likewise imagines that basis— which is "belonging to the self"— as permanent, and the self as its master,
other forms of conceiving also arise. For, by means of this apprehension of the object as "mine," the relationship of belonging to the self is made manifest.
By the word "delights" (*abhinandati*), craving (*taṇhā*) and adherence through views (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*) are included; thus, in order to show these, he said, "he relishes and misapprehends.
Furthermore, the occurrence of this pair should be understood as taking place without confusion by way of consciousness-arising dissociated from views;

or else, even within a single consciousness-moment, it occurs through the predominance of this or that factor according to prior formative tendencies (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), just like the predominant mental factors (*adhipatidhamma*).
“Occurrence”: in this sense, namely, in the sense of delighting by way of craving and views. “This”: this phrase, “one delights in earth.

“The elucidation of phenomena by those specific modes” refers to the elucidation of phenomena for those disciples by those specific modes through which, when the elucidation is performed, there is a special attainment.
However, for those [disciples] by whom [it is understood] by only one mode...

When the analysis of the Dhamma is performed, there is a specific attainment; having stated that even for them, it is the "sovereignty over the Dhamma" (*dhammissaratā*) to analyze other aspects without exception, which is the "elegance of the teaching.
Therefore he said: "Having first shown the arising of defilements by way of conceiving (*maññanā*), he now shows it by way of delighting (*abhinandanā*).

"In the element of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhātuyā*) means in the state of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). For that [enlightenment] [comprehends] all knowable phenomena according to their true nature.
It sustains and supports; and it sustains the entire continuum of phenomena known as "beings to be trained" from falling into the suffering of the states of misery and the suffering of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, that which is itself the element (dhātu) whose mode of occurrence is unerring is intended here by the term "dhammadhātu.

For path-knowledge has omniscience as its proximate cause, and omniscience has path-knowledge as its proximate cause—this is what is called "perfect enlightenment" (sammāsambodhi). "Well-penetrated" means...
The meaning is: because it has been thoroughly penetrated, or because it has been correctly attained.

*Maññanā* (conceptualization) is the occurrence of mental construction regarding an object by way of longing (*abhikaṅkhana*), exertion (*sampaggaha*), and misapprehension (*parāmasana*). Among these, the mental construction consisting of the insistence "mine" and "I" is *parikappanā*.
That by which there is attachment (*ajjhosāna*) is *abhinandanā* (delight). This is the distinction between them. [These views] are indeed not in contradiction with the Suttas and other scriptures.
The phrase beginning with “And this has been said” was stated in order to show, by means of a sutta, that one’s own judgment (*attanomati*) should be sought and not another.

However, the fixed nature of the teaching—such as the pairs of teachings on causes with reasons, associated causes, and so forth—which serves to manifest the elegance of the instruction, must be determined [separately]. “Of that” (*tassa*) means “by that” (*tena*).

This genitive case (*sāmivacana*) refers to the agent (*kattari*) due to its connection with the word “known” (*ñāta*). “Therefore” (*tasmā*) means “because of the lack of full understanding” (*apariññātattā*).
Regarding the phrase “not fully understood,” the full understanding that was mentioned by way of negation is, in its actual meaning, threefold.
To explain this both in terms of its essential nature and its mode of occurrence, he says, beginning with “For that which...”.
Therein, the wisdom by which one fully understands—that is, delimits—the plane of insight is “the wisdom of full understanding.”

Full understanding as the known (*ñātapariññā*). For this [understanding] makes the various phenomena belonging to the three planes known, understood, and clear by thinking, "This is the plane of insight";
it knows them by delimiting them according to their characteristics, functions, and so forth, and according to the classification of internal and external.

However, in this context, it should be understood by way of the earth element; thus it is said, "He fully understands the earth element," and so on. Full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).

Wisdom that knows by way of scrutinizing. For that [wisdom] knows the five aggregates of clinging—which have impermanence and so forth as their intrinsic nature—by way of scrutinizing and by way of comprehending them through their surrounding aspects such as impermanence, having delimited them. "By the highest path" means by the path of Arahatship;
for that [path] abandons desire and lust without remainder. Alternatively, "by the highest path" means by that which has become supreme.

"By the path" means by the supramundane path; for it shows that wisdom which effects abandonment through total eradication is, in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), the full understanding as abandonment, regardless of whether [the path] is mundane or supramundane.
By the phrase "determination of name-and-form," it should be understood that the discernment of conditions is also included therein. Regarding name-and-form...
Because of the state of defining by way of causes. For that too is indeed the very definition of name-and-form by way of the cause-condition.

Thorough knowledge by scrutinization occurs by way of the contemplation of aggregates and so forth, because it has the nature of contemplation by way of impermanence and so on. "Therefore" means because those thorough knowledges do not exist;
or alternatively, "therefore, due to lack of thorough knowledge" means because earth is not thoroughly known, therefore, due to that lack of thorough knowledge.
"He conceives of that earth as earth and delights in it.
The commentary on the section on earth is finished. [Now follows] the commentary on the sections on water and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *āpo āpo*: here, it is called *āpo* because it flows (*appoti*) or because it causes to flow (*appāyati*). That which exists within a particular aggregate remains pervading it by way of cohesion, or the meaning is that it causes it to grow.
*Adhi* [in *adhi-ajjhattam*] means "over" or "with respect to"; *atthānam* means "of things. *Pati* [in *paccattam*] means "each" or "separately," as in "each for oneself.
By both [terms], he speaks specifically of that which is included within the continuity of a sentient being. In such expressions as *āpo āpogataṃ*, it refers simply to cohesion.
Water (*āpo*): because it has attained the very nature of water, it is "water-ness" (*āpogata*); the meaning is that it reaches the state of water by its own intrinsic nature.
Moisture (*sineha*): by way of its function of moistening; because it has attained the very nature of moistening, it is "moisture-ness" (*sinehagata*).
"The binding quality of matter": this is the state of being a binder for inseparable matter; the meaning is a cohesion by way of non-dispersal. "Grasping": as delimited [by the sense base].
One who grasps the sign in such a way that the learning-sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) is obtained within a water-circle (*āpomaṇḍala*).

"As stated" refers to the "water" mentioned here in the phrase "in water. For that is water together with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra-āpa*), not the water mentioned in the context of the "water-kasiṇa" (*āpokasiṇa*). "The rest" is the detailed explanation of the nature of the conventional designations for the object and the water. It is also the explanation of the meaning of the textual passage beginning with "He understands water as water," and so forth, in their respective places.
The analysis of conceiving (*maññanā*) is exactly the same as that stated for the earth kasiṇa.
Therein, it was stated, "One perceives the earth kasiṇa," and so forth; here, it should be stated, "One perceives the water kasiṇa," and so forth.
And therein, it was stated, "He perceives 'earth,'" whereas here it should be stated, "He perceives 'water,'" and so forth.
Such is the distinction; the rest is exactly the same. Therefore it was said: "It is just as described for earth.
To show what the distinction here is, the words beginning with "only" (*kevala*) were spoken. Therein, "root-juice" (*mūlarasa*) is the juice produced in dependence upon a root.
The same method applies to trunk-juice and so forth. Milk and the like are well known. However, as in the *Bhesajja-sikkhāpada* (the Training Rule on Medicines),...
There is no such restriction here: whatever is milk is simply milk. The same principle applies to the rest as well. "Earthly" refers to water situated in pits and so forth.
"Atmospheric" refers to rainwater that has not yet reached the earth; once it has reached the earth, it is simply "earthly.

And by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "spoken thus," [the author] includes snow-water, the water that destroys the world-cycle, the water within the earth, and the water that supports the earth, and so on.
It also includes what was not mentioned previously.

Regarding the phrase "heat as heat": here, it is called *tejo* in the sense of heating (*tejana*). Heating means the capacity for burning, cooking, and so forth, which is the sharpening [of the senses] and is termed "warmth.
"By which" means by that feverish state of heat when it is provoked. "Is tormented" refers to this body.
"It burns all over" means it becomes heated by way of the occurrence of one-day fevers and other such ailments.
"By which one grows old" means that by this [fever], this body reaches a state of decayed faculties, loss of strength, and the presence of wrinkles and so forth.
"By which one is consumed" means that when it is provoked, this body is consumed all over, and that person thinks, "I am being consumed."
He longs for anointing with the hundredfold refined *sappi*, *go-sīta*, *candana*, and so forth, as well as the breeze from a palm-leaf fan.

And by means of that [wind], whatever has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion—whereby what was eaten, such as boiled rice and the like; what was drunk, such as beverages and the like;
what was chewed, such as flour-based snacks and the like; or what was tasted, such as mangoes, honey, molasses, and so forth, properly reaches full maturation.
The meaning is that it undergoes differentiation into the states of chyle and so forth.
Herein, "fever" (*santāpa*) is the state of heat in the body that exceeds its natural warmth; "burning fever" (*paridāha*) is the great conflagration occurring by way of consuming the body;

"centenally washed ghee" (*satadhota-sappi*) is ghee that has been heated a hundred times and then placed in water; [and the bodily constituents are] chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The [nutriments] beginning with taste (*rasa*). Among these, the first three are produced by all four [causes], while the last is produced by karma alone.

It is called "gone to heat" (*tejogata*) because it has attained the state of heat. "Heat" (*usmā*) refers to the mode of being warm; it is "gone to heat" (*usmāgata*) because it has attained the state of heat itself. "Warmth" (*usuma*) refers to intense warmth;
that very thing is "gone to warmth" (*usumagata*), meaning it has reached the state of warmth by its very nature.
"A wood-fire" (*kaṭṭhaggi*) is a fire that has wood as its fuel. The same method applies to "splinter-fires" (*sakalikaggi*) and so forth.
A "rubbish-fire" (*saṅkāraggi*) is a fire arisen dependent on refuse. An "Indra-fire" (*indaggi*) is a lightning-fire. "Heat" (*santāpa*) is either the heat of a flame or the heat of glowing embers.
"Solar heat" (*sūriyasantāpa*) is sunshine. "Heat from a pile of wood" (*kaṭṭhasannicayasantāpa*) is the heat arisen dependent on a heap of wood.

The same method applies to the remaining [elements] as well. Regarding the phrase "and those thus described": by the word "and" (ca), it includes even those not explicitly mentioned, such as the fire that destroys the world-cycle at the end of an aeon, the fires of hell, and so forth.
As for the expression "it blows, therefore it is wind" (vāyo): here, it is called "wind" (vāyo) in the sense of blowing (vāyana). What is this so-called "blowing"? It is expansion and movement.
Or, some say that "vāyana" means moving. "Upward-moving winds" are the winds that ascend, which set in motion belching, hiccups, and so forth.
"Downward-moving winds" are the winds that descend, which carry away feces, urine, and the like. "Winds residing in the belly" are the winds outside the intestines.
"Winds residing in the bowels" are the winds inside the intestines. "Winds following the limbs and members" follow along the network of the veins (*dhamanī*).
The winds that pervade every part of the body from limb to limb, producing such functions as contracting and extending;
the "knife-winds," which operate like a butcher’s knife, cutting through the joints and ligaments;
the "razor-winds," which cut and split the heart-flesh like a razor; and the "upplaka-winds," which tear out the heart-flesh.

In-breathing (*assāsa*) is the air entering through the nostrils; out-breathing (*passāsa*) is the air exiting through the nostrils. Here, all the preceding [factors] arise from four causes, whereas in-breathing and out-breathing arise solely from consciousness.
"The state of wind" (*vāyogataṃ*) means wind itself as the state of wind; the meaning is that they have attained the nature of wind by their very own essence. "Rigidity" (*thambhitattaṃ*).

"Of form" means the state of rigidity of inseparable material form (*avinibbhogarūpa*). "Eastern winds" are winds coming from the eastern direction. The same method applies to the western and other directions as well.
Regarding "dusty" and so forth: together with dust they are "dusty" (*saraja*); free from dust they are "pure" or "dustless" (*araja*).

"Cold" refers to that which arises from the cold season, or that which is produced within a mass of cold clouds. "Hot" refers to that which arises from the hot season, or [that produced] within a mass of hot clouds.
Or they are born as heat. "Mild" means gentle, thin winds; "intense" means powerful winds. "Black" refers to those arisen within black clouds;
some say this is a designation for those by which one who is struck becomes black in complexion.
"Veramba winds" are winds blowing from above a league's distance. "Wing-winds" are even the winds produced by the flapping of flies' wings.
"Supaṇṇa-winds" refers to the winds of the Garuḷas. Although these too are indeed merely the wind from their wings, they are mentioned separately because of their preponderance.
"Palmyra-fan winds" refers to winds produced by anything shaped like a circle, whether made of palmyra leaves or made of other materials.
"Fanning-winds" refers to winds produced by a fan made of palm-leaves. Furthermore, these palmyra fans and fanning fans [are used] even when [the wind] has not yet arisen...

They produce wind, and they also turn back wind that has already arisen. Here too, the word *ca* (and) includes, even though not explicitly stated, the wind that supports water, the wind that destroys the world-system, the wind that fans the flames, and so forth.

Furthermore, in this context, regarding the phrases "he conceives [it] as water," and so on, it is possible to analyze the types of conceiving according to the method explained in the section on earth—namely, "he conceives 'I am water,' he conceives 'water is mine,'" and so forth—by means of the three modes of conceiving.
It is said, "to be analyzed," and it is stated that "the rest is exactly according to the method already described.
Therefore, following the method explained therein, the analysis of conceiving (*maññanā*) should be clarified as appropriate within these three sections.
"By this much" means by this specific teaching consisting of four sections. The word *ca* (and) indicates a distinction.

By this, he illuminates the specific distinction that is about to be explained. "Yvāyaṃ" means "this which," referring to the connection with the statement that the mode called *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) has been taught.
Furthermore, in order to show what that *lakkhaṇa*-mode is, the passage beginning with "vuttamhi" was stated.
Therein, "vuttamhi ekadhamme" means: in whichever single phenomenon (*ekadhamma*) among the wholesome states and so forth, or among the aggregates and so forth.

In the Sutta, it is stated either by way of its own form or by way of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "Those phenomena which have a single characteristic" means that whatever phenomena—whether by way of being wholesome and so forth, or by way of being the aggregate of form and so forth—possess a characteristic identical to that aforementioned phenomenon.
"All are spoken of" means that all phenomena, whether by way of their nature as wholesome and so forth, or by way of their nature as aggregates and so forth, are indeed spoken of in the Sutta.

Even those not explicitly mentioned by her are considered as having been mentioned because they share the same characteristic; the intention is that they are brought forward for the purpose of commentary.
And here, "having a single characteristic" is stated as "having a common characteristic.

By this, one should understand that even for those things not explicitly mentioned—such as being associated with it, having a common function, a common cause, a common fruit, or a common object—they are to be distinguished as if they had been mentioned.
*Iti* means "in this manner. Therefore he said: "Thus, in the *Netti*, the extraction called the 'Characteristic' (*lakkhaṇa*) is stated.
However, in the *Netti-pāḷi*, the reading that has come down is: "Whatever phenomena have a single characteristic, that extraction is called the 'Characteristic'.

"By way of that" means by way of that extraction of characteristics. "Because it does not transcend the characteristic of matter" means because it shares the same nature as the essential quality of being subject to transformation (*ruppana*).
By the Blessed One speaking thus. These are the views stated as: "One regards form as self.

And here, it should be understood that by the very demonstration of the conceiving of the view of personality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), the conceivings of craving and pride based on the entire category of form are also demonstrated.
For it has been said: "But in that very basis conceived through his conceiving of the view..."
“From one who arouses affection and conceit, craving, conceit, and the conceiving of ‘I’ are also to be understood.

Alternatively, by saying that one “conceives and delights in earth, water, fire, or air as ‘mine,’” according to the method already stated, the conceiving of craving based on the entire category of form has been expressed;
and following from that, the conceiving of conceit has also been expressed. Thus, the other types of conceiving should also be determined here in this manner.
The commentary on the section on water is finished.
Commentary on the section on the elements (bhūta): 3.
By means of the phrases beginning with “he conceives earth, he conceives in earth,” [it is shown that] one regards form as self (*rūpaṃ attato samanupassati*).
Because the personality-beliefs (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), such as "one regards self in form," have been determined [in the Suttas], it is said:
"Having thus stated the conceiving that has formations as its basis by way of form. In those formations, "among beings" means among those beings who possess clinging to them.
"In the elements" means in the four elements, earth and so forth. In passages such as "born, become, conditioned," the word *bhūta* [is used].

It is seen in the sense of arising; however, when accompanied by a prefix, it means "vast" in such passages as “The noble one performs abundant merit,” “mostly despised by the bhikkhus,” and so on; it means “injury” in “Sambhūta Sāṇavāsī,” and so on;
it means “designation” in “Abhibhūta Māra, the battle is won,” and so on; and it means “crushing” in “This naked Pāṭikaputta is indeed ruined,” and so on.
In the word *parājaye* (in defeat), it is seen in the sense of experiencing, as in “experienced pleasure and pain”; in “made manifest, manifested by wisdom,” it is seen in the sense of making clear.
All these [meanings] are included in the phrase “in trees, etc.”; they should be understood as being comprised by the word “etc.
Furthermore, in such passages as “Time devours beings” and “Beings in the world are a mere heap,” the word *bhūta* denotes sentient beings (*satta*) without distinction.
Since specific types of beings have already been included above by terms such as "gods" and so forth, it is said here that those remaining are to be understood by the word *bhūta* (beings);
thus he says, "but not without distinction. For this very reason he says: "For those beings below the realm of the Four Great Kings are intended here by the term *bhūta*.
Indeed, that class of beings which possesses all four modes of birth (*yoni*) and is worthy of being produced through all four modes of birth—within that [class], this...
“Designation of beings” (*bhūtasamaññā*) refers to their arising by way of birth from eggs and so forth.
“Beings” (*bhūte*) refers to those beings indicated by the aforementioned location.

By the phrase “perceives as beings,” it is shown that—taking up the worldly convention “beings”—there is a perception through distorted cognition (*viparītasaññā*) such that conceiving (*maññanā*), such as craving and so forth, can arise therein.
This same point can be understood by following the method explained below in the passage, "One perceives from the earth"; thus he says, "by the very method already stated.

Just as the Suddhāvāsa deities do not appear in this teaching because they are always absent [from the lower realms], so too the denizens of hell do not appear because they are not the basis for any conceiving (*maññanā*).
By this very principle, it should be understood that certain types of *petas* are also not included here.

Others, however, say: "Their inclusion here is indeed intended on account of the underlying tendency toward views (diṭṭhimaññanā) and the adherence to them," according to the method stated in the Sutta beginning with, "He dwells enjoying what he has acquired.
One "lusts" (rajjati) by generating passion for that object through the distorted grasp of "beautiful" and "pleasurable. Thus, one who lusts here does so not merely by way of seeing alone.
Showing that one is indeed lustful even by way of smelling and so forth, he said: “Having seen... pe ... having smelled.

In this context, lustfulness by way of smelling and so forth should be understood as occurring through the odors and garlands experienced by those [senses], through the enjoyment of those objects which are of a discordant nature, and through the act of recollecting them according to how they were experienced.
Thus, when such things exist, one conceives by means of the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).

The meaning is that one conceives through the conceiving of craving for the elements (bhūta) by generating desire and lust for them according to the stated method, relishing their practice, delighting in them, welcoming them, and remaining attached to them;
or else, by way of such a method as thinking, "May such a state be mine in the future," one brings about delight therein. Regarding what has not yet been attained:
The state of being a wealthy kṣatriya and so forth; "success" and "failure" refer to high and low status by way of birth. "Burns" means it establishes [itself].
"Such pride as this" refers to that pride which has arisen thus: "Previously I was equal to him, but now he is superior and I am inferior.
This is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride), for like an excessive burden, it [weighs upon] the previous [state].
The meaning is that, based on a similar [object], it is called "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*).

Regarding the terms "permanent" (*nicca*) and so forth: they are permanent because of the absence of arising; stable (*dhuvā*) because of the absence of death; and eternal (*sassata*) because of their existence at all times.

Alternatively, they are permanent as the opposite of impermanence; stable due to their state of firmness; and eternal due to their equality with eternity, [being free] from transformation through aging and so forth.

He conceives of them as being non-existent and subject to non-change. "All beings" (*sabbe sattā*) refers to all without exception—such as camels, oxen, donkeys, and so forth—in the sense of being sentient (*sañjana*).
"All living things" (*sabbe pāṇā*) refers to all without exception—spoken of by way of "one-facultied living things," "two-facultied living things," and so on—in the sense of breathing (*pāṇana*).
"All creatures" (*sabbe bhūtā*) refers to all without exception who have come into being (*bhūtā*) or been born (*sañjatā*) within egg-shells and the like.
"Beings. All that live—rice, barley, wheat, and so forth—are "living beings" (*jīva*) in the sense of being endowed with life.

For regarding them, he perceives them as living through their state of growth. "Without mastery, without power, without energy": this shows that they possess neither self-mastery, nor strength, nor energy.
Regarding the phrase "transformed by necessity, conjunction, and inherent nature," here "necessity" (*niyati*) means fixedness, like an unbreakable thread or an indivisible gem.
"Unabandoned nature" means that their original character has not been discarded. "Conjunction" (*saṅgati*) refers to the meeting together of the six classes of beings therein.
"State" (*bhāva*) is simply their inherent nature: such as the sharpness of thorns, the roundness of wood-apple fruits and the like, and the variegated colors of beasts and birds;
such is the meaning. Thus, through destiny (*niyati*), conjunction, and state, they have undergone transformation and reached various diverse forms.
It shows that whatever is destined to come to be, comes to be exactly in that way; and whatever is not destined to come to be, does not come to be.

By the phrase "only within the six classes of birth" (*chasvevābhijātīsu*), it shows that beings experience pleasure and pain only while remaining within these six classes of birth—such as the dark class of birth (*kaṇhābhijāti*) and so forth—and that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain.
By the word "or" (*vā*), [it indicates] the distinctions such as the end and so on.
It includes adherence to views (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*).
By the word "rebirth" (*upapatti*), it shows that one desires companionship with beings in this or that class of beings.

By the phrase "the arising of happiness" (*sukhuppatti*), however, it shows the arising of happiness for one who has been reborn in this or that state. [This is expressed] by such statements as "some beings are eternal," and so forth.
This shows the view of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatikadiṭṭhi*). However, by the phrase "I am one among the beings," it shows the fourth doctrine of partial eternalism.
"From whatever source" means from whatever source, such as the distinction of a Supreme Person (*issarapuruṣa*) and so forth. Here too, only a single conceiving (*taṇhāmaññanā*) is obtained.
The possibility of other types of conceiving (*maññanā*) should also be determined according to the method explained below.

Because it must be stated that one "rejoices through craving and views regarding the very elements (*bhūta*) already mentioned," he says, "in the very same manner as stated. The construction (*yojanā*) should be made thus:

"He who fully understands the aggregates (*khandha*), which constitute the basis for the designation of elements, understands them by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*)," and so forth.
The construction should be made. However, others here maintain that even the "community of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) is included by the term "beings" (*bhūta*);

thus, they demonstrate the analysis of conceiving [the self] by way of trees and so forth, as well as by way of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). That [interpretation] is not found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "By way of the distinction of levels, etc.
means by way of the classification of specific levels, specific rebirths, and so on. "By means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means by means of what is produced through a specific kind of merit.
By its influence. Furthermore, although the word *deva* occurs in such passages as "when the sky was clear and free from clouds" (*viddhe vigatavalāhake deve*) referring to the cloudless atmosphere;
in "the god rains drop by drop" (*devo ca thokaṃ thokaṃ phusāyati*) referring to a rain-cloud;

and in "this, O King, is the prince" (*ayaṃ hi deva kumāro*) referring to a member of the kshatriya caste—as in the passage "endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he sports about, as it were a god" (*pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgibhūto paricāreti devo maññe*)—[it is used here in a different sense].
Having come here from among the deities of rebirth, the term "deities" (deva) would otherwise include all beings entitled to that designation without exception;

therefore, in order to show those intended here, the phrase beginning with "they are of three kinds" was stated. The intention is that the remaining six classes of sense-sphere deities are what is meant by "deities" here, as the others have been excluded by other words in the text.
Among the beings included under the expression "beings who are deities" (bhūtā devā):

It is said, "They should be understood in the manner explained in the section on the primary elements (bhūtavāra)," because the three characteristics are also present in the mode of occurrence of the conceivings beginning with craving (*taṇhā*).
In such passages as "The wife of a certain lay follower was beautiful," the word *pajāpati* occurs in the sense of a housewife;
whereas in such passages as "Pajāpati, the giver of desires, may my offspring be golden-colored," it occurs in the sense of a conceptual construction imagined by those holding wrong views.
In such passages as “you should look at the crest of the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the gods,” they refer to the eldest of the gods; however, here they say it means “the lord.
Since Brahmā is mentioned later on, that [previous interpretation] is merely their own opinion. “Of the gods” (devānaṃ) refers to the gods beginning with those of the Four Great Kings.
By the word “etcetera” (ādi) in “of the Great Kings etcetera,” Sakka, Suyāma, Santussita, Sunimmita, and Vasavatti are included. “Of them” (tesaṃ)...

Of the great kings and so forth. "Among those reckoned as beings" means among those reckoned as beings in the sensual plane (*kāmabhūmi*). "The state of *pajāpati*" means the condition of being a *pajāpati*.
For one who utters conceit by way of the state of *pajāpati* is said to "conceive the *pajāpati* through the conceiving of conceit.
It was stated that only one type of conceiving of views (*diṭṭhimaññanā*) is applicable; however, for one who desires proximity to or co-residence with a *pajāpati*, [other types would apply].

It can be understood that craving, conceit, and the conceiving of "otherness" also arise for one who resolves the mind toward becoming such [a state], and for one who regards oneself as superior in relation to the success that is thus to be attained. And by the phrase "whatever phenomena," he refers to vitality, beauty, and so forth.
Regarding the term "Lord of Beings" (*pajāpati*), here too the possibility of other types of conceiving should be understood according to the method explained below.

“Brūhita” means grown great. “By special qualities” refers to distinguished qualities such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and so forth, by virtue of being superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).

Although the word *brahma* generally denotes something distinguished without qualification, the phrase beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated to show the specific ways in which it occurs when associated with particular qualities.
“Sahassa” means one who is the sovereign lord over a thousandfold world-system (*sahassiyā lokadhātu*).
"First-born" means born by means of the sublime first jhāna, or else first born in the plane of the first jhāna.
It should be understood that [the term] "included" refers to the primary ones, since it is established that even non-primary things are included by virtue of some connection.
And here, "Brahmā" is intended to mean Mahābrahmā; for he, by reason of his beauty...
Because he possesses great longevity and because he is a "great Brahmā" due to his greatness compared to the Brahmapārisajja and others, he is called Mahābrahmā.
Those who stand in the position of his chaplain are the Brahmapurohitas; those who exist within the assembly as attendants are to be understood as the Brahmapārisajjas.
Because he exists as a single preeminent individual, the conceit that "I am Brahmā" occurs in him, just as it does in Pajāpati.

It is said: "They are to be understood in the same manner as described in the section on Pajāpati. For indeed, because they share the commonality of being many individuals, the sections on the Ābhassara devas and others are stated to be similar to the section on the Bhūta devas.

Alternatively, the Ābhassarā are so called because they have the nature of shining with the aforementioned radiance. As for the term "Ekatalavāsino" (Dwellers on One Level), this refers to the levels of the intermediate jhānas.
This was stated because there is no distinction between lower and upper levels; however, their respective abodes are indeed limited.

They are called *Parittābhā* (Limited Radiance) because they possess limited radiance compared to the Ābhassara deities. They are called *Appamāṇābhā* (Immeasurable Radiance) because they possess immeasurable radiance. *Subhā* means beautiful radiance.
Like a mass of gold, they are resplendent, thus they are *Kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā* (Resplendent like a Mass of Gold). In that regard:
Regarding the term *subhakiṇhā*: it should have been called *subhakiṇṇā*, meaning "strewn with beautiful radiance" (*sobhanāya pabhāya kiṇṇā*);
however, by shortening the vowel of the word *bhā* and changing the final letter *ṇa* to *ha*, it is stated as *subhakiṇhā*. Furthermore, *subhā* refers to a single, dense, and unshakable radiance.
Those for whom this radiance is limited are the *parittasubhā* (Limited Radiance). Those for whom this radiance is immeasurable are the *appamāṇasubhā* (Immeasurable Radiance).
"Vipulaphalāni" means having results such as abundant peace, happiness, long life, beauty, and so forth.
Although gods, brahmās, and others also overcome their opposites through the fruit of merit and the fruit of meditative absorption (*jhāna*),

this teaching is presented here with reference to those for whom the designation "overcomer" (*abhibhū*) is well-known and established among worldlings (*puthujjana*) and non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*).
Pointing this out, he said: "This is a designation for the non-percipient existence.

Just as in the section on Pajāpati, the occurrence of conceiving was shown by such statements as "here someone [conceives] in Pajāpati alone," so too here it is possible to show that; therefore he said: "The rest is exactly according to the method stated in the Pajāpati section.
The commentary on the section on the elements (bhūta), etc., is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Base of Infinite Space, etc. 4.
Thus, while demonstrating the sequence of planes by way of the seven types of noble persons, [the author], determining the reason for not including the Suddhāvāsa deities, said:

"Thus the Blessed One," and so forth. Therein, "non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed" means both non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). Although...
The Suddhāvāsa deities indeed have lifespans of many thousands of eons; however, from the perspective of the maximum limit, they have lifespans of only sixteen thousand eons and no more.

Therefore, he said, "having lifespans of several thousands of eons. Furthermore, although the phenomena such as the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) occur within the realms of sense-desire and fine-materiality, they do not receive the designation of that specific plane because they belong to the formless realm (arūpāvacara). Thus, [the author] specifies, "only those reborn there," in order to exclude them.
It has been stated. The intention is that they should be understood according to the method explained in the section on the "Masters" (*abhibhūvāra*), as appropriate.

For here, qualities such as being beautiful (*vaṇṇavantatā*) are not possible. Regarding the phrase "according to the method explained in the section on Pajāpati," here pride and conceit (*mānamaññanā*) are to be understood through such statements as, "I am formless, having abandoned the perception of form and repulsion."
The commentary on the section beginning with the base of infinite space is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the section beginning with "seen and heard":
it is stated "also in detail" because the demonstration of the basis for conceiving by way of form is considered to be a summary. That too...
For, just as the inclusion of the passage beginning with "where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air,
nor the base of infinite space," this constitutes a concise demonstration of existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*).
"Seen" refers both to that which has reached the completion of the act of seeing performed through the eye-door, and that which the pair of eyes sees.

"It will be seen" means that if there is the possibility of seeing, one would see; it is stated as "seen at all times" because there is no desire for a specific qualification, just as in the expression "milked.
Therefore he said: "This is a designation for the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). And this method should also be applied to the [spheres of] sound and so forth.
"Beings" (*satta*) means those who are attached or clinging to forms and so on; thus they are "beings. Furthermore, this is also a general term in the sense of "binding" (*sañjana*).
The word *satta*—because it is qualified by its object as "in female form"—should here be understood as denoting a man.
*Rattā* means colored, stained, or impassioned by desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*), which causes a transformation of the mind just as dye colors a cloth.
*Giddhā* means greedy, having become greedy through longing and covetousness due to their inherent nature of yearning; they have fallen into greed. *Gadhitā* means bound or fettered.

Bound to the object by greed as if it were difficult to release; "infatuated" means having become, as it were, unconscious through the influence of the defilements, having no other function, and having fallen into a swoon or delusion;
"clinging" means remaining as if one had swallowed and digested the object, making it as if it were not shared with others.
"By this" refers to the appearance of golden color and so forth. "Auspicious" or "inauspicious."
"Such is seen as auspicious, such is inauspicious. Regarding the phrase "by way of regarding self in form":
this refers to taking feeling and other non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), or all phenomena excluding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), as self;
and then, by imagining either the internal or external sense-base of form as the locus for that [self], thinking: "This self of mine is in this..."
The statement "conceiving in the sense-sphere of visible form" was spoken with reference to this method: "one conceives in what is seen.

Just as in the cases of "one conceives from earth," etc., the occurrence of conceiving was shown as "of oneself or of another together with their equipment," so too can it be shown in the cases of "one conceives from what is seen," etc.;
therefore he said, "it should be understood by the same method stated in the section on earth."

“Having struck” (*āhatvā*) means having followed after the object; the sense is “having reached it. Therefore he said, “having approached” (*upagantvā*). “In mutual contact” (*aññamaññasaṃsilese*) means not being far away, like the eye and visible form or the ear and sound, but rather being in close proximity to one another.
“Known solely by the mind” (*manasā viññātaṃ kevalaṃ*); for the other [objects] are also known by the mind.
In order to include that as well—since it is not comprised within the designation of the remaining seven bases—he says, “or of a mental object” (*dhammārammaṇassa vā*).
It has been stated. Since the inclusion of supramundane states would follow in both alternatives, he said: "But here, only that which is included within identity (sakkāya) is obtained.
"In detail" refers to the detailed exposition of the modes of occurrence of the conceivings (maññanā). "Therein" means in these sections on what is heard and so forth.
The commentary on the sections on what is seen, what is heard, and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Unity (Ekattavāra), etc., 6.

Regarding the "Section on One Who Has Attained" (Samāpannakavāra): this refers to the occurrence during the attainment [of jhāna], that is to say, the occurrence of fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere jhānas.
For that [attainment] is called "unity" (ekatta) because it occurs with a single mode toward a single object.
And having understood it thus, it should be seen that the occurrence of fruition-jhāna (vipākajjhāna) is also included here by the very mention of the section on those who have attained [jhāna].

By the "section on those who have not attained" is meant the occurrence of sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma); for even with access-concentration (upacārajjhāna), the mind is said not to have properly reached unification (ekatta).
“Yojanā” means the application of conceiving (*maññanā*). “Having broken apart” means having analyzed. “By the method of the Teaching” means by the method of the Canon (*pāḷi*).

In this regard, the conceivings are to be understood by following the procedure stated in the passages beginning with “he conceives of unity,” etc., according to the method of “he regards feeling as self,” and so forth;
whereas in the passages beginning with “he conceives of diversity,” etc., they are to be understood by following the procedure stated in the method of “he regards form as self,” and so forth.
And by the method of the commentaries as stated in the *Pathavī-vāra* and other sections— namely, “He conceives ‘I am feeling,’ he conceives ‘feeling is mine’,” and so forth,
and “He conceives ‘I am form,’ he conceives ‘form is mine’,” and so forth— this is the meaning. Therefore, it says,
“having investigated accordingly,” which refers to whichever method of application is possible regarding the states of unity and diversity.
The meaning is: "having investigated in accordance with that. "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. "Others" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*.

The connection is: "they speak of adherence to views. For an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), what is called "conceit" (*maññanā*) occurs only by way of the object as it presents itself after having broken through the identity-view (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*);
therefore, in that case, there is no [distinction] such as "this is the method of unity" or "this is the method of diversity."
In such passages as "by way of analysis alone, the self is perceived as a unity," it is the perception of the self's own unity or diversity that is stated;
it does not refer to the state of unity or diversity belonging to the dogmatic adherence to views that occurs in the form "unity" or "diversity.
Thus, it should be understood that both of these are not intended here.
Showing that whatever the aforementioned worldling is able to grasp in its entirety is called "all" (sabba) by virtue of its being graspable without remainder,
he said, "that very same," meaning "the all of personal existence" (sakkāyasabba). Furthermore,
because there is an absence of disenchantment when one does not see the danger in all phenomena of the three planes, [there remains] the contemplation of gratification.
“Craving indeed increases,” he said; thus, “experiencing gratification in everything, one conceives through the conceiving of craving for everything.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases.
By means of the conceiving of having created it, thinking “All this has been created by me,” one regards oneself as superior and so forth through that [conceit].
One indeed conceives of that which is fashioned by pride (*māna*), because without the conceiving of what is fashioned, such pride cannot arise; thus it is said:
"One who conceives of what is fashioned by oneself conceives everything through the conceiving of pride.

By the phrase "everything does not exist," etc., the word "etc. includes fatalism (*niyativāda*) and other such views. By the statement "My self is great," [one conceives] of the self from all [perspectives].
He shows the doctrine of the manifestation of power (*vibhūtipavattivāda*).

By way of the view that "everything belongs to everything," he says, "The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the section on earth," demonstrating that here too such conceiving (*maññanā*) is possible in such a manner as: "I am in everything; my possession and impediment are in everything; another is in everything; another's possession and impediment are in everything."

Furthermore, one who holds the view, "This entire world is made of man," imagining his own origin or emergence from everything comprised by what is called "man," conceives in every respect through the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). However,

for one who generates affection and pride toward that very basis conceived through the conceiving of views, there arise the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*) and the conceiving of pride (*māna-maññanā*).
And this should be understood. Furthermore, imagining that very same "all" to be one's self, agent, or master, one conceives "all is mine";
likewise, by delighting through views and craving, one delights in all. In this way, the occurrence of these conceivings is to be understood here.

That is personality (*sakkāya*). For those who propound Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī*) conceive of the five aggregates—when accompanied by the highest degree of pleasure—as Nibbāna;
yet in actual fact, that is merely personality itself. "In one way" means having spoken of all five types together as a single unit by way of their nature as Nibbāna.
"Since" (*yataḥ*) means because. "By the five strands of sensual pleasure" means by the five [objects] beginning with agreeable forms.
By means of the components of sensual pleasure, or by means of bonds. "Fully endowed" (*samappito*) means being thoroughly joined and remaining closely attached.

"Possessed" (*samaṅgibhūto*) means being equipped with them. "He enjoys" (*paricāreti*) means that he moves and directs his faculties as he pleases among those strands of sensual pleasure and components of desire, leading them here and there.
Alternatively, it means he dallies, delights, and plays. Here, the strands of sensual pleasure are twofold.

Both human and divine. Human [pleasures] are like those of King Mandhātu; divine [pleasures] are like those of the king of the gods who wields power over the creations of others (*paranimmita-vasavatti*).
For they proclaim that for those who have attained such sensual pleasures, there is the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna-sampatti*).
Therefore he said: "To this extent... it is. "This very life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived phenomenon (*paccakkhadhamma*); therein—

In this context, it is a designation for that which has attained a personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*) means the pacification of suffering within this very existence;
it is Nibbāna in the present life. "Supreme Nibbāna in the present life" (*parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*) means the highest, most excellent Nibbāna in the present life;

the meaning is that one has attained that. It is said to "come in five ways" by way of the pleasure of the aforementioned strands of sensual desire (*kāmaguṇa*) and the pleasure of the fourfold meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
And by way of this, it is presented in the Pāḷi in five modes. "Relishing Nibbāna" means relishing it with the conceiving that it is the supreme happiness and the escape.
One also conceives of Nibbāna thus: "When this Nibbāna is attained, one is not born, does not age, and does not die."
Grasping it with the thought, "There is nothing beyond this which is the supreme consolation," one conceives [it] as Nibbāna.
One conceives, "This Nibbāna has been attained by me; therefore, Nibbāna is mine. For that very reason, one delights in that Nibbāna through the delighting in views.
This, first of all, is here the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*). Furthermore, regarding that very thing conceived through the conceiving of views...
For one who generates affection and conceit toward a physical basis (*vatthu*), craving, conceit, and the conceiving of "I" (*maññanā*) must also be eliminated.

"Of such a kind" (*yādiso*) means "of whatever form," that is, by which [characteristics] such as loathsomeness and so forth it should be seen; this is the meaning. "This" (*eso*) refers to this very thing.

By this, he states that its existence is established through direct perception for both himself and those listening to him. Of the phenomena such as visible forms (*rūpa*) that exist together with their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)—such as the unattractive (*asubha*) and so forth—...

“Body” (*kāya*) is “identity” (*sakkāya*), namely the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*). “In that way” (*tathā*) means by way of its mode of existence, such as its repulsiveness and so forth.

“All conceiving” (*sabbamaññanā*) refers to all the various kinds of conceiving through craving that occur regarding objects differentiated by their specific characteristics, such as earth and so on, and by distinctions like their essential nature or limitations.
“Loathsome” (*jeguccha*) means worthy of loathing; by this, he shows its state of being impure, foul-smelling, and repulsive. “Sidura” means...
Its nature is to break up moment by moment. By this, he shows its impermanent, unstable, perishable, decaying, and fragile nature.
"This" refers to personal existence (*sakkāya*). "Suffering" means it is not pleasant; by this, he shows that its mode of existence is one of hardship, headache, and affliction.
"Without a leader" means it is devoid of a guide; by this, he shows its mode of existence as empty of self and lacking essence. "That" refers to personal existence.

"As an opposite" means as the contrary of its own nature; the meaning is: as beauty, permanence, pleasure, self, and so forth. "Grasping" means one who grasps; therein, the meaning is: one who adheres by way of grasping beauty and the rest.
Now, in order to clarify all three types of conceiving through similes, the passage beginning with "as beautiful" was stated. Therein, just as in a great conflagration...

And just as a moth’s falling into a fire brings about vast misfortune due to its perception of it as beautiful and pleasant, so too does craving’s conceiving toward such a personal body (sakkāya) [bring about misfortune].
This meaning is shown by the passage: “As beautiful... conceiving through craving.
A worm that has found a heap of dung, even when that [dung] is not excellent, produces the appearance of it being excellent and [conceives] itself—

Having established a perception of permanence regarding this personal existence (sakkāya), which possesses manifold disadvantages and is destined for certain dissolution, the fool—intoxicated by the pride of success—conceives conceit therein. It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: “The perception of permanence... [and so on]... conceiving by means of conceit.
Just as a foolish person, whose mental constituent is deluded, might see his own reflection in a mirror and think, “This, I suppose...”
The owner of the mirror, thinking, "If I were to stand here holding this, it might even cause me harm," discarded it and fled;
yet, while there was nothing at all present there, he grasped it as if it were something real.

This illustrates the point that this fool, grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*sakkāya*), is like that person; this is shown by the passage: "There is a conceiving through the view of 'self'... and so forth.
It is subtle because it is subtler even than the bondage of Vepacitti. Therefore the Blessed One said: “O monks, the bondage of Māra is indeed very subtle.
“Much” means exceedingly or many times. Even while struggling, one does not transcend *sakkāya* (the existing body), because one does not transcend *saṃsāra*.
As it was said: “Those recluses, monks, who [assert] the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of the conscious being...”
“They describe [it], yet they run right around after mere personal existence (*sakkāya*), just like that dog on a leash,” and so forth.

For just as the abandoning of craving and views—the leaders of *saṃsāra*—is possible within the seven types of annihilationist conceptualizations, it is likewise possible within the eternalist conceptualizations;
thus, there is some way for one who follows such views to achieve liberation from existence. Therefore it was said:
“‘He does not transcend personal existence (sakkāya).
‘Sasa’ means this very worldling. ‘Niccaṃ’ means at all times.
‘Taṃ’ means therefore, because of not transcending birth and so forth for one who is mired in personal existence. ‘Asātato’ means from suffering.”

"Seeing this thus": seeing that very personality (sakkāya), which has the nature of being unattractive, impermanent, suffering, and non-self, with the wisdom of the Path accompanied by the wisdom of insight (vipassanā) as it truly is in the manner described.
"Having abandoned": having abandoned all conceivings (maññanā) by way of complete eradication. "Is liberated from all suffering":
he is liberated from the entire suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha).
The commentary on the section on unity and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the first method is finished.
The commentary on the second method of the section on the trainee (*sekha*).

7. *Uddesa* is the statement of the intended meaning without specifying it; *niddesa* is the statement after having specified it. Thus it was said: "‘Ya’ is the word of *uddesa*; ‘so’ is the word of *niddesa*.
The sense of *sampiṇḍana* is the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). And since conjunction occurs by way of commonality (*sabhāgatā*), it was said:
"by way of the commonality of the object" (*ārammaṇasabhāgena*), that is, by way of the commonality or similarity of the object.

The meaning [of the term *sekkha*]. It indicates one in training (*sekkha*) because a general designation is restricted to a specific instance, and because that expression refers to the domain of those in training.
"In what sense" means: since the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is the object (*attha*) to be sought after by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), therefore the meaning is:

in what sense, by what intrinsic nature, or by what characteristic does one become known as a "trainee"? Furthermore, because a person [is designated] through the attainment of the qualities of a trainee...
There is the occurrence of the designation "one-in-training" (sekha); therefore, it is said, "One is 'in-training' because of the acquisition of the qualities of one-in-training.
The qualities of one-in-training refer to right view and the other factors within the four paths and the three lower fruits.
Thus he said: "By means of right view of one-in-training... [and so on]... to this extent, bhikkhu, one is a trainee. This is according to the method of the Abhidhamma.
Having shown the characteristic of a trainee (*sekha*) by way of the definition, he now says “Furthermore,” etc., in order to show it also by way of the method of the discourses (*suttanta*).
Therein, by the phrase “he trains,” he shows that one who possesses the three trainings and has not yet completed his training is a trainee.
Therefore he said, “he trains,” and so forth. And here, the repetition “he trains, he trains” is for the purpose of illustrating constant association with the trainings.

This is a reduplicated expression. Alternatively, *sikkhā* is training; he whose virtue (*sīla*) consists of that is a *sekkha*. For he, because his training is not yet completed and because he is intent upon it, is exclusively one whose nature is to train.
He is not like an *asekkha*, whose training is finished and who has laid aside the desire for it;
nor is he like the ordinary person who has abandoned training and is not intent upon it. Now...
Or, one who is born into the noble birth within the three trainings, or exists therein, is a *sekkha*. Alternatively, *ikkhā* is that by which one sees;
it is the right view of the path and its fruit. One who possesses such seeing is a *sekkha*.
This refers to one who fulfills the practice in accordance with the way leading to the cessation of suffering, beginning with virtue (*sīla*) and ending with insight (*vipassanā*).

It is called the "conformity practice" (*anuloma-paṭipadā*) because it conforms to the supramundane way of practice; one who brings it to fulfillment by accomplishing that [practice] is thus described.
Now, in order to show that practice by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), the passage beginning with “endowed with virtue” (*sīlasampanno*) was stated.
Therein, “endowed with virtue” means being possessed of the virtue of restraint according to the *Pātimokkha*, or one whose *Pātimokkha* virtue is complete. For as for the virtue of the *Pātimokkha*:
Here, it is intended as "virtue" (*sīla*) because of its preeminent nature.
