One is "guarded in the doors of the sense faculties" by closing the six sense bases—the mind being the sixth—through the prevention of the occurrence of covetousness and other defilements toward objects such as visible forms.

One is "moderate in eating" by knowing the proper measure in food through [reflecting on] seeking and so forth. Having become free from sloth and torpor, one applies the mind to the meditation subject day and night.
He is devoted to the practice of wakefulness through application. To show how the practice of wakefulness occurs, it is said:
"In the first watch of the night... [and so on] ...he dwells. As it has been said: "And how is he devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day; at night..."
“During the first watch he purifies [his mind] by walking meditation... [and so on] ...thus, bhikkhu, one is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
Regarding this meaning, however, it refers to the sense of whether one “conceives” or “does not conceive,” as defined by the state of being expressible.
A worldling (*puthujjana*) is not intended here, because it is said: “one who has not attained his heart’s goal, yet yearning for the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
Because it exists through association with the mind (*manas*), lust is "mental" (*mānasa*); alternatively, taking "mind itself" as "mental," consciousness is "mental.

The supreme path is "mental" because it completely cools and eradicates conceit (*māna*). Furthermore, the state of being "mental" should be understood for *arahantship* because it is produced by that [path].
"Renowned among people" (*janesu*) means famous throughout the world of all beings; the sense is that its fame has spread far and wide.
“Unsurpassed” (*anuttara*) means there is nothing superior to this. Since that which is most excellent is absolutely without equal, it is said:
“‘Unsurpassed’ means excellent; the meaning is ‘without equal. “Of one who yearns” (*patthayamānassa*) means of one who thirsts.
“Longings” (*pajappitāni*) refers to the longings of pride. For, in whatever object the conceit of yearning—that is, the conceit of one who yearns—arises, [that is what is meant].
The intention is that in that very state, such mental hankerings as "I am superior" and so forth arise. *Pavedhītaṃ* means agitated.
*Pakappitesu* refers to objects conceptualized by the imaginings of craving and views. *Sotaṃ* is the stream of defilements;
for when that is cut, the other streams are indeed cut as well. *Viddhastaṃ* means destroyed; and that [destruction] is even to the extent of a single hair-raising tremor.
Showing that it means "without remainder," he said "made devoid of residue" (*vinaḷīkataṃ*); the meaning is "made such that nothing remains.
Here, the aspiration intended by the term *adhimutti* (resolute confidence) is evident as *patthanā* (longing), which is why "inclined toward that" (*tanninno*) and so forth were stated;
it is not, however, because the wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) itself constitutes resolute confidence. "Resolutely confident" (*adhimuccanto*) means "fixing one's conviction" (*okappento*).
“Of all aspects inverted” means: by way of being the opposite of all the modes that one would grasp, such as “beautiful,” “pleasant,” and “permanent”;
the meaning is that it apprehends the mode of the intrinsic nature of phenomena in its entirety, but in an inverted manner. “By means of distinguished knowledge” means:
unlike non-discerning or false cognitions, it neither fails to reach the intrinsic nature of phenomena nor does it go beyond it.

Rather, it means: by means of a distinguished knowledge that has attained a state of direct confrontation with the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva), and by means of the full understanding through investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) based upon the full understanding through knowing (ñāta-pariññā), together with a portion of the full understanding through abandoning (pahāna-pariññā).

Therefore he said: “‘Earth’... [as before] ...it is so stated. “The state of earth” (pathavī-bhāva) refers to the state of being to be directly known (abhiññeyya) regarding earth; for it is the earth characterized by its specific mark (lakkhaṇa-pathavī) that is intended here.
Furthermore, its state of being fully understood (*pariññeyya-bhāva*) has been grasped by the passage beginning with “‘It is impermanent,’ etc.

Having directly known (*abhiññatvā*) means having directly known by means of the lower path-knowledges through the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning. Regarding the term *māmaññī*: it is called *mā* because one conceives “I” (*maññati*) due to the conceivings (*maññanā*) that have not yet been abandoned;
however, because one does not conceive due to those [conceivings] that have been abandoned, it is called *amaññī*. Thus, one who both [possesses] *mā* and is *amaññī* is *māmaññī*.
Thus, the meaning here should be understood through the analysis of the words. In this context, it cannot be said that "by whichever part he did not conceive, by that same part he conceives";
nor can it be said that "by whichever part he conceives, by that same part he did not conceive.
To show the meaning where the negation is primary, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It should not be said that he both conceives and does not conceive. This is the primacy of the negation.
And herein, it should be understood that this is because even those conceivings (*maññanā*) which are present are weak. For this very reason, it was said:
"But the others have become attenuated. Furthermore, *mā* is a particle (*nipāta*), and since particles have multiple meanings, it is said with the intention:
"In this sense, this word has been inserted as a particle. And regarding the term "inserted" (*nipātetvā*), it refers to the determination of its classification as a root (*pakati*) and so forth.
The meaning is: "having shown the matter through direct perception itself, rather than by means of inference.
By the phrase "like an ordinary person" (puthujjana), he indicates that the conceiving (*maññanā*) associated with the craving and pride to be abandoned by the higher paths has not been rejected.
Alternatively, "let him not conceive" (*mā maññī*) is a statement of prohibition regarding a hypothetical action, as in such expressions as "let them not cook," "let it not decay," and so forth.

"...as it were, he would not conceive"—this is what is meant. For just as an ordinary person (puthujjana) must be said to "conceive" because conceiving has not been entirely abandoned, and just as one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) does not conceive at all because conceiving has been entirely abandoned, so it is not with the trainee (sekkha).
For him, some forms of conceiving have been abandoned while others have not; therefore, due to the presence of both states, he is in both ways.

It should not be said [that he conceives]. But surely, because both states exist, he should be said to conceive in both ways? No. For those [defilements] that have not been abandoned have reached a state of attenuation even for him;
therefore, he would not conceive by means of them either, because of the absence of even the more prominent conceiving, let alone by the others.
Thus the Blessed One said, "Let him not conceive. Therefore it was said: "'Let him not conceive'—this is a statement negating a hypothetical action."
The meaning is that one should not conceive [of it], as in such expressions as “may they not cause me suffering” or “may I not decay.

And this non-conceiving of his is due to the fact that the object is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*), not because it has already been fully understood like the state of one beyond training (*asekha*).

For where something must absolutely be fully understood and is capable of being so understood, no misconceptions contrary to that [understanding] can arise in an ordinary person (*puthujjana*). Therefore he said:
“I say that it is to be fully understood by him.
“Because he has entered the fixed course” means because he has entered the fixed course of rightness; the meaning is that he has descended into the stream of the Path.

“Because he is destined for full enlightenment” means because he has the higher paths and full enlightenment as his refuge; the meaning is that he has a natural inclination, a tendency, and a leaning toward its attainment.

By both [of these], he shows that for him, the remaining types of full understanding (*pariññā*) are necessarily absent. "To be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) means existing in the state of being something that must be fully known, or that which is capable of being fully understood.

Its opposite is "not to be fully understood" (*apariññeyya*). By the phrase "as in the case of an ordinary person" (*puthujjana*), he shows that for the "ordinary person" intended here, there is no suspicion at all of the state of having things to be fully understood, because such a person is not qualified [for this practice].
“Do not rejoice”—here too, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
The commentary on the second method of the section on those in training (sekkha) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the third and subsequent methods of the section on those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
8. It is "shared" (*sabhāga*) by virtue of commonality such as having seen the Truths (*diṭṭhasacca*).

Having explained the meaning of the term *arahant* according to the method of etymological analysis (*niruttinaya*) as being far from defilements (*kilesa*), he says "And this has been said," etc., to bring it into agreement with the Canon (*pāḷi*).

In that context, they are "evil" (*pāpaka*) in the sense of being base and in the sense of leading to an unhappy destination (*duggati*); they are "unwholesome" (*akusala*) in the sense of being blameworthy and in the sense of being produced through lack of skill (*akosalla*).
They are "defiling" (*saṃkilesika*) because they are subject to defilement, or because they are connected with it.

They are "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavika*) because they have the habit of producing renewed existence, or because they are subject to the fruit of renewed existence. They are "with distress" (*sadarā*) because they proceed together with affliction and feverish burning.
They are "having a painful result" (*dukkhavipāka*) because their ripening is painful, harsh, or difficult to bear. [They lead] to birth, aging, and death in the future.
“By their increase, there is birth, aging, and death. In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood.
While this is indeed an exposition of the Suttanta, the method of the Abhidhamma is the non-figurative (nippariyāya) approach; showing this, he said, “The four taints,” and so forth.
“Completely cut off and subsided” means that they are not merely completely cut off, but are also subsided by the function of the Path.
He also eliminates even that which is similar to the fruit.

Associating with the Noble Ones (*ariya-saṃvāsa*) means emulating the conduct of one’s teachers through the purification of virtue and other such practices. Associating with the Noble Path (*ariya-magga-saṃvāsa*) is simply the practice of the Noble Path itself. The so-called "ten abodes of the Noble Ones" (*das’ ariyāvāsā*) refer to the five factors of abandoning and so forth, with reference to which it was said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these ten abodes of the Noble Ones, which the Noble Ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in."

Which ten? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is possessed of six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has shaken off individual speculative dogmas, has utterly renounced seeking, is untroubled in his intentions, has tranquility of bodily formations, and is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom. These, monks, are the ten abodes of the noble ones.”
"Vussati" means "lived" (*vusita*); it refers to the Noble Path and the Noble Fruit.

Because he possesses these, the Arahant is called "one who has lived" (*vusitavā*), according to the desire for an expression of excellence. "What is to be done" (*karaṇīya*) refers to full understanding, abandoning, developing, and realizing.
That, moreover, should be understood as being sixteenfold, because it is to be performed by means of the four paths regarding the four truths. Therefore he said:

“To be accomplished by means of the four paths. Of one who is rightly liberated (*sammāvimutta*): of one who is well-liberated by means of the wisdom of the fruit of the supreme path (*aggamaggaphala-paññā*) through the modes of complete eradication (*samuccheda*) and subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).

Of one whose mind is peaceful (*santacitta*): of one whose mind is thus calmed from all the distress and fever of the defilements (*kilesa*). Of the monk whose defilements are shattered and whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), for whom the duties such as full comprehension (*pariññā*) have been performed.
There is no further accumulation or re-making; for that very reason, nothing further to be done exists or is found.
"Burdens" (*bhārā*) means they are like burdens in the sense of causing one to sink down; for it is said: "The five aggregates are indeed burdens," and so forth.

"Dependent upon oneself" (*attupanibandhaṃ*) means dependent on one's own wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), because [the burden] is included within one's own continuum (*sasantāna*). "Self" (*attānaṃ*)...

"Non-abandonment. Although this [non-abandonment] occurs in all blameless states (anavajjadhamma), it is especially prominent in Arahantship—which is supreme and characterized by an unshakable nature that is not subject to decline—and not in others. Showing this, he said:
"Or, in its sense as the ultimate goal," meaning by way of being the highest state.

The method of the discourses (*suttantanaya*) is a figurative method (*pariyāyanaya*). Thus, in order to show the fetters (*saṃyojana*) by way of the non-figurative method (*nippariyāyanaya*), he said: "the fetter of lust for existence, envy, and avarice," and not "lust for form" and so forth.

They fetter one to states of existence (*bhava*) by acting as conditions for the rounds of defilements, kamma, and kammic results, binding one in such a way that escape is not granted. For even though other factors also serve as conditions for them, [they cannot bind] without [these three].

The fetters exist as the conditions for those [actions]; and through those fetters, which are comprised within the lower and higher categories, there arises the determination of karma that produces this or that existence, as well as the determination of existence itself.
Furthermore, since even actions performed by one whose fetters have been severed do not produce existence, it is precisely these fetters that should be understood as having the sense of "binding."

"Having rightly known" means having known, according to reality, suffering and the rest exactly as they are to be known, by means of the wisdom of the supreme path which consists of full comprehension.
"Liberation of mind" is the relinquishing of all defilements of the mind. "Inclination toward Nibbāna" is the fixing of the mind upon Nibbāna;
it is the state of being directed toward, leaning toward, and tending toward that [Nibbāna]. "That" refers to earth and so forth. It has been fully understood (*pariññāta*).

It is not something unknown like for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), nor is it something yet to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) like for one in training (*sekkha*). Therefore, it is "because of its being fully understood" (*pariññātattā*).
The fourth, fifth, and sixth sections are called the "Nibbāna Sections" because they proceed by way of describing the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*) in various places.

Therein, non-conceptualization (*amaññanā*) occurs because earth and the other elements have been fully understood; that full understanding, moreover, comes about through the destruction of lust and the other defilements.
Showing that the text proceeds by way of illustrating this meaning—that [the fruit] is accomplished—he said:

"Having joined 'it is fully understood by him' with all the phrases, it should then be joined again with 'through the destruction of lust, he is one who has transcended lust. This same method applies to the others.
In this context, "to the others" refers to the fifth and sixth sections. If this is so, why is the text not seen in this way?
He said: "But as for the teaching, it is 'concise' because what is stated in one place is indeed stated everywhere.
One is not "free from lust" by the destruction of lust, because lust has not been entirely abandoned; for he is merely one whose lust is suppressed.
Furthermore, the mention of "outsiders" here is because such a state is found among them, not because that state is found exclusively among them. Now, as for that which...
The application of the meaning for all the phrases beginning with “its full understanding has been achieved” has already been stated;

however, in order to show the application of the meaning for the section on Nibbāna even without those, the passage beginning with “And just as” was spoken. Therein, “he does not conceive conceiving” means that conceiving does not proceed.
Although conceiving is that which is to be conceived by conceiving, the meaning here should be understood as its being included within its own objective basis (vatthu).

Even if the teaching on the door of Nibbāna proceeds without taking up the term "full understanding" (*pariññā*), nevertheless, since the very accomplishment of full understanding is demonstrated by such phrases as "through destruction" (*khayā*), what is the distinction between them? Addressing this objection, he says, "And here," and so forth.

This was stated for the purpose of showing the completion of the development of the path; for the intention is that full understanding is nothing other than the function of the path. The others... [etc.]
"He should be known by way of the praise of one who is free from lust, etc. "Or by two reasons" means by the two reasons already mentioned.
"Of him" refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "This distinction" refers to the distinction that will now be stated.

Although the one whose taints are destroyed is invariably free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, nevertheless, it is by way of the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) that his freedom from lust and so forth become distinguished.
To show that they receive the status of being so described, he says, "In three ways," and so forth.

By seeing the danger in lust through such statements as "One who is lustful does not know the true goal," one perceives that "Lust indeed arises through an attachment to pleasure, and pleasure is suffering due to its changeability;
how much more so the other [forms of craving]. Thus, seeing the danger in lust along with its causes is the sign for the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).
And because contemplation of suffering is the antidote to longing, it fulfills the desireless liberation; thus he said, "In regard to lust...

[he] becomes free from lust. Likewise, by seeing the danger in hatred through such statements as "one who is hateful does not know the true goal," and seeing that "hatred indeed arises dependent on suffering, and both of these are unstable and fleeting," [he becomes free from hatred].
"Decaying" (*pabhaṅgu*) refers to the vision of danger in faults that possess a cause; this is the sign for the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).

And since the contemplation of impermanence fulfills the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*) by being the antidote to the signs of permanence and so forth, it is said: "In faults... [it] becomes.

Likewise, for one who sees the danger in delusion through such statements as "the deluded person does not know the meaning," [one considers]: "Delusion is indeed the failure to grasp things according to their true nature (*yathāsabhāva*)."
“Wandering about”: the suppression of delusion is the sign for the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*);

and because the contemplation of non-self is the antidote to the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*), it fulfills the emptiness liberation (*suññatā-vimokkha*). Thus he said: “In delusion... [etc. ...he becomes free from delusion. “This being so” means:
if freedom from lust and the other qualities have been stated by way of the classification of liberations, then this being so. “Therefore” means: because.

This was not stated by way of restricting [the classification] to the liberations that are the doors to liberation; therefore, with the words "Whatever belongs to the Arahant," and so forth, he shows the meaning that the teaching of the three sections was formulated by analyzing whatever may arise for an Arahant.
Having thus shown the basis for the teaching of the three sections—the distinction of the one whose taints are destroyed—by way of the analysis of liberation, now...

Even though there is no differentiation therein, he says "without distinction," etc., showing the basis for the differentiation between the object of full understanding (*pariññā*) and the object of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*).
Therein, it is said that "equanimous feeling" is specifically the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and has delusion as its basis: "formations...
delusion. The rest is easy to understand because it follows the method already explained.
The commentary on the third section concerning those whose taints are destroyed is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the seventh section concerning the Tathāgata. 12.
By means of which specific qualities, acting as signs, this designation "Tathāgata" is applied to the Blessed One:
To demonstrate this, it was said: "The Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons," and so forth.
For all the names of the Blessed One are derived solely from his qualities. As it has been said:
"Countless are the names of the Great Seer, According to his qualities."
“By virtue of its quality, a name should be borne, even if it be a thousand names.

Regarding the phrase *tathā āgato*: here, the word *tathā* (thus) is used for the purpose of establishing a simile by way of determining the manner [of arrival]. For a general description settles upon a particular instance;

thus, the word *āgato* (come/arrived) has the sense of “having proceeded in that manner,” not the sense of “having attained knowledge,” as in the case of the expression “the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇaṃ*).”
It does not mean "coming" in the sense of physical movement, as in "The Great Ascetic has arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans," and so forth.
In this context, the word *tathā* (thus) is used for the purpose of establishing a simile by way of determining a specific mode;
thus, because compassion is predominant, he shows in a general way, by way of an illustration, the path of arrival of previous Buddhas through the medium of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* have an absolute relationship [of correlative reference], he first spoke generally, saying, "Just as [the path] has come down to all the world...," and then,

showing that same method by way of the six Perfectly Enlightened Ones— Vipassī and the others— who are well-known and proximate through their frequent mention in such discourses as the Mahāpadāna Sutta, he said, "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī... and so forth.
In this context, "by that aspiration" refers to the great aspiration of bodily resolve endowed with eight factors, namely:

human birth, possession of male gender, completion of the requisite causes, meeting with a Teacher, going forth into homelessness, perfection of qualities such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), the service rendered, and the desire for it.
For the bodily aspiration of all Perfectly Enlightened Ones is fulfilled by this very method.
Having thus explained the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" by way of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), he now speaks the passage beginning with, "Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī...
[and so on]... just as the Blessed One Kassapa fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*)," in order to demonstrate it by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*).
Furthermore, at this point, for the sake of generating proficiency among those versed in the Suttas regarding the path of practice for the Great Vehicle of Awakening (*mahābodhiyāna*), [he says]:
The discourse on the perfections (pāramī) should be told; however, that [discourse], endowed with all its aspects, has been explained in detail in the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka.
Therefore, those who desire it should understand it according to the method stated therein.

Just as in the past, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones such as Vipassī and others, having established themselves in the perfection of the initial resolve (abhinīhāra), [practiced] the path of practice that is utterly purified in its entirety...
Thinking of this meaning—that just as all the perfections (pāramitā) were fulfilled by him alone, so too have they been fulfilled by our Blessed One—it was said:

“Having fulfilled the thirty perfections. Although the sacrifice of limbs and so forth also constitute the perfection of giving, the phrase “five great sacrifices” is used both to show their specific nature as acts of renunciation and to demonstrate that they are exceedingly difficult to perform.

The eyes are mentioned separately from the limbs; likewise, although there is a commonality in the nature of relinquishing what is possessed, the relinquishing of wife and children is mentioned separately from the relinquishing of wealth and kingdom.

[This concludes] the accomplishment of the higher knowledges and meditative attainments together with the preliminary practice consisting of fulfilling the duties of going and returning, and so forth.

*Pubbayoga* (former application) is the accomplishment of an especially distinguished practice in giving and so forth; *pubbacariyā* (former conduct) is that same conduct, which is included in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*.
Some say that *abhinīhāra* (the aspiration) is the former application, while the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary wandering by way of physical seclusion, is the former conduct.
[It is accomplished] by way of discerning both giving and so forth, as well as fewness of wishes and so forth, along with the disadvantages and advantages of saṃsāra and nibbāna.
The proclamation of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhāna*) is discourse that proceeds by way of establishing and maturing beings for the three types of enlightenment;

the practice of benefiting kinsmen (*ñātatthacariyā*) is likewise through the power of compassion alone. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes the practice of benefiting the world (*lokatthacariyā*) and so forth.

[This occurs] by way of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatañāṇa*) and by way of proficiency in blameless spheres of action, crafts, and branches of learning (*sippāyatana-vijjāṭṭhāna*).

The movement of knowledge (*ñāṇacāra*) consists of the practice of wisdom (*buddhicariyā*), which occurs by way of familiarity with the aggregates, bases, and so forth, and by way of investigating the three characteristics.

In its essential meaning, however, this is simply the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); it is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*). "Culmination" (*koṭi*) means a limit, in the sense of the highest excellence.
The connection is: "having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness. Therein, "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*) means having generated.
"Having cultivated" means having increased. By the mention of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, he shows the path of approach brought to its culmination.

Alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness and the rest should be understood as being accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). Herein, by the phrase "by which resolution," etc., he shows the beginning of the path of approach;
by "the perfection of giving," etc., he shows the middle; and by "the four foundations of mindfulness," etc., [he shows the end].
It should be understood as "the conclusion.
"Just born" means having been born for a mere moment, having only just been released from the hands of humans, not merely having emerged from the mother's womb;
for as soon as the Great Being had emerged, first the Brahmās received him with a golden net. Of them...
From the hand [of the Bodhisatta], the Four Great Kings received it upon an antelope-skin rug; from their hands, men received it upon a *dukūla* cloth cushion;
and having been released from the hands of men, it settled upon the earth. As the Blessed One said in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*:
"When the white parasol"—that is, the divine white parasol—"was being held aloft" (*anudhārīyamāne*), that is, while it was being carried.
And here it should be understood that by the mention of the sunshade alone, the five insignia of royalty—the sword and the rest—are also included.
For at that time, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the yak-tail fan, the turban, and the headcloth were all presented together with the sunshade;
only the sunshade and the other objects were seen, not those who held them. "All directions" means the ten directions.
The directions. This surveying of all the directions is not to be understood as occurring after the seven steps were taken.
For when the Great Being was released from the hands of men, he looked toward the eastern direction. There, gods and humans, honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, said:
"Great Man, there is no one here equal to you, much less anyone superior. Thus...

Having surveyed all directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—and having seen no one equal to himself anywhere, he proceeded with the stride of a seven-step gait toward what he declared to be the northern direction.
"Foremost" (*āsabhi*) means supreme. "Chief" (*agga*) means the very first. "Eldest" (*jeṭṭha*) and "best" (*seṭṭha*) are synonyms for that same quality. "This is my last birth."
“There is now no further becoming”—with these words, he prophesied the attainment of Arahatship in this very life.
He demonstrates in detail, beginning with the words “For indeed,” the meaning that was stated briefly as being the precursor to many distinguished attainments. In that context, “here” refers to:
“A thousand-spoked wheel with many spokes...”
The gods held a parasol in the sky;
golden-handled fly-whisks were waved about,
yet those who held the fly-whisks and the parasol were not seen.
Regarding this verse: because the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) alone moves unimpeded everywhere, it is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*);
thus he says, "for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. Likewise, by the statement "this Blessed One also went...
[as far as] by way of being a preliminary sign," it is shown that these specific qualities arising by way of natural law (*dhammatā*) at the time of birth are common to all Bodhisattvas.
He shows that these are indeed the outflows (*nissanda*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"He strode" means he went. "Marus" refers to the gods. "Equal" means equal or similar by virtue of the equality of his surveying;
for just as the Great Man surveyed one direction, so too did he survey the remaining directions—there was no obstruction whatsoever in his surveying.
"Ahosī" means "was. Or, "sama" (even) means it is appropriate to look [at them], in the sense of being free from unevenness (*visama*).
For at that time, no unsightly, hideous, or uneven forms appeared before the Bodhisatta in the directions such that they would be inappropriate to look upon.
Having thus explained the term *Tathāgata* by means of the word *gata* in the sense of bodily movement as "one who has gone thus," now...
In order to show that [the goal] by way of the progression of knowledge, he said, "Or else," and so forth.

Therein, "by means of renunciation" (nekkhammena) refers to an arising of wholesome consciousness dominated by non-greed. For here, wholesome states are what is meant by "renunciation," not the act of going forth and so on;

they call it the "first jhāna. "Having abandoned" (pahāya) means having relinquished. "Gone" (gato) means attained; the meaning is that one has entered upon the further distinction. "Having abandoned" (pahāya)...
Or it is the cause of abandoning, or it has the characteristic of abandoning. For this word *pahāya* (having abandoned) has the sense of both cause and characteristic.

Here, the "going" (*gata*) spoken of as "gone" means either penetration or practice, which is caused by the abandoning of sensual desire and so forth; and it is characterized by that very abandoning of sensual desire and so forth.

This same method applies to expressions such as "having split open" (*padāletvā*) and others. By "non-ill will" (*abyāpādena*) means by loving-kindness (*mettā*). By "perception of light" (*ālokasaññāya*)...
By making [the hindrances] disappear through mental attention and by the presence of the perception of light; by non-distraction, that is, by concentration;
by the discernment of states, that is, by the precise determination of states such as the wholesome and so forth. Some also say: "by the discernment of name-and-form together with their conditions.
Thus, through the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire, there arises the first jhāna described in the passage beginning, "having abandoned covetousness for the world," and so on.
Having shown the Blessed One’s state of being a Tathāgata through the preliminary practice, he now says “by knowledge,” etc., in order to show that state together with the means—
the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights. For when delusion, which acts as a bond for the comprehension of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt,
is removed, the perception of impermanence and the other [perceptions] are accomplished for one who stands in the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*).
Likewise, there is [joy] through the sign of delight in the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*).

In this context, the statement, "When lack of delight is dispelled, there is the attainment of the *jhānas* and so forth," indicates that the removal of discontent and the shattering of ignorance are the means for the attainments and insight (*vipassanā*).
However, the presentation in reverse order is for the purpose of showing that ignorance—which has the nature of an obscuration—is included even among the obscurations mentioned below.

It should be seen thus: because they obstruct entry into the dwelling of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-vihāra*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are like door-bolts; therefore it is said, "having thrown open the bolt of the hindrances.
In the passage stating, "Having reflected and deliberated by night, one applies oneself to work by day," reflection and deliberation (*vitakka-vicāra*) are intended as the "smoke";
therefore it is said, "the smoke of reflection and deliberation. Even though [this occurs] only in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna...
Suffering is abandoned in the access to the fourth jhāna, and pleasure is abandoned in the fourth jhāna itself; however, with reference to their complete abandonment, it is said:
"Having abandoned pleasure and pain by means of the fourth jhāna.

Contemplation of the impermanent as "impermanent" is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*); it is the observation of the impermanence of the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

This is the name for insight that has been set in motion after having been grasped. "Perception of permanence" refers to the false perception occurring in the form of "permanent and eternal" with respect to conditioned phenomena.
By means of the term "perception," the inclusion of views and consciousness should also be understood. This same method applies to those that follow as well.
"Contemplation of disenchantment" refers to the contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming disenchanted with conditioned formations.
They delight in craving accompanied by rapture. "By means of the contemplation of fading away" means by means of the contemplation that occurs in the mode of becoming dispassionate toward formations.
"By means of the contemplation of cessation" means by means of the contemplation of the cessation of formations;
or else, it is the contemplation in such a way that formations simply cease and do not arise again in the future as renewed existence.
Contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*). For this very reason it is said: "By means of the contemplation of cessation, one causes [the formations] to cease; they do not arise.

For this desire for liberation (*muccitukamyatā*) has now reached the stage of power. Contemplation that occurs in the mode of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*);

for this is the reflective stabilization (*paṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā*). "Grasping" (*ādāna*) is the seizing [of things] by way of permanence and so forth. [This refers to] the continuity, the collection, the function, and the object.

The apprehension of unity by way of [the continuity of] existence is the perception of compactness (*ghanasaññā*). Accumulation (*āyūhana*) is the act of constructing (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*). Transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the attainment of a particular state.

The perception of stability (*dhuvasaññā*) is the apprehension of a firm nature. A "sign" (*nimitta*) is the apprehension of formations as having a concrete form, due to their being perceived as a mass through the density of the collection and so forth, and due to their delimitation of their own functions.
"Aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) refers to the aspiration of passion and so forth; in its essential meaning, however, it is craving (*taṇhā*).
Inclination toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāresu ninnatā*). Adherence (*abhinivesa*) refers to the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*).

Higher wisdom as the discernment of phenomena (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is the investigation of all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth. Adherence to grasping at the essential (*sārādānābhinivesa*) is the perversion of perceiving essence in what is essenceless.
The adherence that the world has arisen through the creation of a Lord (*Issarakutta*) and so forth is the adherence of delusion (*sammohābhinivesa*).
Some, however, say that "adherence through delusion" (*sammohābhiniveso*) is the occurrence of doubt, as in the passage beginning, "Did I exist in the past?

Adherence through attachment (*ālayābhiniveso*) is the grasping at conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) as a shelter and protection. Because of the statement, "Delighting in attachment, rejoicing in attachment," attachment is craving;
and it is precisely this [craving] that functions by way of adhering to the eye and so forth, and to visible forms and so forth.

Some say that "clinging to the storehouse" (ālayābhinivesa) refers to the knowledge that occurs [thinking], "Such formations are to be relinquished"; this is the contemplation of reflective discernment (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā).
Because it is free from the round of existence (vaṭṭa), it is "turning away" (vivaṭṭa), namely Nibbāna;

the contemplation that occurs by taking that as its object—known as the act of contemplating—is the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā), which is the state of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). "Clinging to conjunction" (saṃyogābhinivesa) refers to [clinging] toward formations by way of conjoining.
"Settling down" (*nivisanaṃ*). "Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*) means associated with views by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of abandonment (*pahāna*).

"Gross" (*oḷārika*) is said in relation to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those abandonable by seeing would be gross in comparison to those to be abandoned by the second path.
"Subtle" (*aṇusahagata*) means minute. This is said in relation to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths. "All defilements" (*sabbakilesa*) refers to all remaining defilements.
For defilements abandoned by the first and subsequent paths are not abandoned again.

Hardness is the state of being rigid. Oozing is the state of being fluid. That wind by which a particular part of the body becomes distended, like a bellows by a worldly wind, or that which constitutes rigidity, is *vitthambhana* (distension). Even though [it] exists...

Regarding the state of contact between elements belonging to one group and those belonging to another group: for those things whose delimitation is "space as the limit of form" due to the distinctness of each respective element, that [space] is indeed not in contact with them;
otherwise, there would be no inherent nature of delimitation for the elements, because they would attain a state of pervasiveness.
Non-pervasiveness itself is non-contact; thus, in whichever group the delimitation of the elements occurs, [that space is not in contact].
The state of not being touched by those [other elements] is the characteristic of non-contact. Therefore the Blessed One said, in the description of the space element:
"Not touched by the four great elements.
Impingement (ruppana) is the arising of something dissimilar when there is a convergence of opposing conditions. Because volition is predominant among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations...
This was stated by way of volition (cetanā): “the characteristic of the formative activity of formations.
For in the *Suttantabhājanīya* of the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregate of formations, it is volition alone that is analyzed, beginning with the words, “volition born of eye-contact,” and so forth.

And volition has the characteristic of formative activity. As it is said: “In this context, what is the meritorious formative activity? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere,” and so on.
Pervasion (*pharaṇa*) is the state of being widespread. "In lack of faith" (*assaddhiye*) means by reason of lack of faith; the locative case is used here in the sense of a cause.

This same method applies to the terms "laziness" (*kosajje*) and so forth. "The characteristic of tranquility" (*upasamalakkhaṇa*) means the characteristic of the subsiding of the fever of body and mind.

When the higher mind (*adhicitta*), free from lethargy and agitation, is proceeding, equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanā*) is the reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) resulting from the absence of engagement in exertion, restraint, or encouragement.
Because it cuts off partiality; because right speech—
being of a nature that embraces, as the opposite of harsh and non-embracing speech such as lying which has the function of deceiving— is oily through its own nature,
it [benefits] both the associated states and the listeners of the well-spoken words conditioned by right speech.

"It grasps the person" is stated as its characteristic of grasping (*pariggāhalakkhaṇa*). Bodily activity (*kāyikakiriyā*) originates something that is to be done, and it itself is the arising and the joining;
thus, the characteristic of origination (*samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇa*) should be understood in relation to the abstention known as right action (*sammākammanta*).
Alternatively, "origination" (*samuṭṭhāpana*) is the lifting up of the associated mental states by means of bodily activity.

It is like the lifting of a burden. Purity (*suddhi*) or cleansing (*vodāna*) is the occurrence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) for a living being, or of the associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*), or indeed of the livelihood itself.
Exertion (*paggaha*) is the correct uplifting of the mind together with its associated states, not allowing it to fall into the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa-pakkha*).
“Formations” (*saṅkhārā*) here is intended to mean volition (*cetanā*), as it is said: “The characteristic of formations is volition.

Inclination is the state of being directed toward an object. Proceeding is the act of occurring. For it is by way of the bases (*āyatana*) that the occurrence of mind and mental factors—termed “the self” (*āya*)—takes place.

Regarding craving as having the characteristic of a cause: its nature is to be the cause that generates the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); however, for the Path, its nature is to lead to Nibbāna. This is the distinction between them.

The characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*) is the non-perverted intrinsic nature. Its single flavor (*ekarasa*) is the state of not overstepping one another and being neither deficient nor excessive. It is indeed serenity and insight joined in yoke (*yuganaddha*); some also say it is faith and wisdom, characterized by exertion and non-distraction.

"Exhausted" (*khīṇa*): it is the path (*magga*), so called because it exhausts the defilements. "Non-arising" (*anuppāda*): it is the fruit (*phala*), so called because its culmination is the state of non-arising.

"Tranquility" (*passaddhi*) is the subsiding of the defilements. "Of desire" (*chandassa*): of the desire consisting in the wish to act. Its characteristic as a root is the state of being a foundation; its state is that of origination.

The characteristic of origination (*samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇa*) is the state of being the cause for the arising of associated states by way of presenting an object. "Conjunction" (*samodhāna*) is the mode in which [states] are to be grasped through the meeting of the sense-object and so forth;
it is what is called "concourse" (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, it is "conjunction" because associated states are brought together (*samodahanti*) equally or simultaneously by means of it;
that is, contact (*phassa*). "Confluence" (*samosaraṇa*) is that wherein they meet and assemble.
It is said thus because, in the absence of feeling, the associated states do not proceed; they are as if gathered together for the purpose of experiencing feeling.
The characteristic of being "foremost" (pamukha) is the state of leadership among the associated states, like the peak of rafters.
Therefore, it is "surpassing that" (tatuttari), meaning superior to those associated states; for wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme excellence.

"Phenomena" (*dhammā*). "By way of liberation" (*vimuttiyā*) means by way of the fruit (*phala*). For that [fruit] is the essence (*sāra*) by virtue of being the ultimate excellence of the essence consisting of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).

It should be understood that this analysis of characteristics (*lakkhaṇavibhāga*) has been made according to the various discourses (*sutta*) concerning the six elements, the five jhāna-factors, and so forth, and in accordance with the method transmitted in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
For even though some phenomena have already been explained previously, they are mentioned here for the purpose of clarifying another perspective (*pariyāyantara*).

It is shown again. And for that very reason, by way of such Sutta passages as: “Wholesome states have zeal as their root, are originated by attention, converge upon contact, and culminate in feeling”;
“Wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme”; “This holy life has liberation as its essence”;
and “For, friends, the holy life has Nibbāna as its refuge and Nibbāna as its consummation.”
“It is the characteristic of desire as its root,” and so forth, was said.
The “such-dharmas” (tathadhammā) are the four noble truths because their intrinsic nature is non-perverted. They are “such” (tathā) because they possess that nature.

They are “not otherwise” (avitathā) because they do not have a false nature. They are “not different” (anaññathā) because they are devoid of any other mode. This is the sense of being produced and fully realized through birth as a condition.
The meaning of "arisen" (*sambhūta*) is the state of having come forth from what has been produced through birth, occurring in conjunction with its own appropriate conditions;
that is the sense of "subsequent occurrence. Alternatively, the compound *sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho* means both the sense of being arisen and the sense of being fully brought about.
Birth does not exist without aging-and-death, nor does it arise from anything other than birth; thus, it is the sense of being arisen through the condition of birth (*jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho*).

And thus, "it arises from birth" means the sense of being arisen with birth as its condition; the meaning is that whatever birth serves as a condition in whatever way, there is a manifestation corresponding to that.

Regarding "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations," here too it is not that ignorance is not a condition for volitional formations, nor do volitional formations arise without ignorance; which...

In whatever way ignorance serves as the condition for whichever formations, this is the meaning of ignorance’s "condition-meaning" (*paccayaṭṭha*)—that is, its state of being a condition (*paccayabhāva*).
The connection is that the Blessed One knows and sees that [conditionality] in all its aspects. "By him" means by the Blessed One. "That which is being analyzed" refers to...

It should be applied. "That" refers to the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "desirable, undesirable, and so forth," neutrality (*majjhatta*) is included;
likewise, it includes the divisions of past, future, and present; limited (*paritta*), internal (*ajjhatta*), external (*bahiddhā*), both, and so on. "By way of the terms as they occur" means:
"The visible-form base is seen, the sound base is heard, the odor base, taste base, and tangible-object base..."

Because of the statement, "All that is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized by the mind," the terms "seen" (*diṭṭha*) and "cognized" (*viññāta*) are applicable to the object-base of form (*rūpārammaṇa*).
The object-base of form—whether desirable, undesirable, or neutral; limited, past, future, or present;
internal or external; seen or cognized—is form, the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*), the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), the appearance of color, and that which is visible.
"By many names such as 'with resistance,' 'blue,' 'yellow,' and so forth.
"In thirteen sections" refers to the thirteen sections of exposition (*niddesa*) found in the *Rūpakaṇḍa*.
And because in each section there are four methods of defining (*vavatthāpana*), he says, "by fifty-two methods. It is exactly thus.

Because of his seeing things without error and because of his teaching that cannot be overturned. By showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and the past through the statement "I know, I have directly realized," it should be understood that the occurrence of knowledge in the future is likewise stated.

The word *vidita* (known) should be understood as not specifying a particular time, as in the expressions "seen, heard, sensed" (*diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ*), and so forth. "It did not appear" means [not appearing] by way of a self or what belongs to a self.

He did not approach [them]. The derivation of the word *tathāgata* should be understood as follows: he is called a *Tathāgata* because he sees, knows, and goes toward those phenomena—such as the objects of form (*rūpa-ārammaṇa*) and so forth—exactly as they are in their intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāva*) and their specific mode (*yathāpakāra*).

However, some maintain that the term is formed by the elision of the syllable *dassi* and the addition (*āgama*) of the syllable *ā* to *āgata*, according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*) or by the application of the *pisodarādi* rule (Pāṇini 6.3.109).
Having done so, they praise [the Buddha] as "the Tathāgata.

Because it is faultless, it is irreproachable (*anupavajja*). Because there is nothing to be added, it is not deficient (*anūna*). Because there is nothing to be removed, it is not redundant (*anadhika*).

Because of its perfection in meaning, phrasing, and so forth, it is complete in every respect (*sabbākāraparipuṇṇa*). "Not otherwise" means that it is exactly as it was stated: "just so" (*tathaiva*).

He accomplishes [it] through exclusion (*vyatireka*). By this, he shows the quality of unerring teaching: that which was spoken for a certain purpose is accomplished exclusively for that purpose; thus, "just as it was spoken by the Blessed One, so it is exactly like that.

Regarding the phrase *gada-attha*, this shows that according to the method of etymology (*nirukti*), the letter *da* has been changed to *ta* in the expression "one who speaks what is thus" (*tathaṃ gadati*)—hence, *Tathāgata*.
"He has gone thus" (*tathā-gata*) means he is a *Tathāgata*. "Gone" (*gata*) here means the activity of body and speech.
When "thus" (*tathā*) is stated, because of the inseparable connection between the words *yaṃ* (which) and *taṃ* (that), the meaning "in this way" (*yathā*) is indeed present;

and since bodily and vocal actions conform to one another, when there is a desire for expression, the body stands in relation to speech, and speech stands in relation to the body through their state of mutual connection.
Showing this meaning, he said, "Of the Blessed One," and so forth. In this sense, the meaning that he is a "Tathāgata" because of being one who speaks thus (tathāvādītā) is also established.
Since that has already been shown previously by another method, he said, "Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of acting thus (tathākāritā).
By the phrase "horizontally in immeasurable world-systems," he indicates that which some [hold] to exist horizontally, as well as above and below.

They say "world-systems" (*lokadhātuyo*); he refutes that. "Consisting of the elegance of teaching" (*desanāvilāsamayo*) means the elegance of teaching itself, just as in expressions such as "consisting of merit" (*puññamaya*) or "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*).

Since particles (*nipāta*) function by indicating the meaning of a word when placed in proximity to a denotative term (*vācaka-sadda*), the word *gata* itself expresses the sense of "understood" and the sense of "past"; thus he says, "Gata means understood and past."

Alternatively, from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) up until perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), because there was an absence of decline, defilement, or turning back during this interval in the practice of the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment (*mahābodhiyāna*), he has gone according to his aspiration; thus, having practiced in accordance with that resolution, he is the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, by virtue of his great supernormal power (*mahiddhikatā*), through the attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and by way of unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇatā*).

Furthermore, because there is no resistance whatsoever [to his will], he is the "Tathāgata" because the movements, goings, and activities of his body, speech, and mind proceed exactly as he desires. Moreover, since in the world words such as *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*,
and *ppakāra* are seen to have synonymous meanings, this Blessed One is also a "Tathāgata" because he is of the same kind (*tathāvidha*) as the Blessed Ones Vipassī and the others.
Furthermore, just as those Blessed Ones were so constituted, this Blessed One is likewise so constituted; thus he is the Tathāgata.
Alternatively, since "true," "real," and "such" (tatha) is a designation for knowledge, he is therefore the Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) by means of such knowledge (tathena ñāṇena).
In this way, too, the meaning of the word Tathāgata is to be understood.
Just as Vipassī and the other Great Seers went forth, having abandoned the stains of sensual desire and the like by means of concentration and knowledge,
so too did the Sakyan Sage, the bearer of radiance.
He has gone thus (tathā-gata), therefore he is called a Tathāgata. And likewise,
that which possesses the characteristics of the elements, sense-bases, and so forth, according to the distinctions of individual essence, commonality, and classification;
The Victor has attained self-existent knowledge;
thus the Sakyan bull is called the Tathāgata.
With his all-seeing eye, he [perceives] the truths as they truly are.
Likewise, because he has fully manifested this specific conditionality through his own unerring knowledge exactly as it is,
he is therefore the Victor, the Tathāgata.
Even in world-systems of manifold divisions,
regarding the range of the Victor’s sense-sphere of visible forms and so forth,
there is a vision of exactly the same variety.
Therefore the Tathāgata is Samantalocana.
And because he speaks the Dhamma exactly as it is,
he acts in accordance with his own words.
He proceeds having surpassed the world with his virtues;
for that reason, the Tathāgata is the Leader of the World.
Accordingly, according to his resolve and according to his inclination—
Because his speech proceeded with a subtle state of mind,
the Jina is called "Tathāgata" because he is just as he was previously toward the Great Seers.

The meaning of the terms beginning with *ārakatta* (remoteness) should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the commentary on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
By the phrase "having perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena," there is indicated his unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*)—
which is independent of the instruction of others, capable of awakening to all phenomena in every aspect, and functions only when there is a desire [to know].
The attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has been demonstrated.
But is not unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) other than omniscient knowledge? Otherwise, the statement that "the six uncommon knowledges are the Buddha-knowledges" would be contradicted.
It is not contradicted; for it is intended to show that they possess a state of uncommon knowledge distinct from others by way of differences in their objects and modes of occurrence.

Because a single knowledge is described in two ways. For that very same knowledge is called "omniscient knowledge" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) because its object is the entirety of conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception;
and it is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) by way of its unimpeded movement therein due to the absence of any obstruction.
As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "It is omniscient knowledge because it knows everything—conditioned and unconditioned—without remainder."
"Because there is no obstruction therein, it is 'unobstructed knowledge' (anāvaraṇañāṇa)," and so forth; therefore, there is no difference between them in meaning.
This must certainly be accepted in this way, for otherwise, both omniscience and unobstructed knowledge would result in being obstructed and having as their object only a limited range of phenomena.
Indeed, there is not even the slightest obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge, [which is] unobstructed knowledge.

Furthermore, if it were not an object for all phenomena (*asabbadhammārammaṇa*), then in those places where it does not function, its state of being "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*) would simply not exist due to the presence of an obstruction.
Alternatively, let there be another kind of unobstructed knowledge distinct from omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);
however, in this context, by virtue of its unimpeded operation everywhere, "unobstructed knowledge" refers specifically to omniscience itself, and through the attainment of that—

The Blessed One is called the All-Knowing (sabbaññū), the All-Seeing (sabbavidū), and the Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha), not merely because of his simultaneous awakening to all phenomena.

Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "This designation 'Buddha' is a realization-based appellation attained by the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree together with the acquisition of the knowledge of omniscience. This is due to the attainment of the knowledge capable of awakening to all phenomena.
For indeed, there was in the Blessed One’s continuum the capacity to penetrate all phenomena without exception.
Here it may be asked: "Does this knowledge, when it arises, arise all at once regarding its entire object, or does it do so successively?
What of this? If, first of all, it were to arise all at once regarding its entire object—distinguished as past, future, present, internal, external, and so forth—...
If conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) and the conventional designation of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata-sammuti-dhamma*) were to appear together as one,
there would be no distinct comprehension through differentiation, like one looking at a cloth from a distance; and if that were the case,

for those practicing insight (*vipassanā*) with the thought "all phenomena are non-self," all phenomena would not appear to the Blessed One in their undetermined form, as they do when viewed under the aspect of non-self.

It follows that [knowledge] becomes the object of knowledge. As for those who say: "The Buddha's knowledge at all times proceeds with respect to the established characteristics of all knowable phenomena, being free from conceptual construction; it is because of this that he is called 'all-knowing.
And having accepted this, the statement, 'The Naga is concentrated while walking, and concentrated while standing,' is also well-said."

For them too, the aforementioned faults do not cease. Because it would have as its object only that which possesses the characteristic of being present, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have only a partial range, since past and future conventional phenomena lack that [present] state; therefore, it is not tenable that his knowledge occurs all at once.

If, on the other hand, knowledge occurs sequentially regarding the entire range of objects, even that is not tenable. For [it cannot be said that he knows] by way of genus, plane, individual essence, and so forth...

When the objects of knowledge—which are divided into many categories according to direction, location, time, and so forth—are grasped in succession, their complete and exhaustive penetration becomes possible because the objects of knowledge are infinite.

However, as for those who claim: "The Blessed One is omniscient because he has made one portion of the objects of knowledge directly perceived through non-deception regarding the meaning, and having resolved that it is likewise in the remainder by means of defining it," [this is not so].
And that knowledge is not inferential because it is free from doubt; for they say that in the world, inferential knowledge is accompanied by doubt—but that is also incorrect for them.

For if all objects were beyond direct perception, it would be impossible to determine that "it is so" regarding the remainder after having made one part of the knowable object directly perceived and then resolving upon it through non-contradiction.
For that which remains is not directly perceived (*paccakkha*). If even that were directly perceived, its status as "the remainder" would not exist—is this not so?
All of this is irrelevant. Why? Because it concerns an investigation into what is not an object [of such perception]. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"The domain of the Buddhas, monks, is inconceivable; it is not to be thought upon. Whoever should think upon it would fall into madness and distress..."

“...would he be a partaker? This, however, is the definitive conclusion here: whatever the Blessed One desires to know—whether in its entirety or in part—knowledge regarding that proceeds through direct perception by virtue of its unimpeded operation; and there is constant composure due to the absence of distraction.
Furthermore, if everything desired to be known were not within his range, his mode of operation would not be bound to his own wish.

And it must certainly be accepted as such, because of the statement: "All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, the desire, the attention, and the arising of consciousness of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Furthermore, even the Blessed One’s knowledge regarding objects of the past and future is direct perception (*paccakkha*) itself, since it is devoid of inference, scripture, conjecture, or conceptual grasping.

But surely, even on this view, when one desires to know everything, the Blessed One’s knowledge would have to proceed all at once toward its entire object in an undifferentiated form; thus, would it not fail to avoid the aforementioned fault? No, for that has been cleared away.
Indeed, that domain of the Buddha has been established as inconceivable. Otherwise, his mode of functioning would be identical to that of the knowledge of ordinary people.
The inconceivability of the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would not exist;

therefore, although that [knowledge] has all phenomena as its object, it proceeds having made those phenomena well-defined as if they were the object of a single phenomenon—this is what is inconceivable here.
And the knowledge is infinite, just like the knowable. For this has been said: "As far as the knowable extends, so far..."
"Knowledge. To the extent that there is knowledge, to that extent there is the knowable. Knowledge has its limit in the knowable; the knowable has its limit in knowledge.

Thus, because he has perfectly and personally awakened to all phenomena—whether taken together, individually, simultaneously, or sequentially, according to his wish—he is the "Perfectly Self-Awakened One" (Sammāsambuddha).
"Those" refers to the aforementioned divisions beginning with earth. "Thoroughly known" (*pariññāta*) means known completely, all around, and in every aspect;

the meaning is that it is known without leaving anything remaining of that which ought to be thoroughly known. Indeed, this very same meaning is demonstrated by the phrase "thoroughly known as far as" (*pariññātanta*);
thus he said, "What is called 'thoroughly known as far as'... and so forth. By each respective path...

The statement that "there is no distinction in the abandoning of defilements" is said with reference to the commonality between Buddhas and disciples regarding the fact that the specific defilements to be abandoned by each respective path must be abandoned by that very path; it is not because there is an absence of distinction in the abandoning of defilements by Buddhas compared to disciples.
For it is only the Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhā) who abandon the defilements along with their latent tendencies (savāsanā), not [the disciples].
"Disciples. "Only a single portion" means only that which has entered into one's own mental continuum (*santāna*).

For even by means of the mere full understanding (*pariññā*) of those phenomena included within one's own continuum, the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths is accomplished. Therefore it was said:
"In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world and I proclaim the origin of the world," and so forth. Even [a portion] the size of an atom...
...pe... they say that there is no [place] from which the Buddhas’ great diamond-like knowledge proceeds by way of its 360 million facets.
The commentary on the seventh method of the section on the Tathāgata is finished.
The commentary on the eighth method of the section on the Tathāgata.
13. *Purimataṇhā* (prior craving) is the craving produced in previous existences that serves as the cause for the present individuality (*attabhāva*).

By the inclusion of this [craving], it should be understood that ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), along with clinging (*upādāna*), are included within the past portion [of the cycle].

"Herein" refers to the phrase "from becoming, birth. By that [phrase], through the heading of "birth" in the expression "from becoming, birth," [the future portion is indicated] by way of the "becoming of rebirth" (*upapattibhava*).

“By the aforementioned state of rebirth. “Of one who has come to be” means of one who has been generated. Since that [being] is called a “sentient being” (satta), it is therefore stated as “of a sentient being” (sattassa).

And by the phrase “knowing thus,” he shows that even here in the expression “of one who has come to be, aging-and-death,” the word “having understood” (iti viditvā) must be brought forward and connected.

Although the aggregates of clinging belonging to the three planes are to be included and comprehended within the eleven instances beginning with "whatever form," they were nevertheless comprehended by the Blessed One by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) through such questions as, "When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? With what as condition does aging-and-death arise?
And dependent origination is so called because it is the state of being both the process of occurrence and the cause of that occurrence.
There are only the first two truths; therefore, clarifying that their realization is "the penetration of the mode of conditionality through the absence of conceiving," he said:

"That which [he realized] at the foot of the Bodhi tree... and so forth. They are called "summarizations" (*saṅkhepā*) because ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are summarized therein;
or alternatively, because in the past, causes and so forth were summarized as simply "cause" and "fruit."
In brief, they are ignorance and so forth, and consciousness and so forth. The word *saṅkhepa* (brief/section) should be understood as a designation for a part.

Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'sections'. Furthermore, these four sections belong to it: the section of causes in the past, the section of results in the present, the section of causes in the present, and the section of results in the future; thus it is called "having four sections" (*catusaṅkhepa*). That...

It has four groups (*catusaṅkhepa*). It has three connections (*sandhi*)—namely, the connection between cause and fruit, the connection between fruit and cause, and again the connection between cause and fruit—thus it is "three-connection" (*tisandhi*);
that is "three-connection. It has three periods (*addhā*) distinguished as past, present, and future, thus it is "three-period" (*tiyaddha*);

that is "three-period. Although not explicitly stated by their own names, ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth, are included within each respective group by virtue of being mentioned therein.
"Modes" (ākāra) means those by which [the conditions] are manifested; or alternatively, "modes" are the ways (pakāra) in which past causes and so forth appear.
Having made five modes for each of the four summaries, there are twenty modes belonging to this [conditionality], thus it is "twentyfold" (vīsatākāra); that is the twentyfold mode.

"All this" means this entire condition, including its divisions such as the four summaries, without exception. "By way of the characteristic of condition" means by way of the state of being a condition (paccayabhāva).
The meaning is: by way of being a condition for its own fruit, which is rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), characterized by inseparability (*avinābhāva*).

For just as ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other factors do not become conditions for consciousness in the absence of craving (*taṇhā*), so too craving does not [function] in the absence of ignorance and the others.

Here, by the mention of "suffering" (*dukkha*), consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are included; and by the mention of "existence" (*bhava*),...
And since craving, volitional formations, and clinging have already been included [in the previous discussion], they are not mentioned here as they follow the same method already stated.
Now, in order to clarify those twenty aspects according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi*, the passage beginning with "Thus these" was spoken.
Therein, "in the previous kamma-existence" (*purimakammabhavasmiṃ*) means in the prior kamma-existence; the sense is: while being performed in the kamma-existence of a past birth.
Delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*): that delusion regarding suffering and so forth at that time, by which one who is bewildered performs an action—that is ignorance.

Accumulation is volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*): those prior volitions, such as giving gifts and so forth, by way of preparing the requisites for a gift and so on, while performing various actions—these are the volitional formations.
However, the volition of one who places the object to be given into the hands of the recipients is existence (*bhava*).
In the case of a single adverting and impulsions, the preceding volition is "accumulation" (āyūhana) and the "formations" (saṅkhāra), while the seventh is "existence" (bhava).
Alternatively, any volition whatsoever is "existence," and its associated mental factors are "accumulation" and "formations. "Attachment" (nikanti) is craving (taṇhā):
that longing and aspiration for the fruit of the rebirth-existence while one is performing an action is what is called craving. "Approaching" (upagamana) is clinging (upādāna).

That which is the condition for kammic existence—namely, the approaching, grasping, and clutching that occurs in such a manner as, "Having performed this kamma, I shall enjoy sense pleasures in such-and-such a place; I shall cease [here]"—this is called *upādāna*.
Regarding "volition is existence" (*cetanā bhavo*), it refers to the volition stated at the conclusion of the exertion (*āyūhana*) described in the two alternative explanations of the meaning.
In the third [link], however, volition associated with the effort of accumulating (āyūhana) is existence (bhava).

Thus, these five factors—namely, the five factors beginning with delusion (moha) as previously stated—are established in the past kamma-existence and serve as conditions for rebirth-linking here and now; this is the meaning.
Herein, "rebirth-linking consciousness" refers to that consciousness which is called "linking" (paṭisandhi) because it arises by way of linking to another existence;
this is "consciousness. "Descent of name-and-form" refers to the descent of material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, as if they were coming and entering;
this is "name-and-form. "Sensitivity as sense-base" refers to this by way of the five sense-bases, beginning with the eye.
It has been said: "Contact is that which has touched, touching the object; this is contact.
"Feeling is that which is felt"—that is, the resultant feeling arisen together with either the rebirth-linking consciousness or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases;
this is feeling. Thus, these... [etc. ...conditions: these fivefold groups of phenomena beginning with consciousness arose in the previous existence.

The meaning is: "They arise here now, in this present state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), by way of the state of being a condition for that performed karma—that is, for the cycle of karma (*kammavaṭṭa*)—due to its being a condition.
Here, because the sense bases (*āyatana*) have reached maturity, there is no delusion; thus, at the time of performing the karma, there was no confusion regarding the matured sense bases.

This is shown. For the mental activity of a young person is predominantly characterized by the *bhavaṅga* (subconscious life-continuum) and is generally not capable of accumulating karma that produces another existence.
By the phrase "at the time of performing an action," all delusion that serves as a condition for karma is included, not merely that which is associated [with consciousness].
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the *padayojanā* (word-by-word arrangement): it is by means of the connection between the words beginning with "therefore" (*tasmā*). Regarding the "conclusion of the meaning":
this refers to the conclusion of the teaching's meaning in this eighth section. Regarding "delight" (*nandī*): it refers to all forms of craving (*taṇhā*) spoken of in this way;

that is, for all cravings expressed in the singular number due to the commonality of their sense of "delighting," there is a distinction based on the continuity, the object, the associated states, and the mode of occurrence.
Of all the various types of craving. "Synonyms for destruction" means they are synonyms for abandonment by eradication;
for it is said, "by ultimate destruction. "This is common to the function of the four paths":
the meaning is that these terms, such as "destruction," are a general designation for the function of abandoning shared in common by the four noble paths. However, of those...
Showing that the phrase beginning with "through dispassion" (virāgā) was stated in order to demonstrate the sequential occurrence of the paths by way of their respective functions, he said:

"Thereafter... [and so on]... should be connected. Likewise, although terms such as "destruction" (khaya) and the rest are synonymous with "abandonment," the inclusion of these alternative terms for destruction and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating the complete abandonment, without remainder, of craving—which is distinguished by its various objects that are to be abandoned.

Showing what "what" refers to, he said, "Go," and so forth. Since craving—which serves as the cause for the aforementioned production [of suffering] and so on—has been abandoned, the statement regarding its destruction and so forth, being spoken as an illustration of that abandonment, does not in any way contradict the nature of phenomena (dhammatā);
thus it is said, "nothing is contradicted."
“Devoid of a superior” means being devoid of a superior—that is, of anything more excellent—because it is capable of surpassing itself.
And this state of being devoid of a superior is due to its own preeminence; thus he says, “the most excellent.
Just as the prefixes *sam-* and *sām-* express the meanings of the words “unerring” (*aviparītam*) and “individual” (*sāman*), so too do they express the meanings of “praiseworthy” and “beautiful.”
He said: "Rightly, it is praised as the awakening of one’s own self, and it is a beautiful awakening.
Here, the tree is called *bodhi* because one awakens to or penetrates the Four Noble Truths—or indeed all that is to be known—under it;

furthermore, the path is *bodhi* because one awakens by means of it, and likewise for the knowledge of omniscience. However, Nibbāna is *bodhi* because it is that which is to be awakened to. This is the analysis of the grammatical derivation (*sādhanavibhāga*) in this context.

It should be understood that the word *bodhi* is indeed used even in the sense of a designation (*paṇṇatti*), as in such examples as "Prince Bodhirāja" and so forth. "Others" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*.
Furthermore, the reason for providing examples of the prefixless form when explaining the meaning of the word *bodhi* together with its prefixes has already been stated above.
