Alternatively, because it is supramundane (*lokuttara*) and because there is no further path beyond it—just as there are lower paths [leading up to it]—it may be said: [siyā...]
With reference to the doubt, "Is it indeed the unsurpassed enlightenment?", the words beginning with "of the disciples" were spoken in order to dispel that [doubt]. Since the Path—
when being accomplished together with certain specific types of knowledge (ñāṇa) that are the fruits of the perfection of the aspiration (abhinīhāra), along with all [other factors]—
is as if it were bestowing upon the Noble Ones (ariya) those respective specific knowledges and so forth, its quality of bestowing all virtues is [established].

It has been said. By this, he shows that the path to arahantship—accomplished through the perfection of a unique resolution and followed by unsurpassed qualities—is called "unsurpassed enlightenment" (anuttarā bodhi).

Disciple-parami-ñāṇa is knowledge not shared with other disciples; it is the exclusive knowledge belonging only to the great disciples. One becomes a paccekabuddha by having awakened to the truths individually.
[They are] Paccekabuddhas. But is it not the case that all Noble Ones (ariya) penetrate the Truths individually, because the Dhamma is to be personally realized?
True; however, this was not said with reference to such a penetration as that.

Rather, it refers to how disciples penetrate the Truths by depending on another—that is, through the voice of another—whereas for them [the Paccekabuddhas], there is no path of vision without the voice of another.

Because they do not arise [as Buddhas], and because these [Paccekabuddhas] do not fully awaken to the Truths by way of being a support for others as the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) does, but rather, having become independent, they penetrate the Truths without being leaders;
therefore it is said: "They are Paccekabuddhas because they have awakened to the Truths individually."
“Itīti” means that which is made or uttered; thus, it is the word *iti*. The intention is that it has the sense of a reason (*kāraṇattha*) in an unrestricted form;
therefore, it is said “*yasmā cā*” (and because). Previously, however, the word *iti* was taken in the sense of a manner (*pakārattha*), as in “having known thus”;
here too, it is appropriate to take it in that same sense of manner. How so? [As in] “having understood.”

Indeed, the word *hi* should be understood here in the sense of a reason (*hetuatthe*), as in such expressions as “having seen with wisdom” (*paññāya cassa disvā*) or “having drunk ghee, strength arises.
Therefore, even when the word *iti* has the sense of a manner (*pakāratthe*), the meaning “because dependent origination has been understood” is certainly obtainable.
In the phrase “having understood dependent origination” (*paṭiccasamuppādaṃ viditvā*), the word *viditvā* likewise carries the sense of a reason as previously stated.

The interpretation of the meaning is indeed appropriate. Here, in the first alternative, having stated the reason for the absence of conceiving (*maññanā*) as being the state of knowing the meaning of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), it is shown that because dependent origination rooted in craving has been demonstrated, the abandoning of craving is indicated here as the cause for the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*);
therefore, the conclusion beginning with "he does not conceive of earth" follows.
It should be understood thus. However, in the second interpretation, it is stated that the feeling of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādavedanā) is the cause for the abandoning of craving;

this demonstrates the meaning that there is an absence of conceiving regarding enlightenment in relation to enlightenment itself. This is the distinction between these two alternative interpretations;
therefore, it is said: "Delight is the root of suffering."

Addressing the objection, "From where is that obtained?", he says, "In whatever place," and so forth. This is the methodological principle (*sāsanayutti*) because such a connection is seen even within the Dispensation (*sāsana*). For in the world as well, the inseparable relationship between the pronouns *yam* (which) and *tam* (that) is established.

He says, "I declare that he has thus fully awakened," because the state of having attained full awakening is what is grasped there; and because it would be impossible for one who is not omniscient to teach in this manner, he says, "Displaying the knowledge of omniscience," and so forth.

"Endowed with the elegance of teaching through various methods" means it is endowed with: (1) various textual methods (*tanti-naya*) distinguished by the divisions such as the section on worldlings (*puthujjana-vāra*);

(2) various methods of meaning (*attha-naya*) distinguished by the divisions such as characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*kamma*), craving (*taṇhā*), and conceiving (*maññanā*); and (3) the elegance of teaching established by the specific designations of rejoicing (*abhinandana*), the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), and so forth.
By the phrase "he taught in such a way that they did not understand," this too refers specifically to the elegance of the Blessed One’s teaching.
He contemplates it. Regarding the phrase "that very earth," here the mention of "earth" is merely illustrative, as it applies by way of water and so forth as well.
Furthermore, their doubt should be resolved by considering such questions as: "What kind of earth is intended here?
Why are only the primary material phenomena (bhūtarūpa) mentioned, and not the remaining material phenomena? Alternatively, how are they named?
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "manner. By this, it should be understood that all the arising of their doubts is encompassed within this sutta.
*Anta* means a boundary; the meaning is the limit or demarcation of the teaching, which is called the "connection" (*anusandhi*).
*Koṭi* means the extreme limit; the meaning is the conclusion of the teaching. By both [terms], the connection of intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*) within the sutta is indicated.
He says, "according to the connection.

"An intermediate talk" (*antarākathā*) refers to some other discourse occurring between the attention to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), the recitation (*uddesa*), or the interrogation (*paripucchā*).

"A digression" (*vippakathā*) means one that is unfinished and has not reached its conclusion. "According to the occasion for doubt" (*kaṅkhaṇānurūpena*) refers to those assembled at the Dhamma assembly at that very moment.
"In accordance with the inclinations of the bhikkhus. "This" refers to the *Mūlapariyāya-jātaka* which is now being spoken of.
"Famous in all directions" means one who has become preeminent in all quarters due to his wisdom. "Brāhmaṇa":
he is called a brāhmaṇa because he "breathes forth the *brahman*" (*brāhmaṃ aṇati*), meaning he recites the mantras. "Of the three Vedas" refers to the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, and the *Sāmaveda*.
"Pāragū" means one who has gone to the further shore, the limit, both in terms of meaning and phrasing.
"Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhā" means together with the *nighaṇḍu* and the *keṭubha*; [it refers to] those. *Nighaṇḍu* is the treatise that elucidates synonyms for trees and so forth.
*Keṭubha* is the elaboration of ritual procedures, the treatise that provides assistance to poets. "Together with the analysis of syllables" (*saha akkharappabhedenā*)...

"Of those [Vedas] classified according to their phonemes (sakkharappabheda)," the meaning is: "of those together with their training rules (sikkhā) and etymologies (nirutti). Regarding the phrase "with Itihāsa as the fifth":

having made the Āthabbana Veda the fourth, "Itihāsa"—which consists of ancient narratives connected with such expressions as "Thus it was said (itiha asa), thus it was said (itiha asā)"—is the fifth of these;
thus they are "those for whom Itihāsa is the fifth. It proclaims the word and the remaining grammar.
One who recites and understands is a master of words, an expert in exegesis (*veyyākaraṇa*). *Lokāyata* refers to the science of caviling (*vitaṇḍasattha*).

The *Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa* is a treatise that elucidates the characteristics of Great Beings, such as the Buddhas. One who is not deficient in these and who fulfills them completely is called "without deficiency" (*anavaya*).
*Manta* refers to the Vedas. Although the Veda is threefold—namely *manta*, *brahma*, and *kappa*—only the *manta* is the root Veda.

The *brahma* is the exposition of its meaning; therein, the prescription for the performance of sacrifice according to the stated method is the *kappa*. Thus it is said: “In the *manta*, that is, in the Veda.

“Wise” means possessing wisdom (*paññā*). For they, by virtue of their broad wisdom, make manifest and grasp—meaning they master—a vast amount of text measuring many thousands, such as two thousand verses and so forth;
and by virtue of their fleet-footed wisdom, they grasp it quickly and swiftly.
Because of their sharp wisdom, they investigate thoroughly without failing;
and because of their perfection in mindfulness and equanimity, what has been grasped by them neither perishes nor is forgotten.

"All crafts" refers to everything that has come to be reckoned as a craft in the sense of being something to be learned—namely, the eighteen branches of knowledge and so forth—including even the external sciences that are considered to lead to liberation.
Because it does not bring about liberation, he said, "beneficial for this life and the future.
"Having become united" means having gathered together in a compact manner, just as friends do. Thinking, "If it were grasped in this way, it would conflict with the beginning;
if in this way, it would conflict with the end," one should reach a conclusion that is consistent from beginning to end regarding the meaning intended to be known.
Being unable to grasp it, they did not see its beginning nor its end.
"Lomasāni" means possessing body hair; the meaning is that they have thick hair on their heads and beards. For even head-hair is included under the term "body hair," as in the expression:
"Purity is to be achieved by touching [removing] the hair and nails. "Kaṇṇaṃ viya" means "like the ear"; "kaṇṇa" here refers to wisdom (*paññā*); having heard by means of that [wisdom].
It is said, “One who has ears is one who possesses wisdom,” because it accomplishes what ought to be done.

Since the lifespan, beauty, and other qualities of sentient beings diminish as time passes, it is therefore said, “it devours their lifespan...,” treating that [time] as if it were an agent acting over a period.

“Having fully understood” means having understood the Dhamma to be taught—distinguished by categories such as the wholesome and so forth, or the aggregates and so forth—as well as the dispositions, latent tendencies, conduct, and liberation of those to be trained.

And having understood, as it truly is, the nature of what ought to be taught to them, I teach the Dhamma; that is, I speak the True Dhamma which brings about welfare pertaining to this present life, the future life, and Nibbāna.

"Not without direct knowledge" means: unlike those outsiders who, because they are not Fully Enlightened Ones, do not know the aforementioned method and thus speak whatever is struck by mere logic, followed by mere inquiry, or produced by their own ingenuity.
"I do not teach" is the meaning. "With its source" (*sanidāna*) means with its cause;

or, according to the inclination of those to be trained, or by way of a question, or by way of the occasion for the teaching, it means with its sign, accompanied by reasons and examples. "With its demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) means with its escape and with its counteracting;
the meaning is that I teach having made it truly demonstrative by means of the counteracting of opposition. Others [explain it differently].

However, some say that [the teaching] is "accompanied by the miracles of psychic power, reading minds, and instruction according to what is appropriate," yet there is no teaching that is devoid of the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
Instruction (*ovāda*) is teaching for one's benefit; that itself is the instruction (*anusāsanī*).

Alternatively, instruction concerns matters not yet entered into [by the listener], while instruction (*anusāsanī*) concerns matters already entered into. Or else, the first teaching is instruction (*ovāda*), and the other is the instruction (*anusāsanī*).
"Enough indeed" is appropriate. "He reached the conclusion" means he attained the accomplishment of the purpose.
The commentary on the eighth method of the section on the Tathāgata is finished.
This, then, is the commentary on the hidden meaning according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Commentary on the Guide (Nettippakaraṇa):
Now we shall provide an exposition of the meaning of the text according to the method of this treatise.

Furthermore, this exposition of the meaning becomes much easier and more readily understood once the origin, purpose, and receptacle of the teaching, as well as its summarized meaning, have been determined.
Therefore, we shall first determine the origin and other factors of the Sutta teaching. In this regard, the origin is the arising of conceit based on the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*);
the purpose is the crushing of conceit. For it is said in the Commentary: “He undertook the study of the scriptures...
[etc.]…” Furthermore, for those to be trained (*veneyya*), there exists the personality-view (*sakkāya*) which is divided into the categories of earth and so forth, and the elements and so forth.

The origin [of this treatise] is the lack of understanding regarding the distinction in the occurrence of the worldling and the noble ones—beginning with those in training—by way of conceiving and non-conceiving along with their causes;
its purpose is the understanding of the aforementioned distinctions.

For indeed, the purpose for those to be trained is the understanding of the distinction in the occurrence of the aforementioned types of persons by way of conceiving and non-conceiving along with their causes, with respect to the subject matter described above.
Furthermore, "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) refers to the source of the teaching. That is twofold: common and uncommon.
Therein, the common [origin] is also twofold, distinguished as internal and external. Among these, the common internal origin is the Great Compassion of the Lord of the World.
For it is by being impelled by that [Compassion] that the Blessed One undertakes the teaching of the Dhamma to those who are to be trained.
The thought arose. It was with reference to this that it was said: "Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye," and so forth.

And here, even at this stage, the inclusion of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) should be understood, because it arises for the purpose of ferrying beings across the great flood of *saṃsāra* by extending the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma. Just as...
And likewise, great compassion, as well as the knowledge of omniscience, the ten powers of knowledge, and so forth, should be described as having their internal origin in the act of teaching.

For the Blessed One, knowing all knowable phenomena, the various ways in which they are to be taught, and the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings exactly as they are, delivers diverse methods of instruction in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained, through his skill regarding what is possible and impossible and other such matters.
"He set it in motion. However, the external, common origin was the entreaty of the Great Brahmā Sahampati, who was surrounded by a retinue of ten thousand Brahmās.

For after that entreaty, the Master of Dhamma, having allayed the indolence born from reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, became intent upon teaching the Dhamma. The uncommon [origin], moreover, is divided into internal and external.
It is indeed twofold. Therein, the internal [aspect] should be understood as both that great compassion and that knowledge of teaching by which this sutta was set in motion.
The external [aspect], however, is the arising of conceit among five hundred monks of brahmin birth on account of their mastery of the scriptures; that has already been stated in the commentary.
The purpose (*payojana*) is also twofold: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).

Therein, the common purpose extends in sequence up to final Nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*), owing to the savor of liberation found in the Blessed One’s teaching. For this very reason, it is said: “This is the aim of the Tathāgata;

this is the aim of his counsel,” and so forth. By this alone, there is the cessation of the wheel of saṃsāra, the setting in motion of the Wheel of the True Dhamma, and the refutation of false doctrines such as eternalism.
Having right speech as its primary aim, it uproots the unwholesome roots, establishes the wholesome roots, closes the doors to the states of misery, opens the gates to heaven and liberation,
pacifies the outbursts of defilements, eradicates the underlying tendencies, fulfills the original promise by saying "I am freed,
I shall liberate others," thwarts the desires of Māra and his adversaries, and crushes the doctrines of the heretics.
The inclusion of purposes such as "establishing [others] in the Buddha’s Dhamma" and so forth should be understood here.
However, what is unique is the crushing of the pride of those monks. And this has been stated in the Commentary:

"The Blessed One, skilled in teaching, began the discourse titled 'The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena' for the purpose of breaking their pride. Both of these [purposes] apply specifically to Bāhiya alone.
If, however, one were to consider even that purpose residing within the mental continuum of those to be trained— which is termed the accomplishment of the power of the teaching—
as indeed the purpose of the Compassionate Blessed One himself, because it consists in the fulfillment of his intention through the achievement of the intended goal,
then by this method its status as internal [to the Buddha] should also be understood.

Furthermore, the origin [of the teaching] is the failure of those to be trained—both the worldling and the noble ones, whether trainees or otherwise—to understand the distinction in the way conceiving occurs through the presence of causes within the person (sakkāya), which is divided by the classifications of earth and so forth, as well as the elements and so forth.
The purpose of this sutta is the understanding of the aforementioned distinctions; this meaning has already been stated. For, in the case of those to be trained in the manner described...

The comprehension of the distinctions in the modes of occurrence of conceiving and non-conceiving—along with their causes—in the case of the persons described above as they relate to objects, serves as the motive for this teaching;
for it is said that "a teaching has as its ultimate purpose the accomplishment of that [comprehension].
Indeed, whatever fruit is to be achieved by a teaching is called its "motive" (payojana), because the teacher is impelled toward the teaching by the desire for that fruit. Likewise:
It is the non-abandonment of conceivings by those susceptible to instruction, both entirely and partially; the failure to see the danger therein;
the lack of knowledge regarding the specific modes of occurrence within the five aggregates (sakkāya) through the various expressions of unrestrained conceivings;
the lack of knowledge regarding the practice for those whose conceivings have been abandoned therein; and the lack of comprehension of the structure of conditions by way of craving.
And such purposes as these should be understood here.

Those who do not know the practice of the Fully Enlightened One regarding the functions—such as the full understanding (pariññā) of unconditioned phenomena and the non-manifestation of conditioned phenomena—within the three planes;

who are intent upon hearing, retaining, and familiarizing themselves with what is not the True Dhamma, and are averse to hearing, retaining, familiarizing themselves with, and penetrating the True Dhamma; [for them...]
And those to be trained are the vessels for this teaching. As for the meaning of the summary, however:

by the passage beginning with "the uninstructed," [it refers to] the frequent application of improper attention, association with the roots of unwholesomeness, being encompassed by sluggishness and restlessness, intensification of that which is not bound by skillful means, possession of wrong adherence, the lack of purification from ignorance and craving, the non-cessation of the three rounds of existence, and the non-separation from the taints, floods, yokes, ties, underlying tendencies, the arising of craving, and the clingings.
The ploughing up of the fallow land of the mind, the bondage of the mind, delighting in [sensual] objects, the failure to transcend the hindrances, the non-abandonment of the roots of dispute,

the non-eradication of underlying tendencies, the failure to transcend false states, dependence on phenomena rooted in craving, engagement in unwholesome courses of action, and the state of body and mind being agitated by the fever of all defilements—
these and other such things are thus illustrated. By the passage beginning with “One perceives earth as earth,” there is a description of the wanderings of craving.
Conceit, lamentation, adherence to perversity, defilement, the grasping of a self-identity, the designation of the characteristics of a fool, the pursuit of manifesting the three crookednesses,

the illumination of the opposites of what is beneficial, the indication of the three kinds of reliance, and the discourse on the destruction of the taints— these and others are thus elucidated. This concludes the commentary on the sixteen modes of exposition.
1. Commentary on the Section on Teaching:

In this context, those designations (paññatti) based upon the phenomena of the aggregates of clinging—which are divided into the primary elements such as earth and so forth—are spoken of by way of their function of establishing designations and by way of the specific suffering of birth, aging, and death;
these phenomena of the three planes, excluding craving, constitute the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).

Craving, as described by way of conceiving (*maññanā*), delighting (*abhinandanā*), and relishing (*nandī*), is the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). This, first of all, is the method according to the Suttas.

In the method of the Abhidhamma, however, it includes not only the aforementioned craving, but also ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest as illustrated by the passage beginning with "the uninstructed person" (*assutavā*);

the pride and views included under the term "conceiving"; and the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) included under the term "existence" (*bhava*). All these together constitute [the truth of origination].
The defilements and volitional formations are the truth of origination. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation.

The truth of the path is indicated by the mention of noble states, by the mentions of full understanding, the bhikkhu, those in training, and direct knowledge, and by the mention of perfect enlightenment.
However, some extract the truth of cessation from the mentions of the destruction of craving and so forth; that [interpretation] is not in accordance with the Commentary.
There is no contradiction here, because the function of the path—consisting of the destruction of craving and so forth—has been explicitly set forth.
In this context, gratification is shown by way of the origin, danger by way of suffering, and escape by way of the path and cessation;
the fruit is the shattering of the conceit of those bhikkhus; and likewise, the purpose is that which was stated as "the realization of the aforementioned divisions," and so on.
Because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that [understanding], the variety of the teaching is the means for determining the true nature of the four types of persons as they really are.
Furthermore, by way of showing the activity of worldlings and others regarding earth and so forth, this is the Blessed One’s instruction here:
"Earth and so forth must be fully understood in every respect, and conceiving (maññanā) must be abandoned. This is the "Teaching Mode" (desanā-hāra).
2. Explanation of the Mode of Conveying Investigation (Vīmaṃsā-hāra):
The inclusion of the term "all" is because conceiving (maññanā) is the cause for the non-distinction of individuality (sakkāya), and because nothing therein remains unexhausted.

The inclusion of the term "dhammas" is because they maintain their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), and because they are devoid of a sentient being and a life-principle (nissatta-nijjīva). [The inclusion of the term "bases"] is because they lack a foundation and because they serve as unique causes.

The term *mūla* (root) is used because it is the primary cause and because it gives rise to the purpose of the teaching; the term *pariyāya* (method) is used because it is present and because it gives rise to the sense of a gift (*sampadāna*);
the word *vo* (you) is used because of their presence and because it gives rise to the sense of a recipient;

the address *bhikkhave* (O monks) is used because they possess such qualities and because they are brought face-to-face with the teaching; and the phrase *desessāmi* (I shall teach) is used because he is capable of teaching and for the sake of arousing mindfulness in them.
“Confessing” (*paṭijānanam*) refers to the state of having admitted what is to be confessed; and because one confesses according to that admission, there is the reference “that” (*tam*).
It is said “listen” (*suṇātha*) because it is something to be heard, and because it absolutely accomplishes the purpose of hearing.
It is said “carefully” (*sādhukam*) because it is to be honored, and because the goal is achieved only through careful practice. [It is said] because the Dhamma is to be attended to with the mind.

And because all attainments are dependent upon that, it is said, "Pay attention. Because the teaching has been fully understood, its state is clearly manifest, and because there is the possibility of a detailed exposition of its meaning, it is said, "I shall speak.
Because the word of the Blessed One is to be received with the head by the world including the devas, and because it accomplishes the intended purpose, it is said, "Thus."
It was said. Because the Teacher is the locus of supreme reverence, and because reverence toward him constitutes a sublime merit, it is said, "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*).
Because the monks were certain that he would act accordingly, and for the sake of rhetorical ornament, it is said, "indeed" (*kho*).
Because they had to acknowledge what was heard, and because they had practiced in that manner, it is said, "they replied" (*paccassosuṃ*), owing to the fact of direct perception.
It is called "this" because all [of it] is made into a single whole.
It is called "here" with reference to the world, because the person being spoken of is included within the world and has the world as his support.
It is called "unlearned" (assutavā) because of the absence of proficiency in penetration and the absence of proficiency in the scriptures.

He is called a "puthujjana" because he is separate (puthu) or because of his common state among people. He is called "ariya" because of his freedom from ignoble qualities and his possession of noble qualities.
Because of the absence of the practice that produces the state of an ariya, and because of the lack of skill and self-restraint therein, it is said, "one who has not seen the ariyas," and so forth.
[He is distinguished] by listening to the non-existent dhamma and possessing the existent dhamma, together with the virtuous (sabbhi).

And because it is from association that one becomes [a true person], it is said, "of good persons. Because of the absence of the practice that produces the state of a good person, and because of the absence of skill and self-control therein, it is said, "one who has not seen good persons," and so forth.
Since the conceivings based on earth are the root of the conceivings to be mentioned below, and of the conceptual proliferations (*papañca-saṅkhā*), [it is said]: "earth as earth..."
It is said, “he perceives. Because the blind worldling has not abandoned the notions of “I-making” and “mine-making” anywhere at all, it is said, “he conceives earth,” and so forth.

This is because [the person] was not previously grasped [as a distinct entity], because [the object] is grasped in its generality, and because the person shares the same objective nature as earth and the other elements.
And because it is obtainable, it is said, "whoever. Because that which was grasped without specification must be specified and identified, it is said, "he.
Because he perceives the fear in saṃsāra with particular intensity and because the destruction of the defilements is possible for him, it is said, "a bhikkhu.
Because he is endowed with the trainings and has attained the state of one in training, he is called "a sekha" (one in training).

It has been said. Because the arahantship to be attained by the mind has not yet been reached, and because it is still to be attained, it is called "one whose mind has not yet reached its goal" (*appattamānasa*).
Because it cannot be surpassed by anything else, and because it stands having transcended all that is suitable for transcendence, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).

Because it is secure and auspicious through yoga—that is, through meditation—and because it is free from the perils of the yoke of sensual desire and the rest, it is called "the security from bondage" (*yogakkhema*).
It is said. Because of the exertion toward the arising of desire, it is said "aspiring.
Because of dwelling entirely in all postures for that purpose—namely, in the dwelling of serenity (samatha), the dwelling of insight (vipassanā), and the divine dwelling—it is said "dwelling.
Having completely overcome, by means of knowledge, both the state of being further to be directly known and the state of being further to be fully understood for one in training (sekha)...

Because he knows, it is said that "he directly realizes" (*abhijānāti*). Because a trainee (*sekkha*) lacks any state of conceiving that has not been entirely abandoned, it is said that "he should not conceive.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained. Following this method, the analysis for all subsequent passages should be made.
For indeed, by following the *Aṭṭhakathā* and its commentary on the hidden meaning (*līnatthavaṇṇanā*), this matter can be understood.

We have not elaborated [on this] for fear of excessive prolixity, so that it may be discerned by the wise. Thus is the Mode of Conveying Investigation (vicaya-hāra) by way of the analysis of each term.
3. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Reasoning (yutti-hāra):
It is logical that personality (sakkāya) is the root of all conceivings (maññanā), because the diversity of the world is merely a conceptual construction.

The state of being a blind worldling (*puthujjana*) is appropriate for one devoid of the two kinds of erudition (*bāhusacca*), because his nature consists in the production of manifold defilements (*kilesa*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Or, the absence of the aforementioned types of erudition is appropriate for a worldling as described, because they exist when that [erudition] is present.
In this regard, it is appropriate for the uninstructed worldling to lack vision of the Noble Ones (*ariya*) and true persons (*sappurisa*), because he lacks the qualities that constitute a Noble One.
And because he has not seen and has not practiced the noble state, such perception as "I am earth," "earth is mine," or "another's earth" is appropriate for him regarding the earth,
since the notions of "I-making" and "mine-making" have not been entirely abandoned. For one who perceives in this way,
having grasped the earth by means of performing agriculture and so forth, it is in various ways...

The occurrence of conceiving is logical because conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhā*) has its source in perception (*saññā-nidāna*). For one who conceives, it is logical that the basis [of his existence] remains uncomprehended, since there can be no abandoning of conceiving without full comprehension (*pariññā*).
The same principle applies to such passages as “one perceives water as water,” and so forth.
For one whose training is incomplete, it is logical that the mind’s goal has not been reached, because the task has not yet been accomplished. This applies to the trainee (*sekha*).
For one who is mindful, the aspiration for security from bondage is appropriate because of the state of being intent upon that [goal].
Likewise, his direct knowledge (*abhijānanā*) of earth is appropriate because he acts with moderation regarding full understanding (*pariññā*) and abandoning (*pahāna*).

For that very reason, it is appropriate to say to him, "Do not conceive," because, just as with the full understanding of the object-base (*vatthu*), the abandoning of conceiving (*maññanā*) has not yet been completed. This applies to the learner (*sekkha*) regarding earth...

The state of being fully understood (*pariññeyyatā*) is appropriate because it is possible to fully understand [them] and because they have not been fully understood in every respect. The same method applies to such expressions as "water as water" and so forth.

For one who is endowed with arahantship and the like, the higher knowledge (*abhijānanā*) of earth and the other elements and the absence of conceiving (*maññanābhāva*) are appropriate because those phenomena have been analyzed (*saṅkhātadhammattā*), because all defilements have been abandoned in every respect, and for that very reason, his state of being free from lust (*vītarāgādibhāva*) and so forth [is appropriate]. From that...
And because dependent origination has been correctly penetrated—this is the Mode of Conveying Reason (yuttihāra).
4. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Footings (padaṭṭhānahāra):
The footing for any conceiving is personality (sakkāya); the footing for conceivings is unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra).
The absence of the two types of hearing is the proximate cause for the state of a blind worldling; that is the proximate cause for not seeing the Noble Ones;
that is the proximate cause for lack of skill in the Noble Dhamma; that is the proximate cause for lack of discipline in the Noble Dhamma.
The same method applies here as well regarding the phrase "not seeing true persons. The perversion of perception is the proximate cause for conceiving.

For the conceptual proliferation of designations has its source in perception (*saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā*). And among the various conceivings (*maññanā*), the conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*) is the proximate cause for the other types of conceiving, because of the statements:
"the agitation and vacillation of those who have fallen into craving" and "with craving as condition, there is clinging.

Furthermore, it is only for one who has fallen into craving that the mental chatter of pride, such as "I am superior," and so forth, occurs. Or rather, all conceivings whatsoever [arise from craving].
It is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for all conceivings (*maññanā*). For, according to the statement, “With clinging as condition, craving arises,” view is also the proximate cause of craving.
And because of the statement, “I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā,” and so forth, pride is also the proximate cause of view.

Likewise, according to the statement, “When there is the thought ‘I am,’ there occurs the thought ‘I am thus,’ there occurs the thought ‘I am such,’ there occurs the thought ‘I am otherwise,’” and so forth.
The state of being the proximate cause for conceit is indeed found in craving as well. The qualities of those in training (*sekha*) are the proximate cause for the partial abandonment of conceiving.
The qualities of those beyond training (*asekha*) are the proximate cause for the complete abandonment of conceiving. Kamma-existence is the proximate cause of birth.
Birth is the proximate cause of aging and death. The realization of the mode of conditions as they truly are is the proximate cause of perfect enlightenment.
“Basis” (padaṭṭhāna): this is the Mode of Conveying the Basis. 5. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra):
In the phrase “The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena,” by the mention of the “root” or by the mention of the “exposition of the root,” [it is shown] how craving, conceit, and views—

Just as [the term] "unlearned" includes the absence of both the scriptural and realized True Dhamma in that person, so too should the inclusion of the True Dhamma of practice be understood; for they share a single characteristic by virtue of being the True Dhamma.

Likewise, the inclusion of defilements such as hatred and delusion should be seen as pertaining to the factors rooted in identity (*sakkāya*), because they share a single characteristic by virtue of being roots of identity.

[It] has the characteristic of not wishing to see the Noble Ones and so forth. By the phrase "unskilled in the noble Dhamma," ignorance—which acts as an obstruction to the realization of the noble Dhamma—is indicated.
By the phrase "undisciplined in the noble Dhamma," the absence of noble discipline is indicated. Furthermore, in its actual meaning, this is simply non-practice according to the noble discipline;
thus, by all three terms, wrong view, doubt, and [the other defilements] regarding the aforementioned objects are indicated.
And they are indeed included. By that inclusion, all unwholesome states (akusala-dhammā) are also included, because they share the same characteristic of being defilements (saṃkilesa-lakkhaṇa).
The same method applies here to the phrase "one who does not see noble persons.
The statement "he perceives earth as earth" is a demonstration of how perception serves as the cause for the conceiving of views (diṭṭhi-maññanā) and so forth.

In this context, just as perception (*saññā*) is a cause of these [conceptions], so too are applied thought (*vitakka*), contact (*phassa*), ignorance (*avijjā*), improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), and so forth;
thus, by way of their being causes of conceptions, they are included here according to their actual meaning, since they share a single characteristic.

By the term "he conceives" (*maññati*), craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*) are included, because they have the nature of defilements (*kilesa*). By the inclusion of those very [defilements]...
The inclusion of doubt and the rest should also be understood, because they share the same characteristic as defilements (*kilesa*).

Likewise, because craving has the nature of a cause (*hetu*), by its inclusion alone the inclusion of all remaining unwholesome causes should be understood, because they share the same characteristic as causes.

Similarly, because craving and views have the nature of taints (*āsava*) and so forth, by their inclusion alone [the inclusion] of the remaining taints, floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), fetters (*gantha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and so on, should also be understood.
The inclusion [of all things] should be understood because they share the same characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇa*), owing to their nature as taints (*āsava*) and so forth.

Likewise, by the statement "one conceives of earth," etc., since earth and the other elements have the nature of form (*rūpa-sabhāva*), and since the conceivings (*maññanā*) directed toward them have form as their object, by the mention of those [elements], the conceivings that have the entire aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) as their object are also shown;
for they share the same characteristic as the desire (*āsa*) whose characteristic is having form as its object.
In this same way, the conceiving (*maññanā*) regarding the objects of the sense bases, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), and so forth, should also be determined.

Regarding the term "not fully understood" (*apariññāta*), it should be seen as a negation of the abandoning of the defilements bound up with that [object], by means of the negation of full understanding (*pariññā*). This is because, through the function of the Path, full understanding and abandoning possess a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇa*).
By this method, the single characteristic should be determined accordingly for the remaining cases as well. This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇo hāro*).
6. Explanation of the Catubyūha-hāra:

Having grasped the meaning based on the mere appearance of the words regarding such subjects as earth and so forth, and failing to perceive the profundity of the Dhamma, they become deceived by listening to what is not the true Dhamma and the like;
thus, they turn away from listening to the true Dhamma, from retaining it, from familiarizing themselves with it, and from reflecting upon it.

The introduction to this teaching is those to be trained who do not understand the distinction in practice among worldlings, trainees, non-trainees, and Tathāgatas regarding the bases such as earth and so forth.

[The Buddha’s intention was: "How indeed might they, being freed from the aforementioned faults and understanding the aforementioned distinction, proceed toward the welfare of both worlds through right practice? This is the Blessed One’s [purpose] in this regard.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Etymology (*nirutta*) is the analysis of words; it is [to be understood] according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and its *Līnatthavaṇṇanā* commentary regarding the introductory phrases such as "Thus" (*evaṃ*) and so forth, and the textual phrases such as "The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" (*Sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*), for fear of excessive prolixity, we have not elaborated upon them here, as they are easily understood through those works.

There are five kinds of connection (*sandhi*): by way of word (*pada*), word-meaning (*padattha*), teaching (*desanā*), arrangement (*nikkhepa*), and sutta. Among these, [the connection] of a word with another word...

Connection (*saṃbandha*) is the junction of words (*pada-saṃdhi*); likewise, the connection of the meaning of one word with the meaning of another word is "connection of meanings" (*padattha-saṃdhi*), which is called the "connection between action and its factors" (*kriyā-kāraka-saṃbandha*).

The connection of a discourse containing various transitions with those respective transitions is [transition of discourse], whereas for a discourse containing a single transition, the connection between what precedes and what follows is "transition of teaching" (*desanā-saṃdhi*). This is as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
It is analyzed in three ways: “connection by way of question, connection by way of intention, and connection according to the sequence.

Furthermore, in this context, intention should be understood as twofold: one’s own intention and the intention of another. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated below in the commentary on the *nidāna*.
Connection by way of presentation (*nikkhepa-sandhi*) is to be understood by means of the four modes of presenting a discourse (*sutta-nikkhepa*).
The connection between the suttas (*suttasaṇḍhi*) here should be understood by way of the first placement alone.
But why is the *Mūlapariyāyasutta* placed first here? This inquiry is not without application anywhere;

moreover, because identity-view (*sakkāya*) is rooted in conceiving (*maññanā*), and all conceiving occurs there divided into many different categories, and not [in the same way] for that which has its own specific object.

This teaching— which generates an extraordinary sense of disenchantment and dispassion toward the conceivings that differentiate earth and so forth, despite the fact that not even a trace of essence exists therein—
and which elucidates the qualities of the trainees and the Tathāgata above—
is a discourse on the Suttanta that specifically unravels views; therefore, it demonstrates from the outset the lack of essence in the grasping of views together with its basis.
Furthermore, this sutta was placed first as a manifestation of the specific qualities of all the Noble Ones (ariya). Moreover,

it was placed first because it manifests the danger and the benefit regarding the process of proceeding and returning by way of the conceiving (maññanā) within the five aggregates of clinging (sakkāya),
and because it distinguishes the practice of all individuals.
Furthermore, the correlation of one teaching with another teaching is also a "connection of teaching" (*desanā-sandhi*), which should be understood as follows:
"This unlearned worldling... [omitted] ...rejoices in *nibbāna*"—this is one teaching.
"In this case, monks, the unlearned worldling... [omitted] ...is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true person regarding what should be attended to..."—this is another teaching.
He does not understand phenomena that should be attended to, and he does not understand phenomena that should not be attended to.
Not understanding phenomena that should be attended to and not understanding phenomena that should not be attended to, he attends to those phenomena that should not be attended to...
[and so on] ...either the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, or the arisen taint of sensual desire increases.

This accords with the teaching: “Either the taint of existence that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of existence that has already arisen increases; either the taint of ignorance that has not yet arisen arises, or the taint of ignorance that has already arisen increases. Likewise:
“It is to be expected that he will attend to the sign of the beautiful; from attending to the sign of the beautiful, lust [arises].”
This accords with the teaching: "If one does not restrain the mind, it will become agitated; thus, with lust, hatred, delusion, blemish, and a defiled mind, one will pass away.
Likewise: "Friends, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises. What one feels, that one perceives; what one perceives..."

This accords with the teaching: "He thinks about that; what he thinks about, he proliferates; what he proliferates, from that as a source, the tendencies toward conceptual proliferation assail the person.
Likewise: "Here, monks, the uninstructed worldling...
not trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, regards form thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'"
One regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as "this is mine, this am I, this is my self.
Furthermore, regarding that which is seen... [and so on] ...regarding that basis for views, one thinks: "That is the world, that is the self;
after death I shall become permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same for all eternity."
This accords with the teaching: “He too regards it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.

And this is the teaching: “Bhikkhus, even that bhikkhu... do not delight in Nibbāna. “In this case, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘All phenomena are not worth adhering to. And so it is, Lord of Devas.”
When it has been heard by a bhikkhu that "all phenomena are not worth adhering to," he directly knows all phenomena;
having directly known all phenomena, he fully understands them;
having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he contemplates those feelings as impermanent.
This accords with the teaching: “He dwells contemplating fading away, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment.
And this teaching—“That monk, bhikkhus, who is an arahant... I say he is fully enlightened”—accords with the teaching:
“But the well-taught noble disciple, bhikkhus... [dwells] in accordance with the Dhamma of the true person.”
One who is well-disciplined regards form as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards feeling... [and so on] ...perception... [and so on] ...volitional formations... [and so on] ...consciousness as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, attained, sought after, or explored by the mind—that too one regards as: "This is not mine..."
He regards it thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

Even regarding that basis for views—namely, "That world, that self, shall become after death eternal, stable, everlasting, not subject to change, remaining just so for all eternity"—he regards even that thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
"Thus, seeing it in this way, one does not become agitated"—it is through such teachings that [this method] is brought into harmony; this is the Fourfold Array (catubyūha) method.
7. Commentary on the Method of Turning Back (āvattahāra):
By the phrase "the uninstructed worldling," there is an inclusion of improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) by way of the rejection of proper attention (yoniso-manasikāra).

It is illuminated. By the passage beginning with “one who does not see the noble ones,” the embracing of bad persons and so forth is illuminated by way of the rejection of reliance upon good persons and so forth.
Among these, by the first method, the failure of the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) is described; by the second, the failure of the application (*payoga*).

By the former, the cycle of defilements (*kilesa-vatta*) is indicated, and from that, the cycle of kamma-result (*vipāka-vatta*)—whereby the entire wheel of saṃsāra revolves. “The earth... [and so on].

By the passage beginning with "he conceives" (*maññati*), three kinds of conceiving (*maññanā*) are stated therein. Among these, conceiving by craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*) is the grasping of craving as "this is mine";
conceiving by conceit (*mānamaññanā*) is the grasping of conceit as "I am this"; and conceiving by view (*diṭṭhimaññanā*) is the grasping of views as "this is my self.
Therein, through the grasping of craving, nine states rooted in craving—beginning with "dependent on craving, there is seeking"—recur.
By means of the grasping of conceit, the nine types of conceit beginning with "I am superior" recur.
By means of the grasping of views, the twenty-based personality view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) beginning with "one regards form as self" recurs.
And among the three types of grasping, that perception by which the grasping of craving is suppressed is the perception of suffering, the contemplation of suffering. By means of that perception—
The suppression of the grasping at conceit is the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), which is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).

However, that perception by which the grasping at views is suppressed is the perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*), which is the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*). In this regard, from the dissimilarity to the first grasping, it turns toward the door of liberation of the wishless (*appaṇihita-vimokkhamukha*);
from the dissimilarity to the second grasping, it turns toward the door of liberation of the signless (*animitta-vimokkhamukha*); and from the dissimilarity to the third grasping...
It turns toward the gateway to liberation that is emptiness.
By the inclusion of the "trainee" (sekha), noble right view is comprised;
by that, the hearing of another's voice and wise attention are illuminated. Through the hearing of another's voice, one turns into a learned noble disciple, and through wise attention—
Nine states rooted in appropriate attention recur, as does the fourfold wheel of excellence.

By the inclusion of the phrase “let him not conceive,” which signifies the abandonment of conceiving in its unfinished state, the destruction of certain taints (*āsava*) is illustrated; and along with that, the states of one liberated by faith, one attained to vision, and the body-witness recur.

By the passage beginning “an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed,” the aggregates of virtue and so forth of the non-learner (*asekha*) are shown, through the perfection of the aggregate of virtue and the rest.

And the ten qualities that make one a protector recur here. By the negation of conceiving in the phrase "he does not conceive," the correct practice regarding the five aggregates of clinging—namely, "this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—is shown;
and by that, the complete exhaustion of attachment, the eradication of the mind [of craving], and the removal of views are especially demonstrated.
The wishless, signless, and emptiness liberations recur.

By the passage beginning with “The Tathāgata,” the qualities of omniscience are manifested; because they are inseparable from that [omniscience], the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the unique knowledge, and the uncommon Buddha-qualities recur.
By the passage beginning with “Craving is the root of suffering,” the cycle of existence and its cessation are explained together with their causes.
The four noble truths revolve through the discernment of the causes for both occurrence and cessation.
By the phrase "through the destruction of craving" and so forth, the abandoning of one thousand five hundred defilements is implied, as they are associated with that [craving].
Furthermore, this is because it is stated: "Through the complete destruction of all cravings, he fully awakened to perfect enlightenment."

By the statement beginning with “‘Delight is the root of suffering,’ having understood thus,” the fact that the experience of the mode of conditions—which is the cause for the absence of conceiving—is a range of knowledge not shared by disciples is demonstrated;

thereby, the Blessed One’s great diamond-like knowledge, which traverses the four hundred and twenty-four million meditative attainments, turns back. This is the “Turning Back” (āvatta) method of interpretation.
8. Explanation of the Analysis:
Regarding the phrase “the exposition of the root of all phenomena,” here “all phenomena” refers to the phenomena of the three planes, since it is the personality-group (sakkāya) that is intended.
The basis for conceiving them is the sign of conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā-nimitta), because of the world’s diversity. These are the wholesome and unwholesome [phenomena].

The indeterminate (*abyākata*) is threefold. Among these, the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the wholesome is wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth; for the unwholesome, it is unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) and so forth;

and for the indeterminate, it is kamma, existence, adverting, and derived matter (*bhūtarūpa*), and so forth. Therein, the wholesome are threefold according to plane by way of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so on; likewise are the indeterminate. However, those that are not associated with consciousness (*acittuppāda*) are exclusively of the sense-sphere.

Likewise, there are unwholesome states (*akusala*). The "unlearned" (*assutavā*) is threefold by way of the absence of the functions of learning (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), penetration (*paṭivedha*), and hearing (*suta*).

The "worldling" (*puthujjana*) is twofold according to the distinction between the blind and the virtuous. The "noble ones" (*ariya*) are threefold through the division of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), the Solitary Buddha (*Paccekabuddha*), and the Disciple (*Sāvaka*).

The "one who does not see" (*adassāvī*) is threefold by way of the absence of vision through the eye of flesh (*maṃsacakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). The noble Dhamma (*ariyadhamma*) is threefold—consisting of the Path (*magga*), Fruition (*phala*), and Nibbāna—or ninefold.
There are five kinds of proficiency in the noble Dhamma by way of hearing, retention, familiarity, attention, and penetration;
one who lacks these is unskilled. The noble Dhamma-Vinaya is twofold—by way of restraint and abandonment—or tenfold;
one who lacks this is undisciplined in the noble Dhamma. Here, the analysis of the proximate causes has already been shown below. [Regarding] "of true persons..."

The same method applies to such passages as "one who does not see" (*adassāvī*). In the passages beginning with "he conceives the earth" (*pathaviṃ maññati*), the classification of the bases for conceiving (*maññanāvatthu*) is already presented in the Canon;
likewise is the internal classification beginning with the internal and external [bases].
As for conceiving (*maññanā*), it is briefly threefold by way of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*); but in detail, there is the conceiving of craving (*taṇhāmaññanā*).
To that extent, craving for sensual pleasures (kāmataṇhā) is of eight hundred kinds; likewise, conceit and estimation (mānamaññanā) are also [eight hundred kinds] according to such passages as:

"When there is the thought 'I am,' there occurs the thought 'I am thus,'" and so forth. By the passage beginning with "When there is the thought 'I am,' there occurs the thought 'I am thus,'" the three types of conceptual proliferation (papañca) are both mentioned and explained.
By this, it should be understood that the view-estimation (diṭṭhimaññanā) is also stated to be of eight hundred kinds. Furthermore, ...
The ninefold nature of the conceit of "I am superior" and so forth regarding one who is superior, as well as its manifold nature through internal subdivisions, should be understood.
This meaning is to be clarified in the commentary on the section concerning inferiority.
Furthermore, the sixty-two-fold nature of the conceit of views, as presented in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, and its manifold nature through internal subdivisions, should be understood.

Regarding the term “not fully understood” (*apariññāta*): here, the manifold nature of full understanding should be understood both by way of the types of full understanding such as understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), etc., and by way of the distinctions in misapprehension such as the obsession with form, etc. Likewise, there is the classification of those in training (*sekha*) by way of the eighth person and so forth, and the classification of those beyond training (*asekha*) by way of those liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), etc.
This is the analysis of the factors (*dhamma*) herein. Furthermore, there is the analysis of the proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*) and the analysis of the planes (*bhūmi*).
"It should be understood according to the method already stated. This is the Mode of Analysis (vibhattihāra).
9. Commentary on the Mode of Reversal (parivattahāra):
In the phrase "The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*), "all phenomena" (*sabbadhammā*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*). Of these...
And the root causes are craving, conceit, and views. Thus, the uninstructed worldling... [as before] ...is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones.

As long as the grasping of craving, conceit, and views—by way of regarding the five aggregates of clinging as beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and self, thinking "this is mine, this I am, this is my self"—is not utterly cut off, so long...
For them, there was no superior continuity of such a kind ever before obtained even in a dream. But when, through the contemplation of things as foul,
as suffering, as impermanent, and as non-self— in the form of "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—
the contemplations of the wishless, the signless, and the voidness, having exerted themselves for the attainment of the Noble Path, proceeded;
They proceed until, because they reach a state of absolute non-designation, there is for them a cessation of the continuity [of existence].
Therefore it was said: "By 'all phenomena' the five aggregates of clinging are included; and their root cause is craving, conceit, and views.
Likewise, the uninstructed worldling... being undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, conceives of the earth through all three types of conceiving.
As long as one delights even in Nibbāna, that object remains uncomprehended by him through the three kinds of full comprehension (*pariññā*).

However, for one by whom that object has been fully comprehended through the three kinds of full comprehension, he does not conceive of it in the same way as the other. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"But, monks, the well-taught noble disciple... well-trained in the Dhamma of the True Person... [regards] form..."
“One regards it thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. [One regards] feeling... [and so on] ...being without craving, one does not tremble.

A trainee should not conceive of earth, nor should he rejoice in anything up to Nibbāna; and an Arahant and a Perfectly Enlightened One do not conceive of earth, nor do they rejoice in anything up to Nibbāna.
In regard to the things that are objects of conceiving, whether partially or entirely...
And because the realization of abandonment is produced through the successful realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*).
But for one who lacks even complete or partial full understanding regarding those bases, how could there be abandonment?

Such a person, according to their own conceptualization, conceives by means of unrestrained imaginings, thinking "this is mine," and so forth. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Here, monks, the uninstructed..."
“The worldling... not trained in the Dhamma of the true person, regards form as ‘this is mine, this am I, this is my self’;
he regards feeling... perception... and so forth. This is the Mode of Conveying Reversal (Parivattahāra). 10. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra)

“‘All phenomena’ (sabbadhammā), ‘entire phenomena’ (sakaladhammā), and ‘phenomena without remainder’ (anavasesadhammā)” are synonymous expressions; “‘The exposition of the root’ (mūlapariyāya), ‘the root cause,’ and ‘the uncommon cause’” are synonymous expressions;
“‘The exposition of the root’ (mūlapariyāya) or ‘the teaching on the root,’ ‘the teaching on the cause’” are synonymous expressions;
“‘Vo’ means ‘to you’ (tumhākaṃ tumhaṃ)” is a synonymous expression; “‘O bhikkhus,’ ‘recluses,’ ‘ascetics’” [are synonymous expressions].
“‘I shall teach,’ ‘I shall speak,’ ‘I shall describe’—these are synonymous expressions;
‘Listen,’ ‘Lend an ear,’ ‘Attend by means of the door of the ear’—these are synonymous expressions; ‘Well,’ ‘Properly,’ ‘Carefully’—these are synonymous expressions;
‘Apply the mind,’ ‘Fix it in the heart,’ ‘Direct your attention’—these are synonymous expressions.”

“I shall speak,” “I shall discourse,” and “I shall analyze” are synonymous expressions; “So be it, venerable sir,” “Excellent, venerable sir,” and “Very well, venerable sir” are synonymous expressions;
“They listened,” “they accepted,” and “they received” are synonymous expressions.
In this manner, synonyms should be stated for all terms. This is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra).

11. Explanation of the Conveying of Designation (*Paññattihāra*) Regarding the phrase "The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*): here, "all phenomena" (*sabbadhammā*) refers to the phenomena of personal existence (*sakkāyadhammā*).

These are designated in five ways by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), in twelve ways by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), and in eighteen ways by way of the elements (*dhātu*). "Root" (*mūla*)— [...]*

Or, the conceiving (*maññanā*) expressed as "the Exposition of the Root" (*mūlapariyāya*) is designated in three ways by way of craving, conceit, and views, and in many ways through their internal subdivisions.

Alternatively, "all phenomena" (*sabbadhammā*) is a designation for the inclusion of phenomena belonging to the three planes; "Exposition of the Root" (*mūlapariyāya*) is a designation for their origin;
"to you" (*vo*) is a designation for the recipient; and "I shall teach, I shall speak" (*desessāmi bhāsissāmi*) [is a designation for the act of teaching].
The designation by admission; the designation as an injunction, namely, “Listen and pay close attention”;

the designation as being averse to realization and the designation as being averse to the scriptures, namely, “the uninstructed”; the designation as ignoble, namely, “the worldling,” which is both the designation of the rejection of the noble Dhamma and the designation of the absence of the noble Dhamma; and [the designation] “of the noble ones.”
There is both non-uniform designation (*asama-paññatti*) and uniform designation (*sama-paññatti*). Among these, non-uniform designation is the designation of the Tathāgata;

uniform designation should be understood as eightfold, by way of the Paccekabuddhas and those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*), etc. The phrase beginning with “one who has not seen the Noble Ones” (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*) is a designation by way of the negation of seeing and cultivation (*dassana-bhāvanā*);
the phrase beginning with “he conceives of earth” (*pathaviṃ maññati*) [is a designation] of the five...

There is the designation of relinquishment and the designation of origin regarding the aggregates of clinging, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the faculties that come under comprehension; likewise, there is the designation of function regarding the perversions,
the designation of manifestation regarding the obsessions, the designation of fruit regarding the defilements, and the designation of growth regarding the formative activities.

The designation of the gratification of craving; the designation of the agitation of views; the designation of the vision and the designation of the development of those who are "trainers"—namely, the followers by faith, those liberated by faith, those who have attained vision, and body-witnesses;
the designation of the stability of the qualities of trainers in one who is "not yet attained in mind";
the designation of the penetration by wisdom in one who "aspires to the unsurpassed security from bondage"; and [the designation] of "directly knowing."

The designation of the states to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-dhamma*) as "to be directly known"; the designation of suffering as "to be fully understood" (*pariññā*); the designation of its origin as "to be abandoned" (*pahāna*);

the designation of cessation as "to be realized" (*sacchikiriyā*); the designation of the path as "to be developed" (*bhāvanā*); the designation of the negation of conceivings as "do not conceive" (*mā maññī*);
and the designation of the origin as "to be abandoned. In this manner, it should be expanded for the remaining terms as well. This is the Mode of Conveying Designation (*paññatti-hāra*).
12. Explanation of the Mode of Conveying Entry (*Otaraṇahāra-vaṇṇanā*) Regarding the phrase "the exposition of the root of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*):

here, "all phenomena" (*sabbadhammā*) refers to the five mundane aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*), the twelve bases (*dvādasāyatanāni*), the eighteen elements (*aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo*), the two truths (*dve saccāni*), the nineteen faculties (*ekūnavīsati indriyāni*), and the twelvefold formula of conditional relations (*paccayākāro*).

This is the introduction to the teaching by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, through the inclusion of all phenomena (*sabbadhamma*). Alternatively, what is called "the root" (*mūla*) or "the exposition of the root" (*mūlapariyāya*) refers to conceiving (*maññanā*);
in terms of meaning, these are craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*).

Since these are included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), this is the introduction by way of the aggregates. Likewise, the statement "inclusion by way of the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*)" is the introduction by way of the bases (*āyatana*).
And there is entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*). By the term "unlearned" (*assutavā*), ignorance (*avijjā*) and other factors that act as obstacles to learning are included.
By the term "worldling" (*puthujjana*), those defilements (*kilesa*) and volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) through whose generation and so forth one is called a worldling are included.
By the phrase "one who has not seen the noble ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*) and so forth, those defiled phenomena (*kilesadhamma*) [are included].
By way of these [defilements], there arises in the Noble Ones the state of being "one who has not seen the Noble Ones" and so forth;

since those views, conceits, ignorance, and so on are included, it should be understood that they are all comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), according to the method previously stated.

Regarding the passage, “He perceives, he conceives, he cognizes, he does not conceive,” here too, because perceiving, conceiving, cognizing, and contemplation are included within the aggregate of mental formations...

The entry [into the teaching] should be understood in the manner already stated. Likewise, by the mention of "those in training" (*sekkha*), the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those in training are included;

and by the mention of "the Worthy One" (*arahant*) and so forth, those beyond training (*asekkha*) are included. Thus, there is entry by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), and entry by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, should also be understood.
Similarly, by the negation of conceiving through craving and grasping in the phrase "he does not conceive," the contemplations on suffering and so forth are indicated.
By means of those [terms] taken up, one should understand the entry via the door of the wishless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) and so forth.

By the term "thoroughly understood" (*pariññāta*), the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) are grasped as they function through the duty of full comprehension; thus, one should understand the entry via the doors of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
Through the mention of delight (*nandi*), existence (*bhava*), and craving (*taṇhā*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*) is grasped.

By the mention of suffering (*dukkha*), by the mention of birth, aging, and death, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is grasped; by the phrase "through the destruction of cravings" (*taṇhānaṃ khayā*) and so forth, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is grasped;

and by the mention of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is grasped. Thus, there is an entry [into the teaching] by means of the Noble Truths. This is the Mode of Conveying the Entry (*otaraṇa-hāra*). 13.
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying the Purification (*sodhana-hāra*)
“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the exposition on the root of all phenomena... Here, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling...
perceives earth as earth. This is the introduction (*ārambha*). “Having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth [to be his].
This is the purification of the words (*padasuddhi*), not the purification of the introduction (*ārambhasuddhi*). Likewise: “He conceives [in] earth, he conceives [from] earth, he conceives earth...”
“He thinks ‘it is mine’ and delights in the earth”: this is purity of phrasing, not purity of undertaking. “For what reason? Because it is not fully understood by him, so I say”:
this is both purity of phrasing and purity of undertaking. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
This is the Mode of Conveying Purification (Sodhana-hāra).
14. Commentary on the Conveying of the Foundation (Adhiṭṭhānahāra):
In the phrase "The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*), the inclusion of "all phenomena" (*sabbadhamma*) is the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) in its general sense.

However, the specific expressions such as "earth, water," and so forth, are particularizations that do not diverge from that [general foundation]. Likewise, "Exposition of the Root" (*mūlapariyāya*) is the foundation in its general sense.
The resolution; not having differentiated that, there is the specific statement: "He conceives of earth... pe ... he delights in it.
And as for "he conceives of earth," this is the general resolution because conceiving is common to all types of grasping such as craving;
not having differentiated that, there is the specific statement: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Thus also the words of other Sutta passages [should be understood].
Having brought [the terms] together, the specific term must be determined. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well. "A trainee" (*sekha*) is a general designation;
without specifying that, the specific terms are "body-witness," "attained-to-view," "liberated-by-faith," "follower-by-faith," and "follower-of-dhamma.
Likewise, "a trainee" is a general designation; without specifying that—
The specific statement is: "In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with right view that is still in training...
[and so on] ...he is endowed with right concentration that is still in training. The term "arahant" is a general designation;

without specifying that, the specific statements are: "one liberated in both ways," "one liberated by wisdom," "one possessing the three true knowledges," and "one possessing the six direct knowledges."
“An arahant (khīṇāsava)” is a general designation; without specifying that, it is further qualified by the specific statement:

“The mind was liberated even from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the mind was liberated even from the taint of existence (bhavāsava),” and so forth. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
“He directly knows (abhijānāti)” is a general designation; without specifying that, it is further qualified by the specific statement: “he conceives (maññati).”

For the state of being free from conceiving (*maññanābhāva*) is established through the penetration of abandonment (*pahānapaṭivedha*), and the penetration of abandonment is not possible without the penetrations of full understanding, realization, and development.
Thus, all the specific super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) are effectively included by the negation of conceiving.
Likewise, "Arahant" is a designation in a general sense; without qualifying that, the specific statement is: "Because he is free from lust, because he is free from hatred..."

“Because of being free from delusion. In this manner, the determination of the general and the specific should be understood for the remaining terms as well. This is the Mode of Conveying the Foundation (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra).
14. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying the Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra):

Regarding the phrase “The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena,” here “all phenomena” refers to those phenomena included within the mundane (pariyāpanna), which are divided into the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

It is threefold. Among these, for wholesome states, the causes are wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth; for unwholesome states, the causes are unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) and greed (*lobha*) and so forth;

among the indeterminate, for resultant states, the cause is their respective karma, while for others, the causes are the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), adverting (*āvajjana*), and attention (*samannāhāra*), etc.
And herein, conditions such as reliance upon a true person (*sappurisūpanissaya*) are included within the category of "cause" itself; they are contained therein.
It should be understood that [the term] is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). The fact that the conceits mentioned as "roots" (*mūla*) serve as causes is indeed stated in the Canon itself.

Among the conceits, however, the conceit of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*) has the contemplation of gratification (*assādānupassanā*) as its cause; for it is said: "In one who contemplates gratification in things conducive to fettering (*saññojaniya-dhamma*), craving increases. The conceit of pride (*māna-maññanā*) has greed dissociated from views (*diṭṭhi-vippayutta-lobha*) as its cause.
The cause for [the conceit] "I am" is simply its occurrence by way of association. The cause for the conceit of views is the grasping of the principle of unity and so forth as they truly are not.
The cause for the state of being a worldling is the lack of hearing [the Dhamma]. That [lack of hearing] is caused by the habit of not seeing the Noble Ones;
that [habit] is caused by lack of proficiency in the Noble Dhamma; and that [proficiency] is caused by lack of discipline in the Noble Dhamma. And this entire succession of causes—

Regarding earth and the other [elements], these are the causes for the three types of conceiving (*maññanā*)—namely, "This is mine," "I am this," and "This is my self"—whereas the states of being a trainee (*sekkha*), one beyond training (*asekkha*), and so forth, are the causes for the partial and total absence of conceiving. This is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*).
16. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropana-hāra*)

In such passages as “The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena,” by the inclusion of the term “root-exposition,” by the inclusion of the term “the uninstructed person,” and by the inclusion of the terms “perception,” “conceit,” and “full understanding,” the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) are shown.

And these, in brief, are threefold: the defilement of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkilesa*), the defilement of views (*diṭṭhisaṃkilesa*), and the defilement of misconduct (*duccaritasaṃkilesa*). Therein, the defilement of craving [is the cause] of the defilement of craving and the defilement of views...

And misconduct is the proximate cause for the corruption of views; likewise, the corruption of views is the proximate cause for the corruption of craving, the corruption of misconduct, and the corruption of views;
and the corruption of misconduct is also the proximate cause for the corruption of misconduct, the corruption of craving, and the corruption of views.
Among these, the corruption of craving is [to be understood] by way of its meaning as...
Greed itself is the corruption of greed, which is analyzed through numerous synonyms such as: "greed, being greedy, the state of being greedy, lust, being lustful, the state of being lustful.
Likewise, view itself is the corruption of views, which is analyzed through numerous synonyms such as:
"a state of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, vacillation of views," and so forth. Furthermore, there are...
[This] is analyzed through sixty-two divisions, beginning with the words, "O monks, some recluses and brahmins...
