Furthermore, the corruption of misconduct (*duccarita-saṃkileso*), in terms of its meaning, consists of both unwholesome volition (*dussīlya-cetanā*) and the mental states associated with that volition;
it is described by many methods such as "misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, bodily irregularity, verbal irregularity," and "killing living beings, taking what is not given," and so forth.
And they are analyzed into many different categories.

Among these, serenity (*samatha*) is the antidote to the corruption of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa*), insight (*vipassanā*) is the antidote to the corruption of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa*), and virtue (*sīla*) is the antidote to the corruption of misconduct (*duccarita-saṃkilesa*).

Furthermore, those states such as virtue and the rest are included here by the mention of "thorough knowledge" (*pariññā*), by the mention of "those in training" (*sekkha*), and by [the mention of] "arahant," and so forth.
And they are included by the inclusion of "ariyaness" and so forth. Therein, by means of virtue (*sīla*), the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct is accomplished;

likewise, the abandoning by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and the abandoning of transgression (*vītikkamappahāna*). By means of serenity (*samatha*), the abandoning of the defilement of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkilesa*) is accomplished;

likewise, the abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) and the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhānappahāna*). By means of insight (*vipassanā*), the abandoning of the defilement of views (*diṭṭhisaṃkilesa*) [is accomplished].
In the same way, there is the abandonment by cutting off and the abandonment of latent tendencies. In that regard, for one established in virtue during the preliminary stage, there is serenity;
for one established in serenity, there is insight; however, at the moment of the Path, they occur simultaneously.
For it is only when bodily and verbal actions are thoroughly purified and the livelihood is thoroughly purified that serenity and insight [arise].
Those who have begun [the practice] and are conceiving the embryo, as they reach maturity, cultivate insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*).

As the cultivation of insight leading to emergence reaches its fulfillment, it joins with the Path (*magga*). At the moment of the Path, the cultivation of serenity and insight (*samathavipassanā*) reaches completion.
Then, through the fulfillment of the cultivation of serenity and insight at the moment of the Path, all defiled phenomena (*saṃkilesadhamma*) without exception—
"They sever [the fetters] and realize cessation, which is Nibbāna. This is the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropana-hāra*).
The commentary on the sixteen modes of conveying is finished.
Commentary on the Fivefold Method (*pañcavidha-naya*).

1. Explanation of the Mode of Conversion by Way of the "Joyful Turn" (*Nandiyāvaṭṭanaya*) In passages such as “The Exposition of the Root of All Phenomena,” by the inclusion of “the root of all phenomena” and the inclusion of “conceiving” (*maññanā*), craving, conceit, and views are included.

For it is shown that even among the modes of conceiving, conceiving itself is the cause; this is the meaning demonstrated here. By the passage beginning with “The uninstructed person,” ignorance, conceit, and views [are indicated].
Or else, all defiled phenomena (*saṃkilesadhamma*) are included by the mention of perception (*saññā*) as something not fully understood.
In the phrase, "One whose taints are destroyed, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted," the taints (*āsava*) and fetters (*saññojana*) are taken in their own form;

likewise, craving (*taṇhā*) is included by the mention of delight (*nandi*) and by the mention of craving itself. Thus, here both craving and ignorance (*avijjā*), along with their associated states, are included both in their own form and by way of synonyms.
In this context, the specific basis for craving (*taṇhā*) is material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), while for ignorance (*avijjā*) it is immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
These, however, have already been shown by the inclusion of "all phenomena" and by the inclusion of "earth and so forth. Their antidotes are serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*);

the manner in which these are to be grasped has already been demonstrated above. The fruit of serenity is liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*), and that of insight is liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*).

For these [factors] are spoken of as being distinguished by such terms as "dispassion toward lust" (*rāgavirāga*); their inclusion here should be understood from the expressions "liberated through right knowledge" (*sammadaññāvimutta*) and "one who is free from lust" (*vītarāga*).

In this context, craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), while it should be understood that the factors belonging to their side are included by the mention of those very two.
The material and immaterial phenomena (*rūpa-ārūpadhamma*) of the aforementioned classifications, which serve as the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for them, constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
The non-occurrence of these is the truth of cessation; the practice that leads to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path.

Furthermore, by the mention of craving (*taṇhā*), the unwholesome side should be understood here by way of deceit, guile, conceit, overweening pride, intoxication, negligence, evil desire, association with evil friends, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and so forth;
and by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), it should be understood by way of distorted attention, anger, resentment, denigration, spite, envy, and avarice.
The unwholesome side is to be understood by way of such factors as harmfulness, harsh speech, the view of existence, and the view of non-existence;

conversely, the purification side is to be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated—namely, by way of lack of guile, lack of deceit, and so forth, as well as by way of non-perverted attention and so forth—and likewise by way of the faith faculty and the other faculties belonging to the side of serenity (samatha), and the perception of impermanence and the others belonging to the side of insight (vipassanā). This is the ground of the "Conversion of Relishing" (Nandiyāvaṭṭa).
2. Explanation of the Tipukkhalanaya:

Among the states belonging to the categories of craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) that have been grasped according to the manner described above—both in their essential nature and by way of synonyms—craving is greed (*lobha*), and ignorance is delusion (*moha*).
When there is craving, [the other defilements] are established just as pus is present when blood exists, because they are associated with ignorance.

"Malice" (*āghāta*) is hatred (*dosa*); thus, when the three unwholesome roots are grasped, the wholesome roots are established by their very opposition, as well as through the full comprehension of the negation of conceiving (*maññanā*) and so forth.
Here too, it is stated: "Greed, or all the wholesome and unwholesome roots associated with the taints (*āsava*), constitute the truth of origination;
and the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), which are produced by them and serve as their basis and objective sphere, constitute the truth of suffering," and so on.
The application of the truths (saccayojanā) should be understood. As for the fruit here, it consists of the three liberations (vimokkha).

Furthermore, the unwholesome side is to be led [to understanding] by means of the three unwholesome roots, through the threefold misconduct, the defilement-stain of corruption, and unwholesome perceptions, thoughts, and so forth. Likewise, the wholesome side is to be led by means of the three wholesome roots, through the threefold good conduct, even and wholesome perceptions, thoughts, the true Dhamma, concentration, the doors to liberation, the liberations, and so forth.
This is the ground of the Tipukkhalo method.
3. Explanation of the Lion’s Play (Sīhavikkīḷita) Method:

Regarding the phenomena associated with craving and ignorance that have been grasped according to their essential nature and their various modes in the manner already described—specifically, by way of craving and views, there are the perversions [of perception] that take the unattractive to be "attractive" and suffering to be "pleasurable"; and by way of ignorance and views...
By way of these [perceptions], the perversions (vipallāsā) should be understood as perceiving the impermanent as "permanent" and the non-self as "self.

Because they are the opposites of those [perversions], the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānāni) are established by means of the faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom, which are accomplished through the full understanding of the negation of conceiving (maññanā), the rejection [of views], and so forth.
In that regard, four types of persons (puggalā) are to be demonstrated by means of the four faculties. How so? There are two kinds...
For one who is driven by craving has dull faculties, while one driven by views has sharp faculties.

Of these two, the first—grasping at the perverted notion of "beauty" in what is actually foul—enters the fixed course of rightness by discerning the true nature of the body through the power of mindfulness and thereby uprooting that perversion.
The second—grasping at the perverted notion of "pleasure" in what is actually suffering—[proceeds in the same manner].
By means of the power of energy— which consists of the restraint of energy described in the passage beginning with “he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire”—
and by dispelling that perversion, he enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). Thirdly, one who grasps what is impermanent as “permanent” through an incorrect apprehension,
having a concentrated mind by means of the power of concentration, [dispels] that perversion by discerning the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).
Uprooting [the view of self], he enters the plane of the Noble Ones. The fourth [type of practitioner],

who falsely adheres to the notion of "self" within the mere heap of phenomena such as contact— which are devoid of self because they are merely a dense mass of continuity, groups, functions, and objects—
destroys that false adherence by means of mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold alternative (catukoṭika-suññatā) and realizes the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala).

Here too, the application of the Truths (*saccayojanā*) should be understood as follows: the Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*) consists of the perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*), the perception of pleasure (*sukhasaññā*), and the four perversions (*vipallāsa*);
while the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*), which serve as their basis and object, constitute the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*).

Furthermore, the fruit here consists of the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). Through the four perversions of mind, there arise the four taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), bodily ties (*kāyagantha*), wrong courses (*agati*), the arising of craving (*taṇhuppāda*), the thorns of clinging (*sallupādāna*), the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the lack of full understanding (*apariññā*), and so forth.

The unwholesome side is to be led [to its conclusion]. Likewise, the purification side is to be led by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the fourfold abiding in jhāna, the factors conducive to happiness, the immeasurables, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and so forth.
This is the ground for the "Lion’s Play" method (sīhavikkīḷita-naya).
4–5. Commentary on the Two Methods of "Directing the Gaze" and the "Goading Hook."

Furthermore, through the establishment of these three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), the two methods of expression (*vohāranaya*) are necessarily established as well. For it should be understood that all five methods are thus included:

the "surveying of directions" (*disālocana*) is the examination of the phenomena that constitute the directions of the methods of meaning; and the "hook" (*aṅkusa*) is the bringing together of those [phenomena].
Thus, the five methods are joined.
The commentary on the fivefold method is completed.
Regarding the commentary on the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*:
this discourse belongs to the sixteenfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna*—namely, that which pertains to defilement, penetration, the state beyond training, and indeed all [four] states.
Or, regarding the phrase "the exposition of the root of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*), it should be understood that by the inclusion of "all phenomena" (*sabbadhamma*),

even mundane wholesome states are comprised therein. Furthermore, in the *Suttanta-paṭṭhāna* consisting of twenty-eight sections, one should understand that there is a presentation of knowledge and the knowable based on all phenomena—
both mundane and supramundane— including the views and cultivations of our own school, the questions to be answered, and the wholesome and unwholesome states that are either permitted or prohibited.
The commentary on the *Nettānaya* is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Mūlapariyāyasutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Sabbāsavasutta*.

14. *Apubbapadavaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Unprecedented Phrase): This refers to the commentary and analysis of the meaning of a new or unprecedented phrase (*apubbapada*), because it has not been previously grasped by way of a commentary on the meaning.
For it is said: "Having abandoned the matter that has come again and again. *Nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā*:

It means either those that have become places of residence, or those that were formerly places of residence; or else, those that have arisen or been produced in a place of residence are "those that have become places of residence" (*nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā*). In that regard—

The meaning is "measured out. Just as Kākandī, Mākandī, and Kosambī are so called—namely, the city measured out at the dwelling place of the seer Kākanda is called Kākandī, that measured out at the dwelling place of Mākanda is called Mākandī, and that measured out at the dwelling place of Kusamba is called Kosambī—in the same way, he shows that it is Sāvatthī.
Because it is to be enjoyed by bringing [the food] near and placing it close at hand.

"Upabhoga" (enjoyment) refers to the sentient physical basis (the body). "Paribhoga" (use) refers to insentient objects such as lower and upper garments, because they are to be used completely and at all times.
By this method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), he explains the establishment of the word *Sāvatthī* as meaning "all things exist here.

Regarding "in conjunction with a caravan": it means the meeting of the caravan with the city; the sense is that the caravan has arrived at that city. [This was said] when questioned by the people of the caravan.
"Accumulated" (*samohita*) means gathered together. "Delightful" (*ramma*) means beautiful both inside and out due to the excellence of its ground and the excellence of its parks and groves.
"Worthy of being seen" (*dassaneyya*) means worth seeing and fit to be beheld due to the excellence of its street layout and the excellence of its palaces, gabled houses, and so forth.
[It is also so called] due to the excellence of the objects for enjoyment and use, as well as the comfort of living there.
And because it delights the minds of those dwelling there permanently as well as other beings, it is called "delightful" (*manorama*).

"With ten sounds" refers to these ten sounds: the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, kettledrums, conchs, drums, lutes, singing, and the sound of clapping hands, along with the sounds of "eat," "drink," and "chew. "Not secluded" (*avivitta*) means not isolated.
The meaning is: "resounding at all times.
"Attained growth and abundance" means it has attained growth through the increase of the beings dwelling there;

by that very growth, it has reached a state of vastness, meaning it is crowded with many people and teeming with inhabitants. It is "prosperous" (iddha) due to the excellence of its wealth and requisites.
It is prosperous due to the state of having abundant alms-food at all times.

It is described as "delightful" (*manorama*) once again to show that it has become pleasing even for all those who are wretched, destitute, mendicants, and beggars—even down to those who subsist on discarded scraps—because their desires are fulfilled there, let alone for those established in power.
Regarding the phrase "from Alakamandā," this refers to the ten cities of the Great King Vessavaṇa, such as Āṭānāṭā and others.
There is a city named Alakamandā, which in the world is called simply Alakā.

Just as that city is the dwelling place of those who have performed meritorious deeds and has attained such excellence through its delightful groves and so forth, so too is Sāvatthī; thus it is said, "like Alakamandā.
"Of the gods" refers to the gods of the Four Great Kings who belong to the retinue of Vessavaṇa.
By the word *jināti* (“he conquers”), it is shown that the term *jeta* is an agent-noun (*kattusādhana*), just like the word *sota* (“ear”). “Of the king” means by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Having attributed the victory pertaining to the king, the prince was called *Jeta* because he had conquered (*jitavā*).

By the phrase “because of its auspicious poetic nature,” etc., it is shown that the word *jeta* is used in the sense of “to be conquered” (*jeyya*). “Because of the fulfillment of all desires” means by means of all objects of enjoyment and utility.
"By means of a radiant state" means by means of being endowed with wealth. Even those who are prosperous may be stingy and give nothing;
therefore, he says "by means of the absence of the stain of stinginess," which means by the absence of stains such as lust and hatred, as well as the absence of stinginess.
Furthermore, even those who are prosperous and not stingy may lack qualities such as compassion and faith, and [thus] withhold their own possessions from others...
"He would not give," he said, "because of his possession of qualities such as compassion. "By that" means by the giving of alms to the destitute.
Etymologically, however, because the state of being something to be given is established at all times, he is called Anāthapiṇḍika because he possesses alms for the destitute (*anāthapiṇḍa*).
Regarding the perfection of the five factors of a monastery: "not too far, not too near, well-served by paths for coming and going."
One factor is: “by day it is not crowded, and by night there is little noise and little sound”; one is:
“there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things”; one is: “while dwelling in that lodging, robes...
requisites arise without difficulty”; and one is: “in that lodging, elder bhikkhus who are learned dwell. Thus, by these—
Because it is endowed with the five factors of a suitable dwelling. If Jetavana is truly Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, why did he say “for that [grove]”?

[The answer begins with] “For that,” and so forth. From the time it was purchased, that grove belonged to Anāthapiṇḍika alone; so why is it described as belonging to both? [The answer begins with] “In Jetavana,” and so forth.
“Even though that plot of land was purchased by the Great Merchant for ten million pieces of gold, the trees...”
"But because it was not sold by Jeta, it received the designation 'Jetavana,'" they say.
He asks about the occasion for the delivery of this sutta out of a desire to explain why it was spoken; for the general reason for the Blessed One’s teaching is already well known.
What, then, is this "occasion for the delivery of a sutta"? It is one's own inclination (*attajjhāsayo*). [It may also be] through others...
The teachers say that the Blessed One taught this sutta of his own accord, without being requested.

However, because he perceived the defilement of the minds of the bhikkhus and thought, "By means of this teaching, these bhikkhus will purify their defilements and proceed toward the destruction of the taints," this teaching was commenced;
therefore, it is said to be according to the inclination of others.

Others [hold this view]. However, both [interpretations] are appropriate, for the possibility of different combinations arising from one’s own inclinations (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth has already been shown below.
"Of those bhikkhus" refers to the bhikkhus who received the Dhamma at that time.

"Purification from defilements" (*upakkilesavisodhana*) means the purification of the mind from the defilements of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). For first, the Blessed One, by means of the gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*) and so forth...
Having removed the defilements from the practice, he subsequently gives a teaching that is pre-eminent, just as one plows a field after clearing away stumps, thorns, thickets, and the like;
therefore, the intention is that the teaching proceeds by this sequence rather than merely stating the meditation subject itself.
"Becoming a restraint" means it is the cause that has the nature of restraint, such as the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and so forth; and that, in terms of its actual meaning, is—
It should be understood that this refers to vision and so forth. "Restrained" means properly or in every way prevented from proceeding by not allowing them to occur.
And because such states are called "shut" through the closing of the doors of their occurrence, it is said, "having been established.
Thus, [the text describes] the non-absolute restraint which serves as the cause for absolute restraint.
Having shown that, he now shows absolute restraint (*accantika-saṃvara*).

He says: "By whatever cause there is the non-arising, cessation, destruction, and abandoning—which is in fact merely the non-occurrence—of those taints (*āsava*) that would otherwise arise when such seeing and so forth exist;
and that [non-occurrence] has seeing and so forth as its cause. Thus, he speaks of that which is designated as non-arising and cessation.
"They go to destruction, are abandoned, and do not proceed; that is the meaning of 'cause'. Regarding "from the eye...

up to from the mind": although there is the occurrence of wholesome states and so forth within the cognitive processes (*vīthi*) of eye-consciousness and so on, as well as the mental consciousness processes (*manoviññāṇa-vīthi*) associated with them, it is only the outflows such as the *kāmasava* (the outflow of sensual desire) that flow forth like pus from a wound, by way of their nature as impure matter.
They flow; therefore, they alone are called "taints" (āsava). For the word *āsava* is conventionally established in the sense of a liquid that trickles or flows.
Regarding the phrase "from the level of phenomena up to the lineage-consciousness" (*gotrabhu*): this is stated because [the taints] do not proceed beyond that into the paths and fruits.
For these, proceeding through phenomena by way of their objects, do not go further than that. [Objection: But do they not proceed beyond that into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth?
Why? Because even those mundane states previously taken as objects are included within the category of "with taints" (*sāsavabhāva*), and thus there is no state beyond them.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the term "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) here, the preliminary stages (*parikamma*) leading up to the change-of-lineage, the exalted emergence (*vodāna*), the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*), and the preliminary practice are intended. Alternatively, only the change-of-lineage preceding the first path is taken here, representing the limit of the boundary.

Beyond that, however, it should be understood that because of the similarity between the path and its fruit, the occurrence of the taints (*āsava*) is obstructed in other paths—whether occurring in the cognitive process of the path, the cognitive process of attainment, immediately after cessation (*nirodha*), or in the fruits and in *nibbāna*.
"Flow" (*savanti*) means they go; the meaning is that they proceed by way of making [an object] their objective support (*ārammaṇa*). The vowel *ā* has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).

The *avadhi* (limit) is twofold, distinguished as *mariyādā* (exclusive limit) and *abhividhi* (inclusive limit). Among these, the *mariyādā* [limit] functions by excluding the action outside [the boundary], as in:
"It has rained from Pāṭaliputta. The *abhividhi* [limit], however, functions by pervading the action, as in:
"The fame of the Blessed One extends even unto the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). And it is this sense of *abhividhi* that is understood here by the prefix *ā-*.
It is said: "The meaning is 'making internal'.
Regarding "wine and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood as including *sindhava*, *kādambarika*, *kapotikā*, and others.

"The state of having been stored for a long time" means being surrounded by age, that is, antiquity. Regarding the phrase "ignorance was not," and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here includes [the passage]: "Bhikkhus, in the past..."
The sutta, “No limit is discerned for craving for existence,” is included here.

By showing that the taints of ignorance and existence have long been present, it is shown by implication that the taint of sensual desire, which exists as a concomitant of those two, has also long been present.
Furthermore, when other aforementioned phenomena such as conceit and so forth are occurring by taking space and objects as their basis, [the same applies].

It should be understood that the term *āsava* (taint) is conventionally established only for these [three], because they alone possess the quality of pervading through the grasping at self and what belongs to self,
and because they possess a resemblance to taints by way of producing intoxication; it is not the case that the *diṭṭhāsava* (taint of views) is not included here,
since the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) is already included by the inclusion of the *bhavāsava* (taint of existence), just like craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
"Extended" means beginningless. "Pouring forth" means bearing fruit.
For there is no suffering of saṃsāra whatsoever that could arise without the taints (āsava). And "the former ones here" refers to the first three among these four ways of describing the meaning.
"In which" refers to those passages from the Sutta and Abhidhamma; therein, they apply specifically to the defilements (kilesa).
This is because the three meanings previously stated are possible. The latter [etymology]—“it flows as the long-lasting suffering of saṃsāra”—is the etymological derivation that has been stated.
It also applies to *kamma*, because the flowing forth of suffering is common to both defilements (*kilesa*) and *kamma*.

"Visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the aggregates (*khandhā*) that have become manifest; those existing in the visible phenomena are "pertaining to the visible phenomena" (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
"Roots of dispute" means those things that serve as the fundamental causes of dispute: anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, presumption, pride, and arrogance.
"By which there might be rebirth among the gods" connects to: "by which kind of karma, defilement, or taint there might be my rebirth or arising among the gods.
"Or a gandhabba, a bird, a wanderer through the air"—this is understood by changing the grammatical case (from the instrumental to the nominative).
It should be joined [to the preceding]. And here, all destinies belonging to the gods—excluding those of the *yakkhas* and *gandhabbas*—are included by the term "gods.
The connection is as follows: "the remaining unwholesome states" refers to those unwholesome states remaining after unwholesome kamma, which are stated to be "taints" (*āsava*).

"For the sake of warding off" means for the sake of preventing. Regarding the phrase "calamities brought about by others... misfortunes," this [refers to] if the Blessed One [had laid down] the training rule...

One should not prescribe [them]; for by doing so, there would arise various kinds of worldly misfortunes such as the censure of others caused by the practice of unrighteous conduct, taking what is not given, killing living beings, and so forth;

and there would also arise various kinds of great suffering experienced through the fivefold bonds, penal servitude, and the like, which result from being reborn in the hells and other realms on account of those very same causes.

It was said with reference to these. "But these" refers to these outflows (*āsava*), which consist of various forms of afflictions such as sensual lust and so forth, as well as karmic actions belonging to the three realms and calamities such as the disparagement of others. "Wherein" means in that portion of the Pāḷi, such as the Vinaya.
"In what way" connects to the fact that they have been handed down in two kinds and other ways in other Suttantas.
"Nirayagāminiyā" means "leading to hell," as in the *Āhuneyyasutta* of the *Chakkanipāta*. For there, the taints (*āsava*) are presented in six ways;
by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra*), the variety of the meaning denoted by the word "taint" is called "variety" (*pabheda*) in the term "taint" (*āsava-pada*).

Alternatively, since the word "term" (*pada*) has the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*), the meaning is: "in the term 'taint' [meaning] in the division of words or in the division of meanings regarding the types of taints."
"Tathā hi" means "therefore"; it refers to the act of restraining, closing, or preventing from proceeding.

By that very reason, when restraint such as virtue (sīla) is intended, the phrase "having restrained the door" is mentioned because of the commonality of the state of blocking by way of preventing [unwholesome states] from proceeding.
As for the passage beginning with "restraint of virtue" (sīlasaṃvara), although it was already stated below in the commentary on the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*, [it is repeated here].
Desiring to provide a complete commentary on the meaning of this sutta, he speaks again. He says:

"It is indeed appropriate that the purpose of virtue (*sīla*), mindfulness (*sati*), and knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is restraint (*saṃvara*), because it is presented as such in the Canon; but how is it so for patience (*khanti*) and energy (*vīriya*)?
Thus he says, "And of those," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: even though [the text says], "He is patient... [and so on]... toward cold," and "When a thought of sensual desire has arisen..."

In the exposition beginning with “he does not tolerate,” the method of restraint (*saṃvara*) for patience and energy has not been mentioned; however, since they are included under the phrase “the restraint of all taints” (*sabbāsavasaṃvara*) in the summary (*uddesa*), they do indeed possess the nature of restraint.
Since the nature of restraint for virtue, mindfulness, and wisdom was previously shown through a different textual passage, it is now [shown] by this sutta as well.

To show that this state has been grasped, the passage beginning with “Moreover” (*apicā*) was stated. Patience, energy, and restraint have already been mentioned by way of the Pāli text through such expressions as “he is patient with cold,” and so forth.
However, the phrase “that which is not a proper seat and that which is not a proper resort” refers here to the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*);

this refers to a secluded, concealed seat in an unsuitable place where the basis [of the offense] is indeterminate, as described in the passage beginning with “in whatever kind of [place],” and so forth.
And that which was previously mentioned as improper—namely, frequenting the domain of prostitutes and so forth—is what is referred to in the passage, "he avoids it by means of wise reflection.
However, the meaning here in this sutta is that this avoidance constitutes the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).

For by avoiding unsuitable seats, the avoidance of improper conduct is expressed; and the avoidance of improper conduct and its objects is the restraint of virtue consisting in good behavior (*cārittasīla*).

For thus, in the analysis of the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), when the Blessed One stated, "He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," he demonstrated the perfection of conduct and resort (*ācāra-gocara-sampatti*) by first analyzing and showing improper conduct and improper resorts through such statements as, "There is improper conduct; there is an improper resort.
And this should be understood as a demonstration of the whole by means of a part, like a demonstration of the ocean or the mountains.

Regarding the phrase "restraint through knowledge consisting in reflection everywhere" (*sabbattha paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaro*), it should be stated here that "appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is restraint through knowledge consisting in reflection.
For in the exposition on what is to be abandoned by seeing, there is no mention of "reflection," but rather it is said, "he attends appropriately.
And in meaning, appropriate attention is indeed nothing other than restraint through knowledge consisting in reflection.
However, this would be appropriate if the meaning were understood in this way. Some, however, say:
"In every instance where the phrase 'here one reflects wisely' occurs, it is said with reference to all of those that 'in all cases, reflection is the restraint of knowledge'.
According to their view, [the passage] beginning with "one attends wisely, thinking 'this is suffering'" is subsumed under the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*).
Furthermore, if there were no inclusion [of these], the statement, "Seeing, utilization, development, and restraint through knowledge," would be contradicted;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood exactly according to the method already stated.

By the phrase "restraint through knowledge is reflective consideration in all instances," it is shown that the knowledge which exists in all seven stations constitutes restraint through knowledge, while virtue and the other factors are described by way of avoidance and so forth.
The meaning "restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) and so forth" has thus been shown.
Since this would result in a confusion of the restraints, it was stated, "by including what was not previously included," in order to show them without such confusion;

for the specific types of restraint—avoidance, excellence, endurance, and removal—are included under the categories of "restraint of virtue" and so on. The meaning is: "by including those that were not [previously] included. Now, as for those not included...
Showing it according to its form, he said: "seeing, utilizing, and developing.

By this—by means of the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) and so forth, acting either as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or as a cause (*kāraṇa*)—the wholesome phenomena (*dhamma*) are those wholesome and unwholesome states.

For, by means of the restraint of virtue and so forth, acting as a condition through the point of co-nascence (*sahajātakoṭi*) or the point of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭi*), wholesome states that have not yet arisen...
The meaning is that phenomena proceed toward arising and thus arise; likewise, unwholesome phenomena proceed toward cessation and thus cease.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is said: "Taints that have not yet arisen do not arise, and taints that have already arisen are abandoned";
thus, only the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome phenomena are mentioned, not those of wholesome phenomena.

"Are they [the defilements] arising, etc.? This should not be viewed in that way. For by such passages as, "But for one who attends wisely, monks," the arising of wholesome states is indeed demonstrated;
it is simply grasped here because the restraint of the taints (*āsava*) is taken as the primary factor.
Thus, even at the conclusion, it says: "Those taints that are to be abandoned by vision have been abandoned by vision," and so forth.
It is concluded by making the abandoning of the taints (*āsava*) itself the primary effort.
Regarding the phrase "of one who knows and sees": here, even "seeing" is intended as seeing with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*) alone, not with the fleshly eye or the divine eye;
thus he says, "the two terms have the same meaning. Even though this is so—that is, even though the two terms have the same meaning—[he still uses both].
“Characteristic of knowledge” (*ñāṇalakkhaṇa*) means the intrinsic nature of knowledge; the meaning is the awakening to the object according to its true nature.

Therefore he said: “For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. “Power of knowledge” (*ñāṇappabhāva*) means the majesty of knowledge; the meaning is the function of knowledge, which is the illumination of the object.
For this very reason he said: “When phenomena are disclosed by knowledge. And by the phrase “of one who knows and sees,” it is stated by way of knowing and seeing.

He said, "The teaching proceeds by way of a reference to persons (puggalādhiṭṭhānā)," meaning that it points out the person by taking into account the characteristic of knowledge and the power of knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "of one who knows and sees": since "proper attention and improper attention" will be explained [later], this refers to the knowing of the object of proper attention and the seeing of the object of improper attention. And furthermore, of these two—

Since what is intended here is the nature of the means for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), this meaning—that [the destruction] occurs by way of producing [the path] and not merely by way of the object—is logical;
thus he said: "Appropriate attention... this is the essence herein.
Having said "of one who knows," it should be understood that here "knowing" does not refer to mere hearsay, verbal expression, or conceptual reflection; rather—

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the term "of one who sees" (*passato*) is stated in order to clarify that, just as with visible forms and so forth, one makes right attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and wrong attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) directly manifest through eye-consciousness, and that "seeing" occurs by way of their arising. For elsewhere too it is said:
"Of one who knows thus and sees thus; knowing, he knows; seeing... [and so on].

In such passages as, "One who knows thus and sees thus [knows] those who do not know and do not see," these two terms have come down as a means of illustrating the general and specific functions of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*).
"Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* residing at Abhayagiri.
For they maintain that "one who knows by means of concentration (*samādhi*) and sees by means of insight (*vipassanā*) knows by knowing and sees by seeing; thus, through knowing..."
They proliferate [with such views] as, "Calm is insight" and so forth. "Those" refers to those proliferations (*papañca*).
"In this meaning" means when the meaning of this sutta passage—beginning with "of one who knows"—is being determined according to its method of presentation.
They are not tenable because the Pāḷi states that knowing and seeing have, respectively, wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as their respective objects.
The abandoning of the taints (āsava) is the absolute abandoning of the taints. Furthermore, since this is their non-arising, their total exhaustion, and their non-existence, it is said:
"the absolute destruction of the taints, their non-arising, the state of being exhausted, and their absence.

"Following the straight path" refers to one who recollects the lower paths together with insight, which have become straight through the abandoning of the crookedness of the defilements as well as the crookedness of body and so forth.
That itself is his training. Regarding the phrase "the first knowledge in destruction" (*khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ*): immediately after that, there is "higher knowledge" (*aññā*).
This means that in the supreme path known as destruction (*khaya*), the knowledge included therein arises first; immediately following that, however, is the higher knowledge of Arahantship.
Although only the word "in destruction" (*khayasmiṃ*) is stated in the verse, it refers to one who is "destroyed" (*khīṇo*) of the taints (*āsava*) by way of their total eradication.
"The path is called destruction," he says, thus stating: "The path is spoken of as the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). A "recluse" (*samaṇa*) is intended here as one who has stilled evil.
Since such a person is one whose taints are destroyed, the phrase "through the destruction of the taints" is stated as a figurative expression for the fruit;

however, in the literal sense, the destruction of the taints is the path, and the fruit is that which is to be attained by means of it. By this very point, it should be understood that Nibbāna also possesses the nature of the destruction of the taints.
Regarding the phrase “of one who knows and sees,” the restriction intended here is that it applies only to one who knows and only to one who sees;
it is not otherwise, because there would be no distinction [in the result] and because it would establish what is undesirable. To show the fruit of this restriction, he said:
“But for one who does not know and does not see, I do not say [it applies]; such is the meaning.”

By this, it is shown that improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is what is excluded here, and that proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) is the single, decisive cause for the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).
By this—namely, by the statement "not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see"—what is it that is rejected? What are they? [They are those who say:
"Both fools and the wise, having run on and wandered through the cycle of existence, will make an end of suffering; there is no cause, there is no condition."
"Beings are purified," and so forth. For among those [views], some maintain that purification from saṃsāra occurs merely through a transition of birth or a transition of existence;
others [hold it occurs] by way of Īśvara, Pajāpati, Kāla, and so on.
All of this should be understood as being included right here under the heading "from saṃsāra, etc."
"By the first two phrases" means by these two phrases: "of one who knows, of one who sees. The "means" (*upāya*) is stated;
it is understood from the context as being for the "destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*). "By this" means by these two phrases: "not of one who does not know, not of one who does not see.
For that which is the non-knowing and non-seeing of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) is indeed the non-means for the destruction of the taints.

Because of not practicing for suchness and because of practicing wrongly. [Objection: Is it not the case that, since "for one who sees" implies that unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) does not arise, the prohibition of the improper means was already stated by the previous [phrase] when "seeing" is intended? [Response:
It is not so, because the non-arising of unwise attention is itself a means, consisting in the guarding of the faculty of the eye and so forth through the power of mindfulness.
Thus, through the power of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) alone, there is an absence of knowing what is unreal by way of [perceiving things as] permanent and so forth.

Therefore he said: “In brief... it comes to be. Therein, “in brief” means concisely; the sense is that it is without elaborating upon the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya* and *byatireka*).
Knowledge... is shown because by the words “of one who knows,” etc., knowledge itself is taken up. If this is so, then this—
How is the passage beginning with “restraint” (saṃvara) to be understood? There is no fault here, for this teaching was given in order to show that knowledge is the primary factor;
likewise elsewhere it is said in detail: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you noble right concentration with its support and its equipment.”

“Of a substance-like nature” (*dabbajātika*) means having the quality of a substance (*dabbarūpa*). For that which is called “substance” (*dravya*) is referred to in such passages as, “A substance perishes, not a non-substance,” and so forth.

Alternatively, “of a substance-like nature” means having an essential character, or possessing a suitable virtue and conduct. As it was said: “Dabba, it is not those who are merely ‘substances’ who unravel [the problem] in this way.
“Standing at the head of the duties” means making duty one’s supreme limb or taking it as one’s primary responsibility. For whoever...

If one makes umbrellas and such for fellow celibates who do not know how to maintain a pure livelihood, or for oneself to ward off wind, heat, and so forth, it is said that one acts while standing at the head of the practice (*vatta*).

It should not be said that these lack a proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), because they serve as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) by way of being qualities that provide protection. For it is said: "Those various high and low [requisites] of fellow celibates..."
"tasks to be done, he is skillful therein," and so forth.

*Upāya-manasikāra* (skillful attention) is the attention that serves as the cause for the arising of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). *Paṭhama-manasikāra* (initial attention) is the attention that constitutes the path to that very [arising].
Regarding "as impermanent, etc., among the impermanent": this refers to the essential natures of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), foulness (*asubha*), and non-self (*anatta*).
"Regarding phenomena" means by way of their non-perverted nature, such as "impermanence, suffering, foulness, and non-self.
"In conformity with the truths" means by way of being favorable to the clear realization of the truths.

"The turning of the mind," and so forth, refers to the occurrence of wholesome javanas at the mind-door that have arisen prior to that [realization], which serve as the conditions for the turning and are designated by the term "fruit."

It is spoken of in that way because, by means of it, there is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of the wholesome. For it is called *āvaṭṭanā* (turning toward) because it turns the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) toward the object.

It is called *anvāvaṭṭanā* (repeated turning toward) because it turns [the mind] repeatedly. It is called *ābhogo* (mental inclination) because it inclines toward an object other than that of the life-continuum.
It is called *samannāhāro* (attention) because it attends to [the object]. That very same object, arising as it does while following after itself—

"He attends to and establishes [it] in the mind" is *manasikāra*. "This is called" means that this, characterized by attention to the path of means (*upāyapatha*), is called "wise attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*);
by means of which a person is able to bring to mind the truths such as suffering.
Regarding "due to unwise attention being repugnant to the truths," it is because it does not conform to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths. The rest...
It should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
"Connection" (*yutti*) means logical proof through reasoning (*upapattisādhanayutti*); the sense is "reason. For this very reason, he says "because," and so forth.
"In this" refers to this passage: "Bhikkhus, [through] improper attention... they are abandoned. "Therein" is an introductory phrase for the statement. But why is it here?
This is the exposition of the summary; it is said, beginning with “properly,” with reference to the objection regarding the turning [of the mind].
Therein, the term *manasikāra* (attention) is common to both; intending this, it was said: “first, by means of these two terms, ‘properly’ and ‘improperly.
For “properly” refers to proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), and “improperly” refers to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), because they follow upon those [terms] therein.

And because it is about to be explained. Although there is a commonality in the arising of misfortune in [the realms of] existence and so forth, one should understand that the triad of similes beginning with the ship is employed to show the predominance of the person (*puggala*) therein, and then, by reversing that, to demonstrate the distinction [between them].
They say that "cakkayantam" refers to a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*) brought [for irrigation].

“Unarisen” means unproduced. Its non-arising should be understood as being due to a specific object (*ārammaṇa*), not by way of the generality of objects such as visible forms, nor by way of the taints (*āsava*) themselves.
Therefore he said: “An object never experienced before... [etc.]... For otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there would be no such thing as taints that have not arisen.
“Basis” (*vatthu*) refers to the cause for the arising of taints, which is divided into those with consciousness and those without consciousness.
“Object” refers to the objects that have become object-conditions, such as material form and so forth.

Now, in order to show that the category of the "unarisen" (anuppanna) can also be understood by way of the taints (āsava), the passage beginning with “even though previously experienced” was stated. “Natural purity” means the state of being pure by nature, established through the removal of defilements by virtue of one’s previous conduct.
“Recitation” (uddesa) is the reciting of the text; “interrogation” (paripucchā) is the explaining of the meaning. “Study” (ajjhayana) is mastery (pariyatti).
New work consists of sewing robes and so forth; it also includes application to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), as well as appropriate attention (yonisomanasikāra).
"By such [attention]" means by that kind of attention—such as "this is a pleasant object"—by which the taints of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the others might arise.
The increase of the taints should be understood as their intense obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna); and that occurs through frequent arising and repeated practice, whereby they become habituated.
Having reached a state of abundance, crushing, spreading, and covering, they create darkness;

arising again and again according to the principle of a single continuum, they are said to be "arisen and increasing. Therefore it was said: "Arising again and again, they are called 'arisen and increasing.
"Other than this" means other than the grasping of oneness in those things that arise repeatedly.
Otherwise, there is indeed no growth because of the momentary nature [of phenomena].
And the phrase "he knows" indicates the absence of agitation regarding the Dhamma. The expression "only for the agent" means only for one who is properly engaged in yoga.
By the words "But for whom... and so forth, he states the aforementioned point—which was spoken without specific reference—by demonstrating the practice of an ancient, preeminent person.
To make it more evident, it is said: "Just as in the case of the Elder Mahātissa, who dwelt at Maṇḍalārāma," and so forth.
For that serves as a cause for fellow practitioners to practice accordingly in the future; hence such a matter is mentioned.
"In that very place" means in Maṇḍalārāma itself. "Having asked his teacher" means having asked his own recitation teacher for the purpose of receiving a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having asked permission to depart. "Having paid homage to the teacher" means having paid homage to the Elder Mahārakkhita, the giver of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"The sequence of the recitation" refers to the series of recitations as they had been undertaken. At that time, it seems, many people would have them recite together all at once by way of oral recitation, and then practice the recitation of the Dhamma by way of mental rehearsal (*manosajjhāya*). In this regard, this Elder, owing to his wisdom...
He was a burden-bearer for the monks who were taking up the recitation. Thinking, "Now that I am a non-returner, what need have I for recitation?", he did not fall into discouragement;

instead, on the second day at the time for recitation, he approached his teacher. Regarding the phrase "arisen [defilements] are abandoned," here "arisen" refers to those similar to what has arisen, not to those currently present.
For it is not possible [to abandon] the outflows (āsava) while they are presently manifest.

He says, "But for those... there is none," because abandonment through the Path is possible [only for certain types of defilements]. Those that are "presently arisen" (vattamānuppannā) possess the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution].

There is no abandonment of them by means of practice; rather, for those that are destined to arise, their non-arising due to the destruction of their conditions is what constitutes abandonment by that [practice].
16. If this is so, what is the purpose of the second clause? The inclusion of both clauses is for the purpose of demonstrating the possibility of the arisen and unarisen states of the taints (āsava).
And it is for the purpose of showing the classification of what is to be abandoned by means of the classification of what abandons. Therefore he said: "Taking this very term.
"Another as well" refers to mindfulness-restraint and so forth, which are other than knowledge. "By seeing"—this is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause;
he clarifies that meaning by using the instrumental case "by means of seeing," which expresses the cause. "This is the method" refers back to that same meaning.
"By seeing" means by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). For that [path] is called "seeing" because it first sees Nibbāna.

Even though the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*) sees it earlier, it is not called "seeing" because it does not perform the function of abandoning the defilements that must be done after seeing.
Indeed, that knowledge is the functional equivalent of the path's adverting consciousness, due to their commonality in having Nibbāna as their object.

This was said, not with reference to the penetration of Nibbāna; therefore, "seeing" refers to that which has not yet reached the stage of development through the repeated generation of the Dhamma-eye.
And the Dhamma-eye is the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of performing its functions, such as full understanding (*pariññā*); thus, it is the realization (*abhisamaya*) of that.
Consequently, there is no attainment of the state of seeing for the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) here. This investigation is [explained] later in the Commentary itself.
It will come. "In all cases" refers to passages such as "they are to be abandoned by restraint. "By restraint" means by means of restraint;

and here, "restraint" should be understood as the restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*). "Practice" (*paṭisevana*) is that by which one practices; it is the knowledge of being intent upon the requisites.
"Endurance" (*adhivāsanā*) is that by which one endures or tolerates; it is non-hatred (*adosa*) occurring in the mode of tolerating cold and so forth, having that as its primary characteristic.
Or, it is the four wholesome aggregates (*kusalakkhandha*). It is called "avoidance" (*parivajjana*) because one avoids by means of it;

it refers to volition (*cetanā*) operating through the avoidance of wild beasts and the like, or the four wholesome aggregates operating in that manner. It is called "dispelling" (*vinodana*) because one dispels or pierces away sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth by means of it;
it is wholesome energy (*kusala-vīriya*). Regarding the Dhamma of the Four Truths seen through the first path:
It is called "development" (bhāvanā) because it arises by way of cultivation; this refers to the remaining three paths. For they do not see anything that was previously unseen;
thus should the etymological meaning of "seeing" and the other terms be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the taints to be abandoned by seeing.

17. Showing that even though objective phenomena (ārammaṇadhammā) are being taken as objects by wholesome and unwholesome states, they attain that state [of being objects] only through the door of adverting (āvajjana), he explains the meaning of the term "manasikaraṇīye" as "āvajjitabbe" (to be adverted to).

They are "worthy of attention" (manasikaraṇīyā) because they deserve to be attended to insofar as they bring about welfare and happiness; conversely, they are "not worthy of attention" (amanasikaraṇīyā). Thus he says: "amanasikaraṇīye."

"In the opposite case" refers to the remaining phrases, such as "not understanding the phenomena that should be attended to," and so forth. Since attention directed toward wholesome phenomena (*kusala-dhamma*) by way of [perceiving them as] beautiful, pleasant, permanent, and so on, is blameworthy because it is a cause for relishing and the like, and brings about harm and suffering;

whereas attention directed toward unwholesome phenomena (*akusala-dhamma*) by way of [perceiving them as] impermanent and so on, is blameless because it is a cause for disenchantment and the like, and brings about welfare and happiness—therefore, "from the standpoint of the phenomena..."
Having said, "There is no fixed rule," he stated, "But there is one in terms of its form.

Since the particle *vā* is generally seen in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*)—as in such passages as, "Monks, I shall become either a god or another god"—and not in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), he provides an example of its use in the sense of conjunction with the words beginning "Just as... (*yathā*).
Thus it has been said. And having established this, this sutta passage is cited as illustrating the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

"The taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) means the taint regarding sensual pleasures, which are reckoned as the five strands of sensual pleasure; hence he says, "lust pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure.

However, it would be more appropriate to say that, setting aside the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), all greed is the taint of sensual desire. As for "in the fine-material and immaterial existences," this is due to the distinction between karma and rebirth.

In both types of existence, whether material or immaterial, there is desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). "Craving for meditative absorption" (*jhāna-nikanti*) refers to the gratification of absorption (*jhānassāda*).

The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) is the lust that arises in one who relishes [existence] by thinking, "This state is beautiful, permanent, and eternal," and which is accompanied by the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
Thus, because all views are subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism, they are included within the taint of existence alone.

The intention is that the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is included because of its coexistence with greed (*rāga*). However, others say that "the taint of views is also included within the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).

Furthermore, since it is stated here that "the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises in four types of mental states associated with greed but dissociated from the four types of wrong view," one must investigate whether greed associated with wrong view possesses the nature of the taint of existence; for [otherwise], [greed] associated with sensual desire...
In passages such as "perception and attention" (*saññāmanasikārā*), the meaning of "concomitance" (*sahagata*) is the sense of taking something as an object (*ārammaṇakaraṇattha*).

If this were the case, there would be no inclusion of the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) within the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). For it is not logical to include that [taint of views] when its association, its state of being bound, and so forth are absent.
Therefore, following the aforementioned scriptural authority, it is appropriate that greed associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhigatasampayuttalobha*) is also the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
It may be so. For the outflows of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) and the rest, which are the causes of suffering pertaining to both the present life and future lives, are also stated in two ways.

Furthermore, in the *Abhidhamma* exposition of the outflow of sensuality, the meaning "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) can be understood as "in the sensual objects consisting of the three planes (*tebhumaka*), which have become the objective supports for sensual lust, views-lust, and so forth.
For the craving that arises therein does not, in its entirety, receive the name "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) and the rest.

"It is not obtained. However, if greed (*lobha*) were to exist even as dissociated from the taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taints of existence (*bhavāsava*), then when it arises in states of consciousness dissociated from views (*diṭṭhigata*), the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) associated with it would have to be described as dissociated from the taints—just as [the taint of ignorance] associated with grief, doubt, or restlessness is described as dissociated from the taints.
Thus, in the four types of consciousness-moments accompanied by greed and dissociated from views...
“Arising delusion may be associated with the taints (āsava), or it may be dissociated from the taints.

One cannot say that lust accompanied by views is not the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), because of the statements: “The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed,” and “Dependent on the taint of sensual desire, there are the taints of views and ignorance.
Furthermore, what is the distinction between covetousness (abhijjhā) and lust for sense-pleasures (kāmarāga) in terms of their being two taints or one taint?
It may be that there is no state of being both an *āsava* and a non-*āsava* [in the case of covetousness]; thus, the existence of covetousness as a non-*āsava* must be examined.

For in the Abhidhamma, there is no seventh or ninth question stating: "States that are both *āsava* and non-*āsava* are a root-condition for a state that is an *āsava*, and for a state that is both *āsava* and non-*āsava*.
And in the enumeration, it says: "Seven in the case of the root-condition (*hetu*)."

It was not stated as "nine. However, if greed associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi-sampayutta*) were a non-outflow (*no-āsava*), then the seventh and ninth questions would also receive an answer, and in the enumeration it should have been stated as "nine in the case of root-cause" (*hetuyā nava*);
yet it was not so stated. And when greed dissociated from wrong view (*diṭṭhi-vippayutta*) is a non-outflow, what ought to be stated has indeed been stated. But because...
The teaching of the Suttantas is indeed a discourse by way of a method (*pariyāya-kathā*), not a discourse devoid of method (*nippariyāya-kathā*) like the teaching of the Abhidhamma;

therefore, in order to show the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) specifically for one whose sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) is powerful, it is said: "The outflow of sensual desire is lust pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure," and likewise regarding "delight in existence" (*bhavābhinandanā*).
By way of generalization, the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) includes the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) within itself; thus, only three taints are mentioned here.

To demonstrate that the latter is included therein, it is said: "In this way, the taint of views," and so forth. For he will likewise state that the taint of existence is the opposite of the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*).
"Ignorance regarding the four truths" is stated according to the method of the Suttas.
It has been said: "For this is an exposition of the Suttanta," or because the past limit (pubbanta) and so forth are included within it.

Just as the outflows of sensuality (kāmāsava) and the rest have been defined according to their meaning, he says "the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇe*) and so forth, showing their arising and increase.

"Attending to them as gratifying" means attending to them by way of gratification through such [notions] as "beautiful" and "pleasant. "By way of being the footing for the four perversions" (*catuvipallāsapadaṭṭhānabhāvena*).
By way of being the objective basis for the perception of the beautiful and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in opposition to the method already stated":

for one who suppresses and eradicates desire and lust through the practice of renunciation preceded by the vision of the dangers in the strands of sensual pleasure—such as, "These sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"—the latent tendency of sensual craving (*kāmāsava*) that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen...

It is abandoned. Likewise, regarding sublime states (*mahaggata-dhamma*) and all states belonging to the three planes, by means of attention to impermanence and so forth preceded by the vision of danger, the outflows of existence (*bhavāsava*) and ignorance (*avijjāsava*)—which constitute the way of escape—do not arise if unarisen, and if arisen, they are abandoned.
Thus, the detailed exposition for the bright side (*sukkappakka*) should be understood as the opposite of the method described for the side of craving.
Why are only three taints mentioned here in this discussion on what is to be abandoned by vision, instead of saying "four" as is done in the Abhidhamma?

In that context, it should be understood that the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) is the opposite of the signless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*), because its nature consists of craving and longing.

As for the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), it is the opposite of the signless liberation because it generally follows the grasping at permanence regarding states of existence and because it is accompanied by attachment to existence.

However, regarding the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), there is nothing at all that can be said about its being an outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*), because ignorance as an outflow is the opposite of the liberation of emptiness (*suññatavimokkha*) due to the power of knowledge established through the perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*).
"In this" means in this discussion on the outflows (*āsava*). "Described" means spoken of.
"By way of non-differentiation" means by way of generality.
18. "Of the taints of sensual desire, etc. means of the taints of sensual desire, etc., which lead to rebirth in the human world and the deva worlds.
However, those taints of sensual desire, etc., which lead to rebirth in hell and so forth, are already included in the phrase "taints to be abandoned by vision.
Alternatively, to the extent that this person is the basis for the taints to be abandoned by vision, to that same extent he is also the basis for the taints of sensual desire, etc.
The phrase beginning with “to this extent” was stated to show that there is no difference in the underlying reality (vatthu) due to a difference in conventional designation (samaññā).

For this very reason, he said, “stated by way of their commonality. But why, when the taints (āsava) to be abandoned through vision are to be shown here, is doubt (vicikicchā) shown by means of the formula “Was I indeed in the past? and so forth? To this he replied, “And here, under the heading of doubt,” and so on. Thus...
Just as doubt arises with sixteen bases, so too does improper attention.
Regarding "existence and non-existence": based on the suspicion of eternalism, one thinks, "Did I exist in the past?"—this refers to the existence of oneself in the past.
Based on the suspicion of fortuitous origination, one thinks, "From whatever point I began... [and so forth].
He doubts the non-existence of himself in the past, wondering, "Did I not exist previously? Why?
Because doubt clings to two modes of apprehension. Furthermore, because it grasps the past as its objective basis, it is shown to rely on the modes of eternalism and fortuitous origination.
Thus, doubt—which functions by moving back and forth and which serves as the cause for never turning away from anything—[is described].
Showing that one should not raise the objection, "Why does he produce [this]?", he said, "The reason why it should not be so stated is this.
That very state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*). If this is so, then it follows that he must possess only improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*);
to address this, he said, "But does not even an ordinary person attend properly (*yoniso*)? In that context, "therein" refers to proper attention.

"Birth, gender, and rebirth" refers to birth as a kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, and so forth; gender as a householder or one who has gone forth; and rebirth as a deva, human, and so forth. "Depending on" means by way of taking [these] as a basis.
At that time, the medium size of sentient beings was the standard measure (*pamāṇika*);

because that [standard] was absent, or because it had passed away from that state, it should be understood as "without measure" (*appamāṇika*). "Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. For they [ask]: "How indeed... by a Lord (*issara*)..."
“Or [they think] it is produced by Brahmā, or by past deeds, or without cause,” they say. Therefore it is said: “They speak of doubting regarding the cause.
For doubt concerning production without a cause is indeed just a misapprehension of the cause. “Succession” (paramparā) means the continuous flow of preceding and succeeding states.
“Duration” (addhāna) is a designation for time; and that should be understood as an accusative case used in the sense of a locative.
"Existence and non-existence": based on the suspicion of eternalism, one doubts the existence of oneself in the future, thinking, "Shall I exist in the future time?";

and based on the suspicion of annihilationism, one doubts the non-existence of oneself in the future, thinking, "In whatever selfhood I am now, shall I not exist beyond that? This should be construed according to the method explained below.
Regarding the phrase "the present time": because it is the temporal present that is intended here, it is said, "beginning with rebirth-linking," and so forth.
Because it proceeds by way of thinking, "What is this? What is this?", it is called *kaṅkhā* (doubt);
one who possesses this is a *kaṅkhī* (one who doubts). Thus he says, "he becomes doubtful. What need for further reflection here? For he is like a madman.
The intention [of the text] is that the term "foolish worldling" (*bālaputhujjana*) was stated specifically as a precaution. He was the son of the chief queen.
Regarding the phrase "they shaved him": they shaved him while he was unwilling and awake, for it was impossible [to do so while he was conscious];
according to the family custom, as is the case with certain ascetics of noble lineage, they say it was done out of fear of the king.

“Became cool”: this is a statement regarding the cause for reaching a state of sweetness. There is also a reading “became white” (*setibhūta*); the meaning is that it attained whiteness by remaining in the water for a long time.
He was like one who, while doubting his own kshatriya status, perceives himself as the son of a charioteer.
With reference to his grasping at himself as “I” when his birth is being investigated, he said: “For in this way there might be doubt. And people also...
"Like kings" means that some people are like certain kings; this is the intended meaning.
It is according to the method already stated, beginning with "in dependence on the mode of configuration," and so forth. "In this regard" refers to the phrase "How indeed am I?
"A living being within" refers to the internal self (antarattāna) postulated by others. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the sixteen *saṃsās*, etc.,"...
It includes such things as the measurement of the body, its circumference, and the size of the atoms of a single grain of rice.

The notion that "the designation of a 'being' has the living soul (jīva) as its object" is merely the opinion of those who hold to false views; in the ultimate sense, however, it has the personal existence (attabhāva) as its object.
Thus he says, "the place of the coming and going of the personal existence," meaning that this is the place from which it has come and where it will go.

19. "In what way this doubt arises": this means that this aforementioned classification of doubt arises in such a manner for one who attends to things inappropriately (*ayoniso manasikaroto*). By this, he states that doubt has its basis in the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*).

For just as doubt proceeds by depending on the adherence to a self—since it takes as its object the modes of eternalism, fortuitous origination, eternalism, and annihilationism—[so too does it arise].

Thus, the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*) also proceeds based on that [ignorance], because the state of being a doubter—which includes the conceit "I was indeed" and so forth—is dependent upon the grasping at a self.
For this very reason it is said: "Because of the firm establishment of unwise attention accompanied by doubt.
The sense of "alternative" (*vikappa*) means the sense of indefiniteness; for it is said: "A certain view arises."
"By way of being very firm" means by way of the extreme strengthening of the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*).
"In this and that" refers to within that particular existence (*bhava*). By the restrictive particle "only the present," the existence [of the self] in the future is excluded;

however, it does not exclude its existence in the past, because since existence persists even there, the grasping for annihilation (*ucchedagāha*) would otherwise still be present. The intended meaning is: "It exists only in the past, not even in the future."
“With the aggregate of perception as its head” means with the aggregate of perception as its chief; the sense is that it makes the aggregate of perception the foremost.
“The aggregates” refers to all five aggregates. “Grasping as ‘self’” means adhering [to the view]: “My self has the nature of perceiving.
Just as an object to be displayed, and just as a lamp illuminating itself, so too the blue and other objects to be perceived—[are illuminated] by the aggregate of perception.
"One perceives even oneself as [identical to] the self"—thus, because one possesses such a view, it is said that one "perceives oneself by means of oneself" due to a particular mode of viewing.
This meaning arises through the grasping of perception and certain other phenomena as "self" or "not-self";
therefore, it is said, "by way of the aggregate of perception," and so forth. And herein, for one who grasps a self as distinct from the aggregates—

The view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) and the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*)—the latter being the grasping of the aggregates as "self"—are thus referred to by the phrase, "all views of eternalism and annihilationism.

"Modes of dogmatic adherence" (*abhinivesākārā*) means modes of perversion (*vipariyesākārā*). By the word "speaks" (*vadati*), he demonstrates his own capacity to awaken beings to their welfare and happiness;
hence he says, "the agent of vocal action. "Vedeyya" means one who feels (*vedeti*); it is derived from *vediyo*, meaning simply "one who feels."
For those learned in the science of grammar consider that such words have primarily the sense of an agent (*kattusādhanata*).

Since that which possesses arising must necessarily possess passing away, and since there can be no permanence when there is both arising and passing away, he said "devoid of arising and passing away" to clarify the intention of one who says "permanent.
"Substantial" means possessing substantiality precisely because of its permanence. "Existing at all times" means...

Existing at all times. "The state of nature" (*pakatibhāva*) means the nature that constitutes its own-being (*sabhāva*), or the nature designated as "nature" as expressed by the words "the speaker," and so forth. "Equal to eternity" (*sassatisama*) means equal to eternity;
the meaning is that it is stable and exists for all time. "It shall remain just so" means in whatever manner it stood previously and stands now.
"In that very same way, it will remain in that manner even in the future"—this is the meaning.
This is a demonstration by direct perception (*paccakkha-nidassana*), made by employing the word "this" (*idaṃ*) to indicate its state of being immediate and perceptible.

"A view itself is a 'gone-to-view' (*diṭṭhigata*)"—he says this to show that the word "gone" (*gata*) is merely an intensification of the term. "One who has gone to views" means one who is included among those with wrong views.
This is the meaning. For this very reason, he said: "Because they are included within the sixty-two views. "The mere going of a view" means the mere grasping of a view.
Just as mountain torrents and water-courses are difficult to exit, so too is the grasping of a view;
thus he said: "It is a 'thicket' in the sense of being difficult to exit. That is called "water"; because one must cross over it after having taken hold of that [grasping].

A wilderness (*kantāra*) is a forest devoid of water; it is also called a "wind-forest" (*pavana*). However, another region of the forest is like a wilderness in the sense that it is difficult to traverse;
thus, he said "in the sense of being difficult to traverse," and so forth, with reference to [wrong] view as well. Piercing through (*vinivijjhana*) means cutting through (*vitudana*).
Being contrary (*vilomana*) means the state of transformation (*vipariṇāmabhāva*). Because its intrinsic nature is unstable, it is wavering and flickering; thus he said "sometimes," and so forth.
The sense of "binding" (bandhana) is the making of one not free from servitude by way of not allowing escape, like the binding of feet and so forth.

The sense of "fettering" (saṃyojana) is the yoking together by drawing back even that which has gone far away through its state of being a condition for the rounds of defilements, karma, and kamma-result; since view is of such a nature, it is called the "fetter of views.
The intention is that he states this while demonstrating the meaning of binding for the sake of accomplishing the function [of the fetters]. Therefore he said:
“...is liberated from the fetter of views... and so forth. In that context, by the phrase “by these,” [the Blessed One] states the conditionality of suffering such as birth and the rest.
