Even after demonstrating the phenomena of suffering, such as birth, in their own nature, the Blessed One—who stated, “one is not fully liberated from suffering”—[intended to show that] the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*) is indeed the cause of all misfortune, highly blameworthy, and the source of all suffering.

In order to show that this meaning has been clarified as being "the root," it was said: "Or rather, what need for much? One is not even liberated from the suffering of the entire cycle of existence. [Objection:

But surely, here by the mention of the fetter of views (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*), the misapprehension of rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) should also be shown; for in this way, through such a demonstration—
Addressing the objection that the taints (āsava) to be abandoned have not been shown in their entirety, he says “because,” and so forth.
Adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is already included by the mention of the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the others, because it has those very taints as its cause.

For one who has not abandoned sensual lust and the rest either for the sake of sensual pleasure or for the sake of purification through existence adheres to rules and observances, thinking, “In this way, there is purification from existence.”
They misapprehend the virtue and observance spoken of in the Sutta thus: “By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity”;
or, “Therein I shall remain permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and persist for ever and ever”;
or, “Purification comes through virtue, purification comes through a vow, purification comes through both virtue and vow. This is what they misapprehend.

In that context, "for the sake of the pleasure of existence and for the sake of purification of existence" means both for the sake of the pleasure of existence (*bhavasukha*) and for the sake of purification of existence (*bhavavisuddhi*).

"Because it is included therein" means because the misapprehension of rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is included by the mention of "views," as in such passages as "for the abandoning of the various types of views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya*).

"Of those" refers to those things to be abandoned by vision. [This was said] to show, by means of a teaching based on persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya*), [the nature of] its opposite. "Of its opposite" means...
For a virtuous worldling who attends [to things] with wise attention.
"Tassa" (of him) refers to the passage beginning with "the learned one. "Tāva" means taking this phrase as the limit, starting from "the learned one" up to the words "this is suffering.

"By the method stated below" refers to the phrases concerning the noble person and the commoner, the noble dharma and the dharma of the commoner, and what is to be attended to and what is not to be attended to.
The connection is as follows: the meaning should be understood according to the method stated here by taking [the terms] from the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* in their proper order.

Regarding "stated in opposition": the meaning should be understood as being the complete opposite of what was stated for these phrases—"the learned noble disciple, one who sees the noble ones, one who sees true persons"—but for the phrases "skilled" and "disciplined," it is not the opposite of everything that was stated.
For an Arahant is, in the direct sense, both skilled in the noble Dhamma and well-disciplined in the noble Dhamma. Therefore it was said:

"He should be understood as a noble disciple who has [overcome] the adverse in every way... pe ...". Knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) is insight that has reached its culmination.
Some, however, say that "insight that has reached its culmination begins from the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*)," but that is incorrect. In accordance with that...
"In the sense of the goal" means in the sense of the Noble One (ariya) appropriate to that person, not by way of penetration; this is the intended meaning.

For this is a "good worldling" (kalyāṇaputhujjana). Just as his status as a "trainee" (sekha) was stated in the Sekha Sutta by way of a figurative expression—beginning with "even one who is a good worldling" and concluding with "he too is called a trainee because he trains"—so too here...

The state of being a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) has been stated. By way of those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), known as the Dhamma and Vinaya of the noble person, or indeed the three trainings (*tisraḥ śikṣāḥ*), which arise through the characteristics of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*), his status as a noble disciple and so forth is stated.
Therefore he said: "by a meaning corresponding to that. Or, [it may be explained] as "a disciple of the Noble One" (*ariyassa sāvako*) by means of the very sense of "noble disciple" (*ariyasāvaka*).

It was said, for example: "The Buddha went to Rājagaha. Furthermore, the inclusion of "insight that has reached its culmination" (*sikhāppattavipassanā*) here is intended to refer to one who, having made insight their primary pursuit, stands upon the path of non-retrogression;
thus, the aforementioned commentary on the meaning is all the more appropriate.

21. Just as one who is intent upon insight by way of the elements is a "meditator on the meditation subject of the elements" (dhātukammaṭṭhānika), and one who is intent upon it by way of the sense bases and so forth is a "meditator on the meditation subject of the sense bases and so forth" (āyatanādikammaṭṭhānika), so too one who is intent upon it by way of the Truths is called a "meditator on the meditation subject of the Four Truths" (catusaccakammaṭṭhānika).

It is called "kamma" because it is to be performed by those seeking to cross over the four floods; it is "bhāvanā" (development). It is "kamma" precisely because it leads to the attainment of distinction.
*Ṭhāna* means cause. Alternatively, in the sense already stated, it is the basis (*ṭhāna*) or the foundation (*avaṭṭhāna*) for the undertaking of meditation;

thus, the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is the undertaking of meditation. One who possesses this [subject] as it proceeds by way of the Four Noble Truths is called "one whose subject of meditation is the Four Noble Truths" (*catusaccakammaṭṭhānika*).

"Non-occurrence" (*appavatti*) means that neither [of these two] occurs therein. "One who has grasped the subject of meditation on the Four Noble Truths" refers to the subject of meditation on the Four Noble Truths according to the scripture (*pāḷito*).
Having grasped it according to its meaning and made it suitable for attention, he stands firm.

"He has ascended the path of insight" means that, having established himself in the vision of name-and-form together with their conditions, he comprehends that very name-and-form as impermanent and so forth. "He directs his mind" refers to the advertence of insight;
therefore, he directs his mind in such a way that the knowledge of insight proceeds, thinking, "This is suffering."
The meaning is "he adverts. But how, in this context, is the meaning "he sees with insight" expressed by the phrase "he attends"?
To this he says: "In this... [etc]... it is said. "In this" means in this sutta.
And "he sees with insight" (vipassati) means that he sees with the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu), observes, in such a way that a further distinction is attained above.
The Path, too, should be mentioned. For while the first two Truths are difficult to see because of their profundity, the other [the Path] is profound because it is difficult to see.
"Adherence" refers to the adherence of insight—that is, the practice of insight. "Having that as its object" means occurring with that aggregate of form as its object.
"Having defined the characteristic according to its true nature" means having defined it unerringly according to its own...

Having placed in the heart, without confusion, the object (ārammaṇa) together with its functions such as delimiting individual essences (sabhāva-chedana) and its characteristics such as ignorance (aññāṇa), this [text] shows that although the delimitation of mind-and-body (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) was performed previously, the establishment of the specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa-vavatthāpana) of phenomena becomes well-established through the discernment of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha);
just as it is said, "that which is bound twice is well-bound. For in this way:

The task of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) is said to be accomplished. Because they have been defined by way of their conditions and the things arisen from those conditions, the state of being accomplished is evident even through the state of being manifest; thus it is said, "having not been, they come to be.

One applies the characteristic of impermanence because there must be an arising of what is non-existent, not of what already exists, and because they possess arising, they are necessarily [impermanent].
Conditions must be sought because their existence is dependent [on them]; since cessation is inevitable when there is arising, there is no room for permanence whatsoever.
And because it is constantly oppressed by the nature of arising and passing away due to its well-established impermanence, it is suffering in the sense of being unsatisfactory.
Therefore he said: "Because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, it is suffering; thus he attributes the characteristic of suffering. In some places...
Regarding the passage on formations (*saṅkhāra*): because it is impossible [to say] of them, "May you not grow old, may you not fall ill," there is no exercise of mastery;

thus he says, "Because there is no exercise of mastery, they are non-self; he applies the characteristic of non-self. "In succession" means by way of the sequence beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
"At that moment" refers to the moment of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). "By a single penetration alone" means by penetrating through a single act of knowledge (*eka-ñāṇa*).
Penetration (*paṭivedha*) is the piercing-through (*nibbijjhana*), characterized by moving without attachment toward an object due to the absence of resistance.

Full comprehension (*abhisamaya*) is the awakening (*avabodha*) characterized by the attainment of the object without missing it. Penetration through full understanding (*pariññā-paṭivedha*) is precisely the knowing that arises from delimiting [the truth] according to the stated method: "This is suffering; this much is suffering; there is nothing beyond this."
This was stated by way of its occurrence, so that there may be no delusion regarding the specific nature and other characteristics of suffering after knowledge has already arisen;
however, it is not because path-knowledge proceeds by way of the formula "this is suffering" and so forth. Therefore he said, "For at that time...
and so on. "Abandoning" (*hāna*) refers to the excellent act of relinquishing (*cajana*) that which has been abandoned such that it need not be abandoned again.
"Cutting off" is abandoning; "penetration by abandoning" means that abandoning itself is penetration in the manner already described.

This too refers to that which strikes down the footprints of those defilements—which, if unabandoned, would prevent the cultivation of the path, and in the absence of such cultivation, would arise—and brings them to the state of non-arising.

It is stated thus because it involves a movement free from attachment due to the absence of any obstruction to the such-like occurrence of knowledge. "Realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) means making directly evident;
it is the taking of an object in its own form, having abandoned hearsay, mere modes of expression, discursive thought, and so forth.

This is the "method" (*tantrī*), which is the grasping [of the object] according to its true nature. That very process, by the method already described, is "penetration" (*paṭivedha*); thus, it is "penetration as realization" (*sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha*).

But this [knowledge] is described thus because, by cutting off that obstruction which it was unable to take cessation as its object due to not having cut off, it proceeds having clearly manifested that [cessation] in its true nature.

Development (*bhāvanā*) means producing and increasing; therein, in the case of the first path, it is in the sense of production, and in the second path and so forth, it is in the sense of increasing.
Or rather, it should be understood in both ways for both cases.

For even the first path, as it proceeds by appropriately increasing the full understanding and so forth that lead to emergence, can be recognized there too as "development" (bhāvanā) in the sense of increasing.

In the second and subsequent paths as well, [it is development] in the sense of producing [the fruit], because of the abandoning of defilements not yet abandoned and because of accomplishing other types of individuals.
Development (*bhāvanā*) is itself penetration (*paṭivedha*) according to the method already stated; thus, "development-penetration.
For this too is spoken of by taking up its very occurrence, just as there is no delusion regarding the specific nature of the path-phenomena once knowledge has arisen.
Let that be for now; [this same principle applies] even to the fruit-phenomena as they occur, in accordance with the path-phenomena already attained.
He becomes one who is free from delusion regarding the true Dhamma as it has been realized. Therefore it is said:
"One who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, fathomed the Dhamma.

And from that point, impelled by the nature of things (*dhammatā*), there arise within him—following the sequence of the path—the reviewings of the path, the fruit, the defilements abandoned, and Nibbāna remaining.

For the phenomena of the truth of suffering consist of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth. And this explanation of the meaning should also be clarified in relation to such passages as “by the full comprehension and realization.

In order to demonstrate more clearly the very meaning already stated—that one realizes [the truths] by a single realization—the phrase “but not by means of mutually distinct knowledges,” and so forth, was spoken.
But the caviller says: "The knowledge of the noble path performs its function by means of distinct realizations regarding the four truths, not by means of a single realization.

For at one time it understands suffering, at another time it abandons the origin, at another time it realizes cessation, and at another time it develops the path; otherwise, for a single knowledge to [perform all these functions] in a single..."
“Performing the four functions simultaneously is not tenable; for nowhere has such a thing been seen or heard in the Suttas.

He should be told: “If the knowledge of the Noble Path realizes the Truths by way of multiple realizations (*nānābhisamaya*) and not by way of a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*), then, that being the case, it would proceed toward each Truth separately at different moments and not at a single moment. If that were so—”

If one were to understand and abandon only a portion of suffering and so forth, it would follow that there is a "gradual realization" (nānābhisamaya), whereby there could be a partial abandonment of the three fetters and so on—which are to be abandoned by the first path and the subsequent paths—resulting in the status of being a "partial stream-enterer" (ekadesa-sotāpatti-maggaṭṭha) and so on.

This would also result in the status of being a "partial stream-enterer" (ekadesa-sotāpanna) and so forth. However, this is not the case, because supramundane wholesome states have an immediate fruit (anantaraphala).
And that [position] is logical. For it is not possible to understand how the very same person is both a stream-enterer and a non-stream-enterer without a difference in time.

Furthermore, this proponent of multiple realizations (nānābhisamaya-vādī) should be asked: "When path-knowledge penetrates the truths, does it penetrate them by way of its object (ārammaṇa), or by way of its function (kicca)? Knowing the answer, he would say: "By way of its function. "By way of its function..."
Having said, "What need is there for a separate realization for one who is penetrating [the truths]?", he should be convinced by a demonstration in successive order.

Then, if he should say, "From the perspective of the object," this being so, the absolute full understanding and eradication of suffering and its origin would not be appropriate for that knowledge—just as they are for insight-knowledge—because it has not yet emerged [from the defilements].
Likewise, the vision of the path [would not be appropriate], for the path does not [arise] by itself.
It is logical that [knowledge] occurs with reference to the self; however, by postulating an intervening path, one falls into the error of instability.
Therefore, while the three truths are penetrated through their functions, cessation is penetrated both through its function and its object.
Thus, for the knowledge of the path that penetrates without confusion, there is no separate realization (nānābhisamaya). For this has been said: "Whoever..."
“Monks, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering,” and so forth. This was not said with reference to seeing at different times;

rather, it was stated for the purpose of establishing that point in the investigation of whether one who possesses the vision of one truth necessarily possesses the vision of the other truths, as in: “Friend, does he who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering... [and] the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?”

Because it was brought forth by the venerable Elder Gavampati, and because the vision of each of the three truths was applied [by him], otherwise—since what was previously seen would not be seen again—the vision of the origin and so forth would have had to be applied.
For the supramundane path does not function like a mundane path by way of performing what has already been done, due to its nature of total eradication; likewise...

One should convince them that "if all-seeing were by means of a single application, it would be the supreme among all forms of seeing, and thus there would be no cessation of seeing"—thereby showing that, both according to scripture and through reasoning, a gradual realization (nānābhisamaya) is not tenable. If they are thus convinced, that is well.
If they are not convinced, they should be convinced by means of a specific discussion on the Abhidhamma.
"By way of cessation as the object" means that the restriction should be understood as "cessation alone as the object," and not "by way of an object.
By this, penetration through the function [of cessation] regarding cessation is established. "At that time" refers to the breakthrough to the truths (*saccābhisamaya*).
"Consisting of twenty bases," etc., is a detailed exposition of those stated as "the three fetters" (*saññojana*). "In regard to the four taints" (*āsava*)...
This is stated according to the method of the Abhidhamma, not according to the method of the Suttas; for nowhere in the Suttas are four taints (āsava) mentioned.

If doubt (vicikicchā) is not a taint, then why was it said: “Bhikkhus, personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances—these, bhikkhus, are called the taints to be abandoned by vision”? To this he says: “to be abandoned by vision,” and so forth.

By the phrase "included herein" (ettha pariyāpannattā), he shows that because it shares the same functional nature as right intention within the aggregate of wisdom, doubt is included here among the taints (āsava).
It is stated that "there is no grasping at a self apart from the personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)," and thus [doubt] is analyzed among the six views... etc.

For that view is "of one function" (ekaṭṭha) both in a single moment of consciousness and within the continuum; therein, the first is "of one function by way of co-nascence" (sahajātekaṭṭha), while the other is "of one function by way of abandonment" (pahānekaṭṭha).
Having determined both of these, the phrase beginning with "from the taints of views" (diṭṭhāsavehi) was stated to show them.
"In every way" (sabbathāpi) means in all modes—that is, in the modes of being of one function by way of co-nascence and of one function by way of abandonment. "The remainder" (avasesa)...
The remaining [taints] are those of view. "The three taints" refers to the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
For it was stated previously: "In regard to the four taints. Therefore, because many taints are to be abandoned here, the plural designation was employed:
"These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by vision. "Of the ancients" means of the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).
And they say, "of the ancient Middle Reciters.
Regarding what should be said concerning [the categories] such as "to be abandoned by seeing," that has already been stated above.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by seeing is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint (Saṃvarāpahātabba-āsava): 22. "By means of restraint, etc. refers to restraint, avoidance, endurance, and elimination.
"Of all" refers to all four noble paths. This discussion concerning what is to be abandoned by restraint and so forth should be understood as the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā).
For it was stated below that the purpose of the Suttanta teaching is "to show the practice for the destruction of the taints, beginning with the purification of the defilements.
Indeed, it is not possible to develop the Noble Path from the very outset;
rather, one who has undertaken virtue and guards the doors of the sense faculties [reflects]: "Having reflected, one pursues one thing; having reflected, one endures another."
“Having reflected, one avoids one thing; having reflected, one dispels another.

Thus, practicing the fourfold foundation of mindfulness as it has been described, one enters the method of comprehension, gradually brings insight to its peak, and exhausts the taints through the sequence of the paths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, just as the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually...”

"It is like a mountain slope that is gradual, not precipitous all at once; even so, monks, in this Dhamma and Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice, and not the penetration of final knowledge all at once.
Here, the word "here" (*idha*) indicates, in every respect, the teaching that serves as the support for a person who is restrained by the restraint of the sense faculties.
It is said, "in this teaching," as a negation of the existence of such [qualities] in other teachings.

"Reflection on danger" (ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā) means the contemplation of danger. "Polished" (sampalimaṭṭhaṃ) means rubbed down. "By way of minor details" (anubyañjanaso) means by way of the various aspects such as hands, feet, smiles, speech, and glances.
For that is called a "minor detail" (anubyañjana) because it manifests (byañjanato) the defilements little by little (anu anu) for one who attends to it improperly (ayoniso).
"Grasping at signs" (*nimittaggāha*) means the grasping of a sign, such as the sign of a woman or a man, or of a sign that serves as a basis for the defilements (*kilesavatthu*).

"By the method of the Discourse on the Burning" (*ādittapariyāyanayena*) should be construed with "the reflection on danger" (*ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā*); that is, it is to be understood according to the method presented in the *Ādittapariyāya Sutta*.

It is not like the term "female faculty" (*itthindriya*), which [derives from] "the faculty of a woman" (*itthiyā indriyaṃ*); rather, this [term] is simply "the eye as a faculty" (*cakkhuṃ eva indriyaṃ*).
"Cakkhundriya" (eye-faculty). "A crow at a watering place" means a crow at a watering place (*titthakāka*); it refers to one that stays fixedly at a river crossing used for crossing over.
The same method applies to "a frog in a pit" and so forth.
Thus, because its mode of existence is bound to that [object], restraint which has the eye-faculty as its fixed locus is "restraint of the eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriyasaṃvara*).
Lack of mindfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*) refers to unwholesome states that are the opposites of mindfulness.

Even though elsewhere the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) may arise uninterruptedly for an incalculable period, it is said in the *Bhavaṅga* section, "having arisen and ceased twice," because between the impact on the sensitive parts of the body, the adverting, and the arising [of the sense-door process], only two instances of the life-continuum consciousness arise; this is the fixed order of consciousness.

However, regarding the moment of javana, since the passage beginning with "if immorality" (*dussīlyaṃ*) and so forth has already been explained here in its entirety for the purpose of avoiding repetition, it should be applied to the six doors as appropriate. For there is no restraint of immorality consisting of bodily or verbal misconduct in the five doors;
therefore, that [restraint] should be applied by way of the mind door, while the other [restraint] should be applied by way of all six doors.
For while unwholesome states such as forgetfulness— which have characteristics opposed to mindfulness— might arise at the five doors,
misconduct consisting of bodily and verbal transgression cannot arise there, because the javanas of the five doors do not produce intimation (viññatti).
The phrase "in what way" (*yathā kinti*) means: by what manner does the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) arising in the impulsion (*javana*) come to be called "non-restraint at the eye-door"?

This is the meaning of the illustration. By the words "in what way" (*yathā*) and so forth, it is shown that just as when there is non-restraint at a city gate, the houses and other structures connected to it become unrestrained, so too, when there is non-restraint in the impulsion, the doors and other factors connected to it become unrestrained.

In the phrase "restraint in what is other" (*aññāsaṃvare*), it demonstrates only the commonality of being unrestrained in what is other, not the commonality of preceding and succeeding moments, nor the commonality of the internal and external.
Furthermore, the relationship [of the doors, etc.,] with the impulsion (*javana*) is to be understood solely by virtue of their being included within a single continuity (*ekasantati*).

By way of being a condition, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth—which were previously produced and are non-existent at the time of the impulsion—are nevertheless existent for the production of the result, just like the eye and other sense bases.
Indeed, that which is currently existing is not called "present" (santa);

therefore, when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so forth are present, the javana that arises subsequently is treated as if it were external, and is thus described as being like the city gate. The other [the life-continuum] is like the houses and so forth within the city.
For although, in the ultimate sense, the javana has no external existence and the other has no internal existence, [it is said]: "This [mind] is luminous..."
From such statements as, "Monks, the mind is defiled by adventitious defilements," it should be understood figuratively that the impulsion (javana),
which is adventitious and arises only occasionally, is external, while the other [the underlying nature],
which is of a different character from that, is internal. Or, when non-restraint has arisen in the impulsion, from that...

However, because the door-moment, the bhavaṅga, and so forth, become the causes for non-restraint (asaṃvara), one should see that after entering by means of the javana—which is like a city gate—the plundering of thieves such as immorality (*dussīlya*) in the door-moment, the bhavaṅga, and so forth, constitutes the destruction of the goods of the wholesome (*kusala*).
For when non-restraint arises, the state of being its cause is perceived in the doors and so forth; and that [non-restraint], at the very moment it arises, [affects] the doors and so forth.
It proceeds precisely by warding off the state of being a support for restraint; this is the manner of occurrence of non-restraint and so forth.

When an object such as a visible form has entered the range of the five sense doors, unwholesome impulsion arises according to conditions, and once the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has subsided, mind-door impulsion occurs, taking that same object and then subsiding into the life-continuum. Again, in that very [object]...
At the door, having determined the object as "woman" or "man" and so forth, the impulsion (javana) sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
On a subsequent occasion, the impulsion runs again by way of attachment and so on.

Furthermore, if a similar object comes into range, an impulsion arises with respect to the visible forms and other objects at the five doors that is exactly like it. With reference to this, it was said: "In the same way..."
"When misconduct and so forth arise in the mind, if there is no restraint therein, the door is likewise unguarded," and so on.
This, first of all, is the explanation of the meaning regarding the side of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The meaning regarding the side of restraint (*saṃvara*) should also be understood by this same method. One who is endowed with restraint is "restrained."
Because it was stated [thus], he said: “‘One who has approached’ is what is meant.

Regarding the phrase “having made into one,” this means having treated as identical in meaning the expression “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. And this very sense is more excellent here, because it accords with the subsequent text.
Therefore he said: “For thus,” and so forth. By the word “yaṃ” (which), together with a change of gender in the pronoun *ādeso*, [the sense is established].
This shows that there is a permutation of the grammatical number; or else, this is a particle used in the sense of the third person plural.

"Afflictive" means causing affliction to the mind and producing mental suffering. The "fever of result" (*vipāka-pariḷāha*) refers precisely to the results that follow from the burning [of defilements], having the aforementioned defilements as their cause.
Furthermore, just as here the taints (*āsava*) and other afflictive defilements and fevers of result are mentioned...
To demonstrate how these [unwholesome states] arise, the passage beginning with "through the eye-door" was stated; that is indeed easy to understand.

Herein, this distinction should be understood: the means of restraint, that which is to be restrained, the restraint itself, the source from which that restraint arises, the locus where restraint occurs, and the fruit of restraint. How so? For "wise reflection" is the means of restraint.

The eye-faculty is to be restrained. By the mention of "restraint," mindfulness is included as that restraint. "Of one unrestrained" indicates the limit of restraint; for restraint is the opposite of non-restraint.
By the mention of "that which is to be restrained," the object of restraint is established here.

For the eye-faculty is restrained by the knowledge of restraint upon a visible-form object; thus, this meaning is established even without being explicitly stated. The absence of the fever of taints, their signs, and the defilements [is the result].
The fruit. In this same way, it should be applied to the ear-door and so forth as well. "In all cases" means in every door, namely, both the mind-door and the five doors.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by restraint is finished.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by careful use.

23. Regarding the passage beginning with "Reflecting wisely on the robe," etc., "reflecting wisely" (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*) refers precisely to the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*) stated as "for the warding off of cold," and so forth.
"Such as this" (*īdisaṃ*) means an object of this kind that is desirable.

"Relishing it through the longing for existence" (*bhavapatthanāya assādayato*) means for one who relishes the object cultivated by way of the longing for existence. "The robe" (*cīvaraṃ*) refers to anything such as an undergarment (*nivāsana*), etc.
"Robe-cloth. "He uses" means he makes use of it by way of wearing it as an undergarment and so forth.
"Only so far as" is a restriction regarding the measure of its purpose. For the purpose of a practitioner in using robe-cloth is indeed only for the warding off of cold and so forth.

"Of cold" means of cold arisen from a disturbance of the elements or from a change in the seasons. "For the warding off" means for the purpose of repelling the physical alteration caused by that [cold].
For the purpose of diversion. "Of heat" means of the heat produced from the warmth of a fire. Gnat-stings and so forth are well known.
Again, the phrase "only as much as" is a restriction regarding the measure of a fixed purpose. For the fixed purpose for the use of the robe is the concealment of the private parts (*hirikopīna*);
the other [purposes] occur only occasionally. "Private parts" refers to the region of the genitals. For in that which...
When a limb is exposed, one is ashamed and feels abashed; because it causes shame, it is called *hirikopīna*. One uses the robe for the purpose of concealing that.

"Almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to any kind of nutriment. For it is so called because, by means of wandering for alms (*piṇḍolya*), whatever portions of alms-food are obtained here and there fall into the bowl;
thus it is a gathering (*pāta*) of what is found in various places, hence it is called "almsfood. "Neither for sport," etc.
"Not for play" means not for the sake of intoxication—that is, not for the purpose of the pride of strength, the pride of conceit, or the pride of manhood.

"Not for beautification" means not for the purpose of plumpness in the limbs and members. "Not for adornment" means not for the purpose of their loveliness; the meaning is: for the purpose of excellence of complexion. And these terms are intended, respectively, for the abandonment of the underlying tendencies of delusion, hatred, shape, color, and lust.

These should be understood [as follows]. Alternatively, the first two [nutriments] are for the purpose of preventing the arising of defilement in oneself, while the other is also for the sake of others.
It should be understood that all four are taught for the purpose of abandoning devotion to the pleasure of sense-desires.
"Of the body" means of the material body (*rūpakāya*). "For its stability and maintenance" means for the sake of its continuous persistence and for the sake of the non-interruption of its occurrence.
For the sake of its long-term endurance, for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

"For the cessation of affliction" means for the purpose of stopping the suffering of hunger. "For the support of the holy life" means for the sake of supporting the holy life of the path of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
"Thus" means in this way, by this means. "I shall ward off old feeling" refers to [the suffering] caused by not having eaten previously.

"I shall ward off the feeling arising from food already eaten, and I shall not give rise to new feeling"—that is, "I shall not give rise to the feeling arising from the condition of food already eaten.
For he consumes food solely for the purpose that what has not yet arisen may not arise.
And herein, "feeling arising from the condition of not eating" refers to the hunger occurring as it naturally does.
Feeling (*vedanā*). For that [feeling] arises by way of increasing more and more in one who is not eating;
even the feeling arising on account of having eaten is characterized by hunger, while feelings such as burning in the limbs or piercing pains do not occur.

For that [feeling], having not arisen due to the condition of eating, will not arise [again]. And their distinction from harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) lies in the fact that they have harmfulness as their characteristic.
"And there will be for me sustenance" means there will be the maintenance of my four postures.

By the phrase "for sustenance," the maintenance of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is expressed; here, however, "sustenance" refers to the non-interruption of the four postures—this is the distinction between them.
"Blamelessness and a comfortable dwelling" [are achieved] by avoiding improper seeking, receiving, and using.

Blamelessness (*anavajjatā*) and a comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*) through moderate consumption. Blamelessness arises from the absence of faults such as discontent, lethargy, yawning, and censure by the wise, which result from unsuitable and immoderate eating;
while a comfortable dwelling arises from the development of physical strength due to suitable and moderate eating.

Blamelessness results from the absence of the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness, by avoiding eating until the stomach is full; [this is achieved] by eating only a measure of four or five mouthfuls.
It is a comfortable dwelling because it brings about fitness for the four postures. For this has been said:
"Having eaten only four or five mouthfuls, one may drink water;
this is sufficient for a comfortable dwelling for a bhikkhu who is resolute."
To this extent, the determination of the purpose and the middle way of practice have been illustrated.

"Recluse’s lodging" (*senāsana*) means both a bed (*sayana*) and a seat (*āsana*). For that place, such as a monastery (*vihāra*), where one lies down, reclines, sits, or remains seated, is a recluse’s lodging.
"For the sake of warding off the perils of climate and for delighting in seclusion": the climate itself, in the sense of enduring it...

"Peril" refers to that which causes physical affliction or mental distraction; or alternatively, it refers to the aforementioned "perils of the climate," as well as the "perils of wild beasts" such as lions and tigers, and the "perils concealed by passion and hatred.
It is for the purpose of dispelling these and for the sake of the bliss of solitude.
Furthermore, this [use of the robe] has the concealment of the private parts with a sense of shame as its indispensable function when using the robe. Thus, once again—
“Just as much as... is what was said.
“Requisites for the support of the sick” (gilānapaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra): it is a “support for the sick” because it functions as an antidote to illness;
it is “medicine” (bhesajja) precisely because it is the material permitted by a physician; and it is a “requisite” (parikkhāra) by virtue of being an accessory and a necessary component for life.
And medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness—this is what is meant. "Of those that have arisen" means of those that have been born or produced.

"Afflictive" means arisen from affliction, from the disturbance of the elements, and from the diseases produced thereby. "Painful sensations" refers to sensations of suffering. "For the sake of reaching the supreme state of non-affliction" is to be construed as:
"I partake [of these] for the purpose of attaining the ultimate condition of being free from suffering. Thus, in brief, it is here.

The commentary on the text should be understood. "Also because of the arising of new feelings" means that it should be understood not only as the fever of karmic result in the future, but also as the arising of new feelings due to overeating, such as those caused by insufficient clothing and so forth.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by use is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Forbearance (24). "Patient" (*khama*) means one who is capable of enduring.

He says, "He wavers, trembles, and abandons the meditation subject," because for one engaged in a meditation subject, wavering is indeed the abandonment of that meditation subject. Even excessive heat he endures; and while enduring it, he does not become like the naked ascetics (*naggasamaṇa*) and so forth.
"He endures it as it were" means that he does so not by abandoning his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), but rather by saying, "He is just like the Elder.
"Walking outside" means walking on the path outside the cave. "Precisely out of fear of heat" means precisely out of fear of the heat of the fires of hell.
Therefore he said, "Having reflected upon the great Avīci hell," and [he thought], "I have experienced that many times, but this [heat] is milder than that."
Having reflected thus: "In this place" means in this state. It should be understood as the heat of fire because the heat of the sun is mentioned later.
"I am one of pure virtue" refers entirely to the thought "I am one of purified virtue," excluding death, and is rooted in non-remorse.
He produced rapture (*pīti*). "Simultaneously with the arising of rapture" means together with the emergence of the rapture of pervasion (*pharaṇapīti*).
"The poison was turned back" means that, overwhelmed by the force of the rapture, it was expelled right from the mouth of the bite. "Right there" means at the very spot where the snake had bitten.
"Having attained one-pointedness of mind" means having reached concentration (*samādhāna*) by way of the method beginning with, "The body of one whose mind is rapturous becomes tranquil."

One who finds delight (*ārāma*) in contentment with requisites (*paccaya-santosā*) and in meditation (*bhāvanā*) because they are the proper objects for such delight is "one who delights in contentment with requisites and in meditation" (*paccaya-santosabhāvanārāma*).
The state of being such is "contentment with requisites and delight in meditation" (*paccaya...rāmatā*); [the phrase ends] with that. A "great elder" (*mahāthera*) is an elder who is more senior.
A "path of speech" (*vacanapatha*) is the path for those who wish to make known the meaning through the very words themselves.
Or, it is "intense" in the sense of being unpleasant; for that which is not pleasant is undesirable and is called "intense.

Thus he explains the meaning of the phrase "of a nature to endure" as being of such a character. "As if starting to split his heart in an instant or a moment" means that, having become a non-returner (anāgāmī), he attained final nibbāna—that is, he attained arahantship and passed away.

"In this way, in all cases" means that in every instance—such as "one touched by heat longing for cold"—the arising of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) should be understood as being caused by signs such as heat;
the intention is that whether it be cold or heat, it is undesirable. When there is grasping at a self, there is grasping at what belongs to a self;
thus he says: "The grasping 'cold and heat are mine' is the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). Enduring when cold and so forth have arrived...
"Enduring them is like bearing them upon oneself," thus it is said: "Having taken them up, one bears them indeed.
"Does not cast off" means does not shake them away. For he who cannot endure cold and so forth is as if shaking them off, casting them away.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by endurance is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Avoidance (25):
"I am an ascetic"—the intended meaning is that one does not think, "I am an ascetic; what is the use of my life or my death?
"Having reflected" means having reflected upon the village area, the purpose, and so forth. "He withdraws" means...
He departs from the vicinity of elephants and other such creatures. A "thorny place" is a location where thorns grow.
"Infested by non-human beings" means corrupted by the presence of non-humans; the meaning is that they are fraught with danger.
"Level" means even; the meaning is that it is not uneven. Or, he committed such improper conduct.
Regarding the phrase "designated as restraint by virtue" (*sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhāta*): what needs to be said here concerning how avoidance constitutes virtue has already been stated above.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "He avoids a fierce elephant," one should understand that even the avoidance of elephants and so forth is indeed conduct-virtue (*ācārasīla*), since it is the carrying out of the Blessed One’s word.
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by avoidance is finished.
Commentary on the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling (26):
"Iti pi" means for this reason; [the taints are to be abandoned] because they arise from improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and because they are accompanied by greed and other [defilements].

The meaning is that this thought is unwholesome for reasons such as being the opposite of the wholesome (*kusalapaṭipakkha*). In this same manner, the meaning should also be understood for [the terms] "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) and so forth.
And here, by the phrase "unwholesome" and so on, he shows the danger of sensual thought pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*);

by the phrase "resulting in suffering" (*dukkhavipāka*), he shows that pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*). By the phrases "it leads to self-affliction" (*attabyābādhāya saṃvattati*) and so forth, it is also by means of this very same [method].
The discernment of danger should be understood according to this method. "Non-endurance" of a sensual thought that has arisen means not allowing such a thought to arise again;
it is appropriate to say that this constitutes its abandoning, its removal, its making an end of, and its disappearance.
Thus, after stating in the text, "he does not endure a sensual thought that has arisen," it continues with "he abandons it," and so forth.
Showing that meaning, he said, "What does one who does not tolerate do? He abandons," and so forth.

Here, "abandoning" refers specifically to suppression (*vikkhambhana*), not to eradication (*samuccheda*); thus, by saying "he dispels" and so on, the meaning is shown as being solely by way of suppression.
"Sensual thought" (*kāmavitakka*) is a thought accompanied by sensual desire, both by way of association and by way of object. Therefore, he said: "connected with sensual desire."

"Thought" (takka), and so forth. "Connected with sensual desire" (kāmapaṭisaṃyutta) means associated with sensual desire in the sense of *kāmarāga* (sensual lust) and bound by sensual desire in the sense of *vatthukāma* (objects of desire).
Regarding "as they arise" (*uppajjamāne*), either the state of the arising of those evil thoughts is being grasped, or there is a grasping of them without remainder.
With reference to the first of these, he says "as soon as arisen" (*uppannamatte*), meaning "just born."
The meaning is as follows. To show that the inclusion of the term "without remainder" (anavasesa) occurs when there is a desire for elaboration, it is said: "even if they have arisen a hundred times.
"Thought of relatives" (ñātivitakka) is the thought that arises with reference to relatives by way of worldly affection, such as:
"Our relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity," and so forth. "Thought of the country" (janapadavitakka) is [the thought]: "Our country has abundant food and a rich harvest..."
By the phrase beginning with “delightful,” it refers to a thought arisen concerning the countryside by way of affection rooted in the household life.

A thought associated with the practice of austerities is a thought for the sake of immortality, [thinking]: “When suffering has been worn away through such things as squatting postures and strenuous exertion, the self will be happy and immortal in the future.

Or, taking that as its object, it is a thought accompanied by the view of the Eel-Wriggler (amarāvikkhepa); thus, it is called an “immortal thought” (amaravitakka) because it is both immortal and a thought.

"Connected with compassion for others" refers to a thought associated with worldly affection—a semblance of compassion that arises toward attendants and others through sharing in their joys and sorrows, and which is bound up with attachment to the household life.

"Connected with gain, honor, and renown" means being associated by way of taking as its object both the acquisition of robes and other requisites, as well as honor and fame. "Connected with non-contempt" means...
“O, may others not despise me; may they not think of me as inferior, but rather hold me in high esteem, as heavy as a stone parasol”—this is a thought that has arisen.

Sensual thought (*kāma-vitakka*) is a mode of desire because its intrinsic nature is the conceptualization of sensual pleasure and because it is preeminent in the occurrence of such conceptualization.

He said: “In this context, the thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*) is the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). “Its specific distinction” means a specific distinction of the taint of sensual desire;

the intended meaning is that it coexists with lust (*rāga*). It is called “removal” (*vinodana*) because by means of it one removes—that is, expels from one’s own continuum—the thought of sensual desire and so forth.
Thus he says: “by removal, which is designated as the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*).”
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by diversion is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the taints to be abandoned by cultivation:
from the statement, “The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation,” [it follows that they pertain to] true knowledge and liberation.
The disadvantage of non-cultivation is that there is no attainment and, consequently, no transcendence of the entire suffering of saṃsāra;

conversely, the advantage of cultivation should be understood through the opposite of what was stated, by way of [the practitioner] becoming a true son of the Blessed One and so forth. "Arisen at the time of the three higher paths" means born at the moment of the second path and those following;
since the context concerns cultivation, the meaning is that they are included within the second path and so on. Is it not [the case that...]?
And since those [factors] are indeed supramundane, why is this qualification made? This is not a qualification; rather, it is that which is to be qualified.
Only the supramundane factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are intended here, and these arise at the moment of the three higher paths.

"For the sake of non-confusion regarding the factors of enlightenment" means for the sake of the absence of confusion regarding the factors of enlightenment in insight, jhāna, the path, and the fruit. According to the mixed method...

When the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are being discussed, the insight-factors of enlightenment and so forth are explained by way of analyzing them through the discernment of seclusion and so on;

they are not [explained as] only the supramundane enlightenment factors that have already been produced. Thus, there is no confusion regarding the factors of enlightenment, because the practice for the development of the factors of enlightenment has been correctly elucidated.
"But here," however, means in this sutta, or in this section. The Supramundane Method (*lokuttaranaya*).
It should be understood in this way because it is predominant in the path of development (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Of the initial terms" means of those terms that stand at the beginning of each respective sentence, such as "the enlightenment factor of mindfulness" (*satisambojjhaṅga*) and so forth.

"By way of meaning" means by way of the specific and general meanings of the word-objects (*padattha*). "By way of characteristics, etc. means by way of their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*rasa*), and manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
*Kamato* means according to sequence. *Anūnādhikato* means exactly as it is. *Vibhāvinā* means by one who is wise.
*Satisambojjhaṅge* refers to the phrase "the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. *Saraṇaṭṭhena* means in the sense of recollecting.
*Upaṭṭhāna* is the state of approaching or not relinquishing an object that is distinguished by such qualities as having been done long ago. It is like a gourd floating in water.
Not allowing [the mind] to wander, but fixing it upon an object that is as immovable as a stone, and then recollecting it, making it not forgotten, and not letting it slip away—this is what is meant.
For this has also been said in the *Milindapañha*: "A treasurer" means a guardian of goods. "He makes it not slip away" means he causes it not to slip away.
"By the Elder" refers to the Elder Nāgasena. "Non-forgetfulness" (*asammoso*) is the activity that is the opposite of forgetfulness; it is not merely the absence of forgetfulness.
"Manifestation as being directed toward the objective sphere" means manifestation as being directed toward objects such as the body and so forth.

"A factor (aṅga) of enlightenment" refers to a constituent part (*avayava*) of the harmony of qualities that constitutes enlightenment, or else it is a cause (*kāraṇa*) for the noble disciple who possesses enlightenment.

Regarding "establishment" (*patiṭṭhāna*) and "accumulation" (*āyūhana*), it is said in the commentary on the *Oghataraṇa Sutta*: "Establishment is by way of defilements; accumulation is by way of volitional formations. Establishment is by way of craving and views..."
Accumulation by means of the remaining defilements and volitional formations. Establishment by way of craving; accumulation by way of views.
Establishment by way of the eternalist view; accumulation by way of the annihilationist view. Establishment by way of dullness; accumulation by way of restlessness.
Establishment by way of devotion to sensual pleasure; accumulation by way of devotion to self-mortification. By way of all unwholesome volitional formations...
"Establishment" means the exertion by way of all mundane wholesome volitional formations;
it should be understood according to those modes not mentioned here. For the phrase "that which is called 'enlightenment' (bodhi)" should be connected [to this].
Regarding the word "awakens" (*bujjhati*), its meaning is "he awakens to" (*paṭibujjhati*); thus he said, "he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements."
Furthermore, that awakening is, in its actual meaning, the penetration of the four truths or the realization of Nibbāna itself; thus he said, "the four," and so forth.
"Like the factors of jhāna and the factors of the path" means that just as the factors themselves are the jhānas and the paths, and not something separate from those factors, so it is here as well.
"Like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot": by this, he shows that the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) is a designation for what does not exist.

“They conduce to enlightenment (*bodhāya saṃvattantī*); thus they are ‘factors of enlightenment’ (*bojjhaṅgā*)”: this is stated by taking the word *aṅga* in the sense of a cause. “They awaken; thus they are ‘enlightenments’ (*bodhiyo*);

these enlightenments themselves are the factors; thus they are ‘factors of enlightenment’ (*bojjhaṅgā*)”; so it is said: “They awaken; thus they are factors of enlightenment. “They awaken after (*anubujjhanti*):
they awaken in accordance with the causes such as insight (*vipassanā*) and the truths that are to be awakened to. They awaken thoroughly (*paṭibujjhanti*): [and so forth].
They "awaken" (*paṭibujjhanti*) because they awaken in the presence of the defilements as their opposite, or by way of being directly manifest.
They "fully awaken" (*sambujjhanti*) because they awaken rightly and without error. Thus should the specific distinctions in meaning of the prefixes be understood.
For the word *bodhi* stands having taken up, in a general sense, the act of awakening associated with all such distinctions.
"Scrutinizes" (*vicināti*) means he investigates [the matter] by means of such [passages] as "This, indeed, is suffering.

"Illumination" (*obhāsana*) is the shattering of the delusion that conceals the true nature of phenomena, just as light [dispels] darkness. That quality (*dhamma*) by whose presence one becomes a "hero" (*vīra*) is "heroism" (*vīrabhāva*).
"Because it is to be set in motion" (*īrayitabbato*) means because it is to be practiced. By way of not allowing oneself to fall into the side of indolence (*kosajja*).
Exertion (*paggaha*) is the grasping of associated states; it is their support and the providing of reinforcement. Sinking is the falling into lethargy;
its opposite, non-sinking, is to be understood as its antidote. It "refreshes" (*pīṇayati*) means it satisfies or increases. Pervasion (*pharaṇa*) is the suffusion of the body with sublime forms.
Joy (*tuṭṭhi*) is called rapture (*pīti*). Exaltation (*odagya*) is the state of being uplifted; it is the lifting up of both body and mind.
The meaning [of "tranquility"] is as follows: "By the allaying of bodily and mental distress" means by the calming and subsiding of bodily distress and mental distress.
Herein, "body" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling.

"Distress" (*daratha*) is a term for agitation (*sārambha*), for the defilements such as restlessness which are conditions for pain and grief, or for the four aggregates dominated by those [defilements]. It is the state of being an antidote to the defilements such as restlessness.
It should be seen thus; and herein, the state of being cool and motionless due to tranquility (passaddhi) should be seen because of the absence of agitation.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "The body is tranquil and unagitated.
From the settling [of the mind]: from the proper settling and placing of the mind. Non-distraction is the non-distraction of the associated states.
That state by which associated states are undistracted is non-distraction. Non-dispersal is its own intrinsic nature of not being scattered.
Cohesion is the bringing about of a state of non-dispersal among associated states, like water for bath-powder.
It has "stability of consciousness" as its manifestation, because of the expression "stability of consciousness"; thus, it manifests as the continuous stability of consciousness.
"By way of equanimity" means by way of a state of indifference. This is the equanimity that is a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga-upekkhā*).

It has the characteristic of reflective discernment because it reflects upon phenomena as they proceed evenly, views them from the standpoint of their arising, and functions by taking on their mode of appearance.

And having done so, because its function of equanimity is predominant—as expressed in the phrase "reflective discernment, stability, and neutrality in grasping"—it is called "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
It has been stated [thus]. "Evenness" (*samavāhitā*) is the state of being a condition for the co-arising of associated states by way of each performing its own respective function.
"Prevention of deficiency and excess" (*ūnādhikatānivāraṇa*) is the state of being a condition for an even flow that is neither sluggish nor agitated.

It is said to have "the cutting off of partiality as its function" because it acts as if severing the bias toward uneven arising among the associated states. Equanimity itself is the state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāvo*).

Because they are beneficial, desirable, and to be sought after in every instance—namely, in both the side of dullness and the side of agitation—they are called "universally beneficial" (*sabbatthika*);

that which is universally beneficial is *sabbatthika*. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, which proceed simultaneously and must be mentioned in sequence according to the order of their verbal occurrence, the reason for mentioning the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*) first, without stating anything else first, is as follows:
The phrase "of all" and so forth is stated because the cause is the state of being beneficial to all. By "all," those belonging to the side of lethargy (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*) are meant;
otherwise, [one might think] even all [other factors] are conditions for all.
The objector asks, "Why are only seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) mentioned? and thus suspects that faith, greed, and so forth might also possess the status of factors of enlightenment.
The other [author], showing that these factors are helpful for the cultivation of the enlightenment factors beginning with mindfulness, said:

"Because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation, and because they are beneficial in all circumstances," and so forth. Therein, "of lethargy" means of a mind that has shriveled up, failing to enter the path of cultivation due to excessive laxity of energy and so on.
For at such a time, the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity should not be cultivated; indeed, by these [factors], that [lethargy] is...
"A small fire is difficult to extinguish, just like [a fire fed by] wet grass and the like. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, suppose a man wished to kindle a small fire, and he were to throw wet grass into it," and so forth.
However, the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture should be developed with dry grass and the like.
Just as a small fire, when dormant, is well-kindled by these [factors], so too is the sluggish mind well-aroused by them. Therefore it was said: “But in that case,” and so forth.
Therein, the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others should be understood according to their respective nourishment (*āhāra*).
For this has been said: “There are, monks, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena... for the increase of the joy enlightenment factor... and so forth.

"...it conduces [to enlightenment]. In this context, the attention that proceeds by way of penetrating the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena] develops the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment and the others.
Regarding "of restlessness": because it does not plunge into the state of being established in coolness through the excessive exertion of energy and so forth of the mind.
At that time, the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture should not be developed.
For by means of these, the mass of fire becomes difficult to extinguish, just as it would be with dry grass and the like. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, suppose a man wished to extinguish a great mass of fire, and he were to throw dry grass into it," and so forth.
The enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, however, are to be developed;
for by means of these, the agitated mind becomes well-composed, just as a mass of fire is extinguished by wet grass and the like. Therefore it was said, "But when," and so forth.
Here too, the development of the enlightenment factors of tranquility and the others should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For this has been said:
“There is, bhikkhus, bodily tranquility and mental tranquility... [and so on] ...which lead to the increase of the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

In this context, having observed the manner in which tranquility and the other factors previously arose, one develops the enlightenment factors of tranquility and so forth by attending to them in such a way as to bring about their arising. This is what is meant by “developing.”
The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, however, is of great assistance in all circumstances.

For it protects the mind from falling into lethargy through states such as tranquility that belong to the side of dullness, and from falling into agitation through states such as the investigation of phenomena that belong to the side of restlessness.
Therefore, it is like salt seasoning in all curries, and like a minister with general jurisdiction in all royal affairs.
It is desirable in every respect. Therefore he said: “And mindfulness, monks, I call ‘all-beneficial.
The connection is: “having known, what is to be known. Growth means expansion, increase, and repeated arising;
thus he said, “he generates it again and again. Causing it to reach full development, he brings it into being. Seclusion (*vivittatā*) means the state of being secluded.

That which is separated from what is to be separated, and that which remains after having been separated—both of these are here called "secludedness" (*vivittatā*) by virtue of their commonality in the state of being secluded.

Among these, the former is a collection of phenomena (*dhammasamūha*) endowed with the activity of separating—which is termed "seclusion" (*viveka*) because it is the very act of separating from what is to be separated;
it is understood as seclusion precisely through that activity of separating. The other, however, is entirely...

Because of its nature of being secluded from this and that. In this context, whichever aggregate of states (*dhammapuñja*) in which the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*) occurs through the act of secluding itself, that occurs only by depending on what is reckoned as seclusion (*viveka*)—that is, by way of the aforementioned state of being secluded;
but the others [the remaining factors] do so by way of being inclined toward it and having it as their object. Thus it is said, "dependent on seclusion. Or alternatively, by way of seclusion...

The jhāna that has arisen is called "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*); likewise, the enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*) that proceeds by way of seclusion should be understood as "dependent on seclusion" (*vivekanissita*).
And the sense of dependence (*nissaya*) should be understood in terms of the path and fruit, by way of insight and the path [which act as their support].

Just as in the expression "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), there is the arising of conditions even though there is no temporal sequence of before and after, so too here [the factors] have a single undivided dharma as their basis.

“Dependence arises through cultivation. “This very thing” means seclusion itself. For seclusion (*viveka*), abandoning (*pahāna*), discipline (*vinaya*), dispassion (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*) are synonymous.

Having stated that [the enlightenment factors] are dependent on the seclusion of factor-seclusion (*tadaṅga-viveka*), eradication-seclusion (*samuccheda-viveka*), and escape-seclusion (*nissaraṇa-viveka*), there is no mention of their dependence on the seclusion of subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*), because the enlightenment factors to be cultivated—such as “he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor” and so forth—are what are spoken of here. Of one who has cultivated the enlightenment factors...
For those factors of enlightenment that constitute the fruit and are to be realized, their function is seclusion through subsiding.
As for "by inclination": it is because of the great inclination [thinking], "I shall realize Nibbāna.

Although at the moment of insight (vipassanā) the mind has conditioned phenomena as its object, yet having clearly seen the danger in conditioned phenomena, there is a resolute leaning toward Nibbāna, which is their opposite.
It is because of one’s underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) that [the jhānas] are dependent on seclusion as an escape, just as the mind of a person overcome by fever tends toward coolness.

They are not prohibited in the case of jhānas based on kasiṇa objects and so forth when they are rooted in insight (*vipassanā*), because mindfulness and the other factors therein partake of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*).
However, if they are not extracted [from their mundane state], jhāna—unlike insight—is not a proximate cause for the path to enlightenment, nor is it...
Likewise, they do not extract the absolute cause, nor do they omit it on the grounds that the function of jhāna—unlike the function of insight—is not the Path.
Furthermore, it should be understood that by the mention of the kasiṇas here, the formless attainments dependent upon them are also included.
For it is appropriate to say that these too serve as bases for insight and partake of penetration, since they possess the quality of being inclined toward that [liberation].
For to the same extent that there is a leaning toward Nibbāna, there may also be a leaning toward the fruit.
The statement beginning with, "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere? is also a proof of this meaning.
It is said that the word *vossagga* has two meanings—renunciation and leaping forward—thus indicating the twofold nature of relinquishment (*vossagga*). For relinquishing (*vossajjana*)...

It is abandonment, and it proceeds without apprehension due to its state of being relinquished; therefore, at the moment of insight (vipassanā), abandonment of the opposite side occurs by way of "factor-substitution" (tadaṅga), and at the moment of the Path (magga), it occurs by way of "total eradication" (samuccheda).

Likewise, at the moment of insight, it should be understood as "relinquishment" because of its tendency toward that [object], and at the moment of the Path, it is "relinquishment" because of its nature of being released through taking [the object] as its support.
“In the manner already described” means by way of its partial eradication (*tadaṅgasamuccheda*) and by way of making it inclined toward and taking that as its object.
Since the meaning of the word *vossagga* (relinquishment) has already been explained previously, he says “by the entire phrase.

“Transforming” refers to the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), while “transformed” refers to the moment of the path (*magga*). He says “ripening” because transformation (*pariṇāma*) is indeed ripening (*paripāka*).

"And matured. "Maturity" refers to the state of being sharp and keen in nature, whereby one is able to abandon the defilements that have acquired their capacity through repeated practice, and is able to leap into Nibbāna.

Therefore he said, "For this," and so forth. "This method" refers to that which was stated regarding the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) in the passage beginning with "dependent on seclusion by way of its own constituent part" (tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ);
[it applies] to the remaining factors as well, such as the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga).
“This is the method” means that it should be applied there in this way.

Having thus explained the mixed method for the sake of non-confusion regarding the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) for beginners, he now says “But here,” etc., in order to clarify the meaning by way of the supramundane enlightenment factors that have been produced.
“But here” refers to this *Sabbāsava Sutta*.
The path itself is subject to change through relinquishment, because it is the path of development that is intended here. And "that" refers to the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
"From the standpoint of eradication" means from the standpoint of cutting off.
Because the taint of views is to be abandoned by the first path, it is stated as "the three taints. Even those [three] are indeed incapable of leading to a state of loss.
It should be understood that [the fetters] leading to the states of misery are abandoned by mere seeing.

Although the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are for the most part identical with the path, it is stated here in terms of those path-phenomena which possess the specific nature of the factors of enlightenment;

thus, taking the individual factors of enlightenment as being associated with the three paths under the heading "development of the factors of enlightenment," he says "associated with the three paths."
The commentary on the taints to be abandoned by cultivation is finished.

28. "Praising": because the abandoning of the taints is extremely difficult to achieve, he praises it by means of that very difficult task. "Of him" (assā): of the bhikkhu who has abandoned the taints.
"Advantage" (ānisansa): the source of benefit culminating in the destruction of suffering, beginning with the cutting off of craving.
By these brief explanations of abandoning and so forth. "Generating enthusiasm" means:
thus generating an effort accompanied by reverence toward that abandonment of the taints (*āsava*), which is both praiseworthy even by the Lord of Dhamma and of great benefit.
"Abandoned by seeing alone" means abandoned precisely by seeing. Therefore it was said: "One does not perceive them as abandoned when they are not yet abandoned."

The distinction between the second and first alternatives should be understood by way of the connection with the taints (*āsava*) and the restraints of the taints (*āsavasaṃvara*), respectively, through the word "all" (*sabba*).
"Through the clear realization of vision" means through the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā*), by way of accomplishing the function of full understanding.
Therefore he said, "by way of function," which means by way of penetration free from delusion. "Samussaya" refers to the body or the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

A mind accompanied by blameless joy and gladness deserves to be called "one's own" (attano) because it brings about welfare, whereas its opposite does not because it brings about harm; thus, with reference to a state of consciousness associated with joy, he says, "with uplifted minds" (*attamanā*) means "with one's own [minds].
Therefore he says, "with contented minds. Alternatively, "with uplifted minds" means that the minds are seized by joy and gladness. And because of those...
Being grasped is simply being associated; therefore it is said, "the mind associated with rapture and joy.
Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning should be understood as being easy to comprehend because it follows the method already stated.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Sabbāsava-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta 29.

"Therefore, having shown that" means: since a commentary on a sutta becomes clear when it is spoken after showing the occasion for its delivery (suttanikkhepa), and since the occasion for the delivery of this Dhammadāyāda Sutta is based on a specific incident (aṭṭhuppattika), therefore, that occasion—
"Having shown" means "having explained. Regarding "gain and honor":
some say it refers to the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) consisting of gain and honor; others say it refers to the occasion regarding gain and honor.

For the Blessed One taught this discourse having made as the occasion that abundance of requisites which had arisen among the monks at that time on account of gain and honor. "The great rain-cloud of pairs" (*yamakamahāmegho*): [this refers to the *Yamakapāṭha*].
With its hundred layers below and its thousand layers above, it is a great cloud-mass in pairs.
It remains wherever the Blessed One dwells for a fixed residence, and when he goes on a journey, it follows after him.
This is because the monks, for the most part, have fulfilled the accumulation of the perfection of giving for a hundred thousand eons or even more.
"Then great gain and honor arose," as it is said: "In this way, for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well.
"Honored" means having received honor. "Venerated" means having received veneration. "Revered" means highly esteemed and beloved in the mind.
"Worshiped" means worshiped both with offerings such as garlands and with the offering of the four requisites. "Respected" means having attained respect.
For he to whom they respectfully bring even specially prepared and most excellent requisites is "honored" (*sakkata*).
He toward whom they present those gifts while establishing a sense of reverence is "respected" (*garukata*). He whom they love in their minds and hold in high esteem is "esteemed" (*bahumata*).
He for whom they perform all these acts by way of worship is "worshiped" (*pūjita*). [He is honored] by way of salutation, rising from one's seat, joining the palms in *añjali*, and so forth.
They perform the highest forms of homage; thus he is honored. The world behaves in this manner toward the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Therefore it is said: “Then at that time... [up to] ...requisites.
Having attained the pinnacle and the summit of gain and fame means having reached the highest point and the excellence of both gain and fame.
"Those for whom requisites such as robes are to be held in high esteem are 'requisite-honourers' (paccayagaruka); the meaning is that they have a 'fleshly eye' (āmisacakkhu).
Those who are greedy and infatuated with requisites, practicing for the sake of obtaining an abundance of requisites, are 'requisite-abundant' (paccayabāhulika).

The intention is that [this conduct] was evident even to the Blessed One by way of his natural behavior, since otherwise there would be no such thing as that which is not evident. This is by way of reflecting on the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva)."

The "arousing of a sense of urgency regarding the Dhamma" (*dhammasaṃvega*) is the knowledge of self-reproach that has arisen; here, however, it should be understood as occurring through the monks' sense of gain and honor.
"The practice of the ascetic’s duty" (*samaṇadhammavutti*) means the performance of the ascetic’s duty. "That" refers to the teaching on being an heir to the Dhamma.
A "mirror for the entire body" (*sabbakāyika-ādāsa*) is a mirror suitable for seeing the whole body by way of reflecting its image.

"Paternal inheritance" (*pitu-dāya*) means that which must be given by a father; those who take from that [inheritance] by virtue of their worthiness (*arahabhāva*) are "heirs" (*dāyādā*), namely sons.
And while in the world that [inheritance] consists only of material things (*āmisa*), in the Teaching it consists of the Dhamma as well.
Therefore, having rejected therein whatever is blameworthy and not leading to liberation, the Blessed One spoke, enjoining the monks toward that which is leading to liberation and blameless.
“Be my heirs to the Dhamma, monks, not my heirs to material things. To be an heir to my Dhamma means to plunge into my Dhamma;
the sense is that one is a partaker of a share of the Dhamma. For thus he will say: “The master of the very portion of the Dhamma.
“A Dhamma that has been produced” means a Dhamma determined as such by its commonality with the Dhamma, insofar as it possesses the quality of being undefiled, unsurpassed, and so forth.
A *pariyāya* is that by which one makes known [the meaning] after having turned it around according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); it is a hint or a reason for a hint.

Because of the absence of such [a hint], the "non-figurative dhamma" (*nippariyāyadhamma*) is so called because, through the attainment of the Path, it absolutely prevents falling into the states of misery and so forth.

The other, being the opposite of what was stated, is the "figurative dhamma" (*pariyāyadhamma*), because it leads, through succession, to falling into the suffering of the miserable states and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

By way of exclusion.
