For just as mundane wholesome states such as giving and virtue are produced with the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa) as their aim, and thus—even if one does not actually achieve that [turning away]—are called "indirect dhammas" (pariyāya-dhamma) by way of being the cause for producing the state that achieves it;
so too, those things produced with the round (vaṭṭa) as their aim are [so called], because they are to be specifically grasped by craving and the like.
In the world, "material things" (āmisa) are well known as clothing, food, and so forth.

Showing that this [friendship] and what resembles it are called "figurative material things" (pariyāyāmisa) by way of being a designation for their status as the cause of specific fruits, he said: "But this which... [etc. ...this is called figurative material thing.
This is because of such statements as: "All of this, Ānanda, is indeed the holy life, namely, having virtuous friends."
It is said that even though the supramundane Dhamma is realized by disciples, it deserves to be called the Teacher’s alone; thus it is stated:

"Even the Dhamma in its ultimate sense belongs only to the Blessed One. For even regarding the right attention that serves as the condition for the vision of the Dhamma in disciples, the specific condition—namely, the voice of another—is dependent upon the Tathāgata. Therefore, although the Dhamma is penetrated by them, it belongs only to the Master of the Dhamma.
It is appropriate to say this. Therefore he said, "By the Blessed One," and so forth.

In that context, "of the path not yet arisen" refers to the Noble Path that had not arisen—due to its non-attainment—from the time of the disappearance of the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa until this present arising of a Buddha.
"One who causes it to arise" means one who brings it about. Furthermore, this bringing about of the path by the Blessed One—

It is said, "the arouser of the unarisen path, the declarer of the undeclared path," in order to show that this is not like the Paccekabuddhas, whose [knowledge] is restricted only to their own mental continuum, but rather extends to the mental continua of others.

Furthermore, this arising and arousing of the path is in fact nothing other than knowing it in its true sense, because it consists in penetration through non-delusion; thus it is said, "knower of the path, seer of the path."
Furthermore, because his recounting [of the path] is extremely skillful, it is said that he is "skilled in the path" (*maggakovida*).
They are "followers of the path" (*maggānugā*) because they follow the path exactly as it was traveled by the Teacher; this is due to the Blessed One’s own perfect realization of that path.
They are "those who have followed along" (*pacchāsamannāgatā*) because they have subsequently, later on, properly and continuously followed and practiced it.

"Knowing, he knows": he knows precisely that which is to be known, categorized as the objects of direct knowledge (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth, because his practice is directed toward absolute welfare.

"Seeing, he sees": likewise, he sees precisely that which is to be seen. Alternatively, "knowing, he knows" means that by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he knows exactly what is to be known;
for with partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*), one does not know everything with absolute certainty. Seeing...

"He sees" means that he indeed sees what is to be seen by means of the five eyes known as the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the wisdom eye (*paññācakkhu*), the Dhamma eye (*dhammacakkhu*), the Buddha eye (*buddhacakkhu*), and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

Alternatively, "knowing, he knows" means that unlike others who, being subject to perversion (*vipallāsa*), know even while knowing through the influence of perversion when they speak of the full understanding of sense-desires and form, the Blessed One does not do so. The Blessed One...

But because he has abandoned the perversions, he knows what should be known as knowing, and because there is an absence of views and seeing [in the conventional sense], he sees what should be seen as seeing;
this is the meaning. He is "become the eye" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he consists of the eye of wisdom, because he has attained that [eye], and because he produces it among beings;
thus, in the sense of being a guide for vision, he has become like the eye of the world. He is "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*) in this very same way...
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Dhammas" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), and "Brahmā" refers to the Path (*magga*).

Because [the Buddha] has arisen through them, or because he has attained and realized them, and because he causes their arising in the world, he should be known as "become Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) and "become Brahmā" (*brahmabhūta*).
He is called "the Speaker" (*vattā*) because he speaks the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; he speaks while causing the penetration of the Truths to proceed for a long time.

He is the one who sets it in motion. "The guide to the goal" means he is the one who extracts and demonstrates, or leads others to, the ultimate truth (paramattha) known as the nature of phenomena (dhammatā) and Nibbāna.
"The giver of the Deathless" means he gives the Deathless by arousing the realization of the Deathless among sentient beings;
thus, he is the giver of the Deathless. He is the Lord of Dhamma because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) are dependent upon him.
“Whatever attainment of Nibbāna there is, all that is obtained by this;
the ripening of merits is blissful, and one’s intention succeeds—
connected with Nibbāna, it bestows every kind of excellence.”

Having heard such words of the Blessed One, the monks understand that the merit of giving and so forth is based on the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭasannissaya*), and not otherwise; thus it is said: "Even the Dhamma of the method... he obtains.
Furthermore, even the acceptance by monks of allowable requisites such as robes and the like—understanding that "such things should be used"—does not occur without the word of the Blessed One.
"How could there be enjoyment [of it]?"—to this he says, "Even as a figurative gift (nippariyāyāmisam)," and so forth.
The fact that the figurative gift belongs to the Blessed One is demonstrated precisely by the fact that the figurative Dhamma belongs to him.
The connection is: "showing that very state of ownership. Therefore, because it is received as something dependent on oneself, it is one's own possession.
"And therein": in that spiritual gift (*dhammāmisa*).
"One for whom conditions are supreme" means one for whom the requisites such as robes and so forth are the highest, in the sense of being the most excellent to be attained;

or, it refers to those superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) such as fewness of desires, which are beyond the reach of others—thus he is "one for whom conditions are supreme," meaning one who values gain. "In the arising of craving" refers to [craving] for robes and so forth.
"Or else, monks, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of robes; or craving arises in a bhikkhu because of almsfood, lodgings, or the pursuit of this state of being or that state of being.
Regarding these four bases for the arising of craving thus stated, "fewness of wishes and so forth" refers to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, and the like.
*Tattha* means "in that exhortation" or "among those monks who have received the Dhamma. Alternatively, the construction may be understood as:
"or for those to whom it will belong there. In this latter case, *tattha* should be taken to mean "in that exhortation.

The underlying intention is [the prevention] of the arising of misfortune through being an heir to material things (*āmisa-dāyāda*), and [the promotion] of the arising of benefit through being an heir to the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāyāda*).
And there is the longing. Therefore he said, “He sees,” and so forth. Therein, “of those who have stumbled over material gain” means of those who have practiced wrongly for the sake of material gain.
“In the past time” refers to the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.

The story of the monk Kapila is to be clarified by the *Kapila Sutta* and by the *Lakkhaṇa Sutta*, beginning with the words, “Even his outer robe becomes ablaze,” and so on. One who is heavy with material gain [is so] because of its low worth.

The construction is as follows: like a counterfeit coin, he lacks luster and does not shine with the splendor of a recluse; and like extinguished embers, he is devoid of radiance. "From that" means from the state of being burdened by conditions.
"With a mind turned away" means with a mind that has withdrawn [from worldly things]; the meaning is "one who lives in austerity.

"Heirs to the Dhamma"—at this point, there is an implicit restrictive statement (*avadhāraṇa*); by that restriction, the excluded matter is [as follows]: *Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an introductory remark for a subsequent section.*

In order to clarify this, the prohibition against being "heirs to material things" is shown. Likewise, in order to clarify it, it is also shown in the explanations of the intended purpose and the benefits;
similarly, through the explanation of the dangers, the prohibition against being "heirs to the Dhamma" is shown. "To be referred to" means to be spoken of by placing [the preceding] below.
Regarding the word *ādiyā*: since the vowel *ā* here has the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), therefore, by one who is devoid of being an heir to the Dhamma...
Because this distinction—whether as the cause or the instrument for the state of being heirs to material things—is a separation and a definition made by the wise, it is said:
"They should be treated separately. Therefore he said: "It is meant that you would be censurable by the wise.
"I have compassion for you... [etc. ...you are not heirs to material things" is the manifestation of his own compassion toward the bhikkhus.
The "making soft" of those [faculties] refers to the practice beginning with “I too by that,” which makes them even softer than before; thus he says, “for the sake of making them exceedingly soft.
The “Nāḷaka practice” and so forth refer to the modes of conduct described in the *Nāḷaka Sutta* and other discourses.

Since these practices were undertaken by the Elder Nāḷaka and others, they constitute a mode of life characterized by supreme austerity (*paramasallekha*) and are therefore extremely exalted practices; for this reason, they are mentioned here in connection with the practice of being an heir to the Dhamma (*dhammadāyāda*).

They are cited by way of illustration. "Acting as witnesses" means that when this practice is being described, they act as witnesses by providing direct evidence for those who might lack faith, thinking, "Is there anyone else besides me who practices?
"In this" refers to the statement beginning with, "And you, monks, are my heirs to the Dhamma. "The rest" refers to the section on the bright side (sukkapa-kkha) beginning with, "And you, [monks]."

The textual passage has been brought forward. "By way of the opposite of the method stated" means by way of the counter-position to the method stated regarding the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) as follows: "Because of being heirs to the Dhamma, not because of being heirs to material things.
"Having heard the praise" means having heard the commendation of the person who practices accordingly, just as [it was done] for him along with his retinue.
Having heard of the Venerable Upasena’s practice and his firmness in virtue. By the phrase "nipātapada" (a particle), he indicates that the word *idha* (here) has no specific referent.

"Pavārito" means one who has been refused. For when someone who is eating, being satiated by the food, refuses the food brought forward by the server, he is said to be "refused" (*pavārito*) by that refusal. Therefore he says: "Pavārito... pe..."

“It is said. It is called *pavāraṇā* because by means of it—one uses various modes such as seeing and so forth—to restrain [faults], to cause [the Sangha] to be requested [for forgiveness], and to provide for the meal;
it is the relinquishing of oneself and the granting of opportunity for the purification of offenses.

Since it is stated that this should generally be performed by those who have completed the rains-retreat (*vassa*), it is therefore called the “Pavāraṇā of those who have completed the rains-retreat. One *pavāreti*: one requests the requisites.

*Pavāraṇā* means "invitation," such as an invitation with robes and other requisites. Alternatively, *pavāraṇā* is a "prohibition" (*vāraṇā*) joined with the prefix *pa-*. It is the prohibition against eating, accompanied by four factors beginning with the state of having interrupted one's meal.

Since that [prohibition] is the cause for an offense arising from eating what is not left over (*anatiritta*), it is therefore called "the invitation regarding what is not left over" (*anatiritta-pavāraṇā*).
The invitation for eating as much as one desires is the "invitation regarding eating as much as desired" (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*).
The meaning is: "the rejection of food brought [to him] by one whose meal is finished.
Because of the word "one who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*), it is intended here that the completion of the meal is what is meant; thus he says, "full" means "full with food.
The same principle applies here to the word "finished" (*pariyosita*): "finished with food," that is, "finished with the act of eating."
In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, in order to make the intended meaning clear, the elision of the word *bhojana* (food) is mentioned.

*Dhāto* means "satisfied. *Sādhakāni* means "indicative. Through the inclusion of *suhitatā* (being well-fed) and *yāvadatthatā* (having eaten one’s fill), the terms *bhuttāvita*, etc., are understood;
or rather, by the inclusion of *bhuttāvita*, etc., the others are made known. Thus, there exists between them the relationship of indicator and indicated (*ñāpaka-ñāpetabbatā*).
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “yo hi” was stated. Thus, by means of all six phrases, food that fills the belly has been shown;
however, this is by way of a hypothetical supposition (*parikappanā*). For the Blessed One does not eat in such a manner. Therefore he said: “All of this has been stated as a supposition.
And regarding the two meanings, “it might be so, or it might not be so,” it is stated that both are possible here: “here, both are [possible].”
“It is appropriate. *Atha* means immediately after; the sense is: “immediately after my meal.
Since that refers back to the time already mentioned, it is stated as “at that time. *Apparuḷhaharite* means devoid of green grass and such things that are growing.
And this word *appa* has the sense of absence, as in the case of *appiccha* (“having few desires”) and so forth.
In the phrase "even when spoken" (*kathitepi*), the particle *pi* has the sense of including what has not been stated. By this, it includes such things as "equalizing" (*vāpasamīkaraṇa*).

For this word *vutta* is seen in the sense of "equalizing" in expressions such as "but not yet answered" (*no ca kho paṭivutta*); in the sense of "livelihood" in expressions such as "feathered, living on what others give" (*pannalomo paradattavutto*);
and in the sense of "departure" in expressions such as "the withered leaf fallen from its bond" (*paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto*).
In such passages as “*gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitaṃ*,” it occurs in the sense of being set forth as the word of the Buddha (*pāvacana*);
however, in common usage, as in “*vuttaṃ parāyaṇaṃ*” (Mahābhāṣya 7.2.26), it is seen to mean study.
Herein, the state of being an heir to the Dhamma is not precluded by the eating of almsfood; rather, it is [precluded] by disregarding the eating of almsfood.
Regarding the phrase "practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*), he spoke thus—"he should spend [his time] on almsfood... etc."—to show the reason for it.

In that context, "he should spend" means he should pass the time through application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, he said: "having reflected upon the simile of the burning head," which refers to the *Ādittasīsūpama-sutta* (the Discourse on the Simile of the Burning Head).
*Kiñcāpi* is a particle identical in meaning to *yadipi*. Since a particle, wherever it is employed in a sentence, indicates the specific sense that ought to be expressed therein,

it is stated here— by way of indicating the sense being spoken of through the granting of permission and praise in the phrase beginning with "alms-food"— that "it is a particle in the sense of granting permission and praise."

However, regarding the commencement of the praise for permission (*anuññā-pasaṃsā*), it might be said that [the phrase] "for the purpose of inspiring confidence" (*asambhāvanattha*) was stated because confidence was already manifested in the preceding [passage],
and because this [present passage] is superior and conforms to that.
How can the refusal of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta-paṭikkhipana*) occurring on a single occasion be the cause for long-term fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth?
With reference to the prompting (codana), he says “For him, indeed,” and so forth. In this context, “excessive desire” (atricchatā) means:
one who desires here is *atriccha*; the state of being such is *atricchatā*. In terms of its meaning, it is the longing for the gains of others. For it has been said:

“Dissatisfaction with one’s own entire acquisitions and longing for the gains of others—this is the characteristic of excessive desire. “Evil desire” (pāpicchatā) is the intention to gain credit for qualities that one does not possess.
One who has evil desires is called *pāpiccho*; the state of being such is *pāpicchatā*. As it is said:
"The conceiving of non-existent qualities and lack of moderation in receiving gifts—this is the characteristic of evil desire.
One who desires great objects, or whose desire is great, is called *mahiccho*; the state of being such is *mahicchatā*. With reference to this, it was said: "The conceiving of existent qualities..."
"Lack of moderation in receiving is the characteristic of great greed"—this is the construction [of the sentence], meaning that by reflecting [in this way], he will restrain himself;
thus, the refusal of almsfood will lead to the welfare of that bhikkhu.
Just as a person of great greed cannot be supported by those who provide requisites because of the nature of his demands for them, so too...
"Even by himself" is said in the sense of seeking conditions; thus it is said: "He is difficult to support, both for himself and for his attendants.
Because of the way he makes use of what is given in faith, he throws it away in another's house.
"With an empty bowl" means that after giving whatever he has received to those families from whom he receives alms in return, [he returns with an empty bowl].
The intention here is that, having received nothing there, he enters the monastery with an empty bowl and lies down due to the weakness of hunger.
One’s own easy maintenance should be understood by way of the consumption of requisites as they are obtained and the avoidance of further seeking;
the easy maintenance of supporters should be understood by way of attaining contentment without showing contempt for the requisites as they are obtained.

"Kathāvatthūni" means the bases (vatthu) for discourses connected with fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and so forth; thus, they are "bases for discourse" (kathāvatthūni), which are simply fewness of wishes and the like.
"Three" refers to three such bases for discourse. "Abhisallekhikā" means that which thoroughly scrapes away (sallikhati) the defilements (kilesa);

thus, it is "abhisallekha," which is the collection of qualities such as fewness of wishes. That which possesses this is "abhisallekhikā," [so called] because it leads to the thinning out of great desire and other such faults.

"Appropriate" means being associated with fewness of wishes and so forth. "Conducive to the removal of mental hindrances" means that by causing the hindrances—which obstruct the arising of wholesome states of mind—to become distant, they are conducive (*sappāya*) to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), which are designated as the "removal of mental hindrances.
Alternatively, they are "conducive to the removal of mental hindrances" because they are helpful and suitable for bringing about the manifestation of the very mind of serenity and insight.

"Leading to utter disenchantment," and so forth, is stated in order to show the benefit of disenchantment and the rest, by which this discourse is called "austerity-inducing" (*abhisallekhika*) and "conducive to the removal of mental hindrances.
Therein, "to utter disenchantment" means for the purpose of becoming utterly weary of the suffering of saṃsāra.
"To dispassion and cessation" means for the purpose of the fading away of that very [suffering] and for its cessation.
"For the sake of peace" means for the sake of the subsiding of all defilements (*kilesa*). "For direct knowledge" means for the sake of directly knowing everything that is to be directly known.
"For full enlightenment" means for the sake of the full enlightenment of the four paths. "For Nibbāna" means for the sake of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*).

For among these, insight (*vipassanā*) is first stated by the first three [terms], then the path (*magga*) by the next three, and Nibbāna by the remaining one. Thus, serenity (*samatha*) and insight are the beginning...
This shows that all these superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma), which culminate in Nibbāna, arise for one who has attained the ten bases of discourse (dasakathāvatthu).

"They will fulfill" means they will lead to that state by way of their intrinsic nature and their efficacy. For qualities such as fewness of desires (appicchatā), once arisen, will conduce to that end in the future.
Thus, there is both the fulfillment of the bases of discourse and the fulfillment of the training (sikkhā).
This should be understood in the manner already stated.
"The deathless Nibbāna" refers to the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

The other [Nibbāna], however, is fulfilled through the completion of the qualities of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*). Furthermore, the fulfillment of Nibbāna here is spoken of figuratively (*pariyāyato*) by way of the fulfillment of the qualities that bring it about.

[These qualities] are to be understood. Now, in order to illustrate by way of a simile that perfection of qualities which results from the gradual increase of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth, he says, "Just as if" (*seyyathāpi*), and so on.
Therein, "rainy-season cloud" (*pāvussaka*) refers to one that has arisen during the months of the rains; for such a cloud does not appear for long.

"Mountain clefts" (*pabbatakandarā*) refers to rivers and streams that flow intermittently or continuously, originating from the vicinity of mountains. "Lakes and branches" (*sarassatākhā*)... [text fragment].
Where water comes from a higher elevated place and both stands and flows—those are *kusobbhas*, small ponds.
*Kunnadīs* are small rivers flowing out from the foot of a mountain; for they fill the great rivers as they descend into them.
"An heir to the supreme Dhamma" means the state of being an heir to the supreme, most excellent Dhamma.
Or the supreme inheritance of the Dhamma. "Those bhikkhus" refers to those bhikkhus who receive the Dhamma.
"Applying" means applying them through the fundamental qualities such as fewness of desires and so forth.
"Having grasped" means having taken it up by way of retention—both in terms of the meaning and the phrasing—and having grasped it without error. "Having compared" means...
Without deviating from my own intention according to the sequence of my teaching.

"Just as you thought here" means just as you thought regarding this teaching on the heirs of the Dhamma, so too did you think when entering the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) elsewhere for the purpose of praising the Dhamma.
"With a single intention" means with a common purpose. "With wisdom" means with discernment (paññā). This teaching is the foremost, and so forth.
This was said because the Blessed One supports the Dhamma-Senāpati (the General of the Dhamma) by his very qualities.

"By the movement of the mind" means by the transformation of the body through the power of the mind, by means of the resolve that makes the body conform to the state of the mind, thinking: "Let this body become like this mind.
But how can the body, which functions slowly, [conform] with the mind, which changes rapidly?
"Does it have the same destination? It does not have the same destination in every respect.
For just as, when the mind transforms the body, the mind does not have the same destination as the body in every respect;
for at that time, the mind cannot persist for the duration of a moment of material phenomena—which proceed slowly—without ceasing from its own moment established by its intrinsic nature. "This..."

However, by means of the resolution, "Let this body be like this mind," because the body—which is slow-moving—is made to follow the mind, the mind continues to proceed in a continuous stream, conforming to the body's movement until it reaches the desired location;
thus, the mind is said to be "transformed" by having its course directed according to the body. Likewise, [one resolves]: "Let this body be like this mind."

By means of the resolution, “Let it be so,” because the perception of lightness and the perception of subtlety have already been accomplished, the body does not turn slowly like those who have not developed the bases of psychic power;
rather, it proceeds in such a way that it reaches the desired place quickly in just a few mental moments.
Thus, the body is said to be transformed by its very conformity with the mind, though not in a single moment of consciousness.
Thus it is for the sake of continuity. And by doing so, even the simile of the frequent bending and stretching of the arms becomes more appropriately fitting without resorting to figurative usage;

otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the nature of things (*dhammatā*). For it is not possible, even by the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), to alter the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of phenomena;
however, it is possible to alter their state (*bhāva*).
31. “Having understood the intention of the Blessed One and the disposition of the bhikkhus”—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Just as one considers the place and the time, the Great Elder likewise expounds the Dhamma after considering the recipient.

Regarding the word “pakkantassa” (of him who has departed), he says “pakkantassa sato” (while he was gone) and so forth, showing that this is a genitive used in the sense of disregard. “Kittakena” means by what measure.

Since that measure is the delimitation of the object to be measured, he said: "‘Kittāvatā’ is a word of delimitation. Regarding the phrase "the particle *nu* [expresses] a question," this is stated because it is understood that this very particle *nu* occurs here in the sense of a question.
For the meaning manifested here by the particle *nu* is the same as the meaning of the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ*—namely, the measure of the object to be measured.

And here, the side of defilement consists in not training in seclusion and being an heir to material things; the side of purification consists in training in that [seclusion] and being an heir to the Dhamma.
"By means of the three kinds of seclusion" is a mention of the triad of seclusions because the pentad of seclusions is included therein.
However, if the pentad of seclusions were mentioned, bodily seclusion would not be included in its own specific form.

Or rather, because it depends upon that [seclusion], the Teacher spoke of "by means of the three kinds of seclusion" and so forth, by way of demonstrating the specific seclusion being employed at that time.
Why was it said, "even one or another"? Is it not the case that the status of being an heir to the Dhamma is not accomplished by bodily seclusion alone? No;
for it is precisely bodily seclusion as supported by the other two kinds of seclusion that is intended here. And having done so, the inclusion of mental seclusion is also [justified].

It is established. For it is not by the mere attainment of mundane jhānas that one is intended to be a literal heir to the Teacher’s Dhamma; rather, that status is intended through the attainment of Nibbāna.

Therefore, all training in seclusion within the Dispensation is said to incline toward Nibbāna, lean toward Nibbāna, and tend toward Nibbāna; hence it is said: "even any one of the three kinds of seclusion."
Just as there is darkness when there is no light, so too, when there is no inheritance of the Dhamma, there is only the inheritance of material things;
thus he says, "they become merely heirs to material things. This same method applies to the bright side (sukkapakkha) as well;

this refers by extension to the commonality of meaning obtainable from the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) by way of its shared characteristics, not to a specific meaning, because that would be dissimilar, or rather, it refers specifically to the particular meaning by means of a method of illustration through a dissimilar example.
“Any one of the three kinds of seclusion”—this is not found here. For although there are three kinds of seclusion, only one of them, or one supported by the other two, is found here.
“Even from afar” means even from a distant place.
Therefore he said, “even from across the border,” and so forth. Regarding the word “let it occur to you”: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

In view of its dependence on the word *paṭi*, "Sāriputta" is in the accusative case; however, showing that the meaning should be understood as being in the genitive case, he says, "of the venerable Sāriputta himself.

By the phrase "let there be a portion," he shows that the prefix *paṭi* has the sense of "portion" (*bhāga*), because meanings such as "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth are not applicable here.
Therefore, he says, "thus it accords with the rules of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*)."
“May it be seen” means may it be seen by means of knowledge; or the meaning is “may it be perceived. “May it be established” means may it stand present before knowledge.
“They shall learn” means they shall bring [the text] to the lips. For “learning” (*uggaha*) is the act of bringing [the words] to the lips.
“They shall master” is a synonym for that very same thing. Alternatively, “mastering” (*pariyāpuṇana*) is the establishing or placing of the meaning in the mind through questioning and so forth.
“An expression of cause” means an expression made by way of being a cause for what has been stated above, according to the rule: “The instrumental case is used for the cause.
The reference back to the meaning already stated is performed by means of the word *taṃ* (that). Therefore he said, “Because,” and so forth.
“In one single manner” means in one single mode, namely, that which consists of taking [the gift] as a share of material goods, established by the fact of giving material goods. That very...

Indeed, it was with this aspect in mind that he said, "This is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One. Otherwise, that same meaning would have been stated by the Elder in a single aspect as well: "While the Teacher dwells in seclusion, his disciples do not train in accordance with seclusion.

"By three aspects" means by the three ways of not training in accordance with the three kinds of seclusion, which constitute the practice for those who are heirs to material gifts. "To this extent" refers to: "In this case, friends... [and so on]."
By the mere recitation of the summary of the dark side ending with "they do not train accordingly," [the teaching] is extensively analyzed;
it is perfectly demonstrated because it has been explained without remainder.

Now, regarding the objection that since the Teacher himself was included by the Blessed One in the summary, he was not explicitly demonstrated, he says "And yet... and so forth, referring to that very point.

"Showing favor to his disciples" means: out of compassion for his disciples, thinking, "The Teacher’s disciples are heirs to his material goods," and even for the sake of protecting the Teacher from the doctrines of others, [thinking], "You must become heirs to the Dhamma. The construction is:
"That is not fitting for the disciples because it is a lack of proper conduct. "This is the method" refers to what was stated beginning with, "To this extent, this Blessed One... and so forth.
The demonstration of the connection [between sections] occurs by way of showing the analysis of the meaning of the summary (uddesa) in the dark section (kaṇhapakkha);
the same method applies to the light section (sukkappakkha), for that is the intended meaning of "demonstrating the connection. Therefore he said:

"This, first of all, is the application of the sequence of the connection here," which means the connection between the teaching of the summary taught by the Teacher and the sequence of the connection taught by the Great Elder (Mahāthera).
And here, the connection should be understood exactly as it follows.
Regarding the phrase "for one who is utterly secluded": just as seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhi*) is absolute for the Teacher, so too are the other forms of seclusion absolute for him.
"Training after" (*anusikkhana*) means filling [the training] again and again; by way of its opposite, he says "they do not fulfill," meaning they do not bring it to full growth.
The meaning is that they do not fulfill [the training]; or rather, the meaning is that they do not maintain it.
For to the same extent that they do not train in seclusion, to that same extent they do not cultivate it, or they receive the designation "they do not maintain it.
But why, in this context, is there a mention of bodily seclusion alone—using an undifferentiated expression—as was done in the summary statement, "they do not train in seclusion"?

With reference to the prompting (*codana*), he says “If, however,” and so forth. Regarding the question: there would be no distinction from the question itself because no differentiation is found in the response.
But is it not the case that no distinction is found in the Canon at all, since the statement “they do not train in seclusion” is an undifferentiated expression?
No; for it is clarified by means of another phrase. Thus he says: “And of those states,” and so forth.
"The side of the answer" (*byākaraṇapakkha*) means the side of the response. And the response is not an indistinct indication like the question;

rather, the intention is that it is the analysis of the meaning as intended. "By this phrase" means that by the phrase "they do not train in seclusion," he shows bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) being left unfulfilled; the same method applies here to "mental seclusion" (*cittaviveka*) and "seclusion from the substrates of existence" (*upadhiviveka*).

And here, the statement "they do not abandon" is an expression of the absence of abandoning regarding those phenomena to be abandoned; it illuminates the absence of seclusion characterized by abandoning.
Having stated that, the subsequent statement "having set aside their duty toward seclusion" further illuminates the absence of a superior degree of seclusion beyond that.
By showing the absence of both these types of seclusion through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) in the passage beginning with "and of whatever phenomena," [the text establishes] "seclusion."
By the phrase "they do not train accordingly," it should be understood that the absence of physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*), which is the root of the two kinds of seclusion, is demonstrated.
Because they take up and grasp various requisites in great measure due to the non-disappearance of craving, they are called "luxurious" (*bāhulika*);

they are "luxurious" precisely because they are "luxurious" (just as one is called a "Vinayika" because of his expertise in the Vinaya). Furthermore, they are so called because they are constantly engaged in efforts for the sake of having an abundance of requisites.

Therefore, he said: “They have set out for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth. Because they grasp the training loosely and without firmness due to a lack of reverence for it, they are called “slothful” (*sāthalikā*). “Loose” (*sithila*) is a neuter abstract noun;

alternatively, the formation of the word *sāthalikā* should be understood by way of the word *sāthala*, which has the same meaning as *sithila*. [The term is used] in the sense of “not understanding” (*avagamana*).
“In the sense of going downwards,” that is to say, by way of being part of the lower realm (*orambhāgiya*).
“In seclusion from acquisitions” means being secluded from acquisitions due to the relinquishing of all acquisitions.

“Having laid down the burden” means having abandoned their exertion. “Indiscriminately” means without specifying any particular distinction, referring to them simply as “disciples” (*sāvaka*) without differentiation; whereas “specifying” refers to terms such as “elders” (*thera*) and so forth.
“From ten years onwards” means starting from the age of ten. “In sovereignty” is used here as in such expressions as “the position of a merchant chief” or “the position of a general.
An “unerring marksman” is one who hits the mark by means of a slight indication. “In stability” means in persistence. “In the moment” means at that very instant.
He says “by way of being dependent on that” because it exists in the relationship of support and supported. “The cultivation of equanimity.”

Indifference toward the seven formations is also a means for attaining the unconditioned; conversely, the adornment of robes and so forth does not lead to the fulfillment of seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka).
Therefore, he said: "Not fulfilling [the requirements for] robes, bowl... and so on. "Therein" refers to the section concerning the Elder (Thera-vāra).
"Here" refers to the sections concerning the Middle and New (Majjhima-navaka-vāra). For it is said: "At the time of being a middle-aged elder," and so forth.
32. And in this "dark side" (*kaṇhapakkha*): it refers to the dark side in this section of exposition (*niddesavāra*), not to the dark side in the section of enumeration (*uddesavāra*).

However, the meaning to be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated for the dark side in the section of enumeration is shown by the extended application (*atidesa*) stating, "This same method applies to the bright side (*sukkapakkha*) as well.
"By the method of the stated opposites" means [by the method beginning] "they do not train in, nor fulfill, bodily seclusion," and so forth.

By way of the opposite method to the meaning already stated, [it is said] in the manner beginning with, “They train in and fulfill physical seclusion,” and so forth. “In this” means in this bright fortnight (*sukkapakkha*). “In brief” means a summary of the meaning.
“By a succession of leagues” means by a sequence of leagues—one, two, three—due to being far from the vicinity of a village. “Wilderness and forest tracts” means...

"In the forests" means those that have become thickets of trees. "Remote" (*pantāni*) means secluded. "The time fit for approaching" refers to the time of being worn out by old age, because of the lack of capacity for the long journeys of going and returning to the alms-village.
[By this,] they generate confidence in the providers of requisites, thinking: "Alas, what a gift given to those endowed with such virtues!
"Praiseworthy" (*pāsaṃsā*) means worthy of praise. "This Great Elder as well," and so forth, is one [instance].
This is stated according to those who, having pointed out one who is more senior among those dwelling in heedfulness, speak [of them].

"He has entered a secluded place" means that he goes out in the evening after having cultivated wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*); this is the intended meaning. He performs the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, not some other duty;
he brings forth the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), not vain mental attention. "In every way" means from the beginning.
Thus, by means of that very factor, he separates the mind from the defilements;
then, through suppression, through eradication, and through pacification, he fulfills mental seclusion in every way. By the phrase "he wears rag-robes," he shows the absence of luxury;
by the phrase "having taken up the teaching without laxity," he shows the absence of negligence; [and] "one who is free from hindrances."
By the phrase "having laid down the burden through this descent" and "the attainment of fruition," etc., he shows that seclusion is the precursor.

33. Regarding the words "Therein, friends": here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. By this, the subsequent teaching proceeding in the manner of "Greed is evil," etc., is exhaustively included without remainder.
As for the question "What is the connection?": it is that which was [taught] by the Blessed One from the side of defilement...
The teaching beginning with, “Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things,” which brings about the practice of being an heir in the Dhamma, was first set forth;
that [teaching] was then analyzed by means of the exposition-teaching adorned with eighteen rounds, beginning with, “When the Teacher dwells in seclusion...”;
and thereafter, by means of the subsequent teaching following the method beginning with, “In this regard, friends, greed is evil... and so on.
He asks about the connection. "Thus" means: on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkhe*), by way of showing the absence of abandonment through the phrase "they do not abandon";
and on the side of purification (*vodānapakkhe*), by way of showing the presence of abandonment through the phrase "they abandon.

Thus, in order to show specifically those phenomena (*dhamma*) which were mentioned generally by the word *dhamma* along with the relative pronouns *yaṃ* and *taṃ*—the specific nature of which had not yet been determined—he says:
The Exposition (*yojanā*). Regarding the phrase "these are those":
why are only greed and the rest mentioned here as states to be abandoned, when there are other states to be abandoned such as delusion, wrong view, doubt, and so forth? It is true that they exist;

however, because they are associated with greed and the others, they are already included by them and thus mentioned. Alternatively, the reason for including only these here will become clear further on.
Now, in order to show the connection by way of accumulation (*upacaya*), the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated.

Therein, as for that quality of being an heir to the Dhamma which is pleasing to the Teacher among his disciples—that has not been extolled by saying, “He develops the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so forth;
rather, it has been spoken of by saying, “They train themselves in seclusion, they abandon those [unwholesome] states, and they are not luxurious,” and so forth.
It was stated that "the Dhamma was taught by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya) below.
Furthermore, [the teaching] beginning with, "They do not abandon those things, being forerunners in falling away," was taught by way of a figurative expression regarding material gain (āmisa).

Also, [the teaching] beginning with, "May there be almsfood for me," and "They become luxurious," was taught even by way of a non-figurative expression (nippariyāya) regarding material gain. Alternatively, this is the Blessed One’s rejection of being an heir to material gain...
The state of being an heir to the Dhamma has been stated, as well as that which was stated by the Great Elder himself while analyzing its meaning—namely, the training in seclusion and so forth.
Both of these were spoken in order to clarify them by way of their causes, beginning with the words: "In this regard, friends, greed... and so on.
For it is through the cessation of the cause that the side of defilement ceases, and through the accomplishment of the cause of cessation that the side of purification is brought about.
“Demonstration of the past teaching” means the reference back to the teaching as it was taught by the Elder in the past.
For this very reason, he said: “It is said: ‘Of the Teacher who is secluded... [and so on] up to ‘of the teaching.
Therein: regarding that which was stated specifically in the phrase, “Of those states for which the Teacher has declared abandonment,” therein the states to be abandoned are greed and so forth.
These have been stated in general terms. "Base" means inferior. For greed is by its cause, condition, intrinsic nature, fruit, and outflow, of a defiled character;
or it is "evil" in the sense that it brings about suffering in the future.
"Characterized by covetousness" means characterized by the intense longing for an object; for by it one covets, or it itself covets.
Or, the mere state of being greedy is called "greed" (*lobha*). Its function is clinging to tastes and so forth; its manifestation is non-renunciation;
its proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that lead to fetters. It has the characteristic of corrupting; thus, it has the characteristic of becoming hostile toward an object.
For it is by means of this that beings become corrupted, or it itself becomes corrupted, or it is the mere state of being corrupted—this is called "hatred" (*dosa*).
Among these, hatred has the nature of spreading like poison, or the nature of burning its own support;

it is manifested as malice and has the objects of resentment as its proximate cause. By the statement beginning with "Among those," there is shown the fact that greed and hatred must be abandoned absolutely.
The phrase "it arises when one obtains requisites from an heir of material goods" is said with reference to the fact that greed has the nature of grasping at an object, by way of craving.
However, with reference to persistent hankering (*anugijjhana*), it is said: “He longs for what he has not obtained. The construction is to be supplied by bringing in the phrase:

“In the non-attainment of requisites, he becomes an heir to material things (*āmisadāyāda*”). Regarding the word “not obtaining,” one should apply the construction here by changing the case-ending of the word “requisites” (*paccaye*).
“Afflicted” (*vighātavatā*) means afflicted by the frustration of desire, according to the statement: “Not to obtain what one desires is also suffering. Greed (*lobha*).
"And there is an object to be given, [but] he is an heir to material things"—this is the connection. This same method applies to the following phrase as well.
And "object to be given" is merely an illustration, because greed can arise in him even on account of the seven kinds of playfulness and so forth.
"Dependent on craving comes seeking; dependent on seeking comes gain"—these and others are the nine rooted in craving. It fulfills...

“An heir to material goods” (*āmisadāyāda*) should be understood as a modification of the grammatical case. The five types of stinginess are stinginess regarding one’s dwelling (*āvāsamacchariya*), and so forth.
“The path” (*magga*) refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). For it goes while slaying the defilements (*kilesa*); it is sought after by those seeking Nibbāna;
or, by way of the clear realization of its attainment (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), it itself seeks out Nibbāna. Thus, in the primary sense, it is called “the path.”
"One extreme" (*eko anto*) means one side that is unmixed with the other, or one end by virtue of its inferiority or wretchedness.

Granted, other wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*) do not reach these extremes because they are dissociated from them—they are indeed free from them—but this [state] does not even approach ultimate liberation;
thus he said, "it is liberated from these extremes. Therefore: "because of being liberated from the two extremes."
The statement "you exist in the midst of these" is said because the Path is liberated from both extremes, not because it is included within them;
for it is to be practiced by those seeking escape from the suffering of saṃsāra.

"In that way" means that just as greed is one extreme—both in the sense of being unmixed with the other [extreme] and in the sense of being base—so too is devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure. This same method applies to the remaining [extremes] as well.
The non-approaching of the path should be understood precisely as the complete non-arising of those extremes.
"By the method previously stated" refers to the method explained earlier in the passage beginning with, "He does not approach these two extremes.

"Of the truths" refers to the four noble truths. "In the sense of being the guide for vision" refers to vision, which is distinguished by such categories as full understanding (*pariññā*) and clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
"In every way" means in the sense of leading and in the sense of proceeding. "The maker of the eye" means the producer or the bringer-to-fulfillment of the Dhamma-eye.

Although this [Dhamma-eye] is not different from the Dhamma-eye even when there is a path, it should be understood that it is stated by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because a meaning established through its constituent parts is said to be "produced by the whole. For he will say accordingly:

“For the path itself leads to the goal of the path, because it performs the task that must be done by means of the path. “For the sake of knowledge” means for the sake of knowing things as they truly are.
Hence he said: “in the sense of making known. For making known is the bringing about of a state of specific understanding (*visesañāta*).
“By way of pacification” means by way of pacifying through complete eradication, just like the state of suffering and so forth being fully understood (*pariññeyya*) and so on.

The state of being "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) is also made manifest by means of the path itself; thus he says, "because it shows that all four truths are to be directly known," the meaning being "by way of their full penetration" (*vibhāvana*).
"Full enlightenment" (*sambodhi*) is the path, because one "awakens by means of this. "For its sake" means for the sake of the function of the path.
For there is nothing other than the path that performs the function of the path. Therefore he says, "Indeed, it is the path itself," and so forth.
Alternatively, when right view arises, it gives rise to the other [factors] by way of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth;

the same applies to the remaining path-factors. In this way, too, the "conduciveness to the path" should be understood. Regarding "for the sake of realization through direct experience": this means for the sake of the direct experience known as realization (*sacchikaraṇa*).
Or, "for the sake of Nibbāna" refers to Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*); by the term "for the sake of peace" (*upasamāya*), Nibbāna with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbāna*) is included.

They come [to this conclusion] by means of the method of meaning already stated in the passage beginning with “For that is of the truths. “In this context” refers to the phrases such as “the maker of vision.

The essence is beautiful and not to be discarded. “Other than this” refers to the elaborate commentary on the meaning, such as “it is the maker of vision because it effects the purification of view through the full understanding of suffering,” which is intended solely for the sake of detailed exposition.

Regarding the phrase *ayameva*: here, by the word *ayaṃ* (this), he demonstrates that both himself and others have direct personal experience (*paccakkhabhāva*) of the Noble Ones’ path within that assembly.
For the word *ayaṃ* expresses immediate proximity. "For the purpose of negating another path" means for the purpose of negating the existence of any other path leading to Nibbāna;
for here, "negation" (*paṭisedhana*) refers to the exclusion of [the existence of] such a path.
Because no other path is obtainable, its non-otherness consists in its being common to the Buddhas and others. Therefore, Brahmā Sahampati said:
“The one who sees the end of birth knows the single path, the compassionate one who seeks the welfare [of beings].”
"By this path they have crossed over in the past, those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood.

By the term *ārakatta* (being far removed), he states the derivation of the word *ariya* according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*). The phrase "for the abandoning of enemies" (*aripahānāya*) is merely a statement of the meaning.

It is called *ariya* because enemies (*arī*) of evil nature go away (*yanti*) or depart by means of it. In the phrase "taught by the *ariya*," the term *ariya* refers to the Blessed One, for the enemies of evil nature go away from him.

In the phrase "for the attainment of the state of an *ariya*," the word *ariya* is to be understood as established through the elision of the final member of the compound; that is, one who performs what is noble (*ariyakara*) is an *ariya*.
Since the designation "path" (*magga*) applies to the collection of path-factors, and the collection is...
He said, "It is called 'endowed with a collection' because it is possessed of eight factors";
therefore, it is "eight-factored" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because these eight factors, which are its own constituent parts, belong to it.

However, since from the ultimate standpoint (paramattha) the path is the factors themselves, it is stated that "it is not separate from the factors," just as one says, "the Veda has six limbs. This is an illustration by way of similarity.
But showing this, he said, "like the fivefold musical instruments," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the fourfold army and other such things.
He states the derivation of the word according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*): "he goes killing. "He seeks" (*maggati*) means he searches for.
For the Noble Path, when it takes Nibbāna as its object, is as if it were searching for it. It is sought (*maggīyati*) by those who desire Nibbāna.
This is because one begins by performing merit that serves as the necessary condition for turning away from saṃsāra, and then practices for that purpose.

By the phrase "it is understood" (*gammati*), he states the grammatical derivation according to the reversal of beginning and end, just as in the word "kakū. Having stated, "‘Seyyathidaṃ’ is a particle," he asks, "Which are those eight factors?

because that particle is common to all genders, cases, and numbers. But surely, when the factors are combined, they constitute the Path; even one deficient in as few as seven factors [is not the Path].

"Is it because of the absence of the noble path? This is true in the sense of the penetration of truth; however, because they act as conditions for the path by each performing its own respective function, even individually they are indeed the path.
Thus he said, "For each single factor is indeed the path," otherwise, even when combined, their function as the path would not be possible.
Now, in order to support this very point with the canonical text:
It is said: “It is both the path of right view and the cause.
Its characteristic is right seeing—that is, the vision and penetration of the four truths by way of full understanding, realization, and so forth, without error.
It is right and non-erroneous regarding the associated states that have Nibbāna as their object.

That which has "directing onto" (*abhiniropana*) as its characteristic of absorption (*appanā*) is "characterized by right directing onto. Because false speech and so forth have the function of deceiving and the like, they are harsh and non-comprehensive;

right speech, being of a gentle nature as the opposite of those qualities, correctly comprehends the associated mental states and the people who hear the well-spoken words conditioned by right speech.
Thus, right speech is "right comprehension," and that which has this as its characteristic is "characterized by right comprehension."
Just as bodily action (kāyika-kiriyā) gives rise to something that is to be done and itself constitutes an arising or an effort,
so too right action— characterized by right origination— is the joy of abstinence known as right conduct (sammākammanta).
Alternatively, "origination" (samuṭṭhāna) is the lifting up of associated states, just as bodily action involves the lifting of a burden.

Right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification because it is the purification or cleansing of a living being or of associated states, or because it is the purification or cleansing of the very occurrence of the life-process through livelihood itself.

Right effort is the exertion or providing of support by not allowing one to fall into the side of indolence, but rather by uplifting the associated states. It is the act of approaching and remaining fixed upon the object.
Or, non-relinquishing is its manifestation. Right placing (samādhāna) is the correct or even placing of associated states upon the object.
One rightly intends (saṅkappeti) and directs associated states toward the object, thus it is right intention (sammāsaṅkappo).

One speaks rightly by means of this, thus it is right speech (sammāvācā). One acts rightly by means of this, thus it is right action (sammākamma); that itself is the basis for right action (sammākammanta).
One lives rightly by means of this, thus it is right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*). One strives and exerts oneself rightly by means of this, thus it is right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*).
One remembers and recollects rightly, thus it is right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*). The mind becomes concentrated rightly by means of this, thus it is right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*);
in this way, the etymological definitions of right intention and the others are to be understood.
“Wrong view” means every kind of wrong seeing. Regarding the phrase “the defilements that are its opposites,” here the word “its” (*taṃ*) refers to right view.
For it is not the defilements that are the opposites of wrong view, but rather of right view.

And the inclusion of “ignorance” (*avijjā*) is because ignorance is the foremost among those phenomena that cause defilement. Thus he said: “Bhikkhus, ignorance is the precursor of unwholesome states.”
"Through the attainment of states. This is because of non-delusion, by means of the eradication of delusion which obstructs vision.
And herein, by the phrase "he abandons wrong view... etc.," the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) is shown;

by the phrase "he takes Nibbāna as his object," the realization of verification (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) is shown; and by the phrase "the associated states... etc.," the realization of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) is shown.

This demonstrates the function of right view. However, it should be understood that the "clear realization through full understanding" (pariññābhisamaya) is already stated by implication, due to its being an immediate consequence.
How, then, can a single moment of knowledge proceed while accomplishing four functions simultaneously?
One should not say: "Such a thing is not seen in the world, nor is there any such scriptural authority. For just as a lamp, in a single moment—
In an instant it burns the wick, consumes the oil, dispels the darkness, and reveals light;

thus should this knowledge be understood. "The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering, it is knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, it is knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and it is knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is the scriptural passage.

An illustration should be given here: Just as right view, having proceeded separately with regard to suffering and the other truths during the preliminary stage, proceeds at the moment of the Path accomplishing the function of all four knowledges as a single unity;

so too, right intention and the others, having been named "intention of renunciation" and so forth during the preliminary stage, proceed separately by way of abandoning intentions of sensual desire and the rest.
Having arisen separately, they proceed at the moment of the path (magga-khaṇa) accomplishing three or four functions respectively.
As for right concentration (sammā-samādhi), however, it proceeds as something distinct both in the prior stage and at the moment of the path.

While it is certainly true that all unwholesome states are opposites of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), nevertheless, in the description of the function of right view, this is done by way of showing its direct antithesis.
The inclusion of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) has been made. For that very reason, it is said:

"and the defilements opposed to it. Those defilements whose non-eradication would prevent right view from arising should be understood as the defilements opposed to it, because they are associated with wrong view by being conjoined with it.
This same principle applies even in the description of the functions of right intention and the others.
This is the method. By way of the path of stream-entry and so forth, these four [paths] are grouped together as a single unit due to their commonality as supramundane paths.
Greed and hatred are the truth of origination; that which has them as its origin is the truth of suffering; the state of abandonment is the truth of the path;
and that wherein such abandonment occurs is the truth of cessation—these are the four truths. But why, in this context, are greed and hatred [singled out]?
Why is there a separate treatment at the beginning? First, the separate treatment is according to the inclinations of those individuals who awaken in such a way;
it is for the purpose of showing that through these faults of greed, one becomes an heir to material things, whereas by abandoning them, one becomes an heir to the Dhamma;

and it is also for the purpose of showing that, by following that sequence, there is thus a gateway to liberation for each [fault] through its connection with the Four Noble Truths. This applies to the remaining sections as well.

The same method applies here. However, its mention first should be understood because it is extremely coarse and thus most manifest, because it is the root of other evil states that will be mentioned, and because it is associated with them.
"Characterized by anger" means having the nature of being provoked; the sense is the mind's state of malice (*byāpajjana*). "Fury" (*caṇḍikka*) is ferocity.
The meaning is "the absence of the Kurus. Its function (*rasa*) is the production of resentment in the mind through such thoughts as "he has done me harm," and so forth.
Its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) is the destruction of one's own or another's continuity, appearing like an enemy who has found an opening.
It is called "binding" (*upanandhana*) because it acts like a binding that fastens repeatedly in various ways.
For it has been stated thus: "Its flavor is the non-relinquishing of resentment; its manifestation is the state of continuous connection with anger.
Regarding the phrase "at another time, enmity," etc., by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the commentary on the meaning of the explanatory terms such as:
"enmity, the state of being enmity, fixing, placing, establishing, reconnecting, continuous connection, strengthening," and so forth.
It is "clinging" (*saṅgayhati*). For a person possessed of resentment (*upanāhasamaṅgī*) burns like a flaming torch of chaff because he does not let go of his enmity;
moreover, his mind, even when being washed, is never purified—like a clear hide or like a rag smeared with soot.
Its characteristic is the smearing over of the virtues of others, having a nature that smears away the virtues of others just as a water-sponge [absorbs] water.
It should be understood that one who has become such [a person] first smears himself with excrement, just as excrement strikes back at its own maker who is striking it.
For he is called "one who smears" (*makkha*) because he smears over the virtues within his own continuum and those of others.
"Taking up the yoke" (*yugaggāha*) is the grasping of an equal burden; it is the imposition of what is not equal and what does not exist. "Making even" (*samīkaraṇa*) is the act of leveling.
It is said, "it has the manifestation of establishing one's own virtues by means of the measure of others' virtues," because it establishes itself by means of the measure of others' virtues.
For in this way, as if biting at the virtues of others, it makes them equal to its own virtues;
thus it is called *paḷāsa* (envy).
Envy (*issā*) is the disparaging of another’s success; it is the grudging of another’s prosperity. It is called envy because one envies another’s success and cannot endure it.

Thus, it is said to have the characteristic of intolerance toward another’s success. In that context—namely, regarding another’s success—it has non-delight as its essence and the function of being the opposite of delight.
Its manifestation is aversion, such that one does not even wish to look upon another’s success.
From non-giving. Its characteristic is concealment, because of the inability to endure others sharing in one’s own prosperity.
"Non-pleasing" (*asukhāyanam*) means not bringing pleasure, but rather causing pain; the intended meaning is "not making known.
"Concealment of committed evil" (*katapāpapaṭicchādanam*) is the hiding of the evil already done, such as bodily misconduct and so forth. Of that evil...
It stands as an obstruction, thus it is "having that obstruction as its manifestation" (*tadāvaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā*); this refers to deceit (*māyā*).
A person endowed with this is like a coal covered by ashes, like a stump hidden by water, or like a sword concealed by a rag.
It is the proclaiming of qualities not actually possessed; that is, the displaying of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth that do not exist within oneself.

Because of that deceitfulness possessed by a person who dwells performing actions according to his own whim through the pretense of possessing qualities he lacks, it is difficult to discern him such that one cannot know whether he is "thus-minded" or "thus-acting";
therefore, one cannot know his belly or his back. Hence it is said:
"With the left side he is a boar, with the right side a goat."
"He has a trunk but no tusks; he is an old bull by his horns"—thus one is like the *yakkha*-boar described in this way.
The state of inflation of the mind is its state of rigidity and coarseness. "Living without support" means living without restraint. By way of a lack of gentleness...
It presents itself as lack of gentleness, or it presents itself as the state of lacking gentleness; thus it is "presented as lack of gentleness. This is *thambha* (stiffness).
A person endowed with this is stiff like a python that has swallowed the head of a plough, or like a leather bag filled with air;
even upon seeing those worthy of respect, he does not wish to bow down, but moves only within his own limits.
Excellence in performance (*karaṇuttariya*) is the superior action of performing a task. Hostility (*vipaccanīkatā*) is, specifically, the state of being antagonistic.
For when someone does something to another, an aggressive impulse arises by way of performing an act twice as great in response.

Arrogance (*unnati*) is the lifting up [of oneself] by way of such forms as superiority. For even contempt (*omāna*) functions in this same manner through the medium of performance, by way of self-exaltation.
It occurs as follows: the act of making "I" (ahaṃkaraṇa) through such thoughts as "I am superior," which is an exaltation, is *ahaṅkāra*.
Excessive elevation after having overcome others is *abbhunnati*. With reference to this, it was said: "In the first stage one regards oneself as inferior;
in the subsequent stage, one regards oneself as superior."
Intoxication (*mattabhāva*) is the state of the mind’s being intoxicated in dependence upon birth and so forth;
or, that phenomenon by virtue of which a person is called "intoxicated" is intoxication. Its function is the grasping of intoxication, its purpose being the act of grasping intoxication.
For intoxication, while occurring as if grasping its own mode of intoxication to the associated phenomena, likewise [grasps] the person who possesses it.
It is as if one were actually doing so. Because one treats a person unfavorably under the influence of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), it is like a state of mental madness;
thus, it is manifested as madness. "Relaxation of the mind" (*cittavossagga*) is the letting go of the mind without restraining it with mindfulness;
the meaning is that it is devoid of mindfulness. The non-reinstatement of the aforementioned relaxation is repeated relinquishment.

The "bestowing of relinquishment" refers to these [states] beginning with anger (*kodha*), or even those beginning with greed (*lobha*). Regarding "characteristic and so forth": this refers to the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*rasa*), and manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
As for the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), it is not mentioned because it consists of other phenomena (*dhammantara*).

The etymological derivation—such as "it is angry, thus it is anger (*kodha*)," or "it harbors resentment, thus it is resentment (*upanāha*)"—is indeed easy to understand and therefore has not been stated; however, in terms of meaning, anger is simply hatred (*dosa*), and likewise is resentment.

For their distinction is made merely from the perspective of their mode of occurrence: malice, spite, and impetuosity are mental states arising as a manifestation of that [mode], associated with aversion;
deceit, fraud, obstinacy, pride, and negligence are mental states arising as a manifestation of that [mode], associated with greed.
Obstinacy (*thambha*) is a particular kind of conceit, because it is to be understood as a state of rigidity of the mind; likewise is pride (*mada*). For it is said: "Conceit..."
This has been explained in the *Vibhaṅga* by such passages as "conceit" (*maññanā*).

However, since pride (*māna*) and excessive pride (*atimāna*) are taken separately here, those phenomena that occur in the mode of intoxication (*majjanākāra*) alone should be understood as "intoxication" (*mada*). The fact that the remaining [factors] are distinct phenomena is indeed evident.
But why are only these eight dyads taken here; are there no other defiled phenomena (*kilesadhamma*) besides these? No.

[The previous section] stated that [these things] do not exist; however, since these [following things] lead more specifically to defilement for one who inherits material gifts (*āmisa-dāyāda*), the passage beginning with “specifically” (*visesato*) was commenced to demonstrate the manner in which greed and the other [defilements] arise in such a person, thereby clarifying that distinction.
In this context, “herein” (*ettha*) means among these [defilements] such as greed. The intended meaning is “not obtaining material gifts. “Anger arisen even beyond that” means...
Having brought [the words together], they should be connected. "Even though existing" (santepi) means even when present. "Is envious" (issaṭi) means she generates envy.

"Becomes corrupt" (padussati) is a synonym for that very same thing; for it is defined as "she envies, she hates, she becomes corrupt," and so forth. Or, because one who generates envy is necessarily one whose mind is corrupted, it is said "she becomes corrupt. "Assa" means...
"An heir to material goods. "One who has practiced in this way" means one who has practiced the course of conduct consisting in the proclamation of non-existent qualities.
"Incapable of being exhorted" shows that what is called "obstinacy" (*thambha*) is a state of being difficult to speak to (*dovacassakaraṇa*).

"He says something by way of giving exhortation. By the phrase "through obstinacy... [they] imagine," he shows that obstinacy is a specific kind of conceit (*māna*); through obstinacy... [they] imagine.
The meaning is "or by means of a cause. "Being intoxicated" (*matto samāno*) means being in a state of intoxication. By the phrase "he becomes negligent through sensual pleasures...
etc.," it is shown that through the power of intoxication he falls into negligence (*pamāda*) with absolute certainty.
By the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), through the very demonstration of the sequence of the arising of greed and so forth in one who inherits material goods, [it is shown] here in the text... them.

It should be understood that the sequence of the teaching has also been shown. The connection is: "He is not liberated from these alone, but rather from other such evil states as well. What, then, are those? They are: meager desire, excessive desire, and so forth.
Thus, since the inheritance of material things brings such great danger, one should generate an even stronger sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); this is the instruction in this context.

It is to be understood. "In this" means in this sutta. "In all places" means in all sections. "Without distinction" means it should be understood that by this very method of applying the Truths (sacca-yojanā-naya) shown here first, it is to be applied in all sections.

"The ground for proficiency in the cultivation of knowledge" refers to the knowledge [arising] from the detailed analysis of the specific distinctions of the Path, such as its eightfold or sevenfold nature.

"Familiarity" (paricaya) in the sense of repeated practice is "familiarity with knowledge" (ñāṇaparicaya); it is for the sake of its proficiency and skill. "In this" means in the Noble Path. "Distinction" (bheda) means difference.
"Order" (kama) is the sequence of the teaching of the factors. "Method of development" (bhāvanānaya) is the procedure of development.
Expanding upon the meaning briefly stated as "sometimes eightfold, sometimes sevenfold," he says again, "For this... and so forth.
In this context, "by way of the supramundane first jhāna" means by way of the supramundane first jhāna.
Furthermore, since some of the factors of jhāna are of the very nature of the Path, it is impossible to speak of jhāna as being entirely separate from the Path;
therefore, instead of saying "accompanied by the supramundane first jhāna," it is said simply "by way of the supramundane first jhāna."
It has been stated. Alternatively, "by way of the supramundane first jhāna" means that having become supramundane, it is by way of the first jhāna;

this is how the meaning should be understood here. For the Noble Path becomes eightfold by way of the first jhāna—either the one that served as the basis for insight or the one that was directly comprehended. Alternatively, [it refers] to a dry-insight practitioner who has attained jhāna.

Alternatively, for one who has attained jhāna, the Noble Path that arises through the comprehension of the first jhāna—without making it its basis—or through the comprehension of miscellaneous formations, possesses eight factors.

Showing that its state of having eight factors is due to its being based on the first jhāna, he says, "by way of the first jhāna. In the same way, the meaning of "by way of the remaining jhānas" should be understood accordingly.
If the Noble Path is sevenfold as well, then why is it stated in the Pāḷi as "eightfold" alone?

To this he says: "Because of the description of the highest [standard]," and so forth. And just as here there is a distinction between the eightfold and sevenfold [paths] by way of the path of practice (*paṭipadā*), so too there should be understood a distinction between the sevenfold and sixfold [paths] by way of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), because of the sixfold nature [of the path] when based on jhānas devoid of rapture (*appītika*).
However, since the teaching has come down according to the path, this distinction was not mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"Beyond this" means beyond these eight factors at the maximum; at the minimum, however, there is no path-factor beyond seven.
[Objection: But in the section on the fivefold path in the *Maggavibhaṅga*, only five path-factors are mentioned, and in the *Mahā-Ṣaḷāyatana-sutta*...
“Whatever view such a person has, whatever intention such a person has, whatever effort such a person has, whatever mindfulness such a person has,
whatever concentration such a person has— that is his right concentration,” having said this, [the Buddha] then spoke of right speech and the others by way of their preliminary stage:
“But prior to that, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood have already been well-purified.”
"Is it true that they have come? "It is true; however, that was said by way of showing the additional function of those five factors that cause right view and the rest to be performed.
Therefore, it should be understood that the statement 'there is no path-factor beyond this' is well-said, for there is no noble path devoid of right speech and the other factors."
"Of all wholesome states" (*sabbakusalānaṃ*) means of all wholesome phenomena (*dhamma*). This genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Among those various wholesome states—classified according to the sense-sphere and so forth—that right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is the best. Indeed, it is because of its excellence that it is said: "They say that living by wisdom is the best way to live.
However, there is no need to state that the right view of the Path (*magga-sammā-diṭṭhi*) is the most excellent of all.

"In the wholesome section" means at the moment of the arising of the wholesome. It is "the forerunner" because, by awakening to the true intrinsic nature of wholesome and other phenomena, it acts as a guide for the associated states.
For this very reason, it is said: "One understands right view as right view," and so forth.
That right view is its source; thus, it is "born from that," namely, right intention. For, by way of right seeing—
He possesses right intention (*sammāsaṅkappo*). "Produced from that" means produced with that as their source.
Even though they are produced with that as their source, they are called "produced by that" because the term for the cause is applied figuratively to the cause of the cause;
thus he said, "the remaining factors are produced from that. Therefore he said, "of right view," and so forth. For just as right seeing [is the cause] of right thought...
...is a specific condition (*visesa-paccaya*). Likewise, right thinking is a specific condition for right comprehension;

right comprehension for right origination; right origination for right cleansing; right cleansing for right effort; right effort for right establishment; and right establishment is a specific condition for right mindfulness.
Therefore, each preceding [factor] is a specific condition for each succeeding one.
