By the phrase “it is a specific condition,” these factors beginning with right view are shown to have been stated in sequence for the purpose of demonstrating their nature as specific conditions.
The "method of development" (bhāvanānaya) refers to the procedure of development that proceeds by way of the union of serenity and insight. For this—

The method of development occurs at the moment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). However, regarding the sequence of development prior to that, for some it is preceded by serenity (*samatha*), while for others it is preceded by insight (*vipassanā*).
To demonstrate that method, the passage beginning with “Someone here” (*koci*) was commenced.

Therein, the first [method] is stated from the perspective of one whose vehicle is serenity (*samathayānika*), and the second from the perspective of one whose vehicle is insight (*vipassanāyānika*). Therefore, he said: “Here, someone,” and so forth.
"Those" refers to calm (samatha), concentration (samādhi), or the factors of jhāna—this is the meaning. "Associated with those" means associated with concentration or associated with jhāna.

And this method is stated with the understanding that, for the most part, those whose vehicle is serenity (samathayānika) apply themselves to insight (vipassanā) by way of the formless (arūpa), and even there, by way of jhāna.
"Developing insight" refers to the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).
Having begun by increasing the nascent insight as it has been attained, the path arises; that is, the mundane preliminary path (pubbabhāgiya-lokiyamagga) emerges.
One cultivates it by way of the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā); one develops it by way of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā);

one practices it repeatedly by way of the contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā). Alternatively, one cultivates it by way of the knowledge of the appearance of fear (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa); one practices it repeatedly.
By way of insight leading to emergence. The fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are exhausted according to the sequence of the paths.
By the restrictive phrase "without having produced serenity," access concentration is excluded, but not momentary concentration;
for without momentary concentration, insight is not possible. "By the fulfillment of insight" means by insight...
"By way of fulfillment" means by way of reaching the state of leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminibhāva*).

"Of those arisen therein" refers to the factors such as right view that have arisen at the moment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*); this genitive case is used here for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇa*).

"As the object of relinquishment" means by way of being the object of relinquishment (*vavassagga*). Relinquishment (*vavassagga*), release (*vossagga*), renunciation (*paṭinissagga*), and liberation (*apavagga*) are synonymous in meaning.
"One" means Nibbāna; therefore, the sense is "by making Nibbāna the object.

"One-pointedness of mind" refers to the right concentration of the Path (magga-sammāsamādhi). For the Noble Path is exclusively concentrated because it completely eradicates the defilements that are the causes of non-concentration.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
At that time, concentration and wisdom are "yoked together" (yuganaddha), because their state of equal flavor (samarasatā) is what is desired.

For at the moment of the Path, concentration is not to be regarded as predominant in its function as it is in the development of serenity (samatha-bhāvanā), nor is wisdom to be regarded as predominant as it is in the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā).
Rather, by virtue of their equal flavor—in the sense of neither one overstepping the other—both are like a pair yoked together.
They proceed together. Therefore it was said: “Tranquillity and insight are indeed coupled together.
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscure in the Commentary on the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Bhayabherava Sutta*.
34. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ*: thus [ends] the *Bhayabherava Sutta*. What is its introduction (*nikkhepa*)? Some first say: "The introduction is occasioned by a question.

For questions are of two kinds, distinguished as manifest and unmanifest. Therein, that teaching which is preceded by the word "what" (*kiṃ*) and expresses a matter intended to be known as the cause for the discourse—that is a manifest question, such as: "What, indeed, here... [and so forth].

"Wealth is the best thing for a man," and so forth. However, that teaching where the intended meaning—the object desired to be known—is revealed by a verbal formulation consisting solely of words without the word *kiṃ*, is an "unmanifest question.
For the meaning desired to be known is called a "problem" (*pañhā*) or a "question" (*pucchā*); therefore, in this context, [passages] such as "O Master Gotama... and so on [are examples].
The statement that "the placement [of the question] was dependent on a query because it was not evident" is without reason;
for that brahmin, when speaking such words as "These, Master Gotama," did not say them while being perplexed, doubtful, or fallen into uncertainty regarding the matter.
Rather, he spoke while proclaiming his own state of confidence and great respect toward the Blessed One concerning the point as he had determined it. Therefore, he said:
“‘He gained confidence in the Blessed One,’ and so forth. ‘In the monastery’ means in the dwelling place. ‘Without interruption’ means while it was still ongoing;
the meaning of both phrases is that it occurred during the spring. This position of family priest was obtained along with the *uṇhīsa* turban and other regalia;
thus they say, ‘It was given to him by the king. Therefore he said: ‘That [was given] to him by the king…’”
"Given. "Brahma" refers to the Veda. That [Veda], moreover, is threefold by way of *manta*, *brahma*, and *kappa*.
Among these, the *manta* is primary because of its status as the root; those which are recited by the Aṭṭhakas and others are [the *manta*], while the others arise dependent upon them.
Therefore, only those are included when one says, "he recites the *manta*. For they are called "*manta*" because they must be spoken with restraint. This very same...
The word *hi* functions as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), thereby rejecting such etymologies as "born from Brahmā" and so forth.

Alternatively, in the phrase "by which reason," this is the instrumental case used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). For the meaning of a cause is the instrument of an action, whereas the meaning of an instrument is not like that of a cause;
therefore, the action of approaching here has the purpose of attaining various specific distinctions of excellence.

In expressions such as “he dwells by means of food,” it is appropriate that this instrumental case has the sense of a cause (hetu), and not the sense of an instrument (karaṇa), because the latter is untenable here;

thus it was said, “or for whatever reason,” and so forth. Because the Blessed One possesses the fruit of the True Dhamma—which is constantly active, unsurpassed, sweet, abundant, and ambrosial—the Blessed One is compared to a great tree perpetually bearing sweet fruit;
and by the very act of taking [the fruit] with the intention of enjoying that sweet fruit...
"For the sweetness of the fruit of the great tree has been grasped.
"He approached" (*upasaṅkami*) means he had approached. For one who goes to some place out of a desire to reach it approaches by passing over various points;
thus he receives the designation "he approached. Therefore he said: "It is meant that he 'went' (*gato*)."

The meaning is "having approached. Regarding the phrase "having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*), he says, "the indication of the completion of the act of approaching," because it is a designation for a prior action.
"From there" means from that place which was reached and described as "he approached.
"Asking whether [all is] bearable and so forth" refers to how the Blessed One asked, "Is it bearable for you, brahmin? Is it sustainable? and so on.
The construction is as follows: by inquiring after [the Blessed One’s] health and so forth, he shared a mutual joy with that brahmin through his initial greeting;
and by imitating that, the brahmin likewise shared a mutual joy with the Blessed One.
To illustrate that mutual sharing of joy by means of a simile, it was said, "like cool water," and so on. Therein:
“Greeted” (*sammodita*) means brought together. “In unity” (*ekībhāva*) means the state of equality and uniformity through the act of greeting. “Endurable” (*khamanīya*) he asks:
“Is this body—consisting of four wheels and nine doors—capable of enduring, given that by its very nature it is difficult to bear due to its momentary perishability?
“Supportable” (*yāpanīya*) refers to [the body] which, being dependent on the requisites for life, is maintained by a long continuity...
"Is it for maintenance?"—meaning, "Am I able to maintain myself? "Is there little affliction?"—meaning, "Is there an absence of ailments such as headaches?
"Is there little sickness?"—meaning, "Is there an absence of a painful livelihood? "Is there lightness of movement?"—meaning, "Is there ease in undertaking various duties?

"Is there strength?"—meaning, "Is there possession of the power appropriate for those tasks? "Is there a comfortable dwelling?"—meaning, "Is there a state of living at ease?"—in each of these instances, the word *kacci* [is used].
Having thus applied [the terms], the meaning should be understood.
Rapture that has reached its peak is simply *pīti* (rapture). Fresh rapture is *pāmojja* (gladness). It is called *sammodanika* because it produces or creates joy (*sammodana*);
he says "because it generates joy" to mean that very thing is *sammodanīya*. It is *sammodanīya* because it is to be rejoiced in (*sammoditabba*). This...
However, in order to show the meaning, he said, "because it is appropriate for mutual greeting. "Because it is to be remembered" means because it is to be recollected.
Although one should say "saraṇīyaṃ," it is stated as "sāraṇīyaṃ" by lengthening the vowel. "Because it is pleasant when being heard" refers to its sweetness upon first contact;

"because it is pleasant when being recollected" refers to its delightfulness when subjected to thorough investigation. "Because of the purity of the phrasing" means by virtue of its being the natural expression [of the Dhamma].
He spoke of the eloquence of that discourse; "by way of the purity of the meaning" means by way of the meaning's freedom from defilement.
"By many methods" means by many reasons.
By the negation of both "too far" and "too near," "not too far and not too near" is understood; however, that [distance] is, at its minimum—
It should be seen by the clashing together of the outstretched hands of both. "Having extended the neck" means having extended it by way of turning the neck.
Regarding "these," he says "ye ime" and so forth, showing that the vowel *i* has been elided here due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
"Noble by birth" refers to those born into high families; thus he says "born into high families. They are "noble" by virtue of the perfection of their conduct.
They are sons of good family who possess proper conduct; therefore he said, "endowed with conduct.

Even in a family that is not well-known anywhere, both types [of qualities] exist among the monks intended by that brahmin; thus he said, "But here, for both reasons, they are indeed sons of good family.
Regarding the word *saddhā*, it is in the instrumental case used in the sense of an instrument (karaṇa), so he said, "by means of faith" (*saddhāya*); or else, *saddhā* means "having believed."

The meaning is as follows. In this interpretation, it should be understood that the expression in the Pāḷi is given by means of the elision of the syllable *ya*. The term "from the state of a householder" (*agārato*) means from living as a householder;
this designation is formed either by the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) or by a figurative usage based on dependence (*nissayūpacāra*).

Since the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*), characterized by the habit of begging and so forth, accompanies the act of going forth (*pabbajjā*), he says, "the going forth and the state of being a monk," thereby including the state of being a monk along with that which is concomitant with it.
Regarding the characteristic of the formal ritual (kammavācā), however, when the state of being a bhikkhu is intended, the word "and" (ca) should be understood as having a conjunctive sense.

By the phrase "the state of one who is homeless," the specific excellence of virtue, conduct, and qualities based on the going-forth (pabbajjā) is included; here, the prohibition of occupations such as agriculture and cattle-rearing is to be understood through terms like "non-arising" (anuppāda).
Furthermore, in the inclusion of the remaining factors, [it refers to] the going-forth by way of taking the refuges and so forth, and by way of taking the refuges and so forth...
Because there are many different types of full ordination (*upasampadā*), he says "in every way" (*sabbathāpi*), meaning by various modes.

He says "the leader" (*nāyaka*) because he leads by means of practicing the path, not by physical movement; the meaning is that he is one who brings about the attainment of Nibbāna through right practice.

"By performing what is beneficial" means by conduct that is beneficial for this life and so forth. "Grasping" refers to [the grasping] in the higher training of virtue (*adhisīla*) and the rest, to an absolute degree...
Showing that it is not a mere matter of speaking but of enjoining, he said "one who causes to grasp" and then "one who trains.

Showing that "following the view" means following after a view, he said "conformity with seeing. The Blessed One’s teaching, which comprises the three trainings, is called "view" because it was seen by him;
it is "conviction" (khanti) in the sense of being acceptable to each person, and "liking" (ruci) in the sense of being pleasing to them.
“Ruci, those who have that very same view, inclination, and preference as the Blessed One’s disciples,” he said, beginning with “yaṃdiṭṭhiko.
This is connected [to the previous statement] by the words “Esa kira alattha” (He, it is said, obtained).

The phrase “like a son of the gods” and so forth serves to clarify the state of renunciation mentioned by the words “through faith” and so on, by demonstrating the absence of any kind of decline. Having gone forth from home through faith...
"Having gone forth" (*pabbajitvā*) is a statement of the cause for being exceedingly joyful and so forth.
"Content with the mere requisites of food and clothing" (*ghāsacchādanaparamatāya santuṭṭho*) should be understood as a statement of the cause for being free from suspicion and apprehension.
The repetition of words in the phrase beginning with "Thus it is" (*evametaṃ*) should be understood as being made by way of encouragement or by way of inspiring confidence.
For thus the word *evaṃ* is stated to have the sense of acceptance and the sense of rejoicing. In the phrase *mamaṃ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative;
or rather, this should be regarded as a particle having the same meaning as *maṃ*.

By the word *ādīni*, the term *ādi* includes those who have not made a livelihood their profession and so forth. "Of such [people] alone" means of those whose nature has been manifested through faith and renunciation, such as being free from covetousness and the like.
Not for others who are covetous by nature. For this has been said:

"Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to follow closely behind another bhikkhu, step for step, holding onto the corner of his outer robe, yet he were covetous, with intense lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, and with corrupt intentions..."
“[One who is] unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unguarded faculties—such a person is far indeed from me, and I am far from him.
Regarding the phrase *durabhisambhavāni*: having plunged [into the world], they are difficult to achieve because the intended goal cannot be realized; thus, they are “difficult to accomplish.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that “they are difficult to endure because dwelling there itself is suffering,” in order to show that the very act of residing therein is the suffering.
“Araññavanapatthāni” means forest groves that have attained the characteristics of a forest (*arañña*). For the word *vanapattha* also applies to a cluster of trees forming a thicket;
thus, the inclusion of the term *arañña* [is made]. “Kiñcāpi” is a particle used in the sense of granting permission or possibility. What does it grant permission for?

It grants permission for the absence of the conventional definition [of forest], namely: “that which is outside the village is the forest. Therefore he said, “in the non-conventional sense,” and so forth.
What does it imply? It implies the fulfillment of the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññakaṅga). For that which fulfills the forest-dweller’s practice is specifically called “the forest.
Therefore he said, “That which is five hundred bow-lengths,” and so forth. “Having gone out beyond the threshold-stake” means having gone out from the threshold-stake;
the meaning is, starting from the outside of that. “Beyond the threshold-stake” (bahi indakhīlā) [is explained as follows:]...
They say that where there are two or three boundary stakes, the limit begins from outside the stake; where there are none, it begins from the spot appropriate for such a purpose.
However, since there is no danger or terror within the human precincts starting from the boundary stake, it should be understood that this [external limit] is not intended here.
“Near a village” (gāmanta) means in the vicinity of a village. “A place not within the range of activity” (anupacāraṭṭhāna) means a place that is not to be frequented for the sake of daily duties.
Therefore he said: “where neither plowing nor sowing is done.
By the word “remote” (pantāni), it is stated that, since the synonym “bounded” (pariyantānaṃ) has been included here in the text, [the commentary] says: “setting aside this one synonym, ‘bounded’...”
Furthermore, this alternative term "dūrānantika" (remote from noise) should not be included, because its meaning is already encompassed by the term "pantāni" (secluded).
If that were the case, it would follow that terms such as "na manussūpacārānaṃ" (not frequented by people) would also have to be excluded;

therefore, its exclusion should be understood on the basis of the word itself. "Paviveka" means separation in various ways (pakārato), or separation by various means (pakārehi), [from] the manifold objects of form and so forth.
The seclusion of one’s own body from the various modes of deportment such as going and so forth occurs even for one who is walking, standing, or sitting alone.

Precisely because of the multiplicity of things to be secluded and the diversity of the modes of seclusion, these are grasped as a unity and expressed by the singular term “seclusion” (*paviveka*). Thus it is said: “Seclusion is difficult to achieve.”

The meaning is that they do not find pleasure in practicing seclusion (*paviveka*). "In solitude" (*ekībhāve*) means in a state of being alone. "Delighting in pairs" (*dvayaṃdvayārāmo*) means one who takes delight in the state of two-by-two.
"As if they carry them off" (*haranti viya*) means as if they seize them by causing distress. Therefore he said, "as if they devour them" (*ghasanti viya*);
the intention is that they have come as if to eat them by producing fear and anguish, like *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, *pisācas*, and so forth.

"Of such a person" means of one who has not attained concentration (*samādhi*). "By the sounds of grass, leaves, wild animals, and so forth" refers to the various terrifying and frightening sounds of grass, leaves, and the like stirred by the wind, as well as the terrifying forms of stumps and the like appearing in the guise of *yakkhas* and other spirits.
Thus, performing what is called a difficult and hard-to-achieve task.
"Ah, these are wonderful!"—thus he was struck with amazement.
Commentary on the Section on Physical Actions (Kāyakammantavāra):
"In sixteen instances" refers to the sixteen reasons that will be explained in the Pāḷi beginning with "Whatever [monks]... and so forth.
Impurity of bodily action and so forth, for those dwelling in the forest, are particularly conducive to distraction because they are causes of mental terror;
however, purity of bodily action and so forth, due to the absence of such [terror], are conducive to non-distraction for them.
Therefore he said, "Because of the fault of impurity of bodily action," and so on. And the phrase "the sixteen" refers specifically to the side of purification.
Thus it was said after taking [the point]. The inclusion of "defilement" (*saṃkilesa*) is also for the purpose of showing purification (*vodāna*).

"Devoid of discerning the object" (*ārammaṇapariggaharahitānaṃ*) means being devoid of the knowledge of discerning that object—such as an impure bodily action seen in the forest—in the manner taught in the Canon by the passage beginning, "Whatever beings... "Endowed with the discernment of the object" (*ārammaṇapariggahayuttānaṃ*): here...
The meaning should be understood by reversing what was stated above. "By himself" refers to the Blessed One; the sense is "he lies down.
"Such as that" means one who is fit for the discernment of the object.
"Awakening" (*sambodha*) is that by which one awakens; thus he says, "by attaining the Noble Path. This depends upon the realization of the supreme path.

"The attainment of the omniscient knowledge of the Buddhas" is what is meant by the phrase "of one who has not yet attained full enlightenment," which means "of one who has not yet penetrated the Four Noble Truths.

It is called *bodhi* because it is worthy of being awakened to as the entirety of all that is to be known; and because a being (*satta*) possesses a special distinction therein through great heroism and other qualities, it is called "the being who awakens.
Therefore, he said "perfect self-enlightenment" (*sammāsambodhi*), and so forth. This is because [the Buddha] has reached the state of certainty.

"From the time he set out, the Great Beings practiced in such a way that their path on the Great Vehicle of Awakening was neither conducive to decline nor conducive to stagnation, but rather conducive to distinction and conducive to penetration; because they practiced thus, they were inclined toward awakening like a bull heading down a slope.
Therefore it is said: 'As if clinging to awakening as if to a living being. Hence he said: 'Of Dīpaṅkara,' and so forth. By the convergence of the eight qualities..."
“Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause, meeting with a Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal”—
by the combination and convergence of these eight factors which constitute the constituent parts of the resolution (*abhinīhāra*).

“Those who have entered upon the going-forth” means those who have approached the going-forth. By that mere going-forth alone they are recluses, not because of having stilled evil; this is what he shows.
He says “or those who address others as ‘sir’” to indicate that here it is those who are merely by birth that are intended as brahmins.

For they are of a habit of saying “Sir! Sir!”; therefore he says, “He is one who addresses others as ‘sir,’ provided he is one who possesses something. Regarding “such as the killing of living beings,” etc.:
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and unchaste conduct (*abrahmacariya*) are included.

Furthermore, the qualification "impure" (*aparisuddha*) refers to bodily action (*kāyakamma*), not to killing living beings (*pāṇātipāta*) and so forth; for there is nothing whatsoever—neither the act of killing living beings itself nor its preliminary application—that can be called pure.
It is "fearful" (*bhaya*) in the sense of being something to be feared, and "terrible" (*bherava*) in the sense of bringing about cowardice.
“With hatred as its cause” means having hatred as its cause. For here, the word *sa-* is used with the anusvāra (*m*). Therefore, he said: “as the cause of its own hatred.
It is called “blameworthy” by way of fear, which is characterized exclusively by mental terror; for mental terror is exclusively blameworthy and is also called “fear” in the sense of being terrified.
“Insecure” refers to both of these [hatred and fear]. Mental terror also...
For both the body and the mind bring harm and are thus insecure; likewise, so too is an object that is terrifying.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, these two meanings are applied according to their respective order.

It is said: "They 'summon' (*avhāyanti*) because they act as if summoning fear and terror by bringing about the arising of mental dread through the sign of a terrifying object imagined by oneself. Thus it is stated: "They summon."
“They call out. *Tete* refers to the relatives, friends, and others of the people who have been killed. Regarding *gacchaṃ*: they say it is a large thicket of thorns that has become dense;
however, some say *gumbaṃ* is not very large. But *gacchaṃ* should be understood as a grass forest, for it is said, “*gacche* means in grown grass”;
whereas *gumbaṃ* is a place filled with thorny shrubs and the like, where nothing has grown. *Baddhā* means bound; *vadhitā* means slain.
As if bound and being beaten with a palm-leaf whip.
Regarding the phrase "na kho pana": here, *kho* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), while *pana* is used in the sense of distinction (*visesa*). By this, he shows:
"Unlike other recluses and brahmins, I am not one whose bodily action is impure; [rather,] in remote forest and woodland retreats..."
"Furthermore, it is not that I do not resort to lodgings; rather, having become one whose bodily action is entirely pure, I resort to them.
This is how the construction of the meaning should be understood here. For by that emphatic statement, "I am one whose bodily action is pure," he demonstrates the clarified meaning.
"I am one among them" means that by virtue of that purity of bodily action, he is one among those Noble Ones.
“I am one of them”: by means of the purity of his bodily action, the Mahāsatta includes himself among the Noble Ones (ariya).
For at that time, the Bodhisatta’s bodily action was purified to the extent of reaching the state of supreme effacement (paramasallekha);
likewise were his verbal actions and so forth purified, such that Māra, though seeking a flaw, followed him incessantly for six years without finding any opening. Therefore he said:
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step;
yet I could find no opening in the mindful Sambuddha.
*Bhiyyo* means more, further, or increasingly. *Bhītatasitā* refers to those whose bodies are trembling due to fear and calamity.
They have bristling hair; however, because they are not terrified or trembling due to the absence of fear and calamity, they remain with unbristled hair, standing in safety and security.
Thus, their attainment of safety or state of well-being becomes manifest through the state of having smooth hair (*pannaloma*);
therefore, it is stated in the Pāli as "smooth-haired" (*palloma*). Hence he said, "the state of smooth hair," and so forth. And herein, I attained even more smoothness in the forest.
"Living in seclusion" is the description of the formal undertaking (*paṭiññā*). "I am one whose bodily action is purified" is the demonstration of the cause (*hetu*).

"For those noble ones of yours" is the demonstration of a similar example (*sadisūdāharaṇa*). "Whatever recluses or brahmins there may be" is the demonstration of a dissimilar example (*visadisūdāharaṇa*).
The remaining [passages] are to be understood as the elucidations of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*); this is the analysis of the logical reasoning (*yutti*) here. By this—
The exposition of the reasoning should be understood according to this method for the remaining sections as well.
The commentary on the section concerning bodily action is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section concerning verbal action, etc.
36. Regarding the phrase "by means of impure lying and so forth," whatever needs to be said there has already been stated according to the method explained above.

However, in order to show—by way of the designation "fear and terror"—the various modes of occurrence of those acts, such as lying and the rest, which are included by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the passage beginning with "How...
was stated. Whatever needs to be said concerning that has also already been stated above.
“In goods” means in goods that are either animate or inanimate. “Having generated” means having generated an improper greed known as covetousness through the power of one’s own transformation.
“Having become angry” means having become angry at another by way of thinking about their destruction;
for in this way, there might later arise a suspicion such as, “Those whom we have wronged will now pursue us,” and so forth. “These...”

"‘I think they wish to take possession of our property; I think they wish to bring about our ruin’—this should be understood as referring to such mental action (*manokamma*) by which others perceive the arising of covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and ill will (*byāpāda*) in them from afar.
Granted that covetousness and the rest [of the unwholesome roots] also arise at the time of the occurrence of unwholesome bodily and verbal actions..."
They indeed continue to occur; however, at that time, they are either on the side of volition (*cetanā*) or are not included in conventional usage (*abbōhārika*).

Thus, the application was made by way of covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth specifically in the section on mental action (*manokamma-vāra*). Alternatively, just as there is an absence of the status of verbal action (*vacīkamma*) and so forth for killing and the like even when they occur through another door [the mind], so too there is an absence of the status of bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth for covetousness and the like even when they occur through another door; rather, they possess the status of mental action (*manokamma*).
However, since they are established in this way, covetousness and the rest are mentioned only in the section on mental action (manokamma). For it has been said:
"Actions move through the doors; the doors do not move through the doors.
Therefore, actions are distinguished from one another by means of the doors."
Although in the Commentary, in the section on livelihood, the mention of "fear and terror" is applied specifically to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation—
based on the words, "Whatever recluses or brahmins there may be"— nevertheless,

it should be understood that the application [of these terms] extends to outsiders as well as to householders. For even among householders, [fear arises] by way of the violation of the laws of birth, family, and country.
Wrong livelihood can indeed be found in other ways as well; and it is precisely through such failure in livelihood—or by other means—that their dwelling in the forest might otherwise become possible.

(37) Having thus shown fear and terror by way of the eightfold virtue of livelihood (*ājīva-ṭhāmaka-sīla*), the teaching is expanded thereafter in order to show that same fear and terror by way of the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth. Explaining the meaning of this, he says, "From here onwards," etc. Therein, by way of the hindrances...

The meaning of "it was said again" is this: if even mere purification of virtue brings about the absence of fear and terror for one dwelling in the forest, how much more so when one has abandoned the hindrances and attained either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*)?

Thus, the teaching is expanded further above in order to show that the absence of fear and terror is caused by the perfection of concentration, due to the state of unwholesome mental action having ceased.
The intention is that although covetousness and ill will have already been mentioned, they are stated again by way of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
He says, "those whose nature is to covet the goods of others and so forth," because the word *jhā* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of coveting (*abhijjhāyana*).

"In sensual objects as bases" means in sensual objects which serve as the bases for the defilement of sensual desire, namely, visible forms and so forth. "Those with dense defilement-passion" refers to attachment (*ajjhosāna*) due to its firm roots and the difficulty of being released from it.

They have abundant defilements and sensual desires. Herein, covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is the longing for objects not yet attained; it is intense lust (*tibbasārāga*), an adherence to objects of success.
For those persons overcome by greed, due to their intense concern for themselves and because they are overwhelmed by greed, their mental objects remain undetermined and the objects are not discerned.
Thus, having failed to examine each respective object in the forest, they dwell [there], [failing to see] ropes and such things as they truly are.
They do not perceive it. Therefore he said, “of them,” and so forth. It manifests through the state of a peaceful mind; for thus it was said, “with agitated minds.

“We are now lost!”—thus they tremble and quiver, as if being oppressed by something that has come upon them; in this way, in the sense of attributing that fear and terror to themselves, they summon and call out to it.
Referring to this construction, he said, “the rest is exactly the same.”

Regarding the Pāli phrase “I am one who is free from covetousness”: because his mental disposition has long been accustomed to non-greed, his mind does not cling to anything—like a drop of water on a lotus leaf—and thus the meaning is:
“I am one who is without longing for anything. 38. “By the abandonment of the natural state” means by the abandonment of the natural state known as the state of complete purity.
For when a state of blamelessness is abandoned by the arising of a blameworthy state, the mind has lost its blameless nature.

"With corrupted minds" means having minds that have become putrid due to being defiled by the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*); hence he said, "It becomes followed by defilements... [and] putrid.

"With corrupt mental intentions" means having mental intentions whose minds have been corrupted by hatred, like urine mixed with poison. "In the manner already stated" refers to: "Those [states] have undetermined objects..."

...by the same method stated in the section on covetousness (*abhijjhālu-vāra*) beginning with the words "they are," etc. For just as by way of greed (*lobha*), so too by way of hatred (*dosa*) and the rest, they have undetermined objects.
"In all places" means that it should be described in all instances, both below and above.
39. From the statement, "That which is the unwieldiness and unworkability of the mind," *thina* (sloth) is [defined] by way of the mind's state of illness.
He says, "by sloth which has become a sickness of the mind," because it goes to the state of being seized [by illness].

Likewise, because of the statement, "whatever unwellness or unwieldiness of the body," he says, "by torpor which has become a sickness of the remaining mental body," since torpor specifically goes to the state of being seized by the sickness of the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
And here, the inclusion of the word "remaining" is for the purpose of excluding the mind.
Furthermore, this drowsiness should be understood as bringing sickness even to the physical body, because it is the cause of sleep.
For it is described as "sleep is a state of restlessness. Therefore he said, "They become full of sleep.
(40) "Of a restless nature" means having a habit of restlessness and an unstable character; for restlessness has instability as its essence.

Therefore he said, “with a flickering mind,” and so forth. Here, in the phrase “with an unpeaceful mind,” it is appropriate to include remorse (*kukkucca*), because by way of commentary, remorse also functions as a factor that prevents the mind from being peaceful.
The intention, however, is that restlessness (*uddhacca*) is included by its very own nature.
41. This fifth hindrance is indeed one alone, namely, doubt and perplexity (*kaṅkhā-vicikicchā*).
If this is so, why was it stated as two? To this he says: “‘What indeed... and so forth.

From the state of doubting—that is, from the state of being in suspense—it is called *vicikicchā*, because “one is distressed (*kicchati*) while investigating the intrinsic nature of phenomena by means of this,” or because “the healing (*tikicchā*) has departed.”

42. Having thus shown the absence of fear and terror through the perfection of concentration by way of describing the absence of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the subsequent teaching beginning with “Those who indeed...
is now expanded in order to show the absence of fear and terror through the perfection of wisdom (*paññā*) by way of describing the absence of self-exaltation and so forth.
To clarify that meaning, [the commentary] begins with “Those who exalt themselves,” etc.
It has been said [that they] "exalt" by means of grasping through the conceit of "I am. Therefore he said, "they place them in a high position.

Regarding the sections on sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt, [the method] being taken up is similar to that in the section on covetousness; therefore, without touching upon that there, he said "How do they...
and so forth, in order to show that there is something different in the section on self-exalting.
43. *Chambhanaṃ* means trembling; it is a powerful terror of the mind that serves as the cause for the body’s state of trembling.
Those who possess this are called *chambhī*. Therefore, he said, “stiffness of the body,” and so forth. *Bhīrukajātikā* means those whose nature is to be fearful.
And this very same fear of what is blameworthy arises by way of producing a state of trembling in the body and a state of rigidity in both the mind and the body.
“*Chambho bhīrutā*” (trembling is fearfulness) is what is said; thus, the ascetics and brahmins possessing that quality are called “*chambhī bhīrukajātikā*” (trembling and of a fearful nature).
Here, however, fear and dread (*bhayabherava*) are taken in their literal sense.
44. He states that the word *lābha* has an objective derivation (*kamma-sādhana*), meaning “that which is obtained” or “that which is reached. It is to be done or given with respect (*sakkacca*).
"Honour" (sakkāra). "Illuminating its meaning": this illuminates the fact that for one dwelling in the forest having abandoned gain and so forth, there is no calling out of fear or terror.
He, it is said, receives the name "Piyagāmika" because he is dear to the village solely due to his reputation for gain.
"Released from work": because he is worn out by old age, he is unable to perform labor and has thus been dismissed by his masters.
45. They are called *kusītā* because they sink down (*sīdanti*) in a contemptible way due to their failure to practice right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
Energy (*vīriya*) is the state or activity of a hero (*vīra*), or it is that which should be impelled or set in motion according to the proper method; thus, it is right effort.

Those who are deficient in this are "of inferior energy" (*hīnavīriyā*). Bodily energy (*kāyikavīriya*) is the energy that functions by way of originating bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), such as in performing duties, walking meditation, and so forth.
It should be seen. The energy that occurs by way of attention to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) while sitting or lying down is mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*).

In this context, the author said "the lazy" and so forth, showing that the former is particularly evident as the opposite of indolence (*kosajja*), while the latter is evident as the undertaking of energy (*vīriyārambha*).
For those of inferior energy, due to their very laziness, they are unable even to perform the mere definition of the object.

46. "Lost mindfulness" (*naṭṭhassati*) means unobtained mindfulness; it is said thus because, due to a deficiency in conditions, even though mindfulness exists, one is incapable of performing the function of mindfulness.
"Not clearly comprehending" (*asampajāno*) means one who lacks clear comprehension.

He says, "devoid of wisdom," because this negative particle *a-* is used here to indicate the cessation of that association (the prefix *sam-*), just as in such expressions as "states without cause" (*ahetukā dhammā*) or "a residence without a resident monk" (*abhikkhuko āvāso*). [Objection: Is it not...?
The sixteenth section is the Chapter on Wisdom; this is the Chapter on Mindfulness. Regarding the question, "Why is wisdom included on the side of defilement?
he says, beginning with "And of this," etc. This is indeed the distribution of mindfulness, namely the fourteenth section;
however, since wisdom here is merely mindfulness that is weak, it is said "without clear comprehension" (*asampajāna*) for the purpose of illustrating the weakness of mindfulness.
These were stated by way of negation. Now, in order to make this very meaning more evident, the passage beginning with “is twofold” was stated.

47. Showing that the mind is said to be “evenly and rightly placed” upon the object through either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), and not otherwise, he says: “‘Unconcentrated’ means devoid of access and absorption concentration. “With wandering mind” means...
"Of unsettled mind. Previously, restlessness (*uddhacca*) was taken up by way of its commonality with the nature of an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) in the phrase "restless, with unpeaceful mind";

here, however, it is stated as the mental agitation caused by restlessness due to the absence of concentration (*samādhāna*), in the phrase "unconcentrated, with agitated mind"—this is the distinction between them.
"In the manner previously stated" refers to what was said before: "For by means of restlessness, the mind wavers over a single object."
"Like a banner on a flagstaff by the wind," according to the method stated [in the Sutta].
"Everything is exactly as before" refers to the similarity with what was said in the section on covetousness within the discourse on the proclamation of fear and terror. 48.

Regarding the term *duppaññā* (of poor wisdom): here the prefix *du-* has the sense of absence, as in "dussīla" (immoral) and so forth, and not as in "duggati" (bad destination) or "duppaṭipanna" (wrongly practiced).
To show that it is like a term of reproach, it was said, "This is a designation for those lacking wisdom (nippaññānaṃ)," and then it was stated, "But there is no such thing as corrupted wisdom.
"Those" refers to the unwise (duppaññā). "In all cases" means in all four alternative readings.
Or, *ela* is said to mean fault (*dosa*). Therefore he said, "That speech which is gentle and pleasant to the ear. For likewise, virtue is called "faultless-limbed" (*nelaṅga*).
It has been said. And those who speak with poor wisdom speak only faulty speech because of their lack of intelligence. For this very reason, it says, "one who speaks ill-spoken words.
Therefore, the meaning here should also be understood as follows: because they possess a mouth that is "ela" (foolish), they are called "elamūga" (fools and mutes).
By way of contrast to that wisdom on account of which one is said to be "endowed with wisdom," [the following is stated].
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “no ca kho” was stated. One might ask: "Are not Bodhisattvas endowed with the wisdom of extensive insight (vipassanā-paññā)?
Indeed they are; however, at that time the Bodhisattva had not yet initiated the practice of insight, and it is not the wisdom of insight that is intended here.
Therefore, it is said: “no ca kho vipassanāpaññāya.”

However, some here say: "The section on faith was not included because those devoid of faith and those with impure bodily actions, etc., do not possess a specific cause for summoning fear and terror, nor does the state of being faithful constitute a feather-like [insignificant] factor.
That is not the reason. For one who has faith in the fruit of kamma, relying precisely on the fact that kamma is one's refuge, regards fear and terror as even less than a blade of grass.

If one were to think thus, one would fall into error. However, because energy and the other factors do not arise without faith, that faith—which serves as their decisive support (*upanissaya*) and is co-nascent (*sahajāta*) with them—is already included by the mention of those very factors; therefore, it is not mentioned separately.
For this reason, it is also not mentioned even in the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) for jhāna. What need is there to speak of this faith? Indeed...
In this context of discerning the object, that [consciousness] is not to be included; therefore, it was not extracted here by the Master of the Dhamma.

In this way, a definitive decision should be made regarding other similar instances as well. For the exposition of the Suttantas consists of a teaching given according to the sequence [of the subject matter].
The commentary on the discussion beginning with the section on verbal action is finished.
The examination of the sixteen bases as objects is finished.
49. Regarding the description of lodgings and so forth by way of fear and terror:

"In such nights" refers to the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight and others. "Sixteen objects" means the sixteen bases that serve as objects. "In such nights" refers to the fourteenth day and so forth.
He speaks with reference to the nights that will be mentioned below. The same principle applies here to the phrase "in such a lodging.

Regarding the word *yā*, since it is an indefinite pronoun used as a general reference, the subsequent use of the word *tā* functions as a specific designation (*niddesa*), just as one might say "those [which were] previously mentioned. Therefore, it is said:

"Both *yā* and *tā* are terms for the nights themselves, serving respectively as the general reference (*uddesa*) and the specific designation (*niddesa*). In the word *abhi*, the sense is that of a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇatthe*), as in the expression "and other well-known [persons]."
[This is] as in [the passage beginning] "brāhmaṇamahāsālā" and so forth. But how is the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇatthā) to be understood here?
It is called a "characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) because one is characterized by it; thus he says, "by the fullness of the moon," and so forth.

By the fullness of the moon on the full-moon day and by the waning of the moon on the new-moon day. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of the moon's half-disk, its seizing upon stars, and so on.
It should be understood thus. The intention is that the prefix *abhi-* alone conveys the sense of "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) by means of the word it qualifies.
"From the first day onwards" means starting from the first day of the month of Pāṭipada.

Since the accuser was not characterized during the time of the Blessed One but became characterized at a later time, it is on account of that state of being characterized (*abhilakkhaṇīyatā*) [that he is so called].
One raises the objection: “Why was the fifth [uposatha] not included by the Blessed One, who sees all?

The other replies with the phrase “because it is not of all times,” intending to show how, when the [uposathas] that occur at all times—such as the fourteenth and so on—are being observed, how could one that does not occur at all times be included?
“In such cases” means in those instances described as “renowned” and so forth; [it is included] by virtue of being presided over by a deity.

Because parks and such things possess the status of a shrine (*cetiya*) for the world, he said, "in the sense of being worthy of worship. Since people for the most part designate such trees at the gates of villages and so forth as shrines, he said, "at the gates of villages, market towns, and so on," and so forth.
They are called "terrifying" (*bhiṃsanaka*) because they strike fear into ordinary beings by causing terror through the mere sight or the mere hearing [of them].
Therefore he said, “They produce fear,” and so forth. That from which one fears is *bhaya*; it is extremely terrifying (*sappaṭibhaya*) and formidable (*bherava*).
“Worthy of being offered prayers and oblations” means fit for the performance of various sacrificial rites and acts of dedication. “Flowers, incense...
[down to] the surface of the earth”—this is a demonstration of making offerings with well-prepared items such as rice-cakes (*suppa*) and the like. “Pounding” means striking.
The intention is that he makes a sound with blows from his horns and hooves.

Here, the name "path" refers to all four-footed animals, not specifically to particular types of deer such as the *rohit* and so forth, as in the expressions "the skin of a bear," "the skin of a deer," or "the skin of a sheep.
"Having shaken" means having shaken it by rubbing the tip [of the horn]. And here, the mention of the peacock is intended to be illustrative (*upalakkhaṇa*).
He said: "Here, the inclusion of all birds is intended. "This is the method" means that just as the word *vā* (or) in the phrase "a peacock or...
has the sense of an unstated alternative, so it is here in "a deer or..."; he says this with reference to the fact that the word *miga* (deer) is used in its specific sense.
"From this point on" refers to the thought of seeking out fear and terror, beginning with the words: "What if I were to [spend] those nights... and so forth.
"From the beginning" means from the start of the search. For even in the phrase "May I perhaps see something fearful and terrifying," it is the object itself that is the fear and terror.

Just as an object that is pleasant is called "pleasant" in such passages as "form is pleasant, fallen into pleasure, immersed in pleasure," and so on. How is it that by the mention of "fear," the mention of the "form-object" is also included?
He said: “And of the limited,” and so forth. Because of the statement “it comes,” some maintain that from the beginning of the search onwards, the object is intended as “this fear”;
however, because it is intended as being seen by the eye in the phrase “he might not see it,” the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
“Desiring fear” means [desiring it] by way of investigation. I...
"I dwell desiring a ground for fear"—what is the purpose of this? The intention is: "Even such an apprehension of fear is improper for me.

Regarding the phrase "in whatever way he has become" (*yaṃ pakāraṃ bhūto yathābhūto*): here, that "way" (*pakāra*) is appropriate in the sense of the postures (*iriyāpatha*), because it is presented as such in the Canon;
thus he says, "in whichever posture he has become. The word "of one who has become" (*bhavitassa*) is [an explanation of] "of one who has become" (*bhūtassa*).
This should be understood as having the same meaning as the word *pada*.
Showing that the word “*samaṅgībhūtassā*” is stated as “*bhūtassā*” by means of eliding the preceding part of the compound, he said, “or *samaṅgībhūtassa*.

Regarding the phrase “in an object of fear and terror,” this refers to an object regarded as fearful and terrifying. The passage beginning with “the Great Being did not even stand still” is intended to show how he would overcome it, just as he had thought: “being thus, he would dispel it.”
Likewise, there is the demonstration of the state of being thus practiced.
Regarding the "succession of postures," they say it is standing, walking, sitting, and lying down;

however, the reverse succession should be understood as follows: first lying down, then sitting, then standing, and finally walking. As for the "proximate succession": standing is proximate to walking, and sitting is proximate to standing.
Going is proximate to sitting and lying down; sitting is proximate to lying down.
Here, however, standing is proximate to going, going is proximate to standing, lying down is proximate to sitting, and sitting is proximate to lying down;
these are to be understood as being taken by way of immediate proximity, while the others are by way of succession. As for the postures of a bhikkhu, they follow the order in which they are attained.
They are spoken of in this way by way of successive arising.
The commentary on the description of the lodgings and so forth, by way of fear and terror, is finished.
The commentary on the dwelling in non-delusion.

50. Furthermore, this subsequent teaching beginning with “There are, however,” was expanded in order to show that this total absence of fear and dread in me is specifically due to my nature of non-delusion; this is the connection here.
By the phrase “for meditators at points of delusion,” he shows that for those who do not meditate, there is simply no need to speak of such points. The word “atthi” (there is) is a particle.
The plural form is also used, as in such passages as "In this body there are head-hairs," which is stated here to show the meaning of the word *santi* (they exist).
One might ask: do they exist by way of possessing the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution]? No; thus he says, "They are found (*saṃvijjanti*), they are apprehended (*upalabbhantī*).
Even such things as these are found within the vast world-system, and they are apprehended because they can be grasped by knowledge. "One who has attained the white-kasiṇa" means...
He is one who has attained the measureless white kasiṇa; for thus, light appears to him on all sides.
"Preparatory work" (parikamma) refers to the stage prior to attainment. He thinks, "I shall emerge when the sun has gone this far," yet he is not skilled in delimiting the duration;
he merely arouses the attention, "I shall emerge during the day. Everything becomes clear.
The object is vivid, as if one were seeing it with the divine eye. "Not clear" should be understood here by way of the opposite of what was stated above.
"Perceiving thus": perceiving "day" when it is night, and "night" when it is day.
"Sitting within his lodging at night"—here the word "night" must be supplied. By means of a small seat and so forth, or by other...
Or by means of causes. It is deep, like the interior of the earth, concealed by dense forests, and covered by thick layers of forest nets;
the light of the sun has vanished, and thus "time" implies that it is day even without being explicitly stated.
As for the phrase "a state of delusion is of many kinds," he says: "one of the various states of delusion."

The division of day and night was well-established for the Bodhisatta, even down to the smallest measure of a lava, a tuṭi, or a khaṇa; likewise, the division of the portions of the day and night was established according to the duties he himself had to perform and according to his knowledge of the time.
At the time of two finger-breadths [of shadow] on the time-post, he strikes the watch-gong for the sake of the Saṅgha’s performance of their respective duties.
"Muggara" refers to the mallet used for striking the gong. The watch-stick falls when it has been set in motion by other bhikkhus.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Until other monks enter the dining hall, he goes to his place for the midday rest (*divāvihāra*) and practices the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Regarding the phrase "yaṃ kho taṃ": here, *yaṃ* is an indefinite designation (*aniyamuddesa*), while *kho* is used for emphasis; thus the meaning is "whichever person" (*yameva puggalaṃ*).
*Tanti* is a word expressing the manner in which it is being spoken. *Mamevā* means "me alone. *Asammohasabhāvo* means non-delusion that has become one's very nature.
Because it was stated [in the previous verse] that he had "arisen," it is said here "in the world of humans.

*Paññāsampattiyā* means by virtue of his own quality of wisdom (*paññāguṇa*), which possesses the capacity to know what is beneficial as it truly is; it is not merely through his aspiration alone that he desires the welfare [of others], but rather—

Showing this through his practice, he said, "one who teaches what is beneficial. However, the desire for their welfare by way of his inner disposition is shown by the phrase "out of compassion for the world.

Since the happiness of enjoyment never occurs without the means of subsistence, and since the gift of such means is caused by the perfection of generosity, he said, "by the perfection of generosity...
[he is] a donor. By the perfection of loving-kindness, he is protected through the bestowing of benefit; by the perfection of compassion... [he is protected].
[The Dhamma] is protected by removing suffering. Now, one might raise the objection: "Was it not already stated previously that [the Dhamma is for] 'welfare and happiness'?
Why then is this mentioned again? With reference to this objection, he says: "By the inclusion of gods and humans here," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that whereas previously welfare and the rest were shown without distinction, they are now shown specifically along with their purpose.
He said, "Because it is the ultimate reality," meaning that there is no goal higher than Nibbāna. It is called "beneficial" (*hita*) because one goes toward (*hinoti*) Nibbāna;
it is the Path. He said, "Because there is no happiness beyond it," referring to the Noble Fruit (*ariyaphala*), which is the supreme happiness.
The commentary on the dwelling in non-delusion is finished.
Commentary on the Preliminary Stage of the Practice (Pubbabhāgapaṭipadāvaṇṇanā): 51.
"Abiding in non-delusion" (*asammohavihāra*) means a mode of conduct free from delusion, or alternatively, the enlightenment characterized by non-delusion.

"That" refers to the practice consisting of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "From the preliminary stage onwards" means starting from the exertion of energy during the preliminary phase of that cultivation.
"Kecīti" refers to those residing in the Uttaravihāra.
"Bodhimaṇḍe" means at the place where the state of being the "maṇḍa"—the essence—of the knowledge known as "bodhi" was attained.
"Caturaṅgaṃ" means endowed with the four factors described in such passages as, "Let skin, sinews, and even bone remain. "Paggahitaṃ" means exerted.
Without making the undertaking slack, it is grasped by means of the state of exertion known as firm perseverance. Therefore he said:
"It is meant that it proceeds without slackness. "Unshrinking" means uncontracted, not having fallen into contraction through laziness.
"Established" means having approached the object by way of non-floating, which is to say, by way of plunging into it. Therefore he said:
“By way of being directed toward the object. Because it proceeds by way of destroying confusion, it is not confused;

thus, it is "unconfused" (*asammuṭṭhā*). Although the body becomes tranquil through the tranquility of the body, just as the mind [becomes tranquil] through the tranquility of the mind, nevertheless, when bodily tranquility arises, it arises together with mental tranquility.
Not without [it]; therefore it is said: "by means of the arising of tranquility of body and mind.

The physical body (*rūpakāya*) also becomes tranquil, because the tranquility of the body brings about the calming of both bodies. And that body is "free from distress" (*vigatadaratha*), meaning free from the distress of the defilements (*kilesa*).
For when the mental body (*nāmakāya*) is free from distress, the physical body also has its distress and fever (*pariḷāha*) subsided.

It is "well-placed" (*sammā āhita*): having severed the distraction (*vikkhepa*) consisting of the mind's running hither and thither among various objects, it is properly placed by bringing about a state of non-distraction toward a single object alone. Therefore he said, "well-established," and so forth.
The mind's lack of one-pointedness is its flickering due to distraction; since that does not occur when there is one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), he said...

"Single-pointed, immovable, and unwavering. By this much—namely, by the demonstration of the accomplishment of the functions of energy, mindfulness, tranquility, and concentration through the passage beginning with "But he has aroused"—is it not the case that the accomplishment of the functions of faith and wisdom must also be intended as part of the preliminary practice for jhāna?
True, they are intended; however, because their accomplishment is established without being explicitly stated as an immediate prerequisite, they are not included here.
For without faith, the undertaking of energy and the other factors would simply be impossible; and if they were not embraced by wisdom, there could be no state of undertaking through wisdom.

Likewise, since non-slackness, non-confusion, and so forth pertain to energy and the rest, it should be understood that the function of wisdom is already accomplished here by the inclusion of non-slackness and the other qualities.
Alternatively, in the development of jhāna, the function of concentration should be considered predominant.
It should be understood that the preliminary practice for jhāna has been explained right up to the conclusion of concentration (samādhi) in order to demonstrate this.

Since it has already been stated, it need not be repeated here; for it has been said that the *Visuddhimagga* constitutes a portion of this commentary, and thus this meaning has already been expressed.
As for the word "dwells" (*viharati*), it occurs because the term "monastery" (*vihāra*) is used in the sense of an abode. Here, however, it occurs as "a dwelling place" (*vihāsa*).

Because it indicates the essential meaning (atthuddesika), he said "the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing" (ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhāna), implying that this is indeed never abandoned by any Buddha.
Since the fourfold distinction of formless jhānas, which proceeds by way of the development of dispassion for form, is included within the fourth jhāna, he said "the four jhānas.
It is indeed logical that one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) serves as the basis for insight (vipassanāpādaka), just as it serves the purpose of ascending to the planes of existence (bhavokkama).
The statement "the four jhānas" is made by way of those [qualities] that are common to all four jhānas.
However, the status of being a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and the status of being a basis for cessation (*nirodha*) belong exclusively to the fourth jhāna;
how then is it said that these are common to the four jhānas? Because they exist as successive supports. For even a proximate cause of a proximate cause is itself considered a proximate cause.
It is said that even a cause of a cause is called a "cause," just as it is said, "the seven were accomplished by means of grass.
And by taking this approach, the inclusion of the eight attainments in the description of the purpose is justified. "Bases for one-pointedness of mind" means bases for the concentration of the mind;
the meaning is "bases for dwelling in happiness in this very life. For it is through the heading of one-pointedness of mind that dwelling in happiness in this very life is [intended].
This was said with reference to one whose taints are destroyed through dry insight (sukkha-vipassaka). Therefore he said: "With one-pointed minds, we shall dwell happily for the day.
"Bases for the ascent to existence" means bases for rebirth within the realms of existence.
Since even prior to approaching the seat of enlightenment, the Bodhisatta had previously produced the fourth jhāna in his final existence, [he did so here].
At that time, however, it had only just been produced; it was not yet a basis for insight (vipassanā) and so forth.

Therefore, it was stated as being distinguished from that [other attainment] by saying, "produced at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "A basis for insight" means a basis for insight at the commencement of insight.
The same principle applies here to "a basis for direct knowledge" (abhiññā). For indeed, at the very first commencement of the Buddhas, by means of the foundational jhāna—

It served a specific purpose; it was not for the sake of attaining the higher paths, the fruition-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*), the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), or the mastery of supernormal powers (*vaḷañjana*) beyond that.
For from the moment of attaining full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), every function of knowledge and concentration is dependent solely upon mere wish.
"Accomplishing all tasks" means accomplishing all tasks such as the successive dwellings (*anupubbavihāra*). "Bestowing all mundane and supramundane qualities" means...

In this context, it should be understood that the fourth jhāna is the bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities upon the Blessed One precisely because it serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) and direct knowledge (abhiññā).
For path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) has omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause, and omniscience has path-knowledge as its proximate cause;
thus, full enlightenment (abhisambodhi) occurs when omniscience is attained, and at the very moment of its realization, all the Buddha-qualities came into the hands of the Blessed One.
And the attainment of the path is supported by the fourth jhāna.
The commentary on the preliminary practice and so forth is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discourse concerning past lives.
52. "Of two clear knowledges" means of the two clear knowledges known as the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).

"Word-by-word commentary" (*anupada-vaṇṇanā*) refers to a commentary on each word of the canonical text (*pāḷi*) that explains those clear knowledges. "The method of development" (*bhāvanā-naya*) is the procedure for their production.
The phrase "he directed" (*abhininnāmesi*) and so forth is stated in order to show the reason for connecting the personal pronoun "so" (*so*) with the word "I" (*ahaṃ*).

It has been stated. Or, in the Pāḷi, when the phrase "he directed" (*abhininnāmesi*) is understood as the application of a supreme person by supplying the word "I," its meaning becomes clear; thus it is said, "He, I.

"He directed" (*abhinīhari*) means that having withdrawn the mind from the object of jhāna, he sent it toward past lives; the meaning is that he made [the mind] incline toward past lives, tend toward past lives, and lean toward past lives.
The aggregates that have dwelt in previous births are "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*).
"Dwelt" (*nivuttha*) means having resided in, experienced, or arisen and ceased within one's own continuum;

or it refers to phenomena that have "dwelt" by way of being objects [of consciousness], whether cognized by one's own consciousness—as in the recollection of past lives (*cutūpapāta-anussati*)—or cognized by the consciousness of another, as in the recollection of the *vaṭumaka* tree and so forth. That past life is [recalled] by means of which mindfulness...
He recollects; the knowledge associated with that [recollection] is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).
"Of one returning" means of one who, having gone as far as desired by way of recollecting past lives, returns again.
"Therefore" is a reference to the stated meaning by way of its causal status; what is meant is that it is the state of reviewing for one who is returning.
"Arising here" means arising here in this final existence (*carimabhava*). "Immediately after" refers to the immediately preceding past.
"There" means in such-and-such an existence. "Arose" means I was born. "By those deities" means by the Tusita deities. "Of the same clan" means of the same clan as the Tusita [deities].
This refers to that which produces rebirth in the world of the gods at the stage marking the conclusion of the continuum (*santāna*) of the Great Bodhisattvas.
It is with the intention that one is not afflicted by unwholesome karma alone that it is said, "But suffering is indeed the suffering of formations" (*saṅkhāradukkha*).
Furthermore, even for sons of gods possessing great merit, there is certainly contact with undesirable objects at times such as when the signs of their passing appear;
thus, it cannot be said that "the occurrence of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) never exists. [The text continues: "Fifty-seven... etc.
"Finite" (pariyanta) is said here with reference to the calculation of human years. However, by the calculation of divine years, it is only four thousand.
All the aggregates (khandha) in past existences, as well as the names and clans associated with them, are included within "past lives" (pubbenivāsa).
He said: "What does it make known? Former abodes. Delusion is called "darkness" in the sense of concealing;
this is done by treating it as being "like darkness. It is called "making light" because it must be understood in the sense of producing illumination;

that is, illumination itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning it must be produced in the state of illumination by its own conditions. The remainder is words of praise, referring to the specific modes of activity in dispelling their opposites.

It is stated [as such] because of its awakening. By the phrase "ignorance has been dispelled," it should be understood that this meaning—that *vijjā* (true knowledge) is so called in the sense of "seeing"—is also illustrated.
Since it is said "true knowledge has arisen," this shows that ignorance is the opposite of true knowledge;

and it demonstrates that this opposition exists by virtue of ignorance being that which is to be abandoned and true knowledge being that which abandons. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
By this, darkness is dispelled and destroyed. Why? Because it refers by extension to this meaning: "because light has arisen.
*Pesitattassa* means of one whose mind is released toward the accomplishment of the intended goal. *Yathā appamattassa* implies that this applies to anyone else like me who is likewise heedful.
The commentary on the Discourse on Past Lives is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye: 53.
"Here" refers to what was stated in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*. The construction is: "Herein, this is the distinction. It is exactly as previously stated: "'Maitrī'..."

By the passage beginning with “by me,” etc., it is shown that there is no function or purpose for the preliminary work (parikamma-kicca) as described by such statements as, “Having emerged from the fourth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā),

one should advert to the very last sitting posture,” and “Having made the jhāna based on the kasiṇa object fully capable of being directed toward [the higher knowledges] in every way. There is no need for this here.
The intention is that there is no explanation of the meaning here in the commentary on the text regarding that method of cultivation, because such cultivation is not intended here.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the divine eye is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

54. *Vipassanāpādaka* means that which serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for insight (*vipassanā*). And insight is threefold, according to the distinction between the persons who possess it.

For the insight of Great Bodhisattvas and Pacceka-Bodhisattvas is of the nature of self-originated knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), because it is developed through knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*).

In others, however, it arises from the instruction of another (*paropadesa*), because it is developed through knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). Setting aside [the former],...

In the *Visuddhimagga*, these various methods for discerning the elements— which were taught in many ways through the door of the formless attainments (such as "having emerged from one or another of the remaining fine-material or immaterial jhānas" regarding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception)—
are likewise explained in manifold ways through various systems by means of one or another of those doors for discerning the elements. [This applies] to the Great Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, by way of its division into twenty-four million four hundred thousand aspects, it becomes the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which is not shared with others, exceedingly profound, subtle, and delicate;

it takes up the embryo of preliminary knowledge that serves as the foundation for the noble path-knowledge (ariya-magga-ñāṇa) which is the support for omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and it reaches full maturity. This is what is described in the commentaries...
This is called "Great Vajira-knowledge" (mahāvajirañāṇa).

And because it serves as the foundation for the twenty-four hundred thousand varieties distinguished by their modes of occurrence, the meditative attainments (samāpatti) that the Teacher enters daily—numbering two hundred and forty million—are called his "daily functional attainments.
This is the mode of insight practice (vipassanācāra) of the Buddhas, as described in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*, the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.
It has been shown by way of brief indication; it should be grasped from there by those who seek it.

Because it exhausts and utterly severs the taints (*āsava*), it is the "destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*); this refers to the Noble Path. By way of the highest description, the inclusion here is of the path of Arahantship.
Demonstrating that "knowledge regarding the destruction of the taints" is *āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*, he says: "In that regard, this..."

Having said "knowledge," he stated "designated by way of that" (*tappariyāpannā*) to show that the locative case in "destruction" (*khaye*) refers to the substratum (*ādhāra*), not to the object (*visaya*).
"This is suffering" is a demonstration of how the Noble Truth of Suffering was apprehended through direct perception at that time.
"So much is suffering" is a demonstration of how the Noble Truth of Suffering was apprehended through direct perception at that time. So much...
“Suffering” is the demonstration of its state as having been grasped after being delimited. “Not more than this” is the demonstration of its state as having been grasped without remainder.

Therefore he said, “All suffering-truth,” and so forth. “By penetration through the characteristic of its own essence” means by penetrating without confusion the characteristic that is reckoned as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
And “penetration without confusion” means, for instance, when that knowledge is occurring...
Thereafter, no delusion remains regarding the specific nature and characteristics of suffering; such is its occurrence. Therefore, it is said: “He directly knew it as it truly is.
“Having reached that state” means having approached that Nibbāna which, in the sense of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for the Path, serves as its cause.
For when a person possesses both [the Path and its fruit], it is said that they have attained both. Alternatively, “having reached” (patvā) [is explained as follows]:
The cause for reaching [it]. "Cessation of occurrence" (*appavatti*) means the sign of non-occurrence; or, it is "cessation of occurrence" because they do not occur therein, namely, Nibbāna.
"Of that" refers to the cessation of suffering. "Leading to the wholesome" (*sampāpaka*) means truly leading to what is wholesome by way of realization.
"By way of defilements" means by way of the defilements known as the taints (*āsava*). Since the taints are a synonym for the truth of suffering, because they are included within it.
There is also a way of explaining the remaining truths through their origination and so forth; therefore, it was said: "by way of a method" (*pariyāyato*).
The construction is: "showing [them] as the truths. And here, only the taints (*āsava*) are mentioned because the passage begins with "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
For indeed, liberation from the taints is stated as the very head of all liberation from defilements. "This is suffering"—thus [it is] according to reality.
Because the mixed path is taught here by the passage beginning with "he directly knew," it is said that "he speaks of the path that has reached its culmination together with insight.
Furthermore, since the penetration of the truths was at that time already in the past, although it is stated "he directly knew [them] as they truly are," the phrase "knowing thus,
seeing thus" is used by taking them as being present at the moment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

The description was made by way of the present time. And although that [moment] is indeed past-time from the moment of the path onwards until the present, its being past-time for the very first time should be understood by way of the moment of the fruit; thus he said:
"By the words 'was liberated,' he shows the moment of the fruit. Alternatively, "of one who knows and sees" is a description of the cause: the cause of knowing and the cause of seeing.

The construction is: "the mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*). Here, by the inclusion of the "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*), it should be understood that the "taint of views" (*diṭṭhāsava*) is also included, since the view of existence (*bhavaditthi*) is likewise subsumed under it, just as lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) is.

[This is indicated] by the phrases beginning with "one whose birth is destroyed" (*khīṇājāti*). "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the knowledge of reviewing. "Ground" (*bhūmi*) means the place of occurrence. Not...
The intention is that for him, past birth has been exhausted through the cultivation of the path. Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because it was already exhausted previously.
The construction is not that future birth is exhausted; rather, he raises an objection by way of a figurative interpretation (*lesa*), seizing upon the commonality of being "future.
Therefore, he says: "Because there is no effort regarding the future. However, what is intended here is a specific kind of future [birth], namely—
And even the effort for abandoning is indeed obtained. Therefore, he said: "But that which of the path," and so forth.

"In the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences" is a mention of the three existences (bhava) for the purpose of showing, by the method already stated, that birth has been exhausted without remainder. "That" refers to the aforementioned birth.
"He" refers to the Blessed One.
