“Dwelling in the holy life” (brahmacariyavāsa) here refers specifically to the actualization of the path as the holy life; thus he said, “It is finished.

When right view proceeds by way of accomplishing the tasks such as full understanding regarding the four truths, the activity of right intention and the other factors also proceeds in accordance with the clear realization of full understanding regarding the truth of suffering, and by way of the clear realization of abandonment and so forth regarding the remaining truths.
The occurrence [of the path] is indeed evident. Therefore it was said: “by means of the four paths, by way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development.
Regarding the term *itthattāya*: these modes (*pakāra*) are *itthaṃ*; their state is *itthattaṃ*; the meaning is “for the sake of that,” as it were.
Those modes intended here are full understanding and so forth, which constitute the activity of the noble path; thus he said: “for the sake of becoming thus possessed of the sixteen functions.”
For these [factors] become manifest and appear to one who reviews the path through the power of that path;

and among full understanding and the rest, abandonment alone is primary because the others have that as their purpose. Thus he said, "for the destruction of the defilements. Alternatively, this was stated by way of reviewing the defilements already abandoned.
Regarding the phrase *itthattāya*, he said "from this state" (*itthabhāvato*), taking the dative case in the sense of the ablative. Another...

[The first two lines refer to] the future. These five aggregates, however, which are designated as the final existence, "remain though fully understood"—by this he shows their lack of a foundation. For a foundation is rooted in non-comprehension. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical nutriment, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness becomes established therein."
"Virūḷhaṃ," and so forth. For this very reason, he said, "Like trees whose roots have been cut," and so on.
The intention is that it is encompassed by the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), and not merely [the attainment] like the first two knowledges.
The intention is that he shows this by way of conclusion; for its essential nature has already been shown previously by means of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa).
The construction is: “having included the knowledge of the past” because it possesses the nature of having the past as its object and because it exists in relation to that [past].
Therein, “knowledge of the past” is unimpeded knowledge regarding the past portion, which consists of the aggregates, bases, and elements of the past.
“By the divine eye” means by the knowledge of the divine eye together with its peripheral range. “The present portion and the future portion” [are likewise explained].
"Knowledge regarding the present and the future" means knowledge concerning the present and the future.

By the phrase "all mundane and supramundane qualities," one should understand that there is an inclusion of all other qualities exclusive to a Buddha— such as the power of knowledge (*bala-ñāṇa*), the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadhamma*), and so forth— just as with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), because they stand having transcended and overcome the entire world.
Therefore he said, "having included all the qualities of omniscience.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the reasons for dwelling in the forest (*araññavāsa*).
55. Regarding the phrase *siyā kho pana te brāhmaṇa*: here, *siyā* is a particle synonymous with *appevā*;

therefore, the meaning is: "Brahmin, it may well be that such a thought occurs to you. As for the word *kadāci* (at some time) used in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), that too was stated with reference to this very same sense; it is not intended as a reason, but rather refers to the matter imagined by the Brahmin.
Having set aside [the opponent's view], he states his own intended reason. "Atthavaso" means that which has the purpose as its fruit because it exists dependent upon it;

or alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as "the cause. By the phrase "his own dwelling in happiness in this very life," the Teacher demonstrates his own delight in seclusion; thus he said, "What is called 'this very life'... and so forth.
In that context, "of the abidings in the postures" (*iriyāpathavihārānaṃ*) means of the occurrences of the postures.
For these occurrences are called "abidings" (*vihārā*) because they carry away the suffering arisen in one posture by interrupting it with another posture.
And by the phrase "out of compassion for future generations," [the Buddha] refers to that which was previously stated by the brahmin: "Your Reverence Gotama is their leader... [and so forth]."

When it was said, "He follows the example of what he has seen," the Teacher concluded his teaching by following the sequence of the narrative and showing, as a conclusion, that very point which had been accepted by himself in such terms as, "It is so, O Brahmin.
The commentary on the reason for dwelling in the forest is finished.
Commentary on the Expression of Gratitude for the Teaching (Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā) 56.
When the teaching had thus been concluded, the brahmin, manifesting his confidence in the Blessed One therein, said, "Excellent" (*abhikkanta*), and so forth.

Regarding the word *abhikkanta*, he explained that it means "transcended" (*atikkanta*) or "gone beyond" (*vigata*), stating that "it is seen in the sense of destruction" (*khaye*). For it is precisely for this reason that [the Buddha] said, "He has gone out" (*nikkhanto*).
"The first watch," it is said. "More excellent" (*abhikkantatara*) means exceedingly desirable and delightful.
And such a beautiful and auspicious thing is called "splendid" (*sundara*); thus he says, "it is seen in what is splendid. "Who?
(*ko*) means which one among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth. "Me" (*me*) means my. "Feet" (*pādāni*) means the feet. "By means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means by this [power].
With such divine power (*deviddhi*). "By fame" (*yasasā*) means by such a retinue and circle of attendants. "Blazing" (*jalanti*) means shining brightly.
"By his lovely appearance" (*abhikkantena vaṇṇena*) means by an exceedingly beautiful, desirable, and handsome complexion; that is, by the color of his skin and the luster of his body.
"Illuminating all directions" (*sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā*) means illuminating and radiating light throughout the ten directions, like the moon and like the sun.
The meaning of the verse is: "making a single radiance and a single light. *Abhirūpe* means in one who is of sublime form or endowed with perfect form.
In expressions such as "Thief! Thief! or "Snake! Snake!", there is reduplication (*āmeḍita*) due to fear. In expressions such as "Pierce! Pierce! or "Strike! Strike!", it is used in anger;
in expressions such as "Excellent! Excellent!", it is used in praise; and in expressions such as "Go! Go! or "Reap! Reap!", it is used in haste.

In expressions such as “Come, come,” it signifies curiosity; in expressions such as “Thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha’,” it signifies wonder; in expressions such as “Come forward, venerable sirs, come forward, venerable sirs,” it signifies laughter;
in expressions such as “Where is my only son, where is my only son,” it signifies sorrow;

and in expressions such as “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! it signifies confidence (*pasāda*). The particle *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*samuccaya*) for what is not explicitly stated; by this, censure, disrespect, and so forth [are included].

The inclusion [of these terms] should be understood. Therein, in expressions such as "wicked, wicked," it is used in the sense of censure. In expressions such as "handsome, handsome," it should be understood as being used in the sense of disrespect.
Showing that this is not stated twice by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), but rather by way of two distinct meanings, he says: "Then..."
He spoke the words beginning with “or. This is stated in the neuter gender in view of the word *abhikkantaṃ*;
however, since that speech of the Blessed One is the teaching of the Dhamma, it is so stated. Alternatively, this is merely a demonstration of the meaning;
therefore, the change of gender and case-ending should be understood according to the sense. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Regarding the phrase *dosanāsanato*:
"Because it dispels the defects of the defilements such as lust, and because it brings about the attainment of qualities" means because it accomplishes qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
Since those qualities which the teaching brings about must be shown according to their predominance, in order to first show those that are predominant, it is said:

"because it generates faith (*saddhā*) and because it generates wisdom (*paññā*). For mundane qualities have faith as their foremost, while supramundane qualities have wisdom as their foremost. [This is] through the perfection of the purpose consisting of virtue and so forth.
It is meaningful because it possesses the perfection of intrinsic nature and terminology; it is well-phrased because its verbal expression is easily understood;

it is profound in meaning because its sense is difficult to comprehend due to its subtle and delicate nature; it is pleasant to the ear because its verbal expression consists of sounds that are smooth, soft, and sweet;
it is heart-stirring because its meaning is vast, pure, and lovely; and it dispels pride and arrogance.
It is cool with compassion because it does not exalt oneself, crushes the stubbornness and agitation [of pride], and does not disparage others;

and because it pacifies the fever of passion and other defilements in others through its operation with the intention of their welfare. It is bright with wisdom because it dispels the darkness of the defilements.

It is delightful to the senses because its voice is as sweet as the song of the cuckoo; it is capable of withstanding scrutiny because its meaning is perfectly pure and free from internal contradictions.

Because it is pleasant when heard due to its initial attractiveness, and because it is beneficial when investigated due to its capacity to withstand scrutiny and its being prompted by an inclination toward welfare.

By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etc. includes: the turning back of the wheel of saṃsāra, the setting in motion of the wheel of the True Dhamma, the shattering of false doctrines, the establishing of right doctrine, the uprooting of unwholesome roots, and the planting of wholesome roots.

The inclusion [of the benefits] should be understood as follows: from closing the doors to the states of misery (*apāya*), from opening the doors to the path to heaven (*sagga*), from the pacification of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and from the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"Placed face downwards" means placed face downwards by someone. "Naturally facing downwards" means naturally born facing downwards.

"Should open up" means he should make it wide open. "Taking by the hand" means that without saying, "Go facing eastward or facing northward," and so forth, he should take him by the hand and say, "This is undoubtedly the path; go in this manner.
"The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight" means the fourteenth day of the waning moon.
One should turn upside down that which was overturned—a vessel that lacked a support for what was to be placed within—by means of providing it with a state of support.

The two phrases, "turned away from the True Dhamma because it arose face-downward" and "fallen into the non-True Dhamma because it was set face-downward," should be applied accordingly, not according to their numerical order.
Granted, sensual desire and the other [hindrances] are also [to be abandoned].
While there are various things that conceal, wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is especially concealing; thus it is said, "concealed by the thicket of wrong view.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the supreme fault.

The entire path leading to the states of misery is a "bad path" (kummagga), in the sense that it is a contemptible path. Because they are the direct opposites of right view and so forth, wrong view and the rest [are so designated].

The eight states of wrongness are the wrong path. For it is precisely with reference to their being the opposites of both [the right path and the right practice] that it is said: "by one who is pointing out the path to heaven and liberation.
A lamp dependent on ghee and the like is not as bright as one dependent on oil; thus, the term "oil-lamp" is used.
"By these modes" means by these ways of comparison, such as those involving turning upside down, turning upright, concealing, uncovering, and so forth.

Or rather, by these aforementioned methods—namely, the discernment of the sixteen objects, the dwelling in non-delusion, the manifestation of the divine dwellings, and the manifestation of the qualities of his own omniscience under the heading of the manifestation of the threefold clear knowledge—he said: "The Dhamma has been proclaimed in many ways.
The commentary on the expression of appreciation for the teaching is concluded.
*Pasannakāravaṇṇanā*:
"An act of faith" (*pasannakāra*) means the honor that should be performed by those who have faith. "Refuge" (*saraṇa*) means a resort; therefore he said "the ultimate resort" (*parāyaṇa*).

And since the state of being an ultimate resort occurs through the prevention of what is harmful and the accomplishment of what is beneficial, he said: "The protector from suffering" (*aghassa tāta*).
"And the provider of welfare. Regarding "of evil" (*aghassa*), they say it means "of suffering," but it is more appropriate to take it as "of sin.
Furthermore, this is a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative. In this context, the word *gami* is not transitive (taking two objects) like the root *ni* and others;
therefore, just as one says "he leads the goat to the village," one cannot say "I go to Gotama for refuge."
However, one should say, “I go for refuge. Here, the word *iti* is indicated as being elided;

its meaning is shown by the statement, “by this intention,” etc., demonstrating that it signifies both the act of going and the resorting [to the Triple Gem] with that purpose, as well as knowing it to be so.
In that context, regarding the phrases beginning with “I resort,” each subsequent term is an explanatory synonym for the preceding one. Resorting...

Approaching with the intention of seeking refuge, attending upon, remaining in his presence, and serving by performing duties and counter-duties—in this way, he illustrates in every respect the state of having no other refuge.
To the question, "How is the meaning 'I awaken' obtained from the word 'I go'?", he says: "For those who... and so forth.
By the two phrases "one who has attained the path" and "one who has realized cessation," only those established in the fruit (phalaṭṭha) are shown, not those established in the path (maggaṭṭha).
Showing this, he said: "and for one practicing according to the instruction. But is it not said that even a "good worldling" (kalyāṇaputhujjana) practices according to the instruction?
Although it is so said, [in the strict sense] it refers to those established in the path.

Thus they alone should be so described, and not the others, because of their lack of entry into the fixed course of rightness (*niyāma*). For it is said of them alone that they "sustain [beings] so that they do not fall into the states of misery.
Indeed, the possibility of liberation from the states of misery arises through the entry into the fixed course of rightness.

Regarding the word *akkhāyati* (it is declared), here the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner. By this, [the passage continues]: "To whatever extent, monks, there are conditioned phenomena..."
Or it includes the sutta passage: “Whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them. Or, by the word “in detail,” this is included.
And here, both the Noble Path—by virtue of its being the means of deliverance—and Nibbāna—by virtue of being the cause for the accomplishment of that goal—are called “Dhamma” in the primary sense.
For it is by obtaining Nibbāna as its object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) that [the Path leads to liberation].

The Noble Path accomplishes that purpose; and the Noble Fruits do so because, as stated in the passage beginning "since by that faith which has not yet subsided," they have the function of pacifying and abandoning the defilements already eradicated by the Path, they are conducive to deliverance, and they culminate in deliverance.
As for the Dhamma of the scriptures, it is the cause for the attainment of the Dhamma of deliverance.
In this manner, the status of being the Dhamma is indeed obtained; showing that this matter is established by the text itself, he said, "Not only...

and so forth. Since all lust—including its divisions such as lust for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*)—is dispassioned toward and abandoned by means of this, it is called "the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāga*).

The path has been explained. Because craving—termed *ejā* (agitation)—and sorrow, which is characterized by inward brooding, have been entirely exhausted upon its arising, the fruit is described as "unagitated" (*aneja*) and "sorrowless" (*asoka*). It is "not repulsive" (*appaṭikūla*) because it demonstrates non-opposition;
thus, the meaning is that it is unopposed by anything, or that it is desirable and sublime. This is because it proceeds in a state of proficiency and because it manifests distinguished qualities.
Or it is well-mastered. As it is said: "O Brahmā, perceiving harm, I did not speak the sublime Dhamma among men, though it was well-mastered.
The construction is: "All the aggregates of Dhamma have been told.
By way of the combination of view and virtue: "This noble view is leading; it leads the practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering."
Regarding the view described thus: "He dwells having attained conformity of view with such a view," and regarding the virtues described thus:

"Those virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration—he dwells having attained conformity of virtue with such virtues."
The meaning is: by way of the cohesion of their virtues (*sīla*) and by way of the commonality of their view and virtue. "Cohesive" (*saṃhata*) means joined together.
For noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), even if they are situated far apart anywhere, they are indeed cohesive through the harmony of their own qualities.
And those eight persons who see the Dhamma—by way of pairs of men there are four, and by way of individuals there are exactly eight of these noble ones of the Dhamma.
He was a seer of the Dhamma through his direct vision. There are three acts of going for refuge by virtue of going for refuge three times with the thought, "The three things are my refuge.
He "declared" means he made known what was in his heart by means of speech.
The commentary on the expression of faith is finished.
The commentary on the discourse on going for refuge states: "In order to achieve proficiency regarding the goings for refuge, the refuge... [etc.

...should be understood," because proficiency in that regard arises from the analysis of the refuge’s object, its classifications, its fruit, its defilements, and its divisions, as well as from the analysis of the person who goes for refuge. Thus it was said.
Because it is impossible [to practice] without going for refuge itself. But why is purification (*vodāna*) not included here?

Is it not the case that the analysis of purification also brings about skillfulness in that regard? True, this is so; however, it is not included because it is already indicated by implication through the inclusion of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
For those causes of their defilement, such as ignorance and so forth, when they have not arisen in every respect—

Purification comes about through the non-arising [of unarisen states] and the abandoning of those already arisen. This term should be understood by way of the word *sara* (to run/flow) in the sense of "hurting" (*hiṃsa*).
Having stated, "It is a refuge (*saraṇa*) because it hurts (*sarati*)," he spoke the words beginning with "those who have gone for refuge" (*saraṇagatānaṃ*) to resolve the inquiry:
"Of whom does this hurting consist? How? And of what? In that context, "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-bhaya*). "Terror" (*santāsa*)...
“Mental terror. Because mental suffering has already been included by that [term], “suffering” here refers to bodily suffering.
“The affliction of miserable destinies” refers to all suffering comprised within the miserable destinies. All of this will be clarified later in the discussion on the fruits.
“This” refers to the word “refuge.”
Having thus shown the meaning of the word *saraṇa* (refuge) without distinction, the passage beginning with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) is stated now to show it with distinction.
"By engaging in what is beneficial" means by directing one toward the goal through such instructions as, "Monks, dwell possessed of perfected virtue" (*sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharathā*).

And "by turning away from what is harmful" means through such [instructions] as, "The ripening of the taking of life is indeed evil, and the future state is evil. (*pāṇātipātassa kho pāpako vipāko pāpakaṃ abhisamparāyaṃ*) etc.

By means of seeing the danger [of worldly things] and so forth, and by turning away from what is harmful. "It destroys fear" means that it eliminates, by preventing its occurrence, the calamity caused by the non-engagement with or engagement in what is beneficial or harmful.
The Dhamma known as the Path destroys fear by ferrying beings across the wilderness of existence (*bhava-kantāra*);
the other [Dhamma] destroys fear by providing consolation for sentient beings—this is the construction [of the meaning]. "Of those who act" refers to [the act] by way of giving and by way of worship.

And it destroys the fear of beings by bringing about the attainment of abundant fruit for the honors offered to them; for its intention is that it possesses the state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
“By this method also” means by this reason as well, which has been explained through analysis:
namely, the occurrence [of the thought] therein, “The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is practicing rightly.”
Confidence in the Triple Gem is *tappasāda*; that same Triple Gem is "heavy" (*garu*) to him, thus it is *taggaru*; the state of being so is *taggarutā*.

Both that confidence and that veneration are *tappasādataggarutā*, [and] by means of them. Having shaken off the defilements through the removal of wrong views, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so forth, he is one whose taints are destroyed.
By way of the mental mode: "That very Triple Gem is my supreme resort, my destination, my refuge, and my shelter. Thus it proceeds.
Taking refuge (*saraṇagamana*) is a mental state proceeding in the form of having that as its ultimate resort; it is so called because "one goes by means of this to what is a refuge.

"One who possesses that" means one endowed with that aforementioned mental state. "Thus he approaches" should be understood to mean that he thus associates with, serves, and honors [the Triple Gem], or else that he thus knows and awakens to it. And here, by the mention of "serene confidence" (*pasāda*), mundane taking of refuge is expressed.
For that [faith] has confidence as its primary factor, not knowledge. By the grasping of weightiness, it is supramundane.
For the Noble Ones regard the Triple Gem with weightiness—due to their recognition of its qualities—just as one regards a stone parasol; therefore, it should be connected thus:

by means of confidence in that [Triple Gem], defilements are dispelled through suppression, and by means of the weightiness of that [confidence], they are eradicated through cutting off. Furthermore, "having that as one's supreme resort" here means having that as one’s final goal.
It should be understood that by this [term], the fourfold going for refuge to be explained hereafter is included.

Alternatively, since "clarity" (pasāda) and "veneration" (garutā) are indicated without distinction, the inclusion of both verified clarity (aveccappasāda) and the other kind is effected by the mention of "clarity," and likewise by the mention of "veneration";
thus, both terms should be applied to both types of going for refuge.

The construction is: "It succeeds at the moment of the path. By the phrase "having Nibbāna as its object," it shows that, in actual fact, the attainment of the Four Truths itself is the supramundane going for refuge.

For therein, the phenomenon of Nibbāna is realized through the penetration of clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) by way of realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and the phenomenon of the Path is realized through the penetration of clear comprehension by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); it is precisely while being thus penetrated that they establish the state of being a refuge.

Furthermore, the qualities of the Buddha that fall within the range of disciples are realized through the clear comprehension of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*); likewise for the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha. Therefore he said:
"It succeeds in its function with respect to the entire Triple Gem. And it succeeds simultaneously, not successively like worldly things;
the intention is that it is penetrated by a penetration free from delusion. As for those who say, "No... [the text continues].

"If it were argued that 'the going for refuge proceeds having Nibbāna as its object, but because the Path has been attained, it is considered already attained—just as certain types of mundane knowledge, such as the threefold lore (tevijjā) and so forth'—then for them, the going for refuge would be merely mundane and not supramundane;
and that is incorrect, since both kinds must be admitted. Here, "that" refers to the mundane going for refuge.
The acquisition of faith occurs through such statements as, “The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened,” and so forth.

“Rooted in faith” means that right view—preceded by the aforementioned faith—is seen correctly and according to the proper method through the mundane awakening to the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma’s perfect nature as Dhamma, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice.
By the phrase “right view rooted in faith,” it is indicated that [this] has the aforementioned characteristics supported by faith.

This shows that wisdom is the mundane going for refuge. Therefore he said, “It is called the straightening of view,” because it is by means of this that view itself is made straight through its own conditions. Or, it is the straightening of view because view is straightened by means of it;

thus, it is a mental state proceeding in such a manner. And having established it in this way, [the definition] “a mental state proceeding in the mode of having that as its ultimate resort” is also [established].
The statement is thus established. However, it should be understood that the inclusion of "right view preceded by faith" is because the arising of the thought has that [faith] as its primary factor.
By the phrase "acquisition of faith," he shows the going for refuge dissociated from knowledge—such as that of children encouraged by their mothers and others;
by the phrase "right view," he shows the going for refuge associated with knowledge.
That is mundane going for refuge. "Self-surrender" (attasanniyyātana) means that by which the self is surrendered, relinquished, and renounced;

it is the rectification of views as previously described. One who has that Three Jewels as his ultimate resort and refuge is "one whose resort is that" (tapparāyaṇa), whether that refers to a person or a state of consciousness.
The state of being such is "having that as one's resort" (tapparāyaṇatā); it is precisely the rectification of views as previously described.
"Taking refuge" (*saraṇa*) means that by means of this [act], one enters into the state of a student (*sissa*) or the state of a resident pupil (*antevāsika*);
thus it is "the entering into the state of a student. "Prostration" (*paṇipāta*) means that by means of this, one bows down with the very intention of going for refuge.

In all instances, the meaning should be understood precisely through the rectification of views as previously described. "Relinquishing oneself" (*attapariccajana*) refers to [the relinquishing] of one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*) for the sake of crossing over the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

Relinquishment. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. The restriction "only to the Buddha and so forth" should be stated accordingly for the other specific types of going for refuge;
for in this way, the exclusion of others is established.
Having thus shown the surrendering of oneself and so forth by one way, [the author] now shows them by other ways as well.

The passage beginning with “Moreover” (*apica*) has been commenced. By this, he shows that even through other methods, the surrendering of oneself (*attasanniyyātanā*) and so forth are indeed the same, because the meaning (*attha*) is not different.
Regarding the phrase “of Āḷavaka and others,” the word “others” (*ādi*) should be understood as including Sātāgiri, Hemavata, and the rest.

But surely these individuals, such as Āḷavaka and the others, attained refuge only by means of the Path (*magga*); how then can their going for refuge be characterized as having that [Nirvāṇa] as their ultimate resort (*tapparāyaṇatā*)?

Is it so stated? It is stated thus because even through the taking of refuge by means of the Path, [the Buddha] has made known the mode of having that as one’s ultimate resort in such passages as, “I shall wander from village to village.
Regarding the phrase “by way of relatives...,” here [the four bases are] by way of relatives, by way of fear, by way of teachers, and by way of those worthy of offerings.

The word "by way of" (*vasena*) should be applied to each [term] individually. Therein, "by way of relatives" (*ñātivasena*) means by way of the state of being a relative. The same applies to the remaining [terms].

"By prostration to those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena*) means by prostration caused by the quality of being worthy of offerings. "By the others" refers to the three types of prostration proceeding from the state of being a relative and so forth.
To show in detail the meaning briefly stated by the words "by the others" and so on, [the text] begins with "Therefore" (*tasmā*).
It has been stated. "He pays homage" is a statement defining the characteristic of prostration (*paṇipāta*). "Of such a kind" refers to what pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*);

for the intention is that one who expects instruction pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*) or leading to liberation (*niyyānika*) performs prostration only toward those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
"The classification of going for refuge" means the analysis of going for refuge.
The Noble Path itself is the supramundane going for refuge; thus it is said: "The four fruits of recluseship are fruition-results.
"The destruction of all suffering" means the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
"This" refers to the vision of the Noble Truths as stated thus: "One sees the four Noble Truths with right wisdom."
"By way of not approaching what is permanent," etc., means by way of not grasping [anything] as permanent. "No possibility" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause.
"No occasion" (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition. By both terms, he negates the very reason. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to the reason by which.
"One endowed with right view" (*diṭṭhisampanna*) is a stream-enterer endowed with the path-view. "Any formation" (*kañci saṅkhāraṃ*) refers to those belonging to the four planes of existence.
"Even a single conditioned formation among conditioned formations"—to "approach as permanent" means one would grasp it as "permanent.
To "approach as pleasant" refers to the grasping of it as pleasant by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), namely: "The self is absolutely happy and free from disease after death.
However, with a mind dissociated from such views, the noble disciple [approaches it] for the sake of allaying the fever [of suffering].
Just as a refined brahmin, terrified of a rutting elephant, might approach a dung heap thinking it to be something pleasant, so too [the fool] approaches some formation as pleasant.
In the section concerning the self, instead of saying "some formation" (*saṅkhāra*) for the purpose of including the descriptions of the kasiṇas and so forth, it is said "some phenomenon" (*dhamma*).
In these sections as well, the delimitation should be understood either by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes. Whatever...
For whatever a worldling grasps by way of clinging, from that very thing the noble disciple undoes his clinging. Regarding the terms "mother" and so forth:
it is the biological mother who is meant; the biological father; and an Arahant who is a human being and has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava).
But could a noble disciple take the life of another? That is impossible; however, this is stated for the purpose of showing the great blameworthiness of the state of being a worldling.
This was said for the purpose of illustrating the fruit for a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). "With a malicious mind" means with a mind corrupted by the intent to kill.
"He should shed blood" means he should shed even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly from a living body.

"He should cause a schism in the Saṅgha" means [he should cause a division] in the Saṅgha that shares the same communal affiliation and stands within the same boundary (*sīmā*), [by means of] a formal act (*kamma*) or a recitation (*uddesa*).

When it is said, "by means of five reasons—namely, by way of verbal communication, by proclamation, and by the drawing of lots—one might cause a schism," the meaning is that it is impossible for one to take another teacher—that is, another founder of a sect—as "this is my teacher.
Furthermore, the meaning is that those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha will not, on account of that, go to a plane of misery; rather, they will fill the hosts of devas.
“By ten bases” means by ten causes. “They overcome” means they prevail. “Also by way of the Velāma Sutta, etc.
refers here to the passage beginning: “Of eighty-four thousand golden plates, silver plates, and bronze plates, each filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion;
of eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with every ornament... [and so forth].
By way of relinquishing eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand milch cows,
eighty-four thousand maidens, eighty-four thousand couches, eighty-four thousand millions of garments,
and immeasurable food consisting of various kinds of hard and soft edibles, for more than seven months...
A gift given to a single stream-enterer (sotāpanna) bears greater fruit than a great almsgiving held at the time of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, performed continuously for seven years;

a gift given to a single once-returner (sakadāgāmin) bears greater fruit than a gift given to a hundred stream-enterers; a gift given to a single non-returner (anāgāmin) bears greater fruit than that; a gift given to a single arahant bears greater fruit than that;
a gift given to a single paccekabuddha bears greater fruit than that; and a gift given to a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha) bears greater fruit than all those.

This is according to the Velāma Sutta, which elucidates this meaning: "Giving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha bears greater fruit; making a monastery for the sake of the Saṅgha of the four quarters bears greater fruit; and going for refuge bears even greater fruit.
For it is said therein: "Householder, the gift that the brahmin Velāma gave—that great gift—"
“Whoever should feed one person endowed with right view, this would bear much greater fruit than that,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “the Velāma Sutta and others,” by the word “others,” the inclusion of the *Agga-ppasāda Sutta* and similar discourses should be understood.
Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the non-knowing of the qualities of the Triple Gem; it is delusion (*sammoha*) regarding them, such as thinking, “Is he a Buddha or not? etc.

By the phrase beginning with “Buddho,” doubt (*vicikicchā*) refers to uncertainty; wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is a distorted apprehension resulting from the conceptualization of his qualities as being non-qualities.
By the word “etc. (*ādi*), disrespect and lack of reverence are included.

“Not of great radiance” means not brilliant; the sense is that it is impure and unpurified. “Not of great expansion” means not sublime. “Blameworthy” (*sāvajjo*) is by way of views, craving, and so forth.
It is with fault. Worldly going for refuge, like the undertaking of training rules, lasts only as long as life itself without any fixed limit of time;
therefore, it is said that its destruction occurs with the breaking up of the aggregates: "It is blameless at the time of death.
"It" refers to the blameless destruction of the going for refuge. Although it is blameless, it does not yield a desirable fruit; thus it is said: "It is fruitless."
The commentary on the discourse on going for refuge is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the discourse on the procedure for lay followers (*upāsaka*): "Who is a lay follower? is a question concerning the essential nature; therefore, it is effectively asking, "What is the defining characteristic of a lay follower? "Why? is a question concerning the cause.
This shows by what cause for application (*pavattinimitta*) the term "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) is conventionally established for that person.
"What is his virtue? means: what kind of virtue does this lay follower have; by what extent of virtue does he come to be called "endowed with virtue"?
"What is his livelihood? means: what is his right livelihood? Furthermore, that [right livelihood] comes about through the avoidance of wrong livelihood.
"He too may be analyzed": what is his failure? It is a failure of that virtue or of his livelihood.
For there is either an injunction or a prohibition regarding what immediately follows. "What is his success?"—the same method applies here as well.
"Whoever it may be": anyone among the Khattiyas and so forth. In this context, the sole cause is the going for refuge, not distinctions such as birth and so on.

He shows [this]. "By means of worship" means by means of attending upon [the precepts] through that very act of going for refuge, through performing them with diligence, and through being endowed with respect, reverence, and esteem.

"Abstentions" (*veramaṇiyo*): "Vera" refers to misconduct such as killing living beings; because they ward off (*maṇanato*), destroy (*hananato*), and eliminate (*vināsanato*) that, they are "abstentions.
These are the five abstinences (*viratiyo*), because abstention is the primary element of that virtue. For this very reason, he said:
In various instances, it says, "he abstains.
"Wrong trade" means that which is not right trade, improper trade, and unsuitable trade. "Having abandoned" means having relinquished by simply not engaging in it.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means not departing from the Dhamma; by this, he also rejects any other livelihood that is contrary to the Dhamma.
"Evenly" means without unevenness. By this, he shows that one's livelihood is maintained by avoiding misconduct such as bodily unevenness and instead practicing good conduct through bodily evenness.
"Sword-dealing" refers to the trade of selling weapons, whether one has made them oneself, had them made, or obtained them already finished.
"Sword-dealing" also refers to the sale of human beings. "Meat-dealing" refers to butchers and the like.

The trade in animals refers to the sale of meat after having reared deer, pigs, and so forth, and prepared it. The trade in intoxicants refers to the sale of whatever intoxicant one has mixed or obtained.
The trade in poisons refers to the sale of poison after one has either mixed it or acquired it.
Among these, the trade in weapons is said to be not to be done because it is the cause of harming others; the trade in living beings is [not to be done] because it renders them non-independent.
Meat is a trade for slaughter because it is a cause for killing; liquor is a trade for negligence because it is a basis for heedlessness.
"Of that very thing" refers to both virtue, characterized by the five abstinences, and livelihood, characterized by the five wrong trades.
"Failure" means breach or corruption. "By which" means by which practice. "Outcaste" refers to an outcaste lay follower (*upāsaka-caṇḍāla*).

The lay follower Malanta. "Base" means inferior among lay followers. Lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) is the opposite of faith regarding the Buddha and so forth, as well as regarding karma and its results;
it is wrong resolve. One who possesses such lack of faith as described is "faithless.
One who possesses the aforementioned failure in virtue (*sīla-vipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīva-vipatti*) is "immoral. "By this view and so forth, this..."

“...will be an auspicious sign”—thus one who possesses the auspicious signs of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, which are termed the superstitions imagined by foolish people, is a “superstitious person. “He believes in auspicious signs” means he places his trust in auspicious signs categorized as those seen and so forth.
“Not in action” means he does not place his trust in the fact that one is the owner of one’s own actions (*kammassakata*). “Outside of this” means outside of this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha.

"Externally" means in the systems of outsiders (*bāhiraka*). "He seeks out one worthy of offerings" means he searches for one who has entered upon a wrong course, perceiving them as being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇāraha*).
"He performs a prior service" means he first performs wholesome actions such as giving and honoring.
And here, by treating the seeking of one worthy of offerings and the performing of a prior service as one, five qualities are to be understood.

Success should be understood as the opposite of what was stated regarding failure. However, this is the distinction: in the sense of producing delight for all four assemblies, the lay follower (*upāsaka*) alone is a jewel;
thus, he is a "lay-follower-jewel" (*upāsaka-ratana*). By virtue of the fragrance of his fame and renown arising from the splendor of his qualities, the lay follower alone is a lotus;
thus, he is a "lay-follower-lotus" (*upāsaka-paduma*). Likewise, he is a "lay-follower-white-lotus" (*upāsaka-puṇḍarīka*).

“Ādimhi” means in the sense of the beginning. “Koṭiyaṃ” means at the ultimate limit. “Vihāraggena” means by way of the division of the dwelling—specifically, by way of the division of each respective place of residence, such as:
“For those living in this chamber, this particular jackfruit comes to fruition,” and so forth.
“Ajjataṃ” means simply “today.”
By the phrase "endowed with life" (*pāṇehi upetaṃ*), he shows that this taking of refuge extends to the very end of his life;
having said, "As long as my life continues," and so forth, he further honors that Triple Gem with his life.
Then, clarifying the intention that had arisen in that brahmin—namely, "I shall protect my taking of refuge"—he spoke the words beginning with "For I... and so on. [End of section on] *pāṇehi*.
"For 'having gone for refuge' means: as long as my life-breaths endure, so long have I gone for refuge. And in going for refuge, it is not by mere words, nor by a single arising of the thought;
rather, even by renouncing one's life, one has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts—thus should the meaning here be understood."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Method for Lay Followers is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta.
57. Regarding the phrase "The Venerable Sāriputta": here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*), meaning "starting with this.
By this, it includes the entire sutta beginning with "He addressed the bhikkhus. Therefore, he says, "the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta. What is its source of origin?
It is his own personal inclination (*attajjhāsayo*). For the Great Elder himself initiated this teaching without being requested by others. However, some say:

“Having seen some bhikkhus with defiled minds, this teaching was undertaken both for the purpose of abandoning the defilement of their minds and for the sake of ensuring that such defilements do not arise again in the future for others. Thus, regarding “in all the suttas”:
just as here in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, so too in all the suttas following this one, only the commentary on words not already explained or previously mentioned is provided. Therefore he said:

“*Tasmā*,” etc. “Delimitation by counting” means delimiting by means of enumeration. For here, having divided sentient beings—who are of two kinds according to whether they have little dust in their eyes (*apparajakkha*) or much dust in their eyes (*mahārajakkha*)—into two further groups each according to whether they know what is beneficial (*atthaññū*) or what is harmful (*anatthaññū*), the term “four” is used as an exhaustive inclusion.
One should not take them to be proponents of a personal entity (*puggalavādin*) like the Vajjiputtakas and others; rather, one should penetrate the meaning in accordance with worldly convention.

Because the teaching was undertaken by way of what is appropriate for those capable [of understanding], and because this method of teaching is dependent upon the Teacher, he said "For this... and so forth, showing that it is thus.

*Commentary on the Discussion of the Teaching of the Conventional and the Ultimate:* In this context, the teaching of the conventional is the "conventional teaching" (*sammutidesanā*), and the teaching of the ultimate is the "ultimate teaching" (*paramatthadesanā*). Regarding the word "therein" (*tattha*):
[The distinction is] between the teaching of the conventional and the teaching of the ultimate, not between the conventional and the ultimate themselves. Therefore he said:
"Such is the teaching of the conventional; such is the teaching of the ultimate. Herein, this is the definition of the conventional and the ultimate:

that which, when broken or when its parts are analytically separated by the intellect, no longer retains its designation—that is the conventional, consisting of the various categories such as pots, cloths, and so forth.
The ultimate meaning (paramattha) is the opposite of that. For this method is not applicable to the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of hardness, contact, and so forth;

rather, it is said that “‘person’ (puggala) is a conventional teaching (sammutidesanā),” because the designation ‘person’ is applied in dependence upon the phenomena such as form (rūpa) as they occur in the manner of a collection and a continuity.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Phenomena possessing the nature of arising and passing away are not permanent.
He said: “‘Impermanent’ is a teaching in the ultimate sense (paramattha). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

But is it not the case that the teaching on the aggregates (khandha) is also merely a conventional teaching (sammuti)? For the meaning of “aggregate” is the meaning of a “heap” or the meaning of a “division,” is it not? True, this is so;

however, this designation “aggregate” is based upon the ultimate sense—just like the appropriate designation for contact and so forth—and is thus more proximate to it than designations such as “person” (puggala).

It is not that they are far apart; rather, their inclusion within the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) has been stated. Alternatively, by means of the term "aggregates" (*khandha*), only those phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) which are derived from them are included.
But is it not the case that all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature ascend to the teaching only through the door of conventional designation (*sammuti*), and not directly?

Would it not follow, then, that the entire teaching is merely a teaching of convention? This is not so; for the classification of the teaching is made according to the classification of the phenomena to be taught.
Because it is intended [as such], and because a sound does not manifest its meaning without some cause for its occurrence (*pavatti-nimitta*).

"Having heard the teaching by way of conventional designation" means having heard the teaching set forth through the door of conventional designation, beginning with, "In this case, a certain person is one who torments himself, devoted to the practice of self-torment," by way of generating knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). "Having penetrated the meaning" means...
Having penetrated, in accordance with that, the meaning known as the Four Truths together with insight and the Path;
"having abandoned delusion" means having abandoned delusion without remainder along with those defilements associated with it.
"The distinction" refers to the distinction known as Nibbāna and the distinction known as Arahantship. "Of them" means of such disciples. "By way of the ultimate sense" [refers to]: "These five..."
“...the faculties, monks,” and so forth, by way of ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*). The remainder is exactly as stated in the immediately preceding method.

“In that regard” means in that teaching by way of both conventional designation (*sammuti*) and ultimate reality (*paramattha*). “Skilled in the languages of various regions” means one who is proficient in the various dialects of different countries.
“Of the three Vedas” is merely an illustration; the intended meaning is “of the three Vedas and also of technical treatises (*sippagantha*).”
For he will explain the acquisition of crafts later on. Alternatively, having included the crafts within the Vedas, it is said "of the three Vedas.
By stating "they are hidden in you, O Seizer," he refutes the false doctrine that the Vedas exist only as something to be recited and do not exist anywhere in a tangible, present form;
thus he demonstrates that even the Vedas persist precisely by way of being subject to recitation. Of various kinds...
"Having various local dialects" means that these [beings] have various local dialects (*desabhāsā*).
"Ultimate reality" (*paramattha*) means the supreme, highest meaning; it is the actual nature (*yathābhūtasabhāva*) of phenomena (*dhamma*).

"Conventional designation" (*sammuti*) is established merely by worldly convention. If this is so, one might ask: "How can conventional discourse be true? To this he says: "Because of worldly convention," referring to worldly common usage (*lokasamañña*).

Because it proceeds by depending [on convention]. For, through the common usage of the world (*loka-samaññā*), making something known without dogmatic insistence (*abhinivesa*)—like the teaching of a certain portion of the *Sutta*—is not false, since that usage cannot be overstepped.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "One should not insist on local dialects; one should not overstep common usage.
"Of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) means of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "True causes" (*bhūta-kāraṇā*) means according to their actual intrinsic nature.
Because it proceeds by depending [on them]. "To one who employs conventional designation" means to one who speaks the common worldly usage such as "person," "being," and so forth.
"For the purpose of illustrating moral shame and dread" means to make manifest, by way of their function, the qualities of moral shame and dread in the duty of protecting the world.
For since their function is evident only within the continuum of a sentient being, that must be stated by means of a discourse having the person as its basis.
This same principle applies to the rest as well. For when an action arises within a particular occurrence of consciousness, the arising of its fruit occurs only within that very continuum;
this is "the ownership of one's own actions" (*kammassakatā*). Thus, there is neither the destruction of a consciousness already performed nor the acquisition of what was not done;

this must be illustrated precisely through discourse that refers to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā kathā*). Furthermore, the performance of meritorious deeds and so forth by those beings, which constitutes individual human effort (*paccattapurisakāra*), is also [to be understood] by way of the continuum.
This should be illustrated by a discourse that is specifically focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), because it is something to be accomplished [by him].
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of illustrating the *ānantariya*": the fruit that arises immediately after death is called "immediate" (*anantara*);

those [deeds] connected with that immediate [fruit], which have the nature of performing what is immediate through the production of that [fruit], or whose purpose is immediate, are the *ānantariyas*, such as matricide and so forth.
For the purpose of illustrating those [factors]. For even they, because they must be accomplished by way of a continuity (santāna),

are to be illustrated only through discourse that has the person as its basis, such as "he deprives his mother of life," and likewise "he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and so forth,
as well as "he recollects his manifold past lives, even one birth," and so forth.

The discourse on the purification of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), and the offering (*dakkhiṇā*)—which proceeds with such statements as, "There is an offering that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient"—should be understood as being expressed solely by way of a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), because its domain is the continuum of sentient beings (*sattasantāna*).
Furthermore, even when speaking of ultimate reality (*paramattha*) through such statements as, "There are eight types of persons (*purisapuggala*);
there is no person who is liberated at times (*samayavimutta*)," one does so for the purpose of not abandoning conventional worldly usage (*lokasammuti*).
He spoke on the discourse concerning the person (*puggalakathā*).

By this, it should be understood that the purpose of the remaining discourses mentioned by him lies in their being based upon the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), as they are included under the general category. Granted, all of this has been stated with reference to those who have not fully understood the basis;
nevertheless, such a teaching is also conducive to ease for those who have fully understood the basis.

"Mahājana" refers to the worldly multitude. They do not know because they lack the analytical discernment of the compact mass [of aggregates] and fail to clearly perceive the functional nature of phenomena (*dhammakicca*).
In that regard, they fall into delusion by becoming caught in doubt, thinking, "What indeed is this? How indeed is this?

Due to their adherence to contradictory views, they become adversaries. However, those who know through conventional discourse on matters long familiar do not fall into delusion, nor do they become adversaries.
They do not abandon conventional usage because they illuminate the ultimate truth by way of conventional expression.
"Worldly designation" (*lokasamaññā*) refers to that by which something is known, designated, or expressed in common usage through the adoption of a name; it is by means of such worldly designation.

"Worldly terminology" (*lokanirutti*) refers to that which is determined, fixed, or spoken as an expression for the elucidation of various meanings by the world; it is within such worldly terminology.

It is called "worldly expression" (*lokābhilāpa*) because it is expressed by the world; that is, it exists as a worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*). It is said to be "existent" (*santa*) precisely because it stands within that worldly expression and has not been abandoned, rather than being grasped according to ultimate reality (*paramattha*) as the proponents of a person (*puggalavādin*) do.

Here, the word *santa* occurs in the sense of being "exhausted," as in "for one who is exhausted for a long distance of a league" (*dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ*), and... [this sentence continues]... "and this..."
In such passages as, "This applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have become stilled and calmed," it occurs in the sense of having ceased;
in such passages as, "This Dhamma realized by me is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime," it occurs in the sense of being the objective domain of peaceful knowledge;

in such passages as, "Of one who is ever peaceful and mindful," it occurs in the sense of the subsiding of the defilements; and in such passages as, "The peaceful indeed proclaim [it] to the virtuous."
In such passages as, "O monks, these five great thieves are existing and are found," it refers to existence; here too, it refers precisely to existence.
And since this is spoken in connection with a person, he says, "it exists by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*)," showing that it is according to common worldly usage.
Furthermore, this word *atthi* should be understood as a particle (*nipātapada*), as in such phrases as, "There are head-hairs in this body."
...as it were. In order to show the meaning of the word *saṃvijjamānā* (“existing”), he said “being found” (*upalabbhamānā*). For whatever exists is found.
“Limbs” (*aṅga*) refers to the stains (*aṅgaṇa*), such as lust and so forth, because by means of these, the persons possessing them go to a state of degradation.

It is called a stain (*aṅgaṇa*) because it anoints (*añjati*) or smears; it is dirt and the like. It is called a stain because, by its persistence, it manifests (*añjeti*) that which is situated therein.

*Aṅgaṇaṃ* means an open space or a cleared area of ground. Because they represent specific modes of manifestation for hatred and so forth, and because they occur frequently in various ways, these are "sharp defilements" (*tibbakilesā*).

"Evil" (*pāpakānaṃ*) means base or inferior. "Unwholesome" (*akusalānaṃ*) means those arisen from lack of skill or proficiency. "Within the range of desire" (*icchāvacarānaṃ*) means those that proceed by way of desire.
"Together with the *aṅgaṇa*" means it exists together with the aforementioned defilement which has received the name *aṅgaṇa*.
One does not even know that "they exist" because of the absence of such appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).

In order to show that the state of being dangerous must be specifically understood regarding those defilements (*kilesa*) whose existence there is, it is said: "These are called defilements," and so forth.
In that context, "hard" means harsh; "wild" means cruel. "Should not be grasped" means should not be produced. "According to their actual nature" means...
"According to their true nature" means by way of their actual mode of being. "In this manner" refers to the manner described in such passages as "these are called defilements," and so forth.
"By whatever or by whichever" means by whatever means, whether in new construction works or in the study of the scriptures, the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), and so on.

"Therein" is a locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*). Showing that this specification is from within the aggregate of both the pure and the impure, he says: "among the four types of persons."
Having said this, he spoke again—"or when those two [factors] are accompanied by faults"—in order to show a portion of that very same point.
For that pair is first distinguished by way of their inferior and superior status, because they were mentioned first. Indeed, distinction occurs in some cases from something, by means of something.
58. Although elsewhere it is said: "The producer is the cause (*hetu*); the supporting factor is the condition (*paccaya*); the uncommon is the cause; the common..."

In such passages as, "The cause is similar, the condition is dissimilar; the cause is prior in time, the condition arises simultaneously," the terms "cause" (hetu) and "condition" (paccaya) are explained by way of their distinctions;

however, here, as in the passage, "Bhikkhus, the four great elements are the causes, the four great elements are the conditions for the manifestation of the aggregate of form," the words "cause" and "condition" [are used synonymously].

To show that they have the same meaning, it is said: "By both [terms], he asks for the reason itself. In this context, "by both" means by the two expressions "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*).
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asks because he wishes to expand the teaching.

"Kiñcāpi" is a particle used in the sense of granting permission or showing esteem. What does he grant permission for? Even though the state of having blemishes is the same for both of them... [of that]...
The superiority and inferiority of those [beings] is caused by their understanding and lack of understanding. What does he appreciate?

He appreciates the Elder’s ability to make the meaning of what was asked clear, having adorned it with various causes and similes due to his diverse ingenuity. Therefore he said, "He does not understand," and so forth.
Both cause (*hetu*) and condition (*paccaya*) exist for the state of superiority and inferiority; for even the fact that they are to be described in such a way is itself based on that [state].
59. This is the reason for the inferiority and superiority of those two persons. To show this more clearly by means of similes, he says:
"This" refers to the failure to abandon a blemish due to the absence of the arousal of energy, which is being discussed immediately following the sutta.
Therefore he said: "With reference to the desire... etc. "Desire characterized by the wish to act" means that which is designated as the wish to act (*kattukamyatā*).
It refers to the wholesome desire for phenomena that arises by way of the wish to abandon the courtyard [of defilements].
"He will not generate" means he will not produce it. Since wholesome effort is strong because of desire, he says: "He will not exert an effort stronger than that.
The intention is: how can one who does not even generate the desire perform the corresponding effort?
“Firm energy” is energy that has reached the state of exaltation; it is steadfast energy.

By the very mention of “with blemish,” since the blemishes are the basis for the defilements and thus the mind is defiled, the separate mention of “defiled” indicates a particularly intense state of defilement;
hence he said, “one whose mind is thoroughly defiled. This also applies to the phrases “one with a soiled mind,” and so forth.
The phrase “by those very [causes]” should be supplied and connected [to the context].
“Staining” (*malaggahaṇa*) refers to the state of being difficult to remove, like the cloth used for wiping a mortar or like a rag soaked in fat; it is the state of being soiled.

“Affliction” (*upatāpana*) means pressing, harming, making non-expansive, obstructing, and burning by producing distress and feverish heat. “Time” (*kāla*) means the duration; that is, the time as it was grasped.

The exhaustion of one’s personal existence (*attabhāva*) means the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyukkhaya*). "He will do" means he will set it in motion; what is meant is that he will reach [that state].
And being thus situated, he is said to "die," as in "he will give up his life.
*Seyyathāpi* is a particle used for indicating a simile. Showing its meaning, he said "just as if" (*yathā nāma*). [The phrase] "by dust and so forth... [is explained as follows:]

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), things such as sweat (*jalla*) are included; by the word "etc. in the phrase "by rubbing and so forth" (*ghaṃsanādīhi*), things such as wiping with ashes (*chārikāparimajjana*) are included.
Just as in expressions like "a beautiful maiden should be given," the sense of excellence is understood even through a word that indicates excellence without explicitly stating it;

therefore he said, "it means 'more thoroughly defiled by dirt' (*malaggahitatarā*). The term "question for inquiry" (*paṭipucchāvacana*) is a specific type of question seeking permission (*anumatipucchā*).
"Being treated thus" means being brought to a state of defilement through not being used, not being cleaned, and being placed on a dusty path.
"Applying the simile" means applying the comparison as it has been presented by making it equal to the object of comparison;
the meaning is "correlating. "A person with blemish" refers to a person who, within that very existence, is one who does not become pure.
Just as a bronze vessel brought from a shop to a household becomes increasingly defiled because it fails to obtain the purification available there,
so too, he shows that a person who has departed from the household life becomes increasingly defiled because they fail to obtain the purification available through the going-forth (pabbajjā).

He said, “In a defiled bronze bowl,” and so forth. As for what is called the state of being more thoroughly defiled, it may arise either through a failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*) on the part of one who has gone forth, or through any one of the failures in conduct, view, or virtue (*ācāra-diṭṭhi-sīlavipatti*); thus, in order to show all of this collectively, he said, “Of that person,” and so forth.
For by the mention of the transgression of an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*), even certain failures in view are included.
"‘There is inclusion’ means: for one standing in this failure of livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*). By this method, it should be stated accordingly for the remaining cases as well.
This teaching of the Great Elder is common to all assemblies; therefore, it should also be applied by way of the householder.
In that context, showing the state of being even more defiled when it has reached its maximum degree, [he says]: ‘the committing of an immediate offense (*ānantariya*) such as matricide,’ etc."

He said: "Without having purified" means without having purified the continuum of the mind, which is defiled by the *kilesas*, in such a way that purity of one's own virtue (*sīla*) or view (*diṭṭhi*) might arise.
"A person capable" means a person who, through the possession of supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and so forth, is a person of purity within that particular existence (*attabhāva*).
"Making it the beginning" means he says that the cleansing by washing, scrubbing, and so on, has that [initial stage] as its starting point. "The place of purity" is where...
Or it is not sprinkled with dust. "Having performed a punitive task" means having performed a punitive task such as, "So much water or sand must be brought.
"Standing here" refers to one who stands in pure virtue (*sīla*). By means of the virtues of right conduct and practice, purification of virtue is shown;
for even through the practice of conduct, there may be the suppression of blemishes. For it is thus:
The state of being pure and cleansed in the case of a defiled bronze bowl is stated by way of a simile.
Dwelling in a remote lodging is the suppression of the defilements and the prevention of them by means of their specific antidotes. Regarding the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry...
[and so on] ...up to the realization of arahantship, in all seven instances, the phrase "like the state of being pure and cleansed" should be supplied and connected.
For one who has gone forth, purification consists, at the very least, in the purification of virtue;

or else, through dwelling in seclusion by means of application to a meditation subject, it consists in the attainment of jhāna, or in the development of insight, or in the attainment of the fruits of recluseship.
"Conducive to lust" means that which serves as a cause for the arising of lust. He says "desirable object" with reference to an object that is discordant [with one's temperament].
"In that" means in a desirable object. "One whose mindfulness has failed" means one who is muddled in mindfulness (*muṭṭhassati*). "That sign" refers to the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*).

"He will advert to it" means he will advert to it inappropriately (*ayoniso*). "By himself, unmixed with another" means here the cutting off of the continuity of wholesome states (*kusalavāra*) itself should be understood as "reviling.
"The rest" refers to the passage beginning with "with blemish, with a defiled mind," and so forth. "In accordance with the method already stated" means...

According to the method stated in the first instance. "All" refers to the entire series of similes and their correlations, beginning with the matricide and ending with the performance of an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed.
"Because of the absence of excessive separation" means because of the absence of forgetfulness; the meaning is "because of the presence of established mindfulness. "The rest" refers to... [so]...
“Non-attachment,” and so forth. According to the second section, [it is explained] by means of washing, scrubbing, soft ash, rubbing, and so on.
The passage beginning with “Who indeed... comes by way of a question, whereas this [present section] comes by way of a conclusion; this is the only difference. 60.
“Stain” (aṅgaṇa) has been elucidated there and there only by name, but not by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) or its classification (pabheda).
With reference to the analysis [of phenomena] from the perspective of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is said: "by one who wishes to make them manifest in their various modes.

"Of those that range according to desire" means of those that proceed by way of desire. "Of those that have entered" means of those that have entered into the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*).
However, because they arise there by way of conditions, they are said to be "occurring"; thus he says, "of those that occur."
“Of various kinds” means of many sorts, both by way of the diversity of objects and by way of the diversity of modes of occurrence. By which cause?
Not only the desire for gain, but rather merit and being honored and esteemed should be understood as the causes here;
showing this, he said, “And even by nature,” and so forth. Therefore, it is not just anyone who desires gain who acts in this way...
This shows that one who possesses merit generates a state of mind such that he is worthy of respect. The elders report [the offense] to the middle-ranking monks out of fear of concealing a fault;

likewise, the middle-ranking monks report it to the junior monks. However, because of their own junior status, the juniors report it to the *vighāsāda*s (those who eat leftovers) and others, saying, "Look at the deed of your elder!
The *vighāsāda*s and others [are those who live] in the presence of such a person...
“They have come for the purpose of receiving exhortation,” they announce to the bhikkhunīs. Regarding the phrase “May the bhikkhus not know me”:
the construction is “May the bhikkhus indeed not know me; oh, that the bhikkhus might not know me!

As for the expression “ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ,” here the word *kho* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), and the word *pana* is a mere ornament of speech (*vacanālaṅkāra*); thus he says, “it is certainly so.”
It is according to the method explained in the previous commentary on the section concerning the arising of desire.
Showing that the word *iti* here has the sense of an immediate cause, he says, "by this reason. And this is a reference specifically to anger and resentment.
"Of such persons" means those who are overcome by anger and resentment; this is the intended meaning.

*Anurāhoti* means in a suitable secluded place. It is precisely to show this meaning that the words "on the outskirts of the monastery" and so forth were spoken. *Purimasadisamevā* means exactly similar to the previous method of application stated in the passage beginning with "one who desires gain.

Regarding the state of being a person against whom one is charged and the charge itself, he said, "He is equal, meaning he is guilty of an offense," because the one who is charged and the one who charges share the same status by virtue of both having fallen into an offense.
Due to his desire to charge him, it must be with one who is a suitable counterpart.
The words beginning with "this" (*ayam*) were spoken in order to clarify the reason.

Furthermore, he says "moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, showing that he does not desire equality solely on account of being subject to an offense, but rather in another way as well. Or, [he thinks] "he is one who has a counterpart" (*sappaṭipuggala*) by means of another counterpart.
For he desires: "Only one who has a counterpart should accuse me," thinking, "In this way, I shall [deal] with him together with his counterparts."
Thinking, "Having become of one intention, I shall be able to say or do something against him.
However, in this context, *appaṭipuggalo* should be understood to mean that there is no rival (*paṭipuggala*) to him; thus he is "without a rival.
The connection is that the word "aho vata" is seen [in the text], because this person stands in the conduct of desire.
Because of the statement, "He should teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus," it is said, "And that too by way of seeking consent.
For the Blessed One does not intend for this to be questioned regarding any transgression in the manner of, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you...
and so forth. Nor does he intend for the path, the fruit, or insight to be made an interval—that is, for the cultivation of the path or the realization of the fruit.

He does not wish for the Blessed One to question him by making as the intervening cause either the practice of insight that has reached its peak (*sikhāppatta-vipassanā*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or even the attainment of a meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

He wishes to be questioned by way of receiving an affirmative response through such questions as "Is the permanent impermanent? and so forth; he wishes to be questioned in a manner that is straightforward.
The meaning is as follows: "He sees them bringing [it]" is the connection. Because they are incapable monks, they will expel him from the Teaching.
"That excellence" refers both to the excellence of his retinue and to the excellence of honor and respect being shown by the monks.
"Having taken it, they enjoy it" means when a distribution is being made by me. "It becomes evident of its own accord" means having gone there himself.
The intention is that she shows herself before the bhikkhus, but when a bhikkhu is staying in front, she simply goes while keeping him in her foreground.
"Dakṣiṇodaka" refers to the water for the guest-offering being brought forward from the front. Since the particle *eva* is used here, a restriction (*niyama*) is intended elsewhere;
or, taking the inclusion of the particle *eva* for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), [the sense is] "I alone shall receive it," meaning "I shall certainly receive it."
With the intention that this restriction should be understood in this way, he said: "The wish 'May I alone obtain [it]' is not a very grave offense.
Otherwise, if the restriction were taken according to the literal sense, the meaning here would be simply "Others should not obtain it.
"He is pleasing" (pāsādika) is a statement showing the reason for his being offered the best seat and so forth.

"Anumodanā" (thanksgiving) refers to a discourse on the Dhamma that should be delivered by way of expressing thanksgiving on auspicious and inauspicious occasions. "Khaṇḍānumodanā" (partial thanksgiving) refers to a portion of such a thanksgiving. This occurs at the mere utterance of the Elder, without saying, "May he who has previously been thanked give thanks.
"In such places" means in the dwelling places of those who are virtuous and learned.
"All-night discourses" (sabbarattikāni) are so called because they are delivered throughout the entire night. "Skilled in discernment" refers to those skilled in various points of doubt.
"Skilled and expert in the resolution of various questions for the removal of doubt"— when those various preachers of the Dhamma were requested to speak in turn,
he was unable to find an opportunity because he had not been requested by the one who summons for the Dhamma, thinking, "This one is competent. And they should perform it respectfully—
meaning that the monks should perform toward me such acts as salutation, rising from one's seat, joining the palms, and respectful homage.
They perform it; they should perform it with due respect. And whatever requisites they prepare for me, they should also make them beautiful and properly prepared—this is the meaning.
"Heavy" means it should be treated as weighty as a stone parasol.
"This method" refers to this method of honoring and so forth mentioned by the words "they should honor," etc. "By that" means for that reason.
The meaning is that only one who possesses specific qualities such as great learning (bāhusacca) is worthy of honor and so forth.
"Of such a kind" means of this sort, characterized by the manner described in the passage beginning with "dear and venerable.

"They would act in this way" means they would perform the aforementioned acts of honor and so forth, as described in the passage beginning with "they would honor. "This is the method" means that this very same procedure which was stated in the section on the monk applies here as well. In the sections following this...

In the sections beginning with the "Bhikkhunīvāra," the restriction should also be understood here in the same manner as explained below: "May I alone be the recipient. Regarding the excellence of the alms-food, it is by way of the condiments and so forth;
thus he says, "filled with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, and so on. [This refers to] beds, chairs, and so forth.
This is merely an illustration; for even things such as a favorable climate, sheltered spots, smooth surfaces, and closed doors, gates, windows, and so forth, constitute excellent lodgings.
Alternatively, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), those [other factors] should also be understood as included.
"In all cases" means in all four of those sets of requisites.
61. "Having seen bodily action": this does not mean that bodily action itself is cognizable by the eye;
