Therefore, he asks, wishing to clarify the reason for taking greed (*lobha*) first when showing [the defilements] by beginning with greed.
"From the first arising" means because it arises for the very first time in each respective existence.

For beings, there is indeed an attachment directed toward the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) exactly as it was obtained, just as there is a reviewing directed toward the specific attainments such as *jhāna* as they were achieved.
Therefore he said, "of all beings," and so forth. "The others as applicable" means that the others—ill-will and so on—arise according to their respective conditions.
The meaning is that there is no fixed rule for them, such that they arise immediately after this or that [state] from the very beginning, as is the case with greed.
Now, addressing the inquiry as to whether these sixteen are the only defilements of consciousness or if there are others, he says "And not only these...
and so forth, showing that there are indeed others. If this is so, why are only these many mentioned here?
Showing [the defilements] by way of their modes of manifestation, he said: "By this, however... it should be understood.

By this, it should be understood that sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, doubt, self-exaltation, disparaging others, timidity, cowardice, lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), desire for one's own welfare, evil desire, and great desire, etc., are included.
72. "Having shown the corruption" means: the corruption stated in brief by way of demonstrating the course of what is corrupted.
Having shown by way of analysis. "Showing purification": here too the method is the same. "Having known thus":

having known by means of preliminary wisdom and the wisdom of the two lower paths, according to their intrinsic nature, origin, cessation, and the means to cessation—that "covetousness is improper greed and is exclusively a defilement of the mind. "He abandons": here—

Showing that what is intended is indeed absolute abandonment (*accantappahāna*), he said: "He abandons by means of the noble path through the mode of abandonment as total eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
By "by means of the noble path" is meant by the non-returner path (*anāgāmimagga*). For it is by that [path] that abandonment is intended here in all instances.
The "sequence of defilements" (*kilesapaṭipāṭi*) here refers to the order of the teaching regarding the defilements. The "sequence of paths" (*maggapaṭipāṭi*) refers to the four noble paths.
There is the sequence of the teaching, the sequence of practicing that teaching, and the sequence of the arising of that practice.
In this context, the "sequence of defilements" refers to the demonstration of the abandonment of various defilements by various paths without regard for the order of the paths;
it is not the sequence of the arising of those defilements. Here, it is the sequence of the teaching.

Showing this, he said, “Covetousness is unrighteous greed,” and so forth. Furthermore, showing that the demonstration of the abandoning of specific defilements by whichever path they are abandoned through the successive order of the paths constitutes a demonstration of their abandonment according to the sequence of the paths,
he said, “By the stream-entry path,” and so forth.
"In this place," however, refers to this section on abandoning, which begins with the words, "But that bhikkhu, monks...

"These defilements" refers to these aforementioned defilements, whether they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry or by the remaining paths, according to the sequence of the paths shown below.
Among those, for those [defilements] to be abandoned by the third path, they are [abandoned] by the path of non-returning alone.

There is nothing further to be said regarding their abandonment. However, since the author intends to explain later the reason why those [defilements] abandonable by the lower paths are included here—while excluding those abandonable by the highest path—he asks: "Why has only that which is abandonable by the third path been taken up?
He replies: "This is the origin here, following the traditional lineage. This refers to this sutta in this context.
"In the proper place" means that which has come from the lineage of the teachers (*ācariyapaveṇi*), the path of discourse; "the source of meaning" and "the reality of the meaning"—this is the sense.
Therein, wishing to state later the reason for including here those [defilements] to be abandoned by the lower paths, he says "And that...

and so forth, showing the justification for not including those to be abandoned by the highest path (*aggamagga*). "By that" means by the fourth path. "The rest" refers to ill-will (*byāpāda*) and the others.
"Yepīti" refers to malice (*makkha*) and so forth. "Of those thoughts that originate them" means of those mental arisings that give rise to malice and the rest.
In this context, the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*) originate malice, spite (*paḷāsa*), envy (*issā*), and avarice (*macchariya*).

Specifically, one becomes deceitful and fraudulent through greed for the five strands of sensual pleasure; and such lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is abandoned without remainder only by the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*).

Therefore it was said: “Because the consciousnesses that originate them have not been abandoned. The connection is: “Those too are well-abandoned. The word “that” (taṃ) refers to the abandonment by the first path itself;
it is not linked with what precedes or follows because, in the phrase “to the extent of his [realization]” (*yathodhi kho*), the term *odhi* denotes the three paths.
The so-called “unshakable confidence in the Triple Gem” belongs to a stream-enterer, just like the virtue dear to the noble ones.
Some say that since those factors were explained later in terms of abandonment, the "abandonment" mentioned here must refer only to suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*).

However, this is merely their personal preference, because the specific abandonment of the verified confidences (*avecca-ppasāda*) has already been demonstrated by way of the aforementioned abandonment; and this point has indeed already been clarified through reasoning below.

74. Each [defilement] should be applied with each [term], because the vision of even a single defilement from its own intrinsic nature and so forth constitutes a gateway to the way out (niyyānamukha), as has been explained below.

Having spoken of abandonment by means of the non-returning path (anāgāmimagga), confidence (pasāda) was extracted; therefore it was said: "The supramundane confidence (lokuttarappasāda) has arrived by means of the non-returning path. If this is so, [then...]
Why is it said that "the mundane [faith] arises"? Because it proceeds in the manner of the expression, "Such indeed is the Blessed One," and so forth, which is mundane.

For only that confidence which has Nibbāna as its object is supramundane. By showing that the expression "Such indeed is the Blessed One," and so forth, refers to the mundane, while the expression of "unshakable confidence" (aveccappasāda) refers to the supramundane, he demonstrates a confidence that is a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. Unshakable...
Confidence that arises from knowing the qualities of the Triple Gem as they truly are is "confidence through penetration" (*aveccappasāda*).
Because it has been brought about by the Path, it is unshakable and invincible by anything; therefore, it is described as "immovable and imperishable.
In this context, the supramundane [confidence] functions by its very activity in utterly destroying delusion regarding the qualities of the Buddha and so forth.

The other [type of recollection] is by way of the object, having those as its basis. "That method" means that particular mode in which it has arisen for him. "Bases of recollection" (anussati-ṭṭhānāni) means subjects of meditation consisting of recollection (anussati-kammaṭṭhānāni). 75.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "joy and so forth," knowledge and the rest are included. Because it is a place where thieves frequently roam...
The inclusion of the word "border" (paccanta). "Reflecting" means reflecting as a king does, thinking: "In such-and-such a place, these and those thieves were destroyed in such-and-such a manner.

He shows that the word *yathā* expresses a desire for detail (*byāpani-icchā*), while the word *kho* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). "Whatever limit" (*yo yo odhi*) means "according to the limit" (*yathodhi*). *Yathā* is used in the sense of specification. *Kho* is used for restriction. Thus he demonstrates.
He said, “It is only fourfold by way of its respective categories,” and so forth. By this, he shows that the same should be understood for the terms “vomited” (*vanta*) and the rest.
To explain the meaning stated in brief as “by way of its respective categories,” he began with “two categories” (*dve odhī*), and so on.
Therein, “that which is to be abandoned by a particular path” means that which is to be abandoned without remainder by whichever path it may be. This is by way of abandoning without remainder.
For there is no admixture of the defilements to be abandoned by one particular path with those to be abandoned by other paths;

otherwise, those [defilements] which are to be abandoned by higher paths due to their respective underlying tendencies (anusaya) would already have abandoned their nature of leading to states of deprivation and so forth by the lower paths, and thus they would be mixed by way of abandonment.
Therefore, the same principle applies here as well: "by that very [path], they are abandoned. "And even beyond that" means:

Furthermore, it is "upward" because of the arising of joy from the sign of abandoning (*pahānanimitta*). Because its function operates specifically toward the opposites (*paṭipakkha*), it is called "downward" (*odhi*);
thus, the three lower paths are referred to as "downward. The passage beginning with "For those... is an exposition of the very meaning already stated.
"Of this bhikkhu" refers to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). Therefore, it was said: "abandoned by the three lower paths."
Some take even what has been vomited; it is said to be "vomited" (*vanta*) in order to show that this is not the case.

For one does not take back again that which has been vomited by oneself. Therefore he said: "by way of showing the state of not being taken up. Something that has been vomited might still be attached to the continuum (*santati*);
it is said to be "excreted" (*mutta*) in order to show that this is not the case. Therefore he said: "from the continuum..."
"By way of liberation. Even though something is liberated, it might remain somewhere like one who has been released from bonds;
to show that this is not the case, the term "abandoned" (*pahīna*) is used. Therefore he said: "By way of showing non-abiding anywhere.
Just as when something is poorly relinquished, it is called "re-relinquished" (*paṭinissaṭṭha*) once it has been properly relinquished after being taken up again.

Thus, it is called "relinquished" (*paṭinissaṭṭha*) for the purpose of showing that what was surrendered through insight (*vipassanā*)—being as if taken up—is abandoned by the Path and thereby relinquished.
Therefore he said: "by way of showing the relinquishing of what was previously taken up.
It is not relinquished behind one's back like a base person, but rather it is relinquished right in front [of the eye]; this is for the purpose of showing that.

“It has been relinquished” is what was stated. Therefore he said, “or facing toward,” and so forth. “Because it is to be approached” means because it must be attained exclusively by one who desires for oneself welfare and happiness.
“Because of upholding” means by supporting those possessed of it from falling into the states of misery (apāya).
A “book” (gantha) is called a “Veda” (veda) because “by means of this they know. One who has gone to, or entered upon, the Vedas—that is, knowledge—is a “Vedaga” (one who has reached the Vedas).
“Abhijānāti” means he would know. “Vedajātā” means those in whom joy has arisen. Knowledge is called “veda” because it is that by which one knows what is to be known.
Joy is called “veda” because it finds and experiences the flavor of the object.
“Arisen” means arisen in dependence upon verified confidence (aveccappasāda). They experience the aforementioned kind of joy as “somanassa.”
“Knowledge consisting of joy”—it is of exactly the kind thus described. *Atthaveda* means knowledge regarding the *attha* (benefit), that is, the fruit which is the result of the cause.

*Dhammaveda* means knowledge regarding the *dhamma*, that is, the cause. Therefore he said: “The cause of confirmed confidence,” and so forth. Here, the words *dhamma* and *attha* are used as synonyms for cause and fruit;
it is in order to show this meaning by means of the Pāḷi itself that he said: “For it has been said,” and so forth. That very...

"Meaning and the Dhamma": this refers to what was stated as "meaning" and "Dhamma," namely, the cause for verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*) and the aforementioned abandonment of defilements (*kilesappahāna*).
"Feeling" refers to the feeling consisting of joy and knowledge, which arises from the benefit of the aforementioned meaning and Dhamma.
"Gladness" denotes fresh rapture (*pīti*). By the phrase "by way of the mode of reviewing," it indicates reviewing.

In this context, it should be understood that it is called "Dhamma" because its intrinsic nature is blameless (*anavajja*). "Rapture arises" refers to rapture of a powerful kind that does not depend on external conditions.
"With a gladdened mind" means with a mind satisfied by sublime surges of rapture that bring about tranquility (*passaddhi*).
"The body" refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "With distress calmed" means with distress thoroughly pacified due to the removal of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*).
It is the concentration of the mind based on such reviewing that is intended here; thus he said, "it remains as if absorbed and immovable.

(76) Granted, the statement, "I am endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, I am endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, I am endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha," is also merely an exposition of the mode of occurrence of that reviewing;
however, this [latter] refers specifically to the Triple Gem.
The phrase "uppannasomanassādippakāsanapadaṃ" refers to the words that reveal the manifestation of arisen joy and so forth. The phrase "Yathodhi kho panā" (But as far as...
is also stated with the intention of revealing the specific mode of reflection; thus it was said: "Now, having revealed... [as far as] ...having revealed.
It can be understood that all four sections are stated both by way of revealing the mode of reflection and by way of showing the benefits such as joy and so forth, for both purposes.

Because it has been so stated. Even though the Noble Path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness and does not arise again, because its opposite has been thoroughly abandoned by it, one who possesses that path is said to be of a nature not subject to falling away precisely by virtue of having that morality and so forth;
thus he says, "He shows the aggregate of morality associated with his Non-Returner path," and so on. [This is seen] in such passages as, "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature."
Just as the word *dhamma* here signifies a synonym for concentration (*samādhi*), it is said: "It shows the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom.

For indeed, by making the associated mental states non-disturbed, non-dispersed, and non-distracted upon a single object, and by placing them evenly and correctly, it is worthy of being called *dhamma* because it maintains them in that way. Thus it is called *dhamma*.

"Of many kinds" (*anekarūpānaṃ*) means of various types. "Obstacle" (*antarāyo*) refers either to the non-attainment of what has not yet been attained, or to the loss of what has already been attained;
showing that neither of these two exists here, he says, "of the path," and so forth.
"That does not become an obstacle for him" means that for that non-returner, the consumption of alms-food does not become an obstacle.
Because one enjoys [the object] after having reflected with a reflection that has reached its highest excellence (*ukkaṃsagata*).
Showing that this reaching of the highest excellence for him is due to the destruction of opposing factors, he said: "Because his mind is purified by the Path.
"In this" means in this absence of obstacles. This very state of having a purified mind is the cause. And here, "neither for him..."
By this statement, "it becomes an obstacle," it is established that the aforementioned abandoning occurs precisely through the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga).
For in the case of a non-returner, sensual lust (kāmarāga) has been abandoned entirely;

because of the absence of craving for tastes (rasataṇhā), the enjoyment of such almsfood does not, in any way whatsoever, become an obstacle to the attainment of the supreme path. "Just as, monks, with a cloth... [and so forth].
Speaking thus, the Blessed One connects it to the simile of the object presented by himself at the beginning.
He says, "It is clear (*accha*)," meaning it is translucent due to its purity from impurities such as mud, moss, and algae; conversely, "it is turbid" means the opposite of that.
Regarding the cloth, he says it is "brightly shining" because it is free from defilement through its radiant color, and "luminous" because of its brilliance.
He said, "It is called 'purified' because it possesses luminosity," meaning that it attains the state of being described as "purified.
"One should bind the lamp" means one should secure the charcoal pan with a thin coating of clay or similar material so that it does not break due to pieces of wood, embers, and the like.
It is like lightning produced solely by the friction of gusts of wind from the Verambha winds after emerging from a mass of clouds.

The radiance is the radiance of a meteor; however, because that [radiance] arises due to the cause of the friction produced by the force of two currents of wind, it is therefore stated by way of its cause as "the meteor is the force of the wind.

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the sequence of connection" (*yathānusandhivasena*) and so forth: the sequence of connection that corresponds to the teaching (*desanā*) set forth is the "sequence of connection" (*yathānusandhi*).

"By way of that. For just as the demonstration of the opposite is a suitable teaching—because it correctly establishes what is to be proven—even when the teaching begins with the positive side, so too should it be understood as an "inversion of dissimilar factors" (visabhāgadhammāvatta) within the application of the method of turning back (āvattahāra).
Expanding upon the meaning briefly stated in the words, "The teaching has come down according to the sequence of connection" (yathānusandhivasena), [the author says:]
In connection with that, he said “For three,” etc., in order to show the other relevant points as well. “Externally” means regarding external objects.
“Absence of agitation” means the absence of agitation caused by craving and views.

“By way of the sutta answered” means by way of the sutta answered beginning with, “Here, a bhikkhu [regarding] someone’s...”. “By whatever state” refers to states of defilement such as impatience, etc., among the states of purification such as virtue, etc.
And by whichever state [it may be]. By the phrase "the six direct knowledges have been attained," he shows the alternative stated as "by way of a corresponding state";
by the remaining [phrases], he shows the alternative stated as "by way of the opposite. For the instruction on the simile of the saw is the opposite of impatience;
likewise, the counterpart to wrong view is the thought: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

By way of emptiness (*suññatākāra*). The same method applies to the other two as well. The teaching on defilements (*kilesa*) given below—“When the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected”—has already been presented.
“All” means without remainder. “In every way” means by every mode, such as the contemplation of danger and benefit, the recognition of the faults of individuals, and so forth.

From the statement, “Loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be developed for the abandoning of ill-will (*byāpāda*),” and so on, it follows that loving-kindness and the others [are the remedies] for ill-will, cruelty, and lustful attachment (*ratirāga*).

The opposites. Since the Blessed One, by means of the passage beginning with “He exists,” taught the attainment of the supreme path for a non-returner (anāgāmin) after bringing the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths to its culmination, he said “Now, of this... and so forth in order to demonstrate that.

Regarding the phrase “the dhammas of the divine abodes” (brahmavihāra-dhamma): it refers both to the divine abodes themselves and to the dhammas concomitant with the divine abodes. Therefore, he said, “by way of name.”
"Having determined" (vavatthapetvā) should be connected by supplying the word "having brought. For in such contexts, the term "name" (nāma) refers to the four immaterial aggregates (arūpino khandhā).

By this method, he indicates the procedure for discerning all remaining derived phenomena (upādāyadhammā) based on the primary elements (bhūta)—that is, all phenomena belonging to the three planes (tebhūmakadhammā), with the exception of craving which is to be abandoned—by way of their intrinsic nature (sabhāvato vijjamānaṃ).

Having made that a matter of personal direct experience, by virtue of its being penetrated as it truly is through knowledge, there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as it has been defined according to reality, [established] with the thought "this exists.
For this very reason, it is said: "To this extent, the definition of the truth of suffering has been accomplished by him.
And this statement is restrictive; it is not like the conventional designations of the world, such as "being," "woman," or "man," which [do not apply] beyond this.

That which is conceptualized by outsiders—such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth, or substance (*dravya*) and so forth, or the soul (*jīva*) and so forth, or the body (*kāya*) and so forth—does not exist in the ultimate sense;

rather, it is said that "it truly exists. "He understands" means that first, in the preliminary stage, he understands in various ways by way of characteristics, functions, and so forth, as well as by way of the classification of the factors to be received;
subsequently, however, he understands while penetrating [reality] by way of the clear realization of full comprehension (*pariññā-abhisamaya*).
"Exclusively inferior" refers to unwholesome states because they are the root of suffering both in the present and in the future; therein, craving is especially so.
Thus it is said: "Piercing the origin of suffering, one understands: 'There is that which is inferior.
Because it has been brought to a state of preeminence by its own conditions, the Noble Path itself is called "exquisite" (paṇīta) in this sense.

He said: "Investigating the means of abandonment, one understands that there is something sublime. If it were stated [simply] as "sublime in the sense of being supreme," the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca) might also be included;
however, since that is already included by another term, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already explained.

Because the application of insight has been made specifically through the gateway of the immeasurables (appamaññā), it is said: "connected with the perception of the divine abodes" (brahmavihāra-saññāgata).
It has been said: it is indeed appropriate to say, "of all that belongs to the three planes and is associated with perception.

And there is no exclusion here, because that perception also has arrived [at that state]. It is said, "Nibbāna is the further escape," because one stands having transcended, surpassed, emerged from, and become dissociated from the world.
"By way of four aspects" means by way of the four modes beginning with "there is the inferior.

He shows that the sense of knowing through insight-wisdom—which consists in subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*) and is of the nature of awakening—and the sense of seeing through path-wisdom—which consists in the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*) and is of the nature of penetration—are established by their own intrinsic nature.
Thus he says: "Because of knowing the four truths through insight-wisdom and [seeing them] through path-wisdom..."

It is said: "seen. By the phrase "in the same manner as stated in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*," he refers [to that sutta] by way of analogy, because the reading here is similar to the reading of the meaning-words and meanings stated by himself in the commentary on the *Bhayabherava Sutta*.

Thus he says: "He understands: 'The mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire... pe... the mind is liberated even from the taint of ignorance. And herein, since it is said: "The mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire... pe... the mind is liberated even from the taint of ignorance," [the meaning follows accordingly].
By saying “Birth is exhausted,” and so forth, the Blessed One pointed out the fourth path;
therefore, it should be understood that what was stated earlier in the commentary—“And that is appropriate because it points specifically to the fourth path”—is indeed well-said.
“For the purpose of challenging him” means that the Blessed One said to that brahmin, for the purpose of challenging himself, “Ask me.”
Regarding the challenge, "O Brahmin, whatever you have intended here with your mind," the intention is for the purpose of granting him an opportunity.

Since the Brahmin lacks such an underlying disposition (ajjhāsaya) as a support for the teaching—because he is devoid of the three aforementioned connections—it is said, "he stated a separate connection.
[The term] "internally" is used because it has entered the mind. [The phrase] "by the bath that emerges from the defilements" means...
By means of the bath of the water of the Noble Eightfold Path, which washes away the stains of the defilements and acts as a means to pacify the fever of passion and other afflictions;
thinking that she had arrived from the Bāhukā River because she had just now approached the pavilion of the assembly of the Dhamma;
[and] by the removal of the oily moisture through the powder of the crushing of the fruits of the Noble Ones, her roughness toward the world was removed. That [roughness] belongs to her.

"It exists" is what is conventionally accepted as "the world" (*loka*). By the inclusion of the term "conventionally accepted by the world," he illustrates his own false apprehension occurring in the form: "In that way, that river is well-known in the world.
Therefore he said: "It is so accepted because it bestows purity.
Because it brings about prosperity in future lives and so forth through the removal of evil, it is beneficial to the world (*lokya*); thus it is "accepted as *lokya*."
Everything is the same as before. Therefore he said: “It is so designated because it leads to the supreme world.
“Designated as merit” (puññasammatā) means they are designated as “merit” (puñña) because they nourish and purify beings by producing the fruits of a state of being worthy of honor (pujja).

“Precisely for the purpose of illustrating its meaning” means precisely for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of that teaching which was previously presented. [Question: What is the purpose of restating the very meaning already stated?

He said, "For those who delight in verses. Those who do not value prose (cuṇṇika-vacana) and do not understand the meaning when it is spoken in that way, but who value verse-explanations (pajjava-vacana) and understand it when it is spoken in that way, are "those who delight in verses.

"For the purpose of illuminating a specific meaning" means for the purpose of illuminating a distinction; the sense is that it is for the purpose of illuminating something other than the previous teaching.
Since it was stated previously, “Does the venerable Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe?,” the word *bāhukaṃ* alone is what indicates that meaning here.
The remaining words, such as *adhikakka*, etc., indicate specific meanings because they clarify a meaning distinct from that [previous statement].
But why were the words *adhikakka*, etc., not spoken by the Brahmin to the Blessed One here?
He said, “They have been taken,” and so forth with the words “Just as indeed. *Kakka* refers here to bathing paste;
it is called *adhikakka* because they take an abundance of paste there after having bathed. Therefore he said, “By way of the materials for bathing,” and so forth.
*Maṇḍalavāpisaṇṭhānaṃ* means having the shape of a circular lotus pond. *Nadiyo* means separate rivers, not merely bathing places like *adhikakka* and the rest.
"By three terms" means by the terms *Sundarikā*, *Payāga*, and *Bāhukā*. "Four" refers to the four beginning with *Adhikakka*.
"Are indeed stated" means that they possess a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇatā*) according to the intention of the Brahmin, based on the characteristic recognized by the world;

however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), they have a single characteristic because they share the characteristic of carrying away evil (*pāpapavāhalakkhaṇa*). Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth. [Regarding] some purification from evil...
They do not even perform it. For one does not cause that person to purify [the deed] unless one purifies it oneself.
"Not having reached the state of enmity or transgression" means not having reached the status of a course of kamma (*kammappatha*). Therefore he said, "by minor ones.
"Refuting" means warding off that view by demonstrating its inappropriateness. Herein, this is the method of refutation:
Just as any descent into water does not wash away evil, so too any astrological conjunction [does not do so], because there is no counteragent to the causes of evil.
For that which destroys something is its counteragent— just as light is the counteragent to darkness and knowledge is the counteragent to ignorance—
but neither descent into water nor an astrological conjunction is a counteragent to the causes of evil, such as greed and the rest.
Therefore, one must reach the conclusion here that "bathing in water and the like do not wash away evil.

"The Phagguṇī constellation is constant" means the intention is that for one whose virtue and so forth are pure, every day is indeed an auspicious day. "The other" refers to one who is impure by way of virtue and so forth.
"Always the Uposatha" is because of having observed the Uposatha in the manner of the noble ones (ariya-uposatha). "Of the pure" means of one whose mental conduct is completely purified.
"Of one who has performed purification" means one whose conduct of body and speech is completely pure. Therefore he said, "by way of being free from defilement," and so forth.
"Connected with the wholesome" means having attained a state free from fault. "The undertaking of vows" refers to the undertaking of the ascetic practices (*dhutanga*) and so on;
it is accomplished, meaning there is no failure in it. "Bathe in my teaching alone, if you desire absolute purity."
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Therefore, he said "if," and so forth. "Security" (*khemataṃ*) means the state of being secure.
"Act in such a way that all beings attain security—that is, attain fearlessness—through the power of asceticism":

thus, by briefly instructing the brahmin in the aforementioned cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables], the perfection of concentration and the perfection of wisdom, which are inseparable from it, are indicated for him.
And it should be understood that [purity] has been shown. Therefore he said: “Purity of the mind-door has been shown.
Furthermore, in order to show the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) which serves as the support for that twofold perfection, he said: “If you do not speak falsely,” and so forth.

And here, by means of the statements regarding abstinence from false speech, killing, and taking what is not given—beginning with “If you do not speak falsely”—[the perfection of virtue is indicated].
By the method of taking the characteristic (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*), the abstention from the remaining bodily and verbal misconduct is also already stated;

likewise, by the very application of the perfection of the wealth of faith and so forth in the phrase "one who has faith and is not stingy," the application of the perfection of the remaining noble wealth (*ariyadhana*) is also established.
Thus, the qualities that ripen liberation—faith and the rest—are indeed revealed for the brahmin.

It should be understood thus. For this very reason it was said: "By this very practice there is purification from the defilements. The intention is that Gayā is more highly esteemed even than the Bāhukā and other such rivers.
80. "Alone" means without a companion; however, this state of being alone for him is due to his solitary nature (*ekībhāva*), for his companionship with craving has not yet departed.
Therefore it was said: "Before long," and so forth. By the mention of "alone" itself, his physical seclusion (*vūpakkaṭṭhatā*) is expressed.

He said: "Withdrawn by way of mental seclusion. By this, he refers to the practice of wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga) as it has been set forth in such passages as "by walking and sitting during the day," and so on.

For one who has become thus, seeing the three realms of existence (bhava) as ablaze with the eleven fires, he strives rightly, cultivating the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in such a way that not even a trace of negligence remains. With a mind indifferent toward anything conditioned (saṅkhāra), [he applies himself].
The passage beginning with "Appamatto" (heedful) was spoken to show that he dwelt solely intent upon Nibbāna.
Regarding the verses beginning with "Khīṇā jāti" (Birth is destroyed), whatever needs to be said has already been stated above. The remainder is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Vatthasutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the Sallekha Sutta 81.
"Cunda" is the name of that great elder; however, out of respect, he is called Mahācunda, just as [Moggallāna] is called Mahāmoggallāna.
Or else, it is in reference to his own nephew, the elder named Cunda, that this was said of the Venerable Sāriputta.
This great elder brother was known as "Mahācunda," just as [another] was known as "Mahāpanthaka.

Regarding the phrase "in the evening time" (*sāyanhasamayaṃ*), he says "at the time of evening" (*sāyanhakāle*) because the accusative case here functions as a locative. For absolute contact (of the sun) with this [time] is not possible here.
By "the seven formations" (*sattasaṅkhārehi*), he means both the beings—such as co-residents, pupils, and lay followers—and the formations such as visible objects and so forth.
*Paṭinivattitvā* means having retreated. *Nilīyanaṃ* means seclusion, which is the state of being detached from both body and mind.
For "solitude" (*ekībhāvo*) refers to physical seclusion, while "withdrawal" (*paviveko*) refers to mental seclusion.

*Tato vuṭṭhito* means having emerged from that twofold seclusion, either through the arising of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) or by meeting with fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*). *Abhivādāpetvā* means having caused [the other] to perform a salutation.
"Thus" means by way of the aforementioned salutation. "Having raised up" means having lifted [the mind]. One might ask: "Let such salutation be for those whose roots of existence are not yet severed;
but what is its purpose for those whose roots of existence are severed? To this he says: "This is the custom of the Tathāgatas.
By this, it is shown that the Tathāgatas do not wish for the welfare of beings only in the future life, but rather also in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
It should be understood. As for the reason why the Tathāgatas speak thus, he states the cause therein: “For they desire happiness,” and so forth.
“Multitudes of beings” (puthukāyā) means many groups of sentient beings. “Yakkhas” means deities; for they are called “yakkhas” because they are worthy of worship.
“They speak” (abhivadanti) means that they address the very object they intend by turning toward it with wisdom and compassion.
Since what has been grasped [by various views] occurs without restriction, he says "these" while showing them as restricted.

And since "these" is a word referring to what is near and present, he says "as if making them face him"; the meaning is that he makes each respective speculative view, which resides in the mind, as if it were right before his eyes.
Showing that the term "views" (diṭṭhiyo) is stated in the Pāli by means of eliding the first member of the compound, he says "wrong views" (micchādiṭṭhiyo).
Arising among beings when there is a mental state of wrong view, or arising by taking beings as its object, it is said to "manifest among beings.
By the doctrine of self (*attavāda*) means by a statement occurring with reference to a self.
"Associated" means associated by way of being the object both in the grasping and the act of grasping [the notion] that "there is a self," by one who holds wrong views.
When those who grasp a view are grasping it in its acquisition and its teaching, the view becomes associated with the proponent of the view because the view is the object of that doctrine.

The view occurring as "there is a self" is here associated with the doctrine of self (*attavāda*), but the self is not the object of that [view]. And that [view] is associated with the doctrine through its state of being the object, by virtue of the doctrine proceeding in such a manner.

"Associated with worldly doctrines" (*lokavādappaṭisaṃyutta*)— *Note: This passage discusses the technical usage of the term "associated" (*paṭisaṃyutta*) in the context of views (*diṭṭhi*). It distinguishes between the view itself, the doctrine (*vāda*) which articulates it, and the actual entity (the self) which may or may not be the objective referent.*
The same principle applies here as well. Beyond that, there are twenty [views], because of the absence of any basis for the doctrine of self (*attavāda*).

For even among the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), each one is individually grasped as "self"; it is from grasping them in this way—by way of being the support for a self—that these views arise.
However, apart from these, there is no object nor any mode of grasping a self that exists independently of them. Thus: "The self is eternal... and so forth.

And regarding the phrase "the world": having grasped one among [the aggregates] such as form and so forth as either "self" or "the world," one holds it to be eternal, existing at all times, permanent, and stable.
As it is said: "One who propounds a self and a world propounds that 'the self and the world are possessed of form and are eternal,'" and so forth.

Among the terms beginning with "eternal," the first is a grasping of a self by way of the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*), the second by way of the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and the third...

The grasping at a self that proceeds by way of partial-eternalism, or the fourth [type] which proceeds by way of speculative reasoning, or which proceeds by way of the "eel-wriggling" (amarāvikkhepa), is the grasping at a self. "Finite" is by way of its own limitation;

"infinite" is by way of its lack of limitation. "Both finite and infinite" is by way of both those [alternatives], while the other is the grasping at a self that proceeds by way of speculative reasoning.
The construction is: "Because it proceeds in this way, there are eight.
"The very beginning" means the initial act of attention (*manasikāra*). Showing its specific nature, he says: "the very first act of attention mixed with insight (*vipassanā*).
By the restrictive phrase "even without reaching the stream-entry path," he shows what is excluded. From the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda*)...

From the beginning up to the observation of rise and fall—this is what is intended here by "initial attention" (*ādimanasikāra*), because it constitutes the commencement of the cultivation of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
And because it is accompanied by the contemplation of rise and fall, its description as being "mixed with insight" (*vipassanāmisseta*) is appropriate.
The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) is a synonym for "by this much means alone," meaning by the aforementioned initial attention. "Of these" (*etāsaṃ*)...
[This refers to] the views associated with the theories of self (attavāda) and theories of the world (lokavāda) as previously described.
Granted that their abandonment indeed occurs through that [path] by way of "partial eradication" (*tadaṅgavasena*), yet that is not what is intended here; therefore, he asks:

how can there be both abandonment and relinquishment by way of "complete eradication" (*samucchedavasena*)? [The answer is: because all fetters have been completely eradicated, even while being free from overestimation (*anadhimānika*). "The noble Dhamma..."
"Adhimāna" is the conceit "I have attained. Those who possess this are "adhimānikā" (those with overweening pride).

The arising of overweening pride through the attainment of the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbayañāṇa*), and the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that culminates in that [attainment], is what is intended here. Because of that, there is no abandoning of views;
it is for the purpose of establishing this point that he asks the question: "He asks for the sake of abandoning overweening pride. "Is it only at the beginning...? etc.

By saying, "there is relinquishment," as if he were one who has not yet attained realization, he appears as if established in overweening pride; thus it is said, "acting like one possessed of overweening pride.
"He" refers to the Elder. "For their sake" means for the sake of his own pupils, so that they might be freed from this wrong grasp by the Blessed One.
It is said that the Elder, like the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), was together with his own pupils.
He approached the Blessed One.
82. *Yattha* is the locative case used in the sense of a domain (*visaya*). For this is a demonstration of the object (*ārammaṇa*) of views.
Since the aggregates alone are both the plane of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of views and the place where they manifest (*samudācaraṇa*), he said: "And wherein these views..."

The phrase beginning with "they arise" is said with reference to the five aggregates. "Having adhered to form" means having adhered by way of adherence through views, thinking, "This form is my self," and having taken it as an object.

For it is while adhering that view arises, making that [form] its object. In such passages as "That is the self," this refers to form comprised of the eye and so forth, because of its being the basis for the arising of consciousness.

“That is my self; what is pleasant and unpleasant here is experienced by it, therefore it is the world (loka). ‘I shall exist as that very same [self] after passing away in the next world’—in such a state it is permanent (*nicca*);

in its steadfastness it is stable (*dhuva*); because it is always present it is eternal (*sassata*); and because it is changeless it is of an unchanging nature (*avipariṇāmadhamma*)—this is the meaning.
If this was said with reference to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*), how can there be the singular number? To this he says: ‘By way of the object (*ārammaṇa*), etc.’”
“Nānākaraṇaṃ” means that by which something is made different; it is a distinction. “By way of birth” (jātivasena) means by way of arising.
For those things that have not previously been produced, when they arise, they receive a conventional designation because they possess a transformation known as origination.
Therefore he said, “by way of birth,” and so forth. “Cultivated again and again” (punappunaṃ āsevitā) refers to successive births within beginningless saṃsāra.
“Having acquired the habit. By this, he distinguishes the sense of “latent tendency” (*anusaya*) from the sense of “cultivation” (*bhāvanā*) regarding the defilements.

“Becoming firm” means having reached a state of strength. By this, he shows the latent tendencies in terms of their intrinsic nature. Furthermore, “becoming firm” is the unique, specific nature of sensual lust and the other defilements;
for it has been said: “One abandons the latent tendencies when they have become firm. “Not yet eradicated” refers to [the defilements] by way of eradication through cutting off (*samuccheda-vinaya*).
They have not been removed. For it is said that defilements which have not been abandoned and have become firmly rooted are "latent tendencies" (*anusenti*).

By this, he shows that they are capable of arising when their conditions are obtained. "They manifest" (*samudācaranti*) means they overcome [the mind]. By this, he shows that they have reached the stage of transgression.
Furthermore, by the word "they arise" (*uppajjanti*), the state of full obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) is shown.

"Object consisting of the fivefold division of the aggregates" refers to that object of views described by the passage beginning, "Wherein these views arise," which is the fivefold division of the aggregates—
such as the form-aggregate of clinging— that serves as the objective support for those views.
"This is not mine" means that this pentad of aggregates does not belong to me as my property, nor does it exist as a source of attachment or a hindrance for me.

Because it lacks the quality of being graspable. By this, he rejects its status as an object of craving from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), due to its being merely temporary and so forth.
"I also am not this"—this refers to the differentiation of the five aggregates;
the meaning is that "I" is not something to be grasped as "this. By this, he rejects its status as an object of conceit, because of its being impermanent, suffering, loathsome, and so forth.
"This is not my self" because of the absence therein of the nature of a self, and because of the absence of anything that could be grasped as "mine" in the sense of being a possession or a fetter.

"Grasping by craving" (*taṇhā-gāha*) means that by means of this [craving], one grasps "this is mine. "Grasping that" means producing that [grasping]. Therefore he said: "the proliferation of craving" (*taṇhā-papañca*).
"He grasps. It is called *papañca* because it proliferates the continuum and causes beings to linger long in *saṃsāra*.

"Of the kind already described" means of the kind consisting of the eight hundred variations of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*). The intention is that he rejects the *papañca* of craving by demonstrating that the pentad of aggregates lacks the status of being a basis for craving.
This same method applies to the two subsequent phrases as well. "Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*)...
They are "to be abandoned by the abandoning of views. By this, he shows that they are to be destroyed by the first path.
However, craving alone is "conjoined with views," not conceit; and that [craving] is only that which leads to states of deprivation (apāya).

One sees "as it really is" when one sees according to how things exist—that is, in the manner of impermanence, suffering, foulness, and non-self. Therefore, he said: "The pentad of aggregates," and so forth.

"By this very mode" means by the very modes such as being subject to deformation (*ruppana*), impermanence (*anicca*), and so forth. "Even while being grasped" refers to those whose perversions (*vipallāsa*) have not been abandoned.

"By that mode" means by the mode of "this is mine" (*etaṃ mama*) and so forth. "There is none at all" is because of the absence of those perversions regarding the vision of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).
"Of one who sees clearly" means of one who sees thoroughly and pre-eminently, in such a way that it need not be seen again in that same manner.
The abandoning of views does not occur through mere initial attention; rather, for those who are conceited, this [initial] vision is merely a form of conceit.
Explaining the meaning that "this occurs only through the Path," he said: "having shown the abandoning of views by means of the stream-entry path.
"Analyzing" means analyzing the jhānas of those who are conceited by way of their lack of refinement (*asallekhabhāva*). [This refers to] ordinary worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*).
It does not arise because it lacks an agent. It is not [a fault] for noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) because the condition of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) has been abandoned by them.
It does not enjoin one to what is improper, since it enjoins one only to a suitable subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The Elder said: "Whatever purpose the Saṅgha summons one for, that purpose is accomplished here for those who have come and gone while residing there."
Though he was sent by the Saṅgha up to three times, he did not go because of his lack of respect; thus [the Buddha] said, "What is this? and so forth.
For a wise person performs only his own duty in such matters; therefore, he dispatched a certain elder who had gone forth late in life.
"What is this?"—he spoke thus, showing his concern for the matter of not carrying out the Saṅgha’s command, asking, "What indeed is this? He was more than sixty years old.
One who perceives what is not attained as attained is considered to have passed sixty years [of the rains-residence].
Because those who are virtuous associate with the virtuous due to their shared inclinations, the Elder said, "Well done, friend," and performed everything, including the mounting of the elephant.
"Just like him" means exactly like the Elder mentioned immediately before—one who perceives what is not attained as attained and is thus considered to have passed sixty years.
The meaning is as follows. "A cluster of lotuses" (*padumagumba*) refers to a thicket of water-lilies. He entered the palace [thinking]:

"If he were to look around freely, his state as a worldling (*puthujjana*) would be revealed by himself. It is said that at that time, in the Tissamahāvihāra, the elder monks, honoring the words "one's own mind becomes serene," swept the courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) early in the morning and [experienced] such an object of meditation as the joy inspired by the Buddha.
Having generated [this thought], they act accordingly day after day. Therefore it is said, “And at that time,” and so forth.

“Dhammadinna, here he sets down his bowl and robes”—even though he was neither a speaker of such things nor one who had been asked anything by way of hospitality, he acted as if he knew their virtue, just as one might know the virtue of a well in its capacity to provide openings for diving and so on. But you did not know this.
Because he did not even perform the duties of a guest. What kind of agreement (katikā) of the Saṅgha could possibly override the Teacher’s command?
Furthermore, an agreement must be observed without contradicting the training rules (sikkhāpada). "I have no association with those who do not know even this much," he said, and leaped into the air.
As for his thought, "I dwell in effacement (sallekha)," it was as if he were thinking, "May I enter and dwell in the first jhāna."

It has been said: "For that bhikkhu, it is possible that through the conceit of thinking, 'I dwell by means of that very refinement which refines away the defilements through the method of practice known as the first jhāna,' such a state might occur.
This is how the connection here should be understood. "That is not fitting" refers to that [claim] of one possessed of conceit, according to the analysis.
The reflection, "The first jhāna is effacement," is not tenable; it is not logical. Therefore he said, "For it is not," and so forth.

In that context, *sallekha* (effacement) is that which thoroughly and completely scrapes away (*likhati*) the defilements; it is the Noble Path. Insight (*vipassanā*) as the means to that [path] is the practice of effacement (*sallekha-paṭipadā*).
Furthermore, the jhāna which serves as the basis for insight also serves, by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāyena*), as the basis for the path.
It indeed exists. Therefore he said, “Because it brings about insight,” and so forth.
“By way of the factors of jhāna” means by way of the five jhāna factors beginning with applied thought (vitakka).

Although jhāna occurs many times by way of individual moments of consciousness, because it possesses a single adverting [consciousness] and is included within a single cognitive process (vīthi), it is considered a single attainment; thus [it is said]: “Again and again...”
It is said, "by way of attainment. Since the four formless jhānas proceed each upon its own respective object, he says, "due to the absence of a difference in object.
"By means of the two preceding reasons alone" refers to the two types of reasons previously mentioned:
"by way of the jhāna factors" and "by way of repeated attainment."

The factors of those formless jhānas are "peaceful" because they are extinguished by the absence of the fever of the defilements, and their objects are "subtle" due to the excellence of their development.
Therefore, "by way of them" means that those jhānas are peaceful on account of those [factors and objects];
thus it is said: "These abidings are peaceful. "Of all four of them" refers to all four of those formless jhānas.
83. He—namely, that conceited bhikkhu, or another such as an external ascetic or wanderer—is not truly comprehending.
In this context, the conceited one does not comprehend because he perceives what has not been attained as attained;
the other does not because it is outside his domain. "In which" means in which subject of effacement, by way of the forty-four modes beginning with non-violence.
The eight attainments (*aṭṭha samāpattiyo*) are those states that proceed by way of suppressing the defilements (*kilesa*), becoming increasingly peaceful and sublime;

mundane states such as non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) and so forth are not like that. In this regard, the objector, wishing to clarify the point as to why only non-violence and the rest are described as being of the nature of effacement (*sallekha*) and not the others, asks, "But why? and so forth. The other [responds]: "Granted..."

The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are by nature peaceful and sublime; however, because they serve as a basis for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), they are not the practice of effacement (*sallekha-paṭipadā*) regarding the defilements.

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) and the like, on the other hand, are practices that lead to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) and are thus the practice of effacement. Clarifying this point, [the author] said: "Because they have the supramundane as their basis," and so forth.
By means of this very sutta, which demonstrates the distinction between non-harming and the rest compared to the eight attainments, [it is shown how] it is more fruitful...
That variety of types should be understood. For this is said with reference to the greater fruitfulness of the offering due to the greater worthiness of the recipient;

such is the connection. Anticipating the objection, "But is it not stated there that he is 'practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry,' and not that he has 'gone for refuge'?", [the author] says, "From the moment of going for refuge," and so forth. For this has been stated:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: “Even a lay follower who has gone for refuge at the very least is one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.

For when someone, desiring to transcend the suffering of the round of existence, goes for refuge to the Triple Gem with a confident mind, that act serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the higher training in virtue and the rest, and will eventually lead to the attainment of the path of vision.
"An object for violence, etc. means that which we call the object of violence and so forth; "in this object for violence, etc. [is the locative].
"And the extreme wrong view, as well as the initial wrong view among the wrong states"—this is stated with reference to the sequence of the teaching.
"Mixing together" means making them into one by way of their commonality as wrong views. "In that manner" refers to how...
Having combined the wrong view mentioned at the beginning and end of the paths of action with the wrong views stated at their conclusion, [the text] brings together this meaning as a single unit;
likewise, it concludes with the right view stated at the end of those same paths.

"A living being" (*pāṇa*) refers, in conventional usage, to a sentient being, and in the ultimate sense, to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "They deprive of life" means they cause that which has the inherent nature of falling [to perish] by means of their own power.
They cause it to fall prematurely; or, having passed beyond [the boundary], they overcome it with weapons and the like and cause it to fall.
*Adinnaṃ* means the property of another. *Ādiyantī* means they take. *Sallekhati* means he scrapes evenly; the meaning is that he abandons.

This is a discussion of the path of kamma, hence it is called "the destroyer of welfare. It is *pisuṇā* because it makes [relationships] empty of what is dear (*piya-suñña-karaṇato*); it grinds (*pisati*).
She is called *pisuṇā* because she harms other beings. *Pharusā* means harsh; the sense is that she is cruel. *Niratthakaṃ* means devoid of purpose, being free from benefit for oneself and others.
*Micchā* means perverted, occurring by way of [wrong views] such as permanence and so forth. *Pāpikā* means blameworthy.

Because they are exclusively unwholesome, they are censured by the wise, such as the Buddha and others. *Natthi dinnaṃ* and so forth refers to those [views] which have "there is no giving" and so on as their basis.

He speaks of wrong view with ten bases. Its inclusion within the course of action (kammappatha) occurs precisely through its reaching the status of a course of action by way of adherence to the state of non-existence (*natthika-bhāva*).
The self-view (*attadiṭṭhi*) that proceeds in the manner of "form is the self," and so forth, is a non-leading view (*aniyyānika-diṭṭhi*) because it acts as an obstacle to the Path.
It is included within the category of the false (*micchatta*) precisely because of its non-leading nature. "Right" (*samma*) means non-perverted (*aviparīta*).

For that very reason, they are "beautiful" (*sobhana*) and "excellent" (*sundara*), being praised by the wise because they are extolled by the Buddha and others. The rest here should be understood according to the method explained under wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

Because they grasp aspects such as beauty in things like the foul (*asubha*), they are "not-according-to-reality" (*ayāthāvā*) and "not leading to liberation" (*aniyyānika*) due to their arising through improper attention (*ayoniso*). They are "unwholesome" (*akusala*).

“Unreal, non-leading-out, and unwholesome intentions. By this phrase, he extends the application (*atidisa*) of the meaning of "unreal," etc., to various other instances through such expressions as “unreal, non-leading-out, and unwholesome speech,” and so forth.
Here, “speech” (*vācā*) is intended as volition (*cetanā*); likewise for action and livelihood.
Because it mostly proceeds by way of recollecting the past, it is said: “for one who thinks about the past.”
It has been said. For it is said in the world: "That abundant wealth which I once possessed has, however, been largely exhausted through negligence.

By "that which resembles mindfulness" (*satipatirūpaka*) means by that which resembles the arising of mindfulness as described thus: "one remembers what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
"Arising" (*uppatti*) means the arising of consciousness (*cittuppatti*). For the occurrence of a state of consciousness in such a manner is wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*).
Furthermore, that [unwholesome thought] arises either through anger, as in one who harbors resentment thinking, "He reviled me, he struck me," and so forth;
or through lust, as in one who recollects with a sense of beauty according to the method described: "He recalls those former instances of laughing, talking, and playing with women";
or through views, as in one who thinks, "That self of mine is permanent and eternal," and so forth.
"Of one who adheres wrongly" and so forth should be understood as occurring in such a manner.
"By way of thinking about means" refers to the mode of reviewing after having committed an evil deed— either for the sake of remorse, by way of reflecting on the arrangement of tools such as nets,
traps, and snares, or for the sake of joy, thinking "I have done well"— by way of considering the propriety [of the act].

Delusion is ignorance (*aññāṇa*). In this context, however, there is a figurative usage of the term "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), similar to the expression "auspicious" (*siva*) being used for what is "inauspicious" (*asiva*).

Nevertheless, because its intrinsic nature is erroneous, it is specifically called "wrong knowledge" (*micchā-ñāṇa*). The nineteenfold reviewing-knowledge is called "right knowledge" (*sammā-ñāṇa*) because it is a correct observation;
other reviewing-knowledges, such as those regarding the jhānas and so forth, are included within right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) itself.

Merely by having attained the meditative absorptions of the fine-material and immaterial realms, they remain entirely unliberated from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), yet they perceive themselves thus: "We are liberated.

They perceive liberation where there is no liberation—namely, in what is designated as the knowledge of the interval between ordinary men; in the persistence of one's own selfhood devoid of qualities;
or in the state of sharing the same world (*salokatā*) with a Great Brahmā, which consists in being joined to his proximity.
It is "evil" because it is base due to its being exclusively unwholesome. It is "perverted" because it is not according to reality.

"In the manner stated" means by the way described as "being indeed unliberated. In such passages as "we shall here be of right view," etc., the right view of the fruit and so forth are also included within the category of the right view of the path and so forth;
this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "they should be understood as associated with the fruit," and so on.

It has been said. However, there is no contradiction whatsoever in referring to all the states of fruition as "liberation" (*vimutti*) because they are included within the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*).
Here, regarding the basis for effacement known as right liberation (*sammāvimutti*):

if they are stated by way of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), then it is for this reason that only three are mentioned, beginning with the words "one who is covetous" (*abhijjhālu*). [These] have reached the state of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
"Overcome by sloth and torpor. That phenomenon whose presence makes them "excited" is called restlessness;
thus he said, "endowed with restlessness means they are excited. "Discriminating" means determining any nature whatsoever, such as "this is Dhamma" or "this is non-Dhamma," and so forth.
"Habitually resentful" means having the habit of following after the mind of another.
“They utter” means they are envious. “They are deceitful” means they are fraudulent, those who represent themselves as one way when they are actually another.
Since they do not speak according to reality, it is said: “it is meant that they do not speak rightly.
“By the method of the opposite of what was stated” means by the method of the contrary meaning to what was stated [in the preceding verses], such as “not wrathful, but free from wrath,” and so forth.
Because they grasp in opposition and hold contrary views toward these [teachings], their speech is painful; thus they are called "difficult to speak with" (*dubbaca*).

Furthermore, because they are not patient with such speech, it is said: "painful to speak to," and so forth. They are "evil" (*pāpaka*) because of their base conduct or because they bring about suffering.

"By way of the non-Dhamma" means by way of the qualities of an unworthy person (*asappurisa*). By way of being distinguished from oneself, there are the bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) and so forth.

Just as there is the state of being a door for bodily action and so forth, so too, by reason of their possession of unwholesome qualities (*asaddhamma*) such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*), these very things—lack of faith and the rest—are called "unwholesome qualities" (*asaddhamma*). With reference to them, he says, "They have no faith in these," just as one says they are "of poor wisdom.
Those who have heard little of the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth, are "of little learning" (*appassuta*); [this is] by way of what has been heard.

This is untenable. By the phrase "to be grasped as 'there is not'," he shows that this word *appa-* has the sense of non-existence, as in such expressions as "*appa-daṃsa-makasa-vāta-ātapa-sarīsapasamphassānam*" (free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles). Because they do not undertake right practice, they are base and censurable;
they sink and sink down into the side of defilement, thus they are *kusītā* (lazy)—the letter *da* having been changed to *ta*. [They are so called] for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states.
Those who possess energy that has been initiated and exerted for the attainment of wholesome states are "those of aroused energy" (āraddhavīriyā).
Those whose mindfulness (sati) is lost and ruined through non-arousal are "those of muddled mindfulness" (muṭṭhassatī). "Corrupted" means defiled.
Regarding "of poor wisdom" (duppaññā), the state of being corrupted is the state of being destroyed by its opposite; thus it is said, "it means their wisdom is ruined. Below...

Because right view is included by the mention of "right view" through both the wisdom of the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā-paññā*) and the right view of the path (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*), and because here the requisites for insight (*vipassanāsambhāra*)—namely, faith and the rest—are extracted as being accompanied by being easy to speak to and having virtuous friends, it is said: "Here, the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) is to be understood.
Therefore he says: "For it is a requisite for insight," and so forth. He shows that this meaning should be accepted even without regard for formal logical consistency (*yutti*).
He said: "The command of the ancients.
It creates an obstacle for supramundane qualities; that is, it creates an obstacle to the attainment of supramundane qualities. *Sandiṭṭhim*:
one's own view (*saṃ* = *attano diṭṭhiṃ*), or whatever view has been grasped by oneself—this is the meaning. Having transcended its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvaṃ*).
*Parāmāsī* means grasping from others. *Daḷhaggāhī* means one who holds firmly, grasping with the conviction, "This alone is the truth.

*Paṭinissaggī* means one who relinquishes. *Kummova* means just as a tortoise, when touched by anyone regarding its limbs such as its feet, withdraws all its limbs into its own shell and does not extend them outward; even so, this person [thinks], "It is not good for you..."
When told, "It is a crocodile; let it go," he did not release it. Keeping it right there within his own heart, he spoke thus.
"The crocodile-grasp" means the crocodile-seizure. "They grasp" means they hold fast so that the crocodiles do not release what has been caught.
84. “In this way, by forty-four modes” means by the forty-four types beginning with non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Why, then, is non-harming mentioned first here? Because it is the root of all virtues. For “non-harming” is a designation for compassion (*karuṇā*);
and that is specifically the fundamental cause of virtue (*sīla*), because it causes one to desist from immorality (*dussīlya*) characterized by injury to others.
For just as the taking of life is characterized by the harming of others, so too is the seizing of another’s property; indeed, the seizure of wealth is even more grievous than the stroke of a sword.
Likewise, unchastity brings about suffering such as the bearing of a fetus and so forth, whereas there is no need to say much regarding the transgression against another’s wife.
The nature of deceiving others, causing dissension, and striking at their vital points constitutes the harming of others.

This is indeed evident: frivolous speech (*samphappalāpa*) is so because it causes one to grasp what is meaningless and gives rise to what is harmful; covetousness (*abhijjhā*) because it is the cause of taking what is not given and so forth;

ill-will (*byāpāda*) because it is the cause of killing living beings and so forth; and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) because it is the cause of all that is harmful and is characterized by injuring others.
Even one who professes to be righteous commits acts such as killing living beings and encourages others to do the same—how much more so, then, those others?
Immorality, characterized by cruelty, is inferior; non-cruelty, being specifically a powerful cause of virtue (*sīla*), is superior.
Furthermore, since concentration (*samādhi*) has virtue as its proximate cause, and wisdom (*paññā*) has concentration as its proximate cause, non-cruelty is the root of all qualities.
Moreover, for noble-minded, reflective, and wise supermen, both concentration and wisdom—just like their virtue—bring about the welfare and happiness of others.
"They are accomplished" means that compassion is thus the root of all virtues; therefore, it was mentioned first.
Following that, in order to show specifically that "these states originate from non-violence," the factors of the wholesome courses of action (*kusalakammapatha*) were included.
After that, this virtue (*sīla*), which is the root of these qualities, was mentioned, [showing] that by one established in this, these states are to be produced.
The eight rightnesses (*sammatta*) are taken for the purpose of showing [the path]. For one who has entered upon the practice for their purification, this occurs from the very beginning;

thus, seclusion from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-viveka*) is taken for the purpose of showing that. As for why only two hindrances are not included at the beginning, the reason for what was and was not included has already been stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, the distinction between anger (*kodha*) and malice (*byāpāda*) is according to the method explained in the commentary on the Vatthasutta.

It is to be understood thus: here, the purification from defilements (*upakkilesa-visuddhi*) is included in order to show that the achievement of effacement (*sallekha*) occurs through the abandoning of anger and the like;
and the miscellaneous factors (*pakiṇṇaka*) are included in order to show that this [effacement] is accomplished by means of being easy to speak to, having virtuous friends, and heedfulness.
These qualities bring to fulfillment the virtues such as being endowed with pleasant speech, and having cultivated insight (*vipassanā*),...
The true Dhammas (saddhamma) are mentioned for the purpose of showing that they lead to the attainment of the Noble Path.
For one who is thus [endowed with them], this wrong grasp acts as an obstacle to the attainment of supramundane qualities; therefore, it must be abandoned from afar.
In this way, one who attains the Noble Path through the aforementioned right practice brings the state of effacement (sallekha) to its ultimate perfection.
The phrase beginning with “one who clings to his own views” (*sanditthiparāmāsī*) was stated for the purpose of showing this;

thus, the purpose for grasping these forty-four modes of effacement (*sallekhākāra*) and their sequence should be understood. Furthermore, even the mere arising of a thought is of great benefit for those unable to undertake the practice of effacement through actual application;
therefore, he said, “in order to show the great benefit of even the arising of a thought.”
“In wholesome states” means in the blameless states already mentioned, such as non-violence and so forth. “Conforming” means the conformity of the arising of consciousness with body and speech.
“Of those states” refers either to the states such as non-violence, or to those states that occur by way of the arising of consciousness.
Now, in order to show the aforementioned states in detail, the passage beginning with “But why? is commenced.

The phrase "or by body" is stated with reference to one who is unable to make the declaration of going for refuge verbally. This same principle applies to the statement, "One undertakes virtue by body.

And here, it is said that bodily and verbal kamma of such a kind is of great assistance by way of the arising of wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses that are light and proceed in such and such a manner;
it is not [the assistance] of the arising of consciousness in its own intrinsic nature.
It should be understood that this is known as being of great benefit.
"For the attainment of welfare" means for the achievement of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth, or specifically for the attainment of the Noble Path;
for the Noble Path is called "welfare" because it is exclusively beneficial. He says "circumambulation" (parikkamana) to refer to the proceeding by way of avoidance.

“For the sake of remedying and for the sake of avoidance. Non-harming was prepared by the Perfectly Enlightened One through the provision of the means for right vision. “With ease indeed” means without difficulty.
“By this very means” refers to the method stated in the verse on non-harming itself. “All the terms” refers to the remaining forty-three terms.

86. "Unwholesome states that do not produce rebirth-linking" refers to the mental factors associated with restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata-cittuppāda-dhammā*), as well as others that merely yield the result of the course-of-existence (*pavatti-vipāka-matta*).

Or, it refers to those that produce results after rebirth-linking has already been given, or to those such as "lapsed kamma" (*ahosi-kamma*) which, due to a deficiency in conditions, have found no opportunity to ripen and thus do not produce [a result].
"By way of class" means by way of the unwholesome class. "Leading to the lower realms" means leading to the states of deprivation (*apāya*). "So named" means...
By the mention of its name, it characterizes its intrinsic nature, because when the conditions are assembled, it does not deviate from that nature.
Therefore he said: "Because at the time of fruition, it is an undesirable and disagreeable fruition. The wholesome side should be understood in the same manner as stated.
However, this is the distinction: here, the states associated with direct knowledge (abhiññā) produce rebirth-linking; the rest is exactly as previously described.
Regarding the phrase "all unwholesome states": here, with the exception of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), all other unwholesome states serve as the similes;
for cruelty is the subject of the simile (*upameyya*). The same method applies to the phrase "all wholesome states.

By this very means—that is, just as cruelty was stated to be the subject of the simile while the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states were stated to be the similes—by this same principle, the unwholesome...
The unwholesome, such as the taking of life, should be compared to the other [the wholesome], and the wholesome, such as the abstention from taking life, should be compared to the other.
87. Regarding "bringing to final extinction" (*parinibbāpana*): it means the subsiding of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*).
"Mire" (*palipa*) is so called in the sense of being smeared all over; it refers to thick mud, and since that is invariably deep, it is said, "sunk in deep mud."
The five strands of sensual pleasure are called "quagmire" because they cause one to sink, like a quagmire.
Therefore, the application of the meaning in this context should be understood by means of the method of correlating the simile with the subject of the simile as it is now being stated.

For in the phrase "not that cause," the "cause" refers to the state of not being stuck in the mud, whether by hand or foot; however, that [state] does not exist here. This same principle applies to the subject of the simile as well.
In this regard, there might be someone’s reflection: “The monks and others speak by the power of the Blessed One’s teaching.
Having stated, “For the Blessed One himself extracts [the meaning] therein,” he spoke the words beginning with “of the king” in order to clarify that point by means of a simile.

Let alone ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), even for Noble Ones (*ariya*) who have attained the excellence of being at the head of the disciples (*sāvaka-sikhāppatta-viśeṣa*), the teaching belongs to the Teacher alone.

He said “even though” and so forth in order to show what is meant by “teaching. For indeed, the discourses taught by them are the very word of the Buddha, and the noble ones who have attained distinction through their teaching are truly the sons of the Buddha.
“Because of non-observance” means because of not practicing [the training]. “Because of not being trained in the Vinaya” refers to [the lack of respect for] the five Vinayas.
“By way of being trained. Now, since that [training] occurs through the training in the three trainings according to the Vinaya, he said, “He will train in the three trainings.
But what is that? Regarding the statement, “It is possible,” he asked, “What is the possibility?
and replied, “The state of not being mired in what is mired,” and so forth. Because in the Pāḷi it is said, beginning with, “That indeed, Cunda...”

Having taken the general meaning by way of the simile and stated the specific meaning by way of the subject of comparison, he first explains that meaning in common terms with the words, "In this way the meaning is to be understood," and so on;
then, expanding upon it in its uncommon aspect, he says, "What is meant? and so forth.
The phrase "he will extinguish another's intention to harm" refers to one who practices the right conduct known as non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Having seen [this], one who follows the example of what was seen becomes non-harming through the teaching of the Dhamma; it is with reference to such a person that this was said.
For his speech is a prophetic declaration (*ādesana*). Therefore he said: "This which belongs to the harming person... [referring] to one who previously harmed and practiced wrongly.
