By means of the passage beginning "cultivating the path for the abandoning of harm," [it refers to] his own non-harming.
He spoke of [the practice] leading to the final extinction (*parinibbāna*) of violence. Therefore, he said, “As if extinguished,” and so forth.
“In all instances” refers to the forty-three instances that have come down in the text beginning with “one who takes life.
88. “Thus” is a reference to the manner in which it was taught. “Of that” refers to effacement (*sallekha*). In such passages as, “There is indeed, O Brahmin, this method (*pariyāya*),” and so on.
Since the word *pariyāya* has the sense of "cause" (like the word *viya*), he says "the cause of effacement" (*sallekhakāraṇa*).
"By means of them" means by means of the effacements. "Seeking welfare" means by way of bringing about loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Compassionating" means by way of compassion (*karuṇā*).
"Having encompassed" (*pariggahetvā*) means having grasped all around; the meaning is "having surrounded. "Having gone around" (*pariccā*) means having gone all around, that is, completely.

"Having pervaded"—this is the meaning. "Do not be negligent" means: do not fall into negligence through ignorance of the serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) mentioned by the words "you should meditate," or through any other cause for negligence.
For in the dispensation that leads to liberation, even doing what should not be done is negligence. "In a time of misfortune" means:
in a time possessed of the seven kinds of misfortune, such as unsuitable conditions (*asappāya*), and so forth. The five methods are as previously stated.
He said, "Meditate; do not be negligent—this is my instruction to you," because all other qualities of the Dispensation are also included right here.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Sallekha Sutta is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta* 89.

By the restrictive particle "eva" (indeed) in the phrase "the question out of a desire to speak," the other four questions are excluded because they are impossible [in this context] and because the answer is given to the matter exactly as asked; therein, [it is stated]: "This is right view."
Even ordinary people and external ascetics, though not knowing things as they truly are, call one who stands in virtue equal to their own a "person of right view.
"Also by way of hearsay and so forth" means also by way of hearsay, modes of reflection, views, meditative contemplation (*nijjhāna*), and acceptance.
Because one brings about acceptance through meditative contemplation that the meaning of the state as it actually exists is "just so," there is an absolute grasp of things as they truly are.

He says, "Also by one's own direct experience" (*attapaccakkhenapi*), meaning: because the characteristic has been penetrated according to reality, it is by way of being directly experienced by oneself.
By the phrase "taking the word of many," it should be understood that this is a reduplicative usage (*āmeḍitapayoga*) due to its established convention both in the Dispensation and in the world;
and furthermore, taking the confidence in the Dispensation into account, this reduplicative usage should be seen as pertaining to both.
*Attha* means the meaning of the word. *Lakkhaṇa* means its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Upādāya* means having taken [as a basis]. *Sobhanāya* means for the sake of beauty.
*Pasatthāya* means for the sake of praise. Among these, by the first [term], he shows the intrinsic nature of right view, which consists in the awakening to the true nature of phenomena as they are.
For by that [right view], it shines forth, having overcome all phenomena. By the second [term], regarding the associated phenomena...
The state of being a guide. For by that [wisdom], it makes the associated states appear as if they were made of knowledge, and the person possessing them appears like a mass of knowledge;
thus, praise spreads in all directions for him, such as "he is wise, clever, skillful, learned, and discerning. Regarding "knowledge of one's own action as one's own property" (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*):
one who has action as his own is a "possessor of action" (*kammassaka*); the state of being such is "one's own action as one's own property" (*kammassakatā*). In this regard:
Knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is the knowledge that knows: “This karma belongs to sentient beings; this does not belong to them.

Knowledge in conformity with the truths (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) is knowledge in conformity with the truths because it conforms to the penetration of the Noble Truths; it is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
“Not in conformity with the truths” means that the outsider’s right view is not right view in conformity with the truths, because that [true] conformity is entirely absent in him.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of the adherence to the view of self. However, for an outsider, the view that one is the owner of one's karma arises in conformity with the view of self, because it proceeds in such a manner as "there is what is given" and so forth.

But for one within the Dispensation—even for an ordinary person—it is right view by means of both [factors], namely, through the two knowledges beginning with the knowledge that one is the owner of one's own karma; for such a person has entered the fixed course of rightness.
“It is said: ‘the trainee (sekha) is fixed. One should supply the word “right view” and connect it with “the right view of one beyond training (asekha).
To show that among the three types of persons, it is the trainee who is intended here as “one of right view,” he says: “fixed, leading to liberation,” and so forth.
Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned meaning by means of the Pāli, he says: “Therefore it was said,” and so forth. “The two extremes” refers to “eternalism... [and annihilationism].”
“Annihilation, sensual pleasure, and self-mortification”—these constitute the two extremes.

The non-approach to the two extremes of striving for the basis of lethargy and restlessness is already established by implication. “By way of straightness” means by way of the path whose intrinsic nature is straight;

the meaning is: by way of the middle way. Since the inclusion of confidence in the Dhamma necessarily includes confidence in the Teacher and the Saṅgha as well, the word “in the Dhamma” alone [is used].

It is stated thus because of the inseparable connection with that [right view]. Since this person is intended to be "one possessed of right view" (sammādiṭṭhi) by virtue of being endowed with certain right view, and since that [certainty] comes from the escape from the round of existence (vaṭṭa) through the attainment of the turning away from it (vivaṭṭa), he says: "He has come to this True Dhamma.
For Nibbāna is called the "True Dhamma" (saddhamma) because it is the peaceful, ever-present reality; and it is distinguished from other fruits by its uniqueness.
It may be stated by way of a figurative expression. This is his realization through the penetration of the scriptures (*āgama-sacchikiriyābhisamaya*);
and showing that this is accomplished here together with the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) and the others, he said, "All the thickets of views," and so forth.
Therein, by the two phrases "unraveling all the thickets of views" and "abandoning all defilements," he speaks of the realization of abandonment; [and regarding] the cycle of births...
By the phrase "going forth," the realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) is indicated; for the meaning of "full understanding" is the sense of "transcending.
By the phrase "bringing the practice to completion," the realization through development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) is to be understood.
Regarding the expression "delimitation of time": it is delimited, thus it is a "delimitation" (*pariccheda*); time itself as the delimitation is "delimitation of time" (*kālapariccheda*).
The meaning is: "the statement regarding that moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa), which is delimited by the comprehension of the unwholesome and so forth, at the time of emerging from the path.
Therefore he said, "at which time. The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and the unwholesome" (akusalañca) has the sense of conjunction;

by it, he includes the unwholesome roots and so forth that will be mentioned later. As for the expression "the ten unwholesome courses of action" (dasākusalakammapatha), from where does this distinction arise, since no specific distinction has yet been determined?
Is it unwholesome that has been taken up? No, because a general designation does not apply to a specific instance. Or rather, what is the use of this investigation of logic?
For the second section is an exposition in detail of the meaning taught by way of summary in the first section. Therefore he said, "But which, friends," and so forth.
Since supramundane right view is intended here, [it is] that which has cessation as its object.

The meaning is that, by way of the function of understanding through path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), one who penetrates the ten unwholesome courses of action as "this is suffering" is said to "understand the unwholesome" because of [overcoming] delusion. "Of that" refers to suffering, which is comprised of the unwholesome courses of action.
"In that very manner" means by the manner already stated: "by way of the function of understanding whose object is cessation."

Regarding the term *kusala*, this is its etymological meaning (*vacanattha*): it is called *kusala* because it "shakes," "moves," or "agitates" (*salati*) contemptible, evil states (*kucchite pāpadhamme*).
Alternatively, those evil states which "lie down" (*sayanti*) in a contemptible manner are called *kusā*. That which "reaps" (*lunāti*) or cuts off these *kusā* is *kusala*.
Or else, knowledge that thins out (*sānato tanukaraṇato*) what is contemptible is called *kusa*; that which is to be reaped, grasped, and set in motion by means of that [knowledge] is *kusala*.
It is *kusala*. Or, just as the *kusa* grass cuts both parts of the hand that hold it, so too this [term] cuts and severs the side of defilement pertaining to both the arisen and the unarisen;
therefore, because it cuts like the *kusa* grass, it is *kusala*.
Alternatively, it is *kusala* because it flows away from (*salana*) and restrains (*saṃvaraṇa*) base, blameworthy states. By way of wholesome states...
For unwholesome states (*akusala*) are restrained by not occurring at the six sense-doors, with the mind as the sixth.
Or, it is "wholesome" (*kusala*) because it shakes (*salati*), drives away, and removes base or evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*).

Alternatively, "blades of grass" (*kusā*) refers to hatred, greed, and so forth, because they sharpen, whet, and excite such base acts as killing living beings and the like. Through the presence of danger, volition attains a state of sharpness toward killing and other such acts.
It is highly blameworthy. It is "kusala" because it mows or cuts away the *kusa* grass [of evil].

Or, the *kusas* are the faculties such as faith that function by way of performing merit; they are so called because they cut off, bring an end to, and destroy what is contemptible. That which is to be obtained or set in motion by means of these is "kusala.
Alternatively, "ku" refers to the ground (*bhūmi*), and that which is similar to it by virtue of being its foundation is [also called *kusala*].
They are called *kusā* because they burn up and destroy their own support—the continuity of form and the formless—both now and in the future;
thus, *kusā* refers to lust and the other defilements. Because they cut and sever their own support in this way, they are called *kusala*.
For wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*), when accomplished through proper application, utterly eradicate the phenomena of form and the formless by ensuring they do not arise again.
“Root of the wholesome” (*kusalamūla*) means the foundation and cause of the wholesome by way of establishing it firmly;
this is the meaning. “Root of the unwholesome” (*akusalamūla*): here too the same method applies.
Furthermore, “unwholesome” (*akusala*) is that which is not wholesome; it is called unwholesome by virtue of being the opposite of wholesome states.
The meaning of the word must be understood. For it is in this sense that "wholesome" (*kusala*) is said:

in the sense of being healthful, blameless, having a pleasant result, and being born of skill. Thus, the meaning is shown as follows: whatever class of phenomena is not healthful, not blameless, not having a pleasant result, and not born of skill, that is unwholesome (*akusala*).
Likewise, [the meaning of *akusala* is] that which does not have the nature of flowing toward what is contemptible...
It should be understood that this meaning is also shown: "That which is to be carried out by means of grass or with grass, yet is not like the reaper himself—this is called unwholesome (akusala).
"Understanding of the basis" (vatthupajānanā) refers to the penetration and understanding of the basis consisting of suffering and so forth.
He said, "also by way of understanding the unwholesome and so forth," because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those persons who are to be awakened in such a manner.

And for that very reason, the teaching proceeded in brief. However, the mental attention to development proceeds by way of encompassing all material and immaterial phenomena without exception, according to the statement: "Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known. Therefore he said: "Only the teaching," and so forth.
In that context, "penetration through mental attention" refers to the mental attention of insight occurring in the prior stage and the penetration of the Noble Path.

And because there is no anger in anyone, it is stated only by way of expansion; the meaning is that those practicing insight and penetrating the path also penetrate it only by way of the expanded method, due to the absence of any sequence of purification.
"Bhikkhus" refers to the bhikkhus seated in the assembly of the five Nikāyas during the Dhamma-saṅgīti at the Mahāvihāra. "Thera" [refers to...].

In this context, they say "the senior of the Saṅgha. However, according to the method stated in the commentary on the Vatthasutta, the word "they said" (*āhaṃsu*) refers to the bhikkhus who were pupils of the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita. The term "the Elder" (*thero*) refers to the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita;
for he was the one who delivered these various expositions in this Majjhima Nikāya. "As a collection" (*rāsito*) means as a whole; the sense is "in one place."
Commentary on the Unwholesome Courses of Action:

"Unwholesomeness" (*akosalla*) is so called because it is the opposite of "skillfulness" (*kosalla*). It refers to ignorance (*aññāṇa*), because it proceeds from that [ignorance], meaning it arises from unskillfulness.
Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), just as a non-friend (*amitta*) is the opposite of a friend, and likewise, it is the opposite of the wholesome (*kusala*).
The unwholesome (*akusala*) is to be abandoned by means of the wholesome (*kusala*), but it is not because the wholesome itself is to be abandoned;

for it is precisely the wholesome, when perfected through application, that abandons the unwholesome. It is called "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) because it proceeds together with faults such as greed and the like.

It is "having suffering as its result" (*dukkhavipāka*) because its ripening consists of the four aggregates, which are painful and undesirable. In this context, by the term "blameworthy," the state of suffering in the occurrence of unwholesome states is indicated.
By the expression "resulting in suffering," it shows the suffering inherent in the result (*vipākadukkhatā*).
For the former statement is a definition of the unwholesome by way of its occurrence in the present life, while the latter is by way of its capacity to produce a result in a subsequent existence.
Likewise, by the former it shows the unwholesome's impure intrinsic nature, and by the latter, its impure result. By the former, the unwholesome...
It turns [the mind] away from the nature of the wholesome; by the latter, it does so from the nature of the indeterminate, because the latter indicates the possession of karmic fruition.

Alternatively, by the former, through its function of showing the state of being irreproachable, it demonstrates the quality of producing what is harmful as its "flavor" (rasa) in the sense of its activity;
by the latter, through the sense of attainment, it demonstrates the flavor of undesirable fruition. And by the former, in the sense of the mode of manifestation...
By the first [characteristic], it shows the state of being manifested as defilement; by the last, in the sense of its fruit, it shows the state of being manifested as painful result.
Furthermore, by the first, it explains that improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of the unwholesome, for it is from that that the blameworthy arises.
By the last, it clarifies the state of being the proximate cause of other unwholesome states, for that [unwholesome] is the cause of painful result.

"Kāraṇaṃ" means: "Saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ" means possessed of defilements; the meaning is that it is oppressed by the ten bases of defilement, or afflicted by them, corrupted by them, and made impure. And this refers to its having a painful result (*dukkhavipākatā*);
for those who do not believe in this state of having a painful result because it is not directly perceived, [it is shown] by demonstrating the disadvantage through direct perception.
This was said for the purpose of inducing a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). It is common to all unwholesome states.
"Excessive falling" (*atipāta*) means falling even more intensely than that which has the nature of falling by its own essence;

the meaning is that it is a rapid falling, not allowing one to fall slowly. Alternatively, "excessive falling" (*atipāta*) is falling after having been overcome by weapons and so forth. [It occurs] through the magnitude of the application, the object, and so on.
Great culpability arises because of the powerful nature of the volition produced by those conditions.

For the magnitude of the preliminary effort (*payoga*) is due to the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*), which accomplishes its own function through the sudden completion of a single application and has gained proficiency through many occurrences of javanas. This remains so even though at times it may be slight.
When a large living being is killed with equal effort, the volition (*cetanā*) of one who kills a large being arises in an intense mode;
thus, this is the "greatness" of the object. Therefore, both of these [the greatness of the object and the intensity of the volition] occur precisely through the power of the volition.

Even in the aforementioned sequence of conditions, the state of being a great offense (*mahāsāvajja*) should be understood as arising solely from the power of the volition by means of the respective conditions. For, regarding the conditions such as the effort (*payoga*), the object (*vatthu*), and so forth—
Even when the object to be killed is not great, there is great culpability due to the virtue of the victim; conversely, there is slight culpability due to the opposite qualities.
This should be understood as being like the greatness or smallness of the objective basis (*vatthu*).

Furthermore, slight culpability and great culpability should also be applied according to the mildness or intensity of both the defilements (*kilesa*) and the physical effort (*upakkama*). [The factors for killing are: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, and the murderous intent.

They may also belong to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāgiya*), as does the preparatory effort (*upakkama*) instigated by the volition (*cetanā*) to kill. For while the volition to take life consists of five constituent factors (*sambhāra*), this [preparatory effort] should be understood as being devoid of those five factors.
This analysis should also be applied appropriately to the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and the other courses of action.

That which is accomplished by one’s own hand through piercing, striking, and so forth, is "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*); that which proceeds by means of commanding others is "by command" (*āṇattika*).
That which proceeds by means of releasing things such as intestines, weapons, or stones is the *nissaggiya* (relinquishing) type;

that which proceeds by means of causing harm or striking and so forth is the *thāvara* (fixed) type; that which proceeds by means of reciting mantras like those of the Āthabbaniyas and others is the *vijjāmaya* (magical) type;
and that which is produced from the ripening of karma, such as the fang-snap [of a snake] and so forth, is the *iddhimaya* (supernormal) type.

If it is "what belongs to me" that constitutes what is not given when it has been appropriated by another, then how could there be an absence of the perception of appropriation regarding the belongings of an infant lying on its back? To this he says: "Where another... and so forth.

An "other" means one who is either conscious or unconscious, but who is the owner of that object. For even an unconscious person, having acted according to his will during a time of consciousness, [is considered the owner].
"Without punishment" means [one is not punished]. Taking what belongs to another through the recitation of mantras is "consisting of science" (*vijjāmaya*).

Drawing away what belongs to another from them by means of bodily or verbal effort, without mantras, through such a kind of supernatural power (*iddhi*), is "consisting of psychic power" (*iddhimaya*)—thus, six modes of application for taking what is not given have been stated, beginning with "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*).
Regarding the phrase "according to the appropriate [mode]": here, first, the mode "by one's own hand" applies to all five types of theft.

It occurs by way of [the four types of taking]: thus it should be understood that the *āṇattiyo* (commands) and the *nissaggiyo* (relinquishables) are likewise. It is stable (*thāvara*) by way of taking through theft, taking by force, and taking by concealment.
The same should be seen for the rest as well.
Regarding "in sexual misconducts" (*methuna-samācāresu*): this refers to the two kinds of sexual misconduct, namely, lack of contentment with one's own wife and going to another's wife.

This indeed is the distinction intended here: "protected by lineage" means protected by those of the same clan; "protected by the Dhamma" means protected by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma; "with protection" means having a husband;
"with legal penalty" refers to her for whose approach a punishment has been established by the king;

"bought with wealth" means purchased with money for the sake of being a wife; "living by consent" means living according to her own will; "living for the sake of enjoyment" means living for the sake of material wealth.
One who lives in a cloth is a *paṭavāsinī*. One who has taken hold of a water-bowl is an *odapattakinī*.
One who has removed her head-cushion is an *obhaṭacumbaṭā*. One brought as a captive is a *dhajāhatā*. One for a moment is a *taṅkhaṇikā*.
Sexual misconduct committed by overcoming [the other] is a great offense, not so that which occurs through the mutual consent of two people. By overcoming...

They say that even when there is a transgression and the endurance of practicing what is not the path by way of the path, there is no sexual misconduct for one who is being overcome, because of the absence of the prior intention and application for indulgence.

However, the absence of application while the mind of indulgence is present is not a valid criterion, since for the most part there is an absence of the application of indulgence toward a woman. If that were the case, [the fault would apply] to the mind of indulgence that arose previously.
There would be no sexual misconduct on her part even if she were approached, nor on the man's part if there were an absence of the application of service; therefore,

it should be understood that all four requisites are stated by including both those cases where the act occurs through one’s own inclination and those where it occurs through force, with each being threefold.
“Destructive of welfare” is stated by way of the courses of kamma; for this is a discussion of the courses of kamma. “Of him” means of the deceiver.

“False speech” (musāvāda) is the volition [by which one speaks falsely]; in this interpretation, “false” (musā) is the effort of making known an object in a manner that does not correspond to reality, and it is called “false speech” because the volition that originates it is so designated. To speak otherwise than that, he says “another method,” and so forth.
It has been stated. The phrase "due to the unwillingness to give what belongs to oneself," and so forth, is stated by way of the general nature of false speech (*musāvāda*).

Even with the intention of laughter, there is false speech when deception is placed foremost. "Of another" refers to one who is to be informed by means of deception. "That" refers to the application of false speech.

"The state of being empty" means the state of being void due to the absence of joy (*pīti*). Because of its harsh sound, it is not pleasant to the ear; because of its failure in meaning, it is not pleasant to the heart. "Of a defiled mind" means of a mind corrupted by hatred or greed.
"An intention that is exclusively harsh" indicates precisely the state of a corrupted mind; and this corruption of mind is to be understood by way of the absence of the intent to kill.
For if there were the intent to kill, the purpose would be accomplished; in its absence, there may be either the taking of life or malice.
Whatever person in relation to whom harsh speech is employed, the offense reaches its head (is finalized) in their presence. Even when [the victim] is absent, it reaches its head.

Others say, "It is so. In this regard, the following intention would be appropriate: because those who speak disrespectfully in the presence [of the person] possess a powerful state, their volition may be strong, as well as their communication of that meaning to another;

it is not so when [the act is done] out of sight. And just as an apology made at the funeral pyre for one who has been reviled and is dead removes the obstacle of the reproach, so too [does it do so] when done in the absence of the other.
It can be understood that one who is intent [on such speech] necessarily possesses harsh speech.

The word “of that” (tassa) is used for the purpose of clarifying that harsh speech exists precisely because of an exclusively harsh volition. The intention is that it is “wound-cutting” due to its harshness when heard.
Because of the gentleness of the mind, there is no harsh speech [in the technical sense], as it has not reached the status of a course of kamma; however, its status as kamma cannot be denied. Thus...

Having established harsh speech through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the harshness of volition, [the text] now states "by gentleness of speech" and so forth in order to establish that same point through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). "This" refers to harsh speech.

That which has not reached the status of a full course of action (*kamma-patha*) is less blameworthy, while the other is more blameworthy. Likewise, everything is similar to what preceded, with the distinction between the mildness and intensity of the defilements.

Habitual practice means frequent repetition. It is less blameworthy when that for whose sake one has engaged in it is not seized, and more blameworthy when it is seized, because it then reaches the level of a course of action (*kammappaṭha*).
Furthermore, any idle chatter is accomplished through two factors.
Its status as being less or more blameworthy should also be understood by way of the mildness or intensity of the underlying defilements.

It should be understood that one’s own dedication [of merit] occurs through the mind alone. “He destroys the welfare and happiness” means that he destroys the welfare and happiness of whoever produces it.
By the phrase “Oh, may it,” he illustrates the thought of absolute destruction;

for it is through such a cruel manifestation that there is the attainment of a course of kamma. “By the absence of grasping things as they truly are” means by the absence of a grasp according to reality (*yāthāvaggāha*).
By apprehending that which has the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so forth as permanent and so forth. "Views falsely" means one sees it erroneously.
By the phrase "like idle chatter," he shows that [wrong view] is of slight blame when its habituation is weak, and of great blame when its habituation is strong.
"The state of being the opposite of the mode apprehended" refers to the erroneous nature of the mode apprehended by wrong view. "Of the object" (*vatthuno*) refers to that [object].

He speaks of the nature as it is not. "By way of suchness" means that for that theorist, or for that object, its manifestation occurs precisely in the mode grasped [by him], thinking, "It is thus, and not otherwise.
"By way of dhamma" means by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

"By way of constituent parts" means among the constituent parts of the mental factors, such as those beginning with contact as the fifth; the meaning is: "from whichever constituent parts they are. "States of volition" means having the intrinsic nature of volition.
Regarding the phrase "seven in sequence," one might ask: "Is it not the case that volition (*cetanā*) is not mentioned among the courses of action (*kamma-patha*) in the Abhidhamma?
Therefore, is it not improper to consider these seven as courses of action in their sequential order? No, for the reason for its non-mention is something else.
It is not because volition is not a course of action that it is omitted from the category of courses of action; rather, it is because it is only occasionally a course of action.

"It is not always" is said because the status of being a path of action (*kamma-patha*) is not fixed; however, when it does become a path of action, its inclusion within the category of paths of action is not precluded.

Here it may be asked: if the status of being a path of action is unfixed because volition (*cetanā*) is not always a path of action, and thus is not mentioned in the category of paths of action, would that not mean that covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and the rest lack the status of being paths of action?

Does it not follow that because they exist even when [the actual act] has not been performed, their status as a course of action (*kammappatha*) is indefinite, and thus they too should not be mentioned in the category of courses of action?
No, it does not follow; for they are included therein by virtue of their being courses of action and their sharing the same essential nature (*tatsabhāgatā*).
If this is so, should volition (*cetanā*) also be mentioned there? This is true; however, it is already evident as "killing living beings" and so forth, and of that—
It would not be stated that they are "paths of action. For the status of volition as "action" is evident from such statements as: "Bhikkhus, I say that volition is action;
the three types of bodily volition, bhikkhus, are unwholesome bodily action," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is volition itself that functions as the path for the occurrence of good and bad destinations, as well as for the pleasure and pain that arise therein.
The fact that it is called a "course of action" (*kammappatha*) is well known in its capacity as such;

however, the status of covetousness and the rest as good or bad conduct is due to their nature of striving through volition (*cetanā*), and their status as paths to happy or miserable destinations and to the pleasure or pain arising therein is due to their being like the tracks of a wheel following upon the volition—thus, their status as courses of action is not so well known.
Therefore, [the author] shows them precisely by way of that intrinsic nature.
In the Abhidhamma, volition (cetanā) is not mentioned as being part of the collection of courses of action (kamma-patha);

or rather, it should be understood that volition is not mentioned along with them because it does not possess the same nature as they do. "Having reached the root" means having reached the teaching on the roots; the sense is: when the phenomena (dhammas) whose intrinsic nature is that of roots are being discussed.
The statement that “taking what is not given has sentient beings as its object” contradicts this passage from the *Pañhapucchaka-pāḷi*, which says: “The five training rules have only limited objects.
For whatever is the object of unwholesome conduct such as the destruction of life is precisely the same object for the abstention from it;
for abstinence consists precisely in the refraining from the very thing that is to be transgressed. Or alternatively, [the phrase] “having sentient beings as its object” means...
There is no contradiction here, for it is stated with reference specifically to formations (saṅkhāra) designated as "beings" (satta). Thus, it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*:

"As for those training rules (sikkhāpada) mentioned here as having beings as their object, they take as their object only those formations that have reached the designation 'being'. Regarding an object of a different class, such as "woman,"...

Some say that because it is to be grasped as "a person," it has sentient beings as its object. [This is said] with reference to idle chatter such as "one seen, two heard," etc., by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
Likewise, in the phrase "coveting thus" (*tathā abhijjhā*), the word "thus" (*tathā*) also extends to this [phrase], namely "by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized";
it does not indicate that [the coveting] has only conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) among sentient beings as its object, because one covets by way of seeing and so forth.
Even when the wrong view, “There are no beings of spontaneous birth,” occurs, it has formations as its object;
this is stated with the intention that its object consists of the phenomena belonging to the three planes. But how can all phenomena of the three planes be the object of wrong view?
In a general sense. For when the [wrong view] occurs as “There is no fruit or result of well-done or ill-done deeds,” [it takes all such phenomena as its object].
In terms of its meaning, even the phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are indeed included.
Because of their abundance of pleasure, kings say, "Kill the thief," even while laughing; however, since laughter for them belongs to another domain, he said, "It is decisive... [etc]...
"Of some" refers to co-nascent factors such as taking what is not given and so forth. "By way of being an impeller of the associated" means being associated [with them].

In the sense of causing to arise. "Of some" refers to those that are not co-nascent (*asahajāta*). By the phrase "in the sense of the decisive support condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*), it excludes the assistance [rendered] by greed in its capacity as a root (*mūla*).
For the sense of a root is the establishment of a state of being well-founded, and that is invariably concomitant with the nature of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
Therefore, in this context, it should be understood as a "root" because it is like a root; however, in the primary sense, it refers to those previously mentioned as "of some."

The state of being the root for those [factors] that arise together should be understood. By the Sutta passage beginning with "One who is lustful," etc., it is clarified that greed is the root cause of unwholesome states such as the destruction of life;

it does not, however, imply assistance in the sense of being a root [in the strict Abhidhamma sense], because, without distinction, those [unwholesome states] lack the status of being its specific cause or condition.
The commentary on the unwholesome courses of action is concluded.
Commentary on the Wholesome Courses of Action:
*Vera* refers to evil states such as the destruction of life and so forth. For it is called "enmity" (*vera*) because it is the cause of enmity;
one "abstains from" (*veramaṇī*) it because, like someone threatening—"How can you come while I am standing here?"—one restrains it. Therefore, he said: "He abandons."

The term "viramaṇī" was spoken by adding the syllable *eva* according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*) where it should have been "viramaṇī. It is stated thus specifically for the purpose of pointing it out in the *Vibhaṅga*.
Abstinence from what has not been undertaken as a precept, by way of the object to be transgressed as it presents itself, is "abstinence by attainment" (*sampattavirati*).
Abstinence arisen through the act of undertaking is "abstinence by undertaking" (*samādānavirati*). [This abstinence] arises by way of undertaking...

Abstention (*virati*) is the abstention consisting in the undertaking [of precepts]; it is also the abstention consisting in eradication (*samuccheda-virati*), which occurs by way of cutting off the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Fresh meat" (*allasasamaṃsa*) refers to the flesh and blood mixed with the living animal itself. He released [the snake] everywhere out of his equal compassion for all. Having spoken the truth, he made this resolution: "By this utterance of truth, may my mother’s illness be cured.
"Great serpent" (*mahāsappa*) means a python (*ajagara*). Having been released, it departed through the power of his virtue (*sīla-teja*).
“Skill” (kosalla) is said to mean knowledge (ñāṇa), because of proceeding by means of skill or through the approach [to the goal] by way of skill.
“From lying in a vile manner” means from lying down in a vile way, from lying latent, or from proceeding [in that manner].

Although they could have been called “skilled in abstinence” (veramaṇi-kusalā), they were not called “skilled” (kusalā) because the answer must conform to the question; rather, they were called simply “skillful” (kusala).

Although in this context only the abstinences (virati) are mentioned in the text, in the analysis of the training rules (sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga), volition (cetanā) is also brought forward and explained; therefore, taking both together, he said: "Both volitions and abstinences are included.

For when non-covetousness reaches the root and reaches the category of the path of action (kamma-patha), that dhamma called non-covetousness is, from the standpoint of its root, the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha). This is how the meaning should be understood. The same method applies to the other two terms as well.

To show how those things which have misconduct as their object, or have that same [misconduct] as their object, or have the life-faculty and so forth as their object, abandon such misconduct, it is said:
“But just as...,” and so on. “Of one who abstains from covetousness...,” etc., means: of one who abandons covetousness.

For there is no separate abstinence from mental misconduct, since its abandonment is accomplished by non-covetousness and the rest alone. Regarding these—namely, non-greed and so forth—the following should be stated:
That should be understood in the same manner as explained regarding the unwholesome roots.

"The section on absorption" (appanāvāra) refers to the concluding section. "By one method" means by one method among the various meditation subjects for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna), such as the method of the formless (arūpa-mukha) through feeling and so forth.
"With the exception of covetousness, there are nine unwholesome courses of action" (akusala-kammapatha).
It should be stated thus. Or, this word "ten" should be connected with the phrase "wholesome courses of action," as in:

"the ten unwholesome courses of action and the ten wholesome courses of action. For, by the very phrase "excepting covetousness," the ninefold nature of the unwholesome courses of action is already expressed.
Alternatively, this word "ten" may be connected in both ways; for covetousness—

Even mindfulness that is to be abandoned does not transcend the state of being fully understood (*pariññeyyatā*). For it has been said: "Craving for form is a lovely form, a pleasant form," and so forth.
Therefore, by virtue of that state of being fully understood, it is indeed included within the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*);

however, with reference to what is to be abandoned, it is stated as "having set aside covetousness. For this very reason, he said: "But in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*), all courses of action (*kammapatha*)..."
“[It is] the truth of suffering. Because the distinction between them is established by the mode of their occurrence as covetousness and greed, it is said, “these two states.
According to the method of the Suttas, craving is called the “truth of origin”; therefore he says, “the truth of origin in the direct sense.
By the term “non-occurrence,” he refers to the cause of non-occurrence, just as in the expressions “the destruction of lust” and “the destruction of hatred. Because of its conditioned nature...
When the truth of suffering, which has the intrinsic nature of the conditioned, is grasped, the unconditioned truth of cessation turns up as its opposite by way of being non-conditioned;

and when the truth of origination, which is exclusively blameworthy and characterized by accumulation, is grasped, the truth of the path—which is blameless and characterized by dispersal—turns up as its opposite.
Thus, these two should be understood by way of the "turning-back" method of treatment.
Thus it was said. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Netti*:
"When there is one footing, one seeks the remaining footing;
when it turns back toward the opposite, that is the mode of conveyance called 'the Reversal' (*āvatta*)."
"In every way" (*sabbākārena*) means by all modes, such as sensual lust, form-lust, and so forth;
or from all aspects, such as those leading to the states of deprivation and so on; or without leaving anything remaining therein. "In every way indeed" (*sabbākāreneva*) means from every aspect.

"Having extracted" (*nīharitvā*) means having removed; the meaning is precisely "having utterly eradicated. "Without leaving behind any phenomenon whatsoever" (*kañci dhammaṃ anavakārīkaritvā*) refers to any [phenomenon] among form, feeling, and the rest.
The meaning is: having taken [them] as a whole, without making even a single dhamma inseparable and without grasping them individually.
It is by way of the grasping of the conceit "I am," that is, "I am. Since that [conceit] grasps the five aggregates without remainder, it is therefore said:
"by way of grasping as a whole. And since the mind of the supreme path (aggamagga-citta) is spoken of here, he says: "similar to [wrong] view."

Regarding "the underlying tendency to conceit" (*mānānusaya*): just as the view (*diṭṭhi*) functions by grasping form and so forth as "I am this," according to the passage beginning "Whatever is form, that is I," so too does conceit function through such thoughts as "I am superior.
Thus he says: "The underlying tendency to conceit is similar to the view because it proceeds with the thought 'I am'.
It is "delimiting" (*paricchedakara*) in the sense of providing a final delimitation; it is so called because from this point onward there is no further suffering.
"By way of the teaching on the courses of kamma" means by way of the teaching on the Four Noble Truths as it proceeds through the gateway of the courses of kamma.
"By way of the penetration of attention" means by way of the penetration of the path through the attention of insight.
The commentary on the section on the wholesome courses of kamma is finished.
Commentary on Nutriment (Āhāravāra-vaṇṇanā): 90.

"Brings" (*āharati*) means it brings [to existence]; the meaning is that it produces and supports. "Produced" (*nibbatta*) means born. For from that point onward, the worldly convention of "born" is used.
However, from the moment of seizing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) until the emergence from the mother’s womb, [it is called "conceived"].
"Thus far, those who are 'born from birth' (sambhavesino). This, then, is the distinction between those "born from birth" among those born from a womb;

as for others, however, it is stated by way of the first moment of consciousness and so forth. Here, the word "birth" (sambhava) signifies "procreation" in the case of those born from a womb, but signifies "arising" in the case of others.
For they attain "birth" at the moments of the first consciousness and the first posture.
They are said to "seek" (esanti) and "approach" (upagacchanti) rebirth; they have not yet become [fully] realized because they are not well-established in their arising.
This is because all seeking for existence (bhavesanā) has been utterly severed. By the restrictive phrase "they will not exist again," he shows the meaning excluded [by that restriction].
In such passages as "he who has become a consumer of time," the word *bhūta* should be understood as referring to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
And here the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction, as in such expressions as "by fire or by water.
With the intention that the assistance to be rendered by the nutriments consists precisely in establishing the individual existence (*attabhāva*) through their respective conditions, he said:
"The difference in expression... [is] only one. "Of the phenomena arisen in the being" means: in the continuity (*saṃtāna*) of the being.
Regarding "of arisen phenomena": just as when it is said, "it remains for a hundred years," what is meant is that it proceeds by way of continuous succession (*anuppabandha*);
likewise, "for stability" means proceeding by way of continuous succession. Furthermore, since that [stability] is non-interruption, he says, "for non-interruption.
Through the arising of phenomena in continuous succession, the continuum of beings (*sattasantāna*) is said to be sustained.
He said: "For the arising of those that have not yet arisen. These are the terms for stability and support; they are to be understood in both contexts, not according to their numerical order.
Since the nutritive essence residing in the physical basis (vatthu) goes along with it as something to be swallowed, just like the physical basis itself, it is said:

"It is called 'nutriment' because it is to be swallowed. However, with reference to the nutritive essence already produced, it is said: "Edible nutriment brings in the material qualities consisting of the eightfold essence."
He will say: "Coarseness" refers to a lack of nutritive essence (*ojā*), not to the bulkiness of the substance nor its hardness;
therefore, whatever substance has little nutritive essence is coarse. Snakes and the like are to be understood as coarse because they produce suffering.
Regarding horns and so forth that have been discarded for three years, they say their softness consists in their having become putrid, due to being chewed by hyenas and smeared with saliva.
But for those who have become thus, there is softness; for this is the very nature of things (*dhammasabhāva*). The food of snakes is subtle because they consume tender grass and crops.
The food of birds is subtle because they consume seeds of grass and the like. That of border-dwellers is subtle, for even potherbs, leaves, dry stalks, and lotus petals are their food.
For those Paranimmittavasavatti [gods], it is simply "subtle"; that is, not in comparison with anything else, but rather—
"Subtle"—this is the conclusion reached, because beyond that there is no further subtlety.
However, here the grossness and subtlety of nutriment are stated by way of its physical basis (*vatthu*);

and in order to show that this should be understood through its being watery, fiery, and airy respectively, the passage beginning with "And here" was spoken. "Fatigue" refers to the exhaustion of the body arising from hunger.
"Dispels" means it performs the mere act of dispelling that [disturbance]. "But it cannot sustain" means it is not capable of maintaining the body because it lacks substantial nourishment.
"It cannot dispel fatigue" because it does not fill the stomach.
By the phrase "even the sixfold," he indicates that no contact whatsoever is to be left out. Here, [the sequence] follows the very order of the teaching on nutriment.
He says, "It is simply the method of teaching," and so forth, to show that contact and the other factors possess their second and subsequent positions for no other reason than this.
The inclusion of the word "mind" (*mano*) is for the purpose of showing that it is the volition of the mind, not the volition of a "being";

thus he says, "Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) is simply volition (*cetanā*). "Mind" (*citta*) refers to any kind of consciousness whatsoever, and not exclusively to resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*).
Since it was previously stated that "nutriment means condition," he objects with the words, "If the meaning of nutriment is the meaning of condition," and so forth.
Then, as for the question, "Why are only these four mentioned?"—the construction is: "Why are only these four mentioned, and why are only these [four] mentioned?
By the phrase "because they are specific conditions," he shows that, unlike other conditioned phenomena which [contribute] to their own produced effect...

These [other factors] are indeed conditions, but these [nutriments] are both such and otherwise; thus, although their status as conditions is equal, they are "additional conditions" (*atirekapaccaya*).

Therefore, this shows the meaning of why they are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*). Now, in order to demonstrate that status of being an additional condition, the passage beginning with "a specific condition" (*visesapaccayo hi*) is commenced.
The physical nutriment of mouthfuls (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is a specific condition for the material body because it acts as its support (*upatthambhaka-bhāva*).
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: “The four nutriments, by way of supporting both the material and the immaterial, are the nutriment-condition.
For even though they possess the quality of producing, the quality of supporting belongs to the immaterial nutriments and to the nutriment that originates matter born of nutriment;
however, in the absence of the quality of supporting, the nutriments lack the quality of producing. Thus, the quality of supporting [is essential].
Exertion. For even when producing [its effect], nutriment produces it only by way of supporting it through non-interruption; thus, its state as nutriment is precisely its state as a support.
Contact is a specific condition for feeling, for it is said: "With contact as condition, there is feeling.
From the statement "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness," mental volition is a condition for consciousness. Volition is threefold existence...
For it is said: "The mother [is the cause]. However, from the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form," consciousness is the specific condition for name-and-form.
Indeed, in the absence of the consciousness that enters the womb, there is no arising of name-and-form. As it was said:
"If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would name-and-form coagulate in the mother's womb? and so forth.
In order to establish this very point by means of a sutta, the passage beginning with "As it has been said" was stated.
Thus, although the meaning of nutriment (*āhāra*) is the meaning of condition (*paccaya*), these alone are called "nutriments" because they are specific conditions;
having shown their status as specific conditions without differentiation, [the author] now shows them by way of differentiation, beginning with "But what here... and so forth.
It has been undertaken. Even when merely placed in the mouth and not yet chewed, it certainly becomes a condition for the food inside by that much alone.
Therefore, he said: "It arouses eight kinds of material form. "Conducive to pleasant feeling" means beneficial to pleasant feeling.
"In every way" means by way of eye-contact and so forth; that is, according to however many varieties of contact there are.
The nutriment of contact is of every kind; it brings about the three types of feeling as appropriate, and there is nothing that does not provide nutriment.
"In every way" means that here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained regarding the nutriment of contact.

"By way of the threefold continuity" refers to the threefold continuity consisting of the body-decad, the mind-decad, and the base-decad. "By way of the system of co-nascent and other conditions" [is to be understood].

By way of the method of the co-nascent and other conditions. For the rebirth-linking consciousness, while acting as a condition for its own co-nascent mentality (nāma) through the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance, it is said to "nutriment" that [mentality] by way of the nutriment condition;

however, in the case of co-nascent materiality (rūpa), it acts as a condition for the physical basis (vatthu) by way of the dissociation condition—excluding the association condition—and for the remaining materiality by way of the mutuality condition.

The application [of the terms] should be made according to the method already stated, with the exception [of those specified]. The term "those" (*tāni*) is a neuter designation used even for non-neuter things because they are spoken of together with neuter ones.

Only wholesome and unwholesome volitions associated with the taints (*āsava*) have been mentioned. The word "cause" (*hetu*) indicates their status as specific conditions. Therefore, he said: "But without distinction," and so forth.
The same principle applies here as well regarding the statement that "only rebirth-linking consciousness has been mentioned. As it is for each respective [case], so it is here.

The function of nutriment (*āhāra*) for these [mental factors] consists in their being conditions for the fruit in a specific sense; this is stated by the passage beginning with "But in a non-specific sense," which shows that it is so even without distinction.
Therein, "of those phenomena associated with them and originated by them" means: of both the phenomena associated with those [factors] such as contact, and the material phenomena originated by them.
In this context, the inclusion of "associated" should be understood according to what is appropriate, whereas the inclusion of "originated" applies without distinction.

"Supporting, it accomplishes the function of nutriment": thus, while supporting, it originates matter; indeed, its accomplishment of the function of support is achieved solely through the origination of the eightfold nutritive-essence matter (*ojatthamaka-rūpa*).
"Touching, indeed" means performing the very function of touching. "Exerting themselves" means intending and striving.
"Only one who knows" means only one who knows by way of conceiving rebirth (*upapatti-parikappa*).
The construction is: "it accomplishes the function of nutriment. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.

And the accomplishment of the function of nutriment for them is simply the continued occurrence of the personal existence (attabhāva) by way of being the cause for the arising of feeling and so forth.
Why was it stated, "by establishing the body"? Is it not the case that matter born of karma and so forth proceeds only by means of karma and so forth? This is the objection.

Having this in mind, he said: “Even that produced by kamma,” and so forth. Since the maintenance of the material continuity born of temperature and mind is accomplished precisely through the support of the continuity of appropriated matter, it is stated as “of the two material continuities. And with reference specifically to this support, it is said:
“acting as a preserver. For sustenance (yāpanā) is the preservation (anupālanā) that serves as the cause for the endurance of the material body.
"Become the basis for pleasure and so forth" means it is the place where pleasure and so forth arise.

For even an object is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because phenomena that take it as their object dwell there by way of making it their object. "Only while touching" is said because contact has the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of touching;
indeed, there is no occurrence of phenomena apart from their intrinsic nature. [This refers to] the occurrence of feeling.

Since there is no wandering of beings without [feeling], it is said: "Pleasure and so forth... arises. Furthermore, in this discussion regarding the state of non-perception (*asaññībhava*), the state of perception (*saññībhava*) need not be shown;
for even that [state] exists only by way of the occurrence of feeling, which serves as its cause, and thus the reason [for its existence] is not universal.
For it is said: "Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*)... arises for the stability of beings because it brings about the root of existence (*bhavamūla*)."
Therefore, it has been said: "Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is that which cognizes; thus, by way of conceiving rebirth, it is precisely that which cognizes"—this is the meaning of what was stated.
The four fears are to be understood through the discernment of their dangers (*ādīnava*). "Craving" (*nikanti*) means longing.
He speaks with reference to craving for flavors (*rasataṇhā*), for that is powerful regarding edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*). For this very reason, the restriction is made there. One fears.
From this there is fear; indeed, attachment itself is fear because it is the cause of great harm.

Approaching—occurring by way of association among the sense objects, the faculties, and the consciousnesses, as well as among the consciousnesses of the sense objects—is called "fear" because it is the cause for the arising of feeling and the other [mental factors].

The purpose of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is exactly as stated in the method [above]. This same method applies to the remaining two [terms] as well. Accumulation (*āyūhana*) is the act of joining together (*abhisandahana*).
They also call it "provisioning. Because it is the cause for the arising of existence (*bhava*), it is called "fear" (*bhaya*).
"Descent" (*abhinipāta*) is the manifestation [of rebirth] by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in this or that state of existence.

It is called "fear" because it is the root cause of all misfortunes that have the arising of existence as their cause. Now, [the text proceeds] to explain in detail the fearful nature of attachment (*nikanti*) and the others.

The passage beginning with “For what reason? is commenced in order to show this. Therein, “having made an attachment” means having generated a settling (ālaya), that is to say, having produced craving.
“Experiencing contact” means causing the occurrence of contact divided into eye-contact and so forth.
“Relishing contact” means having the habit of relishing contact designated as the tangible object by way of body-contact. By way of body-contact...

Indeed, in order to show that craving for tangibles (*phoṭṭhabba-taṇhā*) occurs among beings, the object of tangibles was singled out in the demonstration of the danger of the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*), by means of the passage beginning, "In those things protected and guarded by others," and so forth.

Alternatively, *phassassāda* means "delight in the nutriment of contact" (*phassāhāra*). For when there is the nutriment of contact, there is delight in the objects of contact for beings, but not when it is absent. Therefore he said, "Rooted in delight in contact," and so on.
It is called "rooted in that" because it is grasped as having the nature of being struck by the fear of birth-signs; the meaning is that it is the sign for the accumulation of kamma.

It "strikes down" (abhinipatati) means it is produced (abhinibbattati). For the initial production of beings in various states of existence, which are like pits of glowing coals, is similar to being struck. "Because it is rooted in that" means because it is rooted in the production of name-and-form.
"Therein" refers to those similes. "Making it a real fact" means not a merely imagined fact, but rather a real one.
Formerly, having accomplished his purpose, while those carrying provisions for the journey were on their way, it was as if the provisions themselves were going;
thus it is said, "Having gone, he brought the provisions to an end. Or, "having gone" means "for the sake of going.
Due to being afflicted by hunger and thirst, they were unable to approach a tree with dense shade and sat down in the sparse shade. Now it is no longer possible...
I was unable to do so because of my extreme weakness. Like a young child who stumbles in his gait, overcome by hunger and thirst, he died even as he was walking.
"Because of having flesh of the same birth" means because of having flesh of the same species; that is to say, human flesh. As for that human flesh...
For that is "repulsive" (*paṭikūla*) in the world because it is loathsome. Thus it is shunned by the wise.
Even among human meats, the flesh of a relative is repulsive due to its unsuitable consumption; even there, the flesh of one’s own son; even there, the flesh of a beloved son;
even there, the flesh of a young child; even there, raw meat; even there, that which has not been prepared with salt; even there...
"Saltless," and even there, "unfumigated"—thus the reason for each subsequent stage being more repulsive than the preceding one should be understood.
"Like the flesh of one's own son": by bringing forth the aspect of repulsiveness, one views it as being like the flesh of one's own son.
"One consumes attachment thereto" means that one exhausts longing for food by means of the Noble Path.
“Sā gāvī” (that cow) refers to the cow mentioned in the Sutta as: “Just as, bhikkhus, a cow... “Uddāletvā” means having torn out.
“Nissāya tiṭṭhati” means it persists by making a dependent condition.

With reference to the fact that all three types of feeling are, in their nature, suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth, he says: “of the suffering of feeling.”

Even a destination esteemed by the virtuous is indeed a state of great feverish distress, by way of the suffering inherent in change and the suffering inherent in formations, as well as by way of the suffering of the defilements;

thus it is said: "The three existences are in the sense of being states of great feverish distress. Just as there are two men who drag [someone] along, so too there are two mental volitions by way of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
One who practices so that mental volition does not arise abandons attachment toward those [volitions].
It should be understood as "he completely consumes.
"Struck by a hundred spears" is a simile; thus, it is the "simile of being struck by a hundred spears," and within that simile of being struck by a hundred spears.
That hundred spears. Of that man. "In a place where [spears] have fallen" means in the spot where the previous spears had fallen. There is no measure to his suffering.
Because it arises repeatedly in manifold ways. "The generation of the aggregates" refers to the repeated arising of the aggregates;

however, their initial manifestation is precisely rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Rebirth-linking consciousness is like a man who has committed a crime, because it is the basis for the arising of various kinds of suffering and because one must undergo those sufferings through it.
Because it functions as the leader among the associated mental states, [it is called the "foremost" of consciousness].
It is called "the arising of suffering. For it has been said: "Mind precedes all phenomena";

thus, one should understand that the act [of renunciation] therein consists in the exhaustion of attachment toward future rebirth, so that consciousness does not proceed by way of rebirth-linking in the future.
"The basis is fully understood" refers to the truth of suffering. "Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" means having the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object.
"Lust" (*rāga*). "It has been fully understood" (*pariññāto hoti*) means it has been transcended through the knowledge that discerns [it].

For when craving for taste (*rasataṇhā*) has truly vanished, craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*) and so forth have likewise vanished. This being so, the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) is indeed severed;
thus, the act of doing so should be seen as the exhaustion of attachment thereto. For when the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) is accomplished, [the fetter is severed].

Thus, the realization of abandonment is established. And showing that when the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) has been abandoned, not even a trace of the lower-tier fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) remains, he said:
"There is no such fetter," and so forth. By this, he shows that the full understanding (*pariññā*) of edible food leads to the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmitā*).
However, showing that the full understanding of the remaining nutriments culminates in Arahantship, he said: "In contact..."

He spoke the passage beginning with “Monks. Therein, “three kinds of craving” refers to these three: craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*), craving for form (*rūpatanha*), and craving for the formless (*arūpatanha*).
To explain in detail the meaning stated in brief as “due to the arising of prior craving,” he began the section starting with “How?
Therein, “produced with craving as condition” means produced by way of the condition of craving. At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it arises due to the arising of prior craving.

Since the arising of the clung-to (upādinnaka) nutriment is already shown by the very demonstration of the arising of nutriments at the moment of their occurrence, that [specific instance] is not mentioned here;
rather, in order to show the arising of craving for those things that are not clung-to (anupādinnaka), the passage beginning with "But because... was stated.
"Here" means in this sutta, where they are spoken of in combination because they are not distinguished [separately]. "Produced by the condition of co-nascent craving" means...

Here, the inclusion of the term "conascent" (sahajāta) is for the purpose of showing that nutriment not acquired by clinging (anupādinnaka-āhāra) is also found even when it is produced by a condition of craving that is not conascent.

However, because that [nutriment] might give rise to doubt due to its commonality with the aforementioned nutriment acquired by clinging—namely, the fact that both are produced by a condition of craving that is not conascent—it was not mentioned;
nor is this the reason why [the Suttanta says], "Dependent on lust, grief arises."

Because it is stated [in the scriptures], and because non-clung-to nutriment is obtained by way of craving as its decisive support (*upanissaya*) and by way of nutritive essence (*ojā*) originating from a mind accompanied by aversion (*paṭigha*).
But how can craving be a decisive support condition for nutritive essence? For nowhere in the *Paṭṭhāna* is a decisive support condition for material form ever mentioned.
This is not a contradiction, for [the definition holds]: "When A exists, B occurs; A is the decisive support for B."
Because the method of the Suttanta is intended here, and because the meaning as previously stated is possible; for this very reason he said, "by the cessation of this... craving.
Since when the cause has ceased entirely, the fruit also ceases entirely, he said, "the cessation of nutriment is discerned.
Because nutriments are a portion of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), the mention of nutriment is itself the mention of the truth of suffering; thus he said, "here..."

“All four truths have been stated in their own form. The teaching on the truths is for the purpose of demonstrating that suffering and the rest are precisely what must be fully understood and so forth;
therefore, showing that the state of being fully understood and so forth regarding aging, death, and the rest must be observed without confusion, he said:
“The truths should be extracted by one who is not confused in any respect.”
The commentary on the section on nutriment is finished.

Commentary on the section on the truths (Saccavāra-vaṇṇanā): 91. "By whichever method he explains": by whichever method—whether by way of suffering and so forth, or by way of aging and death and so forth—he speaks of the noble truths both in brief and in detail. "Suffering" refers to the truth of suffering; it is suffering, not merely a state of suffering.
The commentary on the section on the Truths is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Aging and Death (92):
The expression "of this or that" is stated here according to the desire for detailed analysis; therefore, it is just as one might say, "Village after village is delightful."
When "delightfulness" is stated, all such villages are included;
likewise, when "the birth of those various beings" is stated, all beings are included by way of the transformation designated as "birth. Therefore he said:
"In brief, this is a common description for many beings."

"By way of destiny and birth" means by way of the five destinies (*gati*); and therein, by way of each individual destiny, according to birth-class (*jāti*) such as the *khattiya* and so forth, or the terrestrial devas and so forth, or elephants and so forth.
"Nikāya" is that wherein beings are grouped together, or that by which they are grouped; it is the classification according to clan, school of thought (*caraṇa*), and so on.

"Old age" (*jarā*) is the very nature (*sabhāva*) of the decline of vitality; therefore, "old age" is a designation for the nature characterized as the decline of vitality, by way of manifest old age.

The exposition [is given] because it is grasped by way of brokenness (*khaṇḍicca*) and so forth. *Jīraṇatā* (the state of aging) is simply aging (*jīraṇa*), or else the suffix *-tā* expresses the mode (*ākāra*) of that which is aging.
Therefore he said: “This is an exposition of the mode. That person in whom brokenness has arisen in the teeth and so forth is *khaṇḍito*;
his state is *khaṇḍicca*. One who possesses grey hair is *palito*; his state is *pālicca*.
"Valittaco" means that which has wrinkled skin; the state of having wrinkled skin is "valittacatā. These—wrinkling and so forth—are aging (*jarā*).
"By way of showing the transformations" means by way of showing the decline. "Of the wind" refers to a great mass of wind.
The path traversed by way of wrinkling and so forth is evident; therefore, he shows that the mention of wrinkling and so forth is stated as a description of the function of aging.

And it is not merely brokenness and so forth that constitute aging; rather, from the time of the *kalala* onwards, at the moment when the preceding forms reach aging, succeeding forms arise that correspond to the ripening of those forms, arising as they become increasingly transformed.

Thus, in the course of time, as these highly transformed forms reach their full maturation, those things whose nature is brokenness and so forth arise. These are like the withered state of grass and trees on paths by water and the like.

Those [signs] that have arisen in respect to matured material phenomena—designated as "the path that has reached maturity"—are said to be "the path gone by means of aging," but they are not aging itself.

"By nature" (pakatiyā) means by way of the nature of the ripening of the fruit; or else, the fruit itself is the nature to be reached by aging, and it is by means of that [fruit] that aging is illustrated.
"Very clear" (suppasannāni) means perfectly clear. To show that very clarity in terms of its function, [the text says] "even the subtle," and so forth.
It has been said. For the sharpness and clarity of those faculties is their state of being well-purified. "Agitated" means confused. "Unclear" means incompetent.
Granted that even in material phenomena (rūpa-dhammas) momentary aging is difficult to discern and remains concealed;

nevertheless, because it becomes manifest through its occurrence as a continuous stream (santāna), it is described specifically as "manifest aging. Uninterrupted aging is "uninterrupted aging" (avīcijarā).
"Because of the continuous succession of beings within a continuity (*santāna*).
"In others than those" means in others such as the later decads (*mandadasaka*), etc., as distinguished from the earlier decads (*pubbadasaka*), etc., as previously described.

"From time to time" means, within those very aforementioned types, between the earlier decad and the subsequent decad. "Of the distinctions of color, etc. means of the distinctions of color, shape, tactile sensation, and so forth.
"By way of falling away" (*cavanaka-vasena*): this is stated by extending the word with the syllable *ka*; therefore, it means "falling away is death" (*cavanaṃ cuti*).

However, since that [death] is grasped without distinction as the death occurring in the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences (*bhava*), he says: "It is a general term for the one, four, and five aggregates.
Alternatively, "by way of falling away" means "by way of the person who is falling away" (*cavanakassa puggalassa vasena*). It is simply falling away.

He says, "by means of a term denoting a state (bhāvavacana)," [referring to] "the state of passing away" (cavanatā). "The demonstration of the characteristic" means the demonstration of the characteristic consisting of decay (vaya).
Alternatively, the mode of one who is passing away is expressed by the suffix -tā as "the state of passing away.

It is said that "breaking" (bhedo) is "disintegration" (bhijjana), as in the phrase "the indication of the arising of the dissolution of the aggregates of death" (cutikkhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ). Just as in the case of a broken jar by someone...
In a figurative sense, there is no standing as a solid mass; thus, for the aggregates that have been broken apart, "passing away" (cavana) is what is meant by "disappearance.
Therefore it is said: “‘Disappearance’... is an exposition. That which is called "death" (maccu) is dissolution (bheda), and that which is "dying" (maraṇa) is the relinquishing of life;
having combined both together, it is stated as “death and dying” (maccu-maraṇa). Or rather, this is the meaning here.
It is to be seen. The "action of Time, the Ender," which is spoken of in the world, is *cuti*; the meaning is "death.

Alternatively, because it cannot be transcended, the very moment of passing away is specifically called "Time"; thus its action is, in actual fact, the reaching of the dissolution of the aggregates of death (*cutikkhandhā*).
This was previously explained using conventional terminology in the passage beginning with "Death is the state of passing away" (*cuti cavanatā*).
Now, in order to show that the exposition is indeed by way of the ultimate meaning (paramattha) already produced, it is said:

"to illustrate according to the ultimate meaning. For by the passage beginning with "by way of passing away," the commentary was composed based on conventional designations (vohārādhiṭṭhānā) regarding individuals (puggala).

For those of spontaneous birth (opapātika), there is no laying down of any physical body; rather, there is simply the disappearance of the aggregates (khandha) at the moment of death (cuti), after which—

The continuity of matter produced by temperature does not proceed. Regarding such passages as "with the arising of birth," that which ought to be said can be understood through the same method already explained under "with the arising of craving" and so forth;
therefore, it has not been stated here.
The commentary on the section on aging and death is concluded.
The Exposition of the Section on Birth (Jātivāra): 93.

The passage beginning with "In the sense of being born" (*jāyanaṭṭhena*) is stated in order to demonstrate birth by encompassing all sentient beings through two pairs of terms—namely, according to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and according to the modes of birth (*yoni*).
However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is said: "Birth is so called in the sense of being born (*jāyamānaka*), and in the sense of being fully born (*sañjāyana*)."
Because it is stated as "sañjāti" (arising), it should be understood that there, by means of each single term, one demonstrates birth (*jāti*) having encompassed all sentient beings.
Considering that "sampuṇṇā jāti" (complete birth) is "sañjāti," it is said: "That is appropriate by way of the complete sense bases (*paripuṇṇāyatana*).
By this very [explanation], the incompleteness of the sense bases (*aparipuṇṇāyatanatā*) regarding the birth expressed by the word *jāti* alone should be understood. It is "abhibyattā" (manifest).
“Nibbatti” means arising (*abhinibbatti*); the sense is that arising is manifest. The phrase, “The manifestation of this or that being... [etc.]...
the manifestation,” is a teaching by way of conventional designation (*vohāradesanā*), because it proceeds by way of beings.

Regarding the expression “here and there”: in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), there are two; in the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), there are two; and in the remaining fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*)...
The inclusion [of phenomena] should be understood by way of the five bases arising at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*),
and in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) by way of seven, nine, ten, again ten, and eleven bases according to whether the faculties are deficient or complete.

Even though the aggregates of the death-moment are conditions for the immediately subsequent rebirth-linking states by way of contiguity and other such conditions, [they do not constitute a condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness itself].
However, those origins that do not produce [rebirth] are intended here as "existence at birth" (*upapattibhava*).
Showing that only the productive [origin] is intended by the term "existence," he said: "Kamma-existence, which is the condition for birth, should be understood.
The commentary on the section on birth is finished.
Commentary on Existence (Bhavavāravaṇṇanā) 94.

Existence (bhava) is twofold in the sense of becoming (bhāvana) and being (bhavana). Therein, kamma-existence (kammabhava) is existence in the sense of becoming, because "existence arises from this" (*etasmā upapattibhavo bhavati*).
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) is stated to be existence because "it comes to be" (*bhavatīti bhavo*).
Because it is the cause of that [existence], karma is called "existence" (*bhava*) by way of metaphorical designation for its fruit; this is the meaning stated here.
