In both cases, it is shown that the term "karmic existence" (*kammabhava*) applies to karma because it serves as the cause for the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). "In every respect" means in all possible ways, such as through the distinction of existence as becoming, existence as non-becoming, wholesome and unwholesome existence, existence as a fortunate rebirth, and existence as an inferior or superior state.
It is called "sensuous existence" (*kāmabhava*) because it is caused by sensual craving and because it serves as the objective field for sensual craving.

Furthermore, kamma that leads to rebirth in the fine-material realm is the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*); likewise, kamma that leads to rebirth in the immaterial realm is the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*). The aggregates produced therein are the fine-material and immaterial rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*).
Their status as fine-material and immaterial existences, however, should be understood in the same manner as explained under the heading of "sense-sphere existence" (*kāmabhava*).
The commentary on the section on existence is concluded.
Commentary on Grasping (Upādānavāra): 95. "Grasping" refers to the fourfold grasping.

For just as there is grasping of sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*) for one who performs various karmas leading to rebirth in various happy states due to a delight in sensual pleasures or a delight in existence (*bhavassāda*), so too is there grasping through false adherence to views such as annihilationism (*uccheda*).
All four types of clinging (*upādāna*) serve as conditions for their respective wholesome kamma-existences solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
For unwholesome kamma-existence, they serve as conditions by way of decisive support and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*), whether they are non-conascent, immediate, or both.
As for conascent sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), it serves as a condition by way of conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root-cause (*hetu*).
In seven ways, the remaining types of clinging become conditions there by abandoning their status as root-conditions and adding the path-condition; thus they are conditions in exactly seven ways.
For what is immediate, however, they are conditions by way of the immediate, the contiguous, the immediate-strong-dependence, the absence, the disappearance, and the repetition [conditions].

It should be understood that this "also" (api) refers to the co-nascent and so forth, as the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes them. [This refers to] the sensual desire for the physical basis (vatthu-kāma).

The meaning is that the mind clings (*upādiyati*), or that a person (*puggala*) clings by means of this. "That" refers to the object of desire (*vatthukāma*). The construction is: it is both desire (*kāma*) because one desires it, and clinging (*upādāna*) because one clings to it. "By the method stated" means by the method stated in the Abhidhamma.
The statement "the self is eternal" was spoken in order to point out a subsequent view while one is clinging to a preceding view. Just as...
This view is grasped in a progressively higher and more refined manner by way of strengthening each preceding one; thus, views such as "there is no giving" and so forth are included.

However, the inclusion of the term "self" (attaggahaṇa) refers to the clinging to a self-theory (attavādupādāna), and should not be regarded as a demonstration of the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna).
The phrase "and the world" (loko ca) here refers to that which constitutes the clinging to views, distinct from the grasping at a self, as indicated by the mention of earlier and later views.
It should be understood that this has been said. "Grasping at views" (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is a designation for every form of speculative view, because of the statement:
"All views whatsoever are grasping at views.
They grasp at virtue and observance (*sīlabbata*); that is, they grasp at virtue and observance as "the path to purification. By means of this wrong adherence.

Or it is that [view] itself, accompanied by wrong adherence. Because it accompanies virtue and observance (*sīlabbata*), and because it is a state of firm grasping, it is "clinging to virtue and observance" (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
"From the adherence that 'this is purity'" means from the state of adhering to the notion that "purity in *saṃsāra* comes through such practices as the cow-virtue and cow-observance.
By this, he shows that the adherence, due to its accompaniment by those [practices], is entitled to that designation.

“They say” means they express themselves by saying, “I have a self,” and so forth; that is, by means of this particular speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*). “Merely a doctrine of self” means merely the word “self. By this, he shows that this is merely a verbal basis, namely, the “self” imagined by outsiders.
“Craving is the clinging to sensual pleasures” (*taṇhā kāmupādānassa*): here [it is asked], “What therein is clinging to sensual pleasures?

Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, feverish passion for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and attachment to sensual pleasures—this is called clinging to sensual pleasures.”
From the statement "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*), clinging to sense-pleasures is the intensification of craving (*taṇhā*).

And this intensification of craving is simply the subsequent craving that has become strengthened by way of being the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the preceding craving. However, some say:
"Craving is the longing for an object not yet attained, like a thief reaching out his hand in the dark; [while] grasping at an object already attained..."
“Grasping (upādāna) is like seizing that very same merchandise. These states, which are the opposites of fewness of wishes and contentment, are the roots of the suffering of seeking and guarding.
Therefore, craving (taṇhā), characterized as stated, is a condition for grasping—characterized exactly as stated—which follows immediately after it, by way of decisive support (upanissaya);
it is also a condition by way of object (ārammaṇa) and so forth. However, [craving] is [a condition] for those [states] such as the immediate [condition], by way of being immediate and so forth.
This is the condition. For indeed, every instance of greed (lobha) can be designated by the term "craving" (taṇhā) as well as by the term "sensual clinging" (kāmupādāna).

As for the "remainder"—namely, views-clinging (diṭṭhupādāna) and so forth—one should understand everything according to the method already explained below: that for those [states] that are co-nascent, it is by way of being co-nascent, etc.; and for those that are not co-nascent, it is by way of proximity, decisive support, and so forth.
The commentary on the section on clinging (*upādāna*) is finished.
The commentary on the section on craving (*taṇhā*). 96.
“Eye-contact,” and so forth, is like giving a name to a son based on the mother; it is given to contact (*phassa*) based on its basis (*vatthu*), by way of its support.
Because it is the cause of arising, the object is called "merely the cause of arising," as stated in the passage beginning, "The merchant... by name.

"By way of sensual lust" means by way of being impassioned with respect to the sensual object (vatthukāma). "Relishing form" means that they relish form precisely while taking delight in it through the approval of craving (*taṇhābhinandanā*) regarding the object of form.
They take delight in form by way of the approval of views (*diṭṭhābhinandanā*), such as [regarding it] as permanent and so forth.
"Having died, he will not exist" means that after breaking up, he does not exist again because of non-rearising.

"Likewise for sound, dark [forms], and so on" means that just as craving for forms—due to its nature as sensual craving—is threefold craving according to its occurrence as eternalism-craving, annihilationism-craving, and [craving for] existence, so too are craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, and craving for tangible objects. These are the "wanderings of craving."
"From the manifestation of craving" means craving that proceeds by way of its manifestation.
"Depending on the internal [basis]" means depending on the fivefold internal aggregate (*khandha*). This genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"The thought 'I am' arises" means that, based on this internal fivefold aggregate, there arises from grasping it as a whole through craving, conceit, and views...

"It is 'I am'": this means that when that [basis] exists, such a thought arises. "It occurs as 'I am this'" means that among the kṣatriyas and so forth, one thinks "I am of this kind" by way of craving, conceit, and views; this is the apprehension here without further qualification.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the following are included]: "I am thus," "I am otherwise," "I shall be," "I shall be thus," "I shall be otherwise."

"Otherwise I shall be," "I am not," "I am," "I might be," "I might be thus," "I might be so," "I might be otherwise," "Perhaps I might be," "Perhaps I might be thus," "Perhaps I might be so," "Perhaps I might be otherwise"—
this is the inclusion of these wanderings of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*). Therein, "I am thus" is said with reference to a comparison.
"Grasping" means: "Just as this kṣatriya is, just as this brāhmaṇa is, so am I"—this is the meaning.
"I am otherwise" is a grasping in comparison with one who is not a śramaṇa:

"Just as this kṣatriya is, just as this brāhmaṇa is, I am other than that—either inferior or superior"—this is the meaning. Thus, these two previously mentioned [views] are, by way of the present, [the third and fourth views].
There are four modes of craving’s wandering. Furthermore, the four beginning with “I shall be” are stated by way of the future.
Their meaning should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the preceding tetrad. “Asasmī” means “I am non-existent”; this is a designation for the permanent;
therefore, the meaning is “I am eternal. “Satasmī” means “I am perishing”; this is a designation for the impermanent; therefore—
"I am eternal" is the meaning. Thus, these two are stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism.
The four following views, beginning with "I might be," are stated by way of speculative doubt; they should be understood in meaning according to the method explained for the preceding tetrad.
The four beginning with "Perhaps I might be" are stated by way of aspiration and imagining, thinking, "May I indeed come to be."
These have been stated; they are to be understood according to the same method explained for the preceding tetrad.
Herein, the two views stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism are called "heads of views" (*diṭṭhisīsa*).

However, these four—“I am,” “I shall be,” “I might be,” and “I may not be”—are simply "pure heads" (*suddhasīsa*). Furthermore, there are twelve "rooted in a head," consisting of three triads beginning with “I am thus” (*itthasmī*).

Thus, these eighteen modes of craving’s movement (*taṇhāvicarita*)—namely, two based on views, four based on purity, and twelve based on the head—are to be understood with reference to the internal [aggregates].
"With reference to the external" means with reference to the external pentad of aggregates; for here too, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

By means of this or that form... up to ... by means of this or that consciousness—thus, regarding each one among form and the rest as "I," and grasping the other as a possession or an impediment, one adheres to it as "I am" through craving and so forth;
"by means of this" is the specific distinction here. By means of this term "I am," one adheres to [the thought]: "I am a khattiya" because of my sword, or my parasol, or my consecration.
“Supported by external form, etc. means supported by external forms, feelings, and so forth, which are included within the continua of others.
“Eighteen”: by this term, the eighteen [types of conceit] that proceed in the manner of “I am,” etc., are indicated; these are to be understood in the same way as previously explained.
For the only distinction here is the word “by this”; therefore, having determined them according to the method stated in the passage beginning with “two heads of views,” etc.
[The number] should be understood. However, having combined both together, he said "thirty-six.
By the meaning of the exposition means by the statement of the meaning of the explanatory text (pāḷi) beginning with, "Friends, there are these six groups of craving.

By the detailed exposition of that [text] means by way of the detailed expansion of that exposition according to the eight hundred modes of the movement of craving (taṇhāvicarita). And of that detailed exposition...
"By way of inclusion" means: first, by way of including within six and then within three the eighteenfold classification of the wanderings of craving that was detailed in two ways;
and second, because resultant feeling is intended here specifically as that which is to be relished by the self. For it is precisely that quality of being relished which belongs to it.
In order to explain this, the passage beginning with “How? was stated. “By way of relishing” means by way of delight. “Treating as ‘mine’” means treating as property.

In the phrase “of painters and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (ādi) includes those who provide objects of desirable color. In the phrase “by way of demonstrating crafts and so forth,” the word “and so forth” includes physicians and others;
for physicians [act] by way of providing elixirs and tonics, and by way of supporting [the body] therewith.
And they are givers of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). This word "beginning" (ādi) should be applied individually to each term, as in the phrase "lute-players and so forth.
"Loving their son" means cherishing their son. Here, feeling (vedanā) should be regarded as like the son;

desirable objects such as forms and so on—which serve as conditions for feeling—are like the beneficial ghee, milk, and so forth; and those who provide the sixfold objects of form and so on are like the nurse.
The painters and so forth are to be understood [as metaphors].
The commentary on the section on craving is finished.
The commentary on the section on feeling.

97. Feeling born of eye-contact itself, when taken together as a single mass by way of its divisions into past and so forth, constitutes one "feeling aggregate" (*vedanā-kāya*), just as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) does.

Likewise, those born of ear-contact and so on are included; thus it is said in the Canon: "Friend, these six are the feeling aggregates. Therefore, he says: "Feeling aggregates means collections of feeling. [Those] born from eye-contact...
Feeling born of eye-contact. That, moreover, is both acquired (upādinnā) and unacquired (anupādinnā); since the commentary on the meaning was composed by including both of these, he said:
"This, first of all, is the inclusive explanation here. Now, taking only that which is acquired under the heading "this is the method of result," he said:
"by way of result," and so forth. [In the case of] the mind-door, those associated with the mind-consciousness-element...
[It is] associated with the mind-consciousness element that has that [object] as its object.

"The remaining" refers to the feelings of reception (*sampaṭicchana*) and so forth. Regarding "the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*) and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the immediate condition (*anantara*) and others should be understood.
For contact is a condition for the immediate ones by way of being the immediate condition and so forth, and for the others by way of the decisive support condition.
However, in the case of the mind-door, mental contact is a condition for the feelings that take that as their object by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"Of those without doors" means of those devoid of doors; for there is no door whatsoever for the feelings of rebirth-linking and so forth.
By the phrase "from the arising of the co-nascent mental contact," he states its status as a condition for them from the perspective of the limit of co-nascence (*sahajātakoṭi*).
The commentary on the section on feeling is finished.
Commentary on the section on contact: 98.
Contact that arises dependent on the eye is "eye-contact. "Based on the five bases" means based on the five bases beginning with the eye.
“Supported by the five bases beginning with the eye. The inclusion of the number twenty-two is because this is a discourse on what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*);

the inclusion of the term “mundane” (*lokiya*) is because it is a discourse concerning the process of occurrence (*pavatti*). “Contact associated with resultant mind-consciousness” means contacts associated with resultant mental consciousness (*vipākamanoviññāṇa*).
Since the condition must be clung-to just as that which has arisen from the condition is clung-to, [the text says] “of the six, beginning with the eye.”
"...of the sense bases" is what was stated.
The commentary on the section on contact is finished.
The commentary on the section on the six sense bases.

99. This is merely an illustration; therefore, just as here—in view of the immaterial world—the sixth base and the six bases are intended to be expressed by the single remainder (*ekasesa*) as "the six bases," so too, according to those for whom that which is produced by conditions is clung-to (*upādinna*), while the condition itself is not clung-to (*anupādinnā*), the single remainder should be understood even by way of the external bases: "The sixth base and..."
"Both the sixfold base and the sixfold base are the 'sixfold base. Since the *Visuddhimagga* is a commentary on the meaning of this scripture, he says:
"In the *Visuddhimagga*... it is according to the method already stated. This same principle applies whenever the *Visuddhimagga* is mentioned elsewhere.
The commentary on the section on the sixfold base is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Name-and-Form (Nāmarūpa):
100. "The characteristic of bending" (*namanalakkhaṇa*) means having the nature of bending toward the object, because it does not function without that [object].

"Being affected by change" (*ruppana*) is the arising of something different when there is a concurrence of opposing conditions such as cold and so forth. However, by the phrase "these three," etc., [the author] speaks in a manner common to all mental states (*cittuppāda*).
That is the inclusion of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); therefore, he shows that even those factors which are not common [to all aggregates] are included by implication.

"Having grasped" (upādiyitvā) means having made them a condition. For the very act of making a condition is the grasping of the factors that serve as conditions for that which has arisen from those conditions.
This genitive case-ending expresses a relationship with a collection; thus it is said: "This genitive case-ending is used in the sense of a collection."

Because without that [consciousness], there would be an absence of connection. "Tenā" means "therefore. "All that" refers to all twenty-seven types, categorized as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*).
"Of which mind" refers to the mind in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*). Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) should also be understood as being included therein.

"Of matter" refers to matter in the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*). However, in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*), consciousness is specifically the formative consciousness (*saṅkhāra-viññāṇa*).

Regarding the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*): by way of that [name-and-form], one should understand the conditionality of that respective consciousness for that respective name,
according to what is appropriate— by way of co-nascence and so forth for the co-nascent, by way of immediacy and so forth for the immediate,
and by way of decisive support and so forth for the other.
The commentary on the section on name-and-form is finished.
Commentary on the section on consciousness (101):
The reason for including the resultant [consciousness] of the three planes has already been stated below. "The volitional formation of which consciousness... [and so forth].
Herein, the eightfold formation of sense-sphere merit is the cause for the sixteenfold resultant consciousness of the sense sphere;
the fivefold formation of fine-material-sphere merit is the cause for the fivefold resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere;
and the twelvefold formation of demerit is the cause for the sevenfold unwholesome resultant consciousness. The fourfold...

The imperturbable kamma-formations are a condition, as appropriate, for the fourfold resultant consciousness of the formless sphere—both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence—by way of both kamma-condition and decisive-support-condition. This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The commentary on the section on consciousness is finished.
Commentary on the section on formations (saṅkhāra): 102.
"Characterized by volitional construction" means having the intrinsic nature of being intended; the meaning is that it is characterized by accumulation. "By way of impelling" means...
By way of the impulsion (copana) designated as bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). By this, volition pertaining to the five doors is excluded.
"By way of the differentiation of speech" means by way of the utterance of words; the meaning is: by way of originating vocal intimation (vacīviññatti).

The aforementioned twenty [types of wholesome volition], together with the nine sublime wholesome volitions, constitute twenty-nine types of mental volition (manosañcetanā). "By way of decisive support (upanissaya) for the wholesome... [and so forth].

It has been stated [that it is a condition] by way of co-nascence and so forth; it should also be stated that for some [states], it is by way of the object (ārammaṇa). "By way of co-nascence and so forth" means by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions, as well as by way of the root-cause (hetu) condition.

For those [states] that are immediate, it is a condition by way of the immediate (anantara), contiguous (samanantara), proximity (anantara), decisive-support (upanissaya), absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), and repetition (āsevana) conditions.
By the word "api" (also/even), the decisive-support (upanissaya) condition is included.
The commentary on the section on volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-vāra*) is finished. 103.
To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly as “ignorance regarding the truth of suffering,” the passage beginning with “Therein” (*tattha*) is commenced.
That is ignorance (*aññāṇa*). Although it is something to be abandoned, it is included within the category of what is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
And its truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—meaning both the truth of suffering as the objective basis and the truth of suffering as the associated aggregates—is the object of that ignorance;
for it serves as its supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). Of that [truth of suffering], by way of obstructing the penetration of its characteristic as it truly is...
By way of obstructing the penetration of the conditioned nature that is non-perverted.
By this, he states its state as an impediment to the penetration of the Noble Path, which is termed the "clear realization through full understanding" (*pariññābhisamaya*).

"By the occurrence of knowledge" means by the occurrence of preliminary knowledge in the mode of awakening: "This is suffering; this much is suffering. "In this" refers to the Truth of Suffering. "By non-bestowal" means...
By "non-release. By this, he states that it is also an obstruction to the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anubodha-ñāṇa*).
It should be understood through three reasons because it is included therein.

Here, ignorance regarding the origin (*samudaya*) should be seen in terms of the basis (*vatthu*) by way of the associated aggregates (*sampayutta-khandha*) alone. "By one only" rejects the other three reasons. Even though it is ignorance...
It does not take cessation and the path as its object; how, then, could it possess the quality of being included within them?

However, for one who desires to know them, that [ignorance] which occurs by way of concealing them and by way of causing the apprehension of cessation and the path where they are not present is called "ignorance regarding cessation and the way leading to cessation.
Therefore, he said, "by way of concealing," and so forth. This is its meaning.
It has already been stated. "By its profundity" means by its very nature it is profound.

It is "hard to see" because, due to its lack of a fathomable foundation, it is impossible to produce knowledge regarding its object. However, the first two truths are profound not by their intrinsic nature, but in the sense of being deceptive;
that is, they are hard to see because they appear in a way that is not according to reality. Therefore—
Ignorance arises with respect to that object. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*):

because the characteristic of the true nature of impermanence and so forth is difficult to see within those first two truths, one must supply and connect the words "ignorance proceeds by way of the perversions such as permanence.
Now, in order to show the analysis of the occurrence of ignorance within the truths through an analytical exposition, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) was stated.

In that context, by the locative designation "in suffering" (*dukkhe*), [it is shown]. "By way of inclusion" means because it is to be included within suffering due to its being something to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
By this, he shows the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); for ignorance is selected out as being in suffering, not in anything else.

"By way of basis" means in the sense of a support; for ignorance has suffering as its foundation. "By way of object" means in the sense of a domain, because it proceeds having taken that [suffering] as its object.
"By way of function (*kicca*)": because it proceeds by pervading that [object] through the act of concealing for the purpose of spreading.

In this manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining [truths] as well. "Without distinction (*avisesa*)": because of the absence of distinction; the meaning is that one does not take up any specific mode of occurrence regarding suffering and so forth according to the method already stated.
"By way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*"): by way of its own essential characteristic. For all four truths have the intrinsic nature of non-knowing.
For ignorance is indeed [the taint]. Since sensual lust and lust for existence are the taints of sensuality and the taint of existence, he said, "by way of being co-nascent, etc.
One might ask: "Is it not the case that ignorance itself is the taint of ignorance? How then can it be a condition for ignorance? To this he replied, "arisen previously," and so forth.
The commentary on the section on ignorance is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Taints (Āsavavāra) 104. The meaning of the word *āsava* and an investigation into the taints have already been explained above.

Now, with reference to the objection, "Why is this section stated? Is it not the case that the teaching on dependent origination consists only of ignorance and so forth?", [the author] says, "This section," and so on.
"Initiated. Regarding "in the sections on dependent origination": this refers to the constituent parts of dependent origination.
For the Teacher’s teaching on dependent origination consists of twelve parts.

"By way of showing its condition" means that this [ignorance] is not without a condition like the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) of the followers of Kapila; rather, it is with a condition. Thus, by way of showing the condition even for ignorance: "by way of the origin of the taints (*āsava*)."

Through the arising of the taints (*āsava*) in a past existence there is the arising of ignorance (*avijjā*) now; through the arising of ignorance now there will be the arising of taints in the future.

Thus, because the taints and ignorance proceed from one to another by way of being condition and conditioned, and because the beginning of that *saṃsāra*—which has them as its cause—is likewise without a beginning, the state of being "without end in either direction" (*anamataggatā*) should be understood as established.
"Thirty-two points" means thirty-two causes for the penetration of the truths, or thirty-two meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) on the Four Truths.
"From this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta" refers to that noble right view by which a noble disciple is called one of right view;
since that noble right view is explained here, it is the "Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta," and [the phrase means] "from this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta."

“By way of the exposition of the Four Truths” means by way of the causes for the realization of the Four Truths. “By way of the exposition of Arahantship” means by way of the causes for the realization of Arahantship, such as [the passage] beginning, “Having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust. Therefore he said, “by sixty-four reasons.
The commentary on the section on the taints (*āsava*) is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Sammādiṭṭhi-sutta* is complete.
10. Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta 105.
"Jānapadino" means those who possess a country, or princes who are lords over a country. They are called "Kurus" by way of their lineage (*gotta*).
If their residence constitutes a single country, one might ask how there can be a plural form; thus he says: "By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsaddena*)."
For grammarians (*akkharacintaka*) desire that in such instances the gender and number be appropriate [to the meaning], according to the rule *yutte viya saliṅgavacanāni* (Pāṇini 1.2.51).
This is the conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) here, just as in other cases such as "he dwells among the Aṅgas" and "he dwells among the Mallans.

However, when qualifying that word "country" (*janapada*), which is a term for a genus (*jāti*), it takes only the singular number. As for the phrase "but the teachers of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathācariyā*)," the word *pana* [indicates]...
It is for the purpose of indicating a distinction (*visesatthajotana*). By means of that, because its referent is a plurality of objects, it is thus a plural number;

this indicates the specific detail that will be explained by the words beginning with "But many" (*bahuke pana*). "Having heard" (*sutvā*) means having heard the account handed down through tradition in accordance with the display of the majesty of the Great King Mandhātu.
"While wandering about" (*anusaṃyāyantena*) means while roaming about. "The place of these" (*etesaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) refers to [the place] headed by the moon and the sun.
He speaks of the abode of the Cātumahārājika gods. Therefore he says, “He went there,” and so forth. “He” refers to the Great King Mandhātā.
“That” refers to the sovereignty of the Cātumahārājikas. “Having taken” means having accepted. He questioned the counselor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratanam) again.
They stand on the ground of the gatekeepers because they are appointed for the protection of the four gates of the divine assembly hall (Sudhammā) and the city of the gods.
"Adorned with thousands of celestial trees"—this should also be applied to the phrases "the grove of variegated creepers" (*cittalatāvana*) and so forth.
"It stood upon the earth": having descended, it remained in a place near the earth;
and having stood there, it soon vanished because the King, the Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*), lacked the power to sustain that particular existence for longer. "For a much longer time..."

"Having stood," say others. The state of being a deva appeared because an opportunity had been created for karma that yields its result in the process of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*) and is to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*).
Since a distinction established in a part serves to qualify the whole, even a single kingdom is expressed using the plural number.

They explain the meaning by means of the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) through the letter *da*. "Kammāsa" refers to Kammāsapāda by the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*), just as "rūpabhava" is called "rūpa.
But how is he "Kammāsapāda"? To this he says, "It is said that of him... and so forth.
Regarding the word "tamed" (*damita*), what kind of taming is intended here? He says: "He was restrained from the state of being a man-eater (*porisāda*). And these...
"Theras" refers to the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya; however, they speak thus with reference to Cūḷakammāsadamma.
For Kammāsapāda, the son of a yakkhinī, was tamed there by the Bodhisatta during his time as Prince Alīnasattu.
But Mahākammāsadamma is that place where he was tamed by the King of Bārāṇasī during his time as Sutasoma, through the prevention of his state as a man-eater (porisāda).
Regarding the name: having said "son" (*putta*), the term "born of one's own womb" (*atraja*) is used for the purpose of showing his status as a legitimate son.
As for those by whom the region they inhabited received the name "Kuru-land," those people came from Uttarakuru;
there they observed the five precepts according to the system of protection [they had known], and the later generations followed their example.

Thus, as it continued without interruption by way of the laws of the country, it became known as the "Duty of the Kurus" (*kuruvattadhamma*); and this matter can be illustrated by the *Kurudhamma Jātaka*.
Later on, in order to show where he was first born with a defiled mind, the words beginning with "of the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru" were spoken.
[The word] "where" refers to a certain monastery that served as the Blessed One’s dwelling place.
In that context, the mere description of the village as a resort is the natural function of the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*);
thus, in order to show the meaning of "he dwelt among the Sakyans at the town named Devadaha," he said "from the place of residence" and so forth.
[End of] the commentary on the section concerning the recitation (*uddesavāra*).

106. When it is asked, "Why did the Blessed One speak this sutta?", the question refers to the uncommon origin (*asādhāraṇasamuṭṭhāna*), while the common origin is left unmentioned because it is self-evident.

Since the placement of the sutta (*suttanikkhepa*) is what is being questioned, the other [the commentator] shows by the words "of the inhabitants of the Kurū kingdom," etc., that this placement of the sutta arises from another's inclination (*aparajjhāsayo*). By this, it should be understood that the external origin has been elucidated.
However, the internal and specific [conditions] should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* and other texts.

It is said that at that time, the kingdom of Kuru was endowed with favorable climate and other conditions because, for the most part, the beings dwelling there possessed wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and by the power of merit performed in the past.
Therefore it is stated: "Because of being endowed with the condition of climate and so forth."
By the word "ādi" (etc.), the excellence of food and so forth is included. Some, however, say:

"Due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of having formerly practiced the duties and laws of Kuru, that kingdom—while being for the most part endowed with a favorable climate and other conditions, much like Uttarakuru—became during the time of the Blessed One exceptionally suited to the climate and other requirements.
"Cittasarīrakallatāya" means by way of the health of both the mind and the body.
"Those whose power of wisdom is supported" means those who have obtained the assistance of the majesty of knowledge, or those in whom the fire of wisdom has been repeatedly cultivated.

"In twenty-one instances" refers to the fourteen instances by way of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), one instance by way of contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*), likewise one by way of contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*), and five instances by way of contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*); thus, in twenty-one [instances].

Regarding the stages: "Having included the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in Arahantship" means that by way of the teaching, he has included it in Arahantship so that the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths brings about the attainment of Arahantship.
Just as various flowers such as jasmine and campaka, or the seven treasures such as the mani-gem, placed within golden caskets or golden boxes, [shine] due to the excellence of the vessels...

They shine with distinction and perform their functions due to their pleasant nature; likewise, this teaching of the Blessed One, delivered to the assembly dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru—which has become a distinguished vessel through its perfection in virtue, vision, and so forth—shines all the more and performs its function.
By the passage beginning with “Just as a man,” he shows this meaning. “Therein” means in the kingdom of Kuru.
"By nature" means by way of its own inherent essence; the intention is that this was so even prior to the teaching of this Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*).
"They dwell devotedly" means they dwell according to the Teacher’s instruction—this is the intention.

"With a neglected selfhood" means with a mind that has not been directed toward any appropriate mental attention (such as impermanence and so forth), but rather with a mind that is negligent due to delighting in sense objects such as forms.
It is not fitting to remain so; the intention is that one must abandon dwelling in negligence and become heedful.

Regarding the term *ekāyano*: here the word *ayana* is a synonym for "path. To show that it is not only this word but many others as well are synonyms for "path," he says, "of the path," and so forth. If the word *ayana* is a synonym for "path,"...
Addressing the objection, "But why is it called the 'path'? he says "Therefore," and so forth. In this context, "the single path" means there is only one path;
for there is no other path leading to Nibbāna. [Objection: Is it not the case that "foundation of mindfulness" is intended here as the "path," while there are many other path-factors besides it?
[Reply: True, they exist; however, they are included by the very mention of the foundation of mindfulness.
They are included because they are inseparable from it. For indeed, knowledge, energy, and so forth are included in the *Niddesa*;
however, their inclusion under mindfulness alone in the *Uddesa* should be understood as being due to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

By the phrase "not being a forked path," he shows that this Path, like a non-forked path, lacks the state of having multiple paths and lacks the state of not leading to Nibbāna. "By one" means without a companion.
Lack of companionship is twofold: either by way of the absence of a second self, which is called "physical seclusion" (*vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā*);
or by way of the absence of craving as a companion, which is called "mental seclusion" (*pavivittacittatā*). Therefore he said, "by one who is secluded and whose mind is secluded.
Even a superior person in the world is called "one" in such expressions as "as long as you make others one with yourself," etc.; thus he said, "of the one, i.e., the superior."

If the meaning of "going" (*ayana*) is the sense of escaping from *saṃsāra*, and if that is common to others who possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), how is it [unique] to the Blessed One?
To this he says: "Even though," and so forth. Here, the word "kho" (*khu*) has the sense of restriction;
therefore, the meaning is "in this very [teaching]. For this is merely a difference in the mode of teaching, namely, whether one calls it the "path" (*magga*) or the "going" (*ayana*).
Therefore he said, "But the purpose is one.

"Proceeding by way of various doors and methods of development" means it proceeds by way of the door of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) and so forth, and even therein, by way of the door of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and so forth, according to the method of development.
"The single path" (*ekāyana*) means leading to one [goal]; the meaning is that it leads to Nibbāna. For Nibbāna, because it is peerless and supreme—
And it is called "one. As it is said: "For there is one truth, there is no second," and:

"To whatever extent, monks, there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them. Destruction itself is the end; thus, it is the "end of destruction" (khayanta).
One who has seen the end of destruction regarding birth is a "seer of the end of birth" (jātikhayantadassī). [He sees] all beings without distinction...
"One who sympathizes with what is beneficial" is *hitānukampī*. "They crossed over" (*atarinsu*) means they have crossed over. "In the past" (*pubbe*) refers to former Buddhas, or to the past time.
"That" (*taṃ*) refers to their speech; however, its being expressive of a verbal action (*kiriyāvutti*) is not tenable.
For there is no quality of expressing a verbal action in the word *eka*, which denotes a number, even when it is the primary element—as in expressions such as "even once he might go upwards."
It must be [the reading] "sakim-ayano" with this phrasing. "Having thus construed the meaning" means having thus construed the meaning of the words.
"In both ways" means by the former method and by the latter method. It is not appropriate [in the latter case] because the path intended here exists as something that occurs many times.
Therefore he said, "Why? and so forth. "It goes even many times" refers to the former method.
“The fact that his path is manifold” is a refutation of the latter method. Regarding this term:
it refers either to the statement, “This, monks, is the one-way path,” or to the point of doubt concerning whether it is the preliminary path or the supramundane path.
“The mixed path” means the supramundane path mixed with the mundane.
The Elder Teacher, including the direct cause for purification and so forth, said "the mixed path";
the other [teacher], however, meaning the indirect cause intended here, said "the preliminary path.
"Having heard the sound" means having heard the sound announcing the time, namely, "It is time, venerable sir, for hearing the Dhamma. "Having thus raised [the question]" means...
Thus, they do not wander about carrying [this] as if it were a load of sugarcane, thinking, "Where shall we throw away this sweet thing? without actually throwing it away.

"Is agitated" (*āluḷeti*) means that it becomes stirred up and confused. The "path traveled by one alone" (*ekāyanamagga*) refers to the path of the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamagga*).
When the intended meaning here has been established by this much, for the sake of its further embellishment, [it is said]: "But that [mindfulness], for which there is a preliminary path..."
To demonstrate this, the verses beginning with “The eightfold among paths” have also been brought and placed here from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
“In the sense of going to Nibbāna”: it is called "going to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagamana*) because one goes to—that is, attains—Nibbāna by means of it;
that very thing is the "meaning" (*attha*) because its intrinsic nature is non-perverted. Thus, "in the sense of going to Nibbāna" means in the sense of being the means for the attainment of Nibbāna.

"In the sense of being sought after" means in the sense of being something to be searched for; or alternatively, the reading is "in the sense of being approached," meaning in the sense of being something to be resorted to.
"By lust and so forth": by this, only lust, hatred, and delusion are included, because of the statement, "Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain.
However, by the phrase "by covetousness, improper greed, and so forth," all defilements whatsoever are included.
They have been extracted separately for the purpose of inclusion. To demonstrate the absolute certainty of the meaning stated as "for the purification of beings," he said, "For thus," and so forth.

Granted that "for purification" is a general indication, he said, "But by way of the stain of form," and so on, in order to show that it is specifically the purification of the mind (cittavisuddhi) that is intended here. This is not merely the word of the commentary;
Then, showing that this was spoken as a direct statement (*āhacca-bhāsita*) regarding this matter, he said, "For it is thus," and so forth.
Furthermore, since this purification of mind, when accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and the rest, it is therefore stated:
"for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation," and so on. In that context, "sorrowing" refers to [the grief] caused by the loss of relatives and the like.
Sorrow (*soka*) is the burning of the mind, an inward brooding.

Lamentation (*parideva*) is the prattling by way of wailing—such as "Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?"—due to an excess of sorrow caused specifically by the loss of relatives and the like.

"For the sake of abandoning" (*pahānāya*) is said because its transcendence here consists in not arising again in the future. Furthermore, that [abandoning] brings about its transcendence; this is shown by way of illustration.
Showing this, he said, “This indeed,” and so forth.
Therein, “purify that which was before” refers to the purification of the defilement of craving regarding past aggregates. “Afterwards” means later. “That” means yours.
“Let there not be” means let it not exist. “Possession” (kiñcana) refers to the possession of lust and so forth. By this, [it is meant] regarding those yet to come...
The purification of defilement regarding the aggregates has been stated. "In the middle" means in the interval between those two. "If you will not grasp" means if you will not cling.
By this, the occurrence of clinging within the present continuity of the aggregates is stated. "You will wander at peace":
when there is thus purification of defilement pertaining to the three periods of time, one wanders at peace because all feverish distress has been extinguished.
Having offered [this], you shall dwell [in peace]—thus he concluded the verse with the pinnacle of *arahatta*. Therefore, he said: "This verse," and so forth.
"Sons" means legitimate offspring, or whoever else they may be. "Father" means the progenitor. "Relatives" means kinsmen. This is the meaning here:
whether sons, father, or relatives, for one who is assailed and overcome by the End-maker, Death...
"They do not provide protection; therefore, there is no refuge among kinsmen. For there is no protection from death by means of kinsmen.
Therefore, the intention is: "O Paṭācārā, do not lament fruitlessly with words such as 'both my sons have died,' but rather see the Dhamma according to its true nature."

“Established in the fruit of stream-entry”: at the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching that was delivered in accordance with the truth and was self-exalting, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry adorned with the thousandfold method.
But how did she become established in the fruit of stream-entry by way of the path of the foundations of mindfulness?
To this he says, “Because...,” and so forth. For it is not by means of a discourse on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths [that one is established].
There is the attainment of the Noble Path even without [the presence of] disciples.

However, the phrase "having heard this verse" is stated because this verse was first heard as it was being recited for the purpose of dispelling sorrow; the same method applies to the other verse as well. "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation of wisdom (*paññā*), for that is what is intended here.
Therefore, the contemplation (*anupassanā*) of form and so forth as impermanent and so on is also the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Therefore: "They too" refers to the minister Santati and Paṭācāra.
"Five hundred thieves" means he dispatched five thieves in succession, each accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thieves.
Having entered the forest and searching for the Elder, they eventually came into his presence. Thus he said: "They went and [found] the Elder..."
“...surrounding him, they sat down. The connection is: “Having suppressed the painful sensation, rapture and gladness arose.

For as the Elder was reflecting upon his virtue, the sublime rapture and gladness arising in dependence on that perfectly pure virtue suppressed the painful sensation produced by the breaking of the thigh bone.
“Pādāni” means “the feet. “Saññapessāmi” means “I shall persuade.”
"I shall do. "I am disgusted" means I feel loathing. "I am ashamed" means I feel shame. "Vipassissanti" means I have attained clear insight.
"Of those nodding" refers to those who have fallen into sleep. "Endowed with vows" means endowed with the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
He says "negligence" with reference to nodding. "With mind restrained" means with the higher mind (adhicitta) suppressed. "In the cage"—
Regarding the body: for here, the body is called a "cage" because it is a collection of bones bound together by sinews.

He was a yellow-clad wrestler (*pītamalla*) because he carried a yellow-colored banner and because he possessed a mind skilled in wrestling. Regarding "in the three kingdoms": this refers to the kingdoms of Paṇḍu, Coḷa, and Goḷa.
Wrestlers receive honor and respect in the island of Sihaḷa; thus, [he went] to Tambapaṇṇidīpa.

"Having approached. "Making that very [teaching] a goad" means: having made the meaning proclaimed in the *Tumhāka-vagga*—namely, "form and so forth should not be grasped as 'mine'"—a goad for the elephant of one's own mind.
"He walks on his heels" because, he thinks, "if I sit down, there will be an opportunity for sleep.
"Having explained" means: by way of making known the fruitfulness of his own exertion of energy.
Having inspired his fellow practitioners and declared his own higher knowledge (*aññā*), he spoke these words. To whom did he speak? He says:
"To the Best of Buddhas, the Foremost Speaker in all the world. The passage beginning with "Not yours" and so forth is a demonstration of the manner in which that [teaching] proceeded.
Showing that this is the cause for the absolute stilling of the conditioned formations (*saṅkhārā*), he brought forward the verse: "Impermanent indeed... and so on.

By this, he shows that he is now "healthy" (*aroga*) and "fully extinguished" (*parinibbuto*) due to the absence of the disease known as the moment-by-moment dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"His" (*assa*) refers to Sakka. "Rebirth" (*upapatti*) means rebirth among the gods. It became exactly as it was before because he was reborn specifically in his capacity as Sakka.
"Subrahmā" is his name. Having seen the rebirth of the celestial nymphs (*accharā*) in hell, from that time forth [he maintained] that which was constantly occurring...
He says, “This mind is constantly terrified,” and so forth, referring to the terror within his own mind.
In this context, *utrastaṃ* means frightened or afraid; *ubbiggaṃ* means agitated. Alternatively, *utrastaṃ* means agitated, while *ubbiggaṃ* means shaken along with the body due to fear.
*Anuppannesu* means in those that have not yet arisen. *Kicchesu* means in sufferings. [The suffix -su here denotes] the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
The locative case signifies "the cause for the arising of future suffering"—this is the meaning. The phrase *uppātitesu* is to be construed with *kicchesu*, meaning "when difficulties have arisen";
the intention is that it refers to the sign of suffering having arisen for one's own retinue at that time.
*Bojjhā* means "from awakening," that is, from the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). The word *aññatra* is an ablative (*nissakkavacana*) used in relation to the following term.
Therefore, the meaning is "excepting enlightenment. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "From austerity" (*tapasā*) means from the practice of asceticism (*tapokamma*).
By this, he shows the practice of effacement (*sallekha*), such as the observance of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*), which serves as the means for attaining the Path.

"From restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvarā*) means from the restraining of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth. By this, under the heading of the restraint of mindfulness, he indicates the entire morality of restraint according to the method of the extraction of characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*).

Or it shows the entire fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "From the relinquishing of all" means from the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*) and from the abandoning of all defilements (*kilesa*);
for when the defilements have been relinquished, the cycle of kamma and the cycle of its result are likewise relinquished.
"Safety" means security and freedom from calamity.
It is called *ñāya* because it leads with certainty—that is, it goes toward Nibbāna—or because Nibbāna is known or penetrated by means of it;
thus it is said: "The noble eightfold path is called *ñāya*. It is "devoid of the bondage of craving" because it is free from the bondage known as craving.
For craving binds (*vinati*) the aggregates to the aggregates, or fruit to karma, or suffering to sentient beings, and it sews them together (*saṃsibbati*).
"Vāna" is so called [from the root *vā*, meaning "to weave"].

This is *nibbāna*—the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*)—because there is no weaving (*vāna*) here, or because there is no further weaving for a person once this has been attained. "Realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) means making directly manifest without depending on another; thus he said, "by way of personal direct experience" (*attapaccakkhatāya*).

Now, one might object: "Since 'for the sake of purification' (visuddhiyā) intends the purification of mind (cittavisuddhi), the transcendence of sorrow and so forth are already included by the mention of 'purification' itself;
why then are they mentioned again? Addressing this inquiry, it is said: "In that regard, although... and so forth.
"Skilled in the principles of the Dispensation" means proficient in the Dharma-methods characterized by the truths, dependent origination, and so on.

"He makes known this and that meaning" means that by means of his own skill in teaching, the Blessed One, awakening each and every person capable of being awakened in whatever way they ought to be awakened—

whether in brief or in detail— makes known this and that meaning. "Showing it by making it manifest" means that, disregarding any transgression regarding the meaning, he makes that and that meaning manifest.
He speaks thus, demonstrating this. For the Fully Enlightened Ones do not utter words that must be established through logical proof, such as pointing out the existence of a fault.
"Leads to" (*saṃvattati*) means it arises; the meaning is "it comes to be.

Because there is never any purification of the mind for one who has not transcended sorrow and lamentation—since the accomplishment of mental purification occurs only by way of transcending sorrow and lamentation—he said: "Of sorrows and lamentations..."

“...it comes about through transcendence. However, because sorrow and the rest overwhelm an ordinary person (puthujjana) who is touched by painful states conditioned by mental grief, and because those [states] do not exist when those conditions have been fully understood, it is therefore said:
“The transcendence of sorrow and lamentation is through the subsiding of pain and mental grief. “Of the method” (ñāyassa) means of the supreme path, the third path.
Indeed, through the attainment of that [knowledge], suffering and mental distress cease respectively.

Although the realization of the others (the remaining truths) occurs simultaneously with the realization by way of direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), it is described as being "caused by" the realization by way of direct experience because it is inseparable from it, as in the phrase:

"The attainment of the method is for the sake of the direct experience of Nibbāna. Alternatively, this was said with reference to making [Nibbāna] manifest through the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*): "Of Nibbāna..."
"for the sake of realization. This should be understood as the dative case (the recipient of praise).
"Speaking of praise" means words of commendation. Showing that this was not done only here, but that the Teacher did it elsewhere as well, he said, "For just as...
and so forth. In that context, it is "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*); or, its beginning is good, thus it is "good in the beginning."

The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. It is "possessing the meaning" (*sāttha*) because of the perfection of its meaning; it is "possessing the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) because of the perfection of its phrasing.
It is "entirely complete" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*) because the five aggregates of dhamma, beginning with virtue, are fulfilled and there is nothing further to be added;

it is "utterly pure" (*parisuddha*) because it is free from defilements and there is nothing to be removed. It is the "noble life" (*brahmacariya*) because it is the supreme conduct, namely the life of the Dispensation and the life of the Path.
"I shall explain them to you"—this is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Noble lineages" (*ariyavaṃsā*) means the lineages or traditions of the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas. "Foremost" (*aggaññā*) means they are to be known as "foremost" because of their preeminence over all other lineages.
"Ancient" (*rattaññā*) means they are to be known as "long-standing. "Lineages" (*vaṃsaññā*) means they are the lineages of the Buddhas and so forth.
They should be known. "Ancient" means old, because they are not of recent origin. "Unmixed" means unadulterated, not removed.
"Never before mixed" means they have never been removed by the Noble Ones with the thought, "What is the use of these? "Are not being mixed" means they are not being removed by them even now.
"Will not be mixed" means they will not be removed by them in the future either. "Unreproached... by the wise" refers to those who...
"In the world" means among the wise ascetics and brahmins; "unblamed by them" means not censured or criticized by them.

"By such words as 'purity' (*visuddhi*) and so forth" means by those words that illustrate purity and the rest. "By phrases" means by sentences, or by distinct portions of the Dhamma differentiated by categories such as the meaning of purity.

"Calamity" (*upaddava*) means misfortune. "Purity" (*visuddhi*) means the act of purifying, the abandoning of defilement (*saṃkilesa*). "Memorization" (*uggaha*) is the act of committing [the text] to memory.
*Pariyāpuṇanaṃ* means mastery through familiarity. *Dhāraṇaṃ* is the fixing of the meaning in the heart. *Parivattanaṃ* is recitation.

*Gandhārako* refers to one born in the region of Gandhāra. *Pahonti* means they are capable; "paths that do not lead out" refers to wrong paths, or alternatively, to paths fixed in wrongness and paths not so fixed.
*Suvaṇṇaṃ* is said to include even counterfeit gold. *Paṇī* refers to glass gems as well.
"Gold" includes even that made of bamboo. "Coral" is also said to mean a sprout; thus, these are specified by such terms as "red Jambunada gold.

"Not below that" is because the body and so forth intended here lack the intrinsic nature of feeling and the rest, and because the phenomena of the three planes—body, feeling, mind, and liberation—are taken separately as distinct bases for the perversions in the preceding mentions.
This was said with reference to the undesirable objects of the perversions; however, because there is no fifth object of perversion, he said, "not above.

For here, the classification of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is by way of the classification of their objects. "Three foundations of mindfulness" is a demonstration of the range of meanings for the term *satipaṭṭhāna*, but it does not refer to the specific term *satipaṭṭhāna* as it is used here in the text.

Regarding the phrase "seeing the meaning" (*atthadassana*): in the passage beginning with "the domain of mindfulness" (*satigocara*), the word "beginning" (*ādi*) includes those sections of the Sutta that elucidate the domains of mindfulness stated as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), namely: "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feelings; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness;
with the arising of attention, there is the arising of mental objects. Thus it is also in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

The word "beginning" (*ādi*) should be understood as indicating that there are other remaining portions of the text. "A station for mindfulness" (*satiyā paṭṭhāna*) means a place where mindfulness is to be established.

Since giving and so forth, as well as forms and so forth, and the kasiṇas become stations for one who practices them with mindfulness, he says "a pre-eminent station" (*padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) in order to exclude those.
For the intention here is that the prefix *pa-* indicates the sense of "pre-eminent," as in such expressions as "sublime states" (*paṇītā dhammā*).

"Ariya" refers to the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), who is the best among all beings. "In this" means in this *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta*. He indicates the sutta by means of a portion of it; for therein it is said:
"There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One... deserves. Thus it was said; but with reference to what was it said?
Here, monks, the Teacher, compassionate and seeking their welfare, out of compassion teaches the Dhamma to his disciples... [and so forth].
"Having taken it up, [he says]: 'This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understanding, and they proceed by deviating from the Teacher's instruction.
In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased, nor does he experience displeasure."
And he dwells untainted, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which the Noble One...
[as before] ...is worthy of. Furthermore, monks, the Teacher... [as before] ...says to you: "This is for your welfare. Yet some of his disciples do not wish to listen...
[as before] ...they do not practice accordingly. Some disciples wish to listen... [as before] ...and they practice without deviating from the Teacher’s instruction. In that regard,
Monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure;
he is neither pleased nor does he experience pleasure.
Having avoided both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is called...
The second foundation of mindfulness... [as before] ...is worthy. Furthermore...
[as before] ...for the sake of happiness. His disciples listen attentively... [as before] ...they conduct themselves accordingly.
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences that pleasure, and he dwells untainted.
“Mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is called the third foundation of mindfulness... [as before] ...is worthy.
Thus, being unsprinkled by aversion and attachment, and having transcended both through constant establishment of mindfulness, it is called “foundation of mindfulness.
For it is only in Buddhas that there is constant establishment of mindfulness due to its status as an exclusive quality (*āveṇika-dhamma*).

[This applies] not to Paccekabuddhas and others. The prefix *pa-* indicates "commencement" (*ārambha*); and since commencement is a form of occurrence (*pavatti*), it is said: "the meaning is 'that which is to be set in motion'.
Because mindfulness (*sati*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), that which is to be established (*paṭṭhāna*) by means of it is "the establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
For, according to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacana*), the suffix *-ana* can also have the sense of the object (*kamma*).
Thus, since the sense of the agent is also obtained here, it is said: "It is a *paṭṭhāna* because it establishes (*patiṭṭhāti*).

In that context, the prefix *pa-* illuminates a leaping-forward (*pakkhandana*) distinguished by the sense of existence (*bhūsa*); therefore he says, "the meaning is that it proceeds after having descended and leaped forward.
Furthermore, while praising the word *sati* and the word *paṭṭhāna* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), he says, "Or else," and so forth. By that...
In the first interpretation, it is understood that the word *sati* and the word *paṭṭhāna* have the sense of "recollection" (*saraṇa*).

"In the sense of recollecting" means in the sense of recollecting what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago. "This" refers to that which was stated as "mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*);
this is what is intended here in this passage of the sutta.

"If it is thus": if mindfulness-establishment (*satipaṭṭhāna*) exists only when mindfulness (*sati*) exists—and since mindfulness is a single phenomenon—then why is the plural form "mindfulness-establishments" (*satipaṭṭhānā*) used?
To this he says, "Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness," and so forth. If these mindfullnesses are many, then why is the singular form "the path" (*maggo*) used?
This is the construction. "In the sense of a path" means in the sense of leading out (*niyyāna*). For the phenomenon of the path is that which leads out; for that very reason...
"By virtue of its leading-out nature, it has entered into unity and goes exclusively toward Nibbāna;
and since it is sought after for that purpose by those who desire it, he recalls what was previously stated by himself with the words, 'And this has been said.
In this context, "these four kinds of mindfulness" refers to the fourfold mindfulness consisting of body-contemplation and so forth. "At a later stage" means at the moment of the Noble Path.
"Accomplishing their function": in the preliminary stage, by dispelling perceptions of beauty and so forth regarding objects such as the body, they proceed individually;

then, at the moment of the Path, accomplishing the function of abandoning through the total eradication of all four kinds of perversions simultaneously, they go toward Nibbāna by taking it as their object. It is precisely through this accomplishment of the fourfold function that—

Here, there is an indication of the plural number. And "this being so" means that because it is possible to speak of it as "the path" using the singular number by taking its unity in terms of the path-factor (*magga*), and as "four" by taking its fourfold nature according to the distinction of its objects (*ārammaṇa*), the teaching beginning with "This is the one-way path" and so forth possesses a logical sequence; it is not without a sequence.

This is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). In order to establish the meaning already stated by means of an illustration, he brings forward the sutta passage "the crusher of Māra’s army" and correlates it with the illustration beginning with "just as. The section beginning with "Therefore" is the conclusion.
Specifically, because the body and feeling are the causes for gratification, for the purpose of abandoning them, [one should contemplate] craving toward those bases—the coarse and the subtle.
Because the contemplations on the nature of foulness and suffering are easy for those of dull or sharp wisdom who are dominated by craving,

they are called the "Path of Purification" (Visuddhimagga) for them. Likewise, regarding the mental phenomena that serve as the specific causes for the view based on the misconception that "it is permanent and self," the contemplations on impermanence and non-self—

with respect to their association with lust and so forth, their association with perception, contact, and so forth, and their association with the hindrances and so forth— [are likewise the Path of Purification].

Furthermore, because these [four foundations of mindfulness] are easy for those of dull or sharp wisdom with a view-characteristic (diṭṭhicarita) to practice for the sake of abandoning those [defilements] when they have reached either excessive subtlety or excessive coarseness, they are called the "Path of Purification" (Visuddhimagga) for them.

And herein, just as it is possible for craving to have the mind and mental phenomena as its objects, so too can views have the body and feelings as their objects; thus, even though all four of these...
It should be understood that the specific term is used for the purpose of showing which [factor] is the predominant condition for whichever [craving or view] serves as its basis.

It is said that one who is a practitioner of sharp wisdom and of serenity (samathayānika), while grasping a coarse object, does not remain fixed upon it, but rather enters into jhāna, and having emerged, grasps the feeling (vedanā). Regarding the "coarse object":
"Because it does not settle. However, for one whose vehicle is insight (vipassanā-yānika), the mind leaps into the subtle mind and mental phenomena;
thus, the fact that the paths to purification belong to those with weak or sharp wisdom who take insight as their vehicle is stated through the contemplation of the mind and mental phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "for them there," the word *tattha* here is to be construed with the word "for the purpose of abandoning" (*pahānatthaṃ*). Later, [it says] "for them there..."

Here too, the method is the same. Because the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are especially found in the body, the body is specifically the basis for the flood of sensuality (*kāmogha*).

Because of the grasping at happiness within the various states of existence (*bhava*), there is a craving for existence (*bhavassāda*); thus, feeling (*vedanā*) is the basis for the flood of existence (*bhavogha*).

Because of the specific grasping at a solid continuity, there is a particular adherence to a self in the mind; thus, the mind (*citta*) is the basis for the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*). Regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), because of the lack of analytical separation...
Because phenomena are difficult to realize and their mere nature is hard to penetrate, there arises delusion; thus, phenomena are the basis for the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*).
Therefore, it is for the sake of abandoning them that the four [noble truths] alone have been taught.

And to the extent that the body is the basis for the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*), to that same extent it is the basis for the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*), which leads to suffering.
The underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in feeling;
thus, feeling—consisting of the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations—is specifically the basis for the bodily tie of ill will.

Because there is a misapprehension of a self as eternal through the grasping at permanence in the mind, and because of such views as "purity comes through virtue" and so forth, the mind is the basis for the misapprehension of virtue and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).

For one who does not see what has come to be as it truly is through the delimitation of name-and-form, there arises an adherence to the view that "this is the truth," which consists of the views of existence and non-existence; thus, phenomena are its basis. Through the relishing of pleasant feeling, one becomes indifferent to the next world and gives rise to the misapprehension beginning with "there is no giving"; thus, feeling is the basis for the clinging to views. Through the grasping of the compactness of continuity, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth— ... [the text continues] ... the clinging to rules and observances. Through the grasping of the compactness of the five aggregates, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the self—the clinging to a theory of self arises; thus, the five aggregates are the basis for the clinging to a theory of self. Through the grasping of the compactness of the six bases, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the world—the clinging to views regarding the world arises; thus, the six bases are the basis for the clinging to views regarding the world. Through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of the six bases, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of the world—the clinging to views regarding the objects of the world arises; thus, the objects of the six bases are the basis for the clinging to views regarding the objects of the world. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for existence, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to craving for existence arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to craving for existence. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for non-existence, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding non-existence arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding non-existence. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for both existence and non-existence, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding both existence and non-existence arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding both existence and non-existence. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for neither existence nor non-existence, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding neither existence nor non-existence arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding neither existence nor non-existence. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for sensual pleasures, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to sensual pleasures arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to sensual pleasures. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for form, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding form arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding form. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the formless, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the formless arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the formless. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for cessation, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding cessation arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding cessation. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for eternity, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding eternity arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding eternity. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for annihilation, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding annihilation arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding annihilation. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for both eternity and annihilation, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding both eternity and annihilation arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding both eternity and annihilation. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for neither eternity nor annihilation, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding neither eternity nor annihilation arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding neither eternity nor annihilation. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for pleasure, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding pleasure arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding pleasure. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for pain, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding pain arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding pain. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for both pleasure and pain, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding both pleasure and pain arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding both pleasure and pain. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for neither pleasure nor pain, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding neither pleasure nor pain arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding neither pleasure nor pain. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the seen, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the seen arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the seen.
