Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the heard, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the heard arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the heard. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the sensed, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the sensed arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the sensed. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the cognized, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the cognized arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the cognized. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the past, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the past arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the past. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the future, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the future arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the future. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for both the past and the future, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding both the past and the future arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding both the past and the future. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for neither the past nor the future, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding neither the past nor the future arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding neither the past nor the future. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the internal, in a mind possessed of lust and so forth—through the grasping of the compactness of the objects of craving—the clinging to views regarding the internal arises; thus, craving is the basis for the clinging to views regarding the internal. Through the grasping of the compactness of the craving for the

"Delusion occurs" means that the mind is the basis for the course of delusion; "fear arises through the non-comprehension of the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva)" means that phenomena are the basis for the course of fear.
As for those [courses] not mentioned here, their status as bases should be applied according to the method already stated.

For indeed, the application regarding the bonds (yoga) and the floods (āsava) is identical in meaning to the method stated for the floods, because they are not different in substance. Likewise, this applies to the application of the first flood and the third and fourth bonds.
The application of the body, mind, and mental phenomena as the basis for the other kinds of clinging is exactly according to the method already stated;

likewise, the application of the body and feelings as the basis for desire, hatred, and wrong view is also according to the method stated in the application of the flood of sensual desire and the bodily tie of ill will.
“With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of the body; with the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness [arises].”

Because of the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," the nutriments—edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which constitute the origin of the body and so forth, become fully understood through the thorough comprehension of the body and the rest;
thus he says, "for the sake of the full comprehension of the fourfold nutriment.
This is the method of the treatise (*pakaraṇanaya*), meaning the method of commentary on the Suttas by way of the *Nettippakaraṇa*.
“By way of refuge” means by way of supporting the body and so forth, as well as wholesome states and so forth.

In the sense that “they go to Nibbāna by means of this,” it is called *sati* (mindfulness). In this context, “convergence in unity” (*ekattasamosaraṇa*) refers to the meeting and coming together in Nibbāna, which is a single state and of one nature.
To demonstrate precisely this, the passage beginning with “Just as” was stated. It is the cause for entering into the single Nibbāna.

Or, "sameness" (samānatā) refers to the single state and unity of the foundations of mindfulness; the convergence therein and their sharing of that same nature is "convergence in unity" (ekattasamosaraṇa).
However, in order to show that they are the cause for entering into the single Nibbāna, he said, "Just as," and so forth.

In this sense, refuge, unity, and convergence should be understood as being stated together as the reasons for the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness, whereas in the previous [explanation] they were treated separately.
Or, if the meaning is "by way of going" (*gamanavasena*) in the sense of "as a refuge" (*saraṇavasena*), then that very going is the convergence (*samosaraṇa*).
Or, when the word *sati* is not used in the sense of "remembering," it is simply the state of holding fast (*dhāraṇatā*);

since there is no other meaning for the word *sati*, the former [meaning] is the cause for the existence of mindfulness, while the latter is for its singleness. Thus, even in the case of the convergence in Nibbāna, these two are indeed conjoined.
The causes for the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) have been stated.
The [classification] as fourteenfold, ninefold, sixteenfold, and fivefold is stated by way of the sections on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānapabba) and so forth that appear later in the Canon;
however, through their internal subdivisions and the subdivisions following upon them, a manifold variety of cultivation is indeed obtained.

The resemblance to merchandise for sale in the four directions should be understood as referring to the power of the development of the respective foundations of mindfulness, beginning with body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*).
From such statements as, "Monks, wander in your own range, in your ancestral domain," these phenomena—namely, body-contemplation and the rest—are the "range" of the bhikkhu.
In this regard, it is because of the practice of body-contemplation and the others that one becomes a bhikkhu.
Therefore, by saying "he dwells contemplating the body," etc., he shows the bhikkhu; for that [contemplation] is restricted to the bhikkhu, as it says:

"because it demonstrates the state of being a bhikkhu through his practice. Due to his conformity with the conduct of the Teacher and his reception of the entire dispensation, he is a fit vessel for instruction in every aspect.
"One should walk evenly" means that, having abandoned uneven conduct of body and so forth, one should walk evenly with body and so forth. "Peaceful" means through the subsiding of lust and so forth.
"Tamed" means through the taming of the sense faculties. "Disciplined" means by way of the fourfold path. "Living the holy life" means because of his supreme conduct.

"Having laid aside the rod" means by refraining from the rod of body and so forth. Established in the state of a noble one—such a person, by virtue of having banished evil, stilled evil, and shattered the defilements.
One should understand that "brāhmaṇa," "samaṇa," and "bhikkhu" [are used here].

In such passages as "this body and external name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)," the five aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) are meant; however, in such passages as "he experiences pleasure with the body," the term "body" refers to the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*). Therefore, in order to distinguish it from those, he says, "with the body" means "with the form-body" (*rūpakāya*).

Regarding "unmixed": even though there is a possibility of contemplating feelings and so forth in relation to the body—thinking, "feeling and the rest are also seated here, bound here"—[the phrase "unmixed" serves to exclude them].

The meaning is: "thereafter, [it is] unmixed with what has occurred. Because the word *kāya* (body) refers to a collection and because it is derived from a totality (*samudāya*), the singular form "in the body" (*kāye*) is used for the aspect of foulness (*asubhākāra*).

Likewise, although consciousness (*citta*) is divided into many types by way of its objects and so forth, the singular form "in consciousness" (*citte*) is used by grasping it as a unity through the commonality of the state of being consciousness. Feeling (*vedanā*), however, is divided into the distinctions of pleasure and so on.
They are stated in the plural as "in feelings" (*vedanāsu*) by one who intends to show that they should be contemplated individually; likewise, the exposition proceeds in that same way.
Furthermore, since mental objects (*dhammā*) are of more than fifty kinds and the modes of contemplation are of many kinds, these too are stated using the plural.
This is for the purpose of preventing the grasping of a whole, the over-extension of a designation, and the adherence to seizing a core.

Distinguishing the body from its limbs and parts, those [limbs] from hair and so forth, and hair and so forth from the primary elements and derived matter, he said, "Thus, there is no [self] in the body," and so on.
Even for those who maintain the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), they do not grasp at a whole within a collection of parts such as a palace or a city;
however, some might still run after a mere conventional designation, thinking that there is some entity called a "city."
The example of the city was given to illustrate how conventional designations such as "woman" or "man" are merely a proliferation of names.

Within the aforementioned aggregates—the collection of limbs and members, the collection of hair of the head and body, and the collection of primary elements and derived matter—there is no so-called "body" existing apart from them, let alone women and so forth;
thus he said, "Or a body... is not seen. By the phrase "any phenomenon whatsoever," he rejects [the notions of] a "being," a "life-principle," and so on.

But the whole (avayavī) is rejected by the very rejection of the body. If this is so, how can there be designations such as "perception of the body" and so forth? To this he says: “As has been stated...
they perform [the function]...
When one sees a woman or a man—surely there is no seeing of a woman or a man with the eye? This is true.
However, the phrase "whatever one sees" is stated by way of the perception that occurs as "I see a woman" or "I see a man.

Alternatively, what one sees through wrong seeing—that is, through [wrong] view—is not truly seen; the meaning is that it is not the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), because its nature as form is falsely imagined due to the grasping of a perversion.
Or else, it refers to that which is designated as the aggregate of the primary elements and derived matter, such as head-hair and so forth.
It is not "seen" because it is not cognizable by eye-consciousness; or rather, it is not that which is seen. "That which is seen, he does not see":

the meaning is that he does not see with the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) according to reality that visible object-base (rūpāyatana) which consists of the collection of primary elements and derived matter such as hair and so forth.
"Not seeing, he is bound" means [not seeing] this personal existence (attabhāva) as it truly is with the eye of wisdom.
Not seeing [it thus], one is bound by the fetter of defilements, thinking: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
"Not contemplating other phenomena" means not contemplating other natures; the meaning is that one does not contemplate it in any aspect other than the unattractive (*asubha*) and so forth.
With the words "What is meant? and so on, he makes this very meaning clear. "The earth-body" refers to the earth-element consisting of the parts of the body, such as hair and the rest.
He calls it "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of phenomena (*dhamma-samūha*);

or, taking as a collection the characteristic earth element itself—which exists in many divisions throughout the entire body and occurs in a sequence of before and after—he calls it "body. The same method applies to the "water-body" (*āpo-kāya*) and so forth.
"Of that which is to be grasped in this way" means of that which is grasped by blind fools as "I" and "mine," in the sense of self and what belongs to self.
Now, in order to show body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) by way of the seven modes of contemplation as well, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) is commenced.

Therein, "he contemplates as impermanent" means he contemplates the body arisen from the fourfold origination as "impermanent. When he sees it thus, it is said that he likewise contemplates its aspect of impermanence.
And for one who has become such, [there is the abandoning] of the grasping at permanence...
It is said that "even this does not exist," and thus it is stated, "not as permanent. For it is likewise stated that "one abandons the perception of permanence.
Here, in the phrase "he contemplates only as impermanent," the particle *eva* is indicated by elision; therefore, in order to show the meaning excluded by it, it is stated, "not as permanent.
And one should not suspect here that there is an exclusion of contemplation as suffering and so forth.

Because the particle *eva* functions to exclude its opposite, and because those [other qualities] have already been dealt with in the subsequent teaching, the same method applies to such passages as "he contemplates as suffering" (*dukkhato anupassati*). However, this is the distinction:
since that which is impermanent is suffering, he contemplates that very body as suffering; and since what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates it as non-self. Furthermore, because...
"It is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; it is not to be delighted in, nor should one be attached to it.
Therefore it is said: "One becomes disenchanted, not delighted; one becomes dispassionate, not attached.
Thus, being unattached, he brings about the cessation of lust and does not cause its arising; this is the meaning. And practicing in this way, he relinquishes and does not grasp.

For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth is called "the relinquishment by abandonment and the relinquishment by leaping forward," because it completely abandons the defilements along with the volitional formations of the body and its supporting aggregates through the power of "factor-by-factor" eradication,
and because it leaps forward toward Nibbāna— which is the opposite of those formations—
by seeing the faults in the conditioned and inclining toward it; therefore, one who is endowed with it...
In the manner described, the bhikkhu abandons the defilements and leaps into Nibbāna;
being thus established, he does not take up defilements by way of rebirth, nor does he take up conditioned objects by way of viewing them with aversion.
Therefore it is said: "He relinquishes, he does not take up. Now, regarding those phenomena [which are the objects] of these contemplations...
In order to show that there is abandoning, it says: “Contemplating that as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence.

Therein, “perception of permanence” refers to the distorted perception (viparīta-saññā) occurring in the form “formations are permanent. The inclusion of the term “perception” (saññā) should be understood as indicating the abandoning of the perversions of perception by way of the very same means used for abandoning the perversions of view and mind;
or else, those [perversions] are also to be understood as being included under the heading of perception.
They delight in craving accompanied by rapture. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "he dwells," it is said that this refers to the dwelling in the postures of one who possesses the practice of body-contemplation;
thus he says, "he moves," which means he carries out the postures. Because it pervades [the mind] by way of making it its object, [it is said to pervade] "the three realms of existence."
It has been stated that, by way of their arising, the defilements belong only to the limited plane (*parittabhūmaka*).

Although the abandoning of defilements is indeed "exertion" (*ātāpa*) for right view and the other factors as well, the word *ātāpa* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) only for energy (*vīriya*);
thus it is said: "This is a name for energy. Alternatively, it is because of the way the associated states exert themselves (*abbhussahana*) toward the abandoning of opposing factors.
Because the exertion of energy that is currently occurring is preeminently self-exerting (*ātāpana*), it is energy itself that is so designated, and not other phenomena.

Furthermore, this vowel *ī* in the term *ātāpī* indicates either praise or excellence; thus, by the inclusion of the word "ardent" (*ātāpī*), he demonstrates possession of the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*).

Being "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means knowing correctly, thoroughly, and personally; through the determination of things without confusion, there is an absence of contemplating other phenomena.
"Rightly" means without error; "perfectly" means by way of understanding in all its aspects; "by way of proceeding" means by way of bringing about successive distinctions.

The meaning is: one understands for oneself. If one contemplates by means of wisdom (*paññā*), how is it the "establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*)? To this he says, "For it is not," and so forth.
"Beneficial in all respects" means existing everywhere, because it is desirable in all cases—whether the mind is sluggish or agitated.
Or else, they are "universal" (*sabbatthika*) because all the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) that are to be developed are needed for this [mindfulness].
A bhikkhu who has taken up the meditation subject dwells contemplating the body in the body as previously described, precisely when wisdom has received assistance from mindfulness.

"Internal contraction" (*antasaṅkhepa*) means internal shrinking back; the meaning is indolence (*kosajja*). Regarding the phrase "by means of embracing the means," here [it refers to] the purification of virtue and so forth.
Counting and so forth, as well as proficiency in learning and so forth, are the means; the non-means should be understood as their opposite.
And because one whose mindfulness is established does not abandon the aforementioned means nor cling to what is a non-means, it is said: "One who is muddled in mindfulness...
is incapable. By this [it is meant] that there is no abandoning or grasping in the case of the avoidance and acceptance of means and non-means, respectively.
And because of the state of incapacity of this yogi.
Since mindfulness alone is stated here as the *satipaṭṭhāna*, therefore its associated states, such as energy and so forth, are its factors;
thus he says, "having shown its factor of association. And here, the word *aṅga* (factor) should be understood in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).

And here, by the very mention of mindfulness (*sati*), the inclusion of concentration (*samādhi*) should be understood, because it is comprised within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
Or rather, this teaching is headed by mindfulness; for the abandoning of defilements or the attainment of Nibbāna does not occur through mindfulness alone, nor does mindfulness function in isolation.
Therefore, in this teaching on jhāna, [the inclusion of other factors] is like the mention of "with applied thought" (*savitakka*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the demonstration of the factors of conjunction" (*sampayogaṅgadassana*), the word *aṅga* should be understood as having the sense of a constituent part (*avayava*).
The term "factor of abandoning" (*pahānaṅga*) is used to show the factor that is to be abandoned, as in the passage beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*).

Since what is intended here is the mundane path (*lokiyamagga*) and not the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*), he demonstrates only the preliminary purification (*pubbabhāgiyavinaya*) by saying: "either by abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*)..."

He said, "or. Regarding "of those states": this refers to states such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth; for since those [specific states] were not intended there, it was said, "this was stated by way of a summary of the meaning" (*atthuddhāranaya*).

Since the abandoning of both hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) has been stated without distinction, he said "by way of distinction" (*visesena*) in order to show the specific difference in abandoning stated again for each one individually.
Alternatively, instead of saying "having removed the hindrances," the mention of covetousness and dejection (*abhijjhā-domanassa*) [is used].
Showing the purpose, he said, "by way of distinction," and so forth.

For the purpose of this [treatise] is the abandoning and seeing of attachment and other factors that are direct opposites of the cultivation of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanābhāvanā*). "Based on bodily excellence" means having as its cause the perfection of the physical body, such as beauty, strength, youth, and health.
From the opposite of what was stated, opposition based on bodily deficiency should be understood. "By the cultivation of the body" means by the cultivation of body-contemplation.
For that indeed is intended here as "development of the body" (kāyabhāvanā). By the phrase "by that," meaning by the statement regarding the abandoning of attachment and so forth.
The passage beginning with "for the power of yoga... is an elucidation of the very same point already stated.

"By mindfulness and clear comprehension" refers to the inclusion of both mindfulness and clear comprehension. "A meditation subject of universal benefit" refers to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati).
Loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and the meditation on foulness— this tetrad, when maintained by a practitioner,
is called a "universal meditation subject" because it must be maintained without interruption through the power of extreme circumspection; or else,
serenity is said to be included in mindfulness because it is comprised within the aggregate of concentration.
"Tenā" means together with the text of the *Vibhaṅga*, which proceeds by way of analyzing the meaning of the state (*bhāva*) without taking up the literal meaning of the words (*saddattha*).
"The method of the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathānaya*) refers to the method of explaining the meaning as it is appropriately stated, by way of clarifying even the literal meaning of the words.
"Just as it harmonizes" (*yathā saṃsandati*) means that it harmonizes in every respect, without contradicting [the source] either in terms of its meaning or its underlying intention.
It is to be understood in this way.

Regarding the repetition of "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth: here, because mental states (*nāmadhamma*) are dependent upon feeling as their support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), and because in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) immaterial phenomena exist in dependence on material form, even when the contemplation of the body and so forth is being discussed, [feeling is mentioned].
The second mention of "feeling" is for the purpose of showing the definition [of feeling] as distinct from that [body], and for the purpose of showing the resolution of the compact mass and so forth.
By this, it is shown that one is not a contempler of the body, nor a contempler of mind or mental objects, but rather a contempler of feeling alone;
thus, by showing the mode of contemplation of feeling specifically upon the basis known as feeling, there is a definition through its distinction from other things.
Thus it is demonstrated. Likewise, by not remaining at the level of the mere generality of the existence of feeling—such as:
"At whatever time there is pleasant feeling, at that time there is neither painful nor neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

or at whatever time there is painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time there is no other feeling"—but rather by demonstrating each specific feeling after having analytically separated them.
The resolution of the compact mass and the discernment of its impermanent nature have thus been shown.

By that demonstration of their existence for only a moment, the perception of impermanence, and consequently of suffering and non-self, has been clarified. Regarding the phrase "resolution of the compact mass, etc.," the word "etc.
should be understood to include this meaning as well: for here one is a contemplator of feeling alone within feeling, not a contemplator of other phenomena.

What is meant? Just as a fool might perceive the form of a gem even in a bubble of water that lacks the nature of a gem, this person does not perceive a pleasing form in feelings—even those that are stable, let alone others;
rather, because of their momentary disintegration, lack of mastery, and the oozing of the filth of the defilements, he perceives them in terms of the aspects of impermanence, non-self, and foulness.
It is said that one contemplates suffering specifically through the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*) and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*).
In the same way, the purpose for restating [the contemplation] regarding mental states (*citta-dhamma*) as appropriate should be stated.
By the phrase "But this alone," etc., he shows here the limit of what is to be known, namely, "this much is to be understood. By the words "This is the method" (*esa nayo*), as follows:

The mind and mental phenomena (dhammas) are to be contemplated; one who contemplates them in such a way should be understood as "contemplating the mind in the mind" and "contemplating phenomena in phenomena"—this is the meaning that is extended here.

As for the phrase "he who takes pleasure to be suffering": it refers to a bhikkhu who regards pleasant feeling as "suffering" because of its inherent nature of suffering through change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā).

He saw with the eye of wisdom. He saw suffering as a barb; that is, he saw and perceived painful feeling as a barb because it produces oppression, because it pierces inwardly, and because it is difficult to extract. "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to equanimous feeling.
"Peaceful" means peaceful because, unlike pleasure and pain, it is not coarse and its intrinsic nature is calmed by way of conditions. "Because of impermanence" means...

Having sacrificed [them] because of their non-existence, because they possess arising and passing away, because they are temporary, and because they are the perpetual negation [of permanence], he who has seen them as "impermanent" is indeed a bhikkhu of right vision;
the meaning is that he is one who sees feeling correctly and with complete clarity.
"Suffering" as well means that it is suffering by way of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*). "All that is in suffering" means all that...
"I say that what is felt is included within and comprised by suffering, because it does not transcend the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).

Regarding "both pleasure and pain": since it has been stated that pleasure and so forth possess the quality of pleasure through the knowledge of their stability and change, and possess the quality of suffering through the ignorance of their change and stability, the meaning is that all three should be contemplated as pleasure, and all three also as suffering. [This applies to] form and other objects, desire and other predominant factors, knowledge and other co-nascent phenomena...

It should be connected thus: "by way of the diversity of the various planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth; by way of the diversity of the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional [states], and so forth;

and by way of the diversity of the distinctions such as prompted (sasaṅkhārika), unprompted (asaṅkhārika), with a physical basis (savatthuka), and without a physical basis (avatthuka)," the word "and so forth" (ādi) being used here.

"Of the dhamma of emptiness" (suññatadhammassa) means: of that which has the nature of emptiness as it appears in the section on emptiness, beginning with the words, "There are dhammas," and so forth.

By way of this [phrase], the objection is shown with the words “Granted that here... and so forth, that since [the defilements] were abandoned previously, their abandonment again need not be mentioned;
or else, that because what is abandoned at one place during the moment of the path-consciousness is abandoned everywhere, it need not be mentioned separately for each [moment].
In this regard, the first objection is resolved by the distinction of different persons, while the latter is resolved by the distinction of different moments of consciousness.
For in mundane development, what is abandoned in the body is not necessarily abandoned in regard to feeling and so forth, even if it does not manifest there;
yet, because that covetousness and dejection do not arise therein through the development of the specific antidote, their abandonment must be stated once again.
Thus, "what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the rest" refers to the development of the foundations of mindfulness as the path.
Or rather, it was stated with reference merely to the non-occurrence [of defilements] everywhere through mundane cultivation (*lokiyabhāvanā*).
For in the *Vibhaṅga*, under the four instances, it is said: "The five aggregates are the world.
The explanation of the commentary on the section of the summary (*uddesavāra*), which clarifies the hidden meaning, is completed.
Commentary on the Contemplation of the Body: Commentary on the Chapter on Breathing (Ānāpāna). 107.
Since even among outsiders there exists one portion of this [contemplation], the phrase "for one who produces all modes of contemplation of the body" is used to include every variety.

By this, it includes in its entirety all these fourteen modes that have come down by way of the sections on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-pabba*) and so forth, as well as the modes of internal and other contemplations included therein;
likewise, the modes of the four jhānas having hair and so forth, color, shape, and the kasiṇas as their objects, as stated in the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta*;
and the worldly modes and so forth—all of these are comprehensively gathered. And these modes are found in this very [text].
Regarding the statement, "in the Dispensation, not outside of this," it is said: "the negator of all modes... and the negator [of other].
Therein, "negator of the state of being otherwise" means the negation of the status of another teaching as a support for a person who has produced the contemplation of the body in all its aspects.
By this, he shows that in the phrase "here, monks," the word *idha* includes the sense of the word *eva* (only/exclusively). They exist.
For even single words can be restrictive, as in the expression "one who subsists on air. Therefore he said, "A recluse only here," and so forth.
For one who produces all modes of contemplation of the body is indeed one whose qualities that constitute a recluse are complete.
"The doctrines of others" refers to the various types of doctrines and sectarian positions of outsiders, namely those belonging to other religious systems.
The passage beginning with "For him indeed" was stated to show that forest dwellings and the like are suitable lodgings for meditation.

A "wild bull" (*kūṭagoṇa*) is a bull that is difficult to tame and has not submitted to training. A "false cow" (*kūṭadhenu*) is one that obstructs milking so that, at the time of milking, milk does not flow out completely from the udders.
The "taste" (*assāda*) is the gratification arising in dependence upon visible forms, sounds, and so forth.

The "taste" (rasa) refers to the object of form and so forth. "An object previously practiced" means an object familiarized prior to going forth, or one cultivated throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"One should bind" means one should fasten [the mind]. "By means of mindfulness" means by means of mindfulness that proceeds through the correct observation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "In the object" means in the object of the meditation subject.
"Firmly" means steadily, such that for one who practices with mindfulness, there arises the distinction between access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption (*appanā*).
"Concentration succeeds" means it is made firm.

"The proximate cause for the attainment of distinction and for the pleasant dwelling in this very life" refers to the attainment of distinction by all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddhas,
as well as the pleasant dwelling in this very life attained by others through different meditation subjects.
And it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). The Blessed One is like a teacher of architecture (*vatthuvijjācariya*), because he points out suitable dwelling places for yogis.
A bhikkhu is like a leopard, because by dwelling alone in the forest, he accomplishes his desired goal through the crushing of adversaries.
"The supreme fruit" is said with reference to the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). "Ground suitable for the speed of exertion" refers to the speed of enthusiasm for meditation (*bhāvanā*).
It is the stage that serves as the basis for preparation.

"He trains by means of in-breaths and out-breaths" means: he trains in the application of development by way of understanding the long and short [duration] of in-breaths and out-breaths, by way of experiencing the whole body [of breath], and by way of calming the gross and subtle [breathing];
or, having become such, he practices the three trainings. "In the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths": [this refers to the sign of concentration].

When one focuses on the counterpart sign established by means of the support of the in-breath and out-breath, one grasps the in-breath and out-breath by way of the physical form (rūpa), while applying insight; such a person is called a "worker with in-breath and out-breath.
When one applies insight by way of the immaterial (arūpa), one grasps the factors of jhāna.
The "basis" (vatthu) is the physical body, because it serves as the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors.

Having attained the purified view that "there is no other being or person," and having crossed over doubt by resolving it through the three periods of time— thinking, "This is merely a collection of phenomena; it is not without cause,
nor does it have an improper cause such as a Supreme Lord (Issara), but rather it has ignorance and so forth as its causes"—
he applies the three characteristics by means of the comprehension of aggregates according to the formula, "Whatever form there is," and so on.
Increasing insight by means of the contemplation of arising and passing away (*udayabbayānupassanā*) and so forth, he proceeds gradually through the sequence of the paths.
As for the phrase "or another’s body of inhalation and exhalation," this was stated on the grounds that this passage occurs in the context of the practice of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*);
however, from the perspective of serenity (*samatha*), there is no arising of the sign of absorption (*appanānimitta*) with respect to another’s body of inhalation and exhalation. This...

"Both are not obtained" means that these two factors mentioned as "internal" and "external" are not obtained together as a single object. It is called *samudaya* (origin) because it arises (*samudeti*) from this;
that very thing is a *dhamma* in the sense of being a cause, thus it is a *samudayadhamma* (an origin-factor). [This refers to] the in-breaths and out-breaths.

The physical body and so forth are the cause for its continued occurrence (*pavatti-hetuka*). One whose nature is to contemplate that [body] is "one who contemplates the phenomenon of arising" (*samudaya-dhammānupassī*).
Showing that phenomenon of arising by way of a simile, he says, "Just as if," and so forth. Therein, "bellows" (*bhasta*) means a skin bag. "Gaggarā-nāḷi" means a pipe for blowing a fire.
"Those" refers to the physical body and so forth. Just as the body of inhalation and exhalation is connected to the physical body and so forth as its fruit...
Thus, because they are connected to the body of inhalation and exhalation by way of being its cause, they receive the designation "having the nature of arising in the body";
this is why it is said: "Having the nature of arising... is so called. Alternatively, the word *dhamma* denotes "nature," as in such phrases as "having the nature of birth" (*jātidhammānaṃ*).
Therefore, one who contemplates the body's inherent tendency to arise when the collection of conditions is present is called "one who contemplates the nature of arising."
It has been said. Therefore he says: “And the body born of kamma,” and so forth. And by doing it thus, the locative expression “in the body” (kāyasmiṃ) is justified.
Regarding the phrase “contemplating the nature of vanishing”: although destruction is causeless, when certain causal factors are absent that which would have existed does not exist;

thus, the absence of those [factors], such as the body born of kamma, is figuratively spoken of as if it were the very absence of that [destruction] itself. This is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

The cause of the passing away of the body of in-breaths and out-breaths has been stated. Therefore he said, "Just as in the case of a bellows," and so forth. This, first of all, is the exposition of the meaning according to the first alternative.
According to the second alternative, however, the meaning should be understood even without the figurative application (upacāra).
Like the contemplation of the internal and external, the contemplation of the nature of arising and passing away also has its object in distinct bases.
He said, "It is not obtained at one time," meaning: "Contemplating the arising [of the body] at one time and its passing away at another time.

Regarding the phrase "there is the body," the word *eva* (only/just) is indicated by elision; thus, by stating "there is only the body" and employing this restriction, he shows that it is established as such, saying "not a being," and so forth.
Its meaning is: that which, among form and the other aggregates, due to the state of being attached and entangled, and for others as well...
It is conceptualized by others as a "sentient being" (satta) in the sense of being equipped [with faculties] or because of its association with the qualities of a being.

It is called a "person" (puggala) because it fills that category of beings and because it "falls away" (galanato) due to the nature of passing away and re-arising. It is called a "woman" (itthī) because the womb (gabbha) is "stuck" (thīyati) or "congealed" (saṃhaññati) therein.
It is called a "man" (purisa) because he lies (seti) or exists (pavattati) in the former (pure) part. The conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna) is placed (āhita) [upon it].
“Herein”: as “self” (*atta*); as that which belongs to oneself, as “belonging to self” (*attaniya*). Because another does not exist, it is [designated] as “I”;
because it belongs to me, it is [designated] as “mine. Because there is no other distinct from the aforementioned categories, it is [designated] as “somebody”;
yet when one considers it as “belonging to somebody,” there is no such person at all—there is only the body. Thus, there is only the emptiness of self and what belongs to self.
He makes the body disappear. "In this way" means by the manner described in such passages as "the body alone exists.

"For the sake of the measure of knowledge" means for the purpose of bringing about a measure that is supreme to the knowledge of body-contemplation. "For the sake of the measure of mindfulness" means for the purpose of bringing about a measure that is supreme to the mindfulness engaged in the apprehension of the body.
For, according to the method already stated, [the thought] "the body exists" arises repeatedly in succession.
Mindfulness being established serves to further increase knowledge and mindfulness therein.
Therefore he said: “for the purpose of increasing mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Because this development is the direct antidote to the grasping of craving and views, it is said: “…craving… dwells.”
Being such as he is, he does not see anything in the world that should be grasped as "I" or "mine"; how then could he grasp it?

Therefore he said, "And nothing whatsoever," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even thus," the word "even" (*pi*) indicates a collective sense of what has not been explicitly stated, because there is an absence of such a state as was described below;
thus he said, "taking the subsequent meaning into account. "Thus" (*evaṃ*).
However, he says, "By this... he shows," because the reference is made by way of conclusion to the manner already demonstrated.
Since it is the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) that is intended here, it is stated: "Mindfulness is the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, that mindfulness is the very originator of the craving for whichever personal existence (attabhāva) arises; and in the absence of that [craving], [mindfulness] does not arise.
“Because of its non-existence,” he said: “the prior craving that gave rise to it.
“Non-occurrence” means the cause for non-occurrence; or, it is non-occurrence because nothing occurs therein. “By way of the Four Truths” means by way of the meditation subject of the Four Truths.
“Having ascended” means having climbed up through the succession of purifications; the meaning is, having led the development to its higher stages. “Door of deliverance” (niyyānamukha).
The means of escape from the suffering of saṃsāra.
The commentary on the section on mindfulness of breathing is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section on the postures.
108. "By way of the modes of deportment" (*iriyāpathavasena*): *Iriyā* means moving about, activity; here, however, it should be understood as physical application.
The path (*patho*) for that moving about—the course of its occurrence—is the "mode of deportment" (*iriyāpatho*), namely the bodily postures such as walking and so forth.
For a being, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, performs the action to be done with the body. "By way of these" means by way of the classification of the modes of deportment.

The meaning is as follows. "And furthermore" (*puna ca paraṃ*) means: "Moreover, I shall speak of another meditation subject for the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) that is even more [excellent] than the aforementioned meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing;

listen," such is the intended sense. The phrase beginning with "whether walking" (*gacchanto vā*) is a general statement common to both the mere knowledge of walking and so forth, and the knowledge of the specific details involved in walking and so forth.
Among these, the mere knowledge of walking and so forth is what is meant here.
That is not what is intended; rather, the intended meaning is the discernment of specific states such as going and so forth. To demonstrate this by way of analysis, it is said:

"In that regard, 'desire'... and so on. One does not abandon—that is, one does not relinquish—the perception of a being, which is the grasping at a self based on the notion that "a being exists," because of the presence of the grasping [in the form of] "I am going" or "my going. For that very reason...

One does not remove or eliminate the perverted perception of a self—which occurs in the form “there is a self, an agent, an experiencer”—because it lacks an opposing factor, or because its opposite has not been cultivated.
For one who remains thus, how could there be the state of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and so forth?

Therefore he said: “There is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Now, as for the white side [of the practice], beginning with the words “But for this person,” etc.:
The meaning should be understood by reversing what was stated above. Indeed, in order to explain that very same meaning, the passage beginning with “For this” (*idaṃ hi*) was spoken.

Therein, “Who goes? is a question regarding the agent of the action of going; its purpose is to negate a self characterized by the status of being an agent, since it demonstrates that going is established as a mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*) alone.
“Whose going? has the purpose of negating the apprehension of a self characterized by the absence of agency.
But as for the question "What is the reason?", it is an inquiry into the unerring cause of the act of going which has been rejected;
this is because such causes of going as "the self is conjoined with the mind, the mind with the sense-faculties, and the sense-faculties with their objects" have been refuted.
Therefore he said, "In that regard," and so forth.
No being (*satta*) or person (*puggala*) goes, because it is established that there is only the movement of phenomena (*dhamma*), and because nothing exists apart from them.

Now, in order to demonstrate that it is only phenomena that move, it is said: "by the expansion of the wind-element through the activity of consciousness" (*cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena*), and so forth.
In this context, "the expansion of the wind-element through the activity of consciousness" means that which is both the activity of consciousness and the expansion—the vibration—of that wind-element.
By this [term]. And here, by the mention of "mental action" (*cittakiriyā*), he excludes the vibration of the air-element not bound to the sense-faculties;
by the mention of "vibration of the air-element," he excludes mental action consisting of the differentiation of verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) associated with volition (*cetanā*);
but by both together, he clarifies bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). Having said "he goes," just as one says "he goes" with respect to the body while it is in motion—

The expression "conventional usage" (vohāro) exists; to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "Therefore" (tasmā) was stated. "That" (taṃ) refers to the consciousness that has arisen by way of the desire to go.
"It generates wind" (vāyaṃ janeti) means it generates a material aggregate (rūpakalāpa) in which the wind element (vāyodhātu) is predominant;

and here, this predominance is due to functional capacity (sāmatthiya), not due to quantity (pamāṇa). It performs the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body (sahajātarūpakāya) originated by the consciousness of going.
Referring to the air element as it occurs through a specific mode that serves as a condition, he says, "Air produces intimation.

For intimation is a modification concomitant with intention; and the mention of "air" is precisely because of its predominance as described above, not merely because the air element alone possesses the capacity to produce it.
Otherwise, the status of intimation as derived matter (upādāyarūpa) would be difficult to establish.
It may be so. "Leading forward" (*purato-abhinīhāro*) is the movement of the body from the front part, which is called "advancing" (*abhikkamo*).

Having stated this briefly by way of analogy with the phrase "the same method applies," the passage beginning with "For there too... is spoken in order to explain that very point. "From the starting point" means from the lower limit. "The state of being raised up" (*ussitabhāvo*) is the state of being elevated.
"One who understands thus" means one who understands that the state of walking and so forth occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) produced by mental activity.

For the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion through such understanding, the investigation "it is thus" is spoken of by those who do not know things as they truly are, either by way of a false adherence or by way of worldly convention.
The phrase "but there is," however, is a question-word used for one's own examination.
"There is not" is a word of negation regarding a being by way of a definitive conclusion. As for the phrase "but how," and so forth...
This is the illustration by way of a simile for this same point:

"A boat by the force of the wind. Just as an insentient boat goes to another place by the force of the wind, and just as an insentient arrow shaft goes to another place by the force of the bowstring, so too the insentient body, struck by the wind, [is driven] by the aforementioned wind.
"One who has been taken goes to another place"—thus should the correlation with the simile be understood.
However, if someone were to say, "Just as the boat's movement to another place occurs by means of the oars and the man pushing them, so too does that of the body," let it be so;
for this is indeed the intended meaning. For just as the boat [moves] by means of the oars and the man, whose characteristic is precisely their being joined together...
Movement occurs by way of [the strings], not by way of that which lacks the characteristic of being joined; so it is with the body as well—what loss is there?

Rather, even more so, one gains a footing in the mere nature of phenomena (dhammamattatā), and not in the notion of a "person" (purisa). Therefore he said: "That which is moved by means of the string," and so forth.
Therein, "employed" (payutta) means employed by way of activities such as moving, according to the method explained below. "It stands" (ṭhāti) means it remains still.
"In this" means in this world. "Without cause and condition" means without the causes and conditions such as the mind desiring to go and the air element originated by that [mind].
"Stands" means it would stand. "Goes" means it would go; the connection is "who indeed [could do so]?
Here, the word "what" (kiṃ) has a negative sense; thus, by way of negating standing and going in the absence of causes and conditions, it negates the entire occurrence of phenomena.
It should be understood that by demonstrating the state of being dependent on conditions, not only self-emptiness but also impermanence and suffering are demonstrated.
"Posited" means established or placed in various ways according to the conditions.
"A term inclusive of all" is a term that encompasses all four postures; previously, [the postures] were treated individually.
Because it has been so stated, the meaning is that this is a statement taken from those [previous ones] collectively.
Alternatively, since the first method was stated with emphasis on the postures (*iriyāpatha*), in that case the body was secondary and produced as a consequence;
here, however, the second method is stated to show the body both as primary and as secondary, and the posture as being produced as a consequence. Such is the distinction between these two methods.
It should be understood that "stationed" means occurring.
Even the grasping of the postures is the grasping of the body itself as it exists in those postures, because they are merely specific states of it;
thus it is said: "By grasping the postures, he dwells contemplating the body in the body. For this very reason, here [the body] is treated solely by way of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
The origin and so forth have been extracted. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

Regarding the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), here the term "and so forth" includes the four nutriments (*āhāra*)—namely, "from the arising of craving, from the arising of karma, from the arising of nutriment"—just as one who sees the characteristic of production also sees the arising of the aggregate of form;
likewise, it includes such passages as "from the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form," and so on.
It should be understood that [the four foundations of mindfulness] are comprised of five aspects. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on the postures is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension.

109. "By way of the fourfold clear comprehension" (*catusampajañña*): one who knows thoroughly (*samantato*) or in every manner (*pakārehi*), or who knows clearly and specifically (*pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ*), is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*).

The state of being clearly comprehending is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*), which is knowledge occurring in such a manner. The four clear comprehensions taken together are "the fourfold clear comprehension," by way of which [it is said].
Regarding "going forth" (*abhikkamana*): it is called "gone forth" (*abhikkanta*); thus he says, "It is called 'gone forth' (*abhikkantaṃ vuccati*)."
"Going" means this. Likewise, returning is "returned-to"; thus it is said: "Returning is called turning back.
Turning back refers merely to the act of turning; however, going after having turned back is simply "going.
"Bringing forward" means moving the body by way of going.

“Sampajañña” means right understanding (*sammā-pajānanam*). One who has the habit of performing what ought to be done by oneself through that [understanding] is called “one who acts with clear comprehension” (*sampajañña-kārī*);
thus it is said: “One who performs all duties with clear comprehension. That the word *sampajāna* is a synonym for *sampajañña* has already been stated previously.

“He indeed performs clear comprehension” means that he generates non-delusion regarding such states as “going forth” (*abhikkanta*) and so on. Or, it refers to the action of one who possesses clear comprehension (*sampajānassa kāro*).

"One who acts with clear comprehension" means one who thinks, "This has meaning. That which proceeds together with a meaningful purpose, reckoned as spiritual progress in accordance with the Dhamma—such as the "excellent" and so forth—is "meaningful" (*sātthaka*).
Clear comprehension of what is meaningful is "clear comprehension of the meaningful" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).

Clear comprehension of what is suitable—that is, beneficial and conducive to one's own welfare—is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*), [referring] to the range of the alms-round such as walking forward and so forth.

Furthermore, when one does not abandon the range known as the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) even while engaged in other activities, that clear comprehension is "clear comprehension of the range" (gocara-sampajañña).
Clear comprehension regarding non-delusion in such acts as walking forward and so forth is "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (asammoha-sampajañña). "Having grasped" means having reflected upon.
"In that" refers to the purpose already grasped by way of clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). For "purpose" (attha) is indeed growth in the Dhamma.

Since someone might suspect that the journey intended as "useful" (sātthaka) is necessarily only "suitable" (sappāya), the passage beginning with "First, the visiting of shrines" was commenced in order to dispel that doubt.
"Like painted figures" means like images made by painting, or like figures produced by mechanical devices through various artistic crafts.
"Not looking at" is due to the influence of household-based ignorance (*aññāṇupekkhā*).
It is the improper grasping of an object. With reference to this, it was said: "Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling," and so forth.
Through the crushing by elephants and the like, there is a threat to life; through the sight of disagreeable forms and the like, there is an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

From the day of their going forth, it is the custom for monks to engage in conversation that accords with the Dhamma; however, conversation that does not accord with it is called its "second" [type]. Thus he said, "Two kinds of talk have never before been spoken.

The word "thus" refers back to the entire manner already described, beginning with "But if," and does not refer to what is being said here, namely, "the unattractiveness of the female form to a man" and so forth.
Because it is the locus where the work of yoga proceeds, the object of meditation is called a *kammaṭṭhāna* (basis of action).

He said: "The 'range' is that which is known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Having mastered" means having mastered it by way of perfecting the skill of mastery so that the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises. "Carries" means he sets the meditation subject in motion;
the meaning is that he applies himself to it until his return from the alms round. "Does not bring back" means [from] the enjoyment of food... until...
By going to his daytime sitting place, he does not abandon his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Attending to the body" means caring for the body by washing the face and so forth. "Two or three cross-legged postures" means two or three sessions of sitting, or two or three warm seats.
Thus he said, "causing warmth to arise. "Precisely with the meditation subject as the primary aim" means...
The meaning is: "precisely by means of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), having made the meditation subject the primary focus.

By this, he shows that one does not abandon the meditation subject—which will be explained in the passage beginning with "Even a bowl is insentient"—or whatever [object] is being cultivated as one's practice.

Because a "body-relic shrine" (*sarīracetiya*) is more venerable than a "use-relic shrine" (*paribhogacetiya*), the phrase "having paid homage to the shrine" is stated according to the sequence of prior actions.
For thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “The branches of the Bodhi tree, even if they obstruct the shrine, should be removed.
“For the purpose of winning over people” means for the purpose of winning over people through the favor of the Dhamma, thinking, “If I do not speak, who else will speak to them?
“Therefore” means because the masters of the *Aṭṭhakathās* say, “A discourse on the Dhamma must indeed be delivered,” and because...

Furthermore, there is no discourse on the Dhamma that is not connected to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); therefore, even in the phrase "having performed the expression of appreciation" (anumodanaṃ katvā), the connection is to be understood by supplying the words "by means of the meditation subject as the primary focus.
"By the limit of what is available" means by the highest possible standard, without making distinctions such as "familiar" or "unfamiliar. "In fear" refers to fear from foreign armies and the like.

"Digestive heat" (*kammaja-tejo*) is said with reference to the stomach (*gahaṇi*). It does not enter the path of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-vīthi*) because, due to the body being exhausted by hunger and fatigue, there is an absence of concentration.

"In the remaining places" means in those places other than where the rice gruel was taken. "One after another" (*poṅkhānupoṅkha*) is a term showing the uninterrupted succession of the appearance of the meditation subject;
just as there is no interruption in the continuous sequence of arrows flying one after another, so it is with this as well.
Having laid down the burden in the application of development, and having broken all the foundations by failing to fulfill the duties of practice:
"He is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from lust for the body, and not free from lust for forms;
having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, he dwells addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of drowsiness, [aiming for] some class of devas."
"Having made a resolve, he leads the holy life"—thus it is said of one whose mind is bound by the five kinds of mental obstructions.
"Having practiced" means having engaged in [the practice].
"Desiring their own welfare" means wishing for their own benefit and happiness; the meaning is that they possess the desire for the Dhamma. For "Dhamma" here signifies welfare.

"And pleasure caused by that. Alternatively, "self" (*atta*) refers to a phenomenon (*dhamma*) because it is without distinction for the wise and because it is comprised within the personal existence (*attabhāva*);
those who desire or wish for that are "those who desire self" (*attakāmā*). An *usabha* is twenty *yaṭṭhi*s.
"By that perception" means by that perception of stone; the intention is that they know, "We have come as far as this place. That very same...
The method stated for standing—beginning with "this monk"—is the same for sitting as well.
Even out of fear that those coming from behind might miss their meal, one cultivates proper attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
Thinking, "I shall honor the one who exerted great effort," [one reflects on] the difficult practice performed by the Lord of the World for six years for our sake.
"Thus, I shall worship according to my ability. For the worship of practice (*paṭipattipūjā*) is indeed the worship of the Teacher, not the worship of material things (*āmisa-pūjā*).

The phrase "only standing and walking" is stated with reference to the postures (*iriyāpatha*) that must be maintained; it is not intended as a prohibition against sitting, which must necessarily be done at times such as eating.
Regarding the instruction that one should first observe the streets without looking here and there after having descended into them, he said: "the streets..."
"Having observed. In order to show that which is referred to by the phrase "with a pleasing advance," the passage beginning with "And there... was stated. The connection is:
"He realizes private enlightenment (paccekabodhi), provided he is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya). This applies everywhere in all subsequent cases as well.
In this context, the endowment of supporting conditions for private enlightenment lasts for two incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa).

There was a hundred thousand [aeons] of the accumulation of merit and knowledge pertaining to that; for the chief disciples in the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi), one incalculable aeon and a hundred thousand aeons; for the great disciples, just a hundred thousand aeons;
and for others, the wholesome states conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) produced through the basis of turning away (vivaṭṭasannissaya) in past births. [As for] Bāhiya Dārucīriya—
He was known as Bāhiya because he was born and raised in the outskirts [of the city], and as Dārucīriya because he wore bark garments. Indeed, that venerable one said:
“Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen, there will be merely the seen; in the heard... in the sensed...
in the cognized, there will be merely the cognized. When, Bāhiya, in the seen there is merely the seen...”
“In what is heard... in what is sensed... in what is cognized, there will be only the mere state of being cognized. Then, Bāhiya, you will not be *by* that.

When, Bāhiya, you are not *by* that, then, Bāhiya, you will not be *there*. When, Bāhiya, you are not *there*, then, Bāhiya, you will neither be here, nor beyond, nor in between the two. This, indeed, is the end of suffering.”—to this extent [is the teaching].
Through this teaching, he realized arhatship.
"That" refers to non-delusion. "In this way" means it should be understood according to the manner now being described.

By the phrase "the self goes forward," he shows the delusion regarding going forward that occurs in an ordinary person who is blind to the truth due to their adherence to wrong views, such as thinking, "I am going forward."
However, by way of this grasping through conceit (*māna*), since both of those do not exist without craving (*taṇhā*), confusion is indeed shown by way of grasping through craving as well.
Having said, "Not being thus confused," he spoke the words beginning with "I advance" in order to show that resolution of the compact (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) by which that non-confusion occurs.
In that regard, because of the air element (*vāyodhātu*)...
The fire element (tejodhātu) that has followed [the wind] is a condition for lifting up.
Since the fire element has the nature of moving upward, its state of being followed by the air element occurs during the act of lifting; therefore, he said, "Each one...
[are] powerful," showing that here, by virtue of their functional capacity, these two are predominant while the others are subordinate. Furthermore, because of the fire element—
The air element that accompanies [the fire element] is the condition for carrying away and bringing back.
For the air element moving horizontally has a particularly predominant function in carrying away and bringing back; thus, there is a state of being accompanied by the fire element.
Therefore, showing that between these two [elements] there is a preponderance of capacity here, while the others are deficient, he said: "Likewise, in carrying away and bringing back."

The inclusion of the word "thus" (tathā) refers merely to the state of the fire element and the air element, in order to show the specific distinction between the following and that which is to be followed by mindfulness.
In this context, "lifting up" is the raising of the foot from the place it has stepped upon;

Indeed, even for material phenomena, the moment of occurrence is extremely brief, like the heads of sons of gods who delight in running, chasing each other head-to-head in rapid succession.

Just as the breaking of sesame seeds being crushed is indicated by the sound "paṭapaṭā," so too, for the purpose of showing that conditioned phenomena arise [and pass away], it is said "paṭapaṭāyantā" (breaking with the sound paṭapaṭā). For those things that have arisen necessarily break up.

"Along with matter" is said with reference to those material phenomena that cease simultaneously with the cessation of each respective consciousness—namely, that which arises at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness from that point.
Otherwise, if material and immaterial phenomena were simultaneous, there would be a contradiction with such statements as: "Matter is heavy in its transformation and slow in its cessation."
Likewise, according to such scriptural passages as: "Monks, I do not see even a single other dhamma that changes so rapidly as this mind.
For the mind and mental factors, having the nature of possessing an object, arise only by manifesting—according to their respective capacities—the object that serves as their object-condition;

Cessation [is without object], whereas material phenomena (rūpadhammā) must be shown to be without objects;
thus, the cessation of their state of being demonstrable occurs by means of the sixteen consciousnesses, and therefore their momentary existence (taṅkhaṇāyukatā) is accepted.

This is because the three aggregates have as their condition merely the conjunction with a swift consciousness and its object, and because consciousness has a rapid turnover due to having merely the conjunction with an object, and due to the condition of the sluggish great elements (mahābhūta).
Material phenomena are slow in their transformation, whereas the knowledge of the various elements as they truly are belongs only to the Tathāgata;

furthermore, it is material phenomena alone that are called the "pre-arising condition" (*purejātapaccaya*), and the "post-arising condition" (*pacchājātapaccaya*) also belongs to them alone. Thus, the simultaneity of material and immaterial phenomena is not tenable.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated.
"One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases": that which was the previously arisen consciousness is one thing;

yet, as it ceases, it does so precisely by serving as a condition—such as the immediately preceding condition—for another. Thus, another consciousness arises having obtained its conditions from that [preceding one].
If this were so, one might think there would be an interval between them; therefore he says, "without interruption" (*avīcimanusambandho*).

Just as no interval between waves can be found, such that those who do not understand the distinction think "it is that very same one," so too the mental continuum and the material continuum proceed in continuous succession like the flow of water in a river.
Regarding the term *ālokita*, it is said to be "looking forward" because it is looking directly in front of oneself in whichever direction one is going.

Thus it is said: "Looking (*vilokita*) means looking toward the intermediate directions. [This applies] when performing tasks such as sweeping or plastering, which involves *olokita* (looking down);

Commentary on the Section on Attention to the Repulsive (Paṭikūlamanasikārapabba-vaṇṇanā) 110. "By way of attention to the repulsive" means by way of its loathsomeness. "The repulsive" (*paṭikūla*) is that which is indeed repulsive; it refers to the act of attending to that which has the nature of being repulsive and the aspect of being repulsive.
For even without a word expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*), the meaning of the abstract state is understood.

It is understood just as in the expression "the whiteness of a cloth. Since this was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, it should be understood according to the method explained therein and in its commentary (*Vaṇṇanā*).
A covering made by binding [the skin] with cloth and so forth in the shape of a bag is called a *putoḷi*.
"The manifest aspect" (*vibhūtākāra*) refers to the mode of appearance of the foul state that has arisen after transcending conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*). Regarding the word "iti":
Showing the meaning of the term "aspect" (ākāra), he said "thus" (evaṃ); then, showing that reason in its specific form, he said "by means of the discernment of head-hairs and so forth.
The commentary on the section on the contemplation of the repulsive (paṭikūla-manasikāra) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section on the contemplation of the elements (dhātu-manasikāra).
111. "By way of attention to the elements" means by way of the attention to meditation that proceeds by taking as its object the four elements beginning with the earth element;

the meaning is "by way of the determination of the four elements. For "attention to the elements," "the meditation subject of the elements," and "the determination of the four elements" are one and the same in meaning.
"Cattle-butcher" means one who kills cattle for the sake of a livelihood. "Pupil" means [one so called] by virtue of performing work.
He is a neighbor living near him. Regarding the word *ṭhita* (standing):

However, here it is intended to indicate the mode of occurrence of the material body in whatever way it may be; thus he said, “of the four...”

"As it stands" (*yathāṭhita*) means as it occurs; here, it refers precisely to the state already described.
It is said, "because of being as it stands and as it is directed," with the intention that this refers to "the disposition" (*paṇidhāna*).

Alternatively, "standing" (*ṭhita*) is an illustration of the body’s association with the postures (*iriyāpatha*) known as standing; "directed" (*paṇihita*) is an illustration of its association with the other postures.

Alternatively, "standing" is an illustration of the persistence (*avaṭṭhāna*) at each respective moment of the material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) comprised by the body, according to their own specific functions.
"Paṇihitaṃ" means "placed" (nihitaṃ) in various ways (pakārato) by those respective conditions (paccayehi) according to the function of the conditions;
thus the meaning here should be understood. "Paccavekkhati" means he reviews (pati pati avekkhati); having analyzed with the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhunā), he sees each thing separately.
Now, in order to demonstrate the very meaning already stated by way of analyzing its underlying significance (*bhāvattha*), it was said:
“Just as for the cow-killer,” and so forth. Therein, “of one who rears” means of one who causes [the cow] to grow and increase its flesh through the feeding of bran, rice, cotton seeds, and so on.
“Killed and dead” means having been harmed, it has died; and “dead” means merely deceased. For this very reason, he said:

“Just so”: the designation “cow” does not disappear because the conventional term “cow” still applies even to a cow that has just died, based on its various limbs and members as they were previously situated, since that specific configuration has not yet been destroyed.
They are called *bīla* because they dissolve, break apart, and fall asunder; this is derived by changing the letter *va* to *ba* and the vowel *i* to *ī*.
“Bīlaṃ bīlaṃ katvā” means having made a cavity after each cavity. “Vibhajitvā” means having separated the flesh from the skeletal framework, or having divided the flesh thus separated into portions.
For this very reason, it says: “The perception of flesh occurs. This applies even to one who has gone forth but whose meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is not yet fully mastered.
“Ghanavinibbhogaṃ” means the analysis and separation of what is compacted by way of continuity, mass, function, and substance. “Dhātuso paccavekkhatō” means reflecting according to the elements.

For one who, by means of the resolution of the compact, discerns each element—the earth element and so forth—separately and reflects upon them, they say that "the perception of a being" is a perception occurring by way of the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*).

However, it is indeed appropriate that even the conventional perception of a being should then disappear, because the resolution of the compact is accomplished according to reality. For when this is so:

[this refers to] the discourses that proceed specifically regarding the bloated corpse and so forth, which are cast away in a charnel ground.

To show how that occurs, he said “in the open air,” and so forth. Since the second section on charnel grounds (*sivathika-pabbādi*) is established by way of the state of being devoured and so on, it is stated:
“The application should be made by way of being devoured, etc.”
The commentary on the Chapter on the Nine Cemetery Meditations is finished.

Commentary on the Contemplation of Feelings (Vedanānupassanā): 113.

Regarding the phrase "pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ*): here, it is called "pleasant" (*sukhā*) because it pleases (*sukhayati*), providing gratification to the associated mental states and the body.
The meaning is "it does. Or, it is "pleasurable" (*sukhā*) because it eats well, or because it digs away, or because it afflicts both bodily and mental ailments.
Others say it is "pleasurable" because the granting of space for it is easy. It is "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it feels—that is, it experiences—the flavor of the object.
"Experiencing" means experiencing [the object]. Regarding what should be said about "desire" (*kāma*) and so forth, that has already been stated in the section on the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
The experiencing by one who is clearly comprehending is "clearly comprehending experience.
By the phrase "it is a mere conventional expression," he shows that the statement, "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, I am experiencing a pleasant feeling," is a mere conventional expression.
"Having the bases as their object" means having visible forms and so forth as their object; for feeling has visible forms and so forth as its object.
It is intended as "basis" (*vatthu*) because it is the locus of occurrence. "Assa" means "it would be.
Since there is no agent other than the phenomenon (*dhamma*) itself, he says "feeling itself feels" (*vedanā va vedayati*) to show that the phenomenon alone possesses the status of an agent.
"Sighing" (*nitthunanto*): sighing by way of yielding an opportunity for that [feeling] after seeing the danger in suppressing a powerful surge of feeling.

"Having applied the balance of energy" means: because the energy of endurance (*adhivāsana-vīriya*) is excessive, by reducing it and thereby bringing about a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) with concentration, one applies the balance of energy.
"Together with the analytical knowledges" (*saha paṭisambhidāhi*) means together with the supramundane analytical knowledges (*lokuttara-paṭisambhidā*).
Alternatively, even regarding the mundane ones, he says "together with the analytical knowledges" with reference to their capacity for that [supramundane attainment] at the time of their arising.

“Samasīsī” means having become one who attains final nibbāna simultaneously with the completion of the reviewing stage; the meaning is that he attains parinibbāna in the stage immediately following the reviewing stage.

And just as it was said regarding “pleasant,” so too regarding “painful”—just as it was stated in phrases such as “he feels pleasant [feeling]” with reference to clear comprehension of feeling, so too is it for the painful.
In that context, it is “painful” (dukkhā) because it causes suffering (dukkhayati), [afflicting] both the associated mental states and the body.
"It oppresses" means it afflicts. Or else, it is "painful" (dukkhā) because it eats or digs away bodily and mental ease (*sāta*).
Others say it is "painful" because it is difficult to grant it space. "Immaterial meditation subject" (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) means the discernment of the immaterial;

the meaning is that it is an application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) by way of immaterial phenomena. However, through the material meditation subject, there is also an application of serenity (*samathābhinivesa*).

He said this to show that while [the mind] is generally restrained, it is specifically the adherence to insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) that is intended here: "The discernment of form and the discernment of the formless are both called by this very name.
Regarding the statement "he taught the analysis of the four elements," the word "mostly" (*yebhuyyena*) should also be supplied and connected there.
"Both of those" refers to the two versions of the analysis of the four elements, namely the concise and the detailed. By way of concise attention...
In the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna*, it is presented by way of detailed attention (*vitthāramanasikāra*) in such texts as the *Rāhulovāda* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*.
