By using the term "for the most part" (*yebhuyyaggahaṇa*), it is indicated that there exists a discourse on formless meditation subjects (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*) by way of other phenomena as well;
thus, in order to show this through a classification, the passage beginning with "For it is threefold" was stated. Therein, "adherence" (*abhinivesa*) means "entry."
The meaning is "beginning. For this distinction applies only to the beginning; however, the act of comprehension (*sammasana*) proceeds by encompassing all phenomena without exception.
The phrase "when the meditation subject of form has been encompassed" is stated with reference to the application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) by way of form;
but the application of insight by way of the formless generally belongs to one who is a practitioner of serenity (*samathayānika*).
This [definition] is desirable; and having first discerned the factors of the first jhāna, one subsequently discerns the remaining phenomena.

Regarding "the first impact": since all mental concomitants (cetasika) are dependent on the mind and are spoken of as being of the nature of mental activity, contact (phassa) is called "the first impact of the mind"; thus, the person in whom contact has arisen, or the aggregate of mind and mental concomitants, [is said to be] in contact with the object.
Being touched, one feels it at that very same time through the feeling co-nascent with contact;

however, because contact is the specific condition for feeling and the other mental factors—just as a lamp is for illumination—it is spoken of as if occurring at a prior time, which is what is meant by its characteristic of "launching" toward the object.
"Touching" means by way of the mode of touching the object. For this immaterial dhamma, even though it does not adhere to any single part [of the object],...
Just as the eye [encounters] form and the ear [encounters] sound, consciousness proceeds by touching and impinging upon the object;
thus it is said to have "the nature of impingement.
"Experiencing the object" means experiencing the flavor of the object through its sovereignty, its pervasiveness, and its state as the master.
For contact and the other associated mental states function toward their object only partially, because they consist merely of touching and so forth;
however, feeling functions toward its object without limitation, because it functions by way of experiencing the desirable aspect and so on.
Indeed, grasping an object through the state of touching and so forth is a partial experience, whereas grasping it through the state of being felt is according to one's desire.

Since those apprehensions have the very nature of experiencing everything, one should not urge them to experience their own lordship by performing their respective functions, as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*).
"Discerning" (*vijānantam*) means knowing specifically by way of delimitation;
for consciousness (*viññāṇa*), like a person measuring an object to be measured with a nali-measure, delimits the object.
It proceeds as a process of discerning, not merely as a simple act of perceiving like perception (saññā).

For by means of this [consciousness], there may at times even occur the discernment of the three characteristics. Furthermore, the specific manifestation of these factors—contact and the rest—should be understood through the influence of prior mental application (pubbābhoga) established by particular conditions.
Thus, even though each [of these factors] is individually manifest, he says "therein, of whichever...

and so forth, showing that all phenomena subject to comprehension must be grasped, based on such statements as: "Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known" and "And indeed, bhikkhus, one must fully understand everything.
In this context, the restriction "only those with contact as the fifth" is used because they are included within that category.

Because the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) are already included by the inclusion of "contact" (*phassa*) itself—since contact is common to all mental states—and because therein, by the inclusion of both contact and volition (*cetanā*), there is a comprehensive gathering of all phenomena belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), as volition is their predominant factor.
Thus, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, within the analysis of the aggregate of formations, it says: "Born of eye-contact... [and so forth].
By the passage beginning with "volition," volition alone is analyzed, while the other aggregates are taken in their own form.
Regarding the phrase "dependent on the basis" (*vatthuṃ nissitā*), since the word "basis" (*vatthu*) here refers to the body born of karma (*karajakāya*), one might ask: how is this understood?

To this he says, "With reference to which it was said," and so forth. Where, then, was this said? In the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*. "It" refers to the body born of karma. [That which is] distinct from the five aggregates...
The statement "name-and-form does not exist" is spoken by way of its specific context (*adhikāra*). For otherwise, name would indeed exist even as something distinct from the aggregates.

"Having ignorance and so forth as their cause" means having ignorance, craving, clinging, and so forth as their cause. Having stated powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*) with the passage beginning "he wanders...
by way of the sequence of insight," he then spoke the words beginning with "He" in order to show the further intensification of that insight and the attainment of distinction.
"Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching on the second foundation of mindfulness.
Since it must be explained by way of the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*), the Blessed One spoke by way of feelings.

And among the three aforementioned modes of application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānābhinivesa*), he said "by way of contact" (*phassavasena hi*) and so forth, in order to show that application to the meditation subject by way of feelings is easy, because feelings are clearly manifest (*vibhūta*).
It has been said. "It does not become manifest" is said with reference to such a person for whom, from the very beginning, feeling alone appears more clearly.
For in this way, what was stated—"contact becomes manifest, consciousness becomes manifest"—is not contradicted.
And the phrase "due to the manifestation of the arising of feelings" refers to pleasant and painful feelings.
This is stated by way of [the first two]. For their occurrence is gross, not that of the other.

Or rather, because it must be grasped by means of grasping both of those, the occurrence of the other is also evident to the wise; thus, the inclusion of "of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*) without distinction should be understood.
The passage beginning with "When pleasure arises" is an elucidation of the manifest state of pleasant feeling. At that time, neither...

"One feels a painful feeling": at that time when one possesses a pleasant feeling, one does not feel a painful feeling because it has ceased (in the case of the past) and because it has not yet arisen (in the case of the future), respectively;
furthermore, its non-existence in the present has already been stated.
It is impermanent because it persists for only the moment of its own function. It is produced by conditions having come together and met.

They are conditioned (*saṅkhata*). They are dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) because they have arisen in dependence on conditions such as the physical bases (*vatthu*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*).

Because their nature is to be subject to exhaustion, passing away, dissolution, and cessation, they should be understood as "subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*)... and so forth... up to "subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*).

The five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) are called "the bait" (*āmisa*) because they can be touched by defilements; thus, they are "together with the bait" (*saha āmisehi*) by way of being made into objects.

“Material things. Therefore he said, “dependent on the bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Regarding the passage following this, namely the text beginning with “There is feeling,” he said, “in exactly the same manner as was stated in the section on the contemplation of the body.
The commentary on the contemplation of feelings is finished.
Commentary on the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanā) 114.
"With lust" (*sarāga*) means occurring together with lust by way of association. Therefore he said, "accompanied by greed" (*lobhasahagata*). Regarding "free from lust" (*vītarāga*):
here, while it is true that the term "free from lust" must be understood as the opposite of the term "with lust," [this is so] for the range of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*).
However, because only that which belongs to the three planes is intended here, it says "mundane wholesome and indeterminate," and then clarifies that very intention with the words "But this...
and so forth. The remaining two roots of hatred and the two roots of delusion constitute four unwholesome types of consciousness.
For these lack any association with greed (*rāga*), and thus possess no state of being accompanied by greed (*sarāgatā*), since they are caused by that [greed] as their objective condition.

But it might be argued that because they are associated with that [ignorance], the state of being free from passion (*vītarāgatā*) does not exist at all; rather, here only the state of being dissociated from suffering (*dukkha*) is obtained.
Therefore, he said: "They do not partake of the first term, nor do they partake of the last term. If this is so, does it follow that the understanding is merely partial (*padesika*)?
It does not follow, because those [factors] are included within the intermediate category of suffering. Among the unwholesome roots, [ignorance] exists together with delusion (*moha*).
"It occurs" means it is deluded; thus he said, "accompanied by doubt and accompanied by restlessness.
And because here the phrase "together with delusion" (saheva mohena) implies that the first term is also restrictive, therefore it was stated, "But because... and so forth.

Furthermore, just as through extreme delusion, according to the method of individual application, there is a state of being especially possessed of delusion, [it is called] a "deluded mind" (momūhacitta).

Regarding what ought to be said: specifically, the pair [of unwholesome consciousnesses] associated with doubt and restlessness is called "with delusion" (*samoha*), whereas the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses are not; thus it is stated, "they indeed turn back.

That which is "overcome by sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhānupatita*)—meaning followed or pursued by sloth and torpor through association—is the fivefold prompted wholesome consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika-kusala-citta*); this is "contracted consciousness" (*saṅkuṭita-citta*).
"Contracted mind" (saṅkuṭitacitta) is so called because it proceeds by way of contraction toward its object.

"Associated with restlessness" (uddhaccasahagata) refers to a state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness that has become strong through the influence of specific conditions; otherwise, every unwholesome consciousness would be associated with restlessness.
"Distended mind" (pasaṭacitta) is so called because it proceeds with excessive distraction.
It is called "lofty" (*mahaggata*) because it has attained greatness through its capacity to suppress the defilements, its vast fruitfulness, and its long continuity;
or alternatively, because it has been entered upon by means of great and sublime factors such as aspiration (*chanda*).

Furthermore, it belongs to the planes of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpabhūmika*), because there is nothing greater than that in the world. Therefore he said: "belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. And its counterpart here is—
"It is indeed limited" means he said, "it is not exalted; it belongs to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). "With-surpassable" (sauttara) means together with those that are capable of surpassing it;
by contrast, "unsurpassable" (anuttara) is its opposite. Taking both of these into account, it should be understood as such;
thus he said, "with-surpassable means belonging to the sense sphere," and so forth. By means of concentration (samādhi) capable of suppressing opposing factors, [one attains] correctly...
It is "placed" (āhita) and "composed" (samāhita). Therefore he says, "of which," and so forth. "Of which" means of which consciousness.
That which is not composed by the aforementioned concentration is "uncomposed" (asamāhita). Therefore he says, "devoid of both kinds of concentration.

That which is liberated through liberation-by-its-factors (tadaṅga-vimutti) is wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; that which is liberated through suppression-liberation (vikkhambhana-vimutti) is sublime consciousness. It is with reference to both of these that he says:

“Liberated by means of that factor, suppression, and emancipation. If it were understood that wherever both kinds of liberation are absent, that is what is meant by “devoid of both liberations,” there might be the suspicion that this applies even to supramundane consciousness;
therefore, in order to exclude that, he said: “…there is no possibility at all for its cutting off, etc.
And the absence of such an opportunity should be understood as being intended with respect to the mode of comprehension (sammasana-cāra). As for what follows here:
It is not analyzed in terms of meaning, as it follows the same method already explained above.
The commentary on the contemplation of mind is concluded.
The commentary on the contemplation of mental objects (dhammānupassanā).

115. The meaning that the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) has been demonstrated in five ways by way of showing the classification of phenomena such as those to be abandoned is understood from the Pāḷi itself;
thus, indicating this meaning, [the text says]: "To explain the contemplation of phenomena in its fivefold aspect."
It has been said. If this is so, why are they taught specifically by way of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth?

It is because of the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*). For those disciples for whom the hindrances must first be explained in detail among the phenomena to be abandoned, the Blessed One here first taught the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) with respect to the hindrances. Likewise, even the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) is preceded by serenity (*samatha*).

After that, a further teaching was given regarding the aggregates and sense bases to be fully understood, the factors of enlightenment to be developed, the distinctions such as what is to be fully understood, and the Truths.
Therefore, even the development of serenity (samatha-bhāvanā) is intended here only for the sake of insight (vipassanā);
thus, the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is preeminent in insight and abounds in insight, owing to its classification according to the application of insight.

Explaining the state of having been taught, he says, “Moreover,” and so forth. Therein, the exposition of the mixed apprehension should be understood by way of the aggregates (khandha), the bases (āyatana), and the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).

By the word “also” in the phrase “the apprehension of the perception and formations aggregates,” he includes the apprehension of all five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandha), because the others are included within them.
At the time of understanding that “there is no mingling of the dark and the bright,”...
It is said, "due to the frequent occurrence" because of their constant manifestation. "In what way" (yathā) means by which mode.

Since it is stated, "there is the arising of sensual desire," that refers specifically to the mode of the cause of sensual desire; in terms of meaning, it is simply the cause itself. Therefore, he says, "by which cause.
The word *ca* has the sense of including the meaning that is about to be explained.
*Therein*: in the phrase beginning with “And just as,” which was stated above.

*Even beauty*: even sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). For that [sensual desire] is called “beauty” by way of its own mode of grasping; and because it serves as the sign for other sensual desires that arise in that same mode, it is also called the “sign of beauty.
A desirable object, or form and so forth being grasped in a desirable mode, is the “beautiful object” (*subhārammaṇa*). Of the desired welfare and happiness...
“Improper attention” (*anupāyamanasikāra*) is attention that is not a means. “That” refers to improper attention.
“Therein” refers to both kinds of the sign of the beautiful (*subhanimitta*), which serve as the object to be produced. “Nutriment” (*āhāra*) means a condition.

“The foul too” (*asubham-pi*) refers to the foul jhāna as well, by eliding the latter member of the compound. That [foul jhāna], moreover, exists in the ten types of the insentient foul (*aviññāṇakāsubha*).

And it should be understood that [this perception] occurs with respect to the hair and so forth; for in the *Girimānanda Sutta*, the perception regarding the hair and so forth is called the "perception of foulness" (*asubhasaññā*).

Furthermore, it should be understood here that the inclusion of both the fourfold improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) is made for the purpose of showing them exhaustively.
Among those, [regarding the object of] the foul as "beautiful," and [the object of] the foul as "foul"...
And here, attention (manasikāra) is intended; or rather, the others are included because they are conducive to it.

In the eleven kinds of foulness (asubha), the apprehension of the aspect of repulsiveness, or the practice in such a way that the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) arises therein, is the apprehension of the foulness-sign (asubhanimitta).
It is the application to the development of foulness that brings about access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā).

It is said that by devotion to the meditation on foulness, sensual desire is abandoned because it finds no opportunity to arise, owing to the absence of being overcome by sloth and torpor in one who knows the proper measure in eating.
Furthermore, there is the perception of repulsiveness regarding food dependent upon eating, the seeing of the foul nature of its transformation,
of its basis [the body], and of its state as undigested food in the stomach, as well as the seeing of the body's dependence on food for its maintenance.
He who understands correctly is specifically called "one who knows the proper measure in food," and for him, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is indeed abandoned.

The Elder Tissa, a practitioner of the meditation on the foul (*asubha*), was one who saw teeth-bones. According to the method of the Abhidhamma, all greed (*lobha*) is the hindrance of sensual desire;
thus he said, "by the path of Arahantship."
Even aversion (*paṭigha*) that has arisen previously is considered the cause for the aversion arising subsequently because it serves as the sign of aversion (*paṭighanimitta*).

One is "friendly" (*mitta*) because one feels affection through the act of radiating welfare; that which exists toward such a friend, or that which belongs to a friend, is "loving-kindness" (*mettā*);
[this refers to] that loving-kindness.
The apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness (*mettā-nimitta*) consists in the arousing and maintaining of a diffusion of welfare toward beings through loving-kindness.
Regarding the "limited," "unlimited," and "directional" diffusion: limitation (*odhisakatā*) occurs by way of oneself, one's dearest, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy;

"unlimited" (*anodhisakatā*) occurs when the boundaries have been broken down; and "directional diffusion" (*disāpharaṇatā*) occurs by way of diffusing [loving-kindness] toward one direction and so forth. This is the apprehension of loving-kindness.

It should be understood. Alternatively, with reference to the twofold grasping—namely, the directional extension that is specific (*odhisaka*) by way of a monastery, a road, a village, and so forth, and the directional extension that is non-specific (*anodhisaka*) by way of the eastern and other directions without specifying a monastery and so on—it is said:
"of the specific and non-specific directional extensions. Furthermore, the grasped [space] should be seen as extending as far as the precincts (*upacāra*); for once it has been grasped...

Cultivation is repeated practice. In this context, there are five types based on the categories: "all beings, all living things, all creatures, all persons, and all who have entered upon a personal existence.

Within each of these, when practiced fourfold as "may they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness," there are twenty modes of non-specific pervasion (*anodhisakapharaṇā*) loving-kindness. [Likewise for] "all women,"...
There are twenty-eight kinds or seven kinds according to the classification of beings— namely, men, noble ones, ignoble ones, deities, humans, and those in the states of misery—
or ten kinds according to the classification of directions by way of the ten directions; or, within each direction,
there are four hundred and eighty varieties based on the distinctions of beings and so forth, women and so forth, and enemies and so forth.
The spheres of mastery (*odhiso*) and the coverings (*pāṭalī*) are to be understood.
That improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) by which discontent and the other [hindrances] arise is "improper attention regarding discontent and the rest"; by means of that.
For this is the locative case used in the sense of "that which is to be produced. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. [Discontent] with remote lodgings...
It is the state of avoiding the arising of unwholesome states and the inclination toward more wholesome states. "Bending of the body" means bending the body into an unsuitable posture.

Because its nature is to establish oneself in the practice of wholesome states and because its nature is to wither away their opposites, it is called "the energy of the first undertaking," referring to the energy that operates from the very beginning as the element of initiative. This is because of the mere initial undertaking.
There is no subsiding of laziness nor its becoming established; therefore it is said, "because it has emerged from laziness, it is stronger than that.

Furthermore, because it brings about successive distinctions through repeated arising and becomes exceedingly well-established through habitual practice, it is said, "because it advances to higher and higher stages, it is even stronger than that."
"Grasping the sign in overeating" means grasping the sign of sloth and torpor in overeating;

the meaning is that there is a grasping of the cause and non-cause of sloth and torpor, thinking, "When this much has been eaten, it is a cause for sloth and torpor, but when this much has not been eaten, it is not.
"The daylight of the sun by day" refers to the sign of the sun's light grasped during the day, even when one is attending to it at night.

The meaning here should be understood in this way. Because the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are dependent upon energy, it is said: "Also by talk that is conducive and based on the ascetic practices.

Since remorse (*kukkucca*)—arising through the grieving over what has been done and left undone—brings about a lack of tranquility in the mind, it shares the same characteristic as restlessness (*uddhacca*); thus it is said: "Lack of tranquility means an unpeaceful state; in terms of meaning, this is simply restlessness and remorse.

For one who is well-versed in the scriptures and investigates the discourses and so forth according to both the letter and the spirit, there is the possibility of attaining the knowledge of meaning (*atthaveda*) and the rest.
There is no distraction, and there is no remorse for what has been done or left undone regarding practice according to the rules and the application of appropriate remedies;
thus he said, "By great learning... [etc. ...restlessness and worry are abandoned.
To the same extent that restlessness and worry are abandoned by means of great learning, to that same extent they are also abandoned by means of being inquisitive and knowing the training.

It should be understood that because it brings about the state of being a Buddha and leads to the moral conduct of a Buddha, it is said to cause the abandoning of restlessness and remorse due to its quality of calming the mind.
However, regardless of [the attainment of] Buddhahood itself, those who uphold the Vinaya and dispel remorse are called "spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitta).

Furthermore, since a monk’s distraction is for the most part caused by remorse, [the text says] "because of the abundance of inquiries regarding what is allowable and what is unallowable," and so forth.

By means of the method of training (*vinaya-naya*), qualities such as being one who asks questions (*paripucchakatā*) and so forth are indicated. In the phrase "restlessness and remorse having been abandoned" (*pahīne uddhacca-kukkucceti*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Because remorse (*kukkucca*) is accompanied by mental distress (*domanassa*), its non-arising in the future is stated to occur via the path of the Non-Returner (*anāgāmi-magga*).
That in which something stands or occurs is called a "basis" (*ṭhānīya*); thus, "bases for doubt" (*vicikicchā-ṭhānīya*) refers to those things which are bases for doubt. Regarding doubt...

These are states that have become causes. Alternatively, they are "standpoints" (*ṭhānīyā*) because they persist; thus, "that which has doubt as its standpoint" is *vicikicchā-ṭhānīyā*. In terms of meaning, it is simply doubt itself. For that [doubt] which has previously arisen is the uncommon cause for a similar state of doubt arising subsequently.
Regarding "wholesome and unwholesome": they are wholesome in the sense of being produced through skill (*kosalla*), and unwholesome by way of being their opposite. Those which are unwholesome...
Those that are blameworthy are not to be cultivated and are inferior. Those that are wholesome are blameless, to be cultivated, and superior.
Alternatively, even among the wholesome, those undertaken with inferior zeal and so forth are inferior, while those undertaken with superior [zeal] are superior.

They are "dark" (kaṇha) because they are black, as they cause the mind to lose its luminosity; they are "bright" (sukka) because they are white, as they cause the mind to become luminous. Or, they are dark because they are the cause for birth in a dark state, and bright because they are the cause for birth in a bright state.

The bright [factors]. These very ones are the counterparts. For the dark factors are counterparts to the bright ones by way of being direct opposites, and likewise the bright ones are counterparts to the others.
Alternatively, "dark and bright counterparts" means both the dark and the bright are counterparts.
For pleasant feeling is a counterpart to painful feeling, and painful feeling is a counterpart to pleasant feeling.

Granted that doubt consisting of the eight bases is abandoned through much learning and thorough inquiry; nevertheless, since all other doubts are rooted in doubt regarding the Three Jewels, it is said:
"with reference to the Three Jewels. For when the qualities of the Three Jewels are understood, doubts such as "he is uncertain about the Teacher" cannot possibly arise.
"Knowledge of what has been done" (*pakataññutā*) regarding the Discipline refers to [the absence of] doubt concerning the training.
He says, "even for one who has attained mastery in the Vinaya," because such a person effects the abandonment of doubt as it has been described.

"One who is abundant in resolve (adhimokkha) known as faith that inspires confidence" means one who is frequently resolved by means of the resolve known as faith that penetrates the object worthy of faith.

It should be understood that this "resolving" is simply the production of resolve. Alternatively, resolve (adhimutti/adhimokkha) is the state of being inclined or leaning toward [the object] by means of faith.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the sign of the beautiful, the sign of the ugly, and so forth": the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be applied to each term individually, as in "in the case of the sign of the beautiful and so forth, and the sign of the ugly and so forth.
Therein, by the first "and so forth," there is the inclusion of the sign of repulsion and others;
by the second, there is the inclusion of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness and others. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated according to the established method.
The commentary on the section on the hindrances is finished.
Commentary on the section on the aggregates: 116.
The aggregates are called "aggregates of clinging" (upādānakkhandha) because they are to be clung to by means of the clingings, either by way of making them an object or otherwise. Thus, "form..."
Here, with the intention that the word *iti* has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*, he says, "this is form.
He further says, "This is the complete inclusion of form according to its own nature," meaning, "This much is form; there is no form beyond this.

Alternatively, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of a manner; therefore, by the phrase "thus is form," whatever extent of form there is—whether by way of the primary elements (*bhūta*), the derived matter (*upādāya*), and so forth—[is indicated].

"By way of distinction" means that he demonstrates form by exhausting it entirely along with its divisions. "By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of the intrinsic nature of being subject to transformation (*ruppana-sabhāva*) and by way of the intrinsic natures of the eye and so forth, or of color and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of feeling and the rest," here [the text] says: "He understands feeling by way of its intrinsic nature, thinking:
'This is feeling; this much is feeling; there is no feeling beyond this,'" and so on; thus, "by way of intrinsic nature" means by way of the intrinsic nature of experiencing (*anubhavana-sabhāva*).
It should be applied [to the other aggregates] by way of such phrases as "because their intrinsic nature is pleasant," and so forth.
The commentary on the section on the aggregates is finished.
The commentary on the section on the sense bases (*āyatana*) begins.
117. Regarding "in the six internal and external [bases]": the word "in the six" (*chasu*) should be applied individually to both "in the six internal" and "in the six external.
Why, then, are exactly six of each mentioned? Because of the determination of the doors, objects, and the arising of the groups of consciousness.
For, in the case of a group of consciousness included within the cognitive process of eye-consciousness, the eye-base alone is the door of its arising.
The visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) alone is the object for [the eye-consciousness], and likewise the other bases are the objects for the others.

However, for the sixth [consciousness], the door of arising is a portion of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) known as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and its unique object is the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*).

It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; the meaning is that it enjoys and discerns visible form. It is called "ear" (*sota*) because it hears. It is called "nose" (*ghāna*) because it smells. Because it is the sign of life...

Taste is life; it is called the tongue (*jivhā*) because it causes that life to live. The body (*kāya*) is so called because it is the source (*āya*), the place of arising, for base, tainted phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*).

The mind (*mano*) is so called because it measures (*munāti*) and cognizes its object. Form (*rūpa*) is so called because it manifests itself by undergoing changes in color and revealing its state as something internalized.
Sound (*sadda*) is so called because it flows (*sappati*), is carried along by its own conditions, and reaches the state of being cognizable by the ear-consciousness.
Sound (*saddo*). It is called "odor" (*gandho*) because it makes its own basis fragrant or indicates it. It is called "flavor" (*raso*) because beings taste or relish it.
It is called "tangible object" (*phoṭṭhabbaṃ*) because it is touched. They are called "phenomena" (*dhammā*) because they bear their own characteristics.

Furthermore, all these are called "bases" (*āyatanāni*) in the sense of extending the arrival [of consciousness]. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentary.
And this should be understood according to the method already stated.

Regarding the phrase "he understands the eye": here, "eye" refers to the sensitive eye (*cakkhupasāda*), not the physical eye with its constituent parts, nor the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) and so forth;
thus he says "the sensitivity of the eye. It is with reference to this that it was said: "That eye which is derived from the four great elements..."
“...clarity. The word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for the meanings that will be explained hereafter.

“By way of its own unerring function and characteristic” means by way of both its own unerring function (*rasa*) and its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*); the meaning is: by way of its function of impinging upon visible forms and its characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by visible forms.
In such passages as “dependent on the eye and visible forms,” it is the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) in its aggregate state alone [that is intended].
The plural form "in visible forms" (*rūpesu*) is employed to show that [the eye] is the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, rather than being separate from it;

and by that same method of teaching, although it is stated here as well that "one understands visible forms," nevertheless, taking everything together under the commonality of the state of being a visible form, it says: "and external matter consisting of the fourfold origination."

The meaning has been stated by way of the singular number. Regarding the phrase "by way of its own characteristic": it should be connected as being by way of both the function of being the objective field for eye-consciousness and the characteristic of impinging upon the eye. "Depending on both" means:

the eye, which serves as a condition by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); and visible forms, [which serve as conditions] by way of the object-dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) conditions.

And [the term] "dependent" refers to that which has become a condition. Although this is an exposition of the Suttas, since what is called a "non-figurative discourse" (nippariyāya-kathā) is necessarily based on the Abhidhamma, he speaks according to the Abhidhamma method in order to show the fetters (*saṃyojana*), saying:

"The fetter of sensual lust... up to ... the fetter of ignorance. Therein, lust for sense pleasures is "sensual lust" (*kāmarāga*); it is both "sense pleasure" (*kāma*) and "lust" (*rāga*), hence "sensual lust. That very thing is a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) in the sense of being a bond.
For this [fetter] fetters and binds that person who possesses it to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);
thus, it fetters and binds a being to suffering, or to future existences such as the next life, or karma to its result. Therefore, it is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).

In the same way, the meaning of the fetter of repulsion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*) and the others should be stated accordingly as appropriate. Regarding the phrase "by way of their own characteristic": here—

However, it should be construed by way of one’s own function, which consists in not relinquishing the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and by way of the characteristic, which consists in the aforementioned bondage.

The inclusion of "delight in sensual pleasures" (*kāmassāda*) is for the purpose of turning away from the delight in existence (*bhavassāda*) and the delight in views (*diṭṭhissāda*). "Delighting" (*assādayato*) means while taking pleasure in [it].
“Rejoices” means rejoicing by way of craving accompanied by rapture. By these two phrases, the arising of sensual lust—which serves as the condition for powerful sensual lust—is stated.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. “This object” means this object that is so subtle and so difficult to discern.
“Permanent, stable”—this is merely an illustration; [it is said] because one thinks, “It will be cut off, it will perish.”
The inclusion of such phrases as "of one who takes" should also be understood. "Of one aspiring for existence" means:
"Since this desirable object has become easily obtainable for us in such a state of prosperity (*sampattibhava*), may there be prosperity in the future as well"—thus desiring existence.
The construction is: "It is possible to obtain such [a thing]. "Of one who envies" means: of one who arouses envy or jealousy.
"Being stingy with another" means being stingy by making something not common to others.
"By all nine fetters" refers to those already mentioned.
"And that cause" refers to the manifestation of the sign of beauty, the sign of repulsion, and so forth, as well as the desirable or undesirable objects of form.
"And the appropriate attention born thereof" refers to the cause of each respective fetter. With reference to its being unobstructed, not eradicated, and arisen by way of its own plane, it is said:
"of that which has arisen in the sense of being unabandoned. The state of being currently present is already included by the mention of "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*).
"By whatever cause" means by whatever cause consisting of the cultivation of insight and serenity; for that [cause] is its...

It is the cause of abandoning by way of its being a factor [of the path] and by way of suppression. It is stated that envy and avarice are to be abandoned by the first path because they lead to rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).
If this is so, how is the scriptural passage to be explained: "By the total destruction of three fetters, one becomes a stream-enterer"?
That was stated according to the method of the Suttanta. For the teaching of the Suttantas is an instruction given in accordance with conventional reality.

However, this is an exposition according to the method of the Abhidhamma, so there is no fault here. "Of the gross" means of the coarse, because it occurs through frequent arising, obsession, and intensity.
"Accompanied by the subtle" means having attained a subtle state—that is, a state of minuteness—due to the absence of the aforementioned grossness.
Furthermore, the non-arising of the fetter of restlessness is already stated here, because it is inseparable from the aforementioned fetters.

Showing that the understanding of the ear and so forth by way of their individual essence, specific nature, and characteristic, as well as the understanding of the arising and so on of the fetters conditioned by them, should be understood in the same manner already stated, he refers back [to that] with the words, "The same method applies.
Or, "in regard to one's own states" means in regard to one's own internal sense-base states, or in regard to both types of one's own states. In this...
"By means of grasping the internal bases within the category" means by way of grasping the internal bases;
thus, the grasping of the bases is established in their entirety within one's own and others' continuums.
The same method applies here to "or in the phenomena of another. "Of the base of visible form" refers to the base whose intrinsic nature consists of the nine and a half divisions of material form.
"Should be extracted by the method stated for the aggregate of form"—having brought this forward, it should be connected [to the following].

"In the remaining aggregates" means in the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations. By the expression "by the method stated," this extended application (*atidesa*) clarifies this distinction:

that for the aggregate of form it is "originating from nutriment," for the aggregate of consciousness it is "originating from name-and-form," and for the remaining aggregates it is "originating from contact. However, everything else is the same in all cases.
Just as in the section on the aggregates (khandhapabba), there is no exclusion of supramundane states (lokuttara) included in the text for the section on the bases (āyatanapabba);
therefore, he says, "supramundane phenomena (lokuttaradhammā) are not to be included.
The commentary on the section on the bases is concluded.

Commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgapabba) 118. "Of a being who awakens" means of a being who awakens from the sleep of the defilements, or of a being who penetrates the Noble Truths.
"In the factors" means in the causes, or in the constituent parts. From the moment the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa) arises...

"One who stands on the path to full enlightenment is called a practitioner" (yogāvacara); thus he said, "starting from one who has initiated insight (vipassaka), he is a practitioner for the sake of full enlightenment.

The meaning of the phrase "conducive to the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness" (satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīya) should be understood according to the method stated in the passage concerning "conducive to doubt" (vicikicchaṭṭhānīya). "That" refers to wise attention (yonisomanasikāra). "Therein" (tattha) refers to mindfulness; this is the locative case used in the sense of what is to be produced.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension are "mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension" (satisampajañña). Alternatively, it is the knowledge consisting in the discernment of the purposeful nature of things such as "excellent" (abhikkanta) etc., which has mindfulness as its primary basis.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension: because they bring about the state of acting with mindfulness in all circumstances, they lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*).

Just as the abandoning of contrary states and the cultivation of corresponding states lead to the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, so too does the avoidance of persons devoid of mindfulness and the association with persons who act with mindfulness [lead to the same].

And herein, by the phrase "mindfulness and clear comprehension," etc., he shows this meaning: that being properly engaged and applied therein leads to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
Investigation of phenomena (*dhamma*), or the investigation among phenomena, is *dhammavicaya*; that itself is the enlightenment factor.

Regarding that *dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*, whatever needs to be said concerning [the categories] such as "wholesome and unwholesome phenomena" has already been stated above. In that context, "frequenting of wise attention" (*yonisomanasikārabahulīkāra*) means:

It is an arising of consciousness associated with knowledge that occurs by way of understanding, as it truly is, the respective individual essence, function, and characteristic of the wholesome states and so forth.
For this is called "appropriate attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*) because of its non-erroneous nature of mental engagement;

and because it is directed toward that [object], initial application (*āvajjanā*) is also included therein. Its frequent occurrence is "cultivation" (*bahulīkāra*). "For the sake of further increase" means for the sake of repeated occurrence.
"Vepullāya" means for the sake of expansion. "Pāripūriyā" means for the sake of full development.
"Paripucchakatā" is the state of one who asks questions after having thoroughly investigated [the matter].
Having attended upon a teacher and investigated the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, whatever therein constitutes a point of difficulty, that very thing—[thinking] "this..."

“Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?”—to one who asks thus concerning the meaning of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga) arises.
Therefore it is said: “The state of being abundant in the aggregates, elements, … [and so on].
Regarding the phrase “making the basis pure”: here, the body is the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors; those things bound up with it—
In this context, robes and so forth are intended by the term "bases" (*vatthu*). Making them such that they bring happiness to the mind is the act of making them pure.
Therefore it is said: "of internal and external," and so on. "With aggravated humors" (*ussanna-dosa*) means with aggravated humors such as wind (*vāta*) and the rest.
"Smeared with sweat and dirt" means with both sweat and the bodily dirt known as *jallikā*.
"And smeared. By the word "and" (*ca*), other things that cause affliction to the body are also included. Regarding the phrase "or a lodging" (*senāsanaṃ vā*):

by the word "or" (*vā*), the inclusion of bowls and so forth should be understood. Whether they are not yet objects or have become objects: how can those things be objects for one devoted to meditation?
This is stated in reference to the mental states that arise from time to time; for it is those very mental states [that perceive them].
They lead to the impurity of one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*). Regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*) which serve as the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and so forth:
the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "knowledge also" (*ñāṇam pi*) has the sense of inclusion.

By this, it is shown that not only is that basis (*vatthu*) [impure], but when that is impure, knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is also impure; thus, through the impurity of the support, there is the impurity of that which depends upon it.
It demonstrates the impurity of the subjects due to the impurity of the object.
"Making them equal" means, in terms of function, making them neither deficient nor excessive.

This occurs because, according to the respective conditions, the function of resolve (*adhimokkha*) toward a credible object is more prominent, while wisdom (*paññā*) lacks clarity and energy (*vīriya*) and the other factors are lax.
The faculty of faith is strong. Therefore he said, "the others are weak. "From that" means because of the strength of the faculty of faith and the weakness of the others.
Not allowing [the mind] to fall into the side of indolence, the grasping and providing of support for the associated states is "exertion" (paggaha);
exertion itself as a function is "the function of exertion" (paggahakicca). "It is not able to do" [refers to this].
Having brought [the object] near, it should be connected. Approaching the object is its station;
or, non-relinquishing is its manifestation. Non-distraction is the opposite of distraction, or that by which the associated states are undistracted.

Just as the eye cannot perform the function of seeing the true nature of an object through the medium of a form, so too [wisdom] is unable to perform the function of seeing when it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).

Because of its predominance. For co-arising phenomena that function together while exercising lordship over one another, the accomplishment of their purpose occurs solely through their state of single flavor (*ekarasa*), and not otherwise.

Therefore, he refers back to the aforementioned point by way of its causal nature. "That" refers to the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*). "By means of reflecting on the individual essence of phenomena" (*dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena*)...

When the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) has become strong through the exceptional engagement in resolving upon the qualities such as the loftiness of an object worthy of faith, then, by investigating according to reality the distinctions between conditions and their results, and so forth—thus grasping [things] through their own essential nature and intrinsic character according to the method of "suchness of phenomena" (*evaṃdhammatānaya*)—there is no expansive resolve (*adhimokkha*). This is because: "This..."
This is because the function of wisdom (*paññā*) is preeminent in the thorough knowledge (*parijānana*) of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of these phenomena.

For among the factors that bear the burden [of the path], just as there is a deficiency of wisdom when faith (*saddhā*) is predominant, so too there is a deficiency of faith when wisdom is predominant.
Therefore it was said: "By reflecting on the intrinsic nature of those phenomena... [it] should be diminished."

"Likewise, by non-attention" means: it is said that one does not apply oneself to the development in the same manner in which the faculty of faith became strong while one was devoted to development. Here, the state of the faculty of faith being strong is twofold:
either because its own function exceeds [that of others] due to a particular condition, or because the functions of energy and the other faculties are weak.
In that regard, the method for diminishing [the faculties] is shown in the first alternative; however, in the second alternative,

just as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) became strong because the functions of energy (viriya) and the others were weak when one was attending [to them], so too it should be diminished by non-attention— that is,
by attending in a way that brings about the efficient functioning of energy and the others— thereby making the faculty of faith equal in strength to them.
By this method, the procedure for diminishing [the faculties] should be understood regarding the remaining faculties as well.

Regarding the story of the Elder Vakkali: that venerable one, having performed his duties with devotion through resolute faith (*saddhādhimuttāya*), lived constantly intent on beholding the physical body (*rūpakāya*) of the Teacher.
Then the Teacher said to him: "Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this putrid body? Whoever..."

Having exhorted him with the words, “Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me,” and having directed him toward a meditation subject, the Teacher dismissed him when Vakkali failed to apply himself to it.
Driven away, Vakkali climbed to a precipice in order to cast himself down.
Then the Teacher, while remaining seated as he was, pointed out the futility of his action by emitting a radiance.
“A bhikkhu full of gladness, with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching, shall attain the state of peace, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.
Having spoken this verse, he said, “Come, Vakkali! Being thus sprinkled as if with the Deathless (Amata), he became joyful and elated, and applied himself to insight (vipassanā).
He established [the practice], but because his faith was so powerful, it did not enter the path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*).
Knowing this, the Blessed One purified a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for him and gave it to him so that he might bring his faculties into balance.
By following the method given by the Teacher, he advanced in insight and reached Arahantship through the successive stages of the Path. Therefore it is said: "The Story of the Elder Vakkali."
"And here is the illustration.

"The distinction of other functions" refers to the specific functions such as establishing [the mind] (*upaṭṭhāna*), and so forth. In the phrase "tranquility, etc.," the word "etc. includes the enlightenment factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
"Should be diminished" means that, for example, the state of strength of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is diminished by reflecting upon the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena.

It diminishes; likewise, the preponderance of the energy faculty (*vīriyindriya*) diminishes through the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and so forth, because that [tranquility] belongs to the side of concentration (*samādhi*).

For it, by protecting the preponderance of the concentration faculty from falling into indolence, just as the cultivation of energy and the rest protects the preponderance of the energy faculty from falling into agitation (*uddhacca*), causes it to diminish one-sidedly. Therefore...
It is said: "That which is to be abandoned through the cultivation of tranquility and so forth. This is the story of the Elder Soṇa; that is, the story of the Elder Soṇa the Delicate.
For that venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and dwelling in the Cool Grove, thought:
"My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness merely by means of ease; even by wearying the body, the duty of a recluse [can be fulfilled]."

"must be done," he resolved upon standing and walking meditation alone and applied himself to striving. Although blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he disregarded the pain and exerted firm energy;
yet, because his energy was overly ardent, he was unable to produce any distinction.
The Teacher went there, exhorted him with the "Lute Simile" instruction, and demonstrated the method for applying balanced energy.
Having purified his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he went to Vulture Peak.

The Elder, too, by applying effort with equanimity according to the method given by the Teacher, developed insight and, having brought it to excellence, established himself in Arahantship. Therefore it is said:
"The story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown. "In the others as well" means in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
"Balance" (*samatā*) refers to the state in which faith and wisdom are neither deficient nor excessive in relation to one another, as it does for concentration and energy.

For just as it is specifically required that faith and wisdom—which serve as the two separate "yoke-horses" of the path—do not overstep each other in their respective functions, so that through their equal balance absorption (*appanā*) is achieved; even so it is with concentration and energy.

When there is a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) among the factors belonging to the sides of laziness and restlessness, because they mutually support one another, the absorption (*appanā*) of the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) succeeds perfectly through the absence of falling into either extreme.

The passage beginning with "one who has strong faith" and so forth is a demonstration of the same point by way of its opposite (*byatireka*). Its meaning is as follows: one who is endowed with strong faith but possesses unclarified knowledge...
Thus he has blind faith, not faith based on verified conviction (*aveccappasāda*). For he places his confidence in what is groundless, just like the followers of other sects.
He sides with the faction of the "scoundrel" (*kerāṭika*), that is, the faction of deceit. Overreaching with a wisdom devoid of faith, he imagines such things as:
"Merit consisting in giving arises even by the mere arising of the thought, without the relinquishing of a material object to be given."

Deceived by things that merely resemble the true causes, one who has become thus—his mind dried up and ravaged by craving—does not accept the words of the wise and does not respond to their exhortations.
Therefore it was said: "Like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable.
And just as here the mutual balance of faith and wisdom brings about welfare, while their imbalance brings about harm, so too...
Thus, the equilibrium of concentration and energy brings about non-distraction, whereas their imbalance leads to distraction.
The intention is that when laziness predominates, one does not reach absorption (appanā) because of it. The same principle applies here to the phrase "when restlessness predominates.
"Both of these" refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, and the pair of concentration and energy. "Should be made equal" means they should be made to have an equal flavor (samarasa).
"Of one whose work is concentration" means of one whose meditation subject is serenity (*samatha*). "In this way" means when this is so; the sense is: when faith has become somewhat strong.

"Having faith" means not thinking, "How can absorption arise merely by attending to 'earth'?", but rather having faith and generating faith, thinking, "Surely the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed. "Resolving" means...
Entering into the object as it were, he is resolving by way of conviction, leaping forward.
Strong one-pointedness is required because concentration is the dominant factor in jhāna. "Of both" refers to concentration and wisdom.
Since for one whose work is concentration, the preeminence of concentration requires the preeminence of wisdom as well, he said "even by way of evenness," meaning by way of equality.
The meaning is this: "Absorption" here refers to mundane absorption (*lokiya-appanā*). For that reason, he speaks with apprehension, saying, "It certainly occurs.
However, supramundane absorption (*lokuttara-appanā*) is desired by them precisely through the balancing of these factors. As it is said: "He develops serenity and insight coupled together.
If, specifically, the equality of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, is desired, why does he mention mindfulness? He says: [to show its role].
"But mindfulness must be strong in all cases. "In all cases" refers to the five faculties belonging to the side of sluggishness and agitation.
Since he is taking up only one portion of that which belongs to the side of agitation, he says, "faith, energy, and wisdom";
otherwise, "rapture" would also have to be included. For it is said, "by concentration belonging to the side of laziness," but not "by tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
*Sāti* means "sati" (mindfulness). *Sabbakammiko* means one who is appointed to all royal duties. *Tenā* means by that reason, namely, the sense of being desired everywhere;

this is what was stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). *Sabbatthikā* means those appointed everywhere, or alternatively, those who must be sought after (*atthetabbā*) by means of every factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to the side of non-laxity and non-agitation;
thus, they are *sabbatthikā* because they are to be sought after everywhere (*sabbatthiyā*). *Cittaṃ* refers to wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*).

For when that [mindfulness] exists, it is a refuge and a resort for one who has not yet attained, for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, and for the sake of realizing what has not been realized.
Therefore he said, "manifested as protection," and so forth.

"Those whose wisdom has not plunged into the distinctions of the aggregates and so on" means those whose intellects are not established in the aggregates, bases, and so forth, even by way of extensive learning in the scriptures.
For associating with those of great learning brings about knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

Even one possessing nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassanā*) is certainly called "wise" (*paññavā*) because he stands in knowledge consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*); thus it was said: "Associating with fifty... [persons]...
Because of the profundity of the phenomena to be known, there is the grasping of the profundity of the knowledge that delimits them; thus it was said: "In the profound..."

“...of the profound wisdom that occurs regarding the aggregates and so forth. For that object of knowledge is called the “course of profound knowledge” because one must course therein with such wisdom;
or, the “course of profound knowledge” is the occurrence of that wisdom there in its various modes.
Its “reviewing” is what is meant by the phrase “the reviewing of the distinctions of profound wisdom. Just as one who has attained perfection in mindfulness...
Since he is indeed an Arahant, and thus he alone has attained the full expansion of wisdom, it is said: "The fulfillment of development occurs through the path of Arahantship.
This same method applies to energy and the other factors as well.
By such passages as "They thrust a red-hot iron stake into the hand," [it is shown] the fivefold tortures of binding for a being reborn in hell.
"Most often they perform it first" is said because it is mentioned at the beginning in such discourses as the *Devadūta-sutta*;

thus he says, "starting from the fivefold bond and penal servitude. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the time of transporting carts, etc.," he includes other times when [beings] are oppressed by humans and animals.
"One interval between Buddhas" (*ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ*)—this...
This is stated with reference to beings who are reborn among the *petas* again and again, or because certain *petas*, like certain animals, possess such long lifespans.
For instance, the Naga King Kāḷa beheld the physical forms of four Buddhas.
Thus, for one who perceives these benefits, every attainment—both supramundane and mundane—is dependent solely upon energy (*vīriya*).
Thus it is for one who sees the benefits of energy. "The path of going" refers to the practice of the Noble Path leading to Nibbāna, together with its preliminary stages.
For that is called the "path of going" because it is the way to be traversed and the course to be undertaken by a bhikkhu for the sake of escaping the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Abounding in bodily fortitude" means being intent on making the body firm in whatever manner [necessary]. "Alms-food" refers to the alms-food of the country.
*Piṇḍāpacāyana* (honoring the alms-food) is the honoring of the alms-food by making the gift-givers aware of the great fruitfulness of their deed toward oneself through one’s own proper practice.
*Nīharanto* means taking it out from the bowl-bag. *Taṃ saddaṃ sutvā* means having heard that speech of the laywoman at the door of the leaf-hut.
Remaining [in that state], having heard with the divine ear (dibbasota) through the attainment of the five higher knowledges (pañca-abhiññā):
there are three kinds of excellence—human excellence, divine excellence, and finally, the excellence of Nibbāna. "Will you be able to give? means:

"By means of the meritorious deeds consisting of giving and service performed by you, through attaining the status of a distinguished field of merit, will you attain successive human and divine excellences, and finally, the excellence of Nibbāna?"
"Will you be able to give?"—thus the Elder asks himself. "Smiling," means:
while smiling by way of the joy produced at the conclusion of the reflection, "I have indeed transcended the suffering of the round (saṃsāra) without difficulty.
"One who has practiced wrongly" means one who has not practiced rightly by transgressing the laws of birth, family, and so forth. Thus, just as one who has practiced wrongly...

Just as a son, by that very same improper conduct, becomes an outsider from the family lineage and does not partake in the inheritance from his father, so too the lazy person, through that very state of laziness and being improperly conducted, does not partake in the noble wealth—the inheritance to be obtained from the Teacher.
Only one who has aroused energy obtains it, because of practicing rightly. Thus, the energy factor of enlightenment arises.
The construction [of the commentary] is as follows.

This applies everywhere. "Great" (*mahā*) means great and vast in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), and not shared by others. Showing that this greatness of his qualities became manifest in the world through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*), he said, "Of the Teacher," and so forth.

Since the state of being a son of the Sakyans (*Sakyaputtiya*) arises for one who has gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation by the very act of going forth, he said, "With unbroken... and so forth, in order to show his status as a son of the Buddha.
Avoiding from afar those individuals who are indolent— those who do not know even the mere name of meditation, who are preoccupied with physical strength, who eat as much as they desire,
who devote themselves to the pleasures of sleep and so forth, and who engage in worldly talk— is the avoidance of lazy persons.
[This is contrasted with] those who have initiated energy through the commencement of meditation, such as by means of walking and sitting during the day, and who possess firm perseverance.
From time to time, one should approach [the teacher] and associate with persons who have initiated energy. Therefore, he said: "Having filled the belly," and so forth.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, this pair—reflection on the greatness of one's birth and reflection on the greatness of one's fellow-celibates—is not included;
rather, that pair—dispelling sloth and torpor and reflection on the right exertions—is taken.

It is included. Therein, the reflection on the right efforts is included precisely because of the vision of their benefits, since it consists in seeing that the attainment of both mundane and supramundane distinctions depends upon energy (*vīriya*).

The dispelling of sloth and torpor is included precisely because of being intent upon that; for one who is devotedly engaged in the production of energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is already accomplished as a matter of course.
Therein, [the factors are] the dispelling of sloth and torpor, avoiding persons who are indolent, associating with persons who have initiated energy, and being intent upon that.

Through the application of conditions that destroy opposing factors, the contemplation of the states of woe (*apāya*) and so forth should be seen as producing the energy enlightenment factor (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) by way of providing encouragement.
The rapture (*pīti*) previously arisen is "a basis for the rapture enlightenment factor" because it serves as the cause for the rapture arising subsequently.
It is called "qualities" (*dhammā*); however, because of its manifold occurrence, it is expressed in the plural.
Practice is such that it arises in the same way as those qualities; the attention is that which causes their arising.
Because the recollection of the Buddha culminates in access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), it is said: "up to access. "Pervading the entire body" means...

Pervading the entire body with sublime forms arisen from rapture, the joy factor of enlightenment (pītisambojjhaṅga) arises, pervading the entire body up to the stage of access concentration (upacāra), even for one who is recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma. In this same way,

it should be applied to the remaining recollections and to the contemplation of inspiring discourses (pasādanīya-suttanta), since they too belong to that category by virtue of being bases for liberation (vimuttāyatana).
"By means of attainment... [and so on] "...they practice": this is the demonstration of the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*).

For even when there is a partial pacification of formations (*saṅkhāra*), the attention of development (*bhāvanāmanasikāra*)—occurring through wisdom in such a way that it is capable of suppressing the defilements just as in the case of total pacification—induces access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) and, being endowed with such joy and gladness, constitutes the joy enlightenment factor (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
"...for the sake of arising. "Harshness of heart" refers to a state of heart that is like husks due to the absence of clarity and affection toward inspiring objects;
this is understood through the failure to show respect and reverence toward them, hence he says: "in the harshness indicated by careless performance.

Tranquillity (passaddhi), characterized by the subsiding of agitation of body and mind, is itself the enlightenment factor of tranquillity (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga); [this refers] to that enlightenment factor of tranquillity.
"Consuming excellent food" means consuming excellent and suitable food.
By the mention of "pleasant postures," one should understand the inclusion of suitable postures.
For when that threefold suitability is practiced, it brings about lightness of mind by way of producing pliancy of the body, and thus becomes the cause for both kinds of tranquility (passaddhi).
The view that pleasure and pain among sentient beings occur without cause is one extreme; the view that they arise from an unequal cause such as a Supreme Lord (Issara) is the second.
Without falling into either of these two extremes, the understanding that they arise through their respective individual karma is the Middle Way practice.
That which possesses a neutral application is "neutral-application"; the state of being so is "the quality of neutral-application."
For this [tranquility] brings about two kinds of tranquility by being the cause for the state of a tranquil body after having abandoned the state of an agitated body;
it should be understood that its bringing about these two is described precisely by way of avoiding persons with agitated bodies and associating with persons with tranquil bodies.
When grasped by way of observing the mode of concentration as it has arisen, serenity (*samatha*) itself that has previously arisen is the sign of serenity (*samathanimitta*).
"Distracted" (*byagga*) means that which has various peaks (*agga*) due to wandering among diverse objects; thus, it is called distraction (*vikkhepa*).
For it is said to have non-stability as its essence and restlessness as its manifestation. Because of the absence of one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), it is the opposite of the undistracted.
“Unconfused, concentration”: it should be stated as before that this itself is the sign. Therefore he said: “And in the sense of non-distraction, the sign of non-confusion.

It has been stated that the purification of the physical basis and the balancing of the faculties bring about wisdom; however, they also bring about concentration. Since they bring about wisdom precisely by way of bringing about concentration, it was said: “The purification of the physical basis... should be understood [as such].”
Because skill in the causal process (*karaṇabhāvanā*) is inseparable from skill in protection, and because skill in protection is rooted in that [skill in the causal process], it is said:
"Skill in signs (*nimittakusalatā*) means skill in grasping the sign of the *kasiṇa*. Furthermore, the phrase "of the *kasiṇa* sign" should be regarded as merely illustrative;
for skill in grasping any sign whatsoever—such as the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*)—which serves as the basis for the arising of jhāna, is what is meant.
"Skillfulness regarding signs alone.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "due to excessive laxity of energy, etc.," it includes dullness of application of wisdom and deficiency of joy.
"Its exertion" refers to the arousing of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga*) and so forth, for that sluggish mind.
Extraction from a lapse into sloth. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, the time for the development of the energy enlightenment factor, and the time for the development of the rapture enlightenment factor.”
For what reason? Because, monks, a sluggish mind is easily stirred up by these qualities.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to kindle a small fire were to throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, and throw dry wood into it.
"And if he were to blow on it with his mouth and not sprinkle it with dust, would that man be able to kindle the small fire? "That being so.

And here, it should be understood that the development and arousing of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others occurs by means of their respective nutriment; this has already been explained immediately above.
"By means of over-exerted energy, etc."—by the word "etc.," it includes the possession of strength through the application of wisdom (*paññā*) and the agitation caused by excessive joy.
"Its restraint" is the prevention of that agitated mind from the transgression of agitation by means of arousing the enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*) and so forth.
And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is agitated, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, bhikkhus, an agitated mind is easily calmed by these states.”
“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wished to extinguish a great mass of fire, and he were to scatter wet grass there...
and sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?”—“He would not, venerable sir.”
Here too, it should be understood that the development and arousal of the enlightenment factors, beginning with tranquility, occurs by way of their respective nutriment.

Among these, the development of the enlightenment factor of tranquility has already been explained; that of the enlightenment factor of concentration will be stated [later], and that of the other will be spoken of immediately thereafter.
"Due to the weakness of the application of wisdom" means due to the paucity of the activity of wisdom.
For just as generosity has non-greed as its predominant factor and virtue has non-hatred as its predominant factor, so too does meditation have non-delusion as its predominant factor.
In that regard, when wisdom is not strong, then meditation does not bring about successive excellence; it is like food that has not been properly prepared for a person.

It does not produce delight in the mind of the yogin; therefore, it becomes unpalatable to him. Likewise, through such meditation, he does not properly experience the bliss of tranquility by way of entering the right path;
for that reason also, the mind becomes unpalatable. Hence it is said: "The application of wisdom... [etc. ...becomes unpalatable.
Its treatment consists in the arousal of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and the arousal of confidence (*pasāda*).
Demonstrating this, he said, "The eight bases for spiritual urgency," and so forth.

Therein, since birth, aging, sickness, and death occur respectively in both the happy destinies and the miserable destinies, the suffering of the woeful states (apāya) must be understood as distinct from those, being caused by the fivefold bondages, hunger and thirst, mutual affliction, and so on;
all of this pertains to the present existence of various sentient beings.
"Taken up" means that in the past and future times, the sufferings rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) have been taken up separately.

However, it should be understood that for those beings who subsist on nutriment and who subsist on the fruits of their exertion, the eighth basis for spiritual urgency—the suffering of livelihood which is not shared with others—has been taken up. This is called "encouragement at the proper time."

This is "proper cheering" (*sampahaṃsanā*), which, according to the method stated for the occasion of cheering, consists of cheering correctly by means of both spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and the production of confidence (*pasāda*).
The meaning is that it is the satisfying of the mind of development (*bhāvanācitta*) through the production of confidence preceded by the arousal of spiritual urgency.

"By resorting to right practice" (*sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma*) means by way of the practice of the path of serenity (*samatha-vīthi*) free from lethargy (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*), and being "right" (*sammā*), that is, not uneven (*avisama*).

This is solely by resorting to the practice of development (*bhāvanāpaṭipatti*). Regarding the terms "unlanguid" (*alīna*) and so forth: it is "unlanguid" because of the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of laziness (*kosajja*);

it is "unagitated" (*anuddhata*) because of the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of restlessness (*uddhacca*); it is "not dissatisfied" (*anirassāda*) due to the power of the application of wisdom (*paññāpayoga*) and the attainment of the bliss of tranquility (*upasamasukha*);
and for that very reason, it proceeds evenly toward the object and has entered the path of serenity (*samathavīthi*). In this regard:
One does not fall into exertion through encouragement when there is no sinking, through restraint when there is no agitation, and through cheering when there is no relishing.
It should be understood that it proceeds evenly upon the object because of the absence of both sinking and agitation; it has entered the path of serenity because of the absence of relishing.
Alternatively, it is "not sunk" due to proceeding evenly, and "not agitated" due to having entered the path of serenity. It is "without relishing" because of its entry into the path of serenity.
"This is called equanimity at the appropriate time" means that at the time when one should be equanimous,
this is called "looking on" after having overcome the opposing factor consisting of the mind's preoccupation with exertion, restraint,
and encouragement during meditation. Because it suppresses the opposing factors and because it serves as a basis for insight (vipassanā), even access-concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) [is included].
Since the accomplishment of the function of undertaking [the training] is precisely the means of establishing a person’s state of concentration, he says there, with equal weight:
“access or absorption.
Regarding the phrase “states that are bases for the equanimity enlightenment factor,” whatever needs to be said here should be understood according to what was stated above.
The state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāva*), by way of abandoning both attraction and aversion, is the cause for the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*);
for when that [neutrality] exists, [the factor] is accomplished, and when it is absent, it is not accomplished.

And since that state of neutrality is twofold according to its object, he said: "neutrality toward beings and neutrality toward formations. Furthermore, the opposition to both of these is the development of the enlightenment factor of tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*).

The phrase "thus made distant" is stated as "the state of being neutral toward the seven [types of persons]" and so forth, by one who demonstrates the method of abandoning even while still feeling attraction.
For this very reason, it is said: "avoiding persons who are fond of conditioned formations. Indeed, passion is specifically the opposite of equanimity;
thus it is said: "Equanimity is the path of purification for one who has an abundance of passion."
