"By two ways" means by these two reasons: reflection on one's own karma as one's own property (*kammassakatā*), and reflection on the emptiness of self (*attasuññatā*). "Only by two" is a restriction based on the equality of the number. The state of being ownerless is the absence of self-ownership (*anattaniyatā*).
For if there were a self, the robe or anything else might be called "belonging to the self" (*attaniya*) by virtue of its being something owned by it; however, that [self]...
The intended meaning is that there is none at all. "Anaddhaniya" means not enduring for a journey; it does not last long, but is brief and impermanent—this is the sense.
"Tāvakālika" is a synonym for that very same thing. "Mamāyati" means one makes it "mine";
one remains grasping it with craving, thinking, "It is mine. "Dhanāyanta" means making it wealth, making it a material possession.

This teaching on the foundations of mindfulness is taught by way of the preliminary path; thus, with reference to the factors of enlightenment belonging to the preliminary stage, it is said: "Mindfulness that comprehends the factors of enlightenment is the truth of suffering.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Four Truths begins.
119. "By way of its own-nature" means by way of its non-perverted nature, that is, by way of the characteristic of oppression (*bādhanalakkhaṇa*);
or, whatever its own-nature may be, that is "by way of its own-nature," meaning by way of its own-nature such as being subject to deformation (*ruppana*) or hardness (*kakkhaḷatā*).

"That which produces and originates" means that which produces the suffering characterized by occurrence (*pavattalakkhaṇa*) and that which originates the suffering characterized by the cause (*nimittalakkhaṇa*). "Former craving" refers to [craving] prior to the arising of suffering.
Craving is established as being prior [to its cessation].
Since cessation, when grasped as the non-occurrence of suffering and its origin included within one's own continuity, appears as if it were itself included within that continuity, it is said:
"or the four truths of oneself. [This refers to] another's...
The same method applies here as well. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world, I proclaim the origin of the world, I proclaim the cessation of the world, and I proclaim the way leading to the cessation of the world.
But how does one who is a beginner [perceive] the truths of cessation?

"Grasps" means he grasps a mode established through hearsay and so forth; and by taking it in this way, even when referring to the supramundane factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the act of grasping is not contradicted.

"According to what is possible" means in accordance with what is possible; the meaning is that, setting aside the truth of cessation, arising and passing away are to be understood by way of the remaining truths.
The commentary on the Origin of the Four Truths is finished.
The seven charnel-ground meditations beginning with “a skeleton with flesh still attached” are stated to be subjects for absorption (appanā) because they constitute the meditation subject of bones;
the others, such as the bloated corpse and so forth, are subjects for absorption by their very nature. Thus, only two [of the nine] are [explicitly mentioned].
"Mindfulness of breathing" and "the thirty-two aspects"—these two alone [are intended]. "Adherence" refers to adherence through insight;

that, moreover, is the discernment of the phenomena subject to comprehension. Postures, looking forward, and so forth, are merely specific states of material phenomena and thus do not come within the scope of comprehension, unlike intimation and the like. The hindrances and the factors of enlightenment are not to be discerned at the outset.
It is said: “...the postures... do not arise. By means of the designation ‘hair and so forth,’ the material phenomena that constitute their basis are grasped;

likewise, by means of the designation ‘postures and so forth,’ the material phenomena existing in those states are grasped. And by way of the hindrances and so on, the states associated with them and dependent upon them are grasped.
With this intention, the Elder Mahāsīva said: “Adherence arises even toward the postures and so forth. Is there, then...?

The passage beginning with "metiādi," however, demonstrates that for a beginner, the postures and so forth do not constitute the true nature [of the path], because full comprehension (*pariññā*) is preceded by non-full-comprehension (*apariññā*).

Although the term "bhikkhu" is employed here and there in the summaries and detailed explanations—such as in the passage, "Here, bhikkhus, bhikkhus"—that is for the purpose of showing the state of being a bhikkhu through practice;
the teaching itself, however, is intended to show that it is common to all.
“Whoever, monks”—by saying this, he shows that it is not only a monk; thus he says, “whoever, a monk or...,” and so forth.
*Aññā* (higher knowledge) is the wisdom of the supreme path that has reached its peak, knowing without transgressing the limit of what is known through the path of vision;
because it is the state of the fruit of that [wisdom], he says, “*Aññā* is Arahantship. Even in the case of one who has attained less...
The construction is: "showing the nature of the Dispensation as leading to liberation at the proper time.
138. "Leading out" means bringing to an end.
[From] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is completed.
The commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Vagga is finished.
The first volume is concluded.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Root Fifty of the Middle Collection.
(Second Part) 2.
The Chapter on the Lion’s Roar 1.
Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta (The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar)
139. *Aṭṭhuppatti* is the arising of a meaning (attha) consisting of the occasion for the teaching of a sutta; since that [occasion] belongs to it, it is called *aṭṭhuppattika*.

"On account of gain and honor" means by way of gain and honor, i.e., because of the gain and honor arisen for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha, or for the purpose of producing gain and honor for oneself. "At the lamentation of the sectarians."
It was for the purpose of causing the sectarian teachers (titthiyā) to babble such things as, "Is the ascetic Gotama truly an ascetic?

Having stated that "great gain and honor arose," he spoke the passage beginning with "for it has four measures" in order to show the cause for its arising—that is, its universal beauty (samantapāsādika).
"Four measures" means four standards (pamāṇāni); one who possesses these four measures is "one having four measures" (catuppamāṇiko).
“World-dwelling” (*lokasannivāsa*) means the dwelling together by way of coming together and gathering; the meaning is “the body of beings.

It is a “measure” (*pamāṇa*) because one measures excellence, such as loftiness, by means of it; thus, “form is the measure” refers to the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Because form is its measure, it is “one who has faith in form” (*rūpappamāṇo*).
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “Sound” (*ghoso*) refers to the sound of praise that occurs.
"Coarse" (*lūkha*) refers to the coarseness of the requisites. "Dhamma" refers to the qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
"Of those persons": their "ascension" (*āroha*) means height; and that indeed should be understood as being proportionate at each respective time.
"Circumference" (*pariṇāha*) means a measured circumference by way of being neither too emaciated nor too stout. "Shape" (*saṇṭhāna*) refers to [the configuration] of those various limbs and members.
"Well-proportioned" means the fullness and completeness of all the limbs and members of the body.
"Taking that as the measure" means taking the state of perfection in that form as the standard. "Produces confidence" means it generates resolute conviction (*adhimokkha*).
“By praising another” means by means of words concerning fame and virtue such as, “So-and-so is like this and like that.
“By extolling another” means by means of praise that generates commendation for another in their very presence. “By lauding another” means by means of recounting another’s virtues in their absence.

“By conveying another’s praise” means by conveying another’s praise through a succession of intermediaries, that is, by bringing about the report of another’s reputation through a chain of transmission.
"Therein" means in that sound of praise.

"Coarseness of robe" refers to the roughness of the robe due to its being thick, old, or made of many patches, and so forth. "Coarseness of bowl" refers to the roughness of the bowl due to its having many knots, dents, and so forth.
Or, "various difficult practices" refers to what is undertaken by way of the cultivation of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*), and so on.
"Various kinds of difficult practices. "Or, having seen the virtue":

having seen with the eye of knowledge the purity of good conduct of body and speech by way of the fulfillment of virtue; or the concentration accomplished through the attainment of jhāna and so forth; or the wisdom consisting of insight and direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

This is the connection with the phrase "having seen the Blessed One’s physical form. Even one who takes physical beauty as the measure gains confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone, [seeing him] as produced by the power of merit accumulated over immeasurable time.
Because of his universal loveliness, which arises from a perfection of the physical body that is entirely blameless and complete in every limb—
a radiance that surpasses even the full orb of the moon with its perfect digits on a clear night when the sky is free of clouds;
and a brilliance that outshines the autumnal splendor of the sun’s web of rays, intensified tenfold during the autumn season.
It outshines the solar disk; having surpassed both of them through its state of being brilliantly radiant with the essence of the moon’s rays,
it shines, blazes, and glows, surpassing the mass of radiance of Mahābrahmā, which is capable of illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system in a single moment.

Furthermore, the mention of the sacrifice of limbs and so forth is for the purpose of showing the specific nature of such sacrifice within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), as well as to demonstrate its extreme difficulty.
Within that context, the sacrifice of eyes is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of limbs;
and although they share the commonality of being sacrifices, the sacrifice of wife and children is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of a kingdom. And so on.

By the word "method" (*naya*), etc., one should understand the inclusion of the perfection of causes— such as prior application and former conduct— and the perfection of results, as stated in the passage beginning,
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One," as well as the performance of deeds for the benefit of beings, as stated in the passage beginning, "He teaches the Dhamma.
One has faith in the Perfectly Enlightened One alone, because these aforementioned qualities are not shared by anyone else.
And because of its wonderful and marvelous nature. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
Having said, "Seeing the coarse robe," it was stated, beginning with "If the Blessed One," in order to demonstrate that.
"With a hempen rag-robe" means with a hempen rag-robe discarded after wrapping it around a corpse, which had been taken after shaking off the worms the size of a water-jar.
“Bhāriyaṃ” means heavy; the meaning is that it is difficult to perform. There is a threefold nature of acting, according to whether one is a wife, a young bride, or a middle-aged woman;
or according to whether one is a child, a youth, or an old person. “Hareṇuyūsaṃ” is the juice of the *maṇḍala* (lotus) buds.

The connection is made by bringing in the word “nāma” in the phrase “yāpessati nāmā,” for with the use of the word “nāma,” there is a grammatical application as if referring to the future tense; the actual meaning is simply “he will sustain himself.”
“Appāṇaka” means breathless; it refers to that which has ceased both inhalation and exhalation.
By the inclusion of the terms “jhāna” and so forth, he explains the meaning stated generally as the “qualities of concentration.

The phrase “the taming of Pāṭikaputta and others” indicates that even the attainment of a state free from worldly indulgence through the crushing of pride and arrogance is indeed a form of taming. By the word “and others,”...
This includes [the taming of] Saccaka, Kāḷavaka, Baka, and others. *Bāveru* refers to a region of that name.
*Sarasampanno* means endowed with a voice possessed of the eight qualities.

By this demonstration of his Brahma-voice and his speech like that of the karavīka bird, he reveals—through the method of "taking the characteristic" (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*)—the Buddha’s splendor of teaching, because it is inseparable from the perfection of the remaining characteristics, just as the presence of one characteristic implies the fulfillment of the rest.

“Deprived of splendor” means that their radiance has vanished through the power of the Buddha. “Comparable to the dark fortnight” refers to being overcome by the darkness of delusion for sentient beings, thus resembling the time of the dark fortnight. “The sun” intends to convey that it shines after the sun has risen.
“At a crossroads” means at a triangular street. “At a junction” means at a point where four roads meet.

“Lamenting” means they are uttering incoherent cries by way of wailing; for lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outburst caused by excessive sorrow. “Arising as soon as he arises in the world” means [the Dhamma] arises simultaneously with his arising.
They demonstrate the antiquity of their own doctrinal view.
"In the remaining passages as well" means that in the subsequent sections such as "here is a second ascetic," etc.,

just as the restriction established here in the phrase "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" applies also to the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states," because the meaning is indeed one of exclusive qualification.
Because they are intended [to be included], it is the same here as well. Therefore he said, "The second and the others, too," and so forth.
Since the state of a recluse (*samaṇabhāva*) is, in the non-figurative sense, the attainment of the fruits of recluseship, the four types of recluses are taught here by way of those [fruits].

To support that meaning with another sutta, he said, "Therefore he said," and so forth. [This refers to] the once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) and the others, according to the sequence of practice and the sequence of teaching.

Since "being second and so forth" has been stated, it is not questioned that for a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), "being first" is established by implication. Only those ascetics who have attained the fruit (phalaṭṭhaka) are intended here, because of the inclusion of the term "ascetic who has stilled evil" (samitapāpa).
Why, however, are those standing on the path (maggaṭṭha) and those practicing for that purpose not included here, as they are in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*?
It is due to the disposition of those to be trained (veneyya). For in that [other] case, [the categories were used] for the sake of attaining the path.

The Blessed One said, "One who practices even a portion of the True Dhamma does not exist outside of this; how much less so those established on the paths and fruits," showing that even insight (vipassanā) does not exist outside of this, let alone the paths and fruits.

However, here, by taking only those who have reached the final goal as representing the respective states of a recluse (samaṇa), only the recluses established in the fruits are included, for one established in the fruit is superior to one established on the path.
“...worthy of offerings. This meaning is understood through the very difference in teaching between two suttas. “Empty” (*rittā*) means secluded.

“Hollow” (*tucchā*) means devoid of essence, because there is an absence of the essence of those who have entered the path. They are called “proclamations” (*pavādā*) because people proclaim by means of them;
thus he said, “the four eternalist views,” and so forth, referring to the tenets that illustrate the various views of those following wrong paths. Therein:

What is to be said will follow later. "Those" refers to the recluses as previously described. "In this" refers to the external systems (bāhiraka-samaya) mentioned by the term "the doctrines of others" (parappavāda). "In which" (*yasmiṃ*):
this nominative case form is used in the sense of the locative. "Method" (*ñāya*) refers to the Noble Path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
Therefore, because Nibbāna is known, reached, and penetrated by it, and because it is the cause for attaining Nibbāna, it is called "Dhamma";
thus he says, "of the Dhamma that is the Way.

Regarding those other doctrines and teachings, their state of being non-fields and their state of being fields depends respectively on the absence and presence of the Noble Path, which is perfectly pure.

This is because of the absence and deficiency of both morality and the complete purity of serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*). Both of these are caused by whether the teaching is ill-proclaimed or well-proclaimed;

and that [distinction] is due to whether it has been proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One (*asammāsambuddha*) or by a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). Thus, he shows that because a *pārājika* offense is a cause for the failure of the Teacher, the Dispensation lacks the quality of leading to liberation (*aniyyānabhāva*).

Now, in order to support the aforementioned meaning both through a methodical exposition and by means of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he presents the scripture with the words “Therefore the Blessed One said,” and so forth.
Then, elucidating the Sutta therein by way of a simile, he says “Because,” and so on.
Therein, because for certain lions—specifically—their two front feet perform even the function of hands, he therefore says, “With hands and feet well-colored.”
The lion’s hair refers to the mane, the body-hair.
The wild elephant herd refers to the natural elephant herd, which is also called the *kālāvaka*. A colt refers to a wild horse.
On the slopes of Mount Sineru, there is a lake fifty yojanas in extent covered with *simbali* trees, known as the *simbali-daha*; surrounding it is a vast forest of *simbali* trees.

Referring to that, he said: "In the Simbali-flame forest. He said "not even a single ascetic" to show that while among these ascetics in the grounds of other sects some might not arise, here there is no such alternative;
rather, none at all arise in any way whatsoever. "Worn away by the Noble Path" means fashioned by the arising of the Noble Path. When...
The Noble Path shines forth through the correct practice of those belonging to the Dispensation;
such is the meaning. "Correctly" (*sammā*) means "well. Regarding "well-sounding," he says "by way of cause" (*hetunā*), meaning speaking well after having properly applied the reason.
And that reason must be sought as one that is indeed non-erroneous; thus he says "by way of method" (*nayena*), which means by way of the proper principle (*ñāyena*). And being thus...
Showing that he accomplishes and achieves his intended purpose, he says, "by the cause.
If the roar of the animal lion is called the "best roar" because it is superior to the roars of all animals, certain humans, and non-humans, how much more so the Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata?
To this he says: "The Lion’s Roar means the best roar. This is said even if the status of the animal lion's roar as the "best roar" [is in question].
Because it is desired for its fearlessness and lack of adversaries, the meaning of this very lion’s roar of the Tathāgata is preeminent;
thus he said, "the fearless roar, the unopposed roar. Now, demonstrating the state of being the supreme roar by means of a reason, he said, "For of these... and so forth.
By that, he supports the meaning expressed as "rightly" (sammā). Therein, by the phrase "because of its existence," he establishes the supreme significance of the lion’s roar.
He shows this. For the "actual meaning" (bhūtaṭṭha) is the "supreme meaning" (uttamaṭṭha). Demonstrating that it is precisely because of this actuality that there is a "fearless roar," he said:

"These recluses... [etc. ...is what it is called. Since for one who speaks what is unreal there might be fear or apprehension from some quarter, he demonstrated the non-erroneous nature of the restriction "right here" by saying: "Even for us... [etc. ...it is called a 'non-response'."
He said: "For it is not appropriate to restrict [the meaning] by saying that what exists elsewhere must exist here alone.
(140) *Kho* is used for emphasis; by it, he shows that [the thing] indeed exists. *Yaṃ* is in the nominative case with the sense of the instrumental; thus he says, "by which cause.
A "ford" (*tittha*) refers to the sixty-two views, as well as any other movement of views apart from those.
Because of its non-existence. "Crossing" (taraṇa) is defined as reaching the far shore;

for those who hold wrong views, it is a "floating" (pilavana) by way of repeatedly surfacing and submerging in that very place. Thus he said, "They cross, they float. "Uppādeta" refers to Pūraṇa and others.
They are called "titthiyas" because they are born at a ford (tittha), or because they possess a "ford" consisting of the aforementioned wrong views.
*Titthikā* means those who belong to a *tittha* (ford); thus they are *titthiyā*. *Assāsa* is that by which one breathes here, or it is a refuge (*avassaya*).
The words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are used as demonstrative pronouns; when they are stated in grammatical apposition with the words "by the Blessed One" (*bhagavatā*) and so forth, [the meaning is]:
by whatever state of perfect enlightenment the Blessed One became renowned, having attained the status of a Teacher, he became well-known and manifest.
And, demonstrating that state of perfect enlightenment together with the path by which he arrived, he said: "He who... [etc. ...has attained perfect enlightenment.

Although the terms *ñāṇa* (knowledge) and *dassana* (vision) are here synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*), they are used to show their distinct modes of operation within their respective domains according to specific distinctions; thus, they are presented by way of their unique characteristics and by way of the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjāttaya*).

He spoke the words beginning with "of those various [beings]" in order to demonstrate how they are connected by way of the knowledge of the obscurations to clear vision and direct knowledge (*vijjā-abhiññā*), by way of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) and the fleshly eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*), and by way of the knowledge of penetration and teaching.
In that context, "by one who knows their underlying tendencies and latent dispositions" means by the knowledge of underlying tendencies and latent dispositions;

"by one who sees all knowable phenomena" means by the unobstructed knowledges of omniscience; and "by [the knowledges of] past lives, etc. means by the knowledges of past lives and the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

The physical body of the Blessed One—which was produced by the power of merit not shared by others and which had previously acquired a prior existence through the attainment of unsurpassed knowledge—surpasses even the divine majesty of the gods; thus it is said: "Of all beings...
[omission] ...the seer. "By means of penetrative wisdom" means by means of path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*). For by that, delusion regarding all knowable phenomena has been entirely dispelled.
The subsequent realization is spoken of as if it were the initial realization itself.
"Of enemies" refers to the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*), or the fivefold Māras, or the adversaries of the Teaching—the followers of other sects;
their "slaying" means overcoming them through miracles, rendering them speechless, or remaining equanimous toward them. In this regard, the *Kesivinaaya Sutta* is cited.
This is the illustration. And likewise, it is by one who knows what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), etc.; who sees beings according to their karma;

who is an *arahant* due to the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*); and who is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*) through the non-erroneous realization of phenomena—such as those to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*)—as being "to be directly known" and so forth.
Alternatively, he is "one who knows" by virtue of having unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, and because his bodily actions and so forth proceed in accordance with that knowledge.

By the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), who possesses omniscience—which is established by an inexhaustible presence of inspired eloquence (*akkhayapaṭibhāna*) that serves as the cause for the non-decline of zeal (*chanda*) and the other [faculties], and which is established by the perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*) that proves even the absence of clamor—and who sees through acting with circumspection; thus, the application should be understood also by way of the ten powers (*dasabala*) and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhamma*).
"Yet" refers to the four qualities. "In ourselves" means among us, not among kings, royal ministers, and so forth, as a support.
“Reflecting,” is to be construed as “not reflecting on physical strength.
“Arisen confidence” refers to confidence based on penetration (*aveccappasāda*). For he will say later: “The four factors of stream-entry have been explained.

Granted that those beyond training (*asekkha*) are indeed fellow-practitioners (*sahadhammika*) due to their equal training with those beyond training, yet because they have already lived the holy life (*ciṇṇabrahmacariyatā*), [they are distinguished].
However, because it cannot be said that they "practice the Dhamma together," the section on those beyond training (asekkha) is not included. Regarding the phrase "all these":

all these aforementioned individuals—monks and so forth, as well as ordinary persons (puthujjana) and noble ones (ariya) such as stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and others—are called "those who share the Dhamma" (sahadhammika) because they possess the same Dhamma through their respective trainings (sikkhā).
Now, by way of the noble Dhamma already produced, regarding those who share the Dhamma...

Showing this, he said, “Furthermore,” and so forth. Regarding the vision of the path: through the penetration of the truths by way of full comprehension (*pariññā*), clear realization (*abhisamaya*), and so on, there is no dispute concerning such statements as “there are nine path factors” or “there are eight factors of enlightenment. Regarding “conducting themselves according to a single Dhamma”:

this means conducting themselves according to the same Dhamma. For those who have penetrated the truths, there is no dispute such as, “The Dhamma has been well-seen by me, but it has been poorly seen by you,” and so forth.
For those supreme persons are comprised within the Saṅgha by virtue of their commonality in view and virtue.

By the phrase "those who are fellow-followers of the Dhamma" and so forth, he demonstrates that the excellent practice of the Saṅgha—which was previously mentioned only partially under the heading of "fulfilling [the training] in the precepts"—is actually complete.
For those who are endowed with perfected virtue and possess perfectly purified vision are dear to the wise.

“Agreeable. To this extent, it has been explained in various sections of the Suttas by way of demonstrating confidence in the Triple Gem through such expressions as, “Indeed, friends, there exists... (A.IV.38). 141.
“Confidence in the Teacher”: By the inclusion of the term “confidence,” the qualities that inspire confidence—such as [the statement] “by the Blessed One” and so forth—are also included.

By this, he demonstrates the Buddha’s state of being perfectly enlightened; likewise, by the phrase "confidence in the Dhamma," he shows the Dhamma’s state of being well-expounded, and by the other [phrase], the Saṅgha’s state of being well-practiced.

It should be understood that by means of that mind—which is not found elsewhere—the meaning "the recluse exists only within the Dispensation and does not exist outside of it" has been correctly established. In this regard, the following is said:
The interpretation: Because the Perfectly Enlightened One is our Teacher, therefore, friends, we have confidence in the Teacher;
and because he is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well-expounded—thus we have confidence in the Dhamma;

and for that very reason, we possess the practice of fulfilling the precepts... [and so on] ...we are those who follow the Dhamma... and we are those who have gone forth. Thus, in this context, regarding the Teacher:

“Through confidence in the Dhamma comes confidence in the Dhamma; through that, there is right practice toward the Saṅgha. This principle is not found even in a slight degree among the doctrines of others;
thus, it is only here that one is a true ascetic... [and so on] ... "by ascetics other than these.
It is said "now" because for those who have penetrated the Truths and abandoned attachment, the arising of worldly affection is simply impossible.
If this is so, how is it that such statements as, "Monks, a preceptor should establish a father’s love for his co-resident pupil," were spoken?
This was not said with reference to worldly attachment; rather, because it resembles it, it is expressed by way of the term "love" to denote the affection of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
For the Blessed One does not enjoin monks toward defilement. It is with reference to such love—as it brings about serene confidence and brings forth virtuous qualities—that these words were spoken.

Devotion and serene confidence (*pasāda*) do not exist toward Pūraṇa and the others; rather, it should be understood that what occurs in their case is merely a manifestation of greed resembling serene confidence.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita, by whom the commentary was committed to writing. There is but one Teacher because his qualities are not shared by others;
otherwise, due to the lack of wonder, the very definition of a Teacher would not be fulfilled.
"Having made it distinct" means having separated it from others and made it one's own exclusive possession.
For those who declare, "Our Teacher," it follows as a matter of course that he is not the teacher of others;

likewise, those who claim his status as a teacher in a limited sense, even while desiring his status as a teacher endowed with complete characteristics, are in contradiction [with the full definition] because they seek a state of being a teacher that is inconsistent with that [complete definition].

They are defeated. Regarding "the Dhamma of the scriptures" (*pariyattidhamme*), this refers to the period of the various divisions such as the *suttas*, *geyyas*, and so forth, which possess superior qualities of the Brahma-qualities.
In that context, the phrase "the goat-virtue... [and] the dog-virtue, etc. is stated because, for the most part, other sectarians (*aññatitthiya*) are found to undertake such vows;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of restraints, observances, the fourfold restraint, and so forth. "Excessive intention" (*adhippāyaso*) means excessive.

*Adhippāyo* means that by which one causes to flow (*payasati*) or employs (*payujjati*); it is a distinguished activity to be performed with excellence. Therefore, he said: "the application of the superior.
"The culmination of that confidence" means the finality of that confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma.
Finality (*niṭṭhā*) is liberation (*mokkho*). For those who speak according to the occasion, confidence in the respective occasions and in those who teach them lasts only until that point.
The meaning is the attainment of liberation. Since those who hold views merely imagine a final conclusion (niṭṭha) according to their own respective tenets, he said:
"There is no one who does not proclaim a final conclusion. "Of the brahmins" means of those who propound the doctrine of brahminhood.
Among them, some say that the final conclusion is co-residence with Brahmā; some, proximity to him; and some, union with him.
They say, "It ends there. In this regard, those who maintain the doctrine of co-residence (*salokatā*) and those who maintain the doctrine of proximity (*samīpatā*) are proponents of dual views;
the others are proponents of non-dual views. All of them, however, in actual fact, perceive their final goal as rebirth in the Brahma-world alone.
For they have a persistent adherence to that world as permanent, just as in the case of the Brahma Baka. Therefore it is said: "The Brahma-world is the final goal."
"Brahmaloka" refers to the plane of the first jhāna. "Of the great ascetics" means of the ascetics such as the Vekhanasas.
Just like Mahābrahmā, there is no single most excellent one among the Ābhassara deities on the plane of the first jhāna; therefore, the plural form "Ābhassarā" is used.
"Of the wanderers" means of wanderers such as Sañjaya and others. "One whose mind is infinite" (anantamānaso) means one who has neither an end nor a mind.
Because it is never absent for the Ājīvakas, it is infinite; because it transcends pleasure, pain, and so forth, it is beyond the mind (*amānasa*).
By this, he shows that the mind is defiled by these eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

Whatever needs to be said regarding *papañca* has already been stated above. Here, craving and views alone are intended, as they are the cessation of the notions of "mine" (*mamaṅkāra*) and "I" (*ahaṅkāra*).

Because they are intended [to be included]. Just as greed (*lobha*) alone appears as the single defilement in five places, so too do three defilements—namely, hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), and views (*diṭṭhi*)—appear in two places. For in the passage where it says "of one with hatred" (*sadosassa*), the unwholesome root of aversion (*paṭigha*) is taken;

in "of one who is opposed" (*paṭiviruddhassa*), it is opposition; in "of one with delusion" (*samohassa*), it is the unwholesome root of delusion; and in "of one who lacks clear vision" (*aviddasuno*), [it is ignorance].
“Possessing a garland” refers to a lack of clear comprehension (*asampajañña*). “Possessing clinging” refers to grasping according to the manner of thinking, “There is no gift,” and so forth.
“Delighting in proliferation” is by way of the arising of proliferation (*papañca*).

“In terms of mode” means in terms of the mode of occurrence. Because a specific type of lust is being stated by means of another word, the expression “with lust” (*sarāga*) was mentioned at the beginning.
"Coarse sensual object" means "by way of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure," so it was said. "By way of grasping" means by way of firm grasping.
Because the text comes down in the Canon as a single compound, "of one who is both attracted and repelled" (*anuruddha-paṭiviruddhassa*), the words have been extracted together here.
However, in that context, the meaning should be stated as "of Anuruddha" by way of beauty; for there is no such thing as being repelled [in that sense].

It is by way of its intrinsic nature. "By way of showing the arising of proliferation (*papañca*)" means: proliferation (*papañca*) is the proliferating of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) due to the state of being a condition for the successive arising of defilements, karma, and karmic results;
it is by way of showing that [craving] is the cause for the arising of that [proliferation].
For craving is the specific condition for the arising of existence. "By way of showing clinging conditioned by craving" means: by way of showing clinging which has craving as its condition.
It is by way of seeing the state of craving that serves as the condition for clinging. For this is a description of the specific cause by means of its fruit.

"Thus you should shatter it": why should you thus scatter greed—which consists of sensual lust, craving for existence, and so forth? "By way of making it into craving" means by way of making it into the act of craving, that is, by way of grasping at the aspect of beauty.
For lust that occurs toward an object is called "beauty."
142. It is called "doctrine" (*vāda*) because they speak by means of it; thus, it is a "view-doctrine" (*diṭṭhivāda*). For it is by way of views that those who follow wrong views postulate:
"The self and the world are eternal," and "The self and the world are not eternal. Therefore he said: "There are these two views, monks.
Since there is no view devoid of craving, it is precisely through the influence of craving that one adheres to the notion of the self's eternity.
Having stated this, it was said: "by way of craving and views. "Attached" means dependent. "Approached" means having reached a state of oneness, as it were, by way of not relinquishing them.
"Clinging" means swallowed by that view and, as it were, finalized within its scope.
Therefore he said: "penetrated. Just as sensual clinging is the root of dispute for householders, so too is it for those who have gone forth.
Regarding "clinging to views," he said, "They are opposed to the view of non-existence (vibhavadiṭṭhi). For through opposition to a view, there is opposition to those who hold that view.
Regarding "the momentary origination" as the moment of arising, he said, "the production of views.
And by the very mention of the production of views here, just as the dependent origination of views is made clear, so too is the basis for those views; thus it applies to both.
It should be understood that impermanence, suffering, and non-self have been analyzed.
Showing those which, according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidā*, are called "the eight bases for the origin of conditions," he said, "The aggregates also," and so forth.
Therein, the aggregates are also a basis for views in the sense of being an object, because of such statements as, "One regards form as self. Ignorance also is a basis for views.

Because it functions as a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) and so forth. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the Noble Ones and is unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones," and so on.
Contact (*phassa*) too is a basis for views. As it is said: "That too is conditioned by contact;
experiencing it again and again through contact," and so on. Perception (*saññā*) too is a basis for views. For this has been stated:
“For proliferation and conceptualization have perception as their source,” and so forth, including: “Having perceived earth as earth,” and so on.

Discursive thought (*vitakka*) is also a basis for views. As it is said: “Having applied reasoning to views, they speak of two things—truth and falsehood,” and “He is a reasoner, an investigator,” and so forth.
Inappropriate attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is also a basis for views. As the Blessed One said:
“For one who attends to that in an improper way, one of the six views arises;
the view ‘I have a self’ arises for him as true and definitive,” and so forth. It is called *samuṭṭhāna* because it originates by means of this;

its state is the meaning of origination (*samuṭṭhānaṭṭha*), and [the term is used] in that sense. The passing away of moments is momentary cessation (*khaṇikanirodha*). The passing away of conditions is...
It is the absolute cessation of ignorance and the other [defilements]. Showing that by which this occurs, he says, "the path of stream-entry.
For the four noble paths are, as appropriate, the causes for the absolute cessation of their respective classes of formations;
however, momentary cessation is causeless.
"Benefit" (*ānisansa*) means arising. That, moreover, is twofold: pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).

Among these, that which pertains to the future life belongs to the side of disadvantage (*ādīnava*) due to the afflictions of miserable rebirths; thus, showing the other [the benefit], he said, "with reference to which...
and so forth. Showing even the disadvantage as pertaining only to the present life, he said, "the calamity rooted in the grasping of views," and so forth.
This is the danger (*ādīnava*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the term *ādīna*, there is an inclusion of nakedness, fasting, standing, squatting, and so forth.
If it were said that "one escapes by means of this" (*nissarati etena*), then the path of vision itself would be the escape from views;
however, since that [path] is taken here in the sense of "disappearance" (*atthaṅgama*), it is Nibbāna—escaped from all conditioned things—that is the escape even from views.
Having stated this, it was said: “The escape from views is Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase “by this,” etc., what is to be said follows the same method as explained in the *Anuyogavatta*.
143. “Showing the cutting off of views”: by showing the full comprehension (*pariññā*) of all clinging (*upādāna*), he demonstrates the method for the total eradication of all views.
It has already been stated: “There are four kinds of clinging; these, according to their analytical meaning...”
Having recited the verse: “The concise and detailed [expositions] of phenomena, and their sequence, I shall now elucidate,” it is indeed stated by way of the analysis of the meaning and so forth.

Granted, those outside this [teaching] do not possess such knowledge as: “These clingings are exactly four, and no more than this”; yet, some [of them] nonetheless hold that “sensual pleasures are to be abandoned.”
Some say, "It is wrong to say that there is no other world," while others say, "It is wrong to say that purification comes through rules and observances.
Yet they do not know at all the falsity of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*). Even regarding that which they do know, they do not know its absolute abandonment;
nevertheless, [they fail to understand] everything that is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
They remain merely asserting that "there is something to be fully understood.
To show what kind of practice these people undertake therein, the Teacher said, "There are, monks," and so forth. In this context, *santi* means they exist.
By this, he shows the non-interruption of those speculative theorists (*diṭṭhigatika*) through their continued existence. *Eke* means some. *Samaṇabrāhmaṇā* means...
“Ascetics by virtue of having gone forth, and brahmins by birth alone. “Of all” means the transcendence and abandoning of all clingings without exception.
“They do not correctly proclaim” means that even for those whom they do proclaim [to be liberated], they do not proclaim a correct full understanding (*pariññā*).

Now, in order to demonstrate this meaning in detail, the passage beginning with “some” is stated. Therein, there are the *hotika*, *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, *paramahaṃsa*, *kājaka*, *tidaṇḍa*, *monavata*, *seva*, *pārupaka*, and *pañcamarattika*.
The weavers, the Muggasobhitas, the Cārabākas, the ascetics, the Nigaṇṭhas, the Ājīvakas, the seers, the Pārāyaṇikas, those who practice the five fires,

the followers of Kapila, the followers of Kaṇāda, the liberators from saṃsāra, those who subsist on fire, those who subsist on cow urine, those who subsist on cow dung, those who follow the dog-vow, those who carry water-pots, those who subsist on bats, those who wear a single garment,
those who seek purification by water, those who torment the body, those who seek purification through moral conduct, those who seek purification through meditation, and the fourfold [sectarians].

The ninety-six [heretical views], such as eternalism and so forth, are called *pāsaṇḍas* because they bite with the snare of craving (*taṇhā-pāsa*) or because they obstruct the noble Dhamma (*ariya-dhamma*).
"Sensual pleasure" (*kāma*) refers to the enjoyment of a basis (*vatthu*), meaning the enjoyment of the object of one's activity.

"They practice through theft" means that they practice according to the worldly terminology of common designations such as "stolen hand" (*paṭihatta*) and so forth. "Three reasons" refers to: "There is no... [and so on].
The causes for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakāraṇa*), which consist of specific views proceeding in the manner beginning with "It was given," etc., are [the subject].

"Discussions on meaning" (*atthasallāpikā*) means those that discuss meaning; the intention is that they reveal the discussion of the intended meaning between two parties. For the speech of two people is called a "discussion. Therefore he said, "The earth, it is said," and so forth.

Because the confidence of the sectarians (*titthiya*) toward their own teacher, the Dhamma, and their fellow practitioners—which has been mentioned—is directed toward what is not a proper basis (*anāyatanagatattā*).
The demonstration of a lack of confidence is the severing of confidence. Discourse that proceeds in such a manner is called "discourse that severs confidence.
"Of such a kind" means of a nature that, according to the method described, does not lead to the subsiding of the defilements.

"Dhamma" refers to what is merely a semblance of Dhamma; "Vinaya" refers to what is merely a semblance of Vinaya. For the followers of other sects, standing in deceit and deceiving the world, speak of "Dhamma."

Having spoken something such as, “These seven bodies are unmade and not fashioned by a maker,” and likewise, having prescribed the rules of training for his disciples—such as the *Gosīla*, *Vaggu*, and *Lūkhappaccaka* sections—under the heading of the “Dhamma and Vinaya,” they speak of them;
it is with reference to this that it is said, “in the Dhamma and Vinaya. Therefore, he says: “By both [of these], he shows the teaching to be non-leading to liberation.”

Even for one who wishes to perform a mere trifle of merit, it is to be censured by the wise in this very life and a miserable rebirth is to be expected in the future, because he creates an obstacle by obstructing one overcome by the stain of stinginess;
how much more so for a founder of a sect who strikes a blow at the Wheel of the Conqueror, which brings about escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra?
Showing this meaning—that it applies to one who acts according to that advice—he said, "In a teaching that does not lead to liberation," and so forth.

Showing how that confidence, by way of its own occurrence, does not proceed rightly in the future life, he said, "Even after having lasted for some time, it subsequently perishes"; the meaning is that it is not ultimate, like the confidence born of direct penetration (*aveccappasāda*).
When practiced according to the prescribed method, it leads to rebirth in the animal realm; for the result must indeed correspond to the action.

"The entire variety of causes" refers to the specific types of causes—namely, the wrong practice characterized by the followers of the various founders—that bring about the suffering of the miserable states (apāya). Furthermore, this confidence...
It does not lead [to liberation] because it belongs to the side of wrongness, like faith in a jackal that has drunk liquor.

"Surājallika" refers to the dregs thrown away after straining liquor. He said, "I will deceive this man," with the intention that "Brahmins are greedy for wealth. "A hundred kaṃsas" means a hundred kahāpaṇas.
"Of that" refers to the faith. Since all greed is called simply "clinging to sense-pleasures" (kāmupādāna), he said, "by the path of arahantship..."
"Regarding the full understanding of the abandoning of clinging to sensual pleasures. "Of such a kind" means of a nature that leads entirely to the subsiding of the defilements.
It is called "Dhamma" in the sense of supporting those who practice according to the instructions, by way of preventing them from falling into the states of misery.
It is called "Vinaya" in the sense of disciplining them completely. In this context, it refers to that which leads to the escape from the suffering of existence.

He stood paying homage for two incalculable eons due to his fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*) leading to the enlightenment of a *paccekabuddha*, his long-standing familiarity with the Buddha’s teaching, and his serene confidence of heart toward the Blessed One.
The verse beginning with “O owls,” etc., was spoken by a tree deity. “Having risen at the proper time” means having arisen from his midday rest in the evening.
“He does not go to a miserable destination” means he does not go to an evil state of existence (*duggati*).

"He will not go. [This applies to] the peacock-catcher, the drum-player, and so forth; even the account of the great drum-player and others should be elaborated, beginning with the manifestation of a smile.

"In the ultimate sense" (*paramattha*) means in supramundane phenomena (*lokuttaradhamma*). "But what need is there to say more?"—this refers to taking a sign (*nimitta*) even in phenomena that are ultimate.
For those who hear it. The story of the novice (*sāmaṇeravatthu*): on the very day he went forth, he was bitten by a snake, died, and was reborn in the world of the gods;
this is the story of that novice. "Milk-rice" (*khīrodana*) means rice mixed with milk. "Timbarusaka" is the fruit of the *tinduka* tree. It resembles *tipusa*.
One type of creeper is the *timbarusa*; they call its fruit *timbarusaka*.
*Kakkārika* is a small *elāḷuka*, which they also call *mahātipusa*. *Vallipakka* is the fruit of the small *tipusa* creeper.
*Hatthapatāpaka* is *mandāmukhī*. *Ambakañjika* is sour *kañjika* (sour gruel); they also call it *khaḷayāgu*. *Doṇinimmajjanī*—
"With oil" means with sesame dregs. "A fan" means a square-handled fan. "A palm-leaf fan" means a circular fan made from palm leaves.
"A peacock-feather fan" means a mosquito fan made from peacock feathers.
"In accordance with the method already stated" means that here too, all the various reasons already mentioned are taken together as one.

The Teacher, demonstrating this, said, "For what reason? and so forth; therefore, it should be understood by applying the method stated for that [other] teaching which does not lead to liberation, by way of recollection. 145.
"Full understanding" (*pariññā*) refers to the full understanding of abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*). To show their condition, he says: "the full understanding of the clingings."

*Pahānapariññā* (full understanding as abandoning). What is intended here is their absolute cessation, and since that occurs through the cessation of conditions, [the text] sets forth their condition starting from the root cause.
*Ayaṃ* refers to what is now being stated; it is the meaning of the compound terms such as "what is their source" (*kiṃ nidānā*) found in the passage beginning with "And these...
(*ime ca*). *In all instances* refers to all [passages] such as "from the arising of craving" (*taṇhāsamudayā*).
In these phrases. And by this very inclusion of "all," the inclusion of such phrases as "having contact as their source" should also be understood.
These followers of other sects do not know the origin of even the clingings, much less their cessation;
but the Tathāgata knows, according to reality, both the origin and the passing away of those clingings and their respective conditions. Therefore—

“Right here, monks, is the ascetic... [as before] ...empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics,” thus bringing the lion’s roar he had begun to its conclusion, he shows the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by descending into the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) through the method beginning with, “And these, monks, are the four kinds of clinging,” and then, showing the cessation of the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), he says, “But when... and so forth.
He grasped the pinnacle of the teaching by means of his attainment of Arahatship; showing this meaning, he said, "But because the Blessed One," and so forth. This is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*.
146. Description of the City of Vesālī:
"Aparāparaṃ" means repeatedly. "Because it has become extensive" means because it has expanded by a distance of one *gāvuta* after another.

"Therein" refers to that state of having become extensive. "As soon as it was discarded" means at the very moment it was cast away. "By dangers such as waves" means by the dangers of waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, and sea-monsters.

Furthermore, even though it had come by way of a flow of water, the heat did not depart; and since such heat could only exist because of the presence of consciousness, he thought, "There might be a fetus.
The phrase beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*) is an investigation into the reason for that.
Because of their merit, there was no foul odor, and because of their excellence, there was no state of putrefaction. Due to the children's reliance on merit, [the child emerged] from the thumb.

Milk appeared for him, and he obtained milk-rice. Just as the skin of the Bodhisatta’s mother became clear and radiant when the Bodhisatta had entered her womb in his final existence—so that she was as if skinless—it is said, “they were skinless.
“Of them” refers to the two boys. “Parents” refers to their foster parents. Having consecrated [them]...
They made him king because he had performed deeds that bestow royal success and because he was born into an unbroken royal lineage.
Some say that the deities, urged by the power of the prince’s merit, took possession of him.
Others say it was near the city; at a distance of one *gāvuta* to the west of the city, there was a place with walls and small pavilions, like the Jīvaka Ambavana.
Regarding the phrase "not long after he had departed" (*acirapakkanto*): here, what is intended is not departure to another place, but rather departure from the Teaching (*sāsana*).

Demonstrating this, he said, "having disrobed" (*vibbhamitvā*), and so forth. For that very reason, he said, "from this Dhamma and Vinaya. "In the assembly" (*parisati*) means in the assembly; the meaning is a gathering of people.
When one has entered such a gathering of people, it is called "in the midst of the assembly" (*parisamajjhe*). By means of the mental attention of cultivation (*bhāvanā-manasikāra*).
A "human quality" (*manussadhamma*) is a state that must be produced by humans through their own nature;

or, a "human quality" is a state that brings about human existence—that is, a limited wholesome state (*parittakusala*) that is not sublime. This exists even when a Buddha has not arisen, and it is with reference to this that it is said:
"By a low holy life, one is reborn among Khattiyas. [Thinking], "He is our Buddha,"...
Those who act with a sense of "mine" toward the Buddha are "those who claim the Buddha as their own. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
Regarding the commentary on "superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and so forth:
one who is capable of the noble state, that is, of the nature of an *ariya*, is an *alamariya*. He knows the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and sees it, just as visual consciousness does.
The knowledge and vision that knows and sees things as they are—namely, the three characteristics and the states conducive to full comprehension—is knowledge-vision;
this is insight (vipassanā). The knowledge and vision that knows and sees Nibbāna, or the four truths, through penetration free from delusion is knowledge-vision;
this is the path (magga). As for the fruit (phala), it should be understood in the same way as Nibbāna.
“Knowledge and vision” (*ñāṇadassana*) refers to the knowledge of the goal attained through the path in the sense of direct realization;
it is also knowledge and vision in the sense of omniscience, unobstructedness, and being the universal eye.

What is intended here is the supramundane path, for the intention is that if that were denied, none of the Buddha’s qualities would be possible. Therefore he said: “For he denies that of the Blessed One.”
There is no such thing as a "subtle state" (sukhumadhammantara)—such as jhāna, vipassanā, and so forth—that has been grasped through the assistance of a teacher.

"Struck by reasoning" (takkapariyāhata) means having been struck around and turned over by the mere process of initial application (vitakka), which reasons about each respective object to be shown, thinking, "It will be thus," or "It will be in this way.
Therefore he said, "Having reasoned," and so forth. This refers to mundane wisdom (lokiyapaññā).
The intention is that he permits a discourse on the Dhamma suited to the assembly seated nearby. Therefore, he said, “The ascetic Gotama,” and so forth. *Paṭibhāti* means *paṭibhāna*;
it is the thought of speaking that occurs thus, “I shall speak in this way. Knowledge arising from that thought is *paṭibhāna*.
Because it arises spontaneously in the absence of prior study (*āgama*), it is called *sayaṃpaṭibhāna* (spontaneous inspiration). Therefore, he said: “By this, his...”
"It obstructs direct perception regarding phenomena. "Well-polished" means free from obstruction;
for if there is no contact [with the palate], the sound of speech does not easily issue forth. "The enclosure of the teeth" refers to the two lips.
Because the tongue also does not easily issue forth the sound of speech due to stiffness, he said, "the tongue is soft. It is a sweet voice because of its beauty like the song of the karavīka bird.
"Ela" is said to mean hatred (*dosa*). "Elagaḷā" means that which flows with hatred; "anelagaḷā" means not flowing with hatred, that is, being free from hatred.
The meaning is that it does not cause affliction. He speaks thus while showing the very causes for such coloring.
"The five things" refers to the grasping, hearing, retaining, mastering, and wise attention toward the aggregates and so forth, which constitute the practice of profound knowledge.

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Regarding the phrase "for the one who acts rightly for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering," the word *sammā* (rightly) should be applied in both instances:
"for the one who acts rightly, rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. For indeed, only he who practices the Dhamma rightly attains the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, for that practitioner who acts according to the method described, deliverance is, in its true sense, the very essence of the Dhamma itself.
"Leading out" (niyyāna) means: "That Dhamma... leads out, it goes forth. 147.
"Angry" (kodhana) means one whose nature is to be angry. However, because Sunakkhatta was harsh and spoke with cruel words due to his anger, [the Blessed One] said:
"Angry means fierce and cruel. In that particular existence, there was no proximate cause (upanissaya) for the Path and its Fruits.
"There is none" means that there is no decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits that ought to arise within that particular existence.
In such cases, the Buddhas call him a "foolish man," as in the instances of Sudinna, Lāḷudāyin, and others.
Even when a decisive support exists, if at that moment the path or the fruit is absent, they call him a "foolish man," as in the instances of the elders Dhaniya and Upasena.
But regarding one whose decisive support (upanissaya) has been cut off, there is nothing at all that can be said.
Just as it was said, “The wretched man Makkhali thinks himself a thrower among men,” so too was it said of Sunakkhatta: “But of this one...,” and so forth.
The genitive case here is used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). “By anger” means by way of the cause of anger.
"Bhagavato" is the dative case used in view of the word "kuddha. "Pubbe" means at the time of being a bhikkhu. "Desirous of hearing the sound":
it is said that while he was seeing the forms of the deities in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his divine eye, he saw their movement of the lips but did not hear the sound;
therefore, he became desirous of hearing their voices. Hence it is said: "Desirous of hearing the sound... etc.

"He asked. And because he had previously deafened a virtuous bhikkhu by striking him on the ear with a stone, he was incapable of attaining the divine ear even while performing the preliminary exercises.
With reference to him, it was said: "Knowing that there was no sufficient basis (upanissaya), he did not teach the preliminary exercises.
"He thought" means he thought while emerging from improper reflection through his own wrong deliberations.
Because it awakens one to the state of leading out (niyyānika), the teaching-dhamma is called "leading out" by way of figurative designation as non-distinct from that state.
Alternatively, the teaching-dhamma is "leading out" because the noble path—which is itself the leading out—must be awakened to by means of it.

It demonstrates its own presence through the demonstration of the accomplishment of its function, because it has been made manifest in various instances, and not merely by way of a formal promise. For indeed, according to the offense...
Through the promulgation of various training rules in accordance with the Dhamma and in conformity with the inclinations of those to be trained, through his unerring teaching of the Dhamma,
and through his immediate answering of questions posed by gods and humans in a manner suited to their respective dispositions,
the Blessed One’s omniscience— characterized by the unimpeded range of his knowledge in all respects— is made manifest to the wise.

Likewise, in various instances such as the performance of the Twin Miracle, there are the types of knowledge beginning with the supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*). Therefore, he said, "And of mine," and so forth.

It is called *anvaya* because it follows (*anveti*) by way of conforming to the convention (*saṅketa*) as it was grasped; it goes (*eti*), that is, it knows. Therefore, he said, "the meaning is 'it understands'.
And here, the conformity to convention is [illustrated] by the passage beginning, "by the promulgation of this or that training rule (*sikkhāpada*) according to the offense," and so on.
It is exactly as stated. Thus, the application should be understood:

just as the application was made by means of the knowledge of omniscience, so too should the application be understood in various places through such passages as, "Even such a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) as this, namely my knowledge of the supernormal powers (iddhividhañāṇa)," and so forth.
The commentary on the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and so forth is finished.
148. Commentary on the Knowledge of the Ten Powers:
Although, because the teaching begins from the outset by way of the triad of direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), [the section] following the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) appears above...

One might say that "the three direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) should be mentioned," yet because they are in fact the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjāttaya*), which is identical to the aforementioned triad of direct knowledges in meaning, it is stated:
"the three clear knowledges should be mentioned. Why, however, is it said here: "When these are mentioned, the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) above is not fulfilled"?
Is it not the case that these knowledges, like the remaining direct knowledges, have the sense of directly knowing their own respective objects?

Are they to be described as "higher knowledges" (*abhiññā*) by way of their meaning of unshakability and support, yet as "powers of knowledge" (*balañāṇa*) by way of that same meaning, just as right mindfulness and so forth are [designated] among the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors? This is not so.

For in that case, the teaching was given with the aim of clarifying the specific functions of the phenomena (*dhamma*), whereas here it is given with the aim of clarifying the specific qualities of the Teacher.
It is not possible to speak thus in the teaching because there is no difference in meaning; for some worldlings, the thought might arise:
"What is this? Is the Blessed One, by taking up again the qualities mentioned below, merely demonstrating an excess of qualities?
Therefore, it is well said that "the knowledge of the ten powers is not fully perfected above."
Why is it said that these are "not shared with others"? Is it not the case that some of these [knowledges] also arise for certain disciples?
Certainly they do arise; however, such [powers] as the Buddhas' knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*) and so forth never arise for anyone other than them.
Therefore, they are "not shared with others. For this reason, he said: "These are the powers of the Tathāgata alone. This very...

Indeed, having regard for the aforementioned deficiency [in merit], the designation of "unique qualities" (asādhāraṇaguṇa) is established only in reference to such things as the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa), because that [deficiency] is absent there.
Granted, the equipment of knowledge (ñāṇasambhāra) is a specific condition for the powers of knowledge; however, the equipment of merit (puññasambhāra) is also a condition for them.
Or rather, since the equipment of knowledge itself constitutes an equipment of merit, it is said: "They have come by way of the attainment of the store of merit."

“Pakatihatthikulam” means the entire species of ordinary elephants by strength, including the various types such as those that roam the mountains, those that roam the rivers, and those that roam the forests, known by names such as Gocariya and Kālāvaka. “Of ten men” means of ten men of middling strength.
The connection is made by supplying the words “the bodily strength of one Tathāgata. And regarding the word “of one,” it is as explained in the preceding discussion.
It is stated according to the stream of the teaching because it has been handed down [in the tradition]. Regarding the phrase "the power of the Nārāyaṇa-composition": here, *nārā* refers to reins;
since many various kinds of these arise from this [body], it is called *nārāyana*, which is the thunderbolt (*vajira*).

Therefore, the meaning of "the power of the Nārāyaṇa-composition" is "the power of the thunderbolt-composition. As for the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), however, it has indeed been included in the Canon itself, unlike the physical power (*kāyabala*).
The intention is that this is indeed recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. It is stated: "The seventy-three knowledges mentioned in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* are the seventy-seven knowledges.
However, in that [work], seventy-seven are found in the Nidāna-vagga and forty-four [others];
furthermore, the seventy-three consisting of those beginning with knowledge born of hearing (*sutamaya*) are seen in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, not in the *Saṃyutta*. "And others too" means...

By this, it includes the many classifications of knowledge stated in the *Ñāṇavatthuvibhaṅga* by way of single factors and so forth, as well as those stated elsewhere in such passages as "knowledge of the past limit" and so on, and in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and other texts in such passages as "The Tathāgata understands this; these are the bases of views thus grasped," and so forth.
It also includes the unshakability of both the person and [the teaching] due to penetration according to reality.
Because it exercises superior power over those things to be known by one who possesses them, it is said: "in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.
That which belongs to a bull (*usabha*) is *āsabha*; it is the preeminent state.
They go forward toward it by way of professing omniscience, or the eight assemblies approach it; thus they are *āsabhā*, namely the previous Buddhas. And this, moreover, is the state of the Buddhas.
He speaks only of omniscience. "While standing" means that even while remaining silent, he effectively acknowledges it by his very presence.
"He assents" means he grants permission.
"In the eight assemblies" refers to: "I recall, Sāriputta, having addressed many hundreds of assemblies of khattiyas... [and so forth]."
Regarding the eight assemblies mentioned there: "In that regard, Sāriputta, I do not perceive any sign that fear or trepidation would overcome me.
He "roars the fearless roar" means that by means of the application of knowledge demonstrated later, he roars the fearless roar as one who possesses the ten powers.
This is according to the *Sīhanāda Sutta* found in the *Khandhavagga*.

By the remainder of the sutta, “The four wheels turn for devas and humans,” it is stated that the occurrence of the attainment of fruits through reliance on true persons and so forth, or the occurrence of the attainment of later reliance on true persons and so forth by depending upon earlier reliance on true persons and so forth;
thus, it should be understood that the word *cakra* (wheel) is included therein by the word *ādi* (and so forth). They are shaped like a wheel (*vicakkasaṇṭhānā*).

*Asani* (thunderbolt) is indeed *asanivicakkaṃ* (the thunderbolt-wheel). Regarding the phrase "in the heart-wheel and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood that the term *cakra* (wheel) also applies to the collection of commands and other such things.
For in expressions such as "We shall cause a schism in the Saṅgha, a schism in the wheel" (*cakkabhedaṃ*), the command is called "the wheel";

whereas in expressions such as "the divine wheel" (*devacakka*) and "the asura wheel" (*asuracakka*), it refers to a collection. Because it is the state of having fully penetrated [the truths], the knowledge of the path of Arahatship—
"Realization" (*paṭivedha*) is said to be "that which has arisen at the moment of the fruit" (*phalakkhaṇe*).

By this it is meant that even for the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) already attained, the fulfillment of its function occurs merely through another person’s awakening; thus it is said: "The stream-entry [of Koṇḍañña the Elder]... [and so on]...
is that which occurs at the moment of the fruit. Thereafter, however, until his final *parinibbāna*, the occurrence of the knowledge of teaching belongs to him alone.

It should be understood that this is the "station" of the Wheel of Dhamma once set in motion, just as it is the station of the Wheel-Treasure of a wheel-turning monarch whose wheel has been set in motion.
When it is said, "it stands," is it like a man standing on the ground? No; he says, "because its existence is dependent upon that.
Furthermore, "station" here refers to its acquisition of selfhood and its continued presence, not the cessation of movement; thus he says, "it both arises and proceeds."
Showing where this knowledge of the Ten Powers is set forth in detail, he said, "But in the Abhidhamma," and so on.
The same method applies to the others as well.
"Samādiyantī" means "undertakings"; however, since these are things performed after having been undertaken, he said, "of those performed after having been undertaken."

"Or, 'kamma' itself is the undertaking of kamma (*kammasamādāna*). By this, he shows that the word "undertaking" (*samādāna*) has no meaning not already expressed by the word "kamma," just as the word "gone" (*gata*) has no meaning not already expressed by the word "urine" (*mutta*).
"Gati" refers to the destinies such as hell and so forth. "Upadhi" refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Kāla" refers to the time when the kamma is ready to ripen.
"Payoga" refers to the activity that serves as the condition for the arising of the result.
"Leading to the wrong course" means leading to Nibbāna; for he will say: "Sāriputta, I know Nibbāna, and the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
Even when many people kill a single living being, although the volition of all of them has that very same life-faculty as its object, that kamma is nevertheless of different kinds for each of them.
For among them, one performs [the deed] out of reverence, having conceived a desire for it; another performs it being pressured by others who say, "Come, you too should do it";
and another wanders about as if having the same desire, not offering any resistance.

Among these, one is reborn in hell because of that very action, one in the animal realm, and one in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya). The Tathāgata [knows this] at the moment of the accumulation [of kamma].
In this way—because of the accumulation [of karma] by this mode—he knows: "This one will be reborn in hell; this one in the animal realm;
this one in the sphere of hungry ghosts. Even as they are being reborn in hell, he knows: "This one will be reborn in the great hells; this one in the supplementary hells.
Even as they are being reborn in the animal realm, he knows: "This one will be without feet..."
He knows: "This one will be two-footed; this one four-footed; this one many-footed. Regarding those reborn in the realm of ghosts (pettivisaya), he knows:
"This one will be of parching thirst; this one hungry and thirsty; this one subsisting on what is given by others.
And regarding those karmas, he knows: "This karma will draw forth rebirth-linking; this [karma] will do so after another rebirth-linking has been given."
He knows: “It will ripen as a result of the acquisitions (upadhivepakka).

Likewise, when all the inhabitants of a village offer almsfood together, although the volition of all of them has indeed the almsfood as its object, that karma is nevertheless of different kinds for each of them.
For among them, one performs the act with reverence; the rest is as previously described.
Therefore, some among them are reborn in the world of the devas and some in the human world; the Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of their volitional effort:
"Because of the manner in which this has been volitionally produced, this one will be reborn in the human world, this one in the world of the devas;
and even there, this one in a khattiya family, this one in a brahmin family, this one in a vessa family, this one in a sudda family, and this one among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas."
"Here [is one] among the Nimmānarati devas, here among the Tusita devas, here among the Yāma devas, here among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, here among the Cātumahārājika devas,

here among the earth-devas"— in such ways, at the very moment of accumulation, he knows each respective distinction, categorized as inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, having few attendants or many attendants, and so forth.
Likewise, while they are establishing insight, [the teacher says]: "In this manner, he will not be able to perceive anything else;
he will define only the great primary elements; he will remain at the mere discernment of form; he will remain at the mere discernment of the formless;
he will remain at the mere discernment of name-and-form; he will remain at the mere discernment of conditions; he will remain at insight that has the specific characteristics as its object."
Thus he knows: "This one will attain only the first fruit; this one will attain only the second fruit; this one will attain only the third fruit; this one will reach Arahantship.
Even among those performing the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, he knows: "For this one there will be only the mere preliminary work;
this one will produce the sign; this one will reach absorption itself; this one will take jhāna as a basis..."
He knows: "Having established insight and having applied it, he will attain arahantship. Therefore, he said: "His volition," and so forth.

Because it is desired, because it is desirable, and because it is associated with sensual desire, the element of sensual desire is the *kāmadhātu*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of the element of ill-will (*byāpādadhātu*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), and so on.
"By way of dissimilarity" means by way of having a distinct intrinsic nature. "The world of aggregates, bases, and elements" refers to the world of manifold elements.
The construction is: "He understands, as it really is, the world of various elements, the world of aggregates, the world of bases, and the world of elements.
"This is called the aggregate of form... [and so on] ...this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
Among these, the aggregate of form is of one kind, and the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds. The aggregate of feeling is of one kind, and the aggregate of feeling is of many kinds."
“The aggregate of perception is singlefold; the aggregate of perception is manifold. The aggregate of volitional formations is singlefold;
the aggregate of volitional formations is manifold. The aggregate of consciousness is singlefold; the aggregate of consciousness is manifold.
Thus, first, regarding the world of the aggregates. [And: “This is called the eye-base…pe… this is called the mental-object-base. Therein…”

He understands the world of the sense bases (āyatana-loka) as having many and various characteristics through such passages as, "Ten sense bases belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), two belong to the four planes," and he understands the world of the elements (dhātu-loka) as having many and various characteristics through such passages as, "This is called the eye-element...
pe ... this is called the mind-consciousness-element; therein, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere, two belong to the four planes.
He understands not only the world of conditioned phenomena that are clung-to (upādinnaka-saṅkhāra-loka), but also [the other worlds].
Furthermore, even for the world of non-clung-to formations: "Due to the predominance of this particular element, the trunk of this tree is white;
this is black; this is smooth; this is thorny; this has thick bark; this has thin bark;
the leaf of this is of such-and-such a kind by way of color, shape, and so forth; the flower of this is blue or yellow."
Red, white, fragrant, foul-smelling; its fruit small, large, long, short, round, well-shaped, ill-shaped, soft, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, or astringent;
its thorn sharp, blunt, straight, crooked, copper-colored, black, or white.
He understands by means of such passages as “it happens,” and so forth. For this is the power of the Omniscient Buddhas and others alone, and not of anyone else.

“Diversity of inclinations” (*nānādhimuttikatā*) means diversity of underlying tendencies (*ajjhāsaya*). An inclination (*adhimutti*) is a disposition (*ajjhāsayadhātu*), the very nature of one’s underlying tendency.
Although that is described in two ways in the Canon by way of its general division into inferior and superior, it is nevertheless manifold, being further divided into inferior, superior, and so on.
