He said: "The state of having various inclinations [arises] from inferior and other such inclinations.

In this regard, whichever beings have whatever inclinations, they associate with, frequent, and attend upon those who have those very same inclinations, due to the similarity of their elements (*dhātu*).
Just as this is the nature of the elements of excrement and so forth—that they flow together and unite with excrement and the like—so it is with persons.

This is the very nature of inclination (*ajjhāsaya*): that those of inferior inclinations associate and come together with those of poor virtue and so forth, while those endowed with perfected virtue and so forth associate with those who likewise possess perfected virtue and so forth.
The Blessed One understands, as it truly is, this diversity of their inclinations.

"Increase and decrease" refers to being superior or not superior in terms of capacity due to specific conditions. [This concludes] the description of the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*).
Why is the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) and latent dispositions (*anusaya*)—in the phrase “he knows the underlying tendency, he knows the latent disposition”—taught separately?
It is because of the manifestation of the knowledge of those respective faculties by means of which beings possess various underlying tendencies toward what is wholesome or unwholesome.

And by doing so, the unique and non-common nature of the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties, the knowledge of underlying tendencies and latent dispositions, and the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations is established.

And it is established as a distinct power. In this context, "abode" (*āsaya*) refers to that place where beings dwell—namely, their dwelling-place, which may be either a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*) or knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).
A "latent tendency" (*anusaya*) is a defilement that has become firmly rooted through its state of being unabandoned.
The Blessed One, knowing the abodes of beings, [knows] those various speculative views and the knowledges of insight and the path.
He knows even at the moment of non-occurrence. For this has been said:
“The Blessed One knows one who is indulging in sensual pleasures: ‘This person values sensual pleasures, is inclined toward sensual pleasures, and is intent upon sensual pleasures.
He knows one who is indulging [in renunciation]: ‘This person values renunciation, is inclined toward renunciation, and is intent upon renunciation.’”
He knows one who is practicing renunciation; he knows one who is practicing ill-will, non-ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, or the perception of light.
He knows: "This person is heavy with sloth-and-torpor, inclined toward sloth-and-torpor, and devoted to sloth-and-torpor.
Regarding the first four jhānas, that is, the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) jhānas beginning with the first, it is in the sense of burning away their opposites...
And [they are called] *jhānas* in the sense of closely contemplating the object. This is stated according to the fourfold method. Regarding the phrase "of the eight liberations":
here, the first seven are called "liberations" because at the moment they are fully absorbed, they are liberated from adverse states and because they resolve upon their objects;
however, the eighth is the "liberation by departure," because it is liberated from all perceptions and feelings whatsoever.
[This is] the name. In the fourfold and fivefold systems, the concentration of the first jhāna is called "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra*);

in the fivefold system, the concentration of the second jhāna is "without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*). In both systems, the concentration in the three higher jhānas is "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*).

Regarding the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), they are also given the names "eight concentrations" (*aṭṭha samādhī*) in their respective order, and also the name "attainments" (*samāpatti*) because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).
Because that [state] is absent in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it does not have the name "concentration" (*samādhi*).

A state conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiyadhamma*) is the intrusion of sensual desire and other such states into the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so forth when they are not yet mastered.

A state conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiyadhamma*) is the inclination toward the second jhāna and so forth in the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so forth when they are mastered.
Thus, the plungings into the second jhāna and so forth, by means of perception and attention, have been shown to be factors conducive to decline and factors conducive to distinction;

however, the fact that the jhānas possess those respective natures is expressed by the word *dhamma*. Therefore, he refers back to the very meaning already stated as the reason with the word *tasmā* (therefore).
"Purification" (*vodāna*) refers to purification in the sense of proficiency; for that [proficiency] arises from the first jhāna and the others.
Having emerged [from it], because it serves as a condition for the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth, it is called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*).

As for those who say, "There is no canonical text stating that there is an emergence from cessation into the attainment of fruition," they should be refuted by this canonical text: "For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*). This applies to one who has attained such meditative absorptions.

Being equal [to others], one perceives what is "not obtained" as "not obtained"; being equal [to others] regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), one perceives it as "not a meditation subject";
he should be understood as perceiving even success (*sampatti*) as "failure" (*vipatti*). 149.
"Absorption" (*appanā*) is the conclusion. "It should not be viewed in that way" means it should not be viewed in the manner stated by the opponent.
It should be seen. "He knows each respective function" means he knows how to perform each respective task, such as knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*);
the meaning is that he penetrates each respective object according to its own nature. "And that too" means that which is to be known by those ten powers of knowledge (*dasabala-ñāṇa*).
"Only the result of a specific action" means he knows only the specific result of a specific action; [he knows] the volition and the states associated with that volition.
Taking "kamma" to mean the course of action leading to states ranging from the hells to Nibbāna, he said, "only the delimitation of kamma.

Regarding the phrase "the diversity of elements and the cause of the diversity of elements," it should be understood as a *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (an elliptical compound retaining only one member of a similar class).
For that knowledge knows both of these: [it knows] precisely how [it is said], "Because of the predominance of this particular element," and so forth.
It has been described. "The very delimitation of the truths" means precisely the delimiting of the truths by way of full understanding, clear comprehension, and so forth.
It is not able to apply itself, unlike the eighth and ninth powers; nor can it transform, like the supernormal knowledge of transformation (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) which resembles them.
By this, he precludes its similarity to those powers. Or, it is like the knowledge of jhāna and so on, in that it can both apply itself and transform. Even if...

For although it is stated that the "knowledge of reviewing jhāna, etc., is the seventh power" and thus its state of being accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*) is mentioned,

nevertheless, it should be understood that this was said by including within that category the knowledge associated with jhāna, etc., because there is no reviewing without jhāna and so forth. Alternatively,
not all functions of a power are like the functions of jhāna and so forth, which belong to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
To show that [the ten powers] are unable to perform certain functions, it is said: "Having become jhāna, it cannot enter [absorption]; having become psychic power (*iddhi*), it cannot transform.
This, however, should not be understood as meaning that any one of the powers lacks the nature of either jhāna or psychic power.

Having thus shown the distinction between the knowledge of the ten powers and the knowledge of omniscience by way of their specific functions, [the author] now shows it also by way of the categories of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the different planes of existence (*bhūmi*).
To demonstrate that, it was said, “Furthermore,” and so forth. “In sequence” means starting from the beginning in successive order.
The connection is: “they are to be understood after having provided a word-by-word commentary. Defilement-obstruction (*kilesāvaraṇa*) is fixed wrong view;
the absence of defilement-obstruction is the ground for the attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), while its presence is the non-ground for that non-attainment.
However, showing the reason why both of those are, respectively, "the impossible" (*aṭṭhāna*) and "the possible" (*ṭhāna*), he said: "Because of the mundane...

[etc. ...and because of seeing. In that context, the persistence of mundane right view is the "possible" for the attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), because it is the cause for the absence of the obscuration of defilements.
For that [destruction] does not occur when that [mundane right view] exists, but it does occur when it is absent. By this, its...
The impossibility of its persistence has already been stated. "Of those beings to be trained" refers to those sentient beings who are to be converted.
"By showing the diversity of elements" means by showing the different modes of occurrence of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

To the extent that one knows the diversity of elements, to that same extent one also knows the specific temperaments (*cariyā*). Alternatively, "by showing the diversity of elements" means by showing the diversity of the *dhammadhātu* (the element of phenomena). All...

For indeed, conduct is entirely included within the element of the Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*). Even without employing the formal application (*payoga*), as was the case for the minister Santati and others.

Regarding the phrase "to be attained through the power of the knowledge of the divine eye" (*dibbacakkhuñāṇānubhāvato*): here, for disciples, the preparation (*parikamma*) consists in seeing the red color supported by the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) of another by means of the divine eye, for the purpose of knowing the mind occurring at that time; and this applies specifically to those who are beginners (*ādikammika*).

Since the attainment of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) may occur through the power of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), even though for Buddhas the attainment of the knowledge of the divine eye occurs long before the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa),
nevertheless, they do not perform the preliminary exercises (parikamma) in that manner,

because it is accomplished through the perfection of the three types of true knowledge (vijjā). Among the remaining three higher knowledges (abhiññā), the knowledge of others' minds is [attained] by means of the attainment of the knowledge of the divine eye.
It should be understood that it is stated thus because it attains the status of being something that ought to be said.
Furthermore, by generating the thought, "I shall not speak such words again," one is said to abandon those words;
however, since that meaning becomes manifest through speech, it is stated as "speaking. "I shall not adopt a view" is a rejection of the grasping of views.
He said "abandoning" because the non-arising of a view is itself its abandonment. The intention is that this person who reviles the Noble Ones is already placed in hell;
there is no obstacle whatsoever to his rebirth in hell, for this matter is certain.
"Of him" refers to this state of certainty. "Without the trainings"—that is, without virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and without insight (vipassanā) for their sake.
Because it is impossible for [virtue, concentration, and wisdom] to be attained through anything else, he stated, "Worldly and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom are to be understood.
Then, showing those factors beginning with virtue that are most proximate, he said, "It is also appropriate to exclude them by way of the supramundane alone.
Therefore, virtue and the others included within the supreme path (aggamagga) are to be understood. For one who stands in the supreme path has, in this very life, a single-pointed [certainty].
The attainment of another’s favor; for others, it is not one-sided. *Sampadā* means thorough understanding; the meaning is "accomplishment.
Therefore, "one who has such accomplishment" means one who has brought about such a state of non-disenchantment; this is what is meant. Hence he said, "And for this reason," and so forth.

In that context, "reason" (*kāraṇa*) means logical justification (*yutti*). Herein, this is the determination of the justification: "One who reviles the Noble Ones goes to hell, as does one who takes up [the same offense]..."

"Because it does not exist, just like wrong view. And here, by the statement "without abandoning that speech," etc., and by the non-abandoning of its adoption, he shows that reviling the Noble Ones is an obstacle and brings about harm;

whereas by abandoning it—by confessing the transgression and asking for forgiveness—it becomes free from obstacles and brings about benefit, just as in the case of an offense that has been cleared after confession.
The commentary on the knowledge of the ten powers is finished.
Commentary on the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence:
*sārajjana* is the seeking of refuge due to delusion and fear; it is the state of being confident (*sārada*). Delusion and fear have departed.
"One who is confident (visārado) is so called because he possesses confidence; the state of being such is *vesārajja* (intrepidity).

That, moreover, is the fourfold reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) that occurs based on the security consisting in the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, and the perfection of the specific excellence of teaching. Therefore he said, "In the four instances," and so forth.
"In the demonstrated doctrines" means in the doctrines already stated; for there is only the mere mention of them.
But it is not because of the non-existence of such a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that there is no seeing [of it].

Or rather, regarding those phenomena shown by the Blessed One through the words of another, such as "these phenomena have not been fully awakened to," the word *dhamma* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in the expression "analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Therefore, he said: "by means of the *sahadhamma*, that is, by means of the cause. And here, "cause" should be understood as a logical reason for establishing a proof (*upapattisādhanahetu*).
There is neither an agent nor one who brings about [the result]. "Immeasurable" means non-indicative (*anidassana*).

For that which is indicative is called "measurable" (*pamāṇa*) because it functions as a measure through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*byatireka*). "Sign" (*nimitta*) means the cause of the instigation (*codanā*).

In this context, the instigator is the cause because he performs the instigation; the Dhamma is the cause because the instigation is performed by means of it. Therefore, he said: "Even a person," and so forth.
*Sukhema* means being untroubled by the state of not being obstructed by anything.
They are *antarāyika* because they have an obstacle (*antarāya*) or because they are associated with obstacles.
Since such things are indeed called "obstacle-makers," he said: "They are *antarāyika* because they create an obstacle. An unintentional transgression is not [an offense].
Likewise, having established that it is blameworthy (*sāvajja*), it is stated: "having intentionally transgressed.

The phrase "the seven classes of offenses" (*satta āpattikkhandhā*) and so forth is merely an illustration, because there is no deviation regarding the status of those other four things described as "obstructive" (*antarāyika*).
However, the statement "here, sexual intercourse is intended" is made on account of the specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), just like the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha.

Because if one becomes detached even for a moment upon seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and attains distinction, rather than being attached to sensual pleasures, it is therefore said: "Sexual intercourse... is an obstacle.
In that context, "of anyone whatsoever" means not only of one who has gone forth, but of anyone at all; for thus it is said: "For one devoted to sexual intercourse..."
"One must indeed uphold the Dispensation. "In that non-leading dhamma" means: in that sign of a non-leading dhamma imagined by others.
For this locative case is used here in the sense of a "sign" (nimitta) in connection with an object (kamma-saṃyoga).
The commentary on the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence is finished.
Commentary on the Eightfold Assembly (Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā) 151.

Just as a man’s heroic nature becomes manifest in battle and not while sitting at home, so too the power of the knowledge of intrepidity (*vesārajjañāṇa*) is demonstrated to be present in assemblies of the wise, wherever they may be. Thus, [the text] says: "Of the knowledge of intrepidity..."

He said, "for the purpose of demonstrating power. By the term "the place where they had assembled and were seated," he indicates specifically the assembly of khattiyas who had gathered there by way of referring to the location itself.

The same method applies everywhere; thus, in order to show the meaning already revealed through this extension (*atidesa*), the words "of those belonging to Māra’s host" and so forth were spoken, because the scope of an extension concerns a similar subject.
For just as a collection of khattiyas is called a "khattiya assembly" (*khattiyaparisā*).
This meaning is applicable here, but not so in the case of the phrase "Māra’s assembly" (*māraparisā*); rather, the intended meaning there is "the assembly of Māra" (*mārassa parisā*).
Therefore he said: "Of those belonging to Māra’s host... [etc. ...not of Māras. "Of those belonging to Māra’s host" means of those who are on Māra’s side.
"By way of showing a place of dread" means by way of showing a place that should be feared; thus, the noble Kṣatriyas [showed] their own...
The intended meaning is "by the power of merit. The phrase "the brahmins in the three Vedas" is stated by way of showing that this is not within the domain of others;
for even though kshatriyas and vaishyas may recite the Vedas, they are generally incapable of investigating their meaning.
Why, however, are the assemblies of the Yama gods and others not included here? Because of their intense greed for sensual pleasures and their consequent lack of proper attention (yonisomanasikāra).

For the Yāma gods and others, while indulging in exceedingly sublime sensual pleasures, do not even naturally give rise to the thought of listening to the Dhamma due to their intense craving for them;
yet, drawn by the power of the Great Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, they occasionally perform services such as attending upon them during such great occasions.
It is for this very reason that there is even the teaching of the *Vimānavatthu*.
There were not many instances caused by that [reason]. This was composed with reference to human beings.
Since there is no attainment of distinction among humans in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), he asks: "But does the Blessed One go to other world-systems as well?
The other [responds]: even though they lack the attainment of the noble Dhamma (*ariyadhamma*), because of their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)...
But showing that he goes there and teaches the Dhamma, he says, "he goes to the raw. *Keyūra* is an arm ornament consisting of a golden net interlaced with various kinds of gems.
*Aṅgada* is an arm bracelet scented with various perfumes, or one made entirely of gold. *Chinnassara* means having a broken voice;
*gaggarassara* means having a gurgling voice, like the sound of a person gargling, a harsh voice that is gurgling.
“Another language” is said with reference to their specific dialect. To expand upon what was stated briefly as “investigation arises,” the passage beginning with “this is what is meant” is spoken.

“Having come together” means having assembled. “Conversation” (ālāpa) is speech from the outset; “discourse” (sallāpa) is speech in the form of question and answer. “Discussion” (saṃkathā) is talk that is correct or conventional; “dialogue” (sākacchā) is indeed discussion.
The commentary on the eight assemblies is finished.
Commentary on the Four Wombs (Catuyonivaṇṇanā): 152.

That which is called a *yoni* is so named because, by it, beings—even though they are not actually mixed—become as if mixed due to their commonality of birth (*samājātitā*). Furthermore, that [womb]...
In terms of its meaning, it is a specific mode of the partial manifestation of the aggregates, distinguished by being the place of origin for those born from eggs and so forth;
thus he said, "A portion of the aggregates is called a *yoni* (womb/source). "Born from an egg" is stated with reference to the first birth;
however, regarding the second [birth], the sense should be understood as "born from an egg" or "born while the egg is breaking open. Therefore he said, "They are born having broken out. *Vinā*.
"Without these external conditions, such as eggs and so forth. "As if having flown up and fallen" means as if having arisen and then descended.
Or, because they do not depend on external conditions, those who are skillful in "falling" (upapātana) are *opapātika*; it is these very beings who are called *opapātika* here.
By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of the Great Lotus Prince (*Mahāpadumakumāra*) and others who were born in the impurity of the womb. [This also includes] the *nijjhāmataṇhika* ghosts.

Because they are constantly afflicted by suffering, there is no indulgence in sensual pleasures; therefore, they do not dwell in a womb. Due to their possession of a net-like covering, an embryo does not take shape within their bellies;
therefore, they are exclusively of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), as birth from moisture (*saṃsedaja*) is also impossible for them.
By means of the illustrative expression "like those in hell," he demonstrates that they too are of spontaneous birth. "The remainder" refers to those in the *nijjhāmataṇhika* hell.
With the exception of those [beings] remaining, the rest are those fallen into the states of misery (*vinipātika*).

Since the *yakkhas* are included within the state of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*), the phrase "so too are the *yakkhas*" was stated in order to preclude that [misconception]. For they are neither earth-bound deities (*bhummadeva*) nor beings fallen into the states of misery.
The description of the four modes of birth (*catuyoni*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Five Destinies (Pañcagativannanā) 153.

"To be gone to" means to be reborn. For just as *kamma-bhava* (the existence of karma), although in the ultimate sense it lacks a doer, is established through the concurrence of conditions and is conventionally designated as "done by a being" characterized by a continuity (*santāna*) possessing that [karma], so too is the characteristic of *upapatti-bhava* (rebirth-existence).
Although destinies (*gati*) do not exist in the ultimate sense, they are conventionally designated as "destinies" because those who possess such-and-such kamma must go there by virtue of that kamma.

Having thus shown the meaning of the word *gati* from the perspective of its etymological derivation, the phrase beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) was stated in order to show it also by way of an analysis of its referents (*atthuddhāra*).
In those rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*) classified as hell and so forth, the term *gati* is established; however, it is used elsewhere as well.

The occurrence of the word "going" (gati) exists; having distinguished that by means of the word "going," he says "the going of going" (gatigati), just as one says "suffering of suffering" (dukkhadukkha) or "form of form" (rūparūpa).
Going in the sense of the state of arising is "approaching" (upagamana); thus it is called "the going of production" (nibbattigati). "Going" (gati) refers to the going of consciousness (cittagati).
Therefore he says, "it is called the going of inclination" (ajjhāsayagati), which means the occurrence of inclination (ajjhāsayappavatti).
In the commentary on that [passage], however, the meaning is stated as: "Gati means accomplishment. For this is the canonical text (*pāḷi*) in the *Brahmanimantanika Sutta*.
"Juti" means majesty or power. "Vibhava" means destruction; for it is a "gati" in the sense of "departure.

For this very reason, because of its multiple meanings, one speaks of "the *nibbāna* without residue as the *gati*, the departure, and the destruction of the Arahant," saying: "The *nibbāna* without residue is the *gati* of the Arahant."
Regarding the elements (*dhātu*): "Only two destinations" means there are only two results; thus he said, "This is called the destination of result.
"Ayo" is happiness (*sukha*), in the sense that what arises does so while increasing [well-being]. "Nirayo" is where there is no such "ayo.

Precisely for that reason, showing that there is nothing therein to be delighted in or relished, he said: "In the sense of being without joy (*nirati*), in the sense of being without gratification (*nirassāda*)."
"Niraya" means: "stretched out horizontally" (*tiriyaṃ añcita*); that is to say, unlike gods, humans, and others who are tall vertically, they are long horizontally—this is the meaning.

Going away from (*nir-aya*) happiness, departing, is the state of having passed away (*pecca-bhāva*); it refers specifically to the animal realm of ghosts (*petayoni*), which is the sphere of those who have reached that state of having passed away.
"The abundance of mind" (*manaso ussannatta*) is due to qualities such as mindfulness, gentleness, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

This is because of the state of having cultivated the mind and the state of a mind possessing superior qualities; this meaning, moreover, should be understood in its direct sense (*nippariyāyato*) by way of those dwelling in Jambudīpa.
As it is said: "In three respects, bhikkhus, the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

However, because they shared the same physical appearance and other characteristics with the inhabitants of the minor island, the humans dwelling on the other great islands were also recognized as being "human" (manussa).

for the detailed account, one should follow the method explained in the commentary on the *Vimānavatthu* within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.

"By means of their majesty" (ānubhāvehi) means by means of specific supernormal powers (iddhivisesa) known as divine majesty (devānubhāva). Regarding the phrase "in the animal womb, etc.," here the mention of the animal womb and the realm of ghosts (peta-visaya) refers specifically to the aggregates (khandhas), because those [aggregates] lack such a delimited physical space.

Alternatively, the space may also be understood by way of the particular location where they dwell in a fixed residence, such as forests, oceans, or mountains. By the terms "those who have reached hell" and so forth...
Because it is to be sought by beings, it is called the "path" (magga), and because it is to be practiced, it is called the "way of practice" (paṭipadā);
thus, it is said that each respective action itself is what is being described. By the phrase "and how he has practiced," he indicates the manner in which that action was performed and accumulated.
And here, by the terms "the path leading to hell" and "the way of practice leading to hell," he refers generally to that which conduces to hell.

Having spoken of *kamma*, it should be understood that the passage beginning with “according as one has practiced” was stated in order to show its uniqueness by virtue of its occurrence within a specific individual continuum (*santāna*).
Regarding the term “falling down” (*vinipatanti*), it means they fall helplessly or they fall in an ugly manner.

Now, addressing the inquiry as to why the Blessed One, while demonstrating the knowledge that delimits the five destinies (*pañcagati*), said “and I have taught Nibbāna,” etc., he says “this, however,” and so forth.

The explanation of the five destinies is finished.

“Entirely painful” means exclusively painful, absolutely painful. Showing that these are painful at all times and are not mixed even with a substrate of pleasure, he said: “constantly painful, incessantly painful. “Thick” means not thin; the meaning is “great.”

“By the same method as before” means by the very method stated in the Simile of the Pit of Embers, beginning with: “The animal realm is to be regarded like a pit of excrement.

Because of its smallness. "With a woolen spread" means with a red woolen spread (*uṇṇāmaya-lohita-attharaṇa*).

However, since it would be easily understood if only a portion were stated at the beginning, he said, "Just as he," and so forth.

This was not stated because the experience of unsurpassed bliss is within the range of the divine eye; rather, it was stated by way of figurative expression for the reason that it is simply the seeing of that future state by means of the knowledge of future possibilities (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), which serves as an adjunct to the divine eye.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is simply stated: "Having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand. "But in terms of meaning, they are different," [it is said].
In order to explain the meaning stated in brief, he said, "The happiness of the deva-world," and so forth;
then, showing that this meaning is made clear even by the similes already shown, he said, "Even by way of a simile," and so on.

From the moment the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) arises, having seen cessation, [the practitioner] does so both by means of the reviewing of the path and fruit that have arisen, and subsequently by means of entering into the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
And because the noble disciple is, as it were, lying on the bed of cessation due to the very fact that [the mind] proceeds by relying upon it, he said: "Having gone to the excellent bed of cessation.

155. Because it differs from the three types of connections—such as the connection by way of a question and so forth—it is stated: "by way of a separate connection.
It is not only those who hold the view that "purity comes through the performance of difficult austerities" (*dukkarakārikā*), but also among those who practice such difficult deeds...
To show that he was full of confidence, the words beginning with “apica” were spoken. “Catukuṇḍiko” means one who wanders about on four limbs—namely, on two feet and two hands.
“Chamānikiṇṇaṃ” means scattered upon the ground. “Bhakkhasaṃ” means food.
Because of the departure from evil states such as the stain of stinginess and because of the cultivation of virtues such as loving-kindness, it is called “brahmaṃ,” meaning supreme, conduct.
The holy life (brahmacariya) and generosity (dāna). For these have been spoken of by the Blessed One as being established by the wise.

In the same way, for the remaining [terms], the method of exposition regarding the holy life should be determined and stated as appropriate. What is it like? Of what kind? "Vrata" refers to the vow undertaken.
"Of the well-practiced" means of merit that has been thoroughly practiced. "Success" (iddhi) means power (ānubhāva). "Radiance" (juti) means the brilliant luster of garments and ornaments.
*Sarīrappabhā* (the radiance of the body). *Balavīriyūpapatti* (the attainment of strength and vigor) means being endowed with both physical power and exertion.

Because of that, he is "one who grants desires with his hand": by extending his hand to travelers approaching him, through the merit consisting in showing the site of the gift to the merchant Asayha, his hand now becomes like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*), granting whatever is desired.
He became a giver of desires, one who was sweet-voiced and disposed to bestowing desirable objects.
"By that holy life of mine" means by that supreme conduct consisting of the aforementioned service performed for my body. "Merit" refers to the fruit of merit;
for it is called "merit" because its nature is worthy of honor (*pujja*), or by the elision of the final member of the compound, as in such expressions as "thus this merit increases."
The five training rules (sikkhāpada) are grouped together as "the five training rules," just as one says "three existences" (tibhava) or "three carts" (tisakaṭa).

Regarding the phrase "in the holy life" (brahmacariyasmiṃ), it refers to the teaching of the Dhamma. For that [teaching] is called "holy life" (brahmacariya) because it brings about the state of a Brahmā (brahmabhāva)—that is, the supreme conduct—for those to be trained;
or alternatively, because it is the verbal conduct of the Blessed One, who is a Brahmā.
"A thousand who have abandoned death" means that a thousand [persons] have become abandoners of death by attaining arahantship and thereby transcending the domain of death.

Regarding the phrase "we shall be practitioners of the holy life" (*brahmacārī bhavissāma*), having extracted that holy life (*brahmacariya*) by which they are called practitioners of the holy life, he says:
"The holy life is said to be the abstention from sexual intercourse."
“*Nātikkamāma*”: we do not transgress; we do not overstep even in places where one should not go, nor elsewhere. Therefore he said: “Apart from those [wives], we lead the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
*Amhaṃ*: our. *Attadamanavasena*: by way of taming the mind according to the manner of emulating the Arahants as promised;
the meaning is: by the taming of the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth. Because of its being the supreme conduct that has reached the pinnacle, it is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
The holy life (*brahmacariya*). It is called the holy life because by means of it one practices what is sublime (*brahma*) and supreme; it is the Teacher’s dispensation.
"Of those who are not in haste" means of those who do not hurry, but wait for the proper time and place.

"The hope for the fruit succeeds" means that even regarding a fruit that is very difficult to obtain, the hope indeed succeeds through right application. "I am one whose holy life has ripened" means one whose refined aspiration has been specifically brought to fulfillment.
"One whose noble aspirations are fulfilled. For he is described by way of the "discourse on the holy life" (*brahmacariyapariyāya*) due to his supreme mental conduct.

The intention is that this very passage is the place where it occurs; the meaning is that in the Buddha’s word contained in the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*), this very line of the Sutta is the place where it is stated:
"Vigour is the holy life. For vigour, in that domain, is supreme and has reached the highest excellence.
"And because of such conduct" refers here to the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*).
"Endowed with four factors" means endowed with four factors by way of the fourfold manner of one's own conduct that accomplishes the fourfold difficult practice.

160. Commentary on the Purification of the Round of Existence, etc.:
"By the round of existence" means by wandering through states of being in succession, by way of passing away and re-arising. With reference to this, it was said:

And in the Canon it is said: "By supreme speed, mindfulness, and fortitude," and later: "Thus possessing supreme speed."
It has been stated. By showing that "fortitude" (*dhiti*) is energy capable of accomplishing [its task], he illuminates its association with the aforementioned mindfulness (*sati*).

"Of that" refers to the capacity to see the meaning by way of the scriptures (*āgama*) and the capacity to see the reason by way of logical connection (*yutti*), belonging to the Dhamma of the scriptures which has been well-purified through the aforementioned mindfulness of the destination and fortitude.
"One who has a bow that is firm and steady" is *daḷhadhanvā*; he is here called "one of steadfast nature" (*daḷhadhammā*).
One who takes up a bow for the purpose of destroying enemies is an archer (*dhanuggaha*); he is an archer (*issāsa*) because he shoots (*asati*) or hurls arrows (*issu*).
Thus it is said: "the archer standing having taken up his bow. "Possessing the strength of two thousand" means capable of carrying a load of iron and so forth weighing two thousand *palas*.
Therefore he said, "It is called 'having the strength of two thousand,'" and so forth. "In the staff" means on the staff of the bow.

"As far as the measure of the arrow" means that for as much as is the length of the arrow, at the mere lifting of the bow-staff to that extent, the string-staff is already drawn back, and that burden is released from the ground;

“Mastered the craft” means he has mastered the craft of archery. “Skilled of hand” refers to the steady and unerring discharge of arrows at targets;

“One who has displayed his craft in royal families and the like” means that by him, sitting down (upāsana) after approaching royal families and other such places, [the craft] has been performed; hence it says “one who has displayed his craft in royal families and the like.”
"Thus made" means it has been made light by such means as hollowing out the interior and so forth.

"He looks at" means he gazes upon it. Even though this is so, "their turn is discerned" means that for one who is thus wise, the sequence of questioning—such as "this one asks first, this one second," and so on—is discerned with subtlety.

Now, demonstrating that very appearance through reasoning, he said: "The shadow is four fingerbreadths less than a span," and so forth.
This is because, in a moment as brief as the snap of fingers, there occurs the arising of many thousands of millions of mental states (*citta*).

Having stated, "The Blessed One speaks even before the shadow has exceeded four vidatthis (finger-breadths)," he said, "Let these matters stand for now," etc., in order to show that the Teacher’s mode of teaching is indeed even more rapid than that.
Now, in order to demonstrate the reason for this, he said, "Why? and so forth. By the phrase, "He speaks sixteen words,"...

Now, in order to show the reason for this as well, the passage beginning with "Why?

is stated. *Dhamma* refers to the Pāḷi text. A *pada* (word) is so called because meaning (*attha*) is reached (*pajjati*) by means of it; such is its sense. It is called *byañjana* (phrasing/letter) because it manifests (*byañjeti*) the meaning.
A syllable (*akkhara*). For when it is delimited by the states of phrase, sentence, and syllable, it manifests and makes clear its respective meaning.

This shows that there is never an exhaustion of these [qualities]. "Answering questions" (*pañhabyākaraṇa*) means that by means of this, one answers questions;
it refers to the ready wit (*paṭibhāna*) that functions in such a manner. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess wit that is inexhaustible;
hence it is said, "there is no decline in the teaching of the Dhamma. Therefore he says, "What does this show? and so forth. Likewise, even for one whose final Nibbāna is near...
Because there is a distinction in the teaching of the Blessed One and others, the first word of the Buddha, the middle word of the Buddha, and the final word of the Buddha are exactly the same.
Beyond eighty years of age, the fifth division of the life-span [ends]. 162.
Herein, although the Blessed One [spoke] by way of the proclamation of the marvelous and wonderful by the Elder Nāgasamāla—
It is called the "Discourse on the Horripilation" because it proclaims the state of having one's hair standing on end; nevertheless,

it should be understood that the name "Great Lion’s Roar" was established by the Great Elders of the Council because the teaching was delivered by means of the lion’s roar consisting of sixteen sections,
which manifests the power of the unique wisdom of omniscience and other qualities not shared by others.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāsīhanādasutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta*: 163.
"Beyond that" refers to the Saṅgha consisting of more than three persons, because it has reached the stage of remediation through formal acts (*kamma*) such as those requiring a quorum of four.

This applies even in the cases of "full understanding of forms" and "full understanding of feelings. Granted, [this] is the cause for all the non-Buddhist teachers to proclaim their own full understanding of sensual desire and so forth.
There is no [such] system; however, for those who do have one, it is said: "knowing their own system.

Even if they were unable [to do so], they might still designate the full understanding (*pariññā*) of sensual desires merely through the perception of their ultimate abandonment, while claiming it to be the first jhāna.
For what reason? Because such a scriptural authority and realization (*āgamādhigama*) does not exist.

The same method applies to the full understanding of form and feeling as well. "Vuccetha" means "it would be said. Regarding the second phrase: "or an instruction (*anusāsani*) by way of instruction (*anusāsaniyā*). Thus...

Even regarding the words spoken: those monks, it is said, "will not even master" (na ceva sampāyissanti) means they will not lead [the matter] correctly through various modes, nor will they make it known.
Therefore he said, "they will not be able to speak after having mastered it. Because the question was asked concerning a subject that is not their domain, therefore...

The construction is: "they will fall into [it]. In the phrase "together with the devas," there is an inclusion of the formless (arūpa) devas, for they are superior to worldly devas by virtue of their long life and other qualities.
In "together with Māra," there is an inclusion of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) devas. In "together with Brahmā," there is an inclusion of the form-sphere (rūpāvacara) Brahmas.

In the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins," here the term "recluse" (samaṇa) includes those who have gone forth (pabbajita), while the term "brahmin" (brāhmaṇa) includes those who are brahmins by birth (jātibrāhmaṇa).
Furthermore, by the mention of "gods," conventional gods (sammutideva) are included; by the mention of "human beings," the remainder of the human aggregate is encompassed.
The purpose of the term "the world’s progeny" (lokapajā), however, has already been shown in the Commentary. Otherwise, there would be no such thing as "attainment" (ārādhana);
for outsiders, this [term] refers solely to the realization of the gratification and so forth in sensual pleasures, form, and feeling exactly as they are.
It shows that [the self] does not exist;
how, then, could there be any experience? "Satisfying the mind" means pleasing the minds of others by reporting things as they truly are.

In the sense of being a bond, the "qualities" (guṇa) are said to have the sense of a bond even with respect to the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), because they serve as conditions for the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*); in this context, the sense of "portion" (*koṭṭhāsa*) is intended.
Or, the meaning of "quality" (guṇa) should be understood here. "They cross over" means they go or proceed while crossing.

Since the very states of youth and so forth—distinguished as past and so on—are taken as "qualities of age" by way of their being a collection (*rāsi*), he says: "The meaning of 'collection' is the meaning of 'quality'.

Alternatively, "cognizable by the eye" means they are to be known by eye-consciousness and the consciousnesses associated with its doors. The same method applies to "cognizable by the ear," and so forth.
"Consisting of desirable objects" means that by their very nature they belong to the class of desirable objects, or have attained the state of being desirable objects.
"Lovable" means worthy of being desired. "Heart-stirring" means captivating; by this, one also includes the state of being desirable through mere imagination.
"Of a dear nature" means having a nature that is to be cherished. "Associated with sensual desire" means approached and conjoined with sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
He said, "having made it the object," meaning that [the counting] must be performed in a connected manner.
"Having established a perception" means performing the calculation by making a mental mark (saññāṇa), such as: "When this section beginning with the fingers is grasped, there is a hundred;
when this one, a thousand," and so forth. "Uninterrupted counting" means counting without gaps according to the sequence from "one, two" up to nine.

“Counting by heaps” (*piṇḍagaṇanā*) means counting after having gathered [the items] together by means of totaling, forming groups, and so forth. Therefore he said, “having looked at the field,” and so on.
“Plowing” (*kasī*) refers to the act of plowing; by mentioning plowing, all means of livelihood connected with cultivation are included, which is why he said, “‘Plowing’ means the work of plowing.
“Trade by foot” (*jaṅghavaṇijjā*) refers to trade by way of a caravan on foot, while “trade by land” (*thalavaṇijjā*) refers to trade by way of a caravan of carts.
By the word "etcetera," trade by means of ships, markets, and so forth is included. "Vaṇippatha" means the path of merchants;

the meaning is that it is commerce consisting of the giving and receiving [of goods]. "Issatta" is the work of shooting arrows, a livelihood through the craft of archery; however, here it is called "issatta" because it is like being a lord (issara), namely, a livelihood by means of all weapons.
Thus he said: "the service of attending [to others] after taking up arms. "Porohicca" refers to the duties of a priest and so forth.

Royal service. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all remaining great crafts (*mahāsippa*)—such as the craft of charioteering and the science of archery—as well as minor crafts (*khuddakasippa*), are included.

"Placed before the cold" means made to stand in front of the cold. For one who, for the sake of a livelihood during the cold season, plunges into a cool place, is pursued by the cold just as if by wild beasts and the like; thus, he is as if placed in front of it.
Therefore he said, "Afflicted by cold. The same method applies here to the phrase "preceded by heat" as well.
"Having crawled" means having crept along. "Being struck" means being harmed or afflicted. "Affliction" (ābādha) is the state of being afflicted; the meaning is "torment.
Or, "on account of sensual desire" (kāmahetu) is a neuter abstract expression, just as in the phrase, "the moon and sun revolve unevenly."
The same applies to the remaining two phrases as well. For this very reason, he said: "precisely for the sake of sensual pleasures.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sensual pleasures," a restriction to the preceding word is inappropriate, because it would entail the negation of other conditions; likewise, a restriction to the subsequent word is inappropriate, because it is possible that sensual pleasures might occasionally not be the cause.
Therefore, it is stated: "it certainly arises."
By the word "exerting" (*uṭṭhahanto*), it is said that the energy of exertion (*uṭṭhāna-vīriya*) is meant; thus he says, "by the energy that initiates one's livelihood.

That energy is the energy that initiates one's means of subsistence (*ājīvika*). "Connecting what precedes with what follows" means causing it to proceed uninterruptedly from the very beginning of the undertaking.
"He sorrows with intense sorrow arisen in the mind" means [he sorrows] within through mental anguish (*cittasantāpa*).
He reflects. "By the suffering arisen in the body" means by the suffering that has arisen in the body through the power of that very sorrow.
Or, lamenting various things while uttering that [sorrow] under the heading of grief, he wails. "Beating his breast" means having struck the region of the chest.
The passage beginning with "In vain," etc., shows both the manner of lamentation and the manner of falling into delusion. Having said "Me," he then says "no," which is a plural expression.
Because it can be expressed in either way regarding oneself, or because the statement is confused due to grief. 168.
Here, since sense-pleasures (*kāma*) are specifically understood as objective pleasures (*vatthukāma*), the inclusion of "sense-pleasures" and so forth was made;

however, due to its immediate consequence (*ānantariyatā*), the defilement of sense-pleasure (*kilesakāma*) is also certainly included. Regarding "sword and shield," here the mention of "shield" does not refer only to that which is made of leather.

Or rather, it is the inclusion of that which is bound with leather; however, showing that it includes all weapons and instruments of harm, he said, "such as shields, wooden planks, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of arrows and the like.
"Having equipped himself with a bow and quiver" means having equipped himself with both a bow and a quiver of sharp-pointed arrows, as well as the act of making the bow-staff ready for the string.
They fasten the bows. "A double-array" (*ubhatobyūḷha*) refers to the arrangement of battle formations by two armies.
"While they were flashing" means while they were revolving due to their flashing, caused by their sharp yellow blades.

"The ramparts" (*pākārapādā*) are the defensive works near the walls, which are called "rampart-bases" (*upakāriyo*); these are what are known as "mounds" (*uddāpā*). "With a hundred-fold edge" means...
"By means of many hundreds of teeth" refers to that [device] which has many hundreds of sharp teeth as its roots.
Because of its extreme weight, even ten or twenty people cannot lift it; however, by means of a machine, they lift it, fasten it, and set it down.
Therefore he said, "in the form of eight teeth," and so forth. "They press down" means they push it down.
169. Desiring to live by means of theft, they even break into houses. "Plundering" (nillopa) refers to total plunder;
having surrounded a small village, it is the taking of captives without leaving behind anything at all that can be seized. Therefore, he said "great plunder.
"Robbing the road" (panthaduhana-kamma) is the plundering of travelers by standing on forest paths. For the purpose of inflicting blows, there is the striking with a staff.
For the sake of accomplishing ease. *Kañjiya* is that which is produced from sour gruel; it is fermented rice-water (*āranāla*).

That which is called "sour gruel" (*bilaṅga*)—the vessel into which one pours it—is a *kañjiyaukkhalikā*. A *bilaṅgathāliyaṃ* is a vessel made in the shape of a *bilaṅgathāli* (a bowl for sour gruel).
"Having cut out a piece of the skull" means having made an opening the size of a hot iron ball to be inserted. "The execution of the 'conch-shell-shaven' punishment" refers to this.
The "shell-like" means the punishment of shaving the head like a shell.
The "Rāhu-mouth" means the punishment resembling the sun entering the mouth of Rāhu. The "garland of fire" means the punishment of wearing a garland of fire.
The "hand-torch" means the punishment of holding a torch in one's hand. The "eraka-vine" means the punishment of being wrapped in eraka vines.
The *erakavattasadisa-sarīrato-baddha-uppāṭana-kammakāraṇa* is the punishment of having [the skin] torn from the body and bound [together] like a lotus stalk.
The *cīrakavāsika-kammakāraṇa* is the punishment of making one wear garments made of strips of bark torn from the body.

When performing this, just as they would cut away the bindings starting from the neck and place them at the waist, so too, starting from the ankles, they cut away [the bindings] and [place them] at the waist.
They place [them] there. In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is said: "Having cut [the flesh] starting from the waist, they place [it] on the ankles.
"The execution of the Eneyyaka" means an execution resembling that of the eneyya deer. "Having given iron bracelets" means having fastened iron bracelets [around their arms].
"Pounding with iron spikes" means they drive iron spikes into the joints of the knees and the tops of the feet. *Nti*.

That being who has had such deeds done to him: "the flesh-peeler" means one who has the flesh torn away with hooks; "the penny-man" means one who has his body cut into pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa coin;
"they hack him" means they cut him; "the salt-scorcher" means one who, having been flayed, is subjected to the treatment of being sprinkled with salt.
*Palighaparivattikaṃ*: the act of turning like a crossbar (*paligha*). They make it into a single solid mass by hammering an iron spike.
*Palālapīṭhakaṃ*: the act of twisting the body like a straw mat (*palālapīṭha*).
*Kāraṇikā*: those who carry out the execution. *Katvā palālavaṭṭiṃ viya*: just as those making a straw mat [roll up] a roll of straw.
They wrap it around by way of rolling it up; "they do so" is the meaning. "By hungry ones" means by well-bred dogs that are famished;
for they are strong, capable of speed, and courageous. That which one passes away to (*samparaiti*) by way of kamma is *samparāya*, the other world.
Existence therein is *samparāyika*.
170. Nibbāna is so called because "herein lustful desire (chandarāga) is both restrained and abandoned.
Therefore he said, "For nibbāna... In this context, the phrase "having come to" is stated with reference to the object of him who restrains and abandons lustful desire.
By the words "by means of the three full understandings," it is meant that they will fully understand by means of the full understandings of the known and of investigating.

This possibility does not exist. What need is there to mention the full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*)? He shows this by saying, "for the sake of such a state," meaning for the sake of the state of thorough knowledge (*parijānanakabhāva*).
171. "Not limited" means not deficient. "Vast" means great. If it were for the purpose of showing the excellence of physical beauty, why was the "set of ten beauties" (*vaṇṇadasaka*) not included?
To this he says, "of a woman," and so forth. This is stated to show that [the practice is effective] even when there is a lack of excellence in food and other such factors.
It is said: “Even for one reborn in a destitute family. Little by little, the sense-sphere of color (*vaṇṇāyatana*) becomes clear through the nourishment of the flesh;
thus the flesh of the breasts increases and is produced. It is called “color” (*vaṇṇa*) because it seems to manifest the state of being present in the heart.
That very same thing shines forth through its harmony, enjoyment, and so on, thus it is “splendor” (*nibhā*). Therefore he said: “‘Color and splendor’ means simply color itself.”
It is "bent" (*bhogga*) because it is excessively curved. However, such a body is as if broken, which is why he said "broken" (*bhagga*).
Therefore he said: "By this, he also illustrates its very state of being crooked. It is "one with broken teeth" due to the teeth being cut, split, or some having fallen out.
Because the hair has become white in color, it is called "gray" (*palita*); thus he said "with white hair" (*paṇḍarakesa*).

Regarding the phrase "the designation 'bald' applies when the hair has fallen out in patches," he says "a head with a great bald patch" (*mahākhallāṭasīsa*) with reference to cases where it has fallen out extensively.
Regarding the phrase "limbs marred by moles," he says this with reference to the moles that appear at the time of reaching one hundred years of age.
Since some of those are white and some are black, he says "with white and black moles. The term "afflicted" (*byādhika*) refers to one who is afflicted by a chronic disease.
"Severely ill" means one who is ill with a terminal illness.
"At that time" means at the time of entering and abiding in that jhāna. "He does not intend" means he does not direct his mind toward it.
"Affliction" (byābādha) is so called in the sense of causing harm; affliction itself is "afflictiveness" (byābajjha). That in which there is no afflictiveness is "unafflicted" (abyābajjha).
It is free from suffering. Therefore he said, "precisely without suffering.
174. The aspect of impermanence and so forth refers to the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of change, and the aspect of instability and so forth.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta 175.
Regarding the phrase "Among the Sakyans," whatever needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
Showing this by way of a portion, he says, "For he... In that context, those by whom the princes were called the Sakyas...
Because they were born there, and it is called a "province" (*janapada*) in the sense of being their place of residence, that [explanation] should be stated; thus he said:
"The origin of the Sakyans, however, has been handed down in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. The term "Kapilavatthu" is used according to its former designation.
He states the basis for the plural form of the word "states of greed" (*lobhadhammā*): for greed is [manifested] in various ways.
Due to its specific states and the diversity of its modes of occurrence, it has many classifications such as "desire, lust, craving, attachment, regard," and so forth;
yet, by virtue of its characteristic of greediness, it is called simply "greed" (*lobha*). Therefore, he said: "Greed itself in its various forms.
Likewise, [hatred] is described as "ill-will, hostility, anger, enmity, opposition," and so forth; while delusion is described as "bewilderment, lack of regard, non-reflection."
And by the passage beginning with "Dullness is childishness," etc., he speaks with reference to the various modes of hatred and delusion, saying: "The same method applies to the other two as well.
"Having exhausted" means having taken up completely on all sides. He says "it occurs in the sense of grasping" because this is the meaning here;
"pariyādiyati" means it is utterly destroyed. For those learned in grammar state that the root *dī* has the sense of destruction (*khaya*).
He says, "at each time," because this is a designation made by eliding the repetition (*āmreḍita*).

"Greed, hatred, and delusion" refers to the greed, hatred, and delusion remaining after they have been abandoned by the first path. They are abandoned without remainder; otherwise, what would be accomplished by the second path? This is the intended meaning.
However, seeing them when they have reached the stage of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), one knows, "There is still something unabandoned in me. Thus...
"How is there a perception of abandonment without remainder? To this he says: "One perceives that which has not been abandoned... [etc. ...as such.
Having thus stated how doubt arises for one whose uncertainty has been completely severed by the first path—namely, "What dhamma indeed remains unabandoned within me?"—he states the reason:
"Because of being unskilled in designations (paññatti). For, like remorse regarding the Vinaya (*vinayakukkucca*), [this doubt arises].
Due to unskillfulness regarding designations (paṇṇatti), even Noble Ones sometimes experience a mere measure of doubt, just as those who have not entirely abandoned delusion do.
Showing that there is no purpose in not knowing one's own domain through skill in designations—since this matter is accomplished by mere reflection—he asks: "Is there no reflection for him?"

He said: Since it cannot be said that the other [type of reviewing] does not exist, he stated that "it exists" and, in order to show the divisions obtainable therein, he spoke the passage beginning with "But that...
Therein, "that" refers to the reviewing. "Of all" means of all Noble Ones (ariyas).
To show that while it is not complete in every respect, it is not entirely non-existent, he spoke the passage beginning with "But among these..."
176. "Internal" (ajjhatta) is intended here as one's own internal [domain], thus he said, "in your own continuity" (tava santāne).

"Not abandoned" means not abandoned without remainder. "Two kinds" refers to sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma). For even a sensual defilement, by the very same degree that it is relished, is by that same degree consumed.
177. That which is relished is "relish" (assāda), namely, pleasure. Those in which there is little or only a slight relish are "of little relish" (appassādā). Therefore he said:
“Of little pleasure”: because of the suffering caused by the search [for sense pleasures] and so forth, there is suffering pertaining to the present life;

and because of the performance of misconduct therein, there is suffering pertaining to future lives. Thus, among these sense pleasures, suffering is abundant, hence they are “of much suffering. They are “of much despair,” meaning they are accompanied by much affliction (*parikkilesa*).
Furthermore, those afflictions are indeed many here, even those pertaining to the present life according to the method that will be explained; thus he said: “pertaining to the present life... [etc.]”

"Many. And since those defilements create obstacles to the practice of what is beneficial for one who possesses them, and they function as causes of danger both in this world and in the next world, it is therefore said: "In this present life... many.

"Even though it is thus" means in the manner beginning with "Sensual pleasures have little gratification. "By way of principle" means by way of the Dhamma. "By way of reason" means by way of logical consistency (*yutti*).
"It is well seen" is the connection [of the sentence]. "By insight-wisdom" (vipassanā-paññā) means by the wisdom of the Noble Path.
Since that [wisdom] sees all four truths specifically, it is intended here as "insight" (vipassanā). Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'by the knowledge of the two lower paths'.
"Joy and bliss" refers to the two jhānas possessing joy and bliss. "Two paths" refers to the two lower paths. "Having the nature of turning back" (āvaṭṭana-sīla)...

“He is not one whose nature is to enjoy” means he is not one who turns back [toward sense pleasures]; that is, he is one for whom the desire and lust for sensual pleasures have not been entirely abandoned. Therefore he said, “Why? and so forth.
“The knowledge of abandoning dancers and actors,” etc., refers to the knowledge of contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa*).
179. The gratification (*assāda*) has also been mentioned; for by the phrase “of little gratification,” whatever gratification there may be in sensual pleasures, all of that is [included].
Having grasped it without remainder, its limited nature is shown;
thus, even the danger is stated in brief, because the remaining dangers have been indicated. To speak of that [is] to speak of that escape by means of the phrase "experiencing absolute happiness.
"From these extremes" refers to the presentation of the strands of sensual pleasure by way of the passage beginning, "Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure."

Having shown devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure through the phrase “they remain standing, rejecting seats,” and devotion to self-mortification through the phrase beginning with “they remain standing,” he said [this] in order to show that his entire teaching is free from these two extremes.

Because the perfection of the teaching culminates in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*), he spoke thus by means of the heading of the higher attainment of the fruit to show the whole teaching.
The term *kūṭa* is like a vulture; it is a compound formed by the elision of the middle word (*majjhepadalopīsamāsa*).
As in the expression “sākapatthiva. Regarding the second [term] here: because vultures frequent its peak, it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
Those who stand only upright are those who remain standing in one place from the moment they rise from sitting;
thus he said, “not sitting. “Of the Nigaṇṭha” means of Nāṭaputta. That which has no remainder is “aparisesa” (without remainder).
Thus, because it is merely a term for conditioned existence (*saṅkhā-bhava*), he said "completely conditioned" (*aparisesa-saṅkhāta*).
Since the word *satata* might suggest a continuous occurrence in the sense of permanence, it was stated as "constant" (*samita*);
by this, he shows its uninterrupted occurrence—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
180. "Whatever one does, one knows that"—this is called the wise person’s task of wearing away and casting off suffering. A wise person must know what has been done and what has not been done;
therefore, while you are bringing about the exhaustion of past kamma, you must first know how many such past kamma there are, and then [know] "by doing this much for so long a time..."

By such statements as, "Through asceticism (*tapas*), so many of those [karmic bonds] have been exhausted; now so many remain to be done," it is shown that this method must be delimited by oneself, just as a task to be performed is delimited by a man. Therefore he said: "It should be known by you in the same way.
*Suddhanta* means the pure portion, the exhaustion of karma established through non-influx in the future; from that...
The meaning is "or the destruction of suffering. By the question, "Is there one who has reached the end of purity?

he demonstrates that in the system of the Nigaṇṭhas, there is no abandonment of unwholesome states nor cultivation of wholesome states in any way whatsoever, because of the total absence of the cultivation of purification;
therefore, from where could the occurrence of the destruction of suffering arise?
"Thus, when there is a state of not knowing" means: when there is non-knowing of the manner described by the words "we ourselves were," etc.;
the meaning is: when that [state] is not known by you. "Cruel" (luddā) means terrible. Since they, moreover, perform only base acts through body and speech, it is said:
"of cruel conduct. They are called "blood-stained hands" because they practice actions of that kind.
"Hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, and so forth" refers to hunters and the like. "Harsh deeds" means cruel deeds.
"They go forth among the Nigaṇṭhas" shows that because you previously performed deeds leading to great suffering, you now experience such great suffering as this.

"Vādeti" means "in a view," that is, in a tenet-system (*samaya*). Regarding "by means of happiness, [one attains] happiness": here, "by means of happiness" means by means of the happiness of practice;

the sense is, "by means of a happy practice. "Happiness" refers to the happiness of liberation (*vimokkhasukha*). The intention is this: just as those who attain happiness in this world do so only through practices involving suffering, such as farming and commerce, so too is it with the happiness of liberation.
Because he possessed the excellence of bodily parts (*sarīrāvayava*), he was "Bimbisāra"—that is, the essence (*sāra*) of Bimbi.
Those Nigaṇṭhas... [etc. ...say this with reference to that, yet they do not know the Blessed One’s penetration of the absolute peace and exquisite bliss of *nibbāna*.
"Suddenly" means shouting. "Without reflection" means without having reflected or investigated. Therefore he said: "Having acted impulsively," and so forth.
“Unmixed with other feelings, it is exclusively pleasant, absolute pleasure; he experiences that. Therefore it is said:
“experiencing uninterrupted pleasure. “For the purpose of establishing the discourse” means for the purpose of establishing the discourse thus commenced as “experiencing absolute pleasure.
“In the royal section” means in the section of the teaching delivered concerning the king.
"It is easy to ask about his welfare" means that there is ease in asking questions such as, "If seven days and nights are not sufficient, will six days and nights suffice?

and so forth. The pure section beginning with "I indeed... is included because it comes by way of the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), which is the natural outflow (*nissanda*) of purity.
It is not surprising for one who is able to endure seven days and nights.
"What should be said regarding one day and night?"—this has been stated exactly as it is, because its meaning is plain and easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Anumāna Sutta*.

181. "According to the method stated" means that the meaning of the words should be understood by following the method stated here in the phrases "among the Kurus" and "among the Sakyas," according to the manner [of the commentary] beginning with "the Bhaggas were princes of the realm.
"On the day of the site-selection" means on the day the master of geomancy (vatthuvijjācariya) selected the location for the city in order to establish it. "Then" (atha)... [text continues].
"Later. "The city was built there" means that the city was constructed there without any obstacles.
Taking that very mountain of Susumāra as an auspicious sign (*subhanimitta*), they gave it the name "Susumāragiri.
Because of its resemblance to a crocodile (*susumāra*), there is a certain mountain named Susumāra near that city; therefore, because it has that Susumāra-giri, it is called "Susumāragiri."
Some say it is so called because it is called *bhesakaḷā*. *Bhesakaḷā* refers to the *ghammaṇḍa* shrub; some call it the "white tree.
Because of its abundance, that forest became known specifically as the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
Some say that there was a certain mischievous *yakkha* named Bhesa, and because [the tree] oozed from his [wound], that forest came to be called the Bhesagaḷā Forest.
"Born, grown, and increased in a place where there is no fear to give"—this is the meaning.
"He causes them to desire" means that he arouses in his fellow celibates (sabrahmacārī) the desire to say whatever is censurable regarding himself;
the meaning is that for that purpose, he offers himself to them. First, the beneficial instruction and advice was given; subsequently...
*Anusāsanī* (instruction) has been given. *Ovāda* (advice) concerns the present and the past; *anusāsanī* concerns the future. *Ovāda* is based on a matter already entered [into practice];

the other is *anusāsanī*. "He" refers to that bhikkhu who thus invites [criticism]. One whose speech is difficult to endure toward a person who is contrary, hostile, resentful, and disrespectful is called "difficult to speak to.
Therefore he said, "one who must be addressed with difficulty. Regarding the phrase "by those mentioned above":

"By the sixteen evil qualities mentioned in the passage beginning with 'he is one of evil desires'": "one who takes what is favorable" (padakkhiṇaggāhī) means one whose way of bringing about [results] is favorable;
thus, one whose habit is to grasp from that which is favorable is "one who takes what is favorable. One who does not take what is favorable is "one who does not take what is favorable.
"From the left" (vāmato) means from the left side; the intended meaning is by way of the opposite of what was stated above.
"Of aspirations for esteem through non-existent [qualities]" means: of those things which are aspirations for esteem through qualities that are non-existent and not found.
The prefix *pati-* is a synonym for "individual" (*paccattika*); here, "pervading" (*pharaṇa*) or "striving" (*vāyamana*) refers to standing in such a way. Thus he said:
"It opposes (*paṭippharati*) means it stands opposed (*paṭiviruddho*), having become antagonistic (*paccanīko*). "He disparages" (*apasādeti*) means he casts out or threatens. Being thus...
And because it is called "striking back," he said "he strikes. "He attributes" means that he attributes a fault, which is the counterpart of what was stated by the other, onto the accuser.
"He pursues" means he acts or proceeds by way of concealment; or else, the word *carati* has the sense of concealing itself.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, he says "he conceals. To show the manner of concealing one thing by another, he says "by another reason," and so forth.

In this context, "another reason" means either a statement; that is, he conceals by means of a different reason or statement from that which was stated by the accuser as the reason for exposing the fault of the accused.
"By reason" means by a logical argument that demonstrates the groundlessness of the accusation. "By word" means by making known its meaning.
By the phrase beginning with "Who has committed [the offense]?", he shows the evasion of the question and the resorting to diversion, which is the practice of evading one point with another;

the distinction between these two is that the former is the turning away from the subject matter after having answered, while the latter is the failure to answer at all. Therefore, he says: "Such-and-such a person," and so forth.

Faults are "held back" (*apa-dīyanti*) by it; they are protected, or they are "shorn off" (*lūyanti*) or "cut off" (*chijjanti)—thus it is called *apadāna*. It refers to the application of effort by beings, whether right or wrong. Therefore he said: "by one's own conduct.
(183) *Anuminitabbaṃ* means that which is to be inferred, understood, or known step by step (*anu anu*).

In the phrase "the self is to be inferred," this is the accusative case used in the sense of the nominative. Therefore he said: "to be inferred, to be weighed, to be investigated. "The self is to be inferred."
Or else, one should exercise inferential knowledge regarding oneself. Herein is the method:

"The state of evil desire operating within me brings about unlovability, because it is a state of evil desire, just like the evil desire operating in another. This same method applies to the remaining qualities as well.
Another method is this: by one who desires the state of being beloved by his fellow celibates, evil desire must be abandoned, because it is an obstacle to the purification of virtue.
It is like the abandoning of self-praise and so forth. This same method applies to the remaining qualities as well.

184. “It should be reviewed” means that one should review it three times a day with the eye of knowledge, thinking, “I shall not have evil desires, nor shall I fall under the power of evil desires,” and so on; thus, knowledge should be exercised.
The meaning (*attha*). It should be considered with respect to the abandoning of evil desires and so forth;

and this meaning should be understood according to the fact that the word *tabba* has the sense of a state (*bhāva*), whereas in the commentary it is stated as "oneself" (*attan*) using the accusative case in the sense of identity (*paccatta*).
"By one training" means by one training in all three trainings. Therefore he said, "in wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*).
*Tilakanti* means a mark made with black sesame, white sesame, and so forth. *Sabbappahānanti* means the abandoning of all modes.
*Phale āgate* means when the fruit has arisen. *Nibbāne āgate* means because of the attainment of Nibbāna.

*Bhikkhupātimokkhan*ti refers to the Pātimokkha of those called "monks" (bhikkhus) in such passages as "he is a recluse, he is a monk," and not exclusively of those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
It should not be regarded as applying to those who have gone forth alone. Since this is the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, it is therefore said:
"This [should be done] three times a day," and so forth. It is not permissible to fail to reflect upon it, because it is the absolute cause for one’s own purification.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Anumānasutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta 185.
They are called *cetokhilā* (mental barrenness) because by means of them the mind becomes barren, that is, it falls into a state of rigidity. Therefore, he said:
"Because of the mind's state of rigidity. For when these [hindrances] have arisen, the mind becomes defiled and unpleasant, like a place overgrown with weeds or like a field choked with stumps.
It becomes of great fruit. Therefore it was said: "Because of its state as refuse, because of its state as a stump.

The word "of the mind" (cittassa) should be supplied and connected [to the verb]. "Having bound the mind" means having restrained the mind as if it were bound by obstructing the opportunity for wholesome conduct through the occurrence of craving.
Therefore he said: "as if grasping it after placing it in one's fist. From the perspective of the literal meaning...
But because the mind is bound and restrained by these, they are called "mental bondages" (*cetaso vinibandhā*).

One whose fourfold virtue (*sīla*) is perfectly purified through reaching the state of being unbroken and so forth, and which— due to its quality of leading to distinction— brings about the paths and fruits with little difficulty, like the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita,
such a person attains growth in this Dhamma and Vinaya by means of that kind of virtue.

He said, "Growth by virtue," because one will attain [it]. But for one in whom the Noble Path arises well-established, like a tree with deep-set roots, he has attained growth within the Teaching; thus he said, "Growth by the Path.

One who has reached the Nibbāna of defilements in every respect is an Arahant, having attained the fullness of mindfulness through the complete perfection of the aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and the rest.
He said, "By means of Nibbāna, there is abundance. In the second interpretation, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.

Just as the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas, so too their physical body (rūpakāya), because it is not shared by others and because it is the basis for unsurpassed qualities, remains a ground for doubt for those who have not personally realized it;
thus it is said, "he doubts either regarding the body or regarding the qualities."
