In this context, just as the qualities of the form-body, such as the secondary characteristics (anubyañjana) and so forth, are already included by the mention of the marks of a Great Man because they are inseparable from them—
hence it is said, "adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks"— likewise, all the qualities of the Dhamma-body, with their infinite and immeasurable divisions,
are already included by the knowledge of non-obstruction; therefore, only the inclusion of "omniscient knowledge" (sabbaññutaññāṇa) was made, as it is not something separate.
It should be seen. "He doubts" means he doubts by way of generating a longing, thinking, "O, may these qualities not exist in them, or may they indeed exist.
For the former has a perverted inclination, while the latter has an inclination toward knowledge of things as they truly are.

"Investigating" means desiring to discern them with wisdom that consists of investigation; because of their absence, he encounters difficulty and suffering, and this encounter with difficulty occurs therein.
He said, "Because it is incapable of reaching a decision," meaning "it is not able to resolve. *Vicikicchā* means that which has departed from healing (*cikicchā*).
"Does not obtain resolution" means that one does not attain a determination regarding the qualities by way of conviction, thinking, "It is exactly so.
"Having entered" means having penetrated with wisdom. "To have confidence" means [to think], "The Blessed One possesses the qualities of a body whose form is serene."
It is unable to become clear and free from turbidity. By the term "doubts" (*kaṅkhati*), weak uncertainty is expressed;
by "is perplexed" (*vicikicchati*), middling [uncertainty]; by "does not resolve" (*nādhimuccati*), strong [uncertainty];
and by "does not have confidence" (*na sampasīdati*), it should be understood that the turbidity of the mind arising through all three kinds of uncertainty is expressed.
*Ātappāya*: It burns and heats itself from the beginning, thus it is *ātappa*; it is the element of exertion (*ārambhadhātu*), for the sake of that. *Anuyogāya*:
Applying oneself repeatedly so that there is no opportunity for defiling states is *anuyoga*; it is the element of striving (*nikkamadhātu*), for the sake of that.
Therefore he said: "for repeated application. *Sātaccāya*: so that there may be the attainment of further distinction step by step.
*Satatam*: the state of constant, uninterrupted application; *sātaccaṃ* is the element of perseverance (*parakkama-dhātu*), for the sake of that.
*Padhānāya*: for the sake of that energy known as striving (*padhāna*), which has its power thus increased by the three elements mentioned above and is capable of shattering all defilements.
And herein, the mind does not incline toward ardor due to the aforementioned doubts.
The four terms were taken up to show that they indeed have the meaning of application (*anuyoga*) and so forth, or else to demonstrate their distinctions without remainder.
Some, however, say that the terms beginning with "application" are merely synonyms for "ardor" (*ātappa*).

Up to this point, the Blessed One [has explained] the state of mental barrenness (*cetokhila*), because through doubt regarding the Teacher, the mind becomes like hard refuse or a stump, thereby bringing about unwholesome states and the like.
[The text] shows this. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

Since the practice of the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) is included by the mention of "training" (*sikkhā*), it is said: "in the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and in the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha*).
To show where doubt might arise regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, [the text] says: "the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*)," and so forth.

This has been stated. However, this should be regarded as merely an illustration, since doubt may arise in some regarding that [teaching] even on account of its being conducive to penetration through a traditional lineage.
And just as doubt regarding penetration has been mentioned, it should be understood that it likewise occurs regarding the dhamma of attainment.
For instance, some say: "The jhānas are accomplished through the development of the kasiṇas and so forth."
“Formless attainments are the outcome of the kasiṇas; the fourth divine abiding is the outcome of loving-kindness and so forth”—it is precisely because of such [statements] that one remains in doubt.

And here, it should be understood that the occurrence of doubt pertains only to the designation (paññatti) among the nine supramundane states, because supramundane phenomena are undefiled (asaṃkilesika).
“Of such a kind” means of this sort, namely, what is designated as right practice, straight practice, methodical practice, and proper practice.
The right way of practice. The training in higher virtue and so forth should be understood as being in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma.

For in this way, the distinction between these [trainings] and the trainings of the path and fruit is established. Thus it has been said: "Because by the mention of 'training,' the true Dhamma of practice is included.
And here, just as doubt functions by way of non-conviction and lack of serene confidence regarding the qualities of the Triple Gem and the training, [so too does ignorance].
The stiffness of the mind due to its lack of practice, and its state as refuse and chaff through its occurrence by way of wandering hither and thither,
should likewise be understood as the stiffness of the mind toward fellow practitioners of the holy life through resentment, ferocity, and so forth,
and its state as refuse and chaff through its injuring and opposing them. [There is also] doubt regarding the Noble Saṅgha, and certain [doubt] regarding individuals.

The phrase "there is not" refers specifically to the Saṅgha; and since this teaching on the "stiffness of mind" (*cetokhila*) is given from the perspective of the Dispensation, the "anger" referred to pertains specifically to one's fellow celibates.
186. Just as with sensual desire for objects (*vatthukāma*), so too is sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*) something to be relished;

thus it is said, "even in sensual desire as defilement. Therefore the Blessed One said: "In the world, craving for forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving arises when it arises..."

“Settling down here, it settles down,” and so forth. In the description of sensual desire (*kāma*), all phenomena belonging to the three planes are called “sensual desires” in the sense of being desirable;
however, in this context, only those things that serve as the basis for powerful sensual lust are included by the term “sensual desire.
Just as one’s own body is mentioned separately because it is the basis for being bound [to it], so too are the corresponding material phenomena of others included in the sense of a collection.

He said: "Regarding 'form,' it refers to external form. For just as lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure leads to being bound by the attainment of specific states such as the jhānas, so too does concern for one's own body and concern for external things—such as one's own requisites, kinsmen, and friends—lead to such bondage.
However, some here elaborate [the meaning] by saying, "'Form' refers to the jhāna of form," and so forth. That is incorrect, because those who are bound by the attainment of jhāna...
And because those things which constitute the defilement of virtue are grasped by way of being mental fetters (*cetovinibandha*).
"As much as needed" (*yāvad-atthaṃ*) means for as long as one desires; thus he said, "as much as one wishes, that much.
"That" refers to what has been eaten until the stomach is full. From smearing and from filling. "The pleasure of lying down" (*seyyasukhaṃ*) is [the pleasure] dependent upon lying down.

The pleasure of lying down is the pleasure arising from reclining on one’s side. The pleasure of sitting is the pleasure arising from sitting cross-legged. The pleasure of walking is the pleasure arising from walking back and forth.
The pleasure of looking around is the pleasure arising from turning the head.

The pleasure of sleep is the pleasure arising from sleeping. “By virtue” and so forth is a demonstration of the mode of aspiration. “Taking up vows” is the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and the like. “Austerity” is the exertion of energy; for it is said that this is the practice of austerity in the sense of scorching and restraining the defilements.
"Depending on desire" means: by making desire the burden, desire the chief, and desire the forerunner;

it is "depending on desire" in the sense of its occurrence. "Exertion" (*padhāna*) means those states which are principal in the sense of being chief, or which have attained the state of being principal.
"By those states" refers both to the concentration that occurs depending on desire and to what is called "the volitional formation of exertion."

And by "endowed with the aforementioned energy. "Endowed" (*upeta*) means associated (*sampayutta*). "Success" (*iddhi*) is in the sense of succeeding; the meaning is that it is in the sense of accomplishment and in the sense of acquisition.
"Foot of that success" (*iddhipāda*) means its basis, its foundation. Alternatively, they succeed, are successful, grow, and reach excellence by means of it, thus it is "success";
and because it serves as the basis for further distinctions, it is a "foot. Therefore he said:

“Or, that which has become the basis for success (iddhi) is the ‘basis of success’ (iddhipāda). Regarding the phrase “in the remaining ones as well”: this refers to the basis of success consisting of energy (vīriyiddhipāda) and so forth.

“Its meaning is explained” means it was composed for the purpose of illumination; therefore, the investigation of its meaning should be taken from the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) on the *Visuddhimagga*.
Because concentration is the primary factor among the bases of success, it is said: “the abandoning by suppression is stated.”

It is called *ussoḷhi* (exertion) because of its striving toward the production of those various wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) not yet arisen, and toward the further development of those already arisen;

it is the element of energy that has reached the state of strength. Furthermore, as it serves as the specific condition for the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), it is described as "the fifth" in relation to them.
And since it [functions] in the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and therein at the beginning, middle, and end—

Energy must be accomplished; therefore, he says: "‘Exertion’ (ussoḷhi) shows the energy that must be applied in all instances. Having analyzed the means for accomplishing serenity and insight belonging to the preliminary stage according to the categories of phenomena to be abandoned, he says:
"The five abandonings of mental barrenness and the five abandonings of bondage.
"Capable" (bhabbo) means fit or worthy for the attainment of fruition. "By knowledge" means by path-knowledge. "For the breaking up of the defilements" means of the defilements.
"For the purpose of cutting off. "Of security" means of that which is free from calamity.
"For the purpose of esteem" means the sense of esteem is the sense of conceiving the possibility, thinking, "May it indeed be so.
"For thus" means that in the world, speaking of one thing not as a single number, but together with another number, constitutes elegant speech.

As in the phrase, “two or three drops of water. “Laid down properly” means that she lay properly on top of them for the purpose of warding off external dangers such as wind, without herself causing them any injury with her feet or other limbs.
“Causing them to take on heat” means causing them to absorb heat by means of the warmth of her own body for the purpose of exhausting their moisture and oiliness.
Therefore he said, "made warm. "Thoroughly infused" means they have been completely perfumed with the scent of the cock.

Therefore he said, "made to take on the smell of a cock. And this infusion with the smell of a cock should be understood as "producing the result" through the accomplishment of proper laying and proper incubation.
Since it succeeds only together with those [three factors], it is stated, "by performing the threefold action."
Even though no such wish might arise in the form of "Oh, may these [beings]...

and so forth, nevertheless, because the necessary conditions have been fulfilled, they are indeed capable of breaking through; this is the construction of the sentence. To the question "Why are they capable?", he says: "For since, by that... and so on.
In this context, just as the thinness of the shell is the cause for the light being perceived within, so too is the shell's...

It should be understood that the statement regarding the cause is for the purpose of the exhaustion of moisture and oiliness, as well as for the thinness of the nail-tips and the beak’s mouth and for their hardness.
"Therefore" means because it is perceived within the light and because it has itself reached full maturity.
"The application of the simile" means the correct presentation of the meaning of the simile by means of the thing illustrated (the *upameyya*). "By the meaning" means...

In the sense of being that which is to be compared: just as the performance of the threefold action upon the eggs by a hen is the primary cause for the chicks’ emergence from the eggshells, so too the fifteen factors of exertion are the primary cause for a bhikkhu’s emergence from the eggshell of ignorance;
thus he said: “The state of being endowed with... [the qualities] of that hen. This is by way of the commonality of concealment.

Because ignorance is like an eggshell, the thinning of that ignorance-eggshell occurs by means of powerful insight; this is the time when the knowledge of insight undergoes transformation and attains the state of leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*).
At that time, she is as if bearing the embryo of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*); thus it is said, "the time of conceiving the embryo.
"In the category of mundane direct knowledge" (*abhiññāpakkhe*) refers to the category of mundane direct knowledge (*lokīyābhiññā*). [The term] "supramundane direct knowledge" (*lokuttarābhiññā*)...

"Indeed, he splits the eggshell of ignorance. In this verse, "he strikes the eggshell of ignorance" means that through the elegance of the teaching, he impacts the eggshell of ignorance within the mental continuum of those to be trained, not allowing it to remain in its original place.
"Abandonment by means of reflection" refers to abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*) preceded by abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*). [The term] *pubbabhāgiyā*...
Since the bases for psychic power (iddhipāda) are included in the text, it is said: "The abandoning by suppression is [effected] by means of the bases for psychic power.

However, because of such statements as, "A bhikkhu endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion is capable of breaking out," the supramundane bases for psychic power are already included by the mention of "full enlightenment" (sambodha).
Regarding their inclusion in the Path: when a bhikkhu endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion intensifies his insight (vipassanā), [the bases for psychic power are included].
"Appeared on the path" means having arisen when the path has been reached; or, according to the text, it refers to its appearance through the breakthrough and the realization of enlightenment.

Regarding the phrase "it has appeared in the fruit," the meaning should be understood here in the same manner as previously stated. However, because Nibbāna does not appear in the text [in this context], "escape" and "abandonment" are not included.
The remainder is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Cetokhila Sutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Vanapattha Pariyāya Sutta* 190.

It is called "forest" (*vana*) because it is frequented (*vanīyati*) by those desiring seclusion, or because it is sought (*vanute*) by them as a place of residence for the sake of their own spiritual attainment.
It is called *vana* because it resembles a forest (*vana*). It is called *pattha* because those desiring seclusion settle there for the sake of attaining their intended specific distinction;
thus, a dwelling place in forests, in a dense thicket, is a *vanapattha*. It is called *pariyāya* because it proceeds by encompassing its own fruit;

he says "the cause" (*kāraṇa*) in the phrase "the cause of the *vanapattha*" (*vanapatthapariyāya*). For the *vanapattha*— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
For one dwelling in dependence upon that, there is the cause of dependence (*upanissaya-kāraṇa*). Therefore he said: “He dwells in dependence upon a forest thicket (*vanapattha*).

It is called a "method" (*pariyāya*) because it encompasses and establishes the meaning to be taught; thus, it is a teaching (*desanā*). A teaching that proceeds by taking a forest thicket as its basis is a "teaching on the forest thicket" (*vanapatthadesanā*).
In both cases, the mention of the "forest thicket" is merely for the sake of illustration (*lakkhaṇamatta*).
Because here [in this context], the state of being a cause for cattle and so forth, as well as the state of being the object of the teaching, is obtainable. 191.
"Depending" (*nissāya*) means relying upon (*apassāya*); the meaning is "having made it the support for dwelling in seclusion.

By the words "it does not present itself" (*na upaṭṭhātīti*) and so forth, [the author] indicates the absence of suitability regarding the lodging in that forest retreat, or alternatively, the absence of suitability regarding the climate, other persons, and the hearing of the Dhamma.
[The text] shows this. "Requisites for life" means the requisites, that is, the conditions, for the occurrence of life.
"To be procured" means they must be brought forth and attained progressively through the right method, such as blameless alms-gathering and so forth.
Since those things thus procured are indeed what is meant by "collected," [the author] says "to be gathered. "They arise with difficulty" means they are not easily obtained.
They do not exist. By this, he shows the absence of suitable food and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "during a portion of the night or a portion of the day," he says "in a division of the night or a division of the day" because the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
One should set out only at night, because the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) cannot be accomplished there [during the day].
192–3. *Saṅkhāpīti* (reflection-delight) occurs when one reflects: "The purpose for which I went forth is not being accomplished here; yet robes and other requisites are being acquired.
I did not go forth for the sake of those things; what is the use of staying here?
Furthermore, in the subsequent section, *saṅkhāpīti* occurs [when one reflects]: "The purpose for which I went forth is being accomplished here; robes and other requisites..."
"But if it does not come to fruition, I did not go forth for that purpose"—this is the meaning of "even after reflecting. Therefore he said:
"Having known the state of the non-accomplishment of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*).
Regarding the phrase "that person," [the sense is]: "That person should depart without asking permission; one should not follow after him."
The connection is with the phrase "he should not be followed. For whatever has a connection with someone, it remains so even at a distance.
Regarding the word "that person" (*taṃ puggalaṃ*), by transforming the nominative case (*so puggalo*) into the accusative case, the meaning is:
"one should depart without having asked that person for permission. Indeed, the transformation of case endings occurs according to the requirements of the sense. Having asked him...
"Should depart": here too the method is the same. "Having asked for permission, one should depart" is an exhortation to gratitude and the recognition of what has been done.

(198) "Such a person as this": he shows by the words "even if" and so forth that even if one restrains such a person with disciplinary measures and the like—provided that, by relying on him, a bhikkhu may expect only an increase in virtues and no exhaustion regarding the requisites—he is not to be abandoned.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Vanapattha-pariyāya-sutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta 199.
*Jātivana* means a forest that has grown of its own accord. Therefore he said, "unplanted. *Paṭisallānatthāya* means for the sake of solitude;
that is, for the sake of being alone, or by withdrawing the mind from diverse objects toward the ultimate peace of Nibbāna by means of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
For the purpose of inspiring confidence. "One who has a staff in his hand" is *daṇḍapāṇi*.
To show how he is called "Daṇḍapāṇi," the passage beginning with "For this one... was stated. "Because of his addiction to the staff" means because of his craving for the staff.
For he was a son of Daṇḍa and was highly skilled and renowned in the art of the staff; therefore, he wandered about only carrying a staff. "For the purpose of dispelling fatigue in the legs."
It was for the purpose of removing the fatigue of the legs that had arisen from sitting for a long time in the royal assembly.
"Leaving at will" (*adhiccanikkhamana*) means leaving according to one's desire, not leaving frequently. "Clinging" (*olubbha*) means standing having pressed [the body] down.
To show how he is called "clinging," it is said: "like a cowherd’s boy," and so forth.
200. It is called *vāda* because they speak by means of it; thus he asks, "What is their doctrine? What is their view? (*Kiṃvādī* means what is their view?). "What do they proclaim?

(*Kimakkhāyī*) means what do they declare, or what kind of Dharma-discourse do they give? "Without respect" (*acittīkārena*) means without deference. Showing the reason for asking in such a manner, he says, "Why," and so forth.
"Let this family perish" (*nassatu etaṃ*) means let this clan be destroyed.
"He does not know the meaning": if he were to know the meaning even in part, he might still persist in opposing it by grasping it wrongly.
"That would lead to his harm and suffering for a long time"—this lack of knowledge regarding the meaning is what the Blessed One has in mind.
"Contentious talk" (*viggāhika-kathā*) means talk involving conflict; the sense is that it is talk involving aggression (*sārambha*). Is it not [the case] that in the world, with the Blessed One...
With reference to the challenge that "there are many ascetics and brahmins with various doctrines," he says, "For the Tathāgata...
and so forth. He does not dispute because the causes of dispute—the attachments to sensual pleasures and views—have been eradicated by the Path itself;

yet, due to the absence of those [attachments], the world disputes with the Tathāgata. One who speaks the Dhamma, one who speaks according to reality, does not dispute with those who speak the Dhamma.

Because those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma lack any desire to quarrel, whereas one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma—even if they regard [the other] as no more than a blade of grass—quarrels with them.
Therefore it was said: "Monks, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma does not quarrel with anyone in the world.

But one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma quarrels indeed, because the causes for quarreling have not been severed. And so it was said: "Monks, it is only one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma who quarrels."
Regarding the phrase *yathā ca pana*: here, the word *yathā* signifies "cause," as in such passages as, "And how the arising of unarisen sensual desire occurs, that he understands.

Thus it is said, "by which cause. Alternatively, the mode of the cause is expressed here by the word *yathā*, but since that is in meaning simply the cause itself, it is stated as "by which cause. "This..."
“Kathaṃkathā” (doubt) is so called because it proceeds by asking “how is this? and “how is that?”; it is doubt. One who has no such doubt is “akathaṃkathī” (one free from doubt);

[the Buddha is] addressed as “akathaṃkathiṃ. Regret and remorse were severed by the Blessed One through the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga), while the remorse regarding hands and feet was severed by the highest path (aggamagga) due to the attainment of the unique qualities (āveṇikadhamma). Here, “bhavābhava” refers to existence arising again and again.
He said: "In repeated existence. Since restraint and non-restraint are like fruit and non-fruit, and small and great existences are called "existence and non-existence," he said:
"Or in inferior or superior existence. Existence that has reached growth is called "non-existence," just as [the term] "states beyond training" (asekkhā dhammā) is used.
By "perception of defilements," he refers to the perception of sensual desire and so forth; or rather, the defilements themselves are designated by the name "perception."
It is stated [thus] in such passages as, "Having abandoned perception, one reaches the Deathless" and so forth.

By the phrase "he illuminates his own state of being one whose taints are destroyed," it should be understood that this meaning—that he teaches the Dhamma to others for the sake of their attaining that same state—is also clarified.
"Having brought out and made them play" means both having brought them out and having made them play, or alternatively, having made them play by way of bringing them out. "Tivisākha" (three-branch).
It is called *nalāṭikaṃ* because it arises on the forehead like a frown (*bhākuṭi*) that has three divisions (*tibhaṅga*).
(201) "Kinti nu kho" means "for what reason? The meaning is "by what cause. "Having grasped the connection" means having established the connection of the question.
"Yatonidānaṃ" means "having that as its source" (*yaṃnidānaṃ*), which is to say, "having that as its cause. For in the preceding word, there is the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti-aloṣaṃ*).
The explanation is made by way of having [already] established that the source is the six internal and external sense-bases and so forth; this is precisely the meaning.

They are called "constructions" (*saṅkhā*) because they are known as having the nature of constructions; thus he says, "Constructions are portions. Although conceit (*māna*) is indeed a proliferation (*papañca*) here, he says "associated with the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views" while taking only that which has the nature of relishing (*abhinandana*). For he will say later, "that which is to be relished," and so forth.
"They assail" (*samudācaranti*) means they proceed by completely and utterly exhausting [their object] from above upwards. This particle *ā* has the sense of a limit;
and by that connection, "person" (*purisaṃ*) is used in the accusative case, just as in the passage: "Monks, two types of thoughts assail the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
And craving and the other [defilements], not overstepping their respective modes of occurrence—
They proceed higher and higher by way of repeated practice (*āsevana*). For it is for this reason that they are called "proliferations" (*papañca-saṅkhā*).
Regarding the phrase "in a cause": this refers to the condition for continued existence (*pavatti-paccaya*). "Not even a single base" ... [etc] ... "does not exist" means:

if not even a single base, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), exists as something to be delighted in, to be affirmed, or to be adhered to, then surely it does not exist at all; why then [is it said otherwise]?

“Is it said that ‘they do not exist’? True, they do not exist. However, for worldlings (*puthujjana*) who have not abandoned delighting, welcoming, and clinging, there are sense bases (*āyatana*) of various kinds such as those to be delighted in; therefore, it cannot be said of them that they do not exist.
But for those who have abandoned delighting and so forth, they do not exist in every respect; thus it is said, “If they do not exist. [The notions of] “I” and “mine”...
“It should be delighted in” means it should be approved as “I” through delighting in views, and as “mine” through delighting in craving.
“It should be welcomed” means it should be spoken of by way of giving rise to adherence. Therefore he said: “It should be spoken of as ‘I’ and ‘mine.
“Having clung to” means that view and craving, having entered into the objective basis, have made the two types of grasping as if they were not shared with anyone else.
Therefore he said, "having swallowed and having finished. By this—by the statement beginning with "If there is not here"—he means:

"here" refers to the sense-bases (*āyatana*). By way of showing that craving and the other [defilements] have no basis, the non-occurrence of craving and the others themselves is called the "extinction of defilements" (*kilesa-parinibbāna*).
Therefore the Blessed One said, "This indeed is the end," and so forth; this very thing is what brings about the absence of delight and the rest.

The path, the fruit which is the subsiding of that [defilement], or Nibbāna as its escape—this is the meaning of "the end" (*anto*), signifying the limit, the conclusion, or the non-occurrence of the underlying tendencies such as lust (*rāgānusaya*). Therefore he said: "This... is the end.
"In all instances" refers to all such phrases as "this indeed is the end of the underlying tendency to aversion" (*paṭighānusayānaṃ*) and so forth.
"Seizes" (*ādiyati*) means it is grasped by way of dealing blows and so forth.

"A quarrel that has reached its peak" (*matthakappattaṃ kalahaṃ*) refers to a quarrel that has gone beyond mere brawling and the like, reaching its height by way of piercing with verbal darts and so on; this is to be connected with the phrase "that by which one acts.

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Mere diversity of opinion" (*nānāgāhamattaṃ*) is by way of holding conflicting views; likewise, "mere diversity of speech" (*nānāvādamattaṃ*) is by way of speaking conflicting words.
Thus it proceeds: even toward those who ought to be honored, one fails to show respect and engages in contentious speech, saying "you, you.

Whatever volition one employs when doing something, that is "you, you. "In dependence upon" (*nissāya*) means by way of a condition, such as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); this is the meaning.

Let it be granted for now that the sense-bases (*āyatana*) are the cause for the arising of defilements, because they exist when those [defilements] exist; however, how can they be the cause for their cessation?
But how [is this so]? Anticipating the objection that "there is no inclusion of supramundane states here because only mundane ones are intended," he says, "Even as they are ceasing," and so forth.
Showing that this was stated with reference to their being mere names and signs, he says, "Wherever they arise, right there they cease.
Then, establishing that meaning by means of another sutta, he says, "And this meaning," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by the question on the truth of origination" (*samudayasaccapañhena*), this refers to the exposition of the truth of origination within the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna*. For that [exposition] is called a "question" because it proceeds by way of inquiry, beginning with "Where does it arise? and so forth.
To show that there is no room for an objection such as, "But was not the arising and cessation of craving mentioned there, and not of all defilements?", he says "And just as... and so forth.

By the term "attained by designation" (*laddhavohāra*), he shows that Nibbāna is conventionally designated as "the end" because it is the cause for the non-occurrence of lust and the other defilements.
By this very [term], it should be understood that the commentary has already explained the absence of delight (*abhinandana*) and so forth.

But how can there be the cessation of unwholesome states in Nibbāna, which is escaped from all conditioned things? To this he says: "For whatever is not present in a certain place, that is ceased in that place."
"Indeed, it is so. This meaning, which was stated using the term "cessation" in reference to non-occurrence, should be illustrated by the question on cessation.
For in that context, it is not said that the applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) have ceased after having arisen and then passed away;
rather, they are simply non-occurrent.
"203. ‘Thus-endowed’ (evaṃsampadaṃ) means that which is endowed in this way; this is my request, and it is to be seen thus.
Therefore he said: ‘The meaning is “of such a kind” (īdisaṃ). ‘Knowing, he knows’ (jānaṃ jānāti): by means of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), he knows everything that is to be known.

For, by means of this term ‘knowing,’ which employs a superior designation and an inclusive apprehension, he encompasses the entire range of objects of knowledge without exception; thus, regarding its objective domain—"
It is appropriate that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) alone is the instrument for the act of knowing.

Alternatively, this meaning should be clarified by means of the context and the proximity of the word "Bhagavā. He sees what is indeed to be seen by means of the eyes of knowledge known as the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), the eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*), the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

He who should see, indeed sees. Alternatively, "knowing he knows" means that whereas others, who speak of the full understanding of sense-desire and form while being subject to perversion, know even as they know through the influence of perversion, the Blessed One does not do so.
Rather, because he has abandoned perversion, the Blessed One knows simply by knowing;
and because there is an absence of seeing through [wrong] views, he sees simply by seeing—this is the meaning. By way of being the guide for seeing...

Just as the eye leads beings toward the purpose of seeing, so too, because it is the means for the world to see things as they truly are, he is "become the eye" (*cakkhubhūta*) in the sense of being a leader in the function of seeing.
Alternatively, because he consists of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), or because he has attained the eye of wisdom through his own independent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he is "become the eye.
The meaning of the term "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*) should be understood in exactly the same way. [The word] *dhammā*.

Or, he is "become Dhamma" (dhammabhūta) because he has attained the Dhamma that is not shared with others, since the factors conducive to enlightenment have arisen within him and he causes them to arise in the world.

He is called "Brahmā" because the Path (magga) is so named; since the world has arisen through it and he causes it to arise, and since he has attained it by means of his own self-dependent knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa), he is "become Brahmā" (brahmabhūta).
He is a "speaker" (vattā) because he speaks the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. For a long time...

He is called the "Proclaimer" (pavattā) because he speaks while bringing about the penetration of the Truths. "Having extracted the meaning" means having drawn out the meaning of suffering and so forth, and therein, the meaning of oppression and so forth.

Or, he is the "Giver of the Deathless" (amatassa dātā) because he causes beings to attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, by generating within them the realization of the Deathless. He is the "Lord of Dhamma" (dhammassāmī) because the factors conducive to enlightenment are dependent upon him.
204. Thus, since the summary (uddesa) applies to oneself as well, the Elder said, "That which we...

For the teaching of the Buddhas is common to all the world. Now, in order to show those doors and objects by means of which the conceptual proliferations of perception (papañcasaññāsaṅkhā) assail a person, he provides the detailed exposition (niddesa) by way of the analysis of the sixfold base (saḷāyatanavibhaṅga).

In order to demonstrate its meaning, the passage beginning with “the eye” (*cakkhuñca*) was commenced. Therein, “by way of being a support” means by way of being a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*).
And the support-condition is the sensitive eye-faculty (*pasāda-cakkhu*) alone, not the eye as a composite consisting of fourteen factors or forty-four factors;
thus he said, “dependent on the sensitive eye-faculty. “By way of being an object” means by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

Regarding the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), since it can be anything among the material phenomena produced by the four causes, it is said: "dependent on the material phenomena produced by the four causes.
Herein, while even the eye alone is a condition for consciousness, the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) is always multiple and combined;

in order to show this distinction, [the text] mentions "the sensitivity of the eye" by way of its status as a support (*nissayabhāva*) and "the material phenomena produced by the four causes" by way of their status as objects (*ārammaṇabhāva*).
Thus, a distinction in the phrasing has been made. But what is the reason that the eye is a condition for consciousness even when it is single, whereas visible form is only so when it is manifold?

It is because of the specific nature of their conditioning. For the eye, in being a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the conditions of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), and dissociation (*vippayutta*), acts as a condition only through its state of existence; for when it exists, [the consciousness] arises, and when it is absent, it does not. Wherefore...
It is said that this [condition] is a condition for that by way of the presence and non-disappearance conditions;

however, its dependence on that should not be understood as clinging in a partial manner, because it is formless (arūpa). Rather, it is by way of being bound to that, like students, kings, or men in relation to their teachers, kings, or lords;
while the other conditions are to be understood according to their respective specific characteristics.

Since this state of being a condition does not fail to occur even in a single instance, the Pāḷi says in the singular— "depending on the eye, friend"— to show that even a single eye serves as a condition for eye-consciousness. As for visible form,
although it acts as a condition through the relations of presence, non-disappearance, and antecedence— just like the eye— it has arisen earlier.
Because it is beneficial precisely at the moment it exists, even so, it becomes a condition only when multiple factors are combined,
by way of being an object (ārammaṇa). For that consciousness which arises discerning a conditioning phenomenon—
whether it be of an intrinsic nature or merely a conceptually constructed form— it is [the primary factor] among others, owing to its own nature of possessing an object.

That which is called an "object" (*ārammaṇa*) is so termed because it is to be resorted to (*ālambanīya*) by way of being the cause for the occurrence of consciousness— which is incapable of occurring without having something to resort to. Since the apprehension of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), in whatever manner that may be,

constitutes for consciousness the acquisition of the object-condition, therefore, when eye-consciousness occurs taking visible form (*rūpa*) as its object, it occurs only by making manifest the intrinsic nature of that [form].

And for him, whose mode of existence is dependent on the sense faculties, the apprehension of the objective essence does not occur by way of the color belonging to one or two *kalāpas*, nor even by way of the color belonging to a few *kalāpas*;
rather, it occurs by way of the color that has entered the range of perception in accordance with the mental application (*ābhoga*).
Thus, showing that many forms indeed serve as conditions for consciousness through their collective functioning, [the text says]: "In regard to form, there arises..."
He spoke thus by way of the plural, [saying] “eye-consciousness.

As for what is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: “The visible-object base is a condition, as an object-condition, for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it,” that refers to whatever kind of visible-object base serves as an object-condition for eye-consciousness.
It was said with reference to such [a case]. But what kind [of case] is it? "Aggregated" (samudita) is the meaning that is evident.
And having established this, even that which some say—"Eye-consciousness and the rest have the discernment of the aggregate as their object, not the discernment of the substance"—is well-said.
Nor, in this context, should the state of having an aggregate as its object (samudāyārammaṇatā) be suspected.

Because there is no such thing as the enjoyment (*ābhoga*) of a collective whole, it is the color-phenomena (*vaṇṇadhamma*) that have arisen together which serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
But how can those that are individually incapable become an object-condition when combined? Is it not the case that the blind, who are unable to see individually, cannot see even when combined?
This is not an absolute rule; for even those who are individually incapable [of carrying a burden] can do so in activities such as carrying a palanquin (*sivikā*) when combined.

Because it is seen as being capable [of perceiving]. Furthermore, since it is impossible to grasp the individual color of the hair and so forth where they are situated, yet possible to grasp them when they are gathered together in that very same place, their collective functioning (*saṃhaccakāritā*) is even more clearly evident.
By this, what is the object of eye-consciousness: is it an atom-form (*paramāṇurūpa*), or rather a collection thereof? And so forth.

It should be understood that this is a rejection of the [notion of] instigation (*codanā*). In such passages as, "Dependent upon the ear, friend," the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
"What is called eye-consciousness" means that what is characterized by the cognition of forms based on the eye arises; it is called eye-consciousness.
"From the meeting of the three" means from the coming together and convergence of these three: the eye, the form, and eye-consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "that which is called contact": although it is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*), because it occurs by way of the mode of touching the object, there arises a phenomenon called contact characterized by touching.
"By way of co-nascence and so forth" means: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, and so forth, for that [contact] associated with eye-consciousness;

by way of contiguity and so forth, for that which is immediate; and by way of decisive support, for the other [types of consciousness]. Thus, through its state as a condition, it is "with contact as condition."
Feeling arises with contact as its cause. Since the perceiving of the object occurs at the very same time as the experiencing [of it], it is said:
"Whatever object one feels by means of that feeling, that very same object perception perceives.

However, since the phenomena pertaining to the eye-door are intended here, when there is the grasping of subsequent feelings and so forth arising in succession according to that [process], [the following applies].
Or it expresses a reason: the meaning is that because one feels the object, therefore one perceives it.
For when there is no feeling, the arising of perception never occurs. The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well.

For, by way of applied thought (*vitakka*), one conceptualizes an object—whether existing or non-existing—in accordance with how it has been perceived; and in accordance with how it has been conceptualized...
One who conceives by means of views, craving, conceit, and the conceiving of "otherness" is said to "proliferate. For this very reason it was said:
"One perceives earth as earth," "Having perceived earth as earth, one conceives earth," and so forth; and also:

"Having formulated reasoning regarding views, they speak of the two-fold duality of 'truth' and 'falsehood. This commentary on the meaning is given specifically with reference to proliferation that has reached its full development.
[This] has been explained; however, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is [stated] by way of their extreme weakness.

"By means of the causes consisting of eye, visible form, and so forth" means by means of those things that have become causes, namely, eye-consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, and applied thought.

The mention of "causes" is made because even when they are not acting as causes, they still exist. For once these have been fully understood (*pariññāta*), they no longer act as causes. Therefore, he said:
“*Apariññātakāraṇan*” means that which has not been fully understood through the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). “*Abhibhavanti*” means they overwhelm.

Regarding “*sahajātā honti*,” here, based on such statements as “there is a wholesome aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact,” both feeling and perception must be understood even when they are not co-nascent.
If this is so, then in the phrase “*papañcetī*,” if [it refers to] that which is co-nascent with the five-door impulsion (*pañcadvāra-javana*),...
The objection is raised: "Conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) is intended [here] because they have present objects;
why, then, is there a mention of the past and the future? The other replies with the words, "Because they arise in that same way," and so forth.

In this context, "because they arise in that same way" means that just as conceptual proliferations arise at the eye-door during the present time, so too do they arise at the eye-door in the past and in the future.
The inclusion of the past and future is made because those [consciousnesses] belonging to the eye-door do not arise with respect to past or future eye-objects.

Regarding the phrase "depending on the mind, friends," there are two kinds of mind: the bare life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and that which is accompanied by adverting (*sāvajjana*). For there are two ways of explaining this.
In the discourse concerning the door of arising, the life-continuum that has vibrated twice is called the mind-door, as are the eye and so forth...
It is like [a door] by means of which [the mind] is struck by visible forms and so forth, because it serves as the gateway for the subsequent arising of consciousness therein.

In the discussion on conditions, the *sāvajjana-bhavaṅga* (the life-continuum accompanied by an advertence) is intended—as in such passages as, "There is the wholesome [consciousness] conditioned by mental contact"—for it is the mental contact accompanied by an advertence (*sāvajjana-manosamphassa*) that is meant, not the mental contact of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-manosamphassa*), because the latter is impossible in those instances. With reference to the first method therein, he says: "The mind..."

“Life-continuum consciousness. Regarding the phrase “with phenomena as its object”: some say that by this it is shown that defilements arise only with respect to phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*);
however, that is incorrect, because it has been stated that even designations (*paññatti*) which are the basis for clinging have phenomena as their object.
Here, however, it is said “with phenomena of the three planes as its object” in order to show that phenomena belonging to all three planes are obtainable here, and not [to imply otherwise].
Because a designation (paññatti) lacks an object. This must be accepted as such; otherwise, unwholesome states of consciousness would be called "objectless.

In the discussion on the doors of arising, it was stated that "mental consciousness" refers either to the mental consciousness itself or to the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), because like eye-consciousness and the rest, the adverting consciousness also belongs to the category of a door.
However, in the discussion on conditions, the adverting consciousness is specifically included.
“Or impulsion” is what was stated. In order to show the classification of the co-nascent states within the two methods, it was said, “when adverting is included,” and so forth.
“It is indeed appropriate” means that it is appropriate in the primary sense (nippariyāyato).
As long as penetration of conditions is not possible, specific-nature phenomena (sabhāvadhammā) are known only by way of their conceptual description (paññatti).
He says, "A single phenomenon called contact arises," because he does not designate it individually.
Thus, having designated the concept of contact, he will cause the knowledge that perceives its objective domain to arise.

"When this exists, that comes to be": when this condition, such as the eye and so forth, exists, this conditionally arisen state, such as contact and so forth, comes to be. By way of the twelve sense bases...
By way of the method of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) presented through the twelve bases (āyatana).

"By way of the negation of the twelve bases" means by way of the negation of the twelve bases in the sequence of demonstrating the absence of the condition and the absence of the conditioned, according to the formula: "When this is not, that does not come to be."
"The question was spoken by a disciple" means that this question was spoken by a disciple; for this reason, do not have any doubt.

Alternatively, "the question was spoken by a great disciple who, by explaining in detail the meaning stated in brief and being established as foremost among those [disciples], spoke this question"—for this reason, do not have any doubt regarding this question.
Do not be like those who, when a money-changer is present, determine the value of a coin for themselves; rather, be free from doubt in the very presence of the Blessed One.
(205) They are called *ākārā* because they produce a fruit by way of their respective boundaries; thus, they are causes.
It is said "by separate causes" because the cause for the elaboration (*papañca*) has been specified individually according to the six doors. Alternatively, [the term may be understood as follows:]

Even though a particular fruit is produced by as many factors as there may be—since their status as causes exists only when they are combined, because the fruit arises precisely through their conjunction—it is nevertheless stated that "by individual causes," taking each one to be a cause of it individually.
By "words" (padehi) is meant both the words such as nouns and so forth, and the sentences which are the collections thereof; hence he says, "by the combination of syllables."
For it is the syllables themselves that are delimited, according to their respective functions, into the form of words and sentences within meanings.
"By means of phonemes" (*byañjanehi*) means by means of those letters designated as "phonemes" because they manifest the meaning.

Since these are called "syllables" (*akkharāni*) because they articulate (*akkharana*) a method of expression, he therefore says "by means of syllables" (*akkharehi*). And herein, [it is said] "by these modes and these word-phonemes."

The construction is: "The analysis has the purpose of showing the occurrence of conceptual proliferation (*papañca-samudācāra*), as well as the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).
By "wisdom" (*paṇḍiccanā*) means by means of discernment (*paññā*). Showing the characteristic of a wise person according to such sūtra passages as, "In what way, venerable sir, is one wise?
When, bhikkhu, a monk is skilled in the elements (*dhātu-kusala*)," he said, "By four reasons," and so forth.

"Wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*) has been shown by way of the penetration of the truths; therefore, in order to demonstrate his state of great wisdom (*mahāpaññatā*) by way of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), it was said:
"In great matters," and so forth.
"Sugar-cake" (*guḷapūva*) is a cake made mixed with sugar. "A ball of solidified juice-sugar" (*baddhasattuguḷaka*) is that which has been formed into a lump with honey and sugar.
A lump of clay. It is not to be moistened with honey and so forth, precisely because it must be joined together by those [means].

"Of a contemplative nature" means one whose inherent character is that of a contemplator of the Dhamma. "By the knowledge of omniscience alone" means that, having had the excellence of this sutta determined by the knowledge of omniscience alone, I shall cause its name to be taken.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Madhupiṇḍika-sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Dvedhāvitakka-sutta* 206.
"In two pairs" means having made them into two pairs of sections. Although here one might think, "I have made this one section," [the text continues:]

Because of the statement, "He made this into a second portion," all thoughts (vitakkas) are divided into exactly two portions by way of the distinction between defilement (saṃkilesa) and purification (vodāna).
However, because of their frequent occurrence through repeated arising, the word "having divided into two" (dvidhā katvā) in the Pāḷi is a reduplicated expression;
thus it is stated in the form of a reduplicated expression as "having made them into two pairs of portions. Alternatively, [it refers to] the two portions...

Because of its possessive nature, the Blessed One said, "One should dwell having divided thoughts into two," desiring to grasp each pair that is diametrically opposed as separate entities. Having reflected thus,
he then demonstrated how wrong thoughts and right thoughts were grasped therein without exception and without confusion.
"I made this one portion," he said, "and I made this second portion.

"Associated with sensual pleasures" means conjoined with desire known as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), or bound by desire. The same method applies to the remaining [fetters] as well. However, this is the distinction:
that by which the mind becomes corrupted is ill-will (*byāpāda*), which is hatred (*dosa*). By which beings are harmed, or the harming of them, is cruelty (*vihiṃsā*).
"Violence" (*vihiṃsā*) is a designation for this evil state, which is the opposite of compassion and occurs in the manner of harming others.
"Internal" refers to having internal phenomena as its object; "external" refers to having external phenomena as its object. "Gross" means associated with abundant sensual lust and so forth;
by way of contrast, "subtle" is the opposite of that. Thus, applied thought (*vitakka*) belongs exclusively to the unwholesome side.

By this commonality of being *vitakka* (applied thought), and by the commonality of being unwholesome (*akusala*) therein as well, he shows that they are made into a single class; it is not, however, by way of their being included within a single arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), and so forth.
"Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) is called the first jhāna because it transcends greed (*lobha*); all that is wholesome (*kusala*) is so called because it has emerged from all that is unwholesome.
But here, since what is intended is the opposite of sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), he says: "escaped from sensual pleasures, associated with renunciation."
"Applied thought" (vitakka): this refers to the applied thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka).

"Up to the first jhāna" means that from the initial application of attention up until the attainment of the first jhāna, the applied thought arisen therein is precisely the applied thought of renunciation. And the phrase "the first jhāna" is stated because there is no further applied thought beyond that point.
By means of this, the mind does not become afflicted; or rather, [it is the antidote] to ill-will (byāpāda).
The opposite is non-ill will (*abyāpāda*), which is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the commencement of the cultivation of loving-kindness.

It is called non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) because one does not harm by means of it, or because it is the opposite of cruelty; it is the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the commencement of the cultivation of compassion.
For the Great Bodhisattvas, from the time they set out on the Great Renunciation, having found the opportunity, their intentions were right.
He said, “They proceeded for six years...,” because they occurred with increasing distinction.

Since his knowledge was not yet fully matured, there could occasionally be even the stain of wrong thoughts due to forgetfulness arising from past tendencies; to show this, he said, “Through forgetfulness...
they remained. Just as in a house that is normally closed, when the window is opened even for a moment—

Just as the wind might enter when it finds an opening, so too, within the continuum of the Bodhisatta whose sense faculties were well-guarded, an unwholesome thought arose due to a lapse in mindfulness.
Once arisen, it cut off the continuity of the wholesome state and remained.
Then the Great Being, having immediately dispelled that very thought which had arisen in that moment, [reflected] for the sake of its non-arising in the future: "These are wrong thoughts."
Having delimited these as "right thoughts" according to their true nature, he did not allow any opportunity for wrong thoughts and thus increased right thoughts.
Therefore it was said: "These are mine," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "negligence (pamāda) is the departure of mindfulness (sativippavāsa)," he said: "Of one who is diligent (appamattassa)" means of one who stands in the non-departure of mindfulness.
“Possessing ardor and energy” means possessing the energy that suppresses the defilements.

“With mind directed forward” means having released the mind for the sake of liberation from existence, being indifferent toward both body and life. “Thus he became as before” refers to the manifestation of joy arising in dependence on his own physical form;
yet, due to the greatness of his wisdom and his subtle vision, he did not produce that kind of joy which belongs to the side of worldly, household-based happiness.
"Of one standing in non-full-understanding" means not standing in full-understanding; the meaning is "one for whom full-understanding has not been mastered.

"Applied thought" ... [etc. ... "receives these three names"—the intention is that it cannot be said that wrong applied thought arising in such a person does not harm oneself or harm both, because it does not transcend its own intrinsic nature. This is due to its being the cause for the non-arising of what has not yet arisen and the abandoning of what has already arisen.
"It brings about the cessation of wisdom" means it is "wisdom-cessating. Therefore he said, "of that which has not yet arisen," and so forth.

"It goes to non-existence" refers to abandonment by suppression through the power of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna-bala*). By the words "it ceases" and so on, he speaks of that very same thing.
But by the words "its end is gone" and so forth, he says that at that time it does not function, as if it had been uprooted along with its root.
208. The state of transformation of the mind is the alteration of the mind, the departure from its natural state. Distraction is the mode of non-one-pointedness.
In that context, because the mind—as if being struck—becomes agitated by applied thought (*vitakka*), it is said: "Having grasped that, he engaged in harmful applied thought.
Compassion (*kāruñña*) refers to mental distress caused by the suffering of others. For this very reason, it is said: "In the suffering of others..."
“Compassion (karuṇā) is so called because the minds of the virtuous tremble when [suffering] exists.
This was said with reference to the trembling of the mental continuum that occurs by way of compassionate concern; the intention is not that cruelty actually occurs toward sentient beings.
And “in each such manner” means: in whatever manner a bhikkhu has thought over and pondered, in that very manner...
In that manner, there is an inclination of his mind. For this very reason, he said, "in sensual thoughts and so forth.

He said "he has abandoned" (*pahāsī*) because it is stated with a reversal of tense; thus he said, "he abandons" (*pajahati*). However, his abandonment is already established because the antidote is established;

to show this, "he has abandoned" was stated, just as in the expression, "the villagers took the property when it was ownerless. The phrase "he practiced extensively" (*bahulam akāsī*) follows the same principle here as well.
This is the method. "It bends in this way" means it takes on the very mode of association with sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), or it transforms by way of being associated with sensual thought.

"Kiṭṭha" means plowing; the sense is "plowing" (*kasī*). However, because it is produced from that [plowing], the crop is spoken of as "kiṭṭha" through a metaphorical transfer of the cause to the effect;
thus he said, "in the midst of the crops. "The four fears" refers to execution, imprisonment, death, and disgrace.
“Afflict” means the state of producing harm. “Base” means the state of being inferior. “In their own aggregates” means in one’s own *khandhas*.
“An opening” means the entry of the defilements (*kilesas*). Purification is cleansing from defilement;
that itself is “brightening” (*vodāna*), as it is said: “‘The side of brightening’ is a synonym for that very thing.”
209. All that is wholesome is renunciation (*nekkhamma*) because it is the opposite of all that is unwholesome and because it has emerged from that.

Nibbāna alone is renunciation because it has emerged from all defilements and from all conditioned things. An object such as visible form is like a cramped field of grain because, when there is negligence, it becomes a place where harm arises.
A counterfeit ox is like a deceitful mind because of its nature of being difficult to subdue.

The Bodhisatta is like the wise Gopālaka because of his application of skill in means (*upāyakosalla*). Wrong thoughts (*micchāvitakka*) are like the fourfold fear because they possess a state of dread.
"One whose increase of wisdom exists" is *paññāvuddhika*. That by which the mind is afflicted is *vighāta*, meaning mental suffering;
that which belongs to that side is *vighātapakkhika*. One who does not belong to the side of affliction is *avighātapakkhika*.
“Conducive to Nibbāna, bringing about Nibbāna. “It might become over-exalted” means it would become agitated and distracted;
this is the sense. “I steady it” means I establish it correctly.

To show how, when established, it is called “steadied,” the words “I make it settle down,” and so forth, are spoken. “I make it settle down” means [I remove] the defilements that are the opposites of concentration.
Causing the mind to settle, I settle it within its own objective range. By means of producing a state free from agitation, I make it one-pointed;
I properly and thoroughly apply it so that it is well-fixed upon the object, making it concentrated.
For when the mind is thus concentrated, it is said to be well-placed upon the object and does not fall away from it.

Therefore it was said: "The meaning is 'I shall mount it well. *Mā ugghātīyittha* means "do not be struck," or "do not be removed"; such is the meaning. 210. Regarding the passage beginning with "That very same...

and ending with "...is said": although by this one might think that a single wholesome thought-moment (*kusalavitakka*)—just as at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*)—is shown as if having three names because of the occurrence of its threefold nature, it should not be viewed in that way. For it is a continuous flow (*pabandha-pavatta*)...
Based on the principle of identity, it is said: “That very same [thought], in the sense of being the opposite of ill will,” and so forth.

For among wholesome thoughts of a single class, a thought that has arisen may be called “that very same one” due to its identical mode of appearance, just as one says, “that very same partridge,” or “those very same medicinal herbs.
This is because, at that time, for the Great Being, there was no dependence upon the meditations on the foul, loving-kindness, or compassion.
"Those thoughts are spoken of in this way.
"In dependence upon attainment" means having entered into attainment and then emerged from it; this is the meaning.
The construction is: "insight, too, is tender. Due to the cultivation of the tenderness of serenity and insight, the body becomes weary, [as does] the subsequent [mind].
Because no distinction [in attainment] is being obtained. Therefore he said: "The mind is struck, it is afflicted. Attainment is of great assistance to insight;
for thus it has been said: "Bhikkhus, develop concentration; one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are.
Just as a place of rest dispels the fatigue of warriors, so too, for the purpose of dispelling fatigue, [one uses] wooden planks...

A place for rest should be prepared, such as a wooden platform or shed; however, insight (vipassanā) is more helpful for meditative attainment (samāpatti), because it weakens all defilements by crushing them.
Therefore he said: "Insight, when it has gained strength, protects even meditative attainment and makes it strong. But is it not so?

"Does this not result in the fault of mutual dependence? This is not necessarily so; in order to show that even through mutual dependence the accomplishment of a task is found in the world, the passage beginning with "Just as... was stated.
"Brought to the vicinity of a village" means brought near to a village. Regarding "these cows," only the mere production of mindfulness should be performed.
Just as cattle must be guarded because they might otherwise stray; "at that time" refers to when serenity and insight have attained strength.
With reference to the frequent arising of the contemplations, it is said, "he has ascended as if all at once," yet he actually ascends through the sequence of the contemplations step by step.

215. Thus, having shown his own practice of heedfulness and the extraordinary distinction attained thereby, and having demonstrated the perfection of the fruit together with the perfection of the cause, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with "Just as if" (seyyathāpi) in order to demonstrate the perfection of his service to sentient beings;
this is how the connection here should be understood. [The phrase] "merely by being suitable for the characteristics of a forest" (araññalakkhaṇayoggamattena)...
*Arañña* means a forest (*pavana*). For a forest that has grown large is a *pavana*. "By the four bonds" means by the bonds consisting of hunger, thirst, fear, and the practice [of worldly life].
"Secure" means free from calamity. "Bringing about well-being and freedom from calamity" means it is *sovatthika*.

"Leading to joy" means it brings or leads one toward joy (*pīti*). "Going to a drinking ford" means it goes to a place for drinking water; thus it is *pītagamanīya*. "By branches, etc. means by forests of thorny branches and thorny creepers.

Even though water-blocked [terrain] is not a path, it is mentioned for the sake of reaching a place free from danger (*anāsayagāmitāya*); the others are mentioned also because they lead to a lack of joy (*apītigamanīyatāya*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes what is seized. It is called *okacara* because it wanders in the range of a deer-trapper; it is a wild animal that frequents islands.
A long rope-tether is used so that, upon seeing deer in the forest, one might flee together with them.
"Living here" refers to the deer's dwelling; from that dwelling, they emerge by this path.
"Roaming here" means they take their food in this place. "Drinking here" means they drink water at this watering-place (*nipānatittha*).
"Entering by this path" means they enter the watering-place by this path. [This is] the path.
"Having blocked" means having blocked the natural path. "He does nothing for the time being" means he desires to slaughter all the forest deer without exception.

"Having become ignorant through ignorance" means, because of being shrouded by ignorance, having become devoid of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), and having been led away by the passion of delight (*nandīrāga*), becoming bound to sense objects such as forms.
"The passion of delight is the 'home-ranger' because of its seductive nature; it is the 'wanderer' because of its delusive nature."
He shows this by taking "ignorance" as the subject. "Of them" refers to those who move about and dwell in the forest.
"By means of a branch-breaking" means by means of a branch-breaking with a coarser scent than that [of humans]. Having removed the human odor, it is by the scent of that branch-breaking.
"Thoroughly swept" (sammatta) means thoroughly cleansed and cleared away.

Showing that the Buddhas’ traversing of the path of security and the closing off of the wrong path, though common to all the world, in actual fact depend solely upon individuals who are to be trained (*veneyya-puggala*), he said:
"of capable persons such as Aññāta-Koṇḍañña and others. By "uprooted" (*ūhata*), he meant "completely eradicated" (*samūhata*, *nīhata*), saying:
"cut in two and cast down. By "expelled" (*nāsita*), he meant "made to disappear," saying: "entirely and utterly uprooted."
"Beneficial conduct" (*hitūpacāra*) means the practice of what is beneficial for sentient beings.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Dvedhāvitakka-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Vitakkasaṇṭhāna-sutta*.

216. "By way of the ten courses of wholesome action" should be regarded as a mere illustration, because here even the consciousness of an attainment that has the round [of existence] as its basis is not intended to be included under the heading of "higher consciousness.
Therefore he said: "the consciousness of the eight attainments that serve as the basis for insight.
Alternatively, he shows that only that which is comprised within the unsurpassed human states (anuttara-manussa-dhamma) should be called "natural consciousness" (pakati-citta).

Having stated, "The consciousness arisen by way of the ten courses of wholesome action is simply consciousness," he says, "the consciousness of the eight attainments that serve as the basis for insight," in order to show what is intended here by "higher consciousness" (adhicitta).
It should be understood that the rule [of the suffix] does not preclude the other [meaning] here; thus, "higher consciousness" refers to that which is associated with insight.
"Kece. "Anuyuttena" means by one who is devoted to it, both by way of producing what has not yet arisen and by way of increasing what has already arisen.
"Mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to the fundamental meditation subject (*pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna*). "Viharanto" means dwelling while applying oneself to meditation.

Even though one has not yet attained absorption (*appanā*) through meditation, one is indeed "devoted to higher consciousness" (*adhicittamanuyutto*), because that term is applied even to that purpose.
Those signs by which the fruit, as it were, appears to be prepared in its place of arising are called "causes.
Therefore he said, "the causes. Regarding the phrase "from time to time" (*kālena kālaṃ*): here, *kālena* is used in the instrumental case with the sense of the locative;
thus he said, "at each occasion" (*samaye samaye*). But why was it said that [it] should be attended to continuously? Is it not so? ...pe... Is it not so?

Is this teaching—"five signs should be brought to mind from time to time"—initiated by the Blessed One while demonstrating the method for removing the mud because [the meditation] had entered the path of development (*bhāvanā-vīthi*)?

To the objector who suggests that one "devoted to higher consciousness" (*adhicittamanuyutta*) is so called because they are engaged in development in an uninterrupted manner, [the reply is: because it is stated, "by one devoted to higher consciousness," [it refers to one] intent on development by way of continuity.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). The Teacher said, "from time to time," showing that for a beginner who is devoted to meditation, occasional defilements of meditation might arise;
therefore, these signs should be brought to mind at the appropriate times for the purpose of purifying the mind.
To demonstrate this, he said, "For in the text... and so forth. In that context, "these" refers to these [signs] mentioned in the text.
Five signs have appeared. "Abbuda" refers to a calamity.
"Accompanied by desire" means accompanied by craving-desire and associated with sensual lust. "Regarding the desirable, the undesirable, and the indifferent" means:

regarding the desirable (which is dear) and the undesirable (which is not dear), and regarding that which is viewed unequally—that is, with partiality. "Viewing unequally" occurs by way of ignorance-based viewing rooted in attachment.
It is the improper grasping of the object. It is with reference to this that it was said: “Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity [arises] in the fool, the deluded worldling,” and so forth.
These are the discursive thoughts (*parivitakka*).
“Other than that sign” means other than that new sign which is the cause for the arising of unwholesome thoughts associated with desire and so on. “While attending” (*manasikaroto*)—
For it has been said: therefore, the object is the sign (*nimitta*), or rather, the mode of the arising of consciousness that previously occurred in such a manner.

"The sign dependent on the wholesome" means that the cause for the occurrence of wholesome consciousness should be attended to, should be placed in the mind, should be reflected upon by way of meditation (*bhāvanā*), or should be transferred into the continuum of consciousness. For the foul is the foul sign. Regarding formations (*saṅkhārā*):
"Arising thoughts associated with desire" (uppanne chandūpasaṃhite vitakke) should be connected by bringing [the word] "having brought" (ānetvā).

Likewise, in the cases of "associated with hatred" (dosūpasañhite) and so forth, the respective term should be brought and connected as appropriate. "In whatever place" (yattha katthaci) means "among beings or among formations" (sattesu saṅkhāresu), in whatever place.
"The fivefold decisive support for phenomena" (pañcadhammūpanissayo) means a decisive support (upanissaya) consisting of five kinds of phenomena.
Thus, in order to show in detail the meaning briefly stated by the words "connected with desire" and so forth, the passage beginning with "His hands are beautiful" is commenced.
Therein, having said that "it should be brought to mind as foul," the manner of bringing it to mind is shown by the question:
"In what are you infatuated? By "skin-color" (chavirāgena) is meant by way of the appearance of skin-color, such as the hue of black, brown, and so on.
“Filled with putrid fruit” means it is full of ripe, rotten fruits; alternatively, the reading is “filled with *kalī* fruit.

“By way of being ownerless and temporary” means that this bowl, having gradually undergone changes in color and reached a state of decay, will become perforated here and there, broken, or end up as mere shards. This robe, in due course...
Having undergone a change of color and reached a state of decay, it will become a foot-wiping rag and must eventually be discarded at the end of its handle.
However, if these things had an owner, he would not allow them to perish in such a manner.
Thus, by way of their ownerlessness, and by way of their temporary nature—contemplating them as "this is not lasting; it is merely for the time being"—he attends to them.

“Laying to rest resentment... should be developed”: having dispelled resentment by means of the *Āghātavinaya Sutta*—which comes down in the manner beginning, “Monks, there are these five ways of laying to rest resentment, wherein the resentment arisen in a monk should be entirely laid to rest”—and by means of the *Kakacūpama Sutta*, the *Chavālātūpama Sutta*, and so forth, loving-kindness should be developed.

"Living in dependence on a teacher" (*garusaṃvāsa*) means dwelling in reliance upon a teacher. "Recitation" (*uddesa*) refers both to causing the Dhamma of the scriptures to be recited and to reciting it oneself.
"Questioning regarding what has been recited" (*uddiṭṭhaparipucchanā*) is the inquiry into the meaning of the Dhamma as it was learned.

"Depending on five things" (*pañca dhammūpanissāya*) means in dependence upon the five factors beginning with living in dependence on a teacher. "The element of delusion" (*mohadhātu*) is delusion itself.

"Upanissitabbā" means "to be relied upon," or else this very reading [“upanissayitabbā”] is correct. "Yattappaṭiyatto" means that he is both diligent—having applied himself with zeal in requesting permission to enter the village—and prepared.

"Then his delusion is abandoned" means that for this bhikkhu who has thus applied himself there, that delusion subsequently disappears. "Even in this way" means even by not being negligent regarding the recitation.
"Furthermore, 'thus also' refers to the removal of doubt through inquiry into the meaning. In various places, the meaning becomes manifest;
thus, as the Dhamma is being heard, in those various sections, the respective meaning—such as 'here virtue is taught,' 'here concentration,' or 'here wisdom'—becomes clear.
This [is] the eye, visible form, light, and so forth, for this eye-consciousness."
Regarding the cause: this rice seed, soil, water, and so forth are the causes of this rice sprout.

"This is not the cause" means that the very same eye, visible object, light, and so forth are not the cause of ear-consciousness, and that the very same rice seed and so forth are not the cause of a millet sprout;
thus he becomes skilled in determining what is the case and what is not the case.
"Regarding objects" means regarding meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "These thoughts" refers to sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*) and so forth.

Since all wholesome states are the opposites of all unwholesome states, although one could say they are "abandoned," he speaks with reservation, saying "they are indeed abandoned," because not all [wholesome states] are the direct antidotes to all [unwholesome states].
Therefore, he says "these," and so on.
"Dependent on the wholesome" (*kusalanissita*) means supported by or dependent upon the wholesome.

"Being a condition for the wholesome" is a synonym for that same term; it refers specifically to the aforementioned signs of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) and so forth, which are the causes for the arising of the wholesome.
"On a plank of heartwood" means on a plank made of sandalwood. "A peg placed unevenly" refers to a peg situated there in an irregular manner. "He would strike" means he would hit or drive it out.
