217. *Aṭṭo* means afflicted; oppressed by foul odors and disease. *Dukkhito* means one in whom suffering has arisen.
For this reason as well—that is, because they arise from lack of skill (*akosalla*), are opposed to the wholesome (*kusala*), and are like diseases inherent to the household;
and because these unwholesome states are censurable by the wise, loathsome, reprehensible, lead to undesirable fruits, and result in a lack of satisfaction—they are thus [called] unwholesome.
And [he reflects] that they have painful results. Thus, for various reasons, he examines their unwholesome nature and so forth:
"Behold, Nanda, this body—a mass of suffering, impure, and putrid;
oozing and trickling, it is what fools delight in."
Or by means of such discourses as those that cause revulsion toward the body. By the word "etcetera" [is meant]:
"He who returns anger for anger is worse off than the one who was angry;
he who does not return anger for anger wins the battle that is hard to win."
This also includes such discourses as those on the pacification of aversion (paṭighavūpasamana).
218. "Not recollecting" means non-recollection; "not attending to" means lack of attention. One should sit having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna);
thus, one should sit by means of attention directed toward the meditation subject itself. "A continuous discourse on the Dhamma has been learned."
A discourse on the Dhamma is an aid to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). A "book the size of a fist" is a portable book measuring the size of a fist.
"By attending to" means by directing one's attention. There is no opportunity because that which has been begun must be brought to completion.

The Elder’s view is that reaching the end of what has been begun is equivalent to not having begun it at all. "Of him" refers to the preceptor. Cleaning the mountain cave is a bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
Exerting himself for the purpose of suppressing discursive thoughts, he accumulated three types of action:
the verbal action of reciting the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, and the preliminary work on the fire-kasina for the purpose of performing the duty of visiting [the Elder].

Having understood his intention and the kasina with particular clarity, the Elder said, "In this monastery," and so forth. Thus, everything was accomplished for him exactly according to his desire. The Section on Mindfulness.
[This is] called [the section on] the destruction of the root of thought, because it analyzes the suppression and cultivation of thought through non-attention.
219. "The section on the destruction of the root of thought" (*vitakkamūlabheda-pabba*) refers to the analysis and exposition of the destruction of the root of thought and its own root.
It is called "volitional formation of thought" (*vitakkasaṅkhāra*) because it constructs thought; it is also a condition for thought regarding such things as the sign of beauty.

By means of [the perception of] the beautiful and so forth, there is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Furthermore, that which is called "the stabilization of the formations of thought" (*vitakkasaṅkhārasanthāna*) is the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), such as perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive. Therefore he said: "One should attend to both the root of thoughts and the root of the root.
For one who goes toward the root of the root of thoughts, by way of investigation, [one abandons] wrong thoughts...
The root is the cause of arising for one who proceeds along the path of knowledge.
For one who knows things as they truly are, thoughts do not frequently occur as they did before; thus it is said, "the movement of thought becomes slack.
When that has become slack, one reaches the summit—in the manner already described, the movement of thought having become slack, through that gradual progression toward the root of thoughts...

"As they reach the pinnacle of attaining stability": "all thoughts cease entirely" means that all wrong thoughts either pass away and no longer manifest, or else, through the perfection of development (*bhāvanā*), they are abandoned without remainder.
"Falling at the root of the ear": it has fallen so as to strike near the hare's ear, like one striking the earring on the ear.
It is said that beneath that hare there was a great pit dug by large rats, resembling a subterranean cavern;
because of its falling into this, a great noise arose. Thinking, "The earth is being torn up," they fled.
Thinking, "The earth is splitting," they would investigate it root and branch. Having gone to where this hare had arisen, they [sought] its fundamental cause, thinking: "What if we were to..."
“I shall investigate. When the earth reached the point of breaking apart, [the hare thought], “Who knows?
What will happen? and said, “I cannot do it, Master. For a request from one who possesses authority is gentle and soft.

“He cries out ‘duddubha’” means he makes the sound “duddubha”; this is a term used in imitation of his cry. “Bhadanta” is a term of affectionate address used by the king of beasts; [it means] “O King of Beasts.”
"Bhadante atthu" means "May it be well with you. "Kimetan" means "What is this?"—that is, what is its fundamental cause?

"Duddubhan" is likewise merely a description of its echoing. "Evan" means that just as the hare's splitting of the great earth was baseless, arising from a false apprehension for the sake of making a sound, so too the movement of thought (*vitakkacāro*) is baseless, arising from a perversion of perception (*saññāvipallāsa*).
Therefore he said, "of thoughts," and so forth. 220.
*Abhidantaṃ* means "overpowering tooth"; the meaning is "upper tooth. Therefore he said, "upper tooth.
For that [tooth], like a pestle, functions by specifically overpowering the other [lower tooth] at the time of chewing something.
"With a wholesome mind" means with a mind associated with powerful right intention.

"An unwholesome mind" refers to an unwholesome mind accompanied by sensual thought and so forth. "Should be suppressed" means it should be overcome and restrained so that it does not manifest in the future;
the meaning is that it should be brought to a state where its recurrence is impossible. And who are you, even with long-term cultivation?

Thus, having overcome [the defilements] by thinking, "I am not weak; even though they stand as if having gained a firm footing in my presence, I shall now deprive them of that footing," he spoke of the exertion of energy endowed with four factors, beginning with the words "Willingly, skin and...
in order to demonstrate that manner of overcoming. The term *atthadīpikaṃ* means that which illuminates the purpose of the absolute suppression of discursive thought (*vitakka*).
The simile is the comparison beginning with, "Bhikkhus, just as if a strong man... (Upamanti).

221. Regarding the "section on completion" (*pariyādānabhājanīya*): that which was indicated at the outset—"A bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should attend to five signs from time to time"—therein [is explained] the completion of the time for attending to those signs.
This is an analysis by way of [the practitioner’s] mastery. Alternatively, this is the conclusion, namely, the passage beginning with “Since, monks...”.
For a restatement of the meaning already explained is called a conclusion (*nigamana*). Or rather, the passage beginning with “Since, monks...

was spoken for the purpose of showing the purification of mastery for one who has practiced accordingly. “Teacher-instructor” (*satthācariya*) refers to an archery teacher. For, as in the case of the religious tradition (*sāsana*)...
Just as that which is not a weapon is included under the term "taking up a weapon," so too the art of archery is included within the science of archery (*dhanubbeda*).

It is called a "method" (*pariyāya*) because one proceeds (*pariyāyati*) and reflects upon it. By "path of the sequence of thoughts" (*vitakkavārapathe*), he means the paths of occurrence through the succession of thoughts.

"Mastered by practice" (*ciṇṇavasī*) means mastery gained through cultivation. "Mastery through proficiency" (*paguṇavasī*) means mastery gained through thorough development. [This refers to] right thought alone.
Because one thinks in accordance with what is desired, whereas for the other, there is simply the destruction of the bridge.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta* is completed.
And the commentary on the *Sīhanāda Vagga* is finished.
3. The Chapter on Similes (Opammavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpamasuttavaṇṇanā) 222.

"A wreath" (*moḷi*) means a decoration of hair-crests. "In the air" (*vehāsa*) means in the sky. *Sāti* means a crest (*moḷi*). One who possesses a crest is a *moḷika*; one who is simply a *moḷika* is a *moḷiya*. *Phagguṇo*, however, is the name. *Saṅkhā* means a designation.

In the absence of a wise person, even five or six words of exhortation are said to be sufficient as a measure.
"Having made it accompanied by play" means having made it associated with sport.
"Mixed" (*missībhūta*) means mixed by way of inappropriate association. To explain what was stated briefly as "he speaks dispraise," it is said: "burning, cooking, pounding, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "he also creates a legal dispute" (*adhikaraṇaṃ pi karoti*), the passage beginning with "of these bhikkhus" is given to show how he strives for that legal dispute. Legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*).
"He draws them toward" means he draws those bhikkhus toward the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), or he draws them toward it by causing the legal issue to arise among them.

"Or even a mere recitation of the words" means merely the recitation word by word. "Neither out of a desire for affection" means neither out of a desire to create a state of being beloved in himself by the Teacher.
"Nor with the intention of causing a schism" means not with the intention of causing a schism in the Teacher by that bhikkhu.
"Out of a desire for his welfare" means out of a desire for the benefit of Moḷiyaphagguna.

Regarding "speaking dispraise": this refers to speaking of the faults of the bhikkhunīs. Because they are the basis for desire and so forth, the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are like a house;
thus, they are called "house-dependent" (*gehasita*), being attached to and reliant upon them. Their craving and desire are likewise [dependent].
The desire to act (*kattukāmatā*) and *pīti* (joy) are both forms of craving-desire (*taṇhā-chanda*); however, aversion-desire (*paṭigha-chanda*) is simply their desire to act.
Since passion and the like are causes of transformation for the continuum of consciousness—which is naturally luminous like a crystal gem—they are like an external defilement;
thus he said, "the impassioned mind is transformed," and so forth. "Compassionate" refers to the manifestation of compassion (*karuṇā*).
In passages such as “For one within whom there are no angers,” the word *antara* is a synonym for the mind (*citta*); thus he says, “one whose interior is hatred” means “one whose mind is hateful.
225. Refusing to accept the instruction due to his ill-naturedness, he remained with a mind that was hostile.
“They seized the mind” means they acted in a way that entered the heart. “They fulfilled the aspiration” is the meaning. In one...
At the time of the first enlightenment. "Eating at one sitting" (*ekāsanabhojana*) means eating at a single sitting; it is eating only once.
And that is specifically in the morning, as he said: "One meal before the midday meal," and so forth.

Even food eaten seven times is intended here in this sutta as "eating at one sitting," and not because of the practice of *ekāsanika* (eating at one sitting) in the sense of a single session of sitting.

Regarding "food": in passages such as "the state of being free from flies... and so forth, the word *appa-* has the sense of non-existence; thus he says, "freedom from affliction, freedom from suffering.
"Light effort" (*sallahakauṭṭhāna*) means an effort that is light, easy, and not difficult due to the influence of striving and so forth.
"Not at one time" means not in a single instance, nor at one and the same moment; this is the intended meaning. "Two meals" means...
“‘In the afternoon or at night’ refers to two times for eating. ‘Five qualities’ refers to the five benefits beginning with being free from illness.
‘Merely for the purpose of arousing mindfulness’ means it was done solely for the sake of arousing mindfulness;
there was no repeated exhortation regarding what ought to be avoided.”
“Maṇḍabhūmi” means fertile ground, where crops become grain even without irrigation.
“Yoggācariya” refers to a trainer of draft animals—those animals that are to be yoked to a yoke—and specifically to one who instructs them.
Since village elephants and other such creatures are also called “yoggas,” the text says “charioteers of horses to be tamed. By whichever of the four paths...

He desires [to go]. Among the various modes of movement, such as those characterized by speed, evenness, and so forth—whichever mode he enters, having mounted that very path, he has indeed descended [into it].
He is neither to be restrained by pulling back the reins, nor is he to be pierced with the goad-stick.
"Going alone"—these [horses], when harnessed, move slowly according to my wish, they move evenly, and they move swiftly; thus [he reflects] regarding their hooves.
Having established the perception of signs, the charioteer must simply observe their movement;
he does not direct them there. And by those monks as well: "they abandoned what was to be abandoned. "Sāladūsanā" means those who destroy the *sāla* trees.
There were other creepers standing entwined around the *sāla* trees. "By carrying them out" means by casting them away from the *sāla* grove.
"Well-formed" means endowed with a beautiful shape. "Having bound a boundary" means having established a boundary by way of constructing a water-trough (*ālavāla*).
"A *kipilla* leaf-cup" refers to a leaf-cup made from the *tamba-kipillika* plant. "Carrying dry sticks" [refers to] those within the interior of the water-trough.
(226) She is called "Vedehikā" because she was born and raised in the kingdom of Videha. "Paṇḍā" is said to mean wisdom (*paññā*); she has "gone" (*itā*) by means of that.
The wise say so. *Gahapatānī* means the mistress of the house. *Soraccena* means by self-restraint. *Nivātavuttī* means one who acts with humility.
*Nibbutā* means one whose fever of misconduct has been extinguished. *Uṭṭhāhikā* means one possessed of the energy of exertion. *Kibbisā* means the wicked. 227.
Having thus shown the fault of impatience, [he speaks] even of those whose fame and reputation are spread throughout the world as being "virtuous."
Having explained the disadvantage of intolerance—such as the cause for resentment, the arising of ill-repute, the loss of virtues, and so forth—[he says] "in the path of speech.

"In the path of speech" means in the course of speech, such as at the appropriate time and so on. For even the state of gentleness is a mode of occurrence for speech; thus it is called the "path of speech.
"Of those very times and so forth" refers to those same [conditions]. "Metta" (loving-kindness) is that which has this [kindness] as its essence; it is the arisen mind of loving-kindness.
"These have arisen with minds of loving-kindness. Again, the passage beginning with "At the proper time, monks," etc., proceeds by way of showing the nature of the Dhamma:
"Those who speak for the purpose of exhorting another speak by means of these modes.
"Having resolved" means having released and directed the mind of development toward that person by way of delight. That person is the object.
"Of this" refers to the object of that [meditation], namely, the mind of loving-kindness (*mettā-citta*).

If one objects, "In that case, since its range is limited, how can it be as if its range were unlimited?", he asks, "How does that which has such an object encompass the entire world? The other replies with the words, "By five modes of address," and so forth.
Here, "and its object" (*tad-ārammaṇaṃ*) means the object of that very same mind of loving-kindness.
The word "having done" (*katvā*) should be understood as an ellipsis in the text. Therefore he said, "Again, of that very [person]," and so forth.
He said "sabbāvantaṃ" (all-encompassing) in order to show this meaning: "one who possesses all people, reckoned as the six classes of beings.

"By the vast" (*vipulena*) means by that which has the great multitude as its object. For the word *vipula* is a synonym for "great," and here "greatness" refers to the state of being numerous. Therefore he said:
“With many beings as the object”: this refers to the person who has come within the range of the five modes of address.
“Of the mind” means of the mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*mettā*). And here, the connection is: “We shall dwell with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
To the question “How so? he says: “Having made that person and the entire world the object of that mind, and having resolved upon them.”

228. *Tadatthadīpikā*: This means it illuminates that purpose—namely, for one who stands having correctly developed the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā cetovimutti*), there is no possibility of being affected by any alteration because of his immutability.
*Apabhavaṃ*: It is "not earth" (*apathavī*) because earth does not exist [there].
*Nippabhavaṃ*: It is the total absence of the state of earth in every respect. But why is it said, "but horizontally it is unbounded"?
It has been asked: "Does not each world-system (cakkavāḷa) get delimited by the World-Sphere Mountains? No; because it is connected as a single mass with the earth of other world-systems.
For there is no earth in the intervals between three world-systems—similar to the spaces between three wheels—because those are the states of the Lokantara hells.
In the places connected by the gaps between the World-Sphere Mountains, there is earth.

It is a single continuous mass. For at the time of the eon’s dissolution, even as the earth is being established, it is established as a single continuous mass just like the earth as it currently exists.
Therefore he said: "But it is unlimited across. By this very depth, it is demonstrated that there is nothing beyond the dimensions already described.
229. Regarding "Haliddī," it is said that "whatever is yellow-colored" is intended, because *haliddī* signifies a yellow color.

That which possesses form (*rūpa*) characterized by color is "possessed of form" (*rūpī*); that which is not possessed of form is "formless" (*arūpī*). For this very reason, he says: "because of the negation of the state of being visible. 230.
"Five hundred yojanas" is stated with reference to the point where [the river] enters the ocean from the Himālaya, not from the mouth of Lake Anotatta.
Having taken the depth and the immeasurable water found in other rivers as a point of comparison,

it is said, "profound and immeasurable. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that the phrase beginning with "by this method" (*etena payogena*) is intended solely to demonstrate the absence of anything to be heated by a grass-torch.
231. "Like cotton, like cotton" he says, meaning "equal to the down of the *simbali* tree, to lotus fibers, and to cotton.
"Humming" (*sassara*) refers to the sound that proceeds in such a way; for this is a term for echoing. Likewise with the word "humming" (*bhabbhara*).
All of this is intended to show that it is impossible to corrupt the mind of one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārin*). This is the summary of the meaning here: just as the great earth...
Just as it is impossible for any person to make the earth non-earth, just as it is impossible to place any form in space,
just as it is impossible to heat the water of the Ganges with a grass torch,
and just as it is impossible to make the fur of a cat stiff and harsh to the touch, even so it is with the liberation of mind through loving-kindness when it has been practiced and developed.
Because it has been practiced extensively, no man who comes by any means whatsoever can cause a change of mind once he has been taken into the fivefold path of speech.
232. *Ocarakā* means those who perform base deeds by way of harming others; therefore he said, "those who perform lowly deeds.
*Anadhivāsanena* means by way of intolerance. "He does not act according to my advice" refers to the production of resentment through mental corruption toward another who acts for one's harm.
In my teaching, there is no such thing as one who practices correctly.
233. *Aṇu* means small, slight, or limited. *Thūla* means large or gross.

However, since the intended meaning here is the range of verbal expression, it should be understood according to the distinction between what is blameworthy; thus he said: "whether slightly blameworthy or greatly blameworthy."
They said, "This is not a heavy burden for patience; we see it as 'not being overcome'... and so forth.

"For a long time" means for a long duration; the meaning is "absolutely. And since absolute welfare and happiness are attained only through final knowledge, he said, "reaching the peak by means of arahantship."
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Kakacūpama-sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Alagaddūpama-sutta* 234.
"They afflicted" means they struck. By way of being an obstruction to various attainments, [they afflict] within the continuum of sentient beings.
It is called an *antarāya* because it comes (eti) into the middle; that is, an undesirable consequence such as misfortune pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).

They are "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) in the sense of being connected to that obstruction by way of not transcending it, or they deserve the result of obstruction, or they have the habit of producing obstruction.

Therefore he said: "They are obstructive because they create an obstruction. "Actions with immediate retribution" (*ānantariya-dhamma*) refers to volitional actions whose intrinsic nature is that of immediate retribution.
Herein, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*): that which has its fruit immediately after death is called "immediate" (*anantara*);

those connected with that immediate [result], or whose nature it is to produce that [result] immediately, or whose purpose is immediate, are "those of immediate [retribution]" (*ānantarika*). Those very same ones are called "immediate [offenses]" (*ānantariya*).
Actions themselves are "obstructive" (*antarāyika*), thus they are "obstructive actions" (*kammantarāyika*). They create an obstruction specifically to liberation, not...
Because sexual misconduct lacks the characteristic of leading to heaven. For there is no such thing as a "Dhamma-protected" state for a bhikkhunī.
This has been stated with reference to an ordinary bhikkhunī; however, for a noble one (ariyā), what occurs leads only to the states of misery.
In this regard, the young brahmin Nanda is the illustration. Or rather, it is because both share the same desire that it constitutes an obstruction to heaven.

Furthermore, because they defile the practice aimed at liberation, they constitute obstacles to liberation; moreover, once they have become established through their prevailing influence, even obstacles to rebirth in heaven cannot be prevented.

The views of non-causality (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*), the view of non-action (*akiriyā-diṭṭhi*), and the view of nihilism (*natthika-diṭṭhi*)—when these have reached a state of certainty—are the phenomena of "fixed wrong view" (*niyata-micchādiṭṭhi*). By "rebirth-phenomena," he refers to the arising of the rebirth-consciousness.

And here, the mention of the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and so forth is merely illustrative, because all rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) that is without root-cause (*ahetuka*) possesses the quality of being an obstacle to fruition (*vipākantarāyika*).
For that volition which reviles a Noble One is the "dhamma of reviling a Noble One. "Thereafter" means after having asked for forgiveness.
Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the *Līnatthappakāsanā* commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*. [This continues] as far as the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*).
He confesses that he has committed a *pārājika* offense. He does not emerge from the remaining grave offenses (*sesa-garukāpatti*), nor does he confess the light offenses (*lahukāpatti*).

This is the monk Ariṭṭha. "Mixing essence with essence" means having brought together the blameless essence of partaking in the requisites of life with the blameworthy essence of indulging in the strands of sensual pleasure. "As if placing near" means as if placing a fetter near.
“*Ghaṭento viyā*” is also a reading. “*Upasaṃharanto viyā*” means as if bringing together a similarity, by way of setting aside the state of blamelessness in that which is exclusively blameworthy.
“*Pāpakan*” means blameworthy in the sense of being base and in the sense of leading to an unhappy destination (*duggati*).
It is like one who binds the great ocean by means of constructing a bridge. By means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), it was seen as “blameworthy.”
By using the term "blameless" (*anavajja*), he contradicts that [assertion]. By using the term "entirely free from obstacles," he excludes the knowledge of self-confidence (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).
One who says, "The correct practice of the Noble Path will not be defiled by the thorns of sensual desire," is described as "one who throws stumps, thorns, and so forth onto the Noble Path.
Regarding the training rule known as the first *pārājika*, [the phrase] "unholy conduct" (*abrahmacariya*)...
And in the "Wheel of Command" (āṇācakkam), which consists of instructions such as "having abandoned," they are said to "interrogate" by asking questions; for a question is indeed an interrogation.

Therefore, "establishing" (patiṭṭhāpanam) means causing one to acknowledge again through repetition for the purpose of following up on the tenet already attained; that is, taking hold of it and causing him to adopt it.
"It is as if they were," he said, "they are called 'thoroughly pursuing' (samanugāhanti). However, when that tenet is being examined, even the reason stated for it is merely a semblance of a reason;

thus, his questioning is a "rebuttal" (samanubhāsana). In the sense of burning along with [the fire], it refers to the practice of an improper means (anupāya-ppaṭipatti) which burns both now and in the future.
In the sense of great scorching, it refers to the lack of a stable intrinsic nature (anavaṭṭhita-sabhāvatā). In the sense of appearing only briefly (ittara-paccupaṭṭhāna),...
Because it is delightful for only a moment; because it is subject to being overcome by others in the sense of being merely temporary;
because it crushes all limbs and members in the sense of being the basis for cutting, breaking, and so forth; because it is like a gash in the sense of being a violent laceration;

because it has the nature of piercing through after producing a wound on what was not wounded and entering within; and because it is a sign of harm pertaining both to the present life and the future life.

In the sense of being accompanied by anxiety and fear. "By the strength of that view" means by its state of having become firmly established. "By the misapprehension of that view" means by the misapprehension consisting of that view.
For it is called "misapprehension" (*parāmāsa*) because, having transcended the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), it misapprehends (*parato āmasanena*) what is beyond.
"Adhering" means by means of an adherence of views preceded by an adherence of craving, [thinking] "This alone is the truth here..."
"Having adhered thus" means having insisted upon it. For since insistence is what constitutes being "insistent" (abhiniviṭṭha) regarding that [view], he said, "having resolved" (adhiṭṭhahitvā).
"Even though wishing to say 'there is not'" means even though wishing to deny it out of a desire to conceal one's own tenets. He accepts [the position].
He acknowledges. Regarding the phrase "two kinds of talk," he speaks with reference to deceptive talk;
for since talk that was previously unreal has now occurred by way of talk that is real, it is called "two kinds of talk.
With the words "For whom indeed...? the Teacher shows: "Never before has there been a teaching of the Dhamma for the sake of one such as you or me. Therefore he says, "Of a khattiya... and so forth.

"One who possesses heat consisting of knowledge is 'heated' (*usmī*); one who has been made heated by such conditions—that embryo of penetration within that personal existence—has also been made heated.

Because of this state of being "heated," the Blessed One asks the bhikkhus: "Does the seed of wisdom exist for him in this Dhamma and Discipline? They, rejecting it, say: "By misconduct committed while in a state of transition (*ṭhānagatena duccaritena*)."
Perceiving his state to be struck down by knowledge: "become lusterless" (*nittejabhūta*) means having become lusterless, having reached a loss of splendor.
For that very reason, because he was unable even to look directly at the monks, he stood with shoulders drooping and face cast downward.

Because he was incapable of saying anything in accordance with the Dhamma, he was speechless. "Leading to attainment" (*sampattūpaga*) means bringing about attainment. "Quelling" (*paṭippassambhento*) means restraining.
237. By means of the attainment that creates obstacles, he purifies the assembly through the manifestation of their true nature. He expels and removes those who possess impure views.
This refers to someone who does not know the power of the Buddhas; for such a person might think, "This was said impulsively.
Indeed, there is never such a thing as an impulsive act on the part of the Buddhas. "Assa" means "of someone."
“Of one who has spoken as a bhikkhu. The connection is: “Even having heard it, he might fall into silence; ‘then it might be so’ [is the construction].
“All that” refers to the entire hypothetical formulation stated by the words beginning with “If indeed. “They will not do it” is connected with “he clears the assembly’s conviction.

“Manifesting his conviction” means manifesting it by way of its great culpability. “By means of perception and applied thought” means by way of grasping the signs and secondary characteristics of the beautiful.

[This occurs] through active perceptions and thoughts. Therefore he said, "associated with the defilements of sensual desire. The phrase "sexual intercourse" is stated here by way of primary importance;

however, it also includes the enjoyment of material things (āmisaparibhoga) directed toward objects of a different sex, as it is recorded in such passages as: "Furthermore, he consents to the anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing down of women," and so forth.
“It is impossible that he will conduct himself otherwise than free from sensual pleasures, free from perceptions of sensual pleasure, and free from thoughts of sensual pleasure.
By means of wise reflection, there is no desire or lust here; thus it is “free from desire and lust,” and that is what is meant by “free from desire and lust.
This refers to householders whose virtue is not fixed—those who at times observe the Uposatha and undertake the precepts, but at other times do not.
It creates an obstacle to the undertaking of moral discipline; it involves the enjoyment of sensual objects with desire and lust;
and it acts as a hindrance for monks through lack of reflection, involving the enjoyment of requisites with desire and lust.
"This Ariṭṭha, by means of his misapprehension of the scriptures, slanders us, ruins himself, and generates much demerit."
Thus, showing the fault of a poorly grasped study by saying, "May such perceptions not arise," he spoke.
"They learn" means they recite, bring [the words] to their lips, and memorize;
this encompasses the Dhamma of the study in its ninefold division, beginning with the *sutta*. How is the *sutta* ninefold?
For a discourse with verses is *geyya*, while a discourse without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*;
and there is no discourse that is free from both and devoid of specific designations such as *udāna* that could constitute the *sutta* division.

Furthermore, discourses such as the *Maṅgala-sutta* would not be included in the *sutta* division due to their lack of prose, like the *Dhammapada* and others, or they would have to be included in the *geyya* division.

Is it because they contain verses that they are called "with-verses" (sagāthaka), like the Sagāthāvagga, or likewise like the portions containing verses within the Ubhatovibhaṅga and so forth? It is said in reply:
"Sutta" is a general designation, while others are specific designations;
they possess their own characteristics due to conventional usage, being distinguished by what is associated with them and not by what is other than them.
For indeed, "discourse" (*sutta*) is the general designation for the entire word of the Buddha. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the *Nettippakaraṇa*:
"The investigation of the ninefold discourse. And such statements as, "So much of that Blessed One’s teaching has come down as discourse, included within the discourses;
in our own tradition there are five hundred discourses," serve to establish this meaning. However, regarding its specific parts:

The specific types of discourse, such as *geyya* and the rest, are established by their respective characteristics. For instance, the possession of verses (*sagāthakatva*) is the characteristic that defines *geyya*.
Indeed, even in the world, a collection of stanzas (*cuṇṇiyagantha*) that contains both prose and verse, or contains verses, is called "geyya.
However, when there is an absence of verses, the state of providing an answer after having posed a question is the characteristic that defines *veyyākaraṇa*.
For the answering of a question is called "byākaraṇa" (exposition); exposition itself is "veyyākaraṇa" (analytical exposition).
If this were the case, would it not follow that even the Sagāthaka and other sections—which proceed by way of posing questions and providing answers—would possess the status of veyyākaraṇa?

It does not so follow, because there is no room for the specific designations such as "geyya" (verses in prose interspersed with verse), since [the definition] is qualified by the phrase "when there is an absence of verses."

For instance, in the *Dhammapada* and other works, the designations "Gāthā," "Udāna," "Itivuttaka," and "Abbhutadhamma" are established respectively for those specific types of discourses that consist solely of verse compositions;
even when they contain prose, provided they are joined with verses consisting of joy and knowledge; when they are connected with introductory statements such as "For this was said";
and when they are associated with marvelous phenomena—even though they possess the nature of verse composition.
The designation *jātaka* was established for those discourses that illuminate the power of the Blessed One’s conduct in past births;

and the designation *vedalla* was established for certain *suttantas*—despite their being in the form of question-and-answer sessions and containing verses—because they cause one to obtain knowledge (*veda*).
Thus, by such respective characteristics as the presence of verses and so forth, the designations *geyya* and the rest were established for those various specific discourses.
The specific types [of discourses] following the *sutta* category are the *geyya* and so forth.

However, that which here lacks the characteristics of the *geyya* category and so on belongs to the *sutta* category, because it functions under a general designation by avoiding a specific one. Now, an objection is raised:
"Is it not the case that a discourse containing verses (*sagāthaka*) is *geyya*, while a discourse without verses (*niggāthaka*) is *veyyākaraṇa*? Thus, the *sutta* category would be impossible."

Are they in that same state? No, they are not in that state, because they have been refined. For it was previously refined [in the commentary] that "the status of being a question-and-answer (pucchāvissajjana) constitutes the nature of a *veyyākaraṇa*, with the absence of verses (*gāthā*) as its cause.
And as for what was said—that "because of the absence of verses, the *Maṅgalasutta* and others would not be included within the category of *sutta*"—that is not so.
Because it is so established. For the status of being a *sutta* is firmly established for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others;
they are not renowned as being merely *gāthās* (verses) like the *Dhammapada*, the *Buddhavaṃsa*, and so forth, but rather precisely as *suttas*.

It is for this very reason that the name "called a *sutta*" was given to it in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As for what was said—"because it contains verses, it might be included within the *geyya* division"—that too...
It does not exist, because it must be together with something else. For "together with verses" (sagāthaka) means [to be] with verses;

and as for this "being together," in terms of its actual meaning, it occurs only in relation to something else. Yet, in the *Maṅgalasutta* and other such texts, there is no portion of a sutta devoid of verses that could be called "together with verses.
Nor is there any such thing as a "composite whole" (samudāya). As for what was said regarding the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth...

If it is argued that "there might be an inclusion of the Geyya factor within certain portions of the Sagāthaka," that too is not so. For those verses are distinct, being included within the Jātaka and other categories;

therefore, the Ubhatovibhaṅga and the rest do not possess the status of the Geyya factor by virtue of those [verses]. In this way, the absence of mutual confusion among the factors such as the Sutta and the others should be understood.
“Meaningful meaning” (*atthattha*) refers to the meaning that has become the goal, the meaning as it truly is.

Since some people, due to cognitive distortion (*vipallāsa*), grasp even what is not beneficial as being “beneficial,” it is stated with the qualification “meaningful meaning. “Causal meaning” (*kāraṇattha*) refers to the meaning that serves as a cause;
for example, virtue is the cause of concentration, and concentration is the cause of insight—thus, the meaning that serves as the cause for each respective factor. Therefore he said:
“‘In this place, virtue’ and so forth. By this, he shows that they are unable to understand: “In this place virtue is taught, and that is solely for the sake of concentration;
concentration is for the sake of insight; insight is for the sake of the Path; the Path is for the sake of the Fruit;
and the round of existence is taught solely for the sake of attaining its transcendence. Thus, in the Pāḷi...
By the word “attha,” it should be understood that the meanings of what has been spoken, the purpose, and the application are included.

“They do not grasp” means they do not investigate; they are not capable of the wisdom of reflection (*nijjhāna-paññā*); the intention is that these [teachings] are not to be grasped after having reflected upon them and approved of them with wisdom.
Thus, by means of this scripture, the benefits of resolving disputes are placed above oneself.
They master the Dhamma for the purpose of escaping the censure leveled by others; that is, either to escape from debate or to escape from blame.

"And for whom" means: for the sake of that which is to be attained through the fulfillment of virtue and so forth, or for the sake of the path to be attained through its realization, or for the sake of the fruit to be attained through its realization, or for the sake of the liberation without clinging.
They master the Dhamma; the intention is that they master it by way of the proper method. They do not experience [its benefit], they do not find it.
Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time, by way of being the cause for criticism, conceit, arrogance, calumny, and spite.
239. *Alagadda*: "That which has gone (*gado*) to the extent of being sufficient (*alaṃ pariyatto*)"—thus it is formed by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) and adding the letter *d*.
The mastery (*pariyatti*) for the purpose of crossing over the wilderness of the suffering of saṃsāra is "mastery for crossing over" (*nittharaṇapariyatti*).

One who is appointed to the storehouse is a "storekeeper" (*bhaṇḍāgārika*); like a storekeeper, he is a "storekeeper," one who protects the treasure of the Dhamma. Without regard for any other purpose, he is simply a storekeeper.
The mastery of the scriptures is the mastery of the storekeeper. Regarding the phrase "one who protects the lineage," this is a restrictive definition;

it should be applied to both preceding terms according to the method of the lion’s backward glance, meaning one who merely maintains the thread [of the tradition] is indeed a protector of the lineage.
If the mastery of the scriptures consists in the thorough study of the Buddha’s word for the purpose of maintaining the thread and so forth, why [is it called the mastery of the storekeeper]?

It was stated specifically as “of one whose taints are destroyed”; anticipating the objection, “Does this method not apply to some worldlings (puthujjana) as well?”, he says “But whoever,” and so forth.
“In his own place” means in the place of crossing over. Granted that a worldling might master [the teachings] with the intention, “I shall preserve the tradition”;
however, because he has not yet crossed over from the wilderness of existence (bhava-kantāra) for himself...
The intention is that for him, that mastery of the teachings is indeed called "mastery for crossing over. Therefore he said, "Of the worldling," and so forth.

"They endure contemplation" means they endure the wisdom of contemplation. Having contemplated the qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so on as they arise here and there, and having found them agreeable through wisdom, they are to be grasped according to their true nature.
Therefore he said, "Here, virtue," and so forth. It is not merely well-grasped...

The phrase beginning with "regarding the doctrines of others" (*paravāde*) was stated to show that, by relying on the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*), the realization of the fruits (*phalasacchikiriyā*), as well as the refutation of opposing views and the establishment of one's own doctrine (*sakavāda*), are all accomplished.
Therefore he said: "Having thoroughly refuted with reasoned argument (*sahadhamma*) any arisen doctrine of another," and so forth.
"The desired place" refers to what is intended by way of the unraveling of views (*diṭṭhiviniveṭhana*) and other such matters.
The desired passage from the Pāḷi is: "To release" means to remove.

Even that which does not lead to welfare or happiness is indeed a cause for the welfare and happiness that arises in its absence, because it exists when that [absence] is present. Thus, even a well-seized iron hook should be seen as leading to welfare and happiness.
240. It is called *uttara* because one crosses over by means of it; it is called *setu* because they bind (*sinanti*) or fasten together. Thus, it is the *uttarasetu* (the bridge for crossing).

It is called *kulla* because it carries or brings one to the further shore (*kūla*). It is "bound as a bundle" (*kalāpa*) because it is bound together in the form of bundles made of bamboo, reeds, and so forth.
He says "fine" (*aṇu*) with reference to the fetter that has the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) as its object. "Coarse" (*thūla*)...

The other. "View" (*diṭṭhi*) means seeing things as they truly are; the meaning is "insight" (*vipassanā*). "Thus purified, thus cleansed" means that regarding phenomena belonging to the three planes, one knows:
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus, by the absence of the defilements of craving and views, it is entirely pure;
and because it is pure, it is cleansed. "One should not cling" means [one should not cling] by way of attachment.
One should rely [upon it]. "One should not cherish" means one should not treat it as "mine. "One should not treasure" means one should not regard it as wealth or property.
"In both respects" refers to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Regarding the phrase "in what is not the true Dhamma" (*asaddhamme*) and so forth: the Dhamma of the unvirtuous, those of inferior disposition, is "what is not the true Dhamma. It is the Dhamma of those who dwell in villages.

It is the "village-dharma" (*gāmadhamma*). It is the "dharma of the outcaste" (*vasaladhamma*) because its nature is to rain down defilements (*kilesa*). It is "filthy" (*duṭṭhulla*) because it is corrupted by defilements and because of its grossness.
It is "ending at the water's edge" (*odakantika*) because it concludes with purification by water.
Even when speaking for the sake of the monks with this exhortation, "Even dharmas must be abandoned," he was actually rebuking Ariṭṭha alone.
241. "By way of the threefold grasping" means by way of the grasping of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*).
If this is so, why are only two types of grasping mentioned—namely, "he grasps as 'I' and 'mine'"? This is not the case, because even there, all three types of grasping are indeed stated.
For by the word "I," the graspings of conceit and views are expressed, due to their commonality with the grasping "I am. Views, moreover, are the locus of views.
This is because it serves as the cause for views that have arisen previously, such as the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), and so forth.

Its object (*ārammaṇa*) consists of the five aggregates and objects such as visible forms. As for the conditions for views, they include ignorance, contact, perception, applied thought, improper attention, evil friends, the voice of others, and so on—these being the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) and others for views.
Indeed, this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "Which are the eight bases of views?"
“Ignorance, contact, perception, applied thought, improper attention, evil friends, the voice of another, and the basis for views”—and so forth.
"Having form as their object" means having as their object those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is to be affected by change.
Furthermore, it should not be said that "form is the self," because here the grasping expressed in the phrase "one regards form as self" is not intended [as a literal truth]. He...
For this will be stated later on in the passage beginning, "That which is the basis for views," and so forth.
However, some here maintain that what is intended are these three modes of grasping: "one regards the self as possessing form, form as being in the self, and the self as being in form.
That is incorrect; because form is not the self, yet it serves as the objective support (ālambana) for the grasping of a self, precisely within the very nature of the self.
Or, when the view of self arises directed toward phenomena such as form, it does not arise with respect to a self, because a self is not found in the ultimate sense.

Therefore, taking the view of self to have form and so forth as its object, it is said [that the view of self has form as its object]; however, form itself should not be called "self"—this is the meaning here.
But by the passage beginning, "That which is a basis for views," and so on, it is like insight and subsequent insight (*vipassanā-paṭivipassanā*).
The contemplation of views has been shown.
As for the sense bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles, they are to be grasped by reaching them, because they are the objects of the faculties that go to meet them.
For that [faculty], having reached its own object, grasps it by means of a connection. The remaining seven bases—
That which is "cognized" (*viññāta*) is so called because it is to be cognized by the mind (*manas*). Otherwise, the other [objects] would also be considered cognized.
"Attained" (*patta*) means acquired. "Sought" (*pariyesita*) means searched for. "Discerned" (*anuvicarita*) means reflected upon. Therefore he said, "by the mind.

And here, having shown a fourfold permutation (*catukkoṭika*) by way of the non-rejection of attainment and seeking, and the rejection of them both individually and together, [the text proceeds] with attainment and seeking...
In order to show the analysis of that which has been scrutinized (*anuvicarita*), it is said: "For in the world... and so forth.

That which is obtained after having sought it—first by the mind and subsequently by the body—is called "obtained" (*patta*). That which is not obtained despite having been sought is called "sought" (*pariyesita*) merely because of the state of having been sought.
And that which is neither obtained nor unobtained without having been sought is to be scrutinized by the mind alone.
"Deliberated by the mind" (manasānuvicaritaṃ) is its name.

And since this conceptualization (vikappa) appears as if confused, the phrase "or else" (atha vā) and so forth is stated. "In the sense of having been reached" (pattaṭṭhena) means by way of being reached, by way of the commonality of the state of having been reached.
"Not reached without having been sought" (apariyesitvā nopattaṃ) is called "deliberated by the mind," because of the absence of both reaching and seeking. All [of this].
"Or this" refers to the fourfold [craving] described by the passage beginning with "having sought after, even what is obtained," and so forth.

"By this" refers to the statement beginning with "that which is a basis for views. Craving, conceit, and views having consciousness as their object are stated by way of the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).
To the question, "What is the purpose of grasping [the meaning] by way of the method of elimination? he says: "By way of the elegance of the teaching," and so forth. For those disciples...

When penetration occurs by way of elucidating other aspects—such as the function of the object, associated states, specific fruits, and so forth—without touching upon the actual nature (*sarūpa*) of the phenomena to be taught, [the Teacher speaks] of those [phenomena] by means of those various types of states. However, when penetration occurs by elucidating [phenomena] through a single aspect or their actual nature itself, he speaks of that [aspect or nature];
and because he is the Lord of Dhamma (*dhammissara*), he [speaks] of the others.
And the elucidation of all aspects without remainder is the elegance of the teaching. Therefore, it was said: "Consciousness has been shown by way of objects such as the seen and so forth.
"Basis for views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*) means that view itself is the basis for views; this follows the method already explained below.
That form which this view grasps as "the world and the self"—referring to that form, there is the statement: "That is the world, that is the self."

The word "said" (*vutta*) is to be construed [with what follows]. He stated, "Having passed away, I shall become...," and so forth, according to the doctrine of those who maintain that there is an existence after death (*uddhamāghātanikavāda*).
"I, having gone to the next world, shall be eternal," etc. "Permanent" (*dhuvā*) means stable. "Eternal" (*sassata*) means existing at all times.
"Of a nature not subject to change" (*avipariṇāmadhamma*) means having a nature that cannot be altered by aging or death; the meaning is "unchanging."
“That too is a seeing”: that aforementioned manifestation of views (*diṭṭhidassana*) is grasped as if it were a self (*attā*) by way of the specific grasping of craving and views.
Therefore he said, “This is mine,” and so forth. “Having views as their object” means having views as their domain (*visaya*).

But how can a view have a view as its own object? To this he said, “By means of insight,” and so forth. “At the time of counter-insight” refers to the time of comprehension by pairs (*yamakato*) and so on.

He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). In this context, the engagement of those who hold views (*diṭṭhigatika*) in grasping a view should be understood as being like the engagement of grammarians (*akkharacintaka*) with sound, or like that of Vedic reciters (*vedajjhāyin*) with the Vedic scriptures.
And regarding the word "observes" (*samanupassati*), the construction is that "observing" is its meaning. By that, [it is shown that] observing—
This shows that there are four kinds [of views]. In this context, first, *ñāṇa* (knowledge) is called *samanupassanā* because it contemplates the even and uneven correctly and according to reality.
The others, however, are called *samanupassanā* because they contemplate repeatedly (*anu anu*) by way of defilement.

If that is so, let it be granted for now that the view-obsession (*diṭṭhi-samanupassanā*) is such because of its nature as wrong seeing; but how is it so for craving (*taṇhā*) and conceit (*māna*)? For craving also—
It should be understood that there indeed exists a mode of activity resembling wisdom (*paññā-patirūpikā pavatti*) on the part of beings, which consists in seeing means for performing evil deeds;
through this, deception, fraud, and crookedness become possible. Likewise, pride (*māna*) also elevates itself by viewing things as "superior" and so forth;
thus, there exists a mode of activity resembling wrong view (*samanupassanā-patirūpikā pavatti*) on the part of craving and pride. Regarding the phrase "non-existent": "This is mine."
Thus, when the five internal aggregates— the basis for craving— which ought to be grasped, are no longer found and have perished, one does not tremble,
because fear-trembling, anxiety-trembling, and craving-trembling have been eradicated by the path.
(242) Regarding the phrase "for four reasons," although it was stated that "one does not tremble when [the object] is absent," this is taken together with the other three reasons.
It has been stated. "By four reasons" means by the reasons for explaining the emptiness of the fourfold alternative (catukkoṭika-suññatā).

"Non-existent externally" means when it is not found in an external object. Furthermore, that non-existence of his is either through the destruction of what was obtained or through the non-attainment of what was not yet obtained;
as it says in the Pāḷi: "Alas, it was mine! Alas, that is no longer mine! Alas, it might have been mine! Alas, that I do not obtain!"

It is said that, having analyzed both of those by way of requisites (*parikkhāra*), the passage beginning with “In the destruction of external requisites” was spoken in order to demonstrate the anxiety (*paritassanā*) therein.
Therein, “conveyance” (*yāna*) refers to such things as chariots and carts; “vehicle” (*vāhana*) refers to elephants, horses, and so forth.
“By which defilements” means by which defilements such as the longing for what is non-existent. “May it be thus” means: “O, may it have been thus!”... [ahu vata]...
By such statements as "me," there may be instigation and so forth. Regarding the phrase "views, bases of views, obsessions, misapprehensions, and underlying tendencies":
here, among the views that arise successively, those views which arise later have the previously arisen views as their "bases of views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being their cause;
they are the "bases of views" (*diṭṭhādhiṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being the foundation for them, through the attainment of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
All obsessions of views (*diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna*) are the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that occurs in the form: “Only this is true, all else is false.

They are called *anusaya* because they lie dormant (*sayanti*) within the continuum (*santāna*) due to their state of being unabandoned. In this way, the analysis of the terms such as “bases for views” (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*) should be understood.

Because they are subject to being shaken by craving and the other [defilements], all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are indeed “shaken” (*iñjita*); thus, they are called “all conditioned phenomena shaken” (*sabbasaṅkhāraiñjita*).

The same method applies to the other two lines as well. It is called *upadhi* because suffering is accumulated (*upadhīyati*) therein; thus, the aggregates themselves are the *upadhi*, and so there is "aggregates-as-upadhi" (*khandhūpadhi*).
This same method applies to the others too. And the construction is: "It is by depending on that very thing that craving is exhausted, fades away, and ceases.
In phrases such as "I shall be cut off from name," the words are mere particles, or they express doubt. The word *tāso* refers to the state of being one's own (*attaniya*).
It is both the dread of craving (*taṇhā-parittāsa*) and the dread of fear (*bhaya-parittāsa*). Therefore he said, “For this is a dread,” and so forth. “I might not be, and nothing might be mine”:

it is said that “I” refers to some person who might not exist, and “mine” refers to something that might not belong to him. For this is a demonstration of the remedy for that dread. 243. “To this extent”:
by means of the phrase “When this was said,” etc., [the Buddha spoke] by way of connecting the question with the following: “Bhikkhus, these six...”
Or [it is said] by way of "bases for views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni*), and so forth.

For that [emptiness] also proceeds by showing the state of being terrified at the destruction of the internal aggregates, and then showing the state of being unafraid; thus, even the demonstration of emptiness as the non-performance of what is to be feared is itself a demonstration of emptiness.
It is on account of these [points] that it is said: "Emptiness is explained by way of four alternatives (*catukkoṭikā*). [The text continues with: "Externally..."
“Requisites” (*parikkhāra*) refers to external articles of use for beings, both animate and inanimate.

For they are called “requisites” in the sense of being equipment for the maintenance of life. “Having made them into possessions” means having made them into what is to be possessed by way of the thought, “This is mine.
Every kind of grasping at views—such as “The self is eternal, stable, and permanent,” or “The self is annihilated”—is included here.

Because it is said, “It perishes,” and so forth, that [the view] is indeed dependent upon the view of self; thus it is stated: “The sixty-two views, headed by the view of individuality (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Since it serves as a support for both adherence and the establishment [of a position] through grasping what is not as it truly is, it is called a “support of views” (diṭṭhinissaya), meaning that the view itself is the support.
“One would grasp” means one would grasp it by qualifying it with attributes such as permanence and so forth. Why would one grasp it in this way?
Could it be possible? "In all cases" refers even to these [passages]: "Monks, one would cling to that clinging to a self-theory;
monks, one would rely upon that reliance on views.
"If there were a self" means: if there were a self of which something could be called "belonging to the self" by way of being its possession. In that [self]...
The intention is that while there is a "self," that very self does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). For could it not be said that the self imagined by outsiders is "ultimate"?
Might the five aggregates be [considered ultimate] because they have the nature of being objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*), just like a jar?
And if there were something else distinct from them, would that not necessarily be their opposite? Yet, that [self] does not exist in the ultimate sense.
"It does not exist because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition, like the horn of a horse. Regarding "when there is something belonging to a self" (*attaniye*):
this refers to when some object has been determined as "this is mine," existing in the state of being a possession (*kiñcana*).

For that which belongs to a self is called "belonging to a self" (*attaniya*). Regarding "when there is 'I'": this refers to that which serves as the basis for the conceit "I am," namely, "I am such-and-such."
When something exists whose specific nature has been determined from the ultimate standpoint (*paramattha*), it would be appropriate to grasp it as "mine" by way of its being one's own property.
When "mine" exists, the same principle applies here to "I.

Thus, because a self is not found from the ultimate standpoint, there is nothing whatsoever belonging to a self from the ultimate standpoint; therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are non-self (*anattā*).
It shows that which is not-self-determined, and that which is made by the non-self because of its being not-self-determined. "As real" means from the perspective of the real meaning.
"As suchness" means from the perspective of its true nature. "As stable" means from the perspective of its established nature, being changeless.
"Because, having been, it does not exist" means because, having previously been non-existent, it arises through the convergence of conditions, and then [again...]

Because it does not exist through its own breaking up, it is "not permanent"; thus "impermanent" (*anicca*) means "unstable. For that very reason, it is "subject to arising and passing away," because it proceeds by way of both arising and ceasing.
Here, "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) refers to the departure from one's own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); "momentariness" (*khaṇikatā*) is its temporary duration;
and the absence of a permanent intrinsic nature is itself the negation of permanence. For phenomena that are impermanent, by that very fact of their own...
By way of their impermanent nature, they are said to reject permanence in terms of their actual meaning; for it has been stated: "That which is not permanent is impermanent.

Because of the continuous oppression of matter through arising, aging, and dissolution, its state of suffering consists in the manner of being afflicted. "Torment" (santāpa) refers to the burning and scorching by way of the suffering of suffering and so forth;
it is therefore called "the state of being difficult to bear" (dukkhamatā).
It is established as a basis for suffering because it is the foundation for the three kinds of suffering and for the suffering of saṃsāra.
The negation of pleasure is simply the absence of the intrinsic nature of pleasure. "Subject to change" means having the inherent nature of undergoing transformation through aging and death.
Because this form arises through the convergence of conditions, immediately after its arising, it inevitably reaches aging.
It breaks apart; once broken, it remains broken, and there is no transference of anything whatsoever.

In order to make manifest the quality of being subject to change through the absence of transference—defined as not entering into another state of existence—it is said: "having the nature of entering into the transition of existence.
The abandonment of one's original state, the departure from its own nature, is simply cessation. Thus, [it is] impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
“Form. By this—namely, by the denial that form is the basis for the grasping of craving and so forth, as in the reply, “No indeed, venerable sir”—it is shown that there is no mastery over form here.
For one cannot say: “Let form that has arisen not reach stability; let what has reached stability not decay; let what has reached decay not break up;
let it not be exhausted by arising and passing away. Such is its meaning of non-submission to control (avasavattanattha).
He said, "Venerable sir, they acknowledge that form is non-self by way of its lack of mastery," because it is the cause for the discernment of non-selfhood.
Emptiness (suññatā) is the meaning of emptiness (suññaṭṭha) due to the absence of a dweller, a doer, an experiencer, and a controller;

the meaning of ownerlessness (assāmikaṭṭha) is the absence of anyone who has become a master; the meaning of non-mastery (anissaraṭṭha) is the absence of the state of mastery as previously described; and [it is] the absence of the intrinsic nature of a self (atta-sabhāva) imagined by others.
Such is the meaning of the negation of self.

Since the characteristic of suffering, like the characteristic of impermanence, makes the characteristic of non-self easy to understand through both of them rather than by either alone, the Blessed One, demonstrating that the manifestation of the characteristic of non-self is performed here by means of both, said: [the passage beginning with] "The Blessed One..."

He said, beginning with "No," and so forth. Therein, "by way of impermanence" means by way of the state of impermanence (*aniccatā*); "by way of suffering" means by way of the state of suffering (*dukkhatā*).
"It does not arise" means it is not tenable. To demonstrate that very untenability, he said, "The arising of the eye," and so forth.
Since the proponent of a self (*attavādī*) describes the self as permanent, whereas the eye is impermanent, therefore the eye—
Just as [the eye], so too the self has become impermanent. Therefore he said, "But for whom... and so forth. In that context, *veti* means it passes away, it ceases.
Thus, "the eye is non-self" means that because the eye possesses arising and passing away, it is impermanent;
and because a proponent of a self does not accept that the self is impermanent, the eye is non-self.
Granted that in the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*— “But because, monks, form is not-self, therefore form leads to affliction”—
the suffering inherent in the non-selfhood of form appears to be clearly demonstrated; nevertheless, by the evident logic of “because form leads to affliction,
therefore it is not-self,” the absence of any core of self in form is established through its very state of being subject to affliction.

Because that [state] has been analyzed, and for that very reason, there is no mastery over form in the sense of being unable to exercise control over it—such as [thinking], "May my form be thus; may my form not be thus"—its mode of non-submission is shown. Thus he said:
"He shows selflessness by way of suffering. That which is impermanent is suffering; whatever object is impermanent is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away.
The intention is that whatever is permanent is happiness because of its non-existence [as impermanent], just as Nibbāna is. The phrase "that which" (*yaṃ taṃ*) is a statement of reason;

the meaning is: "because form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, therefore it [is suffering]. Regarding the statement "whatever is suffering, that is not-self," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as explained previously.
By the term "impermanent," it is shown that, like a jar or similar objects, it arises dependent on conditions.
This demonstrates the meaning: "Form is impermanent. By this same method, although it is possible to say "non-self," there is no one who actually says "non-self.
Regarding the phrase "speaking thus, 'it is suffering,'" the appropriate explanation should likewise be stated here as follows:
"Form is suffering because it arises from conditions, just like when one has undergone changes such as an eye-ache, and so forth. It is difficult to see.

It is the non-proclamation [of this]. For even teachers such as Sarabhaṅga and others did not see it; how much less could they proclaim it? This, then, is the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa).

Therefore, he said, "Now and at other times as well," because the three characteristics of form pertaining to the three periods of time were stated by means of the phrase beginning with "Therefore, bhikkhus.
However, since that was stated in such a manner regardless of its specific nature, the distinctions such as "internal" and so forth must also be mentioned.
Or rather, by the word "pi" (also), its inclusion should be understood.
245. "Becomes weary" means he does not find delight. Elsewhere, "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) refers to powerful insight (*vipassanā*);

however, equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) accompanied by conformity (*anuloma*) is called "leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*). To the question, "How then has this arisen here as 'disenchantment'?", he says: "By the insight leading to emergence..."
"‘Yes’ and so forth. By this, he shows that here it is the ‘emergence-leader’ (vuṭṭhānagāminī), due to its reaching the peak of the summit, that is spoken of by the name ‘disenchantment’ (nibbidā).

Having stated, ‘He gradually touches the peak of perception,’ and having stated, ‘Poṭṭhapāda, perception indeed arises first, and knowledge later,’ it is called the ‘peak of perception’ because, among the mundane perceptions of abandoning, it has reached the state of being the summit."

It is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) because it is considered the culmination of the vision of specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*). Beyond that, there is knowledge whose object is the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Therefore he said: "First, Susīma, comes the knowledge of the stability of phenomena; afterwards, knowledge of Nibbāna.
It is called the "factor of striving for purification" (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) because it is the purification from all defilements that act as obstacles to the attainment of the Path.
It is called a "limb" because it has arisen for the practitioner who is striving, or for the cultivation of striving.

It is called "purity by knowledge and vision of the way" because it is the state of purity by knowledge and vision of the way that has reached the highest excellence. Regarding the phrase "the absence of identification":

here, "identification" (tammayatā) means craving; because the process belonging to the three planes of existence is produced by this or that [craving] among sensual craving and the rest, it is called "identified with that" (tammaya).
"Of that" means having made [it] its state. Because it brings about the exhaustion of that craving, insight leading to emergence is called "non-identification" (*atammayatā*).
"Depending on" means making that non-identification the condition. "Resorting to" is a synonym for the same.

"Diversity" (*nānatta*) means of various natures, many, and of manifold kinds. "Based on diversity" means supported by various objects, such as the sense-fields of visible forms and so forth. "Unity" (*ekatta*)...
It has a single nature. "Dependent on unity" means dependent on a single object alone.
"Depending on that" means making that equanimity dependent on unity the condition. "Of this" refers to this equanimity.

"Abandonment occurs" refers to the insight leading to emergence, which is called "non-identification," for one who stands having abandoned all forms of equanimity beginning with the equanimity of unknowing.
It is said that "exhaustion" (*pariyādāna*) refers to the abandoning [of defilements] through the equanimity of the formless-sphere attainments and the equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).

Because the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*) and the reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) regarding all conditioned phenomena have reached their culmination, they are called the "desire for deliverance leading to emergence" and "reflective contemplation.
[These differ] merely in their mode of occurrence according to whether they are weak, medium, or strong; in terms of their actual meaning, however—

The desire for deliverance and so forth have the same meaning; there is only a difference in phrasing. "By two names" means by these two names: *gotrabhū* (change-of-lineage) and *vodāna* (cleansing). "Dispassion" (*virāga*) refers to the Path;

it is called dispassion because by means of it one becomes utterly dispassionate. "By that" means by the Path acting as the cause. "Is liberated" means it is liberated by way of liberation through subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*). Therefore he said, "the fruit has been explained.
"One whose taints are greatly destroyed" (*mahākhīṇāsava*) is a term of praise, just as in the expression "Great King. For the Teacher, in praising him, [uses this title].
“Monks, this is called a monk for whom the crossbar has been lifted,” and so forth, he said.
To explain its meaning, the passage beginning with “Now, of that” was stated. “According to reality” means according to how things truly are.

“In the sense of being difficult to lift up” means by virtue of being impossible for ordinary people to lift up. A crossbar (*paligha*) is so called because it is an obstruction to entering the city of Nibbāna.

"Viyāti" means it is called a "paligha" (crossbar). It is like the designation "auspicious" (*sivā*) given to an inauspicious palm stump (*tālāvatthu*), which—because its head has been cut off—is devoid of leaves, fruit, and so forth. Therefore, he said: "made like a palm tree with its head cut off.

That which has the nature of producing renewed existence (*punabbhava*), or that which deserves the fruit of renewed existence, is "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavika*). Being thus, [it leads] to renewed existence...
"It gives a name" means it says "it brings about renewed existence.

By the phrase "the condition for the aggregates of renewed existence," he shows that the cause is stated by way of a metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*) for the cycle of birth (*jātisaṃsāra*). It is called a "fetter" (*parikkhā*) because it binds the continuum.
"Because of being completely strewn" means because of being utterly scattered and destroyed. "In the sense of having entered deeply" means in the sense of having penetrated into what is profound.
"Having plucked out" means having uprooted. "These" refers to the fetters of sensual lust and so forth. They are called "bolts" in the sense of being fastenings.

One whose banner of conceit has fallen by means of the supreme path is "one whose banner of conceit has fallen. Because the laying down of other burdens has already been indicated by the preceding words, it is said:
"It is intended that he is 'one who has laid down the burden' specifically because of the laying down of the burden of conceit. [This is] by means of the fetter of conceit itself.

The phrase "because of being dissociated" follows the same method here as well. It is stated that "the conceit 'I am' regarding form," and so forth, refers to the conceit "I am" intended as that which proceeds by grasping all five aggregates without distinction.
Just as stakes are erected on both sides of a city gate for the purpose of warding off dangers and for the sake of beauty...
"Having dug it up, they set it aside" refers to the statement: "on a pillar of sand erected at the city gate.
Since the leveling of the ground occurs by the very destruction of the wall, he says: "breaking down the wall and leveling the perimeter. "Thus," and so forth, is the application of the simile.
A "body" (*kāya*) that exists and is found is a "mass of phenomena" (*sakkāya*); it is the pentad of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
The thirty-two tortures are included in the Aggregate of Suffering. There are ninety-eight diseases, beginning with eye disease, head disease, and so forth.
There are twenty-five great fears, beginning with fear of kings. 246.
The continuum of consciousness that cannot be attained [by others] is understood as: "Depending on this, it proceeds in such-and-such a manner."
Thus, regarding the state of having a mind difficult to know: he says "seeking" (*anvesanto*) because they seek [him] individually in the singular number.
A sentient being (*satto*) is also called a "Tathāgata," as in such passages as "the Tathāgata after death.

For just as one sentient being has come to this human state through karma and defilements, so too has another; thus he is called "Tathāgata. He is the "Supreme Person" (*uttamapuggala*), [referring to] the Blessed One.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Even one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*) refers to anyone at all who has destroyed the taints and is intended as a "Tathāgata.

For just as one person, having well-established the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are, has arrived at and attained unsurpassed Arahantship, so too another who has arrived in that same way is called a "Tathāgata."

"Non-existent" (*asaṃvijjamāna*) means unapprehendable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). "Unfindable" (*avindeyya*) means it cannot be found; the sense is that it is difficult to discern.
"I do not designate a 'being' or a 'person' as a Tathāgata" because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the being itself is non-existent—this is the intention.
Why shall I designate anything? Because even the basis for designation (*paññatti-upādāna*), while currently existing, is devoid of intrinsic nature. "Non-arising is security."

Or it is the insight-consciousness directed toward the attainment of the highest fruit (aggaphala-samāpatti), which proceeds by way of leaping into the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) through such phrases as "non-arising is security.

He says "by means of emptiness" (*tucchakena*), because the word *tuccha* is used here in the instrumental case with an ablative sense (*nissakkavacana*). "Discipline" (*vinaya*) means that which disciplines; that itself is the "disciplinarian" (*venayika*).
"Thus-minded" (*tathāmaṃ*) means one who has become thus. For he speaks of the non-existence of a being (*satta*) that exists only in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
One might indeed be called a proponent of the destruction of beings; however, I declare that such a thing does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
Furthermore, I employ conventional designations exactly as the world employs them. Thus, the construction [of the sentence] is:
those ascetics and brahmins who say, "The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist," thereby misrepresent me with what is non-existent, empty, false, and untrue.

When one says that the final consciousness of an arahant who has no rebirth-linking—like a fire that has gone out for lack of fuel—is extinguished (parinibbūta) and cannot be discerned as being supported by "this" or "that," does one thereby become an annihilationist?
I do not say that "I never existed," nor do I say that "nothing exists. This being so, supported by what [could one be an annihilationist]?

The intention here is this: those foolish persons, by saying that they "proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being," misrepresent [the Dhamma] with what is non-existent... [and so forth].

By the mention of the "seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in the phrase "at the seat of great enlightenment," he refers to the seven days [spent there]. By that, [it is implied] from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma...
He speaks of the teaching of the discourses mentioned previously. By the statement, "I proclaim only the Four Noble Truths," he shows that there is no teaching of a Teacher apart from these truths.
