And here, by saying, "Both formerly and now, it is only suffering and the cessation of suffering that I proclaim," the Blessed One implies that he has never at any time said, "The self is annihilated, it perishes."

“I do not say that there is anyone called ‘self. This shows that, such being the case, on what basis do those foolish men falsely accuse [me] with what is non-existent and empty, saying, “He proclaims the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being”?
He says, “others... persons incapable [of understanding] the truths,” meaning “others” refers to those who are not my own, who have become unfit vessels for my instruction.
"By way of intention" (adhippāyena) means that this refers merely to their underlying intent;

it shows that for the Tathāgata, however, acts of resentment and harassment are simply impossible, just as it is impossible to scratch the sky. "Anger" (āghāta) is so called because it strikes the mind.

"Ill-will" (appaccaya) is that by which one becomes dissatisfied. "Discontent" (anabhiraddhi) is that which does not gladden the mind. "Dissatisfaction" (atuṭṭhī) is the opposite of contentment (tuṭṭhi).
A mental state occurring in such a way, or anger itself. "Others" means certain other people.
It is called *ānanda* because they rejoice (*ānandanti*) and delight by means of it; this is a designation for joy (*pīti*).
*Somanassa* is the state of having a beautiful mind (*sobhanamanatā*); this is a designation for mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*). One floats away from the previous state.
It is called *uppila* because it breaks through and attains distinction; that itself is *uppilāvita*, and its state is *uppilāvitatta*.
This is a designation for that worldly, elated joy (*odaggiyā pīti*) by the arising of which body and mind reach a state of inflation, like a bag filled with air.
Because they are unable to penetrate the Truths, [they experience] only suffering.

Being unable to understand that [the mind] arises and ceases and that there is no other thing called a "sentient being," those who hold the view that "there is a self" have not abandoned their cognitive distortions (*vipallāsa*).
The intention is: they revile even the Tathāgata, the supreme object of confidence; how much more so, then, the monks?
247. The abandoning of desire and lust that occurs through the perception of "mine" by way of a false grasp toward the five aggregates which are not-self.

This is because [one realizes]: "This is not ours, nor is it our self. For form, feeling, and so forth are the very basis for the grasping of a self, since there is nothing else apart from them that could be clung to as a self. "This—grass, sticks, branches, and foliage—is not our form, nor is it our consciousness."

Therefore, the construction is: "It is not even 'self' for us. Because the internal basis (vatthu) has been rejected as "not self," the external object is thereby rejected as being "belonging to a self" (attaniya); thus he said, "Even our requisites such as robes do not exist [as ours].
By using the external object as an illustration, it is shown that it is only the pentad of aggregates (khandhapañcaka) [that is under consideration].
"Is it not yours?"—this causes one to abandon [it]. It is not as if one were to pull it out like a bulbous root, nor as if one were to pluck it out like hair.

By this, they intend the abandonment of form and the rest by way of their names. "He causes one to abandon that which has been pointed out by means of the removal of desire and lust"—this he shows in its actual form.
248. "What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? and so forth; this teaching consists of three turns. Up to...

"This point" refers to the passage in the text beginning with "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*). It is called "well-expounded" because it has been explained in a way that is easy to understand; thus he says:
"Because it was well-spoken, it is clear, revealed, and made manifest.
*Pilotika* (rags) refers to cloth that is torn across and cut lengthwise, and for that very reason, it is like worn-out clothing mended here and there with patches and knots.
"Because of the absence of that, he is one whose rags are cut off"; the meaning is that he is devoid of rags.
The stabilization of postures, the non-existent jhānas, and insight are like sewing knots on a practice that has been cut off and no longer exists;
since such things do not exist here, he said, "For here... there is none. "It does not find a footing" means even by way of associating with those who are virtuous.
It cannot find a footing, and indeed there is nothing that can be said regarding its attainment of distinction.
"Sweep away the *kāraṇḍava* grass": discard, without regard, like refuse, the person who has become like rubbish due to their failure in virtue.
And "draw out the dregs": draw out that which has become dross, even when it is mixed in the midst of the nobles and others.
Drive away and cast out this man who has oozing sores like a caṇḍāla! Why?
Because a monastic dwelling (saṅghārāma) is built for those possessed of virtue, not for the immoral; that is the reason.

Therefore, winnow away the chaff—those who are not true recluses yet imagine themselves to be recluses—just as chaff is devoid of inner substance and, though lacking rice, appears like paddy because of its outer husk.
In this way, evil monks, though devoid of internal virtue, appear like monks by means of external requisites such as the saffron robe;
therefore, they are called "chaff. Drive out that chaff, shake it off, and winnow it away.

Having thus expelled those who are not true recluses but merely pride themselves on being recluses through their outward appearance... [and so forth] ...be mindful. In that context, *kappayavho* means:
"Make it allowable; do it"—this is what is meant. "Mindful" (*patissatā*) means being mindful and clearly comprehending (*sampajānantā*) each time, or thoroughly understanding.

Alternatively, "mindful" means being respectful, having mutual reverence for one another. Thus, living in purity with those who are pure, they are harmonious through their commonality of view and virtue.
Gradually, through the maturation of their wisdom, they become prudent (*nipakā*). Of all this...
The meaning is: "You will bring an end to the cycle of suffering; you will attain final Nibbāna.
There is no cycle remaining for them to designate, because the root of the cycle has been completely severed.
They are "followers of the Dhamma" (dhammānusārino) because they recollect the Dhamma, or because their nature is to recollect the Dhamma. The same applies to the followers by faith (saddhānusārino).
It should be understood. "Of one who is practicing" means of one who is engaged in the practice; even one standing on the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) is intended here.
"Excessive" means powerful. "Conveying wisdom" (paññāvāhī): they say it is so called because it brings forth wisdom, or because wisdom carries this person along, thus he is "one who conveys wisdom.
"Preceded by wisdom" means having made wisdom the forerunner. "This is called... refers to such a person as this.
A person who remembers and recollects by means of the Dhamma known as wisdom is a "follower of the Dhamma" (dhammānusārī).
Regarding "carrying faith": they carry faith, or faith carries this person; thus they are called a "carrier of faith" (saddhāvāhī), so it is said.
"Preceded by faith" means having made faith one's forerunner. "This is called... refers to such a person who remembers and recollects by means of faith.
*Sad-dhānusārī*. "Mere faith" (*saddhāmattam*) refers to the mere act of believing in the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment through such passages as, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One.
By the word "mere," it excludes unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*). "Mere affection" (*pemamattam*) refers to the mere satisfaction that arises following the aforementioned course of faith.
Some say it means "endearment" (*sineho*). [The phrase] "to those sitting having thus established insight" refers to [insight] by way of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*) and so forth.
"For those who have initiated insight" (*āraddhavipassanānaṃ*). "A single faith": through the sequence of insight, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is established;
from that very fact, a single, supreme, and sublime faith arises. "A single affection": here too, the same method applies. "As if placed in heaven":

this expresses the infallible quality of their faith and affection, because they lead inevitably to heaven. "The minor stream-enterer" (*cūḷasotāpanno*): [refers to one who has entered the stream but has not yet reached the full fruit].
They say [this] because they are established in the realization of truth by way of a partial aspect. The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Alagaddūpama-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Vammika-sutta*.
249. "Pleasant speech" means conduct that is agreeable. For those of a wise nature, when addressing others with what is dear, they address them as "Sir," or "Beloved of the Gods," or "Venerable Sir.

Therefore, addressing them directly as "Friend," and addressing them from a distance as "Venerable Sir"—this too is a form of agreeable conduct. [This refers to] Mahākassapa, Uruvelakassapa, and others.
Thinking that there were others named Kassapa as well, they asked, "Of which Kassapa? [The answer is] "Of the King," meaning the King of Kosala.
To explain the meaning stated briefly in the phrase "they recognized," the passage beginning with "But this... is commenced.
"Assa" means of Kumārakassapa, or of the recognition mentioned in the phrase "they recognized. "Performing meritorious deeds" refers to [the period of] one hundred thousand eons.
Having been reborn among gods and humans, she cultivated merits such as giving. "When declining" means when [the Dhamma] was falling away.

"The first" refers to the time when she was a young girl. The Teacher entrusted that legal matter to the Elder Upāli so that, through a formal act of the Vinaya, there would be no obstacle to that bhikkhunī’s going forth.
*Paññattivibhāvanā* means the manifestation of that which is known as "Andhavana. *Olīyati* means it contracts or proceeds slowly.
*Bhāṇaka* refers to a reciter (*sara-bhāṇaka*). *Yaṃ atthi, taṃ gahetvā* means: there is no place now to be searched for;
rather, taking whatever exists as it has come down. *Balavaguṇe* means in those of preeminent quality. [This refers to] the Blessed One Kassapa.
Due to the convention established over time and the uninterrupted continuity of its usage, even during this current appearance of a Buddha,
it was known simply as "Andhavana," despite the earth having increased further and further and trees, shrubs, and so forth having grown upon it.
"The practice of the trainee" (sekkhapaṭipada) refers to the practice of purification that brings about the state of a trainee.
The word *aññatara* (another/one) applies to both the obscure and the well-known, as it is synonymous with the word *eka* (one);

thus, to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "abhijānāti" was stated. Furthermore, showing here the extraction of the meaning of the word *abhikkanta* even as it appeared in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*, the commentary on the meanings made in various places below will likewise be applied further on in those respective instances.
He provides an illustration of the method by stating that [the characteristics] should be described in their respective places within the Sutta passages as appropriate.

He says "of the skin" with the intention that the state of having skin resembling gold is already included by the mention of "golden-colored. Others, however, maintain that it is the color-element residing in the skin itself that is grasped here by the mention of "color" in the phrase "golden-colored.
It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is praised (*vaṇṇīyati*), celebrated, and proclaimed; thus, it means praise (*thuti*).

It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is described (*vaṇṇīyati*) and defined without confusion; thus, it is a class of families (*kulavagga*). It is called *vaṇṇa* because by means of it the fruit is described—that is, made manifest according to its true nature;
thus, it is a cause (*kāraṇa*). It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is the description (*vaṇṇana*) consisting of the configuration of long, short, and so forth;

thus, it is shape (*saṇṭhāna*). It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is described—that is, measured—by way of smallness, greatness, and so forth; thus, it is measure (*pamāṇa*). It describes (*vaṇṇeti*) that which is undergoing change (*vikāra*).
It is called *vaṇṇa* because it manifests the state that has entered the heart; thus, it is the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
In this way, the application of the word *vaṇṇa* to various meanings should be understood according to their respective causes for its occurrence.
*Anavasesattaṃ* means entirety, completeness, or totality. Regarding the term *kevalakappa*, some say that those which are almost complete, though not entirely so, are *kevalakappa*.

They say: if this were so, the word *kevala* would have the sense of "without remainder" (*anavasesattha*) alone. However, by joining it with the word *kappa* in a different sense, the phrase *kevalakappā* is formed through the expansion of the compound.
Or rather, they are called *kevalakappā* because they are to be fashioned (*kappanīyattā*) and established (*paññapetabbattā*) as being exclusively such.

"Majority" (*yebhuyyatā*) means abundance (*bahulabhāva*). "Unmixedness" (*abyāmissatā*) means the absence of confusion with what is of a different kind (*vijātiyena asaṅkara*), that is, purity (*suddhatā*). "Non-excess" (*anatirekatā*)...
Being limited to that [object] is the absence of distinction. "Entirely" (*kevalakappaṃ*) means having made it entirely firm.

"Entirely" (*kevalaṃ*) refers to Nibbāna because of its seclusion from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*). Therefore he said: "It has many meanings, such as dissociation (*visaṃyoga*)," and so forth.
One who possesses this attainment of the entire [Nibbāna] is a *kevalī*; one who has realized cessation and whose taints are exhausted.
Furthermore, this word *kappa*—whether with or without a prefix—is intended here to indicate the mere root *okappa*, which is found in the compound *okappanīya*;
otherwise, if one were to list the meanings of the word *kappa* alone, the term *okappanīya* would remain unindicated.
*Samaṇakappehi* means by those designations of "ascetic" established by the Vinaya. *Niccakappam* means at all times. *Paññatti* means...
"Name": this is the name of that venerable one, namely "Kappa. "With hair and beard trimmed" means with hair and beard cut off by means of a razor.
"The two-finger-span rule" (*dvaṅgulakappa*) refers to the allowance for [the shadow] to exceed [the limit] by two finger-breadths once the time of midday has passed.
"Apadeśa" (*lesa*) means a pretext. Even for a radiance capable of pervading everything without exception, there may be a partial pervasion due to some cause.
However, in order to show that this [mindfulness] pervades everything, the word *kappa* is taken here in the sense of "all around"; thus he said, "without remainder, on all sides.

"By the manifestation of the perception of being an ascetic" means by the manifestation arising from the perception "I am an ascetic," or by the designation based on that [perception], or by its cause.
"In the discourse on former practice" (*pubbayoga*) means in the discussion concerning former practice. "This is his proliferation" (*papañca*) means this [proliferation] regarding you.

"The hospitality and the manner of conversation extended toward those who have arrived are our own elaborations (*papañca*). The intention is: 'Without doing even this much, let us practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) alone.
'One who has reached the noble plane' means one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). He speaks with reference to the clansman Pakkusāti."
"Having analyzed" means having made a distinction. "By way of hurried speech" means by way of speaking in haste. This shows that he spoke in haste to indicate:
"This ascetic is difficult to encounter; therefore, his question must be stated quickly, and the Teacher must be questioned quickly after going there.
However, with the words beginning "Or as," he addresses him twice for the sake of poetic ornamentation (*vacanālaṅkāra*).
"Evamāha" means he spoke thus twice: "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu.
Having made the body composed of the four elements (karajakāya) directly perceptible by means of the simile of the anthill, the deity said, "This is the anthill.
However, because she did not state the underlying meaning (bhāvattha), [the Buddha], showing only the literal meaning of the words, said: "Standing before him... pe... this..."
He said, "Yes. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. Regarding "frog": this refers to a land frog;
for it is called *uddhumāyikā* (the bloated one), not a water frog. Because of its habitat, [the Elder] said, "having moved away from the upper wind," so that the wind might not afflict him.
But how did this deity explain these questions to the Elder in this manner? Some say:

They said: "Having grasped the meaning as it was heard through the medium of a simile, and having reflected in his own mind upon the subject of the simile, the Blessed One himself will explain this to him; and that teaching will lead to welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Thus, [the Elder] explained the fifteen questions to the Thera by way of similes alone, beginning with "This anthill," during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa.
It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a certain wealthy merchant, possessed of great riches, who, having buried a vast treasure, installed certain signs there such as a crossbar.
At the time of his death, he informed a brahmin friend:
"I have buried a treasure in this place; show it to my son when he has reached the age of discretion."
Having spoken thus, he passed away. When the friend’s son reached the age of discretion, the brahmin showed him that place.
He dug it up and saw the nāga last of all; seeing his own son, the nāga thought, "Let him take the wealth in peace," and departed.
This matter then became well known throughout the world. At that time, however, this deity was in Bārāṇasī.

Having been reborn in a household of laypeople and having reached the age of discretion, he renounced the world under the Teaching after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, offering his own chest [as a ladder].
Together with five companion monks, he practiced the duty of a recluse. It was with reference to them that it was said: "Five monks having fastened a ladder," and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "Having taken the meaning as it was heard and expressed it by way of a simile," and so forth.
Others, however, say: "The deity, having formulated these questions by means of his own inspiration, explained them to the Elder.
The term *devaputta* is used in the sense of the agent (*nissakka*), because that matter was [posed] as a question by the son of a god (*devaputta*). 251.
That which is produced from the four great elements is called *cātumahābhūtiko*. Therefore he said: "of that which consists of the four great elements."
"Vamati" means it is as if vomiting or disgorging. "Vantaka" means one who has discarded [it].
"Vantussaya" means that which serves as a mound for the lumps of clay vomited by termites. "Vantasinehasambaddha" means bound together by the saliva-slime of what has been vomited.
Regarding the phrase "vomits impure filth," because insects emerge from the mouth and other [orifices], [the word refers to] the insects.
The meaning "it vomits" is indeed obtainable here as well. It is stated [as "vomited by the Noble Ones"] because of the commonality of its physical nature.

Alternatively, since the entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes has been fully understood through the full comprehension of the truth of suffering, the whole body has indeed been vomited up by the Noble Ones through the abandoning of desire and lust.
"All that" refers to that which is propped up by the three hundred bones, bound together by the sinews, and by those...
Being smeared with flesh, enveloped by that raw hide, and colored by that skin—one feels absolute disgust for all of it, including the bones and so forth, such that there is only detachment.
By the phrase beginning with "And just as," he shows this meaning through a simile that ought to be stated: "like an anthill, therefore it is called an 'anthill'."
It is called *sambhava* because it arises from this; it is called *mātāpettikasambhava* because its origin is from mother and father.
Of that. It is called *upacaya* because by means of it there is accumulation; it is called *odanakummāsūpacaya* because boiled rice and sour gruel are its accumulation.

Of that. Because of its unstable nature, of that which is subject to impermanence, [there arise] the disturbances of the elements such as sweat, feces, bile, and phlegm, as well as heaviness and foul odors.
The word *dhamma* should be applied individually to each term as follows: to that which is subject to being rubbed (*ucchādetabba*) for the sake of amusement;
to that which is subject to being massaged and kneaded all over (*parimadditabba*); to that which is subject to breaking (*bhedana*) due to its inherent nature of disintegrating moment by moment;

and to that which is subject to destruction (*viddhaṃsana*) precisely because of its inherent nature of scattering. "By means of thin ointment" (*tanuvilepanena*) refers to the application of ointment as a cosmetic for the body.
"For the purpose of dispelling afflictions of the limbs and members" means for the removal of such bodily distortions arising from that [cause].
Since semen and blood are the nutriment, and anointing and massaging are the conditions for its production and growth as appropriate, he said:

"The materiality born of mother and father... so it is said. The state of being high or low should be applied as appropriate, by way of the accumulation of rice and gruel, and the taking up of anointing and massaging.
"High state" means increase. By the mention of "arising from the mother and father," the origin [of suffering] is shown.

By the others, the low state, decline, and passing away are made manifest. For even the formation of the limbs and members is included in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), because it is a condition for the cycle of existence.
Regarding the phrase "anger is smoke": since anger is spoken of here by way of a synonym for smoke, the word "smoke" applies to anger.
It is said, “smoke-like smoke. *Bhasmani* means ashes. *Mosavajja* means false speech. *Dhūmāyitam* is simply smoke.
One whose desire is her smoke is *icchādhūmāyitā*, [referring to] the people.
The application of the term *icchādhūmāyita* to craving is in the manner already stated. *Dhūmāyanto* means being tormented by the heat of applied thought (*vitakka*), that is, thinking.

The meaning is as follows: *Palipota* refers to the great mire that is difficult to traverse. It is said that it proceeds "firmly rooted" (*timūla*), meaning it moves as if established by three roots and is immovable.

"Dust and smoke have been declared by me": in the sense of producing the nature of dust, they are declared by me as "dust," and in the sense of producing the nature of smoke, they are declared by me as "smoke. Just like natural smoke [is to] fire...
Because wisdom is the state of being the flame for the mass of the fire of defilements; because the smoke of the teaching of the Dhamma is the precursor to the kindling of the fire of knowledge.
"This smokes at night" means that reflecting during the night with reference to the tasks to be performed during the day—this is "smoking at night.

"Of the seven qualities" is stated according to the method found in the Sutta; and the Sutta was spoken in such a way by virtue of the suitability [of the teaching] and the disposition of those to be trained.

Or, because of its being conjoined with that [wisdom], it is so called in relation to the other defilements. "One of beautiful wisdom" (*sundarapañño*) means one who possesses beautiful wisdom by way of the full understanding consisting of knowledge, investigation, and abandoning.
"This" refers to this designation "Teacher" (*satthā*), because he teaches and completely cuts off the phenomena of defilement.
"That" refers to energy (*vīriya*). It follows the course of wisdom alone, because what is intended is only that which is beneficial through wisdom. At the time of undertaking mundane wisdom—

The construction is as follows: mundane energy (lokīyavīriya) is to be taken [as the example], and supramundane energy (lokuttaravīriya) is to be taken at the moment of the occurrence of supramundane wisdom (lokuttarā paññā).
"Illustration of the meaning" (atthadīpanā) refers to the simile that illustrates the meaning of the subject of comparison (upameyya).
"From the village" means from one's own village of residence. "Spells" (manta) refers to Atharva-veda spells; for those brahmins teach them only in the forest.
“Lest others hear,” he thought. He acted accordingly by dividing [the question] into four parts. Thus, in this context, the simile is presented specifically in relation to the "ant-hill" question;
for the remaining questions, it should be understood according to the method explained below.

It is a *laṅgī* (barrier) in the sense of obstructing and warding off; it is a cross-bar (*paligha*). In the "gateway of knowledge" means within the sequence of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "Falls" means...
It proceeds by way of the acquisition of the meditation subject and the interrogation of its meaning.
"By way of the acquisition of the meditation subject" means by means of learning the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths;

"by way of the interrogation of its meaning" means both by way of interrogating the meaning of that [subject] itself and by way of interrogating the determination of the meaning known as insight (*vipassanā*). For interrogation is the desire to know thoroughly. And insight is [the discernment] of all phenomena belonging to the three planes in terms of impermanence and so forth.
"He wishes to know. Thus he speaks of the abandoning of ignorance by way of insight (vipassanā), because there is still more to be done above that;

it is not yet by way of the path (magga). "In the gaps between the creepers" (*valliantare vā*): the word *vā* has the sense of an unmentioned alternative, such as "or in the gaps between the dust, or in the gaps between the clay.

"Merely a slight turbidity of mind" (*cittāvilamattako va*): merely a slight agitation of the mind. "Unrestrained" (*aniggahito*): not checked by the power of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). "Distortion of the mouth" (*mukhavikulanaṃ*).
The contraction of the face; the moving of the jaw leads to the state of muttering within.
Looking toward the directions leads to seeing where one might be struck, for the purpose of warding off or shielding oneself.
"The falling of staffs and weapons" refers to the state of brandishing staffs and weapons over another person. By that anger which is not restrained, [one harms] a mother or others...
Having struck another who should not be struck, one strikes oneself as well, thinking, "Alas, I have done what is improper.

It is with reference to this that it was said: "One brings about the destruction of others and the destruction of oneself. Or rather, this meaning should be understood by way of one who, through the act of striking another who is being killed, incurs the state of being a killer himself; for this is [said] because of the commonality of anger.
It is said: "Having caused another to be killed, one kills oneself. "Reached the highest peak" means reached the ultimate excellence.
Anger itself is the "distress of anger" because it brings about a formidable threat. Therefore he said: "Attained to strength," and so forth.
It becomes like a forked path because it is the cause of non-practice [of the Dhamma].
A wholesome state does not persist because it is merely suppressed by the hindrances.
For one who develops insight preceded by serenity, first there is the suppression of the hindrances by means of serenity;
however, it is insight that actually eradicates those hindrances through the power of substitution (tadaṅga). Thus it is said: "by way of suppression and substitution."
In passages such as "Just as a tortoise [withdraws] its limbs into its own shell," it is specifically the feet and the head that are called the "limbs" of the tortoise;

therefore, he says, "there are only five limbs. Since the practice of insight (vipassanā-cāra) is what is being discussed here, by virtue of the context, only those phenomena subject to comprehension are to be understood;
thus, he makes the qualification, "all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammā)."
It has been said. Therefore the Blessed One said: “This is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging.
It is called *sūnā* because they are heard (*sunanti*) and cut (*koṭṭanti*) therein; thus he said, “upon the slaughter-block (*sūnāya upari*). With the sword (*asinā*) means with the meat-cutter.

“Being struck” (*ghātiyamānā*) means being killed or afflicted. “Having placed them above the objects of sensual desire” (*vatthukāmānaṃ upari katvā*) means having set them apart from the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāmesu*).
Having made a fire-pit, they cut [the wood]; "cut" means chopped. "Pounded" means divided into pieces.
"Abandonment of desire and lust" refers to the abandonment through suppression (*vikkhambhana*) of desire and lust.
"Intoxicated" means deluded and confused. Because of their delusion, they approach with delight and lust, thereby increasing the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Not seeing such dangers as these, they approach the object of delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*) and cause it to increase.
"Bound by delight-and-lust" means being bound by it because of being attached to delight-and-lust. "They stick to the round" means they cling to the threefold round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Because of clinging there, even when encountering suffering, they do not become weary of it nor do they feel revulsion. Herein, [the phrase] refers to abandonment without remainder.
It is said that "the abandonment of delight and lust is spoken of by means of the fourth path.
This is precisely what is clarified in the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* by the passage beginning, "They do not go by way of desire (*chanda*) and so forth.

The passage beginning with "He is the Buddha, the Blessed One" is a demonstration of the manner in which one performs the homage previously stated as "pay homage. "For the sake of awakening" (*bodhāya*) means for the sake of the full awakening to the Four Noble Truths.
Likewise, self-control (*damatha*), tranquility (*samatha*), crossing over (*taraṇa*), and final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*) are to be understood by way of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

However, tranquility and final Nibbāna should also be applied by way of the state without residue (*anupādisesa*). "It became a meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānam ahosi*) means it became a meditation subject for insight (*vipassanākammaṭṭhāna*).
"Of this question" (*etassa pañhassa*) refers to the meaning of this fifteenth question. The same should be stated for the others as well.

Bringing the meditation subject of insight (vipassanākammaṭṭhāna) to its culmination through the qualities of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), he concluded the teaching by following the natural sequence of the discourse, not by following the sequence of the question;
this is the intended meaning. [Objection: But was this teaching not commenced on account of a question? [Reply:
It is true that it was commenced; however, it should be said that "the presentation was occasioned by a question," but not that "it was [concluded] by way of the sequence of the question."
“...is concluded. Because the teaching has not been diverted by way of an intermediate inquiry, the teaching is indeed concluded in accordance with its commencement.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Vammikasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Rathavinītasutta*.
252. The description of being taken possession of by Mahāgovinda is a characteristic mark of it having been taken possession of by the King of Magadha at that time;
for he was indeed his chaplain. Some say that "Mahāgovinda" was the name of a certain ancient king of Magadha.
It is called *Gaha* because it is seized (*gahati*); the city seized by kings is *Rājagaha*. This neuter designation is used in view of the word "city. There are other explanations as well here.
It is called Rājagaha because it became the "house" (gaha) of those [kings] due to being properly established by kings after they had seen it;
or it is Rājagaha because it became the "house" (gaha) of rival kings who approached it as a source for the occurrence of misfortune due to its excellence in protection and other such factors;

or it is Rājagaha because it "shines" (rājate) with the beauty of groves and so forth, and is "grasped" (gayhati) or "appropriated" (pariggayhati) by beings through the sense of ownership due to the comfort of dwelling there. Thus it is Rājagaha.
In such ways as these. The phrase "during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch" is stated by way of the most common occurrence.
It was surrounded by bamboo, and not merely a forest of wooden beams. It was provided with watchtowers (aṭṭālaka) because of the watchtowers established there during the king’s pleasure excursions.
*Janana* means birth; the ground of birth is *jātibhūmaṃ*. Or else, the Great Bodhisatta was born (*ajāyi*) here, and thus it is that very [place].
"Birth-place" (*jātibhūmi*) means the land of birth; "those whose birth-place is this" means those who dwell in that birth-place, thus he said:
"Those whose birth-place is [this] are the inhabitants of the birth-place. To the question, "But whose is this birth-place? he said: "Now, that... and so forth.

Since it is the birth [of the Buddha] that is intended—being unique and not shared by others—and because it is well-known in the world including the devas, the specific object is understood here even without an explicit qualifying term.
He shows that the word *jāti* is understood [in this sense]. Therefore he says: "The Sakyan country, the birthplace of the Omniscient Bodhisatta.
Even there, it is a region situated near Kapilavatthu; thus he says: "Having its source at Kapilavatthu.
[This concludes] the commentary on the state of being a *garudhamma*.
“Of the Sākiya circle” means of the assembly of Sākiya kings. “The ten bases for talk” (dasakathāvatthu) refers to the ten subjects of talk beginning with fewness of desires;
it consists of fewness of desires and so forth. One who is well-established therein is “one who has obtained the ten bases for talk.
“Therein” means in the ten bases for talk.
"Dhammagaru" means one for whom the Dhamma is venerable because it is to be treated with reverence; "dhammagarutā" is the state of being such, and [it is] by that [state].

Having stated, "It is to be known by his inclination," he says, "Indeed, by his reverence for the Dhamma alone," and so forth, in order to show that it is not to be known by inclination alone, but also by bodily and verbal applications.
"Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night..."

In this context, the meaning should be understood through the method of supplying ellipsis (*vacana-sesa*) as follows: “While staying for three watches of the night in the potter’s dwelling, he gave a discourse on the Dhamma.

Otherwise, if the meaning were taken according to the literal occurrence of the words, it would follow that the discourse on the Dhamma was given for three watches of the night; but that is not the case.
For the author will later state: “‘For much of the night’ means for the duration of one and a half watches.”
Just as the specific qualities such as the ten powers are identical among all Buddhas— like refined gold— the practice for the benefit of others,
which is caused by reverence for the Dhamma, is likewise the same. Thus, in this praise of the Blessed One’s reverence for the Dhamma,
[the text] shows the Blessed Kassapa’s reverence for the Dhamma with the words, "The Blessed Kassapa too," and so forth.
"He set out on a journey" means he departed to travel through the countryside.

Because he had set out for a journey through the countryside at an improper time, the King of Kosala and others began to try to stop him; for traveling after the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) is the practice of the Buddhas.
Desiring to receive Puṇṇā’s correct practice, the Blessed One said, "What will you do for me?"
"Ananhāto" means that, out of a desire to hear the Dhamma, he did not perform the bath customary for Buddhas in the evening.

Since the fourfold classification of those who have entered upon the practice is established by the existence of one, two, or all three of the practices for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, it is said:
"And one who has entered upon the practice... is fourfold. For even one who has entered upon the practice preceded by rejection [of unwholesome states] is, in actual fact...

"The purpose is indeed practice. Granted, one who practices for his own benefit makes the Teaching shine through that right practice; however, he does not cause the Teaching to increase because of his state of being free from exertion, nor does he fulfill in every way the wish of the compassionate Blessed One.

For instance, during the first enlightenment, when sixty-one arahants had been born, [the Blessed One thought: "If only there were more noble disciples who could establish the lineage of the Dhamma! Thus, he made a great aspiration for the sake of the future. Therefore, it is the practitioner who fulfills the Blessed One's intention. Furthermore, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma was for the sake of those who would practice; thus, it is the practitioner who causes the Teaching to flourish. Consequently, the purpose of the Teaching is practice alone. It is said: "The purpose of the Teaching is practice; the purpose of practice is the goal; the purpose of the goal is nibbāna. This is the meaning of the verse. Now, as for the words "one who has entered upon the path": although one who practices for his own benefit makes the Teaching shine through that right practice, he does not cause the Teaching to increase because of his lack of concern, nor does he fulfill in every way the wish of the compassionate Blessed One. For example, at the time of the first enlightenment, when sixty-one arahants had arisen...
—“Practice, monks, for the welfare of many,” and so forth; with these words, he directed the monks toward the practice of benefiting others.
Therefore it was said: “The Blessed One does not question such a monk; why? Because he does not stand on the side of the growth of my teaching.
Since a collective remains as if complete even when deficient by a small part, [the text] excludes the Elder Bākula from the fourth group.

It is said, “eighty great elders (asīti-mahātherā) spoke. Alternatively, the designation “eighty great elders” should be understood as applying to the individuals themselves, just as the term “eight attainments” (aṭṭha-samāpatti) applies to their common quality.
In such a context, the speaking of many together and speaking with loud voices was solely for the purpose of pleasing the Teacher’s mind;
thus, showing that those bhikkhus acted accordingly, [the text says] “those bhikkhus [produced] the sound of thunder...”

Having heard this, he said, “...and so forth. “By reason of the esteem for his virtues” means he was esteemed because of the esteem arising from the virtues that will be described hereafter, and not merely on account of some general capability or fitness for tasks.
The commentary on the nature of the heavy rules (garudhamma) is concluded.
In the commentary on *appicchatā* (fewness of wishes), having taken the word *appa* in the sense of "limited," it says: "The phrasing seems to be incomplete. Therefore, he says: "For not of that...
and so forth. Furthermore, it can be understood here that the word *appa* has the meaning of "absence" (*abhāva*), as in [the phrase] "healthiness" (*appābādhata*).
It is as in such passages as “I perceive,” and so forth.

"Desire for this or that" (atricchatā) means desiring this or that. "Praising non-existent qualities" (asantaguṇasambhāvanatā) means making known to others qualities that do not exist in oneself, as if they did exist.
"Faithful" (saddho) means [thinking], "May people know me as one who possesses the distinction of performing duties and observances."
"May he know [this] by means of such things as 'the practice of duties, recitation, and meditation.

"Appreciation for his peaceful qualities" means the manifestation of the qualities existing within oneself—such as virtue (*sīla*) and the ascetic practices (*dhuta-dhamma*)—while remaining established in right conduct. For in accepting [an offering] from such a person, there may even be a lack of moderation.
The intention is that while receiving it, one emerges [in purity] even while others remain unaware.

Having shown the fourfold classification of desire by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) under the heading of "effort for fewness of wishes" (*appicchatāpadhāna*), he again spoke the passage beginning with "another fourfold [classification] of one who has few wishes" in order to show another fourfold classification of desire by way of the person.
"Under the control of the giver" means according to the mind of the giver. "Under the control of the object to be given" means according to the smallness or greatness of the gift.
"His own strength" means his own measure of sustenance.
Not even a single bhikkhu knew [of it], because he had conducted himself perfectly according to the duties of a charnel-ground dweller (*sosānika*). "Uninterrupted" means without break.
"May a second not know me" means that even a second person who was his companion should be unable to recognize him; in such a way...
"I have dwelt continuously in the charnel ground for sixty years; therefore, I am indeed the supreme charnel-ground dweller.

Having agitated the people with a discourse on the Dhamma—by means of such things as causing hair to stand on end, giving shouts of "Excellent!", and tossing up one's robes—he [caused] the great multitude, both those already assembled and others who thought, "How might we hear the Dhamma in the presence of this noble one?", to break into a clamor.

"Having stirred up. "Gone" means he went to his own cell out of fear that [others] would recognize him, thinking, "This is the one who gave the Dhamma talk during that night," and out of fewness of desires regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti-appicchatā*).

"Like three clansmen" means like the three clansmen who lived in harmonious residence in the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove. "Having abandoned" means having abandoned it first through the preliminary stages by means of the abandonment of specific factors (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), and later by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*) itself.
The commentary on fewness of desires is finished.
Commentary on the Twelve Kinds of Contentment:
Since heavy robes and the like do not bring comfort to those who are naturally weak and so forth, but rather cause physical exhaustion,
the use of light robes after exchanging them for others out of necessity— rather than out of a lack of desire— is not contrary to contentment.
He said: "Even while subsisting on what is light, one is indeed content.
Even after obtaining expensive robes or many robes, discarding them and taking others according to the method of what is appropriate does not contradict contentment;

thus he said: "Even while wearing those... one is indeed content. In the same way, regarding the remaining requisites, [this applies] to the descriptions of contentment according to one's strength and according to what is appropriate.

The intention behind including the word "also" (*api*) should be understood. Contentment that is appropriate to one's station is indeed the foremost, because it elevates the underlying tendency toward non-greed (*alobha*).
The commentary on the twelve kinds of contentment is finished.
[Now follows] the commentary on the threefold seclusion (*paviveka*).
"Ekoti" means alone. "Gacchati" (goes) is said by way of minor postures (*cuṇṇika-iriyāpatha*). "Carati" (wanders) is by way of moving outside the monastery;

"viharati" (dwells) is by way of the daytime dwelling (*divāvihāra*) and so forth. "Bodily seclusion" (*kāyaviveka*) refers to the state of having the body withdrawn for one intent upon renunciation (*nekkhamma*) through devotion to meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*), and not merely the seclusion of the jhānas.
Therefore he says, "of those who delight in renunciation. "Of those with pure minds" (*parisuddhacittānaṃ*).
Of those whose minds are purified from the defilements such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Of those who have attained supreme clarity" means of those who have reached the highest, most excellent purity through the removal of the respective opposites of the jhānas beginning with applied thought (*vitakka*). "Of those without substrate" means of those without substrate due to the disappearance of the substrates of defilement (*kilesupadhi*) and so forth.
The commentary on the threefold seclusion is finished.
Commentary on the Five Kinds of Contact (*saṃsagga*):
It is called "contact" (*saṃsagga*) because one sinks down by means of it; it is lust (*rāga*).

Contact that has hearing as its cause, or contact that occurs by way of hearing, is "contact through hearing. This same method applies to the remaining types as well. However, bodily contact is physical touch. "A woman" (*itthī*) refers to a wife (*vadhū*).

"Or a young woman. "To connect" (*sandhānetuṃ*) means to join what precedes with what follows. "By way of the cognitive process of ear-consciousness" (*sotaviññāṇavīthivasena*) is said with reference to the primary act of hearing;
even the lust that arises during the subsequent mental-door impulsion-processes (*manodvārika-javana-vīthi*) is indeed a connection with hearing.
The same principle applies to the connection with seeing. Regarding the Bodhisatta Anitthigandha, by others...
This is an illustration of the contact with hearing that occurs by way of something being spoken. As for the young Tissa, it is by way of his own hearing.
In this regard, showing that the first [case] is to be understood from the Jātaka, he said, "The young man, it is said," and so forth.
"Pierced by sensual lust" means that the dart of passion has been driven into the heart and pierced within.
This is the "contact by sight. He says, "It should be understood thus," making it clear by way of the specific instance.
It is said that in that village, for the most part, the women were beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold; therefore, the Elder said, "If you do not walk about within the village.
Because he had entered very early, she gave him rice-gruel; therefore, as he was going away taking only the gruel, [she said], "Turn back!"
“Venerable sir, please accept almsfood,” they said. “Having requested” means: having requested by saying, “Venerable sir, we do not refuse because we are unwilling to give almsfood;
rather, this is the reason. “Conversation” (*ālāpa*) is initial talk;

“discourse” (*sallāpa*) is that which proceeds by way of question and answer. “A bhikkhunī” is merely an illustration; for any woman whatsoever, sexual intercourse—even if passion has arisen through the use of property belonging to her—is indeed sexual contact (*saṃsagga*).
The commentary on the fivefold contact is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the grasper and the grasped, etc.:
"A monk’s bodily contact with other monks" refers to such things as massaging or rubbing the body. "Bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsagga*) means contact consisting of bodily touch (*kāyaparāmāsa*).
*Gāhagāhaka*: the meaning is "one who seizes those who seize. *Gāhamuttaka*: one who himself is released from those things that improperly entice with material gains.
*Muttagāhaka*: one who seizes those who have been released from the aforementioned forms of attachment. *Muttamuttaka*: one who is himself released from those things that cause release.
[This is] by way of seizing and by way of gathering. They approach from there.
They do not expect any worldly gain on account of being worthy of offerings.

Regarding the phrase "by way of taking [them] into the side of the bhikkhus," it should be connected as "by way of gathering them for the sake of obtaining requisites. "By the method stated" refers to the method stated by the words "with worldly gain," and so forth.
"Position" means one's own state or condition. One does not allow that [position] which has already arisen to be reached [by others], by the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).
By expelling [the defilements], one suppresses them. Therefore he said, "by means of a mantra," and so forth.
The meaning is that just as a person desiring to live does not dwell with a black snake or an enemy, so too one does not dwell with the defilements for even a moment.

The fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) is both mundane and supramundane; likewise is concentration (samādhi). Those which serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā) are called "insight-bases" (vipassanāpādaka).
Just as mundane concentration is included by the mention of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*),
so too supramundane concentration is included by that very same mention of the eight attainments.

For just as the path-concentration (*maggasamādhi*) that proceeds having made the four fine-material jhānas its basis is "based on insight" (*vipassanāpādaka*), so too [the supramundane concentration based on the immaterial jhānas].
It also occurs by taking the formless jhānas as its basis. However, the sequence of attainments (samāpatti) should be understood according to the conventional usage of earlier terminology.
Alternatively, it is so called because one enters correctly (sammā) through the complete eradication of opposites, just as in the case of the "stream-entry path" (sotāpattimagga).

In this way, the mixed nature of both virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) should be understood here, not that of wisdom (paññā) alone. "Liberation" (vimutti) refers to the noble fruit (ariyaphala).
It is stated because of the expression "endowed with liberation. For that [liberation] is to be accomplished in the sense of bringing something to completion, but it is not Nibbāna itself.
And herein, one is content with whatever requisites are obtained through fewness of desires;

through contentment, one uses those obtained without being greedy or infatuated, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. Being thus, by virtue of having a mind that does not cling to anything—
Cultivating seclusion, he dwells unassociated with anyone, whether a householder or one gone forth.
Thus endowed with such an aspiration, he arouses energy for the attainment of what has not been attained and for the realization of what has not been realized.
And while exerting himself, he reviews his own virtue as it was undertaken, and the utter purity of that virtue.
Dependent upon this, non-regret arises; this is his accomplishment in virtue (*sīlasampadā*).
His mind, properly nourished by joy, rapture, tranquility, and happiness rooted in that non-regret, becomes rightly concentrated;

this is his accomplishment in concentration (*samādhisampadā*). Then, knowing and seeing things as they truly are, he becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion...
He is liberated; this is his perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*). His state of liberated mind, however, is his perfection of liberation (*vimuttisampadā*);
and from that liberation comes knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*). Thus, the sequence of these ten bases of discourse (*kathāvatthu*) should be understood.
That which is his possession of these ten bases of discourse is the practice for his own benefit (*attahitāya paṭipatti*). As for their proclamation to others—

This is the practice for the benefit of others. Among these, the former is preceded by knowledge and associated with knowledge, while the latter is preceded by compassion and associated with compassion;
thus, the entire section on knowledge and compassion should be recited.
By means of the ten bases of discourse acting as instruments, he gives exhortation to the bhikkhus: "A bhikkhu, indeed, [should avoid] excessive desire and so forth..."
The meaning is that he instructs the bhikkhus on various topics of discourse by means of such passages as, "Having avoided [these] from afar, one should properly be of few desires.
For while instructing them, he is said to "exhort" those bhikkhus. He indeed exhorts them merely by showing their true nature.
"Having turned over the subtle meaning" means: "In this way too there is fewness of desires; in that way too," and so forth.

Having shown the successive progression of fewness of wishes (appicchatā) by way of fewness of wishes and so forth, it is not possible to make known the subtle and refined meaning designated as "fewness of wishes" therein.
"He makes known" means he makes it known by means of the aforementioned distinctions.
"The reason" refers to that cause by which fewness of wishes succeeds; for among those beginning with great desire (mahicchatā), these are the faults, whereas in fewness of wishes—
"The benefit is this": thus should the vision of both the danger and the benefit be understood. "One who shows" (*sandassaka*) means one who demonstrates right-mindedness through a proper cause.
"To cause to take up" (*gāhetuṃ*) means to act in such a way that [the person] takes it up; the meaning is to establish them therein.
"By way of generating enthusiasm" means that one truly incites them with such vigor that their undertaking becomes steadfast.
"Encourager" means one who inspires. "In those who have conceived enthusiasm" means in those who have developed enthusiasm for fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).

Having spoken in praise, he "gladdens"—that is, he thoroughly satisfies them by various means—after having described the excellence therein and the qualities obtainable in the future; thus he is a "gladdener.
In this way, the application should be made accordingly to contentment and the other [virtues].
The commentary on the “Gāhagāhaka” and so forth is finished. 253.

Regarding the statement, “Such was the praise that arose in the very presence of the Teacher”: by this, it is shown that the praise originated from his qualities as they truly are (*yathābhūtaguṇasamuṭṭhitatā*).
...he shows. "Like one very dull" means like one who is exceedingly unskilled. "Like one very weak" means like one who is exceedingly feeble.
"Like one with a frowning face" means like one with an exceedingly unpleasant countenance.

"Having reflected" (*anumassa*) means having reflected; the meaning is: having thoroughly examined the ten bases of discourse both in their general form and their specific details. As for the examination of these:
"It is as if entering," thus it is said "having entered. The construction is: "praising by one's fellow-celibates is one gain.
The same applies to the remaining [gains]. The intention is that he spoke thus while aspiring out of reverence for the Dhamma.
The commentary on the five gains is finished.
Commentary on the Wandering, etc.
(Cārikādivaṇṇanā) 254. "Abhirataṃ" means delighting; that same word is stated as "abhirantaṃ" without eliding the nasal vowel. This is a bhāvanapuṃsaka (neuter present participle).
There is no such thing as non-delight, nor is there any prolonged dwelling [in the world] after having delighted, because the objects [of defilement] have been thoroughly understood.
For all the Blessed Buddhas are indeed possessors of all things and are not lacking in anything.

Having shown, by way of illustration, both what was already mentioned and what was not yet mentioned in the context of praising the reverence for the Dhamma— such as the Great Kassapa’s going out to meet the Buddha—
and having related in detail the story of the forest-dwelling novice Tissa, [the author] now proceeds to relate the account of the wandering through the countryside.

The passage beginning with “The Blessed One indeed... is commenced. Desiring to go together with those who travel through the air, he said, “Announce [him] as one possessing the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā).

They say that although full ordination (upasampadā) is accomplished by means of a formal act of the Saṅgha, it was stated, “I shall give you the Buddha’s inheritance,” because it is accomplished only by virtue of the Teacher’s command.
Others say, “Even though he was less than twenty years of age, his full ordination...”
They say that the Teacher, granting his consent, said, “I shall give you the inheritance of a Buddha.
“Having ordained him” means having ordained him with the General of the Dhamma as preceptor.
The distance of nine hundred yojanas is included within the Middle Country itself; beyond that is not intended here, on account of its remoteness.
"By way of going. "All around" means on the four sides of the place already traversed.

"For another reason as well" means that because the monks' development of serenity and insight is still tender, he departs from the Middle Circle and enters the Inner Circle for other reasons such as the ripening of the wisdom of those to be trained.
The phrase "by seven [days]" and so forth should be construed according to the sequence stated in the passage beginning with "for one month."
"For the sake of bodily comfort" means for the sake of bringing relief to the body whose elements have become aggravated by residing in one place alone, through the administration of a purgative.

"For the sake of desiring an occasion for the arising of a teaching" means by desiring an occasion for the delivery of a Dhamma discourse, such as those in the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra* (The Simile of the Mass of Fire) or the *Maghadeva-jātaka*. [This was] in the promulgation of the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor.

...as if for the purpose of establishing the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For the sake of awakening those beings capable of being awakened, such as Aṅgulimāla and others. "Fixed wandering" (*nibaddhacārikā*) refers to a wandering undertaken with reference to a specific person who resides in a fixed location. 255.
To demonstrate the state of being unpossessed and the state of not clinging to anything, [he said]: "Having abandoned the herd... like a rutting elephant..."
It is said, “without a companion. This means he was devoid of the duties of a companion, like a lion; thereby it shows his solitary dwelling and his majesty.
However, the reason why physical seclusion could not be obtained at that time should be understood as follows.
The phrase beginning with “by many,” etc., is stated by way of showing his inherent nature. The Elder’s assembly was well-disciplined.
One who has lived with his teacher for a long time conducts himself exactly according to the teacher’s wishes.

Regarding the phrase "even though," etc., he says this because the term *cārikā* (wandering) is conventionally established in the Dispensation to refer to journeys made for stated reasons and in accordance with what is appropriate.
[Furthermore,] regarding a designation that occurs for some specific purpose due to a certain characteristic (*nimitta*), even when applied to another thing that lacks that characteristic—
This is a conventional term for the course of events. Because he had conquered Māra, he was like a great warrior victorious in battle.
"Having approached another" means having approached another bhikkhu for the purpose of reporting, saying, "Inform the Teacher that I have arrived.
While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma that was appropriate and suited to the specific inclinations of each individual.
Demonstrating that he performs [this], he said, “In the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta,” and so forth. Therein, regarding the benefit of the flavor of concord (*sāmaggirasa-anisamsa*):

by means of the passage beginning, “But are you, Anuruddhas, living in concord, in harmony...,” he spoke of the benefit of the flavor of concord. Regarding the benefit of the lodging (*āvasathānisamsa*):
by means of the passage beginning, “[The lodging] wards off cold and heat...,” he spoke of the benefit connected with the lodging. Regarding the attainment of mindfulness (*satipaṭilābhika*).
However, as soon as the Elder Jotipāla had descended into that lowly state, he made a resolution to penetrate omniscience upon the Great Bodhi-seat;
thus, fulfilling the perfections, he arrived here.

Thinking, "Such a lapse into negligence is not fitting for one such as this," just as the Blessed One Kassapa spoke a discourse on the Dhamma so that the Bodhisatta might regain mindfulness, so too did this [Buddha].
The Blessed One delivered to the monks the Ghaṭikāra Sutta, a discourse concerning his former lives.
Therein he set forth four summaries of the Dhamma: "The world is swept away; it is unstable. The world has no shelter and no protector. The world is ownerless;
one must depart, leaving everything behind. The world is deficient and insatiable, a slave to craving. These are the four summaries of the Dhamma.

He spoke. Although these summaries of the Dhamma were spoken by the Venerable Elder Raṭṭhapāla to King Koravya in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, it is stated that they were brought forth by the Blessed One himself and then spoken there by the Elder;
thus it says, “in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta,” and so on. For it is said in that Sutta: “There is, Great King, [that which was taught] by the Blessed One...”
“By the one who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, four summaries of the Dhamma were taught”—this and so forth is the discourse on the benefits of drinking.

Having spoken the expression of thanks with the words, “The fire-sacrifice is the mouth of sacrifices,” and so forth, he then spoke a discourse on the benefits connected with drinking by way of miscellaneous talk.
He spoke of the benefit in solitude, with reference to which it was said: “Then...”

“The Blessed One instructed the Venerable Bhagu with a discourse on the Dhamma,” and so forth. “Infinite method” refers to a discourse on the Dhamma connected with fewness of wishes and other such qualities, which is a method of teaching that is immeasurable.
Therefore he said: “Puṇṇa, this too is just a discourse on fewness of wishes,” and so on, teaching through many modes in various ways.
To show how the Elder understood what was thus taught, he said: “For one who has attained the analytical knowledges... [and so on]... it occurred to him.”
The commentary on the *Cārikā* and following sections is finished.
Commentary on the Questions on the Seven Purifications, §256:
"From that time onwards" means when the monks from his native region spoke in praise of the Elder in the presence of the Teacher.
From that time onwards, his following behind the Elder, keeping close at his heels and looking up at him, should be understood as having been done out of a sense of reverence upon meeting the Elder.
For it is said in the text: "Perhaps he might... and so forth, and "in a state of great haste.
As for what is stated in the Commentary—"hidden in one place," and so on—that is not the reason; for the General of the Dhamma...
He was unable to know by means of his knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) where that elder was sitting.
It is appropriate to consider that even the thought, "I wonder if he will depart without seeing me? arose out of a sense of reverence.
For even a disciple who had come to see the Teacher—such as the Venerable Aññāta Koṇḍañña—[would not have known] that the General of the Dhamma, who was like the Teacher himself, was dwelling there.

There is no one who goes without having seen [the Buddha]. Regarding "for the sake of the daytime abiding" (*divāvihāratthāya*), he says this because the term *divāvihāra* is used in the accusative case in the sense of the dative (the purpose).
257. "In the former conversation" means in the first discourse. "Not established" means not having proceeded.

"The subsequent conversation does not arise" means there is no opportunity for the discourse that ought to be spoken later. He asked about the seven purifications by way of correlating what had been seen.
The purification of knowledge and vision is the Noble Path. Because there is indeed something further to be attained beyond that, it is said:
"Even for one established in the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth, the dwelling in the holy life does not reach its culmination.
Therefore, because the culmination of the dwelling in the holy life has not been reached, he rejected everything—even the seventh [stage].
He rejected the question; there is nothing further to be said regarding the others.

By "Nibbāna without conditions" (appaccaya-parinibbāna), he refers to Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). Now, in order to show the Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna) by another method, the passage beginning with "twofold" (dvedhā) was stated.
In that context, "clinging through grasping" (gahaṇa-upādāna) refers to clinging that consists of firm grasping.
Therefore he said, “the clinging to sense-desires, and so forth. Clinging to conditions (*paccayūpādāna*) refers to any kind of condition.
For that [condition] is called “clinging” because it clings to its own fruit, grasping it by way of clinging. Therefore he said, “What is called clinging to conditions...
[etc. ...conditions. From the statement, “By non-clinging, the mind is liberated from the taints,” [it follows that] the fruit of arahantship...
They speak of "final Nibbāna through non-clinging. It is not associated with clinging;
that is, it is neither conjoined with clingings nor does it arise together with them. It does not cling to any phenomenon;

that is, it does not cling by way of making any phenomenon its object. "In the state of being finally extinguished" means at the conclusion of the final extinction of the defilements to be abandoned by the supreme path.
Because it has arisen. They speak of the deathless element itself as final Nibbāna without clinging;

and while they speak thus, they show that just as for that [element] there is no such thing as a condition, so too for the Nibbāna attained, there is likewise no such thing as a condition, by describing it as "Nirvana without conditions" (apaccaya-parinibbāna) with the words, "This is the end," and so forth.
He then began another question concerning Nibbāna without clinging.
Desiring to establish [the meaning] according to its form.
258. "In all turnings" means in all turnings of questions; the sense is "in the sections on questions. "Precisely that which has the nature of being grasped":

it is called "grasping" (gahaṇa) because one grasps it with such thoughts as "this is mine"; that which is together with grasping is "with-grasping" (sagahaṇa), meaning "subject to clinging" (upādāniya).
Because it lacks any support for the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa), it is said to be "following the round" (vaṭṭānugata). Therefore he said:

"Because even the mere virtue of the fourfold purification is absent. However, one who is established in the virtue that is the necessary condition for the fourfold turning away from the round deserves to be described as being "apart from these states."
The commentary on the question regarding the seven purifications is finished.
Commentary on the Seven Chariots: 259.
This is an ablative expression, as in such phrases as “as far as the remains of the lowest step. *Attha* means purpose (*payojana*).
Here, purification of mind employs purification of virtue because it has that as its purpose.
Purification of virtue is said to have performed its function because it leads to concentration; for purification of virtue is indeed that which conduces to concentration.
"In all instances" refers to all such passages as "purification of mind is only for the sake of purification of view," and so forth, within the context of purification of view.
It should be applied by way of such statements as: "For one who is established, the task of purifying the mind is said to be accomplished.
This is because the city of *sakkāya* (personality-belief) must be transcended, just like the city of Sāvatthī; and because the city of *nibbāna* must be reached, just like the city of Sāketa.
It is like the time when an urgent task arises—something that must be attained in precisely nine moments.
It is the time of assuming the function of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Just as when a king has mounted his seventh chariot at the palace gate in Sāketa, his task is not yet finished;

rather, it would be considered finished only when he has made the necessary arrangements while surrounded by a host of kinsmen and friends and has partaken of delicious food—so too, regarding the defilements [in relation to] the purification of knowledge and vision.

Having discarded [the defilements], at the very time when one possesses the noble fruit that accomplishes their subsiding and abandonment, the task of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is said to be finished. Therefore he said: "The time for the yogin... must be seen.

In this context, the "more than fifty wholesome states" refers to the more than fifty blameless states consisting of contact and so forth, which are included within the arising of consciousness. "In the bed of cessation" means in the bed of *nibbāna*.

“Purifications” (*visuddhiyo*) and “bases of discourse” (*kathāvatthūni*) are identical in meaning; they differ only in phrasing. To demonstrate that they are not different in meaning, the word “thus” (*iti*) was employed.

When it is said, “The Venerable Puṇṇa expounded the ten bases of discourse,” he expounded the ten bases of discourse even while expounding what are called the seven purifications, because they are not different in meaning.

It should be understood that by this very [statement], it is also implied that the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, asked about the ten bases of discourse while inquiring about the seven purifications.
Regarding the question "What (kiṃ) having known did he ask?":
he asked having known, "I am asking about the bases of discourse by way of the sequence of the purifications. [He asked] the Elder who had attained the ten bases of discourse about the purifications.

The construction is as follows: "Is he one skilled in fords who asks by asking only where there is something to be asked, or rather, is he one unskilled in fords who asks in a place that should not be asked about and which is outside his domain—like one who, desiring water, causes people to fall from banks onto places that are not fords?
By this same method, the application of the meaning should also be understood regarding the side of the answers.

It should be understood. Having stated "being skilled in the grounds" and so forth to show the purpose for which this investigation was undertaken, the phrase beginning with "for what reason" (*yaṃ hi*) was spoken to demonstrate that although there is no difference in meaning between the bases for the discourse on purification, this specific distinction exists.
"This very thing" (*tadaminā*) refers to that which was described as "concise" and "detailed."
Now it should be understood according to the method and procedure being stated.
"One purification of virtue" means that among the purifications, the purification of virtue is one distinct category.

Among the ten topics of discourse (*kathāvatthu*), it appears as four topics of discourse because the purification of virtue is impossible without fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and the other qualities. Regarding the "discourse on fewness of wishes," and so forth:
The *Dasakathāvatthu* is included under the heading of "discourses" (*kathā*). Alternatively, it is called *kathāvatthu* because it is a basis for what is to be told.
Thus, by way of its utility or its intrinsic nature, the inclusion of the four *kathāvatthus* should be understood as falling within the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).

The same method applies to the inclusion of the three *kathāvatthus* within the purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*). The five purifications refer to the delimitation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpapariccheda*).
These are the five purifications: purification of view; purification by overcoming doubt, which is the seeing of mentality-materiality with its conditions;
purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, which is the knowledge of insight arisen after abandoning the defilements of insight;

purification by knowledge and vision of the way, which consists of the ninefold knowledge beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall; and purification by knowledge and vision, which is the knowledge of the noble path.
The commentary on the *Sattarathavinīta* is finished.
260. "Having exchanged greetings" means having exchanged greetings with the person about to be mentioned immediately after.
"By way of an impossible supposition" means by way of imagining an unreasonable matter; that is, speaking after imagining a point that was not possible at that time. "Of frequent seeing" means...
"Of constant vision, of fixed vision"—this is the meaning.
"He extolled" means he magnified him by way of his qualities as they were spoken. "Of the elder" refers to the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa.
At this point, for this reason, it was by means of a single phrase for the purpose of manifesting qualities within the domain of a disciple that are not shared with others.
Now, in order to make that very same point more evident, the passage beginning with “amaccañhi” was spoken. “Apacāyamāno” means honoring.
Because it was stated, “having asked each question one by one,” he speaks by way of investigation: “But which is more difficult—the posing of the question or the answering?
“Having made it reasoned” means having established what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. “With its cause” refers to that very same [point].
Synonyms. "Even the question" means that even asking about a matter that ought to be asked in accordance with the Dhamma, having prepared it oneself, is heavy and difficult.
"Even the answer" means that answering in accordance with the Dhamma is also difficult.
For by answering in this way, one satisfies the minds of the wise. Thus the teaching, from the beginning along with its equipment, is concluded precisely according to the sequence of connection.
This is because the teaching was brought to its conclusion by demonstrating virtue at the beginning, concentration in the middle, and wisdom—having attained mastery—at the end.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Rathavinīta Sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Nivāpa Sutta*.
261. *Nivāpa* means "snares" (or bait); one who sets snares is a *nevāpika*, or one whose food consists of snares—a deer-trapper who captures deer by luring them with bait.
*Tiṇabījāni* refers to the seeds of the bait-grass. *Vappaṃ* is that which is to be sown, in the sense of being like a crop to be sown.
[The phrase] "pride and intoxication [thinking], 'Who else will obtain such [a thing] as we do?'"...
"They will fall into negligence" means they will fall into a state of being unwatchful and unsuspecting.
For wild animals are generally apprehensive and anxious when dwelling in places inhabited by other powerful species of wild animals, especially in the vicinity of humans such as hunters;
yet, being bound by craving for taste, they will fall into negligence. "Nivāpa" (bait) is that wherein one scatters [food]; "nivāpabhūmi" is a place where bait is scattered.
Therefore he said, "at the place of the bait. To explain the meaning of what was stated as "to be done according to one's desire," the passage beginning with "It is said that one...
was spoken. Therein, "like a grove of wild rice" means like a collection of wild rice. Wild rice (*nīvāra*) is a species of rice that grows spontaneously in the forest.
"Like a mass of clouds" means like a cluster of clouds. "Solidly compact" means as if gathered together in one place without gaps. "They depart" means...
They depart having become apprehensive and suspicious. "Wagging their ears" is a description of the appearance of those who are not apprehensive.
"A cluster in a circle" means a group standing in the shape of a circle.

262. "Having fashioned" means having imagined by way of a simile. "Mastery" (*vasībhāva*) is the bringing of the deer under one's own control. That itself is "success" (*iddhi*) in the sense of accomplishment, and "power" (*ānubhāva*) in the sense of manifestation.
263. "With fear, with enjoyment" means together with fear (*sabhaya*) due to the consumption of fodder.
"Strength and energy" refers to bodily strength and the energy of exertion. However, in the Commentary, strength itself is called energy. "Strength" here means bodily strength;
and that, in its actual sense, is the wind moving back and forth through the pathways of attention, as stated in the phrase "the wind element moving back and forth."

264. *Sikkhitakerāṭikā* means those who are practiced in deceit; the meaning is "fraudulent. They appear as if possessed of psychic power (*iddhi*) and as if endowed with majestic influence (*ānubhāva*).
They are called *parajanā* because they have become superior to common people; they are great beings (*mahābhūta*). Therefore, he says "yakkhas.
*Samantā sappadesaṃ* means having a location on all sides—a vast dwelling place with spatial extent. As for its being "with a location" (*sappadesa*):
“By way of great spaciousness” means “a great space” has been stated.
(265) “They will strike against” means they will direct the mind by way of perceiving it as “originating from fear”; the meaning is that they will cause it to tremble.
“They will abandon” means they will become free from attachment. “An elder” means one who is advanced in age, being worn out by birth. “Weak” means...
Either by way of disease, or naturally devoid of strength.
Or, because it is like bait, it is called "bait" (*nivāpa*). Or, because it is included within the world and is to be touched by the defilements, it is called "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*).

Because they have become bait within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), [they are called] "the bait of the cycle of existence. It brings [them] under control by means of the strands of sensual pleasure.
“Beings greedy for the strands of sensual pleasure, by the power of that very greed, bring themselves under its control. Therefore he said:
“The snare that moves through the sky, which roams the mind— With that I shall afflict you;
O ascetic, you shall not escape me.”
