They go forth like the first species of deer. Regarding the forest-dweller’s departure with his wife and children—though he is mindful and free from the proliferation of conceptual elaboration (*papañca*)—the text says, “with his sons and wife he goes forth.
(268) Here, the liberation of the mind from sensual desire is intended by the term “liberation of mind” (*cetovimutti*); thus it is said, “Liberation of mind...
[omitted] ...is the arisen inclination. Because they have cast off sensual desires yet once again become submerged in them, they are called the second type of ascetics and brahmins.
The second simile of the species of deer has been told.

269. Regarding the third group of recluses and brahmins, the Blessed One asks, "But what did they do? with the intention that they remained having renounced sense pleasures exactly as they were renounced, and were not submerged in them as the second group was. The others [responded] straightforwardly regarding sense pleasure.
Showing that they were not submerged in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), but were submerged in a figurative sense and enveloped by the net of views (*diṭṭhijāla*),
he said, "villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals," and so forth. Since even the net of views is followed by the net of craving (*taṇhājāla*),
he said, "having surrounded them with the net of views of Māra the Evil One."
271. It should be understood that here, by the term "Māra," the Māras consisting of the aggregates (khandha), defilements (kilesa), formations (abhisankhāra), and the Deva Māra are included.
He "pierced his eyes" by causing them to reach a state where they were incapable of seeing. Therefore he said, "the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight," and so forth.
For although Māra [might try to disturb] the mind of a bhikkhu who has attained any kind of jhāna, it is [only] by depending on such-and-such an object...

"He does not know that it revolves" means he does not perceive its movement; however, with reference to the bhikkhu intended here, it is called "the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight" (vipassanāpādakajjhāna).
"By that same method" refers to the manner already stated, such as "he did not pierce Māra’s eyes," and so forth.
The same principle applies here to the phrase "he has gone beyond sight. And "the eye finds its footing"—here, "footing" (pada) means the object (ārammaṇa).
Because it proceeds by grasping that which is intended, he said, "without a footing, without an object. "He" refers to Māra.
"Having seen" means because of seeing. For the taints (āsava) are not yet fully exhausted by the path through the seeing of the Four Noble Truths;
indeed, they are said to be "exhausted" at the moment of the fruit (phala).

“World” (*loka*) refers both to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*) and the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*). “By way of being entangled” (*visattabhāvena*) means by way of clinging (*laggabhāvena*) and, moreover, by way of being specifically attached (*savisesa-āsattabhāvena*).
Alternatively, with the words “or else” (*atha vā*) and so forth, he explains the term *visattikā* according to the method of a formal definition (*niddesanaya*).

“Entangled” (*visatā*) means spread out; it is “entangled” (*visaṭā*) by way of pervading the three-plane phenomena such as form and so on. Thus, the word *visatā* itself [is used], with the letter *ta* [changed]...
It is stated with the letter *ṭ* [in the word *visatti*]. "Visālā" means extensive (*vipulā*). "Visakkati" means she moves about or endures (*parisakkati*, *sahati*).
For one who is impassioned endures even when struck by the foot, which is the basis for passion. They also say that "visakkanam" means retreating or struggling.
"Visaṃharati" means that, while showing the advantages of sensual pleasures in this or that way, she turns [the mind] away from renunciation through various modes.
It withdraws and contracts the mind; the meaning is that it carries away or brings about poison, which is suffering (*dukkha*).

It is "deceptive" (*visaṃvādikā*) because it causes one to grasp the impermanent and so forth as permanent, thus being deceptive. It has "poison as its root" (*visamūlā*) because it is the cause of the karma that produces suffering;
or, it is "poison-rooted" because its root is feeling (*vedanā*) consisting of the suffering of pain and so forth. This is because it is the origin of suffering.

"Poisonous fruit" (*visaphalā*) means that its fruit is poison. Since craving involves the enjoyment of suffering alone—such as form and so forth—and not the deathless (*amata*), it is called "the enjoyment of poison" (*visaparibhogā*).
In all cases, the derivation of the word should be understood according to its etymological analysis (*nirukti*).
However, to show the primary meaning here, it is further stated: "Or else, 'vast' (*visālā*)," and so on. [The one who has] crossed over...
*Uttiṇṇo*: this word is expanded by means of the prefix (*upasagga*). Alternatively, *nittiṇṇo* means "crossed over without remainder.
*Uttiṇṇo* means "crossed over further and further" by means of various paths. Whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Nivāpa-sutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Pāsarāsi Sutta* 272.

Regarding the phrase "They cry out" (*sādhumayaṃti*), here the word *sādhu* has the sense of a request, not the sense of approval and so forth as in expressions such as "Well done, friend" (*sādhāvuso*).
Therefore, he says, "Crying out [for help]. For this reason, it is stated in the text: "May we obtain... and so forth. They are unable; why? Because of the Buddhas.

For they are venerable; they are supremely venerable, the highest object of reverence, and are not to be approached in just any casual manner. Therefore he said, "Like a lion wandering alone," and so forth.
To explain what was stated briefly as "manifest activity," he said, "For that which... The Blessed One, at all times...
"Did he act thus at all times? No, he did not act thus at all times. To show when he did act thus, it was said:
"At the time of the first enlightenment," and so forth. By the phrase "in a human existence," he indicates a male existence (*purisattabhāva*).
The intention is that there was no such thing as the relinquishing of wealth by the Blessed One while he was living.
“Wreaths and refuse” means withered wreaths and refuse. “Dust and dirt do not adhere” because of the state of his skin being exceedingly clear.
For this has been said: “Because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body. If that is so, why does the Blessed One bathe?
He says: “For the purpose of removing the heat.”
"Vihāra" refers to the Jetavana monastery. They say it was twenty *usabhas*—a quarter of a *gāvuta*.
"At one time" means at some particular arising of a Buddha. "Unwavering indeed" means it did not shift at all because its nature was unchanging;
however, due to the small size of the beds, there were indeed decreases and increases in the area where their legs rested.
By means of golden liquid streams flowing from golden tubes, he demonstrated the proper conduct for bathing, showing that "one who has gone forth must bathe in this manner.

For the Blessed One’s body was the color of well-refined gold; its hands, feet, and limbs were as beautiful as well-purified coral; and his hair and body-hair resembled a row of perfectly pure blue gems.
Consequently, it was beautified here and there by the glow of natural vermilion liquid trickling down.
Covered above by a series of highly precious gems, it shone like a moving peak of the Golden Mountain.
And at that moment, the six-colored rays of light issuing from the body of the One Possessed of Ten Powers streamed and radiated all around for a distance of eighty cubits;
it appeared as if strewn with heaps of gems, jeweled garlands, and powdered jewels, or like a spread-out golden cloth inlaid with jewels.
That place and the wind pervade [the sky] perfectly, as if covered by streams of flowing lac juice; as if crowded with the falling of showers of sparks;
as if densely strewn with *kaṇikāra* and *kiṅkiṇika* flowers; as if colored by the powder of cotton-bark flung up by the force of the wind;
and as if overspread by a canopy of rainbows and lightning flashes. Therefore it is said: "This is called the ground of color," and so forth.
“Meanings” refers to the meanings of the things being compared (*upameyyattha*). “By way of similes” means appropriate similes corresponding to each case that illustrate “it is like this.
“Causes” refers to the reasons that clarify the relationship between the simile and the thing being compared. “Having fulfilled” means having made the description complete.
“Strength” is to be understood from the fact that one cannot say, “he has leaped onto a place where there is no ford.”
273. *Kaṇṇikā* refers to circular spots on the body. *Parikkhārabhaṇḍa* (requisites) is said with reference to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
But does this method exist on the bodies of the Buddhas as well?

It does not; however, the passage beginning with "But for the Buddhas... was spoken to show that this [description] was made for the purpose of illustrating the general rule. This is by way of their movement.
The "leading forth of the body" is the act of departing. "Turning back according to one's intention" is the frustration of that intention.
"By means of a certain perfection" refers to the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*); others say it refers to the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*).
"Of the Great Renunciation" refers to the great departure in his final existence; for that [renunciation] involved a vast mass of wealth and a great [retinue].
Having renounced a vast circle of kinsmen and the glory of a universal monarch,
it is called the "Great Renunciation" because it proceeds for the great benefit, welfare, and happiness of the world— including its gods and Māras—
and because of its greatness due to its venerability.
*Purimaṃ* means the sense expressed by the words: “With what discourse, pray, are you seated together?
Here, the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of exclusion (*byatireke*). By it, he illuminates the fact that the discourse being about to be spoken was interrupted by the question just asked.
The word *pana* is for the ornamentation of speech. For that very discourse by which those bhikkhus were seated together became an intermediate conversation (*antarākathā*).
The unfinished [discussion] is asked about again specifically. "Aññā" expresses the meaning of the word *antarā*.
For this word *antarā* has the sense of "other," as in expressions such as "another place" (*bhūmantara*) or "another time" (*samayantara*);
or else, its meaning is "in between" (*vemajjhe*). "Based on the ten bases of discourse" means: "What is called virtue (*sīla*), how is it to be fulfilled, and what are its..."
By such statements as “defilement and purification,” there is discourse based on fewness of wishes and so forth, and based on virtue and so forth.

An *ariya* is one who is faultless. Alternatively, he is called *ariya* because he is to be sought after (*araṇīya*) by those who desire welfare; or he is called *ariya* because he goes toward (*ayanti*) the noble ones (*ariyānaṃ*).
By means of the mental attention of development (*bhāvanā-manasikāra*), they become silent, not like certain outside renunciants who observe a vow of silence. The second jhāna also...
The noble silence is due to the abandoning of verbal formations. "The root meditation subject" refers also to the meditation subject for development.
"Jhāna" here refers to the second jhāna.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 3:68) "For you who have assembled together, bhikkhus, there are two things"—this teaching was delivered by way of an occasion.
In order to show the connection to the subsequent teaching, he asks about the sequence: "Bhikkhus, there are these two searches—what is the connection?
This "search of yours" refers to the discourse on the Dhamma connected with the Great Renunciation;
that is called your search for the Dhamma, your investigation of the Dhamma, and the Noble Search. "The path to the states of deprivation" means...
The path that brings about what is harmful. "Having broken the sequence of the enumeration" means having skipped over the serial order of the enumeration.
The word *dhamma* has its primary sense [of "nature"] as in such passages as "nibbāna is the nature that does not decay. "Jāyanasabhāvo" means "having the nature of arising";
this is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"In all cases" means that just as there is a singular number by way of a *dvanda* compound in "son and wife," this same principle applies to all terms such as "slave-girl and slave-boy" and so forth.
Because it remains always as gold (*jātarūpa*) without undergoing any change, it is called *jātarūpa*, meaning gold.
Because it is colored (*rañjīyati*) due to its white nature, it is called *rajata*, meaning silver. However, in this context, it refers to gold.
Excepting whatever is fit for use or enjoyment, only silver is thus included. "Bases" (*upadhī*) are so called because suffering is accumulated therein.
By "death," which is reckoned as passing away, he refers to death as the cessation of the aggregates included within a single existence.
However, momentary cessation occurs at every moment; therefore, he said, "as if of beings. "It becomes defiled" means by the poison of corruption.
It will defile itself as it were. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are these five impurities of gold: iron, copper," and so forth.
"Taking the stain" means taking the stain by way of those conditions for being stained through association with them.
The construction is: in the section on the nature of aging (*jarādhamma*), gold is taken because of its subjecting to decay (*jīraṇa*). As for those who...
In the section on the nature of birth (*jātidhamma*), they do not recite "gold" (*jātarūpa*);

however, it should be understood that for them, just as with the others, although it does not appear explicitly in the section on the nature of aging (*jīraṇadhamma*), it is nonetheless included by way of the inclusion of the acquisitions (*upadhiggahaṇa*).

But when spoken of according to those established in full comprehension (*pariggahe ṭhitānaṃ*), the application is indeed possible even for birth, aging, and death, though they are not manifest [in that specific context]. By way of the heading "gold"...
And here, it should be understood that the inclusion of "everything not bound by the faculties" is intended, just as the mention of "sons and wives" implies the inclusion of "friends and companions.
With the words beginning "This, bhikkhus," he demonstrates two types of compound:
"the seeking by the noble ones" (*ariyehi pariyesanā*) or "the seeking of the noble ones" (*ariyānaṃ pariyesanā*), which together constitute "noble seeking" (*ariyapariyesanā*).
"From the beginning" means from that point where the vision of the danger inherent in the state of household life— the root cause of the Great Renunciation— arose.
Since those monks were seated there engaged in a discussion concerning the Great Renunciation,
and since that conversation of theirs had been left unfinished, the Blessed One [recounted] the discourse on the Great Renunciation for them from its very beginning.

He began to speak: "I too, in the past... This specific statement refers to his own experience in his final existence—while his knowledge was still unripened—of enjoying a great prosperity comparable to divine splendor, accompanied by three palaces and a retinue of three kinds of theatrical performances;
it also refers to his subsequent practice of self-mortification through the exertion of striving after he had gone forth. This is the ignoble search.
The same principle applies here as well. Regarding the phrase "the group of five [monks]": they were previously devoted to their respective household enjoyments;

having abandoned those and gone forth, they remained intent on self-mortification. Then, through the Teacher’s teaching on the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, they abandoned even that and sought the Noble Search.

277. Granted that the word *dahara* occurs in the sense of a young child in the passage, “a young boy, a tender infant lying on his back,” yet because it will be stated later, “endowed with auspicious youth,” the stage of youth is what is expressed here by the word *dahara*;
thus he said, “being still young. This is because he was twenty-nine years of age in his first period of life. For as long as... [of birth]...
"Thirty-three years old" refers to the first stage of life. The genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard (anādara), as in the expression: "He went forth while Devadatta was weeping.

Granted that "weeping" (*rodana*) means the shedding of tears, and this is already indicated by the phrase "from those with tearful faces," nevertheless, by stating "while they were weeping" (*rudantānaṃ*), he reveals the occasion for weeping arising from intense sorrow; thus he said this.
"Having wept and been lamenting": "Seeking what is wholesome" means seeking that which is entirely free from fault and leads exclusively to liberation.
"The excellent state" (*varapada*): it is "excellent" (*vara*) in the sense of being sought after exclusively by those desiring escape from the suffering of saṃsāra;
it is a "state" (*pada*) in the sense of being something to be reached. He was tall due to his lofty physique, and [golden-hued] due to his tawny eyes.
"Piṅgala" means one with long, tawny hair. "Dhamma" means the Vinaya; "samaya" is its meaning.
"Having heard, I mastered it" means that by the mere hearing of what was being spoken by him, I mastered it and brought it to the tip of my tongue.
"By the mere repeating" means by repeating it once more. "Jānāti" (he knows) is "ñāṇa"; the discourse on knowledge is "ñāṇavāda."

That is the "declaration of knowledge" (*ñāṇavāda*). Because [the Buddha] has come [to the world] saying, "I declare," the meaning is stated in the Commentary as "I know" (*jānāmi*) by way of the supreme person (*uttamapurisa*).
"Many others too"—many others who know my suchness say, "This one knows this Dhamma," or "He is firm due to his unshakability.
"An attainer" (*lābhī*) means he has understood through the recitation of the Dhamma, owing to his great wisdom.
“He proclaims the path he has himself traveled; he is not one who merely repeats what he has heard”—thus he knew. *Assa* means of the Bodhisatta.
*Etad ahosi* means this occurred to his mind; it means he reflected, [thinking] “Indeed, Āḷāra Kālāma... and so forth.
Because it is impossible to achieve the higher attainments (*samāpatti*) without the lower attainments, [he considered] the seven attainments...
“...made me understand,” he said. “They would apply themselves” means they would devote themselves to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
“He spoke thus” means he spoke these words beginning with “I, friend”; the meaning is that he acknowledged the attainment of the seven meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
“Free from envy” means without jealousy. Through this, he manifested his confidence in the Great Man. Those attainments of the Bodhisatta—
For one who has been reborn and remains there, because of the vastness of his knowledge through familiarity with previous births, their destiny and future state become manifest.
Consequently, the certainty arose in him: "These indeed are included within the round of existence. Therefore he said: "This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment," and so forth.
Even for some, though it may bring about the transcendence of the cultivation of dispassion, it does not lead to their ultimate...
It brings about transcendence, yet it itself is still included within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);
therefore, it does not lead to disenchantment with the round, nor, by that same token, to dispassion, nor to the cessation of evil states such as lust, nor to their pacification;
consequently, it does not lead to the full understanding of those phenomena that ought to be fully understood... [and so forth].
The construction is: “it leads to.
By saying “only as far as rebirth in the base of nothingness,” he speaks by taking the highest among the seven meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Because it is appropriate to seek the state of non-falling (*acuti-dhamma*) again and again after rising [from it], that too is indeed a state not transcending the nature of birth (*jāti-dhamma*).
He said, "The Great Being abandons," and so forth, beginning with "and the state he reaches.

"From that time on" means from the moment he fully understood the course and the future destiny of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). "By way of flies" means by way of the food being infested with flies;
the intention is that he did not resolve to eat [the food]. "With great effort"—this refers to [his staying] there for a few days.
This was said with reference solely to the practice of meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*), and not like others who perform the preliminary work of the kasiṇas and so forth.
For indeed, for Bodhisattvas in their final existence, there is nothing at all difficult regarding the production of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Without having adorned" means having adorned repeatedly, again and again, thinking, "There is no purpose served by this."
278. Regarding the phrase "merely grasped by speech," the meaning here should be understood according to the method explained previously.
279. *Mahāvelā* means like a great shore (*mahāvelā*); the sense is that it is like a vast coastal bank due to its mass of abundant sand.
Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'a great heap of sand. The words *uru*, *maru*, *sikatā*, *vālukā*, *vaṇṇu*, and *vālikā* are synonyms.
The meaning is the same; there is only a difference in the phrasing.
A "senānigama" is a place where an army has marched to or settled; it is a place where an army is stationed. However, this specific designation "senānigāma" is a later convention.
Furthermore, this is an indication of the village used as a resort for alms. "In the subsequent sutta" refers to the Mahāsaccaka Sutta.
But here, the "Bodhi-seat" (bodhipallaṅka) is intended, because it is spoken of in the context of the Noble Quest. Furthermore,
since the specific object of the two terms taken together as "knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) has not been specified, and because the word "mine" (me) is used,
it indicates a specific kind of knowledge capable of awakening all those to be trained, rather than mere knowledge in general.
"It is not merely seeing," he said, "for my omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), capable of seeing all phenomena, has arisen.

Regarding "for the sake of unshakability": because it culminates in liberation, it is entirely incapable of being disturbed by opposing states. Therefore he said, "it is not shaken by lust and the other [defilements].
Furthermore, even with respect to the continuity of the object, there is a distinction among those things that take it as their object, as follows:
“He said ‘in the imperturbable abiding’ because it has an unshakable object.
“The knowledge of reviewing as well” means not only omniscient knowledge, but also the nineteenfold knowledge of reviewing regarding the True Dhamma of penetration as it was attained.
“Penetrated” means by means of self-enlightened knowledge, through the process of direct penetration in the manner of “This is suffering,” and so forth.

"Attained" means having understood it as it truly is. "Profound" means that, like the great ocean, it cannot find a footing for the knowledge of others—except for those who have accumulated and matured the equipment of knowledge. Therefore he said:
"This is a statement negating its superficiality. That which cannot find a footing is, by virtue of being impossible to fathom...
And because it cannot be seen even in its own form, he said, "It is difficult to see precisely because of its profundity.

It is "to be seen with difficulty" (dukkhena daṭṭhabbo), meaning it can be seen only with great hardship by someone. But as for that which cannot even be seen, there is no talk at all of fathoming it and awakening to it step by step;
thus he said, "It is difficult to awaken to precisely because it is difficult to see. It is to be understood with difficulty.

Because awakening is difficult to achieve. In this context, the following passage from the Sutta should be cited: "What do you think, monks, which is more difficult to do or more difficult to accomplish?

Or, it is "peaceful" (santo) because its object is peaceful; it is "extinguished" (nibbuto) because all feverish distress has been extinguished; or it is "exquisite" (paṇīto) because it has been brought to a state of excellence; and in the sense of being non-satiating...
It is like delicious food that is not satiating. And herein, the truth of cessation is "peaceful" and its object is peaceful;
the truth of the path is peaceful and its object is peaceful—thus it is "peaceful as an object.

Because of the absence of defilements and formations whose intrinsic nature is unpacified, and because of its state of being peaceful and sublime due to the extinction of all feverish distress, it possesses the quality of being "unfailing" (asecanaka).
The state of being untormenting is to be seen. Therefore he said: "This pair was spoken of with reference only to the supramundane.

Because it is the domain of supreme knowledge, it cannot be fathomed by mere reasoning; for that very reason, because it is the range of subtle knowledge, it is delicate. And because its intrinsic nature is subtle, it is refined;
and because it is not the domain of fools, it is to be known only by the wise—thus it is "to be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*). They adhere...
They are called *ālaya* in the sense that they are resorted to for the purpose of delight; thus, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) are *ālaya*.

They are called *ālaya* because one clings to them, resorts to them, and takes delight in them; thus, the modes of craving (*taṇhāvicaritāni*) are *ālaya*. "They delight" means they find pleasure, play, and frolic. "Delighting in *ālaya*" means being devoted to *ālaya*.
"With reference to the word *ṭhāna*" means with reference to the term *ṭhāna*. In terms of meaning, however, *ṭhāna* is dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
This is what is intended. It is called a "condition" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands depending upon it;

thus, ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other factors that serve as conditions for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth are meant. These are the conditions for these volitional formations and the rest, hence they are "specific conditions" (*idappaccaya*).

Ignorance and the others are themselves the "state of specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*), just as one says "the god himself is the divinity. Alternatively, it is the state belonging to those specific conditions, namely ignorance and the rest.
The state of being a condition for the fruit, the capacity to produce it, is "this-conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*).

By this, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is shown as having the characteristic of a capable condition. It is called "dependent origination" because the fruit arises dependently (*paṭicca*) from this.
Even by these two terms, the meaning of conditionality among phenomena is clarified. Therefore, he said: "This is the [meaning] of conditions such as volitional formations..."
“Designation. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*.

Regarding the phrase “the stilling of all formations,” etc.: “all” refers to everything denoted by the terms “stilling of all formations” and so forth, and in its ultimate sense, this is nibbāna alone.
Now, in order to show that it is nibbāna, the passage beginning with “for because” was stated. “It” refers to nibbāna.

“Having come” means by reason of its being the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for the Noble Path. “They subside” means they subside by way of the cessation of rebirth-linking (appaṭisandhika-upasama).
Being thus subsided, they are said to be “especially calmed”; hence he says, “they become fully stilled” (vūpasammanti).
By this, he shows that “nibbāna is the allaying of all formations” (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha), because all formations subside therein. [It is] dissociated from all conditioned things.
And the manner in which Nibbāna is the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) should be understood according to the method already explained above.

The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well. "Relinquished" means they have been abandoned by way of complete eradication. "All craving" refers to all craving, including its eight hundred varieties.
"All defilements of lust" refers to all forms of lust that are defilements, such as the divisions of sensual lust (kāmarāga), form-lust (rūparāga), and so forth.

Alternatively, all defilements (*kilesa*) here should be understood as "defilement-passions" (*kilesarāga*), and not merely specific types of greed (*lobha*), because they bring about a state of transformation in the mind.
As it is said: "A lustful mind is transformed; a hateful mind is transformed; a deluded mind is transformed.
They "fade away" (*virajjanti*) means they disintegrate.
Physical fatigue and bodily affliction are to be understood by way of backache, dryness of the palate and throat, and so forth, resulting from sitting for a long time and speaking for a long time.
And this is said with reference to those who do not understand the meaning of the teaching;
however, for those who do understand, even the physical exertion of the teaching is no exertion for the Teacher. Therefore the Blessed One said: "And there is no legal issue concerning me..."
"...he harassed. For this very reason he said: "That which is called teaching those who do not know would be weariness for me.
"Both" means both mental weariness and mental harassment; neither of these exists for the Buddhas because they were utterly eradicated even at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
"Anubrūhanaṃ" means a compounding or a gathering together. "So" is the particle "apissu. "Maṃ" is used in the sense of the genitive (possessive) case through its connection with the prefix *paṭi*.
He said "mine" (*mamā*) as a term of application. Or, they are called *anacchariyā* because they have reached a state of excellence;

for the vowel *a-* also has the sense of excellence, as in the expression "the qualities of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*). Having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramiyo*) for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons solely for the purpose of sharing the Dhamma with the world including its devas, he has now attained the sovereignty of the Dhamma.
In this regard, it should be understood that there is the demonstration of the attainment of non-concern, the wonderful nature of the meaning of the verses, and the attainment of their growth.
For the meaning of the verses is not [merely] through the literal sense; rather, "they became objects of the range" means they appeared before him.
And since appearing before him is a matter of being reflected upon, he said, "they reached the state of being to be thoroughly reflected upon."
If it were indeed an easy practice, why would there be difficulty? To this he says: “But at the time of fulfilling the perfections,” and so forth.
These [things] are difficult to renounce for one who gives them away. Or, *ha* is a particle used in the sense of “clever” (*byatta*).
Some say it has the sense of certainty (*ekamsattha*). Thus, *ha byattaṃ*, or with certainty (*ekaṃsena*), it is sufficient (*alaṃ*)—meaning useless—for such a Dhamma attained through hardship.
"Taught" (*desita*) is the construction [of the term]. Or, *hala* is a word synonymous with *ala*, as in "I say they are *hala*" (*halanti vadāmī*) and so forth.
"By those touched by lust and hatred" means by those overwhelmed and contacted by lust and hatred, as by a snake touched by its venom.
"Followed by lust and hatred" means pursued by lust and hatred.

Because they are stained by passion for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and stained by passion for existence (*bhavarāga*), they are shrouded by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); because they are stained by passion for views (*diṭṭhirāga*), they are possessed of a distorted adherence.
"They shall not see" means they will not penetrate the Dhamma as it truly is.

"To cause them to grasp thus" means to make them know the Dhamma as it truly is according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) through [the teaching] beginning with "impermanent. Their being overcome by lust and hatred is likewise due solely to their state of delusion.
He said, "Enveloped by a mass of darkness.
To clarify the reason for his falling into a state of indifference toward teaching the Dhamma, he himself raises the objection beginning with "But why," and so forth.
In that context, the phrase "in an unrecognized guise" refers to his not having entered into the status of a disciple of the Blessed One.
"In another form. Some say "in the guise of an ascetic," but that [guise] would surely vanish upon the attainment of Arahatship.
There are three reasons for falling into indolence: the strength of the opposing factor, the profundity of the Dhamma, and an excessive reverence for it.
To demonstrate these, the passage beginning with "For he... was commenced. (In this context, the opposing factors...)
Indeed, the defilements such as lust and the rest are so called because they create obstacles to right practice.

Due to their powerful nature, having been cultivated for a long time, and being difficult to purify from the continuum of sentient beings, they—like intoxicated elephants—overpower and overwhelm weak men, leading them to ruin and disaster;
[they do this] within a well-constructed, dense settlement measuring many hundreds of yojanas in length and breadth.

They even lie down upon a thorny difficult path. However, the passage beginning with "Then for her" (*athassā*) was spoken to demonstrate the difficulty of purification due to its far-reaching divisions and its stubbornness to sever.
In that context: a gourd filled with sour gruel because it is not polished on the inside;

a jar filled with buttermilk because it has been kept for a long time; a rag soaked in fat because it is weak and saturated with oiliness; and a hand smeared with ointment because it is mixed with oil.
These are said to be difficult to purify because they are of inferior quality by way of their continuity as a mass of form and because their defilement is of recent duration;
however, the defilement by the *kilesas* (defilements) is even more difficult to purify because it is beginningless and lies latent. Therefore he said, "extremely defiled.
And just as they are more difficult to purify, so too are they deep, hard to see, and difficult to penetrate.
The aforementioned similes are inferior similes.
Through the removal of opposing factors, even a profound Dhamma may become clearly manifest. However, the removal of opposing factors is dependent upon right practice;
that [right practice] depends upon hearing the true Dhamma; and that [hearing the true Dhamma] is contingent upon confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma.

He said "Furthermore" (*apica*) and so forth to show that [the eye] is caused by the entreaty of those worthy of respect, and that it is the sign for the Brahma-invocation regarding the practice of the Dhamma by beings in the womb.
"Little dust" (*apparaja*) refers to that which has little passion-dust (*rāgaraja*) and other defilements; thus, it is an "eye with little dust," meaning the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).

Having established that they possess such a nature, the meaning of "those of a nature with little dust" (*apparajakkhajātiko*) is elucidated by the passage beginning with "consisting of wisdom" (*paññāmaya*).
Alternatively, the etymological meaning of the word may also be possible as follows: those whose nature consists of having little dust, such as passion (*rāga*), are "of a nature with little dust.
Together with the taking of refuge and the dedication for the welfare of others, the ten bases of meritorious action beginning with giving (*dāna*) amount to twelve.
It is said, “by way of the twelve bases for the performance of merit.

By means of their own inspired intuition— hammered out by reasoning and followed by inquiry— [the teachings] were conceived by six teachers such as Pūraṇa and others, who claimed the status of teachers but were defiled by the stains of passion and so forth,
and who remained in the state of being poets of thought through the composition of mere wordplay.
It is said that they deceived the world, which had become curious upon hearing the rumors of the Buddha’s great renown;
standing in hypocrisy and claiming omniscience, they proclaimed whatever was contrary to the Dhamma as being the Dhamma. Therefore he says: “For they, having arisen earlier,” and so forth.
“Open this”: this [gate] of the city of Nibbāna, which has been closed since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation...
“Open wide the great door of the Noble Path” means: open, that is, reveal it, by means of the hand of the teaching of the True Dhamma.
He said, “as upon the summit of a rocky mountain,” because a rocky mountain is high and firm, unlike a mountain of earth or a mixed mountain.
“The palace made of Dhamma” refers to the supramundane Dhamma; for that indeed brings about complete confidence.
And it is like a palace in the sense of having ascended above all phenomena (*dhamma*). Alternatively, the word *dhamma* here refers to wisdom (*paññā*).
For that [wisdom] is defined in the Abhidhamma as a "palace" in the sense of having ascended above. Thus it is said:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, free from sorrow, one looks down upon the sorrowing people."
“As one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground, so does the wise man look upon the foolish.
“Arise! means: arise from the state of weariness caused by falling into a contraction known as indifference toward the teaching of the Dhamma.
283. *Abhipatthanā* (aspiration) is the earnest entreaty made after having attended upon those worthy of honor, for the sake of a more weighty purpose.
Since that too, in its essential meaning, is simply a request, he said: "‘Entreaty’ means ‘asking.
Because this pair of knowledges does not have as their object merely a limited portion [of the world] and belongs exclusively to the Buddhas, they are called the "Buddha-eye"; thus he said:
"For these two knowledges are named the Buddha-eye. Regarding "the three path-knowledges," [this refers to] the lower ones.
The name "Dhammacakkhu" (the Eye of Dhamma) is applied to the three knowledges of the path because they consist merely in the seeing of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

Since those knowledges are described as being like lightning, whereas the knowledge of the supreme path—having reached the culmination of the function of knowledge—is not a mere seeing, it is not called "Dhammacakkhu"; therefore, it is described as being like a thunderbolt.
"By the method stated" means by the method stated here regarding those "with little dust in their eyes.
Since those with dull defilements are called "those with little dust in their eyes," therefore those with abundant defilements should be understood as "those with much dust in their eyes.

They are sharp, keen, and clear because of their capacity to destroy opposing factors; by way of the opposite of what was stated, they are blunt. The "modes" such as faith refer to the various ways of believing and so forth.
He says: "Sundara" means beautiful. In the *Sammohavinodanī*, however, it is stated: "Those whose factors such as disposition (*āsaya*) and so forth are beautiful are 'of good form' (*svākāra*);
those who are the opposite are 'of two-fold form' (*dvākāra*). This should be understood as being entirely consistent with and in agreement with this commentary on the meaning.
"Reason" (*kāraṇa*) refers to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), or else to the Truths (*sacca*).

"Ayaṃ panettha pāḷī" (But this is the text here) means that in the exposition of the meaning of the terms "those with little dust in their eyes" and so forth, this is the text that elucidates that meaning.
The strength of the factors that bring about the maturation of liberation—such as faith and the rest—occurs precisely through the weakness of the unwholesome states that are their opposites;
and the strength of those [unwholesome states] occurs through the weakness of faith and the rest.

The presence or absence of those qualities that ripen for liberation is shown in the Pāḷi by way of the classification into those with little dust in their eyes (*apparajakkha*) and those with much dust in their eyes (*mahārajakkha*), and so forth.
The aggregates (*khandha*) and so on are themselves the world (*loka*) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.

The world consisting of the state of prosperity (*sampattibhava*) is the "world of prosperity"; this refers to the state of rebirth known as a happy destination (*sugati*). It is called "prosperity" because prosperity arises by means of it.
The world of the origin of success consists of the kamma-process existence that leads to a happy destination.
The world of the origin of failure consists of the kamma-process existence reckoned as a miserable destination that leads to a miserable destination.
Furthermore, having analyzed the world by way of single and dual categories and so forth, it was stated, "One world," and so on. [These refer to] nutriment and the rest.
For conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), which subsist by means of nutriment, are called "the world" (loka) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. Herein, regarding the statement "one world:

all beings subsist by means of nutriment," according to that discourse which is expressed in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhānā kathā) concerning the dependence of the activity of all conditioned phenomena on conditions, all conditioned phenomena constitute one single world, because there is no other mode [of classification]. Regarding the statements "two worlds," and so forth—
The meaning should be understood by this method. Furthermore, Nibbāna is not included here by the mention of "name" because its intrinsic nature is non-luminous (*aloka-sabhāva*).
But would it not follow that even the Path and the Fruits are "worldly" (*loka*) in this context—since they are said to be "subsisting by nutriment"—because they exist in dependence on conditions?

It does not so follow, because here the term "world" (*loka*) is intended to refer specifically to those phenomena belonging to the Truth of Suffering which are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*). Alternatively, ...
"Does not break up, does not disintegrate"—that which is grasped in such a way does not exist; thus it is called "the world" (*loka*).

For those who are free from such grasping—the supramundane (*lokuttara*)—there is no state of being "worldly. The aggregates that serve as the objects of clinging are the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*).
"Ten bases" (*dasāyatanāni*) refers to the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*). The rest here is easily understood.

Because one whose inclination is toward the turning away from the round (vivatta-jjhāsaya) intends this, and because for such a person all kamma of the three planes appears as something to be censured and abandoned, it is said:
"All volitional formations are blameworthy; all kamma leading to existence is blameworthy.
In each of the five dyads beginning with those of little dust in the eyes and those of much dust in the eyes, ten [types of persons] are grouped together, making fifty.

"It is said that he knows these five faculties by their modes. Alternatively, it is stated thus because he knows the relative degrees of the faculties—faith and the rest—by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

And herein, as the Blessed One adverts [to beings] by way of their being "few with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkha*) and so forth, or their being "capable" (*bhabba*) and so forth, those beings appear to him in groups, not individually.

"Uppalinī" means "that in which there are blue lotuses (*uppala*)," referring to both a grove and a body of water; however, since it is a body of water that is intended here, he says "in a blue-lotus grove.
Those which grow and increase while remaining submerged within the water are called "those nourished while submerged" (*antonimuggaposīni*).
They are "explained" in the sense that they are elucidated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, or stated right here [in the commentary] by the words "and others as well," and so forth.
*Ugghaṭitaññū*: "Ugghaṭita" means the breaking open of knowledge; the meaning is that one knows as soon as knowledge has been broken open. *Vipañcitaññū*:
one who knows the meaning only when it is explained in detail (*vipañcita*) and expanded upon. *Neyyo*: one who is to be led by means of brief indications (*uddesa*) and so forth.
*Saha udāhaṭavelāya*: "at the very moment of being uttered"; that is, as soon as it has been spoken. *Dhammābhisamayo*: the realization of the Dhamma, namely, the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

"Realization together with knowledge. Regarding "this is called": when the summary matrix (mātikā) is established by way of the method beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness," a person capable of attaining arahantship by directing knowledge according to the sequence of the teaching is called "one who understands through a condensed [explanation] (ugghaṭitaññū).
Regarding "this is called": this refers to the matrix established in brief.
Setting aside the detailed analysis of the meaning, a person capable of attaining *arahantship* is called "one who understands through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*).

"By way of summary" (*uddesato*) means by reason of a summary; that is, for one who is being given a summary or causing a summary to be given. "By way of inquiry" (*paripucchato*) means for one who inquires into the meaning.
"The realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually" (*anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti*) means the attainment of *arahantship* occurs step by step.

There is no realization of the Dhamma through that birth; thus, with that personal existence (*attabhāva*), he is unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit, or even at least meditative absorption (*jhāna*) or insight (*vipassanā*).
This person is called "one for whom the word is the limit" (*padaparamo*); this person is so called because for him the word (*pada*)—that is, the mere letter—is the limit.

"By the obstruction of kamma" means by the fivefold karma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). "By the obstruction of ripening" (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*) refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) without roots.
Since there is no penetration of the Noble Path even for those with two roots, rebirth-linking with two roots should also be understood as "an obstruction of ripening.
"By the obstruction of defilements" (*kilesa-āvaraṇa*) refers to fixed wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). "Lacking faith" (*assaddha*)...
Those devoid of faith in the Buddha and the others. "Lacking desire" (*acchandikā*) means lacking the wholesome desire for the wish to act.
The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of being "lacking desire. "Lacking wisdom" (*duppaññā*) means being deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*).
However, even one whose life-continuum wisdom is complete, if that life-continuum does not serve as a condition for the supramundane (*lokuttara*), is likewise "lacking wisdom."

"Unable to enter into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states" means they are incapable of entering—that is, of attaining—the path known as the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
"Not by the obstruction of kamma," and so forth, should be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated.
It is the door to Nibbāna, the path for entering it; it has been opened and set forth by the self-existent knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa) through the proximate cause of great compassion.
Because it has been realized. "Let them release their faith" means: let them enter into their own faith; the meaning is, let them establish the mode of believing.
"Well-functioning" means it is capable of proceeding with ease and without difficulty. "I thought:

'I have not spoken, nor shall I speak,'" [refers to] the thought associated with the teaching of the Dhamma that proceeded thus from the seventh week. 284. "'I shall teach the Dhamma'—[this refers to] the thought connected with the teaching of the Dhamma that had thus proceeded."
However, because it arose specifically on the eighth week, it is said, "on the eighth week.
This is not because there exists a distinct eighth week characterized by specific functions as there are for the other weeks.
They "open" means that through the intervention of deities, their limbs and members are opened, and they manifest clearly to people, breaking out from their sleep.

The meaning is as follows: Having displayed what is known as the "Earth-Turning Shrine" caused by the intensity of the thought that arose—"I shall not return until I have attained Buddhahood"—and having spoken of the three kingdoms by way of the Śākya, Koliya, and Malla dynasties, she departed for the foot of the tree, that is, the foot of the *nigrodha* tree; and as she was departing, the Great Being showed her his form.
Regarding the taking of the golden platter, she departed, saying, "That has already been relinquished by you.
"Having spent the day in meditation" means having dwelt in the day's abiding by entering into various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is according to the method set forth in the Sutta beginning with: "Let skin, sinew, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up."
Having resolved upon fourfold energy, [the Nāga king] approached, completely enveloping him, and said: "Arise, Siddhattha! I [am the owner] of this couch."
Having said, "This is suitable," he pointed to his own retinue while establishing his witness there, exclaiming all at once, "This alone is suitable!
This alone is suitable! Hearing that, the Great Being...
[as before] ...stretched out his hand. With reference to this it was said:
“This earth is insentient, it does not know pleasure or pain;
yet by the power of my gift, even it shook seven times.

Having purified the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), the connection [of the text] is established by bringing [the subject] forward according to the method of the lion’s backward glance (*sīhāvalokana*). [This refers to] the cycle of existence and its cessation (*vaṭṭavivaṭṭa*).

"Having reflected" refers to the mental attention directed toward the Four Noble Truths. "For the purpose of this cross-legged posture" indicates the specific excellence attained by means of the cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*).

For there, without relinquishing the bliss of liberation that has reached its peak, and while periodically attending to the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), he sat in a single cross-legged posture. "Of some" refers to those who have already attained the Path.
Excluding those deities who have realized cessation and know the qualities of a Buddha even in part,

for others there are yet further factors that establish Buddhahood. From the full moon of Visākha onwards, day and night, for those whose state is constantly concentrated upon the qualities of a Buddha,
there are other means of accomplishing Buddhahood— the realization of the state of being a Buddha such that others perceive, "This one is a Buddha."
The construction is: "Are there indeed phenomena to be eliminated?
"With unblinking eyes" means with eyes free from blinking due to the unwavering expansion of clarity resulting from the thrill of joy in the Dhamma.
"On the jeweled walkway" refers to the walkway made of jewels constructed by the deities. And therein, of the seven treatises consisting of jewels...
They say that because of the realization of the jewel of the Dhamma with its infinite methods, that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya.
"In this way" means in the manner about to be described. The comparison is stated because, due to the rays of six colors emerging from his tusks, he was like the Chaddanta elephant lineage.

"Of the same size as the lower storey of the Lohapāsāda" means it was the size of the very first lower storey of the nine-storeyed Lohapāsāda. However, in the *Khandhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated there that it was "of the size of the interior of the treasury chamber.
"Paccaggha" means brand new. Some say it is called "paccaggha" because each individual item is of great value;
that is not correct, for the Blessed Buddhas do not accept or consume things of great value. Regarding the term "piṇḍapāta": [text continues].
He speaks with reference to both the stirred drink and the honey-ball. "This is a thought" refers to the reflection: "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
"By wisdom" means by the state of being wise, which consists in the attainment of proficiency through the mastery of meditative attainments.

"By proficiency" means by way of the state of being competent, which is reckoned as functional wisdom (*pārihāriyapaññā*) and is a condition for the attainment of meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

"Wise" (*medhāvī*) should be understood here as one endowed with *medhā*, which is reckoned as the wisdom of a three-rooted rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the wisdom regarding what is to be done in each particular instance.
"A great loser" (*mahājāniyo*) means one who suffers great loss. Also, [the term] "footsteps of the coming... [is used].

"‘It does not exist’—this is what must first be said; then, even if I were to go there, having gone, he would lack even the clarity of hearing to hear the Dhamma being taught there"—this is the construction [of the sentence].
But is it not possible for the Blessed One, through his own power as a Buddha, to make them understand the Dhamma?
Yes, it is not possible; for without the voice of another, [the teaching] cannot reach the disciples.

The realization of the Dhamma occurs [only through these conditions]; otherwise, there would have to be a realization of the Dhamma even for one devoid of the other conditions, but that is not the case.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, there are these two conditions for the arising of right view:
the voice of another and wise attention within oneself. In the Canon, it is stated that Rāma alone was a master of the meditative attainments.
"He has arrived, but not for water"—this was said by the Bodhisattva on account of the time of their meeting.

For even while he had previously been dwelling there engaged in his practice, having heard that the Great Being had quickly attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
When the Great Being subsequently departed from there, he applied himself and strove, and before long...
He produced the eight attainments (*samāpatti*). Therefore it was said: “He saw that he had been reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*)”;
this is to be connected with the phrase “these eight brahmins. “Possessing six factors” (*chaḷaṅgavā*) means one who knows the six factors.

“The mantra” (*manta*) refers to the words of a mantra. The word “having reflected” (*nijjhāyitvā*) is an ellipsis; the meaning is “having deliberated. “They declared” (*viyākariṃsu*) means they spoke.
“According to the words of the mantra” means in accordance with the Vedic utterances designated as *lakṣaṇa-mantras*. “Gone” means those who have practiced.
Unable to determine [the truth] according to the fixed rule stated in the passage, “There are only two destinations, no other,” the brahmins followed exactly what was prescribed;
they did not expect the Great Man to attain Buddhahood. But these, Koṇḍañña and the others—
Because they have reached the certainty that "the Buddha will surely appear," they have transcended the words of the mantras.
"A full bowl" refers to a gift given out of joy. "Free from doubt" means free from conceptual construction; it is not a twofold doubt.
"At the time of sowing" means at the time of planting. Taking the best [grain] there for the purpose of sowing, he gave the gift.
This refers to the offering of the first-fruits of the seed. The same principle applies to the first-fruits of the threshing floor and so forth. Regarding the grain and fruit:

it is at the time when they are not yet over-ripe, that is, at the time of threshing. "Threshing" (*lāyana*) refers to the threshing of the standing crop. Just as what has been reaped is made into a handful and bound together by way of a braid, that braiding is called "braiding" (*veṇikaraṇa*).
A "braid" (*veṇi*), however, is a bundle bound for the purpose of being carried by men. On the day of placing those bundles on the threshing floor, the "first-fruits" (*agga*)—
*Khala-agga-dāna*: Having taken the best portion from the threshing floor. *Bhaṇḍa-agga-dāna*: On the day of making a heap of the harvested rice, taking the best portion and giving it as an offering.
*Koṭṭha-agga-dāna*: On the day of putting the grain into the storehouse, giving an offering. "Having extracted" means having extracted the grain from the threshing floor.
"Because the nine foremost offerings were given"—this is for the purpose of establishing his status as the foremost among those of long-standing seniority (*rattaññū*).
This is stated because [the Buddha] acted while practicing the perfections of his disciples in accordance with the resolution he had made.
For when any of the three types of Bodhisattas reach the culmination of their respective perfections, whatever merit or demerit they have performed results in a very heavy ripening;
and furthermore, how could the status of being foremost among those of long-standing seniority be established without the Dhamma being realized first?
"Indeed, these five bhikkhus are very helpful"—this, moreover, is merely a recollection of assistance based on familiarity, similar to the recollection of Āḷāra Kālāma. 285.
He opens [the door] in the middle. Therefore he said, "in a place three gavutas apart. When it is not being joined, the accusative case is used.
It does not take the nominative case because, in this context, the dative case is intended due to its connection with the word *antara*.
Therefore he said: "But because it is joined with the word *antara*, the accusative case is used.

Having overcome all phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*) by means of the clear realization of full comprehension (*pariññā-abhisamaya*), [he transcends] the phenomena of the four planes (*catubhūmaka-dhamma*).
Because all knowable objects have been abandoned in their entirety through the abandonment of the veil of the knowable, I have known them with omniscient knowledge.
Even that which is not to be abandoned—namely, the wholesome and the indeterminate—is said to "not exist" because it has been abandoned by the destruction of the defilements bound to it;
thus he says, "He stands having relinquished all phenomena of the three planes. "From the perspective of the object" means by way of making it an object.

"Although there is no instruction from another regarding the attainment of even mundane states such as that of the Lord of the World, there is not even a trace of supramundane states in him," thus he said, "I have no teacher regarding supramundane states.
"A counterpart person" (paṭibhāgapuggala) means a person who serves as a substitute by way of qualities such as virtue and so forth. "With a cause" (sahetunā):
By means of the Dhamma together with its wonders. "By way of method" means by the procedure beginning with direct knowledge (*abhijānanatā*).
"The four truths" is said because there is no object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) apart from them. "A Buddha himself" means awakened by his own self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*).

"Become cool" due to the absence of feverish distress (*pariḷāha*). For that very reason, he is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*). "I shall strike" (*āhañchanti* = *āhanissāmi*) [the drum] for those who are to be trained (*veneyya*).
The Teacher’s preaching of the Dhamma, having made a proclamation for the attainment of the Deathless (*amata*), is called the "Deathless Drum" (*amatadundubhi*).
"One of infinite knowledge who has conquered the defilements" is *Anantajina*.
"It might even be so named"—the intention is that such a jewel of a form as this ought to possess such knowledge. For this became the condition for his going forth; he had performed his duties.
This is the meaning. For the Blessed One set out on that path on foot for the purpose of meeting him.

"Endowed with constituent parts" means endowed with the limbs and members known as the various bodily parts. "Is distressed" (*aṭṭīyati*) means he becomes distressed; the sense is that he falls into mental grief (*domanassa*).

"Reborn in the Aviha [heaven]" means those who have taken birth among the Aviha deities. "Liberated" means liberated by the liberation of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala-vimutti*). Having abandoned them...

“They attained divine union with their human bodies”: those such as Upaka, having abandoned the human personal existence (attabhāva), were reborn in the Aviha heaven immediately upon abandoning the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana).
Then, through the attainment of the supreme path, they transcended the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) by means of divine union. 286. “They established [the rule]”:
they made a formal determination (saṇṭhaṃ kiriyākāraṃ) that “he is not to be saluted,” and so forth. Therefore he said:
“*Katikaṃ akaṃsu*”: from the standpoint of their former exertion, that is, from having previously undertaken difficult practices.
“*Pabhāvitaṃ*”: it is originated by speech; the meaning is the utterance of words. [He said this] so that they would not be despondent, thinking, “This one will not attain any distinction.
“Do not think, ‘We shall go wherever we please. “*Obhāso*”: the light of insight (*vipassanā*). “*Nimittaṃ*”: the sign.
The sign of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-nimitta*). "By a single word" means by a single expression.

Having gained mindfulness [with the thought], "By him nothing wrong has ever been spoken even in the past," he became one who speaks according to reality (*yathābhūta-vādī*), and thus reverence arose [in others].
He remained within the monastery itself, being looked after by those monks like a young boy. "Mala" means defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
“Nīhaṭabhatta” means one for whom alms-food has been brought out from the village and offered;

[thus it refers] to the Blessed One by that name. “This much of the path of discourse” means the entire course of the teaching, beginning with “Monks, there are these two searches” and ending with the phrase “there is now no further becoming. Although here—“You too... [the text continues:]
“The Noble Search is your search, insofar as you have entered upon the path that I and the group-of-five monks have entered upon”—this is the word of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
By this [statement], however—“Bhikkhus, being myself subject to birth... [and so on]...
I attained the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; then, bhikkhus, the group-of-five monks... [is explained].

It is said: "The Blessed One spoke of that Noble Quest which you and the group of five have now ascended upon the path, even as I did," because the meaning of this very passage from the Sutta—“When the bhikkhus were thus exhorted by me... [and so on]... they attained Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage... there is now no further existence”—has been fully elucidated.
"Your search" (*tumhākaṃ pariyesanā*). He brought this up showing only this single connection. 287.
"Even for those who have gone forth" (*anagāriyānam-pi*) means even for those who have renounced the world.

There is a "noble-less search" (*anariya-pariyesanā*) by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, because of enjoying them with attachment and so forth. There is also a noble-less search by way of wrong livelihood; therefore...
The phrase "by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure" is stated for the sake of specification, because enjoyment characterized by desire and lust is intended here.
Now, in order to identify the strands of sensual pleasure among the four conditions, the passage beginning with "Therein... is stated.

"The flavor of enjoyment" refers to the joy and mental happiness derived from the condition of enjoyment. However, this is termed "flavor" (rasa) by virtue of its similarity to a taste, based on its being grasped as such.

It is spoken of [as such], but not by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Based on grasping it as an intrinsic nature, joy and gladness would have a mental state (*dhamma*) as their object, not a flavor (*rasa*) as their object.
"Enjoyment without reflection" means enjoyment devoid of reflection; the meaning is that it is enjoyment by way of being infatuated and so forth, without regard for the purpose of this [object].
"Infatuated" (*gadhitā*) means bound by craving. "Deluded" (*mucchitā*)...
They have fallen into fainting, delusion, and negligence. "Plunged" (*ajjhogāḷhā*) means thoroughly immersed; they remain having entered into each respective object.
"Not seeing the danger" means not knowing the fault in enjoyment accompanied by desire and lust.
"The escape" (*nissaraṇaṃ*) is that by which one escapes—that is, transcends—the danger caused by unreflective enjoyment; it is the knowledge of reflection.
“Pāsarāsi” means a heap of snares. For when a hunter sets a snare, he does not set only one, nor does he set it in only one place;
rather, having observed the paths by which various deer approach, he sets many snares here and there.
Therefore, taking them as a single unit in the mind, it is called “a heap of snares. Or, [it refers to] a net.
Because of the great number of sand particles, it is called a "heap of sand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Pāsarāsi Sutta* is completed. 7.
The *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta* (The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint).

288. *Setaparivāra* means having a white covering; the meaning is that it has white-colored ornaments. Previously, however, in the phrase “white ornaments,” the ornamentation of the horse was taken [as the referent];
here, it refers to the ornaments to be made on the components of the chariot, such as the wheel-rims, the felloes, and so forth.
*Evaṃ vuttena* means by what was spoken in this manner—namely, in the sequence beginning with “with a white [horse], indeed”—in the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya. *Nātimahā*.
For the sake of ease in moving about the battlefield. "The warrior and the charioteer"—this refers to two; or with the one who hands him weapons, three.
He circumambulates the city for the sake of beautifying the city. This, it is said, was the established custom handed down through tradition, perfected by birth, belonging to that Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi.
Therefore he said: "After this many days," and so forth. By way of this custom...
The city-dwellers also act accordingly. Those engaged in reciting auspicious words concerning merit are the *māṅgalikas*. Those who wish for a state of well-being (*suvatthi*) are the *sovatthikas*.
By the word "etc.," those such as bards (*vandīs*) are included. Regarding "the attainment of fame and glory":
this means by the attainment of fame and the attainment of glory; that is to say, by the attainment of a retinue and the attainment of the splendor of wealth.
He set out toward the city at his own time for alms-round. Regarding the phrase "he thinks he is wise," the word *maññeti* here is a particle (*nipātapada*) synonymous with *maññati*.
Showing its meaning by supplying the word *iti*, the author says:
"he thinks [thus]: 'I am wise. This is stated in the form of a question seeking consent; therefore, he says: "or rather not?"
“Venerable Vacchāyana, what do you think of the discernment of the ascetic Gotama?”—repeating this very point that had already been stated, he said, “I consider him wise.
Therefore it was asked: “Does Venerable Vacchāyana consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or not?
The intention is: “Speak to him as you see fit.”
“I am who?”—this shows that [the matter] is beyond his scope. Regarding the phrase “And who?,” he says “From where?
because it is a nominative singular used in the sense of a cause or source. Likewise, he says, “By what means shall I know? the intention being:
“That means by which I might know the analytical clarity of the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama does not exist in me. It is the Buddha alone [who knows].
Even if one were so, it would not be possible for one who is not a Buddha to know in every way the power of a Buddha’s knowledge.

For this has been said: "But, monks, that by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata is trifling, insignificant, merely a matter of virtue; there are, monks, other qualities that are profound and difficult to see."
“Difficult to awaken to... [and so on] ...by whom one might rightly speak the true praise of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the phrase “In this regard,” it refers to the expression: “He too must surely be such as that. “Praised, praised” means he is praised by his own very virtues which are themselves praiseworthy;
it does not mean by his reputation. The sense is that he is worthy of praise precisely because of the nature of his praise.
Therefore he said, "Of all virtues," and so forth. "The jewel-treasure" refers to the jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
The second alternative, "or by those who are praised," is taken in order to show that [this quality] is praised even among those who are themselves praised in the world including the devas.
"Araṇīya" means purpose; that which dwells in that very [purpose] is "vasa" (abode); thus it is "atthavasa," meaning that which constitutes the benefit (*ānisamsa*) of each respective application.
He said, "They bear fruit" means "they have purpose and benefit. Alternatively, *atthavaso* is that which has purpose (*attha*)—as defined by the characteristics already stated—as its basis (*vaso*);
thus it is a cause. "One who dwells in the elephant forest" refers to one who lives in the forest where noble elephants roam for the purpose of capturing them.
"One whose craft is unmastered" refers to one who has not trained in the art of elephant-lore, [relying] merely on seeing a footprint that is long and wide.
“‘Great indeed, sirs, is this nāga!’—this is because [the person] reached a conclusion based on what had been said up to that point. However, regarding the passage spoken later by the Blessed One:

a man who has mastered his craft and comes as a forest-guardian of elephants, having understood the deceptive nature of the term ‘nāga’—which refers to something long, broad, high, and inhabited—he does not reach a conclusion at that much alone;
rather, he reaches a conclusion only upon seeing a great elephant. Thus, knowledge is attained.”

"Herein" refers to the steps of knowledge (*ñāṇapada*); these are the jhānas and so forth attained through the discipline (*vinaya*) because they have been disciplined within the Dhamma and Vinaya by wise Kṣatriyas and others.

For these are the places trodden upon by the teaching-knowledge of the Tathāgata, that elephant among scents. However, the number "four" is given because only those of four types—wise Kṣatriyas and so forth—are included here as those to be trained (*vineyya*).
289. Regarding individuals, the designation "wise" (*paṇḍita*) is based precisely on their skillfulness in wisdom (*paññā*) and their capacity to perceive subtle meanings;
thus it is said, "capable of penetrating subtle internal meanings. Here, the word *kata* has the sense of "accomplished" (*nipphanna*).

That which others proclaim here, or by means of which they proclaim, is "the proclamation of others" (*parappavāda*), that is, the doctrine of others (*parasamaya*). Alternatively, the proclamation made by others is "the proclamation of others" (*parappavāda*).
"Crushing the doctrines of others through debate" refers to both of these taken together, as stated in the Pāḷi;
thus he says, "both when one has understood the doctrines of others and when one has cultivated skill in debate with others.

The meaning is that [this knowledge] is accomplished in regard to the systems of others and in crushing the doctrines of others. "Like a hair-splitter" means resembling a hair-splitter; therefore he says, "similar to an archer who splits a hair."
"Of the hair" (*vālasya*) means of the hair known as "hair" (*vāla*) belonging to one who is split in many ways.
"As if splitting" means as if those splitting a physical object such as a jar with a mallet or similar tool; the intention is that they are splitting the points of view (*diṭṭhigatāni*) definitively.
"They ask a formulated question" means they ask a question composed of words [with the thought]: "We shall ask after having made the hidden meaning concealed."
The passage beginning with “dupadampi” was spoken in order to demonstrate this. That by which one speaks is *vāda*; it means fault (*dosa*).

That which is questioned is *pañha*; it means meaning (*attha*). That by which one questions is *pañha*; it means sound (*sadda*). Taking both of these together, he said, “in such a question,” and so forth.
Furthermore, by saying “one should ask thus, one should answer thus,” he demonstrates the mastery of the training in questioning and answering.
“Seyyo” means “superior”; the intended meaning is that it is the highest gain.

Having thus stated that others do not dare to ask the Blessed One a question even out of fear of the destruction of their own doctrines, he now begins with the words “Moreover” (*apica*) and so forth to show that they do not dare [to ask] even without the destruction of their doctrines.
The mind becomes serene; others even desire to entrust their own persons to him, because that loving-kindness is similar to the radiation of limited loving-kindness (*odhisaka-mettā*).
"Endowed with vision" means endowed with the state of being seen, due to the quality of supreme vision;
the meaning is that they are exceedingly beautiful to behold.
"Disciples by way of going for refuge" means disciples by way of mundane going for refuge; however, discipleship by way of supramundane going for refuge will come later.
And that [discipleship] is spoken of with reference to those who have gone forth, whereas here it is with reference to householders;
in both cases, discipleship should be understood as being through going for refuge. For they see the danger of blame and the next world.
“Noble sons”: there are also noble sons of such conduct. By the word “even slightly,” he explains the meaning of the phrase “we shall not forget.
It is called an *udāna* because it is uttered by way of rapture and joy; or rather, an utterance (*udāharaṇa*) is an *udāna*. Therefore he said:
“he uttered an utterance (*udāhāraṃ udāhari*”). “Of this Dhamma”: of this true Dhamma of penetration, which is preceded by the true Dhamma of practice.

The phrase "the elephant’s footprint simile" refers to the Dhamma being described by way of its resemblance to an elephant’s footprint. "By this much" means by the mere path of discourse spoken by that wanderer.

Granted, even by that path of discourse spoken by him, the Dhamma described as resembling an elephant’s footprint is indeed complete, because it has been proclaimed as leading to Arahantship; however, it is [complete] only in brief, not in detail.
He said: "It is not complete in detail by this much alone.
If the teaching was begun in the same manner as the elephant's footprint simile is completed in detail, then why was it not stated that he is "skilled"?
(This is the objection. 291. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "also in length," he indicates that they are short even in height; for they have low bodies. [They are] tall.
*Uccakā*: "Nisevana" means that which is resorted to, or that which is resorted to therein; here, "resorting" refers to rubbing for the purpose of removing itching.
Therefore he said: "the place rubbed on the part of the body. *Uccā* means not low; the meaning is "possessing height.
*Kāḷārikā* means having sparse teeth; the meaning is "having unevenly spaced teeth. Therefore he said: "of the teeth," and so forth. *Kaḷāratāya* means...
*Viraḷatāya*: "arañjitāni" means colored; the meaning is "scratched. *Kaṇerutāya*: by way of having the shape of a bud.
"Ayaṃ vā": here the word "vā" has the sense of resolving a doubt, just as in other instances such as, "Of these ascetics and brahmins, this one is the most foolish, the most deluded," and so forth.
“Like an elephant forest” means like an elephant forest that serves as the place where the tracks of great elephants, dwarf-elephants, and so forth are seen.

This is because the teaching of the Dhamma, from the beginning up to the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), serves as the place where the tracks of the Tathāgata and those of other external wanderers (*paribbājaka*) are seen.
“From the beginning” means starting from the words “Listen to that. “The skilled elephant-forest keeper” refers to one who knows the elephant forest well.
Like a practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara) because of grasping a measure by way of seeking. "Standing upon the head" means standing at the conclusion of this sutta.
"In this place too" refers even to the point where the meaning of the simile is introduced with the words, "Even so, O brahmins," and so forth.
"Svāyaṃ" takes the mere word *idha*, not the word *idha* as it is to be qualified. For he will say [later]:
“In some cases it is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. It is said with reference to the world because it is expressed in grammatical apposition with the word *loka*.
In the remaining two phrases, however, it should be understood that they are expressed with reference to this or that [object] merely by the proximity of other words.
“Space” refers to a certain location, as the Indasāla Cave is intended here. It is merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
Because even the pointing out of an occasion is impossible.
The specific meanings of terms such as *tathāgata* have already been stated in the *Mūlapariyāya-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*.
Since the *tathāgata* is included within the category of sentient beings, [it is said]: "In this context, however, the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*) is intended."
Having said that, in order to show the particular class of beings and the particular location in which he arises, it was stated:
“Even when arising in the world of beings,” and so forth. Therein, “in this very world-system” (*cakkavāḷa*) means in this very world-sphere (*lokadhātu*).
