“It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise in a single world-sphere... [and so on].

In the passage, "They would arise neither before nor after [one another]," the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*), which serves as the field of birth, is referred to as "a single world system.
However, here, referring specifically to this very world system, it is said, "in this very world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*).

For in the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) consisting of the Three Baskets (*tipiṭaka*) as established at the three councils, there are two types of fields: the field of objective range (*visayakhetta*) and the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*).
Regarding "the field of birth" (*jātikhettam*): among the three kinds of fields, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) apart from this one;
however, there is a sutta stating that they do not arise [elsewhere]. How so? Because [the Buddha] spoke such words as, "I have no teacher, no one equal to me is found;
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One," while standing within this world-system.

When the Blessed One asked, "But, friend Sāriputta, is there now another ascetic or brahmin who is equal to the Blessed One in regard to perfect enlightenment?"—having been thus questioned, venerable sir, I would say, "No. To show the reason for this, he said:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that in a single world-system there should be two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
By showing this sutta, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) has stated that, setting aside this world-system which is the birthplace of Buddhas,
there is no arising [of a Buddha] elsewhere.
Among the four alternatives stated beginning with "by Sujātā," the first alternative is presented by way of demonstrating a practice closer to the state of Buddhahood.
It is said: for one who stands on the practice that is closer [to the goal] is said to "arise," because arising is certain;

how much more so for one standing at the very summit of the practice. The second [explanation] is by way of showing the practice that is close, starting from the going-forth that brings about the state of Buddhahood.
The third is by way of showing the practice for the state of Buddhahood, starting from the fulfillment of the qualities that constitute a Buddha.
For there is no such thing as the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment for Great Beings starting from their rebirth in the Tusita heaven.
It begins from the undertaking of the fourth quality that produces a Buddha.

Indeed, it is from the attainment of the state of certainty regarding enlightenment onwards that wise people can say, "A Buddha is arising," because the arising is certain; just as they say, "He stands..."
In the phrase "The mountains stand; the rivers flow," the present tense is used by taking into account the non-interruption of the actions of standing and flowing.
Likewise, in the four alternatives, the expression "it arises" (*uppajjati*) is stated by taking into account the non-interruption of the action of proceeding toward arising.
"The state of having first arisen" refers to [the dhamma] prior to all the specific qualities that will be mentioned hereafter.
First, there is the specific quality of existence known as the arising of the Tathāgata.
"That Blessed One" refers to the one whose qualities have been extolled in such terms as "the Tathāgata, the Arahant," and so forth; that is the Blessed One.
"This world" is not said with reference merely to the world present before the eyes of the multitude, but rather it includes everything without exception.
The phrase beginning with "together with the devas" (*sadevaka*) was stated in order to show this. Therefore he said: "He now points out what is to be said.

"Because they have been born" (*pajātattā*) means because they have arisen through their own respective kamma and defilements. The inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere devas (*pañcakāmāvacaradeva*) is by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*), since the others are already comprised by other terms.
Furthermore, in the compound *sadevaka*, the analysis is according to its parts (*avayava-viggaha*), while the meaning of the compound (*samāsa-attha*) is the whole.
The inclusion of the six classes of sense-sphere deities is according to the principle of proximity; for he was born there and dwells there.
The same method applies here as well regarding the inclusion of the Brahmakāyika and other Brahmās.

The mention of "adversaries, enemies, recluses, and brahmins" is merely illustrative, as it includes by implication those who are not adversaries—namely, recluses and brahmins who have not yet stilled or abandoned their evil.

Because it is included [in the compound]. Granted that, due to the qualifying terms such as "together with the devas," the word *loka* is understood to have "beings" as its referent because those terms share a common grammatical connection (*tulyayoga*), nevertheless, since this compound is found even in cases of non-common connection—as in "having hair" (*salomako*) or "having wings" (*sapakkhako*)—the inclusion of the word "progeny" (*pajā*) is stated to demonstrate that there is no such deviation;
thus he says: "By the term 'progeny,' the world of beings is grasped."
Formless beings, dwelling in their own imperturbable state (*āneñjavihāra*), receive this etymological derivation:

"they shine, thus they are gods" (*dibbanti ti devā*). Therefore it was said: "By the inclusion of 'together with the devas,' the world of the formless-sphere devas is included. For that very reason it was said: "into the company of those devas who have reached the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*).
By the inclusion of "together with Māra," the world of the six sense-sphere devas is included, because of its particular distinction.
Because of falling under the power of Māra. The world of the *rūpa*-brahmās is included because the world of the *arūpa*-brahmās has been mentioned separately.

"By way of the four assemblies" means by way of the four assemblies consisting of kṣatriyas and so forth. However, the other four assemblies are already included by the mention of those beginning with "together with Māra.
The remaining world of all beings consists of the various classes such as nāgas, garuḍas, and so on.

Having thus far shown a *yojana* by taking the world part by part, he now says, "Moreover, in this regard," etc., in order to show a *yojana* by taking the world as a whole, according to its various specific distinctions. Therein, "by way of the highest limit" means by way of discerning the most excellent degree.

For among the five destinations (*gati*), the world of the devas alone is the best. Even there, the formless beings (*arūpin*) are [the best] because their defilements and suffering have been cast far away.
They are far superior to others by such distinctions as "possessing a dwelling that is peaceful, sublime, and imperturbable," and "extremely long-lived.
The passage beginning with "Brahmā of great majesty" refers to the Great Brahmā within the ten-thousandfold world system; for it is said, "from the perspective of the highest limit.
"Unsurpassed" (anuttara) means the most excellent, namely the nine supramundane states (lokuttara). This is the sequence according to the development of the states.
The sequence of the phrases beginning with "together with the devas" is according to their existence and according to the inclinations of others.

"In three ways" means by way of the three modes consisting of being accompanied by devas, Māras, and Brahmās. "In the three phrases" refers to the three phrases beginning with "together with the devas.
"By this or that mode" means by this or that manner, such as being together with the devas and so forth. It is precisely the triple world (tedhātuka).
The construction is: "‘Exhausted’ (pariyādinnaṃ), however, [is] what the ancients have said.
Regarding "direct knowledge" (abhiññā), this is a designation with the elision of the letter *ya*; its meaning here is "having directly known" (abhijānitvā). Thus he says:

"By direct knowledge, having known by means of superior knowledge" (*adhikena ñāṇena*). "The rejection of inference and so forth" means the rejection of inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), postulation (*atthāpatti*), and so on.
Because they possess a single measure [of knowledge]. For the Blessed Buddhas have direct perception of everything due to the unimpeded range of their knowledge regarding all things.
"The unsurpassed bliss of seclusion" refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

He said, "even having abandoned," because the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is sometimes interspersed with that [bliss]. Indeed, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, at whatever moment the assembly...
He either gives a cry of approval, or reviews the Dhamma as he has heard it;

having delimited that moment by means of the preceding portion, he enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Then, emerging from that attainment according to his delimitation, he teaches the Dhamma starting from the very place where he stood.
"Teaching" (*desanā*) is the act of instructing and awakening [others] through methods such as commands directed toward those who are to be exhorted;
this should be understood by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). Thus he said: "First, regarding teaching, even of a four-line stanza," and so forth.

"Instruction" (*sāsana*) is the act of guiding according to the nature of the person to be guided—such as their specific transgressions—and the disciplining (*vinayana*) thereof by means of the removal of defilements through their very cause (*tadaṅga-vinaya*), and so on.
"It should be understood by way of the dhamma of practice," he said, [beginning with] "virtue, concentration, and insight. "Of the wholesome" means of those skilled in the path;
or alternatively, "of the wholesome" means of those that are blameless (*anavajja*). By this, the inclusion of the dhammas that are fruits is also established.
Virtue and view are the "basis" because they are the root of the further-human states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). In each respective sense...
The Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) is established by way of verses and by way of discourses as a continuous succession of words with defined limits;
it is this very thing that is called "teaching" (*desanā*) here. Its specific meaning, however, consists of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; thus he said: "For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma...
he shows Nibbāna. In that context, "having shown virtue" means that by the mention of virtue, [the path] together with its requisites is indicated.

Virtue has been taken up. Likewise, by the inclusion of the Path, the "Path" is understood as including its requisites; thus, by both of these, the meaning of the entire scripture is encompassed without remainder.

"By that" means by the demonstration of virtue and so forth. For here, it is intended that the quality of being "good in the beginning" and so on refers to the teaching in terms of its purpose (*atthavasena*).
"The speaker’s disposition" means the speaker’s state of being, his establishment through the act of speaking.
It does not teach what is beneficial because that teaching lacks the purpose of leading to liberation (*niyyāna*).

"Connected with a single consonant, etc. means either connected with consonants of a single type—such as those classified as soft (*sithila*) and so forth—or connected with consonants of two types, like the Tamil language;
or it consists entirely of labial consonants, since it must be spoken everywhere with the lips closed (*niroṭṭha*).
Like the Kirāta language, it is "without consonants" (abyañjana) because it consists entirely of vowels suitable for utterance, like the Yavana language;
or, because it consists entirely of aspirated consonants due to its being accompanied by anusvāra everywhere, like the Mleccha languages such as Pārasika;
and since all these [languages] function only by means of partial consonants and thus have incomplete consonantal systems, they are termed "without consonants."
"Without smearing" means without scraping off, without destroying, or without letting it go—that is the meaning.
Whatever meaning the Blessed One teaches, even a single verse or a single sentence, in order to make that meaning known, he teaches it by making that teaching entirely complete in every respect;
thus, regarding all cases, he said: "Even a single teaching is not incomplete."

“There is not. By “established in the nature of rescuing” means by a mind that is fixed in the nature of pulling out [beings] from the side of defilement and from the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
“Therefore”: because the entire teaching, which comprises the three trainings, is intended here as “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*), therefore.
Having joined all the terms in grammatical apposition with this word “holy life,” [one should explain] the meaning.
He said, "One who shows [the Dhamma] teaches the Dhamma... [as follows]... he reveals it; thus the meaning should be understood here.
Right practice in the Teaching is possible only for one whose conceit has been cast far away, not for one of a conceited nature; therefore he said, "because of having humbled conceit.
"Because of being abundant" means because of its frequent occurrence. Intoxications based on wealth, health, and so forth are easy to abandon.

"Because the sign does not remain stable, the pride of those born into noble families—whether Kṣatriyas or Brāhmaṇas—even though they have gone forth, is difficult to abandon when based on the knowledge of their birth; thus he said: 'For the most part...
they exercise pride. 'By way of being of different birth' means by way of being of low birth. 'They are unable to stand firm' means [they cannot attain] complete purity."
They are unable to guard their virtue. For it is by means of virtue that one is established in the Teaching;

or rather, "to be established" means to be established in the supramundane state through the penetration of truth. For those who possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) are for the most part well-born, not ill-born.
“Completely pure” means entirely purified in every respect due to the absence of defilements, because it demonstrates the absolute abandonment of lust and the other [defilements].

“He acquires faith” means he believes by way of the faith of ordinary worldlings (*pothujjanika-saddhā*). For those of a wise nature, the establishment of faith is preceded by the grasping of the excellence of the Dhamma, owing to their state of having the Dhamma as their authority and being confident in the Dhamma.
“A husband and wife live together” means, as one might say, “husband and wife.”
When this is stated, it is understood that only two [types of people] are included by way of the master of the house and the mistress of the house.
However, regarding a man who has several wives, what should be said there? It is stated as "two" for the purpose of showing that even with just one of them, dwelling is cramped.

[The terms are used] in the sense of being "possessive" (sakiñcana) due to lust and so forth, and in the sense of being "obstructed" (sapalibodha) due to fields, land, and so forth. Of the dust of lust and the like...
Since the state of being the path of arrival is itself the state of the place of arising, these two explanations are identical in meaning; there is only a difference in phrasing.

By the sense of "non-adhering" means by the sense of not clinging, that is, by the state of being unbound. Having thus shown the confinement and the open space of household life and the life of renunciation respectively by way of their being the locus for the occurrence of the unwholesome and the wholesome, [the text now proceeds] regarding the occurrence of the wholesome...
Thus, in order to show them by way of what is possible and what is impossible, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” was stated.
A “concise explanation” (*saṅkhepakathā*) is a commentary on the meaning without extracting the words one by one. “Even for a single day” means even for the duration of a single day.
“Having made it unbroken” means having made it free from breach by not committing even a mere *dukkaṭa* offense.
“Untainted by the stain of defilements” means having made it undefiled by way of the defilement of craving and so forth.
“Having clothed himself” means both having put on the lower garment and having wrapped himself in the upper robe. “House-dwelling” (*agāravāso*) is *agāra* with the elision of the latter member;

that which brings about its increase is “beneficial to the house” (*agārassa hitam*). “Mass of wealth” (*bhogakkhandho*) means a heap of wealth, a collection of wealth. “In the sense of binding” refers to [the son] as a “son”...

By the phrase beginning with "relatives" (*nattā*), it refers to [the bond] through affection, in the sense of being connected with limits. They are called *ñātī* (kinsmen) because they are known as "these are ours.
It is a *parivaṭṭo* (turning) in the sense of revolving by way of grandfather, father’s son, and so forth.
Although the word *sikkhā* (training) is a general term, due to its proximity to the word *sājīvo* (livelihood), it is used here in view of the specific distinctions that will be explained below.

And it is said that [the training] is indeed included within the qualification: “The training of the bhikkhus, which is termed higher virtue (adhisīla). It is called *sikkhā* in the sense of that which is to be trained in (*sikkhitabba*).
It is called *sājīva* because they live together (*saha ājīvanti*) therein. “By way of the state of training” means by way of both the training (*sikkhā*) and the mode of livelihood (*sājīva*).
“Fulfilling the training” means fulfilling the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*). “And not transgressing the mode of livelihood” refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
The meaning is: being one who does not transgress the Blessed One’s word, namely the training rule stated as "the body of words, the body of definitions, and the body of phonemes.
And it is precisely this pair that is called "training" (*sikkhanā*). Among these, the non-transgression of the communal life (*sājīva*) is the condition for the fulfillment of the training;
for from that, there is the fulfillment of the training up to the [attainment of the] Path.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished by way of formal undertaking. From the very moment they are abandoned... [etc. ... "is abstinent":
by this he shows the simultaneity of the abandonment and the abstinence. If this is so, how is it that "having abandoned" is an expression referring to a prior time?
It is because it must be understood in that way. For when the relationship of cause and effect among phenomena is considered, even those things that are co-nascent [are related as such].

Since the apprehension of the relationship between condition and the arisen-from-conditions occurs precisely through their sequence of priority and posteriority, there is a designation of "prior time" for the act of abandoning in relation to the conditions—such as moral shame (*hirī*), moral dread (*ottappa*), and wisdom (*ñāṇa*)—by way of the mode of the occurrence of that apprehension;

and there is a designation of "subsequent time" for the act of abstaining in relation to the abstinences (*virati*) which have arisen from those conditions. Thus it is said: "Having abandoned, he is refrained."

It has been said. Or, "having abandoned" (*pahāya*) is stated by way of the time of undertaking [the precept], while "abstaining" (*paṭivirato*) is stated by way of the subsequent engagement with the matter to be transgressed. Or, "having abandoned" is as in:
"Having destroyed the mass of darkness, this sun has risen."
It should be understood according to the sense of simultaneous time, as in such passages as: “He speaks with the radiance of his complexion; having illumined [the world], he has arisen.
Alternatively, *pāṇātipāta* (killing of living beings) is that by which a living being (*pāṇa*) is slain;

it is a defiled state of mind (*saṃkilesadhamma*), primarily consisting of volition (*cetanā*), which serves as the cause for the destruction of life, such as shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), and cruelty (*vihiṃsā*).
Having abandoned that by means of undertaking [the precept], he is "restrained" (*virato*)—by this restriction, he shows the boundlessness of that abstinence in terms of time and so forth.
For while others who have undertaken abstinence may, due to an unstable mind or for the sake of gain, livelihood, and the like, break their undertaking, this one does not.
Rather, from the very moment it is abandoned, he remains restrained from that point onward.
In such passages as "having abandoned taking what is not given," the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
*Daṇḍa* means striking or the act of striking with a staff. Here, even specific types of weapons such as clubs and the like are intended by the term "specific weapon.
Therefore he said: "With the exception of the staff, all remaining implements [are included]. Regarding the harming of others, which is termed "striking":
He said, “for the purpose of harming others,” and so forth, as a statement regarding the laying down of sticks and weapons in order to illustrate the state of having abandoned them.

“From the state of violence” means from the state of causing affliction. Regarding the term “conscientious” (*lajjī*), it should be understood that in this context, *ottappa* (fear of wrongdoing) is also implied by the mentioned *lajjā* (shame).
For there is no lack of shame (*alajjana*) that is devoid of both disgust for evil and fear of evil.

Or rather, for one who—by virtue of reverence for the Dhamma and because that Dhamma is dependent upon oneself and has oneself as its sovereign—performs the function of moral shame (*lajjā*), there is no need to say that he performs the function of dread of blame (*ottappa*), which has the world as its sovereign; therefore, he is simply called "one possessed of shame" (*lajjī*).

Why is it said, "he has attained a heart of compassion (*dayā*) and loving-kindness (*mettā*)"? Is it not the case that the word *dayā* appears in such expressions as "without compassion" (*adayāpanna*)?

"Does it proceed from compassion? This is true; however, this word "compassion" (dayā), when used with the sense of protection included within it, proceeds as both loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā).
Thus, what is spoken of here is that which proceeds as loving-kindness. It is called *mettā* because one is moistened (*mijjati*) and softened (*siniyhati*);
that which possesses this is *mettaṃ*. One who possesses a mind of loving-kindness (*mettaṃ cittaṃ*) is *mettacitto*.
Its state is *mettacittatā* (the state of a mind of loving-kindness); the meaning is simply "loving-kindness" (*mettā*).
By the phrase "compassionate toward the welfare of all breathing beings," he shows that this abstinence is boundless by way of its objects.

"Breathing beings" (*pāṇabhūta*) refers to those born as living creatures. "Compassionate" (*anukampaka*) means one who feels compassion. Furthermore, because loving-kindness is a specific condition for compassion...

Therefore it was said: “precisely by that state of having become compassionate. Thus, the possession of those qualities—shame (*lajjā*), loving-kindness (*mettā*), and compassion (*karuṇā*)—by which the abstention from taking life is accomplished, has been shown; it should be understood as being together with the qualities of the backbone.
Here one might ask: why is the singular designation used in the phrase “having abandoned the taking of life,” when [the objects] are not without remainder?
Is it abstaining from the destruction of living beings that is intended here? For it has been said: “He dwells compassionate and sympathetic toward the welfare of all breathing beings.
Is it for this very reason that the commentary provides the plural designation, “compassionate through welfare toward all breathing beings”?
True, this is so; however, in this case, the singular designation was made at the beginning of the text by way of the commonality of the state of being a breathing being.

Since multiplicity is already understood through the presence of the word "all," the meaning was stated in the commentary using the plural form—not because a general designation was not made, but in order to demonstrate it according to the desire for specific terminology.
Furthermore, this distinction in expression was made in order to show this particularity:
that from a general standpoint there is the undertaking of restraint, and from its specific standpoint there is the classification of restraint.

This is to be understood. "He dwells" (viharati) means that, being in the manner described, he carries on (harati) and maintains (pavatteti) his personal existence by interrupting with another posture the suffering arisen in one posture;
this is the meaning. Therefore it is said: "He moves about (iriyati) and protects (pāleti).
It is not only through the application of body and speech that there is grasping; rather, his desire also has as its object things that have been relinquished.
To show this, it was said, “even by mind,” and so forth. A *thena* is one who steals (*thenaṃ karoti*); thus, a thief.

Regarding the phrase “by one who has become pure” (*sucibhūtena*), purity here—due to the context and the proximity of other words—refers to the abstaining from the defilement of theft; hence he says, “by one who has become pure through the very absence of theft.
Although it is true that such qualities as “being modest and compassionate” are not explicitly mentioned here, they are understood by virtue of the context.

However, it should be understood that this has already been stated in terms of its meaning. For just as shame and the other [virtues] are specific conditions for the abandoning of killing, so too are they for the abandoning of taking what is not given;
therefore, that passage from the Canon should also be cited. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well.
Alternatively, by the phrase "having become pure," the possession of shame, moral dread, and so forth, as well as the abandoning of shamelessness and the like, is indeed already stated.
It should be understood that [the terms] such as “lajjī” (conscientious) are not mentioned here.
“Aseṭṭhacariyaṃ” means the conduct of those who are ignoble, or an ignoble conduct. “Mithuno” refers to that which goes toward (ayati) those who are like a pair (mithuna) in the manner described;
it is the aforementioned misconduct. By the phrase “ārācārī methunā,” [it is implied]: “In this regard...”
"O Brahmin, one person... [as before] ...does not engage in the act of sexual intercourse with a woman;
yet he consents to being rubbed, massaged, bathed, and anointed by a woman;
he relishes that, he desires it, and he finds satisfaction therein"—thus, there is also the abstention from the seven forms of sexual union mentioned in such passages.
It should be understood as "shown.
By means of truth, truth: the latter verbal truth is connected with the former verbal truth because there is no interval between them due to their lack of falsehood.
Therefore he said, "For whoever," and so forth. It is not made firm like turmeric dye; here, this is because of the instability of the discourse.
It should be understood as being like the color of turmeric, not like a person. The same principle applies here in the phrase "like a line on stone.
*Saddhāyika* means that wherein faith (*saddhā*) goes or proceeds; thus it is *saddhāyika*, just as one says "Venayika" (one who follows the discipline).

Alternatively, *saddhāyika* means that which is to be approached by faith, meaning "one who is to be trusted. The intention is that he incurs the state of being subject to censure because of his deceptive speech.
"Anuppadātā" means one who provides support; or, one who provides [support] by way of following along. But whose following and providing?
Since it is said "of those joined together," it is understood to be of the connection (*sandhāna*). Therefore he says, "one who provides support for the connection.
For, by way of following along, there comes to be the establishing, the protecting, or the strengthening of the connection through the providing [of support].
Therefore it was said: “Having seen two people in harmony,” and so forth. It is called an *ārāma* because they delight (*āramanti*) therein; thus, it is a place for enjoyment.
However, since this meaning can be obtained even without the vowel *ā*, it was stated: “The Pāḷi reading ‘samaggarāmo’ also exists;
this is precisely the meaning here.”
"Herein"—referring to:
"The chariot with faultless parts, white canopy, and single wheel rolls on;
see him approaching, free from distress, with the stream cut off and unbound."
In this verse, virtue is referred to as “nelaṅga. For this very reason, the householder Citta said:
“Venerable sir, ‘nelaṅga’ is a designation for virtues. They are called “sukumāra” because they are soft due to their lack of harshness.
In the phrase “purassa esa,” the word *pura* should be understood as denoting the inhabitants of that city, as in expressions such as “the village has arrived. For this very reason he said:
“Of those living in the city. It is called *manāpā* because it nourishes and increases the mind; thus it is said, “those which cause the growth of the mind.
The passage beginning with “speaking at the proper time” demonstrates the practice of one who abstains from idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).

For even speech that is beneficial may fail to bring about its purpose if employed at an improper time; therefore, it conforms to speech that does not communicate what is harmful, and thus [it is included in] idle chatter.

It is said that one who abandons [unwholesome speech] must avoid speaking at the wrong time; thus it is said, "one who speaks at the right time" (*kālavādī*). Even when speaking at the right time, one must avoid what is untrue, as it accomplishes both kinds of harm;
thus he says, "one who speaks what is true" (*bhūtavādī*). And for one speaking what is true, it is shown that only that which brings about welfare in this world and the next should be spoken;
thus it is said, "one who speaks what is beneficial" (*atthavādī*). Even when speaking what is beneficial, [it should not be] merely based on worldly matters...
It is stated as "one who speaks on the Dhamma" (dhammavādī) for the purpose of showing that one should speak having relied upon and based it on the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).
And it is stated as "one who speaks on the Vinaya" (vinayavādī) for the purpose of showing how that meaning is dependent upon the supramundane Dhamma;
for the meaning being spoken of is by way of the fivefold restraint-vinaya and the fivefold abandonment-vinaya.
"Because it is the cause for attaining Nibbāna, it is supported by supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma).
To show that only when endowed with such specific qualities does the meaning shine forth when being spoken—and that it becomes effective in its function, and not otherwise—it is said:
"one who speaks words that possess a foundation. Now, in order to clarify that skill in teaching, he says: "at the proper time," and so forth.
For one who, having observed the distinctions in categorical and other types of answers regarding the subject matter of speech that has descended through questions and so forth,

and who— by means of a discourse that is limited and well-defined in form yet capable of encompassing a more extensive, profound, noble, and ultimate exposition— elucidates the application of setting aside, the reasons for doing so, examples, and the reconciliation [of views] according to the appropriate occasion,
establishes others in the Dhamma as it truly is in accordance with the power of their own knowledge, is called "skilled in teaching."
In this way, the interpretation of the meaning here should be understood.
Having thus explained the seven root training rules (mūla-sikkhāpada) in their proper sequence, although the subsequent teaching includes the abandoning of covetousness and so forth,

the restraint of the sense faculties, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the practice of wakefulness, the text proceeds by setting those aside and explaining only the virtue of conduct (ācāra-sīla).

In order to explain that meaning, it was said: “From the destruction of seeds and the destruction of the community of living beings,” and so forth. Therein, the *gāma* (community) of seeds—that is, their collection—is the “seed-community.
The *gāma* (community) of *bhūta* (living beings)—that is, the collection of trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth that have arisen and come into being—is the “living-being-community.

Now, are not trees and the like not *jīva* (living souls) because they lack consciousness? And is it not the case that they lack consciousness because they lack movement (*paripphanda*), as [is seen] when they are cut?
They are to be understood as such because of their growth, because they belong to a different species [from living beings], and because they are not included within the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Furthermore, since growth is found even in coral, stones, and salt, this is not a reason for them to possess the nature of a living being (*jīva*).

Their grasping of objects is merely a mental construction, like the dreaming of a *ciñcā* tree; likewise with their longings (*dohala*) and so forth. In that regard, why is there the undertaking of destroying seeds and the destruction of the community of living beings (*bīja-gāma-bhūta-gāma-samārambha*)?

Is abstention desired? Yes, because it is befitting for a recluse and because it protects the beings dwelling therein. For this very reason, he said: "For people, O foolish man, perceive life in a tree," and so forth.

Root itself is the seed; thus it is "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*). It is also called "root-seed" in the sense that the root-seed is its [source]. The same method applies to the remaining [types of seeds] as well. "Creeper-seed" (*phaḷubīja*)...

The term *pabba-bīja* (joint-seed). Because it serves as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when combined with other conditions, the word *bīja* (seed), which is conventionally established for a substantial fruit capable of sprouting, is applied by extension to certain roots and so forth to achieve that same meaning.

Therefore, in order to exclude [the application of the term] to roots and the like, it is specified by the single term *bīja* as "seed-seed" (*bīja-bīja*), just as one says "matter-matter" (*rūpa-rūpa*) or "suffering-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*).
And so it is. But why, in this context, is only the "seed-creepers" (bījagāma) specified after having extracted both the "seed-creepers" and the "living-creepers" (bhūtagāma)?
This should not be viewed in that way; for did we not say: "A root that is itself a seed is 'root-seed' (mūlabīja), and that which has a root-seed as its [origin] is also 'root-seed'"?
Therein, by the first [term], the seed-creepers are specified, and by the second, the living-creepers.

This [seed] is twofold: root-seed (*mūlabīja*) and so forth. It should be understood that it is taught by way of a general designation as "root-seed," or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*). For this very reason, he says, "of the fivefold," and so on.
"Of blue grass, trees, and so forth" means of both fresh grass and fresh trees, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and so on is intended.

"Eka-bhatta" means a single meal; one who has that is an "ekabhattika. Since such a person might also eat at night, the phrase "restrained from the night" (*rattūparato*) is stated in order to exclude that possibility.

Furthermore, since one who eats only after midday might also be considered an "ekabhattika," the phrase "abstaining from eating at the wrong time" (*virato vikālabhojanā*) is stated to exclude that as well. [This applies] from the time of sunrise until...
This time of midday is called the time for eating that has been practiced and traditionally observed by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas;
any other time is *vikāla* (the wrong time). However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), because eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase, it is stated:
"When midday has passed until the setting of the sun, eating is called *vikālabhojana* (eating at the wrong time)."

“The Blessed One’s teaching, which proceeds in the manner beginning with ‘The non-doing of all evil,’ does not conform to the viewing of dancing and such things that arise from extreme passion”; thus he said, “because it is contrary to the teaching.

Dancing performed by oneself and dancing caused to be performed by others are both included in the Pāli by the single word *nacca* (dancing) due to their commonality as dancing; likewise for the words *gīta* (song) and *vādita* (instrumental music).
Thus he said: "By way of dancing and causing to dance, etc. By the word "etc.," singing, causing to sing, playing instruments, and causing to play instruments are included.
Furthermore, here hearing is also included under seeing by the method of "residual inclusion of the dissimilar" (virūpekasesa-naya).
Alternatively, because the five consciousnesses have the nature of perceiving their respective objects, even the act of hearing is subsumed under the designation of "seeing."
“Seeing” is what was stated. Therefore he said: “By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not cognize any phenomenon other than the mere impact [of the object].
Hearing music that is not frivolous is sometimes permissible; thus he said: “Seeing that which is frivolous.
For it is likewise stated in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Books (*Khuddakapāṭha*): “That which is connected with the Dhamma...”
“Singing is permissible, but a teaching associated with singing is not. Regarding the phrase “whatever”:
it refers to any flower, whether strung together or not. “A kind of perfume” means a substance belonging to the class of perfumes.
Because of the expression “whatever” applied to that as well, it shows that any kind of ointment or the like—whether made from meat or not—is not permissible.
*Uccā* is another word having the same meaning as the word *ucca*. It is called *sayana* (bed) because one lies (*seti*) upon it.
High beds (*uccāsayana*) and large beds (*mahāsayana*) are intended here as those unsuitable for a renunciant; thus he says, "exceeding the proper measure and having an unallowable covering.

Furthermore, it should be understood that here the term "seat" (*āsana*) is included within "bed" (*sayana*). For when the support [the bed] is prohibited, that which rests upon it [the seat] is also prohibited.
The actual act of using them is indeed prohibited; therefore, it is stated simply as "high and luxurious beds and seats.
However, in terms of meaning, it should be understood that the abstention from sitting or lying down on such things used for enjoyment is what is shown.

Alternatively, this expression is a singular remainder (*ekasesa*) based on the sense: "both high and luxurious beds and seats, and high and luxurious beds and seats" is "high and luxurious beds and seats."
It is as in the case of the statement, “With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]”;
or it should be understood that because the act of sitting precedes the act of lying down, the term “lying down” includes the act of sitting as well.

By the word “iti” (thus) in the phrase “a wooden māsaka,” he indicates that such things are included which are used in common parlance. [The phrase] “having them taken by others” refers to having them received through others.
And since the purpose of receiving (*paṭiggahaṇattha*) is found even in the consenting to what has been set aside, he said:
"He neither takes it up himself, nor causes it to be taken up, nor consents to what has been set aside. Alternatively, there are three kinds of receiving:
by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, receiving by body is taking up; receiving by speech is causing to be taken up; and receiving by mind is—
Regarding the phrase "accepting" (*sādiyanan*): having taken all three types of acceptance together, it is stated as "acceptance" (*paṭiggahaṇa*); thus he says, "he does not accept it," and so forth.
This same method applies to the phrases "acceptance of raw grain" (*āmakadhañña*) and the others.
Since secondary grains such as *nīvāra* are included within the primary grains such as *sāli*, it is said "of seven kinds. "I allow you, monks, five..."
Because it is stated, "fats such as bear fat, fish fat, otter fat, pig fat, and donkey fat," this is called what is specifically permitted (*odissa-anuññāta*).
However, because it is further stated that "it must be received at the proper time," its acceptance is allowable.
Regarding the phrase "when there is a requisite," he said, "except for what is specifically permitted."

*Sarūpena vañcanam* (deception by appearance) means deception by means of a semblance; this is the meaning. *Aṅgakūṭaṃ* (deception by limb) is deception by means of a limb, that is, a part of one's own body.
*Gahaṇakūṭaṃ* (deception by grasping) is deception by way of seizing. *Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ* (concealed deception) is deception having made it hidden.
*Akkamati* means to press down; the connection is "presses down in the prior stage."
*Hṛdayanta* refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as the *nāḷi*. *Sikhā* is the very peak raised up when measuring sesame seeds and other substances with the *nāḷi* and similar measures.
*Sikhābheda* is the breaking of that [peak]. "Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* and the residents of the Uttaravihāra.

*Vadha* means tormenting by means of blows from the fist, slapping, and so forth; the meaning is "afflicting. Indeed, the word *vadha* is seen to have the sense of "tormenting," as in: "Having struck himself..."

In passages such as “having killed, she weeps,” etc., although there is a commonality in the state of being unclaimed, women, boys, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth, are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the specific categories of things that should not be accepted by those who have gone forth (pabbajita).

Likewise, although there is a commonality in the state of taking what is not given because it is taken from another, false scales and so forth are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the specific varieties of taking what is not given; however, it is not so with the category of killing living beings (pāṇātipāta).
There is a purpose for taking up the term "killing" again; for it cannot be said that there is "self-exertion" in that case and "exertion by another" here, because of the statement:
"The volition that originates bodily and vocal effort consists of six types of effort. Therefore, the meaning as previously stated is appropriate here.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "'Killing' means causing death," and that too refers simply to striking.
And it is possible to understand [the term] with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*), since the word "killing" (*māraṇa*) is seen to be used in the sense of "injuring.

(294) Showing that, when the robes and alms-food are respectively indicated as being merely for the maintenance of the body and the stomach, it is possible for them to serve that purpose among the eight requisites without distinction, he says: "All these," and so forth.
These nine requisites and so forth are also characterized by fewness of wishes and contentment; for therein there is neither great desire nor discontent.
He dwells happily in the four directions; thus, those four directions become for him a state of happy dwelling.
Or, he is "four-faced" (cātuddisa) because he perceives that [the Dhamma] exists everywhere.

Furthermore, he is "non-resistant" (appaṭigha) because he does not strike back at beings or at conditioned phenomena out of fear. He is "contented" (santussamāna), being one who finds satisfaction by means of the twelve kinds of contentment. "With this or that" means with things high and low.
As for "dangers," there are external ones such as lions and tigers, and internal ones such as sensual desire and so forth.
Because he overcomes physical and mental calamities, he is "enduring" (*sahita*) toward dangers. Because of the absence of fear that causes rigidity, he is "fearless" (*acchambhī*).
Being alone and without companion, he is therefore "like the horn of a rhinoceros" (*khaggavisāṇakappa*); the meaning is that he should "wander" (*careyya*).
A bird whose wings are severed, or whose wings have not yet grown, is unable to go; thus, by the word "winged" (*pakkhī*), [the term] "bird" (*sakuṇo*) is used.
Having specified that the bird is mentioned in the text, he says, "a bird possessed of wings.

To show that this monk is one for whom there is no enjoyment of stored-up goods and no setting aside of anything with a view toward future use, he says, "But here is the summary of the meaning," and so forth.
They are called *ariya* because they go away from (*apenti*) those faults, or because they are far removed (*āraka*) from them; thus they are *ariya*.

He said: "By the noble means by the faultless. "Internal" means within oneself. "Faultless happiness" is spiritual happiness (*nirāmisa-sukha*), because it is free from the thorns of the defilements (*kilesa*).

295. Restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) is desired only for one who is established in the aforementioned restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), because the former is based upon the latter and because the latter acts as its protector.
Thus it was said: "Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue..."
“Monks. Regarding the remaining phrases, such as “he does not grasp at signs,” and so forth:
since this was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, it should be understood according to the method explained in its commentary, the *Līnatthappakāsinī*.

Because the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) is characterized by the avoidance of grasping at signs and so forth regarding visible forms and other objects, there is the quality of being unsoiled by defilements and a state of ease.
And his state of unconfused happiness has been described.

296. "Perfection of requisites" means the complete fulfillment of requisites. "These four" refers to the restraint of virtue, contentment, restraint of the sense faculties, and mindfulness and clear comprehension;
these are the four provisions for dwelling in the forest. [This is] the state of being spoken of by the animals.
[One] incurs [this offense], as in the case of the father and others of the sage Isisiṅga. "By forest-dwellers" means by female forest-dwellers.
They cause them to hear terrifying sounds; while they do not flee at that moment, they seize their heads with their hands... [and so on].

It is either a "black spot" consisting of a transgression of the formal rule (paṇṇatti), or a "mole" consisting of wrong thought (micchā-vitakka). "That" refers to rapture (pīti), which he contemplates as passing away because it appears as a manifestation of the state of being dissolved (vibhūta-bhāva).
“Secluded” means secluded from people; therefore he said, “empty. And that seclusion is to be characterized by the absence of sound;
thus he said, “with little noise and little clamor. A lodging that serves as a dwelling place in the sense of being a place to dwell in is a “monastery-lodging” (*vihāra-senāsana*).
Beds and chairs made of masāraka wood and so forth, as well as the mattresses and pillows spread upon them, are connected to those beds and chairs.
“Beds and chairs” refers to lodgings. “Rugs and so forth” refers to lodgings that are spread out upon the ground because they are to be spread there.
“Tree roots and so forth” refers to lodgings in the open air, such as walking-grounds (*caṅkama*), because these are places where one must retreat.

Having said, “Showing what is suitable,” he spoke the words beginning with “For therein” in order to clarify that very suitability. “Unroofed” means not covered even by a roof of bricks or the like, nor even by tree branches.
“Behind the meal” means behind one who is eating the meal. “The posture with the thighs bound” refers to sitting by way of binding the thighs below.

Since the placing of the lower body straight is already indicated by the word “sitting,” he says, “having placed the upper body straight,” because here the word *kāya* (body) refers specifically to the upper body. That...
However, in order to show the straightening [of the mind] by way of its essential nature and its purpose, the passage beginning with “eighteen” was stated.
“They do not bend” means they do not incline. “It does not fall away” means it does not disappear; it does not overstep the path.
For that very reason, through the attainment of successive excellence, the meditation subject reaches growth and expansion. “Near the mouth” means in the vicinity of the mouth.

[He fixes it] either on the tip of the nose or the upper lip. Here, the prefix *pari-* has the same meaning as the prefix *abhi-*, which is why he says “facing the meditation subject” (*kammaṭṭhānābhimukha*);
the meaning is that, having turned away from external diverse objects, one holds the meditation subject alone in front of oneself.

The prefix *pari-* has the sense of embracing (*pariggaha*), as in such words as “guide” (*pariṇāyikā*). It also has the sense of emerging (*niyyāna*), in the sense of going forth from the opposite [side]; therefore—

"Having established mindfulness that has grasped the thirty modes of deliverance in every way, such that it is free from confusion and has abandoned confusion"—this is the meaning. "By way of suppression":
here, suppression means non-arising and non-occurrence, not [suppression] by way of an antidote.
"Abandonedness. And by "abandonedness," it is said with reference to a state resembling what has been abandoned; that is, the non-attainment of jhāna.
Nevertheless, this [state] is not devoid of covetousness by its own nature (*sabhāva*) like eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*);
rather, it is so by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore he said: "not like eye-consciousness. "In the same way" means that just as eye-consciousness, by its own nature...
"Free from covetousness and free from ill will" does not mean that these have been suppressed by meditation; it is not like that.
Rather, the meaning is that this consciousness is "free from ill will" because it has been purified by meditation, and it is likewise "free from sloth and torpor," "unagitated," and "without doubt.
"Both of these" refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
297. Regarding the phrase "having cut them off, they cause them to fall": here, "cutting off" and "causing to fall" mean precisely the non-arising of those wisdoms that have not yet arisen.

Thus, the hindering states (nīvaraṇa-dhammā), which serve as the causes for the non-arising of sublime and unsurpassed wisdom, as well as certain limited wisdoms, likewise destroy the capacity for the others; such is the nature of wisdom.
The [hindrances] have been described as "weakening. This first jhāna is also called a "footing for knowledge" (ñāṇapada) because knowledge reaches its footing here;
it is called a "range of knowledge" (ñāṇavaḷañja) because knowledge operates within this range. 299.
One has not yet reached the ultimate goal, for there may still be places entered by the knowledge of outsiders. If this is so—
To the question, "How is it that he has not reached a final conclusion regarding the state of path-knowledge, which is not shared by others? he says, "Even at the moment of the path," and so forth.

"He has reached a final conclusion regarding the Three Jewels" means that, with respect to the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice, he has arrived at a final conclusion—that is, a certainty—by means of knowledge.
Although, in this context, [this is already achieved] entirely by the first path alone...
Because doubt has been abandoned, no noble disciple whatsoever possesses either uncertainty or perplexity;
however, while the knowledge of an Arahant who has attained the fullness of wisdom penetrates his own domain with particular distinction, that is not the case for non-returners and others.
Therefore, with reference to the attainment of a definitive certainty of knowledge regarding the Three Jewels in its most eminent form, [it is said]: "by means of the supreme path..."
It is said that "the arrival at the ultimate goal therein has been explained. Furthermore, whatever remains unexplained here is indeed easy to understand.

The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷahatthipadopama-sutta* (The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint) is completed. 8. Commentary on the *Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta* (The Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint).
300. Regarding the term *jaṅgalānaṃ*: here, that region of land which is devoid of moisture, not marshy, and hard and parched due to the absence of water is called "jungle" (*jaṅgala*).
Because of its abundance, the entire region of land here is called "jungle.
Those born in or existing in that jungle are "jungle-born" (*jaṅgalā*); [the phrase refers to] those jungle-born [elephants]. For in this way, it includes even the elephants that roam by rivers.
The inclusion is established; for just as those things to be combined are included by the mention of "wilderness-dwellers," so too are the agents who combine them included.
By the phrase "those that move on the surface of the earth," he does not exclude those that move in water, because their feet are invisible.

Although the term "living beings" (pāṇānam) is a general expression, it is understood specifically as a qualifier due to the proximity of the other word "classes of footed creatures" (padajātāni); thus he says, "of living beings possessing feet."

In passages such as “muttagatam,” the word *gata* (gone) is as if it has no other meaning [than what is implied], and the word *jāta* (born/arisen) likewise has no other meaning; thus he says, “*padajātāni* means ‘words’.
*Samodhānaṃ* means a complete inclusion or a being contained within. “By its greatness” means by its vastness.

“Wholesome states” (*kusalā dhammā*) refers to states that have blameless and pleasant results, not merely those states that are blameless. This is according to the method presented in the *Kusala-ttika* (The Triplet on the Wholesome).
For here, wholesome states (*kusala-dhammā*) are to be understood, not according to the method presented in the *Bāhitika Sutta*.

Why was it stated that "the compendium is fourfold," when surely only a single-fold compendium is intended here? No; because the word itself was taken without grasping its meaning, and thus its meaning remained undetermined.
First of all, the word "compendium" (*saṅgaha*) is fourfold by way of its own referents; this is what is meant here.

Meaning (*attha*). Alternatively, meaning itself—when its specific distinctions have not yet been determined and it has reached a state where it must be grasped by way of a general characteristic—has attained the status of being expressible by the word "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) in this context;
thus there is no fault. However, once the specific distinction has been determined, that [meaning] would possess only a single mode, and not prior to that.
"Inclusion by genus" (*sajātisaṅgaha*) means inclusion of what belongs to the same genus, or the inclusion of those belonging to the same genus.
In the *Dhātukathāvaṇṇanā*, however, it is stated simply as “the grouping by genus” (*jātisaṅgaho*). This was said because the word “genus” (*jāti*) is a term that requires a complement;
thus, when it is said “the grouping of the genus,” it is understood to mean “of its own genus,” since no other related term has been mentioned.
Here, however, in order to make it clear—as in the commentary on the *Rūpakaṇḍa*—it is stated as “the grouping by its own genus” (*sajātisaṅgaho*).
It has been said. "Sañjāti" means that which is born therein; "sañjātisaṅgaho" is a grouping by way of birth, meaning a grouping according to the specific class of birth.
When it is said, "All charioteers," all chariot-warriors are grouped together as one because of their common activity of fighting with a chariot.
When it is said, "All archers," all bowmen are grouped together as one because of their common activity of piercing with a bow.
He said: "In this way, the inclusion is by way of function. "Included within the aggregate of form" means it shares a single inclusion with the aggregate of form;
it is counted as the aggregate of form itself. The meaning is that it has been grasped.
It partakes of one and a half truths because it constitutes a portion of both the truth of the path and the truth of suffering. Even though it is included within a portion of the truths...
"It is indeed included within the truth" means "because it is included within the truths.
Now, in order to illustrate that meaning by means of both the teaching and worldly analogy, the passage beginning with "Just as... was spoken.
Therein, the phrase "This, monks, consists of more than one hundred and fifty training rules" refers to the number of training rules prescribed at the time when that discourse was taught.
It has been stated; beyond that, however, there are more than two hundred training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

Because they are included within the trainings, [they fall under] the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*). And here, the proposition that "one who trains in virtue also trains in the three trainings" is an incorrect assertion.
For in that context, he who abandons what is to be abandoned and enters into restraint regarding what is to be restrained—this is his [training].

The training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). The non-distraction of the mind therein is his training in higher consciousness (*adhicitta-sikkhā*). The investigation therein is his training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*).
Thus, it is shown that this clansman trains in the three trainings exactly as they are found in their own nature, not merely by way of their being included within one another.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "The restraint of one who has become such..."
“Herein, that which is his training in higher virtue is the training in higher virtue; the concentration of one who has become thus is the training in higher mind;

the wisdom of one who has become thus is the training in higher wisdom. One trains in, cultivates, develops, and makes much of these three trainings upon that object, by means of that mindfulness and that attention. Here, however, of the truths—
Is it because they are included within [the training] that, by the mere fact of being denotable by the word "truth," they are included in the count among the four truths?
No; for even there, only the training in higher virtue is obtained in the primary sense, while the others are so only in a figurative sense.
Therefore, it is said: "because they are included within the trainings."
The statement that they "are included within the four noble truths" is said with reference to their not being separate from them, but rather being contained within them.

And by taking it in this way, the elephant-footprint simile shown in the passage beginning, "Just as [all footprints are encompassed] by a single elephant's footprint," should be understood as being established.
This refers to those phenomena which have entered into the count, even if they are found in one, two, or three of the truths.
It should not be understood solely by way of the triad of the wholesome; rather, it should be understood according to the terms that are applicable within the respective triads and dyads.
In this context, the phenomenon included in the count of one truth is to be seen as the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*);
those included in the count of two truths are the wholesome phenomena, likewise the unwholesome phenomena, and the indeterminate phenomena; and [those included] in three...
Conditioned phenomena are included within the truths; in this same way, this meaning should be explained by dividing it appropriately according to other triads and dyads.

Therefore he said: "Even in one... they are indeed included. For a single part, because it is contained within the whole, receives inclusion under the general term as a collective, just like a particular. Therefore he said: "Of the truths..."

"Because it is included within. As for the sequence of the teaching: having listed the Noble Truths, there is the analysis of the five aggregates of clinging by way of the exposition of the Truth of Suffering.
And therein, by way of the exposition of the aggregate of form, there is first the analysis of the internal earth element. This is the sequence of this teaching.
301. However, in order to clarify this by means of similes, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated.
Therein, "well-born" (*sujātaṃ*) means beautiful; the intention is that it is well-proportioned and well-rounded. "Pieces" (*pesiyoti*) refers to segments.
"Taking the belly portion because of its softness" means taking the part of the interior due to its pliability. "And the other four portions" refers to the other four among the five divided sections.
"And the other three portions" refers to the other three portions among the four divisions initially distinguished.

"By the simile of the king’s son" means by the simile of the king’s eldest son. "It" refers to the ornament. "Legitimate" (orasa) means born from the breast, produced by the noble lineage generated through effort.
"Born from the mouth" means born from the teaching of the Dhamma that has issued from the mouth; or [born] from the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas.

He is born from the noble Dhamma which is his source; for that very reason, he is "born of the Dhamma" (dhammaja) and "fashioned by the Dhamma" (dhammanimmita). Because he has been received as a true heir to the Teacher’s Dhamma alone, he is a "heir to the Dhamma" (dhammadāyāda).
Therefore, it is said: "not an heir to material things" (no āmisadāyādo). The word "him" (tam) refers to the statement beginning with "the Blessed One’s son.

Because he stands preeminently in the sequence of successive states through qualities such as great wisdom, one who speaks correctly and in accordance with reality—being able to speak thus—should say [the following].

The construction is as follows: he attends upon more than a thousand bhikkhus, who are serving the Sugata, the Fully Enlightened One, who—by the removal of the dust of passion and so forth—is the Dhamma free from dust, and who teaches Nibbāna, which is "fearless" (akutobhaya), and that which leads to Nibbāna.
Having said, "One should serve and associate with them," he states the reason for this: "The bhikkhus are wise and helpful. Being wise, they are not of little learning;
rather, they are helpful through their exhortations and instructions. Thus, the first simile refers specifically to the Elder himself.
The first [term] was stated with reference to the Blessed One, while the second was stated with reference to both the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. 302.

"Internal" (*ajjhattika*) means included within the continuity of one's own being. By the two terms "internal" (*ajjhatta*) and "individual" (*paccatta*), the specific personal phenomena of each individual are expressed;
thus he said, "Both of these are indeed synonyms for 'one's own' (*niyaka*). However, because they are included within one's own continuity...
“Internal” (*ajjhatta*) means that which occurs with reference to or directed toward the self (*attā*), by way of its having attained the state of being graspable as a self;
it is “individual” (*paccatta*) because it is included within the respective continuum of each sentient being. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
“It is ‘internal’ because it occurs within the self, and ‘individual’ because it occurs in dependence upon each self. “Hard” (*kakkhala*) means rigid.
Because it serves as a support for those things co-nascent with it through its state of rigidity, it is called "rigid" (*thaddha*).
"Gone to hardness" (*kharigata*) means gone into—that is, included within—those things whose intrinsic nature is hard; the meaning is that its very nature is hard.
Furthermore, because it appears in a harsh manner due to its hard nature, it is called "harsh" (*pharusa*). It is "clung-to" (*upādinna*).
This is the "body-decad. Among these, that which is originated by kamma is, in the primary sense, called "clung-to" (*upādinna*); the other is "not clung-to" (*anupādinna*).
However, both of these are here shown to be "clung-to" in the sense of being grasped, seized, and adhered to by craving and the rest;
thus it is said, "The body-decad, indeed," and so forth. In this context, "clung-to" means firmly adhered to.
“Mine” is what is grasped; “I” is what is clung to.

“For one who takes the elements as his meditation subject” means for one who maintains the meditation subject of the elements by way of the analysis of the four elements. “In this” means in this meditation subject of the elements.
“In the three sections” means in the three types of sections; for those [sections] are not three or four sections.
“Of the kind described” means of the kind described by the passage beginning with “head-hairs, body-hairs.

“Due to their diverse intrinsic natures” means that although there is a commonality in their hardness, they possess diverse intrinsic natures as members of the aggregate consisting of head-hairs and so forth, owing to their analysis into constituent parts. “Attachment” (ālaya) means concern. “Lust” (nikanti) means longing.
“Aspiration” (patthanā) means the aspiration of craving. “Obsession” (pariyuṭṭhāna) means the obsession of craving. “Grasping” (gahaṇa) means...
Sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*). "Adherence" (*parāmāsa*) means grasping from another [source]; it is a wrong conviction, not a powerful underlying tendency (*ālaya*) and so forth.
If this is so, why is the external earth element analyzed in detail in the *Vibhaṅga*?

Because the teaching there proceeded by way of detailed exposition according to the nature of the dhamma (*yathādhammadesanā*), whereas here the teaching is abbreviated according to the method of sequential exposition (*yathānulomadesanā*).
"Having joined, he shows" means having brought them together, he shows them. "That" refers to the internal earth element.
There is the grasping of it as pleasure [only] when one thinks, "It is not my self.

For once the characteristic of non-self is established, the characteristic of suffering and the characteristic of impermanence are also necessarily established among conditioned phenomena, because they are inseparable from it. "He makes a spectacle" means he performs a distorted or ugly action.
It causes movement. Since that, in its actual sense, is simply vibration, he says, "it vibrates.
"Its" refers to the internal earth element. The absence of consciousness becomes evident through the observation of it as being merely an element.
"Both of these" refers to both types of earth element.
“More distinguished than that” means more distinguished than that external great earth; the meaning is “lighter. “Is disturbed” means it is agitated.
“Melting away” means going to dissolution like salt in natural water.
“Following after the water” means following the water, having the same course as the water. Therefore he said, “it becomes just water. Non-existence itself is non-existence; it does not exist.
Or, it is a phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is non-existence; its state is "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatā*). Its nature is decay, destruction, and passing away;
thus it is a "decay-phenomenon" (*vayadhamma*). Its state is "decay-phenomenon-ness" (*vayadhammatā*), which in meaning is simply destruction.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Therefore he said: "By all these terms, only the characteristic of impermanence is stated. [This refers to] the state of being destroyed.

However, because they must be explained, although only the characteristic of impermanence has been stated according to its own form (*sarūpato*), he says "But that which... and so forth, showing that the others too have indeed been stated by way of their meaning (*atthato*).

It stands for only a moment (*matta-khaṇa-matta*); thus it is "momentary" (*mattaṭṭha*), meaning its duration is only a moment; it is "momentary" (*mattaṭṭhaka*) in the sense of having a very brief duration. It is "extremely momentary" (*ati-ittara-khaṇika*).

This is the meaning. Therefore he said, "of that which has a limited duration. "By the limitation of duration" means by way of its characteristic of lasting for no more than the occurrence of a single moment of consciousness (*citta*).
For, in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), the life-moment of sentient beings is delimited by the mere moment of the occurrence of a single consciousness.
Therefore he said, "For this... and so forth.

"Life" means the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "Pleasure and pain" means pleasant and painful feelings (*vedanā*); for equanimity (*upekkhā*) is also included within pleasure and pain because of its desirable or undesirable nature.
"Individual existence" (*attabhāva*) refers to the remaining phenomena, excluding life, feeling, and consciousness.
"Entirely" means unmixed with the state of a self (*attaniya*). "Associated with a single consciousness" means accompanied by a single moment of consciousness.
"Consisting of a single moment of consciousness. Because it lasts for only a single moment, the "moment" (khaṇa) of life and so forth proceeds as something light and extremely brief;
this is the meaning of "proceeds and passes away. The word "this" refers to the statement in the verse.
For the life of sentient beings proceeds only while obtaining the successive movement of inhalation and exhalation.

It does not occur when these [qualities] are not obtained; therefore, it proceeds only while being bound to the in-breath and out-breath. Likewise, it proceeds only while obtaining the balanced state of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

For, through the excessive disturbance of any one of the others—such as the water element and so forth—within the earth element, even a man endowed with strength may have a body that is either rigid, or has a body that is moist and putrid due to diarrhea and the like, or is overcome by a great fever, or has its joints and ligaments severed.
Or, having offered [the oblation], he reaches the end of his life. Life proceeds only for one who obtains solid food at the appropriate time;
for one who does not obtain it, it comes to exhaustion. Furthermore, life proceeds only while consciousness is active, not when that [consciousness] is inactive.
Here, by the word "iti" in the phrase "jīvitam iti," [the inclusion of] being bound to the postures, being bound to cold and heat, and so forth [is indicated].
Inclusion. For life proceeds only when the four postures maintain their equilibrium;
however, through the excessive intensity of any one of them, the life-formations (āyusaṅkhārā) are cut off.
Likewise, [the body] proceeds only when cold and heat maintain their equilibrium; but for one overcome by extreme cold or extreme heat, it fails.
"Of that which is grasped by craving": by this statement, which points out its status as a conditionally arisen phenomenon, he clarifies its very nature of momentary dissolution.

Because they are the direct opposites of the graspings of craving through the contemplation of suffering, the grasping of conceit through the contemplation of impermanence, and the grasping of views through the contemplation of non-self, these graspings are dispelled with absolute certainty by these three contemplations respectively.
He said, "It does not even exist. This is a demonstration of the occurrence of seeing the disappearance of the external earth element that has arrived.
"Grasping" means the grasping of the elements. "Establishing" means beginning or teaching. The construction is: "he shows power in the ear-door.
By way of showing the power of the practitioner of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he demonstrates the majesty of the meditation subject itself.
"Striking with speech" is said because of the presence of force at the ear-door. "Force" refers to the state of being without volition in the internal earth element just as in the external one;
it is the lack of reaction even when someone reviles or strikes one, like a tree.
"By way of its state of having arisen as it occurs" means by way of its state of being present at that time. "By way of its state of having arisen as a manifestation" means...
When that undesirable sound-object has come within range, there is javana-feeling (javana-vedanā) at the ear-door by way of its arising as the act of taking an object;
this is because it is stated [in the texts] that "feeling is suffering. For it is said, "by way of decisive support" (*upanissaya-vasena*).

"Feeling and so forth" refers both to the feeling mentioned here in the phrase "feeling is impermanent," as well as perception (*saññā*) and the other mental factors. These, indeed, share the same plane (*bhūmi*) as contact (*phassa*).
It is not the feeling mentioned previously. The object is the element itself; thus, it is the objective field (visaya) reckoned as the earth element, just as it was defined.
"Enters" means that the insight-consciousness enters by way of comprehension, [perceiving it] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
By this, he expresses the absence of outward distraction; however, by the word "becomes confident," he refers to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

"Entering the path" (vīthipaṭipannataṃ). "It stabilizes" (santiṭṭhati) refers to its abiding through the attainment of successive distinctions and through its immovability due to the overcoming of opposing factors.
"It is liberated" (vimuccati) refers to its specific release from the grasp of craving, conceit, and views.
In the commentary, however, the meaning is stated by way of origination: "it attains resolution" (adhimokkhaṃ labhati) regarding the object within the ear-door.
"Having come into the range of the senses": this is the vision of the root by means of fundamental full understanding (*mūlapariññā*).
Through the ear-doors, when one adverts improperly, greed arises toward a desirable object and aversion toward an undesirable object by way of the act of adverting and determining;
however, in the mind-door, there occurs lust and so forth [thinking] "woman," "man. For that, the impulsion of the five doors is the root—all of it.
Or [it may arise] from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so forth. Thus, thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) occurs by way of the root of the impulsion in the mind-door.
However, thorough knowledge as adventitiousness and temporary occurrence should be understood as applying only to the impulsion in the five doors, by way of its prior state and its subsequent state.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, has already been stated in the commentary on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhāna*).

Even for one who has performed the preliminary grasping by way of comprehending the elements as they truly are, if improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) should arise due to the force of habituation since beginningless time;
"having reached the function of determining" means having attained the state of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*).

Having received repetition (*āsevana*) once or twice, it does not [function] as a condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). For a rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata-ahetuka-citta*)...

There exists [a condition] that serves as the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya). If such were the case, then in the Paṭṭhāna, within the "Dependent" (paṭicca) section of the wholesome triad (kusalattika), it would have had to be stated:
"With path-condition, two in repetition; with repetition-condition, two in non-path. However, it is instead stated: "With path-condition, one in repetition;
with repetition-condition, one in non-path. And here, in the phrase "one or two," the mention of "one" (eka) serves to exclude [the possibility of] two.
This is stated for the sake of linguistic elegance. For in the second section on "Futility" (Mogha-vāra), the process of adverting does not occur only once;
rather, the mention of "once" refers to its occurrence twice, and the mention of "twice" refers to its occurrence three times.
In that context, when it occurs for the second and third times, it is as if it has already acquired the habit of repetition.
However, since the statement, "Having reached the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana), after receiving one or two rounds of repetition,
the mind sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)," might be said by way of the second "flood" (ogha) section, and since that occurs precisely due to the weakness of the object,
this is established as such in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*. But here, because of the power of the sharp insight (anupassanā), there is no arising of unwholesome states.
If one attends improperly due to the impossibility [of the object], there may be an improper determination rather than a proper one;
and in that case, during its occurrence, the impulsion (javana) would not arise with respect to a large or very large object—this meaning should be understood after careful consideration.

Or, even if one assumes this [object] to be of two kinds, if it were [so] in the section on dependence (*paṭicca-vāra*) and so forth within the triad of feelings (*vedanā-ttika*) in the forward order (*anuloma*), [the following applies].

It might have been said, "With respect to the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), there are two [factors] that are not path-conditions; with respect to the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*), there are two that are not repetition-conditions," yet this was not said.
For if even determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) were a repetition-condition, it would follow that wholesome and unwholesome states could also be so.
Indeed, a state that is fit to receive the condition of repetition does not become a repetition-condition merely by being a phenomenon (*dhamma*).
It has not been stated that [the wholesome and unwholesome] are conditions by way of repetition for determining consciousness; moreover, it is actually excluded by the statement:
“Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises, not by way of repetition as a condition. Dependent on an unwholesome state...
[and so on] ...not by way of repetition as a condition. Furthermore, even if it were argued that this was stated specifically with reference to states of different feeling, even so—
