For example, just as it is stated: "Adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya)," so too it could be stated:
"[it is] a condition by way of repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya). If it is argued that this was not stated because of a difference in genus (jāti-bheda), [we reply:

no, for just as there is a state of repetition-condition for sense-sphere states toward form-sphere states and so forth despite a difference in plane (bhūmi-bhinna), so too there is such a state despite a difference in genus.
It would indeed have to be stated [as such]; and by way of that which is of non-distinct type, just as it is said:

"Adverting is a condition for root-cause-accompanied aggregates by way of proximity-condition," so too it would have to be stated: "[it is] a condition by way of repetition-condition. Yet it is not so stated.
Therefore, even in the triad of feeling, it is said: "By way of repetition-condition, there is one [condition] for the Path, but not [in the case of] the Path itself."

When determining by way of enumeration that there is "only one" [condition] for the path-condition in relation to the repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), this section on the "futile" (*mogha-vāra*) must be understood after careful investigation, because voṭṭhabbana lacks the status of being a repetition-condition.
However, voṭṭhabbana is *āvajjana* (adverting) because it turns toward the stream of the path-resultant continuity; from that, there arises a dissimilar *javana* (impulsion).
From the perspective of its function, it could be designated as "attention" (*manasikāra*);

however, if that were the case, the *Paṭṭhāna* would not have stated, "Advertence (*voṭṭhabbana*) is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition," but rather would have simply stated "adverting" (*āvajjanā*).
Furthermore, that [adverting] is the object-prenascence for four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*) following the stage of advertence.

The determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), which has arisen taking form and so forth as its object because it was unable to become [a full cognitive process], stands in the place of the impulsion (*javana*) and then descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "Standing in the place of the impulsion" means that it occurs twice in the place where the impulsion would normally arise;
it does not mean by way of being an actual impulsion. And here, "having received repetition" (*āsevana*) is used in the same sense as repetition itself.

This meaning has already been stated [under the heading] "cultivation" (*āsevana*). Because of its expansive nature, it is precisely its occurrence two or three times that constitutes its similarity to cultivation here.
For it is said that its capacity to originate intimation (*viññatti*) is due to this expansiveness.
Although expansive, because it does not occur many times like the impulsion (*javana*) and because it is not well-established, it does not possess the status of cultivation in the primary sense.

The phrase "it occurs" is not stated here for the purpose of its repetition; rather, it is stated figuratively in the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), just as the term "path" is applied to the fruition-consciousnesses.
This refers to the work of insight meditation performed even once, by way of not giving rise to lust and the other defilements, as expressed in the passage beginning with "even if."

The practitioner of yoga acts thus. "Reached the peak" means having attained the summit. Because he is not overwhelmed by opposing factors, he possesses sharp insight through the clarity of his insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

The object is indeed grasped; for the mental adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*)—having the function of determining the absence [of the object] after the impulsion (*javana*) has occurred with the thought, "Thus my impulsion has impelled"—serves as the basis for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), or likewise through the process of adverting itself.
Having relinquished that object, at that very moment the original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) becomes the grasped object.
However, "by way of the second" refers to the case of one who is not an extremely keen vipassaka,
as described in the passage beginning, "another’s impulsion (javana) runs once by way of lust and so forth," where it is said, "his mind leaps into the element-object (dhātārammaṇa)" and so on.

Because it is stated in this sutta: “When he is practicing for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions, then at some time or other, due to a lapse of mindfulness, memories and intentions associated with acquisitions may still occur. But, Udāyi, the arising of mindfulness is slow;
nevertheless, he quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.”

In the *Laṭukikopama-sutta*. For in its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), after raising the objection: "Let those who are stream-enterers and so forth abandon [the defilements] first; how does an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) abandon them?", it says:

"Indeed, one who has begun insight meditation (*vipassaka*), when defilements suddenly arise through a lapse of mindfulness, feels a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: 'Defilement has arisen even in a monk such as myself,' and then exerts energy."
The meaning stated is: "Having increased insight, he eradicates the defilements by means of the path; thus, he is said to abandon.
Therefore it was said: "Because this is found in this sutta, beginning with the words 'his mind leaps forward toward the element as its object,'" and so forth.
And this meaning should be understood according to the medium course in the development of the faculties (indriyabhāvanā).
"By way of comprehension" means by way of the comprehension of the elements (*dhātu*).
Having encountered an undesirable object such as verbal abuse occurring through the cutting of vital parts and so forth, the person suffers at the ear-door;
likewise, having encountered an undesirable object such as beating or striking, he suffers at the body-door.
“They act upon” means they act entirely upon it from above. This so-called acting upon with disagreeable things is simply an attack by way of beating, striking, and so forth;

thus he says, “they attack,” which means they afflict. “Of such a nature” means that its very nature is such that it undergoes a change as soon as it is touched even slightly by the striking of hands and so on.
[This is illustrated] by the passage beginning, “Monks, even with a two-handled saw... and so forth.
The giving of exhortation (*ovādadāna*) is unique to the Buddhas alone and not shared with others; thus it is said:

"Even one who recollects, 'This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One'... even one who recollects the exhortation of the simile of the saw. Some say this is because it is the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*).
However, that which consists in being without malice and remaining unshaken even toward people who are like the bristles of a saw—that is the Teacher’s instruction (*satthusāsana*).
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: even when recollecting, one is indeed recollecting the Dhamma characterized by right practice.
By "the qualities of the bhikkhu," he refers to the quality established through the attainment of the noble Dhamma.
And since that is the quality of all Noble Ones (ariya), it is said that even when recollecting that, one is recollecting the Saṅgha.

What is intended here is insight-equanimity (vipassanupekkhā). Therefore, the meaning is that because equanimity supported by the wholesome does not settle [there], one does not obtain equanimity toward all formations by way of insight.

"Six-factored equanimity" (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) means "six-factored equanimity-like," due to the commonality of being without perturbation toward the desirable and undesirable. Hence he said, "But this... and so forth.

He establishes [the mind] in the six bases of equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhāṭhāna*), falling into a state of gladness by thinking, "It is a gain for me! It is well-gained by me! and so forth. 303. *Āpogataṃ*:
Water is so called by way of binding (*ābandhana*); because it has gone to the nature of water, it is *āpogata*.

Or, the meaning is that it has attained the state of water by its very own nature. For that moist and liquid state, which is reckoned as the nature of water, exists within the earth-element together with its constituents (*sasambhāra*) and within water and so forth together with their constituents.
It exists in all water; therefore it is said, "pervading all waters, it has the characteristic of the state of being moist," which means the characteristic of the state of fluidity.
Regarding the phrase "it agitates" (*pakuppati*), he says "it increases by way of a flood" with reference to its natural agitation.
Thus he says, "this is its natural agitation. However, to show the other [type of agitation], [he speaks of] "the time of the dissolution of the water-world" (*āposaṃvaṭṭakāle*).
The passage beginning with "panā" has been stated. Regarding the term "ogacchanti," here "ogamana" (going down) is intended in the sense of exhaustion, not merely going downwards;
thus he says, "reaching the hearth... etc. 304.
"Gone among all fiery elements" means gone among all portions of the fire-element, which are divided into many types by way of fuel and so forth.
"Occurrence. Just as *pīti* itself is *pītigata*, so too *tejo* itself is *tejogata*; the meaning is that it is merely an occurrence by way of heating.

In the same way, *āpogata* and *vāyogata* are to be understood; thus he said "in the former," and so forth. "By way of being subject to one-day fever, etc. means by way of the various types of aging such as one-day fever and the like.
"Born with heat" means overcome by heat. "He ages" means he becomes decrepit. By way of the fire element (*tejodhātu*).

In order to show that the occurrence of aging within this body should be understood by way of manifest aging while it is still occurring, the passage beginning with “deficiency of the faculties” was stated.

“The state of having wrinkles and grey hair” means the condition of having wrinkles and grey hair, as well as the loosening of the limbs and members. “By one who is provoked” means by one who is agitated.
Ghee is that which has been extracted after heating it a hundred times and repeatedly throwing it into cold water.
They say that *sata-dhota-sappī* (clarified butter purified a hundred times) is [the remedy]. The state of heat that exceeds the body’s natural temperature is *santāpa* (fever);
the great burning that proceeds by way of consuming the body is *paridāha* (consumption)—this is the distinction between them. *Asita* means swallowed;
*khāyita* means chewed; *sāyita* means tasted. "It undergoes proper digestion" refers to a digestive system (*gahaṇī*) that is well-balanced in its maturation.
This is stated by way of [the stomach] not digesting properly; it should also be understood by way of a digestive fire (*gahaṇī*) that digests irregularly.

"By way of the state of chyle and so forth" means by way of the states of chyle, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, and semen. "Separation" (*viveka*) refers to the state of being distinct, the state of being mutually dissimilar.
During the transformation of food divided into the categories of what is eaten and so forth, there arises chyle; depending upon that, the element of chyle (*rasadhātu*) [arises].

The meaning is "it arises. In this way, regarding the transformation of the nutrient essence (*rasa*), everything should be understood by applying [the same analysis] starting from "blood" and so forth.

"Haritantam" means simply "green"; the word *anta* is used for metrical expansion of the phrase, just as in the cases of "forest-limit" (*vananta*) and "discourse-text" (*suttanta*). "Cammanillekhanam" refers to the slough that has been scraped off the skin and discarded.
Regarding the phrase "vomiting, hiccups, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes the winds that cause belching, spitting, and so forth.

It should be seen. Regarding the phrase "feces, urine, and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the wind that expels bile, phlegm, pus, and the like, as well as the heat-wind.

Although the word *kucchi* is a synonym for the belly (*udara*), since the word *koṭṭha* refers to the interior, the remaining portion of the belly is what is meant here by the word *kucchi*; thus he says, "lying in the belly."

"Because the inner winds are outside the outer winds. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "bending, stretching, etc.," all bodily activities such as looking forward, looking around, lifting, and so forth are included.
"Ossavana" means that water flows out from it; it is the edge of the covering. "Here" (*idha*) means in this place.
(306) "The state of being devoid of a sentient being" (*nissattabhāva*) means the absence of a self-made entity. For the four elements, as they have been shown, are merely non-self (*anattaniya*).
This shows the meaning: "consisting of elements, devoid of a sentient being, and lifeless.

"Surrounded" means standing surrounded, being encompassed. Therefore he said, "These," and so forth; the intention is that sticks and other materials are placed there by way of a particular arrangement.
Otherwise, the conventional designation "house" would not exist. Therefore he said, "But in the case of sticks and so forth," and so on. For what purpose [this was stated] in the Pāḷi...
The passage beginning with “Just as, friends,” and so forth, was commenced; in order to make that meaning clear, the passage beginning with “Just as firewood, etc. was stated.
Granted that below, by the phrase “of the body consisting of the seven [nutritive] essences,” and so forth, derived matter (*upādārūpa*) was also mentioned both generally and partially;
likewise, feeling and the other [aggregates] were not mentioned while being defined as aggregates (*khandha*), and craving (*taṇhā*) was treated in the same manner.

By way of its nature as the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). However, the other truths have not been explained in their entirety. For this very reason it was said: "Below... [they] were not explained.
When the clarity of the eye (*cakkhupasāda*) has ceased means when the clarity of the eye has perished. "Impaired" (*upahata*) means afflicted by things such as eye-worms (*pubbakimi*).
"Obstructed" (*palibuddha*) means covered by the arising of eye-secretions (*pubba*) and so forth, even without [the worms]. "Corresponding" (*tajja*) means...

"Suitable for that" means suitable for the arising of eye-consciousness. Attention, which arises when a visible object has come into the range of the eye, exists only when the eye exists—even though it is dependent on the heart-base—and does not exist when it is absent;
therefore, it is said to "arise in dependence on the eye. Just as the revolving of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) [occurs] through its object-condition...
Thus it is said, "dependent on the eye and visible forms," that there is also a condition of confidence (*pasāda*). "That" refers to the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) at the eye-door.

"Of one engaged in something else" means of one intent upon another object. "Appropriate to that" means appropriate to those [factors], namely the eye, the visible form, and the mental advertence (*tadābhoga*).
The intention is that he shows the four truths both by way of their essential nature (*sarūpato*) and by way of their implication (*atthāpattito*).
"Tathābhūta" means one who has become such, or one who has attained such a state; the meaning is: of one who is endowed with such a mode of conditions, just as visual consciousness arises.

"Matter arisen from the three" refers to matter arisen from temperature, kamma, and nutriment. And this [is said] even though, at that time, there is also matter arisen from the mind that is turning back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
This is stated merely by taking the absence of matter produced by eye-consciousness.
"It goes into inclusion" means that, like a city, it enters into the state of being included within the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) in the kingdom [of consciousness].

Because it is said "of one who has become thus," feeling and the other [mental factors] are associated specifically with eye-consciousness, and consciousness itself is specifically eye-consciousness. "Volitional formations" (saṅkhārā) refers to...

The intention is that volition is mentioned [first] because the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) has volition as its primary constituent. Furthermore, in that context, contact, the life-faculty, attention, and mental stability are also indeed phenomena belonging to the aggregate of formations.
"Taken together" (*ekato saṅgaho*) means counting them as one as "the five aggregates.

"Coming together" (*samāgamo*) means their convergence according to their respective conditions. "Assemblage" (*samavāyo*) means the state of being gathered together through their mutual relationship as conditions.
“Dependent origination” (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) means that which causes phenomena arisen in dependence to arise; it is the mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*).

It is said, “He who sees dependent origination,” and so forth, because one who sees the conditioning phenomena also sees the phenomena arisen in dependence upon them, and one who sees those [latter] also sees the conditioning phenomena. “By way of making a wish” means by way of craving (*taṇhā*).
"By way of making it a basis" means by way of making it an object of dependence. "By way of making it an object of attachment" means by way of being enamored with it.
"Having plunged into" means by way of grasping firmly—as if having entered the object, as if having swallowed it, and as if having finished consuming it.
It is called "the removal of desire and lust" (*chandarāgavinaya*) and "the abandoning of desire and lust" (*chandarāgapahāna*) because therein desire and lust are removed and abandoned.
Nibbāna. "Having brought" means it should be taken by way of inclusion, having been brought forward according to its meaning even though it does not appear explicitly in the text (*pāḷi*).
Showing the method of bringing it forward, he said, "That which, among these... and so forth. "Among these three points" refers to the three points of realization (*abhisamaya*) as previously stated:
pleasure, pain, and so on. "View" is [to be understood] by way of the realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*), and so forth.

Right view is the turning [toward the truth] and the seeing of things as they really are. In this same way, right intention and the other factors should also be understood according to their respective roles.
"Penetration by means of development" means penetration through the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not merely by taking [the object] as a mental support (*ārammaṇa*).
"This is the path" refers to the eightfold path that proceeds by way of penetrating the four noble truths. "Even at this point" means thus, within a single eye-door (*cakkhudvāra*).
By means of the apprehension of the physical basis (*vatthu*), and by bringing the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths to its culmination,
the Blessed One’s teaching has been extensively, abundantly, and perfectly fulfilled and practiced.
It is said that the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), having arisen and ceased, becomes the condition for the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana-citta*).
“Even that which has ceased”: this is said with reference to one who is overcome by a heavy sleep, meaning it remains in a state of dullness on the path.

However, for one who is seized by monkey-drowsiness, the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) might occasionally serve as a condition for adverting. “At the very time of the life-continuum” means at the very moment the life-continuum is occurring;
[this applies] to those who are proficient in jhāna, proficient in meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), or proficient in texts.
Mental attention (manasikāra) occurs even without deliberate application (ābhoga), simply through the state of proficiency.

For instance, when one is reciting a text that has been mastered as if it were continuous, because of being occupied with something else, there is no observation such as, "this much of the text has been covered; this much remains.
The phrase "arising from all four [bases]" refers to all material form arising from the four bases, not as previously described.

The intended meaning is "arising from three [causes] alone. Because they are the forerunners and because they are gross, contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*) alone are taken as the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), not because others are absent.
"Comprehending only a portion" means touching upon the teaching by way of explaining only a single part, without having fully explained the matter as it was listed below. "In this place" means...
In the context of explaining the meaning as it was indicated by way of the six sense bases, beginning with "Friends, the eye is internal," and so forth;

"the teaching below is deficient" refers to the entire range of meanings that were omitted by way of the detailed exposition, such as "derived form, the four immaterial aggregates, and the three higher Noble Truths. By way of this or that sense base...

The eye-door and so forth [are explained] according to their respective doors. Since the teaching, having been commenced by way of the Four Noble Truths, was concluded by way of the Four Noble Truths as well, he said:
"He brought the sutta to its conclusion precisely following the sequence of the connection.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Mahāhatthipadopama-sutta* (The Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint) is completed.
9. Commentary on the Mahāsāropama-sutta 307.
*Nacirapakkante*: not long after he had departed; that is, not long after he had gone away. *Saliṅgeneva*:
by means of his own former outward signs, such as the shaving of the head and the wearing of the saffron robes. *Pāṭiyekke jāte*: because his conduct and views had become corrupted.
After the performance of the *pakāsanīya-kamma* (act of reconciliation), he became distinct and separate from those similar to other sectarians (*aññatitthiya*).

"A son of good family" (*kulaputta*) means a son of good family by birth alone. "Untainted" (*asambhinnāya*) means free from contamination; the meaning is that it is devoid of the intermingling of castes.
Here, under the heading of "birth," suffering based on birth is stated; thus he says: "One who has gone down" (*otiṇṇa*) is one into whom birth has entered within.
For once a being is born, from the very moment of birth, he is afflicted as if pierced within by the suffering caused by the fact of birth.
The same principle applies to aging and the other [stages of existence]. "Gains" (*lābhā*) refers to the four requisites being obtained;
the "well-made state" or "thoroughly prepared state" refers to the excellence of those four requisites when they are being acquired. "Praising" (*vaṇṇabhaṇana*) means the extolling of virtues.
“Unrenowned” means they are not known by way of being esteemed; this is a demonstration of the absence of the production of gain and so forth.
Therefore he said: “They do not receive even a mere measure of food and clothing. “Of little influence” means they have little power.
That state of having little influence becomes manifest through the absence of both excellence in leadership and excellence in retinue. In that regard, regarding excellence in retinue...
Showing the absence [of such things], he said, "having few attendants.

Since some, through ignorance or by obtaining what is not known, perform even that which is not essential (asāra) though it ought to be done, he spoke the phrase "that which is to be made essential by means of the essential" for the purpose of distinguishing it from those;
showing this, he said, "such as axles, wheels, yokes, ploughs, and so forth."
“Of the holy life” (brahmacariyassa) means of the holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings.

For this great tree—whose heartwood is the path and its fruits, whose sapwood is knowledge and vision, whose bark is concentration, and whose outer bark is virtue—the four conditions, being restless by nature and prone to creeping about, are called the “branches and foliage. “By that very [means]” means by the very production of gain, honor, and fame.
"In this Dispensation, 'the essence is my attainment' means that the so-called essence to be realized has been reached through the production of gain and so forth;
thus he has attained complacency, having finished what was to be done.
(310) "Knowledge and vision" refers to the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), which is vision consisting of knowledge that functions by way of realizing the object.
"Subtle form" refers to the form of deities and so forth, or any other form of a subtle nature. Therefore he said: "At least...
they dwell," for here, by way of a superior description, the divine eye is taken as "knowledge and vision. 311.
Regarding the phrase "he attains the non-temporal liberation" (*asamayavimokkha*), in order to show what is intended here as "non-temporal liberation" by means of the text itself:
“What is ‘liberation independent of time’? and so forth is said. For the eight [attainments], there is both a time for entering them and a time when they are not entered;
however, for liberation by means of the path, there is neither a specific time nor a non-time.
For one whose faith is powerful and who has initiated insight (vipassanā), it occurs whether they are walking, standing, sitting, or eating.
It should not be said that there is no penetration of the paths and fruits;

thus, for one who is liberated by way of the liberation of the path, there is neither time nor non-time [for it], and therefore it is "liberation at any time" (asamayavimokkha). Hence he said, "The mundane attainments," and so forth.
It is "unshakable" (akuppa) because it does not waver and does not perish; its nature is such that it never undergoes decline. By way of the subsiding of all defilements—
“Liberation of mind” means *cetovimutti*. Therefore, he said, “the liberation that is the fruit of arahantship. This meaning is the purpose of this;
thus it is “for this purpose,” namely the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Dispensation, and this [liberation] is its ultimate pinnacle.

Since the teaching was concluded with a fruit that serves as a metaphor for the core of what was undertaken, he said, “he brought the teaching to a conclusion according to the sequence of connection (*yathānusandhi*). As for what is here...
The meaning has not been analyzed; that is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the Mahāsāropama Sutta is completed.
10. The Commentary on the Cūḷasāropama Sutta.

312. *Piṅgaladhātuka* means having a tawny nature or a tawny complexion; or it means "tawny-eyed. *Saṅgha* refers to a community of those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*), not in the sense of being gathered together by virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.
They are called *saṅghina* because they possess a *saṅgha* that serves as their retinue.
*So eva* means that very same one designated as a community of those who have gone forth. *By way of training in conduct* means by himself...
"By means of training in practices such as the fabricated observance of nakedness (*acelakatā*) and so forth.

"Renowned" (*paññātā*) means renowned both by way of the precepts they have undertaken for themselves and by way of the views they have acquired through understanding. "Causers of [wrong] views" (*laddhikarā*) means those who give rise to that wrong view.
"Of many people" (*bahujanassa*) means of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*). For them, there is not even the perfection of scripture (*āgama*), so how could there be realization (*adhigama*)?
He said, "the blind worldling (puthujjana) alone," referring to "the uninstructed, blind, foolish worldling.
For the wise do not place their confidence in that which is unworthy of confidence. A *maṅgaladāsa* is a slave who performs the duties to be done for the sake of auspicious ceremonies.
*Tantāvūtānaṃ* means those woven after spreading out the warp. *Gaṇṭhanakilesa* is the defilement of bondage within saṃsāra.

"Thus having spoken" means thus having admitted, or thus having held as a view. "Leading out" (niyyānika) means being conducive to the state of deliverance and possessing the quality of being incontrovertible;
the intention is that they do not constitute grounds for reproach. The construction is to be supplied by bringing in the words "if they were not leading out.
Because their claim to omniscience was untrue, he said that by stating its falsity, no purpose whatsoever was achieved for that brahmin.
“Because there is no purpose [in teaching] by way of stating that these [states] lack the quality of leading to liberation.

(318) One whose underlying intention (*ajjhāsayo*) is attached to the base worldly pleasures, and not to *nibbāna*, is one with a sluggish intention (*līnajjhāsayo*). Because he lacks intense reverence for the training, he grasps the Dispensation (*sāsana*) in a lax manner.
(323) “Below” refers to the Mahāsāropama Sutta immediately preceding this. The states of the first jhāna and so forth serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka*).
They are the proximate cause for insight (*vipassanā*). "Here" means in this *Cūḷasāropama Sutta*.

"Having cessation as their basis" refers to non-returners (*anāgāmin*) or arahants who are capable of attaining the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Therefore" means because they have cessation as their basis.
It should be understood that the states beginning with the first jhāna are superior to knowledge and vision.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Cūḷasāropama Sutta is completed.
And the Commentary on the Opamma Vagga is finished.
4. The Mahāyamaka Vagga.
1. Commentary on the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta 325.
A village that serves as a place of residence for kinsmen is a *ñātiko*; that very same thing is a *nātiko*.
It is said that the village belonged to those whose ancestor had established it as a common property for his own kinsmen; therefore, it was known as a "nātiko."
Then later, it was divided into two parts by two heirs and enjoyed by them. Therefore he said:
"Two villages for the two sons of the younger and elder uncles. *Giñjakā* means bricks; a dwelling made of bricks is a *giñjakāvasatha*.
It is said that in that place, the clay was unmixed with gravel, pebbles, sand, and so forth, being neither hard, but soft and fine.
The pottery vessels made by her were as strong as if they were made of stone;

therefore, those lay devotees had long and broad bricks made from that clay, and having set up the doorposts, windows, shutters, and beams with them, they constructed the entire palace using only bricks, without any other building materials. Hence he said, "With bricks alone," and so forth.
The Gosiṅga Sāla Grove: this refers to the protected forest that received the name "Gosiṅga Sāla Grove.
"Of the chief tree" means of the *sāla* tree which was like a lord of the forest. "The flavor of concord" refers to the bliss of seclusion characterized by qualities such as harmony.

In the *Upakkilesa Sutta* of the *Upari Paññāsa*, the period of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is described; here, in the *Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta*, the period of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is described.

It has been explained. For those great elders, though they had accomplished their task, dwelt there considering their own dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*), the following of others' example by others, cultivating supreme seclusion (*viveka*), and experiencing the flavor of concord (*sāmaggirasa*).
"Then" (*tadā*) means at the time of the teaching of the *Upakkilesa-sutta*. "Those" (*te*) refers to the sons of good family headed by Anuruddha.
"Having obtained gratification" means having obtained gratification through the course of progress in insight (vipassanā).
For when insight proceeds by bringing about successive distinctions, it brings about an extraordinary degree of rapture and mental joy. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"From whatever [aspect] one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates..."
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless.
Having "found a footing" means through the attainment of the paths and fruits. For when the paths and fruits are attained, one is said to have found a footing in the Dispensation, and not otherwise.
Granted that Sāriputta and Moggallāna were included among the Great Disciples, yet by virtue of their status as the Chief Disciples, theirs—
The separate mention of "the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the General of the Dhamma," is for the purpose of showing their distinction.
For even when there is a common connection, those who possess special qualities are mentioned separately, as in: "Brahmins have arrived; Vāsiṭṭha has also arrived.
Even though they are mentioned separately from those [eighty], the mention of "the eighty great disciples" includes a small deficiency or excess.
Or it does not enter into calculation. "At the very least" (antamaso) is said because he is close in conduct due to his role as an attendant to the Dhamma-treasurer.
"Troops" (anīka) refers to an elephant troop; the meaning is a multitude of elephants from among the elephant troops.
It is said, "like a black lion escaped from the herd," because a black lion generally wanders apart from the herd. However, the maned lion...
"Like one wandering alone. "Like a cloud severed by the wind" means like a fragment of a cloud the size of a mountain peak that has been torn away by the wind.

"By grasping at those" means just as a desire arises for food in one who is hungry, for drink in one who is thirsty, for warmth in one touched by cold, for coolness in one touched by heat, and for happiness in one who is suffering.
In the same way, having seen the Kosambī monks of the Blessed One’s community fallen into mutual dispute, while others were living in concord, he directed his attention [to them];
these three clansmen came into his field of vision, and desiring to uplift them, he approached them.
Thus, through this sequence of practice, it became the means for the discipline of the Kosambī monks. Therefore, he said: “Of them...”
"Because of taking it up. By this very [phrase], "out of compassion for future generations," it should be understood that this reason as well has been described only in part.
"Having exalted" means having distinguished by way of praising with the qualities as they truly are, having made them superior;
this is a repetitive expression (āmeḍita-vacana) in the sense of praise.
That forest is protected by one appointed by the owner of the woods; it is a grove that is guarded and preserved, unlike the great forests and such which are unowned.
Those who have set out for their own welfare through the various categories of virtue and so forth are seekers of their own good, not those who have not abandoned attachment;
thus he said, "desiring their own welfare. Therefore he said, "For whoever," and so forth. "Should destroy" means should ruin.
“Weak people” means people who are weak in wisdom, the ignorant. “Those” refers to the miracles that appeared during the various births and so forth.
“Having concealed them with the interior of his robe” means as if hiding them within a chamber known as a robe;
for the majesty of a Buddha is not concealed merely by being covered with a robe. Rather, it was done in such a manner [thinking], “Lest anyone should know this majesty of a Buddha.”
Having concealed himself by means of a supernormal feat (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*), the Blessed One departed; thus it was said. Therefore he said: "He went in the guise of a stranger.
Regarding the word *abhikkamatha* ("come forth"), he says "come hither from here," because it expresses an injunction toward the state of being face-to-face.
The body of the Buddhas is as beautiful as a perfectly pure birth-gem; there is no stain whatsoever that needs to be removed.
To the question, "For what purpose did the Blessed One wash his feet? he replied, "Of the Buddhas," and so forth.
Alternatively, the term *Anuruddhā* is stated according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*), since the single remainder of dissimilar forms (*virūpekasesa*) is also accepted;
and by doing so, the use of the plural number is also justified. "The posture is comfortable" means because of the lightness of the body.
The fourfold posture is also easy to maintain. "It sustains life" means that life has the characteristic of sustaining;
it sustains this body-frame, causing it to proceed with ease.

"Whether it be a ladleful of gruel or a spoonful of alms-food"—this was said by way of describing the maintenance of life through mixed food obtained by the "crocodile's gait" (makaravutti) mode of living. Therefore he said, "He asks about the practice of wandering for alms."
"They meet each other" means that although both groups are distinct in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), their differences are difficult for ordinary people to discern;
they remain as if completely blended together, like milk and water mixed.
Therefore he said: "They do not exist separately; they approach as if they were one. "Loving eyes" (*piyacakkhu*) are eyes that manifest affection.
One is called "dear" (*piya*) because one loves (*piyāyati*) or because one ought to be loved.
When the Blessed One asked, "In what way? and so forth, he did so inquiring about the sole cause for living in harmony; thus it is said, "'In what way? is a question regarding the cause.

It refers to that specific manner in which these very actions and so forth, accompanied by loving-kindness (*mettā*), manifest toward one another. With reference to this, he said, "'In what way' (*kathaṃ*)."
Question. For thus, later on, the answer was spoken by the elders beginning with, "In this way indeed, Bhante.
That which has loving-kindness (*mettā*) as its essence is *mettaṃ*, namely bodily action (*kāyakamma*). "Openly" (*āvī*) means manifestly. "Secretly" (*raho*) means not manifestly.
For whatever bodily action one establishes directed toward someone, if that is in their presence, it is manifest; if behind their back, [it is secret].
That is of little light. Therefore he said: "Both openly and in secret" means both in the presence of others and behind their backs.

"The other two" refers to bodily and verbal actions performed behind one's back. The passage beginning with "In that regard" was stated in brief; the words beginning with "For whatever" are spoken to explain that meaning.
Or, it may refer to a place suitable for being looked after by means of sweeping and so forth. "In the same way" means as follows:

It has been stated regarding the performance of loving-kindness through bodily action in one's presence; it is the same here. Friendly conversation consists of talk such as, "I hope you are well," and so forth.
Conversation of hospitality is talk conducted by way of welcoming others so that no deficiency exists between oneself and them.
[For example: "Oh, how wonderful! At that time the Elder gave me exhortation and gave me instruction."
Thus, "recollection-talk" (*sāraṇīya-kathā*) is talk connected with what is to be remembered at another time, or talk connected with the six things that are conducive to recollection.
"Dhamma-talk" (*dhammī-kathā*) is talk connected with the teachings such as virtue (*sīla*), etc., by way of laying down a passage from the Sutta and explaining its meaning.
"Reciting in melody" (*sarabhañña*) is the chanting of a Sutta in a melodic tone. "Questioning" (*pañha*) is the posing of a question regarding a meaning that one wishes to know.
The posing of a question; the answering of that question as it was asked is the "answering of the question.
"Thus attending" means thus bringing it to mind; the meaning is, thus directing loving-kindness toward them.
It is not possible to do so simultaneously, therefore [the directions are] separate. "In the sense of welfare" means by way of the state of mutual welfare, just like one's own.
"In the sense of being without interval" means by way of the absence of an intermediate space or a division. "In the sense of non-obstruction" means by way of the state of being without conflict.
"In the sense of being united" means by way of being joined together. "Having plastered around" means having smeared it with thick or thin coatings of clay.
"Or washing their own robes" means they wash their own robes. "Or plastering around" means they plaster the area around their own leaf-hut.
327. Regarding the phrase "paṭiviruddhā eva" (only those who are at variance), here too the word "yebhuyyena" (for the most part) should be brought in and connected.

"Tesaṃ appamādalakkhaṇaṃ" means their characteristic of non-negligence; that is, their essential nature of being diligent. Regarding the phrase "kacci pana vo anuruddhā samaggā," here too "vo" is merely a particle, or it is a form of the second-person plural pronoun; thus the meaning should be understood as "I hope you [all] are harmonious."
*Samuggapātiṃ*: a bowl resembling a casket. *Vattapaṭipatti*:
the practice of duties consisting of sweeping the courtyard both inside and outside the leaf-hut.
*Paṭivisamattameva*: just enough for one’s own maintenance. *Osāpetvā*: having put [the food] inside. *Pamāṇameva*: just the measure required for one’s own maintenance.
"Having abandoned in the manner stated" means having abandoned according to the method set forth in the Pāḷi.
"Binding hand to hand" means binding one's own hand to the other person's hand by means of a firm grip.
"Vilaṅghaka" refers to the hand; it is called *vilaṅghaka* because one causes [the other] to reach another place (*desantara*) by means of it. Thus, the hand itself is the *vilaṅghaka*.
*Hatthavilaṅghaka*: by that which leaps from hand to hand.
"Having made it unbroken" means having made it continuous by way of the occurrence of the hearing of the Dhamma over the course of those three days.
"This" refers to the statement beginning with "Now, every five days. It occurs on every fifth day.
Every five days. By the Elder Anuruddha when questioned by the Blessed One. "In the very places of negligence" means in the very places where others are negligent.
The phrase "in the very places of negligence" was stated; then, in order to make that same meaning clearer, the words beginning with "for others...
were spoken. "Bases for the production of proliferation" means bases for the production of verbal proliferation (*kathā-papañca*) through the occurrence of loose talk.

These are the points for negligence regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Even there, the Elder demonstrates the perfection of his own characteristic of heedfulness by saying, "Venerable sir, we do not practice in a way contrary to the meditation subject.
However, the phrase "having left this much space" was said because at that time there was no opportunity for entering the meditative attainments (*vihārasamāpatti*) in the monastery.
328. Because meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is intended here, it is stated simply as "the distinction of noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa*).

The Elder said, "What indeed could there not be, venerable sir? because he had pleased the Teacher's mind through his own correct practice, and because that specific attainment was directly evident to the Teacher.
"As long as" (*yāvadeva*) means for whatever duration of time—whether one part of a day or the entire night.
Or for as many as seven days.

329. *Samatikkamāya* means for the sake of complete transcendence. For when there is the attainment of a higher distinction, the lower jhāna is said to have been transcended and its agitation has subsided (*paṭippassaddhi*). Therefore he said, "for the sake of subsiding. *Ñāṇadassanaviseso* (distinction of knowledge and vision).
It should be understood that this is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause.

"From the pleasure of what is felt" means either from the pleasure of jhāna accompanied by feeling, or from the pleasure of the fruit. "Pleasure not felt" is pleasure devoid of feeling, like the pleasure of Nibbāna.
Furthermore, "pleasure not felt" is merely an illustration; it is indeed entirely devoid of all mind and mental factors, being intangible, non-perceptual, and non-conscious.

And thus, even though material phenomena are still occurring therein, because it is insentient and entirely devoid of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkha), the attainment of cessation is said to be more peaceful and more sublime.
Therefore he said: “The pleasure that is not felt is more peaceful and more sublime. By this, it was stated: “And from this,” and so forth.
330. The Blessed One spoke specifically on the benefits of concord (*sāmaggī-rasa-anisamsa*) because it was in accordance with his disposition.
*Anusāvetvā* means having properly announced [the matter] by way of approaching [him]. Alternatively, the reading is *anusaṃsāvetvā*, which has the same meaning.
Then, having turned back—thinking, "At present, the Blessed One’s intention is for solitary dwelling," and thus capturing the Teacher’s mind—they said, "Right here..."

"Stay! Having turned back from the place where he had been dismissed, [he spoke]. Regarding the phrase "ordination and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes full ordination (*upasampadā*), purification (*visuddhi*), the practice of the ascetic virtues (*dhutanga*), the application to the meditation subject (*kammatthāna*), the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the liberations (*vimokkha*), the attainments (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), the cultivation of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*), the realization of the fruit (*phala-sacchikiriyā*), and so on.

Regarding the phrase "even having attained," the particle "even" (*api*) implies that this applies even to those things already attained. Regarding the phrase "being ashamed by talk of one's own qualities":

although he had attained these things by relying upon the Blessed One, [he was ashamed] because the discourse on the Dhamma would illuminate the Teacher’s lack of hostility toward his disciples. The Blessed One...
The construction is: “even though she was shrinking away from talk about manifest virtues. “Deities” refers to those deities who have attained various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
“My mouth falters” means my mouth is capable of speaking; the sense is that it is fit for discourse.

(331) “Thus arrived” means thus arrived in the *Āṭānāṭiya Sutta*. “Enveloping” means reproaching. “Being envious” is said because he thinks: “She is being envious, unable to bear even the Blessed One’s announcement of her own virtues.”
"01. Their gains": the gains of those Vajjian kings and the people dwelling in the Vajji kingdom—namely, their human birth, their residence in a suitable locality, and so forth;
and for the Blessed One and the three sons of good family, the gains consisting of seeing, paying homage, giving, hearing the Dhamma, and so on. "Well-gained are these gains" is the construction.
"One should recollect with a confident mind": having inspired confidence in the mind regarding the virtues of that family, such as their moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.
One should recollect them. It was said of them: "Bhikkhus, I declare that even this recollection is of great benefit to those bhikkhus.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Mahāgosiṅga Sutta*.
"332. *Kocideva* means: whatever village might be a grazing village (*gocaragāma*) situated in the vicinity of the Gosiṅgasālavana;
therefore, because it is not fixed, a grazing village is not included here, but rather the place of residence is indicated. For that very reason, this has the forest as its source.
*Sabbattha* means: in both the world of the gods and the world of humans. *Thirakārakehi* means: [factors] that make the Dispensation (*sāsana*) firm."
By those who bring about steadfastness. "Born at the end of hearing" means because they were born through noble birth at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma, which contains the four truths.
They are called *sāvakas* (hearers) because they hear the Dhamma in such a way that the thorough knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-bāhusacca*) succeeds.
Like the sun, they dispel the darkness of delusion by being radiant with the rays of brilliant qualities. Like the moon, they do so by possessing qualities that are delightful, charming, and cool.
Because of the subsiding of the fever of the defilements; because of the established nature of the Dhamma through its depth, stability, vastness, and manifold qualities, like the ocean;

and because of the Elder’s renown due to the greatness of his qualities—and since that greatness of qualities is to be known precisely according to the method handed down in the Suttas—it was said, beginning with "not only," in order to demonstrate this in detail. "The Sīhanāda Sutta" [is found] in the Majjhima Nikāya.
The *Mahāsīhanāda-sutta* has been included. The *Therapañha-sutta* is the *Sāriputta-sutta* found in the *Aṭṭhakavagga* of the *Suttanipāta*.
The *Therasīhanāda-sutta* is the *Sīhanāda-sutta* delivered by this Elder in the presence of the Teacher during his journey through the countryside.
The *Abhinikkhamana* [refers to] that very Elder’s great departure together with a vast circle of kinsmen and a vast circle of wealth.
The renunciation of the household life is the Great Renunciation. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. *Yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "whoever this may be.
"Taking along monks of great wisdom" means that, it is said, even the monks in the retinue of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera were themselves of great wisdom.
For beings come together according to their own elements (*dhātu*). This same method applies to the phrases "himself a possessor of psychic power," and so forth. This...
The purpose [of this discourse] should be illustrated by the *Dhātusaṃyutta*:

while seated on his sickbed on Vulture Peak Mountain, the Blessed One looked out at Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others who were staying around him for protection and walking back and forth with their respective retinues, and addressed the bhikkhus: “Do you see, bhikkhus, Sāriputta?”
“...walking to and fro together with many bhikkhus. “It is so, Bhante. “All these bhikkhus, monks, are of great wisdom”—all this should be recited in full.
“At the edge of the forest” means at the edge of a grove. “Meghavaṇṇāya” means having a blue luster, like [the radiance] of one rising from the surface of the ocean.

This was said with reference to its presence [in proximity]. Because it functions by means of an irradiation of light near the summit of the mountain of the world-sphere (*cakkavāḷapabbata*), it is said to be "on the summit of the eastern mountain of the world-sphere," not because the lunar disk actually moves upon the summit of the mountain of the world-sphere.
If that were the case, the light of the moon and sun would also pervade even the hells of the world-intervals (*lokantarika-niraya*). As for its height...
Indeed, the moon and sun move from the very center of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.

It is said that "as if being sprinkled with lac juice" because the radiance of the *sāla* flowers is exceedingly red. "As if singing along" means as if approaching and singing in the manner of paying homage.
"What delight indeed today? refers to the delight of meditative absorption (*jhāna-samāpatti*) itself; or rather—
He thought: "She delights in discussing the Dhamma; she delights in teaching the Dhamma.
With a radiance that had reached the pinnacle of supreme beauty, like two lunar disks;
with a splendor of virtues that was exceedingly pure and brilliant, like two solar disks; and with a majestic power like that of two Chaddanta elephant-kings.
Like two lions because of their majestic power; like two tigers because of their fearless conduct.
"All in full bloom" means everything is blossoming on all sides.
333. A "discourse-locale" (*kathā-upacāra*) is a place where discourse approaches or proceeds—that is, a range of hearing; that is the discourse-locale.

"Delightful" (*rāmaṇīyaka*) means simply that which is charming. "Ujjaṅgalā" refers to a rough or barren place. "Dosinā" means those who have gone away from faults; here, the letter *t* has been changed to *n*.
"Devalike gandhā viya" means like the scents in the world of the gods.
"Dibbā" means existing in heaven (*divi*). "The two elders" refers to the Elder Sāriputta and the Elder Ānanda. Let the Elder Ānanda, for his part, take care of me.
How did the Elder Sāriputta speak from the standpoint of one whose taints (*āsava*) were not yet exhausted?
This was not out of attachment rooted in affection for his home, but rather out of respect for his virtues; thus, there is no fault here.
"An inquiry for consent" (*anumatipucchā*) means an inquiry made for the purpose of obtaining consent. In that regard, since even what is unrighteous (*adhammika*)...
The other is not permitted to refuse the consent of one who is senior; therefore, that [senior] must indeed grant permission.
For this reason, it says: "This is called the inquiry for consent," and so forth.
"Starting from the junior" means starting from the youngest. *Paṭibhāna* is that which appears or presents itself; as intended—
This is the meaning; this is the inspired response (*paṭibhāna*). It will not reach the summit or attain full expansion because it was spoken by those established in partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*).
It will reach the summit and attain full expansion because it is in harmony with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
To clarify this very point by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated. In that context, the adversaries are struck with fear.
*Aṭṭa* means that by which things are afflicted; it is a term for a legal decision. *Gāmabhojaka* refers to the village chief of the village where he was born.
*Janapadabhojaka* refers to the provincial governor of the province where he was born.
*Mahāvinicchaya-amacca* refers to the chief justice minister in the capital city of the kingdom in which that province is located.
"General" means the general of that king to whom the minister belongs. Likewise for "viceroy.

This, however, should be understood as stated here according to the ordinary course of events, in conformity with the meaning of the simile. It does not circulate from one to another because it has already been adjudicated by one authorized to adjudicate.

*Pāḷi* is so called because it is the "lineage" (*āḷī*) of excellent strings of speech, since it awakens the meaning of virtue and so forth that are preeminent and sublime, and because it was spoken by the Buddha and others according to their true nature and etymology; thus, it refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
*Anusandhi* is the connection of a subsequent meaning with a preceding meaning. Furthermore, through the medium of the meaning, it also applies to sections of the scriptures.

There is indeed a connection (*anusandhi*), and it is fourfold: by way of connection between what precedes and what follows, connection through questioning, connection through intention, and connection as it naturally occurs.
Furthermore, the linking together of the respective teachings in their sequence is "the preceding and following" (*pubbāpara*).

Each term—by way of the text (*pāḷi*), by way of the connection, and by way of the sequence—should be applied accordingly. "Mastered" (*uggahita*) means grasped repeatedly, both in terms of the phrasing and the meaning.
"Taken" means it has been grasped by the heart both through mastery and through inquiry; this is the meaning.

It is "heard" (*suta*) because it is to be heard by those seeking escape from the suffering of saṃsāra; it refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures. One who "bears that" is a "bearer of what is heard" (*sutadhara*).
For one who is a bearer of what is heard, what has been heard becomes established in him, well-established; therefore it is said, "he is the foundation for what is heard. Thus he said:
“*Yassa hi*,” etc. That which is accumulated without even a single word or a single syllable being lost is a “collection” (*sannicaya*).

One in whom such a collection of what has been heard exists is a “repository of learning” (*sutasannicaya*). “Having entered into” (*ajjhosāya*) means having penetrated [it]. “Remains” (*tiṭṭhati*) means it is not forgotten.
“Firmly established” (*ṭhitā paguṇā*) means well-mastered or committed to memory. “Unwavering” (*niccalitaṃ*) means not subject to change. “Having compared” (*saṃsanditvā*) means with others...
"Having synthesized" means having penetrated the meaning by means of thorough inquiry. "Like the flow of the Ganges" is said because there is no obstruction to its continuity;
alternatively, the reading is "like the flow of the *bhavaṅga* (subconscious life-continuum)," the meaning of which is that it proceeds with natural ease.
Here, mastery through mere verbal recitation of a portion of the sutta or of the sutta itself is not intended; rather, what is intended is mastery by way of sections (*vagga*) and so forth.

He said: “The ten suttas... recited. The meaning is that they were recited verbally after having observed them by way of [noting] “ten suttas have been traversed; ten sections have been reached,” and so forth.
“Mentally scrutinized” means examined again and again, contemplated part by part, and reflected upon mentally.
“Appears like a visible form” means it becomes clear to the eye as if it were a visible form.
Having offered [the sacrifice], it becomes manifest. "Well-penetrated" means having made it free from roots and free from thicket, it has been thoroughly penetrated according to its true nature.
A "phrase" (*pada*) is so called because meaning is reached and known through it; that very same thing is called a "phrasing" (*byañjana*) because it clarifies the meaning. Thus he said:
"A phrase itself is 'phrase-phrasing' (*padabyañjana*) because it is the phrasing of the meaning. The perfection of the phrasing consists in the completeness of the syllables.
But that fulfillment should be understood in this way; thus he said, "without omitting the ten kinds of analytical insights regarding the phrasing.
"Bringing another [text] as an objection" means that one cites a sutta other than the one just presented that is inconsistent with it.
"One applies it to its meaning" means that one investigates the meaning of that very sutta which was cited. His discourse is incomplete.

It is called "name" because the meaning is not yet complete. By means of the commentary on the meaning of the sutta exactly as it was set forth, even when introducing another sutta, one does not go outside [the subject] by even a single word. "Without smearing" means without destroying.
Having well-established each respective meaning and showing it, it is as if delimiting it with a ruler. [This refers to] the exceedingly profound meaning.
It is like one directing water into a deep channel. For if the boundary were overtopped by a shallow channel, the water would flow elsewhere.
Like a noble Sindhu horse, he repeatedly praises a single word through numerous methods, as if trampling upon that word;
for such a horse, by its galloping gait, moves along while trampling step after step.

By way of the method of discourse, his speech is called "complete" because it is perfect in every respect—being complete in terms of the Dhamma, the meaning, the connection, the sequence, and the teacher’s mastery.
"With continuous [speech]" means with words that are fluent and unimpeded. It is neither too fast nor too slow, but uninterrupted and of a single flavor.

He spoke the words beginning with "The monk who... in order to show that one speaks with fluent discourse only when preaching the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations of the assembly, and not otherwise.
The examples of speaking very rapidly—such as "as if churning a fire-drill" or "as if eating hot food"—refer to skipping over what has already been grasped, and so forth.

Regarding the explanation: for just as a lizard moving through the spaces between old leaves might sometimes be seen, so too the commentary on the meaning of certain passages is not found in some places.
"Leaving aside" means setting it aside. By the words "And whoever," etc., he shows that the discourse was not delivered in a single form.
"The fire of the hungry ghosts" refers to the fire issuing from the mouths of those hungry ghosts who are consumed by parching thirst. "It spreads" means...
He does not fall into a state of dejection. Like one afflicted by some disease and suffering pain, he groans;
"like one crying out" means like one making a loud outcry. It is called "uninterrupted" because it proceeds without ease.
"Abiding by the method given by the teachers" means not relinquishing the grasp of the teachers' instructions, and [reciting] exactly as the teachers commented upon each respective sutta.

The meaning is: "He explains by that very same method. "Making the stream unbroken" means: having made the continuity of the discourse uninterrupted according to the method stated below, beginning with "neither too fast nor too slow," and so forth.

"For the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*)"—by this, he shows that the conclusion of that discourse is *arahantship*. "By such a [method]"—this is not a singular number; it refers to that many [methods].
It should be understood thus; rather, showing that [the qualities] occur in the characteristics (lakkhaṇa), it is said: "by a hundred such monks, or by a thousand monks.
By the phrase "with cross-legged posture" (pallaṅkena), the meaning is "by way of the term 'cross-legged posture'"; that is, "by means of the seat with cross-legged posture.
By the phrase "in this manner," he refers by extension to the meaning common to other sections, while that which is not common will be stated later.
334. It is called an *ārāma* because one delights (*āramati*) therein.

335. "Constantly frequented" means regularly resorted to. "In the courtyard of the palace" means in the open space of the palace. "Established upon the hub" means established on the ground at the hub. "The intervals between the spokes" refers to the gaps between the spokes, the intermediate spaces between each spoke. 336.
One is a forest-dweller (*āraññika*) by having undertaken the forest-dwelling ascetic practice (*araññadhutaṅga*), not merely by the fact of living in the forest.

337. "They do not encourage" means they do not discourage; the meaning is that they do not ask one another questions with the intent of discouraging each other. "One who conducts" means one who is proficient. 338.

"Supramundane dwellings and attainments" refers to the elder’s attainments of the fruit of Arahantship; however, in a figurative sense, it should also be understood as including the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
339. A cry of approval was given to the Elder Ānanda. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Just as Ānanda himself would answer correctly..."
“...should explain,” and so forth. “Sammā” means well; the intention is that it is according to one’s own inclination (*ajjhāsaya*).
For whatever has been spoken according to one’s own mind is said to be “well-spoken. Indeed, one who acts accordingly and speaks accordingly shines through the attainment [of virtue].
Therefore he said, “only what is suitable for oneself,” and so forth. A learned monk (*bahussuta*) [explains] therein, in various discourses, the virtues (*sīla*) and so on—
Because these [factors] are well-known in the places where they occur, one who practices according to the instructions fulfills them;

thus he said, "In the places where virtue occurs," and so forth. The meaning is: having caused insight to take up the womb [of the path] by means of the flowing forth of the path, etc., and having brought it to maturity.
340. Expanding upon the point stated briefly by way of analogy with the words "The same method applies," he said, "For the Venerable Revata," and so forth.
342. “Various kinds of defilements” (nānappakāre kilese) means various kinds of defilements such as hatred, delusion, and so forth. “Having shaken off” (dhunitvā) means having dispelled them.
343. The connection is: “The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna explained it thus.

Without taking the entire consciousness occurring within the cognitive process of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa-vīthi*) to be “eye-consciousness,” rather, consciousness that is dependent upon the eye alone is “eye-consciousness.”
Immediately following that is reception (*sampaṭicchana*), immediately following that is investigation (*santīraṇa*), and so forth;

thus there is a diversity of consciousness consisting of distinct moments of mind, each possessing extremely brief durations. There is also a diversity of aggregates and so forth, known as the distinction between one aggregate and another.

For example, having attained the first jhāna upon the earth-kasiṇa, one likewise attains the third jhāna; in such cases, without skipping over the object, it is simply the jhāna itself [that changes].
Ascending by skipping over one stage at a time is called "jhāna-leaping" (*jhānokkantika*).

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa, and then again that same [jhāna] in the fire-kasiṇa, and so forth—ascending through the jhānas in this manner while skipping over the objects of meditation itself—is called "object-leaping" (*ārammaṇokkantika*).
[This continues] from the description "the first jhāna has five factors" up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
The definition of factors (*aṅgavavatthāna*) is the defining of the factors of jhāna alone as being fivefold.
The definition of the object (*ārammaṇavavatthāna*) is the defining of the mere object alone, such as: "This is the earth-kasiṇa... [and so on]... this is the white-kasiṇa.
The transition of factors (*aṅgasankanti*) is the attainment of the other jhānas right there after having first attained the first jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa. In the earth-kasiṇa... [and so on].

Having attained the first jhāna, one then enters that same jhāna upon the water-kasiṇa; in this way, the attainment of the same single jhāna upon all the kasiṇas is the "transference of the object" (*ārammaṇasaṅkanti*).
As for "expansion in one direction" and "expansion in both directions," these are found in the teaching on the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth;
for in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, when the Blessed One analyzes the feeling aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*), he takes the triads and places them within the dyads.

Having taken two [factors] at a time, he included them in the triads; this is "increment by one" (*ekatovaḍḍhana*). He spoke of both the triads and the dyads by means of the method of "double increment" (*ubhatovaḍḍhana*);

this is "double increment. Thus, it should be understood for the remaining aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth, according to the method as it appears in the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa* and the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. Therefore, he said: "Only for one who is an Abhidhammic teacher of the Dhamma..."

"Manifest. Because he lacks proficiency regarding the three characteristics within the phenomena possessing intrinsic nature—such as the aggregates (khandhas)—as well as regarding designations (paññatti) and other systems, he does not know, "This is our own doctrine;
this is the doctrine of another. For that very reason, he contradicts his own doctrine... [and so on] ...and contradicts other doctrines.
However, through proficiency in the aggregates and so forth, one who is versed in the Abhidhamma does not contradict his own doctrine... [and so on] ...nor does he contradict other doctrines.

344. One is able to bring the mind under one's own control because it is capable of grasping [the object] through the powers of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) and meditative development (*bhāvanā*).
Now, in order to clarify this matter by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) and agreement (*anvaya*), the text says, "But the one of weak wisdom," and so forth.
In that context, *sabbānassa* means "of all his. *Visevitavipphanditāni* refers to both the writhings of the poison of the defilements (*kilesa*) and the writhings of misconduct (*duccarita*).
“Having broken” means having crushed. “Externally” means outside of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), upon a variety of external objects.
Regarding the word “by way of” (*pariyāyena*): here the word *pariyāya* has the sense of a cause, as in such passages as “There is, brahmin, this way (*pariyāya*)”;
thus he says, “there is a beautiful cause. If the Blessed One—“Here, Sāriputta... [and so on].
By saying, "The bhikkhu, having returned from his almsround after the meal," and so forth, he spoke with reference to his own Great Bodhi Throne.
This being so, it follows that the Saṅghārāma should be graced by the Fully Enlightened Ones alone and not by others; thus he said, "Moreover, the later generation," and so forth.
That which has practice as its essence for the sake of Nibbāna is "practice-essence" (paṭipattisāra); that [is what is meant].
The essence is practice. "In the primary sense alone" means without any figurative or secondary manner, but by the principal method itself.
One who sits having made a firm resolve, thinking, "I shall not rise until I have attained arahantship," rises only after attaining it.
It is such a person as this that makes this Gosiṅga Sāla Grove resplendent, for all undertakings in the Dispensation have that as their purpose.

The purpose [of the teaching] is as follows: having begun with the practice that brings about the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayāvaha*), he brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely through the destruction of the taints;
thus, he completed the teaching according to the natural sequence of the connection (*yathānusandhi*).
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāgosiṅgasutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mahāgopālaka Sutta 346.
*Tattha* means "in the Gopālaka Sutta. *Tisso kathā* means three commentaries; the meaning is that there are three ways of explaining the meaning of the sutta.
*Ekanāḷikā*: that which has each word as its stalk (*nāḷa*) and root (*mūla*) is thus designated; or alternatively, each individual word is a stalk.
It is called *ekanāḷikā* because its path is the extraction of the meaning (*atthaniggamana*). Therefore he said: "the explanation of the meaning of each single word.

It is called *caturassā* because it possesses four corners or divisions (*aṃsa*) which are the means for discerning the meaning. Therefore he said: "the explanation after having tied [the words] into a set of four.
It is called *nisinnavattikā* because it possesses a sequence (*vatta*) of what has been undertaken while sitting in a fixed order; as it was undertaken...
The meaning is: "one who brings each point to its respective conclusion. Therefore, he said, "having shown the wise cowherd," and so forth.
"Of each single word" means a commentary on the meaning of each individual word, without stating the combined meaning of many words by way of showing the summarized sense (*piṇḍattha*).
This is applicable in all cases. "Having bound them into a tetrad":

Having applied this tetrad—namely, the pair of simile and subject of the simile in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), and likewise in the bright side (sukkapakkha)—this [method] is found in such suttas as these.

First, some say that "reaching the conclusion" means: having shown the simile in the dark side, and since a simile is intended solely for the purpose of providing a counterpart to the subject of the simile, one brings forward the meaning of the subject of the simile and then presents the description of the defilement-side.

"And for the purpose of clarifying the side of purification" means that even the bright side (sukkapakkha) is brought forward by distinguishing between the simile and the subject of the simile (*upameyya*), thus concluding the meaning of the sutta.
This same method applies to the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*) as well, when showing the subject of the simile and proceeding to the conclusion and so forth.
Others, however, [hold that] one should conclude each respective instance of the simile and its subject separately for both the dark and bright sides.
They say that "the conclusion" refers to the reaching of the end of the discourse. "Ayam" (this) refers to those who sit in a circle.
"Iha" (here) means in this *Gopālaka-sutta*. "The practice of all teachers" means that it has been practiced and commented upon by all former teachers, and the text proceeds exactly in that manner.

They are called "aṅgas" because they are known as constituent parts (*avayava-bhāvena*), that is, portions. Furthermore, since these [parts] here possess a nature associated with fault (*sāvajja-sabhāva*), [they are so designated].

Therefore he says: “By means of factors (aṅgehi) means by means of groups of qualities (aguṇakoṭṭhāsehi). A herd of cattle (gomaṇḍalaṃ) is a collection of cows. To tend (pariharituṃ) means to protect.
Furthermore, that tending consists of wandering about while having taken possession [of them]; thus he says: “having taken possession, to wander about.
Increase (vaḍḍhiṃ) refers to the abundance of cattle, the growth characterized by the great quantity of milk products. That which appears as “this much” is form (rūpaṃ).

Since both measurement and delimitation are aspects of the body’s form, he says, “either by way of counting or by way of color. He does not search because he simply does not know that it has perished.
In the phrase “blue,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning with”; by this, colors such as white, brown, and so forth are included.

Regarding the phrase “bows, spears, spikes, and so forth,” here the reference is to the practice of archery masters who mark their targets with bows when shooting at cattle; [and likewise] for the groups of the Kumārabhṛtyas...
The mark of the spear made on cows belongs to the groups of the Sattis; the mark of the spit made on cows belongs to the groups of the Issaras and Bhattas—this is the construction [of the sentence].
By the word "etc. (ādi), one includes the marks of the axe, the discus, and so forth, made on cows by the groups of the Rāmas, Vāsudevas, and others.

"Blue flies" refers to tawny flies or simply small flies. It is called *sāṭikā* because one is afflicted (*saṭati*) or pained by it; an increased *sāṭikā* is an *āsāṭikā*. Thus he said, "increasing," and so forth.
*Vākena* means with a leaf-plate. *Cīrakena* means with a rag. *Antovasse* means within the rainy season.

*Niggāhaṃ* means free from crocodiles and other such predators. *Pītaṃ* refers to the state of having drunk water. *Sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ* means fraught with danger and peril due to lions, tigers, and the like.

"Five days have passed for this," thus it is *pañcāhito*; that very [period] is the "five-day turn" (*pañcāhikavāro*). In the same way, the "seven-day turn" (*sattāhikavāro*) is to be understood. "A frequented place" (*ciṇṇaṭṭhānaṃ*) means a place where one has traveled or a place where one’s range of movement has been established.
"The father’s place" (*pituṭṭhānaṃ*) means the duty to be performed by a father; the meaning is "the task to be done by a father.
"Taking [them] according to their pleasure" (*yathāruciṃ gahetvā*) means they go having taken [them] to a grazing ground or across a river in accordance with the cows' own inclination.
“Gobhatta” means rice mixed with cotton-seed, husks, and so forth, which is fit for a cow to eat; by the mention of “rice,” the rice-gruel (*yāgu*) is also included.
To show the two modes mentioned as “in two ways,” it is said: “either by way of enumeration or by way of origination.
Thus, having divided birth (*jāti*) into two—as “accumulation” and “continuity”—the heart-base is [treated].
Having taken them up, they are thus presented in the commentary on the *Rūpa-kanda* as "the ten bases and the fifteen subtle material phenomena.
The "twenty-five material components" (*rūpakoṭṭhāsa*) are portions of matter because they possess their own specific characteristics and lack mutual confusion.
Alternatively, they are called "material components" because they do not occur individually but occur only in the form of groups (*kalāpa*). And as for the term "components" (*koṭṭhāsa*), it means...
*Aṃsā* means parts or components. Alternatively, *koṭṭha* refers to the body;
its parts, such as the hair and so forth, are called *koṭṭhāsa* (sections), and other components are likewise called *koṭṭhāsa* because they are like sections. *Seyyathāpi* introduces a comparison.

In that context, *rūpaṃ pariggahetvā* means having grasped the aforementioned form by means of knowledge according to its specific characteristics. *Arūpaṃ vavatthapetvā* [means] having defined that form...
Having defined the four aggregates— feeling and the rest— which arise depending upon and taking an object as their support,

as "the formless"; and having discerned both the material and the immaterial by further determining that therein whatever has the characteristic of being affected (ruppana) is "matter," while what is other than that is "the formless," and that there is nothing whatsoever apart from these two, whether a self or anything belonging to a self.
The construction is as follows: having observed that both of these are "with conditions" by means of conditions such as ignorance,

and having applied the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, he who is unable to bring the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to its culmination through the sequence beginning with the comprehension of aggregates (kalāpasammasana) does not progress.

"Such a form has a single origination": the eye-base, the ear, nose, tongue, and body-bases, the femininity-faculty, masculinity-faculty, and life-faculty—these eight types [originate] by way of kamma; the two, namely bodily intimation and verbal intimation, [originate] by way of consciousness.
Such is the extent of form that has a single origination. The sound-base alone [originates] by way of temperature and consciousness.
[Materiality] has two origins. The materiality consisting of lightness, malleability, and wieldiness has three origins:
temperature, consciousness, and nutriment. The bases of visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility; the space element; the water element;
and physical nutriment—this much materiality has four origins: temperature, consciousness, nutriment, and kamma. [The materiality of] integration, continuity, and decay... of materiality.
