“Impermanence”: by this much he does not know that this form does not arise from anywhere.

Regarding the phrases “not knowing form by way of its origination,” and so forth, it should be understood according to the same method explained in the passages beginning with “not knowing form by way of enumeration.
“Characterized by karma”: one whose characteristic is the evil deed committed by oneself is “characterized by karma”; such a person is a fool.
For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool. Which three?
He thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken speech, and performs ill-done deeds. These, indeed... are the characteristics.
One who has good conduct as his own performed karma as his characteristic is a wise person (*kammalakkhaṇo paṇḍito*). And this too has been said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three...”
“Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person. What are the three? He is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds.
These, indeed... [are] the characteristics of a wise person. Therefore it was said: “Wholesome and unwholesome karma is the characteristic of the wise.
Regarding the phrase “having avoided fools, he does not associate with the wise”: having avoided foolish persons...
One who desires their welfare should serve the wise, yet he does not do so. To show that for one who has become such, this is a disadvantage, it is further stated:
"Having avoided the foolish," and so forth. In this context, if something conforms to what was permitted by the Blessed One as "this is allowable for you," then it is allowable (*kappiya*).
If something conforms to what was prohibited as "this is not allowable for you," [then it is unallowable].
That is unallowable (*akappiya*). That which arises from skillfulness is wholesome (*kusala*); its opposite is unwholesome (*akusala*). That very same [unwholesome] is blameworthy (*sāvajja*);
the wholesome is blameless (*anavajja*). From the perspective of offenses, the first two classes of offenses are heavy (*garuka*);

other than those, they are light (*lahuka*). From the perspective of the nature of phenomena (*dhamma*), that which is greatly blameworthy is heavy; that which is slightly blameworthy is light. That which has a remedy is accompanied by a task to be performed (*satekicca*).
Irremediable and incurable. A cause that follows the nature of things (*dhammatā*) is a valid reason; anything else is not a reason.

"Not knowing that" means not knowing what is allowable and what is unallowable, what is grave and what is light, and what is curable and incurable—one who does not know this is unable to guard morality even after making it perfectly pure.
Not knowing what is wholesome and unwholesome, what is blameworthy and blameless, and what is a reason and what is not a reason, [one is likewise unable] regarding the aggregates and so forth.
Because of his unwholesome state, he is unable even to discern form and the formless, let alone take up a meditation subject and develop it.
Therefore, he said: "He is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it.

Having arisen in a personal existence that resembles a cow-pen, wrong thoughts are like gadflies because they are the cause for the arising of suffering there; thus he said: "Having removed the gadfly of unwholesome thought."

Because of the statement, “‘A boil,’ monks, is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging,” one must cover with the restraint of mindfulness the wound that is the personal existence, from which the impurity of the defilements trickles out through the six doors—just as a boil from which pus trickles out through six openings is covered with a piece of cloth.
But this person does not do so; thus it is said: “Just as he...”
Just as a cowherd does not cover over the forest, so too one does not accomplish restraint.
Just as smoke, arising in dependence upon fuel, being soft and subtle, enters various crevices and pervades them,
dispelling the danger of gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like for living beings, and serving as the precursor to the emergence of a mass of fire—
In the same way, the teaching of the Dhamma— arising in dependence upon the collection of material and immaterial phenomena that serve as its fuel—
is subtle and refined; it penetrates and pervades each respective aggregate and sense base,
dispels the dangers of beings such as wrong thoughts, and is like smoke, being the precursor to the emergence of the net of the fire of knowledge.
He said, “Smoke,” meaning that the cowherd does not produce the smoke of teaching the Dhamma.

*Upaṇisinnakathā* (seated discourse) is the appropriate Dhamma talk to be given to one who has approached and sat down near oneself. *Anumodanā* (thanksgiving) is the discourse of rejoicing in the merit of giving and other such deeds already performed.
*Tato* means because of the failure to perform such things as Dhamma talks. “One who is learned...”
Why was it said, “they do not know him to be virtuous”? Is it not true that one should not even give a discourse on the Dhamma for the purpose of making oneself known?
That is true; indeed, one should not do so. However, this was said with reference to the fact that when the Dhamma is spoken with a pure intention, the listener comes to know the speaker’s virtue.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“They do not recognize a wise man who does not manifest himself, being mixed with fools;
let him manifest and illuminate the Dhamma, and raise high the banner of the seers.
Here, *tittha* means a crossing, a place for descending into rivers, ponds, and so forth, for the purpose of bathing and the like. Just as...

Just as water washes away the bodily impurities of beings who have entered it, dispels their fatigue, and produces purity, so too do those of great learning wash away the mental impurities of beings who have entered their presence with the water of the Dhamma, dispel their fatigue, and produce purity;
therefore, they are like a ford, a *tittha*. Thus he said: "being a ford."
"Learned bhikkhus. Regarding the phrase "how should the phrasing be applied," venerable sir: how should this phrasing, this word, be applied to this meaning?
In what manner has it become a designator of this meaning?
Alternatively, there is the reading "nirūpetabbaṃ"; the intention is that it should be examined: how is this natural linguistic expression established (*niruḷha*) in this context? Of this...
"What is the meaning of what was said? asks regarding the literal meaning (*saddattha*). "In this place" means in this section of the Canon (*pāḷipadesa*).
"What does the Canon say? asks regarding the underlying meaning (*bhāvattha*). "What does the meaning illuminate? refers either to the underlying meaning or the conventional meaning (*saṅketattha*).
"He does not inquire further" means he does not ask at all by way of a question intended to sever doubt. "He does not question further" means...
He does not explain or reveal his desire to know himself thoroughly; therefore he said, "he does not make it known. "Those" refers to the learned bhikkhus.
"Exposition" means speaking by analyzing the meaning; thus he said, "they do not show it by dividing it up.
"Not made plain" means not made manifest by knowledge—secret and concealed. "They do not make plain" means...
They do not make it plain, as if they were dredging the silt at the root of Sineru or revealing the water that supports the earth.

Thus, having shown by way of a figurative expression how those who are "learned" (bahussuta) are called "those who abide" (tittha), the passage beginning with "And just as" is now stated to show how they actually abide (titthanti) in that very same sense in a non-figurative sense. Dhammo.
For by means of this they cross over to that which is called Nibbāna, the "tank"; thus it is called a "ford. Therefore the Blessed One, having become wise, said:
"When the tank of the Deathless exists, And the stains of the defilements have been washed away, If one does not seek out that very tank, It is no fault of the tank of the Deathless."
One who does not know the manner of entering the Dhamma—which is like a ford for crossing over to Nibbāna—is said to "not know the Dhamma-ford.
Regarding the phrase "drunk and undrunk," he does not know or perceive the state of the cattle in the herd as being either drunk or undrunk;

for it is said that one who does not perceive [this] does not obtain it. Having stated, "he does not perceive the benefit," the author spoke the words beginning with "having gone to the head of the Dhamma-listening" in order to demonstrate the manner of his non-perception.
He says "noble" (ariya) with reference to the phrase "this is supramundane. Alternatively, by the principle of proximity, there is a negation of the immediately preceding rule;

or else, the word "noble" should be understood as a synonym for "faultless. As for "eightfold," it should be taken both separately and collectively, considering the eight factors individually and as a whole, due to their being eight factors and because of their predominance. And having done so, even for the sevenfold noble path—
The summary is established.
In such passages as "the four foundations of mindfulness," the foundations of mindfulness are stated without distinction.

Among these, those having the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena as their objects are mundane; those that proceed by way of destroying delusion regarding them and have Nibbāna as their object are supramundane.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: "These are mundane, these are supramundane.
"He milks dry" means that, not knowing the proper measure in receiving gifts, he milks dry some donors by causing a loss of faith and others by causing a loss of requisites.
"Approaching with speech" is *vācābhihāra*. "Approaching with requisites" is *paccayābhihāra*.

By the statement, "They do not show respect toward us," he demonstrates the lack of correct practice of the Dhamma among these junior monks, because they fail to establish fatherly affection for their teachers and preceptors.
And by indicating that absence of reverence for the training, he shows their unfitness as recipients of support;
and by that, the elders' lack of concern for them. For [support] does not arise through qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
Having attained stability in the Teaching, they assist fellow celibates who do not deserve assistance, or they provide assistance that is useless.
Therefore he said, "newly ordained bhikkhus. "The sequence of Dhamma discourses" refers to the path of miscellaneous Dhamma discourses handed down through tradition.
It is a secret text connected with the truths, the seven rebirths, and the modes of conditions, which elucidates emptiness (*suññatā*). "By way of the reversal of what was stated" means...
“By way of the negation of the prohibition stated in such passages as ‘one who does not know form’ (na rūpaññū), that is, by way of its non-apprehension.

Having joined [the meaning] means: having joined the meaning by such statements as “‘One who knows form’ means one who knows form either by number or by color,” and “his herd of cattle does not diminish, nor is he excluded from the enjoyment of the five products of the cow. It is to be understood thus.
The meaning in each respective section should be understood as appropriate.
The Elucidation of the Obscure Points in the Commentary on the Mahāgopālaka Sutta is completed.
4. Commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta.
350. *Celukkāhi*: by means of torches made of cloth. It is called *Ukkacelā* because the cloth has become like torches there; it is the name of the city.
"The entire Ganges becomes manifest" means that it appears clearly to the ordinary eye (*pakaticakkhu*);
however, to one with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) or the all-around eye (*samantacakkhu*), it remains manifest no matter where the Blessed One is seated.
"Sotthi" means free from calamity. "Vaḍḍhi" means non-decline. "Ārogya" means health, the absence of disease.

One whose dwelling place is the Magadha country is "Māgadha"; one who is Māgadha is thus called "Māgadhika. There is no such thing as being ill-behaved in terms of wisdom (*paññā*), because it is entirely irreproachable;
therefore, in this context, the prefix *du-* signifies non-existence, as in words such as "dussīla" (immoral), whereas the word *jāti*— [refers to birth].
And because it has the sense of "nature," he said, "having the nature of being devoid of wisdom" (*nippaññasabhāvo*).

Because the word *saddo* has the sense of "beginning," he said, "he began to cross" (*patāresi* = *tāretuṃ ārabhi*), since the cows had not yet reached the opposite shore. "Of the beautiful Videhas" (*suvidehānaṃ*) means of the lovely Videhas.
It is said that the kingdom of Videha was beautiful due to its excellence in the appearance of the terrain and its delightful forests and so forth. "Āmaṇḍalikaṃ."
"Having done so" means having turned back and fallen into a whirlpool, circling about in a circular form.
Because some cows were not left behind but were carried away by the river current, it is said: "They met with decline and destruction.
For even if a few cows had remained, there might have been an increase in the herd over time. "A place of rest" means a place for dispelling fatigue.
"Standing on the bank" means she had not yet reached the ford because she was unable to grasp it.
"He was not called 'healthy'" means that all the cows were lost in the river current without even a single hair being left behind.
Those who do not know those aggregates, bases, and elements upon which the conventional designation "this world" is based are "unskilled in this world."
It is said: "In this world, they are unskilled and incompetent regarding the aggregates, elements, and bases. This same method applies here as well in the phrase "unskilled in the world beyond";
thus he says, "The same method applies to the other world too. It is called the "domain of Māra" (māradheyya) because Māra dwells therein.
And here, "Māra" should be understood as the defilement-māra (kilesamāra), for the formative forces of the aggregates (khandhābhisaṅkhārā) constitute his mode of existence.

"Māra the Death" is already included [among the others]; and it is by way of "Māra of the Defilements" (kilesamāra) that Māra the Son of the Devas (devaputtamāra) exercises sovereignty over the sensual realm (kāmabhava).
"Of them" means of those who are unskilled in this world and so forth. Showing them according to the highest possible description, he said:
"By this, six teachers are shown."
351. "Powerful cattle" (*balavagāvo*) means powerful bovine forms. These, moreover, are both tamed oxen and milch cows; thus he said, "tamed oxen and milch cows.
"Unborn cattle" (*avijātagāvo*) means those that have not yet given birth. "Calves" (*vacchaka*) refers to small calves.
This word *ka* has no specific meaning here; therefore he said, "young calves. "Lean and weak" (*kisābalaka*) means feeble.
352. "Having cut off Māra’s stream of craving" means having completely severed the stream known as craving associated with the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*).

"Standing after exhausting three portions" is said with reference to non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Regarding "in all instances," this refers to the stages of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the eighth-rank practitioner (*aṭṭhamaka*).
Therein, however, they stand having exhausted two portions of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, respectively.
Having exhausted one portion, they remain; thus it should be said that they exhaust the first portion.
They recollect the Dhamma, or their nature is to recollect the Dhamma, thus they are "followers by Dhamma" (dhammānusārino). And here, by "Dhamma," wisdom (paññā) is intended.
They recollect faith, or their nature is to recollect faith, thus they are "followers by faith" (saddhānusārino).

Regarding the word "knowing" (*jānato*): since the object of the act of knowing is not specified here, it is intended by way of context to refer to all specific objects of knowledge without exception;
thus he says, "by one who knows all phenomena. Because it is devoid of inner pith and because it stands upright like a reed, it is called a "reed" (*naḷo*);
[the Buddha] has made this reed of pride vanish—thus he says, "made free from the reed of pride. Regarding the phrase "seek safety": here, by means of the four...

Because it is free from danger through the yogas, "security" (khema) refers here to Arahantship. Furthermore, "aspiration" (patthanā) means the aspiration of desire (chanda), not the aspiration of craving (taṇhā);
thus he said, "One should aspire to Arahantship with the desire to act.

For one who has already attained it, there is no obstacle whatsoever to that attainment. Having begun the teaching with the aim of reaching the further shore in safety, [he speaks] for the sake of attaining security.
Because the teaching had reached its conclusion, he brought the discourse to an end by following the natural sequence of the narrative.
The exposition of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta.
353. "By means of the swan-wheel disguise" (*haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena*) means by means of being concealed by a swan-wheel; the meaning is "in the form of a circle of swans.
They speak by means of this, thus it is "discourse" (*vāda*), which is the path. What do they speak? An answer (*uttara*). Hundreds of discourses are "hundreds of discourses" (*vādasatāni*).
"The Nigaṇṭha has five hundred discourses, the Nigaṇṭhī has five hundred discourses"—thus both the Nigaṇṭha and the Nigaṇṭhī have five hundred each.
Wandering about after having mastered hundreds of doctrines, they questioned him regarding their practices (*kiriyā*); however, his status as a Nigaṇṭha was known from his outward marks (*liṅga*).
Therefore he said, "I shall put forward my doctrine.
"Attending" means by way of sweeping and so forth. "Too early" (*divātarā*) means excessively early in the day. "Whose question? Whose answer?"
When the female wanderers said, "Let it be so," the Elder said, "The question has indeed come to us. A question is the first position in a debate;

since you are devoted to debate, delight in debate, and wander about with your banner raised, therefore the first position in the debate has come to us. Even so, because of your status as women, [the first position]—
Demati said, "But you women should ask first. Those female wanderers, each asking two hundred and fifty questions, asked a total of one thousand questions.

Just as there is nothing difficult for a sharpened sword in cutting the stalk of a water lily, so too was there nothing difficult for [the Buddha], who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) among his wise disciples.
Regarding the Elder Dhammasenāpati, who stands at the head [of the Saṅgha], in his answering of questions as conceived by worldlings:
"What is heavy? To this he said, "The Elder with the sword," and so forth.

Therein, "having made it free from tangles and knots" means that he explained it after disentangling it in such a way that those [questions] would no longer be able to form tangles or knots there again. This is the Elder.
Seeing the Elder’s lucidity of wisdom— how, like one lighting a thousand-fold lamp in a darkness endowed with four factors,
he answered questions that were outside the scope of others and shrouded in gloom the very moment they were asked— the women,
unable to maintain their deception because it was the Elder’s final existence, said, "Venerable sir, we know only this much. To the Elder...
"Object" means the range of the Elder’s wisdom.

"They saw neither end nor limit" means that because what ought to be called "one" was actually manifold, they did not see—that is, they did not know—the sense of that question as having such an end or such a final limit.
The Elder, observing their underlying intention...
Seeing their inclination toward the going-forth (pabbajjā), he asked, "What will you do now?
He was one of even superior wisdom; that is, by virtue of his familiarity with the paths of debate and his intelligence, his wisdom was superior to theirs.

The "path of speech" (kathāmaggā) is the path of debate (vādamaggā). Therefore, through various modes of discourse, he [addressed] the speech—the path of debate—with respect to those various opposing doctrines and so forth.
One who says "I speak" is a talkative disputant (*bhassappavādaka*). One who says "I am wise" is one who speaks thus: "I am wise, clever, and learned.

Whatever prediction he utters according to the movement of the stars—that is, through his knowledge of time based on the course of the constellations—such as predicting, "On such-and-such a day there will be an eclipse of the moon;
there will be an eclipse of the sun," and so forth; he is one who gains [reputation] as a "sage" (*sādhuladdhika*).

It is beautiful by virtue of its perfection of knowledge. "Imposed" means that the argument, having been subjected to faults such as the admission of a premise (*paṭiññā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the demonstration (*nidassana*), is thus placed upon [the opponent];
it is "self-imposed. By the proponent who imposes these points of fault, there may even be an agitation of the elements (*dhātukkhobha*) in the opposing debater;
through mental distraction, he is "shaken" by that very intention toward the fault. "Pillar" (*thūṇa*) refers to the body.
He said this thinking, "It has been shaken. For "pillar" (*thūṇa*) is a designation for blood, bile, and phlegm, because they support the entire body and its limbs.
Furthermore, there is a method of debate called the "pillar-step" (*thūṇapada*), which those who adopt a line of argumentation employ.
But Saccaka, standing in hypocrisy and bewildering others by means of his own various modes of disputation, said, "And if the pillar," and so forth. [This was] for the sake of the disciples.
The Vinaya is the code of training (sikkhāpada), and that is the teaching of the Dhamma; thus, this alone is his instruction.
Inquiring about the Dispensation (sāsana) of the Perfectly Enlightened One through the gateway of the Vinaya and so forth, Saccaka said, "But how, sir, did Assaji... and so on.
Then the Elder [said to him]: "The discourse on the three characteristics is a teaching of the Dhamma unique to the Buddhas, not shared by others."

And there, when I have initiated a discourse on impermanence, Saccaka—unable to endure it, making a clattering noise out of hollow pride—will come into the presence of the Blessed One taking the Licchavis with him.
Then the Blessed One, crushing his argument and establishing that "all is impermanent," will preach the Dhamma; at that time, he will abandon his false doctrine and proceed upon the right path.

Having reflected, "I am established," and wishing to show the Blessed One’s instruction associated with the characteristics of impermanence and non-self, he said, "It is so, sir Aggivessana," and so forth.
But why was the characteristic of suffering not included here? To this he replied, "The Elder, however," and so on. [This provides] an opportunity for objection.
To explain what was stated briefly as "it occurs," the passage beginning with "the paths and fruits" was spoken.
Therein, "by way of a figurative expression" means by way of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*). "This one" refers to Saccaka.
"This is not indeed your teaching" means that this which you adhere to is not called your "teaching of the Omniscient One" (*sabbaññu-sāsana*), because it does not provide escape from suffering.

Now, this is indeed called the "Great Place of Execution" (*mahāāghātana*); however, because it is designated as great suffering, it is called the "Ussada Hell," that is, the hell of the protrusions (*ussadaniraya*).
Therefore, there is no hope for happiness for you. "Rising up, rising up" means having exerted yourselves;
"wander about, roam about" means while wearing out only suffering, experiencing nothing but suffering in every respect. All of this belongs to him.
This is merely a false conceptualization. Why? Because here, the discourse is called "the literal" (nippariyāya) precisely when it is connected with the truth of suffering.
For it is for the sake of fully understanding that [suffering] that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.

The paths and fruits are suffering only in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*)—on account of their conditioned nature according to the principle "whatever is impermanent is suffering"—but not in the literal sense. Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth.
The intention is that it is improper to hear [this] because it is a false doctrine.
354. "Sahā" refers to a hall for instruction on matters of state; it is also called a *sandhāgāra*, meaning a hall for the assembly of royal families.
The meaning is: "in that *sandhāgāra*. At such a time, at such an occasion, they deliberate upon the affairs of state here.
*Sandhāgāram*: the meaning is "in that assembly hall" (*santhāgāre*). *Paṭiṭṭhitam*: it is established as being "impermanent and non-self.
*Idāneva piṭṭhim parivattente*: turning his back right now, meaning he was turning away from the Blessed One’s forehead and assuming an averted posture.
*Surāghare*: in a house for the production of liquor. *Piṭṭhakilañjam*: a mat for placing flour upon. *Vālam*: a winnowing fan.

"For the purpose of making a hempen garment" (*sāṇasāṭakakaraṇatthaṃ*): it is called "making a hempen garment" (*sāṇasāṭakakaraṇaṃ*) because they make a hempen garment by means of it; thus, it refers to the thread, for the sake of that.

"Those among whom there is hemp" (*sāṇavākā*): these are hemp-sticks. Having taken them, they engage in a kind of play similar to the washing of hemp, such as "the breaking of *uddāla* flowers" and "the breaking of hemp.
"In what manner is that venerable one?"—meaning, having become of what sort?

Being such as he was, how could one who exists in the state of a *yakkha* or similar being—possessing spiritual qualities far superior even to those of the Supreme Person in the world, the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), by challenging him to debate—possibly have attained that state?
But this one, appearing in the form of a *pisāca* due to his lack of power, what is he saying now after having slept for all this time and only today waking up? This is the intended meaning.
Therefore he said, "Is it a *yakkha*?
and so forth. (355) "At the great time of midday" means at the vast period of noon, at the moment the sun has reached the middle of the sky.
"Those who exert themselves by day" refers to those devoted to spiritual striving (*padhāna*). "Having shown his routine" means because of his going for his daytime rest after the meal.

Having shown and practiced the duties to be performed previously; "showing the Blessed One" means manifesting great reverence and esteem for the Blessed One, raising both hands in the shape of lotus buds while showing him.
"With reference to that" means with reference to that uncountable number, [saying] thus: "of a great assembly of Licchavis."
It has been said. Is the salutation accomplished merely by striking the ground with the head? "Kerāṭikā" means deceitful.
"Mocentā" means those who cause [others] to be released from the giving of alms. "Like a clod of clay thrown down" means like a lump of clay cast downward.
"Anywhere at all" means not conversing with words appropriate to oneself, but anywhere whatsoever.
356. It is called *desa* because it is seen as "this is the fruit of that," and it is designated by means of it; thus it is a cause.
Precisely because it is the place where that [fruit] occurs, it is called an *okāsa* (occasion). Therefore, he said: "some *desa*, some *okāsa*, some cause.
In such passages as "it is impossible, there is no occasion (*anavakāsa*) for this," the word *okāsa* is used to mean a place or a cause. They do not say "when you wish."
Because his admission has as its object all phenomena without exception. “Tumhaṃ” means “yours. Regarding “yakkhas...
pe... paribbājakānaṃ,” the interrogative phrases such as “Ask, friend, whenever you wish” should be applied here in their respective order.
“Having known this world and the next for himself”—this the Great Being said after having shown hell and heaven directly before their eyes.
"Truly, I shall tell you how it is, just as one who is skilled would;
that is, I shall speak in the same manner as the All-Knowing One, who is supremely skilled, knows and speaks.
As for the reason why [the king] might or might not act—being unaware of both the cause and the non-cause—the King may do so or not; however, I shall tell you," he said, "And the King... or not."
"Speaking according to the very method already stated" means that while he would have spoken the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) by way of the triple-turning exposition, here,
in order to avoid the ground for the claim that "the disciple Assaji spoke in one way, whereas the ascetic Gotama spoke in another," the Elder,
without touching upon the characteristic of suffering, spoke only of the characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*) and non-self (*anatta*) according to the very method already stated.
When the Blessed One said, "Form is not-self... down to:

consciousness is not-self," Saccaka, not accepting that, wishing to establish his own position by means of a standard of comparison—just as one might say "a gayal is like a cow"—making himself the object of comparison, said, "An illustration occurs to me, Master Gotama; give me an illustration. "Give it to you," [the Blessed One replied].
"I shall provide an illustration," [the Blessed One thought], "for through an illustration some wise men understand the meaning of what is said"—this is the intention.
By means of an illustration or by any other standard of measure, it is impossible to establish your self, because even a measure for yourself is unapprehendable;
thus he said, "Let it occur to you, Aggivessana. For just as the self...
No such thing as a "self" is found in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), because it is absolutely unapprehendable;
likewise, neither the person who points this out nor the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it is found. Therefore he said, "Bring forth that simile with confidence";
the intention is that by doing so, your doctrine of self (*attavāda*) does not gain a firm footing.
Whatever bodily merit or demerit is seen to be found in a person is known by that to be his materiality;
likewise, whatever experience of pleasure or pain is seen to be found in a person, whatever perception of blue and so forth is seen,
whatever lust, hatred, and so on are seen, and whatever discernment of an object is seen— [all these are known by their respective characteristics].
A person is apprehended; by that it is known that "this person exists as a conscious being.
Thus, a self characterized by form and so forth experiences the result of good and evil deeds—happiness and suffering—in this or that body.
This must be accepted in this way, for otherwise the connection between action and its fruit would not be logical. This is the meaning.
Showing this, he said, “What does this illustrate? and so forth. In that context, “they” refers to sentient beings (*satta*). “Depending upon” (*patiṭṭhāya*) means relying upon.

By first stating that the person is the self in terms of form and so on—saying, “This person is the self by way of form”—and then subsequently saying, “depending upon form,” and so forth, this Nigaṇṭha contradicts his own position;
for he demonstrates the non-difference between the basis (*patiṭṭhāna*) and the one who stands upon it (*patiṭṭhāyaka*).
Form and the other aggregates have the nature of feeling and so forth, and they constitute the self because of the perception of meritorious and other actions through dependence upon them.

Herein, those forms and so forth which are designated as "beings" and are seen to have the nature of a self—just as in the case of deities and the like—are those depending upon which meritorious and other actions are perceived;
whereas those which are designated as "beings" but are other than that [self] and lack the nature of a being—just as in the case of pieces of wood, logs, and so forth—are seen to be otherwise.

Thus, showing that the point to be established must be supported by a reason, he said, "The Nigaṇṭha brought forward an illustration," meaning that he "brought forward a simile having made it very well-reasoned.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the seeds and the vegetation were mentioned as analogous examples because his doctrine holds that even seeds and vegetation possess life, just like the human activities described as "productive of strength" (*balakaraṇīya*).

If, however, those things which are to be observed as being accompanied by the state of supporting the living being (jīva) and by the state of being set in motion [by it] are intended to be "with life" (sajīva),
rather than merely by the state of being set in motion, then it should be understood that when one says,
"tasks that require strength," this is brought forward as a dissimilar example.
There is no one capable of shattering the doctrine of self and establishing the state of non-self, owing to the unique quality of the Sugata.

However, that which those belonging to the present dispensation perform according to their ability—both of these two—is by standing upon the method bestowed by the Buddhas and following their teaching.
"Having turned back" means having brought out; the sense is "having set apart. "The entirety of Vesālī."
He says that all the people living in Vesālī are "supported" by way of the formal act of dependence (*nissaya-upacāra*), just as one might say, "the village has arrived.
"Having gathered together" means having collected them, that is, having taken them as a single unit.
"Having established" means having caused him to give his formal admission (*paṭiñña*) in such a way that he does not disregard that doctrine.

The word *ghāti* has the sense of "killing" (*hiṃsana*). Therefore, those skilled in grammar, having derived the word *tāya* from it, desire the formal derivation (*rūpasiddhi*) as *ghātāyanti* (they cause to kill), and thus he says "one worthy of being killed" (*ghātārahaṃ*).

This same method applies to [the terms] *jāpetāyaṃ* and so forth. In the phrase "he is worthy to speak" (*vattituñca marahati*), the letter *m* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*padasandhi*) of the words.
He illuminates [the meaning] by way of distinction; that is to say, instead of merely saying "it occurs" (*vattati*), he says "and it is worthy to speak" (*vattituñca*).
By the second phrase, "māra-hatī," he explains [the state] as distinguished by what was spoken by the Blessed One.
"Pāsādikaṃ abhirūpaṃ" means endowed with a most desirable form in all its limbs. For that very reason, it is "susajjitaṃ," meaning it always maintains a well-adorned appearance.
By the words "dubbaṇṇaṃ" and so forth, he shows what kind of thing is being referred to when it was said, "of such a kind."
"In this case" refers to the grasping of the reason: "Do you have mastery over that form? For this is the reason taken up by the Blessed One:
"Do you have... [etc. ...let it not be. By this he shows that form is non-self because it does not admit of mastery;
for whatever does not admit of one's mastery is seen to be precisely non-self, just as that aforementioned prosperity [was shown to be]. "Vāda" means fault.

He will bring about a rebuke. "His head shall split into seven pieces" means that because he was causing vexation by failing to answer when questioned by the Tathāgata during a discussion on the Dhamma,
on the third occasion his head split into seven pieces by way of natural law (dhammatā), as happened to him upon approaching the presence of the Blessed One while claiming omniscience.

But why did Vajirapāṇi stand there? Out of compassion, like the Blessed One, he created a massive and terrifying form and stood in the air before him brandishing his thunderbolt, thinking, "I shall frighten him and make him abandon this view.
He did not wish to split his head; for indeed, no one can do any harm in the presence of the Blessed One.
However, because the Blessed One asks only questions that are strictly in accordance with the Dhamma, it is therefore stated in the commentary simply as "when asked.
"Blazing" (*āditta*) means burning.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "eyes, nose, etc.," [the inclusion of] hair and beard resembling the head of a ram and so forth is intended.

He includes [this]. Having stated, "For the purpose of making [Saccaka] abandon his view," he said "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, showing that this arrival was not by his own will, but rather by way of the promise he himself had previously made in the presence of Mahābrahmā.
"That" refers to Vajirapāṇi. It is the cause for turning Saccaka back on his promise. "Are there others too? and so forth.
This shows Saccaka’s state of investigation. For had he seen it without investigating, he might have said, "It is a great *yakkha*," which would have been inappropriate for him;

however, having observed the fearlessness of others and concluded, "Surely they do not see the *yakkha*, therefore fear has arisen in me alone," he acted according to what was appropriate and fitting.

358. *Upadhāretvā* means having observed the matter that is to be explained. *Eseva nayo* means that the same method applies to formations (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) as it does to perception (*saññā*).
*Vuttavipariyāyena* means the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated, such as: "May there not be unwholesome painful feeling;
may there not be unwholesome perception associated with mental grief," and so forth. *Sappadaṭṭhavisam* means... [the poison of one bitten by a snake].
The poison that has fallen upon the bodily parts of all beings at the place where they were bitten by a snake. "Adhered" (allīno) means stuck together.
"Approached" (upagato) means not departed. "Clinging" (ajjhosito) means remaining after having swallowed and fully digested it.

"He would know thoroughly" (parito jāneyyā) means he would know from every side, in every way, leaving nothing whatsoever remaining. "Having encompassed" (parikkhepetvā) means by way of bringing about the state of non-arising in the future.
Having exhausted it entirely. Being thus, he brings about its destruction and passing away; therefore it is said: "having brought about destruction, passing away, and non-arising. 359.
Because his own doctrine lacks essence, or because the essence he has postulated is absent, it is empty and devoid of inner substance.
"Deformity" means the unsightliness, the faulty state, and the blameworthy nature resulting from [wrong] view and conduct.
Having placed them upon those [stones]. *Sinnapatta* means a thin leaf. *Vipharita* means split open.
*Asārakarukkhaparicito* means one who has practiced the splitting of sapless trees such as the *palāsa*. *Thaddhabhāvaṃ* means the state of being fully ripened;
the meaning is "the state of being sharp. *Natthi* (it does not exist) should not be said to mean "it never exists. *Parisati* means...
In the midst of the fourfold assembly. For it is said: "having fastened a knot, with her body covered.
"As if mounted on a machine" means as if mounted on a machine made of bamboo for the purpose of explaining [the Dhamma].
360. "Quarrels of views" (*diṭṭhivisūka*) means the trifles of views. "Wandering in views" (*diṭṭhisañcarita*) means the beating of views. "Fluttering of views" (*diṭṭhivipphandita*) means...
“Movements of views. “Having known their intention” means having understood the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) of those Licchavi youths by their very movements.
That is why he said, “These,” and so forth. 361.
That knowledge, upon the attainment of which a person becomes confident in the Teacher’s dispensation and cannot be led astray by others—that is knowledge.
Having taken the word *vesārajja* to mean "the state of one who is confident," he said:
"One who has attained *vesārajja* is one who has attained knowledge. For this very reason, because there is no other to be relied upon by him, he is "independent of others" (*aparappaccaya*).

Because there is no other attainment to be believed by him, he is "one for whom there is no other refuge" (*aparappattiya*). Granted that "the stage of the trainee" and "the stage of the adept" are indeed the conventional terminology of the Dispensation (*sāsana-vohāra*).

He does not know. However, because it was stated that he "sees" (*passati*)—thereby indicating that the act of seeing has been completed—he understood, "The duties of a bhikkhu are not yet finished by this much alone.
Therefore, he again began the question, "But to what extent [is it finished]?
For this reason, it was said: "Because it was stated 'he sees,'" and so forth.
"Seeing things as they truly are" is *dassana* (vision). It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttariya*) in the sense of being preeminent;
thus, vision itself is the unsurpassed, which is "the unsurpassed vision" (*dassanānuttariya*). Alternatively, it is the unsurpassed among all forms of vision, hence "the unsurpassed vision.
And here, "worldly wisdom" (*lokiyapaññā*) should be understood as insight-wisdom (*vipassanāpaññā*), for that is said to be "unsurpassed" in the sense of being superior to all other worldly wisdoms.
The same method applies to the mundane paths and the unsurpassed states as well.
Now, in order to show all three kinds of the unsurpassed in their primary sense (nippariyāya), it is said: “Only the pure supramundane,” and so forth.

Although all supramundane phenomena possess the quality of being unsurpassed, by way of the highest description, the wisdom of the supreme path is called the unsurpassedness of vision, because there exists nothing higher than that.
Therefore he said, “the right view of the path to arahantship. “The remaining path factors” means the remaining factors of the path to arahantship;

for these, having reached their culmination, are the practice leading to Nibbāna. “Liberation as the fruit of the supreme path” means the liberation that is the fruit of the path to arahantship, namely the fruit of arahantship.
“Of one whose taints are destroyed” means of one whose taints are completely exhausted. “Vision of Nibbāna” means...

He speaks of the clear realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) by means of the right view of the supreme path. In that context, "path factors" refers to the eight path factors.

And it is even slight. Because the apprehension of form is coarse, he demonstrates the apprehension of the formless.

And in demonstrating it, because feeling is proximate, and specifically because of its being the essence of pleasure and because the mind is attached to the gratification of existence, he produces and demonstrates it by way of feeling for Sakka.
"In the sense of arising and passing away" means by way of their nature of rising and falling, through their ceasing after having arisen. "Impermanent" means unstable.

The characteristic of impermanence is impermanence itself, which is the state of arising and passing away. "Therefore" means because the knowledge that sees the five aggregates as subject to destruction and passing away is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), and the person who possesses that [knowledge] is one who contemplates impermanence; therefore.
“Fading away through destruction” (*khayavirāga*) means fading away in the sense of destruction, which is the crumbling of formations.

That by depending upon which there is a complete fading away from all formations—that is *nibbāna*, the absolute fading away. Regarding the phrase “also in the case of the contemplation of cessation”:
having indicated that “the same method applies,” he explains it in part, saying, “For cessation also... [is] twofold indeed.”

He said: To show that here "relinquishment" (*paṭinissagga*) refers to the very same relinquishing (*vossagga*) mentioned in the context of the restraint of all taints (*āsava*), he said, "Relinquishment is called relinquishing," and so forth.

Relinquishing by way of total giving is insight (*vipassanā*). Relinquishing by way of leaping forward is the path, because it leaps forward into absorption (*appanā*) through its own power, as no other state possesses that quality.
"It" refers to the path. "By way of object" means by way of accomplishing its function.

Because it takes [Nirvana] as its object. For in this way, the absence of both leaping forward (*pakkhandana*) and relinquishment (*vossagga*) in other states that take Nirvana as their object—distinct from the Path—is established.
Alternatively, it is by two reasons: by relinquishing and by leaping forward.

The relinquishing of all aggregates should be understood as occurring through the abandoning of the defilements bound up with them. "The mind leaps forward" refers to the mind associated with the Path.
He says this with reference to the mind. Both of these are forms of relinquishing (*vossajjana*).

"One who possesses both" refers to one who possesses insight (*vipassanā*) and one who possesses the path (*magga*). Just as the relinquishment and renunciation (*pariccāga-paṭinissagga*) of defilements is obtained through insight—according to such statements as "by the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence"—so too is there the relinquishment of the aggregates that are to be produced by those defilements in the future.

Relinquishment through giving up (*pariccāga-paṭinissagga*) should be explained [first]; however, relinquishment through leaping forward (*pakkhandana-paṭinissagga*) is to be understood by way of the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-gāmini-vipassanā*), which is the exclusive cause found on the path.

On the path, both of these are obtained in their primary sense (*nippariyāya*) precisely because they have arrived through the proper method (*ñāyāgata*). Therefore, he said: "The person possessing both," and so forth.

In response to the questioner’s underlying intention, he said, “He does not cling to anything in the world,” meaning that here the act of clinging by way of sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*) is being rejected;
thus he said, “he does not cling by way of craving (*taṇhā*). Alternatively, since there is no clinging by way of craving, clinging by way of views (*diṭṭhi*) would have no scope at all;
therefore, it was stated simply as “by way of craving. “He does not misapprehend (*na parāmasati*)”: [this refers to]...
He does not grasp; nor does he misapprehend by way of dogmatic adherence (*diṭṭhiparāmāsa*), such as [thinking] "it is permanent," and so forth.
"He spoke quickly in brief" means that he spoke without elaboration, in accordance with the listener's disposition. 391.
"Having approached" (*abhisamāgantvā*) means having approached the knowable by means of direct knowledge (*abhimukha-ñāṇa*), having understood it as it truly is. Therefore, he said:

“Having known”: because he makes it understood in accordance with the assembly; that is, by making it understood in a manner precisely suited to a large or small assembly capable of receiving the Dhamma.
“It does not go beyond the limit” means it does not proceed further.
“Do not go in vain”—this is stated by way of the natural law (*dhammatā*), not by way of the Teacher’s personal intention. For this is one [instance].
Regarding the eight qualities of the Teacher’s vocal sound, namely, its pervasiveness throughout the assembly:
there is not even a space that is perforated, fissured, or open; the reason for hearing the Blessed One’s voice has already been stated.
Therefore: because of the reasons thus described.

That which has five components is *pañcaṅga*; that which is fivefold is *pañcaṅgika*. Since specific types of lutes such as the *mahatī* and others are also merely *ātatā* (stretched), they are specified as "covered with leather.
A single-sided [lute] includes the *kumbha*, *thūṇa*, *daddara*, and so forth. Being covered with leather and bound with strings is what is meant by *ātatavitata* (stretched and spread).
Therefore he said, "the *paṇava* and others bound with strings," and this applies to the *gomukhī* and others as well.

In this very context, the inclusion [of musical instruments] should be understood. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "bamboo and so forth," the inclusion of conch shells, horns, and the like is intended.
By "drums and so forth" (*sammatādi*), the inclusion of the *sammatāḷa*, the bronze cymbal (*kaṃsatāḷa*), the stone cymbal (*silāsalākatāḷa*), and others is meant.

Among these, the *sammatāḷa* is a drum made of wood. The bronze cymbal (*kaṃsatāḷa*) is made of metal. The stone cymbal (*silāsalākatāḷa*) is a cymbal played with a stone or an iron plate. "Well-applied" (*samappito*) means properly applied.
He is endowed with it; therefore he says "approached" (*upagata*). He is endowed with five hundred musical instruments by way of attendance.
And because one who is thus constituted is said to be "attended" or "possessed" by them, it is stated that "endowed" (*samaṅgībhūta*) is a synonym for that very term.
"He causes to move around" (*paricāreti*) means he causes [them] to move all around. But what does he cause to move, or how does he cause them to move? To this he says:
“...he causes [the music] to be played... and so forth. In that context, “from here and there” means from this or that musical instrument and among those various musicians.
“Having removed” means having restrained the musicians. Therefore he said, “having caused them to be made silent.
He goes on his journey to the celestial realms precisely out of compassion for both deities and humans. This meaning is to be illustrated by the *Vimānavatthu* (Stanzas on the Mansions).
392. “Perhaps because of our own business, dear Moggallāna, we are not very busy, even though we have much to do.
Furthermore, “because of the business of the gods” means that we are especially busy with the business of the Tāvatiṃsa gods themselves.
Some of the deities who dwell on the earth are also protected by Sakka.
He said, “starting from earth,” because they must be determined. “Restricting” means determining.
To show that task in its specific form, he said, “of the deities,” and so forth. “Of them” refers to the daughters of the deities, the sons of the deities, and the female attendants.

“Those who provide ornaments and adornments” means those who arrange for ornaments and adornments. There is no need for a legal proceeding (court of inquiry), because there is an absence of doubt itself.
Whatever category of meaning, though well-mastered by way of repeated study and so forth, does not appear—that is, does not manifest at all to the eye of wisdom—this is the sense.
"Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. "A thrill of joy and spiritual urgency" means a spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arising from joy, not a state of mental terror.
"Drawn up together" (*samupabyūḷha*) means fallen together or plunged in together by way of engaging in battle.

And because one who has become thus is gathered together as a multitude, it is therefore said: "assembled, formed into a heap. Regarding the phrase "in the immediately preceding personal existence" (*anantare attabhāve*):
this refers to the second Sakka-existence, [distinguished] from the Sakka-existence immediately prior to it by virtue of the commonality of being a Sakka-existence.

It is stated as if they were one for the sake of inclusion; otherwise, it would have had to be said, "in the third personal existence," for the personal existence of Magha was indeed the third from this point.
Alternatively, because it immediately followed that personal existence in which the battle between the devas and asuras took place, it is said, "in the immediately subsequent personal existence.
[This was done] through service to mother and father and so forth, out of a desire for the welfare of beings.
His conduct was like the conduct of a Bodhisattva. "Seven vows" (*satta vatapadāni*) means seven sections of vows.

"Great drinking" (*mahāpāna*) means the drinking of a large quantity of liquor. "Gall-bladder drinking" (*gaṇḍapāna*) means the drinking of *gaṇḍa*-liquor; the meaning is excessive drinking. "Surrounding" (*pariharamānā*) means encircling.
"Railing-foundation" (*vedikāpāda*) refers to the railing enclosures at the edge of Mount Sineru. In the five...
"At the spots" means at the five decorative locations; he established guards there by means of Nāgasena and others.
(393) "Delightfulness" means the state of being delightful. "On pillars of masāragalla" means on pillars made of kabamaṇi gems.
"In jars made of gold and so forth" refers to [the arrangement] such as "on silver pillars, jars made of gold; on gold pillars, jars made of silver," and so on.
In small jars made of gold and other materials, there were figures of animals. *Pamatta* means intoxicated to the point of being excessive; thus he said, "exceedingly intoxicated.
*Nāṭakaparivārena* means with a retinue of celestial nymphs (*accharā*).
By both terms, *acchariya* and *abbhuta*, the very manner of causing wonder is expressed; therefore, it is the state of having become wonderful and marvelous that is meant.
"Of a nature to cause amazement" means that they have experienced wonder and astonishment; thus, their mental states have arisen in such a way.
"Of arisen joy" means that joy has arisen in them caused by that wonder and astonishment. "Agitated" means that agitation (saṃvega) has arisen.
Since this agitation is a wavering of the mind from its previous state, it is therefore called "shaken" (calita).
394. "The darkness was dispelled": by witnessing the miracle, [the people] developed great respect for right practice, thinking, "Oh, how great is the Elder’s power of psychic potency!

Furthermore, by giving rise to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), thinking, "Even though we have received such a teaching as this, we remain intoxicated by the vain pride of wealth," the darkness of delusion was dispelled—that is, destroyed. "These" refers to the Great Elder.
"And Sakka"—these two were fellow practitioners (*sabrahmacārino*) because they shared the same holy life.
"Among those who are renowned" means among those well-known—such as the Four Great Kings, Suyāma, Santusita, Paranimmitavasavatti, and Mahābrahmā—one [of them];

the intention is that it was not just anyone. Because it was concluded by means of the very dhamma that had been undertaken, he brought it to a close according to the natural sequence of the discourse.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is completed.
8. Commentary on the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta 396.
"Mere adherence" means mere false grasping, not the dogmatic insistence of a view. "Eternalist view" means the dogmatic insistence on permanence.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha. The construction is: "having spoken, they bring [the matter] together. "Bringing together" means concluding.
"Right there, in each case" means they cease right within those respective states of existence; they do not transmigrate to another state of existence.
The intention is that consciousness, however, remains of an undifferentiated nature and is not something else. "From this world" means from this personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Another world" (*paraloka*) refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*) designated as a future birth. "He runs on" (*sandhāvati*) means that, due to its continuity, it proceeds as if unconnected by anything;
by this, he speaks of the transition from this world to another world. "He wanders about" (*saṃsarati*) refers to the coming back from another world to this one.

Alternatively, "he runs on" expresses the transition between different states of existence (*bhava*), while "he wanders about" signifies the moving from one place to another within those various states.

By stating, “When there is a condition, [consciousness] comes to be,” and so forth, he demonstrates the dependent-originated nature of consciousness through both positive and negative concomitance, thereby rejecting its eternal nature.
Regarding the phrase “he spoke what was not spoken by the Buddha,” this refers to the ground for schism wherein it is asserted:
“That which was neither uttered nor spoken by the Tathāgata, he now declares as having been uttered and spoken by the Tathāgata.”
"It will appear" means he shows [this]. "He strikes a blow at the Conqueror’s Wheel" means that by asserting permanence—saying, "This very consciousness...

is not other"—he strikes a blow, driving in a wedge against the Teacher’s Wheel of Dhamma set in motion in such a manner as: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; form, monks, is impermanent," and so forth. It has been seen as impermanent by the knowledge of omniscience.
By asserting that consciousness, which has been proclaimed [by the Buddha], is permanent, one obstructs the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).

One deceives people who desire to hear—the people who desire to hear the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*), which is the exclusive means for the attainment of the Noble Dhamma—by causing them to cling to the notion of permanence.
For that very reason, by rejecting that [path of insight] on the Noble Path, the course of the Noble Dhamma, one falls down sideways.
398. Explaining the self as it is grasped under the heading of consciousness, he said, "That which, venerable sir," and so forth.

In that context, terms such as "speaker" (vada) and "feeler" (vedeyya) are modes of adherence to the eternalist view (sassataditthi). "Speaker" means one who speaks; the meaning is an agent of verbal action.
For by this term, [the Buddha] demonstrates the capacity for awakening to the welfare and happiness of sentient beings through the means of being an agent.
It shows itself. "Vedeyya" means one who feels; the sense is that it knows and experiences.
For grammarians consider such words to have the agent as their primary derivation (*kattusādhana*). "Vedayati" means it experiences this or that which is to be experienced.
"Tahiṃ tahiṃ" means in those various realms of existence, matrices, destinies, stations, abodes of beings, and classes of beings.
399. Because Sāti remained adhering to that doctrine, his state of having the conditions severed and his state of not growing in the Dhamma should be understood.
"Below" is said with reference to the commentary on the Alagaddūpama-sutta. The same method applies to the phrase "below" where it is mentioned further on as well.
"A separate connection" means a connection that is distinct and not mixed with the three other connections; it is a single, independent connection. Is it not...?
And is this also merely a connection by way of intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*), because it proceeds according to Sātissa’s own inclination? No;

because it does not proceed by way of the gateway to liberation (*niyyāna*). For other connections—such as those concerning the teaching, the question, and so forth—proceed by placing liberation at the forefront through questions and the like.
Since that is absent here, it is said: “a separate connection. “Clearing away the assembly’s misconception” means whatever...

This was Sāti’s view. By purifying the assembly’s view through the demonstration of its absence, Sāti became known as one who had been expelled from the community by that very act of purifying the assembly’s view.
(400) As for the phrase "whatever it may be," although this refers to the apprehension of conditions and phenomena without distinction, [it is said]: "It is reckoned simply as consciousness."

However, because it is stated [elsewhere] that "it goes," it should be understood that what is grasped here is the collection of conditions consisting of the specific conventional signs for each respective consciousness.
Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: "It receives the designation 'eye-consciousness' alone," and so forth.
Alternatively, all other conditions for each respective consciousness, which are restricted to their particular sense-door, are also included here by the phrase "whatever it may be."
In that context, however, because it is unique [to each], it is designated by that very term; thus it is said, "it is called 'eye-consciousness' and so forth.
"Due to the absence of transition between doors" means the absence of consciousness moving from one door to another.
This is stated by way of showing the method for the purpose of easy understanding by those of dull intellect, according to a coarse approach. For present consciousness never actually vanishes.

The subsequent consciousness does not transmigrate because it fails to arise when the conditions for its arising—such as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and others—are absent.
"In the same way" means: just as a fire burning in dependence upon fuel is extinguished right there when without fuel and does not transmigrate anywhere, so too is this case.
Why was it said, "By the deficiency of conditions, it ceases right there," and not [that it transmigrates]? Because here...
The cessation of non-arising is not intended here as the cessation of such [a state], because that kind of cessation is not what is meant in this context; rather, it is momentary cessation.

And is that not due to its intrinsic nature, rather than being caused by a lack of conditions? True, that is so; however, what is intended here is the cessation of consciousness—whether it pertains to a particular sense-door—without it transferring to another door, but ceasing right there. And as for those conditions...

By virtue of this [absence], there must be consciousness through the intermediate opening; because that [consciousness] does not exist for them, there is the apprehension of a deficiency in conditions.

Therefore, the construction is as follows: due to the deficiency in conditions, the ear-consciousness and so forth do not transfer to the ear and other [senses], nor do they attain the designation of "ear-consciousness" and so on.
By this, it is shown that whatever consciousness [arises] by virtue of the completeness of conditions such as the eye and visible forms is designated as "eye-consciousness."

It goes, and it ceases right there and then because its existence is merely temporary; since it lacks the conditions such as the ear and sound, how could there be the designation "ear-consciousness" and so forth?
Thus, it is shown that because it does not persist in that way, how could there be any transmigration of it? "In the occurrence of consciousness" means in the process of the arising of consciousness.
"Merely a transition between doors" means that I do not say there is even a mere transition from one door [of sense] to another therein.

Because it breaks up right there, and because the condition possesses arising, and because cessation is necessarily present when there is arising, impermanence is demonstrated in the sense of non-existence after having been. 401.
“Consciousness has been described by me as dependently arisen; apart from conditions, there is no consciousness.”

Since the fact that consciousness is conditioned (*saṅkhata*) has been demonstrated both through positive and negative concomitance by the phrase "its arising," he says, "having shown its state of having conditions.
Here, what is intended by the term "become" (*bhūta*) is that which is born and produced by causes and conditions;
in terms of meaning, this refers to the five aggregates, because there is nothing apart from them that possesses conditions. And as for those five aggregates...
The Blessed One said that this—both for himself and for those bhikkhus—is "this has come to be" (*bhūtamidam*); thus he said, "This is the pentad of aggregates.
It brings its own fruit, therefore it is *āhāra*, meaning a condition. That from which something comes into being is its *sambhava*; thus, "having food as its source" (*āhārasambhava*).
Therefore he said, "the arising of conditions" (*paccayasambhava*). [And: "the cessation of those conditions."
The non-arising and cessation of that condition—by means of which condition, such as ignorance, the pentad of aggregates comes into being—is what is meant.
However, momentary cessation is independent of a cause.
The particle *no* is an indeclinable used to indicate doubt; thus he said, "Is this real, or is it not real? This is real.
By the phrase "Is it not? (*nossūti*), a mode of doubt of this kind is grasped: "Is this merely the pentad of aggregates, or rather is it a self or what belongs to a self?
But by the phrase "Is it not produced from its nutriment?

(*tadāhārasambhavaṃ nossūti*), just as a mode of doubt regarding whether this element is caused or uncaused is grasped, so too is a mode of doubt regarding whether it has an irregular cause (*visamahetuka*) grasped.

It should be understood that the mode of apprehension is one of doubt. Even the theory of a discordant cause (visamahetu) is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, equivalent to the doctrines of intrinsic nature (sabhāva), necessity (niyati), chance (yadicchā), and so forth, because it is merely a conceptual construction by others and because what exists ultimately is devoid of causes.

By the phrase "is it not subject to cessation?", [the text] addresses the uncertainty regarding impermanence, such as: "Is this existing thing impermanent, or rather permanent?"—thus referring to impermanence itself.

It should be understood that by depending [on these], the mode of doubt is apprehended; for instance, the mode of doubt—"Is this suffering, or is it not suffering? Is it non-self, or is it not non-self?"—is indeed apprehended as well.
This is because the state of suffering and so forth necessarily exists in what is impermanent, whereas both of those [suffering and non-self] are absent in what is permanent.
"By way of the characteristic of its own true nature" means by way of its unerring essence and its specific characteristic.

The meaning is: both by way of function and by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Although wisdom that serves as the foundation for insight (*vipassanā*) is itself insight, it is stated as "of insight-wisdom" (*vipassanā-paññāya*).
"By its own essence" means by way of intrinsic nature; "by its characteristic" means by way of the general characteristic (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*).
Therefore he said: "for one who sees correctly through insight-wisdom. "In the manner already stated" refers to [the phrase] "by way of the characteristic of its own essence as it truly is."
In the same manner as previously stated. "Whosoever" means whichever bhikkhus were in that assembly. "Discerned" means they correctly reflected upon it. "By them" means by those bhikkhus.

"Therein" means in that wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). "The state of being free from craving" means the absence of craving—the abandonment of the grasping of craving that thinks, "This is mine.
By this also, the Blessed One [said]: "O bhikkhus, even regarding phenomena..."
“I praise only the abandoning of craving; yet this misguided man Sāti stands upholding a perverted view that increases craving even for his own individual existence,” thus he rebukes Sāti.
“By seeing the true nature” means by seeing the non-perverted nature of phenomena.
“By seeing the condition” means by seeing the cause, that is, by seeing the cause and condition in their entirety. “One would adhere” means...
One would rely [on them] by way of craving and views. Therefore he said, "by means of craving and views. "You would cherish" means you would maintain them with the play of possession.
Therefore he said, "you would dwell playing. "Desiring like wealth" means generating desire—craving—as if it were wealth or property.
Therefore he said, "you would fall into greed. "You would produce a sense of 'mine'" means...
"You might generate a fixed adherence through craving and views, thinking, 'This is mine.

Nor was it taught for the purpose of grasping through attachment; for the grasping of that subtle and refined Dhamma of insight would indeed occur only through attachment, not through gross craving—thus it is said, 'through attachment.'"
402. Because the fruit comes from this, it is a condition (*paccaya*); that is, every specific cause. Thus he said, "showing the condition for the aggregates.
Indeed, everything up to ignorance is shown here as their specific cause.

Furthermore, [the exposition] proceeds from the beginning to the end, and from the end back to the beginning, by way of showing the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*), both in forward and reverse order.

It is shown that dependent origination has been demonstrated through various methods, and it is further indicated that even the defilement which serves as the sign for grasping at permanence is not found here.

That too has the same meaning as what was stated; thus, the passage from the text beginning with "And these, monks, are the four nutriments" up to "born of craving" has already had its meaning explained in the commentary on the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta. The remainder...
This is included by the very statement: "Because the discussion on dependent origination has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

404. Whatever needs to be said regarding such passages as "When this exists, that comes to be" should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Udāna) in the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
407. "Running back" (*paṭidhāvana*) means a resort; it refers to craving and views directed toward one's own past, the prior time from which one has come.
"Returning" (paṭigamana) is the meaning. [Objection: But is it not the case that "running back" (paṭidhāvana) is mentioned in the Canon by way of doubt (vicikicchā)?

[Reply: True, it is mentioned; however, since that [doubt] has craving and views as its cause, it is stated "by way of craving and views. "Therein" (tattha) means in that knowledge and vision thus attained.

"The state of being unshakable" (niccalabhāva) means the state of being well-established and the state of being unshakeable by the winds of the doctrines of the sectarians (titthiyavāda). "Venerable" (garūti)—
"Endowed with many virtues. "Burdensome like a stone umbrella": this refers to following [the teacher] out of mere faith (*saddhāmattaka*), not out of verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
"Duty" means the duty toward the Teacher. "Of the brahmins" means of those brahmins who possess birth.
"Taking up vows" means taking up vows such as the *magava* and others. "Curiosities of views" means by way of adhering to various respective views.
“‘This is true, this is true’—such things are curiosities to be grasped. Thus they are relinquished:
“Just as the instruction was given to you by me, so too, having relinquished your vows and other observances, what else would you grasp beyond that?
It is known by one’s own knowledge: having abandoned dependence on others, it is known exactly as it is through one’s own wisdom. And being such...
"Seen by oneself" means it has been seen through one's own direct experience; thus he said, "seen by oneself with the eye of wisdom.
"Clarified by oneself" means that the state of that meaning has been brought to personal manifestation by those bhikkhus.
"Led" means led by means of an effort following the teaching of the Dhamma. "By me" is an instrumental case used for the agent. "By the Dhamma" means by way of the reason.
"This statement" refers to this statement beginning with "visible here and now" (*sanditthiko*). 408.

That would be a ground for delusion for this world. "By way of convergence" means by way of coming together. It is called a "womb" (*gabbha*) because it develops as the state of an individual existence (*attabhāva*);

it is a continuity of phenomena (*dhammapabandha*) in the stages of the embryo such as the *kalala*, and the continuum of a sentient being (*sattasantāna*) is so called because it is dependent upon that.
The term “womb” (*gabbha*) is used here just as one says, “the beds are shouting.
It should be understood that the mother’s womb is called “womb” because it is the locus of support for that [embryo], or because it is like a womb.

For just as a chamber is called a “womb” because it is a place of residence for beings, so too the mother’s womb is called a “womb” because it is the place of residence for those born from a womb until their birth.
*Yamekarattiṃ*: on which single night. This is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, or in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
*Paṭhamaṃ*: at the very first moment, at the instant of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). *Gabbhe*: in the mother’s womb. *Māṇavo*: a sentient being.
The mention of "night" is because, for the most part, beings take rebirth-linking during the night. *Abbhuṭṭhito*: one from whom the clouds have risen; one who is clear.
The intention is that he has indeed arisen toward death by way of its very presence. "He goes" means that the youth goes; from the first moment onward, he simply proceeds.
"Going thus, he does not turn back" means that as he goes in this manner, he does not turn back even for a single moment;
rather, he approaches nothing other than death—such is the meaning of the verse.
This was said with reference to the time of conception, not merely the day of the attachment of the embryo according to worldly convention.
Now, in order to make this very point more clear, it is said: “It is said that in whatever [place] of the woman...
and so forth. Therein means in that womb-site. Having formed means having been produced. Having broken up means having been aborted while still ungrasped as a fetus. For this [woman]...
The nature [of the womb]. "The site is pure" means that the site of the womb is pure because of the flowing of blood and the absence of disease.
Because the site is pure, for several days thereafter it remains a field, since there exists only a small amount of residual blood sufficient to establish the formation of the embryo.
But how is the existence of the arising [of the embryo] established? To this he says: "In that..."
"At the proper time," and so forth. Even within the female continuum, the semen-element (*sukkadhātu*) is indeed found. Therefore he said: "Even by the touching of the limbs, a boy is born.
Just as Sāma the Bodhisatta was born through the mother’s touching of her navel, and Maṇḍabya was born through Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s touching of her navel.
A *gandhabba* is so called because of its scenting; it refers to the being that arises at the moment of conception by means of the manifestation of the sign (*nimitta*).
It is called a *gandhabba* because it "wanders" (*abbati*) or proceeds by means of karma leading to existence, which has received the name "scent" (*gandha*) due to its indicative nature;
it refers to the being who arises there. Hence he said, "the being who has arrived there.
"By the driving force of kamma" means driven and led toward that state by the impelling force of what is termed kamma, which brings about rebirth there. "With great danger to life" means...
By the distress of giving birth—that is, by the great and heavy uncertainty consisting of doubt regarding life, which arises in the form: "I shall live, or shall I not live?
Shall I or my son?"—he refers to that place as the "breast-region. It is called *kīḷana* because they play (*kīḷanti*) with it;
*kīḷanaka* is simply another term for *kīḷana*.
409. *Sārajjati* means he becomes one whose mind is lustful (*sārattacitta*). *Byāpajjati* means he becomes one whose mind is malevolent (*byāpannacitta*).

Mindfulness regarding the body (*kāyasati*) is mindfulness that has as its object the nature of that collection of thirty-two impurities, such as head-hairs and so forth, within the body. *Anupaṭṭhapetvā* means not having established [it], which is to say, not having investigated the body according to its true nature.
*Parittacetaso* means one whose mind is limited or broken by defilements; therefore, he says, "one whose mind is unwholesome."
These are unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*). "Cease" means they have reached cessation.

"Rejoices by way of craving" means he delights, facing toward [the object] by way of craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). "Speaks out" means he speaks, having become attached to this or that object by way of craving.
"Clinging" means having entered into the object by way of craving as if it were not shared with anyone else.

Therefore he said, "having swallowed and having finished. Regarding the question, "How does one delight in suffering?", it should be understood here that one who delights in the cause of suffering is said to "delight in suffering.

However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), in order to show that as long as a person's delighting view and craving regarding suffering have not been abandoned, for that long they are said to "delight in suffering," [it says...]
It is said: “One who grasps ‘I am suffering’ or ‘suffering is mine’ indeed rejoices.

By this, he shows that the rejoicing therein is caused by those two types of grasping. “Once again” means once more. It has two connections: by way of the connection between fruit and cause, and by way of the connection between cause and fruit.
This refers, both in terms of meaning and in its own form, to the present summary of the fruit, beginning with the words “there is descent into the womb.”
And because the other two [summaries] were taught by way of their common form (*sarūpena*), he said, “the three summaries.

(410–414) Since the meditation subject for a monk who is a practitioner of serenity (*samathayānika*) has been explained here in brief, up to Arhatship, by way of feelings (*vedanā*), he said, “Bear in mind this liberation through the destruction of craving (*taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti*) in its condensed form. “This liberation through the destruction of craving...”
And it is said that the Blessed One spoke the teaching exactly as it was taught: "This... [etc. ...is the teaching on liberation.
If this is so, how is the teaching itself liberation? He says: "For the teaching... [etc. ...is called liberation.

By virtue of which craving that monk Sāti was caught in the great net of the eternalist view, even though the hands of all the Buddhas were being held out to him, that [craving]—[the teaching cuts through].
"It has become difficult to remove," he said, [referring to the phrase] "entangled in the great net of craving, in the snare of craving.
"The great net of craving" means in the great tangle of craving. "In the snare of craving" means in the trap set by craving. And being thus situated, one is as if placed within it;
hence he said, "entered within, included inside. The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Mahāassapura Sutta 415.
"Jānapadino" means those who possess a country, or princes who are lords of a country; they are called Aṅgas by way of their clan.
[This is] the name. If their dwelling place were a single province (*janapada*), how could there be the plural number? To this he says: "By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsaddena*).
