For etymologists (*akkharacintaka*) desire gender and number as if they were appropriate in such instances [according to Pāṇini 1.2.51].
This is the conventional usage here, as in the expressions: "He dwells among the Kurus" and "He dwells among the Mallans. But regarding its qualification...
In the case of the word *janapada* (country) and the word *jāti* (birth/species), there is only the singular number. Therefore he said, "in the country of the Aṅgas.
Some say that *assa* means stones; since those were beautiful (*sundara*) there, the town was called "Assapura.
Others, however, say it is called "Assapura" because a noble horse (*ājānīya assa*) entered the king's capture there. Why?
That was indeed the name of that town. However, because there was no fixed place for the Blessed One to reside there, it is simply stated that "he dwelt having made that his alms-resort village.
For thus in the Pāḷi, it is merely the alms-resort village that is mentioned:
"There is a town of the Aṅgas named Assapura."

In the passage beginning with "By such virtue," etc., by the mention of "virtue" (*sīla*), he refers to the virtue of restraint (*vāritta-sīla*). By this, he indicates right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
By the mention of "conduct" (*ācāra*), he refers to the virtue of performance (*cāritta-sīla*). By this, he indicates perfectly pure bodily and verbal behavior.

By the mention of "practice" (*paṭipatti*), he indicates right practice as comprising serenity, insight, the path, and the fruit. By the term "the conscientious" (*lajjino*), he indicates the underlying cause rooted in the aforementioned virtue and conduct.
By the word *pesalā* (virtuous), he indicates their purity; by the word *uḷāraguṇā* (of lofty virtues), he indicates the perfection of their practice.
The phrase "speaking in praise of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" is said because those lay followers were for the most part devoted to extolling the virtues of the bhikkhus;
yet they were indeed also deeply devoted to the True Dhamma and the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therefore, he said: "Those who have the Buddha as their own... (*Buddhamāmaka*).
“Dhamma is my own. For those who have full confidence in one of the three objects (vatthu) necessarily have full confidence in the other two as well, because they are inseparable from them.
“In honoring the alms-food” is a figurative expression, just as one says, “the ghee must be guarded from crows”;
therefore, what is meant is “in honoring the requisites. For by means of one’s own correct practice, [one honors] the deed of the donors of the requisites.
In this context, what is intended by "honoring with almsfood" is the act of making [the practice] yield great fruit.
"Those things that make one a recluse" (*samaṇakaraṇa*) means those which produce the state of a recluse; the sense is that they are the makers of the state of a recluse.
Furthermore, since these must be produced and developed within one's own continuum, it is said: "having undertaken them, fulfilled them. And here, the inclusion of the term "recluse" (*samaṇa*)...
He says, "the ascetic who has stilled evil," meaning [he is such] by virtue of being an ascetic, not merely by the outward appearance of asceticism.

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇakaraṇa*, the meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. Furthermore, this distinction between "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) and "brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is only in terms of the phrasing; that is to say, it is a difference in expression, not in meaning.

"The qualities to be performed by an ascetic" (*samaṇadhamma*) refers to those qualities that must be accomplished by one established in the duties of an ascetic. As for "whoever... [the text continues].

For one who is well-established in the state of a recluse (samaṇabhāva) consisting of the lower training, the duties to be performed by that recluse as described are stated precisely by way of those states of a recluse consisting of the higher training which are to be accomplished.
Indeed, with reference to their bringing about the state of a recluse, it was said: "And these too are truly the makers of a recluse. But here, however, [it refers to] Mahāassapura.
The teaching has been set forth in detail by way of moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), and so on;

that is to say, the teaching on the qualities that constitute a recluse (*samaṇakaraṇadhamma*)—consisting of the purification of bodily, verbal, and mental conduct through moral shame and moral dread, restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and the jhānas and true knowledges (*vijjā*)—has been taught in full detail, not merely in brief as in the Third Book (*Tikanipāta*). By the mention of the "fruit" (*phala*) itself, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is included. That...
Furthermore, by way of the exalted description, the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) should be understood as fourfold.

By the inclusion of "benefit" (ānisansa), the causes such as being dear and agreeable are indicated. "The meaning of that very thing" is the exposition of the meaning of that very state which is not deceptive. With the words beginning "For one who... and so forth, he explains the meaning by way of contrast (byatireka).
"By this much of a place" means by this much of a passage in the Pāḷi. Regarding shame (hirottappa) and the rest, [the explanation follows] further in the Pāḷi.
"Of the qualities that make one a recluse" (*samaṇakaraṇadhammānaṃ*) means: "He spoke in praise" (*vaṇṇaṃ kathesi*) means he described their virtues and benefits.
"In the manner stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna*" means in the manner stated in the commentary on the *Satipaṭṭhāna*, beginning with the words: "Furthermore, this is merely a statement of praise.
(416) "That by which one feels shame" (*yaṃ hirīyati*) means that by which, as a cause, one feels disgust. This is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental.
Or it is stated with a reversal of gender; the meaning is "the Dhamma. In the phrase *hirīyitabbenā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative;
the meaning is "that which is fit to be felt shame for," namely bodily misconduct and so forth. The same principle applies here to the phrase *ottappitabbenā*.
*Ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā* means that shame (*hirī*) has its origin within oneself (*niyakajjhatta*), arising from birth and other such factors. As for *bahiddhā*...
Bahirddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ is shame that has its origin outside oneself, having another being as its source.

Attādhipateyyā means "having oneself as the dominant influence," occurring by making oneself the authority. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā means "established in the nature of modesty," abiding in the nature of loathing evil.
Because it is characterized by deference, *patissava* is the act of listening with respect when someone of authority says something.
"With respect" (*sappatissavaṃ*) means accompanied by respect; it is any kind of reverence that consists of or has the nature of respect.
And since *hiri* (moral shame), arising through the contemplation of the greatness of birth and so forth, functions therein by way of reverence, it is said to have "respect as its characteristic.
"Established in the nature of fear" means abiding in the state of having the nature of fearing evil.
Because its characteristic is the fear of faults and the seeing of them as fearful, one who fears faults and sees them as fearful is called *vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvī*;

such is the nature of moral dread (*ottappa*). Furthermore, the fact that moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) originate internally and so forth is stated precisely because they are evident in various instances;
it is never the case that they are dissociated from one another. For there is no feeling of shame that is devoid of fear, nor is there fear of evil that is devoid of shame.
Or it is "shamelessness. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

They are called "world-guardian qualities" (*lokapāladhammā*) because they protect the boundaries of the world. "White" means pure, producing a state of radiance; or they are "white" because they are the cause for rebirth in a white (noble) caste.
"Confusion" means the mixing of conduct and the boundaries of propriety. "Divine qualities" (*devadhammā*) are those qualities that bring about the state of a deva.

“Possessed of bright qualities” (*sukkadhammasamāhita*) means endowed with the aforementioned bright qualities. “Peaceful” (*santa*) means those whose faults have been stilled. “True persons” (*sappurisa*) means peaceful people; for the virtuous (*sādhava*) are so called because they accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others.

Since a whole cannot exist apart from its parts, and since the whole must be designated by means of its parts, the phrase “instruction and full ordination” (*ovādūpasampadā*) refers to a portion of that which brings about instruction and full ordination.
“Here” (*idha*) means in this horse-stable. These are the qualities of moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
“Samaṇadhammā” (the qualities of a recluse) is stated thus, taking them to be the qualities that produce the fundamental state of a recluse; for they are taken up first for that reason.
That Noble Path by the attainment of which one becomes a recluse in the primary sense is called “sāmañña” (recluseship), because it is the recluse’s work and practice.
Furthermore, because it is the fruit of that [path], and because it is to be sought after (araṇīya) by making it its object, [it is also called sāmañña].
The fruits and Nibbāna are the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*). It is called the "destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhaya*) because it destroys lust; this refers to the Noble Path.

It is also called the "destruction of lust" because lust is destroyed therein; this refers to Nibbāna. However, the fruit should be regarded as the "destruction of lust" by way of metaphorical designation based on its cause.

The same method applies to the "destruction of hatred" (*dosakkhaya*) and the "destruction of delusion" (*mohakkhaya*). The "goal of recluseship" (*sāmaññattha*) is the goal that constitutes recluseship; [it refers to] the Path, which is the essence of recluseship.
“Meaning” (attha) refers to the meaning of recluseship (sāmaññattha). He says, “Both the path and the fruit, taken together, are called the meaning of recluseship.

This is stated by way of the highest possible description (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa), for here even the preliminary practice consisting of virtue and so forth is included under the term “the meaning of recluseship.
For this very reason he said, “if there is something further to be done. “I declare” (paṭivedayāmi) means I make known again and again.
417. “By way of the courses of action alone” means by way of the nature of unwholesome courses of action;

therefore, since it is not proper for a bhikkhu to perform even such unwholesome action, the intention is that he desists from it precisely because of its being a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*). “Bound by the training rules” means by the promulgation of the training rules.
[He should desist] from throwing a hand, a stick, or a clod of earth at a water-jar or a bowl belonging to crows.
"Blows upon all this" should be understood as a mere illustration;
for the causing of distress to other living beings, wherever they may stand, such as by lifting them up and so forth, is all included here precisely under the state of impure bodily conduct.
"Exposed" (*uttāna*) means it stretches upwards and upwards; and one who is thus situated has produced a trunk like that of a *sāla* tree in a place where nothing else can grow.
Because it rises higher and higher, becoming increasingly prominent, it is said: "lofty and manifest" (*uggato pākaṭo*). "Uncovered" (*anāvaṭo*) means not obstructed. Therefore he says:
"unconcealed" (*asañchanno*), meaning it is not to be covered. It is "uniform" (*ekasaddiso*) by virtue of its purity.
It is "without gaps in between" (*antarantare chiddarahito*) because of the continuity of correct practice from beginning to end. It is "restrained" (*saṃvuto*) through bodily restraint.
Because it is free from secondary defilements (*anupakkilesa*). Therefore he said: "By closing the door to the defilements (*kilesa*).

418. Herein, just as even a slight bodily action such as making a sarcastic sound brings about impurity of bodily conduct by disturbing one's austerity (*sallekha*), and mere wrong reflection does the same for mental conduct, so too does any mere talk on topics that do not lead to liberation [bring about impurity].
It should be understood that speaking falsehood with the intention of joking is not included here, because it brings about impurity in verbal conduct by disturbing one’s austerity (*sallekha*);
for speaking falsehood with the intention of joking is already prohibited by the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) themselves. 420.

Furthermore, a certain kind of livelihood is also excluded by way of the courses of action (*kammapatha*). However, that is not overly coarse, as it was not included in the sections on bodily and verbal conduct.

It should be understood that [this] was not included because it follows the method already stated. As for those who say, "It was not included because such [a person] is unfit for monks," that is incorrect;
for if that were the case, it would follow that he should also not be included in the section on bodily and verbal conduct.
The question, "Eat! Drink!", indicates one's own desire to eat and so forth, since it is a figurative statement (*pariyāyakathā*).
The agitation of the ascetic’s austerity arose. 422.
One who, having abandoned improper search, seeks requisites righteously and justly, is called “one who knows the measure of search.
One who receives while knowing the measure of the donor, the gift to be given, and oneself, is called “one who knows the measure of receiving.”
One who uses [the requisites] after reflecting thoroughly is said to be "one who knows the proper measure in using.
(423) "In one section" means in that single section designated as the middle watch of the night. They are described as "lying on their left side";
there is no such thing as lying on the right side, because the right hand is incapable of performing the necessary functions such as supporting the body.
This was stated by way of the male.
By the phrase "on account of his preponderance of fire," he shows the lion’s fearless nature.
For other timid animals, having entered their own lairs, lie down in whatever manner they can, preceded by fear; but the lion, because of his fearless nature, acts with mindfulness.
Like a monk, he lies down having established mindfulness. Therefore he said, "With two feet placed before," and so forth.
One lies (*seti*) there in the sense of proceeding in a state of non-exertion; thus it is a *seyyā* (bed). The fourth jhāna itself is the bed. But what is that fourth jhāna?
It is the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*). For, having stood upon that and having increased insight (*vipassanā*), the Blessed One gradually...
Some say that the Tathāgata attained the highest path (aggamagga) and thus became one who has "arisen" (jāta); however, this is not the primary meaning of the term *seyyā*.
Others, taking the statement that "the Blessed One passed away immediately after the fourth jhāna," claim that the mundane attainment of the fourth jhāna is the Tathāgata’s *seyyā*;
if that were so, it would follow that the Tathāgata’s *seyyā* occurs at the very moment of his final Nibbāna.
Furthermore, the Blessed One did not frequently dwell having attained the fourth jhāna; rather, it is the jhāna of the highest fruit (*aggaphala*) that is intended here by the term “fourth jhāna.

In this regard, just as for sentient beings sleep is characterized by lying down and occurs through a series of *bhavaṅga* consciousnesses—and that is their primary mode of existence, being the natural state since birth—so too is this case.

Thus, the fourth jhāna—the consummation of the Blessed One’s noble lineage, which is his predominant mode of conduct and constitutes the highest fruit—should be understood as the “Tathāgata’s posture.
By “lion’s posture,” he means the “best posture,” hence he says “the supreme posture. 426.
“Debt-free” means free from the roots of debt. “Of these” refers to those roots of debt. “Limit” means the remainder.
Cutting off the four postures by preventing their occurrence. "Afflicts" means oppresses.
"Pained" means one in whom suffering has arisen. "Little strength" refers to a mere measure of strength;

for this word *mattā* has the sense of "little," as in such expressions as "the relinquishing of a little pleasure," whereas the word *mattā* in the sense of "strength" is not a separate meaning. The rest [is as follows]: "For he, being released from that bond..."
This was said with reference to what should be stated as: "For one who attends [to the object], both of those arise," and so forth.

"In all instances" means in all instances remaining after those already mentioned. "He goes wherever he wishes" (*yenakāmagāmi*); this is a grammatical designation (*niddesa*) formed without eliding the nasal (*anunāsika*), meaning *yena-kāma-gāmi*.
One whose service (*bhujissa*)—that is, the application of oneself according to one's own pleasure—is desired here is a *bhujissa*, which is to say, a master (*sāmika*).
However, because it belongs to another, it is called "one's own" [in the sense of being under one's control].
Because it is difficult to cross, they cross over (*tārenti*) upon it; thus he says, "a long waterless road.
"He destroys" means he acts in such a way—by misusing the food and so forth—that nothing remains of the principal debt. In whom...

In the case of the basis for lust: that person, by means of that basis for lust—whether a man with respect to a woman, or a woman with respect to a man—should be regarded as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is like a debt, because it causes oppression.

"He does not find" means he does not know. "You should afflict" means you should cause an affliction to his state of ease; the meaning is "you should obstruct. Ill will (*byāpāda*) should be regarded as like a disease, because it is similar in its destruction of happiness.

It is "of manifold methods" because it is adorned with various causes and means, and because it possesses the diversity of the principles of the Dhamma, such as the aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination, and so forth.
"In the hearing of the Dhamma" means in the discourse on the Dhamma; for a discourse is called "hearing" in the sense that it is something to be heard.
Thus, herein virtue is analyzed, thus are the meditations and direct knowledges, and thus are insight, the path, and the fruits.
He does not know the beginning, middle, or end of that hearing of the Dhamma. "Having risen" means having concluded.
"Oh, the reason! refers to the reason taken up by way of the presentation of proofs in accordance with the respective propositions (*paṭiññā*) here and there.
"Oh, the simile! refers to the supporting examples and so forth, such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*byatireka*), which serve to establish that very reason.
Torpor and drowsiness (*thīnamiddha*) should be regarded as a prison, because they are an obstruction to the escape from suffering.

Since there is no hindrance of remorse (*kukkucca-nīvaraṇa*) that is devoid of restlessness (*uddhacca*), or since restlessness and remorse share the same function, nutriment, and opposite, he spoke the words beginning with "by one who is ignorant of what has been laid down in the Vinaya" while showing the object of remorse. For just as restlessness...
It causes the non-quiescence of the mind, and remorse does likewise. Just as thoughts of relatives and so forth are the nutriment for restlessness, so too are they for remorse.
And just as serenity is the antidote to restlessness, so too is it to remorse.
Restlessness and remorse should be regarded as slavery, because they bring about a state of lack of freedom.
"Uncertainty with sixteen bases has entered into uncertainty with eight bases," thus he said, "uncertainty regarding eight points.
"Being uncertain" means being in doubt. "Having resolved" means having gained conviction. "To grasp" means to comprehend the object of faith.
"Approaching" (*āsappana*) is approaching directly; "creeping around" (*parisappana*) is creeping all around.
By both phrases, he speaks of the very mode of non-desire of the mind.
That by which the mind does not plunge into the path leading to the secure state is "non-plunging" (*apariyogāhana*);
that phenomenon by virtue of which the mind becomes paralyzed through being apprehensive and suspicious is "paralysis" (*chambhitatta*). Thus he says: "of the mind..."
"...arising. "Like a road through a wilderness" means it should be regarded as a road through a dangerous wilderness because it is a cause for non-attainment.
"Debtless" (*aṇaṇo*) means there is no debt (*aṇa*) here;
the state of being so is "debtlessness" (*āṇaṇya*), which is the non-maintenance of any debt whatsoever. "One whose work is successful" (*samiddhakammanto*).
The term *palibodha* means that which obstructs or hinders; here, the letter *r* has been changed to *l*.

It refers to a state of non-freedom, and its root or cause is the "root of the obstacle" (*palibodhamūla*). "Having developed six things" means having generated and increased six qualities, such as the apprehension of the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*).
Furthermore, "having developed six things" also includes the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness (*mettānimitta*) and so forth.
It should be understood that "six things" are stated in each respective instance. "Abandons" means he abandons by way of suppression. Therefore he said:
"While being trained in the rules of conduct and so forth," and so on. "In another's property" means in an object belonging to another, or in another's domain.
For these five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed another's domain for a bhikkhu. The abandoning of sensual desire is like a state of debtlessness.

It is said [that the abandoning of ill-will is like health] because it brings about the absence of the basis for what is dear. The training rules, such as the *ācārapaññatti*, are those that ward off failure in conduct.

It is said [that the abandoning of sloth and torpor is like release from bondage] because it brings about a state of composure in body and mind, and because it brings about a state of restraint in the mind.
He spoke of the abandoning of restlessness and remorse as being like a slave, because it brings about the state of mastery over the mind.

"Like grass" means treating it as if it were grass; "disregarding" means not taking it into account. He spoke of the abandoning of doubt as being like a land of security, because it serves as the cause for right practice by virtue of being free from suspicion and apprehension.
427. That which is produced and cast into the womb is the *kara* (the source); that which is born from the *kara* is the *karaja*, namely, the physical origin derived from the mother and father.
The meaning is as follows: others say it is called "born of karma" (*karaja*) because it arises from the mother’s act of maintaining the body's form.

In either case, the term "body born of karma" (*karajakāya*) refers to the materiality of the four continuities (*catusantatirūpa*). It makes moist, thus it is "moistening" (*tinta*); what here is this state of being moistened? He says:
"it lubricates" (*sneheti*), meaning it causes nourishment through the lubrication of joy (*pītisneha*). Therefore he said: "the joy and happiness occurring everywhere."

"...makes. Here, by the fact that the entire physical body is suffused with sublime matter produced by rapture (*pīti*), the presence of the rapture and pleasure that produce it is shown to pervade everywhere.
The same method applies to "it permeates" (*parisandeti*) and so forth; for there too, "it flows all around, moistens, and lubricates" refers to the rapture and pleasure pervading everywhere.
The meaning should be understood according to the context through the passage beginning with "he makes," and so forth.

"He fills" means he fills this physical body (karajakāya) with rapture and pleasure, just as one fills a bellows with air. "He touches on all sides" means he touches this physical body with rapture and pleasure.
Regarding the term *sabbāvato*: the letter *a* has been changed to *ā*; thus, it means "possessing all parts. Therefore, he says, "possessing all constituent parts" (*sabbakoṭṭhāsavato*).
The meaning is: "one who possesses all things such as flesh and so forth. It is not called "unpervaded" because it is entirely permeated by the forms (rūpa) arisen from joy and happiness.
The construction is: "skilled in both making and joining, capable of bringing [them] together.
By means of the hand that forms a lump through the rubbing of bathing powders, the vessel should be pressed.
It is said, "it becomes [so]," meaning "it breaks for one who intends it. "Anugatā" means entered into. "Parigatā" means soaked through on all sides, everywhere.
Because of its state of being soaked, that which has an equal interior and exterior is called "santarabāhirā" (with interior and exterior).
"Sabbatthakameva" means in every respect. And it is not "dripping," because it is moistened with only a measured amount of water. And here, the bathing-powder ball...
The first-jhāna bliss should be seen as water that has soaked through the body born of kamma, becoming like water of a combined volume.
428. "Water welling up from below and rising" means water that rises after welling up from the bottom of the lake by way of a thick stream.
"Water welling up within" means [water] that wells up only inside the lake, not by way of a thick stream.
It is that which breaks forth from the openings of veins whose water has risen. "The path of arrival" refers to the route by which [the water] comes from rivers, lakes, caves, springs, and so forth.
429. It is called *uppalinī* because there are clusters of blue lotuses (*uppalagaccha*) here; it means water. This is the analysis of the term here;
for instance, in the world, one with red eyes is called "one with white-lotus eyes" (*puṇḍarīkakkha*). However, some say: "The red lotus is the *paduma*, and the white one is the *puṇḍarīka*."
They say: "The body born of kamma is like the blue lotus and other flowers; the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.
This meaning also should be understood as being clarified by the very extension [of the phrase] "by the previous method. 430.
"In the sense of being free from defilement" means by way of not being stained by dust, dirt, and so forth, that is, by its state of being unstained (*amalīnabhāvena*). Even though it is unstained...
It is said that "in the sense of luminosity" because some substrate has a luminous intrinsic nature. "Pervasion by temperature" means pervasion by warm temperature.
Since the physical body is touched by the bliss of jhāna everywhere, like a cloth touched by temperature, he says, "the physical body is like a cloth.
Therefore, the very point stated by the passage beginning with "like a cloth" is here given as the reason.
The meaning is that he touches [it] because the body born of kamma resembles a garment, and the bliss of the fourth jhāna resembles the pervasion of temperature.
Furthermore, because it possesses a peaceful nature and because knowledge is supreme here, equanimity is also included within bliss;
thus, the mention of "bliss" is made even in the case of the fourth jhāna. This is because of the statement: "He sits pervaded by purity and clarity."
The similarity of the fourth jhāna consciousness to a cloth has been stated.

With reference to the contact of the bhikkhu’s body by means of the material phenomena produced by the fourth jhāna, it was said: “That material phenomenon produced by it is like the pervasion of heat.
However, the meaning that the bhikkhu’s kamma-born body is like a man’s body was not included because it is obvious; or rather, it was indeed already included.
Because it is said: “Just as in some cases... [the body] becomes touched.
(431) Regarding the simile for the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*): this refers to the illustration shown for the knowledge of past lives.

The mention of performing work on that very day is for the purpose of showing that even for an ordinary person, such an event is generally evident. By mentioning only the three villages visited on that day, [it is implied that the rest is clear].

It should be understood that it is shown that through the great resolves (*mahābhinīhāra*), the deeds performed by others who have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) within the three realms of existence (*tīsu bhavesu*) are for the most part manifest. 432.
"Face-to-face doors" (*sammukhadvārā*) means doors facing one another. "Moving from one to another" (*aparāparaṃ sañcaranteti*) means according to their respective functions.

“Moving back and forth from here and there. Furthermore, “from this house... [etc. ...by way of entering”—this is stated by way of showing the range of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*).
“Standing between two houses” means standing in the middle of the alleyway that serves as the space directly facing the doors of two houses. For if one of those has a door facing east...
For another person facing west, standing in the middle of the street directly in front of him and facing either south or north,
those men entering or leaving would be clearly visible to that sighted man with ease; in the same way,
for one endowed with the knowledge of the divine eye, beings passing away and being reborn are clearly visible.

Just as that man is seen entering at one moment and seen exiting at another, so too for this person, it should be understood that there is a vision of passing away at one moment and a vision of being reborn at another.
The connection is made by supplying the words "clear to knowledge" (ñāṇassa pākaṭā). "Of that" refers to knowledge.
433. "The mountain peak is for the most part contracted and shriveled":
here, the summit of the mountain is called "the mountain contraction" (*pabbata-saṅkhepa*), or the area included within the mountain is the "mountain contraction.
"Untroubled" means free from turbidity. Since that lack of turbidity arises from the absence of mud, he says "free from mud" (*nikkaddama*). Even when [the waters] are standing still...
"Even when the cows are sitting. "Existing" means being available. The others—whether standing or sitting—are called "wandering" according to the convention of wandering together.
"Only while standing, never while wandering. "Both"—this refers to both the oyster-shell and the shoal of fish;
they are said to be "standing," but the intended meaning is that they are also "wandering. Or rather, what is the point of this?
Regarding "association," one should understand here that it refers to taking whatever is obtained.

For the construction should be made as follows: by way of the pebbles and gravel, [the text says] "standing"; and by way of the oysters, shells, and schools of fish, [it says] "both standing and moving.
434. *Bhikkhu*: one who has broken the defilements (*kilesa*) is a *bhikkhu*. For in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), he is one whose name is "ascetic" (*samaṇa*). In this regard:
One who has completely stilled all evils by means of the Noble Path is a *samaṇa*. Therefore it is said: "Because of having stilled evil.

The Perfectly Enlightened One is called *brahmā* in the sense of being supreme; that which comes from him is the Noble Path, and because he has known that path through the penetration of non-delusion, he is a *brāhmaṇa*.
For by virtue of possessing that [path], there is for him the state of having banished evils. Therefore it is said: "Because of having banished evil."
“A brahmin. One who has bathed with the water of the Noble Eightfold Path and washed away the defilements is a *nhātaka* (one who has bathed).
Because it has been penetrated by means of the realization of abandonment, it is said to be "gone beyond" (*gatatta*); therefore he said, "because it is known" (*viditattā*).

Because it has been completely suppressed within the continuum by means of abandonment through eradication, it is said to be "flowed out from" (*nissutatta*); therefore he said, "because it is struck down" (*apahatattā*), for the defilements have been destroyed by way of establishing a boundary.
The meaning is: because the defilements have been completely eradicated in every respect by means of the noble paths. Therefore he said, "because they are slain" (*hatattā*).

"Because they are far removed" (*ārakattā*) means because of their state of being well-abandoned and utterly separated. Therefore he said, "because they have become distant" (*dūrībhūtattā*). Both [terms] should be applied to both meanings:
one is "noble" (*ariya*) because the defilements are far removed, slain, and become distant; likewise, they "deserve" (*arahanti*). That which...
Herein, it has not been analyzed according to its meaning; that is easily understood because its meaning is plain.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahā-assapura-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Cūḷa-assapura-sutta*.

435. *Purimasadisameva* (just like the previous one): Having seen the reverence, esteem, and humble service shown by the inhabitants of Assapura toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [the Blessed One] spoke this sutta while enjoining the bhikkhus to honor those who provide almsfood.
Thus, it is exactly the same as what was stated regarding Mahāassapura in the previous sutta.
*Samaṇānaṃ anucchavikā*: suitable for recluses, appropriate for the state of being a recluse.
“The practice in conformity with recluses” means the practice that is favorable to the Noble Path, which is designated as the state of a recluse for recluses.
“These states” refers to these evil states mentioned in the text, such as covetousness, ill will, and so forth.
“Arising” means arising right now, let alone having been cultivated within the mental continuum. “In what is soiled” means in that which is impure and defiled. “Seized by stain” means...

*Gahitamale*: those whose stains have arisen. *Samaṇamala*: the stains of the ascetics, meaning the defilements of their state as ascetics. *Dussanti*: they become corrupted, fail, or perish. *Samaṇadosa*:
the faults of the ascetics, meaning that which corrupts their state as ascetics. *Kasaṭe*: in what is essence-less. *Nirojeti*: it renders powerless or devoid of energy. *Apāyā*:

because they have departed from security (*yata*) and happiness (*sukha*), they are called *apāya*; these are the states such as hell and so forth. They "deserve" (*arahanti*) that as their fruit, or that is their purpose (*payojana*).
"Leading to the states of woe" (*āpāyikā*). The "bases" (*ṭhānāni*) are covetousness and so forth; therefore he said, "to the state of woe," and so on.

Because they are conducive to feeling included within an unhappy destination by way of being its cause, they are called "producing an unhappy destination" (*duggativedaniyāni*). Hence it was said: "of the conditions for resultant feeling in an unhappy destination.
They move with sharpness like a *vekantaka* [thorn], having a core that pierces; "they move" (*ayanti*) means by means of the iron hook (*ayoghaṃsakena*). Of the *koñca* birds...
It is said that whatever is hard or sharp remains within the womb; for indeed, their excrement causes even bone and stone to melt away.

Therefore it is said: "making the *koñca* birds eat it. It is said that this iron powder burns with difficulty even by means of fire, but by the power of the medicine, it would burn easily. Therefore it is said: "well-trained..."
And smiths, having obtained much raw material for their handiwork, fashion it,” and so forth. It becomes extremely sharp;
they cut through any kind of iron bond as easily as if it were a piece of soft wood. Because it is stitched together with the skins of hares and wildcats, it is called a *saṅghāṭī*;
thus he said, “*Saṅghāṭiyā* means ‘of silk’ (*kosiyā*). It is completely covered (*pariyonaddha*).
“Covered all around” means concealed. “Entirely enveloped” means shut off from every side. (437) “Dust” is adventitious dust.
“Filth” is the salt, sweat, and other impurities arising on the body. One who has not removed this dust and filth by virtue of having undertaken a vow is a “dust-and-filth-wearer” (*rajojallika*);
it is to such a person that he refers when saying, “one who bears dust and filth. Water...
The meaning of "of one descending," and so forth, has already been stated in the commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.
Regarding the phrases "all this" and so on, the intended sense is that "all this" refers to the undertaking of vows.

Since all this has been spoken solely from the perspective of external systems (bāhirasamaya), therefore, "one who wears a saṅghāṭī" means one who wears a garment called a "saṅghāṭī" because it is stitched together from pieces of rags.
This is the meaning. For in the Pāḷi it is stated simply as "of one who wears a saṅghāṭi robe," not "of a bhikkhu. Therefore he said, "In this [case]," and so forth.
But why were only the undertaking of vows such as wearing a saṅghāṭi robe rejected by the Blessed One here?
This is an illustration of the method, because other practices, such as the five-fold heat and the vow of silence, are established by their very rejection. Others say:

But they say: "When it was said, 'Monks, I do not call one a recluse merely because he wears the outer robe (saṅghāṭi),' someone sitting there who held the views of another sect thought, 'Is he perhaps speaking of nakedness?
while others thought, 'Is he perhaps speaking of being covered in dust and dirt? Thus, according to the inclinations of those thinking various things,"

“The Blessed One rejected these very undertakings of vows here [in this life]. Regarding “one who has a *saṅghāṭi*”: it means one who possesses a *saṅghāṭi* by way of using it as an undergarment (*nivāsana*) or an upper robe (*pārupana*).
Therefore, he said, “a cloth that is a *saṅghāṭi*,” and so forth. Friends and others might make a *saṅghāṭi* for him according to his own preference;
later, when he has reached the age of discretion, they would encourage him toward the state of being a *saṅghāṭi*-wearer.
438. One sees oneself as purified because of the absence of the manifestation of covetousness and other such defilements.
However, one cannot say that one is "purified" in the sense of being completely severed from them by the Path.

"Gladness" (pāmojja) refers to fresh joy; for when one sees the purification of the mind through the suppression of the defilements by means of one's own right practice, gladness arises, which is a state of satisfaction.
Therefore he said, "the aspect of satisfaction. "Rapture" (pīti) refers to powerful rapture that brings about tranquility (passaddhi).
By the phrase "the mental body becomes tranquil," he speaks of both types of tranquility. "Experiences" (vediyati) means one feels or finds.
Now, because the mind has attained purification from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through that [rapture], he said, "it is as if it has reached absorption" (appanā). [This] arose elsewhere...

The phrase "by way of the connection" (*yathānusandhinā*) is stated because the teaching was concluded below by means of the opposites of the unwholesome qualities (*asaddhamma*), through the commonality of being high or low and the mere fact of having moved to another place.
In the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*, the Path is compared to a lotus pond, beginning with the words, "Just as, Sāriputta, there might be a lotus pond," and so forth, in the application of the simile.
This is because it is said: "This person has practiced in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has ascended that path, whereby there is the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

For just as men who have come from the eastern and other directions, upon reaching that lotus pond, become pure in body and free from feverish distress, even so those who have come from families such as the *khattiya*s and others [reach purity] through what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
By resorting to the Dhamma-vinaya, the teaching, they become pure in name-and-form and free from the fever of the defilements.
Therefore, because all defilements have been stilled (*samita*), one becomes a supreme ascetic (*paramattha-samaṇa*). The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷa-assapura-sutta* is completed.
The commentary on the Mahāyamaka-vagga is completed.
5. Cūḷayamaka-vagga 1.
Commentary on the Sāleyyaka-sutta.
439. "When a great crowd of people had gathered" means that a vast multitude had assembled;

some thinking, "We shall make the prince laugh by showing him amusing performances," and others thinking, "We shall watch that play. "Divine dance" (*devanaṭa*) refers to celestial music (*gandhabba*).
"Based on the words 'Is it well? and 'It is well'" refers to the exchange of questions and answers such as, "Is all well? and "Yes, all is well."
Because they spoke what was skillful from the very beginning, those people received the designation *kusala*.

Since the princes were the lords (*issara*) of those *kusala* people, they are called *Kosala*. They were born among the *Kosalas*. "Their dwelling"—all of this is according to the method already explained above.
Therefore he said: "That region is called Kosala."
Regarding the phrase "wandering on a journey," although it is a general term, because of the statement "with a great [retinue]... he entered that place," it is established as having a specific sense;
thus he says, "wandering on a journey without haste. "With a great [retinue]" means great both by greatness of virtue and by greatness of number.
For in that assembly of monks, some were endowed with virtue by way of the training in higher morality, and likewise some were endowed with virtue and concentration.
Some say that because of the greatness of his virtues—being endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom—that assembly of monks was great;

yet, without referring to that, he said "of a hundred" and so forth to show only the greatness of its number. It is called a *samosaraṇa* because people gather there (*samosaranti*) for the sake of their livelihood connected to another village;
it is a village, a residential village. "That" refers to the Sāla brahmin village. "Vihāra" refers to [the dwelling] of the Blessed One.
“Place of dwelling. “Therein” means in this Sāleyyaka Sutta. “Unspecified” means not restricted to such-and-such a monastery, mountain, or foot of a tree;
it is stated without specifying its particular form. “Therefore” means because it is unspecified.
Showing the meaning established by implication through a hypothetical assumption, he says, “there will be a grove of trees.”
The meaning is "it would certainly be.
He said, "They perceived... they knew," showing that "they perceived" means they perceived by way of hearing.
Because every sentence has an implicit emphasis as its result, he said, "merely for the purpose of completing the meter."
"Or it is a particle. By the phrase "in the sense of restriction," however, he shows that the word *kho* is included for the purpose of restricting the intended meaning.
When the word *assosuṃ* (they heard) is joined with the word *kho*, it becomes as if blossomed, adorned, and embellished;
it is truly "fulfilled. And by means of that, the preceding and following words become well-connected, which would not be the case if it were not included.

He said: "It is merely for the sake of completing the meter and for the smoothness of the phrasing (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*). The word *matta* has the sense of excluding other qualifications (*visesa-nivatti-attha*).
By this, he shows that it indicates nothing more than that; however, by the word *eva*, he shows the exclusivity of the smoothness of the phrasing.
Those born and raised in the hall (*sālā*) are the *Sāleyyakas*, just as there are the *Katteyyakas* and the *Ubbheyyakas*.
"Because evil has been stilled" means because evil has been completely, without remainder, and along with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*), stilled.
For in this way, the Blessed One’s stilling of evil is distinguished from the stilling of evil by outsiders, those free from passion, and those in training (*sekha*) and beyond training (*asekha*).

Since particles have many meanings, he said, "The particle *khalu* is used here in the sense of tradition," meaning it is a term for traditional recitation. "Mere address" refers to words of affectionate speech; [it is called such] because of being spoken with affection.
Here, it is [addressed] as "bho," or "āvuso," or "devānaṃ piyā. Regarding "by way of clan" (*gottavasena*):
here, that which protects is "clan" (*gotta*). For the designation and the cognition occurring as "Gotama" protect and preserve [the person] by virtue of having a single referential object;
thus it is the "Gotama clan" (*gotamagotta*). Just as cognition does not function without an object that serves as its referent, so too the designation [does not function without it].
Because it is that which constitutes the denotation, it is said that "it protects" (tāyati) or "guards" (rakkhati) those [members].

In its essential meaning, however, it should be understood as a common form belonging to that specific clan—one that has been handed down from the original progenitor of that clan and is shared by all members included within it.

It is a designation for a high-born family because it reveals a lineage of Kṣatriyas that is exalted and extensive. For [the term] originates from the Great King Mahā-Sammata, who was the very first of all Kṣatriyas.

From its foundation, the Sakyan royal family has been unsurpassed and most exalted. "By any loss" means it was never overcome or eclipsed by any kind of decline, such as the loss of kinsmen or the loss of wealth.
For it is well known in the world that at no time did such a loss ever occur to that family, and that at the time of his Great Departure, it was in a state of supreme prosperity.

"Renowned. The statement "gone forth from the Sakyan clan" is spoken to illustrate that the Blessed One went forth out of faith, because it demonstrates that he went forth having abandoned a vast circle of kinsmen and a great mass of wealth.
And here, by the word "ascetic" (*samaṇa*), the Blessed One’s state of being highly esteemed by discerning people is shown, because it illustrates his state of having stilled evil.
By the word "Gotama," there is the indication of his being of the most noble lineage as perceived by worldly people.
Regarding the term "abbhuggato" (eminent), here the prefix *abhi-* is used in the sense of describing a particular state (*itthambhūtākhyāna*).

Furthermore, because of its connection with that [prefix], the accusative form "bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ" is identical even when expressing the sense of a genitive (*sāmī*), since it indicates the connection with that particular state; thus, it is said to be "in the sense of describing a particular state."
Thus it was said. Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘of that venerable Gotama. *Kalyāṇa* means auspicious (*bhaddaka*). And its quality of being auspicious is due to its sublime object;
thus he said, “endowed with auspicious qualities. For here, “endowment” refers to having that as its object.
The same method applies here for the word *seṭṭha*, just as in the phrase, “the word ‘Bhagavā’ is the best. “Bhagavā...”
Because he proclaims and makes resound the qualities through the words beginning with "Arahant," it is called "fame" (*kitti*) as a sound (*saddo*); thus he says, "or fame itself" (*kittiyeva*).
For the word *sadda* is also a synonym for *kitti*, as in the passage: "The sages, possessed of virtue and asceticism, have a sublime reputation.

"A cry of praise" (*thutighoso*) means an utterance of eulogy. "Having overwhelmed" (*ajjhottharitvā*) means having overcome [all others] by way of the absence of opposites and by being unique, not shared by any other.

"Thus, the Blessed One": he who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the Lord of the World—who received the name "Blessed One" (bhagavā) for reasons such as his possessing good fortune;
he is the Blessed One. For "the Blessed One" is the designation of the Teacher's name.
For it has been said: “‘Bhagavā’—this is not a name given by his mother,” and so forth. But later, “Bhagavā” is indeed a praise of his qualities.

Thus, in order to show that those Buddha-qualities which are exceedingly renowned throughout the world including the devas have been analyzed in various ways by means of such terms as “Arahant” and so on, one should join the word *itipi* with each individual term; hence he said: “*Itipi*...”
“He is an Arahant, thus he is the Fully Self-Awakened One... [and so on] ...thus he is the Blessed One. Here, as in such passages as “Thus this is real;
thus this is true,” the word *iti* has the sense of an immediate and direct cause, while the word *pi* has the sense of inclusion, because it indicates the multiplicity of those qualities.
These are the grounds for perceiving those qualities for those of wise nature who are endowed with faith.
Showing that these [qualities] are indeed directly perceived, it says: “It means ‘by this and that reason,’ and so forth. From the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Of these” refers to the terms “arahant,” and so on. The detailed exposition of the meaning should be taken from that very work.
For that same reason, it is stated in its commentary: “He is an arahant because he is far away (*āraka*); he is an arahant because he is near (*āraka*).”

The meaning of such terms as "arahant" should be understood in detail through such passages as: "Because there is nothing remaining to be removed, and because he himself has removed [all defilements], there is for him no further rebirth among the destinations—that is, no going into seclusion—or, because he is worthy of praise, he is 'arahant'.
And on this subject, there are these verses:
“Those men who are of inferior aspiration do not practice rightly;
the Blessed One is far removed from them, and for that reason he is considered ‘Arahant.
Those who practice rightly, whose inclinations are well-guided—”
The Blessed One is near to them, and by that [nearness] he is the Arahant, the Victor.
Those of evil nature are called "arahā" because they must be shunned by the virtuous;
because he has utterly abandoned them, the Blessed One is considered an Arahant.
Those noble ones who have realized the true Dhamma and whose range is pure—the Lord is never separated from them;
for that reason, he is considered "Worthy" (Arahant).
Or else, it is because for him there is no going into seclusion at all within saṃsāra.
One for whom birth and death have been abandoned is considered an Arahant, a Sugata.
Since there is no one equal to him in virtues within the world including the devas,
he is therefore called "Arahant" because of his excellence, the supreme among bipeds.
Far from those of dull intellect, yet near to those who understand;
because of having thoroughly abandoned secrecy, because of being beyond the state of one who is not worthy,
and because of the absence of secrecy regarding states of existence— the Conqueror is praised as the Worthy One (Arahaṃ).
"Sundara" means beautiful. And that [beauty] is to be understood as bringing welfare and happiness to one who sees it; thus he said, "bringing welfare, bringing happiness.
In that context, "bringing welfare" means bringing the welfare associated with the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (paramattha).
"Bringing happiness" means bringing the various kinds of happiness included therein. "Tathārūpānaṃ" means of such a kind. By which [kinds...].

However, in order to show that the Blessed One, being endowed with these qualities, is in every respect utterly inspiring to the world of the fourfold measure, the passage beginning with "even by many" was stated.

Therein, by the phrase "one who has realized as it really is... [and is] an Arhat," he expresses the Blessed One’s quality of bringing forth confidence in those beings for whom the Dharma is the measure and those for whom austerity is the measure; by the other [phrase], he expresses it for the others.
Regarding the statement, "Even a mere sight is good," the story of the Kosiya bird should be told here.
Regarding the thought, "If we can obtain even a single word to hear, it will be even better," the story of the Maṇḍūka deva-putta should be told here.
This was stated by way of general rule—that the questions of householders come in this manner—because for the most part, householders [act in this way].
They ask in this manner. The same method applies to the questions of the homeless ones (*anagārika*). By the passage beginning with "As they were unable...
and ending with "...he answered," [the Buddha] shows the Teacher’s method of rebuking those brahmins and householders.
For, because they preferred brevity, he gave a concise teaching; not understanding the meaning through that, they requested an extensive teaching, and their preference for brevity was such.

Because that conceit [of being] "one who considers himself wise" has no footing in one who does not understand the meaning of what has been taught as it was explained, the Blessed One—having devised a method for subduing their conceit—answered the question in brief, and not because he failed to perceive the need for a full exposition.
Therefore he said, "Those who consider themselves wise," and so forth. Since you have made a request of me...
The intention is that he did not understand the meaning stated in brief.
In expressions such as “a singlefold basis for knowledge,” the word *vidha* has the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*);

and by applying a transposition of case and number, it is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the nominative case as “threefold. However, the actual meaning is expressed through the instrumental plural.
"It should be seen" is said [in the commentary] as "threefold, by way of three components. Alternatively, the word *vidha* has the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*).

Because it has the sense of manner, having brought about a unity by taking either the commonality of being unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct—which are found there—or the commonality of being door-related to the body, it is stated as "threefold.
However, when the distinction of the manners is taken into account, it is stated simply as "threefold" (*tividhā*).

It exists. Regarding the phrase "by means of the body" (*kāyena*): here, "body" (*kāya*) is intended as the *copana*-body (the functional body), and that serves as the door for unrighteous conduct (*adhammacariyā*), because such conduct does not occur without it.
Furthermore, in the expression "by means of the body," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

For although that intimation (*viññatti*) originates from volition (*cetanā*)—which is termed "unrighteous conduct"—it is not [included] among any of the twenty-four conditions (*paccaya*) mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna* in relation to volition.

It becomes a condition; however, since that volition designated as "bodily action" proceeds while thus occurring, it serves merely as a conventional designation for its cause, because it is to be characterized by way of that door.

Alternatively, "by means of the body-door" (*kāyadvārena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of a specific state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*), meaning "by means of the body acting as a door" or "by means of that which has become the body-door."

“Unrighteous conduct” (*adhammacariyā*) means that by means of this one practices what is unrighteous; it is volition proceeding in such a manner. Furthermore, “unrighteousness” (*adhamma*) should be understood as the preliminary effort (*payoga*) originating from that [volition].
“Dhammas” are those things not departed from the Dhamma; those which are not Dhammas are “unrighteous” (*adhamma*). Since it is both unrighteous and a form of conduct, it is “unrighteous conduct.
It is “equal” (*sama*) in the sense of being leveled against its opposite; or “equal” (*sama*) means similar, identical, or appropriate.

Good conduct (*sucarita*). That which is departed from evenness, or is contrary to it, is uneven (*visama*); it is misconduct (*duccarita*). That very same uneven practice is "uneven practice" (*visamacariyā*).

Regarding all the dark and bright passages—referring to all the dark passages that have come down through both the enumeration and the exposition, beginning with: "There are four kinds of unrighteous and uneven practice by way of speech"—[it is said]: "O householders, there are three kinds... [and so forth].

And in all instances where the term *sukka* (white) occurs, whether in the brief enumeration (*uddesa*) or the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), such as in the passage beginning, “Through the body there is conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, conduct in accordance with the Dhamma.
*Ruddo* means one who causes others—who are dependent on him—to weep (*rodeti*) and shed tears because of his cruel deeds;
thus he is *luddo*, having changed the letter *r* to *l*. He is *kakkhaḷo*, meaning cruel. He is *dāruṇo*, meaning harsh. He is *sāhasiko*, meaning one who acts with violence.
Even if they are not smeared [with blood], one who is habituated to killing others is called "red-handed" (*lohitapāṇi*).
Just as one who is habituated to giving is called "pure-handed" (*payatapāṇi*) even when his hands are unwashed for the sake of giving to others;

so too, "striking" (*pahāra*) refers merely to the act of dealing a blow, whereas "struck" (*hata*) refers to the killing of another through a fully developed strike. Demonstrating this, he said "in the struck," and so forth. Therein:
“Attached” means firmly adhered to or devoted to.
That by virtue of which there is the designation of ownership as “another’s” is that property. For what is taken in a general sense is specified by that very designation of ownership;
thus he says, “belonging to another. [The phrase is] “another’s wealth and requisites.”
Or rather, this is a single compound word meaning "whatever belongs to another," specifically the wealth or requisites of another.
"By those others" means by those to whom it belongs. He says, "Theft is the designation for the mind that steals," referring to that by virtue of which a person is called a "thief.
The meaning is: by way of what is reckoned as theft, and not by way of trust, temporary borrowing, and so forth.
The word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative (*avuttavikappa*). By this, it includes the state of being a renunciant (*pabbajita*) and so forth. "By this means" refers to such cases as:
when the mother is dead or lost, she whom the father protects is "protected by the father";

when both parents are absent, she whom the brother protects is "protected by the brother"—it is with reference to these and similar instances that he speaks. "Families of the same class" refers to the act of marriage.
Families that are similar. Or, by means of those such as kings who have established punishments for the purpose of seeing [the offense].

According to the definition of misconduct (*micchācāra*) stated in the *Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta* as: "The volition of transgressing against an unapproachable place, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of an unrighteous state. "For the sake of hands, feet, etc. means for the purpose of breaking [or injuring] the hands, feet, and so forth.
"For the sake of wealth" means for the purpose of obtaining wealth. "For the sake of birth" means for the purpose of [securing] a lineage.
“Gain” (lābha) means that food and clothing are obtained; thus it is gain. “Something” (kiñcikkha) refers to even a mere trifle of material goods.
Therefore he said, “or whatever,” and so forth. “Knowing indeed” means knowing that there is falsehood in that object.
“Bulges” (aṇḍakā) are called the swellings on a tree that resemble eggs; just as they are hard, uneven, and ill-formed, [so too is the offense].
In the same way, speech that proceeds by way of reviling and disparaging is called "eggs. Therefore he said, "Just as on a tree with defects," and so forth.
"Harsh" means rough; moreover, its harsh nature is due to being a cause for ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and because of that, it is putrid.
Therefore he said, "Just as if," and so forth. "Pungent" means undesirable. "Disagreeable" means not increasing the mind's delight.

For that very reason, it is a producer of faults and a cause for the arising of mental corruption. "In the vital organs" (*mammesu*) means in those things such as birth and so forth, which are like vital organs because suffering arises through their being struck.
"Causing attachment" means causing attachment for one who speaks thus with the underlying intention of saying "I say this," and not merely according to the literal phrasing.
It is "near to anger" because it serves as its cause. "By speech accompanied by hatred" (*sadosavācāya*).
The synonyms for "faulty speech" (*sadosavācā*) are given according to the fault that originates it.

"At the wrong time" (*akālena*) means at an inappropriate time. "Based on no reason" (*akāraṇanissitaṃ*) means fruitless; for a result is said to be "based on a reason" because of its invariable concomitance with it.

That which is based on no reason is fruitless; this is the meaning of "frivolous speech" (*sampha*). "One who speaks what is not the true nature" (*asabhāvavattā*) means one who speaks what is not as it really is.

"Connected with non-restraint and lack of discipline" means being devoid of restraint and discipline; it refers to one who speaks neither to themselves while listening nor to others in a way that brings about restraint and discipline.
"To deposit in the casket of the heart" means to deposit [the teaching] by causing it to enter the mind, as it is beneficial and conducive to welfare.
"At an improper time" means when speaking the Dhamma, [speaking] before or after the specific purpose for which the matter should have been spoken at a particular time.

It is the wrong time for him; he speaks at an improper time. "Without a source" (anapadesa) means devoid of a scriptural reference, such as saying, "The Blessed One spoke thus in such-and-such a sutta.
"Without a limit" (apariccheda) means lacking a boundary.
To show how speech might be without a limit, the words "or a sutta," and so forth, were spoken. "Upalabbha" means to pursue or to inquire.
"Only external talk" means: without touching upon the discourse that constitutes the very body of the Sutta or Jātaka in which it is placed, [discussing] only talk that lies outside of it.
"Having brought to completion" means having reached full growth. "The lineages and Jātakas" mean that they remain as roots that have grown and spread further. "Having brought forward" means:
from the Sutta in which it was placed, [bringing forward] something else by way of a relevant simile or illustrative material for the application.
"Having brought [the robe]," means: "In order to make it known that this was said for this purpose," he makes it known to whoever is able.
"To tell him" means: it is permissible for such a preacher of the Dhamma to speak extensively. "Not based on the meaning" means:
not conducive to the welfare of oneself or others.
Covetousness generally occurs by way of seeing what belongs to others; thus it is said, "he looks with covetousness.

Or, while coveting, he covets the object of his covetousness as if seeing it directly before him, even though it is situated somewhere else; thus it is said, "he looks with covetousness. This is the classification of the path of action (*kammappatha*).
It does not exist as a full course of action; it is merely greed itself, because it does not proceed to its completion through the process of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).

However, in order to show how there is a breach of the path of action, the passage beginning with "But when... was stated. "Dedicates" means that one grasps [the object] as being one's own property and directs it toward that end.
"With a corrupted mind" means a mind brought to ruin by ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Therefore he said: "with a mind that has become putrid. Ill-will...
For poison, like [blood], produces putrefaction in the blood-mind.

"One whose mental intention is corrupted by hatred" means one whose mental intention is defiled by poison, such as the irritation caused by ghee and so forth. "Let them be slain" means let them be killed.
"Let them meet with execution" means let them meet with death. "Or let them not even exist" means let them cease to be in every way. Therefore he said: "Let there not be even anything at all."
The meaning is: "May they reach complete destruction. "By the mere thought 'may they be slain,' etc. means by the very thought of their total destruction.

"One of wrong view" means one whose view has arisen through improper reflection (*ayoniso*). And since such a person holds a view that is the absolute opposite of what is wholesome, he is called "one who sees what is unwholesome.
"One of perverted vision" means one who grasps things in a way that is contrary to the true nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*). "There is no giving," etc. [is said].
He says, "He speaks with reference to the absence of fruit for what has been given," because giving was mentioned under the heading of "things to be given.
But how does he reject the gift of material things such as food? This same method applies to the terms "sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) and "offered" (*huta*).
A "great sacrifice" (*mahāyāga*) is a great gift common to all. "Hospitality" (*paheṇaka-sakkāra*) is the honor that should be rendered to guests. "Fruit" (*phala*)...
There is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*nissandaphala*). "Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to a similar fruit.
"For one staying in the next world, this world does not exist" means that for one staying in the next world, this world obtainable through karma does not exist.
"For one staying in this world, the next world does not exist" means that for one staying in this world, the next world obtainable through karma does not exist. He states the reason for this:

“All are cut off right there, right then. These beings, wherever they abide—whether in various states of existence (*bhava*), modes of birth (*yoni*), or destinies (*gati*)—are cut off right there; they perish by way of the cessation of arising and passing away.
“By way of the absence of fruit” means by way of the absence of the fruit of either proper or improper conduct toward one’s mother and father: “There is no mother, there is no...
When he says, "There is no father," it is not because there is no mother or father, nor because of the absence of right or wrong conduct toward them, for they are directly evident in the world.
He said, "There are no spontaneously born beings," in order to show that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble;
it is not preceded by passing away and coming back. Thus he said: "Having passed away..."
"He says that there are no beings who are reborn. A true ascetic, knowing things as they really are, ought to be restrained without speaking anything to anyone;
otherwise, it would be mere boasting. What can one person do for another?
Likewise, there is no opportunity at all for achieving anything for oneself, since everything perishes right where it is.
He said: “Those who... [as before]... proclaim this. “To this extent” means by way of the designation beginning with “there is no giving,” and so forth.
“Having ten bases” (*dasavatthukā*): that which has ten bases (*vatthu*)—namely, ten things—that are to be rejected, is “having ten bases.
441. Non-covetousness and the others have their meaning already explained below, and thus their meaning is self-evident.
442. One who goes together or moves along with others is a *sahabya*; one who acts in concert is a *sahavattanaka*. The state of being such is *sahabyatā*, meaning "acting together. Thus it is said:
"one would attain the state of being together" (*sahabhāvaṃ upagaccheyya*). A collection or assembly of Brahmas is the *brahmakāya*;
because they are included within that [assembly], they have gone there, and are thus called *brahmakāyikā*. Granted, this should indeed be the designation for the entire class of Brahmas.

However, because the second jhāna level and those above it have already been mentioned by the phrase beginning with “the Ābhā [devas],” he says, “of the Brahmakāyika devas,” meaning the devas of the first jhāna level, according to the maxim of “the cow and the ox” (where the specific is included in the general).
There are no separate devas named “Ābhā”; rather, they are grouped together as one under the common characteristic of possessing radiance (*ābhāva*), namely the Parittābhā and the others.
Taking this as it occurs [in the texts], this is a designation, namely "light" (*ābhā*), just as [the terms] "Brahmakāyika" [are used for] the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities.
Furthermore, by the word "etc. in the phrase "of the Parittābhā, etc.," it includes the following canonical passage: "of the Appamāṇābhā deities" and "of the Ābhassara deities.
"Not taking them together" means either as "light" (*ābhā*) or as "unity of body and diversity of perception" (*ekattakāya-nānattasaññī*).

Or not taking them as a single unit. "Of those very ones" means of the very deities mentioned as "radiant. "Grasping by way of division" refers to the inclusion of the Parittābha and other groups by way of showing that the cause is differentiated into the divisions of inferior and so forth.

Thus, having shown the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), the Blessed One [taught] the practice of Dhamma, the practice of equanimity, the path leading to a happy destination based on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-nissita*), and [the path] based on the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa-nissita*).

Having established the practice leading to the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayagāmipaṭipadā*) and having demonstrated the destruction of the taints through the shattering of the three realms of existence, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
"Standing here" means standing in this exposition of the practice of Dharma and the practice of equanimity.

"The twenty-six divine worlds are to be combined" means that all twenty-six divine worlds are to be gathered together. "Twenty Brahma-worlds" refers to them according to the categories included within their respective realms of existence.
The meaning is: twenty Brahma-worlds, twenty Brahma-classes. By the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*):

the arising [of these realms] is shown by means of the ten courses of wholesome action as appropriate—both as those that serve as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for karma and as those that are merely decisive supports.

Of the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*): of the three types of sense-sphere good conduct (*kāmāvacara-sucarita*). And here, the inclusion of the "sense-sphere" is with reference to mental good conduct.
“By the result itself” (vipākeneva) means that its arising occurs through the very production of the result, and not merely by way of being a decisive support (upanissaya).
In order to explain the meaning stated as “by way of decisive support,” it was said: “The ten courses of wholesome action,” and so forth.
In the phrases “having developed the second [jhāna], etc.,” the word “established in virtue” (sīle patiṭṭhāya) should also be brought forward and connected. Why?

Now, although it is stated here [in the *Visuddhimagga*] by way of "proximate cause" (*upanissaya*), does not the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*—in such passages as, "By means of the first jhāna, the abandoning of the hindrances is virtue;
abstention is virtue; volition is virtue; restraint is virtue;
non-transgression is virtue"—and so forth, set forth virtue in all the jhānas? By way of that [virtue], even the higher deva-worlds...

Is it to be said that [the path] arises as a result of kamma-vipāka? No; because it is taught for the sake of full understanding (*pariññā*), and its being taught for the sake of full understanding has already been demonstrated in the *Visuddhimagga* by such passages as "where there is abandoning" and so forth.

For likewise here too, in the passage beginning "The ten courses of wholesome action are indeed virtue" (*sīla*), the fact that virtue is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for existence in the realms of form and the formless is clearly elucidated.

It is not because it has not been produced. But why, when classifying the specific types of existence (*bhava*) according to the practice of Dharma characterized by development (*bhāvanā*), is the non-percipient existence (*asaññabhava*) not included?

To this he says: "But the non-percipient existence... is not specified. For outsiders, due to their lack of vision of things as they truly are, imagine the non-percipient existence to be liberation from existence;
having developed the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) leading to that state, they are reborn among the non-percipient beings.
This is the summary here; however, whatever remains to be said should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā* and its commentary.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* on the commentary to the *Sāleyyaka-sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the Verañjakasutta 444.

*Verañjavāsino* means "inhabitants of the village of Verañja. Some, however, state that the meaning is "those who dwell in various kingdoms (*vividha-raṭṭha-vāsino verañjakā*)," and according to their opinion, the text should read "*verajjakā*. *Aniyamita-kiccena* means "with an unspecified purpose."
“By this name”—it is not by such a restricted function [that the distinction is made]. This is the distinction:
he shows that this is the distinction in the method of teaching between these two suttas, one based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) and the other based on the phenomenon (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*);

however, the meaning and the underlying method of teaching are undifferentiated, like gold that has been melted down. But why does the Blessed One teach a discourse based on the person in some instances?
Is it sometimes an exposition based on the Dhamma? Yes, due to the elegance of the teaching and the disposition of those to be trained.

For the Blessed Buddhas have attained such pedagogical skill that they teach the Dhamma by sometimes adopting an exposition based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) and sometimes an exposition based on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), according to their preference.
However, for those to be trained who have not yet entered the sequence of the Dispensation, they provide an exposition based on the person.

They teach. For those who have entered [the stream], there is the teaching based on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). Those [teachings] concerning conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) are based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), while the other is based on ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).
The former is conducive to compassion (*karuṇā*), while the latter is conducive to wisdom (*paññā*). Or else, the former is for those of the lineage of faith-followers (*saddhānusāri-gotta*);

for they take the person as their measure. The latter is for those of the lineage of Dhamma-followers (*dhammānusāri*). Or [it is for] those whose conduct is dominated by faith (*saddhācarita*), who are masters of the world (*lokādhipati*).
By way of the person’s temperament, it is expressed in terms of the person; by way of those whose dominant influence is wisdom, it is expressed in terms of the Dhamma.

Furthermore, the former are of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), while the latter are of definitive meaning (*nītattha*). Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, having considered various specific circumstances, teaches a twofold teaching in each respective instance.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta is completed.
3. Commentary on the Mahāvedalla Sutta 449.
*Gārava* is the state of being weighty; it is the quality of being held in high esteem, like a stone parasol. One who possesses such esteem is "one who has reverence" (*sagāravo*).
"Patissava" is the act of listening with respect when something is said by a venerable person; "sappatissava" means together with such listening.

It refers to any act of showing respect that consists of, or is similar to, that listening. The phrase "sagāravasappatissavacanaṃ" means the speech of one who possesses both reverence (*gārava*) and respectful listening (*sappatissava*).
Alternatively, *gārava* is the state of showing respect; thus, the speech of one who possesses such reverence and respectful listening is "sagāravasappatissavacanaṃ. By this—

This shows that such speech proceeds from one who possesses reverence by their very nature. Elsewhere, the word *du-* also has the sense of censure, as in expressions like "suffering" (*dukkha*) or "a bad son" (*dupputta*);
however, in this context, that sense is not possible because there is an absence of corrupted wisdom.
Thus he says, "there is no such thing as 'corrupted' (*duṭṭha*) wisdom. In cases such as "immoral" (*dussīla*), it has the sense of non-existence.
Regarding the word *du*, it is said: "The meaning is 'one of little wisdom' or 'one devoid of wisdom. Regarding the word *kittakena*: by what measure?
Since that measure serves to delimit the object to be measured, and since the particle *nu* indicates a question, one says:
"'Kittāvatā nu kho' is a question concerning the delimitation of the cause. [And: "By how much, indeed..."
The meaning is: "It is said thus. By the phrase "an inquiry into the delimitation of causes," the general nature of the inquiry "to what extent" is shown, but not its specific nature;

therefore, in order to make known the specific character of that inquiry, [the author] shows all the inquiries found in the *Mahāniddesa* by way of extracting their meanings, beginning with "And as for inquiries... [He then says: "That which has not been seen..."

That by which one illuminates what has not yet been seen is "illumination of the unseen" (*adiṭṭhajotanā*); this is a question. "Corroboration of what has been seen" (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanā*) is the making of a determination by means of discussion.
That by which doubt is cut off is "doubt-remover" (*vimaticchedanā*). A question for the sake of consent is a "question for consent" (*anumatipucchā*).
For in a question such as "What do you think, monks?", consent is being asked by way of "Is it your consent? (i.e., do you agree?).
