A question asked out of a desire to explain is a "question asked with a desire to explain.
A "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) is any essential nature that one wishes to know. "Unknown" (*aññāta*) refers to the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge.

"Unseen" (*adiṭṭha*) refers to the state of not having been seen as if by direct perception through that which constitutes seeing. "Unmeasured" (*atulita*) refers to [the state of] not having been measured [with the thought], "This is so much."
"Untested" means not having been weighed by that which serves as a scale. "Unexamined" means not having reached the completion of the cognitive act through that which serves as an investigation.
"Unclear" means the state of knowledge being unmanifest. "Unclarified" means the state of not having been made manifest by knowledge.
Here, the question intended is one for the purpose of correlating what has already been seen, not for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen or for cutting off doubt.
To explain how this meaning is to be understood, he says, “The Elder,” and so forth. “Deciding for himself” means deciding specifically upon the meaning of those questions by himself alone.
“This sutta” refers to this sutta adorned with twenty-five questions;
it does not mean that he brought it to its conclusion in its entirety by himself. “Having himself raised the question, himself...”
In the phrase "one who decides," the author says "some indeed" and so forth to show that there are four permutations (*catukkoṭika*).
"Is able only to formulate a question" means he knows only the method of questioning. "Is not able to decide" means he is unable to reach a conclusion;
the meaning is that he does not know the method of answering. "A point of distinction" means a position unlike others.
"Equal to the Elder" means there is no disciple equal to the Elder.
"Having compared" means having joined together or made equal; the meaning is that he did not deviate from the way in which omniscient knowledge functions therein.
"Sporting" means performing a graceful play (*līḷā*). [This was said] because of his attainment of the preeminent state among those who discourse on the Dhamma.
Therein, with the grace of a Buddha, as if through unimpeded knowledge, he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma while guiding the four assemblies.
"Without deviating this way or that" means without deviating even slightly from the path of the discourse as it was mastered, but rather according to the very order in which it was mastered.
Hence he said, "the tip of a staff," and so forth. "A single footpath" means a space just sufficient for the placement of a single footstep.

"Daṇḍakasetu" means a bridge made of a single row of pillars. By bringing forward the textual passages from below and above, one arranges the Buddha’s word contained in the Three Piṭakas in ascending and descending order.

Having set down a verse or a textual passage similar to the Jātassara lake, one brings forward various similes and reasons therein, and by means of those textual passages, one awakens and causes them to arise.
It was said: "As if causing five-colored flowers to bloom in a lake, or as if lighting a thousand lamps on the summit of Mount Sineru.
Regarding the phrase "in a single lifting of a foot" (*ekapaduddhāre*): it means at the moment of lifting a single foot. By way of words (*pada*), there are six million words;
by way of verses (*gāthā*), there are fifteen thousand verses. "As if drawing them up and taking them" means not plucking the flowers individually.
It is like one who, having pulled together a garland of flowers, gathers them all in one place; therefore he said, "all at once.
"Of those possessed of movement" means those endowed with an eminent course of knowledge. "Of those possessed of steadfastness" means those endowed with the power of retention.
"Excelling in infinite methods" refers to the infinite variety [of teachings] by way of dependent origination, the arisen, the spoken meaning, Nibbāna, fruition, functional states, and so forth.
It has been increased and accumulated through endless methods regarding the engagement with sense objects. The construction [of the simile] is:
"like a boat placed at a ford for those seeking to cross the four floods. He speaks of the "chariot of thoroughbred horses yoked in a thousand" with reference to the Vejayanta chariot.
Since it was stated in the question using the reduplication "one of dull wisdom, one of dull wisdom" according to the method of desiring an answer, therefore—
The General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), answering the matter asked, spoke using a reduplication—“he does not understand, he does not understand”—in accordance with the nature of the question.
Therein, showing that the word *iti* has the sense of a reason, he said: “Because he does not understand, therefore he is called one of dull wisdom.
“This is suffering”: this refers to the five aggregates of clinging, which are the Noble Truth of Suffering.
And that, in brief, is just this much: deformation, feeling, perceiving, volitional formation, and cognizing.
Beyond this, there is no class of phenomena whatsoever called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Thus, by means of the wisdom of the Noble Path, one should see it as it truly is, according to its essential characteristic and the sequence of its occurrence, and by way of the characteristics of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changeability.
One does not understand it. When the remaining conditions come together, it arises and originates;
since this is the origin by way of the occurrence of saṃsāra, it is said to be “that which brings about the suffering of occurrence,” meaning it is the producer of the truth of suffering.

“By way of its specific characteristic according to reality” means both by way of its function of causing non-interruption as it truly is, and by way of its characteristics of aggregation, source, conjunction, and obstruction.
"Having reached this state" means by reason of this cause for the non-occurrence [of the defilements]. "Ceases" means it ceases by way of non-arising cessation;

therefore he said, "the non-occurrence of both. "By way of the characteristic of its own true nature" means by way of its characteristic as the deathless essence exactly as it is, and by way of its characteristics as escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless. "This is the path" means this...

It is called "the way" (*paṭipadā*) because one proceeds by means of it, beginning with right view and characterized by the convergence [of the factors]. It "goes toward the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodha*);
that is, it proceeds by way of the clear realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering.

"By way of the characteristic of the essential nature as it truly is" means by way of the essential nature of bringing about the abandonment of defilements exactly as they are, and by way of the characteristic of having the vision of the cause of deliverance as its dominant influence (*adhipateyya*).

And he does not understand. "In the subsequent section" means in the second section. "By this same method" means by the method stated in the first section, such as "This is suffering; this much is suffering," and so forth.
For there, because it is a description of one lacking wisdom (*duppañña*), the teaching comes down by way of the negation of understanding;
here, because it is a description of one possessing wisdom (*paññavant*), it is by way of understanding—this alone is the distinction. "In this" refers to the second section.
"From hearing" means he acquires the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from hearing it. For the acquisition of its meaning occurs by way of hearing the text.

The passage beginning with "setting aside craving" is an illustration of the manner of that acquisition. "He applies himself" means he applies himself by way of the application of insight (*vipassanā*);
he establishes the meditation subject of insight. "He does not turn away" means there is no application of intent toward turning away (*vivaṭṭa*).
It exists because it is not its object.
"This one" refers to the practitioner whose meditation subject is the Four Noble Truths. "The five aggregates" means the five aggregates of clinging.

Although the application of insight (*vipassanā-abhinivesa*) is manifold—being categorized by way of the aggregates, the eye and so forth, and feeling and so forth—it is easy to perform and easy to understand; therefore, that [application] is presented by way of the four elements.
To show this, he said, "having descended by way of the meditation subject of the elements.

"He defines 'form'" means that he delimits it without confusion as "form" in the sense of being subject to change (ruppana). "Having that as their object" means those [mental states] that proceed taking that form as their object.
"He defines 'name'" means that he defines the tetrad beginning with feeling as "name" in the sense of bending (namana). Like one splitting a twin palm tree trunk...

Having split them apart like a pair of twins, one defines, delimits, and discerns name-and-form (nāmarūpa), thinking: "These two phenomena alone exist—namely, the formless and the form; herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self. To this extent, purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) has been shown.
Furthermore, this name-and-form is not without cause, because it does not exist everywhere, at all times, or in every respect.
Therefore, it is with cause. By what kind of cause? Not by an unequal cause such as a Creator God (Issara) and so forth.
Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*. Because it has a cause, it is "with condition" (*sapaccaya*).

"Ignorance and so forth" refers to ignorance, craving, clinging, the nutriment of kamma, and so on. "In this way" means in the manner stated by the passage beginning with "But that [is] this... and so forth.
Having defined, delimited, and discerned both the conditions, beginning with ignorance, and the conditionally arisen phenomena, beginning with material form and feeling.
For this has been said: "With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of material form; with the arising of craving there is the arising of material form.
Up to this point, he demonstrates the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi*).
"Having arisen" means having arisen through the concurrence of causes and conditions. "In the sense of non-existence" means in the sense of perishing immediately thereafter.
"Impermanent" means impermanent and unstable. "He attributes the characteristic of impermanence" means he ascribes the universal characteristic known as impermanence to those five aggregates.
"Thereafter" means after the attribution of the characteristic of impermanence, or from that state of impermanence itself.
"By way of being oppressed by rise and fall" means that they are painful, undesirable, or suffering because of the cause of being repeatedly oppressed moment by moment through arising and ceasing.
"By way of not being subject to mastery" means by way of not being subject to the mastery of anyone.
"Non-self" (anattā) means that it is not itself a self, nor does it have any self belonging to it; thus it is non-self. "Having applied the three characteristics" means...
Thus, having attributed the threefold common characteristic to the five aggregates— due to impermanence being the state of suffering, and suffering being the state of non-self—
one who "comprehends" (sammasanto) means one who, by the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall, abandons the defilements of insight that have arisen,
distinguishes between what is the path and what is not the path, and comprehends formations through the sequence of insight beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall.
Immediately after the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), one attains the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga).
"By a single penetration" means by penetrating with a single knowledge alone.

Penetration (paṭivedha) is the piercing through, characterized by moving without attachment toward the object due to the absence of resistance. Full realization (abhisamaya) is the awakening characterized by attainment without missing the mark.

“Penetration by full understanding” (*pariññā-paṭivedha*) is the penetration consisting in knowing according to reality, having delimited [suffering] thus: “This is suffering; this is the extent of suffering; there is nothing beyond this,” in the manner already described.

And this is stated with reference to its occurrence such that, once knowledge has arisen, there is no longer any delusion regarding the specific nature and other characteristics of suffering; however, it does not refer to the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Because it proceeds by way of [the formula] beginning with “This is suffering. Therefore he said, “And at that moment,” and so forth.

Abandoning (*pahāna*) is the excellent (*pakaṭṭha*) act of relinquishing, casting off, or cutting off, because that which has been abandoned need not be abandoned again. Abandonment-penetration (*pahāna-paṭivedha*) is penetration (*paṭivedha*) in the sense of abandoning, according to the method already stated.
This too [is a factor] by which, when a defilement is not yet abandoned, the cultivation of the path does not [proceed].

It must be so; and it is said thus because, in the absence of the cultivation of the path, when one strikes down and brings about the state of non-arising for whatever [defilement] might arise, there is no obstruction to the occurrence of knowledge, owing to its unimpeded movement.
Realization (*sacchikiriyā*) means making directly evident; it is the taking of an object in its own form, having abandoned hearsay, modes of expression, discursive thought, and so forth.
“‘This is it’ is grasping [the object] according to its actual nature; that very same [grasping], by the method already described, is penetration as realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha).

This too is spoken of in this way because, by cutting off whatever obscuration prevents knowledge from being able to take cessation as its object, that [knowledge] proceeds having clearly manifested its own true form.”

Development (bhāvanā) means both arousing and increasing. In this context, development in the sense of arousing occurs in the first path; in the sense of increasing, it occurs in the second and subsequent paths;
or alternatively, both meanings should be understood to apply to both.

For even the first path proceeds by increasing—according to its specific requirements—the knowledge of emergence, the knowledge of the course, the full understanding, and so forth; thus, it is also development in the sense of increasing therein.

"Bhāvanā" can indeed be understood. In the second and subsequent [moments] as well, it is "development" (bhāvanā) in the sense of producing [the path] by means of abandoning defilements not yet abandoned and by accomplishing another person; that very same thing, according to the method already stated, is "penetration" (paṭivedha), thus it is "penetration-by-development" (bhāvanā-paṭivedha).
This too is such that, once knowledge has occurred, there is subsequently no delusion regarding the specific nature of the path-factors.
This is said with reference to the process [of realization]. Let alone the path-phenomena as they have been attained;

even while remaining in the fruits as they occur, this person remains free from delusion, just as when the true phenomena (sacca-dhamma) were being attained—even though he is still a trainee (sekha). Therefore it is said:
"He has seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma. And as for his phenomena...

For those [arahants], once they have taken as their object the True Dhamma as it has been realized, there subsequently arise, from the path-series onwards, the reviewing knowledges (*paccavekkhaṇā*) of the paths, fruits, the abandoned defilements, the remaining defilements, and Nibbāna.
For the phenomena of the Truth of Suffering consist of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth.

And this explanation of the meaning should also be clarified in relation to such passages as "by the clear comprehension of full understanding" (*pariññābhisamaya*). "By way of function" means by way of non-delusion. "By way of having cessation as its object" means...

Here, in the phrase "also by way of the object" (*ārammaṇatopi*), the word "also" (*pi*) should be understood as being elided; for penetration without delusion is obtainable even regarding cessation (*nirodha*).
"Of this" refers to the person who takes the four truths as his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Wise" (*paññavā*) is stated because it is intended here in its primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) of possessing wisdom. "From the text" (*pāḷito*) means from the Dhamma.

"From the commentary" (*aṭṭhatoti*) means from the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "From the connection" (*anusandhitoti*) means from the respective connection in each respective sutta. "From the sequence of before and after" (*pubbāparatoti*) means from the linking of what follows with what precedes.
Furthermore, the sequence of before and after here should be understood according to the order of the recitation (*saṅgītikkamena*).

Alternatively, it is because the latter portion is linked with the former portion within each specific teaching itself. "One whose temperament is consciousness" (*viññāṇacarito*) means one whose temperament is characterized by cognizing or investigating.

Because of the abundance of investigation and conduct within the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas, one cannot be called "possessed of wisdom" (paññavā), owing to the absence of the wisdom that has entered the Path.

"Arahantship this very day"—the intention is that it is limited and too quick. He belongs to the side of those possessed of wisdom because of the presence of the terminology relating to the trainee (sekha).
However, in the Sutta, only penetration is mentioned, as it is presented by way of the clear realization of the Truths.
"Esā" refers to the noble person (ariyapuggala) mentioned in the preceding [verse]. "The mind that performs the action" means the mind that brings about the action of cultivation (bhāvanākamma).
"It cognizes even pleasant feeling": who feels? Whose is the feeling? For what reason is there feeling?

By way of apprehending the non-existence of even that [feeler], one [contemplates] pleasant feeling according to its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), its arising (samudaya), its passing away (atthaṅgama), its gratification (assāda), and its danger (ādīnava).
And by discerning and grasping [feeling] as it truly is, one is said to "know pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
Since the term "foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna) characterizes the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, its meaning should be understood through that;
therefore, its meaning should also be understood in the commentary upon it according to the stated method. And this is indeed so.
Consciousness cognizes an object other than feeling as well;

however, because in the preceding section insight was demonstrated by way of the material form (rūpa), it is here demonstrated by way of the immaterial (arūpa) with the words, "It cognizes 'it is pleasant,'" and so forth, either to show this or according to the intention of the questioner.
"Conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭhā) means associated (sampayuttā). Therefore he said: "In the sense of union, by way of the characteristics of simultaneous arising and so on. "Disjoined" (visaṃsaṭṭhā) means...
They are dissociated. "Having broken" means having destroyed by seeing [them] as belonging to a different plane, or having completely shattered them.
"He asks about the state of being associated" means he asks about the state of association of the five sense-consciousnesses included within that arising of consciousness.
If this is so, how is there an occasion for the question, given that there is no possibility of even suspecting a state of non-association?

No, because a state of being mixed and conjoined is found among the path-wisdom and path-consciousness, as well as the insight-wisdom and insight-consciousness, occurring within the same moment of consciousness (*cittuppāda*).

"Having separated" means having distinguished them from one another. The statement "it is not possible to show a difference" is said solely with reference to their state of being conjoined, and not to a difference in their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
However, their distinction by way of difference in intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is indeed evident. Therefore, he said:
"Either by way of object (ārammaṇa), or by way of basis (vatthu), or by way of arising (uppāda), or by way of cessation (nirodha).

Now, in order to show that very same difference in intrinsic nature more clearly through the distinction of their respective domains (visaya), he stated: "But of each of those," and so forth. "Domain" (visaya) means the place of occurrence, the sphere of mastery.
By this [term], it is stated that both consciousness and wisdom act as forerunners in various contexts.
Granted, insight (vipassanā) performs its function only by means of wisdom, and the path (magga) is never alone but always accompanied by consciousness;
nevertheless, among mundane phenomena, consciousness is predominant because it functions there with the character of a leader.
For it is said that he is the "king presiding over the six gates"; likewise, among supramundane states, wisdom is preeminent because the destruction of opposing factors depends specifically upon it.

For this reason, right view alone is taken first among the factors of the Path. And this is the distinction in their mode of occurrence according to their respective objects; such also is the method of their presentation.
He said, "The Fully Enlightened One too," and so forth, to demonstrate that this was shown not only by the elders but also by the Blessed One himself.
Where wisdom is not applicable, there is no need to inquire about the mind, as in such cases as, "Bhikkhu, with what state of mind are you [speaking]?
However, where wisdom is applicable, there too the manifestation occurs by way of the mind.
For example: “He steadies the mind internally, settles it, unifies it, and concentrates it, at whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen,” and so forth.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, in order to show exhortation by way of contrast—by way of the mind regarding mundane phenomena and by way of wisdom regarding supramundane phenomena—it asks: “Which...?”
“Those bhikkhus have attained wisdom,” and so forth, is what was said. It should be understood that this was stated by way of the majority.
For in some instances, even mundane states are designated by way of wisdom—as in such passages as:

“For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire still occur; this is wisdom partaking of decline,” and so on. [They are also designated] by way of perception.
—“In such passages as ‘the perception of a bloated corpse’ or ‘the remaining perceptions of the material and immaterial,’ are these states identical in meaning or different in meaning?
Likewise, even supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are sometimes designated by way of the term “consciousness” (citta), as in:
“At whatever time one develops supramundane consciousness”; and likewise by way of contact (phassa) and so forth, as in: “At whatever time one develops supramundane contact...”
In such passages as, “He develops feeling, perception, and volition,” and so forth.

Regarding the four factors of stream-entry: these are association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—these being the four causes for the path of stream-entry.
Granted that other mental states such as mindfulness and so forth are also desirable when these [factors] are present.
Because they cannot exist without those [other factors], nevertheless, it should be understood that faith (saddhā) is particularly effective in performing its function here.
For it is faith alone that attends upon the virtuous person, hears the true Dhamma, applies wise attention, and practices in accordance with the Noble Path;
therefore it is said: "In this context, the faculty of faith is to be seen."

In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining faculties as well. Regarding "in the four right endeavors" (*sammappadhāna*): it refers to the cultivation of the fourfold right endeavor.
The same method applies to "in the four foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.

And here, just as faith is among the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*), so too is energy in the cultivation of the right endeavors, and mindfulness in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness—as in: "Possessing mindfulness, one should remove [unwholesome states] in the world..."

Because of the statement, "covetousness and dejection," mindfulness should be desired as predominant in the preliminary stage by way of its function. Likewise, for one whose task is concentration, concentration is required;
and since it is said that "the cultivation of the Noble Truths is the cultivation of wisdom," wisdom should be desired as predominant therein in the preliminary stage.
This meaning is evident; however, at the moment of attainment, [all factors] are equal, just as with concentration and wisdom.
The state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) among the faculties, beginning with faith, is indeed what is intended.

For this reason, the term "here" (*ettha*) is employed in various places in such passages as "herein the faculty of faith. By the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), that specific context is referred to, namely the equality of the faculties and so forth.
"In their own respective domains" means precisely within each one's own objective sphere. Thus, both mundane and supramundane phenomena have been explained; here, the mundane phenomena are discussed.
And supramundane states are described according to their various specific modes of occurrence. This is what is meant:

when the five faculties, with faith as the fifth, occur together, it is stated that among those objects, each one is to be regarded as predominant due to the preeminence of its respective function—faith and the others—not all of them at once.
In this same way, other mundane and supramundane states are also [to be understood] according to their own [respective functions].
"It is understood by way of the specific modes of activity regarding their respective objects.

Now, in order to clarify through similes the pre-eminent functions of the faculties such as faith in various contexts, the passage beginning with "Just as" was spoken. Herein, this is the correlation of the similes:
the five companions, with the king as the fifth, are like those that bring about the maturation of liberation.

The five faculties. Their simultaneous entry into the path of insight, like the simultaneous crossing of a street for the sake of play, is the simultaneous entry of the faculties into the path of insight.
Just as among companions, the first and so forth move about each in their own respective homes, so too do faith and the others take precedence after attaining the factors of stream-entry and so on.
Among companions, the silence of the others here and there [is analogous].
It is like the conformity of the remaining faculties to that [faculty] in their respective instances. It is the state of following the function of that faculty which has become the precursor.
For at that time, their function is not manifest as it is in the case of the water elements and so forth within the earth and other material constituents;
rather, the function of faith and the other [faculties] alone remains clearly evident, having been established previously by such conditions.

Because the mental continuum has been conditioned. And here, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is mentioned by taking the king as an illustration, in order to show that for one who practices insight meditation (*vipassanākammika*), cultivation is specifically dominated by wisdom. The phrase "Thus... and so forth is the conclusion of the meaning as it has been attained.

"Even consciousness of the path" refers even to the consciousness associated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) which leads to the diminution of defilements. "In the same way, it cognizes that" means:

One understands the true nature of reality (saccadhamma) precisely by way of the method beginning with "This is suffering," because it is comprised within a single arising of consciousness and because it is conducive to the Path.
Regarding the phrase "that which one understands," here both understanding (vijānana) and full comprehension (pajānana) are intended as being comprised within the arising of insight-consciousness;
they are not, as in the expression "that which one fully comprehends" [in the context of the Path], comprised within the arising of Path-consciousness. Thus he said: "That which..."
“Included within formations,” and so forth. “In the same way” means by way of the method beginning with “impermanent.

Because they are comprised within a single arising of consciousness and because they constitute insight, there is “arising together” (ekuppādatā), which means they proceed simultaneously with identical conditions. Precisely for that reason, their ceasing together at one and the same time is “ceasing together” (ekanirodhatā).
Their proceeding in dependence upon one and the same physical basis is “having a single basis” (ekavatthukatā).
"Having a single object" means occurring by taking one and the same object as its basis. Here, the word for cause (*hetu*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

By this, it establishes the state of being conjoined through their simultaneous arising and so forth. This expression also serves to include everything without exception; thus, even by these three [characteristics], the characteristic of association is indeed established.

This was stated with reference to the wisdom of the Path (*magga-paññā*), for that is exclusively to be cultivated (*bhāvetabbā*) and not to be fully understood (*pariññeyyā*); however, as for wisdom in general...
Since the states associated with it also share its nature by virtue of being something to be developed, he says, "But that which is associated with it," and so forth.

Although the consciousness associated with it likewise proceeds by way of the development of insight-wisdom, its state of being fully understood is stated because it does not transcend the condition of being something to be fully understood. For this very reason, he said:
“Even that knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Even so— meaning,

even though there is this general inclusion under the term “feeling” (*vedanā*)— only those feelings belonging to the three planes and included within the range of contemplation (*sammasanacāra*), and thus being the objective domain of the knowledge of contemplation, are intended here.
Because the teaching was undertaken for the sake of bringing benefit to his fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī). For it has been said: "For those seeking to cross over the four floods," and so forth.

This same method applies to wisdom (paññā) as well. Here, in order to establish by means of a Sutta the point that the words "pleasure" (sukha) and so on have as their object the corresponding mental states, it is said:
"And form... and so forth. "Entirely painful" (ekantadukkha) means exclusively undesirable; for that very reason, it is called "painful" (dukkha) due to its nature of suffering.

It is suffering. Because it has fallen upon and entered into painful feeling by way of being made an object, it is "fallen upon suffering" (*dukkhānupatita*) and "entered into suffering" (*dukkhāvakkanta*).
The construction is: "it would not be unentered into by pleasure. In the phrase *nayidaṃ*, *idaṃ* here is merely a particle.
*Sārajjeyyuṃ* means they would produce lust (*sārāga*). "Pleasure" (*sukha*) is desirable both by its intrinsic nature and as an object. From lust...
“They bind” means that, by reason of intense lust, they are bound by whichever of the ten fetters (saṃyojana) is appropriate.
“The fetters become defiled” means that, through being thus bound, they become defiled by way of the defilement of craving and so forth;
the meaning is that they are oppressed and tormented. “Object” refers to an object that is desirable, undesirable, or neutral, respectively.

“Pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure” has been stated. Having thus shown all five aggregates without distinction as having pleasure and so forth as their objective supports (*ārammaṇa*), the passage beginning with “Moreover” (*apicā*) was spoken in order to show that feeling (*vedanā*) alone has pleasure and so forth as its objective support.
Since this was spoken from the perspective of ordinary people, it says, “having made the preceding pleasant feeling the objective support. However, for one who has attained distinction...
One indeed takes even future pleasant feeling as an object. This has been stated in the commentary to the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna):
"For when one experiences the object of feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say that the person possessing that [feeling] experiences it.
"Of all perception" means of all perception belonging to the four planes. "Of all-pervading perception" means in every arising of consciousness.
Of the perception of occurrence. "In the cloth" (*vatthe vā*): by the word *vā*, he includes the color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*). "Causing to arrive":
bringing it near to either access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*). "The perception that arises": even the perception that arises as "blue form," "blue with form as its object."

"Because it does not include all" means because it does not include all feelings, perceptions, and consciousnesses. "That which has come to the stage of reasoning" refers to that which stands by way of the process of reasoning involved in spinning thread or the process of reasoning involved in weaving thread.
"That which has come to the stage of winding and so forth" refers to that which has come to the stage of winding the thread and so forth.
Precisely because they have been let go, they are not grasped; at the very moment wisdom is made to attain association with consciousness.
For that very reason, it is made to obtain association even with feeling and perception. It perceives that very [object] because of its state of being conjoined.
Regarding the phrases "it perceives" and "it cognizes," one should supply the word "it understands" (*pajānāti*), since a distinction will be stated by way of understanding as well.
And this term "knows" (*jānāti*) is indeed used here without distinction; however, there is a distinction in terms of meaning.

It should be so understood. For, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the prefix (upasagga) qualifies the meaning expressed by that verb or noun through its function as an indicator (jotaka), not as an expresser (vācaka).
Therefore he said: "The specific distinction of its meaning of 'knowing' (jānana) should also be understood.
By this, the terms *saññā*, *viññāṇa*, and *paññā* are included within their respective meanings of knowing, each according to its own nature.
And he shows that these are the final conclusions regarding the distinguished objects. Therefore he says, "Perception, indeed," and so forth.
In the phrase "mere perceiving" (*sañjānanamattameva*), the word *matta* (mere) serves to exclude qualifications, thereby excluding the modes of cognizing and fully understanding;
the word *eva* (indeed) emphasizes that these distinctions never exist for this [perception]. Therefore he says, "Impermanent, suffering," and so forth.
In that context, since perception itself is unable even to perform the function of consciousness, how could it perform the function of wisdom?
Therefore, it is said that "it is unable to bring about the penetration of the characteristics," but it is not said that "it brings about the manifestation of the Path.
Consciousness, while occurring with respect to an object, does not proceed by way of perceiving merely blue, yellow, and so forth, in the manner of perception.
Then, because another similar distinction is indeed understood there as well, he says "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) and so forth.
But how does consciousness bring about the penetration of the characteristics? By means of the path shown by wisdom.

For when insight (*vipassanā*)—which has the characteristics as its object—proceeds after having penetrated the characteristics many times, it does so through familiarity due to their becoming proficient.
Insight can also arise with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, just as when one is reciting a familiar text, the sections that have already passed by are no longer clearly perceived.
Furthermore, the phrase "penetration of the characteristics" (*lakkhaṇapaṭivedha*) is stated merely with reference to taking the characteristics as an object, not to their actual penetration.
"Having ascended" means by way of the successive stages of knowledge beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
Having begun [its function], it is unable to bring about the manifestation of the Path because its intrinsic nature is non-awakening.

It perceives the object only by way of full comprehension (*avabujjhana*), not by mere perception (*sañjānana*). Likewise, it brings about the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*) not by mere discernment (*vijānana*), but by exerting itself through its own unique power (*ānubhāva*) which is not shared with others, it also brings about the manifestation of the Path.
Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned point by means of a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as” (*yathā hi*) was spoken.

Therein, “one whose intelligence has not arisen” (*ajātabuddhi*) means one whose intelligence regarding conventional usage has not yet developed. “Enjoyment and use” (*upabhogaparibhoga*) means that which is fit for enjoyment and use;

the meaning is that which is suitable for obtaining the objects of enjoyment and use. A “counterfeit coin” (*kūṭa*) is an imitation of a *kahāpaṇa* coin made of copper, bronze, or similar materials. “Valuable” (*cheka*) means of great worth.

*Karatoti* means "half-value" (*aḍḍhasāra*). *Saṇhoti* means "of a soft nature" (*mudujātiko*), that is, "even-value" (*samasaṃsāro*). The word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādiattho*); by it, there is an inclusion of "foot-value" (*pādasāra*), "other-foot-value" (*paropādasāra*), "half-value," and so forth.

Furthermore, one who knows [this] recognizes that form even upon seeing it... [omission] ...and also knows, "It was made by such-and-such a teacher," because the *heraññikagrantha* (the goldsmith’s manual) has been well-mastered.
"In the same way," and so forth, is the application of the simile. Without making a distinction between the perceptions (*saññā*)... [omission].
Because it grasps the object as a mere lump, it is said to be like a child’s seeing a coin;

for that [perception] is said to have the presence of the object as it appears as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*). Consciousness (*viññāṇa*), because of its capacity to grasp certain specific distinctions within the object, is said to be like a villager’s seeing a coin.
Wisdom (*paññā*), however, because of its complete comprehension of the object...

It is said to be like the sight of a coin by a money-changer. "Of these" refers to perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and wisdom (*paññā*). "Distinction" means a distinction in their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
It is difficult to penetrate by means of natural wisdom (*pakati-paññā*); by this very point, he shows their extreme subtlety.

"Occurring with respect to a single object" means occurring with respect to one and the same object. By this, he demonstrates that they have an undifferentiated sphere of activity and an undifferentiated time.
By clarifying their inseparable occurrence, he indicates precisely how difficult they are to penetrate. "Determination" (vavatthāna) means establishing [them] without confusion.
"This is contact... pe... this is consciousness" is merely an illustration;
or, the word "iti" has the sense of "beginning," by which the inclusion of the remaining factors should be understood. "This" refers to the act of determining formless phenomena.
"Than that"—referring to what was stated regarding the extraction of sesame oil and so forth; "than that. If it is more difficult, how then [is it so]?
To this he says, "But the Blessed One," and so forth.

(451) "By that which has escaped" means by that which has emerged and is no longer connected to itself. "By that which is relinquished" means by that which, through not assuming the state of being a condition, is as if relinquished.

Because there is no connection with that which has arisen by way of condition (*paccayuppanna*). The ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used to indicate the point of departure (*apādāna*); the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) is used to indicate the agent (*kattū-attha*).
Sensuous-sphere mind-consciousness cannot be definitively stated as "this is connected with the five doors," whereas fine-material-sphere consciousness is not like that;
therefore, it is said that the latter alone is "escaped from" (*nissaṭa*) the five faculties. Thus he said.

“By means of the fourth jhāna consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). The mention of the fourth jhāna is because it serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for that very [consciousness] of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).
It is called “purified” specifically because it is free from defilement; for it is particularly purified by being devoid of secondary defilements (upakkilesa).
Therefore, he said, “by means of that which is free from secondary defilements. That which is to be known is the knowable (neyya), within one’s own and others’ continuums.
The meaning is that this must be known as an excellence; it is to be awakened to, or it is to be made known.

Alternatively, "to be led" (*neyya*) means that it is to be led into one’s own continuum, or to be set in motion. Therefore he said: "It is possible to produce [it]. For when one is established herein, it succeeds.
"Separately" (*pāṭiyekka*) means individually, in the sense of each successive dhamma. "Due to the absence of misinterpretation" (*abhinivesābhāvato*).

Because of the impossibility of a fixed adherence to insight (*vipassanā*). "By way of groups" means by way of the method of insight known as the "comprehension by groups" (*kalāpa-sammasana-naya-vipassanā*).
"A bhikkhu" refers to a disciple; for in that context, the "insight into phenomena according to their sequence" (*anupada-dhamma-vipassanā*) is impossible for a disciple, but not for the Teacher.
Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "He relinquishes" means he abandons through the abandoning of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) bound to those [phenomena].
"Having come into his hands" means being like something that has come into one's hands; the meaning is "being near.

For when the Lord of the World was seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the invincible throne, having applied insight by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) through the passage beginning, "Alas, this world has fallen into trouble," he [perceived] by way of thirty-six thousand million aspects in accordance with the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) to be attained.
While engaging in the contemplation of the Great Bodhisatta’s knowledge called *mahāvajirañāṇa*, he contemplated the phenomena of the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) one after another;

immediately following that, he also contemplated the phenomena of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) again and again. Therefore, he said, “The Blessed One, moreover,” and so forth.

“More than fifty” means fifty-two. Now, it should be understood here that certain phenomena, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest, are included among those beginning with contact as the fifth (*phassapañcamaka*).

Although they are included even among the factors of jhāna and so forth, it is stated thus because, through their specific distinctions as various conditions, they become like separate phenomena (dhammāntara).
For instance, in supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness-arising, the state of nine faculties (navindriyatā) is spoken of.
"By way of extracting the factors" means by way of extracting the jhāna-factors, enlightenment-factors (bojjhaṅga), and path-factors (maggaṅga) that are obtainable therein.
Alternatively, the word *aṅga* signifies a "constituent part"; therefore, "by the extraction of the constituents" means by the extraction of the constituent parts beginning with contact as the fifth.
"As many as are the perceptions and attainments" refers to however many jhāna-attainments accompanied by perception there may be;
because they emerge from these and reach the state of being fragrant, there is for those to be trained a penetration of final knowledge (*aññā*) and the attainment of Arahatship to that same extent.

"In the sense of being a guide for seeing" means: like one who, taking hold of the end of a blind man's staff, points out the path, it is by way of its guiding nature, which consists in seeing the true nature of phenomena as they are.

Or, just as that [staff] is the eye for him, so too is wisdom (paññā) for sentient beings. Therefore he said, "by wisdom that has become the eye. Wisdom associated with concentration is "concentration-wisdom" (samādhi-paññā).

And here they say that "concentration" refers to formless-sphere concentration (*ārūppasamādhi*); however, it is more appropriate to consider the application of comprehension (*sammasanapayoga*) as "jhāna-concentration.
"Insight-wisdom" is wisdom that has become insight. One understands through the function [of wisdom] within the attainment of concentration and wisdom;
moreover, according to the statement, "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are," one understands through non-delusion. In this regard:

"By way of function": by way of the function of making an object within the range of the field of experience. "By way of non-delusion": because it dispels delusion regarding associated states, as in the case of the experiencing of joy and so forth.
"For what purpose? means "for what aim?"—thus he says, "What is its purpose?
"In phenomena to be directly known" means those things to be known directly by way of awakening to their specific characteristics and essential natures.

Regarding the phenomena such as the aggregates (khandhas) and the bases (āyatanas): "He fully understands" means he knows them directly and without confusion by way of their specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and their general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa).
By this, he expresses the function of full understanding through knowledge (ñātapariññā).

"To be fully understood" means they are to be known by way of delimitation as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. "He fully understands" [means] according to the passage beginning: "Whatever form... is impermanent in the sense of destruction," and so forth.
Having delimited [them], one knows. By this, he states the function of full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).
"In phenomena to be abandoned" means all evil phenomena, beginning with the perception of permanence and ending with those to be destroyed by the path of Arahantship.

"One abandons" means one abandons them thoroughly; the meaning is that one both suppresses and eradicates them. By this, he states the function of full understanding as abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). Furthermore, this wisdom is both mundane (*lokiya*)...

There are three kinds of supramundane [knowledges], and he himself states their distinction. "By way of function" means by way of the function of the object through the mode of direct higher knowledge (*abhijānana*).

"By way of non-delusion" means because they dispel delusion regarding the objects to be directly known and so forth, according to their respective powers. Because they proceed by making Nibbāna the object, they are free from delusion regarding the objects to be directly known and so forth;
thus he says, "The supramundane [knowledges] are by way of non-delusion."

452. Because the view of self-agency (*kammassakatā*) and right view based on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-nissita*) are not intended here—as this is a discourse on the turning away from the round—it is said:
"by means of both the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*) and the right view of the path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*). "From another" means from another teacher or from a disciple;
it refers to the sound of the Dhamma being received. Therefore, he says: "listening to the Dhamma that is conducive. For that...
It is able to serve as a condition for right view, not just any voice from another.

"Appropriate attention" (upāyamanasikāra) refers to that kind of preliminary attention by which the discernment of name-and-form and so forth are accomplished. And showing that this is a condition for right view specifically in the sense of being a restrictive factor, rather than an all-inclusive one, he says: "But for the Paccekabuddhas... and so on. "Only in appropriate attention" means...

By means of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), it excludes only the "voice of another" (*parato-ghosa*), and not the specific proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna-visesa*), because the word "only" (*eva*) serves the purpose of excluding its opposite.

"Having obtained assistance" means having received conditions such as a support (*nissaya*) and so forth, as appropriate. Because it is grasped by way of being assisted by insight-right-view (*vipassanā-sammā-diṭṭhi*), [the term applies] to the right-views of the paths;

and among those, it refers specifically to the right-view of the path of Arahantship. For a positive injunction (*vidhi*) applies to what is immediately preceding, while a prohibition (*paṭisedha*) [applies to what follows].

Or: the "complete knowledge of others' minds" (*cetopariyāya*) is established exclusively in regard to the concentration of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-samādhi*) and the states that are its requisites.

"Right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) refers to the right view of the path of Arahantship. "At the moment of fruition" (*phalakkhaṇe*) means at the two kinds of moments of fruition: the immediate and the subsequent.
It is called "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) because by it the mind is liberated from all defilements through the process of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).
With the exception of the wisdom of the supreme fruit (*aggaphalapaññā*), all remaining phenomena of the fruits are [the basis]. Therefore he said: "It has liberation of mind as its fruit.
The construction is as follows: "The fruit and benefit is that which is reckoned as liberation of mind;
the fruit and benefit is the abandoning known as subsiding, which consists in the liberation of the mind from all defilements. And here, by the term "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*):

Only the abandoning is taken up; previously, the factors that abandon were mentioned. Otherwise, if the fruit-factors themselves were taken as the benefit, the subsequent statement would be redundant.
In the phrase "the benefits of the fruit of liberation through wisdom," the meaning should be understood in exactly the same way. [This applies to] right speech, right action, and right livelihood.

Because its nature is virtue (*sīla*), it is especially helpful to concentration (*samādhi*); likewise, right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is helpful because its nature is meditative absorption (*jhāna*), for it is designated as "absorption" (*appanā*).

However, since right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) and right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) belong to the side of concentration itself, he said, "The remaining factors should be understood as the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*). This is the virtue of the fourfold purification, which leads to the attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
The basis for this is the virtue of the fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*). The same method applies to learning and the other factors as well.
"Conversation" (*saṃkathā*) is speaking together by way of announcing the movement of one's own mind; it is precisely this conversation that constitutes "discussion" (*sākacchā*).

However, since these are here connected to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he says: "discourse on the meditation subject... etc. In that context, the failure of the meditation subject to proceed through its course even once—
*Khalaṇaṃ* is stumbling; *pakkhalanaṃ* is falling repeatedly; the discourse on the cutting off of both is the *khalanapakkhalanachedanakathā*.
"Of one who fulfills" means of one who maintains and increases [the practice] by making it dependent upon turning away from the world (*vivaṭṭanissita*).

"Of one who listens" means of one who listens so that the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as it was received may reach full development (*phāti*); for it is precisely for this reason that "listening to the Dhamma that is suitable" is stated.
"Of one performing the work" means of one performing the work of devotion to meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*).
In all five instances, the word "end" (*anta*) should be understood as indicating the sense of "cause.

For in this way, the simile of water being mentioned by the phrase "just as," and so forth, would be appropriate. "A water-trough" (*udakakoṭṭhaka*) is a basin for watering plants. "He binds it firmly" means...
Having made it neither loose nor too tight, neither too large nor too small, he joins it together.
"He makes it firm" means that when pouring water, he makes the basin more solid so that the water does not leak out from here and there.
"A dry stick" refers to the dry tip of a branch from that very mango grove. "An anthill" refers to a nest of copper-colored ants.
A spade is a hoe. Virtue is like the binding of the trench because it serves as the foundation for the means of increasing right view.
Hearing the Dhamma is like the pouring of water because it nourishes development (*bhāvanā*).

Serenity (*samatha*) is like the making firm of the embankment because it brings about the strengthening of the embankment of virtue, which is the basis for the aforementioned development. For one who is concentrated...

For virtue becomes more stable. This is because, like the removal of creepers and the like growing nearby, it removes the stumbling, slipping, and cutting away that occur in the meditation subject, thereby clearing away obstacles to successful development.
It is like digging up the roots, for the cultivation of the seven contemplations digs out craving, conceit, and views, which are the roots of those obstacles. And here, since—
For one of perfectly pure virtue who is devoted to the meditation subject, it is necessary to hear the Dhamma that is conducive to it;
from that, one should engage in discussion regarding the meaning as it has been heard; from that, through the purification of the meditation subject, the accomplishment of serenity arises;
from that, for one who is concentrated and has begun insight, there is the fulfillment of insight; and for one whose insight is fulfilled, there is right view of the path.
"Paribrūheti" (he causes to grow) means that this sequence should be understood as having been taught because these factors are mutually related and because he has grasped them directly. 453.
"What does he ask here?"—here, since the teaching has thus led [the listener] to the fruit of Arahatship, [he asks]: "But how many, friends..."
The meaning of "being" (*bhava*) when asking about existence is: what kind of connection (*anusandhi*) does he ask about based upon?
For that very reason, having stated, "the connection has gone back to the root," he spoke the words beginning with "one of poor wisdom" (*duppañño*) in order to clarify his intention.

Here, "one of poor wisdom" is intended as one who has not penetrated the Truths (*sacca*), not merely one who is dull-witted. In the phrases "existence of sense-desire" (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, there is a distinction between karma and rebirth.
Showing that both types of existence (bhava) are intended, he said, "kamma leading to sense-sphere existence," and so forth.
Regarding this, whatever needs to be said should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentary.

As for "of renewed existence" (*punabbhavassa*): it refers to the continuity of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭapabandha*), which has received the name "renewed existence" because it comes into being again and again, repeatedly, and successively.
Therefore he said, "I shall ask about the cycle of existence here. "Rebirth" (*abhinibbatti*) means arising by way of existence, birth-place, destiny, and so forth.
"In this or that" refers to various states of existence and the like. "Delight" (*abhinandanā*) is the cause of delight through craving (*taṇhā*).
By the phrase "there is going and coming," etc., he shows the successive deaths and rebirths of beings within the realms of existence and so forth. "By the destruction and cessation" [of that].

By means of non-arising cessation, which is termed "absolute destruction. Both of these [terms] should not be stated [in this context], because the time for the clear realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) and the clear realization of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) is extremely close.
However, it may be so stated by way of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of cause and effect phenomena.

For just as the disappearance of darkness has the lighting of a lamp as its cause, so too the cessation of ignorance has the arising of true knowledge (*vijjā*) as its cause; and cause and effect phenomena, though simultaneous, [are related in this way].
They are expressed as prior and posterior times, just as: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises"—this is the function of the condition and the conditioned.
Here, in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), going is cut off by final Nibbāna.
There, in the fine-material and immaterial realms, coming is cut off by final Nibbāna. Both going and coming are cut off entirely.
Because there is no further arising of successive states. 454.

Regarding the discourse on turning away (*vivaṭṭakathā*), it is appropriate to explain that the first jhāna—attained by one who has reached turning away and remains therein—is the means for achieving cessation (*nirodha*) for one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) according to the highest description; thus he said: "But which, friend?"

"What is being asked here? and so forth. For immediately after that, the factors associated with and abandoned by the first jhāna are asked about by the bhikkhu who is about to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Definition of factors" (*aṅgavavatthāna*) means the definition of the jhāna factors.
"Delimitation of components" (*koṭṭhāsapariccheda*) means that the delimitation of the components—the phenomena beginning with contact as the fifth—which are found therein, must be known.
In this jhāna, one should know that "so many factors are present" and "so many have ceased. Regarding the "factors that are helpful or unhelpful":
these are the factors that are helpful and those that are unhelpful for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

For since the attainment of cessation is to be reached by means of sixteen modes of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*) and nine modes of concentration (*samādhicariyā*), it is through those respective modes of knowledge and concentration...
The states that must be transcended are the non-beneficial factors; those that effect the transcendence are the beneficial factors.

By means of these, the mind and mental concomitants—having reached a state of extreme subtlety with only the residual formations remaining for the attainment of the peak of existence (bhavagga-samāpatti), which is progressively more and more tranquilized—cease for the allotted duration of time and enter into non-occurrence. "Of that" refers to...

Regarding cessation (*nirodha*): "antecedent condition" (*anantarapaccaya*) means similar to an antecedent condition. For there is no dhamma whatsoever that is called an antecedent condition for cessation.

However, that manner in which the mind and mental factors cease at that time was due to the previously mentioned volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) as the cause of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti*);
thus, that [attainment] acts as if it were its antecedent condition. Therefore, that...
It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "the six attainments," this is because it is considered a commentary on the Sutta Piṭaka as spoken according to the method of the Suttantas.
However, one ought to say "the seven attainments"; otherwise, this could not be called "four-factored.
Or, "having shown the method" means having demonstrated the method by way of showing the beginning and the end.

455. Having thus clarified the basis for cessation, [the author] now shows that the text proceeds by way of questioning the five sensitive organs (pasāda) first—by way of their individual nature, their specific characteristics, their specific objects, and their refuge—in order to inquire about the conditions for the five organs within the internal cessation due to their lack of continuity:
"Questioning the five sensitive organs based on consciousness."

He said: "Regarding 'range and object' (*gocara-visaya*): here, while the term 'range' (*gocara*) may indeed depend on frequent practice therein, and the term 'object' (*visaya*) depends on its state of being nothing other [than that], there is thus a distinction between the states of 'range' and 'object.
However, when analyzed, both have the very same nature as an objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
Therefore, he said: 'the object which has become the range. 'Of each one' (*ekaekassa*) means one for one, another for another."

This is the meaning. For this word *eka* has a different sense here than in such passages as "some thus declare" (*ittheke abhivadanti*), and so on. The phrase beginning with "If indeed" (*sace hi*) is an expression of hypothetical imagination (*abhūtaparikappa*).

In that context, "having combined" (*samodhānetvā*) means having brought together into one. By the words "even without a mouth," etc., he shows what is called an illustration by way of conversational inquiry (*atthasallāpika-nidassana*).
Just as the eye sees form only when presided over by consciousness (*viññāṇādhiṭṭhita*), [so too...]
It is not only that consciousness dependent on the eye sees, while other [consciousnesses] do not; thus he said, "Direct it toward the clarity of the eye.

By this, he shows their joint action (*saṃhaccakārita*) therein. Or, when he says "whether blue or yellow," he speaks with reference merely to the knowledge of the specific nature (*sabhāva*) of blue, yellow, and so forth.
The cognition "it is blue" or "it is yellow" belongs to visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).

[It] does not exist at all because of its lack of conceptualization. This refers to these [mental states], such as eye-consciousness and so forth. This is a question regarding the supported (nissita) by way of the support (nissaya);
for in this way, the inquiry into the experiencing of objects is made possible. Therefore, he said: "Eye-consciousness," and so forth.
Eye-consciousness and the others are incapable of experiencing their respective objects by way of attachment and so forth; therein—
And because there is no capacity [to do so], they do not turn back from anything as if they were retreating;

thus it was asked, "What do these turn back from? Having spoken of the impulsion-consciousness (*javana-mano*) as the resort for both the five-door process and the other [mind-door process] in general, that specific quality of its being a resort through which the occurrence of passion and so forth takes place is found where it is distinguished.

Showing this, he said: "or the mind-door impulsion-mind. Regarding the phrase "in this door," it is because in the eye-door the impulsion becomes attached, or feels aversion, or is deluded, whereby non-restraint such as ignorance arises therein.
"In that" means in the state of the impulsion-mind itself being the refuge. "Weak tax-collectors" refers to royal officials of inferior power.
A *yojjana-kahāpaṇa* is a kahāpaṇa received on the day one is appointed to the service of attendants.
A *bandha-kahāpaṇa* is a kahāpaṇa received upon the release of one who was bound by shackles.
A *māpahāra-kahāpaṇa* is the fine to be paid by one who refuses someone striking him, saying, "Do not strike me. All of these [fines] apply to the common village folk.
He said, "or eight kahāpaṇas," and so forth, to show that when it is obtained in this way, it amounts to that much. "Consisting of a hundred pieces" means consisting of a hundred karīsa-measures.
This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. The passage beginning with "Therein... is a connection of the simile, which is easy to understand. 456.
"Five clear-visions in the midst of cessation" refers to the five clear-visions occurring in one who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"In the occurrence of the functional-constituted process" means in the occurrence of those phenomena that produce functional processes such as impulsion (*javana*).
"They are strong conditions" means they act as conditions by way of the postnascent, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions;

they are strong conditions by virtue of their supporting nature. "Dependent on the life-faculty" means [dependent] on that which has become a condition by way of the faculty, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.

The fivefold clarity (pasāda) persists in dependence upon the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). Without the life-faculty, it does not persist, because for one devoid of the life-faculty, there is an absence of the material aggregate produced by kamma.
Therefore, since heat proceeds only when sustained by the life-force characterized by preservation, and not when unsustained by it, heat exists in dependence upon vitality (āyu).
It remains. "Depending on the flame of the net (jālasikhā), light becomes manifest":

this means that depending on the aggregate of the primary elements designated as the "flame of the net," which occurs simultaneously with it, the color-element (vaṇṇadhātu) known by the name "light" is known through such modes as "it blazes," "it dispels darkness," and "it reveals forms. "Depending on that light" refers to that aforementioned kind [of light].
Having obtained light as a condition, the flame of the net becomes manifest—clearly visible as "small," "great," "straight," "crooked," and so forth.

The fire born of karma (kammaja-tejo) is like the flame of the net because it has that [the body] as its support; the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is like the light because it is dependent upon that [the fire].
Now, in order to show the connection between the simile and the thing illustrated, the passage beginning with "The flame of the net... was stated. Having taken hold of the light...
By the word "arises," it is shown that just as light arises simultaneously with a flame, so too does the life-faculty arise simultaneously with the heat born of karma (*kamma-ja-usmā*).
Since the light dependent on the flame exists only when that flame is present, it is as if the light were produced by it;
thus he says, "by the very light generated by itself. Here, "heat" indeed refers to that which is originated by karma.

The fire element (*tejodhātu*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) dependent upon it, and that which protects it—referring to these, he said: "By means of the life-faculty, which arises from the great primary elements born of karma, there is the protection of heat.
It is not only for the sake of momentary duration, but also for the sake of the non-interruption of the continuity [of existence] that the life-faculty is the cause;
thus he said: "It maintains the activity of the karma-born heat even for a hundred years. Heat is the [support] of vitality...

Since it exists as a condition only when accompanied by the remaining primary elements (*mahābhūta*), he says "the primary elements. Likewise, since vitality (*āyu*) is a condition for heat only while sustaining the co-nascent matter, it is said that "it sustains the primary elements. 457.

It is vitality itself that, by way of being a condition such as the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) and so forth, is called "conditioning" (*saṅkharaṇa*) because of its sustaining of co-nascent phenomena.
The life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*). The use of the plural number is because they occur within material groups (*rūpakalāpa*) that are divided into many hundreds of thousands of types;
thus, it is "of many kinds. They experience the flavor of the object (*ārammaṇarasa*), and are therefore "to be felt" (*vedanīya*), just as [in the expression] "leading to liberation" (*niyyānika*).

Hence he said: "feelings are mental states" (*vedanā dhammā*). The plural designation is used because they are distinguished by the divisions of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. Of these—life-formations and feelings—...

For one who has attained the attainment of absolute cessation (ekantanirodha), death must occur because feeling (vedanā) has ceased. However, because the formations of life (āyusaṅkhārā) have not likewise ceased, there could be no entering into cessation at all;
how much less could there be emergence from it? Therefore, it is said in the Discourse: “And those friends,” and so forth.
Emergence is recognized by the arising of perception, feeling, and the rest. Now...
To clarify that matter in detail by means of a simile, the passage beginning with “yo hi” was stated. “Having become disenchanted” means having become weary of the falling upon various objects.
“By way of the time as it was delimited” means when the delimited time has arrived. “Conditioned by the material life-faculty” means being a condition consisting of a faculty.
The immaterial phenomena are like the movement of a net because of their fiery nature and because they illuminate the sense object.

The prior volitional formation for the attainment of cessation is like a stream of water. The material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is like extinguished embers, because it does not shine due to its mere state of warmth.
"Arrival at the delimited time" means the approaching of the time as it was delimited.
The apprehension of the occurrence of matter is by way of its corresponding rebirth alone. "They abandon this material body" means from this...
The physical forms and bodies pass away and do not continue.

They are conditioned by the body, thus they are "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhārā*), because their existence is dependent upon it. They construct speech, thus they are "verbal formations" (*vacīsaṅkhārā*);

for having first applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one breaks forth into and speaks speech. They are conditioned by the mind, thus they are "mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhārā*).

Because their existence is bound up with that [consciousness]. Just as the cessation of matter is not explicitly enjoined when there is an injunction for the cessation of mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*), so too the cessation of consciousness is not explicitly enjoined, because it is distinct from them. Therefore, the cessation of those associated with consciousness is not absolute, since it does not occur when thought (*vitakka*) and the rest cease.
As for what was said, "speech remains unceased," that too is not the case; for they are "constructing speech."

For verbal formations have ceased; when they have ceased, how could speech not cease? But as for the mind, even though mental formations have ceased, because it is not conditioned by them, it continues to function just as it does during the cessation of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
This is the opponent’s intention here. [He argues that] an immediate offense (*ānantariya-kamma*) would be committed, because the mind has not ceased, and depending upon it—
"And because material phenomena have not departed, they are indeed still called 'living'. "Without making a dogmatic adherence to the literal expression" means:

without making a dogmatic adherence to the idea that the Sutta is of "definitive meaning" (*nītattha*)—thinking, based on the statement "mental formations have ceased," that "only those [formations] have ceased, not the mind"—but rather by standing in the system of the Teachers (*ācariya*). "Of the Teachers" refers to those who have come down through the lineage of tradition.
The meaning is: "having stood in the intended sense. "Should be examined" means that the unerring meaning of a word from one sutta must be investigated by means of the context of other suttas.

For instance, based on the expression "the state of non-perception" (*asaññabhava*), one would not grasp the meaning here as being "only perception is absent there, while the others—mind and mental factors—are present. And likewise, regarding the phrase "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

Regarding the statement, “Only perception (saññā) is of that kind there, not contact (phassa) and the rest,” this meaning is not accepted here because the teaching is given under the heading of perception.
Likewise, here too, the expressions “mental formations (cittasaṅkhārā) have ceased” and “the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha)” are merely the headings of the teaching.
However, the unerring fact here is that all mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika) indeed cease therein.
The meaning must be understood, because through such prior volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), all mind and mental factors cease therein.
By this, it is shown that the previous logical statement, "Because of otherness" and "Because of its absence," is incorrect due to a failure to understand the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
Therefore he said: "For the meaning is the refuge, not the letter."

“Afflicted” means oppressed. “Smeared” means defiled. The exhaustion of the sense-faculties resulting from the impact with their objects is to be illustrated by the eye’s seeing of bright colors, subtle dust, and so forth.

For instance, when a fire is burning in front during the heat of the day and a loud-sounding drum is struck, the eyes cannot endure it as if they were being split, and the ears likewise [cannot endure] the sound. “By the tip of the nose... [refers to the olfactory faculty].
People say, "It is as if they are being struck. 458.
The Fourth Jhāna of the Form Realm itself, when it proceeds by way of the cultivation of dispassion toward form, is the Formless Jhāna;

thus, in providing the answer regarding the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) answered with the words, "With the abandoning of pleasure," and so forth.
By way of departure and disappearance, conditions are "conditions by departure," such as the abandonings of pleasure and so forth.

By way of attainment, however, there are the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere among the kasiṇas and the three lower immaterial attainments; for it is not possible to attain the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without having attained those.
Regarding "the fruition attainment that emerges from cessation": from cessation...
The emergence is the attainment of fruition reached through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). For that is called "the signless liberation of mind" (*animittā cetovimutti*).
Just as direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is the outflow of serenity (*samatha*), the sublime abode of equanimity (*upekkhābrahmavihāra*) is the outflow of loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness;

the formless attainments (*āruppa*) are the outflow of the kasiṇas; and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the outflow of both serenity and insight (*vipassanā*), so too is [this] the case for insight.

The fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) is the outflow-result (nissandaphala); thus he said, "by means of the attainment of fruition which is the outflow of insight" (vipassanānissandāya phalasamāpattiyā).

Since what is called an "object" (ārammaṇa) is specifically the sign for the arising of phenomena that possess objects, he said, "of all signs" (sabbanimittānaṃ), meaning "of all objects such as form and so forth.
Because there is no sign of any conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhāra) here, it is "signless" (animitta), that is, unconditioned (asaṅkhata).

He said, "The element," referring to "the element of Nibbāna, which is free from all signs. He spoke with reference to the attention (manasikāra) co-arising with the attainment of fruition, not to the attention of adverting (āvajjana-manasikāra).
For the latter cannot occur here, because [fruition] arises immediately after the conforming consciousness (anuloma).
"In this place" refers to the beginning, middle, and end of the cessation mentioned here; it is taken here as its conclusion.
In the place where it has been grasped. "By two powers" means by the powers of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"And three formations" refers to the three formations beginning with the bodily formation (*kāya-saṅkhāra*). "By sixteen modes of knowledge" refers to:

contemplation of impermanence, suffering, non-self, disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away; and the path of stream-entry... up to ... the attainment of the fruit of arahantship.
"By these sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge. "By nine modes of concentration" means by the nine modes of concentration beginning with the concentration of the first jhāna.
"Mastery-wisdom" (vasībhāvatā-paññā) is that mastery over a person's conduct in the aforementioned modes;
such [wisdom] has been explained—this is the construction. "Explanatory discourse" (vinicchaya-kathā) refers to the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) proceeding by way of detailed analysis.
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentary.

The attainment of mastery is the attainment of dwelling by way of the noble dwellings (*ariyavihāra*). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of stability" (*ṭhitiyā*), here "stability" is intended in the sense of continuity (*pabandha-ṭhiti*), not in the sense of momentary stability (*khaṇa-ṭhiti*).
Why? Because it is an attainment (*samāpajjana*). Hence he said: "'For the sake of stability' means for the sake of long-term persistence."
