"Limitation of duration" means the prior delimitation of time, thinking, "I shall spend this much time in meditative attainment.

"By way of the signs of visible forms, etc. means by way of the signs of form and so forth that are available as appropriate among the signs of kamma, the signs of kamma-result, and the signs of destiny.
In that context, because all six kinds of objects are found within the sign of kamma, it says "of all signs."
It is not stated that all objects must be attended to together or exclusively; for this is a statement of definition, just as one says, "This medicine should be given if I should have an illness.
By the phrase "it perceives blue," etc., there is the perception of beings of those respective colors through the medium of apprehending blue and so forth.
It is said that "the mental attention to the state of non-ill will and so forth is illuminated," because it says, "For at this point, the immeasurable liberation of mind (cetovimutti) is explained.
Here, the connection is that "nothingness (ākiñcañña) is explained. Regarding "here emptiness (suññatā)" and "here the signless (animittā)," the same method applies.
"This" refers to the statement of meaning spoken in such passages as, "Here there is nothing else called new," and so forth. "These" refers to...

The "immeasurable deliverances of mind" (appamāṇacetovimutti) and so forth. "Of a single name" means having one and the same name, which is intended here [to refer to those] that have different verbal expressions.

"A single phenomenon" refers to the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. "Of four names" means having the names beginning with "immeasurable deliverance of mind. "This" refers to this meaning. "Immeasurable" means without limit;
or even with a limit, it is "immeasurable" in the sense of not being restricted to "only so much. "Without remainder" refers to the attainment of the foul (asubha).
Because it is not apprehended as something distinct [from the mind]. Although the object of the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) is indeed a "something" (*kiñcana*),

for the "something" that consists in the impact of an object, even the objects known as the counterpart signs (*paṭibhāganimitta*) of the attainments of foulness are like physical forms (*sabimba*), possessing a structural form (*viggaha*) that constitutes a "something."

It appears after being offered, but not so for this one. [Objection: Is it not true that even for the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the first formless attainments (*paṭhamāruppa*), there is no object that serves as a counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*)?
[Response: True, there is none; however, this [state] is not described in that way because its object is a counterpart sign, as is the case with the consciousness of the first formless attainment.

"By oneself" means by one's own self. That which exists by means of this is called "self" (*attā*); it is both a designation (*abhidhāna*) and a conceptualization (*buddhi*). Thus, it is a "being" (*bhāva*), namely, the self.
The word *bhāva* is also a synonym for *attan* (self); thus he said, "designated as *bhāva*, *posa*, *puggala*, and so forth.

Regarding these four—immeasurable concentration and the rest—it was stated that "their diversity is manifest. To show this diversity in terms of plane and object, the passage beginning with "But as to the meaning" was spoken.
It is not to be described by way of being limited (*paritta*) and so forth, nor by way of being past (*atīta*) and so forth, nor by way of being internal (*ajjhatta*) and so forth.
"Whose object is this?"—it is "of an indeterminable object" because it has as its object Nibbāna, being the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"So much" means it is of such a limited measure due to being defiled by lust and the other [fetters]; the meaning is that it is shallow and a limited state of mind (*parittacetaso*).

"Nibbāna too is indeed immeasurable" is connected [to the previous statement] by supplying the words "because of the absence of anything that could serve as a measure. "Unshakable" refers to the liberation of the mind (*cetovimutti*) of the fruit of Arahantship.
Because it cannot be shaken by opposing factors. Regarding the word *kiñcati*, since the root cited for the agent is in the sense of "crushing," he says, "it crushes (*kiñcati maddati*).
To show its usage, he states, "It is said that people... and so forth.

Due to their density as a collection and so on, and because they possess a delimited scope of their own function, the formations (*saṅkhārā*) appear as if they were possessed of a physical form; [this is] for the purpose of grasping at permanence and so forth.
In its substantial nature (*vatthutā*), it is called the "sign of permanence" and the "sign of pleasure," and so forth.

However, insight (*vipassanā*)—by effecting the resolution of that compact mass and dismantling the grasping at permanence and the rest—is said to "eradicate the sign. This is because of the absence of the object, which was the compact sign.
Why is it not included in the *Ekattapada-niddesa* (Exposition of the Single-Word) in the Pāḷi?
"Emptiness" (suññatā) is the liberation of mind (cetovimutti). "In all cases" means in the explanations of the immeasurable liberation of mind and so forth.
"By way of object" means that they are identical even by way of their objects, not only by way of their intrinsic nature and essential character.

"By this method" refers to the method obtained from the perspective of the object, such as "immeasurability" and so on. "But in another place," however, [it is used] because it is the cause for the application of terms such as "nothingness" (ākiñcañña).
Through another cause, when immeasurable and sublime sounds arise, they belong to this liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*). This same method applies to the others as well.
"By this way" means by the way of being expressed through those respective designations.

Having reached the peak of the teaching—which, by way of the vision of the truths, had arisen according to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*)—by means of Arahantship, he brought the teaching to its conclusion exactly following the sequence of the connection (*anusandhi*).
Furthermore, whatever herein has not been analyzed according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Mahāvedalla-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Cūḷavedalla-sutta*.
460. Since this teaching proceeds by way of questions and answers, the passage beginning with "But who...

has been stated in order to explain, as a whole, the questioner, the answerer, and the occasion for the question. "Lay follower-ship" (*upāsakatta*) refers to the state of being a lay follower who has not yet entered the path.
"Of them" refers to the eleven myriads. One whose faculties are tranquil and whose mind is peaceful through the tranquility that has reached the path.
“Will something happen to the noble son today? she thought, as she looked down the street.
She extended her hand to support him—that is, to take hold of his hand—out of her habitual practice.
“Externally” refers to something else that is dissimilar to herself. “By one who causes division” means by one who speaks maliciously.
Thinking, "It should not be proclaimed," he reflected out of a desire for little attainment (*adhigamappicchatā*). Then, out of compassion for him, he thought, "If indeed I... and so forth.

"This Dhamma" refers to this supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*). "The proximate cause" (*upanissaya*) is the wholesome state conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) that has been accumulated with a view toward turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
[He thought: "If I have such a proximate cause, it is possible to attain this; even if I do not have it..."
Thinking, "It will be a supporting condition for the future," she was urged on by a perfection of causes that shone within her like the flame of a lamp inside a jar long cultivated;
thus impelled, she said, "If this is so, grant me permission to go forth.
Through the merit accumulated over a very long time, gain and honor arose. This is because of his being endowed with a resolute aspiration—thus [regarding] the Elder Sujāta.
Because she had performed an act of supreme honor toward the Chief Disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara, saying,
"May I be a partaker of the Dhamma seen by you," and because she had made a perfect resolve consisting of a formulated aspiration by giving a gift conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*),
she did not suffer for very long while developing her meditation subject; through the ripening of her insight (*vipassanā*), she was not delayed for long.
*Kilamittha*. To explain this very point that has been stated, the passage beginning with “from here on” (*ito paṭṭhāya*) was spoken.
“By the second journey” means by the second journey undertaken for the purpose of banishment.
“Having brought forward” means having brought forward as the meaning of the question. “Sakkāya” means one’s own body (*sakāyaṃ*). “Something placed near” (*upanikkhittaṃ kiñci*).
"Accepting the site" means as if actually accepting it. "Single-noose" (*ekapāsakā*) refers to a single knot;
for such a one is easy to untie, whereas one with many nooses is difficult to untie. The mention of a "single noose" is intended to show that its release is easily accomplished.

"Standing on the ground of the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidāvisaye ṭhatvā*) indicates by this that the Elder Nun possessed the fully developed analytical knowledges (*pabhinnapaṭisambhida*). "Being the condition" (*paccayabhūtā*)...

It should be understood that Visākha thought, "It is not possible," and so forth, because the Elder’s specific attainment was beyond his own range, even though it had become a condition by way of its object and other factors.

[This is] by means of the answer to the question on the analysis of the truths (*saccavinibbhoga*), which consists in the discernment, differentiation, and distinction of phenomena included within the truths from what is other than them.
By means of answering the question concerning the analysis [of the aggregates]. "Two truths" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin.
"Having turned back" means having reversed [the order]. "A knotty question" refers to a question that has become like a knot due to its difficulty of penetration.
It is not that very same clinging which constitutes those five aggregates of clinging, because a part cannot be the whole, and [clinging] is a part of the whole.
And because it lacks the state of being a part [of those aggregates]. Nor is clinging something other than the five aggregates of clinging, because it is a part of them;
for a part does not exist apart from the whole. By the words "If it were that very same thing," etc., he demonstrates the fault in both positions.
"The nature of form and so forth" means the nature of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as the nature of contact, volition, and the rest.
"Grasping might exist. "Apart from [the aggregates], it might exist" means if grasping were to exist as something entirely separate from the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*).

"In another system" refers to the doctrine of a particular school (*nikāyavāda*). The statement "a latent tendency (*anusaya*) is dissociated from consciousness" is merely an illustration, because within that school's doctrine, even things such as the nature of mind, its absence, and consciousness itself are claimed to be dissociated from consciousness. Thus he explained.
“Indeed not, friend,” and so forth, he answered by way of the presence of desire and lust directed toward the aggregates (*khandha*).

He did so without digression, because his speech arose from a definitive determination of the meaning and the Dhamma; without being diffuse, because he was not confused regarding any of those points; as if kindling a thousand lamps by dispelling the darkness of delusion concerning the subject of the question;
and without leaving anything obscure, because he made clear the state of both the objects of clinging and the act of clinging for ordinary people.
It is hidden (*gūḷha*). It is concealed (*paṭicchanna*) because it resembles something covered for some who have not grasped the convention.

It is struck by the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇāhata*) because its object is the dhamma as affected by the three characteristics. It is profound (*gambhīra*) because it is the domain of profound knowledge. It has gained a footing through the penetration of the Noble Truths.

Thus, they have attained self-confidence (*vesārajjappatta*) because of the state of having seen the Dhamma and so forth. They have crossed over because the holy life (*brahmacariya*) has been fully lived.
"You too, in a future time, will dwell in Nibbāna"—thus she stands at the summit of existence (*bhava*).
Having extracted the phrase "regards form as self," he explains its meaning by means of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* passage beginning with "Herein, a certain person...
In that context, "regards as self" means he regards it as "self" (attā), [identifying it] with the selfhood (*attabhāva*).
He regards [it as such]. He designates himself as "I. For the proponent of self (attavādī) describes the self as that which is the basis for the notion of "I";

therefore, when he says "that form which is 'I'," he regards that which is called "my form"—thinking "that I am"—as his self, and thus he regards both the form and the self as non-dual and not different, thinking "that is my form. Regarding it in this way...
And thus, it follows that either the self is like form, or form is like the self, in that both are impermanent.
"Flame" (*accī*) refers to a crest of fire. If that were color (*vaṇṇa*), it would be cognizable only by the eye and not by the body;

or else, if color were also cognizable by the body and other senses, then because it would be non-different from the flame, the simile would be as inappropriate for the holder of the wrong view as the thing being illustrated. "By the vision of views" means by what is termed wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
He sees by means of vision, not by means of the contemplation of craving, conceit, or wisdom.

Having grasped formless states such as feeling and so forth as "self," he regards the self as possessing form because it is dependent upon form— just as a tree possesses shade because the shade is dependent upon the tree—
and because it is subordinate to form, just as fragrance exists in a flower because it is dependent upon the flower.

Because form is dependent on the self, one regards form as being in the self. Just as a casket is the support for a gem, so too, considering form to be the support for the self, one regards the self as being in form.

By the phrase "the same method applies," he extends by analogy the previously stated points: that feeling and the other aggregates are not different from the self, that they are its support, and that they are dependent upon it.
It is stated that "the formless is the self" because, as in the phrases "possessing feeling" and so forth, there is an absence of being mixed with form.
It is stated that "the self is a mixture of form and the formless" because the remaining formless factors, together with form, are apprehended as the self.

The view of annihilationism is stated because of the perception of the destruction of form and the other aggregates. For this very reason it was said: "If one were to say, 'Form is the self,' that is not tenable."
“‘My self arises and passes away’—thus it occurs to him,” and so forth. “In the remaining cases” means in fifteen instances.
The eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is stated because that which is grasped as having form, etc., has not been specifically determined [as to its nature].
Whatever basis a theorist (*diṭṭhigatika*) regards as the self, for the most part he regards that as permanent and happy.
[The worldling] indeed regards [them as self]. However, because the disciple has clearly seen that "all phenomena are non-self" by way of the opposite of that [view], he does not regard form as self;
being thus established, he regards it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and likewise regarding feeling and the other aggregates, [the Blessed One] said, "Form is not self," and so forth.
Thus, the view of existence (*bhavaditthi*) is also ignorance and the craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*).
In the discourse on views, it is stated: “By this much there is going,” and so forth; and in the discourse on the abandoning of views, it is stated:
“By this much there is no going,” and so forth.
Since the very same matter mentioned below was being questioned, it was said: “It should be answered by the Elder having asked a counter-question.”

The passage beginning with “Upāsakā” was spoken in order to show the method of inquiry. “By way of practice” means by way of being the path leading to the cessation of self-identity (*sakkāyanirodha*).

The word “by way of” (*vasena*) should be applied to each term: by way of the conditioned and the unconditioned, by way of the mundane and the supramundane, and by way of the included and the unincluded. In this context, while it is true that there is no path called “unconditioned,” what then is conditioned?
Or was it stated thus by way of the question, "Is it unconditioned (asaṅkhata)?"? By the word "noble" (ariya) itself, the supramundane nature of the Path is established;
however, since the path-factors included within the aggregates that comprise [the Path] might still be mundane, the term "mundane" is used here.
Although only the term for what is comprised is found in the Canon, and not the term for what is not comprised, those...
However, since those [factors] mentioned by way of being included are not actually included, it should be understood that the commentary employs the term "not included" (*asaṅgahita*).
Regarding the terms "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) and so forth: that which is made by conditions having come together and combined is "conditioned.
And such a state is the preliminary volition of the person possessing it; thus, "my path is eightfold."
"May it be sevenfold"—it is "willed" by way of the state of having been willed. It is also "willed" by co-nascent volition (*sahajātacetanā*), because that [volition] serves as its cooperative cause;
for that very reason, it is "planned" and "exerted. Because it is produced by conditions, it is "made" and "generated.
By one who "enters," meaning by one who correctly enters and arouses [it] within one's own continuum. Thus, by all seven terms, it is precisely that which is generated by conditions.
It shows the noble path.
Because there is a portion of the aggregates that is not included [in the path], the path is "with portions" (*sappadesa*).

Because these [aggregates] have no such portions, the aggregates are "without portions" (*nippadesa*). For a "portion" (*padesa*) is that by which a whole is indicated; it is a part. This [path] proceeds, hence it is called the "path. Because it is with portions...
"Because it is a part. "By means of the remaining parts" means by way of the constituent parts of the whole, since it exists as a whole composed of those parts.

Just as a city, being a part of a kingdom, is included within the kingdom because it is contained therein, so too the Noble Path, being a part of the three aggregates, is included within the three aggregates because it is contained therein; this is shown by the phrase "as the kingdom includes the city. "By way of common genus" means by virtue of having a common nature.

The meaning is: "precisely because they share the same nature. Herein, the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)—when understood according to its divisions stated as "nine thousand million" and so forth, and by way of the abstinence consisting in the undertaking of what has been attained—is "without exception" (*nippadesa*).

However, the virtue of the path (*maggasīla*) is "with exception" (*sappadesa*), being only the eighth factor, right livelihood, and consisting merely of the abstinence that is a total eradication (*samucchedavirati*).
The aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*) [is considered] by way of the limited (*paritta*), the sublime (*mahaggata*), and so forth.

Furthermore, because it possesses many divisions by way of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), and so forth, it is "without limitation" (*nippadesa*); however, path-concentration (*maggasamādhi*) is exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*) and thus belongs only to absorption concentration, making it "with limitation" (*sappadesa*).

Likewise, the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*) is "without limitation" because it possesses many divisions by way of the limited (*paritta*) and the sublime (*mahaggata*), as well as by way of knowledge consisting in what is heard (*suta-maya-ñāṇa*) and so forth;
however, path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) is exclusively supramundane and consists only of that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Thus, these [factors] are well-placed. "By its own nature" means that it is unable to settle by its own essence or by its own power without depending on a cooperative cause—that is, when not supported by energy (*vīriya*) and not established by mindfulness (*sati*).
"The function of exertion" refers to the act of uplifting the state of consciousness so that it does not fall into the side of indolence.
The function of non-floating (*apilāpanakicca*) is the function of not floating away from the object.
"Born together" means co-nascent (*sahajāta*). Effort (*vāyāma*) is like a companion who leans forward by placing his back [against one];

this is because it serves as a specific condition for absorption (*appanā*) regarding the object of concentration (*samādhi*). Mindfulness (*sati*) is like a companion standing by placing his shoulder against one; [it serves as a specific condition for concentration regarding the object].
Because it serves as a condition through its firm occurrence. As "activity" means the activity of assistance.

"Having struck" means having struck the object; for thus applied thought has "striking" as its function, and the practitioner is said to "make the meditation subject struck by reasoning, struck by applied thought. "Here too" refers to right view and right intention.
"By way of activity" means by way of the activity of assistance of the kind already described.

"The destruction of the grasping at signs such as beauty and pleasure" is the accomplishment of the four functions. "By way of being a condition" means by way of its state as a conascence-condition and so forth.
"Precisely by way of accomplishing the four functions" is a demonstration that it is the energy of the Path alone that is taken [as the subject]; for that is indeed one and the same.
Having performed the four functions, it is an "equipment" (parikkhāra) both by virtue of its aforementioned nature as a benefactor and in the sense of being an accompaniment.
By the phrase "of the states associated with the Path," there is the inclusion of the Path-factors themselves, and not merely of the contact and so forth associated with them.
"Occurring in a single moment of consciousness" means occurring in a single moment of consciousness by way of the arising of the Path-consciousness.

"By seven knowledges" means by the knowledges associated with the seven impulsion-moments that have reached the highest excellence, or else by the seven knowledges of contemplation (*anupassanā-ñāṇa*).

"Initial cultivation" (*āsevanā*) is the initial practice; thereafter, "development" (*bhāvanā*) is the increase, and "repetition" (*bahulīkamman*) is the frequent performance—this is the intended meaning when he says, "with another mind," and so forth.
This is the meaning to be grasped after having determined it according to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
A sutta whose meaning requires further interpretation is *neyyattha*; one whose meaning is to be taken according to the literal expression is *nītattha*.

"If this were so" means: if this sutta were *nītattha*, and if cultivation (*āsevanā*) and the other factors occurred through separate moments of consciousness, then it being so—cultivation and the rest occur through the arising of the mind many times, not just once; thus he said, "a single moment of consciousness," and so forth. In this regard, this is [the explanation]:
The summary of the meaning: A consciousness that proceeds by way of repetition might continue to proceed by way of repetition even for a very long time;
likewise for those proceeding by way of frequent cultivation and by way of repeated practice.
And herein, there is no fixed rule that only this many consciousnesses proceed by way of repetition, while only this many proceed by way of cultivation or by way of repeated practice.
It is possible. Thus, for one who asserts that the Noble Path consists of multiple thought-moments (cittakkhaṇa), this fault is unavoidable.

However, just as in the prior stage, the functions of right view and the other factors—such as full understanding—which operate across various thoughts, achieve their respective fourfold functions at the moment of penetration and occur within a single thought-moment;
so too, by way of the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) occurring during insight (vipassanā).

For those teachers who maintain that the acts of cultivation (*āsevana*), development (*bhāvanā*), and frequent practice (*bahulīkamman*) are each restricted to a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*) at the time of penetration (*paṭivedha*), there is no fault;
for the function to be performed by cultivation and the others is accomplished in that very same single moment of consciousness.

Therefore he said, "or they are restricted to a single moment of consciousness," and so forth. "If it perceives" (*sace sañjānāti*) means if it undergoes the state of perception (*saññatti*). "Gruel" (*yāguṃ*).
The intention is that he should be urged with the words "Drink! because he is incapable of engaging in a discussion on the Dhamma. 463.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of meritorious formations, etc.": by the word "etc.," one includes bodily volition and so forth, as well as the bodily formations characterized by them;
it does not refer only to non-meritorious and imperturbable (āneñja) formations. Because they are connected with the body, they are "formed" (saṅkharīyati) by means of the body.
It is not because they originate from the body; for those phenomena originate from the mind.
And the phrase "is produced" is said with reference to their presence when the body exists and their absence when it does not. "Speech" refers to the sound of speech.
"Constructs" means generates. Therefore he said, "produces. For a mind devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*) is unable to produce the sound of speech.

He is able. By the phrase "because they are bound up with consciousness," he shows that consciousness acts as the supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and so forth for them, and that it is the conditioning of the mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra-saṅkharana*).
"Mutually mixed": although the bodily formations and the others are distinct in meaning, they are mutually mixed by virtue of being the objects denoted by the terms "bodily formation" and so on;

thus, they appear as if non-distinct. For this very reason, they are agitated, intermingled, indistinct, unmanifest, difficult to illustrate, and hard to make known. "Taking up, grasping, releasing, and pushing away."
Whatever there may be that is to be grasped by the body, having brought about and accomplished these— namely,
grasping (gahaṇa) which is termed "taking up," releasing (muñcana) which is termed "letting go," and moving (copana) which is termed "shifting according to circumstances"—
the formations (saṅkhārā) that proceed from the body and are formed by the body are called precisely "bodily formations" (kāyasaṅkhāra). This refers to the shifting of the jaw.
The movement of the jaw. "Utterance of speech" means the emission of words; because they construct speech, they are here called "verbal formations" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*). 464.
The word "will enter" refers to the future state of cessation being near; for there is no purpose in excluding what is near and grasping what is distant.
This is because it includes the consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), which serves as the basis for cessation.

With the intention that one enters cessation starting from [the attainment of] the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is said: "By two phrases, the time of entering the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is stated.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "the mind has been developed," here there is the inclusion of the mind that delimits the duration, because the others do not exist immediately prior [to that specific state].
For [it is not so] by means of the minds that have attained mastery over the two powers, knowledge, concentration, and conduct.
Without the consciousness that delimits the duration [of the attainment], it becomes a state of non-consciousness.
"By the remaining formations" means by the bodily formation and the mental formation. They cease precisely in the second jhāna by way of non-arising cessation (anuppatti-nirodha).
The same principle applies to the others as well. The word "will emerge" (vuṭṭhahissanti) has as its object the future state of being near to emergence.

Because there is no purpose in grasping what is distant after having avoided what is near. And because the emergence from cessation is delimited by a single moment of consciousness, it occurs only within that [period];
thus he said: "By the two words, the time of internal cessation is stated.

Likewise, "the mind becomes developed" means that for exactly as long as the period has been delimited, there is a state of being without consciousness, and beyond that, there is a state of being with consciousness.
In that way, the preliminary consciousness for cessation has been produced.
"Having reflected" means having reflected and knowing that this alone must be done, [they attain] mere non-occurrence.
"They attain" means they enter into the state of being without consciousness. Now, why do they attain it for only seven days? Because of the making of a temporal limitation.
And this is because, for beings who subsist mostly on food, the appropriated continuity [of the body] lasts for seven days from the food eaten on a single day.
As for the statement that "all attainment of fruition does not arouse inhalation and exhalation," he said "it does arouse them" to indicate that this is not the case.
But as for that which he does not arouse, showing this, he said: "However, of this... [etc. ...he does not arouse.
Therein, "of this" refers to the bhikkhu who has entered the attainment of cessation mentioned here in the text.

Since there is no fixed rule that his attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) must consist of the fourth jhāna, he said: "What does this matter? and so forth. "Indeterminate" (abbohārika) means because it has reached a subtle state of being.

Some say that they cannot be designated as "existent. However, because the attainment of fruition immediately following cessation—which is not itself the fourth jhāna—does not arouse inhalation and exhalation by means of the practice of concentration such as the fourth jhāna that serves as its basis, these two are said to be "beyond designation" precisely due to their non-existence.
And it is by making this point that even the demonstration of the fruit of the attainment brought forth in the case of the Elder Sañjīva is [consistent].
It is well-established. Therefore he said: "This was stated precisely with reference to the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Regarding the phrase "at the time of the occurrence of functional [kamma-resultant] impulsion": here, "the occurrence of functional [kamma]" refers to the manifestation of bodily and verbal intimation; "at the time of its occurrence" means at the moment of its arising.
They are unable to formulate speech because their initial application and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) do not produce intimation.

"With qualities" means with flavor; "with its own nature" is the meaning. What is called "emptiness" (suññatā) is the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), because it is empty of lust and the other defilements.
Likewise, it is "signless" (animittā) due to the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, and "wishless" (appaṇihitā) due to the absence of the wishes for lust and so forth;
thus he said, "The same method applies to the signless and the wishless as well. The signless and the wishless have Nibbāna as their object.
Having done so, in the attainment of the fruit that has arisen, the contact is called "signless contact" and "wishless contact";
this meaning is extended by the phrase "the same method applies.
Insight into emptiness is the contemplation of non-self because it sees the selflessness [of phenomena]; insight into impermanence is the destruction of the sign of permanence.
Because it rejects the aspiration for pleasure, the contemplation of suffering is signless; thus he said: “Emptiness...

[and so on]... is also called insight. “He emerges from the impermanent” means that, by means of the emergence-leading path which grasps the aspect of impermanence in formations, he emerges from both the sign and the occurrence through either single-sided or twofold emergence. “Having discerned as impermanent” means...
And this was said with the intention that "even this is not invariably so. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
He says, "The same method applies," with reference to the application [of the formula] such as "the path of wishless insight" and so forth, and "the path of emptiness insight" and so forth.

Otherwise, a conceptual alternative (*vikappa*) would arise, because, due to the absence of a fixed determination of the arrival [of the fruit], it would result in a lack of definition. For in this way, there are three...

"Contacts contact": this is an indefinite statement meaning that "three contacts named emptiness and so forth contact," given that they receive their names from both their qualities and their objects.
It is fitting and logical (*sameti yujjati*) because a single contact possesses three names.

Nibbāna is called "seclusion" (*viveka*) because it is secluded from all conditioned things; thus, it is termed "seclusion from the substrata" (*upadhiviveka*). "Inclination" (*ninnatā*) is the state of being turned away from its opposite and directed toward that [Nibbāna]. "Sloping" (*poṇatā*) is the act of leaning toward it, and "inclining" (*pabbhāratā*) is the state of being released from that [opposite].

465. Because it arises from the material body (rūpakāya) that proceeds toward visible forms and so forth via the eye and other [senses], pleasure associated with the five doors is called "bodily" (kāyika).
That which arises from mental contact at the mind door is called "mental" (cetasika). It is described as its own nature because it makes one happy.
"Illuminating the state of being sweet" means making manifest the state of being desirable. "Illuminating the state of being experienced" means revealing the state of being an experiencer.
For it is feeling itself that experiences the object in the ultimate sense, while the object is simply that which is to be experienced.
With reference to such explanatory statements as "suffering" being a description of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva), he says, "the same method applies.

"Pleasantness of duration" means pleasant by virtue of its persisting or remaining, not merely by the moment of its duration. Therefore he says, "the state of existence is pleasant. "Suffering of change" means...
They are suffering through their transformation and their passing away, not by way of the moment of cessation. Therefore he said: "The state of non-existence is suffering.
For those who have not fully understood the basis [of feeling], the cessation of pleasant feeling appears as suffering. This point can be illustrated by separation from what is dear.
The same principle applies here to the statement: "Stability is suffering; transformation is happiness. Therefore he said: "The state of existence is suffering."
"Non-existence is happiness. For the cessation of painful feeling appears as happiness to sentient beings. Thus they say:
"By the subsiding of that illness, oh, happiness has arisen! "The state of knowing" means understanding according to the actual nature of things.
For one who knows a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there is happiness because of its subtle nature, just as [there is] for others in that regard.
The perfect awakening to phenomena by way of their specific characteristics and their general characteristics is the supreme happiness. Therefore it was said:
"From whatever [aspect] one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who knows."
Regarding the phrase "the state of not knowing," the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated here.
For suffering is an abiding in delusion. Another method: the "state of knowing" refers to the existence of knowing, that is, of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

For feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, when associated with knowledge and supported by knowledge, is pleasant and has a desirable aspect. As it is said: "It is both desirable and has desirable fruit. The "state of not knowing" [is its opposite].
Regarding the term "suffering" (*dukkha*), the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated here.

As for the question, "Which underlying tendency (*anusaya*) underlies?"—among the seven underlying tendencies, such as the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), which one proceeds by way of being an underlying tendency?
For they are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie latent within the continuum (*santāna*) by virtue of not having been abandoned; [they do so] upon obtaining a corresponding cause.
The meaning is "they arise. By this, it is shown that they are capable of arising when the necessary conditions are obtained.
For defilements that have not been abandoned do indeed arise when the conditions are met. Therefore he said: "In the sense of being unabandoned, they are as if asleep.
And these should be understood as future defilements in the primary sense, while those that are past and present are included by virtue of having that same nature.
Thus they are called. For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena (*dhammā*) due to a difference in time.
If the meaning of "underlying tendency" (*anusaya*) were merely the state of being unabandoned, would it not follow that all defilements (*kilesā*), being unabandoned, would be underlying tendencies?

We do not say that the meaning of "underlying tendency" consists in the mere fact of being unabandoned; rather, underlying tendencies are those defilements that have become firmly established by virtue of being unabandoned. This...
The state of being firmly established (*thāmagamana*) should be understood as the unique characteristic of lust and the other [defilements] themselves;

for this reason, it is said in the Abhidhamma: "He abandons the underlying tendency that has become firmly established. The word "it" refers to the underlying tendency of lust. "Not abandoned" expresses the sense of lying latent by way of its state of being unabandoned.
And because its basis, the aggregates, has not been fully understood, it finds no footing in those that have been fully understood. Therefore he said: "Not in all..."
“Because that [tendency] has not been abandoned in relation to pleasant feeling. And this sense of *anusaya* (latent tendency) is intended here in terms of its object (*ārammaṇa*). Therefore he said:
“The meaning is that it does not arise by taking all pleasant feeling as its object.

Furthermore, the sense of *anusaya* should also be understood in terms of its basis (*vatthu*), which is called “acquired by the plane” (*bhūmiladdha*). For this reason, it is stated in the Commentary:
“‘Ground’ (*bhūmi*) refers to the five aggregates belonging to the three planes that have become the object of insight (*vipassanā*).

‘Acquired by the ground’ (*bhūmiladdha*) refers to the class of defilements capable of arising within those aggregates; for it is by them that [the path] is said to be ‘acquired by the ground,’ and thus it is called ‘ground-acquired.

However, this is not so by way of being its object (*ārammaṇa*); for by way of being an object, all [defilements], whether past or future, would be [considered abandoned] even when they have been fully understood (*pariññāta*).”

Furthermore, defilements arise with reference to the aggregates of those whose taints are destroyed, just as they arose for Soreyya the merchant, Nanda the young brahmin, and others with reference to the aggregates of Mahākaccāna, Upāli, Upavāṇa, and so forth.
If that [object] were called "acquired by the plane," then since it could not be abandoned, no one would ever abandon the root of existence;
rather, it should be understood as "acquired by the plane" by way of its objective basis (vatthu).
"Wherever aggregates arise that have not been fully understood through insight, there, from their very arising onwards, the defilements that are the root of the round underlie them.
It should be understood that these are 'ground-attained' in the sense of being unabandoned," and so forth.
By the statement "This method applies everywhere," it is shown that [the underlying tendency] is not unabandoned with respect to all painful feeling, nor is all suffering [unabandoned].

He extends the application [of the analysis] with the words, “It arises depending on feeling,” and so forth. Whatever needs to be said therein should be understood according to the method already stated.

Regarding the question of abandonment asked in various places—namely, “The underlying tendency (anusaya) which underlies a particular state, when it is abandoned, is said to be abandoned in that state”—he says with reference to this: “‘What is to be abandoned?’—this is what is called a question of abandonment.”
“By a single explanation” means by a single response beginning with, “Here, friend Visākha, secluded from sensual pleasures...
He answered two questions: the question regarding underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) and the question regarding abandonment.
“He abandons lust by that” is one response; “the underlying tendency to lust does not lie latent there” is another.
The answer proceeds here according to the sequence of abandonment, rather than following the sequence of the questions.
The passage beginning with "In this case" (*idha*) is stated in order to explain in detail the meaning briefly expressed as "he answered two questions.
Therein, by the phrase "having made it thus suppressed," it is meant that having suppressed lust so that it does not arise again;

Having thus suppressed it, one eradicates it by means of the Path; by way of this, it is shown that one may say: "One abandons lust through that [Path], and the underlying tendency to lust does not lie latent therein.

Among beings who are being violently swept away by the four floods—namely, the flood of sensual desire and so forth—or indeed by the flood of the existence of saṃsāra, that [Nibbāna] is what must be reached after crossing over; moreover, because of its firmness, it serves as a foothold.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “The brahmin has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land.
Because they are of many divisions—such as the division of emptiness (suññatā) and so forth—the plural designation “unsurpassed” (anuttaresu) is used in the Pāli;
thus, after stating “the unsurpassed liberations,” it is further stated as “in arahantship” because all of them share the commonality of being the state of arahantship.
In this context, the suffix -e is used in the locative sense. "Of one who establishes an aspiration" means of one who sets up an aspiration thinking, "O, may I attain arahantship";
the meaning is "of one who aspires. Here, the word *anta* in *paṭṭhapentassa* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
But how does an aspiration directed toward arahantship arise? No [ordinary] aspiration has arahantship as its object.

Having made [a resolution], an aspiration arises because [the object] has not yet been attained and is not within one's reach. However, the aspiration arises directed toward that form which has been conceptually imagined.
When it is said, "It arises with longing as its condition," this refers to an indirect (paramparā) condition;
it is stated that there is no direct conditionality, and thus it is said: "It does not have the establishment of the aspiration as its proximate cause."
"...arises. However, this grief is to be cultivated because it serves as the sign for the abandoning of the unwholesome and the increase of the wholesome.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Grief, O Lord of Devas, I declare to be of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated. Those that succeed in three months are "three-monthly" (*temāsika*). The same applies to the remaining two phrases.
The same method applies here. Regarding the phrase "in this invitation": it refers to this particular occasion of the *pavāraṇā*.
"Pure invitation" (*visuddhipavāraṇā*) means an invitation proceeding with the thought, "I am pure. For this is the invitation belonging exclusively to those who are *arahants*.
Having stated "nor by dejection," etc., he shows that there is no state of being an abandoner of anything that need ever be abandoned.
This was stated by way of a method; explaining that, he said, "But this," and so forth. Whatever remains to be said here will be explained in detail later.
"Having taken up the practice" means having made an aspiration, having established a resolve.
"Reflects" means he speaks while encouraging himself by way of exhortation. "A state inferior in virtue" means...
The intention is: "What deficiency in virtue do you have compared to others who are practicing for arahantship?
"Suparisuddha" means perfectly pure, like a well-polished birth-gem, because it is unbroken and so forth.
"Supaggahita" means that energy is well exerted, because there is never any slackening. "Paññā" refers to insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) regarding its opposites.
Being unassailable, unblunted, sharp, and clear, it proceeds and functions having become heroic in the contemplation of formations (*saṅkhārā*).
"By way of method" means by way of that mental grief being a proximate cause for Arahantship. Since "lying latent" here is intended in the sense of the object, he said:
"It does not arise taking that as its object. In this context, non-arising is what is called "abandoning."
It is said: “The meaning is that the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) has indeed been abandoned therein.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), which is to be suppressed by the third jhāna, is itself eradicated by the Noble Path;

therefore it is said, “having suppressed the underlying tendency to ignorance,” and so forth, either because it resembles an underlying tendency or because of its similarity to one. The same principle applies here to the phrase “having suppressed the underlying tendency to lust (*rāgānusaya*). In the fourth jhāna—
It is called "does not underlie" because there is no performance of the duty that ought to be performed therein.
466. Therefore—the intention is [that it is an obstacle] by way of its opposition, its intrinsic nature, its function, and its condition.
It is described as a "dissimilar counterpart," as in such passages as "states with black and white counterparts. They are called "darknesses" because they are like darkness.

They are "few" by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). They are "unmanifest" (*avibhūta*) and "not evident" (*apākaṭa*) because they lack a gross state (*anoḷārikabhāva*). For that very reason, they are "difficult to illuminate" (*duddīpanā*) and "difficult to make known" (*duviññāpanā*).
"Such as these" means precisely like equanimity (*upekkhā*); just as equanimity is not gross like pleasure and pain, so too ignorance (*avijjā*) is not gross like lust and hatred.
Rather, the meaning is that they are like darkness—unmanifest, difficult to illuminate, and difficult to make known.
A similar counterpart (*sabhāgapaṭibhāgo*) has been spoken of in such instances as “an aspiration, an echo,” and so forth.

“In whatever places” means in whatever places such as suffering (*dukkha*), or in whatever objects of knowledge (*ñeyyaṭṭhāna*). A dissimilar counterpart (*visabhāgapaṭibhāgo*) is like light being the counterpart of darkness, or a remedy for affliction.
By “clear vision” (*vijjā*), path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) is intended; by “liberation” (*vimutti*), the fruit (*phala*) is intended. Thus he said: “Both these...”
“Dhammas are without taints. Regarding the phrase “in the sense of being without taints,” etc., it may also be said “in the sense of being sublime.
For that [state] is common to both liberation and Nibbāna; indeed, even the dissimilarity of liberation from the perspective of the unconditioned aspect of Nibbāna can be found there.
The intention is: “You have gone beyond the question; you are asking what should not be asked. This refers to the limit or measure of questions.
Not standing in a place where it was appropriate to grasp [the answer], he who questioned beyond that point was unable to reach the limit of the questions.

Regarding the phrase "of a nature not having a counterpart" (*appaṭibhāgadhammassa*): in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), it refers to that which has no counterpart (*appaṭibhāga*) by way of a similar counterpart (*sabhāga*).

A similar counterpart to Nibbāna has been stated by way of the future and so forth; however, there certainly exist conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) that are dissimilar (*visabhāga*). Therefore, in the primary sense—
Thinking that he asked the question with reference to something that is similar or analogous, it was said, "You have fallen into error," and so forth.
For how could there be, in an absolute sense, the existence of anything similar to Nibbāna—which is unconditioned, without a foundation, and exclusively permanent?
Therefore, he said, "This so-called Nibbāna," and so on.

Regarding the word *viraddho*: here, because there was no certainty [in her mind] that she would ask about a similar or analogous point, she asked the matter she had intended to ask while having missed it; the meaning is not that she asked out of ignorance.

By this, it is shown that all the questions below were indeed posed with knowledge, according to the method of correlating what has been seen. However, the Elder Nun, elucidating each of those matters she had asked about according to their true nature—
Having followed the Teacher’s knowledge of the teaching, he then gave his answer. “Plunged into Nibbāna” (*nibbānogadha*) means having plunged into Nibbāna and remaining there;
thus he said, “within Nibbāna, entered into Nibbāna. “Of this holy life” (*assā brahmacariyassa*). 467.
To show the wisdom (*paṇḍicca*) mentioned here as being possessed by them, it was said, “skilled in the elements” (*dhātukusalā*), and so forth.

For this very reason it was said: “In what way, venerable sir, is one wise? When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense-bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible—in that way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is wise.
This refers to the greatness of wisdom of the Elder Nun, who had attained the analytical knowledges of one beyond training (asekkha).
In order to show that [the Blessed One] stands having fulfilled the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), it is said: “Regarding great matters,” and so forth.

“By royal officials” means by those persons appointed to the king’s service. “By striking speech” means by the speech uttered by the Teacher after striking [upon] the instruments of action and so forth.
Whatever is not analyzed here according to its meaning is easily understood because of the method already stated below.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Cūḷavedallasutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta 468.
“‘Dhamma’ refers to the things grasped”: whether it be the Dhamma or something else, that which proceeds as a grasping held fast is called “dhamma.”
It is simply conduct. "At the moment of accumulation" means at the moment of the occurrence of that phenomenon which has been grasped. "Pleasure" means without difficulty;
therefore he said, "easy to perform. "Resulting in suffering" means ripening into an undesirable fruit. 469.
Just as the apprehension of their respective objects by the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, is established by their own nature, [so too is this].
The same applies to the mind as well. There is no fault in perceiving those sense objects as having desirable forms, nor do they give rise to any fault within the human existence;

such is the doctrine of those recluses and brahmins. Thus he said: "There is no fault either in sensual pleasures consisting of objects (vatthukāma) or in sensual pleasures consisting of defilements (kilesakāma).
There is no danger in enjoying sense objects after relishing them, nor is there any obstacle whatsoever resulting from that.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "They reach a state of being drinkable" means they come to the condition of being enjoyed.
For this prefix *pā-* has the sense of enjoyment (*paribhoga*), and the suffix *-tabba* functions as an agentive noun; thus the meaning is: "they enjoy it according to their desire.
Even defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*), when being relished, is included within object-desire (*vatthukāma*); however, it is by way of defilement-desire that these [objects] are to be relished.

He said: "By means of the defilement-desire, there is a state of being drunk upon the object-desires. In the phrase "by means of the defilement-desire," the instrumental case is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding "a state of being drunk upon" (*pātabyatā*), which means "to be consumed," the meaning here too should be understood according to the agent (*kartṛ*).

"Having made a crest" (*moḷiṃ katvā*) means having made a crest by way of binding the hair. "By ascetic female wanderers" (*tāpasaparibbājikāhi*) means by those who have entered the ascetic wandering life (*pabbajjā*). *Pariññaṃ*...
"Proclaiming" (*paññapenti*) is a synonym for the phrase "they have declared its abandoning" (*pahānam āhaṃsu*); thus it is said, "they proclaim its abandoning and its transcendence.

By this, he shows that what is intended here by "abandoning" is the thorough understanding of these sensual pleasures exactly as they are—as impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—and not merely their absence. "Māluvā-sipāṭikā" means a split creeper-vine.
“A bundle of *māluvā* fruit. “He would fall into terror” is said with reference to the occurrence of the deity dwelling in the tree;
for at that time, it occurred to her thus: “Resembling *koviḷāra* leaves” means having the shape of large *koviḷāra* leaves.
This was said by way of their shape, for *māluvā* leaves are indeed larger than *koviḷāra* leaves.
And they become denser. Having produced a great burden by virtue of being vast, abundant, dense, and massive—this refers to the *māluvā* creeper.
"A mass" (*ogha*) means the state of density that serves as the cause for hanging down from below.
The mention of the Andhavana and Subhagavana forests is because of their well-known renown. Among the species of grasses such as the coconut palm and others.
The observation of eating refers to the grasping at the rising of ants; thus he said, "they might rise.
"As if playing" means as if playing along with the flowing stream. Now, as if rejoicing, "I shall now overwhelm you," she flows on, quivering here and there.
Even the contact is pleasant due to its softness, smoothness, and delicacy.
"It is pleasant even to see it" because of its dense and thick massing of leaves.

"She became joyful" means that previously she had fallen into a state of terror due to the fear of the destruction of existence based on hearsay; now, being enticed by the sight of its excellence, she became joyful.
"She would make a canopy" means she would create a lattice-work by weaving [the leaves] lengthwise and crosswise. And being thus situated, because of its being covered with dense leaves—
"It is like a parasol," he said; thus, "it would stand in the form of a parasol. "The entire tree" means the whole tree, including all its branches and twigs above.

"Descending" means descending by way of wrapping around. "With branches descended as far as the root" means that, having bent down under the weight of the *māluvā* creeper, it climbs back up again with branches that have descended as far as the root of the tree. "All the branches... [and so forth].
Wrapping around all the branches—below, in the middle, and above—it entangles them by weaving them together in the manner of a network or a web.
Thus, by weaving them one after another, it completely covers them.

Having placed all the branches below and standing itself on top, it would shatter under its own great weight when the wind blows or when the rain falls. This is called the "palace with eight branches."

The celestial mansion was suspended from a branch. Since the Teacher here introduced a past incident as a simile by saying, "Just as if, monks," and so forth, it was therefore said, "But this celestial mansion," and so on.
471. "Of a nature with intense passion" means that, because it cannot be removed through reflections, it is a state of lust characterized by a powerful, overwhelming disposition.
"Born of lust" means produced from the sign of lust. "Every time he sees an object" means every time he sees a discordant object.
"He seizes upon the sign" means he seizes upon the sign in terms of its secondary characteristics, which serves as the cause for the arising of defilements.

However, out of respect for the training, he does not follow the path that leads away from those defilements; for that very reason, he [abides by] what has been commanded by his teachers and preceptors.
He indeed performs the disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma). Therefore it was said: “But he does not commit a transgression.

Regarding “taking by the hand, etc.”—this refers to performing acts such as taking the hand, saying, “Come now, let us go to such-and-such a place and examine what you have said and what I have said,” and so forth;
it is not done on account of compassion or loving-kindness (mettā). “One of a deluded nature” means one whose inherent character is thick with delusion (moha).
472. "By the law of karma" means by the law of karma established in previous births, which is determined by such factors as the predominance of greed.

Now, in order to show that predominance of greed and so forth through its divisions, the passage beginning with "For one who... is commenced. Therein, "at the moment of accumulating karma" refers to the time of performing the deed.
"Greed is powerful" means that greed becomes predominant due to the efficacy of the corresponding combination of conditions.
“Non-greed is weak” means that its opposite, greed, is strong. But how do these two—greed and non-greed—which are direct opposites of one another, arise in a single moment?

This should not be viewed as occurring in a single moment; rather, it is said thus by taking the moment of attachment and the moment of exertion as being simultaneous. This same method applies [to other pairs].

Regarding "in the sense-spheres": "to exhaust" means he is unable to overcome [the defilements]. For non-greed (*alobha*), which is associated with a volition (*cetanā*) occurring through such factors as unattached generosity—thinking, for instance, "this is so beautiful, so vast, and so precious that it cannot be given to another"—is truly unable to exhaust greed (*lobha*).
As for the non-arising of hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*), this occurs simply by obtaining the appropriate conditions for their non-occurrence.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are powerful. Therefore, because greed, hatred, and delusion are weak, we refer back to the very reason already stated.
"He" refers to one who possesses those qualities. "By that karma" means by that wholesome karma which has greed and so forth as its decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"One of pleasant virtue" means one who is amiable; he expresses that same meaning by way of a synonym as "one who is not prone to anger."
Weak non-greed and non-hatred are not able to completely eliminate greed and hatred, whereas powerful non-delusion is able to completely eliminate delusion;
thus, the meaning of the extended application (atidesa) should be understood according to the method stated in the first section, as appropriate.
"By the same method as before" means by following the method previously stated. "Corrupt" means prone to anger. "Harsh" means slow-witted. "Virtuous in pleasure" means one whose virtue is pleasant.

And here, with respect to greed (*lobha*), there are three single factors—namely, hatred and delusion (*dosamoha*), greed and hatred (*lobhadosa*), and greed and delusion (*lobhamoha*)—and three pairs—namely, hatred and delusion, greed and hatred, and greed, hatred, and delusion (*dosamoha*, *lobhadosa*, *lobhadosamoha*). Thus, on the unwholesome side (*akusalapakkha*), there are seven instances according to the predominance of greed and so forth;
likewise, on the wholesome side (*kusalapakkha*), there are fourteen instances according to the predominance of non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth. Among these, non-greed, hatred, and delusion...

By the arrival of the third, second, and first sections regarding the side of the wholesome— namely, "non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion," "strong non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion"— the sections on the predominance of hatred, the predominance of delusion,
and the predominance of both hatred and delusion are already included. Likewise, by the arrival of the third, second, and first sections regarding the side of the unwholesome—

namely, "greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion," "greed, hatred, and non-delusion," and "greed, non-hatred, and delusion" being strong— the sections on the predominance of non-hatred, the predominance of non-delusion, and the predominance of both non-hatred and non-delusion are included.
"Already included" means that by including three sets each within the unwholesome and wholesome sides, eight sets have been shown.

As for the other forty-nine sets—such as those where greed and non-greed predominate—which would have to be shown by way of their mutual admixture, they are not shown precisely because they are impossible;
for [they cannot occur] "within a single continuum without an intervening change of state."
Thus, [the statements] such as "greed is strong and non-greed is weak" are appropriate.

Alternatively, their status as strong or weak may be understood either by way of their opposites or by way of their co-nascent states. In this regard, greed is strong because it is not overcome by its opposite;

likewise, hatred and delusion are strong because they are not overcome by non-hatred and non-delusion. Non-greed and the others, however, are strong because they do not allow greed and the others to overcome them. And for all of them...
The state of being powerful relative to co-nascent phenomena is due to their proceeding with a predominance of concentration belonging to the same class. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“Greed is strong, non-greed is weak; hatred and delusion are strong, non-hatred and non-delusion are weak,” and so forth.

Furthermore, this state of being weak or strong in them should be understood as resulting from previous decisive support (*upanissaya*) and the way the underlying tendency (*āsaya*) has been cultivated.
For this very reason, he said, "by way of the sequence of kamma. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷadhammasamādāna-sutta* is completed. 6.
Commentary on the *Mahādhammasamādāna-sutta* (The Greater Discourse on the Undertaking of Dhamma).
473. Thus, those who have such desire (*kāma*)—that is, longing, wishing, or craving—are "those with such desire" (*evaṃkāmā*).

Those who have such inclination (*chanda*)—that is, liking, delighting, or disposition—are "those with such inclination" (*evaṃchandā*). It is a conviction (*laddhi*) that comes toward, or having adhered to, approaches in various ways;
this is the intended meaning. For that conviction adheres to the object to be grasped, thinking "it is exactly thus. By that...
They approach in that manner; having brought [the matter] into their own hands, they remain there and do not let it go.

Those whose underlying intention (*adhippāya*) is such as this when they are being spoken to are "those with such an intention" (*evaṃ-adhippāyā*). They have the Blessed One as their root—that is, their cause—for the realization of these things as they truly are;
thus they are "rooted in the Blessed One" (*bhagavaṃ-mūlakā*). Therefore he said: "For it is by depending on the Blessed One that we understand and penetrate these teachings."

"Our teachings" (*amhākaṃ dhammā*) is said because they are to be realized by oneself through those [teachings]. For the knowledges that realize things as they truly are regarding what is to be cultivated are related to the one who realizes them;

and these are rooted in the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), because their object is not accessible to anyone else. Therefore he said: "Formerly, by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa," and so forth.
"Those for whom the Blessed One is the guide" (*bhagavaṃnettikā*): the Blessed One is their leader. "Leaders" (*netā*) refers to the teachings to be cultivated.

One who leads the continuum to what is wholesome is a "trainer" (*vinetā*). A trainer is one who removes [the mind] from the continuum by means of those states that should not be cultivated; or alternatively, one who trains by way of "training through substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgavinaya*) and so forth.
One who inclines is one who proclaims for the sake of both leading toward and removing: "These states should be cultivated; these should not be cultivated.
Therefore he said, "according to their true nature," and so forth.
It is a "refuge" (*paṭisaraṇa*) because they resort to it; those for whom the Blessed One is the refuge are "those who have the Blessed One as their refuge.
Alternatively, it is a "refuge" because one resorts to it individually by way of penetrating its true nature;
those for whom the Blessed One is the refuge are "those who have the Blessed One as their refuge. "By way of penetration" means by way of that which is to be penetrated.
"Even though it is not actually in his mouth, he speaks as if it were," thus [the author] said: "Contact comes, Blessed One;
what is my name? Regarding the word *paṭibhātu*, because of its dependence on the prefix *pati-*, the accusative case "Bhagavantam" is used;
however, showing that the meaning should rather be understood through the genitive case, he said: "Of the Blessed One (*bhagavato*)," [meaning] "let it occur to [him]."
"And let there be a share for the Blessed One. The intention is: "For this is the share of the Blessed One, namely, the teaching of the Dhamma;
but our share is its hearing. Some, however, state that the word *paṭibhātu* means "let it appear," or "let it be seen by knowledge," or "let it be taught.
And *upaṭṭhātu* means "let it present itself to knowledge."
474. "To be relied upon" (*nissayitabba*) means that which should be depended upon by way of being produced within one's own continuum.
For it is by relying upon the third and fourth undertakings of dhamma that the prosperity of beings increases both now and in the future.
"To be resorted to" (*bhajitabba*) is a synonym for the same. Or, "to be cultivated" (*sevitabba*) is said with reference to reliance upon noble persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and wise attention.
"Bhajitabba" means the meritorious states such as giving, which are the conditions for that [bliss]. 475.
"In reverse order" means that the Teacher’s method of teaching is to first show the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) and subsequently show the phenomena of purification (*vodānadhamma*);
just as one says, "Release the left hand, take hold of the right," so too is it by way of this reverse order.
And that indeed [is explained] in terms of the first two ways of undertaking things; however, regarding the latter two, the matrix (mātikā) is set forth in their proper sequence.
"By the very nature of the thing" (yathādhammarasena) means by the very individual essence (yathāsabhāva) of the phenomena to be abandoned and the phenomena that abandon.

For the individual essence (sabhāva) is called "nature" (rasa) because it is to be tasted (rasitabba), that is, to be known according to its true state. Having first shown the phenomena to be abandoned, immediately thereafter—

The sequence of the teaching is the demonstration of the abandoning factors, [showing] that "these states are abandoned by these [factors]. Grasping (gahaṇa) means taking up (ādiyana), which is the production [of a state] within one's own continuum. 478.

Regarding the approach of one who is terrified of execution, punishment, and so forth, as well as the subsequent departure after having committed misconduct—the prior and subsequent volitions (cetanā) [are involved].
Through this [volition], sexual misconduct becomes painful to experience; likewise, for one afflicted by envy, malice, and so forth, it occurs through the volition directed toward another’s property.

In the same way, this should be understood accordingly for covetousness and wrong view as well. "Of the three kinds of volition" refers to the volitions that finalize the preceding and succeeding actions.
Regarding the four volitions that finalize—namely, taking what is not given, false speech, malicious speech, and idle chatter—[the result is experienced in the present life].
The method [of classifying them] as "associated with pleasure" or "associated with equanimity" has not been set forth here because it is already established [elsewhere].
Furthermore, the statement "here, mental grief itself is suffering" is said by taking into account that both the preceding and succeeding volitions are closely associated with mental grief;
however, with reference to those that are not so close, it says, "for one who engages in seeking," and so forth.

This has been stated. By this very fact, it should be understood that the preceding and succeeding volitions of wrong conduct, covetousness, and wrong view are shown to be proximate to, and included within, the volition that brings about final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*).
"Searching" (*pariyeṭṭhi*) refers to the quest for garlands, perfumes, and so forth—the objects to be transgressed—in the case of wrong conduct and the like;
and the quest for weapons and so forth—the means of killing—in the case of killing living beings and the like.
For one who is undertaking [the action]. Since their pursuit may also occur through what is not difficult to do, he speaks with apprehension, saying, "It is indeed permissible.
479. "There are pleasant feelings" means that there are also pleasant feelings; this is the intended meaning.

Since it is possible for those volitions to be non-pleasant feelings, he uses the apprehensive expression, "There are indeed pleasant feelings. And here, "pleasure" refers specifically to mental joy (*somanassa*).
This was stated on the grounds that both the preliminary and subsequent volitions are indeed accompanied by joy;

however, this refers specifically to the six types of misconduct excluding sexual misconduct. Regarding sexual misconduct, however, the statement that "even bodily pleasure is permissible" is a dangerous expression, as it pertains to the preliminary and subsequent stages of that very act.
480. With the intention that there might be even bodily suffering for him by way of the fever of hatred (*dosaja-pariḷāha*), it is said:
"Even while grasping, he is pained. Or else, referring specifically to mental suffering, it is said:
"Pained and depressed," in order to show its repeated arising.

"In all ten instances" means in all ten components or sentences. Since association with equanimity is also possible, the statement "they are indeed associated with pleasure" here is a cautious expression.
For one who abstains from taking life, even the body may be free from distress and fever;
thus, bodily experience (*kāyika-paṭisaṃvedanā*) can also arise as a result of the condition of abstaining from killing and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "even with pleasure" (*sahāpi sukhena*), bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) is indeed included here as well.

(482) *Tittakālābu*: a bitter gourd; it is so called because its bitter taste is loathsome due to the fact that when consumed, it causes madness and other such afflictions. It "will not be pleasing" (*na ruccissati*) because of its undesirable taste and its undesirable fruit.
(483) "Gives flavor" (*rasaṃ deti*): it shows or makes manifest the flavor.

484. *Pūtimuttaṃ* means urine that is putrid by nature. *Taruṇaṃ* means that which, falling in a stream, is warm; by this he indicates its upper part is urinated. For urine, when being discharged from the urinary passage, becomes warm through the heat of the body.
485. *Yaṃ bhagandarasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ lohitaṃ pakkhandatīti*: this refers to the blood that flows out due to the discharge of blood associated with the disease of fistula-in-ano (*bhagandara*).
*Pittasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ lohitaṃ pakkhandatīti*: this is to be connected by supplying the word [blood].
486. *Ubbiddha* means far away. For when the obscurations such as clouds and mist have vanished, space appears as if lofty and far-reaching;
hence he said, "having become distant. *Tamaṃyeva tamagataṃ* is like [the expressions] *gūthagataṃ* (gone to excrement) or *muttagataṃ* (gone to urine).
While analyzing this fourth undertaking of the Dhamma, it shines, glows, and radiates.
Because the wholesome course of action has been shown by way of analysis.

"Like a *saṅgara* tree" means like a *kandamāda* tree. "By way of *sarabhañña*" means by way of reciting word-for-word without analyzing the meaning. "Of one who is reciting" means of one who is vocalizing.
"In the sound" refers to the sound of the recitation. The deities were unwilling to announce the distinction they had attained.
Thereupon, it vanished right then and there. "On that day" means on the day the Teacher taught [this discourse].
Thus, because it was the sign of her own attainment of distinction, this deity cherished this sutta. The rest is self-evident.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Mahādhammasamādāna-sutta is complete.
7. Commentary on the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta 487.
"One who investigates the meaning" (*atthavīmaṃsaka*) is one who discerns meanings such as his own welfare and the welfare of others.

"One who investigates conditioned phenomena" (*saṅkhāravīmaṃsaka*) is one who investigates conditioned states by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), their general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), and their classification into bases (*āyatana*) and so forth. "One who investigates the Teacher" (*satthuvīmaṃsaka*)... [is one who investigates the Teacher].
One who examines the Teacher is one who considers him thus: “The Teacher is such-and-such by way of his qualities. “An investigator” means one who reflects.

That which delimits the mind according to its divisions, such as being with lust and so forth, is “penetration of minds” (*cetopariyāya*). Therefore he said, “delimitation of consciousness” (*cittapariccheda*).
Because one who has attained the knowledge of penetration of minds [knows]: “This consciousness has arisen after that; this [consciousness] arises after that,” regarding another’s...
He understands the arising of consciousness; therefore it is said, “The penetration of minds (cetopariyāya) means the section on consciousness.
For the word *pariyāya* also carries the sense of “turn” or “occasion,” as in such passages as: “Ānanda, who has the turn today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?

There is also the reading *cittacāraṃ*, which means “the movement of consciousness. “For the purpose of discerning in this way” means for the purpose of investigating in the manner that will now be described.
"Dependence on a spiritual friend" means the powerful support for living the holy life (brahmacariya) that is designated as a "spiritual friend.

By the phrase "half by one's own power," it is meant that half of the holy life accomplished through such a person is achieved by the power of one's own qualities that bring liberation to maturity. "Half by the power of the spiritual friend" means...
But the other half is accomplished through the power of the instruction of that good friend (kalyāṇamitta) in reliance upon whom the holy life is lived;
the meaning is that it is perfected. This matter is established in the world itself. For the worldly say:
“One quarter is accomplished by the teacher, for one quarter is due to his power;”
"Those who serve that [ignorance] are cooked foot by foot;
they are cooked gradually," so they say. "By his own nature" means by his own individual essence (*sabhāva*); the meaning is "by means of knowledge. "Good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*):
one who has a friend (*mitta*) who is good, noble, and beautiful is a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*); the state of being such is "good friendship," which is the quality of possessing a good friend.
Kalyāṇasahāyatā (association with good friends) is the proceeding or activity together with virtuous persons endowed with qualities such as moral virtue (sīla).
Kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā (alignment with the good) is the proceeding toward them with body and mind through a state of inclination, leaning, and tendency.
"Mā hevan" means "do not speak thus"; the sense is: "Do not say, 'It is only half of the holy life. Regarding the phrase "tadaminā," here "taṃ" refers to...
The letter *da* is a mere particle used for euphonic junction (*padasandhi*), inserted by changing the vowel *i* into the vowel *a*.
"By this too" means by that which is now being stated. "By way of method" means by way of reason. In order to show that reason now, the passage beginning with "For me" (*mamaṃ hi*) was spoken.
And just as here, showing that the support of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta-upanissaya*) alone is the distinguishing factor even in other suttas, [he says] "of the bhikkhus..."

He said, beginning with, “Even while speaking of the perfection of external factors,” and so forth.
