Therein, “factors conducive to the maturation of liberation” (vimuttiparipācaniyadhammā) refers to those qualities that bring about the maturation of liberation, which is to say, Arahantship. “Requisite” (paccaya) refers to medicinal requisites for the sick.

“Of great birth” (mahājacco) means one born of a noble family. “Physical conduct” (kāyiko samācāro) refers to such acts as approaching and departing, which are refined by mindfulness and clear comprehension, as well as ordinary conduct. For one who investigates...
For the investigator. "Cognizable by the eye" means that it is to be known by following the path of the eye-door.
The same method applies here for "cognizable by the ear. "Defiled" means afflicted, tormented, corrupted, and soiled by the defilements such as lust;
the meaning is that they are stained. Since those [states] are possessed of them, he says, "associated with the defilements. If...
Since these [qualities] are not cognizable by the eye or the ear, he says "But just as... and so forth to explain how they are described thus in the Canon.

Even bodily and verbal conduct are called "defiled" precisely because they are originated by a defiled mind; for such a metaphorical designation is applied even to that which has that [mind] as its cause, just as one might say, "lump-sugar is phlegm.
However, it is not [defiled] by way of concealment, thinking, "Let no one else know of this unseemly thing of mine."
“They are not found. Having said, “Venerable sir, we do not find anything to criticize in the Blessed One,” he spoke the words beginning with “For the Blessed One...
to show that there was nothing to be criticized. For it may be that one whose path is undeveloped is to be criticized, but not one whose path is developed.
This young brahmin Uttara followed him, thinking, “I will even criticize the Buddha and then depart. Thus he thought.
Because he had not remained steadfast in his own words on the day of the Great Renunciation, Māra, seeing no fault whatsoever, spoke thus:
"For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step;
yet I could find no opening in the mindful Sambuddha."

"Sometimes dark, sometimes bright": for one who is unable to maintain perfectly pure right practice exactly as it was undertaken, bodily conduct and so forth are at times dark and impure, and at times bright and pure;
thus they are "mixed" (vomissaka) by way of being interspersed from time to time. "Free from defilement" (nikkilesa) means devoid of secondary defilements (upakkilesa), being unstained by them.
“Blameless” (*anavajja*) means being free from fault (*vajjarahita*). “For a long time” (*dīgharattaṃ*) is the accusative case used to express continuous duration.
“Has attained” (*samāpanna*) means having properly attained (*sammā āpanna*), having become possessed of it (*samaṅgībhūta*); hence he says, “endowed with” (*samannāgato*).

Acting like a forest-dweller (*āraññaka*) for the sake of concealing his own unbecoming conduct, [he displays] “his maintenance” (*parihāra*), which is the state of being attended upon by people with sublime honors and respect.
"Atidappito" means excessively puffed up and arrogant due to such esteem from people.
"Na ittarasamāpanno" means he knows [this]. Why? Because virtue (sīla) must be known over a long period of time, not by a short one.
Now, by way of its practice throughout many births, the Tathāgata has for a long time been established in this wholesome state (kusala-dhamma).
In order to show that this was exceedingly wonderful for him, it was said: "And this is not wonderful," and so forth.
"In a forest village" means in a small village located in a forest region. There, in order to show the uninterrupted nature of their daily wandering for alms, it was said:
"They wander for alms. The same [explanation] applies here as well regarding the word "drinking."
This is the method. Salt is difficult to obtain because of the ocean’s distance.
At that time, it is said, there were sixteen thousand villages in the kingdom of Videha, all of them large ones. Therefore he said: “Having abandoned sixteen thousand full villages.
Now, why do you reproach me by saying, “Why are you making a hoard now?”—it is because he desires the object [of the gift].
Without revealing that [intention], he said, "Salt... do not do this. Gandhāra, wishing to clarify his purpose, said, "What have I done, O Queen of Videha?
The other, clarifying his own intention, spoke the verse beginning with "Having abandoned... The other replied, "I am speaking the Dhamma."
"Gāthā" refers to all these verses of their questions and answers. In that context, "pasāsasi" means you instruct as if stirring [the mind].
"Na pāpam upalimpati" means evil does not smear [him] because of the absence of mental agitation. "Mahatthiyaṃ" means connected with great benefit.
"No ce assa sakā buddhi," etc., is from the *Vedehaisī*: "The teacher, standing for my welfare, [taught] the Dhamma..."
“...speaking thus” is the demonstration of the manner of emerging through wise reflection (*yoniso*). Therefore he said, “And having spoken thus,” and so forth. “Renowned” (*ñatta*):
in the world, that which is known or celebrated is *ñāta*; the state of being *ñāta* is *ñatta*. “Attained” (*ajjhāpanna*) means approached.
By the mention of “renown,” it is shown that the expansion of fame and the excellence of retinue are manifested; therefore he said, “fame and the perfection of retinue. How?
"What is the purpose? What is the fault here?"—this is the intended meaning.

"Piercing here and there" means that, being intoxicated by the pride of fame and the pride of retinue, whether in a village, a monastery, a secluded place, or in the midst of the Saṅgha, he jostles other bhikkhus, thinking:
"My feet are such that they occupy the very space where the feet of others should be."
“Touching”: he walks as if touching the ground with the tips of his feet out of a desire not to touch it. “He inclines” means that, because of his humble conduct, he bows down;

he is not arrogant and is free from stiffness. “The state of having nothing” means that, having reflected upon the inclination toward having nothing—thinking, “One who has gone forth should indeed possess the knowledge of having nothing and have no possessions”—he remains such even in gain and such even in loss.

"Tādī" means one who is the same at all times; just as he was when there was no gain, so too is he when gain is obtained—thus he is "tādī," being identical in every respect. This remains true even when there is fame or when he has a large retinue.
Having become fearless (*abhaya*), he is "withdrawn" (*uparata*); because fearlessness itself entails a cessation from [fear], he is withdrawn due to having abandoned the causes of fear.
Furthermore, this is not for a mere short time, but rather he is "absolutely withdrawn" (*accantūparata*) because he is withdrawn forever.
Rather, having reflected upon the object that ought to be feared, one has desisted from it out of fear of that. The defilements themselves are the "fear of defilement" because they are to be feared.
This same method applies to the others as well. The phrase "seven trainees" implies that even the seven trainees have desisted through fear, let alone the worldling (puthujjana).
“Thaṇḍilapīṭhaka” means a bench similar to a bed on bare ground; that is the meaning. “Nissāya” means leaning against it, having made that his support.
It was not noticed by the resident monk who was standing at the door looking between the two benches.
“Asaññatanīhārena” means without a restrained manner. [He thought: “He has entered the lower bed while being afraid of me.”
Thinking, "He will be," he looked down at the lower bed. He coughed, thinking, "As you go outside, do not utter abuse and thereby produce demerit.
"To endure" means that even though he saw such a state of supernatural power, he was unable to endure his own anger, even while making a crackling sound.

"By the absolute destruction" means by virtue of being free from lust through the complete destruction of lust. "Without restraining by means of reflection" means by virtue of being free from lust without having first warded off the obsession of lust through the power of reflection.
In the manner thus described, there is the absence of defiled bodily conduct and so forth, as well as transgressions;
this is the purification of conduct, which, due to its long-standing practice, is known even when it occurs in association with others.

Because they are unstained and because they investigate the state of cessation through fearlessness, they are called *ākārā*—the means by which the intended meaning is made known (*ñāpīyati*) in its various aspects (*pakārato*).
These are the reasons that establish [the conclusion] through valid proof (*upapatti-sādhana*).
Furthermore, since they are defined by their function of making known the specific meaning as it is accepted, they constitute the fundamental causes (*mūla-kāraṇa*) for those [conclusions].
And while demonstrating the types of inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*), the Blessed One said, "But what, venerable sir, are your modes (*ākāra*) and what are your inferences (*anvaya*)?
Explaining this meaning, he said: "Modes are reasons; inferences are subsequent understandings.
For just as in the world one follows—that is, knows by inference—the unseen fire from the seen smoke, so too does the investigating bhikkhu [infer]: "The Blessed One..."

Just as one follows and knows through inference the state of fearlessness and detachment by seeing the uniformity [of the Teacher's attitude] toward those who dwell alone, whether they are practicing well or practicing poorly; so too,
one follows and knows through inference the state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) and the excellence of the Saṅgha’s practice,
based on the Teacher’s unerring teaching of the Dhamma, which reaches neither disparagement nor praise regarding persons who are practicing well or practicing poorly.
He knows; and knowing thus, the Tathāgata has ceased through fearlessness because he is entirely free from lust.
For whoever is free from lust for something does not see any fear on account of that—just as Brahmā sees no fear on account of the realm of sense-desire.
Likewise, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, teaches the Dhamma without error; the Dhamma is well-expounded because it leads exclusively to liberation.
He knows the Triple Gem as it truly is in terms of its qualities, thinking: "The Saṅgha is well-practiced because of his unwavering confidence.
By "bondage through group-attachment" is meant being bound and occupied by the attachment known as concern for a group, such as: "My co-residents (saddhivihārikā) and my pupils (antevāsikā).
By "that and that practice" is meant the good practice described as "those who are well-gone and those who are ill-gone."
And [there is] wrong practice. *Ussādanā* means exalting on account of one's virtues. *Apasādanā* means disparaging.

By the phrase "in both cases by way of what is based on the household," it is not precluded that there may be exalting on account of virtues—such as saying, "Monks, Mahākaccāna is wise"—for the purpose of encouraging others toward right practice, nor is it precluded that there may be censuring according to the offense for the sake of future restraint.
The intention of the investigator (*vīmaṃsaka*) also proceeds by way of investigation. The one who investigates the root (*mūlavīmaṃsaka*) does so because he is a proponent of causes (*hetuvāditā*).
Because the one who investigates the "knot" (*gaṇṭhivīmaṃsaka*) has not heard it from another, it is said: "he has reached a conclusion through the speech of another alone.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "by one who does not know the penetration of another's mind. By this [statement], it is shown that only a Tathāgata should be questioned.
Having brought inference (*anumāna*), which was previously stated in its general sense, to its highest excellence, he speaks.
For this inference has reached its peak, namely, the inferring of the meaning that is not within the domain of ordinary persons, based on the non-deceptive nature of the words of the Omniscient One.
Indeed, meaning is threefold: some is established by direct perception (*paccakkha*), which is the personally experienced, unindicatable mode of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

One [type of object] is established by inference (*anumānasiddha*), such as the impermanence and other characteristics of sound and so forth, which are proven by means of the dependence on conditions well-established in the case of jars and the like.
Another is established by conviction (*okappanasiddha*), such as the afterlife, Nibbāna, and so forth, which are objects of faith that are entirely unseen by ordinary people.
In this regard, when the word of a Teacher concerns what is established by direct perception (*paccakkhasiddha*) and what is established by inference...

He does not deceive regarding the matter because his activity is non-perverted; by his word, the trustworthy purpose is accomplished, for the qualities of a Teacher are for the most part of a trustworthy nature due to their absolute possibility.
"This is my path" refers to this minor quality of mine consisting of the eightfold morality of livelihood; this [path] belongs to one who does not know the minds of others.
For a monk who investigates, this is the range of my knowledge, the path of my knowing.
"This is his resort" means that his resort in me is only this much and not beyond this. For even in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, the Blessed One specified only the eightfold morality of livelihood.
"This much is the path" means that the path is only this much. One who is established in morality thinks, "This is mine," or "By this morality..."
Thinking, "I shall become a god or some other kind of deity," one clings through craving;
because one does not transcend that craving due to the lack of a cause for either the state of distinction or the state of penetration, one is said to be "made of that. Therefore he said:
"Not made of that, not with craving," and so forth.

He teaches by making it increasingly superior (*uttaruttara*) through its quality of bringing about higher and higher distinction in what has been heard, and by making it more sublime (*paṇītatara*) through the progressive refinement of that distinction. "With its opposite" (*savipakkha*) means having an adversary by way of the relationship between that which is to be abandoned and that which abandons.
"Having warded off the dark, [it is] the bright"—this category of phenomena is called "dark," and of this...
"This white [dhamma] is what abandons"—thus, having excluded the black, one speaks of the white; and having excluded the white, one speaks of the black:
here too the method is the same. However, in this context, it should be stated as "that which is to be abandoned by this. "With exertion" means with activity (*sabyāpāra*).
For in the continuity (*saṃtāna*) of volitional consciousnesses, where ignorance, craving, conceit, and so forth have not been severed, there is activity and exertion.
The meaning is "having the nature of producing a result. "In that Dhamma taught" means in that mundane and supramundane Dhamma taught by the Teacher.

"Having directly known" means having understood through the distinguished wisdom of the path that specific portion, which constitutes a part [of the whole], namely the Dhamma of penetration consisting of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna.
"By means of the Dhamma of penetration" means by means of the path. "In the Dhamma of teaching" means in the preliminary stages that have been set forth as the teaching.
He reaches a conclusion regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment, thinking: "Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.

He gains confidence in the Teacher, thinking: "The Blessed One is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One who teaches the Dhamma without error, far surpassing even those previously inspired by the faith of ordinary people. And he gains confidence in the fact that it leads to liberation, meaning precisely from the suffering of the round of existence.
Because it brings about deliverance (*niyyānāvahattā*). Regarding the phrase "crookedness, etc.," the word "etc. includes all other faults expressed by the term "improper conduct" (*asāmīci*). 490.

"By these reasons for examining the Teacher" means by these aforementioned reasons for scrutinizing the Teacher, namely: "by his purity of bodily conduct and so forth, and by his successive, increasingly sublime, and unerring teachings of the Dhamma.
"By the phrases that collect the syllables" refers to those very same [teachings].
By means of words characterized as collections of syllables that bring about the understanding of causes.
"By the syllables spoken here" means by those syllables known as *byañjana* (expressions), which manifest the meaning as it has been stated in this sutta.
"Conviction" (*okappanā*) is characterized by conviction, because it enters into the object of faith and becomes serene. It is the root of faith.

"By name" means that the cause for faith—which consists of unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda)—is called its "root"; thus, the causes for believing are such things as perfectly pure conduct of body and so forth.
"Firm" means being well-established because of the total eradication of opposing factors. "Unable to be carried away" means incapable of being removed.
He said, "by a recluse who has stilled evil," and so forth, because there is nothing at all to be said regarding other recluses, brahmins, or devas.
Because he had previously heard that “Māra approaches for the purpose of harassing certain Buddhas and their disciples,” he thought, “This Māra has come.
However, because he was questioned by a noble disciple endowed with great spiritual power, he was unable to utter a falsehood.
“These” refers to those already mentioned, such as the recluses who have stilled evil, excluding [the others]. “Investigation of the true nature” means investigation according to reality.
"Unmistaken investigation. "By way of its very nature" means by way of its actual nature, that is, by way of its qualities as they truly are. "Thoroughly and correctly" means properly.
"Investigated" means examined. The rest is easy to understand.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Vīmaṃsakasutta*.
8. Commentary on the Kosambiya Sutta 491.

"Because it was possessed by the *kosamba* tree, therefore the city came to be designated as 'Kosambī. Alternatively, Kosambī is the dwelling place of the seer Kusamba; because the city is situated not far from that [place], it is called Kosambī.
Regarding the phrase 'in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita': who was this merchant Ghosita, and how was the monastery built by him?"

In order to show Ghosita the merchant, starting from his renunciation, his exhortation, his response, and his attainment, the passage beginning with “There was a country named Addilaraṭṭha” is commenced.
“Delineated by fields” means delimited here and there by the land of the fields.
“Going” means going along the boundary of the fields. “Abundant milk-rice” means a great quantity of milk-rice; and that—
Because he had eaten very little on the way, his digestion was weak; being of such a nature, he was unable to digest the heavy and oily food.
Therefore, it says, "being unable to digest it," and so forth. He was born into a wealthy and beautiful family, and became known as the merchant Ghosita.
Thus, the story of the merchant Ghosita is told here in brief; for the detailed account, however, is found in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

"By way of intention" means by way of the process of intending. "Of one whose body is exhausted by food" means of one whose body is exhausted by the cause of food; the meaning is, of one whose body is exhausted through the depletion of food. "In an empty place" means in a secluded, comfortable spot devoid of people.
"Quarreling is the preliminary stage of a dispute" means that the abuse which serves as the cause for a quarrel, and what is similar to it, is called quarreling.

Unpleasant action is what is called quarreling (*bhaṇḍana*). "By way of grasping and touching hands," etc., means by way of grasping and touching each other’s hands after having become angry, or by way of excessive binding and so forth.
"Fallen into a state of contradictory speech" refers to those who have entered into dispute (*vivādāpannā*) by saying things such as, "This is the Dhamma.
Therefore he said, "that which has become contradictory," and so forth. Or, because it is dependent upon the mouth, it is called speech (*vācā*) here.
“Mukha” (mouth) is intended here; thus he says, “by the arrows of the mouth,” meaning by the arrows of speech.
“Saññatti” means making known—that which is to be made known as “this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya. “Nijjhatti” means the contemplation of that [Dhamma] according to its true nature.
However, it is stated in the Commentary: “This is merely a synonym for ‘saññatti.’”

If, thinking "I shall confess," one perceives an offense due to being easy to speak with and a desire for training, [the Teacher] said this with the intention that the side of non-offense is also possible here, saying, "There is no offense for you. However, it is indeed an offense. Therefore he said:
"He had the view of non-offense regarding that offense."
492. "By way of quarreling and brawling" means by way of the cause of quarreling and brawling. It proceeds according to the sequence of the connection (*yathānusandhi*);

for since quarreling and brawling are opposites to the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīyadhamma*), the subsequent teaching—which brings about their pacification—is indeed appropriate to the preceding teaching.
Thus, the teaching of the subsequent Sutta proceeds according to the sequence of the connection. "Worthy of being remembered" means fit for recollection.
“Fellow celibates” (*sabrahmacārīnaṃ*) means those who share the same Dhamma. “Creating endearment” (*piyakaraṇā*) means making what is dear into something even more worthy of being loved.
“Creating respect” (*garukaraṇā*) means making what is venerable into something even more worthy of being revered. “For the sake of gathering” (*saṅgahaṇatthāya*) is connected as follows:

because they possess the specific qualities of the bases for gathering, they lead to the gathering of fellow celibates. “For the sake of non-dispute” (*avivādanatthāya*) is because they constitute the bases for gathering.

It is not for the sake of dispute. And since they possess the quality of embracing [others] which is the cause of non-dispute, the state of concord and the absence of schism among fellow practitioners of the holy life is established by virtue of them;
thus he says, "For the sake of concord," and so forth. It is called *mettā* because by means of it one is gladdened (*mijjati*) or made affectionate (*siniyhati*);

it is the state of a friend (*mittabhāva*). That which has *mettā* as its purpose is *mettaṃ*, namely, bodily action (*kāyakamma*). For that [action], moreover, is originated by a consciousness accompanied by *mettā*.
Therefore it was said: "Bodily action should be performed with a mind of loving-kindness.
These instances of loving-kindly bodily action and so forth are presented here with reference to monks, because the text speaks of what should be established by monks.

By the mention of "monks" alone, it should be understood that fellow practitioners (sahadhammika) other than monks are also included. For a monk, every blameless bodily action is indeed comprised within the category of conduct pertaining to higher practice (ābhisamācārika-kamma).

He said: “Bodily action by means of a mind of loving-kindness... and so forth. Since the veneration of shrines (cetiyas) and Bodhi trees when performed according to the rules of conduct is similar to loving-kindness, going for the sake of that [veneration] is called "loving-kindness as bodily action.
By the word "etc.," it includes other acts of homage toward shrines, Bodhi trees, and monks—whatever physical activity proceeds by way of loving-kindness—that remain unsaid.
The intention is that even the word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka is being spoken. The three types of good conduct are the good conduct of body, speech, and mind.
By the word "thinking," he shows that even mere thinking in this way constitutes loving-kindness as mental action, let alone the cultivation practiced according to the prescribed method.
"Approaching the state of a companion" means being in their presence; for it is while they are actually performing [the practice] that one approaches the state of a companion before them.
It is called bodily action (*kāyakamma*). Rather than simply saying "the deity," one adopts the expression "the Elder Deity" (*devatthero*) to indicate stability through his virtues.
The term "possessive speech" (*mamāyanavacana*) is speech that makes known the sense of "mine.

For mental action (*manokamma*), which is entirely hidden from view, its manifestation (*sammukhatā*) occurs solely by way of generating intimation (*viññatti*); and yet, in the world, this is considered bodily action.
Without touching upon well-known gestures such as the movement of the hands, he said, "opening the eyes," thereby showing that the occurrence by way of vocal expression was not included.
"Gains" (*lābhā*) are those requisites obtained; they are requisites whose acquisition is pure. Even when being properly received, they do not...
Because they are not "righteously obtained" (*dhammaladdhā*), the term "righteously obtained" is stated in the Canon in order to preclude that [misappropriation].
One who eats without having made a distinction between the gift and the recipient is called "one who enjoys what is undivided" (*appaṭivibhattabhogī*). Therefore he said:
"There are two kinds of divisions," and so forth. By the phrase "dividing with the mind," he means: "Even by a mere arising of thought..."
It shows that "dividing" means "having divided," let alone from the point of the actual application.
By the words "while receiving... he sees," [the author] establishes a shared understanding starting from the moment of arrival.

For in this way, sharing in common is easily accomplished, and his duty of endearing conduct (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) becomes well fulfilled. "Vatta" refers to the practice of fulfilling the duty of endearing conduct.

“Must be given” means it must certainly be given. To show that even a designated gift (*odissaka-dāna*) is not prohibited in all cases for one who has impediments—because it is impossible for one with impediments to fulfill [the precepts] due to their own obstacles—the words beginning with “But by him” were spoken.

By the word “also” (*pi*) in the phrase “even if he does not give,” it is shown that it should be given to one who is immoral (*dussīla*) provided that there is a need. For indeed, what is called a “gift”...

Nothing was forbidden to anyone. There was a village named Mahāgirigāma on the side of Nāgadīpa. To dispel their anxiety, he said: "Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the qualities that are conducive to harmony...
[and so on] ...the food in my bowl is never exhausted. Having heard this, those elders [realized]: "He is one who has fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony..."
Thus they understood. It is said that even in his youth he was one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*);
and in order to demonstrate that this practice was not barren, he said, "These will come to me.

He said, "Do not worry about whether they have gone or not," thinking, "I am one who fulfills the qualities conducive to harmony; by means of what falls to my portion, all these bhikkhunīs shall be sustained."
Regarding the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), the terms "beginning," "end," and "middle" are stated according to the sequence of the canonical text (*pāḷi*) as it has been recited;
for there is no other sequential order for these classes of offenses.
"Torn at the edge" means like a garment torn at its hem or fringe; "fragmented" means possessing fragments or being broken into pieces.
Or: the same method applies here for "with holes" as well. "Mixed with a dissimilar color" means that half or a third part has a blended color;
"speckled" (*kammāsa*) means interspersed here and there with drops of a dissimilar color—this is the distinction between these two.
By the very expression "liberation from the slavery of craving," he indicates that those virtues are a supporting condition for turning away (*vivaṭṭupanissaya*). "By making [them] free" means...
By this [phrase], he shows that this is an exposition using the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*), [namely] "slaves" for "acts that make one a slave.

Because they are not the domain of the ignorant, it is said they are "praised by the wise. Because they are not misapprehended by craving and views—that is, because they are not misapprehended by the craving-misapprehension such as, "By this virtue I shall become a god or some other kind of god"—[it is said they are praised]. By this virtue... [I shall become a god...]
"Having sacrificed there, I shall become permanent, stable, and eternal"—this is because [the view] is not clung to by means of the adherence to views (*diṭṭhiparāmāsa*).

To urge that it *is* clung to, he says: "They lead to concentration," for what is called virtue (*sīla*) is for the purpose of accomplishing concentration through the succession of states such as non-remorse.
"Commonality" (*sāmañña*) is the state of being the same; by way of the state of the fourfold complete purity (*paripuṇṇacatupārisuddhi*), [it is so called].

Because there is no difference [between them], like that of refined gold in its center, there is a commonality through virtue; this is "commonality in virtue" (*sīlasāmañña*). One who has gone to, or approached, that is "one who has attained commonality in virtue" (*sīlasāmaññagata*). Therefore he said: "one whose virtue has attained a state of equality.
"This view which... refers to this very view which is directly evident both to me and to you, in the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths.
The view—namely, “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self,” as well as “The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
the Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha has practiced the good way”—is the commonality (*sāmañña*) of being of a like view.

It is the foremost because it is the preeminent state among the other qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*). This is because when this [view] exists, those [other qualities] are successfully accomplished.
It is a *saṅgāhika* (supporting) because it supports and maintains them by means of that very [structure], having prevented the rafters from falling apart; thus it is a *saṅgāhika*.

It is a *saṅghāṭanika* because it possesses the state of being a roof-peak (*saṅghāṭa*) by way of its uppermost part. It is called *saṅghāṭanika* because "the act of roofing (*saṅghāṭana*)" belongs to these [rafters];
or alternatively, the reading is *saṅghāṭaniya*, meaning it is "connected to the roofing" (*saṅghāṭane niyutta*), thus it is a *saṅghāṭanika*.
Having changed the letter *ka* into the letter *ya*, it is placed in the *saṅghāṭanī*. It is expressed in the neuter gender because it is taken in its general sense.
(493) Even the right view of the first path has this same nature; since there is nothing further to be said regarding the right views of the other paths, he says, "this view of the stream-entry path.
By "even by this much" (*ettāvatāpi*), he means even by the state of having a mind obsessed by each one of the [defilements] such as lust.
One is indeed said to have a mind obsessed, let alone by two or many such obsessions.
"In all cases" means in all eight sections. "Well-established" means established correctly so that the cultivation of the path leads to the subsequent full awakening to the truths.
Therefore he said, "for the awakening to the truths. That knowledge is: "Indeed, there is nothing for me..."

This is the knowledge of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) that occurs by way of the passage beginning with "that obsession" (*taṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ*). It "belongs to the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ*) means it belongs only to the Noble Ones;
for in their case, even a partial abandonment [of defilements] is worthy of being called such. Therefore he said, "not of worldlings" (*na puthujjanānaṃ*).
It is called "noble" (*ariya*) by taking the sense of "born among the noble ones. It is called "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because its cause is supramundane.
For this very reason, he said, “But for those who...,” and so forth. For in that way, it is not shared by worldlings (*puthujjana*).
Therefore, he said, “because of the non-existence of worldlings. “In all instances” means in all the other six sections.

(494) “Individually” (*paccattaṃ*) means separately within oneself, in my own mind alone. Therefore, he said, “in one’s own mind. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends [the principle] to the meaning: “I obtain *nibbāna*—the subsiding of the defilements—individually within my own mind.”

495. Regarding the phrase "by such a view as this": he said, "by such a view as this—namely, by a view such as the view of the path of stream-entry"—meaning that it is a reference back to the sense of the expression "endowed with such a view.

496. "By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of the intrinsic nature of being fixed in the five training precepts and so forth. "By way of formal acts of the Saṅgha" means by way of formal acts of the Saṅgha such as the practice of *mānatta* penance and so forth.
"A youth" (*dahara*) means a fool. "A boy" (*kumāra*) means a child. Since the term "youth" (*kumāra*) is used for both a young child and a young adult, therefore...
"Slow-witted" is what was said. For one is slow-witted due to dull faculties (*mandindriyatā*). Therefore he said, "due to the dullness of the eye, ear, and so forth.
Even so, since some who are in the prime of youth may also have dull faculties, the term "lying on his back" (*uttānaseyyako*) was stated in order to exclude them.
If he is lying on his back, how does he step upon coals? It is simply the touching of the coals, however it may happen, that is meant here.
Regarding the phrase “walking about,” he said “hither and thither,” and so forth. “Of people” means of elderly people.
His hand does not move quickly because his hands are calloused. He withdraws it quickly because his body is soft and supple.
He endures [the situation] with a view toward some purpose.
497. "Of various kinds" means both large and small. "Right there" refers specifically to tasks such as plastering with lime.
"The cooking of alkaline substances" is for the purpose of preparing the lime and other materials; "the fetching of water" is for the purpose of washing and so forth;

"the making of a pit" is for the purpose of applying a coating of turmeric-colored minerals. "Strong aspiration" means a firm desire. "A calf" refers to a young bull born from a cow that has recently calved.
“Apacināti” means he looks toward; the meaning is that he gazes. Therefore it is said, “he looks around” (*apaloketi*).

“He inclines toward that” means he inclines precisely toward the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth, because he performs even various high and low duties solely by way of fulfilling the conduct of moral habit (*cāritta-sīla*), and because he engages in them solely by way of wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
He stood in the presence of the Elder because, due to a lack of wise attention, he thought, “I will converse with this one or that one.”
498. He said, "endowed with strength," meaning that strength itself is what constitutes strength.
"Having created a state of need" means having produced a state of need characterized by a particular distinction through that Dhamma.
"With the whole mind" means with a complete and exhaustive mind, because it occurs throughout—namely, at the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching.
500. *Sabhāvo* means the unique, individual nature (*āveṇika-sabhāva*) of a noble disciple because it is not shared with worldlings.

*Suṭṭhu samannesito* means thoroughly investigated. *Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya* means by the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the meaning is "by the state of having realized it. Therefore he said, "by the knowledge that has realized the fruit of stream-entry."

These are specific types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) regarding the first path and fruit, distinguished by their modes of occurrence. For this very reason, it is said: "by means of the seven great reviewing knowledges. This, then, is the common explanation of the teachers:
that the reviewing knowledges described as "this is his first knowledge," and so forth, are indeed reviewing knowledges and not path knowledges; such is the tradition handed down through succession.
The commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the explanation of the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) of this text are common to and shared with the former teachers. Regarding that, he states the reason:

"For there is no such thing as a supramundane path consisting of many moments of consciousness. If it were to consist of many moments of consciousness, there would be a gradual realization (*nānābhisamaya*);
and if that were the case, one would reach the abandonment of only a portion of the three fetters and so forth. Thus, [it would contradict] the noble path...
Because of having an immediate fruit, it would follow that there is a state of being a "partial stream-enterer" and so forth, or else there would be a multiplicity of fruits;
all of this is untenable. Therefore, the Noble Path consists of only a single moment of consciousness.
As for the scriptural passage upon which the caviller relies to reject the single-moment nature of the Noble Path:

Showing this, he said: "Because of the statement, 'For seven years... For by one who says that the defilements are cut off while they are still light, it is effectively admitted that the abandonment of defilements occurs quickly, whereas the cultivation of the path proceeds slowly.
In that case, if the defilements were abandoned merely by the commencement of the cultivation of the path, what would be the use of the remaining cultivation of the path?
[The view that] they might be useless [until later] and that the abandoning of defilements occurs only afterwards—while claiming that defilements are easily severed—is incorrect;
for [the Buddha] will later say, "for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. Furthermore, it is because he acknowledges the sutta [as authoritative].
"Without having cultivated the path" means without having cultivated the Noble Path by making it complete. "Having understood the meaning and the flavor" refers to the unerring meaning of the sutta.

Thus is the essence of the meaning; having understood that as it truly is, and having thus refuted the arguments of the caviller (vitaṇḍavādin), the statement beginning with "These seven knowledges" was spoken in order to conclude the very point already stated. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* commentary on the *Kosambiya-sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the Brahmanimantanika Sutta 501.
The view that occurs in the form, “The self and the world are eternal,” is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
“Together with the body” means together with that state of existence as a Brahmā. “The abode of Brahmā” refers to his own domain as a Brahmā. “The impermanent as permanent.”
It speaks [of the self] because, due to impermanence, it does not manifest as a self. "Firm" (*thira*) means strong; the meaning is that it is essential because of the absence of destruction.
Because there is no arising or transformation, it is ever-present. "Absolute" (*kevala*) means complete. Therefore he said, "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*).
Alternatively, "absolute" means unmixed with birth and so forth; the intention is that it is devoid of them. Precisely because of the absence of arising and so forth, it is by nature non-perishing.
There is no one being born, or... pe... being reborn, because of their eternal nature. For he asserts that those inhabitants of that place possess an eternal nature along with the place itself.
"The three planes of jhāna" refers to the planes of the second, third, and fourth jhānas.
For the specific types of the fourth jhāna plane are the non-percipient beings, the Pure Abodes, and the formless realms. "He obstructs" means [he obstructs] even while it exists.
Being unaware of what is common [to others], he rejects it, saying, "It does not exist. "Gone with ignorance" means gone together with, or proceeded along with, ignorance;
for this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). Therefore, he said, "endowed with. "Ignorant" means one who lacks knowledge.
"Becoming blind" means having become blind due to being deprived of the eye of wisdom, or having reached a state of blindness.
502. This was said with reference to the uninterrupted continuity of the Blessed One’s dwelling in Subhagavana, [expressed as]:
"Knowing that he was dwelling in Subhagavana. However, therein, with reference to the Blessed One's absence at that time, it says:
"Looking about, wondering where he had gone. By the phrase "seeing him going to the Brahma-world," it refers to a sequence of several moments of consciousness.
This shows that the Blessed One’s journey to the Brahma-world occurred [over time], not in a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*).
Nor is it intended here that the mind is transformed by means of bodily movement—as stated in the passage beginning, "Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm.
Whatever else needs to be said on this point has already been stated below. Regarding the word *vichanda*:
"Departure from desire. "Repelled" means intimidated by the overturning of his adherence to views.
By the words "one who has come upon me," he acted as a support.
"Having entered" means having overcome his personal existence (*attabhāva*) by way of possession. For it is because of such overcoming that he—
It is said, "having entered the body," because it is as if one has entered the body itself.

For when deities, *yakkhas*, *nāgas*, and so forth possess a being, they suppress that person's ordinary course of mental activity consisting of physical actions, and by means of their own supernormal power (*iddhānubhāva*), they cause that person to perform whatever they desire, such as laughing or speaking; and while causing them to do so, they act according to the mind of the person possessed.
Some say that it should not be said [to be] "of oneself," because the power of success born of karma is inconceivable.

Others, however, maintain that just as at that time the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth belongs only to the person who has been possessed (*āviṭṭha*), so too does the occurrence of the functional mind (*kriyāmayacitta*) belong only to him;
yet, through the power of the possessor, its ordinary nature is transformed. For thus, a person of great power—
They are unable to possess [the corpse]; however, in the case of raising it from the dead, they enter the physical body and cause it to move by the power of their knowledge (*vijjā*).
But the rising of the physical bodies of Kora the kṣatriya and others, as well as their uttering of speech, occurs solely through the power of the Buddha.
For the powers of the Buddhas are indeed inconceivable. Thus, he stands having overcome [them].
He stands having overcome the entire world by means of his own majesty. "Jeṭṭhaka" means preeminent; or, because he is endowed with such majesty, he is supreme.
He "sees," thus he is "the Seer" (Dasa). Because there is no desire for specific terminology, the word *dasa* has as its scope everything without exception;
hence it is said, "he sees all. "All people" refers to the entire body of beings, which has received that name. [He] dwells...
He causes [beings] to turn; because he is supreme and a creator, he brings them under his own control. He is the *issara* (lord) because his nature is to rule over the world.

He is the *kattā* (agent) by virtue of being the one who causes beings to perform their actions. He is the *nimmātā* (creator) because he fashions the entire world with its distinction between the stationary and the moving.
He is the *seṭṭha* (supreme) because he is praised in the world for his distinguished qualities. And since such a one is the most exalted, it is said: "the highest" (*uttama*).
Because the creation of beings occurs in such and such a way, like their gathering together and dispersing, he said, “You are a khattiya,” and so forth.
One who is *vasī* is one who has mastery over his own mind through proficiency in the jhānas and other attainments. *Bhūtānaṃ* means of those who have been born.

Those who are worthy of birth (*bhavaṃ abhijātaṃ arahanti*) are the *bhabyā*, the seekers of existence; [the text refers to] those *bhabyā*. Therefore he said, “Beings born from eggs and from a womb,” and so forth.

“Earth and the other elements are permanent, stable, and eternal. Those beings who censured them by saying ‘they are impermanent,’ and so forth, being loathsome of them, became destined for states of misery at the time of death due to their speaking of things as they are not.
But those who praised earth and the others by saying ‘they are permanent, stable,’ and so forth, because they spoke of things as they truly are, attained the Brahma-world,” said Māra the Evil One.

Desiring to separate [beings] from them, he clarifies the danger in the thorough understanding and exposition of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by way of earth and so forth, both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*).
Therefore, he said, "Those who revile the earth," and so on. And here, Māra, by the mention of the elements such as earth and the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), refers to the human world;
by the mention of *bhūta*, to the realm of the Four Great Kings; and by the mention of *deva*, to the remaining worlds of the sense-sphere gods (*kāmadevaloka*).
By the mention of "beings" (*pajā*), his own station is included; by the mention of "Brahmā," the Brahmakāyika devas are included.

However, it should be understood that the Ābhassara and other higher realms were not included by him simply because they were outside his range. "By way of craving and views" means by way of delighting in craving and delighting in views.
Those who delight—that is, those who take pleasure—thinking, "This is mine, this is my self."

Or, they are of a nature to rejoice. "He displays the power of psychic potency (*iddhānubhāva*) to those standing under the instruction of Brahmā" means that he displays the power of psychic potency produced by those Brahmās assembled there because they stand under the instruction of that Great Brahmā.
"By glory" (*yasena*) means by power; "by splendor" (*siriyā*) means by beauty. "He led me to the assembly of Brahmās" refers to such [a state].
The assembly of Brahmās [spoke] because of their perfection in sovereignty and other qualities; therein he exhorted me.

"By the killing of the great multitude" means by the power that destroys the qualities which are the necessary conditions for the great multitude’s turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). "Infamy" means the opposite of fame, the power of actions that result in ill-repute.
(503) "A full hundred years" refers to a lifespan of one hundred years. "He lies near" is *upasaya*; it is simply a dwelling place (*upassaya*).
Regarding the term *opasāyika*, as he said "one who is a remover" (*venayiko*), he explained it as "one who lies near" (*samīpasaya*).

To show that the inclusion of the word "lying" (*saya*) here is merely illustrative, he stated "when I am going," and so forth. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the sense of "conducting" (*vattanattha*) should be understood.
"Lying on my ground" (*mama vatthusmiṃ sayanako*) means one who conducts himself within my domain or sphere. "Having pushed aside" (*bāhitvā*) means having made [it] low.
"Having overcome. Regarding the term "a cluster of *jajjharikā* plants": here, *jajjharikā* refers to a species of shrub that grows spreading across the ground.
"By this" refers to the statement beginning with, "If you, O bhikkhu... This one is Brahmā. "Entices" means he wins over.
"Disparages" means he rebukes. "By the remaining phrases" refers to these: "one who dwells in the very place [of the offense], one who may be treated as one pleases, and one who is to be excluded."
"With your feet": "You will take up my protection" means you will be my guardian.
"Lakuṇḍakataran" means one who is lower, inferior in conduct and physique.
He does not see anything capable of even touching him, let alone possessing the power of knowledge; such is the intended meaning. "Nipphattiṃ" means...
"Resulting" (*nipphajjana*) means "fructifying. For that [result] is called a "destination" (*gati*) because it is to be gone to and attained by way of its cause.
"Majesty" (*ānubhāva*) means "power" (*pabhāva*). For that is called "splendor" (*juti*) in the sense of shining and illuminating.
One is called "of great influence" (*mahesakkha*) because one is declared to be "a great lord" (*mahesi*) due to overcoming others by means of great majesty. And this—
He said, "of great fame and great retinue," because he surpasses others through the perfection of his renown and the perfection of his following.
"They circumambulate" means they revolve keeping Mount Sineru to their right. Regarding the word "disā" (directions), this is an accusative plural used in the sense of a locative;
thus he said, "shining in the directions. This is either by means of their own radiance or by means of their divine splendor. "By them" refers to the moon and the sun.
"By that measure" means by whatever measure constitutes one world-system known as a *lokadhātu* illuminated by the moon and sun;
by that measure. This *cakkavāḷa* is the most excellent, supreme, and preeminent place for the arising of Buddhas;
therefore, the deities who are mostly reborn here surpass the deities in other *cakkavāḷas*.
They proceed. For indeed, Brahmā Sahampati, accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand Brahmās, approached the Blessed One.
Therefore he said: "In this thousandfold world-system, your authority prevails.
Now, in order to show the nature of that exercise of authority which was stated as "your authority prevails here," [the text] says: "And you know both the higher and the lower," and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, showing that the meaning should be understood by bringing the word *ettha* (here) from the first verse, he said:
"In this thousandfold world-system. "High and low" means superior and inferior by way of birth, family, appearance, wealth, retinue, and so forth.
By the phrase "this one is prosperous, this one is an ordinary human," it is shown that he knows the higher and lower states of beings according to their actual form.

This shows that [the knowledge] is not by way of full realization (*samudāgama*). However, as for what he will say—“the coming and going of beings”—that is stated with reference merely to the knowing of the taking up and laying down of beings in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), and not to the knowing of kamma and its result (*vipāka*).

For if he were to know it by way of full realization, he would have to know his own [coming and going] as well, yet he does not possess such [knowledge]; thus he said: “‘In this state of being’ (*itthambhāva*)...”
"This is the world-system" (*cakkavāḷa*), and so forth. It is called "lust" (*rāga*) because it is conjoined with lust, or because it possesses lust;

one whose nature is to be free from passion is "dispassionate" (*virāgī*); [the phrase] "to him who is dispassionate toward lust" refers to that. You are named Sahassibrahmā because you know only this minor world-system (*lokadhātu*).
The word "from" (*tāya*) is used in the instrumental case to express the source. "Of four cubits" (*catuhatthāya*) refers to the measure of cloth that can be made by many hands using a loom.
He restrains [the mind] by thinking: "One who strives to make a ragged cloth four cubits long and two cubits wide is like one attempting to submerge his ankles in water;
not knowing the proper measure, he is frustrated. (504) "That body" refers to that very same collection.
"Even when reaching the state that ought to be known" means: "This is mine, unique and not shared with others."

"Let alone such specific virtues as morality and the rest; even having attained such a mundane and limited field of knowledge as this, he is 'nīceyyo,' meaning one who is exceedingly low among these [others].
Its abstract state is 'nīceyyatā' (the quality of being lowly). Thus he said: "But from where could there be in me a state of being even lower than you?"
"One reborn below" means one who, having passed away from higher and higher realms, has obtained rebirth in a lower one.

To show this matter stated in brief in detail, he said, "when the arising of a Buddha has not yet occurred. "Having made [the aspiration] for rebirth below" means having made an aspiration for rebirth below.
Just as when someone has committed many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), that which among them is the weightiest and most powerful—
That [factor] alone gives the rebirth-linking; the others, however, merely provide support for it and do not give the rebirth-linking themselves.

Likewise, when the four fine-material jhānas have been developed, that one which is most predominant—whether through zeal, aspiration, resolve, or other means, and thus accompanied by volitional effort—that alone gives the rebirth-linking; the others, however, do so because they find no opportunity for it.
They provide reinforcement but do not provide rebirth-linking; rather, it is by means of the very jhāna produced therein that there is the manifestation of renewed existence in the future.
Thus he said, "having developed the sublime third jhāna. "Therein" means in the Subhakiṇha Brahmā-world.
"Again, there" means in the Ābhassara Brahmā-world. "At the first time" means at the first moment of that existence. "Both" means...
Both [the place] where one was born in the past and the kamma performed by oneself that served as the cause for being born there—
having forgotten both because of the great length of time, one "passes" or "proceeds" [through it]. This refers to the activity occurring at the moment of its occurrence,
taking that specific moment of the action as the basis.
*Apāyesi*: he caused [them] to drink. *Pipāsita*: thirsty. *Ghamma*: during the hot season. *Sampareta*:

overcome by the heat of the summer and by thirst. *Taṃ*: that gift of water. *Vata-sīlavatta*: a vow that has become a duty through the act of undertaking it, and a virtuous practice because it has been habitually observed as a state of moral conduct.
*Suttappabuddho va anussarāmī*: "I remember as if just awakened from sleep"—that is, like one who has just woken up after having slept.
"I recall your dream from your former existence by means of my knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*);
the meaning is that I see it directly, as if with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
"Karamara" means those who have been brought back after being plundered. "Kammasajja" means prepared for battle; the meaning is "one who provides weapons."

"At Eṇīkūla" means at a spot on the bank of the Ganges that had acquired the name "Eṇīkūla" due to the abundance of *eṇī* deer. "Being led away as a captive" means being led from one's own place by thieves for the purpose of making them a prisoner or a slave.

"Having established a friendship through marriage alliances" means having formed a bond of friendship with them. "While we were thus sporting, the Ganges elephant became enraged"—they did not even perceive this thought in me. "The roar of the *susukāra*" refers to the terrifying hissing of the *susū* snake.

*Gahitanāvan* means a boat that has been seized—that is, held fast—in order to obstruct its course with the intent to harm it. *Luddena* means by one who is cruel. *Manussakappa* means [the act] out of a desire to harm the people who have boarded the boat.

*Baddhacaro* means one whose conduct is bound [to another]; therefore he said, "a pupil. *Taṃ nissāyeva* means that even though he was being attended upon by the king, he abandoned the king and relied solely on that pupil.
*Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññī* means he thought and esteemed him thus: "This one is truly wise and endowed with the observance of vows."
"In various states of existence" means in diverse and distinct individual existences (*attabhāva*).
"Categorically" means with absolute certainty. "'This is my life-span' means this aforementioned life-span as it occurs in various respective existences is mine.
Not only do you know my life-span, but you also know all else that is to be known; there is nothing unknown to you.
Indeed, there is a reason for this. For you are the Buddha, the Fully Enlightened One. If it were not so, how could this matter be known?
For it is precisely because of your state as the Fully Enlightened One that this blazing, radiant majesty stands illuminating the entire Brahma-world and shining with celestial splendor;
thus he proclaimed the Teacher’s peerless equality.
“By way of the earth-nature” means by way of the earth-essence. Therefore he said, “by way of the earth-characteristic.

And here, since there is a need to grasp Nibbāna by way of the non-characteristic of earth—both generally, through such phrases as “the stilling of all formations,” and specifically, through “wherein there is no earth”—he says “of the earth” in order to exclude that [non-characteristic] and to grasp the characteristic of earth that is not shared with anything else.
It is said, "by way of the earth-nature. "Did not reach" means he did not attain it. Here, "reaching the earth" refers to grasping it as "this is mine," and so forth;
thus he said, "he did not grasp it through the seizures of craving, views, and conceit. "Because of being one who speaks" means because of having a habit of speaking.
"Having pointed out every single syllable" refers to [the passage] beginning with, "O Brahmā, I have indeed seen everything," and so on.
The Blessed One, having demonstrated by way of repetition the word *sabba* thus: "If, dear sir, you have not experienced everything in its entirety," [the opponent] seizes upon a fault in the letter;

for when the Blessed One employed the word *sabba* with reference to the *sakkāya-sabba* (the all that is the basis of identity), [the opponent]—by means of a shift in meaning based on a literal totality (*sabbasabba*) and through the commonality of the denotability of the word *sabba*—seizes upon a flaw in the phrasing.
And thus he apprehends a fault. Therefore he said, “But the Teacher,” and so forth.
In that context, if one asks of the world without remainder, “Does everything not exist? on the grounds that everything has not been experienced, [the response is:

if everything were unexperienced and unattained in its totality and its entire nature, then it would be nothing at all, like a flower in the sky. Now, if for him there exists something unexperienced...
If there exists anything not experienced by way of its entirety, then this statement “all” is false;
the intention is that such a thing would not truly be "all. Therefore he said, "May it not be empty for you," and so forth.
[The opponent thinks: "I shall speak of 'all,' yet I shall speak of that which is not experienced; I shall say both 'all' and 'not experienced.'"

And I shall explain [this], for what fault is there here? This is the intended meaning. "Bringing forward the reason" means pointing out the reason for the existence of that which has not been experienced by anyone as a universal.
"To be known" means it is to be known specifically through the knowledge of reviewing the path and fruit, owing to its distinction from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*).
"Invisible" (*anidassana*): this refers to Nibbāna in the dyad of "visible" and "invisible."

The phrase "because it does not come within the range of eye-consciousness, it is called 'non-demonstrable'" is stated with the intention of showing its association with the second term [of the compound].
Alternatively, it is "non-demonstrable" (anidassana) because there is no demonstration (nidassana) of it due to its being devoid of all conditioned things (saṅkhata).
It is "infinite" (ananta) because there is no end to it. Thus it was said: "And that," and so forth.
“Beings” (*bhūtāni*) means those produced by conditions. “Unproduced” (*asambhūtam*) means not produced by conditions; the meaning is “Nirvana.

Because of the absolute absence of causes for the state of being dimly radiant, it shines forth from all sides; thus it is “all-shining” (*sabbatopabham*). Therefore he said, “Because of Nirvana,” and so forth.
For it has been stated: “Darkness is not found there. “Only abundant” (*pabhūtam eva*) means by way of its preeminent state.
It exists precisely by way of its supreme state. Because it does not point out [anything else] due to its formless nature, it shines forth from every direction and is found everywhere;
thus it is called *sabbatopabhaṃ*. Therefore he said, "in the eastern direction and so forth. It is called *pabha* because they enter (*pavisanti*) into it;
this is stated by changing the letter *sa* to *bha* and eliding the letter *vi*. Therefore he said, "of the bathing place..."

"By name. "He established his own position": by saying, "Thus everything was spoken by me, even that which has not been experienced," the Blessed One, while refuting Brahmā—who had grasped at fault out of haste and without reflection because he did not understand the intended meaning—established his own position, asserting: "That [criticism] is wrong."
"Whatever has been grasped": this refers to the various graspings such as "this is permanent," and so forth.

Having been made to relinquish these by the Teacher—who refuted them by pointing out the defects in each instance—and finding no doctrine of his own to accept as a refuge, he wished to conceal his defeat;
thus, desiring to perform a playful display of psychic power (*iddhi*), he abandoned his argument.
"If you are able to vanish from me," the intention is, "but you will not be able [to remain].

"Desiring to go to the root-rebirth" means desiring to stand with his own natural physical form (*attabhāva*); for that is called the "root-rebirth" because it is similar to what is produced at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Of others" refers to other Brahmās belonging to lower bodies. He did not give [the gift] by means of a body that had been specially fashioned (*abhisaṅkhata-kāya*).
"Let it be; let it not be in its natural form"—thus he resolved in his mind.
Because he was unable to remove that conditioned body, he began to create a darkness to conceal his physical form. The Teacher dispelled that darkness.
Therefore it is said: "Or the root-relinking," and so forth.
"Bhavevāhan" means "I [will remain] in existence itself. Showing that this word "eva" (itself/only) is used in the sense of exclusion (*aṭṭhāna*), he said:
"Having seen fear in existence itself," meaning having seen, with the eye of knowledge, the fear of birth and so forth in all forms of existence exactly as they are.

"Sattabhava" refers to existence known as a "being" (*satta*). For the designation "being" is applied to the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) when it has the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) as its condition.
They discern liberation (*vibhava*). Even while seeking it, because they have not yet attained the means, they see only existence (*bhava*).

Or rather, the meaning here should be understood as follows: seeing "existence" for those beings who seek non-existence (*vibhava*), and seeing "arising in existences" for those beings who seek liberation (*nibbāna*) as non-existence. They do not welcome it, because there is no mode of welcoming such as "O, what happiness! [in this state].
He did not adhere; this is a term for a characteristic (*lakkhaṇavacana*). Or, since the word *abhivāda* has the sense of "entering" (*gāha*), he said, "he did not enter," meaning "he did not seek.
Here, by the mention of "existence" (*bhava*), the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is indicated; by the mention of "delight" (*nandi*), the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);

by the mention of "non-existence" (*vibhava*), the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and by the phrase "they did not cling to delight," the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is made manifest. Thus he said, "Thus, the four..."
"Proclaiming the Truths. This was the Teacher’s demonstration of the analysis of the Four Noble Truths through this verse.
However, as he proclaimed the Truths in detail according to the inclinations of those Brahmās, he brought them to insight and reached the climax of his teaching with the attainment of Arahantship.
And of those Brahmās, some attained the fruit of Stream-entry, and some the fruit of Once-returning.
Some were established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and some in arhatship (arahatta). Therefore it was said:

"The Teacher taught the Dhamma, proclaiming the Truths," and so forth. "Astonished" (acchariyajāta) means having become struck with wonder. "Existence with its root" (samūlaṃ bhavaṃ) refers to existence together with its roots, namely craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā).
"They have transcended my domain" (mama vasaṃ ativattitāni) means they have completely surpassed my sphere through the path that transcends the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
They have been transcended. But how does he know their attainment of the noble plane? From grasping the method:
"When the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma, revealing the peril in saṃsāra and the benefit in nibbāna, he makes nibbāna as if already seen by those people who are ready to be trained;
his teaching is not barren, it is not fruitless, like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra."
"And by his command, those who abide [in the path] are no longer seen within saṃsāra"—thus he knows through inference based on grasping the method.

"If you have awakened thus" means: just as you speak of the perfect awakening to truth for others, so too, in accordance with yourself, you stand having penetrated the Dhamma through self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) as one who has awakened. "Do not bring that Dhamma [to me]"—meaning do not lead me toward that Dhamma.
He did not cause her to attain the realization of a disciple regarding the Dharma she had penetrated.
By "this," Māra refers specifically to the aforementioned establishment in the Brahma-world; showing this, he says, "When [the Buddha] has not arisen," and so forth.

However, "establishment in the states of woe" refers to those who have gone forth as ascetics among the Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and other sectarians, or anyone else who, having gone forth, practices wrongly.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*) toward the person. "Unarisen" (*anuppanna*) means not yet produced; the sense is "not yet attained.

"By way of non-prolixity" (*anullapanatāya*) means by speaking such a reply that Māra is unable to utter anything further in response. "By an invitation-word" (*nimantanavacanena*) means by a word of persuasion.
It is either a sublime (*brahma*) and supreme (*seṭṭha*) invitation, or it is one where there is an invitation from Brahmā.
The Discourse on the Invitation by Brahmā. Whatever herein has not been analyzed according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the Discourse on the Invitation by Brahmā is completed.
10. Commentary on the Discourse Rebuking Māra (*Māratajjanīyasutta*).
506. “He has entered the granary”: because it is a place for excrement, the “abode” (āsaya) is called a “granary” (koṭṭha);
here, the interior of that is the “granary. Having entered in a manner suited to it, he is said to have “entered accordingly” (anupaviṭṭha).
For having fashioned a subtle body appropriate to that [place], he has entered there. “As if very heavy” means as if extremely heavy. This is because the vowel *u* has been changed to *o*.
The meaning is that this description is considered exceedingly weighty. Or rather, the reading is *garugaru viya* (like something very heavy).

By the elision of the latter member of the compound, *māsabhattaṃ* means "a month's worth of food"; it is considered to be "filled" (*māsācitaṃ*) or "satiated" (*pūritaṃ*) by that month's food. Therefore he said: "like the belly of one who has eaten a month's worth of food.
To show the meaning without the elision of the latter member, [he says]: "a bag filled for a month."
"Like a ripe mango," it is said; "like a ripe mango" means like a ripe mango in a bag. The intention is:
"What indeed is this heaviness in my womb, what is this pus, how indeed was it born? "By means" (*upāyena*) means by way of the path, by way of the method.
However, to show the lack of means (*anupāya*) as its opposite, the passage beginning with "If, however" (*sace pana*) was stated. [He considered] himself alone...
Or, having intended [the Saṅgha], he said, "Do not harm the Tathāgata. For just as the Noble Saṅgha is called "Tathāgata" in such passages as, "The Tathāgata is worshipped by gods and humans;
let there be well-being for us who revere the Saṅgha," so too are the noble individuals included therein.
And just as the former two Chief Disciples [remained] for one hundred thousand plus one aeons...
"He has come having fulfilled the perfections for incalculable eons; this Great Elder has likewise come," thus he is called "Tathāgata.
"He stood right against the door" means he stood on the outside of the door. 507.
Tree-deities are a lower class among the Cātumahārājika devas; therefore, because they have become accustomed to it, the scent of humans [is familiar] to them.
He said, "not too disgusting," referring to "the deities dwelling in the sky. "Causes affliction" means it produces suffering. "A city-dweller" means one who is delicate.
"Well-groomed" means entirely pure in appearance. "The share of kinsmen" means a portion for relatives.
The intention is that in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, there is no being whatsoever who is not entitled to a share among kinsmen. This refers to: "You are my nephew..."
"Hosī" is this word. "By way of lineage" means it is said by way of this succession: that he was my nephew at that time and is now standing in the position of Māra.
Or, "vesamaṃ" means a different burden or a distinct duty. Therefore he said, "dissimilar to others.
"Without difficulty" means simply with ease. "Those who go along the paths" are called *pathāvino*.
"Ettakena" means by this much, namely, by way of the funeral pyre. "Udakaleṇa" means a cave formed by water dripping down.
"Samāpattito" means from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). "Samāpattiphala" means the fruit of the attainment of cessation. 508.
"By ten grounds of abuse" means by all ten grounds of abuse, not omitting even one of them. "Paribhāsatha" means revile.
"Reproach them" means: strike at them with words that leave nothing out. "Afflict them" means: produce suffering in their minds.

"Of these" refers to those bhikkhus; the intention is that by your reviling and so forth, defilements arise in the bhikkhus, whereby Māra Dūsī gains an opportunity here. They are worthy of receiving this [reproach].
They are called *ibbhas* because they are like *ibbhas* (outcasts) due to their lowly livelihood; however, they are referred to as "householders" (*gahapatika*) because they live with their wives.
They are "black" (*kaṇha*) because they belong to a dark birth-status. They are "footless" (*apādaka*) because they are born from the feet [of the earth].

They are "born lazy" (*ālasiyajātā*) because they have become indolent by not performing work such as farming or trade. A "drain for discharging dung" (*gūthaniddhamanapanāḷī*) refers to a channel from a cesspool.
The place of exit for excrement.
Human beings would not possess unwholesome states because they lack such an underlying intention (*abhisandhi*). This meaning has already been stated:
by the power of the possessor, the mental continuum (*cittasantati*) of the one possessed undergoes a transformation. "An object of a dissimilar nature" means:
A female form in the presence of monks, or a male form in the presence of nuns— such things,
or anything else unsuitable for those who have gone forth and discordant with their state— is called "an object for remorse," meaning a condition for remorse in those who see it.
"A stick smeared with plaster" means a stick from a winnowing-basket coated with plaster.
510. "By way of joy" means by way of joy based on the household life. "Alteration" means a state of elation.
"In the same manner as before" refers to the method previously stated, beginning with: "If Māra, having become intent upon the bodies of human beings...
If Māra alone were to act in such a way, it would not be for the welfare of human beings, but rather for Māra's own sake; however, [the Buddha acts] without becoming intent upon their bodies.
He showed such a pleasing object that inspires confidence. Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. 511.
"By one who has cultivated the perception of foulness" means: the jhāna accompanied by the perception that occurs regarding the entire body as foul is the "perception of foulness";
by that which is cultivated, that is, thoroughly developed. "By the mind" means by the consciousness (*citta*). "Abundantly" means frequently. "Dwells" means...
"For one who dwells frequently in the attainment of the foul" (asubha-samāpatti) is the meaning. "It recoils" means it contracts, because it remains fixed there due to its aversion.
"It shrinks back" means it retreats. "It turns away" means it desists; for that very reason, it does not extend forward.
"By craving for flavors" means by craving whose object is sweet and other such tastes.

The perception of non-delight in the entire world (*sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā*) is the development of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*) that proceeds by way of disliking the three realms of existence (*bhava*).

This is the contemplation of revulsion (*nibbidānupassanā*). "In the world’s diversities" (*lokacitresu*) refers to the various wonders of the world, such as elephants, horses, chariots, palaces, gabled houses, and so forth, as well as delightful parks and groves.
"With lust calmed" (*rāgasantāni*) means with lust stilled. "With hatred and delusion calmed" (*dosamohasantāni*)... [refers to those whose hatred and delusion are likewise stilled].
The same method applies here as well. This way of taking up the meditation subject is suitable for all of them.
"Having taken a pebble" means a handful of broken stones; by the term "pebble," he refers to a quantity of broken stone sufficient to remain within the fist, as stated:
"stone the size that stays inside the fist. The meaning is "contained within the fist. For this is the minimum size for a stone.

*Hatthināgo* means a great elephant. Some say that the word *nāga* has the sense of "great. Alternatively, it is called *hatthināgo* for the purpose of distinguishing it from [other types of] *ahināgas* (serpent-nāgas) and so forth.
The phrase beginning with *yathā hi* was stated in order to explain the meaning already expressed: "having turned around with his entire body, he looked back. Regarding the word *na*, he said:
"In this context, the word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)," thus [he said]: "not even the measure..."
"‘Sahāpalokanāya’ means ‘by this statement’; the intention is that by taking up this mere statement [he said it]. ‘Uḷāre’ means ‘of sublime qualities.
For, with the exception of the Blessed One, there was no one else at that time in the world with its devas possessed of such distinguished qualities.

‘Visuṃ visuṃ paccattavedaniyo ayasūlena saddhiṃ bhūtāni cha phassāyatanāni etassāti’: [it refers to him] who possesses the six bases of contact, together with the iron stake, each of which is individually experienced."

The six bases of contact are suffering. Because that exists here, it is "possessing the six bases of contact" (cha-phassāyatanika), referring to hell. Therefore he said: “In the six bases of contact... [the] condition.

It strikes together (samāhanati) thus it is "struck together" (samāhata); because many hundreds of varieties of spears are struck together here, it is "where spears are struck together" (saṅkusamāhata), referring to hell.
It is "to be felt" (vedaniya) because it stands as a specific condition for feeling.
"Individual-experienceable" (*paccattavedaniya*) means that which is to be experienced individually by itself, without an agent or an instrument.
"Together with the iron stake" (*ayasūlena saddhiṃ*) means together with the iron stake that has come from the region of the feet, striking continuously, and which is held by fifty people;
it [the head] has come from the region of the head. And this is said because of the commonality of the state of being an iron stake.

The singular number refers to the fact that only a single spike fell. By the phrase "having reflected on this matter," he speaks of the support (*nissaya*) using the conventional expression for what is supported (*nissita-vohāra*).

"Thus it was said" means it was said thus: "Then you would know: 'I have been boiling in hell for a thousand years. "Of emergence" (*vuṭṭhānimam*) means existing in emergence; the meaning is "final" (*antima*). Therefore he said: "the feeling of the emergence from the result" (*vipākavuṭṭhāna-vedanā*).
The meaning is that the conclusion of the result (*vipāka*) is feeling (*vedanā*). It becomes more painful, like the great intensity [of heat] at the moment a lamp is extinguished.
513. Having struck and beaten. "Producing individual feelings" means producing great suffering individually.
Niraya is that which has gone away from *aya* (going); it is to be illustrated by the *Devadūta Sutta*. Its commentary, however, will be given later by himself.

"He will come. But the Great Elder, having brought forward this past-life account and seeking to demonstrate the power of his own knowledge while intimidating Māra, spoke the verse beginning, "He who fully understands this. Its meaning is as follows:

he who possesses great supernormal powers (mahābhiñña), having placed this karma and its fruit directly before him like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand, [sees it] through direct perception.
He knows this: because his defilements have been utterly destroyed, the monk is the foremost disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One;
yet, by having assailed and provoked one of such sublime virtue, you, O Māra, who are black due to being possessed of entirely dark and evil qualities, will experience great suffering in the future.
"Making water the basis" means that, through the common karmic fruit of the beings reborn there, it is the water of the great ocean itself [that serves as their dwelling].
Having made a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For indeed, those [palaces] endure for an eon (*kappa*). Therefore he said, "enduring for an eon.

"Of them" means of the celestial mansions (*vimāna*). He knows this—the abode of the aforementioned celestial mansions, the excellence of those nymphs (*accharā*), and its cause—having made it directly manifest to himself (*attapaccakkhaṃ*). "He shook with his big toe" refers to [the palace] at Pubbārāma, belonging to Visākhā.
With his big toe, he shook the great palace adorned with a thousand chambers that had been built by the Great Female Lay Disciple (mahā-upāsikā).
Therefore it was said: "This is to be illustrated by the Sutta on the Shaking of the Palace.
As for the word "this," the various meanings of the verse beginning with "He who [shook] the Vejayanta" are to be illustrated by the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta itself.
Immediately after that assembly of Brahmās had thought thus, they went to the Sudhammā Hall of the Brahmā-world in that Brahmā realm.
"They too" refers to Mahāmoggallāna and the others. "Each in their respective directions" means:
the Elder Mahāmoggallāna in the eastern direction, the Elder Mahākassapa in the southern direction, the Elder Mahākappina in the western direction, and the Elder Anuruddha...

"In the northern direction," and so on: thus the four elders sat down in the four directions all around the Blessed One, who was seated in the midst of the Brahmā assembly. "The verse was spoken": the verse beginning with "He who questions Brahmā" was spoken.
"In the *Aññatarabrahma Sutta*": "Now at that time, a certain Brahmā had such an evil [thought]..."
“...a speculative view has arisen,” according to the *Aññatara-brahma-sutta* found in the Mahāvagga.
“He touched with the liberation of jhāna” means he contacted it by means of the knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) which relies upon the liberation of jhāna.
“He touched the forest” refers to Jambudīpa; for Jambudīpa is here called “the forest” because of its abundance of forests. This is the connection.
Therefore he said, "The lord of Jambusaṇḍa. "Of Pubbavideha" means the island of those dwelling in Pubbavideha; the meaning is "the island of Pubbavideha.

Those called "earth-dwellers" (bhūmisaya) are the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna and Uttarakuru, because, due to the absence of houses and possessions, they sleep on the ground itself and not in palaces and such. "Obtained" (paṭilabhi) means he produced [it].
"Do not harbor this hope" means: just as Māra’s hope in the past was so, even so will your hope bring harm for a long time;
therefore, do not harbor such a hope—thus he gave this advice to Māra. The rest is easy to understand everywhere.
(From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya)
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Māratajjanīyasutta* is completed.
The commentary on the *Cūḷayamaka-vagga* is finished.
The sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa* is completed.
The second part is finished.
